01.Maths/Calculus/02.Limits-and-Derivati.title: 02.Velocity Problem
01.Maths/Calculus/02.Limits-and-Derivati.content:
“The velocity problem and the tangent problem appear to be different. But they turn out to be the same problem in disguise — and that disguise is the derivative.”


§1. The Physical Motivation
Suppose a ball is dropped from a tower. Physics tells us its height (in metres) at time t (in seconds) is approximately:
s(t) = 4.9t^2
Question: How fast is the ball falling at exactly t = 2 seconds?
The phrase “at exactly t = 2” is the crux. Speed is ordinarily computed as:
\text{speed} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}}
But this ratio requires two moments in time — a start and an end. At a single instant, both numerator and denominator collapse to zero. We have a \frac{0}{0} problem.
This is not a computational inconvenience. It is a genuine conceptual difficulty that Newton and Leibniz spent their lives resolving. The resolution is the limit.

§2. Average Velocity vs. Instantaneous Velocity
Definition: Average Velocity
Over the time interval [t_1, t_2], the average velocity is:
\bar{v} = \frac{s(t_2) - s(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1} = \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}
This is just slope: the slope of the secant line on the position-time graph between (t_1, s(t_1)) and (t_2, s(t_2)).
Definition: Instantaneous Velocity
Fix a moment t = a. Let h = \Delta t \to 0. The instantaneous velocity is:
v(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{s(a+h) - s(a)}{h}
This is the slope of the tangent line on the position-time graph at (a, s(a)).
The velocity problem is the tangent problem, with time on the horizontal axis.

See also: The Tangent Problem


§3. Worked Example — The Falling Ball
Let s(t) = 4.9t^2 metres. Find the instantaneous velocity at t = 2.
Step 1: Compute average velocities over shrinking intervals.















































Interval [2,, 2+h]s(2+h)\Delta s\bar{v} = \Delta s / hh = 1 (i.e., [2,3])4.9(9) = 44.144.1 - 19.6 = 24.524.5 m/sh = 0.54.9(6.25) = 30.62511.02522.05 m/sh = 0.14.9(4.41) = 21.6092.00920.09 m/sh = 0.014.9(4.0401) = 19.79650.196519.65 m/sh = 0.001——19.601 m/sh \to 0——\mathbf{19.6} m/s
Step 2: Confirm with the limit.
v(2) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{4.9(2+h)^2 - 4.9(2)^2}{h}
= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{4.9(4 + 4h + h^2) - 4.9(4)}{h}
= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{4.9(4h + h^2)}{h}
= \lim_{h \to 0} 4.9(4 + h) = 4.9 \times 4 = \mathbf{19.6 \text{ m/s}}
The ball is falling at exactly 19.6 m/s at t = 2 s. Notice 19.6 = 2 \times 9.8, which is g \cdot t — consistent with Newtonian mechanics (v = gt for free fall from rest).

§4. Visualization
Position-Time Graph and the Secant-to-Tangent Process
s(t) = 4.9t²  (falling ball, position vs time)

  s (metres)
  |
44.1|        * ← s(3), secant endpoint for h=1
  |       /|
  |      / |
  |    /   |  ← secant line (h=1): slope = 24.5 m/s
  |   /    |
19.6|  *←s(2)  (the fixed point P)
  | /|
  |/ |
  |__|___________________________ t (seconds)
  0  2   3

  As h → 0, Q slides down toward P.
  The secant line rotates → tangent line.
  Slope of tangent = instantaneous velocity = 19.6 m/s.

Velocity-Time Graph
Once we compute v(t) = s'(t) for all t:
v(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{4.9(t+h)^2 - 4.9t^2}{h} = 9.8t
v(t) = 9.8t  (linear — constant acceleration)

  v (m/s)
  |             /
29.4|           /  ← v(3) = 29.4
  |          /
19.6|        *  ← v(2) = 19.6
  |       /
9.8|     /  ← v(1) = 9.8
  |    /
  |  /
  | /
  |/_________________________ t (seconds)
  0   1   2   3

  Slope of this line = 9.8 m/s² = g (acceleration due to gravity)


The derivative of position is velocity. The derivative of velocity is acceleration. Differentiation is the engine of kinematics.


§5. The Full Kinematic Chain
Let s(t) be position. Then:
v(t) = s'(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{s(t+h)-s(t)}{h} \quad \text{(velocity)}
a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t) \quad \text{(acceleration)}
For our falling ball s(t) = 4.9t^2 = \frac{1}{2}gt^2:

























QuantityFunctionValue at t=2Positions(t) = 4.9t^219.6 mVelocityv(t) = 9.8t19.6 m/sAccelerationa(t) = 9.89.8 m/s²
The acceleration is constant — this is the defining property of free fall near Earth’s surface. Newton’s second law F = ma with F = mg gives a = g.

§6. Example 2 — Oscillatory Motion
Let s(t) = \sin t (a particle on a spring, say). Find the velocity at t = 0.
v(0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sin(0+h) - \sin 0}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sin h}{h}
This is the fundamental trigonometric limit:
\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sin h}{h} = 1
So v(0) = 1 m/s (in appropriate units). And indeed \frac{d}{dt}\sin t = \cos t, which gives \cos 0 = 1. ✓

This limit is not obvious. It requires the geometric squeeze theorem — the area of a circular sector squeezed between two triangles. See Stewart §3.3.


§7. Example 3 — Negative Velocity (Motion in Reverse)
Let s(t) = -t^2 + 4t (a projectile thrown upward).
v(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{[-(t+h)^2 + 4(t+h)] - [-t^2 + 4t]}{h}
= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{-t^2 - 2th - h^2 + 4t + 4h + t^2 - 4t}{h}
= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{-2th - h^2 + 4h}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0}(-2t - h + 4) = -2t + 4
Analysis:

v(t) = 0 \Rightarrow t = 2: the ball is momentarily at rest (peak of trajectory).
v(t) > 0 for t < 2: ball moving upward (positive direction).
v(t) < 0 for t > 2: ball moving downward (negative velocity).

s(t) = -t² + 4t

  s
  4|    *   ← peak at t=2, s=4; velocity = 0 here
  |   / \
  |  /   \
  | /     \
  |/       \
  *_________*_________ t
  0         4

v(t) = -2t + 4: positive before t=2, zero at t=2, negative after.

The sign of the derivative encodes the direction of motion. Zero derivative = stationary point.

§8. Formal Definitions and Theorems
Definition. Let s : [0, T] \to \mathbb{R} be a position function. The instantaneous velocity at time a \in (0,T) is:
v(a) = s'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{s(a+h)-s(a)}{h}
if the limit exists.
Definition. The speed at time a is |v(a)| — velocity is a signed scalar (or in higher dimensions, a vector); speed is its magnitude.
Theorem (Mean Value Theorem for velocity). If s is continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), then there exists c \in (a,b) such that:
v(c) = s'(c) = \frac{s(b) - s(a)}{b-a}
In words: at some moment, the instantaneous velocity equals the average velocity over the interval. This is the MVT — one of the deepest theorems in calculus.

Practical consequence: if your average speed on a highway is 120 km/h, then at some moment your speedometer read exactly 120 km/h. The MVT is also why radar speed traps work.


§9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning

The velocity problem is not just a physics curiosity. It is the conceptual prototype for how neural networks learn — and how time-series models reason about change.

9.1 Learning as Motion Through Parameter Space
Think of training a neural network as a particle moving through parameter space \mathbb{R}^n. The weights \mathbf{w}(t) evolve over “time” (iterations t), following:
\frac{d\mathbf{w}}{dt} = -\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w})
This is gradient flow — the continuous-time limit of gradient descent. The velocity of the parameter particle at time t is -\nabla \mathcal{L}. Just as v(t) = s'(t) tells us how position changes, the gradient tells us how loss changes as we move through weight space.
The discrete update rule \mathbf{w}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(t)} - \eta \nabla \mathcal{L} is the Euler method for this ODE — the most primitive numerical integration of the velocity problem.
9.2 Momentum Optimizers
In physics, a particle with momentum \mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v} resists sudden changes in direction. The SGD with momentum optimizer is exactly this:
\mathbf{p}^{(t+1)} = \beta \mathbf{p}^{(t)} - \eta \nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^{(t)}) \mathbf{w}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(t)} + \mathbf{p}^{(t+1)}
The parameter \beta \in (0,1) is the momentum coefficient — a “friction” term that decays past velocities. The Adam optimizer goes further: it tracks both the first moment (velocity) and second moment (variance of velocity) of the gradient, adaptively scaling each parameter’s learning rate.





























PhysicsOptimizerPosition s(t)Weights \mathbf{w}^{(t)}Velocity v(t) = s'(t)Gradient \nabla \mathcal{L}Momentum mvFirst moment estimate (Adam’s \hat{m})FrictionMomentum decay \betaEquilibrium v = 0Convergence \nabla \mathcal{L} = 0
9.3 Recurrent Neural Networks and Temporal Derivatives
An RNN processes sequences x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_T and maintains a hidden state h_t that evolves over time. The continuous-time limit is the Neural ODE:
\frac{dh}{dt} = f_\theta(h(t), x(t))
Here \frac{dh}{dt} is literally the instantaneous velocity of the hidden state — exactly the velocity problem. Training Neural ODEs requires differentiating through an ODE solver (using the adjoint method, which is itself a calculus result).
9.4 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
PINNs solve differential equations (which are velocity equations — equations involving s'(t), s''(t), etc.) by training neural networks whose loss includes a penalty for violating the ODE:
\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\sum_i (u_\theta(t_i) - u_i)^2}_{\text{data term}} + \underbrace{\sum_j \left(\frac{du_\theta}{dt}\bigg|_{t_j} - f(u_\theta(t_j))\right)^2}_{\text{physics term (velocity residual)}}
The physics term is zero only when the network’s instantaneous rate of change matches the prescribed ODE. This is a direct application of the velocity problem inside a neural network loss function.
9.5 Finite Differences in Time-Series
The difference quotient approximation:
v(t) \approx \frac{s(t+h) - s(t)}{h}
appears directly as a feature engineering step in time-series ML. First differences \Delta x_t = x_t - x_{t-1} are used to stationarize time series before feeding them to models — removing trends by working with velocities (rates of change) rather than raw levels.
Raw series (non-stationary):         First differences (stationary):
   x                                    Δx
   |    /                               |  *  *     *
   |   /                                | * *   * *
   |  /                                 |*         *
   | /                                  |
   |/_____ t                            |___________ t
   trend present                        trend removed

ARIMA models explicitly include an “integrated” component d — the number of times the series must be differenced to become stationary — because d-fold differencing approximates the d-th order derivative.

§10. The Conceptual Unity
The table below shows that the velocity problem, the tangent problem, and the learning problem are all the same thing:















































Context”Position""Time/Input”Difference QuotientLimitKinematicss(t)tAverage velocity \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t}Instantaneous velocity v(a)Geometryf(x)xSecant slope \frac{\Delta f}{\Delta x}Tangent slope f'(a)ML training\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w})\mathbf{w}Finite diff. gradient approx.True gradient \nabla \mathcal{L}Time seriesx_ttFirst difference \Delta x_tInstantaneous rate of changeNeural ODEh(t)tDiscretized state update\frac{dh}{dt} = f_\theta(h,x)
They are all the same limit. The derivative is the universal language of change.

§11. What the Velocity Problem Teaches Us


Instantaneous quantities are limits of average quantities. There is no shortcut. The real number v(a) exists only because the difference quotient converges.


The sign of v encodes direction. Zero velocity = critical point (maximum, minimum, or inflection in time).


Acceleration is the second derivative. One differentiation gives velocity; a second gives acceleration. Higher derivatives encode higher-order structure of motion — and of functions.


Differential equations are velocity equations. Newton’s law F = ma is s''(t) = F/m — an equation constraining the second derivative of position. Virtually all laws of physics are written this way.


In ML, the gradient is velocity through loss landscape. Training dynamics, optimizer design, and convergence theory are all kinematics in disguise.



References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §2.1. (The tangent and velocity problems; the definition of derivative.)
MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.02 Multivariable Calculus. Lecture Notes. (Vector-valued velocity; rates of change in higher dimensions.)

01.Maths/Calculus/02.Limits-and-Derivati.title: 03.Limit of a Function
01.Maths/Calculus/02.Limits-and-Derivati.content:
“The limit is not about what happens at the point. It is about what the function is trying to become. This distinction — between the value and the approach — is the philosophical heart of analysis.”


§1. The Motivating Crisis
Consider the function:
f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}
At x = 1: the numerator is 0, the denominator is 0. The function is undefined at x = 1.
And yet — something is happening near x = 1. Factor:
f(x) = \frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1} = x + 1 \quad \text{for } x \neq 1
The function wants to equal 2 at x = 1, even though it doesn’t exist there.
This “wanting” is the limit. Calculus is built on making this precise.





































xf(x) = \frac{x^2-1}{x-1}0.91.90.991.990.9991.9991undefined1.0012.0011.012.011.12.1
The values approach 2 from both sides. We write:
\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^2-1}{x-1} = 2

§2. Informal Definition
Informal Definition. We write \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L and say “the limit of f(x) as x approaches a equals L” if we can make f(x) as close to L as we like by taking x sufficiently close to a (but x \neq a).
Three things to note immediately:

x \neq a is mandatory. The limit is about approach, not arrival. The value f(a) is irrelevant — f need not even be defined at a.
Both sides. x must be able to approach a from the left and from the right, and both approaches must yield L.
L must be a finite real number (for now — we will extend to \pm\infty).


§3. The Formal \varepsilon-\delta Definition
The informal definition uses phrases like “as close as we like” and “sufficiently close.” These are meaningless without precision. The \varepsilon-\delta definition eliminates all ambiguity.
Definition (Cauchy-Weierstrass). We say \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L if:
\forall \varepsilon > 0,\ \exists \delta > 0\ \text{ such that }\ 0 < |x - a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon
Parsing the Definition

\varepsilon (epsilon) measures the tolerated error in output: how close f(x) must be to L.
\delta (delta) measures the required precision in input: how close x must be to a.
The challenge is: given any \varepsilon > 0 (no matter how tiny), find a \delta > 0 that works.
0 < |x - a| encodes x \neq a.

The ε-δ picture:

  f(x)
  |
L+ε |. . . . . . . . . . . . .
  |          / ← f(x) must stay in this band
L  |        *                     ← the limit L
  |       /
L-ε |. . . . . . . . . . . . .
  |
  |_____|____|____|_____________ x
      a-δ   a  a+δ
             ↑
        x stays in this
        punctured interval
        (x ≠ a)

  For every ε-band around L,
  we must find a δ-interval around a
  such that f maps the punctured interval into the band.

\varepsilon-\delta Proof: Example
Claim: \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 3} (2x - 1) = 5.
Proof. Let \varepsilon > 0 be given. We need |f(x) - 5| < \varepsilon whenever 0 < |x - 3| < \delta.
Compute: |f(x) - 5| = |(2x-1) - 5| = |2x - 6| = 2|x - 3|
So |f(x) - 5| < \varepsilon \iff 2|x-3| < \varepsilon \iff |x-3| < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2}.
Choose \delta = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2}. Then:
0 < |x-3| < \delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \implies |f(x) - 5| = 2|x-3| < 2 \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon \quad \blacksquare

The key technique: work backwards from |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon to find the required \delta. The algebra determines \delta; then you write the proof forwards.


§4. One-Sided Limits
Sometimes f approaches different values from the left and from the right. We need finer tools.
Definition. The left-hand limit is:
\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = L \quad \text{(x approaches a from below)}
Definition. The right-hand limit is:
\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L \quad \text{(x approaches a from above)}
Theorem.
\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \iff \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = L \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L
The two-sided limit exists if and only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal.
Example: The Heaviside Function
H(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \ 1 & x \geq 0 \end{cases}
\lim_{x \to 0^-} H(x) = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^+} H(x) = 1
Since 0 \neq 1, the two-sided limit \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} H(x) does not exist.
H(x):

  1 |          *————————————
    |          |
  0 |————————  |
    |__________|____________ x
              0

  Left limit = 0, Right limit = 1 → no two-sided limit.

Example: The Absolute Value
f(x) = \frac{|x|}{x}
\lim_{x \to 0^-} \frac{|x|}{x} = \frac{-x}{x} = -1, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{|x|}{x} = \frac{x}{x} = 1
Limit does not exist at 0.

§5. When Limits Fail to Exist
There are three canonical failure modes:
Case 1: Jump Discontinuity
Left and right limits both exist but are unequal. (Heaviside function above.)
Case 2: Infinite Oscillation
f(x) = \sin!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \quad \text{as } x \to 0
sin(1/x) near x = 0:

  1 |  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
    |  oscillations become
  0 |  infinitely rapid
    |  as x → 0
 -1 |  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
    |________________________ x
    -0.1  0  0.1

The function oscillates infinitely between -1 and 1. Neither one-sided limit exists. No limit.
Case 3: Divergence to Infinity
\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{x^2} = +\infty
This is a convention — we say the limit is +\infty to describe the behavior, but +\infty is not a real number. The limit does not exist in \mathbb{R}; we are describing how it fails.

§6. Limit Laws
Once we know the limit of simple functions, we can build complex limits algebraically.
Theorem (Limit Laws). If \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L and \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M, then:





































LawStatementSum\lim [f + g] = L + MDifference\lim [f - g] = L - MConstant multiple\lim [cf] = cLProduct\lim [f \cdot g] = L \cdot MQuotient\lim [f/g] = L/M, provided M \neq 0Power\lim [f^n] = L^nRoot\lim \sqrt[n]{f} = \sqrt[n]{L}, provided L > 0 for even n
Corollary (Direct Substitution Property). If f is a polynomial or rational function and a is in the domain of f, then:
\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)
This is the content of continuity — for “nice” functions, the limit and the value agree.

§7. The Squeeze Theorem
Theorem (Squeeze / Sandwich Theorem). If:
g(x) \leq f(x) \leq h(x)
near a (but not necessarily at a), and:
\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = \lim_{x \to a} h(x) = L
then:
\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L
The Fundamental Trigonometric Limit
Claim: \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1.
Proof sketch (geometric squeeze).
For 0 < x < \pi/2, compare areas:
\text{Area}(\triangle OAB) \leq \text{Area(sector } OAB) \leq \text{Area}(\triangle OAT)
\frac{1}{2}\sin x \leq \frac{x}{2} \leq \frac{1}{2}\tan x
Divide by \frac{1}{2}\sin x > 0:
1 \leq \frac{x}{\sin x} \leq \frac{1}{\cos x}
Take reciprocals (reversing inequalities):
\cos x \leq \frac{\sin x}{x} \leq 1
As x \to 0: \cos x \to 1 and 1 \to 1. By squeeze:
\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1 \qquad \blacksquare
Geometric squeeze:

        T
        |  \
        |    \
        |      \  ← tan x
     1  |     *  \
        |   /  \   \
        | /  sector \
        |/  x    \   \
        O——————————A——— (unit circle)
        
  Triangle OAB ≤ Sector ≤ Triangle OAT
  (1/2)sin x   ≤  x/2   ≤ (1/2)tan x

Corollary:
\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos x}{x} = 0
(Proof: multiply numerator and denominator by (1 + \cos x) and use \sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1.)

§8. Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes
Definition. \displaystyle\lim_{x \to +\infty} f(x) = L means: for every \varepsilon > 0, there exists N such that x > N \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon.
The line y = L is a horizontal asymptote.
Examples
\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{x} = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3x^2 + 2x}{x^2 - 1} = 3, \qquad \lim_{x \to \infty} e^{-x} = 0
Technique for rational functions: divide numerator and denominator by the highest power of x.
\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3x^2 + 2x}{x^2 - 1} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3 + 2/x}{1 - 1/x^2} = \frac{3 + 0}{1 - 0} = 3
f(x) = (3x²+2x)/(x²-1):

  f
  |
3 |. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ← horizontal asymptote y=3
  |                  ______________
  |            _____/
  |       ____/
  |  ____/
  |_/__________________________ x
  0        5       10      15


§9. Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes
Definition. \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = +\infty means: for every M > 0, there exists \delta > 0 such that 0 < |x - a| < \delta \implies f(x) > M.
The line x = a is a vertical asymptote.
Example
\lim_{x \to 0^+} \ln x = -\infty, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{x^2} = +\infty, \qquad \lim_{x \to 1^+} \frac{1}{x-1} = +\infty
f(x) = 1/x²:

  f
  |
  |  *   *   ← shoots to +∞ from both sides
  |   \ /
  |    |
  |    |  ← vertical asymptote x=0
  |____|_______ x
      0


§10. Summary of Limit Types
                    LIMIT TAXONOMY
                    
    lim f(x) as x → a
    
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Two-sided limit                              │
    │  lim f(x) = L  iff  lim f = lim f = L        │
    │             x→a        x→a⁻   x→a⁺           │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    DOES NOT EXIST when:
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  • Left ≠ Right (jump)                        │
    │  • Infinite oscillation (sin(1/x) at 0)       │
    │  • Diverges to ±∞ (vertical asymptote)        │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    SPECIAL CASES:
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  lim f(x) as x → +∞  (limit at infinity)     │
    │  lim f(x) = +∞       (infinite limit)        │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘


§11. Connection to Continuity
Definition. f is continuous at a if all three conditions hold:

f(a) is defined.
\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) exists.
\displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a).

Failure of any one condition creates a discontinuity:






























Failure modeTypeExamplef(a) undefined, limit existsRemovable\frac{x^2-1}{x-1} at x=1One-sided limits unequalJumpH(x) at x=0Limit is \pm\inftyInfinite1/x^2 at x=0Limit doesn’t exist (oscillation)Essential\sin(1/x) at x=0
Removable discontinuity is the most important: the limit exists, but f(a) is either missing or wrong. We can repair it by redefining f(a) = L.

The derivative f'(a) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} is a limit of a difference quotient. Every result in differential calculus — every differentiation rule, every theorem — is a theorem about limits in disguise.


§12. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning

The limit is the mathematical foundation of every continuous operation in ML. Understanding limits is understanding why neural networks can approximate, generalize, and converge.

12.1 The Universal Approximation Theorem
The Universal Approximation Theorem states (informally): a feedforward neural network with one hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any continuous function f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} to arbitrary precision.
The word arbitrary precision is a limit statement:
\forall \varepsilon > 0,\ \exists \text{ a network } N_\varepsilon \text{ such that } \sup_x |N_\varepsilon(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon
This is \varepsilon-\delta logic applied to function spaces. Neural networks are approximating the limit of a sequence of functions. The depth of modern networks pushes this from width-approximation toward depth-approximation, but the \varepsilon-precision language is identical.
12.2 Gradient Descent Convergence
For a convex loss \mathcal{L}, gradient descent with step size \eta produces iterates \mathbf{w}^{(t)} satisfying:
\lim_{t \to \infty} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^{(t)}) = \mathcal{L}^*
This is a limit at infinity — the loss approaches its minimum as iteration count grows. The convergence rate determines how fast this limit is approached. For strongly convex \mathcal{L}:
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^{(t)}) - \mathcal{L}^* \leq \left(1 - \eta\mu\right)^t (\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^{(0)}) - \mathcal{L}^*)
The right side \to 0 as t \to \infty (geometric decay). The limit is zero; convergence is guaranteed.
12.3 Softmax and the Limit as Temperature → 0
The softmax function:
\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z}/T)_i = \frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/T}}
with temperature T > 0. Consider:
\lim_{T \to 0^+} \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z}/T) = \mathbf{e}_{\arg\max_i z_i}
As T \to 0^+, softmax approaches the argmax function — a one-hot vector. This is a limit of a continuous function approaching a discontinuous one. It explains why during inference (low temperature) the model becomes more “decisive,” while during training (higher temperature) probability mass is spread more smoothly.
Softmax temperature limit:

  probability
  |
1 |          *  ← T→0: hard argmax (limit)
  |         /|
0.8|        / |
  |       /  |    T=0.1 (nearly argmax)
0.6|      /   |
  |     /    |    T=1.0 (standard softmax)
0.4|    /     |
  |   ——————  |    T=10 (near-uniform)
0.2| ————————  |
  |____________|_______ class index
              argmax

12.4 Vanishing Gradients and Limits
In deep networks, the gradient of the loss with respect to early-layer weights involves products of Jacobians. For sigmoid activations \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}:
\sigma'(x) = \sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x)) \leq \frac{1}{4}
In a network with L layers, the gradient magnitude is bounded by:
|\nabla_{\mathbf{w}_1} \mathcal{L}| \leq \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^L \cdot C
As L \to \infty:
\lim_{L \to \infty} \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^L = 0
This is the vanishing gradient problem — a limit at infinity converging to zero, making early layers untrainable. The solution (BatchNorm, ResNets, ReLU) is fundamentally about preventing this limit from being reached.
12.5 L’Hôpital’s Rule in Loss Analysis
The \frac{0}{0} indeterminate form appears in ML theory. For example, when analyzing the cross-entropy loss:
\mathcal{L} = -\sum_i y_i \log \hat{p}_i
as \hat{p}_i \to 0 for a true class (y_i = 1):
\lim_{\hat{p} \to 0^+} \hat{p} \log \hat{p} = \lim_{\hat{p} \to 0^+} \frac{\log \hat{p}}{1/\hat{p}} \stackrel{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{\hat{p} \to 0^+} \frac{1/\hat{p}}{-1/\hat{p}^2} = \lim_{\hat{p} \to 0^+} (-\hat{p}) = 0
This ensures the loss remains finite (and the KL divergence is well-defined) even at boundary probabilities.
12.6 Activation Functions as Limit Constructions

























ActivationLimit propertyReLU: \max(0,x)\lim_{x\to 0^-} = 0, \lim_{x\to 0^+} = 0; continuous but not differentiableSigmoid: \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\lim_{x\to -\infty} = 0, \lim_{x\to +\infty} = 1; horizontal asymptotesTanh: \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}\lim_{x\to \pm\infty} = \pm 1; bounded outputSoftplus: \ln(1+e^x)\lim_{x\to -\infty} \approx e^x \to 0; smooth ReLU approximation
Every activation function is designed with its limiting behavior in mind — what does it do to very large or very small inputs? That is a question about limits at infinity.

§13. L’Hôpital’s Rule
For completeness — the most powerful tool for \frac{0}{0} and \frac{\infty}{\infty} indeterminate forms.
Theorem (L’Hôpital). If \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = 0 and \displaystyle\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = 0 (or both \pm\infty), and g'(x) \neq 0 near a, then:
\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}
provided the right side exists.
Example
\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1}{x} \stackrel{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x}{1} = 1
This is the derivative of e^x at x = 0 — L’Hôpital confirms the definition.

Warning: L’Hôpital requires the \frac{0}{0} or \frac{\infty}{\infty} form. Applying it to \lim_{x\to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x + 1} = \frac{0}{1} (not indeterminate!) would give the wrong answer.


§14. Precise Proof Technique Summary
When writing \varepsilon-\delta proofs:

Scratch work (backwards): Start from |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon. Simplify. Find what |x - a| <\ ? must be.
Bound complications: If |f(x) - L| involves |x - a| multiplied by something that depends on x, bound that factor by assuming |x-a| < 1 (say), then choose \delta = \min(1, \varepsilon/\text{bound}).
Write the proof forwards: State \delta, assume 0 < |x-a| < \delta, chain inequalities to conclude |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon.

Example with Bounding
Claim: \displaystyle\lim_{x \to 2} x^2 = 4.
Scratch: |x^2 - 4| = |x-2||x+2|. Need to bound |x+2|.
Assume |x-2| < 1, so 1 < x < 3, so |x+2| < 5.
Thus |x^2-4| < 5|x-2|. Need 5|x-2| < \varepsilon, i.e., |x-2| < \varepsilon/5.
Proof. Let \varepsilon > 0. Set \delta = \min!\left(1, \dfrac{\varepsilon}{5}\right).
If 0 < |x-2| < \delta, then |x-2| < 1 \Rightarrow |x+2| < 5, and:
|x^2 - 4| = |x-2||x+2| < \frac{\varepsilon}{5} \cdot 5 = \varepsilon \quad \blacksquare

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §§2.2–2.6. (Limit of a function; limit laws; precise definition; continuity.)
MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.02 Multivariable Calculus. Lecture Notes. (Limits in higher dimensions; epsilon-delta for vector-valued functions.)

01.Maths/Calculus/02.Limits-and-Derivati.title: 04.One-Sided Limits
01.Maths/Calculus/02.Limits-and-Derivati.content:
“The limit does not care where you are — only where you are heading.”


Tags
#calculus #real-analysis #limits #continuity #deep-learning #machine-learning

0. Why Bother? (Motivation Before the Machine)
Before we write a single \varepsilon, let’s feel the problem.
Consider the function f(x) = \frac{|x|}{x}. Near x = 0, the function does not oscillate wildly. It is perfectly calm on either side. To the left, f(x) = -1. To the right, f(x) = +1. And yet, no two-sided limit exists at x = 0.
The classical (two-sided) limit asks: does the function approach a single value no matter how you approach a? One-sided limits ask a more refined question: what does the function approach if I restrict the direction of approach?
This is not a technicality. It is a fundamental distinction that separates differentiable functions from merely continuous ones, smooth activation functions from hard thresholds, and integrable functions from unruly ones.

1. Informal Picture First
    f(x)
      |
  1   |        o————————>     ← f approaches L₂ from the right
      |
  0   |————————x————————
      |         0
 -1   | <————————o            ← f approaches L₁ from the left
      |
      +————————————————> x

The function approaches different values depending on the direction. Neither is wrong — they are simply different one-sided facts.

2. Formal Definitions
2.1 Left-Hand Limit (LHL)

Definition (Stewart §2.2; MIT 18.02 spirit). We say \lim_{x \to a^{-}} f(x) = L if for every \varepsilon > 0, there exists \delta > 0 such that 0 < a - x < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon.

Unpacking the notation.

x \to a^- means x < a and x \to a. The superscript "-" denotes approach from the left (below).
The condition 0 < a - x < \delta encodes: x is strictly less than a, and within distance \delta of a.
We require |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon: the output is arbitrarily close to L.

2.2 Right-Hand Limit (RHL)

Definition. We say \lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x) = L if for every \varepsilon > 0, there exists \delta > 0 such that 0 < x - a < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon.


x \to a^+ means x > a and x \to a. The superscript "+" denotes approach from the right (above).
The condition 0 < x - a < \delta encodes: x is strictly greater than a, and within distance \delta of a.


3. The Bridge Theorem
This theorem is the central link between one-sided and two-sided limits.

Theorem. The two-sided limit \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L exists if and only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal: \lim_{x \to a^{-}} f(x) = L \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x) = L.

Proof.
(\Rightarrow) Suppose \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L. Let \varepsilon > 0. Then \exists \delta > 0 such that 0 < |x - a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon. In particular, this holds when x \in (a - \delta, a) (giving the LHL) and when x \in (a, a + \delta) (giving the RHL). Hence both one-sided limits equal L.
(\Leftarrow) Suppose both one-sided limits equal L. Let \varepsilon > 0. By hypothesis, \exists \delta_1, \delta_2 > 0 such that:

0 < a - x < \delta_1 \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon
0 < x - a < \delta_2 \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon

Set \delta = \min(\delta_1, \delta_2). Then for 0 < |x - a| < \delta, either x < a or x > a, and in both cases |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon. Hence the two-sided limit exists. \blacksquare
Corollary. If \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) \neq \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x), the two-sided limit does not exist.

4. Worked Examples
Example 4.1 — The Signum Function
\text{sgn}(x) = \begin{cases} -1 & x < 0 \ 0 & x = 0 \ 1 & x > 0 \end{cases}
Computing the one-sided limits at a = 0:
\lim_{x \to 0^-} \text{sgn}(x) = -1, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^+} \text{sgn}(x) = 1.
Since -1 \neq 1, the two-sided limit \lim_{x \to 0} \text{sgn}(x) does not exist.
    sgn(x)
      |
  1   |           o————————>
      |
  0   |      •
      |
 -1   | <————o
      |
      +————————————————> x
         -1   0   1
   (open circles = not included; filled = value at 0)


Example 4.2 — The Heaviside Step Function
H(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \ 1 & x \geq 0 \end{cases}
\lim_{x \to 0^-} H(x) = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^+} H(x) = 1.
The two-sided limit does not exist. Note: H(0) = 1 is defined, but it does not affect the limit analysis.

Remark. H(x) is the “hard threshold” activation function. It is not differentiable at 0, precisely because the one-sided limits disagree. This is why sigmoid and ReLU were introduced — to fix differentiability for gradient-based learning.


Example 4.3 — A Piecewise Function with Matching Limits
g(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 + 1 & x < 2 \ 3x - 1 & x \geq 2 \end{cases}
\lim_{x \to 2^-} g(x) = (2)^2 + 1 = 5, \qquad \lim_{x \to 2^+} g(x) = 3(2) - 1 = 5.
Since both agree, \lim_{x \to 2} g(x) = 5. Moreover, g(2) = 3(2) - 1 = 5, so g is continuous at x = 2.

Example 4.4 — An \varepsilon-\delta Proof of a One-Sided Limit
Claim: \lim_{x \to 0^+} \sqrt{x} = 0.
Proof. Let \varepsilon > 0. We need to find \delta > 0 such that 0 < x - 0 < \delta \implies |\sqrt{x} - 0| < \varepsilon. Note |\sqrt{x}| = \sqrt{x} for x > 0. We want \sqrt{x} < \varepsilon, i.e., x < \varepsilon^2. Choose \delta = \varepsilon^2. Then 0 < x < \delta = \varepsilon^2 \implies \sqrt{x} < \sqrt{\varepsilon^2} = \varepsilon. \quad \blacksquare

The function \sqrt{x} only makes sense for x \geq 0, so a right-hand limit is the only sensible notion at x = 0. One-sided limits are not just a technicality — sometimes they are the only thing that exists.


5. One-Sided Limits and Continuity
5.1 One-Sided Continuity

Definition. f is right-continuous at a if \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a). f is left-continuous at a if \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = f(a).

f is (two-sided) continuous at a \iff f is both left- and right-continuous at a.
5.2 The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Connection
The Riemann integral is defined via step functions. The floor function \lfloor x \rfloor (greatest integer \leq x) satisfies: \lim_{x \to n^-} \lfloor x \rfloor = n - 1, \qquad \lim_{x \to n^+} \lfloor x \rfloor = n, \qquad \lfloor n \rfloor = n.
So \lfloor x \rfloor is right-continuous but not left-continuous at every integer. This matters when defining integrals of piecewise functions.

6. Visualizations
6.1 The Anatomy of a One-Sided Limit
   f(x)
     |
 L₂  |  - - - - - - - ○ ··················>   (approaches L₂ from right)
     |                ↑
     |             x = a
     |
 L₁  | <··············○ - - - - - - - -       (approaches L₁ from left)
     |
     +——————————————————————————————> x
                    a


Open circles (\circ): the function does not reach that value at a itself
Dotted arrows: direction of approach
L_1 \neq L_2: two-sided limit fails

6.2 The \varepsilon-\delta Picture for \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L
   f(x)
     |
 L+ε | ......................
     |          /           ← All f(x) must land here
 L   | - - - - /  - - - - -
     |        /
 L-ε | ....../ ...........
     |      /
     +——|——|——————————> x
        a  a+δ

   (Only x ∈ (a, a+δ) is considered)

For every \varepsilon-band around L, there must exist a \delta-interval to the right of a such that f maps that interval into the \varepsilon-band.

7. Connection to Derivatives
The derivative at a point is a two-sided limit: f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}.
We can define one-sided derivatives: f'_+(a) = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}, \qquad f'_-(a) = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}.
f is differentiable at a \iff f'_+(a) = f'_-(a).
Example: ReLU
The ReLU function \sigma(x) = \max(0, x) satisfies: \sigma'_-(0) = 0, \qquad \sigma'_+(0) = 1. Since these disagree, ReLU is not differentiable at 0. This is precisely the “kink.” In practice, one chooses a subgradient (often 0 or 1) at this point for backpropagation.

8. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
This is not decoration — one-sided limits sit at the mathematical heart of several core concepts.
8.1 Activation Functions and the Differentiability Problem















































ActivationFormulaLHL at kinkRHL at kinkDifferentiable?Heaviside H\mathbf{1}_{x \geq 0}01✗ (No gradient)ReLU\max(0, x)derivative 0derivative 1✗ (Subgradient used)Leaky ReLU\max(\alpha x, x)derivative \alphaderivative 1✗ (Subgradient used)Sigmoid \sigma\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}smoothsmooth✓ everywhereGELUx \cdot \Phi(x)smoothsmooth✓ everywhere
The transition from Heaviside → sigmoid → ReLU → GELU is precisely the story of trying to find activations that are (a) nonlinear, (b) computationally simple, and (c) differentiable or at least subdifferentiable everywhere. One-sided limits diagnose exactly where and why differentiability fails.
8.2 Backpropagation and the Chain Rule
Backpropagation is the chain rule applied layer by layer. The chain rule requires derivatives to exist. When activations have kinks (like ReLU), we use subgradients, which are defined via one-sided derivatives: \partial \sigma(x) = \begin{cases} {0} & x < 0 \ [0, 1] & x = 0 \ {1} & x > 0 \end{cases} The value chosen at x = 0 is a convention — the mathematics says the one-sided derivatives disagree there.
8.3 Loss Functions and Piecewise Structure
The Hinge loss used in Support Vector Machines: \ell(y, \hat{y}) = \max(0, 1 - y\hat{y}) has a kink at y\hat{y} = 1. Computing its gradient requires understanding left- and right-hand derivatives at the kink point. One-sided limits are the language for this.
The Huber loss was designed to be smooth everywhere by matching the one-sided derivatives at the transition point: L_\delta(r) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}r^2 & |r| \leq \delta \ \delta(|r| - \frac{1}{2}\delta) & |r| > \delta \end{cases} One can verify: \lim_{r \to \delta^-} L_\delta'(r) = \delta = \lim_{r \to \delta^+} L_\delta'(r). The function is C^1 by design.
8.4 The Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) in Probabilistic Models
In probabilistic deep learning and Bayesian inference, the CDF F_X(t) = P(X \leq t) is always right-continuous: \lim_{x \to t^+} F_X(x) = F_X(t). The left-hand limit \lim_{x \to t^-} F_X(x) = P(X < t) may differ at atoms of the distribution. This distinction matters in variational autoencoders, normalizing flows, and any model that works with explicit probability distributions.
8.5 Learning Rate Schedules
Cosine annealing and step decay schedules for learning rates are piecewise-defined functions. The one-sided continuity at “restart” points determines whether gradient updates are stable across restarts.

9. Common Pitfalls

⚠️ The value f(a) is irrelevant to the limit. One-sided limits depend only on the behavior of f near a, not at a.


⚠️ “Does not exist” is not the same as “equals infinity.” \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1}{x} = +\infty is a precise statement. The one-sided limit exists as an extended real number, even though it is not finite.


⚠️ Notation discipline. \lim_{x \to a^-} and \lim_{x \to a-} (without the superscript) are different things in sloppy notation. Always write the superscript clearly: a^-, a^+.


⚠️ Domain matters. For f(x) = \sqrt{x}, asking for \lim_{x \to 0^-} \sqrt{x} is asking about a region outside the domain. The left-hand limit does not exist (not just equals zero).


10. Summary Theorem Sheet





























FactStatementTwo-sided ↔ One-sided\lim_{x \to a} f = L \iff \lim_{x \to a^-} f = \lim_{x \to a^+} f = LContinuityf continuous at a \iff both one-sided limits equal f(a)Differentiabilityf differentiable at a \iff f'_-(a) = f'_+(a)Monotone functionsLeft- and right-hand limits always exist (may differ)Bounded monotone\lim_{x \to a^{\pm}} f(x) finite for monotone bounded f

11. Practice Problems


(Computational) Let f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 - 1 & x < 1 \ 2x & x > 1 \end{cases}. Compute \lim_{x \to 1^-} f(x) and \lim_{x \to 1^+} f(x). Does the two-sided limit exist?


(Epsilon-delta) Prove rigorously that \lim_{x \to 3^-} (2x + 1) = 7 using the \varepsilon-\delta definition.


(Conceptual) The function f(x) = \sin(1/x) for x \neq 0. Show that neither one-sided limit at x = 0 exists.


(Applied — ML) For the Leaky ReLU f(x) = \max(0.01x, x), compute f'_-(0) and f'_+(0). Is the function differentiable at 0? What subgradient is typically used?


(Proof) Let f be monotonically increasing and bounded above on (a, b). Prove that \lim_{x \to b^-} f(x) exists. (Hint: use the completeness of \mathbb{R} and the supremum.)



12. References


Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §2.2 “The Limit of a Function”; §2.4 “The Precise Definition of a Limit.” — The canonical undergraduate source. One-sided limits introduced informally first, then sharpened with \varepsilon-\delta.


MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.02. Multivariable Calculus. — The treatment of limits forms the analytic foundation before partial derivatives and directional limits, which generalize one-sided limits to higher dimensions.


Rudin, Walter. Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed. Ch. 4 “Continuity.” — For the reader who wants to see this done in full generality on metric spaces.


Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville. Deep Learning (MIT Press, 2016). Ch. 6.3 “Hidden Units.” — The activation function zoo and the role of non-differentiability.

01.Maths/Calculus/02.Limits-and-Derivati.title: 05.Infinite Limits
01.Maths/Calculus/02.Limits-and-Derivati.content:
“Infinity is not a number. It is a direction — and limits are how we speak precisely about directions.”


Tags
#calculus #real-analysis #limits #asymptotes #deep-learning #machine-learning #numerical-stability

0. Motivation: When Functions Blow Up
Consider f(x) = \frac{1}{x^2}.
As x \to 0, the denominator collapses to zero while the numerator stays fixed. The output does not approach any finite number — it grows without bound. But it grows predictably, consistently, from both sides. This is not chaos. It is a precise, describable behavior, and we need language for it.
Infinite limits answer: what does it mean, rigorously, for a function to “go to infinity”?
The answer is not “the limit equals \infty” as if \infty were a number on the real line. It is a carefully crafted statement about the behavior of f(x) for x near some point a.

1. Informal Picture
    f(x)
      |
      |     |        |
  M   | ····|········|·····   ← eventually, f(x) stays above any M
      |     |        |
      |      \      /
      |       \    /
      |        \  /
      |         \/
      +—————————+————————> x
                a

No matter how large M you choose, for x sufficiently close to a (but x \neq a), f(x) > M. The function escapes every finite ceiling.

2. Formal Definitions
2.1 Limit Equals +\infty

Definition (Stewart §2.2; Rudin Ch. 4). We say \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = +\infty if for every M > 0, there exists \delta > 0 such that 0 < |x - a| < \delta \implies f(x) > M.

Reading it carefully:

The role of \varepsilon in the standard limit is now played by M — but M measures largeness, not closeness.
There is no "|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon" because there is no finite L to be close to.
For every finite ceiling M, we can find a neighborhood of a where f exceeds it.
This is not “the limit is undefined.” It is a specific, precise type of behavior.

2.2 Limit Equals -\infty

Definition. We say \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = -\infty if for every N < 0 (equivalently, every M > 0), there exists \delta > 0 such that 0 < |x - a| < \delta \implies f(x) < N.

The function falls below every finite floor.
2.3 One-Sided Infinite Limits
We naturally combine the one-sided approach with the infinite behavior:
\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = +\infty \quad \text{means:} \quad \forall M > 0,\ \exists \delta > 0:\ 0 < x - a < \delta \implies f(x) > M.
\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = -\infty \quad \text{means:} \quad \forall N < 0,\ \exists \delta > 0:\ 0 < a - x < \delta \implies f(x) < N.
All four combinations (\pm\infty,\ a^\pm) are possible. Each is its own precise definition.

3. Vertical Asymptotes — The Geometric Meaning

Definition. The line x = a is a vertical asymptote of f if at least one of the following holds: \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = \pm\infty \quad \text{or} \quad \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \pm\infty.

Key point: a vertical asymptote is a consequence of an infinite limit — not a definition in itself. The limit statement comes first; the asymptote language is shorthand.

4. The Extended Real Line \overline{\mathbb{R}}
In real analysis, one formally adjoins two symbols to \mathbb{R}: \overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup {-\infty, +\infty}.
Arithmetic rules on \overline{\mathbb{R}} (partial):





































ExpressionValue\infty + \infty+\infty-\infty - \infty-\inftyc \cdot \infty, c > 0+\inftyc \cdot \infty, c < 0-\infty\infty + (-\infty)undefined (indeterminate)0 \cdot \inftyundefined (indeterminate)\frac{\infty}{\infty}undefined (indeterminate)

Warning. The indeterminate forms are not undefined because we are ignorant — they are undefined because different functions can approach 0 \cdot \infty with any answer. L’Hôpital’s Rule is the tool for resolving them.


5. Worked Examples
Example 5.1 — The Prototype: 1/x^2
\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{x^2} = +\infty.
\varepsilon-M-\delta proof. Let M > 0. We need \delta > 0 such that 0 < |x| < \delta \implies \frac{1}{x^2} > M.
We want \frac{1}{x^2} > M, i.e., x^2 < \frac{1}{M}, i.e., |x| < \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}. Choose \delta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}.
Then 0 < |x| < \delta \implies x^2 < \frac{1}{M} \implies \frac{1}{x^2} > M. \blacksquare
    f(x) = 1/x²
      |
      |   |   |
      |   |   |
      |   | | |
      |  || | ||
      ||||   ||||
      +—————0————————> x

   Symmetric blow-up from both sides → limit = +∞


Example 5.2 — Asymmetric Blow-Up: 1/x
\lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1}{x} = +\infty, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^-} \frac{1}{x} = -\infty.
The two one-sided limits are +\infty and -\infty respectively. The two-sided limit does not exist — not even as an infinite limit — because the function diverges in opposite directions.
    f(x) = 1/x
      |
      |  /               ← +∞ from the right
      | /
      |/
  ————+————————> x
      0\
       \
        \                ← −∞ from the left


Example 5.3 — Logarithm at Zero
\lim_{x \to 0^+} \ln x = -\infty.
Proof. Let N < 0. We need \delta > 0 such that 0 < x < \delta \implies \ln x < N.
\ln x < N \iff x < e^N. Since N < 0, we have e^N \in (0, 1). Choose \delta = e^N > 0. Then 0 < x < \delta = e^N \implies \ln x < N. \blacksquare

This is why log-loss in machine learning requires the predicted probability \hat{p} to be clipped away from zero. If \hat{p} \to 0^+, then -\ln \hat{p} \to +\infty and the loss explodes.


Example 5.4 — Rational Functions
\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x+1}{(x-2)^2}.
Near x = 2: numerator \to 3 > 0, denominator (x-2)^2 \to 0^+. Hence the ratio \to +\infty.
\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x+1}{(x-2)^2} = +\infty.
Now consider: \lim_{x \to 3^+} \frac{x-5}{x-3}.
Near x = 3^+: numerator \to -2 < 0, denominator \to 0^+. Hence ratio \to -\infty.
\lim_{x \to 3^+} \frac{x-5}{x-3} = -\infty.
The sign rule for rational blow-up:

If \lim_{x \to a} p(x) = L \neq 0 and \lim_{x \to a} q(x) = 0, then \lim_{x \to a} \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = \pm\infty. The sign is determined by the signs of L and q(x) near a.































Sign of LSign of q(x) near aLimit+++\infty+--\infty-+-\infty--+\infty

Example 5.5 — Oscillation vs. Blow-Up
f(x) = \frac{1}{x} \sin!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right), \quad x \neq 0.
As x \to 0, |f(x)| \leq \frac{1}{|x|} \to \infty in magnitude, but the function oscillates. Neither one-sided limit is +\infty or -\infty in a consistent way — the limit does not exist in any sense. Blow-up requires monotone escape, not mere unboundedness in fluctuation.

6. Indeterminate Forms and L’Hôpital’s Rule
When a limit naively produces an indeterminate form, further analysis is required.
The seven classical indeterminate forms:
\frac{0}{0}, \quad \frac{\infty}{\infty}, \quad 0 \cdot \infty, \quad \infty - \infty, \quad 0^0, \quad \infty^0, \quad 1^\infty.

L’Hôpital’s Theorem (Stewart §4.4). Suppose \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = 0 and \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = 0 (or both \to \pm\infty), and g'(x) \neq 0 near a. Then \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}, provided the right-hand limit exists (possibly \pm\infty).

Key Examples
\frac{\infty}{\infty} form: \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln x}{x} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1/x}{1} = 0.

Logarithm grows slower than any power. Used in complexity analysis.

0 \cdot \infty form — rewrite as \frac{0}{0} or \frac{\infty}{\infty}: \lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln x = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\ln x}{1/x} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1/x}{-1/x^2} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-x) = 0.

This is the reason the entropy term p \ln p \to 0 as p \to 0^+ — critical in information theory and cross-entropy loss.

\infty - \infty form — algebraically combine: \lim_{x \to 0} \left(\frac{1}{\sin x} - \frac{1}{x}\right) = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x - \sin x}{x \sin x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos x}{\sin x + x \cos x} \overset{\text{L'H}}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{2\cos x - x \sin x} = 0.

7. Limit Laws Extended to \pm\infty
The standard limit laws extend to infinite limits with care. Let \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = +\infty and \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = L \in \mathbb{R}.








































ExpressionLimitConditionf(x) + g(x)+\infty—f(x) \cdot g(x)+\inftyL > 0f(x) \cdot g(x)-\inftyL < 0g(x) / f(x)0—f(x) / g(x)+\inftyL > 0f(x) + h(x), \lim h = +\infty+\infty—
The dangerous forms \infty - \infty, 0 \cdot \infty, \infty/\infty are not covered — these are the indeterminate cases.

8. Rates of Growth — A Hierarchy
Infinite limits are about how fast functions blow up. This hierarchy is fundamental:
\ln x \ll x^p \ll x^q \ll a^x \ll x! \ll x^x \quad (p < q,\ a > 1, \text{ as } x \to +\infty)
More precisely, for p > 0, a > 1: \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln x}{x^p} = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^p}{a^x} = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{a^x}{x!} = 0.
   Growth rate (schematic, as x → ∞):

   x^x  ↑ fastest
   x!   ↑
   a^x  ↑
   x^q  ↑
   x^p  ↑  (p < q)
   ln x ↑ slowest

   Each is "infinitely smaller" than the one above it.


Why this matters in ML. Exponential blow-up appears in softmax without numerical tricks. Factorial blow-up appears in combinatorial search. Understanding the growth hierarchy tells you which quantities need to be log-transformed, normalized, or clipped.


9. Visualization: Four Behaviors at a Point
Case 1: lim f = +∞ from both sides         Case 2: lim f = −∞ from both sides

   f(x)                                        f(x)
     |   | |                                     |
     |  || ||                                ————+————> x
     | ||   ||                                   |  ||   ||
     |                                           | ||     ||
   ——+————————> x                                |   |   |
     a                                           a

Case 3: +∞ from right, −∞ from left        Case 4: −∞ from right, +∞ from left

   f(x)                                        f(x)
     |  /                                       \  |
     | /                                         \ |
     |/                                           \|
   ——+————> x                                   ——+————> x
     |\                                            /|
     | \                                          / |
     |  \                                        /  |

   (e.g., 1/x)                               (e.g., −1/x)


10. Connection to Continuity and Differentiability
Infinite limits and continuity: If \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = \pm\infty, then f is not continuous at a (continuity requires a finite limit equal to f(a)). This is a type II discontinuity (infinite discontinuity).
Classification of discontinuities:






























TypeDescriptionExampleRemovableLimit exists (finite), but \neq f(a)\frac{\sin x}{x} at 0JumpBoth one-sided limits finite but unequal\text{sgn}(x) at 0InfiniteAt least one one-sided limit is \pm\infty\frac{1}{x} at 0OscillatoryLimit does not exist, neither finite nor infinite\sin(1/x) at 0
Infinite limits and differentiation: By the limit definition, if f'(a) = \pm\infty, we say f has a vertical tangent at a. For instance: f(x) = x^{1/3}, \qquad f'(x) = \frac{1}{3} x^{-2/3}, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0} f'(x) = +\infty. The tangent line is vertical. f is continuous but not differentiable (in the usual sense) at 0.

11. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
11.1 Numerical Overflow and Underflow
In IEEE 754 floating-point, numbers have finite range. When a computation exceeds float32 max (\approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}), the result is inf. This is a computational infinite limit — the mathematical function is fine, but the representation fails.
Softmax instability: \text{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}. If any z_i is large (say, 1000), e^{z_i} overflows to inf. The standard fix: subtract the maximum logit. \text{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i - \max_j z_j}}{\sum_j e^{z_j - \max_j z_j}}. This is valid because \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{e^x}{e^x} = 1 — the limit of the ratio is preserved. The numerical trick is justified by a limit argument.
11.2 Log-Loss and the Entropy Limit
Cross-entropy loss: \mathcal{L} = -\sum_i y_i \log \hat{p}_i.
If \hat{p}_i \to 0^+ and y_i = 1: -\log \hat{p}_i \to +\infty.
The loss blows up. This is an infinite limit at work. In practice, numerical libraries clip \hat{p}_i to [\varepsilon, 1-\varepsilon] for small \varepsilon > 0 to prevent the computation from reaching the vertical asymptote of -\log x at x = 0.
The mathematical fact: \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-\log x) = +\infty — rigorously proved as in Example 5.3.
11.3 Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
In deep networks, gradients are products of Jacobians across layers. Two pathologies arise from infinite limit behavior:
Exploding gradients: |\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}| \to \infty as network depth increases. The product of many matrices with spectral radius > 1 grows without bound — a discrete-time analogue of \lim_{n \to \infty} r^n = \infty for r > 1.
Vanishing gradients: |\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}| \to 0 — the other extreme. Sigmoid saturates because: \lim_{x \to +\infty} \sigma'(x) = \lim_{x \to +\infty} \sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x)) = 1 \cdot 0 = 0. The derivative approaches zero as input grows. The gradient effectively “dies.”
Gradient clipping (for exploding) and residual connections / batch normalization (for vanishing) are engineering responses to these limit behaviors.
11.4 Softplus as a Smooth Approximation to ReLU
\text{softplus}(x) = \ln(1 + e^x).
As x \to -\infty: \text{softplus}(x) \to \ln(1) = 0. As x \to +\infty: \text{softplus}(x) = \ln(1 + e^x) \approx \ln(e^x) = x \to +\infty.
So softplus approximates ReLU. Its derivative is exactly \sigma(x) (the sigmoid), which is smooth and bounded. The infinite limit behavior at +\infty is linear — the same growth rate as ReLU — but the transition is smooth.
11.5 KL Divergence and Infinite Penalties
The KL divergence: D_{KL}(P | Q) = \sum_x P(x) \log \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}.
If P(x) > 0 but Q(x) = 0 for some x: the term \log \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} \to +\infty. Hence D_{KL}(P | Q) = +\infty.
This is not a flaw — it is a feature. It means: if Q assigns zero probability to an event that P says is possible, the distributions are “infinitely different.” Variational autoencoders and variational inference must ensure Q has full support to keep D_{KL} finite. This is an infinite limit providing a hard constraint.
11.6 Weight Initialization and the Spectral Norm
For a linear layer y = Wx, the spectral norm |W|_2 = \sigma_{\max}(W). If weights are poorly initialized, activations can grow without bound through layers: \lim_{L \to \infty} |W^L x| = +\infty \quad \text{if } \sigma_{\max}(W) > 1.
Xavier/He initialization ensures \sigma_{\max}(W) \approx 1, keeping the limit finite. Understanding why initialization matters requires understanding infinite limits.

12. Common Pitfalls

⚠️ \lim f(x) = \infty does not mean the limit “does not exist.” It means the limit exists in \overline{\mathbb{R}} and equals +\infty. In \mathbb{R}, it is true that no finite limit exists — but be precise about which sense you mean.


⚠️ \infty is not a number you can plug in. You cannot write f(\infty) for a function f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}. The expression \lim_{x \to \infty} is a limit, not a function evaluation.


⚠️ Indeterminate \neq undefined. \frac{0}{0} is indeterminate: the limit might exist; we just can’t determine it from the form alone. \frac{1}{0} (with 1 \neq 0) is not indeterminate — it signals \pm\infty (sign depending on the side of approach).


⚠️ L’Hôpital applies only to \frac{0}{0} or \frac{\infty}{\infty}. Applying it to \frac{1}{0} or \frac{3}{\infty} (which are not indeterminate) gives wrong answers.


⚠️ Oscillation is not blow-up. f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\sin\frac{1}{x} is unbounded near 0 but has no infinite limit. “Unbounded” and “limit equals \pm\infty” are different statements.


13. Summary Theorem Sheet

































StatementMeaning\lim_{x \to a} f = +\infty\forall M > 0,\ \exists \delta > 0:\ 0 < \|x-a\| < \delta \Rightarrow f(x) > M\lim_{x \to a} f = -\infty\forall N < 0,\ \exists \delta > 0:\ 0 < \|x-a\| < \delta \Rightarrow f(x) < NVertical asymptote at x = aAt least one one-sided infinite limit at af continuous at aRequires finite limit = f(a); infinite limit \Rightarrow discontinuousL’HôpitalResolves \frac{0}{0} or \frac{\infty}{\infty}; differentiate numerator and denominatorGrowth hierarchy\ln \ll polynomial \ll exponential \ll factorial

14. Practice Problems


(Definition) Prove rigorously that \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1}{x} = +\infty using the M-\delta definition.


(Sign analysis) Determine the sign of each one-sided limit and state whether a vertical asymptote exists: f(x) = \frac{x-3}{(x+1)^2(x-2)} \quad \text{at} \quad x = -1 \text{ and } x = 2.


(Indeterminate forms) Evaluate using L’Hôpital or algebraic manipulation: \lim_{x \to \infty} x e^{-x}, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0^+} x^x, \qquad \lim_{x \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{1}{x}\right)^x.


(Growth hierarchy) Arrange in increasing order of growth rate as x \to \infty: x^{100}, \quad e^x, \quad \ln(\ln x), \quad x!, \quad 2^x, \quad x^x. Justify each comparison with a limit.


(ML connection) Let p \in (0,1) be a predicted probability. Compute \lim_{p \to 0^+} p \ln p and explain why this implies that the entropy H(p) = -p \ln p - (1-p)\ln(1-p) extends continuously to [0,1].


(Proof) Let f be continuous on (a, b) with \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = +\infty. Prove that f is unbounded on (a, a+\varepsilon) for every \varepsilon > 0. (This sounds obvious — make it rigorous.)



15. References


Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §2.2 “The Limit of a Function” (infinite limits); §4.4 “Indeterminate Forms and L’Hôpital’s Rule.”


MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.02. Multivariable Calculus. — Infinite limit behavior reappears in partial derivatives, improper integrals, and the behavior of functions at boundary of domains.


Rudin, Walter. Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed. Ch. 4 — Treatment of limits in \overline{\mathbb{R}}; Chapter on sequences gives the sequence analogue of all definitions here.


Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville. Deep Learning (MIT Press, 2016). §4.1 “Overflow and Underflow”; §6.2 “Gradient-Based Learning”; §8.2 “Challenges in Neural Network Optimization.”


Higham, Nicholas J. Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms, 2nd ed. — For the rigorous treatment of floating-point infinite limit behavior.

01.Maths/Calculus/02.Limits-and-Derivati.title: 06.Limit Laws
01.Maths/Calculus/02.Limits-and-Derivati.content:
“The limit is the soul of calculus — everything else is machinery built on top of it.”


§0. Why This Matters Before We Start
Before we can differentiate, integrate, or train a neural network with gradient descent, we need a rigorous foundation for what it means for a function to approach a value. The limit laws are the axiomatic scaffolding that make all of that possible — not just heuristics, but provable theorems derived from the \varepsilon-\delta definition.

§1. The \varepsilon-\delta Foundation (The Real Definition)

Definition (Stewart §2.4, MIT 18.02 Review Notes). We say \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L if for every \varepsilon > 0, there exists \delta > 0 such that 0 < |x - a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon.

What this is really saying: No matter how tight a tolerance band (-\varepsilon, +\varepsilon) you draw around L, I can find a punctured neighborhood around a whose entire image fits inside that band. The function doesn’t need to be defined at a — we explicitly exclude x = a with the condition 0 < |x-a|.
Pedagogical note to self: Students always confuse “limit exists” with “function is defined at a“. These are completely independent conditions. The classic example:
f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}, \quad a = 0
f(0) is undefined, yet \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1. This will matter enormously when we study derivatives (which are themselves limits of difference quotients at points where the quotient is 0/0).

§2. The Limit Laws (Theorems, Not Postulates)
Let \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L and \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M, where L, M \in \mathbb{R}. Then:













































LawStatementInformal NameL1\lim_{x \to a}[f(x) + g(x)] = L + MSum LawL2\lim_{x \to a}[f(x) - g(x)] = L - MDifference LawL3\lim_{x \to a}[c \cdot f(x)] = cLConstant Multiple LawL4\lim_{x \to a}[f(x) \cdot g(x)] = L \cdot MProduct LawL5\lim_{x \to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{L}{M}, provided M \neq 0Quotient LawL6\lim_{x \to a}[f(x)]^n = L^n, n \in \mathbb{Z}^+Power LawL7\lim_{x \to a}\sqrt[n]{f(x)} = \sqrt[n]{L} (with domain conditions)Root Law
Two Trivial But Essential Base Cases
\lim_{x \to a} c = c \qquad \text{(limit of a constant)} \lim_{x \to a} x = a \qquad \text{(limit of the identity)}
These two facts, combined with L1–L7, are sufficient to evaluate the limit of any polynomial — which is the content of the Direct Substitution Property.

§3. Proof of the Sum Law (Full \varepsilon-\delta Proof)
This is the one proof every analyst should be able to reproduce from memory.
Theorem (Sum Law). If \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L and \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M, then \lim_{x \to a}[f(x)+g(x)] = L + M.
Proof.
Let \varepsilon > 0 be arbitrary. We need |f(x) + g(x) - (L+M)| < \varepsilon.
By the triangle inequality: |f(x) + g(x) - L - M| \leq |f(x) - L| + |g(x) - M|
Strategy: make each piece < \varepsilon/2.
Since \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L, for \varepsilon/2 > 0, \exists, \delta_1 > 0 such that: 0 < |x-a| < \delta_1 \implies |f(x) - L| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}
Since \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M, for \varepsilon/2 > 0, \exists, \delta_2 > 0 such that: 0 < |x-a| < \delta_2 \implies |g(x) - M| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}
Set \delta = \min(\delta_1, \delta_2). Then for 0 < |x-a| < \delta: |f(x)+g(x) - (L+M)| \leq |f(x)-L| + |g(x)-M| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon. \qquad \blacksquare

Note: The \min trick — taking the smaller of two deltas so both conditions hold simultaneously — appears constantly in analysis. It’s the workhorse move.


§4. The Squeeze Theorem (Sandwich Theorem)
This deserves its own section because it’s not derived from L1–L7; it’s an independent tool for limits that can’t be evaluated directly.
Theorem (Squeeze). Suppose h(x) \leq f(x) \leq g(x) near a (except possibly at a itself), and \lim_{x \to a} h(x) = \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = L. Then \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L.
Canonical example:
\lim_{x \to 0} x^2 \sin!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)
Since -1 \leq \sin(1/x) \leq 1 for all x \neq 0: -x^2 \leq x^2 \sin!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \leq x^2
Both -x^2 \to 0 and x^2 \to 0 as x \to 0. Therefore by Squeeze: limit = 0.
    y
    |      .·' x²
    |   .·'
    | ·  ← f(x) trapped here
    |·_____________________ x
    |·
    | ·
    |   '·.
    |      '·. -x²

The function f(x) = x²sin(1/x) oscillates but is
squeezed to 0 as x → 0.


§5. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Polynomial (Direct Substitution)
\lim_{x \to 3}(2x^2 - 5x + 1)
By L1, L2, L3, L6, and the base cases: = 2\lim_{x\to 3} x^2 - 5\lim_{x\to 3} x + \lim_{x\to 3} 1 = 2(9) - 5(3) + 1 = 18 - 15 + 1 = \boxed{4}
Example 2 — Indeterminate Form 0/0 (Factor and Cancel)
\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}
Direct substitution gives 0/0 — the Quotient Law does not apply (since M = 0). Instead:
\frac{x^2 - 4}{x-2} = \frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2} = x + 2, \quad x \neq 2
Now the Quotient Law’s obstruction is gone (we’re looking at a different function that agrees with ours near x=2 but not at x=2, which is all a limit cares about):
\lim_{x \to 2}(x+2) = 4

Key Insight: Cancellation is valid here because in the limit, x \neq 2. Limits are inherently punctured neighborhoods.

Example 3 — Rationalization Trick
\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x+4} - 2}{x}
Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate \sqrt{x+4}+2:
\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x+4}+2}{\sqrt{x+4}+2} = \frac{(x+4)-4}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} = \frac{x}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}+2}
\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}+2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4}+2} = \frac{1}{4}
This exact computation is the derivative of \sqrt{x} at x=4 from first principles.

§6. Visualization — What Limits “Look Like”
Case 1: Limit exists, function defined at a
        f(a) = L  ✓
        
    L ──────────●──────────
               /
              /
    ──────────────────────► x
              a

Case 2: Limit exists, f(a) undefined (removable discontinuity)
        
    L ──────────○──────────    ← hole at x=a
               /
              /
    ──────────────────────► x
              a
    Example: sin(x)/x at x=0

Case 3: Limit does not exist (jump discontinuity)
        
   M  ──────────●
               
   L  ──────────○
               
    ──────────────────────► x
              a
    Left limit ≠ right limit
    Example: floor function at integers

Case 4: Limit does not exist (oscillation)
        
    L ────────────────────
           ~~~~
          ~    ~         ← oscillates, never settles
         ~      ~
    ──────────────────────► x
              a
    Example: sin(1/x) at x=0 (without the x² factor)


§7. One-Sided Limits
Definition. The right-hand limit: \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L \iff \forall \varepsilon>0,; \exists \delta>0: 0 < x-a < \delta \implies |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon
Theorem. \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L if and only if \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = L = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x).
This is the two-sided characterization. It’s the tool for checking limits at points of potential discontinuity, like piecewise functions.
Example: f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & x < 1 \ 2x - 1 & x \geq 1 \end{cases}
\lim_{x \to 1^-} f(x) = 1^2 = 1, \qquad \lim_{x \to 1^+} f(x) = 2(1)-1 = 1
Both sides agree \Rightarrow \lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 1. (And f(1) = 1, so f is actually continuous here.)

§8. Limits at Infinity
\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L \iff \forall \varepsilon>0,; \exists M>0: x > M \implies |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon
Key results used everywhere:
\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{x^p} = 0 \quad \text{for } p > 0
\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{a_n x^n + \cdots + a_0}{b_m x^m + \cdots + b_0} = \begin{cases} \frac{a_n}{b_m} & n = m \ 0 & n < m \ \pm\infty & n > m \end{cases}
Technique: divide numerator and denominator by x^{\max(n,m)}.
Example: \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3x^2 - x}{2x^2 + 5} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3 - 1/x}{2 + 5/x^2} = \frac{3-0}{2+0} = \frac{3}{2}

§9. Continuity — The Payoff of All This
Definition. f is continuous at a if:

f(a) is defined,
\lim_{x \to a} f(x) exists,
\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a).

All three conditions are independent. The limit laws immediately give us:
Corollary. Every polynomial is continuous everywhere. Every rational function is continuous on its domain.
The Direct Substitution Property is precisely the statement that for continuous f: \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a) — you can just plug in.

§10. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning

This section earns its place because every claim below traces back directly to the limit laws.

10.1 The Derivative = A Limit
The entire edifice of backpropagation rests on one limit:
f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}
This is an indeterminate form 0/0. Without limit laws (specifically the algebraic manipulation of 0/0 forms), we cannot differentiate anything. Every weight update in gradient descent is:
w \leftarrow w - \eta \cdot \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w}
where \partial \mathcal{L}/\partial w is a partial derivative — a limit.
10.2 Activation Functions and Limits at Infinity
The sigmoid activation is: \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}
Its behavior at the saturation regime: \lim_{x \to +\infty} \sigma(x) = 1, \qquad \lim_{x \to -\infty} \sigma(x) = 0
These horizontal asymptotes (limits at infinity) explain the vanishing gradient problem: in the tails, \sigma'(x) \to 0, so gradients vanish in deep networks. ReLU was introduced precisely to avoid this — \text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0,x) has no saturation for x > 0.
The limit \lim_{x \to 0^-} \text{ReLU}'(x) = 0 \neq 1 = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \text{ReLU}'(x) shows ReLU is not differentiable at 0 — a one-sided limit problem. In practice, subgradients handle this.
10.3 Loss Landscape and Continuity
For gradient descent to work at all, the loss function \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) must be continuous (so small changes in weights don’t cause catastrophic jumps in loss). The limit laws guarantee continuity of compositions of continuous functions — since neural networks are compositions of affine maps and continuous activations, the overall network function is continuous. This is not obvious without limit theory.
10.4 Batch Normalization — Limits and Stability
Batch norm computes: \hat{x}_i = \frac{x_i - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_B^2 + \varepsilon}}
The \varepsilon > 0 in the denominator is there to prevent division by zero (i.e., to avoid the case M = 0 where the Quotient Law breaks down). As \varepsilon \to 0^+, the expression approaches the true normalization — this is a limit in its own right, and the chosen \varepsilon is a practical \delta.
10.5 Universal Approximation and Limits
The Universal Approximation Theorem (Cybenko, 1989) states that a single hidden layer network with enough neurons can approximate any continuous function f: [0,1]^n \to \mathbb{R} to arbitrary precision \varepsilon > 0. The phrase “arbitrary precision \varepsilon” is the limit definition in disguise — the theorem is fundamentally an \varepsilon-approximation result whose roots lie exactly in the \varepsilon-\delta language.
10.6 Convergence of Training — Sequences and Limits
When we say “the model converged,” we mean the sequence of loss values {\mathcal{L}_t}_{t=1}^{\infty} satisfies: \lim_{t \to \infty} \mathcal{L}_t = \mathcal{L}^*
This is a sequential limit — the analogous notion to \lim_{x \to a} but for discrete sequences. The \varepsilon-\delta definition becomes the \varepsilon-N definition: for every \varepsilon > 0, there exists N such that t > N \implies |\mathcal{L}_t - \mathcal{L}^*| < \varepsilon. Same idea, different setting.

§11. Common Errors and Traps






























ErrorWhy It’s WrongCorrect MoveApplying Quotient Law when M=0Law requires M \neq 0 — denominator limit must be nonzeroFactor, rationalize, or use L’HôpitalConcluding limit DNE from one approachMust check all paths (not just x \to a^{\pm})For functions of two variables, this gets much worseWriting \lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a) alwaysOnly valid if f is continuous at aVerify continuity explicitlyCanceling (x-a) before the limitValid because x \neq a in a limit; often forgotten in explanationAlways note “since x \neq a in the limit…”

§12. Summary Map
ε-δ Definition
      │
      ▼
  Base Cases: lim c = c,  lim x = a
      │
      ▼
  Limit Laws (L1–L7)
      │
      ├──► Direct Substitution Property
      │           │
      │           └──► Continuity
      │
      ├──► Algebraic Techniques (factor, rationalize, conjugate)
      │           │
      │           └──► Evaluating 0/0 forms  ──► Derivatives
      │
      └──► Squeeze Theorem
                  │
                  └──► Limits of oscillating/bounded functions


§13. Problems (Self-Check)
Easy:

Prove the Constant Multiple Law (L3) from the \varepsilon-\delta definition.
Evaluate \lim_{x \to -1} \frac{x^3 + 1}{x + 1}.

Medium: 3. Use the Squeeze Theorem to show \lim_{x \to 0} x \cos(1/x) = 0. 4. Prove that if \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L > 0, then f(x) > 0 in some punctured neighborhood of a.
Hard: 5. Give a function f such that \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) exists but f is discontinuous at every rational number near 0. 6. Prove the Product Law (L4) from scratch. (Hint: write f(x)g(x) - LM = f(x)[g(x)-M] + M[f(x)-L] and apply the triangle inequality.)

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Cengage Learning. §§2.2–2.5.
