01.Maths/Calculus/04.Applications-of-Dif.title: 01.Minimum and Maximum Values
01.Maths/Calculus/04.Applications-of-Dif.content:
“Nature is thrifty in all her actions.” — Pierre Louis Maupertuis
Personal note: Every optimization algorithm in machine learning — gradient descent, Adam, RMSProp — is, at its core, a machine trying to do what we’re about to describe rigorously. Understanding this chapter is understanding the soul of modern AI.


§1. The Absolute Extrema — Definitions
Let f be a function defined on a domain D \subseteq \mathbb{R}.

Definition 1.1 (Absolute Maximum). A value f(c) is the absolute maximum of f on D if f(c) \geq f(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in D.


Definition 1.2 (Absolute Minimum). A value f(c) is the absolute minimum of f on D if f(c) \leq f(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in D.

The absolute maximum and minimum are collectively called extreme values or absolute extrema.
Remark. Existence is not guaranteed in general. Consider:

f(x) = x on (0,1): no maximum, no minimum — the interval is open.
f(x) = \frac{1}{x} on (0, \infty): no minimum.
f(x) = \sin(x) on \mathbb{R}: maximum value 1 achieved at infinitely many points, but the set of maxima is well-defined.

This motivates the fundamental existence theorem.

§2. The Extreme Value Theorem

Theorem 2.1 (Extreme Value Theorem — EVT). If f is continuous on a closed, bounded interval [a, b], then f attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on [a, b].
That is, there exist c, d \in [a, b] such that f(c) \leq f(x) \leq f(d) \quad \text{for all } x \in [a, b].

Why both conditions are necessary:

























Condition droppedCounterexampleWhat failsContinuityf(x) = \begin{cases} x & x \in (0,1] \ 2 & x=0 \end{cases} on [0,1]Min not attainedClosed intervalf(x) = x on (0,1)Neither attainedBounded intervalf(x) = x on [0, \infty)No max
Proof sketch. The proof uses two deep facts from real analysis:

A continuous image of a compact set is compact (Heine–Cantor).
A compact subset of \mathbb{R} is closed and bounded, hence contains its supremum and infimum.

Since [a,b] is compact and f is continuous, f([a,b]) is compact, so \sup f([a,b]) and \inf f([a,b]) are attained. \blacksquare

§3. Local Extrema
Global search is hard. We begin locally.

Definition 3.1 (Local Maximum). f has a local maximum at c if there exists \delta > 0 such that f(c) \geq f(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in (c-\delta, c+\delta) \cap D.


Definition 3.2 (Local Minimum). f has a local minimum at c if there exists \delta > 0 such that f(c) \leq f(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in (c-\delta, c+\delta) \cap D.

Intuition. A local max is the highest point in its neighborhood — it doesn’t need to beat everyone, just its neighbors. This is critical in optimization: most algorithms find local extrema, and global optimization is generally NP-hard.

§4. Fermat’s Theorem — The Critical Point Condition

Theorem 4.1 (Fermat’s Theorem). If f has a local extremum at c and f'(c) exists, then f'(c) = 0.

Proof. Suppose f has a local maximum at c. Then for all x sufficiently close to c: f(x) - f(c) \leq 0.
Case 1: x > c. Then \dfrac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} \leq 0, so taking x \to c^+: f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c^+} \frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} \leq 0.
Case 2: x < c. Then \dfrac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} \geq 0, so taking x \to c^-: f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c^-} \frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} \geq 0.
Since f'(c) exists and satisfies both f'(c) \leq 0 and f'(c) \geq 0, we conclude f'(c) = 0. The local minimum case is symmetric. \blacksquare

Warning (Converse is FALSE). f'(c) = 0 does not imply c is an extremum.
Example: f(x) = x^3. Then f'(0) = 0, but x=0 is an inflection point, not an extremum. The function changes sign of its derivative here — it’s increasing on both sides of 0.


§5. Critical Numbers

Definition 5.1. A number c in the domain of f is a critical number (or critical point) if either:

f'(c) = 0, or
f'(c) does not exist.


Why include non-differentiable points? Fermat’s theorem requires f'(c) to exist. But extrema can occur where the derivative fails to exist.
Example: f(x) = |x| on [-1, 1]. The minimum is at x = 0, but f'(0) doesn’t exist (corner point). So 0 is a critical number.
Example: f(x) = x^{1/3}. Then f'(x) = \frac{1}{3}x^{-2/3}, which doesn’t exist at x = 0. The point x=0 is a critical number (it’s an inflection point here, but could be an extremum in other examples).

Corollary 5.1. If f has a local extremum at c, then c is a critical number of f.

This is the contrapositive of Fermat’s theorem combined with the observation about non-differentiable points.

§6. The Closed Interval Method
The EVT guarantees extrema exist on [a,b]. The Closed Interval Method finds them:

Algorithm 6.1 (Closed Interval Method). To find the absolute extrema of a continuous f on [a,b]:

Find all critical numbers of f in (a, b).
Evaluate f at each critical number.
Evaluate f at the endpoints: f(a) and f(b).
The largest value is the absolute maximum; the smallest is the absolute minimum.


Why does this work? By EVT, the absolute extrema exist. By Corollary 5.1, any interior extremum must be a critical point. The endpoints are candidates by default (boundary of the domain). Exhausting all candidates and comparing gives the answer.

§7. Worked Examples
Example 7.1 — Polynomial
Find the absolute extrema of f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 1 on [-\frac{1}{2}, 4].
Step 1. f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x-2).
Critical numbers in (-\frac{1}{2}, 4): x = 0 and x = 2.
Step 2–3. Evaluate:

























xf(x)-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{2})^3 - 3(\frac{1}{4}) + 1 = -\frac{1}{8} - \frac{3}{4} + 1 = \frac{1}{8}00 - 0 + 1 = 128 - 12 + 1 = -3464 - 48 + 1 = 17
Absolute maximum: f(4) = 17. Absolute minimum: f(2) = -3.
Example 7.2 — With Non-differentiable Point
Find the absolute extrema of f(x) = |x^2 - 1| on [-2, 2].
f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 - 1 & |x| \geq 1 \ 1 - x^2 & |x| < 1 \end{cases}
f'(x) = \begin{cases} 2x & |x| > 1 \ -2x & |x| < 1 \ \text{DNE} & x = \pm 1 \end{cases}
Critical numbers: x = 0 (where f' = 0), x = \pm 1 (where f' DNE).





























xf(x)-23-10011023
Absolute maximum: f(\pm 2) = 3. Absolute minimum: f(\pm 1) = 0.

§8. Visualization
8.1 Anatomy of a Function on [a, b]
  f(x)
  │                                    * abs max (endpoint)
  │                *                  /
  │               / \                /
  │    loc max   /   \    loc min   /
  │     *       /     \    *       /
  │    / \     /       \  / \     /
  │   /   \   /         \/   \   /
  │  /     \ /                \_/
  │ /       *   saddle (f'=0,
  │/         inflection)
  ├──────────────────────────────────── x
  a    c₁    c₂    c₃    c₄    c₅    b
       ↑      ↑     ↑     ↑
    loc max  f'=0  loc  loc
             not   min  min
             extr

Legend:

* = critical point (either f' = 0 or f' DNE)
The absolute extremum can occur at a critical point or at an endpoint
A critical point with f'=0 is NOT necessarily an extremum (see c_2 above — inflection)

8.2 Sign Chart for Derivative Analysis
For f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 1:
f'(x) = 3x(x-2)

x:     -∞    0    +∞
       ──────┼──────┼──────
f'(x): + + + 0 - - - 0 + + +
              ↑           ↑
           loc max      loc min

Reading the chart:

f' > 0 \Rightarrow f is increasing
f' < 0 \Rightarrow f is decreasing
Sign change + \to - at x=0: local max
Sign change - \to + at x=2: local min

8.3 Multi-variable Preview (Loss Surface)
In 2D, a loss function \mathcal{L}(\theta_1, \theta_2) looks like a surface. The contour plot below is conceptual:
    θ₂
    │      saddle
    │       ×
    │   ∗           ∗
    │  local       local
    │  min          min
    │
    │       ∗
    │    global
    │      min
    └─────────────────── θ₁

Gradient descent follows -\nabla \mathcal{L} — the steepest descent direction — which is exactly the generalization of f'(c) = 0 to multiple dimensions.

§9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning

This is not a digression. This entire chapter IS the theoretical foundation of machine learning.

9.1 Loss Minimization as the Core Problem
In supervised learning, we train a model with parameters \theta \in \mathbb{R}^n by minimizing a loss function: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \ell(f_\theta(x^{(i)}), y^{(i)})
where \ell is a pointwise loss (e.g., squared error, cross-entropy). Finding optimal \theta^* is exactly an absolute minimum problem.
The critical point condition becomes: \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta^*) = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{(gradient is the zero vector)}
This is Fermat’s theorem in \mathbb{R}^n.
9.2 Gradient Descent — Iterative Fermat
Since \mathcal{L} is typically non-convex and high-dimensional (GPT-4 has ~10^{12} parameters), we can’t solve \nabla \mathcal{L} = 0 analytically. Instead:
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)
where \eta > 0 is the learning rate. This is a discrete approximation to following the steepest descent path toward a local minimum. The fixed points of this update (\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t) are exactly the critical points.
Variants:

SGD (Stochastic Gradient Descent): Uses a minibatch to approximate \nabla \mathcal{L}
Adam: Adapts the learning rate per parameter using first and second moment estimates
RMSProp: Divides by running average of squared gradients

All seek the same thing: a point where \nabla \mathcal{L} \approx \mathbf{0}.
9.3 The Local vs Global Minimum Problem
A deep neural network’s loss landscape is non-convex, so gradient descent finds local minima, not necessarily global ones. This is the direct multi-dimensional generalization of our observation that f'(c) = 0 does not guarantee a global minimum.
Surprising empirical finding (2014–present): In practice, local minima of large neural networks tend to have similar loss values to the global minimum. The more dangerous critical points are saddle points — where \nabla \mathcal{L} = 0 but the Hessian H is indefinite (some eigenvalues positive, some negative). These are the analog of f(x) = x^3 at x=0.
Theorem (informal, Dauphin et al., 2014). In high dimensions, most critical points with high loss are saddle points, not local minima. True local minima with high loss are exponentially rare.
9.4 Second-Order Methods and the Hessian
The second derivative test in 1D:

f''(c) > 0 at a critical point \Rightarrow local min
f''(c) < 0 \Rightarrow local max
f''(c) = 0 \Rightarrow inconclusive

In \mathbb{R}^n, the Hessian matrix H = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L} plays this role:

H positive definite \Rightarrow local min
H negative definite \Rightarrow local max
H indefinite \Rightarrow saddle point

Newton’s method for optimization uses the full Hessian: \theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - H^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)
This converges quadratically near a minimum but costs O(n^3) to invert H — infeasible for large networks. Quasi-Newton methods (L-BFGS) approximate H^{-1} cheaply.
9.5 Convex Optimization — When Local = Global
If \mathcal{L} is convex (e.g., linear regression with MSE loss, logistic regression), then: \text{every local minimum is a global minimum}
This is the analog of: a function with f'' > 0 everywhere on an interval has at most one local (= global) minimum. Convexity is defined by: \mathcal{L}(\lambda \theta_1 + (1-\lambda)\theta_2) \leq \lambda \mathcal{L}(\theta_1) + (1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}(\theta_2), \quad \lambda \in [0,1]
Support Vector Machines and linear models exploit convexity to guarantee finding the global minimum. This is why they have convergence guarantees that deep networks lack.
9.6 Regularization as a Constraint
L2 regularization (weight decay) solves: \min_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta) + \frac{\lambda}{2}|\theta|^2
This is equivalent to finding the minimum of the unconstrained loss subject to |\theta| \leq R for some R — a constrained optimization problem. The method of Lagrange multipliers (multivariable calculus) formalizes this connection, and the critical point condition becomes the KKT conditions in convex optimization.
9.7 Summary Table









































Calculus ConceptML/DL AnalogueLocal minimum of fConverged weights in gradient descentf'(c) = 0\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} = 0 (training complete)Saddle pointThe main obstruction in deep net trainingSecond derivative testHessian analysis, curvature of loss landscapeClosed interval methodGrid search / hyperparameter searchAbsolute minimum on [a,b]Global optimum (convex problems only)Convex functionConvex loss (linear/logistic regression)Gradient descentIterative approximation to critical points

§10. The Second Derivative Test (Preview)
Full treatment in the next section, but the setup:
If f'(c) = 0, how do we classify c?

Theorem 10.1 (Second Derivative Test). Suppose f'' is continuous near c and f'(c) = 0:

If f''(c) > 0: c is a local minimum (f is concave up)
If f''(c) < 0: c is a local maximum (f is concave down)
If f''(c) = 0: inconclusive (need higher derivatives or sign analysis)


Intuition. Near a local min, the graph looks like a upward parabola — f'' > 0 means concave up, i.e., the function curves away from the tangent line upward. This is exactly why gradient descent converges: near a true minimum, the loss surface curves upward in all directions.

§11. Key Theorems — Reference Card






























TheoremStatementConditionsEVTContinuous f on [a,b] attains abs. max and minf continuous, [a,b] closed & boundedFermatLocal extremum at c, f'(c) exists \Rightarrow f'(c) = 0f differentiable at cClosed Interval MethodCheck critical pts + endpoints for absolute extremaf continuous on [a,b]2nd Deriv. Testf'(c)=0, f''(c)\neq 0 classifies cf'' continuous near c

§12. Common Mistakes and Traps

Trap 1. Assuming f'(c) = 0 implies c is an extremum. Counterexample: f(x) = x^3 at x=0. Always check sign change of f'.


Trap 2. Forgetting to check endpoints on closed intervals. The absolute max/min can occur at a or b.


Trap 3. Applying EVT to open intervals or discontinuous functions. The theorem’s conclusion is false without both hypotheses.


Trap 4. In ML: confusing “gradient is zero” with “global minimum found.” In non-convex problems, \nabla \mathcal{L} = 0 only guarantees a critical point.


Trap 5. Using the second derivative test when f''(c) = 0. The test is inconclusive. Use first derivative sign analysis instead.


References

Stewart, J. — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Chapter 4.1: Maximum and Minimum Values.
MIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus (Denis Auroux). Lectures on optimization, critical points, second derivative test in several variables.
Dauphin, Y. et al. — Identifying and attacking the saddle point problem in high-dimensional non-convex optimization. NeurIPS 2014.
Boyd, S. & Vandenberghe, L. — Convex Optimization. Cambridge University Press. (For the connection between calculus extrema and modern ML optimization theory.)


— End of Note —

Next: §Second Derivative Test and Concavity → then Curve Sketching → then Applied Optimization (where ML loss functions live in their natural habitat).

01.Maths/Calculus/04.Applications-of-Dif.title: 02.Fermat's Theorem
01.Maths/Calculus/04.Applications-of-Dif.content:
“To find the maxima and minima of a quantity, one takes the ordinary derivative and sets it equal to zero.” — Pierre de Fermat, c. 1638 (paraphrase)
Personal note: Fermat wrote this before calculus existed — before Newton, before Leibniz. He was computing what we now call derivatives using an ad-hoc “method of adequality.” The theorem bearing his name is the rigorous formalization of his geometric intuition: at a peak or valley, the tangent line must be horizontal.


§1. Motivation — What Does Extremum Mean Geometrically?
Stand on a smooth hill. At the very top, the ground beneath your feet is flat — the slope is zero in every direction. If you’re in a valley, same thing. The tangent plane is horizontal.
In one dimension: if f has a local max at c, then just to the left of c the function is increasing (f' > 0), and just to the right it is decreasing (f' < 0). At the transition point itself, f'(c) = 0.
        f(c) ← local max
       /     \
      /        \       f' changes + → −
─────              ─────
    f' > 0   f'=0   f' < 0

Fermat’s Theorem makes this intuition a theorem — rigorous, with clear hypotheses.

§2. Statement of the Theorem

Theorem (Fermat’s Theorem). Let f be defined on an open interval containing c. Suppose:

f has a local extremum at c (either a local max or local min), and
f is differentiable at c.

Then f'(c) = 0.

Logically: \bigl(f \text{ has local extremum at } c\bigr) ;\wedge; \bigl(f'(c) \text{ exists}\bigr) ;\implies; f'(c) = 0

§3. Complete Proof
We prove the local maximum case. The local minimum case is symmetric (or apply the result to -f).
Setup. Suppose f has a local maximum at c. By definition, there exists \delta > 0 such that: f(x) \leq f(c) \quad \text{for all } x \in (c - \delta,; c + \delta). \tag{$*$}
We are given that f'(c) exists, so the limit f'(c) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} exists (as a finite real number). Since the two-sided limit exists, the one-sided limits both exist and equal f'(c).

Case 1: Right-hand limit (h \to 0^+, i.e., h > 0 small).
For 0 < h < \delta, we have c + h \in (c - \delta, c + \delta), so by (*): f(c + h) - f(c) \leq 0.
Since h > 0: \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \leq 0.
Taking the limit as h \to 0^+ (the inequality is preserved under limits): f'(c) = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h} \leq 0. \tag{1}

Case 2: Left-hand limit (h \to 0^-, i.e., h < 0 small).
For -\delta < h < 0, we have c + h \in (c - \delta, c + \delta), so by (*): f(c+h) - f(c) \leq 0.
But now h < 0, so dividing reverses the inequality: \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \geq 0.
Taking the limit as h \to 0^-: f'(c) = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h} \geq 0. \tag{2}

Conclusion. From (1) and (2): f'(c) \leq 0 \quad \text{and} \quad f'(c) \geq 0 \implies \boxed{f'(c) = 0.}
For the local minimum case: the inequality (*) reverses to f(x) \geq f(c), which flips the signs in Cases 1 and 2, and we again conclude f'(c) = 0. \blacksquare

§4. The Converse is FALSE — This is Critical

f'(c) = 0 does NOT imply c is an extremum.

This is one of the most common errors. Fermat’s theorem is a one-way implication only.
Counterexample: f(x) = x^3 at c = 0
f'(x) = 3x^2 \implies f'(0) = 0.
Yet f is strictly increasing on all of \mathbb{R}: for x > 0, f(x) > 0 = f(0), and for x < 0, f(x) < 0 = f(0). So x = 0 is neither a local max nor a local min — it is an inflection point.
  f(x) = x³

       │      /
       │     /
       │    /
  ─────┼───────── x
       │  /
       │ /
       │/
         ↑
    f'(0) = 0, but NOT an extremum
    (function strictly increasing through 0)

Summary of Logical Structure

























StatementTrue?Local extremum at c + differentiable \Rightarrow f'(c)=0✓ Fermat’s Theoremf'(c) = 0 \Rightarrow local extremum at c✗ FALSE (x^3 counterexample)f'(c) = 0 \Rightarrow c is a critical number✓ (by definition)Local extremum at c \Rightarrow c is a critical number✓ (Fermat + non-diff. case)
The correct chain is: \text{local extremum} \implies \text{critical number} \centernot\impliedby \text{critical number}

§5. Why the Hypothesis “Differentiable at c” is Essential
Fermat’s theorem requires f'(c) to exist. Drop this and the conclusion fails.
Example: f(x) = |x| at c = 0
f has an absolute (and local) minimum at c = 0. But: f'(0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{|h| - 0}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{|h|}{h}
The right limit is +1, the left limit is -1 — they disagree. So f'(0) does not exist.
The minimum occurs at a corner, not a smooth point. There is no horizontal tangent — there is no tangent line at all.
  f(x) = |x|

   \   /
    \ /
     *  ← global min, f'(0) DNE
     |
─────┼───── x

This is why the definition of critical number includes both f'(c) = 0 and f'(c) DNE — to capture all possible extrema locations.
The Full Picture: Where Can Extrema Occur?
\text{local extremum at } c \implies c \text{ is a critical number}
c \text{ is a critical number} \iff f'(c) = 0 ;\text{ or }; f'(c) \text{ does not exist}
Fermat’s theorem handles the differentiable case. The non-differentiable case is separate (but the conclusion — that c is a critical number — holds trivially).

§6. Why the Hypothesis “Open Interval” is Essential
The theorem requires f to be defined on an open interval containing c (not just at c, and not on a closed interval where c is an endpoint).
Why? The proof uses the limit from both sides of c. If c = a is the left endpoint of [a,b], only the right-hand limit is available:
f'(a^+) \leq 0
But we can’t conclude f'(a) \geq 0 from the left (there is no left side). So we can’t squeeze to f'(a) = 0.
Example. f(x) = x on [0, 1]. The absolute minimum is at x = 0 and the absolute maximum at x = 1. But f'(x) = 1 \neq 0 everywhere — including at the endpoints. Fermat’s theorem simply doesn’t apply here, because 0 and 1 are not interior to the domain.
Consequence. This is precisely why the Closed Interval Method must check endpoints separately — Fermat doesn’t cover them.

§7. Visualization: The Full Taxonomy
All points c in domain of f
│
├── f'(c) exists
│   ├── f'(c) = 0  ──────────────────→ CRITICAL NUMBER
│   │   ├── sign of f' changes + → −  → local MAX    ← Fermat applies
│   │   ├── sign of f' changes − → +  → local MIN    ← Fermat applies
│   │   └── sign of f' doesn't change → INFLECTION (e.g. x³ at 0)
│   │
│   └── f'(c) ≠ 0  → NOT a critical number
│                     (cannot be an interior extremum by Fermat)
│
├── f'(c) does not exist
│   ├── corner (e.g. |x| at 0)  ──→ CRITICAL NUMBER (may be extremum)
│   ├── cusp (e.g. x^{2/3} at 0) → CRITICAL NUMBER (may be extremum)
│   └── vertical tangent         → CRITICAL NUMBER (may be extremum)
│
└── c is an ENDPOINT of [a,b]
    └── Fermat does NOT apply → check separately


§8. Examples
Example 8.1 — Polynomial, All Cases
f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3
f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 = 4x^2(x - 3)
Critical numbers: f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0 or x = 3.
Classify x = 0:
Sign of f'(x) = 4x^2(x-3) near x=0:

For x slightly < 0: 4x^2 > 0, (x-3) < 0 → f'(x) < 0
For x slightly > 0: 4x^2 > 0, (x-3) < 0 → f'(x) < 0

Sign does not change → x = 0 is not an extremum (inflection point). f'(0) = 0, Fermat’s conclusion holds, but the converse is false.
Classify x = 3:

For x < 3: 4x^2 > 0, (x-3) < 0 → f'(x) < 0
For x > 3: 4x^2 > 0, (x-3) > 0 → f'(x) > 0

Sign changes - \to + → x = 3 is a local minimum.
f'(x) sign chart:
      − − − 0 − − − 0 + + +
      ──────┼───────┼──────
            0       3
         inflec.  loc min

Example 8.2 — Non-differentiable Extremum
f(x) = \begin{cases} -x + 1 & x < 0 \ x^2 + 1 & x \geq 0 \end{cases}
At c = 0: \lim_{h\to 0^-} \frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0^-} \frac{(-h+1)-1}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0^-} \frac{-h}{h} = -1 \lim_{h\to 0^+} \frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0^+} \frac{h^2+1-1}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0^+} h = 0
One-sided limits disagree: f'(0) DNE. Fermat’s theorem does not apply. Yet f(0) = 1 is a local minimum (approaching from left, f \to 1^+; from right, f \to 1^+ through x^2+1 \geq 1).
Example 8.3 — Verifying Fermat Directly
f(x) = \sin x, \quad c = \frac{\pi}{2}
f'(x) = \cos x, so f'(\pi/2) = \cos(\pi/2) = 0. ✓
f(\pi/2) = 1 is a local (and global) maximum on any interval containing \pi/2. Fermat’s theorem confirms f'(\pi/2) = 0, consistent.

§9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, Deep Learning

Fermat’s Theorem is the theoretical certificate that gradient descent is doing the right thing — and also explains why it can get stuck.

9.1 The Training Objective
In machine learning, we minimize a loss: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m \ell(f_\theta(x^{(i)}), y^{(i)}), \quad \theta \in \mathbb{R}^n
At any interior local minimizer \theta^_ where \mathcal{L} is differentiable, Fermat’s theorem (in \mathbb{R}^n) gives: \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta^_) = \mathbf{0}
This is the necessary condition gradient descent tries to satisfy. Every weight update moves toward making this gradient zero.
9.2 The Converse Failure = The Saddle Point Problem
The converse of Fermat’s theorem fails in 1D with x^3. In high-dimensional ML it fails catastrophically at saddle points.
A saddle point \theta^_ satisfies \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta^_) = \mathbf{0} but is neither a max nor a min — it’s a max in some directions and a min in others. In \mathbb{R}^n for large n, saddle points are exponentially more common than local minima.
  Saddle point in 2D:
  
    θ₂
    │    ╲   ╱   ← increasing in θ₂ direction (local max)
    │     ╲ ╱
    │      ×  ← ∇L = 0 here, but saddle
    │     ╱ ╲
    │    ╱   ╲   ← decreasing in θ₁ direction (local min)
    └──────────── θ₁

Consequence for training: Gradient descent near a saddle point has gradient \approx \mathbf{0}, so updates become tiny — training stalls. This is a major practical problem in deep learning.
Solutions used in practice:

Momentum (SGD with momentum): carries velocity through saddle regions
Adam: uses second moment estimates to escape flat regions
Noise in SGD (from random minibatches): perturbs away from saddle points

All of these are engineering responses to the failure of the converse of Fermat’s theorem.
9.3 ReLU and Non-differentiable Points in Neural Networks
The ReLU activation \sigma(x) = \max(0, x) is not differentiable at x = 0: \sigma'(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & x > 0 \ 0 & x < 0 \ \text{undefined} & x = 0 \end{cases}
This is the neural network version of |x| — a corner. In practice, we use the subgradient (set \sigma'(0) = 0 or 0.5 by convention). Fermat’s theorem doesn’t directly apply at these points, but the critical number concept extends to the non-smooth setting via subdifferential calculus.
The entire field of non-smooth optimization — used when training networks with \ell_1 regularization, ReLU activations, max-pooling — is a generalization of the observation that extrema can occur where f' fails to exist.
9.4 Fermat’s Theorem in Convex Optimization
For convex loss functions (e.g., logistic regression, ridge regression), Fermat’s theorem becomes if and only if:

\theta^_ is a global minimum \iff \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta^_) = \mathbf{0}

This is because for convex differentiable functions, every critical point is a global minimum (there are no saddle points, no local-but-not-global minima). This is the reason logistic regression and linear SVM have convergence guarantees — gradient descent provably reaches the global minimum.
For non-convex deep networks, only the \Rightarrow direction holds (Fermat), not \Leftarrow.
9.5 Summary

































Fermat’s Theorem ConceptMachine Learning MeaningLocal extremum \Rightarrow f'(c)=0Optimal weights have zero gradientf'(c)=0 \centernot\Rightarrow extremumZero gradient ≠ trained model (saddle points!)Non-differentiable extremum ($xOpen interval hypothesisInterior optimum (not boundary of param space)Convex case: f'(c)=0 \iff global minLogistic regression, linear modelsInflection point (x^3 at 0)Saddle point in loss landscape

§10. The Contrapositive — A Useful Form
Fermat’s theorem by contrapositive:
f'(c) \neq 0 \implies c \text{ is NOT a local extremum (for interior points).}
This is algorithmically useful. If you’re doing gradient descent and |\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta)| > \varepsilon, you can certify: \theta is not (approximately) a local minimum. Training should continue.
Conversely, |\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta)| \approx 0 is a necessary condition for convergence — but not sufficient (saddle point!). This is why modern optimizers also monitor the loss value and validation metrics, not just the gradient norm.

§11. Connections Within Calculus
Fermat's Theorem
        │
        ├──→ Definition of Critical Numbers
        │           │
        │           ├──→ Closed Interval Method (absolute extrema)
        │           └──→ First Derivative Test (local extrema)
        │
        ├──→ Second Derivative Test
        │     (f'(c)=0 + f''(c)>0 → local min; classifies critical pts)
        │
        ├──→ Rolle's Theorem
        │     (f(a)=f(b) → ∃c: f'(c)=0; uses Fermat in proof)
        │
        └──→ Mean Value Theorem
              (follows from Rolle's; one of the deepest theorems in calculus)

Rolle’s Theorem proof sketch using Fermat. If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a) = f(b): by EVT, f attains its max and min on [a,b]. If both occur at endpoints, f is constant and f' \equiv 0 (any c works). Otherwise, an extremum occurs at some interior c \in (a,b), and by Fermat, f'(c) = 0. \blacksquare
Fermat’s theorem is thus the seed from which Rolle’s and the MVT grow.

§12. Key Points — Professor’s Summary



The theorem: differentiable local extremum \Rightarrow zero derivative. The tangent is horizontal.


The proof idea: squeeze the derivative between \leq 0 (from the right) and \geq 0 (from the left). Both sides of the derivative limit must agree, forcing f'(c)=0.


The converse is false. f'(c)=0 only gives a candidate. Test the sign of f' around c, or use the second derivative test.


Two hypotheses matter: differentiability at c (corners can be extrema without f'=0), and c being interior (endpoints escape Fermat).


In ML: this theorem is why \nabla \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0} is the training convergence condition — and why convergence to zero gradient is necessary but not sufficient for a good model.




References

Stewart, J. — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed., §4.1. Theorem 4 (Fermat’s Theorem), proof and discussion of critical numbers.
MIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus (Auroux). Extension of Fermat’s condition to \nabla f = \mathbf{0} for functions of several variables; saddle points in 2D.
Dauphin, Y. et al. — Identifying and attacking the saddle point problem in high-dimensional non-convex optimization. NeurIPS 2014. (Empirical and theoretical analysis of why saddle points dominate in deep networks.)
Rudin, W. — Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 5.8. (Analysis-level proof of Fermat’s theorem.)


— End of Note —

Logical chain: Fermat’s Theorem → Critical Numbers → Closed Interval Method → Rolle’s Theorem → Mean Value Theorem. Every theorem in the next sections rests on this one.

01.Maths/Calculus/04.Applications-of-Dif.title: 03.The Mean Value Theorem
01.Maths/Calculus/04.Applications-of-Dif.content:
“The Mean Value Theorem is the midwife of calculus — it delivers the deep connection between a function’s local behavior and its global change.” — Personal marginal note


§1. Motivation — Why Should We Care?
Before the theorem, a question:

If you drive from Dhaka to Chattogram — a distance of roughly 250 km — in 3 hours, must there have been some instant when your speedometer read exactly \frac{250}{3} \approx 83.3 \text{ km/h}?

Intuitively: yes. You can’t average 83.3 km/h without ever hitting that speed.
The Mean Value Theorem is precisely the theorem that makes this rigorous. It is, at its core, a theorem about the relationship between average rate of change (slope of a secant) and instantaneous rate of change (slope of a tangent).

§2. Prerequisites
Before the MVT, we need two foundational results. I’ll state them and prove the first in full.
2.1 Rolle’s Theorem

Theorem (Rolle, 1691). Let f be a function satisfying:

f is continuous on [a, b]
f is differentiable on (a, b)
f(a) = f(b)

Then there exists at least one c \in (a,b) such that f'(c) = 0.

Proof.
Since f is continuous on the closed bounded interval [a,b], by the Extreme Value Theorem (Stewart §4.1), f attains both an absolute maximum M and an absolute minimum m on [a,b].
Case 1: M = m. Then f is constant on [a,b], so f'(x) = 0 for all x \in (a,b). Any c \in (a,b) works. \checkmark
Case 2: M \neq m. Since f(a) = f(b), at least one of M or m must be attained at an interior point c \in (a,b) (not just at the endpoints).
At such a c, f has a local extremum. Since f is differentiable at c, by Fermat’s Theorem (Stewart §4.1): f'(c) = 0
\square
Geometric picture:
    f(a) = f(b)
      *-----------*
     /  horizontal \
    /   tangent     \
   /        *        \
  /        (c, f(c))  \
 a                    b

Somewhere between a and b, the curve must “turn around,” and at that turning point the tangent is horizontal.

2.2 The Mean Value Theorem

Theorem (Lagrange’s MVT). Let f be a function satisfying:

f is continuous on [a, b]
f is differentiable on (a, b)

Then there exists at least one c \in (a,b) such that: \boxed{f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}}

This is the theorem. Elegant. The right-hand side is the slope of the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)). The theorem asserts: the tangent line at c is parallel to this secant.

§3. Proof of the MVT
The proof is a beautiful reduction to Rolle’s Theorem. The key idea: subtract the secant line from f to create a new function that satisfies Rolle’s hypotheses.
Construction. Define the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)): L(x) = f(a) + \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(x - a)
Now define: g(x) = f(x) - L(x) = f(x) - f(a) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(x-a)
Verify Rolle’s conditions:

g is continuous on [a,b] — yes, f is continuous and L is a polynomial (hence continuous). ✓
g is differentiable on (a,b) — yes, f is differentiable and L'(x) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} exists. ✓
Check endpoints: g(a) = f(a) - f(a) - 0 = 0 g(b) = f(b) - f(a) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(b-a) = f(b) - f(a) - (f(b)-f(a)) = 0

So g(a) = g(b) = 0. ✓
Apply Rolle’s Theorem: \exists, c \in (a,b) such that g'(c) = 0.
Compute g': g'(x) = f'(x) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}
Setting g'(c) = 0: f'(c) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} = 0 \implies f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}
\square
The geometric story of the proof:
         f(b)
          *
         /|  ← secant line L(x)
        / |
   f(c)/  |
  ....*.  |   ← tangent parallel to secant
      /   |
     /    |
f(a)*     |
    a  c  b

g(x) measures the vertical gap between f and the secant. At both endpoints this gap is 0. So somewhere in between, the gap must reach a maximum or minimum — and Rolle tells us g'(c) = 0 there, which is exactly f'(c) = slope of secant.

§4. Worked Examples
Example 1 — The Driving Analogy Made Rigorous
Let s(t) = position (km) at time t (hours), with s(0) = 0, s(3) = 250.
Assume s is continuous on [0,3] and differentiable on (0,3) (reasonable physical assumption).
By MVT: \exists, c \in (0,3) such that: s'(c) = \frac{s(3)-s(0)}{3-0} = \frac{250}{3} \approx 83.3 \text{ km/h}
Since s'(t) is velocity, the speedometer must have read exactly 83.3 km/h at some moment t = c.
This is not just intuition anymore — it’s a theorem.

Example 2 — A Polynomial
Let f(x) = x^3 - x on [0, 2].
Secant slope: \dfrac{f(2)-f(0)}{2-0} = \dfrac{(8-2)-0}{2} = \dfrac{6}{2} = 3
MVT guarantees \exists, c \in (0,2) with f'(c) = 3.
f'(x) = 3x^2 - 1. Solve: 3c^2 - 1 = 3 \implies 3c^2 = 4 \implies c = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} \approx 1.155
Indeed c \approx 1.155 \in (0,2). ✓
Note: MVT guarantees existence — it doesn’t say c is unique. Here it happens to be unique in (0,2), but for other functions there could be multiple such c.

Example 3 — Using MVT to Prove an Inequality

Claim: |\sin b - \sin a| \leq |b - a| for all a, b \in \mathbb{R}.

Proof. If a = b this is trivial. Assume WLOG a < b.
f(x) = \sin x is differentiable everywhere. By MVT, \exists, c \in (a,b): \sin b - \sin a = f'(c)(b-a) = \cos(c) \cdot (b-a)
Taking absolute values: |\sin b - \sin a| = |\cos c| \cdot |b-a| \leq 1 \cdot |b-a| = |b-a|
since |\cos c| \leq 1 always. \square
This is the power of MVT for inequalities: you convert a statement about a function’s values into a statement about its derivative, which is often easier to bound.

Example 4 — Uniqueness of Solutions

Claim: The equation x^3 + x = 2 has exactly one real solution.

Existence: f(x) = x^3 + x - 2 has f(0) = -2 < 0 and f(1) = 0. So x = 1 is a solution.
Uniqueness (by MVT / Rolle): Suppose there were two solutions a < b with f(a) = f(b) = 0. By Rolle’s Theorem, \exists, c \in (a,b) with f'(c) = 0.
But f'(x) = 3x^2 + 1 \geq 1 > 0 for all x. Contradiction. ✗
Therefore x = 1 is the unique solution. \square

§5. Important Corollaries
These follow quickly from MVT and are used constantly.
Corollary 1 — Zero Derivative Implies Constant

If f'(x) = 0 for all x \in (a,b), then f is constant on (a,b).

Proof. Take any x_1, x_2 \in (a,b) with x_1 < x_2. By MVT: f(x_2) - f(x_1) = f'(c)(x_2 - x_1) = 0
So f(x_1) = f(x_2). Since x_1, x_2 were arbitrary, f is constant. \square
Corollary 2 — Equal Derivatives Imply Functions Differ by a Constant

If f'(x) = g'(x) for all x \in (a,b), then f(x) = g(x) + C for some constant C.

Proof. Apply Corollary 1 to h(x) = f(x) - g(x). \square
This is the reason antiderivatives are defined up to a constant — a fact that underlies all of integral calculus.
Corollary 3 — Monotonicity


If f'(x) > 0 on (a,b), then f is strictly increasing on [a,b].
If f'(x) < 0 on (a,b), then f is strictly decreasing on [a,b].


Proof (increasing case). Take x_1 < x_2 in [a,b]. By MVT, \exists, c with: f(x_2) - f(x_1) = f'(c)(x_2 - x_1) > 0
since f'(c) > 0 and x_2 - x_1 > 0. So f(x_2) > f(x_1). \square

§6. The Generalized (Cauchy) MVT

Theorem (Cauchy’s MVT). Let f, g be continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and g'(x) \neq 0 on (a,b). Then \exists, c \in (a,b): \frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)} = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{g(b)-g(a)}

Taking g(x) = x recovers Lagrange’s MVT.
This is the key lemma behind L’Hôpital’s Rule. When computing \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} of the form \frac{0}{0}, Cauchy’s MVT provides the justification for replacing the ratio of functions with the ratio of derivatives.

§7. MVT in Higher Dimensions — A Glimpse (MIT 18.02)
In multivariable calculus, the MVT generalizes but requires care. For a function f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}:

MVT for scalar fields. If f is differentiable, then for points \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^n: f(\mathbf{b}) - f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{c}) \cdot (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}) for some \mathbf{c} on the segment joining \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b}.

This is a direct generalization: the gradient \nabla f replaces f', and the dot product replaces ordinary multiplication.
For vector-valued \mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m, the exact MVT fails in general (there need not exist a single c). Instead, one uses the MVT inequality: |\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{b}) - \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{a})| \leq \sup_{\mathbf{c} \in \overline{ab}} |D\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{c})| \cdot |\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}|
where D\mathbf{f} is the Jacobian matrix. This inequality is fundamental in numerical analysis and functional analysis.

§8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning

This is where the theorem stops being “pure math” and starts running your GPU.

8.1 Gradient Descent — The MVT Beneath Every Update
The backbone of training neural networks is gradient descent. Given a loss function \mathcal{L}(\theta) where \theta \in \mathbb{R}^p are the parameters:
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)
Why does this work? MVT tells us exactly:
\mathcal{L}(\theta_{t+1}) - \mathcal{L}(\theta_t) = \nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{c}) \cdot (\theta_{t+1} - \theta_t)
for some \mathbf{c} between \theta_t and \theta_{t+1}.
When the step is small, \nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{c}) \approx \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t), so: \mathcal{L}(\theta_{t+1}) - \mathcal{L}(\theta_t) \approx \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t) \cdot (-\eta \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)) = -\eta |\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)|^2 \leq 0
The loss decreases. The MVT is the mathematical reason gradient descent works — it licenses the approximation that a small step in the negative gradient direction reduces the objective.

8.2 Learning Rate and the Lipschitz Condition
The MVT motivates one of the most important practical choices in deep learning: choosing the learning rate \eta.
If \nabla \mathcal{L} is Lipschitz continuous with constant L: |\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta) - \nabla \mathcal{L}(\phi)| \leq L|\theta - \phi|
Then by MVT-type reasoning, one can show: \mathcal{L}(\theta_{t+1}) \leq \mathcal{L}(\theta_t) - \left(\eta - \frac{L\eta^2}{2}\right)|\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)|^2
The right-hand side is decreasing only when \eta < \frac{2}{L}.

Practical implication: If your learning rate is too large (bigger than \frac{2}{L}), gradient descent is theoretically not guaranteed to converge. This is why learning rate schedules and adaptive methods (Adam, RMSProp) exist — they are heuristic attempts to stay in the MVT-safe zone.


8.3 Backpropagation and the Chain Rule
The chain rule — the engine of backpropagation — is proved using the MVT. Recall:
\frac{d}{dx}[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)
One rigorous proof of this fact proceeds by writing: \frac{f(g(x+h)) - f(g(x))}{h} = \frac{f(g(x+h)) - f(g(x))}{g(x+h)-g(x)} \cdot \frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}{h}
and applying MVT to control the first factor as h \to 0.
In deep learning, every layer’s gradient computation is an application of this chain rule. The entire backpropagation algorithm is the chain rule applied recursively — and the chain rule’s proof leans on MVT.

8.4 Loss Landscape Analysis
Modern deep learning theory studies the loss landscape \mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R} of neural networks. Questions like:

Are there saddle points? Local minima? (Answered using critical point theory — \nabla \mathcal{L} = 0, directly from MVT corollaries.)
How “flat” are the minima? (Studied via the Hessian H = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L}, which is the second-order MVT — Taylor’s theorem.)

The second-order MVT (Taylor with remainder): \mathcal{L}(\theta + \delta) = \mathcal{L}(\theta) + \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta)^\top \delta + \frac{1}{2}\delta^\top H(\mathbf{c})\delta
is used in the analysis of Newton’s method, natural gradient descent, and second-order optimizers like K-FAC.

8.5 Generalization and Lipschitz Neural Networks
In learning theory, the generalization gap (difference between training and test error) can be bounded using the Lipschitz constant of the network. By MVT:
|f_\theta(x) - f_\theta(x')| \leq \text{Lip}(f_\theta) \cdot |x - x'|
Networks with small Lipschitz constants generalize better — this is the theoretical motivation behind spectral normalization (used in GANs) and gradient penalty methods. All of these bound or control the Lipschitz constant, which is defined via MVT.

§9. Summary Table








































ConceptStatementKey UseRolle’s Theoremf(a)=f(b) \Rightarrow \exists, c: f'(c)=0Proof engine for MVTLagrange’s MVT\exists, c: f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}The core theoremCauchy’s MVT\frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)} = \frac{\Delta f}{\Delta g}L’Hôpital’s RuleCorollary 1f'=0 \Rightarrow f=\text{const}Integration theoryCorollary 3f'>0 \Rightarrow f increasingOptimizationMultivariate MVT\Delta f = \nabla f(\mathbf{c}) \cdot \Delta \mathbf{x}Gradient descent analysis

§10. Hypotheses Are Not Optional

A common exam trap — and a deep conceptual point.

The MVT requires both continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b).
Counterexample 1 — Continuity fails: f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x \in [0,1) \ 1 & x = 1 \end{cases} \frac{f(1)-f(0)}{1-0} = 1, but f'(x) = 0 wherever it exists. No c works.
Counterexample 2 — Differentiability fails: f(x) = |x| \text{ on } [-1, 1] \frac{f(1)-f(-1)}{2} = 0, but f'(x) = \pm 1 \neq 0 everywhere f' is defined; f'(0) doesn’t exist.
The hypotheses in theorems are not bureaucratic formalities — they are load-bearing walls.

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Cengage Learning. — §4.2 (The Mean Value Theorem), §4.1 (Extreme Values, Fermat’s Theorem).
MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus. Lecture notes on the gradient, directional derivatives, and multivariate MVT. Available at: ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/

01.Maths/Calculus/04.Applications-of-Dif.title: 04.How Derivatives Affect the Shape of a Graph
01.Maths/Calculus/04.Applications-of-Dif.content:
“The derivative does not merely describe the function — it is the function’s autobiography. Every rise, fall, bend, and inflection is written in f' and f''.”


§1. The Central Philosophy
A function f is a static object — it just is. Its derivative f' is dynamic — it tells you how f is moving at each point. The second derivative f'' tells you how that movement is itself changing.
This hierarchy:
f \xrightarrow{\text{differentiate}} f' \xrightarrow{\text{differentiate}} f''
corresponds to:
\text{height} \xrightarrow{} \text{slope} \xrightarrow{} \text{curvature}
Everything about the shape of a graph — its rises and falls, its peaks and valleys, its bends and straightenings — is encoded in these two derived functions.

§2. The First Derivative — Increasing and Decreasing
2.1 The Theorem

Theorem (Increasing/Decreasing Test). Let f be differentiable on an open interval I.

If f'(x) > 0 for all x \in I, then f is strictly increasing on I.
If f'(x) < 0 for all x \in I, then f is strictly decreasing on I.
If f'(x) = 0 for all x \in I, then f is constant on I.


Proof of the increasing case.
Take any x_1 < x_2 in I. By the Mean Value Theorem, \exists, c \in (x_1, x_2): f(x_2) - f(x_1) = f'(c)(x_2 - x_1)
Since f'(c) > 0 and x_2 - x_1 > 0, we get f(x_2) - f(x_1) > 0, i.e., f(x_2) > f(x_1). \square
(The MVT is doing all the real work here — this is why MVT is called the “workhorse of differential calculus.”)

2.2 Finding Intervals — The Method
To determine where f increases/decreases:

Find all critical numbers: points where f'(x) = 0 or f'(x) does not exist.
These critical numbers partition the real line into open intervals.
Pick a test value in each interval; evaluate f'.
Sign of f' → increasing or decreasing on that interval.

Example. f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 4
f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 = 3(x^2 - 2x - 3) = 3(x-3)(x+1)
Critical numbers: x = -1, ; x = 3





























IntervalTest valuef'Behavior(-\infty, -1)x = -23(-5)(-1) = 15 > 0Increasing ↑(-1, 3)x = 03(-3)(1) = -9 < 0Decreasing ↓(3, \infty)x = 43(1)(5) = 15 > 0Increasing ↑
        ↑           ↓           ↑
  ------+---\-------+-------/---+------
       -1    \             /    3
              \           /
               \_________/


§3. Critical Points and Local Extrema
3.1 Definitions

Definition. A number c in the domain of f is a critical number if either f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) does not exist.


Fermat’s Theorem. If f has a local maximum or minimum at c, then c is a critical number of f.

Important converse failure: A critical number need not yield a local extremum. The canonical example: f(x) = x^3 has f'(0) = 0 but x = 0 is neither a maximum nor a minimum — it’s an inflection point.
f(x) = x³

        |  /
        | /
        |/
--------+--------
       /|
      / |
     /  |

f'(0) = 0, but no extremum at x = 0.


3.2 The First Derivative Test

First Derivative Test. Suppose c is a critical number of a continuous function f.

If f' changes positive → negative at c: local maximum at c.
If f' changes negative → positive at c: local minimum at c.
If f' does not change sign at c: no local extremum (inflection).


Visual mnemonic:
LOCAL MAX:         LOCAL MIN:         NO EXTREMUM:
    *                                     
   / \               ___              ___/
  /   \             /   \            /
 /     \           /     \         __
         \/                \/
f'>0  f'<0         f'<0  f'>0      f'>0  f'>0

Continuing the example f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 4:

At x = -1: f' goes + \to - → local max, f(-1) = 1 - 3 + 9 + 4 = 9
At x = 3: f' goes - \to + → local min, f(3) = 27 - 27 - 27 + 4 = -23


§4. The Second Derivative — Concavity
4.1 Concavity Defined

Definition. A differentiable function f is:

Concave upward on I if f' is increasing on I.
Concave downward on I if f' is decreasing on I.


Equivalently (when f'' exists):

Concavity Test.

f''(x) > 0 on I \Rightarrow f is concave up on I (holds water ∪)
f''(x) < 0 on I \Rightarrow f is concave down on I (spills water ∩)


Geometric intuition. Concave up means the tangent lines lie below the curve. Concave down means they lie above. This is not a cosmetic property — it determines how well linear approximations (tangent lines) over- or under-estimate the function.
CONCAVE UP (∪)          CONCAVE DOWN (∩)
   f'' > 0                  f'' < 0

    curve                  curve
   /      \               /      \
  /        \             /        \
 / tangents \           / tangents \
     below                 above

tangent UNDERESTIMATES   tangent OVERESTIMATES


4.2 Inflection Points

Definition. A point (c, f(c)) is an inflection point of f if f is continuous at c and the concavity of f changes at c.

Necessary condition: If f''(c) exists and (c, f(c)) is an inflection point, then f''(c) = 0.
Warning: f''(c) = 0 does NOT guarantee an inflection point. Again, f(x) = x^4: f''(0) = 0 but concavity does not change at 0 (it’s concave up everywhere).
Example. f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 4
f''(x) = 6x - 6 = 6(x-1)
f''(x) = 0 at x = 1.

x < 1: f''(x) < 0 → concave down
x > 1: f''(x) > 0 → concave up

Concavity changes at x = 1 → inflection point at (1, f(1)) = (1, -8).
Full shape of f(x) = x³ - 3x² - 9x + 4:

      local max (−1, 9)
         *
        / \
       /   \         ← concave down
      /     \
     /  IP   \
    /  (1,−8) \
   /            *    ← inflection
                 \
                  \  ← concave up
                   *
            local min (3, −23)


§5. The Second Derivative Test for Local Extrema

Second Derivative Test. Suppose f'' is continuous near c and f'(c) = 0.

If f''(c) > 0: local minimum at c.
If f''(c) < 0: local maximum at c.
If f''(c) = 0: inconclusive — use the first derivative test.


Why does this work?
If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0, then f' is increasing through 0 at c. So f' goes from negative (before c) to positive (after c) — exactly the first derivative test’s condition for a local minimum.
Proof sketch.
f''(c) > 0 means, by definition of derivative: f''(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x) - f'(c)}{x - c} = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{x-c} > 0
For x near c: f'(x) and (x-c) have the same sign. So:

x < c \Rightarrow f'(x) < 0
x > c \Rightarrow f'(x) > 0

This is exactly a local minimum by the first derivative test. \square
The inconclusive case — three behaviors are possible:





























Functionf'(0)f''(0)Behavior at 0f(x) = x^400Local minf(x) = -x^400Local maxf(x) = x^300Inflection
When the second derivative test fails, go back to the first derivative test. It never fails (as long as f' is defined nearby).

§6. Asymptotes — Behavior at the Boundary
Shape analysis is incomplete without understanding what happens as x \to \pm\infty or as x approaches a discontinuity.
6.1 Horizontal Asymptotes
\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L \quad \text{or} \quad \lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L
implies y = L is a horizontal asymptote.
6.2 Vertical Asymptotes
\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = \pm\infty \quad \text{or} \quad \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \pm\infty
implies x = a is a vertical asymptote. These arise at zeros of denominators, logarithm arguments going to zero, etc.
6.3 Slant (Oblique) Asymptotes
When \deg(\text{numerator}) = \deg(\text{denominator}) + 1, polynomial long division yields: f(x) = (mx + b) + \frac{r(x)}{q(x)}
where \frac{r(x)}{q(x)} \to 0 as x \to \infty. The line y = mx + b is the slant asymptote.

§7. A Systematic Curve-Sketching Algorithm
This is the full synthesis — a procedure that transforms f into a picture using everything above.
Algorithm (Stewart §4.5):

Domain — Where is f defined?
Intercepts — y-intercept at f(0); x-intercepts where f(x) = 0.
Symmetry — Even (f(-x)=f(x))? Odd (f(-x)=-f(x))? Periodic?
Asymptotes — Horizontal, vertical, slant.
Intervals of increase/decrease — Find f', critical numbers, sign chart.
Local extrema — Apply first or second derivative test.
Concavity and inflection points — Find f'', solve f''=0, sign chart.
Sketch — Plot key points, connect with appropriate shape.

Full worked example. f(x) = \dfrac{x^2}{x^2 - 1}
Domain: x \neq \pm 1, so (-\infty,-1) \cup (-1,1) \cup (1,\infty).
Symmetry: f(-x) = \frac{x^2}{x^2-1} = f(x) → even function, symmetric about y-axis.
Intercepts: f(0) = 0 → y-intercept (0,0); f(x) = 0 gives x = 0 → x-intercept (0,0).
Asymptotes:

x \to \pm 1: denominator \to 0, numerator \to 1 → vertical asymptotes x = \pm 1
x \to \pm\infty: \frac{x^2}{x^2-1} = \frac{1}{1-1/x^2} \to 1 → horizontal asymptote y = 1

First derivative: f'(x) = \frac{2x(x^2-1) - x^2(2x)}{(x^2-1)^2} = \frac{2x^3 - 2x - 2x^3}{(x^2-1)^2} = \frac{-2x}{(x^2-1)^2}
Critical number: x = 0 (denominator never 0 in domain).
Sign chart for f'(x) = \frac{-2x}{(x^2-1)^2}: denominator always positive; sign determined by -2x.



































IntervalSign of -2xf'Behavior(-\infty,-1)++Increasing(-1,0)++Increasing(0,1)--Decreasing(1,\infty)--Decreasing
At x=0: f' goes + \to - → local max, f(0) = 0.
Second derivative (after computation): f''(x) = \frac{6x^2+2}{(x^2-1)^3}
Numerator 6x^2+2 > 0 always. Sign of f'' determined by (x^2-1)^3:

|x| > 1: (x^2-1)^3 > 0 → f'' > 0 → concave up
|x| < 1: (x^2-1)^3 < 0 → f'' < 0 → concave down

f'' \neq 0 in domain → no inflection points.
Final sketch:

y
|           |           |
|   \       |     /     |
... *-------+-------* ...   y = 1 (asymptote)
|    \      |(0,0) /    |
|     \     *     /     |
|      \   / \   /      |
|       \_/   \_/       |
|      local max at 0   |
        x=-1       x=1   (vertical asymptotes)


§8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
8.1 Loss Landscape Topology
In training a neural network, the loss function \mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R} (over millions of parameters) has a shape — a high-dimensional analog of the curves we’ve been analyzing. Every concept from this note has a direct counterpart:





































Calculus conceptML/DL counterpartIncreasing/decreasingLoss going up/down during trainingCritical point (f'=0)Stationary point — where gradient descent stopsLocal minimumA solution the optimizer converged toSaddle pointCritical point that is a min in some directions, max in others — a major obstacle in deep learningConcave up region (f''>0)“Sharp” minimum — bad for generalizationConcave down region (f''<0)Descent away from a local maxInflection pointTransition in curvature of the loss curve
8.2 Saddle Points — The Deep Learning Problem
In \mathbb{R}^1, a critical point is either a max, min, or inflection point. In \mathbb{R}^p (high-dimensional parameter space), there is a fourth type: saddle points — points where \nabla \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0} but the Hessian H = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L} has both positive and negative eigenvalues.
Saddle point in ℝ²:
f(x,y) = x² - y²

        ↑ y
        |
  \     |     /     ← concave down in y
   \    |    /
----\---+---/----→ x
   / \  |  / \
  /   \ | /   \    ← concave up in x
        |

At the origin: \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 0, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 0, but it’s neither a max nor a min.
Why this matters: Early deep learning theory (Dauphin et al., 2014) suggested that saddle points — not local minima — are the primary obstacle for gradient-based optimizers. In high dimensions, most critical points are saddle points (the probability that all eigenvalues of the Hessian are positive is exponentially small in the dimension).
SGD and Adam navigate these saddle points through noise and momentum — but the underlying geometry is exactly the second derivative / concavity analysis from §4.
8.3 Sharp vs. Flat Minima and Generalization
The concavity at a minimum predicts generalization:


Sharp minimum (f'' very large): The loss surface curves steeply. A small perturbation of \theta causes a large increase in training loss — and even larger increases in test loss (since train and test distributions differ slightly). Poor generalization.


Flat minimum (f'' small): The loss surface is nearly flat. Small perturbations don’t hurt much. Better generalization.


Sharp minimum:          Flat minimum:
     |                  _____________
     *                 /             \
    /|\               /               \
   / | \             /                 \
  /  |  \           /                   \

  Bad for test        Good for test

This is the theoretical foundation behind:

Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) — explicitly seeks flat minima by perturbing weights and minimizing the worst-case loss in a neighborhood
Weight averaging methods (SWA, EWA) — average iterates to land in flatter regions
Batch size effects — large batch sizes tend to find sharper minima (Keskar et al., 2017)

All of this is concavity / second derivative analysis, lifted to high dimensions.
8.4 Learning Rate Schedules and Curvature
The optimal learning rate at a point is inversely proportional to the curvature (f'') there:
\eta_{\text{optimal}} \propto \frac{1}{f''(c)}
This is Newton’s method: \theta \leftarrow \theta - \frac{f'(\theta)}{f''(\theta)}.
In high dimensions, this becomes \theta \leftarrow \theta - H^{-1}\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta).
Adaptive optimizers (Adam, RMSProp, Adagrad) approximate this by maintaining running estimates of the second moment of the gradient — a cheap surrogate for curvature. The reason they work better than vanilla SGD is exactly that they adapt the step size to local curvature:

High curvature region (f'' large) → small step
Low curvature region (f'' small) → large step

This is the geometric insight from §4 operationalized in code.
8.5 Activation Functions and Concavity
The choice of activation function in a neural network is, in part, a choice about concavity:






























ActivationConcavityConsequenceSigmoid \sigma(x)Concave up for x<0, down for x>0Vanishing gradients; inflection at x=0ReLU \max(0,x)Linear (no concavity)No vanishing gradient; not differentiable at 0GELU, SwishSmooth, with inflectionEmpirically superior; behaves like ReLU but differentiableSoftplus \log(1+e^x)Always concave upSmooth ReLU approximation
The inflection point of the sigmoid at x=0 is the reason sigmoid saturates and causes vanishing gradients in deep networks — the concavity flips, and \sigma'' changes sign there. ReLU eliminates this by having no curvature at all (above zero). The entire history of activation function design is an applied study in concavity.

§9. The Full Picture — Derivative Dictionary
FUNCTION f(x)
│
├─── f'(x) > 0  →  f is INCREASING   (graph rises left to right)
├─── f'(x) < 0  →  f is DECREASING   (graph falls left to right)
├─── f'(x) = 0  →  CRITICAL POINT    (horizontal tangent)
│         │
│         ├── f' changes + → −  →  LOCAL MAX
│         ├── f' changes − → +  →  LOCAL MIN
│         └── f' doesn't change sign  →  INFLECTION (if f''=0 too)
│
└─── f''(x) > 0  →  CONCAVE UP    ∪  (tangents below curve)
     f''(x) < 0  →  CONCAVE DOWN  ∩  (tangents above curve)
     f''(x) = 0  →  POSSIBLE INFLECTION POINT
           │
           └── concavity changes?  →  YES: INFLECTION POINT
                                       NO:  not an inflection point


§10. Why the Hypotheses Matter
The differentiability hypothesis is essential. Consider f(x) = |x| on [-1, 1]:

f'(x) = -1 for x < 0 and f'(x) = +1 for x > 0
f'(0) does not exist
f has a global minimum at x = 0 — but Fermat’s Theorem still holds! (x=0 is a critical number because f'(0) DNE)

The theorems in this note require differentiability, but the extrema can still occur at non-differentiable points — they just can’t be detected by f' = 0 there. Always check where f' fails to exist, not just where f' = 0.

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Cengage Learning. — §4.3 (How Derivatives Affect the Shape of a Graph), §4.5 (Summary of Curve Sketching).
MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus. Gradient, Hessian, and multivariable second derivative test.
