01.Maths/Calculus/05.Integrals/12.Integr.title: 12.Integrals of Symmetric Functions
01.Maths/Calculus/05.Integrals/12.Integr.content:
“Symmetry is one of the most powerful problem-solving tools in mathematics. When a function has it, the integral often collapses to something trivial — or doubles into something clean. Learning to see symmetry before computing is the mark of a mature analyst.”


§ 0 — The Core Idea
Before you touch an antiderivative, ask: does this integrand have symmetry?
If the interval of integration is symmetric about the origin, [-a, a], and the function is either purely even or purely odd, the integral either vanishes immediately or halves. This is not an approximation. It is an exact theorem, and it saves enormous computation.
The result is elementary but its reach is surprisingly wide — from trigonometric integrals to Fourier analysis to the symmetry arguments underlying quantum mechanics and neural network weight initialization.

§ 1 — Even and Odd Functions: Definitions and Geometry
Definitions
A function f defined on a symmetric interval [-a, a] (or all of \mathbb{R}) is:

Even if f(-x) = f(x) for all x in the domain
Odd if f(-x) = -f(x) for all x in the domain

Geometric Meaning
EVEN FUNCTION: f(-x) = f(x)          ODD FUNCTION: f(-x) = -f(x)

   f(x)                                  f(x)
    │     ╭───╮                           │           ╱
    │    ╱     ╲                          │          ╱
    │   ╱       ╲                         │         ╱
────┼──╱─────────╲──→ x               ───┼────────╱─────→ x
    │              ╲  ╱                   │       ╱
    │               ╲╱                    │      ╱
                                          │     ╱
   Mirror symmetry                        │    ╱
   about the y-axis.                   Rotational symmetry
   Graph folds onto                    about the origin.
   itself.                             Graph maps to itself
                                       under 180° rotation.

Standard Examples

































EvenOddx^{2n} (even powers)x^{2n+1} (odd powers)\cos x\sin x\cosh x\sinh x\|x\|x^3 - xe^{x^2}x e^{-x^2}f(x) + f(-x) (symmetrization)f(x) - f(-x) (antisymmetrization)

Remark. Most functions are neither even nor odd. But every function with a symmetric domain decomposes uniquely as a sum of an even and an odd part: f(x) = \underbrace{\frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}}_{\text{even part}} + \underbrace{\frac{f(x)-f(-x)}{2}}_{\text{odd part}} This decomposition is used heavily in Fourier analysis.


§ 2 — The Symmetry Theorems
Theorem (Integrals of Symmetric Functions)
Let f be integrable on [-a, a].
Part (i) — Odd function: f \text{ odd} \implies \int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 0
Part (ii) — Even function: f \text{ even} \implies \int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 2\int_0^a f(x),dx
Proof of Both Parts
Split the integral at 0:
\int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = \int_{-a}^0 f(x),dx + \int_0^a f(x),dx
In the first integral, substitute x = -t, so dx = -dt. When x = -a, t = a; when x = 0, t = 0:
\int_{-a}^0 f(x),dx = \int_a^0 f(-t)(-dt) = \int_0^a f(-t),dt
Therefore:
\int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = \int_0^a f(-t),dt + \int_0^a f(t),dt = \int_0^a \bigl[f(-t) + f(t)\bigr],dt
Case (i): f odd. Then f(-t) = -f(t), so f(-t) + f(t) = 0: \int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = \int_0^a 0,dt = 0 \qquad \square
Case (ii): f even. Then f(-t) = f(t), so f(-t) + f(t) = 2f(t): \int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = \int_0^a 2f(t),dt = 2\int_0^a f(x),dx \qquad \square

Proof anatomy. The entire argument rests on a single substitution x = -t plus the definition of symmetry. This substitution “folds” the left half [-a, 0] onto the right half [0, a], and the symmetry condition tells you what happens when the two halves meet.


§ 3 — Visualization of the Theorem
ODD FUNCTION on [-a, a]:

     f(x)
      │     ╭──────╮  ← positive area = A
      │    ╱        ╲
──────┼───╱──────────╲────→ x
  -a  │  ╱  0         a
      │              ╭──────────╮
      │              │ negative area = -A
      
  Net area = A + (-A) = 0 ✓
  The two halves are mirror images with opposite sign.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

EVEN FUNCTION on [-a, a]:

     f(x)
      │  ╭────╮    ╭────╮
      │ ╱      ╲  ╱      ╲
      │╱        ╲╱        ╲
──────┼────────────────────╲──→ x
  -a        0               a
      │← area A →│← area A →│

  Total area = A + A = 2A = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx ✓
  The two halves are identical.


§ 4 — Worked Examples
Example 1 — Vanishing by Oddness
\int_{-3}^{3} \left(x^5 - 4x^3 + \sin x\right)dx
Check each term: x^5 is odd, 4x^3 is odd, \sin x is odd. Their sum is odd. On [-3, 3]:
\int_{-3}^{3} \left(x^5 - 4x^3 + \sin x\right)dx = 0
No computation required.

Example 2 — Doubling by Evenness
\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos^2 x,dx
\cos^2(-x) = \cos^2(x), so \cos^2 x is even:
= 2\int_0^{\pi} \cos^2 x,dx = 2\int_0^{\pi} \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2},dx = \int_0^{\pi}(1+\cos 2x),dx
= \left[x + \frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right]_0^{\pi} = \pi

Example 3 — Splitting a Mixed Integrand
\int_{-2}^{2} \left(x^4 + x^3 + 3\right)dx
Split by symmetry type: x^4 + 3 is even, x^3 is odd.
= \int_{-2}^{2}(x^4 + 3),dx + \underbrace{\int_{-2}^{2} x^3,dx}_{=,0} = 2\int_0^2(x^4 + 3),dx
= 2\left[\frac{x^5}{5} + 3x\right]_0^2 = 2\left(\frac{32}{5} + 6\right) = 2 \cdot \frac{62}{5} = \frac{124}{5}

Example 4 — A Non-Obvious Odd Function
\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{x^3 + x}{1 + x^2 + x^4},dx
Let f(x) = \dfrac{x^3 + x}{1 + x^2 + x^4}. Check:
f(-x) = \frac{-x^3 - x}{1 + x^2 + x^4} = -f(x)
f is odd. Therefore:
\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{x^3 + x}{1 + x^2 + x^4},dx = 0
The antiderivative of this rational function would be genuinely painful. Symmetry gives the answer in two lines.

Example 5 — Trigonometric Integral (Odd \times Even)
\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^3 x \cos^2 x,dx
\sin^3 x is odd, \cos^2 x is even. The product of an odd and an even function is odd. Therefore:
\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^3 x \cos^2 x,dx = 0

Parity multiplication rules. odd \times even = odd. odd \times odd = even. even \times even = even. This mirrors the sign algebra of {+1, -1} under multiplication.


Example 6 — The Sigmoid
\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{e^x}{1 + e^x},dx
Let \sigma(x) = \dfrac{e^x}{1+e^x}. Note that \sigma(x) + \sigma(-x) = 1, so:
\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{2} + \underbrace{\left(\sigma(x) - \frac{1}{2}\right)}_{\text{odd part}}
The odd part integrates to zero on [-1,1]; the constant \frac{1}{2} integrates to 1:
\int_{-1}^{1}\sigma(x),dx = 1

§ 5 — The Algebra of Even and Odd Functions

















































OperationResulteven + evenevenodd + oddoddeven + oddneither (in general)even \times evenevenodd \times oddeveneven \times oddodd\frac{d}{dx}(even)odd\frac{d}{dx}(odd)even\int_0^x(even dt)odd (with zero constant)\int_0^x(odd dt)even
The derivative/integral rows follow from FTC. If f is even and g(x) = \int_0^x f(t),dt, then substituting t = -s:
g(-x) = \int_0^{-x} f(t),dt = -\int_0^x f(-s),ds = -\int_0^x f(s),ds = -g(x)
So g is odd. \square

Deep pattern. Even functions \leftrightarrow cosines; odd functions \leftrightarrow sines. This is Fourier’s insight: every periodic function decomposes into even (cosine) and odd (sine) components. The integral theorem above is the seed of the orthogonality relations in Fourier analysis.


§ 6 — Extension: Symmetry About x = c
The theorem requires [-a, a] (symmetric about 0). For an interval symmetric about c, shift first.
Theorem (Symmetry About x = c)
Let the interval be [c - a, c + a]. Substitute t = x - c:
\int_{c-a}^{c+a} f(x),dx = \int_{-a}^{a} f(t+c),dt
Now apply the odd/even theorem to \tilde{f}(t) = f(t+c).
Example. \displaystyle\int_1^5 (x-3)^3,dx. Let t = x-3, interval becomes [-2, 2]:
\int_{-2}^{2} t^3,dt = 0 \quad (\text{odd function on symmetric interval})
Example. \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} \sin x,dx. Let t = x - \pi/2:
\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos t,dt = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos t,dt = 2[\sin t]_0^{\pi/2} = 2 \checkmark

§ 7 — Connection to MIT 18.02
In multivariable calculus, symmetry arguments become even more powerful.
Double Integrals over Symmetric Regions
If D is symmetric about the y-axis and f(-x, y) = -f(x, y) (odd in x):
\iint_D f(x, y),dA = 0
Example. \iint_D xy,dA where D is the unit disk. The integrand xy is odd in x, and the disk is symmetric about the y-axis:
\iint_D xy,dA = 0
No Jacobian, no polar conversion, no computation.
Trigonometric Orthogonality
The integrals \displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\sin\theta,d\theta = 0 and \displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta,d\theta = 0 appear constantly in polar and spherical coordinate calculations. More precisely, for integers m \neq n:
\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin(mx)\cos(nx),dx = 0
because \sin(mx)\cos(nx) is odd (odd \times even). This is the symmetry theorem. Every such orthogonality relation in Fourier series for mixed sin-cos terms reduces to this one observation.

§ 8 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
8.1 — Weight Initialization and Symmetry Breaking
With all weights initialized to zero, neurons at the same layer compute identical outputs — the symmetry problem. With symmetric (zero-mean) weight distributions, for any odd activation \phi (e.g., \tanh):
\mathbb{E}_{w \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)}[\phi(wx)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(wx)\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-w^2/2\sigma^2},dw = 0
The integrand is odd in w (odd \times even), the domain is symmetric, so the integral vanishes. The expected output of a \tanh neuron under symmetric random weights is exactly zero. He and Xavier initialization introduce careful scaling of variance, not to destroy this symmetry, but to ensure gradients neither explode nor vanish despite it.
8.2 — Fourier Features and Attention
Random Fourier feature methods (Rahimi & Recht) and positional encodings in transformers rely on the orthogonality of sinusoids. The identity:
\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin(mx)\cos(nx),dx = 0 \quad \text{for all } m, n
holds because the integrand is odd. Positional encodings use alternating \sin and \cos features at different frequencies; the orthogonality (which is the symmetry theorem) guarantees these features carry independent information.
8.3 — Batch Normalization and Odd Activations
After batch normalization, pre-activations are approximately \mathcal{N}(0,1). For any odd activation \phi:
\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[\phi(z)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(z)\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2},dz = 0
Odd activations (\tanh, \text{erf}, \sinh) have zero mean output after batch norm — a statistically clean property. ReLU, which is neither even nor odd, has mean output \approx 0.5 under \mathcal{N}(0,1), introducing a positive bias that must be handled. This asymmetry is one reason batch norm is more critical for ReLU networks.
8.4 — The Sigmoid’s Even-Odd Decomposition
From Example 6 in general: since \sigma(x) - \frac{1}{2} is odd:
\int_{-a}^{a}\sigma(x),dx = a
This has a direct interpretation: under zero-mean inputs, the sigmoid neuron has expected output \frac{1}{2} — a constant positive bias. This saturation at \frac{1}{2} is one reason \tanh (which is odd, with zero mean) is often preferred over sigmoid in symmetric architectures.
8.5 — Score Matching and Stein’s Identity
In score-based generative models (DDPM, score matching), the Stein identity states:
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}\left[\nabla_x \log p(x) \cdot \phi(x)\right] = -\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}[\nabla_x \phi(x)]
When p is symmetric (e.g., Gaussian) and \phi is odd, both sides vanish — one by the symmetry theorem, the other by FTC on an odd function. This gives a zero-value sanity check for score network implementations: certain test expectations should be exactly zero under symmetric data.
8.6 — L^2 and L^1 Regularization
The L^2 regularizer R(\theta) = \sum_i \theta_i^2 is even in each \theta_i. Its gradient \nabla_\theta R = 2\theta is odd — it always pushes symmetrically toward zero, with no directional bias. The L^1 regularizer \sum_i |\theta_i| is also even; its subgradient \text{sgn}(\theta_i) is odd. The symmetry of both regularizers about \theta = 0 is what makes them geometrically unbiased: they penalize deviation from zero equally in both directions.

§ 9 — Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Non-symmetric interval. \int_0^3 x^3,dx \neq 0. The interval [0, 3] is not symmetric about 0. Oddness only kills the integral on [-a, a].
Mistake 2: Not checking the condition. Always verify f(-x) = \pm f(x) explicitly. Many functions look symmetric but are not. e^x is neither even nor odd.
Mistake 3: odd \times odd = even, not odd. \int_{-a}^a x \cdot \sin x,dx \neq 0. The product x \cdot \sin x is even (odd \times odd), so the integral doubles: = 2\int_0^a x\sin x,dx.
Mistake 4: Singularities on the interval. f(x) = 1/x is odd, but \int_{-1}^{1} 1/x,dx does not exist in the Riemann sense. The theorem requires integrability. (The Cauchy principal value is zero, but this is a separate concept.)
Mistake 5: Not decomposing a mixed function. For \int_{-2}^{2}(e^x + x^2),dx: write e^x = \cosh x + \sinh x. The odd part \sinh x integrates to zero; the even part \cosh x doubles. Always decompose before integrating.

§ 10 — Summary
f \text{ odd on } [-a,a]: \quad \int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 0
f \text{ even on } [-a,a]: \quad \int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 2\int_0^a f(x),dx

































ConceptContentProof key stepSubstitute x = -t, fold [-a,0] onto [0,a], use f(-t) \pm f(t)Parity of productsodd\timeseven = odd; odd\timesodd = even; even\timeseven = evenUnique decompositionf = \frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2} + \frac{f(x)-f(-x)}{2}Symmetry about cShift t = x-c, then apply theorem to f(t+c)18.02 extensionOdd integrand over symmetric domain → double integral vanishes; Fourier orthogonalityML applicationsWeight initialization, batch norm, sigmoid bias, score function testing, regularizer geometry

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §5.5 (Symmetry in Integration). Cengage Learning.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Symmetry in double integrals, trigonometric orthogonality. ocw.mit.edu
Rahimi, A. & Recht, B. Random Features for Large-Scale Kernel Machines. NeurIPS 2007.
He, K. et al. Delving Deep into Rectifiers. ICCV 2015.
Stein, C. M. Estimation of the Mean of a Multivariate Normal Distribution. Ann. Statist. 1981.

01.Maths/Calculus/06.Applications-of-Ite.title: 01.Area Between Curves
01.Maths/Calculus/06.Applications-of-Ite.content:
“The area between two curves is conceptually the simplest application of the definite integral — and yet it is where students first learn to read geometry carefully before writing symbols. The formula is trivial; finding the limits and handling sign changes is where the real work lives.”


§ 0 — From Single Curve to Two Curves
In the definite integral, we measured the signed area between f(x) and the x-axis. The x-axis is just the function g(x) = 0. The natural generalization: what is the area between two arbitrary curves f and g?
The idea is unchanged — Riemann rectangles, now with height f(x_i^_) - g(x_i^_) instead of f(x_i^*) alone.

§ 1 — The Basic Formula
Setup
Let f and g be continuous on [a, b] with f(x) \ge g(x) for all x \in [a, b].
The area of the region bounded above by f and below by g on [a, b] is:
\boxed{A = \int_a^b \bigl[f(x) - g(x)\bigr],dx}
Derivation from Riemann Sums
Partition [a,b] with sample points x_i^*. Each rectangle has:

Width: \Delta x_i
Height: f(x_i^_) - g(x_i^_) (top curve minus bottom curve)
Area: [f(x_i^_) - g(x_i^_)],\Delta x_i \ge 0

Summing and taking the limit:
A = \lim_{|P|\to 0}\sum_{i=1}^n [f(x_i^_) - g(x_i^_)],\Delta x_i = \int_a^b [f(x) - g(x)],dx
By linearity of the integral, this equals \int_a^b f,dx - \int_a^b g,dx — the area under f minus the area under g.
     y
     │        f(x) ← top curve
     │    ╭───────────╮
     │   ╱  shaded     ╲
     │  ╱   region      ╲
     │ ╱  ╭──────────╮   ╲
     │╱   │  g(x)     │    ╲
     │────────────────────────→ x
          a            b

  Height of each rectangle = f(x*) − g(x*)
  Area = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x) − g(x)] dx

Why the Condition f \ge g Matters
Without it, f(x) - g(x) can be negative, and the integral gives a signed area (positive where f > g, negative where g > f), not the geometric area. When the curves cross, we must split.

§ 2 — When Curves Cross: Handling Sign Changes
If f and g intersect within (a, b), the formula must be adapted.
Procedure

Find all intersection points by solving f(x) = g(x) on [a, b]. Call them c_1 < c_2 < \cdots < c_{k}.
On each subinterval between consecutive intersection points, determine which function is on top.
Integrate |f(x) - g(x)| on each subinterval (using whichever sign makes the integrand positive):

A = \int_a^{c_1}|f - g|,dx + \int_{c_1}^{c_2}|f - g|,dx + \cdots
More precisely:
\boxed{A = \int_a^b |f(x) - g(x)|,dx}
This is always correct, but the absolute value requires splitting at zeros of f - g.
     y
     │        ╭──── f(x)
     │    ╭───╯  ╲
     │   ╱  A₁    ╲  ╭── g(x)
     │──╱───────────╲╱─────────→ x
     │              │╲    A₂  ╱
     │              │  ╲    ╱
     │              c₁  ╲──╱  c₂
     
  A = A₁ + A₂ = ∫ₐᶜ¹[f−g]dx + ∫ᶜ¹ᶜ²[g−f]dx
  (switch the order in the second integral because g > f there)


§ 3 — Integration with Respect to y
Sometimes the natural variable is y, not x. When curves are expressed as x = f(y) and x = g(y), and the region is bounded horizontally, integrate with respect to y.
Formula
Let f(y) \ge g(y) on [c, d] (right curve minus left curve):
\boxed{A = \int_c^d \bigl[f(y) - g(y)\bigr],dy}
   y
   │
 d─┤    ╭──── x = f(y) (right)
   │   ╱│████████
   │  ╱ │████████
   │ ╱  │████████
 c─┤╱   │
   │    │
   └────┴──────────→ x
     g(y)  f(y)

  Width of each strip = f(y*) − g(y*)
  Area = ∫ᶜᵈ [f(y) − g(y)] dy

When to Integrate in y

When curves are given as x = h(y) directly.
When integrating in x requires splitting into multiple integrals but y gives a single clean integral.
When the region is easier to describe by horizontal strips than vertical ones.


§ 4 — Finding Limits of Integration
The limits come from the intersection points of the bounding curves, or from explicitly stated boundaries.
Solving for Intersections
Set f(x) = g(x) and solve. Always:

Find all solutions in the relevant domain.
Verify which function is on top between each pair of consecutive solutions (plug in a test point).
Sketch before integrating — even a rough sketch prevents sign errors.


Personal note. The single most common error in area problems is not the integration itself — it is setting up the wrong limits or forgetting to check which curve is on top. Sketch first, always.


§ 5 — Worked Examples
Example 1 — Area Between a Parabola and a Line
Find the area between f(x) = x^2 and g(x) = x + 2.
Step 1: Find intersections. x^2 = x + 2 \implies x^2 - x - 2 = 0 \implies (x-2)(x+1) = 0 So x = -1 and x = 2.
Step 2: Determine which is on top. Test x = 0: f(0) = 0, g(0) = 2. So g \ge f on [-1, 2].
Step 3: Integrate. A = \int_{-1}^{2}(x + 2 - x^2),dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{2} + 2x - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{2}
= \left(2 + 4 - \frac{8}{3}\right) - \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2 + \frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{10}{3} - \left(-\frac{7}{6}\right) = \frac{10}{3} + \frac{7}{6} = \frac{27}{6} = \frac{9}{2}
     y
     │        ╭──── g(x) = x+2
   4─┤       ╱██
     │      ╱████╲
   2─┤     ╱██████╲──── f(x) = x²
     │    ╱████████╲  ╱
     │───╱──────────╲╱────→ x
        -1           2

  Shaded area = 9/2


Example 2 — Curves That Cross
Find the area enclosed by f(x) = \sin x and g(x) = \cos x on [0, \pi].
Step 1: Find intersections on [0, \pi]. \sin x = \cos x \implies \tan x = 1 \implies x = \pi/4.
Step 2: Determine which is on top on each piece.

On [0, \pi/4]: test x = 0: \sin 0 = 0 < \cos 0 = 1, so \cos \ge \sin.
On [\pi/4, \pi]: test x = \pi/2: \sin(\pi/2) = 1 > \cos(\pi/2) = 0, so \sin \ge \cos.

Step 3: Integrate. A = \int_0^{\pi/4}(\cos x - \sin x),dx + \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi}(\sin x - \cos x),dx
First integral: [\sin x + \cos x]_0^{\pi/4} = \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) - (0+1) = \sqrt{2} - 1
Second integral: [-\cos x - \sin x]_{\pi/4}^{\pi} = (-(-1) - 0) - \left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = 1 + \sqrt{2}
A = (\sqrt{2}-1) + (1+\sqrt{2}) = 2\sqrt{2}

Example 3 — Integrating in y
Find the area of the region bounded by x = y^2 and x = y + 2.
In x: the parabola opens rightward — solving for the two x-branches is messy. In y, this is clean.
Step 1: Intersections. y^2 = y + 2 \implies y^2 - y - 2 = 0 \implies (y-2)(y+1) = 0, so y = -1, 2.
Step 2: Which is on the right? Test y = 0: x = y^2 = 0 vs x = y+2 = 2. So x = y+2 is the right curve.
Step 3: Integrate. A = \int_{-1}^{2}\bigl[(y+2) - y^2\bigr],dy = \left[\frac{y^2}{2} + 2y - \frac{y^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{2}
= \left(2 + 4 - \frac{8}{3}\right) - \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2 + \frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{9}{2}
The same numerical answer as Example 1 — because the region is the same, just described with a different variable.

Example 4 — Three Bounding Curves
Find the area of the region bounded by y = x^2, y = 2x, and y = 0.
Step 1: Find all pairwise intersections.

x^2 = 2x \implies x = 0, 2
x^2 = 0 \implies x = 0
2x = 0 \implies x = 0

The region has vertices at (0,0) and (2,4).
Step 2: Determine the geometry. On [0, 2]: 2x \ge x^2 \ge 0. The region is between y = 2x (top) and y = x^2 (bottom):
A = \int_0^2 (2x - x^2),dx = \left[x^2 - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = 4 - \frac{8}{3} = \frac{4}{3}

Example 5 — Area Requiring Both x and y Integration
Find the area between y = \sqrt{x} and y = x^2 on [0, 1].
Intersections: \sqrt{x} = x^2 \implies x = 0, 1.
On (0,1): test x = 1/4: \sqrt{1/4} = 1/2, (1/4)^2 = 1/16. So \sqrt{x} \ge x^2.
A = \int_0^1\left(\sqrt{x} - x^2\right)dx = \left[\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{3}

§ 6 — Visualization: The Full Geometry
VERTICAL STRIPS (integrate in x):
                                      
   y │    f(x) ← top                  
     │  ╭────────────╮                
     │ ╱│████│████│███╲               
     │╱ │████│████│████╲              
     │  │████│████│█████│             
     │──┼────┼────┼─────┼──→ x        
        a   x₁   x₂    b             
        
   Each vertical strip has width dx
   and height f(x) − g(x).

────────────────────────────────────────

HORIZONTAL STRIPS (integrate in y):

   y                                    
   d─┤      ────── x = f(y) (right)    
     │  ╭───┤████████                  
     │  │   │████████                  
     │  │   │████████                  
   c─┤  ╰───┤                          
     │  x=g(y)                         
     └──────────────────→ x            
     
   Each horizontal strip has height dy
   and width f(y) − g(y).

────────────────────────────────────────

WHEN CURVES CROSS:

   y                                    
     │   f above g      g above f      
     │ ┌───────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  
     │ │    A₁     │  │     A₂      │  
     │─┴───────────┴──┴─────────────┴─→x
       a           c₁               b  
       
   Total area = A₁ + A₂
   NEVER: ∫ₐᵇ (f−g)dx (this cancels the areas)
   ALWAYS split at each crossing point c₁


§ 7 — Connection to MIT 18.02
In 18.02, the area between curves becomes the foundation for double integrals over general regions.
The area of a region D in the plane is:
A = \iint_D dA
When D is described as {(x,y) : a \le x \le b,\ g(x) \le y \le f(x)}:
A = \int_a^b \int_{g(x)}^{f(x)} dy,dx = \int_a^b [f(x) - g(x)],dx
The inner integral \int_{g(x)}^{f(x)}dy = f(x) - g(x) recovers exactly the area-between-curves formula. So area between curves is the 1D cross-section of a 2D double integral — the limits of the inner integral are the bounding curves.
This connection is crucial: in 18.02, setting up double integrals over non-rectangular regions requires exactly the same skill as finding limits for area-between-curves problems.
Type I and Type II Regions (18.02 Language)




















TypeDescriptionIntegral formType Ia \le x \le b, g(x) \le y \le f(x)\int_a^b\int_{g(x)}^{f(x)} h,dy,dxType IIc \le y \le d, g(y) \le x \le f(y)\int_c^d\int_{g(y)}^{f(y)} h,dx,dy
The choice between Type I and Type II is exactly the choice between integrating in x or y in the area problem.

§ 8 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
8.1 — ROC Curves and AUC
The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is the single most used model evaluation metric in binary classification. The ROC curve plots True Positive Rate (TPR) against False Positive Rate (FPR) as the classification threshold varies.
Mathematically, AUC is the area under a parametric curve:
\text{AUC} = \int_0^1 \text{TPR}(\text{FPR}),d(\text{FPR})
When comparing two classifiers A and B, the difference in performance is:
\Delta\text{AUC} = \int_0^1 [\text{TPR}_A(t) - \text{TPR}_B(t)],dt
This is exactly the area between two curves. A classifier dominates another if this integral is positive — if its ROC curve lies above the other’s everywhere. The area between their ROC curves quantifies by how much.
TPR
 1│         ╭──── Classifier A
  │     ╭───╯████
  │    ╱████████╲
  │   ╱██████████╲─── Classifier B
  │  ╱████████████╲
  │ ╱██████████████╲
  │╱────────────────╲──→ FPR
 0                   1

  Shaded area = ΔAUC = advantage of A over B

8.2 — Precision-Recall AUC
The Precision-Recall curve similarly defines an area metric:
\text{AP} = \int_0^1 P(R),dR
where P is precision and R is recall. The area between two precision-recall curves compares models — a direct area-between-curves computation over [0,1].
8.3 — Wasserstein Distance as Area Between CDFs
For one-dimensional distributions, the Wasserstein-1 distance (Earth Mover’s Distance) equals the area between cumulative distribution functions:
W_1(p, q) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|F_p(x) - F_q(x)|,dx
This is the area between two curves F_p and F_q. The absolute value means it splits at crossings — exactly the procedure in § 2. This metric is used in Wasserstein GANs and optimal transport based losses.
CDF
 1│              ╭──── F_q(x)
  │         ╭───╯
  │     ╭───╯ ████████
  │ ╭───╯████████╲
  │ │████████████ ╲─── F_p(x)
  │─┼─────────────────────→ x
  
  W₁ = shaded area between the two CDFs

8.4 — Learning Curves and Sample Efficiency
When plotting validation loss against training steps for two models, the area between the learning curves measures cumulative sample efficiency:
\Delta = \int_0^T [\mathcal{L}_A(t) - \mathcal{L}_B(t)],dt
If model A has lower loss throughout training, \Delta > 0 and A is more sample efficient. This integral accounts for the full trajectory, not just the endpoint — a model that trains faster but converges to the same loss may have a substantially smaller \Delta.
8.5 — Gain Curves in Ranking Models
In information retrieval and recommendation systems, Cumulative Gain curves measure ranking quality:
\text{DCG}@k = \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\text{rel}_i}{\log_2(i+1)}
The continuous analog is an area under a gain curve. The area between the gain curve of a learned ranker and the random baseline quantifies the model’s lift — how much better than chance the ranking is. This is the area-between-curves formula applied to ranked retrieval evaluation.
8.6 — Calibration and the Area Between Reliability Curves
A well-calibrated model has predicted probabilities that match empirical frequencies. The reliability diagram plots empirical accuracy vs. predicted confidence. The area between this curve and the diagonal y = x (perfect calibration) is the Expected Calibration Error (ECE):
\text{ECE} \approx \int_0^1 |f(p) - p|,dp
where f(p) is the empirical accuracy at predicted confidence p. This is the area between the calibration curve and the line y = x — the splitting at crossings (§ 2) handles over- and under-confidence regions separately.

§ 9 — Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Not finding all intersection points. Solve f(x) = g(x) completely. Quadratics have two roots, trig equations have infinitely many — restrict to the domain and find all of them.
Mistake 2: Wrong sign (not checking which curve is on top). \int_a^b (g - f) instead of \int_a^b (f - g) gives the right magnitude but wrong interpretation. Always plug in a test point between the limits.
Mistake 3: Not splitting when curves cross. \int_{-1}^{1}(x^3 - x),dx = 0 suggests the area is zero — but the curves cross at x = 0, and the enclosed regions have equal area on each side. The actual area is \int_{-1}^{0}(x^3 - x),dx + \int_0^1(x - x^3),dx = 1/2.
Mistake 4: Integrating in x when y is far cleaner. When a region is bounded by x = y^2 + 1 and x = 3 - y^2, integrating in x requires inverting and splitting. In y, it is a single integral. Recognize horizontal strip regions.
Mistake 5: Using the net signed area formula for a geometric area problem. \int_a^b [f(x) - g(x)],dx gives signed area. For the geometric area (always positive), use \int_a^b |f(x) - g(x)|,dx, splitting at every crossing.

§ 10 — Summary
A = \int_a^b [f(x) - g(x)],dx \quad (f \ge g \text{ on } [a,b])
A = \int_a^b |f(x) - g(x)|,dx \quad (\text{general, split at crossings})
A = \int_c^d [f(y) - g(y)],dy \quad (\text{integrate in } y: \text{ right} - \text{left})

































ConceptContentFormulaTop minus bottom (or right minus left in y), integrated over the intervalLimitsIntersection points of the bounding curvesCrossing curvesSplit at each crossing; integrate \|f-g\| on each pieceChoice of variableUse whichever gives a single integral over a simply-described domain18.02 connectionArea between curves = inner integral of a double integral over a Type I/II regionML applicationsAUC/ROC comparison, Wasserstein distance, learning curve efficiency, ECE calibration

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §6.1 (Areas Between Curves). Cengage Learning.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Double integrals over general regions, Type I/II. ocw.mit.edu
Arjovsky, M., Chintala, S., Bottou, L. Wasserstein GAN. ICML 2017.
Fawcett, T. An Introduction to ROC Analysis. Pattern Recognition Letters, 2006.
Guo, C. et al. On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. ICML 2017.

01.Maths/Calculus/06.Applications-of-Ite.title: 02.Volumes
01.Maths/Calculus/06.Applications-of-Ite.content:
“Volume is what happens when you take the area idea seriously in three dimensions. The transition from area to volume is conceptually one step — integrate cross-sectional area — but that one step opens a vast landscape of three-dimensional geometry.”


§ 0 — The Unifying Principle
Every volume formula in this note is a single idea dressed in different clothing:
\boxed{V = \int_a^b A(x),dx}
where A(x) is the cross-sectional area of the solid at position x. Slice the solid into infinitely thin slabs of thickness dx, compute the area of each cross-section, and integrate. This is Cavalieri’s Principle elevated to a theorem.
The only question in any volume problem is: what is A(x)?

§ 1 — Volumes by Cross-Sections (General)
Theorem (Cavalieri’s Principle)
If two solids have equal cross-sectional area A(x) at every x \in [a,b], then they have equal volume, regardless of their shape.
The Volume Formula
Let S be a solid bounded between x = a and x = b. If the cross-section of S perpendicular to the x-axis at position x has area A(x), and A is integrable on [a,b], then:
V = \int_a^b A(x),dx
Derivation. Partition [a,b] with points x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n. The slab between x_{i-1} and x_i has approximate volume A(x_i^*),\Delta x_i. Summing:
V \approx \sum_{i=1}^n A(x_i^*),\Delta x_i
Taking |P| \to 0 gives the integral. \square
Solid S sliced perpendicular to the x-axis:

         A(x) ← cross-section at x
          ╭───╮
    ╭─────╯███╰──────╮
    │████████████████│
    │█████A(x)███████│  ← solid
    │████████████████│
    ╰────────────────╯
    a        x       b
    
    V = ∫ₐᵇ A(x) dx
    
    Infinitely many slabs of thickness dx,
    each contributing A(x)·dx to total volume.


§ 2 — The Disk Method
Setup
Rotate the region under y = f(x) \ge 0 on [a,b] about the x-axis. Each cross-section perpendicular to the x-axis is a disk with radius f(x).
A(x) = \pi,[f(x)]^2
Formula
\boxed{V = \pi\int_a^b [f(x)]^2,dx}
y = f(x) rotated about x-axis:

     y
     │    ╭──────╮
     │   ╱        ╲        Rotate
     │  ╱          ╲  ─────────→
     │ ╱            ╲
     │╱              ╲
     └────────────────── x
     a                b

     Each cross-section is a disk:
     
         ← r = f(x) →
         ╭───────────╮
        ╱             ╲
       │    ○  disk    │  radius = f(x)
        ╲             ╱  area = π[f(x)]²
         ╰───────────╯

Rotation About the y-Axis
If the region x = g(y) on [c,d] is rotated about the y-axis:
V = \pi\int_c^d [g(y)]^2,dy

§ 3 — The Washer Method
Setup
Rotate the region between f(x) \ge g(x) \ge 0 on [a,b] about the x-axis. Each cross-section is an annulus (disk with a hole) — a washer.

Outer radius: R(x) = f(x)
Inner radius: r(x) = g(x)
Cross-sectional area: A(x) = \pi R^2 - \pi r^2 = \pi\bigl([f(x)]^2 - [g(x)]^2\bigr)

Formula
\boxed{V = \pi\int_a^b \bigl([f(x)]^2 - [g(x)]^2\bigr),dx}
Washer cross-section at position x:

     ╭───────────────╮  ← outer radius R = f(x)
    ╱  ╭───────────╮  ╲
   │  ╱    hole     ╲  │ ← inner radius r = g(x)
   │ │    (empty)    │ │
   │  ╲             ╱  │
    ╲  ╰───────────╯  ╱
     ╰───────────────╯

  Area = π(R² - r²) = π([f(x)]² - [g(x)]²)


Common error. The washer formula is \pi(R^2 - r^2), not \pi(R - r)^2. These are different. Always square each radius separately, then subtract.


§ 4 — The Shell Method
Motivation
The disk/washer method slices perpendicular to the axis of rotation, giving circular cross-sections. The shell method slices parallel to the axis of rotation, giving cylindrical shells. For certain regions, shells give a single clean integral where washers require splitting.
Setup
Rotate the region under y = f(x) \ge 0 on [a,b] (with a \ge 0) about the y-axis. A thin vertical strip at position x with width dx sweeps out a cylindrical shell:

Radius: x
Height: f(x)
Thickness: dx
Volume of shell: 2\pi x \cdot f(x),dx (circumference \times height \times thickness)

Formula
\boxed{V = 2\pi\int_a^b x,f(x),dx}
Shell method — rotating about y-axis:

     y
     │    f(x)
     │  ╭──────╮
     │  │██████│ ← thin strip at x
     │  │██████│   width dx, height f(x)
     │  │██████│
     └──┼──────┼──→ x
        x  x+dx

  This strip sweeps a cylindrical shell:
  
       ╭──────────────────────╮
      ╱│                      │╲
     │ │  ← shell radius x    │ │
      ╲│  height f(x)         │╱
       ╰──────────────────────╯
       
  Volume = 2πx · f(x) · dx

General Shell Formula
For rotation about the y-axis with region between f and g (f \ge g):
V = 2\pi\int_a^b x,[f(x) - g(x)],dx
For rotation about the x-axis, integrate with respect to y:
V = 2\pi\int_c^d y,[f(y) - g(y)],dy
Disk vs. Shell: Which to Use?

























SituationPreferred MethodRotating about x-axis, region given as y = f(x)Disk/Washer in xRotating about y-axis, region given as y = f(x)Shell in x (avoids inverting f)Rotating about y-axis, region given as x = g(y)Disk/Washer in yRotating about x-axis, region given as x = g(y)Shell in y
The shell method is typically superior when inverting the function to change variables would be messy.

§ 5 — Rotation About Lines Other Than the Axes
When rotating about the line y = k (instead of y = 0), the radius is the distance from the curve to the axis.

Region above y = k: radius = f(x) - k
Region below y = k: radius = k - f(x)

Example. Rotating y = x^2 about y = -1: V = \pi\int_a^b [x^2 - (-1)]^2,dx = \pi\int_a^b [x^2 + 1]^2,dx
Similarly for rotation about x = k: replace x with |x - k| as the radius in the disk formula, or adjust the shell radius.

The key. Radius always means the perpendicular distance from the curve to the axis of rotation. Draw a picture. Identify the distance formula. Then plug into the universal formula V = \int A(x),dx.


§ 6 — Volumes by Known Cross-Sections (Non-Circular)
Not all solids come from rotation. A solid may have cross-sections that are squares, triangles, semicircles, or any shape.
Method
If the cross-sections perpendicular to the x-axis are known shapes, express A(x) in terms of a characteristic length determined by the base curve, then integrate.
Common cross-section areas:






























ShapeIf side/diameter = sArea A(x)Squares = f(x) - g(x)[f(x)-g(x)]^2Equilateral triangles = f(x) - g(x)\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}[f(x)-g(x)]^2Semicirclediameter = f(x)-g(x)\frac{\pi}{8}[f(x)-g(x)]^2Isosceles right triangle (leg = s)s = f(x)-g(x)\frac{1}{2}[f(x)-g(x)]^2
Example. The base of a solid is the region between y = \sqrt{x} and y = 0 on [0,4]. Cross-sections perpendicular to the x-axis are squares with side = \sqrt{x}:
V = \int_0^4 (\sqrt{x})^2,dx = \int_0^4 x,dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^4 = 8

§ 7 — Worked Examples
Example 1 — Disk Method
Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating y = \sqrt{x} on [0,4] about the x-axis.
V = \pi\int_0^4 (\sqrt{x})^2,dx = \pi\int_0^4 x,dx = \pi\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^4 = 8\pi

Example 2 — Washer Method
Find the volume obtained by rotating the region between y = x and y = x^2 on [0,1] about the x-axis.
Intersections: x = x^2 \Rightarrow x = 0, 1. On [0,1]: x \ge x^2, so R = x, r = x^2.
V = \pi\int_0^1 (x^2 - x^4),dx = \pi\left[\frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^1 = \pi\left(\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{5}\right) = \frac{2\pi}{15}

Example 3 — Shell Method
Find the volume obtained by rotating y = x - x^2 (above y=0) on [0,1] about the y-axis.
Inverting y = x - x^2 for x in terms of y is messy. Use shells.
V = 2\pi\int_0^1 x(x - x^2),dx = 2\pi\int_0^1 (x^2 - x^3),dx = 2\pi\left[\frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^1 = 2\pi\cdot\frac{1}{12} = \frac{\pi}{6}

Example 4 — Rotation About y = 1
Rotate the region between y = x^2 and y = 0 on [0,1] about y = 1.
The axis y=1 is above the region. Distances:

Outer radius (from axis down to y=0): R = 1 - 0 = 1
Inner radius (from axis down to y = x^2): r = 1 - x^2

V = \pi\int_0^1(R^2 - r^2),dx = \pi\int_0^1\bigl(1 - (1-x^2)^2\bigr),dx
= \pi\int_0^1(1 - 1 + 2x^2 - x^4),dx = \pi\int_0^1(2x^2 - x^4),dx
= \pi\left[\frac{2x^3}{3} - \frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^1 = \pi\left(\frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{5}\right) = \frac{7\pi}{15}

Example 5 — Classic: Volume of a Sphere
The sphere of radius r is the rotation of y = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2} about the x-axis on [-r, r]. Cross-sections are disks of radius \sqrt{r^2 - x^2}:
V = \pi\int_{-r}^{r}(r^2 - x^2),dx = \pi\left[r^2 x - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-r}^{r} = \pi\left[\left(r^3 - \frac{r^3}{3}\right) - \left(-r^3 + \frac{r^3}{3}\right)\right] = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3
The familiar formula, derived from first principles. \square

Example 6 — Shell, Region Between Two Curves
Rotate the region between y = x+2 and y = x^2 about the y-axis.
Intersections: x+2 = x^2 \Rightarrow x = -1, 2.
For x \ge 0: shells work cleanly. But the region extends to x = -1 < 0.
For shells about the y-axis with region crossing x = 0, the shell radius is |x|. Split at x = 0:
V = 2\pi\int_{-1}^{0}|x|(x+2-x^2),dx + 2\pi\int_0^2 x(x+2-x^2),dx
In the first piece, |x| = -x for x < 0:
V = 2\pi\int_{-1}^0 (-x)(x+2-x^2),dx + 2\pi\int_0^2 x(x+2-x^2),dx
Computing each (left as exercise): V = \dfrac{7\pi}{6} + \dfrac{8\pi}{3} = \dfrac{7\pi + 16\pi}{6} = \dfrac{23\pi}{6}.

Or: use the washer method in y, where the region is described cleanly as x = g(y) with a single outer-inner pair. This is often cleaner for such problems.


§ 8 — Visualization: All Three Methods Side by Side
DISK METHOD (rotate about x-axis):

  ╭─────────── solid ────────────╮
  │  ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○  │  ← stack of disks
  ╰──────────────────────────────╯
  a                              b
  
  Each disk: radius = f(x), thickness = dx
  Volume element: π[f(x)]²dx

─────────────────────────────────────────

WASHER METHOD (hollow solid):

  ╭───── outer ─────╮
  │  ╭── inner ──╮  │
  │  │   (hole)  │  │  ← washer cross-section
  │  ╰───────────╯  │
  ╰─────────────────╯
  
  Volume element: π([R(x)]² - [r(x)]²)dx

─────────────────────────────────────────

SHELL METHOD (rotate about y-axis):

  y │
    │       ╔══════╗  ← outer cylinder
    │       ║ ╔══╗ ║
    │       ║ ║  ║ ║  ← nested shells
    │       ║ ╚══╝ ║
    │       ╚══════╝
    └──────────────── x
    
  Unroll one shell:
  ┌────────────────────────────┐ ← height f(x)
  │  circumference = 2πx      │
  └────────────────────────────┘
  Volume element: 2πx · f(x) · dx


§ 9 — Connection to MIT 18.02
In 18.02, the volume formula V = \int_a^b A(x),dx is recovered as a iterated integral:
V = \iiint_S dV = \int_a^b\left(\iint_{D(x)} dA\right)dx = \int_a^b A(x),dx
where D(x) is the cross-sectional region at x. This is Fubini’s theorem — the triple integral over a 3D solid factors into an outer integral over x and an inner double integral over the cross-section.
Solids of revolution in cylindrical coordinates. The solid obtained by rotating y = f(x) about the x-axis is described in cylindrical coordinates (x, r, \theta) as {(x,r,\theta) : a \le x \le b,\ 0 \le r \le f(x),\ 0 \le \theta \le 2\pi}. The volume is:
V = \int_a^b\int_0^{f(x)}\int_0^{2\pi} r,d\theta,dr,dx = \int_a^b\int_0^{f(x)} 2\pi r,dr,dx = \int_a^b \pi[f(x)]^2,dx
The disk formula is exactly the triple integral in cylindrical coordinates with the \theta and r integrations carried out first.
The shell formula from cylindrical coordinates. Reordering integration — integrating over x first, then r:
V = \int_0^R \int_0^{2\pi} \int_{x: r \le f(x)} r,dx,d\theta,dr = 2\pi\int_0^R r \cdot (\text{length at radius } r),dr
This is the shell formula. The two methods are the same triple integral evaluated in different orders — Fubini’s theorem.

§ 10 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
10.1 — Volumetric Data and 3D Convolutions
Medical imaging (CT, MRI), LiDAR point clouds, and 3D object recognition all involve volumetric data — functions defined on \mathbb{R}^3. Computing the total mass, density integral, or activation volume of a 3D feature map is:
V = \int\int\int_S f(x, y, z),dV
which reduces to the Cavalieri principle when f = 1 (indicator function). Deep networks processing 3D data (3D CNNs, PointNet, NeRF) operate on discretizations of this integral. Understanding the continuous limit — the true volume integral — is essential for interpreting what these networks compute.
10.2 — Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)
NeRF (Mildenhall et al., 2020) represents a 3D scene as a neural network that maps position (x,y,z) and viewing direction to color and density. The rendered pixel color along a ray is:
C(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f} T(t),\sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)),\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}),dt
where T(t) = \exp!\left(-\int_{t_n}^t \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)),ds\right) is transmittance, and \sigma is volume density. This is a volume integral along a ray — the continuous generalization of the cross-section formula. The density \sigma plays the role of A(x); integrating it along the ray gives the accumulated opacity.
The discrete approximation used in practice is:
C(\mathbf{r}) \approx \sum_{i=1}^N T_i(1 - e^{-\sigma_i \delta_i}),\mathbf{c}_i
This is a Riemann sum approximation of the volume integral — exactly the slab approximation from § 1.
NeRF volume rendering:

  camera → ray through scene → pixel color
  
  ╭──────────────────────────────────────╮
  │ 3D scene (density field σ(x,y,z))   │
  │                                      │
  │  •  •  ●  ●  ●  ●  •  •  •  •      │  ← sample points
  │                ↑ high density        │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────╯
  
  C = ∫ T(t)·σ(t)·c(t) dt  ← volume integral
    ≈ Σ Tᵢ·(1−e^{−σᵢδᵢ})·cᵢ  ← Riemann sum

10.3 — Volumetric Loss Functions in 3D Generation
3D generative models (occupancy networks, signed distance functions, 3D diffusion models) define a loss over a volume:
\mathcal{L} = \int_\Omega |f_\theta(x) - f_*(x)|^2,dV
This is a continuous loss integral — the L^2 distance between two volumetric functions. In practice, it is approximated by Monte Carlo sampling (a Riemann sum), but the object being minimized is precisely the volume integral.
10.4 — Solid Angle and Attention
In graphics and physically-based rendering (which underlies diffusion models trained on rendered data), the solid angle subtended by a surface patch is:
\Omega = \iint_S \frac{\cos\theta}{r^2},dA
This is a surface integral (18.02), but its numerical approximation mirrors the cross-section method: sample directions, weight by the integrand, sum. Attention mechanisms in transformers compute a weighted sum over queries — a discrete analog of exactly this kind of integral over a “solid angle” of context.
10.5 — Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks and Univariate Integration
KAN (Liu et al., 2024) represents functions as compositions of learnable univariate functions placed on edges. Each edge function is implicitly a definite integral (or its inverse). The architecture is motivated by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, which expresses multivariate functions in terms of univariate ones — a decomposition that, in the continuous limit, involves volume integrals factoring into products of one-dimensional integrals (when the function is separable). Understanding when \iiint f(x)g(y)h(z),dx,dy,dz = (\int f)(\int g)(\int h) — which is the separability of volumes — directly informs when KAN representations are exact.
10.6 — Expectation as Volume Under a Surface
In probability, the expected value of f(X, Y) under a joint distribution p(x,y) is:
\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)] = \iint f(x,y),p(x,y),dx,dy
This is the volume under the surface z = f(x,y),p(x,y) in \mathbb{R}^3. Every 2D expectation in machine learning — joint entropy, mutual information, 2D kernel density estimation, bivariate loss functions — is a volume computation. Monte Carlo integration approximates this volume with a Riemann sum over samples.

§ 11 — Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Squaring after subtracting instead of subtracting after squaring. Washer: \pi(R^2 - r^2) \neq \pi(R-r)^2. Always square each radius separately, then subtract.
Mistake 2: Using the wrong radius when rotating about a non-standard axis. If rotating about y = 2 and the curve is y = x^2, the radius is 2 - x^2 (not x^2). Always draw the axis and measure the perpendicular distance.
Mistake 3: Forgetting limits when using the shell method with region crossing x=0. The shell radius is |x|, so negative x must be handled separately. When in doubt, switch to washers.
Mistake 4: Applying the disk formula to a region that isn’t touching the axis. If the region between y=1 and y=3 is rotated about the x-axis, there is a hole — use the washer method, not the disk method.
Mistake 5: Not identifying intersection points correctly. The limits of integration must be the x-values where the bounding curves meet (or the stated boundary). Sketch the region and its rotation before writing any integral.
Mistake 6: Confusing which method integrates in which variable. Disk/Washer rotated about x-axis → integrate in x. Shell about y-axis with y = f(x) → integrate in x. Getting this crossed produces an integral that is either wrong or much harder than necessary.

§ 12 — Summary



































MethodFormulaAxisVariableDisk\pi\int_a^b [f(x)]^2,dxx-axisxWasher\pi\int_a^b ([f]^2 - [g]^2),dxx-axisxShell2\pi\int_a^b x,f(x),dxy-axisxCross-section\int_a^b A(x),dxanyany
\text{All are instances of: } V = \int_a^b A(x),dx









































ConceptContentUnifying principleIntegrate cross-sectional area — Cavalieri’s PrincipleDiskRotation about axis; cross-sections are full disksWasherRotation with hole; subtract inner disk from outerShellParallel-to-axis slicing; circumference × height × thicknessKnown cross-sectionsAny shape: express A(x) in terms of the base, integrateNon-standard axesRadius = perpendicular distance from curve to axis18.02 connectionTriple integral in cylindrical coordinates; Fubini reordering gives disk ↔ shell dualityML applicationsNeRF volume rendering, 3D convolutions, volumetric losses, joint expectations

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §6.2 (Disk/Washer), §6.3 (Shell Method), §6.2 (Known Cross-Sections). Cengage Learning.

Mildenhall, B. et al. NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis. ECCV 2020.
Liu, Z. et al. KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks. arXiv 2024.

01.Maths/Calculus/06.Applications-of-Ite.title: 03.Volumes by Cylindrical Shells
01.Maths/Calculus/06.Applications-of-Ite.content:
“The shell method is what you reach for when the disk/washer method forces you into a contortion you don’t want. It is, in many ways, the more elegant cousin.”


Tags
#calculus #integration #volume #multivariable #ML-connection #stewart #18.02

0. Motivation — Why Another Method?
Recall from Volumes by Disks and Washers that we sliced a solid of revolution perpendicular to the axis, getting circular cross-sections. This works beautifully until it doesn’t.
The failure mode. Consider rotating the region bounded by y = x - x^2 and y = 0 about the y-axis. To use washers, you’d need to express x as a function of y — which requires solving a quadratic. That’s manageable here, but imagine y = \sin(x^2). Inverting that is impossible in closed form.
The fix. Instead of slicing perpendicular to the axis, slice parallel to it. Each slice becomes a thin cylindrical shell. This is the shell method.

1. Geometric Setup — Building the Shell
Take a thin vertical strip of the region at position x, width \Delta x, height f(x).
When you revolve this strip about the y-axis, it sweeps out a cylindrical shell — think of a paper towel tube with very thin walls.
        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  Before rotation: a thin rectangle         │
        │                                            │
        │   x          x+Δx                          │
        │   |          |                             │
        │   |  f(x)    |                             │
        │   |          |                             │
        │   └──────────┘                             │
        │        Δx                                  │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────┘

        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  After rotation about y-axis: a shell      │
        │                                            │
        │         ╔═══════╗                          │
        │       ╔═╝       ╚═╗   ← outer radius x+Δx │
        │      ║  ╔═══════╗  ║                       │
        │      ║  ║       ║  ║  ← inner radius x     │
        │      ║  ║  h=   ║  ║                       │
        │      ║  ║ f(x)  ║  ║                       │
        │      ║  ╚═══════╝  ║                       │
        │       ╚═╗       ╔═╝                        │
        │         ╚═══════╝                          │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Volume of one shell. The shell has:

Inner radius: r_1 = x
Outer radius: r_2 = x + \Delta x
Height: h = f(x)

\Delta V = \pi r_2^2 \cdot h - \pi r_1^2 \cdot h = \pi h\bigl[(x+\Delta x)^2 - x^2\bigr]
Expand: \Delta V = \pi f(x)\bigl[2x,\Delta x + (\Delta x)^2\bigr]
As \Delta x \to 0, the (\Delta x)^2 term is negligible: \Delta V \approx 2\pi x \cdot f(x),\Delta x
The factor 2\pi x is the circumference of the shell at radius x. We are literally unrolling the shell into a flat slab of dimensions: circumference \times height \times thickness.
\boxed{\Delta V \approx \underbrace{2\pi x}_{\text{circumference}} \cdot \underbrace{f(x)}_{\text{height}} \cdot \underbrace{\Delta x}_{\text{thickness}}}

2. The Main Theorem

Theorem (Shell Method — Rotation about the y-axis). Let f be continuous and f(x) \geq 0 on [a,b] with 0 \leq a < b. The volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region under y = f(x) on [a,b] about the y-axis is: V = \int_a^b 2\pi x, f(x), dx

Proof sketch. Partition [a,b] into n subintervals. The Riemann sum \sum_{i=1}^n 2\pi x_i^* f(x_i^*),\Delta x_i approximates the total volume (as shown in §1). By the definition of the definite integral, taking n \to \infty (so |\Delta| \to 0) gives the integral. \square

3. The Mnemonic — CHIT
When using the shell method, write down:
dV = 2\pi \cdot \underbrace{(\text{shell radius})}_{\text{C}} \cdot \underbrace{(\text{shell height})}_{\text{H}} \cdot \underbrace{dx}_{\text{IT (thickness)}}
Circumference × Height × thickness = CHIT (or just think: unroll the shell into a flat box).

4. Worked Examples
Example 1 — The Classic
Problem. Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by y = x - x^2 and y = 0 about the y-axis.
Solution.
First, find the x-intercepts: x - x^2 = 0 \Rightarrow x(1-x) = 0, so x \in [0,1].
Shell radius at position x: just x (distance to y-axis). Shell height: f(x) = x - x^2.
V = \int_0^1 2\pi x(x - x^2),dx = 2\pi \int_0^1 (x^2 - x^3),dx
= 2\pi \left[\frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^1 = 2\pi\left(\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4}\right) = 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{12} = \frac{\pi}{6}

Cross-check intuition. Try setting this up as a washer integral (rotating about y-axis). You’d need x = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1-4y}}{2}. The shell method was clearly preferable.


Example 2 — Non-obvious Shell Radius
Problem. Rotate the region between y = \sqrt{x} and y = x (for x \in [0,1]) about the line x = 2.
ASCII visualization:
y
|         
1 ┤     ╱╲   ← y = √x (above)
  |   ╱    ╲
  | ╱  region╲
  |╱           \__ y = x (below)
──┼──────────────── x
  0      1      2  (axis of rotation)

Shell radius. The axis is x = 2. A shell at position x has radius = 2 - x (distance from x to the axis, which is to the right).
Shell height. h(x) = \sqrt{x} - x (top minus bottom).
V = \int_0^1 2\pi(2-x)(\sqrt{x}-x),dx
Expand: = 2\pi \int_0^1 \left(2\sqrt{x} - 2x - x^{3/2} + x^2\right)dx
= 2\pi \left[\frac{4x^{3/2}}{3} - x^2 - \frac{2x^{5/2}}{5} + \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1
= 2\pi \left(\frac{4}{3} - 1 - \frac{2}{5} + \frac{1}{3}\right) = 2\pi \cdot \frac{8}{15} = \frac{16\pi}{15}

Example 3 — Rotation about the x-axis (Shells Are Horizontal)
Problem. Rotate the region bounded by x = y^2 and x = 1 about the x-axis.
When rotating about the x-axis, the natural strips are horizontal (in y). The formula becomes:
V = \int_c^d 2\pi y \cdot g(y),dy
where g(y) is the horizontal extent of the region at height y.
Setup. The region has y \in [0,1] (by symmetry, consider the upper half and double, or integrate from 0 to 1 with the full horizontal extent).
At height y: the region extends from x = y^2 to x = 1, so g(y) = 1 - y^2.
V = \int_0^1 2\pi y(1 - y^2),dy = 2\pi \int_0^1 (y - y^3),dy
= 2\pi \left[\frac{y^2}{2} - \frac{y^4}{4}\right]_0^1 = 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2}

5. General Formula — Any Axis
The key is always: identify the shell radius and shell height as functions of the integration variable.















































Axis of RotationIntegration VariableShell RadiusShell Heighty-axisxxf(x)x = k (right of region)xk - xf(x)x = k (left of region)xx - kf(x)x-axisyyg(y)y = k (above region)yk - yg(y)y = k (below region)yy - kg(y)
The general template:
V = 2\pi \int_{\text{start}}^{\text{end}} (\text{shell radius}) \cdot (\text{shell height}),d(\text{variable})

6. Shell vs. Washer — Decision Heuristic
                     Is the integrand expressible naturally 
                     in the variable parallel to the axis?
                              /            \
                            YES             NO
                             |               |
                      Use WASHER         Use SHELL
                      (perpendicular     (parallel
                        slices)           slices)

More concretely:

Use washers when rotating about y-axis and x = g(y) is easy; or rotating about x-axis and y = f(x) is easy.
Use shells when the function is hard to invert, or when the shell radius and height are naturally expressed in the integration variable you want.


Personal note: I almost always try the shell method first when rotating about a vertical axis with a function given as y = f(x). The algebra is usually cleaner.


7. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
At first glance, this seems like pure geometric calculus. But the shell method — and integration in general — underlies several fundamental concepts in modern ML.
7.1 Probability Density Functions and Marginalization
In Bayesian ML, we constantly marginalize joint distributions:
p(x) = \int p(x, z),dz
The shell method is conceptually the same decomposition: we decompose 3D volume into infinitesimal shells (2D surfaces × thickness), just as we decompose a joint distribution into conditional slices. The change-of-variables in integration is everywhere in probabilistic modeling.
7.2 Gaussian Integrals and the Normal Distribution
The normalization constant of the Gaussian distribution requires computing:
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi}
The standard proof uses rotation to polar coordinates — which is precisely the spirit of the shell/disk decomposition:
\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2},dx\right)^2 = \iint e^{-(x^2+y^2)},dx,dy = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-r^2} \cdot 2\pi r,dr
That last integrand 2\pi r \cdot e^{-r^2} is exactly the shell method formula in disguise (2\pi r = circumference, e^{-r^2} = height of the “function”, dr = thickness). This is why the Gaussian is so analytically tractable — it separates in polar coordinates.
7.3 Volume of the n-Ball — The Curse of Dimensionality
In high-dimensional ML (think: weight spaces of neural networks), a key geometric fact is:

Most of the volume of a high-dimensional ball lies near its surface (shell).

This is made rigorous by computing the volume V_n(R) of an n-dimensional ball of radius R:
V_n(R) = \frac{\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2 + 1)} R^n
The shell at radius r has “volume” (surface measure × thickness):
dV_n = n \cdot \frac{\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2+1)} r^{n-1},dr
For large n, the factor r^{n-1} concentrates near r = R. The fraction of the ball’s volume within \epsilon of the surface is:
1 - \left(1 - \frac{\epsilon}{R}\right)^n \to 1 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
This is the curse of dimensionality — random points in high dimensions are nearly always near the boundary shell. It explains why:

Distance-based algorithms (KNN) degrade in high dimensions
Sampling from high-dimensional distributions concentrates on shells
Neural networks live in very high-dimensional parameter spaces where geometric intuition from 3D fails

7.4 Radial Basis Functions and Kernel Methods
Many kernel functions in SVMs and Gaussian Processes depend only on |x - x'| — they are radially symmetric. Computing feature map integrals with such kernels uses exactly shell-method decompositions:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} K(|x|),dx = \int_0^\infty K(r) \cdot S_{d-1}(r),dr
where S_{d-1}(r) is the surface area of the (d-1)-sphere of radius r. This is the d-dimensional generalization of our 2\pi r circumference factor.
7.5 Normalizing Flows
Normalizing flows are deep learning models that learn invertible transformations f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d to transform a simple distribution into a complex one. The change-of-density formula uses the Jacobian determinant:
p_X(x) = p_Z(f^{-1}(x)) \cdot \left|\det \frac{\partial f^{-1}}{\partial x}\right|
For radially symmetric flows, this Jacobian computation reduces to a 1D integral — again, the shell decomposition. The shell method is the 1D instance of the general “co-area formula” from geometric measure theory.

8. A Rigorous Note on Validity
The formula V = \int_a^b 2\pi x f(x),dx requires:

f continuous on [a,b] — ensures Riemann integrability.
f(x) \geq 0 on [a,b] — shells have non-negative height; otherwise use |f(x)| or split the integral.
0 \leq a — the axis of rotation (y-axis, x = 0) must not cut through the region. If a < 0, the shell radius isn’t simply x; you need to be more careful about cancellation.

When f can be negative or the region straddles the axis, write:
V = \int_a^b 2\pi x [f_{\text{top}}(x) - f_{\text{bottom}}(x)],dx
and ensure f_{\text{top}} \geq f_{\text{bottom}} throughout.

9. Summary Table








































PropertyShell MethodDisk/Washer MethodSlice orientationParallel to axisPerpendicular to axisElement shapeCylindrical shellDisk or annulusNatural for y-axis rotationy = f(x) given directlyx = g(y) easy to findKey formula2\pi \int r \cdot h ,dt\pi \int [R^2 - r^2],dtHandles hard inverses✓ Yes✗ Often noConceptual imageUnroll shell into flat slabStack coins/washers

10. Quick Reference — Setup Checklist
When you encounter a volume of revolution problem:

 Identify the region (sketch it!)
 Identify the axis of rotation
 Choose method: can I express everything naturally in one variable?
 If shells: write dV = 2\pi \cdot r \cdot h \cdot d(\text{var})
 Determine r = distance from the strip to the axis
 Determine h = length of the strip (top - bottom or right - left)
 Find limits of integration
 Integrate and simplify


References

Stewart, J. — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §6.3 “Volumes by Cylindrical Shells”
MIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus (OpenCourseWare). Lecture notes on change of variables, polar coordinates, and volume decompositions.
Bishop, C. — Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Chapter 2 (Gaussian integral, marginalization)
Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., Courville, A. — Deep Learning, Chapter 5 (curse of dimensionality)

01.Maths/Calculus/06.Applications-of-Ite.title: 04.Volumes by Disks and Washers
01.Maths/Calculus/06.Applications-of-Ite.content:
“Solids of revolution are the first place calculus reveals something the eye cannot directly see: a 2D region, spun through space, carving out a 3D object with exact, computable volume. The disk method is the most direct incarnation of this idea.”


Tags
#calculus #integration #volume #solids-of-revolution #ML-connection #stewart #18.02

0. Conceptual Foundation — Cavalieri’s Principle
Before any formula, here is the geometric principle underlying everything.

Cavalieri’s Principle. If two solids have the same cross-sectional area A(x) at every x \in [a,b], then they have the same volume.

This means: volume is completely determined by the cross-sectional area function. If we can write down A(x), we can compute the volume by integrating it.
\boxed{V = \int_a^b A(x), dx}
This is the master formula. The disk and washer methods are simply the special cases where the cross-sections happen to be circles or annuli (rings).

1. The Disk Method
1.1 Setup
Take a region under y = f(x) on [a,b] and revolve it about the x-axis.
What does a cross-section look like? Slice the solid with a plane perpendicular to the x-axis at position x. The cross-section is a disk (filled circle) with:

Radius R = f(x) (the y-value at that x)
Area A(x) = \pi [f(x)]^2

         y
         |        ╭──────────╮
         |      ╭─╯          ╰─╮   ← y = f(x)
         |    ╭─╯              ╰─╮
         |   ─╯    region        ╰─
─────────┼──────────────────────────  x
         |   a                   b

         ↓  revolve about x-axis

         The solid looks like a "vase" or "football"
         
         At position x:
         
                  ┌───────────┐
                  │     ●─────┤ ← radius = f(x)
                  │           │
                  └───────────┘
                  Disk of radius f(x)

1.2 The Formula
Applying Cavalieri’s Principle with A(x) = \pi [f(x)]^2:
\boxed{V = \pi \int_a^b [f(x)]^2, dx}
Rotation about the y-axis. If instead we revolve x = g(y) on [c,d] about the y-axis:
V = \pi \int_c^d [g(y)]^2, dy
The logic is identical; only the orientation changes.

1.3 Worked Example — The Cone
Problem. Prove that the volume of a cone of radius r and height h is \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h.
Setup. Place the apex at the origin, axis along the x-axis. The slant edge is the line y = \frac{r}{h} x, for x \in [0, h].
Disk radius at position x: R(x) = \frac{r}{h}x.
V = \pi \int_0^h \left(\frac{r}{h}x\right)^2 dx = \frac{\pi r^2}{h^2} \int_0^h x^2, dx = \frac{\pi r^2}{h^2} \cdot \frac{h^3}{3} = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h \qquad \square

This is deeply satisfying: the factor of \frac{1}{3} emerges from \int x^2,dx = \frac{x^3}{3}, not from some geometric trick.


1.4 Worked Example — The Sphere
Problem. Prove that the volume of a sphere of radius r is \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3.
Setup. The sphere is the solid obtained by revolving the semicircle y = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2} on [-r, r] about the x-axis.
Disk radius at position x: R(x) = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2}.
V = \pi \int_{-r}^r (r^2 - x^2), dx = \pi \left[r^2 x - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-r}^r
= \pi \left[\left(r^3 - \frac{r^3}{3}\right) - \left(-r^3 + \frac{r^3}{3}\right)\right] = \pi \cdot \frac{4r^3}{3} = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \qquad \square

2. The Washer Method
2.1 Setup
Now suppose the region is between two curves: y = f(x) on top and y = g(x) on the bottom, with f(x) \geq g(x) \geq 0 on [a,b].
When revolved about the x-axis, the cross-section at x is no longer a full disk — it is an annulus (washer): a disk with a hole punched in it.
        Outer radius: R = f(x)
        Inner radius: r = g(x)

                 ╭──────────────╮
               ╭─╯  ╭──────╮    ╰─╮
              ─╯    │  hole │     ╰─
                    ╰──────╯
               ╰─╮              ╭─╯
                 ╰──────────────╯

        Area = π R² - π r² = π(R² - r²)

Washer area: A(x) = \pi [f(x)]^2 - \pi [g(x)]^2 = \pi\left([f(x)]^2 - [g(x)]^2\right)
2.2 The Formula
\boxed{V = \pi \int_a^b \left([f(x)]^2 - [g(x)]^2\right) dx}
Common mistake. [f(x)]^2 - [g(x)]^2 \neq [f(x) - g(x)]^2. The subtraction is outside the squaring. You square each radius separately, then subtract.
Rotation about the y-axis: V = \pi \int_c^d \left([f_{\text{right}}(y)]^2 - [f_{\text{left}}(y)]^2\right) dy
where f_{\text{right}} and f_{\text{left}} are the right and left boundaries of the region as functions of y.

2.3 Worked Example — Classic Washer
Problem. Find the volume of the solid obtained by rotating the region bounded by y = x^2 and y = x (for x \in [0,1]) about the x-axis.
Find intersections: x^2 = x \Rightarrow x = 0 or x = 1.
On [0,1]: x \geq x^2, so outer radius R = x, inner radius r = x^2.
V = \pi \int_0^1 \left(x^2 - x^4\right) dx = \pi \left[\frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^1 = \pi\left(\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{5}\right) = \frac{2\pi}{15}

2.4 Worked Example — Rotation about a Non-Standard Axis
Problem. Rotate the region bounded by y = x^2 and y = 4 about the line y = 4.
Key shift. The axis is y = 4, not y = 0. The radius of each disk is the distance from the curve to the axis.
The region is bounded above by y = 4 and below by y = x^2, for x \in [-2, 2].
Since we rotate about y = 4 (which is the top boundary), and y = x^2 is below it:
R(x) = 4 - x^2 \quad (\text{distance from } y = x^2 \text{ to } y = 4)
No hole (the top boundary is the axis itself), so this is a pure disk method:
V = \pi \int_{-2}^{2} (4 - x^2)^2, dx = \pi \int_{-2}^{2} (16 - 8x^2 + x^4), dx
By symmetry, = 2\pi \int_0^2 (16 - 8x^2 + x^4), dx:
= 2\pi \left[16x - \frac{8x^3}{3} + \frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^2 = 2\pi \left(32 - \frac{64}{3} + \frac{32}{5}\right) = 2\pi \cdot \frac{256}{15} = \frac{512\pi}{15}

2.5 Worked Example — Revolving About a Vertical Axis (Washers in y)
Problem. Rotate the region bounded by x = y^2 and x = 4 about the y-axis.
The curves meet at y = \pm 2.
At height y: the region runs from x = y^2 (left boundary) to x = 4 (right boundary).
Revolving about y-axis: the outer radius is R = 4, inner radius is r = y^2.
V = \pi \int_{-2}^{2} \left(16 - y^4\right) dy = 2\pi \int_0^2 (16 - y^4), dy = 2\pi \left[16y - \frac{y^5}{5}\right]_0^2
= 2\pi \left(32 - \frac{32}{5}\right) = 2\pi \cdot \frac{128}{5} = \frac{256\pi}{5}

3. General Framework — Any Axis of Rotation
Let d(x) denote the distance from a point at coordinate x to the axis of rotation.








































ConfigurationOuter Radius RInner Radius rAbout x-axis, f \geq g \geq 0f(x)g(x)About y = k (above region), f \leq kk - g(x)k - f(x)About y = k (below region), f \geq kf(x) - kg(x) - kAbout y-axis, f_R \geq f_L \geq 0 (in y)f_R(y)f_L(y)About x = k (right of region)k - f_L(y)k - f_R(y)About x = k (left of region)f_R(y) - kf_L(y) - k
The rule: R is always the radius to the far boundary, r to the near boundary (or zero for the disk case).

4. ASCII Cross-Section Anatomy
DISK METHOD                          WASHER METHOD

   y                                    y
   │    ╭───╮                           │    ╭───────╮
   │   ╱     ╲                          │   ╱ ╭───╮  ╲
   │  │  disk  │                        │  │  │hole│  │
   │   ╲     ╱                          │   ╲ ╰───╯  ╱
   │    ╰───╯                           │    ╰───────╯
   └──────────── x                      └──────────── x
   
   R = f(x)                            R = f_outer(x)
   A = πR²                             r = f_inner(x)
                                       A = π(R² - r²)

          ↑                                   ↑
   "Stack of coins"                    "Stack of washers/rings"


5. Relation to Shell Method — The Complementary Pair
The disk/washer method and the shell method are dual decompositions of the same solid. Given the same solid:



































Disk/WasherShellSlicesPerpendicular to axisParallel to axisElementThin circular slabThin cylindrical shellBest whenFunction easy to express in variable along axisFunction hard to invertExample: rotate y=f(x) about x-axisNatural (integrate in x)Need f invertible as x = f^{-1}(y)Example: rotate y=f(x) about y-axisNeed inverse x = f^{-1}(y)Natural (integrate in x)

Personal heuristic. For rotation about the x-axis with y = f(x) given: use disks/washers (integrate in x, everything is natural). For rotation about the y-axis with y = f(x) given: strongly prefer shells (avoid inverting f).


6. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
6.1 Cavalieri’s Principle → Lebesgue Integration
The master formula V = \int A(x),dx is an instance of Fubini’s theorem: computing a higher-dimensional integral by iterated 1D integrals over cross-sections. In ML, we constantly use this:
\mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim p}[f(x,y)] = \int \left(\int f(x,y), p(y|x), dy\right) p(x), dx
The inner integral is a “cross-section” (conditional expectation at fixed x), and the outer integral averages over all x. Fubini is the theorem that justifies swapping integration order — essential for almost every derivation in probabilistic ML.
6.2 The Gaussian — Disk Slices of the Bell Curve
The normalization of the multivariate Gaussian \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) in \mathbb{R}^d requires:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-|\mathbf{x}|^2/2}, d\mathbf{x} = (2\pi)^{d/2}
The proof proceeds by disk slicing: level sets of e^{-|x|^2/2} are spheres. At radius r, the level set has surface area S_{d-1} r^{d-1} (a generalized “disk”), so:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-|\mathbf{x}|^2/2}, d\mathbf{x} = \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/2} \cdot S_{d-1} r^{d-1}, dr
This is the disk method in d dimensions — integrating spherical cross-sections. The entire theory of multivariate Gaussians rests on this.
6.3 Fisher Information and the Shape of the Loss Landscape
In optimization and information geometry (used in natural gradient descent, second-order optimization for deep networks), the Fisher information matrix is:
\mathcal{F}_{ij}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial \log p(x|\theta)}{\partial \theta_i} \cdot \frac{\partial \log p(x|\theta)}{\partial \theta_j}\right]
For a 1D exponential family, \mathcal{F}(\theta) has a clean geometric interpretation as the curvature of the cross-section of the statistical manifold. The disk/washer decomposition provides the geometric intuition: the Fisher metric measures how the “cross-sectional shape” of the probability simplex changes as you move along \theta.
6.4 Activation Functions and “Solid” Coverage
In neural networks, the effective volume of the activation region of a neuron (the set of inputs that activate it) can be analyzed using disk/washer cross-sections when the decision boundaries are spherical or ellipsoidal (e.g., RBF networks, Gaussian kernel SVMs). The expressivity of such neurons is directly related to the volume of these regions:
V_{\text{active}} = \int_{\text{region}} A(x),dx
Understanding this volume is crucial for capacity analysis.
6.5 KL Divergence — Integration Over Cross-Sections of Probability Space
The Kullback-Leibler divergence:
D_{\text{KL}}(p | q) = \int p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}, dx
is itself an integral of cross-sections. In variational inference (the backbone of VAEs), we minimize:
\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}[\log p(x|z)] - D_{\text{KL}}(q(z|x) | p(z))
The second term has an exact closed form for Gaussians — derived by disk-slicing (the cross-sectional areas of Gaussian ellipsoids integrate cleanly). This is why VAEs are analytically tractable.
6.6 Volume of Confidence Ellipsoids
In Bayesian linear regression and Gaussian processes, the posterior uncertainty is captured by an ellipsoidal confidence region:
\mathcal{E} = {\theta : (\theta - \hat\theta)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\theta - \hat\theta) \leq \chi^2_d(\alpha)}
The volume of this ellipsoid is computed by the washer/disk method after an orthogonal change of variables (diagonalizing \Sigma):
V(\mathcal{E}) = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2+1)} \prod_{i=1}^d \sqrt{\lambda_i} \cdot [\chi^2_d(\alpha)]^{d/2}
where \lambda_i are eigenvalues of \Sigma. The \Gamma function in the denominator comes directly from integrating the disk cross-sections via the gamma integral \int_0^\infty r^{d-1} e^{-r},dr = \Gamma(d).

7. Rigorous Conditions for Validity
The formula V = \pi \int_a^b [f(x)]^2,dx requires:

f continuous on [a,b] — guarantees [f(x)]^2 is Riemann integrable.
f(x) \geq 0 on [a,b] — the radius must be non-negative. If f takes negative values, the radius is |f(x)| (the disk is the same regardless of sign), so replace f(x) with |f(x)|.
For washers: f(x) \geq g(x) \geq 0 on [a,b] — outer radius is genuinely larger, and both radii are non-negative. If g < 0, the formula breaks down; rewrite as distance to the axis.

What if f changes sign? Split the integral at zeros and use |f(x)| throughout. The disk’s radius is always a positive length — the sign of f is geometrically irrelevant.

8. Setup Checklist

 Sketch the region carefully — label curves, identify top/bottom or left/right
 Identify the axis of rotation
 Determine integration variable (x or y) based on which way you slice
 Identify cross-section type: disk (one boundary) or washer (two boundaries)
 Write R(x) and r(x) as distances to the axis (not just function values!)
 Set limits from the intersection points or given bounds
 Write V = \pi \int [R^2 - r^2],dx (or dy) and integrate
 Sanity check: units (\text{length}^3), sign (must be positive), rough magnitude


9. Quick Reference
\text{Disk: } V = \pi \int_a^b [R(x)]^2,dx \qquad \text{Washer: } V = \pi \int_a^b \left([R(x)]^2 - [r(x)]^2\right)dx
\text{In } y\text{: } V = \pi \int_c^d \left([R(y)]^2 - [r(y)]^2\right)dy
Memory hook: “Area of a washer = \pi R^2 - \pi r^2. Volume = integrate the washer area.”

References

Stewart, J. — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §6.2 “Volumes”
MIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus. Lecture notes on cross-sectional area, Fubini’s theorem
Bishop, C. — Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Ch. 2 (Gaussian integrals, ellipsoidal confidence regions)
Kingma & Welling — Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (2013) (VAE, KL divergence for Gaussians)
Amari, S. — Information Geometry and Its Applications (Fisher information, natural gradient)


See Also
