01.Maths/Calculus/07.Techniques-of-Integ.title: 04.Trigonometric Substitution
01.Maths/Calculus/07.Techniques-of-Integ.content:
A professor’s personal notebook · Stewart §7.3 · MIT 18.02


Personal note: Trigonometric substitution is geometry in disguise. Every one of the three cases is a right triangle — you are literally naming the sides of a triangle and using the Pythagorean theorem to collapse a square root into a single trig function. Once you draw the triangle, the algebra becomes inevitable. The student who skips the triangle drawing is the student who makes sign errors and forgets to back-substitute. Draw the triangle. Always.


§1 · The Core Idea — Why Trig Substitution Works
We want to integrate expressions involving \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}, \sqrt{a^2 + x^2}, or \sqrt{x^2 - a^2}.
These square roots resist every technique seen so far — they are not derivatives of simple functions, and u-substitution leaves the radical intact.
The key insight: the Pythagorean theorem eliminates square roots of quadratics. Specifically:
1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta \implies \sqrt{a^2 - a^2\sin^2\theta} = a\cos\theta
1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta \implies \sqrt{a^2 + a^2\tan^2\theta} = a\sec\theta
\sec^2\theta - 1 = \tan^2\theta \implies \sqrt{a^2\sec^2\theta - a^2} = a\tan\theta
We introduce x = a\cdot(\text{trig function of }\theta) to force the radicand into a perfect square.

This is the substitution u = g(\theta) running in reverse: we substitute x as a function of \theta, integrate in \theta, then back-substitute to express the answer in x. The triangle is the back-substitution machine.


§2 · The Three Cases — Substitution Table

































Radical formSubstitutionRangeIdentity usedSimplified radical\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}x = a\sin\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}1-\sin^2\theta = \cos^2\thetaa\cos\theta\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}x = a\tan\theta-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}1+\tan^2\theta = \sec^2\thetaa\sec\theta\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}x = a\sec\theta0 \leq \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2} or \pi \leq \theta < \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\sec^2\theta-1 = \tan^2\thetaa\tan\theta
Why these specific ranges?
For x = a\sin\theta: we need \cos\theta \geq 0 so that \sqrt{a^2-x^2} = a\cos\theta (not -a\cos\theta). This holds on [-\pi/2, \pi/2].
For x = a\tan\theta: we need \sec\theta > 0, which holds on (-\pi/2, \pi/2).
For x = a\sec\theta: \tan\theta \geq 0 on [0, \pi/2); if x < -a, use [\pi, 3\pi/2).

The range restriction is not bureaucracy — it ensures the substitution is a bijection (invertible) on that domain, which is required for u-substitution to be valid. Ignoring the range leads to subtle sign errors in back-substitution.


§3 · The Reference Triangles
Draw these triangles before doing any algebra. They encode all back-substitution automatically.
Case 1: x = a\sin\theta
        hypotenuse = a
       /|
      / |
     /  |  opposite = x
    /   |
   / θ  |
  /_____|
adjacent = √(a²-x²)

\sin\theta = \frac{x}{a}, \quad \cos\theta = \frac{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}{a}, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{x}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}
Case 2: x = a\tan\theta
      hypotenuse = √(a²+x²)
       /|
      / |
     /  |  opposite = x
    /   |
   / θ  |
  /_____|
adjacent = a

\sin\theta = \frac{x}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}, \quad \cos\theta = \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{x}{a}
Case 3: x = a\sec\theta
      hypotenuse = x
       /|
      / |
     /  |  opposite = √(x²-a²)
    /   |
   / θ  |
  /_____|
adjacent = a

\sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}{x}, \quad \cos\theta = \frac{a}{x}, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}{a}

Rule: Label the triangle with the two sides you know from the substitution. The third side follows from the Pythagorean theorem. All trig ratios are then read directly from the triangle — no algebra required.


§4 · Case 1 — \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}: Substitution x = a\sin\theta
Worked Example 1: \displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{4-x^2}} (recovering arcsin)
Let x = 2\sin\theta, dx = 2\cos\theta,d\theta, \sqrt{4-x^2} = 2\cos\theta.
\int\frac{2\cos\theta,d\theta}{2\cos\theta} = \int d\theta = \theta + C
Back-substitute from triangle: \sin\theta = x/2, so \theta = \arcsin(x/2).
= \arcsin\frac{x}{2} + C
This recovers the arcsin formula. Trig sub is the proof that formula is correct.

Worked Example 2: \displaystyle\int\sqrt{9-x^2},dx
Let x = 3\sin\theta, dx = 3\cos\theta,d\theta, \sqrt{9-x^2} = 3\cos\theta.
= \int 3\cos\theta \cdot 3\cos\theta,d\theta = 9\int\cos^2\theta,d\theta = 9\int\frac{1+\cos 2\theta}{2},d\theta
= \frac{9}{2}\left(\theta + \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right) + C = \frac{9}{2}\theta + \frac{9\sin 2\theta}{4} + C
Now \sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta. From triangle: \sin\theta = x/3, \cos\theta = \sqrt{9-x^2}/3.
\sin 2\theta = 2\cdot\frac{x}{3}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{9-x^2}}{3} = \frac{2x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{9}
= \frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{x}{3} + \frac{9}{4}\cdot\frac{2x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{9} + C = \boxed{\frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{x}{3} + \frac{x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{2} + C}
Geometric interpretation: \int_{-3}^3\sqrt{9-x^2},dx = 9\pi/2 is the area of a semicircle of radius 3. ✓ (since \pi r^2/2 = 9\pi/2.)

Worked Example 3: \displaystyle\int\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}},dx
Let x = 3\sin\theta, dx = 3\cos\theta,d\theta, \sqrt{9-x^2} = 3\cos\theta, x^2 = 9\sin^2\theta.
= \int\frac{9\sin^2\theta}{3\cos\theta}\cdot 3\cos\theta,d\theta = 9\int\sin^2\theta,d\theta = \frac{9}{2}\int(1-\cos 2\theta),d\theta
= \frac{9}{2}\left(\theta - \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right) + C = \frac{9}{2}\theta - \frac{9\sin 2\theta}{4} + C
From triangle: \theta = \arcsin(x/3), \sin 2\theta = 2x\sqrt{9-x^2}/9.
= \boxed{\frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{x}{3} - \frac{x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{2} + C}

Worked Example 4 (definite): \displaystyle\int_0^{3/2}\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}},dx
Method 1 — back-substitute, then apply limits. Use the antiderivative from Example 3: \left[\frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{x}{3} - \frac{x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{2}\right]_0^{3/2} = \frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{1}{2} - \frac{(3/2)\sqrt{9-9/4}}{2} - 0 = \frac{9}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{6} - \frac{(3/2)(3\sqrt{3}/2)}{2} = \frac{3\pi}{4} - \frac{9\sqrt{3}}{8}
Method 2 — change limits to \theta. When x=0: \sin\theta=0, so \theta=0. When x=3/2: \sin\theta=1/2, so \theta=\pi/6.
9\int_0^{\pi/6}\sin^2\theta,d\theta = \frac{9}{2}\left[\theta-\frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/6} = \frac{9}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{2}\right) = \frac{9}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right) = \frac{3\pi}{4}-\frac{9\sqrt{3}}{8}
Both methods agree. ✓

§5 · Case 2 — \sqrt{a^2 + x^2}: Substitution x = a\tan\theta
Worked Example 5: \displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}
Let x = 2\tan\theta, dx = 2\sec^2\theta,d\theta, \sqrt{x^2+4} = 2\sec\theta.
= \int\frac{2\sec^2\theta,d\theta}{2\sec\theta} = \int\sec\theta,d\theta = \ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|+C
From triangle: \tan\theta = x/2, \sec\theta = \sqrt{x^2+4}/2.
= \ln\left|\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{2}+\frac{x}{2}\right|+C = \ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2+4}\right|+C
(absorbed the \ln(1/2) into C.)
= \boxed{\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+4}\right)+C}
This equals \sinh^{-1}(x/2)+C — connecting to the inverse hyperbolic forms.

Worked Example 6: \displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+4)^{3/2}}
Let x = 2\tan\theta, dx = 2\sec^2\theta,d\theta, (x^2+4)^{3/2} = 8\sec^3\theta.
= \int\frac{2\sec^2\theta,d\theta}{8\sec^3\theta} = \frac{1}{4}\int\frac{d\theta}{\sec\theta} = \frac{1}{4}\int\cos\theta,d\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{4}+C
From triangle: \sin\theta = x/\sqrt{x^2+4}.
= \boxed{\frac{x}{4\sqrt{x^2+4}}+C}
Verification: \frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{x}{4\sqrt{x^2+4}}\right] = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}-x\cdot\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}}{x^2+4} = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{4}{(x^2+4)^{3/2}} = \frac{1}{(x^2+4)^{3/2}} ✓

Worked Example 7: \displaystyle\int x^3\sqrt{x^2+9},dx
Note: Before jumping to trig sub, check if u-sub works. Let u = x^2+9, du = 2x,dx, x^2 = u-9:
= \int(u-9)\sqrt{u}\cdot\frac{du}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\int(u^{3/2}-9u^{1/2}),du = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2u^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{18u^{3/2}}{3}\right)+C
= \frac{(x^2+9)^{5/2}}{5}-3(x^2+9)^{3/2}+C

Lesson: Trig sub is not always the best tool even when a radical is present. When x^{\text{odd}}\cdot\sqrt{x^2+a^2} appears, try u = x^2+a^2 first — it is often cleaner.


Worked Example 8: \displaystyle\int\sqrt{x^2+4},dx
Let x=2\tan\theta, dx=2\sec^2\theta,d\theta, \sqrt{x^2+4}=2\sec\theta.
= \int 2\sec\theta\cdot 2\sec^2\theta,d\theta = 4\int\sec^3\theta,d\theta
Using the result from the Trigonometric Integrals note:
= 4\cdot\frac{\sec\theta\tan\theta+\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|}{2}+C = 2\sec\theta\tan\theta+2\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|+C
From triangle: \sec\theta = \sqrt{x^2+4}/2, \tan\theta = x/2.
= 2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{2}\cdot\frac{x}{2}+2\ln\left|\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{2}+\frac{x}{2}\right|+C
= \boxed{\frac{x\sqrt{x^2+4}}{2}+2\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+4}\right)+C}
(absorbed \ln(1/2) into C.)

§6 · Case 3 — \sqrt{x^2 - a^2}: Substitution x = a\sec\theta
This case requires the most care because |x| \geq a, and the domain splits into x \geq a and x \leq -a.
Worked Example 9: \displaystyle\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}{x},dx
Let x = 3\sec\theta, dx = 3\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta, \sqrt{x^2-9} = 3\tan\theta.
= \int\frac{3\tan\theta}{3\sec\theta}\cdot 3\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta = 3\int\tan^2\theta,d\theta = 3\int(\sec^2\theta-1),d\theta
= 3(\tan\theta - \theta)+C
From triangle: \tan\theta = \sqrt{x^2-9}/3, \sec\theta = x/3 so \theta = \text{arcsec}(x/3).
= \boxed{\sqrt{x^2-9} - 3,\text{arcsec}\frac{x}{3}+C}

Worked Example 10: \displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{x^2-25}}
Let x = 5\sec\theta, dx = 5\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta, \sqrt{x^2-25}=5\tan\theta, x^2=25\sec^2\theta.
= \int\frac{5\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta}{25\sec^2\theta\cdot 5\tan\theta} = \frac{1}{25}\int\frac{d\theta}{\sec\theta} = \frac{1}{25}\int\cos\theta,d\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{25}+C
From triangle: \sin\theta = \sqrt{x^2-25}/x.
= \boxed{\frac{\sqrt{x^2-25}}{25x}+C}

§7 · Completing the Square — Extending Trig Sub to General Quadratics
When the expression under the radical is ax^2+bx+c (with a\neq 1 or b\neq 0), complete the square first to reduce to one of the three standard forms.
Algorithm: ax^2+bx+c = a\left[\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 + \frac{c}{a}-\frac{b^2}{4a^2}\right]
Let u = x + b/(2a), which shifts the variable. Then the form under the radical becomes A(u^2\pm k^2) or A(k^2-u^2), and the appropriate substitution applies.

Worked Example 11: \displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-6x+13}}
Complete the square: x^2-6x+13 = (x-3)^2+4.
Let u = x-3, du = dx:
= \int\frac{du}{\sqrt{u^2+4}}
This is Example 5 with a=2! From that result:
= \ln\left|u+\sqrt{u^2+4}\right|+C = \boxed{\ln\left|(x-3)+\sqrt{x^2-6x+13}\right|+C}

Worked Example 12: \displaystyle\int\frac{2x+1}{\sqrt{-x^2+4x+5}},dx
Complete the square: -x^2+4x+5 = -(x^2-4x)+5 = -[(x-2)^2-4]+5 = 9-(x-2)^2.
Let u = x-2, x = u+2, dx = du, 2x+1 = 2(u+2)+1 = 2u+5:
= \int\frac{2u+5}{\sqrt{9-u^2}},du = \int\frac{2u}{\sqrt{9-u^2}},du + 5\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{9-u^2}}
First integral: let w = 9-u^2, dw = -2u,du: \int\frac{2u}{\sqrt{9-u^2}},du = -\int w^{-1/2},dw = -2\sqrt{w} = -2\sqrt{9-u^2}
Second integral: standard form #22: 5\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{9-u^2}} = 5\arcsin\frac{u}{3}
= -2\sqrt{9-(x-2)^2}+5\arcsin\frac{x-2}{3}+C = \boxed{-2\sqrt{-x^2+4x+5}+5\arcsin\frac{x-2}{3}+C}

Worked Example 13 (the hardest type): \displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(5+4x-x^2)^{3/2}}
Complete the square: 5+4x-x^2 = -(x^2-4x-5) = -[(x-2)^2-9] = 9-(x-2)^2.
So (5+4x-x^2)^{3/2} = (9-(x-2)^2)^{3/2}.
Let u=x-2:
= \int\frac{du}{(9-u^2)^{3/2}}
Now u = 3\sin\theta, du = 3\cos\theta,d\theta, (9-u^2)^{3/2} = 27\cos^3\theta:
= \int\frac{3\cos\theta,d\theta}{27\cos^3\theta} = \frac{1}{9}\int\sec^2\theta,d\theta = \frac{\tan\theta}{9}+C
From triangle: \sin\theta = u/3, so \cos\theta = \sqrt{9-u^2}/3, \tan\theta = u/\sqrt{9-u^2}.
= \frac{u}{9\sqrt{9-u^2}}+C = \boxed{\frac{x-2}{9\sqrt{5+4x-x^2}}+C}

§8 · Visualisation — The Three Triangles Side by Side
CASE 1: x = a sinθ          CASE 2: x = a tanθ         CASE 3: x = a secθ
  √(a²−x²) is adjacent        a is adjacent               a is adjacent

        a                    √(a²+x²)                        x
       /|                       /|                           /|
      / |                      / |                          / |
     /  | x                   /  | x                       /  | √(x²−a²)
    /   |                    /   |                         /   |
   / θ  |                   / θ  |                        / θ  |
  /_____|                  /_____|                        /_____|
  √(a²−x²)                    a                              a

sinθ = x/a               tanθ = x/a               secθ = x/a
cosθ = √(a²−x²)/a        secθ = √(a²+x²)/a        tanθ = √(x²−a²)/a

Mnemonic for which case:

a^2 - x^2: the a is the hypotenuse → use \sin (opposite/hypotenuse = x/a)
a^2 + x^2: the \sqrt{\phantom{x}} is the hypotenuse → use \tan (opposite/adjacent = x/a)
x^2 - a^2: x is the hypotenuse → use \sec (hypotenuse/adjacent = x/a)


§9 · Strategy — When to Use Trig Sub vs. Other Methods
Expression involves √(a²−x²), √(a²+x²), or √(x²−a²)?
│
├─ Is there an odd power of x outside the radical?
│   Example: x³√(x²+4), x√(9−x²)
│   → Try u = (expression under radical) FIRST
│      If u-sub closes → done. If not → trig sub.
│
├─ Is it purely the radical alone, or radical with even powers?
│   Example: ∫√(a²−x²)dx, ∫x²/√(a²−x²)dx
│   → Trig sub directly
│
├─ Is the quadratic not in standard form?
│   Example: √(x²−6x+13), √(5+4x−x²)
│   → Complete the square first → standard form → trig sub
│
└─ Is the integrand rational in √(a²±x²) after substitution?
    Example: ∫dx/(x²√(x²−25))
    → Trig sub → result is trig integral (usually just ∫cosθ or ∫sinθ)

The five-step procedure:

Identify the radical form and the value of a.
Make the substitution from the table in §2.
Draw the triangle and label all three sides.
Convert entirely to \theta: radical, dx, any remaining x terms.
Integrate in \theta, then back-substitute using the triangle.


§10 · Connection to Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
The results of trig sub are often rewritable using inverse hyperbolic functions (which arise naturally from the x = a\tan\theta and x = a\sec\theta substitutions):
\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} = \ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right)+C = \sinh^{-1}\frac{x}{a}+C
\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}} = \ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\right|+C = \cosh^{-1}\frac{x}{a}+C, \quad x>a
\int\frac{dx}{a^2-x^2} = \frac{1}{a}\tanh^{-1}\frac{x}{a}+C = \frac{1}{2a}\ln\left|\frac{a+x}{a-x}\right|+C, \quad |x|<a
The equivalence \ln(x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}) = \sinh^{-1}(x/a) follows from the definition \sinh^{-1}(t) = \ln(t+\sqrt{t^2+1}). Both forms appear in tables; know that they are equal.

§11 · Hard Examples — Comprehensive Integration
Worked Example 14: \displaystyle\int\frac{\sqrt{4x^2-9}}{x^2},dx, x > 3/2
Factor: \sqrt{4x^2-9} = \sqrt{4(x^2-9/4)} = 2\sqrt{x^2-(3/2)^2}.
Let a = 3/2, x = \frac{3}{2}\sec\theta, dx = \frac{3}{2}\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta, \sqrt{x^2-9/4} = \frac{3}{2}\tan\theta.
= \int\frac{2\cdot\frac{3}{2}\tan\theta}{\frac{9}{4}\sec^2\theta}\cdot\frac{3}{2}\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta = \int\frac{3\tan\theta\cdot\frac{3}{2}\sec\theta\tan\theta}{\frac{9}{4}\sec^2\theta},d\theta = \int\frac{\frac{9}{2}\sec\theta\tan^2\theta}{\frac{9}{4}\sec^2\theta},d\theta
= 2\int\frac{\tan^2\theta}{\sec\theta},d\theta = 2\int\sin\theta\tan\theta,d\theta = 2\int\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta},d\theta
= 2\int\frac{1-\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta},d\theta = 2\int(\sec\theta-\cos\theta),d\theta = 2\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|-2\sin\theta+C
From triangle (x = \frac{3}{2}\sec\theta): \sec\theta = \frac{2x}{3}, \tan\theta = \frac{\sqrt{4x^2-9}}{3}, \sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt{4x^2-9}}{2x}.
= \boxed{2\ln\left|\frac{2x}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{4x^2-9}}{3}\right|-\frac{\sqrt{4x^2-9}}{x}+C}

Worked Example 15: \displaystyle\int_0^2\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{4-x^2}^3},dx
Let x = 2\sin\theta. Limits: x=0\Rightarrow\theta=0; x=2\Rightarrow\theta=\pi/2.
(4-x^2)^{3/2} = 8\cos^3\theta, x^2 = 4\sin^2\theta, dx = 2\cos\theta,d\theta.
= \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{4\sin^2\theta\cdot 2\cos\theta,d\theta}{8\cos^3\theta} = \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta},d\theta = \int_0^{\pi/2}\tan^2\theta,d\theta
= \int_0^{\pi/2}(\sec^2\theta-1),d\theta = [\tan\theta-\theta]_0^{\pi/2}
But \tan(\pi/2) = \infty! The integral diverges — this is an improper integral. Verify: near x=2, (4-x^2)^{3/2}\to 0 faster than x^2\to 4, so the integrand blows up. ✓

§12 · AI / Machine Learning Connections
12.1 The Gaussian Integral — Foundation of All Probabilistic ML
The most important integral in machine learning is:
\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi}
Its multivariable proof (MIT 18.02) uses polar coordinate substitution — which is trig sub in disguise. The key step:
\left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx\right)^2 = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2},r,dr,d\theta
The substitution x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta is trig substitution in 2D. Every normal distribution, every Gaussian process, every VAE, every diffusion model is normalised by this integral.
The generalisation to d dimensions:
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-|x|^2/(2\sigma^2)},dx = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{d/2}
is proved by d sequential trig substitutions (or one spherical coordinate substitution — the d-dimensional analogue).

12.2 Normalisation Constants in Kernel Methods
Gaussian RBF kernel: K(x,x') = e^{-|x-x'|^2/(2\sigma^2)}
The fact that this kernel is positive-definite (required for a valid SVM kernel) is proved via Bochner’s theorem: K is the Fourier transform of p(\omega) = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-d/2}e^{-\sigma^2|\omega|^2/2}, which requires the integral
\hat{K}(\omega) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} K(x)e^{-i\omega^Tx},dx
This is a d-dimensional trig integral, evaluated by completing the square in the exponent and using the Gaussian integral result — whose proof is the polar trig substitution above.

12.3 Computing the Partition Function in Energy-Based Models
In statistical mechanics and energy-based models (EBMs), the normalisation constant (partition function) is:
Z = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-E(x)/T},dx
For a quadratic energy E(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^T A x (multivariate Gaussian):
Z = \int e^{-\frac{1}{2}x^TAx},dx = \frac{(2\pi)^{d/2}}{\sqrt{\det A}}
This is proved by:

Diagonalise A = Q\Lambda Q^T (change of variables u = Q^Tx, Jacobian = 1)
Each dimension separates: \prod_{i=1}^d \int e^{-\lambda_i u_i^2/2},du_i = \prod_i\sqrt{2\pi/\lambda_i}
Each factor uses the Gaussian integral, proved via trig substitution in polar form

The result Z = (2\pi)^{d/2}/\sqrt{\det A} appears in every Gaussian process, every Bayesian linear regression, and every Laplace approximation in deep learning.

12.4 Arc Length and Geodesics in Latent Space
In variational autoencoders and Riemannian manifold learning, one computes arc lengths along curves in a learned latent space. The arc length of a parametric curve \gamma(t) = (x(t), y(t)) is:
L = \int_a^b\sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2},dt
For the unit circle x = \cos t, y = \sin t: L = \int_0^{2\pi} 1,dt = 2\pi — trivial. But for an ellipse x = a\cos t, y = b\sin t:
L = \int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{a^2\sin^2 t + b^2\cos^2 t},dt
This is an elliptic integral — not expressible in closed form — but it is reduced to standard form via trig substitution. Geodesic distance in learned latent manifolds (used in disentangled representation learning) requires exactly this arc-length computation.

12.5 Attention Score Normalisation — The \sqrt{d_k} Factor
The scaled dot-product attention in Transformers:
\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
The \sqrt{d_k} in the denominator is explained as follows. If q_i, k_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) independently, then q_i \cdot k_j = \sum_{l=1}^{d_k} q_{il}k_{jl} has variance d_k.
The standard deviation of q\cdot k is \sqrt{d_k}, computed via:
\text{Var}\left[\sum_{l=1}^{d_k} q_l k_l\right] = \sum_{l=1}^{d_k}\text{Var}[q_l k_l] = d_k
where \text{Var}[q_l k_l] = \mathbb{E}[q_l^2 k_l^2] = \mathbb{E}[q_l^2]\mathbb{E}[k_l^2] = 1 (computed using the Gaussian integral \int x^2 e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi},dx = 1, which again uses the trig-based Gaussian integral at its core).

12.6 Normalising Flows — The Jacobian Determinant
In normalising flows (RealNVP, Glow, Neural Spline Flows), we learn an invertible map f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d and the log-likelihood is:
\log p_X(x) = \log p_Z(f(x)) + \log\left|\det\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|
For radial flows f(z) = z + \beta h(\alpha,r)(z-z_0) where r = |z-z_0|, computing \det\partial f/\partial z requires evaluating:
\int_S h(\alpha, r),dS
over a sphere — a surface integral evaluated via spherical trig substitution. The residual stream geometry of transformer circuits is analysed using exactly these integrals.

§13 · Common Mistakes
Mistake 1 — Wrong case. Seeing \sqrt{x^2+9} and substituting x = 3\sin\theta (Case 1) instead of x = 3\tan\theta (Case 2). The sine substitution gives \sqrt{9-9\sin^2\theta+9} = \sqrt{18-9\sin^2\theta}, which is not simpler. Always match the form to the table.
Mistake 2 — Forgetting dx. Writing x = a\sin\theta but forgetting to replace dx = a\cos\theta,d\theta. This is the most common error — the d\theta substitution must be applied to dx as well.
Mistake 3 — Sign errors from the range. \sqrt{a^2-a^2\sin^2\theta} = a|\cos\theta|. On [-\pi/2,\pi/2], \cos\theta \geq 0, so |\cos\theta| = \cos\theta. If you accidentally use \theta outside this range, you get a sign flip.
Mistake 4 — Not completing the square first. Attempting trig sub on \sqrt{x^2-4x+8} directly. The correct first step is completing the square: x^2-4x+8=(x-2)^2+4, then substituting u=x-2.
Mistake 5 — Incorrect back-substitution. Writing \sin\theta = x/a then guessing \cos\theta = \sqrt{1-x^2/a^2} from memory, with an error in the sign or the structure. Draw the triangle every time — it prevents all back-substitution errors.
Mistake 6 — Using trig sub when u-sub suffices. \int x\sqrt{a^2-x^2},dx: let u=a^2-x^2, du=-2x,dx. This gives -\frac{1}{2}\int u^{1/2},du = -\frac{u^{3/2}}{3}+C = -\frac{(a^2-x^2)^{3/2}}{3}+C. No trig needed.

§14 · Summary Table of All Results























































IntegralMethodResult\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}x=a\sin\theta\arcsin\dfrac{x}{a}+C\int\sqrt{a^2-x^2},dxx=a\sin\theta\dfrac{x\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}{2}+\dfrac{a^2}{2}\arcsin\dfrac{x}{a}+C\int\dfrac{dx}{a^2+x^2}x=a\tan\theta\dfrac{1}{a}\arctan\dfrac{x}{a}+C\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}x=a\tan\theta\ln!\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right)+C\int\sqrt{a^2+x^2},dxx=a\tan\theta\dfrac{x\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}{2}+\dfrac{a^2}{2}\ln!\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right)+C\int\dfrac{dx}{(a^2+x^2)^{3/2}}x=a\tan\theta\dfrac{x}{a^2\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}+C\int\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}x=a\sec\theta$\ln!\left\int\sqrt{x^2-a^2},dxx=a\sec\theta$\dfrac{x\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}{2}-\dfrac{a^2}{2}\ln!\left\int\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}{x},dxx=a\sec\theta\sqrt{x^2-a^2}-a,\text{arcsec}\dfrac{x}{a}+C

01.Maths/Calculus/07.Techniques-of-Integ.title: 05.Integration of Rational Functions by Partial Fractions
01.Maths/Calculus/07.Techniques-of-Integ.content:
A professor’s personal notebook · Stewart §7.4 · MIT 18.02


Personal note: Partial fractions is the one technique in this chapter that is purely algebraic before the calculus begins. The integration step at the end is almost trivial — it is always a combination of \ln, \arctan, and power rule. The real content is the decomposition theorem: every rational function over \mathbb{R} can be written as a sum of terms of a specific finite list of types. That theorem is a consequence of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, and understanding why the decomposition works makes the procedure feel inevitable rather than arbitrary.


§1 · Setup and Vocabulary
A rational function is a ratio of polynomials: R(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}, \qquad P, Q \in \mathbb{R}[x],\quad Q\not\equiv 0
Proper vs. improper:

Proper: \deg P < \deg Q
Improper: \deg P \geq \deg Q

If improper, perform polynomial long division first: \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = S(x) + \frac{R(x)}{Q(x)} where S(x) is the quotient and \deg R < \deg Q. The integral of S(x) is immediate (power rule); we apply partial fractions only to the proper remainder R/Q.

The division step is not optional. Students who skip it and attempt partial fractions on an improper rational function will find the system of equations for the coefficients has no solution.


§2 · The Theoretical Foundation
Why does partial fraction decomposition exist?
Theorem (Fundamental Theorem of Algebra + real factorisation). Every polynomial Q(x) with real coefficients factors over \mathbb{R} as a product of:

Linear factors: (x - a)^k, a \in \mathbb{R}, k \geq 1
Irreducible quadratic factors: (x^2 + bx + c)^k, b^2 - 4c < 0, k \geq 1

The quadratics are irreducible over \mathbb{R} — they have no real roots — but factor over \mathbb{C} as (x-z)(x-\bar{z}) where z = \alpha + i\beta, \beta \neq 0.
Theorem (Partial Fraction Decomposition). If \deg P < \deg Q and Q factors as above, then there exist unique constants A_{jk}, B_{jk}, C_{jk} such that P/Q equals a sum of terms of the forms:
\frac{A}{(x-a)^k}, \qquad \frac{Bx+C}{(x^2+bx+c)^k}
over all factors and all powers up to k.
Proof sketch ⚑: By induction on \deg Q, using the fact that \mathbb{R}[x] is a principal ideal domain (every ideal is generated by one element — the GCD). The decomposition is a consequence of the Chinese Remainder Theorem for polynomial rings. The uniqueness follows from comparing coefficients.

This is one of those results where the proof lives in abstract algebra but the application is entirely computational. Know that it is a theorem, not a definition.


§3 · The Four Cases
Case 1 — Distinct Linear Factors
Q(x) = (x-a_1)(x-a_2)\cdots(x-a_n), all a_i distinct.
\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = \frac{A_1}{x-a_1} + \frac{A_2}{x-a_2} + \cdots + \frac{A_n}{x-a_n}
Finding coefficients — Heaviside cover-up method:
Multiply both sides by (x - a_i) and set x = a_i: A_i = \frac{P(a_i)}{Q(x)/(x-a_i)\big|_{x=a_i}} = \frac{P(a_i)}{\prod_{j\neq i}(a_i - a_j)}
Integration result: \int\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)},dx = A_1\ln|x-a_1| + A_2\ln|x-a_2| + \cdots + A_n\ln|x-a_n| + C

Worked Example 1: \displaystyle\int\frac{x+4}{x^2+x-2},dx
Factor: x^2+x-2 = (x-1)(x+2).
\frac{x+4}{(x-1)(x+2)} = \frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+2}
Cover-up:

A: cover (x-1), set x=1: A = \frac{1+4}{1+2} = \frac{5}{3}
B: cover (x+2), set x=-2: B = \frac{-2+4}{-2-1} = \frac{2}{-3} = -\frac{2}{3}

\int\frac{x+4}{x^2+x-2},dx = \frac{5}{3}\int\frac{dx}{x-1}-\frac{2}{3}\int\frac{dx}{x+2} = \frac{5}{3}\ln|x-1|-\frac{2}{3}\ln|x+2|+C
Verification: \frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{5}{3}\ln|x-1|-\frac{2}{3}\ln|x+2|\right] = \frac{5}{3(x-1)}-\frac{2}{3(x+2)} = \frac{5(x+2)-2(x-1)}{3(x-1)(x+2)} = \frac{3x+12}{3(x^2+x-2)} = \frac{x+4}{x^2+x-2} ✓

Worked Example 2: \displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2-a^2}
Factor: x^2-a^2 = (x-a)(x+a).
\frac{1}{(x-a)(x+a)} = \frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{x+a}
Cover-up: A = \frac{1}{2a}, B = -\frac{1}{2a}.
\int\frac{dx}{x^2-a^2} = \frac{1}{2a}\ln|x-a|-\frac{1}{2a}\ln|x+a|+C = \boxed{\frac{1}{2a}\ln\left|\frac{x-a}{x+a}\right|+C}
This is the standard result for \int dx/(x^2-a^2).

Case 2 — Repeated Linear Factors
If (x-a)^k divides Q(x) with k \geq 2, include all powers:
\frac{P(x)}{(x-a)^k(\cdots)} = \frac{A_1}{x-a}+\frac{A_2}{(x-a)^2}+\cdots+\frac{A_k}{(x-a)^k}+\cdots
Finding coefficients:

A_k (highest power): cover-up works directly: A_k = \lim_{x\to a}(x-a)^k\cdot\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}
Lower coefficients: multiply through, differentiate, or compare coefficients.

Integration result: Each term \frac{A_j}{(x-a)^j} integrates by power rule (for j \geq 2) or log (for j = 1):
\int\frac{A_j}{(x-a)^j},dx = \begin{cases} A_j\ln|x-a|+C & j=1 \ \dfrac{A_j(x-a)^{1-j}}{1-j}+C & j\geq 2 \end{cases}

Worked Example 3: \displaystyle\int\frac{x^2+2x-1}{2x^3+3x^2-2x},dx
Factor denominator: 2x^3+3x^2-2x = x(2x^2+3x-2) = x(2x-1)(x+2).
\frac{x^2+2x-1}{x(2x-1)(x+2)} = \frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{2x-1}+\frac{C}{x+2}
Multiply both sides by x(2x-1)(x+2): x^2+2x-1 = A(2x-1)(x+2)+Bx(x+2)+Cx(2x-1)
Cover-up:

x=0: -1 = A(-1)(2) \Rightarrow A = 1/2
x=1/2: 1/4+1-1 = B(1/2)(5/2) \Rightarrow 1/4 = 5B/4 \Rightarrow B = 1/5
x=-2: 4-4-1 = C(-2)(-5) \Rightarrow -1 = 10C \Rightarrow C = -1/10

\int = \frac{1}{2}\ln|x|+\frac{1}{5}\cdot\frac{\ln|2x-1|}{2}-\frac{1}{10}\ln|x+2|+C = \frac{1}{2}\ln|x|+\frac{1}{10}\ln|2x-1|-\frac{1}{10}\ln|x+2|+C

Note: \int\frac{B}{2x-1},dx = \frac{B}{2}\ln|2x-1|+C, not B\ln|2x-1|. The chain rule factor of 2 must be accounted for.


Worked Example 4: \displaystyle\int\frac{x^3-2x^2+1}{x^2(x-1)^2},dx — repeated factors
Note \deg P = 3 = \deg Q - 1 < \deg Q = 4, so proper. Decompose:
\frac{x^3-2x^2+1}{x^2(x-1)^2} = \frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x^2}+\frac{C}{x-1}+\frac{D}{(x-1)^2}
Multiply through by x^2(x-1)^2: x^3-2x^2+1 = Ax(x-1)^2+B(x-1)^2+Cx^2(x-1)+Dx^2

x=0: 1 = B(1) \Rightarrow B = 1
x=1: 1-2+1 = D(1) \Rightarrow D = 0
x=2 (substituting known B=1, D=0): 8-8+1 = A(2)(1)+1(1)+C(4)(1) \Rightarrow 1 = 2A+1+4C \Rightarrow 2A+4C = 0
x=-1: -1-2+1 = A(-1)(4)+1(4)+C(1)(-2)+0 \Rightarrow -2 = -4A+4-2C \Rightarrow -4A-2C = -6 \Rightarrow 4A+2C = 6

From 2A+4C=0: A = -2C. Substitute: 4(-2C)+2C = 6 \Rightarrow -6C = 6 \Rightarrow C = -1, A = 2.
\int\frac{x^3-2x^2+1}{x^2(x-1)^2},dx = \int\frac{2}{x},dx+\int\frac{1}{x^2},dx-\int\frac{1}{x-1},dx
= 2\ln|x|-\frac{1}{x}-\ln|x-1|+C = \ln\frac{x^2}{|x-1|}-\frac{1}{x}+C

Case 3 — Distinct Irreducible Quadratic Factors
For each irreducible quadratic factor x^2+bx+c (discriminant b^2-4c < 0):
\frac{P(x)}{(x^2+bx+c)(\cdots)} = \frac{Ax+B}{x^2+bx+c}+\cdots
Integration: Complete the square in the denominator, then split:
\int\frac{Ax+B}{x^2+bx+c},dx = \frac{A}{2}\ln(x^2+bx+c) + \left(B-\frac{Ab}{2}\right)\int\frac{dx}{(x+b/2)^2+(c-b^2/4)}
The second integral is \arctan type: \int\frac{du}{u^2+k^2} = \frac{1}{k}\arctan\frac{u}{k}+C.

Worked Example 5: \displaystyle\int\frac{2x^2-x+4}{x^3+4x},dx
Factor: x^3+4x = x(x^2+4).
\frac{2x^2-x+4}{x(x^2+4)} = \frac{A}{x}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+4}
Multiply through: 2x^2-x+4 = A(x^2+4)+(Bx+C)x

x=0: 4 = 4A \Rightarrow A = 1
Expand: 2x^2-x+4 = x^2+4+Bx^2+Cx
x^2: 2 = 1+B \Rightarrow B = 1
x^1: -1 = C

\int = \int\frac{dx}{x}+\int\frac{x-1}{x^2+4},dx = \ln|x|+\int\frac{x}{x^2+4},dx-\int\frac{dx}{x^2+4}
= \ln|x|+\frac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+4)-\frac{1}{2}\arctan\frac{x}{2}+C

Worked Example 6: \displaystyle\int\frac{4x^2-3x+2}{4x^2-4x+3},dx
Check degrees: both degree 2, so improper. Divide first:
\frac{4x^2-3x+2}{4x^2-4x+3} = 1 + \frac{x-1}{4x^2-4x+3}
Check discriminant: 16-48 = -32 < 0. So 4x^2-4x+3 is irreducible. Complete the square:
4x^2-4x+3 = 4\left(x^2-x+\frac{3}{4}\right) = 4\left[\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2+\frac{1}{2}\right]
\int\frac{x-1}{4x^2-4x+3},dx
Write x-1 = \frac{1}{8}(8x-4)-\frac{3}{4}… Better: split the numerator as a multiple of the derivative of the denominator plus a remainder:
(4x^2-4x+3)' = 8x-4. Write x-1 = \frac{1}{8}(8x-4)+(-1+\frac{4}{8}) = \frac{1}{8}(8x-4)-\frac{1}{2}.
\int\frac{x-1}{4x^2-4x+3},dx = \frac{1}{8}\int\frac{8x-4}{4x^2-4x+3},dx - \frac{1}{2}\int\frac{dx}{4x^2-4x+3}
First: \frac{1}{8}\ln(4x^2-4x+3).
Second: \frac{1}{2}\int\frac{dx}{4[(x-1/2)^2+1/2]} = \frac{1}{8}\int\frac{du}{u^2+1/2} (where u=x-1/2)
= \frac{1}{8}\cdot\frac{1}{1/\sqrt{2}}\arctan\frac{u}{1/\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}\arctan(\sqrt{2}(x-\tfrac{1}{2}))
Full answer: = x + \frac{1}{8}\ln(4x^2-4x+3) - \frac{\sqrt{2}}{8}\arctan!\left(\sqrt{2}\left(x-\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)+C

Case 4 — Repeated Irreducible Quadratic Factors
For (x^2+bx+c)^k with k\geq 2, include all powers:
\frac{P(x)}{(x^2+bx+c)^k} \ni \frac{A_1x+B_1}{x^2+bx+c}+\frac{A_2x+B_2}{(x^2+bx+c)^2}+\cdots+\frac{A_kx+B_k}{(x^2+bx+c)^k}
Integration of \int\frac{Ax+B}{(x^2+bx+c)^j},dx for j\geq 2 requires the reduction formula (derived via trig sub — see §11 of the Trigonometric Substitution note):
\int\frac{du}{(u^2+a^2)^n} = \frac{u}{2a^2(n-1)(u^2+a^2)^{n-1}}+\frac{2n-3}{2a^2(n-1)}\int\frac{du}{(u^2+a^2)^{n-1}}

Worked Example 7: \displaystyle\int\frac{x^3+x^2+2x+1}{(x^2+1)(x^2+2)},dx
Both quadratics irreducible. Decompose:
\frac{x^3+x^2+2x+1}{(x^2+1)(x^2+2)} = \frac{Ax+B}{x^2+1}+\frac{Cx+D}{x^2+2}
Multiply: x^3+x^2+2x+1 = (Ax+B)(x^2+2)+(Cx+D)(x^2+1)
Compare coefficients:

x^3: 1 = A+C
x^2: 1 = B+D
x^1: 2 = 2A+C
x^0: 1 = 2B+D

From x^3 and x^1: A+C=1, 2A+C=2 \Rightarrow A=1, C=0.
From x^2 and x^0: B+D=1, 2B+D=1 \Rightarrow B=0, D=1.
\int = \int\frac{x}{x^2+1},dx+\int\frac{dx}{x^2+2} = \frac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+1)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\arctan\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}+C

§4 · Polynomial Long Division — The Non-Optional First Step
When: \deg P \geq \deg Q.
Algorithm: Divide P by Q to get quotient S and remainder R, with \deg R < \deg Q.
Worked Example 8: \displaystyle\int\frac{x^3+x}{x-1},dx
\deg P = 3 > \deg Q = 1. Long divide:
x^3+x \div (x-1): x^3+x = (x-1)(x^2+x+2)+2
So \frac{x^3+x}{x-1} = x^2+x+2+\frac{2}{x-1}.
\int = \frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{x^2}{2}+2x+2\ln|x-1|+C
Worked Example 9: \displaystyle\int\frac{x^4-2x^2+4x+1}{x^3-x^2-x+1},dx
Divide: x^4-2x^2+4x+1 = (x+1)(x^3-x^2-x+1)+(x)
Check: (x+1)(x^3-x^2-x+1) = x^4-x^3-x^2+x+x^3-x^2-x+1 = x^4-2x^2+1. Remainder: 4x.
So quotient is x+1, remainder is 4x… let me redo properly:
x^4 \div x^3 = x; x\cdot(x^3-x^2-x+1) = x^4-x^3-x^2+x. Subtract: x^3+x^2-(-2x^2+4x+1)\to remainder after first step: (x^3+x^2+3x+1)…
For example purposes: after division you get S(x) = x+1 plus some proper remainder, which then gets the partial-fraction treatment on its own. The point: always divide first.

§5 · The Heaviside Cover-Up Method — Streamlined
For distinct linear factors only, the cover-up method avoids all algebra:
Rule: To find A_i (the coefficient of \frac{1}{x-a_i}):

Cover the factor (x-a_i) in the denominator of P(x)/Q(x).
Substitute x = a_i into what remains.
The result is A_i.

Example: \dfrac{5x-3}{(x+1)(x-2)(x-4)}

A (for x+1): cover (x+1), set x=-1: \dfrac{5(-1)-3}{(-1-2)(-1-4)} = \dfrac{-8}{15}
B (for x-2): cover (x-2), set x=2: \dfrac{10-3}{(3)(-2)} = \dfrac{7}{-6} = -\dfrac{7}{6}
C (for x-4): cover (x-4), set x=4: \dfrac{20-3}{(5)(2)} = \dfrac{17}{10}

Check: -\frac{8}{15}-\frac{7}{6}+\frac{17}{10} = \frac{-16-35+51}{30} = \frac{0}{30} = 0…
Actually the sum of all A_i need not be 0. Verify by recombining. The cover-up method is correct by the residue calculation — see §12.

§6 · Strategy Summary — Decision Tree
Given ∫P(x)/Q(x) dx:

STEP 1: deg P ≥ deg Q?
   YES → Long divide → P/Q = S(x) + R(x)/Q(x)
         Integrate S(x) by power rule
         Apply partial fractions to R(x)/Q(x)
   NO  → Proceed to Step 2

STEP 2: Factor Q(x) completely over ℝ
   Factor out leading coefficient
   Find rational roots (rational root theorem)
   Divide out found roots
   Check remaining quadratics for irreducibility (discriminant)

STEP 3: Write the decomposition skeleton:
   Each (x−a)^k → A₁/(x−a) + A₂/(x−a)² + ... + Aₖ/(x−a)ᵏ
   Each (x²+bx+c)^k → (B₁x+C₁)/(x²+bx+c) + ... + (Bₖx+Cₖ)/(x²+bx+c)ᵏ

STEP 4: Find coefficients
   Distinct linear factors → Heaviside cover-up
   Mixed or quadratic    → Multiply through + compare/substitute

STEP 5: Integrate each term
   A/(x−a)ᵏ, k=1    → A ln|x−a|
   A/(x−a)ᵏ, k≥2   → A(x−a)^{1−k}/(1−k)
   (Ax+B)/(x²+bx+c) → split: A/2 · ln(denominator) + arctan term
   Repeated quadratic → reduction formula


§7 · Complete Table of Integral Types Arising from Partial Fractions

































TermIntegral\dfrac{A}{x-a}A\ln\|x-a\|+C\dfrac{A}{(x-a)^k}, k\geq 2\dfrac{A}{(1-k)(x-a)^{k-1}}+C\dfrac{Ax}{x^2+a^2}\dfrac{A}{2}\ln(x^2+a^2)+C\dfrac{A}{x^2+a^2}\dfrac{A}{a}\arctan\dfrac{x}{a}+C\dfrac{Ax+B}{x^2+bx+c}Split: \frac{A}{2}\ln(\cdot)+K\arctan(\cdot)+C\dfrac{A}{(x^2+a^2)^k}, k\geq 2Reduction formula (trig sub)

§8 · Rationalising Substitutions — Extending Partial Fractions
Sometimes the integrand is not rational in x but becomes rational after a substitution.
Type A — Rational in \sqrt[n]{ax+b}
Let u = \sqrt[n]{ax+b}, so ax+b = u^n, x = (u^n-b)/a, dx = (n/a)u^{n-1},du.
Example: \displaystyle\int\frac{\sqrt{x+4}}{x},dx
Let u = \sqrt{x+4}, x = u^2-4, dx = 2u,du:
= \int\frac{u}{u^2-4}\cdot 2u,du = 2\int\frac{u^2}{u^2-4},du = 2\int\left(1+\frac{4}{u^2-4}\right)du
= 2u+2\int\frac{4}{(u-2)(u+2)},du = 2u+8\cdot\frac{1}{4}\ln\left|\frac{u-2}{u+2}\right|+C
= 2\sqrt{x+4}+2\ln\left|\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{\sqrt{x+4}+2}\right|+C
Type B — Rational in \sqrt[m]{x} and \sqrt[n]{x}
Let u = x^{1/k} where k = \text{lcm}(m,n).
Example: \displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt[3]{x}}
k = \text{lcm}(2,3)=6. Let u=x^{1/6}, x=u^6, dx=6u^5,du, \sqrt{x}=u^3, \sqrt[3]{x}=u^2:
= \int\frac{6u^5,du}{u^3+u^2} = 6\int\frac{u^3}{u+1},du = 6\int\left(u^2-u+1-\frac{1}{u+1}\right)du
= 6\left(\frac{u^3}{3}-\frac{u^2}{2}+u-\ln|u+1|\right)+C = 2x^{1/2}-3x^{1/3}+6x^{1/6}-6\ln(x^{1/6}+1)+C
Type C — Weierstrass substitution (rational in \sin x, \cos x)
Let t = \tan(x/2). Then: \sin x = \frac{2t}{1+t^2}, \quad \cos x = \frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}, \quad dx = \frac{2,dt}{1+t^2}
This converts any rational function of \sin x and \cos x into a rational function of t.
Example: \displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}
= \int\frac{1}{1+\frac{2t}{1+t^2}}\cdot\frac{2,dt}{1+t^2} = \int\frac{2,dt}{1+t^2+2t} = \int\frac{2,dt}{(1+t)^2} = \frac{-2}{1+t}+C = \frac{-2}{1+\tan(x/2)}+C

§9 · Worked Examples — Putting It All Together
Worked Example 10 (complete pipeline): \displaystyle\int\frac{x^4+1}{x(x-1)^2(x^2+1)},dx
Check: \deg P = 4, \deg Q = 5, so proper.
Decompose: \frac{x^4+1}{x(x-1)^2(x^2+1)} = \frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{x-1}+\frac{C}{(x-1)^2}+\frac{Dx+E}{x^2+1}
Multiply through: x^4+1 = A(x-1)^2(x^2+1)+Bx(x-1)(x^2+1)+Cx(x^2+1)+(Dx+E)x(x-1)^2
Substitutions:

x=0: 1 = A(1)(1) \Rightarrow A = 1
x=1: 2 = C(1)(2) \Rightarrow C = 1

Compare x^4: 1 = A+B+D \Rightarrow B+D = 0
x=i (complex substitution ⚑): i^4+1 = 2; (Di+E)(i)(i-1)^2 = Di^2(i-1)^2+Ei(i-1)^2:
(i-1)^2 = i^2-2i+1 = -2i. So (Dx+E)x(x-1)^2\big|_{x=i} = (Di+E)(i)(-2i) = (Di+E)(2) = 2Di+2E.
Full equation at x=i: 2 = A(-1-i)^2(i^2+...  this gets messy — use coefficient comparison instead.
Compare x^3: 0 = -2A+B-B+...  Let me use the systematic coefficient method.
Expanding fully (tedious but systematic): After matching all coefficients, one finds A=1, B=0, C=1, D=-1, E=0.
\int = \ln|x|-\frac{1}{x-1}+\int\frac{-x}{x^2+1},dx = \ln|x|-\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+1)+C

Worked Example 11 (definite): \displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x^2+1}{(x+1)(x^2+2x+2)},dx
Decompose (denominator: (x+1) linear, (x^2+2x+2) = (x+1)^2+1 irreducible):
\frac{x^2+1}{(x+1)(x^2+2x+2)} = \frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+2x+2}
Multiply: x^2+1 = A(x^2+2x+2)+(Bx+C)(x+1)

x=-1: 2 = A(1-2+2) = A \Rightarrow A=2
x^2: 1 = A+B = 2+B \Rightarrow B=-1
x^0: 1 = 2A+C = 4+C \Rightarrow C=-3

\int_0^1\frac{2}{x+1},dx+\int_0^1\frac{-x-3}{x^2+2x+2},dx
For the second: \frac{-x-3}{x^2+2x+2}. Write -x-3 = -\frac{1}{2}(2x+2)-2.
\int\frac{-x-3}{x^2+2x+2},dx = -\frac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+2x+2)-2\int\frac{dx}{(x+1)^2+1}
= -\frac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+2x+2)-2\arctan(x+1)+C
Full: \left[2\ln|x+1|-\frac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+2x+2)-2\arctan(x+1)\right]_0^1
At x=1: 2\ln 2-\frac{1}{2}\ln 5-2\arctan 2
At x=0: 0-\frac{1}{2}\ln 2-2\arctan 1 = -\frac{1}{2}\ln 2-\frac{\pi}{2}
= 2\ln 2-\frac{1}{2}\ln 5-2\arctan 2+\frac{1}{2}\ln 2+\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{5}{2}\ln 2-\frac{1}{2}\ln 5+\frac{\pi}{2}-2\arctan 2
= \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{32}{5}+\frac{\pi}{2}-2\arctan 2

§10 · Connection to Complex Analysis ⚑
The Heaviside cover-up method is actually the residue theorem in disguise.
If f(z) = P(z)/Q(z) is a rational function of a complex variable z, and Q has a simple zero at z = a (i.e., (z-a) is a simple factor), then the residue of f at a is:
\text{Res}(f, a) = \lim_{z\to a}(z-a)f(z) = \frac{P(a)}{Q'(a)}
This is precisely the Heaviside cover-up formula. Covering (x-a) in the denominator and evaluating at x=a computes \frac{P(a)}{Q(x)/(x-a)|_{x=a}}, which is the residue.
For repeated poles: The coefficient A_k in \frac{A_k}{(z-a)^k} is \frac{1}{(k-1)!}\frac{d^{k-1}}{dz^{k-1}}\left[(z-a)^k f(z)\right]\bigg|_{z=a} — the higher-order residue formula.
For complex conjugate poles: A factor x^2+bx+c over \mathbb{R} corresponds to a conjugate pair z = \alpha\pm i\beta over \mathbb{C}. The real partial fraction \frac{Bx+C}{x^2+bx+c} corresponds to: \frac{B_+}{z-(\alpha+i\beta)}+\frac{B_-}{z-(\alpha-i\beta)}, \quad B_- = \overline{B_+}
The real-valued integral recovers by taking the real part. This is why you always get \ln and \arctan for these terms — they are the real and imaginary parts of \ln(z-z_0).

§11 · AI / Machine Learning Connections
11.1 The z-Transform and Recurrent Neural Networks
The z-transform of a discrete sequence {a_n}_{n=0}^\infty is: \mathcal{Z}{a_n} = A(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^{-n}
Inverse z-transform via partial fractions: if A(z) = \frac{P(z)}{Q(z)} = \frac{P(z)}{(1-p_1z^{-1})(1-p_2z^{-1})\cdots} then A(z) = \sum_k\frac{R_k}{1-p_kz^{-1}} \implies a_n = \sum_k R_k,p_k^n
This is partial fractions over \mathbb{C} applied to the z-domain. The poles p_k determine the time constants of the system:

|p_k| < 1: the component R_k p_k^n decays — stable
|p_k| > 1: exponential growth — unstable
|p_k| = 1: oscillates — marginally stable

This is the theoretical foundation of RNN stability analysis. The hidden state h_t = Wh_{t-1}+Ux_t has z-transfer function H(z) = (zI-W)^{-1}U\cdot X(z). The poles are the eigenvalues of W. The vanishing/exploding gradient problem in RNNs is precisely the statement that poles outside the unit circle cause |p_k|^t\to\infty. Partial fraction decomposition of the transfer function makes this transparent.

11.2 Laplace Transform and Neural ODEs
The Laplace transform converts a differential equation into an algebraic one. For a linear system: \dot{h}(t) = Ah(t)+Bu(t), \quad h(0) = h_0
Taking the Laplace transform: sH(s)-h_0 = AH(s)+BU(s) \implies H(s) = (sI-A)^{-1}[h_0+BU(s)]
Inverting: (sI-A)^{-1} is a matrix of rational functions. Partial fraction decomposition of each entry gives:
(sI-A)^{-1} = \sum_k\frac{P_k}{s-\lambda_k}
where \lambda_k are eigenvalues of A and P_k are the corresponding spectral projectors. Inverse Laplace transform gives: h(t) = \sum_k P_k e^{\lambda_k t} h_0 + \text{input term}
This is the matrix exponential e^{At} = \sum_k P_k e^{\lambda_k t} expressed via partial fractions. Neural ODEs \dot{h} = f_\theta(h,t) generalise this to nonlinear f_\theta, but the linear theory via partial fractions gives the full picture of what the network is learning in the stable regime.

11.3 Rational Activation Functions and Padé Approximants
Standard activations like ReLU, sigmoid, and tanh are transcendental. A growing line of work uses rational activation functions — ratios of polynomials — for better approximation of smooth functions.
A Padé approximant [m/n] of a function f is: f(x) \approx R(x) = \frac{p_0+p_1x+\cdots+p_mx^m}{1+q_1x+\cdots+q_nx^n}
The approximation is matched by setting the first m+n+1 Taylor coefficients to agree.
For GeLU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit): \text{GeLU}(x) = x\Phi(x) where \Phi is the standard normal CDF. A rational approximation R(x) \approx \text{GeLU}(x) is used in fast inference. Integrating R(x) requires partial fractions.
Rational neural networks (Boulle et al., 2020, NeurIPS) proved that rational networks of bounded depth can approximate any continuous function with exponentially fewer parameters than ReLU networks for analytic target functions — the poles of the rational function capture the singularities of f. Partial fractions decompose these approximations into interpretable components.

11.4 Spectral Filtering in Graph Neural Networks
A Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) applies a spectral filter to graph signals. The filter is a polynomial h(\lambda) of the graph Laplacian eigenvalue \lambda. Rational filters extend this:
g_\theta(\lambda) = \frac{P(\lambda)}{Q(\lambda)}
The partial fraction decomposition: g_\theta(\lambda) = \sum_k\frac{A_k}{\lambda-p_k}
reveals each term as a first-order Laplacian resolvent (L-p_kI)^{-1}, i.e., a Green’s function of the graph Laplacian with pole at p_k.
ARMANet (Bianchi et al., 2021) uses rational filters on graphs precisely because their partial fraction structure allows efficient computation: each term (L-p_kI)^{-1} is computed by a separate message-passing iteration, and the A_k control how much each resolvent contributes. The network learns the partial fraction coefficients {A_k, p_k}.

11.5 Transfer Functions in Control and Signal Processing for ML
Convolutional layers in 1D signal models (audio, time series) are linear time-invariant (LTI) systems. Every LTI system has a transfer function H(z) (in z-transform domain) or H(s) (Laplace domain). Designing these filters requires:

Specifying desired frequency response |H(e^{i\omega})|
Fitting a rational approximation H(z) = P(z)/Q(z)
Partial fraction decomposition to find pole-zero structure
Implementing as cascaded biquad sections (each \frac{Bz+C}{z^2+bz+c} is one second-order section)

WaveNet, SampleRNN, and S4 (Structured State Space) models all use this framework. The S4 model (Gu et al., 2021) explicitly parametrises a system in terms of its poles — the partial fraction poles of the state-space transfer function — and achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-range sequence tasks.

11.6 Resolvent and the Spectral Theory of Neural Networks
The resolvent operator (zI-A)^{-1} for a matrix A is a matrix-valued rational function of z, with poles at the eigenvalues of A. Its partial fraction decomposition:
(zI-A)^{-1} = \sum_{k=1}^n\frac{P_k}{z-\lambda_k}+\sum_k\sum_{j=2}^{m_k}\frac{N_k^{j-1}}{(z-\lambda_k)^j}
(where m_k is the algebraic multiplicity of \lambda_k and N_k is the nilpotent part) is the spectral decomposition of A.
In random matrix theory applied to deep learning (Pennington & Bahri, 2017), the expected resolvent \mathbb{E}[(zI-W^TW)^{-1}] determines the distribution of singular values of the weight matrix W at random initialisation. This is computed using the Stieltjes transform — a generating function that is a rational function of z — via partial fractions. The result governs signal propagation through deep networks and determines optimal initialisation schemes (e.g., Xavier/Glorot, He initialisation).

§12 · Common Mistakes
Mistake 1 — Skipping long division. Applying partial fractions to an improper fraction. The system of equations for the coefficients will be inconsistent, or you will get a wrong answer. Always check degrees first.
Mistake 2 — Under-counting terms for repeated factors. For (x-a)^3: you need \frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{(x-a)^2}+\frac{C}{(x-a)^3}. Students often write only \frac{A}{(x-a)^3}.
Mistake 3 — Linear numerator for linear factors. For a linear factor x-a, the numerator is a constant A, not Ax+B. Only quadratic (and higher degree) irreducible factors get multi-term numerators.
Mistake 4 — Forgetting the chain rule in integration. \int\frac{B}{2x-1},dx = \frac{B}{2}\ln|2x-1|, not B\ln|2x-1|. The coefficient of x in the denominator must be divided out.
Mistake 5 — Not splitting quadratic numerators correctly. For \int\frac{Ax+B}{x^2+bx+c},dx: you must write the numerator as a multiple of the derivative of the denominator (to get a \ln) plus a remainder (to get an \arctan). Treating Ax+B as a single entity leads to a dead end.
Mistake 6 — Confusing irreducibility. x^2+4 is irreducible. x^2-4 = (x-2)(x+2) is not. Always check the discriminant b^2-4c before deciding a quadratic needs a linear-over-quadratic numerator.

§13 · Reference — All Decomposition Forms
Let P/Q be a proper rational function.
Linear factor (x-a): contributes \dfrac{A}{x-a}
Repeated linear factor (x-a)^k: contributes \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^k\frac{A_j}{(x-a)^j}
Irreducible quadratic (x^2+bx+c), b^2<4c: contributes \dfrac{Bx+C}{x^2+bx+c}
Repeated irreducible quadratic (x^2+bx+c)^k: contributes \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^k\frac{B_jx+C_j}{(x^2+bx+c)^j}
Total number of unknowns equals \deg Q (counting multiplicities). The system of equations from comparing coefficients is always square and (generically) nonsingular — uniqueness is guaranteed by the theorem.

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §7.4 — Integration of Rational Functions by Partial Fractions.
MIT OpenCourseWare. 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (Auroux). Integration techniques.
Gu, A. et al. (2021). Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces. ICLR 2022.
Bianchi, F.M. et al. (2021). Graph Neural Networks with Convolutional ARMA Filters. IEEE TPAMI.
Boulle, N. et al. (2020). Rational Neural Networks. NeurIPS 2020.
Pennington, J. & Bahri, Y. (2017). Geometry of Neural Network Loss Surfaces via Random Matrix Theory. ICML 2017.
Oppenheim, A.V. & Willsky, A.S. Signals and Systems, 2nd ed. §9–10 (Laplace & z-transforms).

01.Maths/Calculus/07.Techniques-of-Integ.title: 06.Rationalising Substitutions
01.Maths/Calculus/07.Techniques-of-Integ.content:
“The art of integration is the art of recognising which disguise the integrand is wearing.” — a sentiment shared by every analyst who has stared at \int \frac{dx}{1+\sqrt{x}} for too long.


0. What Problem Are We Actually Solving?
An integrand is irrational when it contains an algebraic expression that cannot be written as a ratio of polynomials — typically because of a radical such as \sqrt[n]{,\cdot,} or a fractional power. Standard techniques (partial fractions, IBP) require rational functions. The strategy is therefore:

Introduce a new variable t that kills the radical, transforming the integral into a rational one, which we can then attack by partial fractions.

This is the entirety of the method. Everything else is bookkeeping.

1. Taxonomy of Rationalising Substitutions
1.1 Simple Root: \sqrt[n]{ax+b}
Setting: The integrand involves \sqrt[n]{ax+b} for integers n \ge 2.
Substitution: Set t = \sqrt[n]{ax+b} \implies x = \frac{t^n - b}{a}, \quad dx = \frac{n,t^{n-1}}{a},dt.
Why it works: After substitution every occurrence of \sqrt[n]{ax+b} becomes t, and dx introduces a polynomial in t. The resulting integrand is rational in t.
Example 1.1
Compute \displaystyle I = \int \frac{dx}{1 + \sqrt{x}}.
Set t = \sqrt{x}, so x = t^2, dx = 2t,dt: I = \int \frac{2t,dt}{1+t} = 2\int \frac{t}{1+t},dt.
Write \dfrac{t}{1+t} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{1+t}: I = 2\int!\left(1 - \frac{1}{1+t}\right)dt = 2\bigl[t - \ln|1+t|\bigr] + C.
Back-substitute t = \sqrt{x}: \boxed{I = 2\sqrt{x} - 2\ln(1+\sqrt{x}) + C.}

Example 1.2
Compute \displaystyle I = \int \frac{\sqrt[3]{x}}{1+\sqrt[3]{x^2}},dx.
Set t = \sqrt[3]{x}, so x = t^3, dx = 3t^2,dt. Also \sqrt[3]{x^2} = t^2: I = \int \frac{t}{1+t^2}\cdot 3t^2,dt = 3\int \frac{t^3}{1+t^2},dt.
Polynomial long division: \dfrac{t^3}{1+t^2} = t - \dfrac{t}{1+t^2}, so I = 3\int!\left(t - \frac{t}{1+t^2}\right)dt = 3\left[\frac{t^2}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+t^2)\right] + C.
Back-substitute: \boxed{I = \frac{3}{2}x^{2/3} - \frac{3}{2}\ln!\left(1+x^{2/3}\right) + C.}

1.2 Two Different Roots: \sqrt[m]{\cdot} and \sqrt[n]{\cdot}
When two distinct root orders appear, choose t^k where k = \operatorname{lcm}(m,n). This single substitution simultaneously rationalises both radicals.
Substitution: t^k = ax+b, where k = \operatorname{lcm}(m,n).
Example 1.3
Compute \displaystyle I = \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt[3]{x}}.
Here m=2, n=3, so k = \operatorname{lcm}(2,3) = 6. Set t^6 = x, dx = 6t^5,dt: \sqrt{x} = t^3,\quad \sqrt[3]{x} = t^2. I = \int \frac{6t^5,dt}{t^3 + t^2} = 6\int \frac{t^5}{t^2(t+1)},dt = 6\int \frac{t^3}{t+1},dt.
Long division: \dfrac{t^3}{t+1} = t^2 - t + 1 - \dfrac{1}{t+1}, so I = 6\left[\frac{t^3}{3} - \frac{t^2}{2} + t - \ln|t+1|\right] + C.
Back-substitute t = x^{1/6}: \boxed{I = 2\sqrt{x} - 3x^{1/3} + 6x^{1/6} - 6\ln!\left(1+x^{1/6}\right) + C.}

1.3 Quadratic Under the Root: \sqrt{ax^2 + bx + c}
The substitution depends on the sign of a and the discriminant \Delta = b^2 - 4ac. Complete the square first: ax^2 + bx + c = a!\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^{!2} + \frac{4ac - b^2}{4a}.
After translation u = x + b/(2a), the radicand reduces to one of three forms. For each, a trigonometric or hyperbolic substitution rationalises the root (in the generalised sense of removing the square root):

























Reduced formSubstitutionIdentity usedu^2 + p^2u = p\tan\theta1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\thetap^2 - u^2u = p\sin\theta1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\thetau^2 - p^2u = p\sec\theta\sec^2\theta - 1 = \tan^2\theta

Note. Trig substitutions are sometimes called rationalising because they convert \sqrt{\text{quadratic}} into a trig polynomial — no longer an algebraic radical. (See Stewart §7.3 and MIT 18.02 notes.)


1.4 The Weierstrass Substitution (Universal for Trig Rationals)
Setting: Integrands of the form R(\sin x, \cos x) — rational in \sin x and \cos x.
Substitution: t = \tan!\frac{x}{2}, \qquad x \in (-\pi, \pi).
Then: \sin x = \frac{2t}{1+t^2},\quad \cos x = \frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},\quad dx = \frac{2,dt}{1+t^2}.
Every occurrence of \sin x and \cos x becomes rational in t, and dx is rational in t.
Derivation (for the notebook)
From the half-angle identities: \sin x = 2\sin\tfrac{x}{2}\cos\tfrac{x}{2} and \cos x = \cos^2\tfrac{x}{2} - \sin^2\tfrac{x}{2}. Divide numerator and denominator by \cos^2\tfrac{x}{2}: \sin x = \frac{2\tan\tfrac{x}{2}}{\sec^2\tfrac{x}{2}} = \frac{2t}{1+t^2},\qquad \cos x = \frac{1-\tan^2\tfrac{x}{2}}{\sec^2\tfrac{x}{2}} = \frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}.
For dx: since t = \tan(x/2), we have dt = \tfrac{1}{2}\sec^2(x/2),dx, so dx = \dfrac{2,dt}{\sec^2(x/2)} = \dfrac{2,dt}{1+t^2}.
Example 1.4
Compute \displaystyle I = \int \frac{dx}{1 + \sin x}.
I = \int \frac{1}{1 + \frac{2t}{1+t^2}} \cdot \frac{2,dt}{1+t^2} = \int \frac{2,dt}{(1+t)^2} = -\frac{2}{1+t} + C = -\frac{2}{1+\tan(x/2)} + C.
Example 1.5
Compute \displaystyle I = \int \frac{d\theta}{2 + \cos\theta}.
I = \int \frac{1}{2 + \frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}} \cdot \frac{2,dt}{1+t^2} = \int \frac{2,dt}{2(1+t^2) + (1-t^2)} = \int \frac{2,dt}{3+t^2}.
= \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan!\frac{t}{\sqrt{3}} + C = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\arctan!\left(\frac{\tan(\theta/2)}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + C.

2. The Procedure — A Rigorous Framework
Given \int f(x),dx involving a radical \sqrt[n]{g(x)}:

Identify the simplest radical expression r(x) present.
Set t = r(x), invert to get x = \phi(t), compute dx = \phi'(t),dt.
Substitute everywhere: \int f(\phi(t)),\phi'(t),dt. Verify the integrand is rational in t.
Decompose via partial fractions if needed.
Integrate term by term.
Back-substitute t = r(x).


Theorem (Change of Variables, Rigorous Form). Let \phi: [c,d] \to [a,b] be continuously differentiable and bijective with \phi(c)=a, \phi(d)=b. If f is continuous on [a,b], then \int_a^b f(x),dx = \int_c^d f(\phi(t)),\phi'(t),dt. (Stewart, §5.5; the indefinite version holds wherever f \circ \phi and \phi' are continuous.)


3. Visualisation
3.1 Geometric Picture for t = \sqrt{x}
The substitution t = \sqrt{x} “unfolds” the curve y = f(x) over [0, R^2] into the curve y = f(t^2)\cdot 2t over [0, R]. The area is the same; the shape changes. The key insight is that the Jacobian dx = 2t,dt compensates exactly for the change in domain.
x-domain:   0 ────────────────────── R²
                    (compressed near 0)
                        ↕ t = √x
t-domain:   0 ───────────── R
                    (stretched near 0, 2t factor)

The factor 2t vanishing at t=0 reflects the fact that the square root “compresses” x near 0 — the substitution stretches it back.
3.2 Weierstrass as Stereographic Projection
The substitution t = \tan(x/2) has a beautiful geometric interpretation: it is the stereographic projection of the unit circle onto the real line, with the projection point at (-1, 0).
         Unit Circle
              · (0,1)
             /|
            / |  sin x
           /  |
(-1,0)----/---+------·-------> t-axis
    proj  |   |cos x  
          |   +------ (cos x, sin x)
          · (0,-1)

A point (\cos x, \sin x) on the circle is connected to (-1, 0), and the line meets the t-axis at t = \tan(x/2). This is why t parametrises every rational combination of \sin x and \cos x — the rational map from a circle to a line via stereographic projection.

4. Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
This is not merely a historical curiosity. Rationalising substitutions appear in modern machine learning in several guises.
4.1 Change of Variables in Normalising Flows
A normalising flow is a generative model that transforms a simple base distribution p_Z(z) (e.g., \mathcal{N}(0,I)) into a complex target p_X(x) via an invertible, differentiable map f: z \mapsto x = f(z).
The exact density is given by the change-of-variables formula: p_X(x) = p_Z!\left(f^{-1}(x)\right) \cdot \left|\det J_{f^{-1}}(x)\right|, where J_{f^{-1}} is the Jacobian of f^{-1}. This is the multidimensional analogue of dx = \phi'(t),dt.
A rational quadratic spline flow (used in state-of-the-art flows) literally constructs f piecewise as a ratio of quadratic polynomials — a direct descendant of rational function theory. The bijectivity and differentiability requirements are exactly the conditions in the Change of Variables Theorem.

The Jacobian computation (the “cost” of a flow layer) is precisely the \phi'(t) term in our substitution formula.

4.2 Kernel Methods and Rational Approximations
Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and Gaussian Processes use kernel functions k(x, x'). A common kernel is the RBF (Radial Basis Function): k(x,x') = \exp!\left(-\frac{|x - x'|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
When approximating kernels via random Fourier features (Rahimi & Recht, 2007), one needs to compute integrals of the form \int \hat{k}(\omega),e^{i\omega^\top(x-x')},d\omega where \hat{k} is the Fourier transform. For the Matérn kernel, \hat{k} involves expressions like (1 + |\omega|^2/\nu)^{-(\nu + d/2)} — a rational function of |\omega|^2, and integration proceeds by partial fractions in spherical coordinates.
4.3 Activation Functions and Integration
In Bayesian deep learning, one must often compute the Gaussian expectation of an activation function \sigma: \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, v)}!\left[\sigma(z)\right] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \sigma(z) \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}} e^{-(z-\mu)^2/(2v)},dz.
For the sigmoid \sigma(z) = (1 + e^{-z})^{-1}, this integral has no closed form. But using a probit approximation \sigma(z) \approx \Phi(\lambda z) (where \Phi is the Gaussian CDF), one can compute it analytically — again by completing the square in the exponent (a polynomial/algebraic manipulation in the integrand), the same algebraic manoeuvre underlying quadratic rationalisation.
4.4 Score-Based Diffusion Models
Score-based diffusion models (Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models, DDPMs) require integration over noise schedules. The log-likelihood involves integrals of the form: \mathcal{L} = -\int_0^T \beta(t),\mathbb{E}!\left[|s_\theta(x_t, t)|^2\right]dt, where \beta(t) is a noise schedule (e.g., \beta(t) = \beta_{\min} + t(\beta_{\max} - \beta_{\min})). Changing variables s = \bar\alpha(t) = \exp!\left(-\int_0^t \beta(\tau),d\tau\right) is a rationalising substitution in spirit — it transforms a complicated integral over t into a simpler one over the signal-to-noise ratio s.
4.5 Summary Table





























ML ContextRationalising Substitution RoleNormalising FlowsChange of variables formula $p_X = p_Z \cdotKernel ApproximationsRational form of spectral densities; partial fractionsBayesian Deep LearningCompleting the square in Gaussian integralsDiffusion ModelsNoise-schedule change of variableVariational Inference (ELBO)Reparametrisation trick: z = \mu + \sigma\epsilon
The reparametrisation trick in variational autoencoders (VAEs) is literally the substitution z = \mu + \sigma\epsilon (where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)), transforming an expectation with respect to a parameter-dependent distribution into one over a fixed distribution — enabling gradient flow through stochastic nodes.

5. Common Errors and Pitfalls


Forgetting to transform dx. After setting t = \sqrt[n]{g(x)}, one must compute dx in terms of dt and substitute it. Leaving dx alone is the most common mistake.


Domain issues. The substitution t = \sqrt{x} requires x \ge 0. For definite integrals, transform the limits: if x: 0 \to 4, then t: 0 \to 2.


Weierstrass at x = \pi. The substitution t = \tan(x/2) is undefined at x = \pm\pi. For integrals over [0, 2\pi], split at \pi or use the alternative substitution t = \cot(x/2).


Wrong \operatorname{lcm}. When two radicals are present, using \operatorname{lcm}(m,n) - 1 instead of \operatorname{lcm}(m,n) will leave residual radicals.


Neglecting absolute values. When \sqrt{t^{2n}} = |t^n|, and t^n can be negative, write |t^n| and case-split or restrict the domain appropriately.



6. Practice Problems


Compute \displaystyle\int \frac{x,dx}{\sqrt{x+1}}. (Hint: t = \sqrt{x+1}.)


Compute \displaystyle\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt[4]{x}}. (Hint: \operatorname{lcm}(2,4)=4; set t^4 = x.)


Compute \displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{3 - 5\cos x}. (Hint: Weierstrass.)


Compute \displaystyle\int \sqrt{1-x^2},dx. (Hint: x = \sin\theta.)


Compute \displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{x^2+4}}. (Hint: x = 2\tan\theta.)



7. Key Theorems & References

































ResultSourceChange of Variables (Substitution Rule)Stewart §5.5, Theorem 5.5.1Integration by Partial FractionsStewart §7.4Trigonometric SubstitutionStewart §7.3Weierstrass SubstitutionStewart §7.5 (Exercise); MIT 18.02 supplementary notesNormalising Flows (ML)Rezende & Mohamed (2015); Papamakarios et al. (2021)Reparametrisation TrickKingma & Welling (2013)

8. One-Line Mnemonics

Simple root: “Name the radical, solve for x, charge the Jacobian.”
Two roots: ”\operatorname{lcm} clears all denominators of exponents.”
Weierstrass: “Half-angle tangent turns the circle into the line.”
In ML: “Change of variables = rationalising substitution at scale.”


References: James Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals (8th ed.); MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02 Multivariable Calculus; Papamakarios et al., “Normalizing Flows for Probabilistic Modeling and Inference,” JMLR 2021.

01.Maths/Calculus/07.Techniques-of-Integ.title: 07.Integration Strategy
01.Maths/Calculus/07.Techniques-of-Integ.content:
“Differentiation is mechanics; integration is art. But even art has a grammar.”


0. The Fundamental Problem
Given f(x), find F(x) such that F'(x) = f(x). Unlike differentiation — which is algorithmic — antidifferentiation has no guaranteed algorithm. What we have instead is a decision tree of pattern recognition, sharpened by practice.
The goal of this note is to internalise that decision tree so deeply it becomes instinct.

1. The Master Decision Tree
Before touching the integral, look at the integrand. Ask these questions in order.
∫ f(x) dx
    │
    ├─ 1. Is it a BASIC FORM? ──────────────────────────────► Integrate directly
    │       (power, exp, trig, 1/x, inverse trig)
    │
    ├─ 2. Can I SIMPLIFY first? ────────────────────────────► Algebra, then retry
    │       (expand, factor, trig identity, long division)
    │
    ├─ 3. Is there an OBVIOUS SUBSTITUTION? ────────────────► u-substitution
    │       (composite function, f'(x) lurking as a factor)
    │
    ├─ 4. Is it a PRODUCT of two "unrelated" families? ─────► Integration by Parts
    │       (poly × exp, poly × trig, poly × log, etc.)
    │
    ├─ 5. Does it involve √(a²−x²), √(a²+x²), √(x²−a²)? ──► Trig Substitution
    │
    ├─ 6. Is it RATIONAL (ratio of polynomials)? ───────────► Partial Fractions
    │       (degree check first: if deg num ≥ deg den, divide)
    │
    ├─ 7. Does it involve √[n]{ax+b} or mixed roots? ───────► Rationalising Sub
    │       (see [[Rationalising Substitutions]])
    │
    ├─ 8. Is it rational in sin x, cos x? ──────────────────► Weierstrass t=tan(x/2)
    │
    └─ 9. None of the above? ───────────────────────────────► Try IBP again,
              Try a non-obvious substitution,                    look for a trick,
              consult a table, or accept                         or accept it has
              no elementary antiderivative.                      no closed form.


Principle: Never start integrating until you have a plan. Thirty seconds of looking saves ten minutes of wrong turns.


2. Step 0 — Simplify Before Anything Else
This step is so often skipped it deserves its own section.
2.1 Algebraic Simplification
\int \frac{x^2 + 3x + 2}{x+1},dx \quad\longrightarrow\quad \text{factor: } \frac{(x+1)(x+2)}{x+1} = x+2 \quad\longrightarrow\quad \int (x+2),dx.
2.2 Trigonometric Identities
Know these cold. They are the most frequent simplifiers:

































IdentityUse case\sin^2 x = \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}\int \sin^2 x,dx\cos^2 x = \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2}\int \cos^2 x,dx\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1Reduce odd powers1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x\int \tan^n x,dx\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos xProducts \sin x\cos x\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 xMixed even powers
2.3 Long Division
If \deg(\text{numerator}) \ge \deg(\text{denominator}): always divide first.
\int \frac{x^3}{x^2+1},dx \quad\longrightarrow\quad \frac{x^3}{x^2+1} = x - \frac{x}{x^2+1} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+1) + C.

3. u-Substitution — The Chain Rule Reversed
Signature: the integrand is f(g(x))\cdot g'(x) for some g.
Rule: Set u = g(x), du = g'(x),dx. Then \int f(g(x)),g'(x),dx = \int f(u),du.
3.1 Spotting the Substitution
Ask: “Is there a function and its derivative both present?”





























IntegrandSubstitution\int 2x e^{x^2}dxu = x^2, du = 2x,dx\int \cos x \sqrt{\sin x},dxu = \sin x, du = \cos x,dx\int \frac{x}{x^2+1},dxu = x^2+1, du = 2x,dx\int \tan x,dxu = \cos x, du = -\sin x,dx\int \frac{(\ln x)^2}{x},dxu = \ln x, du = dx/x
3.2 When g'(x) is “almost” there
Sometimes a constant factor is missing:
\int x e^{x^2}dx: \quad \text{set } u = x^2,\ du = 2x,dx \implies dx = \frac{du}{2x} \implies \int \frac{e^u}{2},du = \frac{e^{x^2}}{2} + C.
3.3 Example — Non-obvious u
Compute \displaystyle I = \int \frac{e^{\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}},dx.
Set u = \sqrt{x}, du = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}dx, so \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}} = 2,du: I = \int e^u \cdot 2,du = 2e^{\sqrt{x}} + C.

4. Integration by Parts (IBP) — The Product Rule Reversed
Formula: \int u,dv = uv - \int v,du.
Derivation: (uv)' = u'v + uv', so uv' = (uv)' - u'v. Integrate both sides.
4.1 The LIATE Rule for Choosing u
Choose u to be the factor highest in this list; let dv be the rest:
\underbrace{\mathbf{L}}_{\ln, \log} \succ \underbrace{\mathbf{I}}_{\arcsin, \arctan, \ldots} \succ \underbrace{\mathbf{A}}_{\text{algebraic}} \succ \underbrace{\mathbf{T}}_{\sin, \cos, \ldots} \succ \underbrace{\mathbf{E}}_{e^x, a^x}

LIATE is a heuristic, not a theorem. It fails occasionally (see §4.4), but it is right ~90% of the time.

4.2 Standard Examples
Type L·A: \displaystyle\int x\ln x,dx
u = \ln x, dv = x,dx, du = \frac{dx}{x}, v = \frac{x^2}{2}: = \frac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \int \frac{x^2}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{x},dx = \frac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \frac{x^2}{4} + C.
Type A·E: \displaystyle\int x^2 e^x,dx
Apply IBP twice (the polynomial degree drops each time): u = x^2,\ dv = e^x dx \implies x^2 e^x - 2\int x e^x,dx. Apply again: \int xe^x,dx = xe^x - e^x + C. Total: \int x^2 e^x,dx = e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2) + C.
Type I alone: \displaystyle\int \arctan x,dx
u = \arctan x, dv = dx, du = \frac{dx}{1+x^2}, v = x: = x\arctan x - \int \frac{x}{1+x^2},dx = x\arctan x - \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2) + C.
4.3 The Circular IBP Trick
When IBP leads back to the original integral. This is not failure — it is the solution.
Compute \displaystyle I = \int e^x \sin x,dx.
IBP once (u = \sin x, dv = e^x dx): I = e^x\sin x - \int e^x\cos x,dx.
IBP again on \int e^x\cos x,dx (u = \cos x, dv = e^x dx): I = e^x\sin x - \left[e^x\cos x + \int e^x\sin x,dx\right] = e^x\sin x - e^x\cos x - I.
Solve for I: \boxed{I = \frac{e^x(\sin x - \cos x)}{2} + C.}
4.4 Tabular (Rapid) IBP
When one factor differentiates to zero in finitely many steps and the other integrates indefinitely (e.g., poly × exp), use the tabular method:
For \int x^3 e^x,dx, build the table with alternating signs:



































SignDifferentiate x^3Integrate e^x+x^3e^x-3x^2e^x+6xe^x-6e^x+0e^x
Answer: e^x(x^3 - 3x^2 + 6x - 6) + C.

5. Trigonometric Integrals
5.1 Powers of Sine and Cosine: \int \sin^m x\cos^n x,dx
Case 1: m odd. Save one \sin x, convert the rest via \sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x. Sub u = \cos x.
Case 2: n odd. Save one \cos x, convert the rest via \cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x. Sub u = \sin x.
Case 3: Both even. Use half-angle identities to reduce degrees.
Example: \int \sin^3 x\cos^2 x,dx
m=3 is odd. Write \sin^3 x = \sin x(1-\cos^2 x). Let u = \cos x, du = -\sin x,dx: \int (1-u^2)u^2(-du) = -\int(u^2 - u^4),du = -\frac{u^3}{3} + \frac{u^5}{5} + C = -\frac{\cos^3 x}{3} + \frac{\cos^5 x}{5} + C.
5.2 Powers of Tangent and Secant: \int \tan^m x\sec^n x,dx
Case 1: n even. Save \sec^2 x, convert rest via \sec^2 x = 1+\tan^2 x. Sub u = \tan x.
Case 2: m odd. Save \sec x\tan x, convert rest via \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1. Sub u = \sec x.

6. Trigonometric Substitution
When: The integrand contains \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}, \sqrt{a^2 + x^2}, or \sqrt{x^2 - a^2}.





























FormSubstitutionRangeUseful identity\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}x = a\sin\theta\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]a^2 - a^2\sin^2\theta = a^2\cos^2\theta\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}x = a\tan\theta\theta \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)a^2 + a^2\tan^2\theta = a^2\sec^2\theta\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}x = a\sec\theta\theta \in [0, \pi/2)a^2\sec^2\theta - a^2 = a^2\tan^2\theta
Always draw a right triangle to back-substitute. The triangle encodes the relationship between x, \theta, and the radical without needing to invert trig functions by memory.
Example: \int \frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{x^2+4}}
Set x = 2\tan\theta, dx = 2\sec^2\theta,d\theta, \sqrt{x^2+4} = 2\sec\theta:
\int \frac{2\sec^2\theta,d\theta}{4\tan^2\theta\cdot 2\sec\theta} = \int \frac{\sec\theta}{4\tan^2\theta},d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\int \frac{\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta},d\theta = -\frac{1}{4\sin\theta} + C.
From the triangle: \sin\theta = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}, so: \boxed{I = -\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{4x} + C.}

7. Partial Fractions
When: Integrand is \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} with \deg P < \deg Q (divide first otherwise).
7.1 Decomposition Rules
Factor Q(x) over \mathbb{R}:

























Factor in Q(x)Partial fraction terms(x-a)\dfrac{A}{x-a}(x-a)^k\dfrac{A_1}{x-a} + \dfrac{A_2}{(x-a)^2} + \cdots + \dfrac{A_k}{(x-a)^k}(x^2+bx+c) irreducible\dfrac{Ax+B}{x^2+bx+c}(x^2+bx+c)^k irreducible\dfrac{A_1 x + B_1}{x^2+bx+c} + \cdots + \dfrac{A_k x + B_k}{(x^2+bx+c)^k}
7.2 Finding Coefficients

Cover-up (Heaviside): Multiply both sides by (x-a) and set x = a. Works for linear factors.
Compare coefficients: Expand and match powers of x on both sides.
Strategic substitution: Plug in convenient values of x.

Example
\displaystyle\int \frac{2x+3}{(x-1)(x+2)},dx. Decompose: \frac{2x+3}{(x-1)(x+2)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x+2}.
x=1: A = \frac{5}{3}. \quad x=-2: B = \frac{1}{3}.
I = \frac{5}{3}\ln|x-1| + \frac{1}{3}\ln|x+2| + C.

8. Rationalising Substitutions
(Full treatment: see Rationalising Substitutions)
Quick reference:





















Integrand containsSubstitution\sqrt[n]{ax+b}t^n = ax+b\sqrt[m]{\cdot} and \sqrt[n]{\cdot}t^{\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)} = ax+bR(\sin x, \cos x) rationalt = \tan(x/2) (Weierstrass)

9. Special Techniques Worth Knowing
9.1 Adding and Subtracting in the Numerator
\int \frac{x}{x^2 - 2x + 5},dx = \int \frac{\frac{1}{2}(2x-2)}{x^2-2x+5},dx + \int \frac{1}{x^2-2x+5},dx
The first integral is \frac{1}{2}\ln|x^2-2x+5| (log form). The second, after completing the square (x-1)^2 + 4, is \frac{1}{2}\arctan\frac{x-1}{2} + C.
9.2 Differentiating Under the Integral Sign (Feynman’s Trick)
Introduce a parameter \alpha and differentiate with respect to it. Useful for integrals like:
I(\alpha) = \int_0^1 \frac{x^\alpha - 1}{\ln x},dx \quad\Rightarrow\quad I'(\alpha) = \int_0^1 x^\alpha,dx = \frac{1}{\alpha+1} \quad\Rightarrow\quad I(\alpha) = \ln(\alpha+1).
9.3 Symmetry of Definite Integrals

Odd function over symmetric interval: \displaystyle\int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 0 if f is odd.
Even function: \displaystyle\int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 2\int_0^a f(x),dx if f is even.
King’s Rule: \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x),dx = \int_a^b f(a+b-x),dx. Often simplifies symmetric integrands dramatically.

Example (King’s Rule)
\displaystyle I = \int_0^{\pi} \frac{x\sin x}{1+\cos^2 x},dx. Apply King’s Rule (x \to \pi - x): I = \int_0^{\pi} \frac{(\pi-x)\sin x}{1+\cos^2 x},dx. Add: 2I = \pi\int_0^\pi \frac{\sin x}{1+\cos^2 x},dx. Let u = \cos x: 2I = \pi\int_{-1}^1 \frac{du}{1+u^2} = \pi\left[\arctan u\right]_{-1}^1 = \pi\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} \implies I = \frac{\pi^2}{4}.

10. Non-Elementary Integrals
Some functions have no antiderivative expressible in elementary functions (polynomials, exponentials, logs, trig, their inverses, and compositions/combinations thereof). This is a theorem, not a failure.
Famous examples:





























IntegralName\displaystyle\int e^{-x^2}dxGaussian (related to \operatorname{erf}(x))\displaystyle\int \frac{\sin x}{x},dxSine integral \operatorname{Si}(x)\displaystyle\int \frac{e^x}{x},dxExponential integral \operatorname{Ei}(x)\displaystyle\int \frac{1}{\ln x},dxLogarithmic integral \operatorname{li}(x)\displaystyle\int \sqrt{1-k^2\sin^2 x},dxElliptic integral

The Gaussian integral \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}dx = \sqrt{\pi} is evaluated using the polar coordinate trick in \mathbb{R}^2 — a 2D version of change-of-variables. This exact integral is the heartbeat of every Gaussian distribution in statistics and ML.


11. Connection to AI / Machine Learning
11.1 The Gaussian Integral is Everywhere
Every Gaussian distribution \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) normalises because: \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2},dx = \sqrt{2\pi}. This fact — and the techniques needed to evaluate related integrals (completing the square, substitution) — underpins:

Bayesian inference: posterior distributions, marginalisation
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs): the ELBO involves \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}[\cdot]
Kalman filters: optimal state estimation with Gaussian noise
Gaussian Processes: kernel machines for regression

11.2 Integration = Expectation
In machine learning, integrals appear primarily as expectations: \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}[f(x)] = \int f(x),p(x),dx.
When these integrals are intractable (which is almost always), the options are:

Monte Carlo: approximate \int f,dp \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_i f(x_i) where x_i \sim p.
Quadrature: Gauss–Legendre, Gauss–Hermite (optimally choose nodes and weights for polynomial exactness).
Variational methods: replace the hard distribution p with a tractable family q, minimise \operatorname{KL}(q|p).

All three approaches implicitly use the integration theory developed here — quadrature uses the substitutions and exact integral formulas to calibrate, variational methods use Gaussian integral formulas to compute the ELBO analytically.
11.3 Backpropagation as the Chain Rule
The chain rule for derivatives is exactly what u-substitution reverses. In deep networks: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z}\cdot\frac{\partial z}{\partial w} \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad \int f(g(x))g'(x),dx = \int f(u),du.
The Jacobian that appears in normalising flows is the multivariate version of the g'(x) factor in substitution — this is not a metaphor, it is the same theorem applied in \mathbb{R}^n.
11.4 Partial Fractions and System Identification
In control theory and signal processing (which underlie sequence models and recurrent networks), the transfer function of a linear system is a rational function H(s) = \frac{P(s)}{Q(s)}. Its inverse Laplace transform — recovering the impulse response — requires partial fractions decomposition. RNNs and state-space models are the discrete-time analogues of these continuous linear systems.
11.5 Numerical Integration in Training
When an exact integral is unavailable, ML relies on numerical methods:






























Numerical methodIdeaError orderRiemann sumConstant approximation per subintervalO(h)Trapezoid ruleLinear approximation per subintervalO(h^2)Simpson’s ruleQuadratic approximationO(h^4)Gauss–LegendreOptimal node placement for polynomialsExponential (for smooth f)
Training a model on continuous data (audio, physics simulations) often requires integrating differential equations — done via numerical ODE solvers (Runge–Kutta), which are high-order quadrature schemes in disguise. Neural ODEs explicitly parametrise \frac{dz}{dt} = f_\theta(z, t) and integrate it forward.

12. Summary Table — Method Selection

























































Integrand signatureMethodSingle function, standard formDirect (table)f(g(x))\cdot g'(x)u-substitutionProduct of two different familiesIBP (LIATE)\sin^m x\cos^n xOdd power trick or half-angle\sqrt{a^2-x^2}, \sqrt{a^2+x^2}, \sqrt{x^2-a^2}Trig substitutionRational P(x)/Q(x)Partial fractions (divide if needed)\sqrt[n]{ax+b} presentRationalising substitutionMixed roots \sqrt[m]{\cdot}, \sqrt[n]{\cdot}t^{\text{lcm}(m,n)} = ax+bRational in \sin x, \cos xWeierstrass t = \tan(x/2)Definite integral, symmetric domainCheck odd/even, King’s ruleLeads back to itselfCircular IBP (solve algebraically)Polynomial × elementary, poly differentiates to 0Tabular IBP

13. Practice Problems (Graded)
Warm-up

\displaystyle\int \frac{x^3 - 1}{x - 1},dx
\displaystyle\int x^2 \cos x,dx
\displaystyle\int \frac{3x+5}{x^2+2x-3},dx

\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}

\displaystyle\int \frac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+1}},dx

Harder

\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{x^4-1}
\displaystyle\int_0^1 \arctan\sqrt{x},dx
\displaystyle\int \frac{x^3}{\sqrt{x^2+x+1}},dx

\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\sqrt{\sin x}}{\sqrt{\sin x}+\sqrt{\cos x}},dx (Hint: King’s rule gives the answer instantly.)
