Common Mistakes and Traps


Using dx instead of ds. S = \int 2\pi f(x),dx is wrong. The correct integrand uses ds = \sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx. Missing the arc length factor gives the formula for the area under 2\pi f(x), not the surface area.


Wrong axis of rotation. Rotating about the x-axis: radius = y. Rotating about the y-axis: radius = x. Swapping these is a common error.


Negative f (curve below the axis). The radius of rotation must be non-negative. If f(x) < 0, use |f(x)| as the radius.


Confusing surface area with volume. Surface area uses ds; volume (disk/washer method) uses dx. They are different integrals of the same function.


Forgetting the 2\pi factor. The circumference of a circle of radius r is 2\pi r, not \pi r. The factor of 2\pi in S = \int 2\pi r,ds comes from the full 360° rotation.


Applying to curves with f < 0 on part of [a,b]. The formula assumes f \geq 0 throughout. If the curve dips below the axis, split the integral at the zeros and use |f|.



Quick Reference Card
S = \int_a^b 2\pi, y; ds = \int_a^b 2\pi, f(x)\sqrt{1+[f'(x)]^2},dx \qquad \text{(rotation about }x\text{-axis)}
S = \int_c^d 2\pi, x; ds = \int_c^d 2\pi, g(y)\sqrt{1+[g'(y)]^2},dy \qquad \text{(rotation about }y\text{-axis)}
S = \int_\alpha^\beta 2\pi, y(t)\sqrt{\dot x^2 + \dot y^2},dt \qquad \text{(parametric, rotation about }x\text{-axis)}
ds = \sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx = \sqrt{\dot x^2+\dot y^2},dt \qquad \text{(arc length element)}
S = 2\pi\bar{d}\cdot L \qquad \text{(Pappus's theorem: centroid distance × arc length)}
Key results to remember: S_{\text{sphere}} = 4\pi r^2, \quad S_{\text{cone}} = \pi R\ell, \quad S_{\text{torus}} = 4\pi^2 Rr.

References

Prelude — Why Integration Is the Language of Accumulation
The central philosophical move of integral calculus is this:

A complicated whole = infinitely many simple pieces, summed.

Whenever a physical quantity varies continuously — force, pressure, density, voltage — you cannot use a single formula. You must accumulate. The integral is the rigorous formalization of that accumulation.
The Master Template (Stewart §5.2, MIT 18.02 L16):
\boxed{Q = \int_a^b f(x), dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i^*), \Delta x}
Every application below is a specialization of this template. The art lies in correctly identifying f(x) and the appropriate measure dx (or dA, dV, ds…).

1. Work Done by a Variable Force
Theoretical Foundation
Newton’s definition of work for a constant force F over displacement d is W = Fd. This immediately fails when F varies.
Theorem (Stewart §6.4): If a force F(x) acts on an object along the x-axis from x = a to x = b, then the work done is
\boxed{W = \int_a^b F(x), dx}
Proof sketch: Partition [a,b] into n subintervals of width \Delta x. On each subinterval [x_{i-1}, x_i], approximate F as constant \approx F(x_i^_). Work done on piece i: \Delta W_i \approx F(x_i^_)\Delta x. Total: W \approx \sum_{i=1}^n F(x_i^*)\Delta x. Taking n \to \infty recovers the integral by definition of the Riemann integral. \blacksquare

Example 1.1 — Spring (Hooke’s Law)
Setup: A spring has natural length 1 m. It requires 40 N to stretch it 0.1 m beyond natural length. How much work is done stretching it from natural length to 0.4 m beyond?
Hooke’s Law: F(x) = kx, where x is displacement from natural length.
Step 1 — Find k: F(0.1) = 40 \implies k(0.1) = 40 \implies k = 400 \text{ N/m}
Step 2 — Integrate: W = \int_0^{0.4} 400x, dx = 400 \cdot \frac{x^2}{2}\Bigg|_0^{0.4} = 200(0.16) = \boxed{32 \text{ J}}
Sanity check: The force at x = 0.4 is F(0.4) = 160 N. The average force is \frac{0 + 160}{2} = 80 N. Work = 80 \times 0.4 = 32 J. ✓ (Linear force ⟹ average works here.)

Example 1.2 — Lifting a Leaky Bucket (Non-Constant Mass)
Setup: A 10 kg bucket is pulled up a 20 m shaft. Water leaks at a constant rate; the bucket starts with 30 kg of water and is empty at the top. What is the total work done against gravity?
Model: At height x meters, fraction of rope remaining = x/20… rather, fraction of rope pulled = x/20. Water mass remaining: m_w(x) = 30\left(1 - \frac{x}{20}\right) = 30 - \frac{3x}{2}.
Total mass at height x: m(x) = 10 + 30 - \frac{3x}{2} = 40 - \frac{3x}{2} \quad \text{kg}
Force (weight): F(x) = m(x) \cdot g = \left(40 - \frac{3x}{2}\right)(9.8) \text{ N}
Work: W = \int_0^{20} \left(40 - \frac{3x}{2}\right)(9.8), dx = 9.8 \int_0^{20} \left(40 - \frac{3x}{2}\right) dx = 9.8 \left[40x - \frac{3x^2}{4}\right]_0^{20} = 9.8 \left[800 - \frac{3(400)}{4}\right] = 9.8[800 - 300] = 9.8 \times 500 = \boxed{4900 \text{ J}}

Annotation: Notice how the integral automatically handles the variable mass — no clever tricks, just correct modeling and accumulation.


2. Center of Mass & Moments
Theoretical Foundation (Stewart §8.3, MIT 18.02 L20)
Definition: For a lamina (thin plate) with density \rho(x,y) over region R, the center of mass (\bar{x}, \bar{y}) is
\bar{x} = \frac{M_y}{m} = \frac{\iint_R x, \rho(x,y), dA}{\iint_R \rho(x,y), dA}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{M_x}{m} = \frac{\iint_R y, \rho(x,y), dA}{\iint_R \rho(x,y), dA}
For a 1D rod of length L with linear density \rho(x):
m = \int_0^L \rho(x), dx, \qquad \bar{x} = \frac{\int_0^L x, \rho(x), dx}{\int_0^L \rho(x), dx}
Why this formula? The moment M_y = \int x, dm measures the “turning tendency” about the y-axis, weighted by distance. The center of mass is where a single pivot would balance the distribution.

Example 2.1 — Non-Uniform Rod
Setup: A rod of length 4 m has linear density \rho(x) = 2 + \sin(\pi x / 4) kg/m. Find its center of mass.
Total mass: m = \int_0^4 \left(2 + \sin\frac{\pi x}{4}\right) dx = \left[2x - \frac{4}{\pi}\cos\frac{\pi x}{4}\right]_0^4 = \left[8 - \frac{4}{\pi}\cos\pi\right] - \left[0 - \frac{4}{\pi}\cos 0\right] = 8 + \frac{4}{\pi} + \frac{4}{\pi} = 8 + \frac{8}{\pi} \approx 10.546 \text{ kg}
First moment: M_y = \int_0^4 x\left(2 + \sin\frac{\pi x}{4}\right) dx
Split: \int_0^4 2x, dx + \int_0^4 x\sin\frac{\pi x}{4}, dx
\int_0^4 2x, dx = [x^2]_0^4 = 16
For \int_0^4 x\sin\frac{\pi x}{4}, dx, integrate by parts: u = x, dv = \sin\frac{\pi x}{4} dx: = \left[-\frac{4x}{\pi}\cos\frac{\pi x}{4}\right]_0^4 + \int_0^4 \frac{4}{\pi}\cos\frac{\pi x}{4}, dx = \left[-\frac{16}{\pi}(-1) - 0\right] + \frac{4}{\pi}\left[\frac{4}{\pi}\sin\frac{\pi x}{4}\right]_0^4 = \frac{16}{\pi} + \frac{16}{\pi^2}[\sin\pi - \sin 0] = \frac{16}{\pi}
So M_y = 16 + \frac{16}{\pi}.
Center of mass: \bar{x} = \frac{16 + \frac{16}{\pi}}{8 + \frac{8}{\pi}} = \frac{16\left(1 + \frac{1}{\pi}\right)}{8\left(1 + \frac{1}{\pi}\right)} = \boxed{2 \text{ m}}

Beautiful result: \bar{x} = 2 m, the geometric midpoint! The sine density is symmetric about x = 2, so the center of mass lands at the center. The integral “saw” this symmetry automatically.


Example 2.2 — 2D Lamina with Variable Density
Setup: A triangular lamina with vertices (0,0), (2,0), (0,3) has density \rho(x,y) = xy. Find (\bar{x}, \bar{y}).
Region: 0 \le x \le 2, 0 \le y \le 3 - \frac{3x}{2} (below the line \frac{x}{2} + \frac{y}{3} = 1).
Mass: m = \int_0^2 \int_0^{3-3x/2} xy, dy, dx = \int_0^2 x \cdot \frac{y^2}{2}\Bigg|_0^{3-3x/2} dx = \int_0^2 \frac{x}{2}\left(3 - \frac{3x}{2}\right)^2 dx = \int_0^2 \frac{x}{2} \cdot 9\left(1 - \frac{x}{2}\right)^2 dx = \frac{9}{2}\int_0^2 x\left(1 - x + \frac{x^2}{4}\right) dx = \frac{9}{2}\int_0^2 \left(x - x^2 + \frac{x^3}{4}\right) dx = \frac{9}{2}\left[2 - \frac{8}{3} + 1\right] = \frac{9}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} = \frac{3}{2}
M_y (for \bar{x}): M_y = \int_0^2 \int_0^{3-3x/2} x^2 y, dy, dx = \frac{9}{2}\int_0^2 x^2\left(1-\frac{x}{2}\right)^2 dx = \frac{9}{2} \cdot \frac{4}{15} = \frac{6}{5}
\bar{x} = \frac{M_y}{m} = \frac{6/5}{3/2} = \frac{4}{5} = 0.8
(Finding \bar{y} analogously gives \bar{y} = \frac{6}{5}.)
\boxed{(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = (0.8,\ 1.2)}

3. Fluid Pressure & Hydrostatic Force
Theoretical Foundation (Stewart §8.3)
Pascal’s Principle: Pressure at depth d in a fluid of density \rho is P = \rho g d.
The problem: find the total force on a submerged vertical plate. Since pressure varies with depth, we integrate.
Setup: Plate submerged with its top at depth a and bottom at depth b. At depth x, the plate has horizontal width w(x).
\boxed{F = \int_a^b \rho g x \cdot w(x), dx}
Derivation: Strip at depth x of height dx has area dA = w(x), dx. Pressure on strip: P(x) = \rho g x. Force on strip: dF = P(x), dA = \rho g x \cdot w(x), dx. Integrate. \blacksquare

Example 3.1 — Trapezoidal Dam Face
Setup: A trapezoidal dam face has its top edge 4 m wide at water surface and bottom edge 2 m wide at depth 3 m. Water density \rho = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s². Find the total hydrostatic force.
Width function: At depth x, the width decreases linearly from 4 to 2 as x goes from 0 to 3: w(x) = 4 - \frac{2x}{3}
Force: F = \int_0^3 \rho g x \cdot w(x), dx = 1000(9.8)\int_0^3 x\left(4 - \frac{2x}{3}\right) dx = 9800 \int_0^3 \left(4x - \frac{2x^2}{3}\right) dx = 9800\left[2x^2 - \frac{2x^3}{9}\right]_0^3 = 9800\left[18 - 6\right] = 9800 \times 12 = \boxed{117{,}600 \text{ N} \approx 117.6 \text{ kN}}

Engineering relevance: Dam engineers must ensure structural supports can withstand this force. The integral gives the exact force accounting for how both pressure and width change with depth.


Example 3.2 — Circular Porthole
Setup: A circular porthole of radius 1 m is centered at depth 5 m on a submarine hull. Find the net hydrostatic force on the porthole.
Setup coordinates: Center at depth 5. Use y measured from center: depth at height y from center is 5 - y. Width at height y: w(y) = 2\sqrt{1 - y^2}.
F = \rho g \int_{-1}^{1} (5-y) \cdot 2\sqrt{1-y^2}, dy
Split: = 2\rho g \left[5\int_{-1}^1 \sqrt{1-y^2}, dy - \int_{-1}^1 y\sqrt{1-y^2}, dy\right]
First integral = area of semicircle = \frac{\pi}{2}. Second integral = 0 (odd function on symmetric interval).
F = 2\rho g \cdot 5 \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = 5\pi \rho g = 5\pi (1000)(9.8) \approx \boxed{153{,}938 \text{ N}}

Note: The 5 meters of depth contributes; the circular shape contributes \pi r^2 area. The depth of the centroid times \rho g times area gives the same answer — this is the centroid shortcut, but only valid when you already know the result! The integral is the derivation.


4. Arc Length & Surface Area of Revolution
Theoretical Foundation (Stewart §8.1–8.2)
Arc Length Formula:
\boxed{L = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}, dx}
Derivation: For a curve y = f(x), partition [a,b]. Each piece has length \approx \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2 + (\Delta y)^2} = \Delta x\sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\right)^2}. Taking the limit as partition is refined gives the formula. \blacksquare
Surface Area of Revolution (rotating y = f(x) about x-axis):
\boxed{S = \int_a^b 2\pi f(x)\sqrt{1 + [f'(x)]^2}, dx}
Each infinitesimal strip of arc length ds = \sqrt{1+[f'(x)]^2}, dx traces a band of area 2\pi f(x), ds.

Example 4.1 — Arc Length of a Parabolic Cable
Setup: A suspension bridge cable follows y = x^2 from x = 0 to x = 2 (units in km). Find its length.
y' = 2x \implies L = \int_0^2 \sqrt{1 + 4x^2}, dx
Trigonometric substitution: 2x = \tan\theta, dx = \frac{1}{2}\sec^2\theta, d\theta, \sqrt{1+4x^2} = \sec\theta.
L = \int_0^{\arctan 4} \sec\theta \cdot \frac{1}{2}\sec^2\theta, d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int \sec^3\theta, d\theta
Using the reduction formula \int \sec^3\theta, d\theta = \frac{1}{2}[\sec\theta\tan\theta + \ln|\sec\theta + \tan\theta|]:
L = \frac{1}{4}\left[\sec\theta\tan\theta + \ln|\sec\theta + \tan\theta|\right]_0^{\arctan 4}
At \theta = \arctan 4: \tan\theta = 4, \sec\theta = \sqrt{17}.
L = \frac{1}{4}\left[4\sqrt{17} + \ln(4 + \sqrt{17})\right] \approx \frac{1}{4}[16.49 + \ln(8.123)] \approx \frac{1}{4}[16.49 + 2.094] \approx \boxed{4.65 \text{ km}}

Example 4.2 — Surface Area of a Cooling Tower
Setup: A cooling tower profile is y = \cosh(x/a) rotated about the y-axis. For a = 1, from x = 0 to x = 1, find the surface area.
y' = \sinh x \implies S = \int_0^1 2\pi x \sqrt{1 + \sinh^2 x}, dx = 2\pi \int_0^1 x\cosh x, dx
(Using \cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1 \implies \sqrt{1+\sinh^2 x} = \cosh x.)
Integration by parts: u = x, dv = \cosh x, dx: = 2\pi\left[x\sinh x - \cosh x\right]_0^1 = 2\pi[\sinh 1 - \cosh 1 + 1] = 2\pi[1.1752 - 1.5431 + 1] = 2\pi(0.632) \approx \boxed{3.97 \text{ m}^2}

5. Electric Charge & Current
Theoretical Foundation
Current I(t) is the rate of charge flow: I = dq/dt. To find total charge from current:
\boxed{q = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} I(t), dt}
Energy delivered to a resistor: \boxed{E = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} P(t), dt = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} V(t) I(t), dt}
Electric potential (work per unit charge) from field \mathbf{E}: V(b) - V(a) = -\int_a^b \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{r}

Example 5.1 — Capacitor Charging
Setup: A capacitor charges with current I(t) = 2e^{-t/3} A. How much charge accumulates in the first 6 seconds?
q = \int_0^6 2e^{-t/3}, dt = 2\left[-3e^{-t/3}\right]_0^6 = -6\left[e^{-2} - 1\right] = 6\left(1 - e^{-2}\right) \approx 6(1 - 0.1353) \approx \boxed{5.17 \text{ C}}
Interpretation: The current is large at t=0 and decays exponentially as the capacitor fills. The integral accumulates this decaying flow.

Example 5.2 — RMS Voltage
Setup: AC voltage V(t) = V_0 \sin(\omega t). Find the root-mean-square voltage over one period T = 2\pi/\omega.
V_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T V_0^2 \sin^2(\omega t), dt}
\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T \sin^2(\omega t), dt = \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T \frac{1-\cos(2\omega t)}{2}, dt = \frac{1}{2}
(The cosine term integrates to zero over a full period.)
V_{\text{rms}} = V_0\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} = \boxed{\frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}}}

This is why household 230 V (in Bangladesh/Europe) means V_0 = 230\sqrt{2} \approx 325 V peak amplitude.


6. Gravitational Potential Energy
Theoretical Foundation (MIT 18.02 L22)
The gravitational force between two masses M and m separated by r is: F(r) = \frac{GMm}{r^2}
Work done lifting a mass from r = R (Earth’s surface) to r = \infty:
W = \int_R^\infty \frac{GMm}{r^2}, dr = GMm\left[-\frac{1}{r}\right]_R^\infty = \frac{GMm}{R}
This is the escape energy — the minimum energy required.

Example 6.1 — Escape Velocity
Setup: Find the minimum launch speed from Earth’s surface (R = 6.371 \times 10^6 m, M = 5.972 \times 10^{24} kg).
Set kinetic energy = potential energy: \frac{1}{2}mv_e^2 = \frac{GMm}{R} \implies v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}
v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2(6.674\times 10^{-11})(5.972\times 10^{24})}{6.371\times 10^6}} = \sqrt{\frac{7.972\times 10^{14}}{6.371\times 10^6}} = \sqrt{1.251\times 10^8} \approx \boxed{11.18 \text{ km/s}}

The integral’s role: The work integral from R to \infty correctly accounts for the decreasing gravitational force — something a simple F \times d calculation cannot do.


7. Moment of Inertia (Rotational Kinetic Energy)
Theoretical Foundation (MIT 18.02 L21)
Moment of inertia I measures resistance to rotational acceleration:
\boxed{I = \int r^2, dm}
where r is the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation.
Kinetic energy of rotation: KE = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2.

Example 7.1 — Solid Cylinder
Setup: A solid cylinder of mass M, radius R, and height h rotates about its central axis. Find I.
Setup: Use cylindrical coordinates. A thin cylindrical shell at radius r, thickness dr: dm = \rho \cdot 2\pi r h, dr, \quad \rho = \frac{M}{\pi R^2 h}
I = \int_0^R r^2, dm = \int_0^R r^2 \cdot \frac{M}{\pi R^2 h} \cdot 2\pi r h, dr = \frac{2M}{R^2}\int_0^R r^3, dr = \frac{2M}{R^2} \cdot \frac{R^4}{4} = \boxed{\frac{MR^2}{2}}
Application: A flywheel engine stores energy E = \frac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \frac{MR^2\omega^2}{4}. Increasing R is more efficient than increasing \omega for energy storage.

Example 7.2 — Thin Rod About End vs. Center
For a uniform rod of mass M, length L, density \lambda = M/L:
About center: I_c = \int_{-L/2}^{L/2} x^2 \lambda, dx = \lambda \cdot \frac{x^3}{3}\Bigg|_{-L/2}^{L/2} = \lambda \cdot \frac{L^3}{12} = \boxed{\frac{ML^2}{12}}
About end: I_e = \int_0^L x^2 \lambda, dx = \lambda \cdot \frac{L^3}{3} = \boxed{\frac{ML^2}{3}}
Parallel Axis Theorem check: I_e = I_c + M(L/2)^2 = \frac{ML^2}{12} + \frac{ML^2}{4} = \frac{ML^2}{3}. ✓

8. Signal Processing — Convolution
Theoretical Foundation
Convolution is one of the most powerful integral operations in engineering:
\boxed{(f * g)(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(\tau), g(t - \tau), d\tau}
Intuition: At time t, the output is the weighted sum of all past inputs f(\tau), weighted by the impulse response g(t-\tau).
Applications:

Signal filtering (audio, image)
System response (input * impulse response = output)
Probability (sum of random variables)


Example 8.1 — RC Circuit Response
Setup: An RC circuit has impulse response g(t) = \frac{1}{RC}e^{-t/RC} \cdot \mathbf{1}_{t \ge 0}. Input: rectangular pulse f(t) = \mathbf{1}_{0 \le t \le T}. Find output y(t) for 0 < t < T.
y(t) = \int_0^t f(\tau) g(t-\tau), d\tau = \int_0^t \frac{1}{RC} e^{-(t-\tau)/RC}, d\tau = \frac{e^{-t/RC}}{RC}\int_0^t e^{\tau/RC}, d\tau = \frac{e^{-t/RC}}{RC} \cdot RC\left[e^{\tau/RC}\right]_0^t = e^{-t/RC}(e^{t/RC} - 1) = \boxed{1 - e^{-t/RC}}
The output rises toward 1, the classic capacitor charging curve — derived directly from the convolution integral.

9. Probability & Statistics (Bridge to ML)
Theoretical Foundation
For a continuous random variable X with probability density function (PDF) f(x):
P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x), dx, \qquad \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x), dx = 1
Expected value: \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x, f(x), dx
Variance: \text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x^2 f(x), dx - \left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty x, f(x), dx\right)^2

Example 9.1 — Gaussian (Normal) Distribution
PDF: f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}
Verify it integrates to 1 (the Gaussian integral):
\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2}, dx = \sqrt{2\pi}
Proof using polar coordinates (MIT 18.02 L25 style):
Let I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2}, dx. Then: I^2 = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}, dx, dy
Convert to polar: x^2 + y^2 = r^2, dA = r, dr, d\theta: I^2 = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/2} r, dr, d\theta = 2\pi \int_0^\infty r e^{-r^2/2}, dr
Substitution u = r^2/2: = 2\pi \int_0^\infty e^{-u}, du = 2\pi
\therefore I = \sqrt{2\pi}. \blacksquare

This double integral in polar coordinates is the engine of all probability theory for Gaussian distributions — and Gaussians are everywhere in ML.


10. Machine Learning & Deep Learning — Where It All Lives

Every topic above has a direct descendant in modern AI. Here we make the connections explicit.


10.1 Gradient Flow & Backpropagation via the Fundamental Theorem
Connection to Work integrals. In optimization, the loss landscape \mathcal{L}(\theta) is a surface. The gradient flow equation: \frac{d\theta}{dt} = -\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta)
describes a “particle” rolling downhill. The total loss change along a path \gamma from \theta_0 to \theta_T is: \Delta \mathcal{L} = \int_0^T \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} \cdot \frac{d\theta}{dt}, dt = -\int_0^T \left|\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\right|^2 dt
This is directly analogous to work done by a force along a path (§1). The gradient is the force; the parameter update is the displacement.

10.2 Convolution in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)
This is §8 directly. A 2D CNN layer computes:
(I * K)(i,j) = \sum_{m}\sum_{n} I(i-m, j-n), K(m,n)
This is the discrete analogue of the continuous convolution integral: (f * g)(t) = \int f(\tau) g(t-\tau), d\tau
In a CNN:

I = input image (or feature map)
K = learned kernel (analogous to impulse response g)
Output = filtered/transformed version of input

Why does it work? Convolution is translation-equivariant: shifting the input shifts the output by the same amount. This is a direct consequence of the integral’s structure: \int f(\tau-a) g(t-\tau), d\tau = (f*g)(t-a).

10.3 Expected Value & Loss Functions
Connection to §9. The empirical risk minimization principle:
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim \mathcal{D}}\left[\ell(f_\theta(x), y)\right] = \int \ell(f_\theta(x), y), p(x,y), dx, dy
The true loss is an integral over the data distribution p(x,y). We cannot compute it exactly (we don’t know p), so we approximate:
\hat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f_\theta(x_i), y_i) \approx \int \ell(f_\theta(x), y), p(x,y), dx, dy
This is a Monte Carlo approximation to an integral — stochastic gradient descent is fundamentally a method for minimizing an integral you can’t compute in closed form.

10.4 Kullback-Leibler Divergence
The KL divergence used in variational autoencoders (VAEs), diffusion models, and information theory:
D_{KL}(P | Q) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty p(x) \log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}, dx
This is an integral of probability densities (§9). For Gaussians P = \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2), Q = \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2):
D_{KL}(P|Q) = \log\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1} + \frac{\sigma_1^2 + (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2} - \frac{1}{2}
Derived by directly evaluating the integral using properties of the Gaussian (completing the square, the Gaussian integral result from §9.1).

10.5 Attention Mechanism as Weighted Average
The self-attention in Transformers (GPT, BERT):
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V
In the continuous limit, this is a weighted integral:
\text{Attention}(q) = \int \frac{e^{q \cdot k(x)}}{\int e^{q \cdot k(x')}, dx'} v(x), dx
This is directly the expected value formula (§9): output = \mathbb{E}[v(x)] under the attention distribution \text{softmax}(\cdot). The softmax is a normalized exponential measure, and the attention output is a weighted average — an integral.

10.6 Moment of Inertia → Batch Normalization
Connection to §7. The variance of activations: \text{Var}[x] = \mathbb{E}[x^2] - (\mathbb{E}[x])^2 = \int x^2 p(x), dx - \left(\int x, p(x), dx\right)^2
This is the second central moment — structurally identical to the moment of inertia formula. Batch Normalization normalizes by \sqrt{\text{Var}[x] + \epsilon}, which is precisely dividing by the “radius of gyration” of the activation distribution.

10.7 Neural ODEs — The Continuous Limit of Deep Networks
Connection to all of the above. A residual network block: h_{t+1} = h_t + f(h_t, \theta_t). As the number of layers \to \infty with smaller steps, this becomes the ODE:
\frac{dh}{dt} = f(h(t), \theta(t)), \qquad h(T) = h(0) + \int_0^T f(h(t), \theta(t)), dt
Neural ODEs (Chen et al., 2018) make this the architecture itself. The forward pass is an integral. Training requires differentiating through an ODE solver — which requires the adjoint method, itself a line integral in function space.

Prelude — The Same Engine, Different World
The physics note established that integration is the mathematics of accumulation. In economics and biology, the same machinery reappears — but what accumulates is different:

























FieldWhat accumulatesMeasurePhysicsForce, pressuredx, dAEconomicsValue, surplus, discounted cash flowdq, dtBiologyPopulation, drug dose, probability of survivaldt, dN
The Riemann sum template is unchanged: Q = \int_a^b f(x), dx = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*),\Delta x
What changes is the interpretation of f and x.

ECONOMICS

1. Consumer Surplus & Producer Surplus
Theoretical Foundation (Stewart §6.1)
Setup: In a market, demand is described by the inverse demand function p = D(q) (willingness to pay) and supply by p = S(q). At equilibrium (Q^_, P^_):
D(Q^_) = S(Q^_) = P^*
Consumer Surplus (CS): Consumers who would have paid more than P^* gain a “surplus” — the difference between what they were willing to pay and what they actually paid.
\boxed{CS = \int_0^{Q^_} D(q), dq - P^_ \cdot Q^*}
Derivation: Partition [0, Q^_] into n small intervals of width \Delta q. In strip i, a consumer buying \Delta q units valued them at \approx D(q_i^_). Surplus on strip i: (D(q_i^_) - P^_)\Delta q. Sum and take limit: CS = \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n (D(q_i^_) - P^_)\Delta q = \int_0^{Q^_}(D(q) - P^_), dq \quad \blacksquare
Producer Surplus (PS): Analogously, producers who would have sold for less than P^_ gain surplus: \boxed{PS = P^_ \cdot Q^* - \int_0^{Q^*} S(q), dq}
Total Welfare: W = CS + PS = \int_0^{Q^*}(D(q) - S(q)), dq

Example 1.1 — Linear Demand & Supply
Setup: D(q) = 120 - 2q, S(q) = 20 + 3q. Find equilibrium and both surpluses.
Equilibrium: 120 - 2q = 20 + 3q \implies 100 = 5q \implies Q^* = 20, \quad P^* = 80
Consumer Surplus: CS = \int_0^{20}(120 - 2q), dq - 80 \cdot 20 = \left[120q - q^2\right]_0^{20} - 1600 = (2400 - 400) - 1600 = \boxed{400}
Producer Surplus: PS = 80 \cdot 20 - \int_0^{20}(20 + 3q), dq = 1600 - \left[20q + \frac{3q^2}{2}\right]_0^{20} = 1600 - (400 + 600) = \boxed{600}
Total welfare: W = 400 + 600 = 1000.

Geometric check: CS is the area of the triangle above P^* = 80 and below the demand curve from q = 0 to q = 20. Base = 20, height = D(0) - P^* = 120 - 80 = 40. Area = \frac{1}{2}(20)(40) = 400. ✓


Example 1.2 — Nonlinear Demand: Market for a Tech Product
Setup: D(q) = \frac{200}{\sqrt{q+1}}, S(q) = 5q + 15. Find Q^_, P^_, and CS.
Equilibrium: \frac{200}{\sqrt{q+1}} = 5q + 15. Try q = 3: \frac{200}{2} = 100, \quad 5(3)+15 = 30. \quad \text{No.}
Try q = 15: \frac{200}{4} = 50, 5(15)+15 = 90. No. Try q = 7: \frac{200}{\sqrt{8}} = 70.7, 5(7)+15 = 50. Getting closer. Try q = 9: \frac{200}{\sqrt{10}} = 63.2, 60. Try q = 24: \frac{200}{5} = 40, 135. Hmm.
Numerically, equilibrium at approximately Q^* \approx 9.64, P^* \approx 62.
CS (exact form): CS = \int_0^{Q^_} \frac{200}{\sqrt{q+1}}, dq - P^_ Q^* = \left[400\sqrt{q+1}\right]_0^{Q^_} - P^_ Q^_ = 400(\sqrt{Q^_+1} - 1) - P^* Q^*

Takeaway: With nonlinear demand, closed-form equilibrium may require numerical methods, but the surplus integral is still analytically tractable once Q^* is known.


2. Present Value & Continuous Discounting
Theoretical Foundation (Stewart §7.8 context)
Money has time value: 1$ received today is worth more than 1received in the future due to earning potential. Under continuous compounding at rater$:
\text{Future value of } $P \text{ at time } t: \quad FV = Pe^{rt} \text{Present value of } $F \text{ received at time } t: \quad PV = Fe^{-rt}
For a continuous income stream at rate f(t) (dollars per unit time):
\boxed{PV = \int_0^T f(t), e^{-rt}, dt}
Derivation: In time interval [t, t+dt], income received \approx f(t), dt. Its present value is f(t), dt \cdot e^{-rt}. Accumulate from 0 to T. \blacksquare
Perpetuity (T \to \infty, constant f): PV = \int_0^\infty f e^{-rt}, dt = f\left[-\frac{e^{-rt}}{r}\right]_0^\infty = \frac{f}{r}

Example 2.1 — Business Acquisition Valuation
Setup: A business generates revenue at rate f(t) = 50{,}000 + 3{,}000t dollars/year (linearly growing). Discount rate r = 0.06. What is the present value over a 10-year horizon?
PV = \int_0^{10}(50000 + 3000t), e^{-0.06t}, dt
Split into two integrals:
Part 1: \int_0^{10} 50000, e^{-0.06t}, dt = 50000 \cdot \left[-\frac{e^{-0.06t}}{0.06}\right]_0^{10} = \frac{50000}{0.06}(1 - e^{-0.6}) = 833333(1 - 0.5488) = 833333(0.4512) \approx 375{,}963
Part 2: \int_0^{10} 3000t, e^{-0.06t}, dt. By parts: u = t, dv = e^{-0.06t}dt: = 3000\left[-\frac{t, e^{-0.06t}}{0.06} + \frac{1}{0.06}\int_0^{10} e^{-0.06t}, dt\right] = 3000\left[-\frac{10 e^{-0.6}}{0.06} + \frac{1}{0.06} \cdot \frac{1-e^{-0.6}}{0.06}\right] = 3000\left[-91.47 + 125.33\right] = 3000 \times 33.86 \approx 101{,}580
\boxed{PV \approx $477{,}543}

Interpretation: If you could buy this business for less than $477{,}543 today, it’s a positive-NPV investment at a 6% discount rate.


Example 2.2 — Continuous Perpetuity
Setup: An endowment fund pays out $$80{,}000/year continuously forever. Discount rate r = 4%$. What endowment size is needed?
PV = \frac{f}{r} = \frac{80000}{0.04} = \boxed{$2{,}000{,}000}
The integral \int_0^\infty 80000, e^{-0.04t}, dt converges because the discount factor e^{-0.04t} decays faster than the constant income grows — a beautiful consequence of the convergence of improper integrals.

3. Total Revenue from Marginal Revenue
Theoretical Foundation
In economics, marginal revenue MR(q) is the revenue from selling one additional unit: MR(q) = \frac{d}{dq}[TR(q)] = TR'(q)
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, total revenue is recovered by: \boxed{TR(Q) = TR(0) + \int_0^Q MR(q), dq = \int_0^Q MR(q), dq}
(Since TR(0) = 0 — zero units sold means zero revenue.)
Similarly, total cost from marginal cost: TC(Q) = FC + \int_0^Q MC(q), dq
And profit: \pi(Q) = \int_0^Q [MR(q) - MC(q)], dq - FC
Profit is maximized where MR = MC — this is where the integrand changes sign.

Example 3.1 — Monopolist Pricing
Setup: A monopolist faces demand p(q) = 100 - q, so TR = pq = (100-q)q = 100q - q^2 and: MR(q) = 100 - 2q MC(q) = 10 + q, \quad FC = 200
Profit-maximizing output: MR = MC \implies 100 - 2q = 10 + q \implies 90 = 3q \implies q^* = 30
Profit via integration: \pi = \int_0^{30}(MR - MC), dq - FC = \int_0^{30}(90 - 3q), dq - 200 = \left[90q - \frac{3q^2}{2}\right]_0^{30} - 200 = (2700 - 1350) - 200 = \boxed{1350 - 200 = 1150}
Cross-check: TR(30) = 100(30) - 30^2 = 2100. TC(30) = 200 + \int_0^{30}(10+q), dq = 200 + [10q + q^2/2]_0^{30} = 200 + 300 + 450 = 950. \pi = 2100 - 950 = 1150. ✓

4. Lorenz Curve & Gini Coefficient (Income Inequality)
Theoretical Foundation (Stewart §6.1 application)
Lorenz Curve: L(x) represents the fraction of total income earned by the bottom x fraction of the population. Properties:

L(0) = 0, L(1) = 1
L(x) \le x (lower incomes earn disproportionately less)
L is convex and increasing

Perfect equality: L(x) = x (everyone earns proportionally).
Gini Coefficient: \boxed{G = 2\int_0^1 [x - L(x)], dx}
This measures the area between the line of perfect equality and the Lorenz curve, normalized to [0,1]. G = 0 is perfect equality; G = 1 is perfect inequality.
Derivation: The area between y = x and y = L(x) is \int_0^1 (x - L(x)), dx. The maximum possible area (perfect inequality: L(x) = 0 for x < 1) is \frac{1}{2}. So G = \frac{\int_0^1(x - L(x)), dx}{1/2} = 2\int_0^1(x - L(x)), dx. \blacksquare

Example 4.1 — Pareto Distribution Lorenz Curve
The Pareto distribution (power law) models wealth concentration. Its Lorenz curve: L(x) = 1 - (1-x)^{1-1/\alpha} \cdot \frac{...}{}
For simplicity, use: L(x) = x^2 (a common textbook model).
Gini coefficient: G = 2\int_0^1 [x - x^2], dx = 2\left[\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = 2\left[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}\right] = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \boxed{\frac{1}{3} \approx 0.333}

Example 4.2 — Empirical Lorenz Curve
Setup: A country’s income data gives the Lorenz curve: L(x) = \frac{e^{2x} - 1}{e^2 - 1}
Verify: L(0) = 0, L(1) = 1. ✓ L'(x) = \frac{2e^{2x}}{e^2 - 1} > 0. ✓ L''(x) = \frac{4e^{2x}}{e^2 - 1} > 0 (convex). ✓
Gini: G = 2\int_0^1\left[x - \frac{e^{2x}-1}{e^2 - 1}\right]dx = 2\left[\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{e^{2x}}{2(e^2-1)} + \frac{x}{e^2-1}\right]_0^1 = 2\left[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{e^2}{2(e^2-1)} + \frac{1}{e^2-1} + \frac{1}{2(e^2-1)}\right] = 2\left[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{e^2 - 1 - 1}{2(e^2-1)}\right] = 2\left[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{e^2-2}{2(e^2-1)}\right] = 1 - \frac{e^2-2}{e^2-1} = \frac{e^2-1 - e^2+2}{e^2-1} = \boxed{\frac{1}{e^2-1} \approx 0.156}
This is a relatively equal distribution (low Gini). For comparison, Bangladesh’s Gini ≈ 0.33, USA ≈ 0.41, South Africa ≈ 0.63.

5. Capital Accumulation & Investment
Theoretical Foundation
If I(t) is the rate of investment (capital added per unit time), then capital stock at time T: \boxed{K(T) = K(0) + \int_0^T I(t), dt}
This is the FTC in action: investment is the derivative of capital, so integrating investment recovers capital. This is identical in structure to \int I, dt = q (charge from current) in the physics note.
Depreciation: If capital depreciates at rate \delta, net capital accumulation: \frac{dK}{dt} = I(t) - \delta K(t) This is a first-order linear ODE, solved by the integrating factor method — but the total investment \int_0^T I(t), dt is still the core integral.

Example 5.1 — Capital Stock Over a Decade
Setup: A firm’s investment rate follows a business cycle: I(t) = 5000 + 2000\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{5}\right) million BDT/year. Initial capital K(0) = 20{,}000 million BDT. Find K(10).
K(10) = 20000 + \int_0^{10}\left(5000 + 2000\sin\frac{\pi t}{5}\right) dt = 20000 + \left[5000t - \frac{10000}{\pi}\cos\frac{\pi t}{5}\right]_0^{10} = 20000 + \left[(50000 - \frac{10000}{\pi}\cos 2\pi) - (0 - \frac{10000}{\pi})\right] = 20000 + 50000 - \frac{10000}{\pi} + \frac{10000}{\pi} = \boxed{70{,}000 \text{ million BDT}}

Observation: The sine investment cycle (booms and busts) contributes zero net capital over a full 10-year period — the integral of a sine over complete periods is zero. The average rate 5000/yr \times 10 yr = 50{,}000 is all that matters.


BIOLOGY

6. Population Growth — Logistic Model
Theoretical Foundation (Stewart §9.4)
Malthusian (exponential) growth: \frac{dN}{dt} = rN
Solution: N(t) = N_0 e^{rt}, which gives N(t) = N_0 + \int_0^t rN(\tau), d\tau — a self-referential integral equation.
Logistic growth: Carrying capacity K limits growth: \frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)
Exact solution via separation of variables:
\int \frac{dN}{N(1 - N/K)} = \int r, dt
Partial fractions: \frac{1}{N(1-N/K)} = \frac{1}{N} + \frac{1/K}{1-N/K}
\int\left(\frac{1}{N} + \frac{1/K}{1-N/K}\right)dN = rt + C \ln|N| - \ln|1 - N/K| = rt + C \ln\left|\frac{N}{1-N/K}\right| = rt + C
Solving for N: \boxed{N(t) = \frac{K}{1 + \left(\frac{K - N_0}{N_0}\right)e^{-rt}}}
Total growth from t=0 to t=T: \Delta N = \int_0^T rN\left(1-\frac{N}{K}\right) dt which equals N(T) - N(0) by the FTC — a useful consistency check.

Example 6.1 — Fish Population in a Lake
Setup: A lake initially has N_0 = 500 fish. The carrying capacity is K = 10{,}000 and growth rate r = 0.3/year. When does the population reach 5,000?
Using logistic formula: 5000 = \frac{10000}{1 + 19, e^{-0.3t}} 1 + 19e^{-0.3t} = 2 \implies 19 e^{-0.3t} = 1 \implies e^{-0.3t} = \frac{1}{19} t = \frac{\ln 19}{0.3} = \frac{2.944}{0.3} \approx \boxed{9.81 \text{ years}}
Total fish-years of stock from t=0 to t=10 (important for fishery management): \int_0^{10} N(t), dt = \int_0^{10} \frac{10000}{1 + 19, e^{-0.3t}}, dt
Let u = 1 + 19e^{-0.3t}, du = -5.7 e^{-0.3t}, dt:
= 10000 \int_{u(0)}^{u(10)} \frac{1}{u} \cdot \frac{du}{-5.7\cdot\frac{u-1}{19}} = \frac{10000 \cdot 19}{5.7}\int_{20}^{1+19e^{-3}} \frac{-du}{u(u-1)}
This becomes a partial fraction integral. Numerically: \approx 46{,}500 fish-years.

Ecological significance: Integrating N(t) over time gives the total biological “resource consumption” or sustainable harvest potential.


7. Drug Concentration — Pharmacokinetics
Theoretical Foundation (Stewart §8.5 type)
One-compartment model: A drug is administered and eliminated from the body. Concentration C(t) in blood plasma:

IV bolus: C(t) = C_0 e^{-kt} (first-order elimination)
Oral/continuous infusion at rate R:

\frac{dC}{dt} = R - kC \implies C(t) = \frac{R}{k}(1 - e^{-kt})
Key pharmacokinetic integral — Area Under the Curve (AUC):
\boxed{AUC = \int_0^\infty C(t), dt}
Why AUC matters: By the bioavailability theorem, total drug exposure = total amount absorbed / clearance. AUC is proportional to the total amount of drug that reaches systemic circulation. It determines both efficacy and toxicity.

Example 7.1 — Intravenous Bolus
Setup: A patient receives a 500 mg IV dose. The elimination constant k = 0.2 hr⁻¹ and volume of distribution V_d = 20 L. Thus C_0 = 500/20 = 25 mg/L.
C(t) = 25 e^{-0.2t} \text{ mg/L}
AUC: AUC = \int_0^\infty 25 e^{-0.2t}, dt = 25 \cdot \left[-\frac{e^{-0.2t}}{0.2}\right]_0^\infty = \frac{25}{0.2} = \boxed{125 \text{ mg·hr/L}}
Half-life: t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{k} = \frac{0.693}{0.2} \approx 3.47 hr.
Concentration at 8 hours: C(8) = 25 e^{-1.6} \approx 5.03 mg/L.
Drug remaining in body at t = 8: V_d \cdot C(8) = 20 \times 5.03 \approx 100.6 mg.
Cumulative amount eliminated by t = 8: \text{Eliminated} = V_d \int_0^8 k C(t), dt = V_d \cdot k \cdot \frac{C_0}{k}(1 - e^{-0.2 \cdot 8}) = 500(1 - e^{-1.6}) \approx 399.4 \text{ mg} ✓ (Total: 399.4 + 100.6 = 500 mg.)

Example 7.2 — Repeated Dosing & Steady State
Setup: A drug is given as IV bolus dose D = 100 mg every \tau = 6 hours. Elimination k = 0.3/hr. Find the steady-state peak concentration.
After n doses, the trough concentration just before the (n+1)th dose accumulates geometrically. At steady state (infinite doses):
C_{\text{min,ss}} = \frac{C_0 e^{-k\tau}}{1 - e^{-k\tau}} = \frac{5 \cdot e^{-1.8}}{1 - e^{-1.8}}
e^{-1.8} \approx 0.1653, C_0 = D/V_d. With V_d = 20 L: C_0 = 5 mg/L.
C_{\text{min,ss}} = \frac{5 \times 0.1653}{1 - 0.1653} = \frac{0.827}{0.8347} \approx 0.99 \text{ mg/L} C_{\text{max,ss}} = C_{\text{min,ss}} + C_0 = 0.99 + 5 = \boxed{5.99 \text{ mg/L}}
AUC at steady state (per dosing interval, using integration): AUC_{ss} = \int_0^\tau C_{ss}(t), dt = \int_0^6 C_{\text{max,ss}} e^{-0.3t}, dt = \frac{C_{\text{max,ss}}}{k}(1-e^{-k\tau}) = \frac{5.99}{0.3}(1 - 0.1653) \approx 19.97 \times 0.8347 \approx \boxed{16.67 \text{ mg·hr/L}}

8. Cardiac Output — Dye Dilution Method
Theoretical Foundation (Stewart §8.5)
Clinical problem: How do we measure cardiac output (volume of blood pumped per minute) without invasive surgery?
Stewart-Hamilton Principle: Inject a known quantity A mg of dye into a vein. Measure its concentration c(t) at the aorta. Then:
\boxed{F = \frac{A}{\int_0^\infty c(t), dt}}
where F = cardiac output (L/min).
Derivation: In a small time interval [t, t+dt], the volume of blood passing the measurement point is F, dt, carrying dye amount c(t) \cdot F, dt. Accumulating all dye: \int_0^\infty c(t) F, dt = A (conservation of mass). Solve for F. \blacksquare

Example 8.1 — Dye Dilution Calculation
Setup: 5 mg of dye injected. Concentration measurements (mg/L) at the aorta:





























t (min)012345678c(t)00.41.84.03.92.81.60.70.1
Approximate \int_0^8 c(t), dt using Simpson’s Rule (h = 1, n = 8): \int \approx \frac{1}{3}\left[c_0 + 4c_1 + 2c_2 + 4c_3 + 2c_4 + 4c_5 + 2c_6 + 4c_7 + c_8\right] = \frac{1}{3}[0 + 1.6 + 3.6 + 16.0 + 7.8 + 11.2 + 3.2 + 2.8 + 0.1] = \frac{1}{3}(46.3) \approx 15.43 \text{ mg·min/L}
Cardiac output: F = \frac{5}{15.43} \approx \boxed{0.324 \text{ L/min}} \approx 19.4 \text{ L/hr}
Note: Normal cardiac output is ~5 L/min at rest; this example uses small numbers for clarity.

Clinical note: This formula is used in hospitals today. The integral cannot be computed analytically from real data — numerical integration (Simpson’s Rule) is essential. This is a direct application of numerical quadrature.


9. Survival & Hazard Functions
Theoretical Foundation
Survival function S(t) = P(T > t): probability that a subject survives past time t.
Hazard function \lambda(t): instantaneous risk of death at time t given survival to t: \lambda(t) = -\frac{S'(t)}{S(t)} = -\frac{d}{dt}\ln S(t)
Key relationship (integrating the hazard): \boxed{S(t) = e^{-\int_0^t \lambda(u), du} = e^{-\Lambda(t)}}
where \Lambda(t) = \int_0^t \lambda(u), du is the cumulative hazard function.
PDF of failure time: f(t) = -S'(t) = \lambda(t), S(t) = \lambda(t), e^{-\Lambda(t)}
Mean lifetime (expected survival time): \mathbb{E}[T] = \int_0^\infty S(t), dt

Example 9.1 — Weibull Hazard Model
Setup: The Weibull distribution has hazard \lambda(t) = \frac{\beta}{\eta}\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^{\beta-1}. With \beta = 2 (increasing hazard — aging), \eta = 5 years.
Cumulative hazard: \Lambda(t) = \int_0^t \frac{2}{\eta}\cdot\frac{u}{\eta}, du = \int_0^t \frac{2u}{\eta^2}, du = \frac{t^2}{\eta^2} = \frac{t^2}{25}
Survival function: S(t) = e^{-t^2/25}
Probability of surviving past 3 years: S(3) = e^{-9/25} = e^{-0.36} \approx 0.698
Mean survival time: \mathbb{E}[T] = \int_0^\infty e^{-t^2/25}, dt = \int_0^\infty e^{-t^2/25}, dt
Let u = t/5: $= 5\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}, du = 5 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2} = \frac{5\sqrt{\pi}}{2} \approx \boxed{4.43 \text{ years}}$$

The Gaussian integral appears again — this time computing the mean lifetime of a Weibull-distributed survival model. The connection to §9 of the physics/ML note is deep: the same \int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}, du = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2} underlies both the normal distribution and the Weibull mean.


Example 9.2 — Median vs Mean Survival (Cancer Study)
For exponential survival S(t) = e^{-\lambda t}:
Mean: \mathbb{E}[T] = \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}, dt = \frac{1}{\lambda}
Median t_{0.5}: S(t_{0.5}) = 0.5 \implies e^{-\lambda t_{0.5}} = 0.5 \implies t_{0.5} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}
Ratio: \frac{t_{0.5}}{\mathbb{E}[T]} = \ln 2 \approx 0.693
This explains why clinical trials often report median survival (robust to outliers) rather than mean — but the mean requires the integral \int_0^\infty S(t), dt, which clinical statisticians compute via numerical integration from Kaplan-Meier curves.

10. Spread of Disease — The SIR Model
Theoretical Foundation
The SIR model (Kermack-McKendrick 1927) partitions a population N into:

S(t): Susceptible
I(t): Infectious
R(t): Recovered (immune)

ODEs: \frac{dS}{dt} = -\beta SI, \qquad \frac{dI}{dt} = \beta SI - \gamma I, \qquad \frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I
Conservation: S + I + R = N (constant).
Total infected over the entire epidemic: R(\infty) = \gamma \int_0^\infty I(t), dt
Final size equation (derived by integrating the SIR equations, dividing, and using separation of variables):
\ln\frac{S(0)}{S(\infty)} = \frac{\beta}{\gamma}(S(0) + I(0) - S(\infty)) = \mathcal{R}_0 \cdot \frac{S(0) - S(\infty)}{N}
where \mathcal{R}_0 = \frac{\beta N}{\gamma} is the basic reproduction number.

Example 10.1 — COVID-style Outbreak
Setup: A university of N = 5000 students. Initially I_0 = 5, S_0 = 4995. Parameters: \beta = 0.0003/person/day, \gamma = 0.1/day.
\mathcal{R}_0 = \frac{\beta N}{\gamma} = \frac{0.0003 \times 5000}{0.1} = 15
Epidemic will occur since \mathcal{R}_0 > 1.
Peak infection time (when dI/dt = 0, i.e., \beta S = \gamma): S^* = \frac{\gamma}{\beta} = \frac{0.1}{0.0003} = 333 \implies \text{peak occurs when } S \text{ drops to } 333
Total fraction eventually infected r_\infty = 1 - S(\infty)/N, solving: \ln\frac{S_0}{S_\infty} = \mathcal{R}_0\left(1 - \frac{S_\infty}{N}\right) \approx \mathcal{R}_0 r_\infty
For \mathcal{R}_0 = 15: r_\infty \approx 0.9999 (essentially the entire population). This is consistent with measles-like dynamics.
Total person-days of infection (cumulative burden, key for healthcare planning): \text{Burden} = \int_0^\infty I(t), dt = \frac{R(\infty)}{\gamma} = \frac{N r_\infty}{\gamma} \approx \frac{4998}{0.1} \approx 49{,}980 \text{ person-days}

This integral is the fundamental healthcare capacity metric. Hospital planning requires knowing not just the peak I(t) but the area under the I(t) curve — the total patient-days. “Flattening the curve” means reducing the maximum of I(t) while the integral (total infections) may stay similar.


Example 10.2 — Herd Immunity Threshold via Integration
The epidemic stops growing when dI/dt \le 0, i.e., S \le \gamma/\beta = N/\mathcal{R}_0.
Herd immunity threshold (fraction that must be immune): p_c = 1 - \frac{1}{\mathcal{R}_0}
For \mathcal{R}_0 = 15: p_c = 1 - 1/15 = 14/15 \approx 93.3%.
Integral verification: The integral \int_0^\infty \frac{dS}{dt}, dt = S(\infty) - S(0) gives the total reduction in susceptibles, which must equal total infections. This is the FTC applied to population dynamics: accumulating the flow dS/dt recovers the stock S(t).

ML & AI Connections

The same integrals from economics and biology recur directly in modern machine learning.


ML.1 — Survival Analysis & Deep Learning (Connection to §9)
Cox Proportional Hazards extended to neural networks (DeepSurv, 2018):
\lambda(t \mid \mathbf{x}) = \lambda_0(t) \cdot e^{f_\theta(\mathbf{x})}
where f_\theta is a deep neural network. The partial likelihood involves:
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \prod_{i:, \delta_i=1} \frac{e^{f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i)}}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{R}(t_i)} e^{f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_j)}}
The baseline survival S_0(t) = e^{-\int_0^t \lambda_0(u), du} is computed via numerical integration (Breslow estimator). The entire architecture depends on the cumulative hazard integral from §9.

ML.2 — Expected Reward in Reinforcement Learning (Connection to §2)
The discounted return in RL is: G_t = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \gamma^k r_{t+k} \approx \int_0^\infty r(t+\tau) e^{-\lambda \tau}, d\tau
This is exactly the present value formula (§2): PV = \int_0^T f(t), e^{-rt}, dt
with discount factor e^{-\lambda\tau} playing the role of e^{-rt}. The Bellman equation is the discrete version of the PV integral. Policy gradient methods optimize this integral.

ML.3 — Epidemic Modeling → Graph Neural Networks
The SIR integral \int_0^\infty I(t), dt is approximated in modern epidemic GNNs (e.g., EpiGNN, 2021) which learn \beta and \gamma from data. The ODE constraints: S(T) = S(0) - \beta \int_0^T S(t)I(t), dt
become physics-informed loss terms. This is neural ODE meets epidemiology — exactly the connection from the physics note’s §10.7 extended to the SIR system.

ML.4 — AUC as a Classification Metric (Connection to §7)
In machine learning, AUC-ROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve) is: AUC = \int_0^1 TPR(FPR^{-1}(t)), dt = P(\hat{p}(x^+) > \hat{p}(x^-))
This is a direct integral — the area under the ROC curve. It measures the probability that the model ranks a random positive example higher than a random negative one. Just as pharmacokinetic AUC (\int C(t), dt) measures total drug exposure, ML AUC measures total discriminative ability.

ML.5 — Gini Impurity & Decision Trees (Connection to §4)
The Gini impurity used in decision tree splits: G_{\text{node}} = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2
is the discrete analogue of the Gini coefficient from §4. The Lorenz curve integral G = 2\int_0^1(x - L(x)), dx measures inequality in income; Gini impurity measures “inequality” (mixing) of class labels at a node. Random Forests and XGBoost both use this integral-derived concept at every split.

ML.6 — Gaussian Processes & Integral Kernels
A Gaussian Process (GP) defines a distribution over functions via a covariance kernel k(x, x'). The posterior mean is: \mu^*(x) = \mathbf{k}(x, \mathbf{X})\left[\mathbf{K} + \sigma^2 I\right]^{-1}\mathbf{y}
The RBF kernel k(x, x') = e^{-|x-x'|^2/2\ell^2} is the continuous generalization of the inner product. Its normalization constant \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2\ell^2}, dx = \ell\sqrt{2\pi} comes directly from the Gaussian integral (§9.1 of the physics note). GPs underlie Bayesian optimization, which is used for hyperparameter tuning in deep learning.

Theorems That Recur Constantly

FTC (Stock-Flow duality): \int_0^T f'(t), dt = f(T) - f(0)
\quad Investment → Capital; Current → Charge; \frac{dN}{dt} → N(t); \frac{dR}{dt} → R(t)
Separation of Variables: \int \frac{dN}{g(N)} = \int f(t), dt — the engine of logistic growth, SIR analysis, pharmacokinetics.
Improper Integrals: \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}, dt = \frac{1}{\lambda} — appears in present value, AUC, mean survival, pharmacokinetics. All require convergence of e^{-\lambda t} as t \to \infty.
Gaussian Integral: \int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}, du = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2} — Weibull mean lifetime, all Gaussian models in ML.

Prelude — Probability IS Integration
There is a profound unity lurking here:

Every quantity in continuous probability theory is an integral.

Probability itself is an integral. Expected value is an integral. Variance is an integral. Information entropy is an integral. The KL divergence is an integral. The evidence lower bound (ELBO) in VAEs is an integral. The likelihood in a Gaussian process is an integral of an integral.
This is not a coincidence — it is the Kolmogorov foundation: probability is a measure, and computing probabilities of continuous events is Lebesgue integration. For us, working at the level of Riemann integration, the statement is:
\boxed{P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f_X(x), dx}
Every formula in this note is a specialization or composition of this single idea.

Part I — Foundations

1. Probability Density Functions — The Central Definition
Definition (Rigorous)
A function f_X: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} is a probability density function (PDF) for a continuous random variable X if:
(i) Non-negativity: f_X(x) \ge 0 for all x \in \mathbb{R}
(ii) Normalization: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x), dx = 1
(iii) Probability via integration: P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f_X(x), dx

Critical remark: f_X(x) is not a probability. It is a density — analogous to mass per unit length. The probability requires integrating over an interval. P(X = a) = \int_a^a f_X(x), dx = 0 for any single point. This is conceptually sharp: continuous random variables have probability zero of taking any exact value.


Example 1.1 — Verifying a PDF
Claim: f(x) = ce^{-3x} for x \ge 0 (and 0 otherwise) is a valid PDF for some c. Find c.
Normalization condition: \int_0^\infty ce^{-3x}, dx = 1 \implies c\left[-\frac{e^{-3x}}{3}\right]_0^\infty = 1 \implies \frac{c}{3} = 1 \implies \boxed{c = 3}
Verify: f(x) = 3e^{-3x} for x \ge 0. This is the Exponential distribution with parameter \lambda = 3.

Example 1.2 — Computing a Probability
Setup: f_X(x) = \frac{3}{8}x^2 for 0 \le x \le 2. Find P(1 \le X \le 2).
Step 1 — Verify normalization: \int_0^2 \frac{3}{8}x^2, dx = \frac{3}{8} \cdot \frac{x^3}{3}\Bigg|_0^2 = \frac{1}{8}(8) = 1 \quad \checkmark
Step 2 — Compute: P(1 \le X \le 2) = \int_1^2 \frac{3}{8}x^2, dx = \frac{3}{8} \cdot \frac{x^3}{3}\Bigg|_1^2 = \frac{1}{8}(8-1) = \boxed{\frac{7}{8}}

2. Cumulative Distribution Function
Definition & Fundamental Theorem Connection
\boxed{F_X(x) = P(X \le x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f_X(t), dt}
Properties (all derived from the integral):

F is non-decreasing (since f \ge 0, adding more area cannot decrease F)
\lim_{x\to-\infty} F(x) = 0, \lim_{x\to\infty} F(x) = 1
F is right-continuous
P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a) — this is the FTC for probability

FTC gives back the PDF: f_X(x) = F_X'(x) \quad \text{(almost everywhere)}
The CDF and PDF are a FTC pair. PDF is the derivative of CDF; CDF is the integral of PDF.

Example 2.1 — CDF of a Power Distribution
Setup: f(x) = 3x^2 for 0 \le x \le 1.
F(x) = \int_0^x 3t^2, dt = t^3\Big|_0^x = x^3, \quad 0 \le x \le 1
Find the median m: F(m) = 0.5 \implies m^3 = 0.5 \implies m = (0.5)^{1/3} \approx 0.794.
Find the 90th percentile p_{0.9}: p_{0.9}^3 = 0.9 \implies p_{0.9} = 0.9^{1/3} \approx 0.965.

Connection to §9 (Survival/Biology note): The survival function S(x) = 1 - F(x) = 1 - x^3 gives the probability of exceeding x. Every concept in survival analysis is the CDF or its complement, computed via integration.


Example 2.2 — CDF from a Piecewise PDF
Setup: f(x) = \begin{cases} x & 0 \le x \le 1 \ 2-x & 1 < x \le 2 \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
(Triangular distribution — note: \int_0^1 x, dx + \int_1^2 (2-x), dx = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1 ✓)
CDF for 0 \le x \le 1: F(x) = \int_0^x t, dt = \frac{x^2}{2}
CDF for 1 < x \le 2: F(x) = F(1) + \int_1^x (2-t), dt = \frac{1}{2} + \left[2t - \frac{t^2}{2}\right]_1^x = \frac{1}{2} + \left(2x - \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{3}{2}\right) = 2x - \frac{x^2}{2} - 1
Check: F(2) = 4 - 2 - 1 = 1. ✓

3. Expected Value & Moments
Definition
For a continuous random variable X with PDF f_X:
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x, f_X(x), dx}
Existence: This integral must converge absolutely — i.e., \int_{-\infty}^\infty |x|, f_X(x), dx < \infty. Some distributions (e.g., Cauchy) have no finite mean because this integral diverges.
Interpretation: \mathbb{E}[X] is the center of mass of the distribution — the balance point of the PDF curve. This is literally the same formula as the center of mass integral from the physics note, with f_X(x) playing the role of linear density \rho(x).

Example 3.1 — Expected Value of Power Distribution
Setup: f(x) = (n+1)x^n for 0 \le x \le 1.
\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^1 x \cdot (n+1)x^n, dx = (n+1)\int_0^1 x^{n+1}, dx = (n+1) \cdot \frac{1}{n+2} = \boxed{\frac{n+1}{n+2}}
Sanity check: As n \to \infty, the distribution concentrates near x = 1, and \mathbb{E}[X] \to 1. As n = 0 (uniform), \mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{1}{2}. Both are correct. ✓

Example 3.2 — Cauchy Distribution Has No Mean
PDF: f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}, x \in \mathbb{R}.
Attempt to compute \mathbb{E}[X]: \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{x}{\pi(1+x^2)}, dx = \frac{1}{\pi} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2)\Bigg|_{-\infty}^\infty
This integral diverges (both tails diverge to \pm\infty). The Cauchy distribution has no finite expected value despite being symmetric about 0.

This is not a mere technicality. In finance, the Cauchy distribution models fat-tailed returns where “the average return” literally does not exist — the empirical mean of samples from a Cauchy distribution never converges, no matter how much data you collect. The divergence of the integral is the mathematics of this phenomenon.


4. Variance, Standard Deviation & Higher Moments
Definition
n-th moment about the origin: \mu_n' = \mathbb{E}[X^n] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x^n, f_X(x), dx
n-th central moment: \mu_n = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^n] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty (x-\mu)^n, f_X(x), dx
Variance (n=2): \boxed{\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2}
Proof of the shortcut formula: \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \int (x-\mu)^2 f(x), dx = \int (x^2 - 2\mu x + \mu^2)f(x), dx = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2\mu \mathbb{E}[X] + \mu^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2\mu^2 + \mu^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu^2 \quad \blacksquare
Skewness (n=3 central moment, normalized): \gamma_1 = \frac{\mu_3}{\sigma^3} — measures asymmetry.
Kurtosis (n=4): \gamma_2 = \frac{\mu_4}{\sigma^4} - 3 — measures tail heaviness relative to Gaussian.

Example 4.1 — Variance of Triangular Distribution
For the triangular distribution from Example 2.2 with PDF f(x) = x on [0,1] and f(x) = 2-x on [1,2]:
\mathbb{E}[X] (by symmetry about x=1): \mathbb{E}[X] = 1.
\mathbb{E}[X^2]: = \int_0^1 x^2 \cdot x, dx + \int_1^2 x^2(2-x), dx = \int_0^1 x^3, dx + \int_1^2 (2x^2 - x^3), dx = \frac{1}{4} + \left[\frac{2x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{4}\right]_1^2 = \frac{1}{4} + \left(\frac{16}{3} - 4\right) - \left(\frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{4}{3} - \frac{5}{12} = \frac{3 + 16 - 5}{12} = \frac{14}{12} = \frac{7}{6}
\text{Var}(X) = \frac{7}{6} - 1^2 = \frac{1}{6}, \qquad \sigma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \approx 0.408 \quad \blacksquare

Part II — The Great Distributions, Derived Rigorously

5. Uniform Distribution
PDF: f(x) = \frac{1}{b-a} for x \in [a,b].
Verification: \int_a^b \frac{1}{b-a}, dx = 1. ✓
Mean: \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_a^b \frac{x}{b-a}, dx = \frac{1}{b-a} \cdot \frac{b^2-a^2}{2} = \frac{(b-a)(b+a)}{2(b-a)} = \boxed{\frac{a+b}{2}}
Variance: \mathbb{E}[X^2] = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b x^2, dx = \frac{b^3-a^3}{3(b-a)} = \frac{a^2+ab+b^2}{3} \text{Var}(X) = \frac{a^2+ab+b^2}{3} - \frac{(a+b)^2}{4} = \frac{4(a^2+ab+b^2) - 3(a+b)^2}{12} = \boxed{\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}}

6. Exponential Distribution
PDF: f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x} for x \ge 0, \lambda > 0.
Normalization: \int_0^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx = \lambda \cdot \frac{1}{\lambda} = 1. ✓
Mean (integration by parts: u=x, dv = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx): \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^\infty x \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx = \left[-xe^{-\lambda x}\right]_0^\infty + \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda x}, dx = 0 + \frac{1}{\lambda} = \boxed{\frac{1}{\lambda}}
Second moment (two integrations by parts): \mathbb{E}[X^2] = \int_0^\infty x^2 \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx = \frac{2}{\lambda^2}
\text{Var}(X) = \frac{2}{\lambda^2} - \frac{1}{\lambda^2} = \boxed{\frac{1}{\lambda^2}}
Memoryless property (unique to exponential): P(X > s+t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)
Proof via integration: P(X > s+t \mid X > s) = \frac{P(X > s+t)}{P(X > s)} = \frac{\int_{s+t}^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx}{\int_s^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx} = \frac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} = e^{-\lambda t} = P(X > t) \quad \blacksquare

7. The Gaussian — Derived from First Principles
The Gaussian Integral: Full Proof
Claim: \boxed{\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx = \sqrt{\pi}}
Proof (MIT 18.02 polar coordinate method):
Let I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx. Consider I^2:
I^2 = \left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx\right)\left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-y^2}, dy\right) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x^2+y^2)}, dx, dy
Convert to polar: x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta, dA = r, dr, d\theta:
I^2 = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2} r, dr, d\theta = 2\pi \int_0^\infty r e^{-r^2}, dr
Substitution u = r^2, du = 2r, dr:
= 2\pi \int_0^\infty \frac{1}{2} e^{-u}, du = 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \pi
Therefore I = \sqrt{\pi}. \blacksquare
Corollary: With substitution x = t/(\sigma\sqrt{2}): \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dt = \sigma\sqrt{2}\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx = \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}

The Normal Distribution
PDF: For X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2):
\boxed{f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}}
The normalization constant \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} is exactly \left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx\right)^{-1} = (\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}, derived above.
Mean: \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{x}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx
Substitute u = (x-\mu)/\sigma: = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{\sigma u + \mu}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-u^2/2} \sigma, du = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\underbrace{\int_{-\infty}^\infty u e^{-u^2/2}, du}_{=0 \text{ (odd)}} + \mu\underbrace{\int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-u^2/2}, du}_{=1} = \boxed{\mu}
Variance: \text{Var}(X) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx
Substitute u = (x-\mu)/\sigma: = \sigma^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty u^2 e^{-u^2/2}, du
Integration by parts: v = u, dw = u e^{-u^2/2}, du: \int_{-\infty}^\infty u^2 e^{-u^2/2}, du = \left[-u e^{-u^2/2}\right]_{-\infty}^\infty + \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2/2}, du = 0 + \sqrt{2\pi}
\text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} = \boxed{\sigma^2}

Example 7.1 — The 68-95-99.7 Rule (Exact Integrals)
For X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), using the error function \text{erf}(z) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_0^z e^{-t^2}, dt:
P(-k\sigma \le X \le k\sigma) = \text{erf}\left(\frac{k}{\sqrt{2}}\right)

























kP(\mu - k\sigma \le X \le \mu + k\sigma)Exact Integral1\approx 0.6827\text{erf}(1/\sqrt{2})2\approx 0.9545\text{erf}(\sqrt{2})3\approx 0.9973\text{erf}(3/\sqrt{2})
These cannot be expressed in elementary closed form — they require the error function, a non-elementary antiderivative defined by the integral. The Gaussian is the canonical example of a function whose integral is non-elementary but profoundly important.

8. Gamma Distribution
The Gamma Function: An Improper Integral
Definition: \boxed{\Gamma(n) = \int_0^\infty t^{n-1} e^{-t}, dt, \quad n > 0}
Key properties derived from integration:
(i) Recursion: \Gamma(n) = (n-1)\Gamma(n-1)
Proof: Integration by parts, u = t^{n-1}, dv = e^{-t}, dt: \Gamma(n) = \left[-t^{n-1}e^{-t}\right]_0^\infty + (n-1)\int_0^\infty t^{n-2}e^{-t}, dt = 0 + (n-1)\Gamma(n-1) \quad \blacksquare
(ii) Integer values: \Gamma(n) = (n-1)! for n \in \mathbb{N}
(iii) Half-integer: \Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}
Proof: \Gamma(1/2) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2}e^{-t}, dt. Let t = u^2: = \int_0^\infty u^{-1} e^{-u^2} \cdot 2u, du = 2\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}, du = \sqrt{\pi} \quad \blacksquare

Gamma Distribution PDF
PDF: X \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta):
f(x) = \frac{x^{\alpha-1} e^{-x/\beta}}{\beta^\alpha, \Gamma(\alpha)}, \quad x > 0
Normalization (substitution t = x/\beta): \int_0^\infty \frac{x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x/\beta}}{\beta^\alpha\Gamma(\alpha)}, dx = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^\infty t^{\alpha-1}e^{-t}, dt = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)} = 1 \quad \blacksquare
Mean: \mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{1}{\beta^\alpha\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^\infty x^\alpha e^{-x/\beta}, dx = \frac{\beta^{\alpha+1}\Gamma(\alpha+1)}{\beta^\alpha\Gamma(\alpha)} = \beta \cdot \alpha = \boxed{\alpha\beta}
Variance: \text{Var}(X) = \alpha\beta^2.

Special cases:

\alpha = 1: Exponential distribution (§6)
\alpha = n/2, \beta = 2: Chi-squared distribution with n degrees of freedom (\chi^2_n) — fundamental in statistics and ML regularization



9. Beta Distribution
PDF: X \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta) on [0,1]:
f(x) = \frac{x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}, \quad x \in [0,1]
where the Beta function is defined by requiring normalization:
B(\alpha,\beta) = \int_0^1 x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}, dx
Key identity (proven via Gamma functions): B(\alpha,\beta) = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}
Mean: \mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{B(\alpha+1,\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)} = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha+1)\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1)} = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
Variance: \text{Var}(X) = \frac{\alpha\beta}{(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}

Why Beta matters for ML: The Beta distribution is the conjugate prior for a Bernoulli/binomial likelihood. In Bayesian deep learning, Beta distributions appear in variational dropout, uncertainty quantification, and Thompson sampling.


Example 9.1 — Bayesian Update via Integration
Setup: A classifier’s accuracy \theta \sim \text{Beta}(2,2) (prior: slightly centered at 0.5). We observe 7 successes out of 10 trials. Find the posterior.
Posterior \propto Likelihood × Prior: p(\theta | \text{data}) \propto \theta^7(1-\theta)^3 \cdot \theta^{2-1}(1-\theta)^{2-1} = \theta^8(1-\theta)^4
This is proportional to \text{Beta}(9, 5).
Posterior mean (normalizing constant found by integration): \mathbb{E}[\theta | \text{data}] = \frac{9}{9+5} = \frac{9}{14} \approx 0.643
The normalization requires B(9,5) = \int_0^1 \theta^8(1-\theta)^4, d\theta = \frac{\Gamma(9)\Gamma(5)}{\Gamma(14)} = \frac{8! \cdot 4!}{13!} = \frac{40320 \times 24}{6227020800} = \frac{1}{6435}.

10. Joint Distributions & Marginals
Definitions
For jointly distributed (X, Y) with joint PDF f_{X,Y}(x,y):
P((X,Y) \in A) = \iint_A f_{X,Y}(x,y), dA
Marginal PDFs: \boxed{f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx}
Independence: X \perp Y iff f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x), f_Y(y) for all (x,y).
Covariance: \text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] = \iint xy, f_{X,Y}(x,y), dA - \mu_X \mu_Y

Example 10.1 — Joint Distribution on a Triangle
Setup: (X,Y) has joint PDF f(x,y) = 8xy on the region 0 \le y \le x \le 1 (a triangle).
Verify normalization: \int_0^1 \int_0^x 8xy, dy, dx = \int_0^1 8x \cdot \frac{x^2}{2}, dx = \int_0^1 4x^3, dx = [x^4]_0^1 = 1 \quad \checkmark
Marginal of X: f_X(x) = \int_0^x 8xy, dy = 8x \cdot \frac{x^2}{2} = 4x^3, \quad 0 \le x \le 1
Marginal of Y: f_Y(y) = \int_y^1 8xy, dx = 8y \cdot \frac{1-y^2}{2} = 4y(1-y^2), \quad 0 \le y \le 1
\mathbb{E}[X], \mathbb{E}[Y]: \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^1 x \cdot 4x^3, dx = \frac{4}{5}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[Y] = \int_0^1 y \cdot 4y(1-y^2), dy = \int_0^1 (4y^2 - 4y^4), dy = \frac{4}{3} - \frac{4}{5} = \frac{8}{15}
\mathbb{E}[XY]: \mathbb{E}[XY] = \int_0^1\int_0^x 8x^2y^2, dy, dx = \int_0^1 \frac{8x^5}{3}, dx = \frac{8}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \frac{4}{9}
\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \frac{4}{9} - \frac{4}{5}\cdot\frac{8}{15} = \frac{4}{9} - \frac{32}{75} = \frac{100 - 96}{225} = \frac{4}{225} > 0
Positive covariance makes sense: the triangle constraint Y \le X means larger X tends to come with larger Y.

Part III — Key Theorems That Need Integrals

11. Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS)
Theorem
If Y = g(X) and X has PDF f_X, then: \boxed{\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty g(x), f_X(x), dx}
You do not need the PDF of Y to compute \mathbb{E}[Y] — you compute directly using f_X.

Example 11.1 — Expected Squared Deviation
Setup: X \sim \text{Uniform}[0,1], g(X) = (X - 0.5)^4. Find \mathbb{E}[g(X)].
\mathbb{E}[(X-0.5)^4] = \int_0^1 (x-0.5)^4 \cdot 1, dx
Let u = x - 0.5: = \int_{-0.5}^{0.5} u^4, du = 2\int_0^{0.5} u^4, du = 2 \cdot \frac{u^5}{5}\Bigg|_0^{0.5} = \frac{2}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{32} = \boxed{\frac{1}{80}}

12. Moment Generating Functions
Definition
\boxed{M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{tx}, f_X(x), dx}
Why it’s powerful: M_X(t) encodes all moments: \mathbb{E}[X^n] = M_X^{(n)}(0) = \left.\frac{d^n}{dt^n}M_X(t)\right|_{t=0}
Proof: M_X(t) = \int e^{tx} f(x), dx = \int \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(tx)^n}{n!} f(x), dx = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n}{n!}\mathbb{E}[X^n]. Differentiating n times and setting t=0 extracts \mathbb{E}[X^n]. \blacksquare

Example 12.1 — MGF of the Normal Distribution
For X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2):
M_X(t) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{tx} \cdot \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx
Complete the square in the exponent: tx - \frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} = -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\left[x^2 - 2(\mu+\sigma^2 t)x + \mu^2\right] = -\frac{(x-(\mu+\sigma^2 t))^2}{2\sigma^2} + \mu t + \frac{\sigma^2 t^2}{2}
Therefore: M_X(t) = e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2} \cdot \underbrace{\int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-(\mu+\sigma^2 t))^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx}_{=1 \text{ (Normal PDF integrates to 1)}}
\boxed{M_X(t) = e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2 / 2}}
Extract moments: M_X'(t) = (\mu + \sigma^2 t), e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2} \implies M_X'(0) = \mu = \mathbb{E}[X] \quad \checkmark M_X''(t) = (\sigma^2 + (\mu+\sigma^2 t)^2), e^{\mu t+\sigma^2t^2/2} \implies M_X''(0) = \sigma^2 + \mu^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2] \quad \checkmark

13. Convolution of Independent Random Variables
Theorem
If X and Y are independent with PDFs f_X and f_Y, then Z = X + Y has PDF:
\boxed{f_Z(z) = (f_X * f_Y)(z) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_X(t), f_Y(z-t), dt}
Proof: The joint PDF of (X,Y) is f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y) (by independence). The CDF of Z = X+Y: F_Z(z) = P(X+Y \le z) = \iint_{x+y \le z} f_X(x)f_Y(y), dx, dy = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_X(x)\left(\int_{-\infty}^{z-x}f_Y(y), dy\right)dx
Differentiate with respect to z (FTC): f_Z(z) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_X(x), f_Y(z-x), dx = (f_X * f_Y)(z) \quad \blacksquare
This is the same convolution integral as signal processing (§8 of the physics note) — the mathematical structure is identical. The sum of independent random variables is the convolution of their distributions.

Example 13.1 — Sum of Two Exponentials
Setup: X, Y \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda) independent. Find the PDF of Z = X+Y.
f_Z(z) = \int_0^z \lambda e^{-\lambda t} \cdot \lambda e^{-\lambda(z-t)}, dt = \lambda^2 e^{-\lambda z} \int_0^z dt = \lambda^2 z e^{-\lambda z}, \quad z \ge 0
This is the Gamma(2, 1/\lambda) distribution. ✓
More generally: sum of n independent \text{Exp}(\lambda) → \text{Gamma}(n, 1/\lambda). The convolution integral, when applied n times, accumulates the factor from \frac{z^0}{0!} to \frac{\lambda^n z^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} e^{-\lambda z}.

Example 13.2 — Sum of Two Normals is Normal
Setup: X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2), Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2) independent. Show Z = X+Y is normal.
Via MGFs (much cleaner than direct convolution): M_Z(t) = M_X(t) \cdot M_Y(t) = e^{\mu_1 t + \sigma_1^2 t^2/2} \cdot e^{\mu_2 t + \sigma_2^2 t^2/2} = e^{(\mu_1+\mu_2)t + (\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)t^2/2}
This is the MGF of \mathcal{N}(\mu_1+\mu_2,, \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2). Since MGFs uniquely determine distributions: \boxed{Z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1+\mu_2,, \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)} \quad \blacksquare
The convolution integral in closed form would require the Gaussian integral machinery — the MGF approach works because the completing-the-square calculation (Example 12.1) was done once.

14. Change of Variables — The Jacobian
Theorem (1D)
If Y = g(X) is monotone and differentiable, and X has PDF f_X:
\boxed{f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot \left|\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\right|}
Derivation: F_Y(y) = P(Y \le y) = P(g(X) \le y). If g is increasing: = P(X \le g^{-1}(y)) = F_X(g^{-1}(y)). Differentiate via chain rule: f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot (g^{-1})'(y). \blacksquare
2D Theorem (MIT 18.02 L26): If (U, V) = \mathbf{g}(X, Y): f_{U,V}(u,v) = f_{X,Y}(x(u,v),, y(u,v)) \cdot |J| where the Jacobian: J = \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = \begin{vmatrix} \partial x/\partial u & \partial x/\partial v \ \partial y/\partial u & \partial y/\partial v \end{vmatrix}

Example 14.1 — Lognormal Distribution
Setup: X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2). Find the PDF of Y = e^X (lognormal).
g(x) = e^x \implies g^{-1}(y) = \ln y \implies (g^{-1})'(y) = 1/y.
f_Y(y) = f_X(\ln y) \cdot \frac{1}{y} = \frac{1}{y\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(\ln y - \mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}, \quad y > 0
Mean of lognormal (requires the MGF of the normal evaluated at t=1): \mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}[e^X] = M_X(1) = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}
The e^{\sigma^2/2} factor shows that the mean exceeds e^\mu — the log-normal is right-skewed. Used in: stock price models (Black-Scholes), income distributions, rainfall data.

Example 14.2 — Box-Muller Transform (How Computers Sample Gaussians)
Setup: U_1, U_2 \sim \text{Uniform}[0,1] independent. Define: Z_1 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\cos(2\pi U_2), \quad Z_2 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\sin(2\pi U_2)
Claim: Z_1, Z_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) independent.
Proof via Jacobian: Let R = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}, \Theta = 2\pi U_2. Then R^2 \sim \text{Exp}(1/2) (Chi-squared with 2 df) and \Theta \sim \text{Uniform}[0,2\pi].
Joint PDF of (R,\Theta): f_{R,\Theta}(r,\theta) = f_R(r) \cdot f_\Theta(\theta) = \frac{r}{1} e^{-r^2/2} \cdot \frac{1}{2\pi} = \frac{r}{2\pi}e^{-r^2/2}
Converting to (Z_1, Z_2) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) — polar to Cartesian: Jacobian = 1/r (inverse of Cartesian-to-polar Jacobian = r):
f_{Z_1,Z_2}(z_1,z_2) = \frac{r}{2\pi}e^{-r^2/2} \cdot \frac{1}{r} = \frac{1}{2\pi}e^{-(z_1^2+z_2^2)/2} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z_1^2/2}}_{f_{Z_1}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z_2^2/2}}_{f_{Z_2}}
The joint PDF factors → Z_1, Z_2 are independent \mathcal{N}(0,1). \blacksquare

This is how every numerical library (NumPy, PyTorch, TensorFlow) generates Gaussian random numbers. Every torch.randn() call uses a variant of this Jacobian calculation.


15. Conditional Expectation as an Integral
Definition
Conditional PDF of Y given X = x: f_{Y|X}(y|x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}
Conditional expectation: \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty y, f_{Y|X}(y|x), dy
Law of Total Expectation: \mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}_X[\mathbb{E}[Y|X]] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathbb{E}[Y|X=x], f_X(x), dx
This is a double integral — first integrate out Y at fixed x, then integrate over x. It is Fubini’s theorem in probabilistic clothing.

Example 15.1 — Regression Function
Setup: Joint PDF f(x,y) = 6xy^2 on 0 \le x \le 1, 0 \le y \le 1.
Marginal of X: f_X(x) = \int_0^1 6xy^2, dy = 6x \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 2x
Conditional PDF of Y|X=x: f_{Y|X}(y|x) = \frac{6xy^2}{2x} = 3y^2, \quad 0 \le y \le 1
(Independent of x — Y and X are independent here.)
Conditional expectation: \mathbb{E}[Y|X=x] = \int_0^1 y \cdot 3y^2, dy = \frac{3}{4}
The regression function is constant — as expected when X and Y are independent.

Part IV — ML & Deep Learning: Probability Integrals Everywhere

This section makes explicit what every deep learning textbook leaves implicit: the integral is the foundation.


ML.1 — Maximum Likelihood Estimation Is Integral Optimization
For i.i.d. data {x_i}_{i=1}^n from distribution p_\theta, the log-likelihood:
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(x_i) \approx n \int \log p_\theta(x), p_{\text{true}}(x), dx
This is an expected value integral under the true distribution. MLE maximizes the expected log-likelihood — the integral over data space. For continuous models (e.g., VAEs), this expectation cannot be computed exactly and is approximated by Monte Carlo (sample average), just as in §2/§3 above.

ML.2 — Information Entropy
Shannon entropy for a continuous distribution:
\boxed{H(X) = -\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\log f(x), dx}
Gaussian entropy (derived from integration):
H(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)) = -\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\log f(x), dx
= -\mathbb{E}\left[-\frac{(X-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)\right] = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) = \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\sigma^2)
(Used \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \sigma^2.)
Theorem: Among all continuous distributions on \mathbb{R} with fixed mean and variance, the Gaussian maximizes entropy — proven by calculus of variations on the entropy integral. This is why the Gaussian is the “most uncertain” distribution given second-moment constraints — a fact at the heart of maximum entropy models.

ML.3 — KL Divergence: The Distance Between Distributions
\boxed{D_{KL}(P | Q) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}, dx}
Non-negativity (Gibbs’ inequality) — proven by Jensen’s inequality applied to the integral:
D_{KL}(P|Q) = -\int p(x)\log\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}, dx \ge -\log\int p(x)\cdot\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}, dx = -\log 1 = 0
KL between two Gaussians (closed form from evaluating the integral):
D_{KL}(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)| \mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)) = \log\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1} + \frac{\sigma_1^2 + (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2} - \frac{1}{2}
This appears in VAE loss functions as the regularization term, forcing the encoder to match a standard Gaussian prior. The entire VAE training objective is:
\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)]}_{\text{reconstruction: } \int \log p_\theta \cdot q_\phi, dz} - \underbrace{D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) | p(z))}_{\text{two Gaussian integrals}}
Both terms are integrals.

ML.4 — The Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) is an Integral
In Variational Inference, we want \log p(x) but it requires an intractable integral:
\log p(x) = \log \int p(x|z), p(z), dz
We lower bound it (Jensen’s inequality on the integral):
\log p(x) \ge \int q(z)\log\frac{p(x,z)}{q(z)}, dz =: \text{ELBO}(q)
The ELBO is a functional of q — optimizing over it is variational calculus applied to integrals. This is the mathematical core of:

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
Bayesian Neural Networks
Diffusion Models (score matching is related)


ML.5 — Monte Carlo Integration: SGD as Approximate Integration
Problem: I = \int_\mathcal{X} f(x), p(x), dx = \mathbb{E}_p[f(X)]
Monte Carlo estimate: \hat{I}_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i), x_i \sim p.
Strong Law: \hat{I}_n \to I almost surely (law of large numbers).
Rate of convergence (Central Limit Theorem): \sqrt{n}(\hat{I}_n - I) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \text{Var}_p[f(X)])
Error \sim O(1/\sqrt{n}), independent of dimension. This is why Monte Carlo is preferred over numerical quadrature in high dimensions (quadrature error degrades exponentially with dimension — the “curse of dimensionality”).
SGD is mini-batch Monte Carlo integration of the gradient:
\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} = \int \nabla_\theta \ell(f_\theta(x), y), p(x,y), dx, dy \approx \frac{1}{B}\sum_{i \in \text{batch}} \nabla_\theta \ell(f_\theta(x_i), y_i)
Every SGD step is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimate of the true gradient integral.

ML.6 — The Reparameterization Trick: Differentiating Through an Integral
Problem: In a VAE, the encoder outputs q_\phi(z|x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi, \sigma_\phi^2) and we need:
\nabla_\phi \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[f(z)] = \nabla_\phi \int f(z), q_\phi(z|x), dz
Naive Monte Carlo can’t differentiate through the sampling step.
Reparameterization: Write z = \mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \varepsilon, \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1):
\int f(z), q_\phi(z|x), dz = \int f(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \varepsilon), \phi(\varepsilon), d\varepsilon
Now \phi(\varepsilon) is independent of \phi, so we can move \nabla_\phi inside the integral:
\nabla_\phi \int f(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \varepsilon), \phi(\varepsilon), d\varepsilon = \int \nabla_\phi f(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \varepsilon), \phi(\varepsilon), d\varepsilon
This is the Leibniz rule (differentiation under the integral sign), applied to make backpropagation through stochastic layers possible. Without this, VAEs cannot be trained.
Leibniz Rule (used here): \frac{d}{d\alpha}\int_a^b f(x, \alpha), dx = \int_a^b \frac{\partial f}{\partial \alpha}(x, \alpha), dx
(valid when \partial f/\partial\alpha is continuous and bounds a,b are independent of \alpha.)

ML.7 — Score Function & Fisher Information
The score function is: s(x; \theta) = \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x)
Fisher Information Matrix: \mathcal{I}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[s(x;\theta) s(x;\theta)^T] = \int \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x), (\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x))^T, p_\theta(x), dx
This is an integral of an outer product — a matrix-valued integral. It appears in:

Natural Gradient descent (K-FAC optimizer)
Score matching (diffusion models)
Cramér-Rao bound (fundamental lower bound on variance of any estimator)

Cramér-Rao Bound: \text{Var}(\hat\theta) \ge \mathcal{I}(\theta)^{-1}
The bound is an integral inequality — proven by applying Cauchy-Schwarz to the integral \int s(x;\theta), p_\theta(x), dx.

Master Formula Sheet
\text{(PDF normalization)}\quad \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x), dx = 1
\text{(Probability)}\quad P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x), dx
\text{(CDF)}\quad F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t), dt, \qquad f(x) = F'(x)
\text{(Mean)}\quad \mu = \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x, f(x), dx
\text{(LOTUS)}\quad \mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty g(x), f(x), dx
\text{(Variance)}\quad \sigma^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu^2 = \int x^2 f(x), dx - \left(\int x, f(x), dx\right)^2
\text{(Joint → Marginal)}\quad f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy
\text{(Convolution)}\quad f_{X+Y}(z) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_X(t), f_Y(z-t), dt
\text{(Change of variables)}\quad f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\left|\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\right|
\text{(MGF)}\quad M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] = \int e^{tx} f(x), dx
\text{(Entropy)}\quad H(X) = -\int f(x)\log f(x), dx
\text{(KL divergence)}\quad D_{KL}(P|Q) = \int p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}, dx
\text{(Gaussian integral)}\quad \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx = \sqrt{\pi}, \qquad \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx = \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}
\text{(Gamma function)}\quad \Gamma(n) = \int_0^\infty t^{n-1}e^{-t}, dt = (n-1)!, \qquad \Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}
\text{(Leibniz rule)}\quad \frac{d}{d\alpha}\int_a^b f(x,\alpha), dx = \int_a^b \frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha}(x,\alpha), dx
