01.Maths/Calculus/10.Parametric-Equation.title: 11.Symmetry in Polar Curves
01.Maths/Calculus/10.Parametric-Equation.content:
“Symmetry is not decoration — it is a theorem waiting to be used. Every symmetry you detect is half an integral you don’t have to compute.”


0. Why Symmetry Deserves Its Own Note
In Cartesian coordinates, symmetry tests are almost trivial: replace x \to -x or y \to -y and check if the equation is unchanged. In polar coordinates, the situation is genuinely more subtle — and more interesting. Because the polar representation of a point is non-unique, the failure of a symmetry test does not mean the symmetry is absent. A curve can possess a symmetry that no algebraic substitution reveals directly.
This is not a quirk to be swept under the rug. It is a precise mathematical phenomenon, and understanding it forces you to think carefully about the difference between a curve (a set of points) and its equation (a representation).

2. The Three Standard Symmetries
There are three symmetries that appear naturally in polar curve analysis, corresponding to the three fundamental reflections of the plane.
          y-axis (θ = π/2)
               |
               |
  ─────────────O─────────────  x-axis (polar axis)
               |
               |

  Three symmetry axes in polar geometry:
  1. About the polar axis (x-axis):      reflection (r, θ) ↦ (r, -θ)
  2. About the line θ = π/2 (y-axis):    reflection (r, θ) ↦ (r, π - θ)
  3. About the pole (origin):            reflection (r, θ) ↦ (-r, θ) or (r, θ + π)


3. Symmetry Tests: The Sufficient Conditions
For each symmetry, there is a sufficient algebraic test. These are conditions on the equation r = f(\theta) that guarantee the symmetry. Crucially, failing the test does not rule out the symmetry.

3.1 Symmetry About the Polar Axis (x-axis)
Geometric meaning. The curve is unchanged under the reflection (x, y) \mapsto (x, -y).
In polar terms: the reflection of (r, \theta) is (r, -\theta). Equivalently (using the non-uniqueness), (-r, \pi - \theta).
Sufficient Test.
\text{If } f(-\theta) = f(\theta), \text{ then the curve } r = f(\theta) \text{ is symmetric about the polar axis.}
Proof. If (r_0, \theta_0) lies on the curve, then r_0 = f(\theta_0). We need the reflected point (r_0, -\theta_0) to also lie on the curve. Indeed: f(-\theta_0) = f(\theta_0) = r_0. So (r_0, -\theta_0) satisfies r = f(\theta). \square
Secondary test (using non-uniqueness): If replacing (r, \theta) with (-r, \pi - \theta) leaves the equation unchanged, the curve is also symmetric about the polar axis.
Example. r = 1 + \cos\theta.
f(-\theta) = 1 + \cos(-\theta) = 1 + \cos\theta = f(\theta). ✓ Symmetric about polar axis.
Example. r = \cos(2\theta).
f(-\theta) = \cos(-2\theta) = \cos(2\theta) = f(\theta). ✓ Symmetric about polar axis.

3.2 Symmetry About the Line \theta = \pi/2 (y-axis)
Geometric meaning. The curve is unchanged under the reflection (x, y) \mapsto (-x, y).
In polar terms: the reflection of (r, \theta) is (r, \pi - \theta). Equivalently, (-r, -\theta).
Sufficient Test.
\text{If } f(\pi - \theta) = f(\theta), \text{ then the curve is symmetric about } \theta = \pi/2.
Proof. If (r_0, \theta_0) is on the curve, we need (r_0, \pi - \theta_0) on the curve. f(\pi - \theta_0) = f(\theta_0) = r_0. \square
Secondary test: replacing (r, \theta) with (-r, -\theta) leaves the equation unchanged.
Example. r = 1 + \sin\theta.
f(\pi - \theta) = 1 + \sin(\pi - \theta) = 1 + \sin\theta = f(\theta). ✓ Symmetric about \theta = \pi/2.
  Cardioid r = 1 + sinθ         Cardioid r = 1 + cosθ
  (opens upward, symmetric       (opens rightward, symmetric
   about y-axis)                  about x-axis)

         ♥                              ♥ rotated 90°
         |                           ────
    ─────O                              O


3.3 Symmetry About the Pole (Origin)
Geometric meaning. The curve is unchanged under the map (x, y) \mapsto (-x, -y), i.e., rotation by \pi.
In polar terms: the reflection of (r, \theta) through the pole is (-r, \theta), which is the same point as (r, \theta + \pi).
Sufficient Test.
\text{If } f(\theta + \pi) = f(\theta), \text{ then the curve is symmetric about the pole.}
Or equivalently: if replacing r with -r leaves the equation unchanged (i.e., f(-\theta) … actually: if -r = f(\theta) implies r = f(\theta), i.e., the equation is even in r).
More precisely:
\text{If } f(\theta + \pi) = f(\theta) \text{ for all } \theta, \quad \text{OR} \quad \text{if replacing } (r,\theta) \text{ with } (-r, \theta) \text{ leaves } F(r,\theta)=0 \text{ unchanged.}
Proof. Under f(\theta + \pi) = f(\theta): if (r_0, \theta_0) is on the curve, then (r_0, \theta_0 + \pi) represents the point diametrically opposite. f(\theta_0 + \pi) = f(\theta_0) = r_0, so this opposite point is also on the curve. \square
Example. r^2 = \cos(2\theta) (lemniscate of Bernoulli).
Replace r with -r: (-r)^2 = r^2 = \cos(2\theta). Equation unchanged. ✓ Symmetric about the pole.
Example. r = \cos(3\theta) (3-petal rose).
f(\theta + \pi) = \cos(3\theta + 3\pi) = \cos(3\theta)\cos(3\pi) - \sin(3\theta)\sin(3\pi) = -\cos(3\theta) \neq f(\theta) in general.
So the sufficient test fails. But the curve still has… wait. Let’s check: the 3-petal rose has 3 petals at 120° apart. It is symmetric about the polar axis (check: f(-\theta) = \cos(-3\theta) = \cos(3\theta) ✓), and about \theta = \pi/3 and \theta = 2\pi/3… but NOT about the pole. A 3-petal rose does not have 180° rotational symmetry — rotating by \pi maps petal to gap.

4. The Critical Subtlety: Sufficient ≠ Necessary
This is the heart of the matter. The three tests above are sufficient conditions. A curve can fail all three tests and still possess a symmetry, because the same geometric curve can be represented by multiple equations.
4.1 A Canonical Example
Consider r = \sin(2\theta) (a 4-petal rose).
Test for symmetry about the pole: f(\theta + \pi) = \sin(2(\theta+\pi)) = \sin(2\theta + 2\pi) = \sin(2\theta) = f(\theta). ✓ Passes.
Test for symmetry about polar axis: f(-\theta) = \sin(-2\theta) = -\sin(2\theta) \neq f(\theta) in general. ✗ Fails.
Yet clearly r = \sin(2\theta) is symmetric about the polar axis — the graph is a symmetric 4-petal rose. Why does the test fail?
Because when \theta is replaced by -\theta, we get r = -\sin(2\theta). This is not the same equation as r = \sin(2\theta). However, the point (-\sin(2\theta), \theta) in polar coordinates is the same geometric point as (\sin(2\theta), \theta + \pi). And \sin(2(\theta + \pi)) = \sin(2\theta). So the reflected point does lie on the curve — but you need the alternative representation to see it.
The correct procedure for r = \sin(2\theta) and polar axis symmetry:
The reflection of (r, \theta) is (r, -\theta). But equivalently it is (-r, \pi - \theta).
Check the second form: does r = -\sin(2(\pi - \theta))… actually let’s be systematic.
The reflected point (r_0, \theta_0) through the polar axis is (r_0, -\theta_0). For this to lie on the curve we need r_0 = \sin(-2\theta_0) = -\sin(2\theta_0). But r_0 = \sin(2\theta_0). So we need \sin(2\theta_0) = -\sin(2\theta_0), i.e., \sin(2\theta_0) = 0. This is not always true.
But! The point (r_0, -\theta_0) can also be written as (-r_0, \pi - \theta_0). Does (-r_0, \pi - \theta_0) lie on r = \sin(2\theta)?
We need -r_0 = \sin(2(\pi - \theta_0)) = \sin(2\pi - 2\theta_0) = -\sin(2\theta_0) = -r_0. ✓
Yes! So the reflected point, in its alternative representation, satisfies the equation. The symmetry is real; the naïve test just didn’t catch it because it only tried one representation.
Summary of what can happen:

  Algebraic test passes  →  Symmetry is definitely present. ✓
  Algebraic test fails   →  Symmetry may STILL be present.
                            Must check alternative representations.


5. Complete Decision Procedure
To rigorously determine whether r = f(\theta) is symmetric about the polar axis, you should check both forms:
About polar axis: symmetric if either

f(-\theta) = f(\theta) (primary), or
Replacing (r, \theta) by (-r, \pi - \theta) leaves the equation unchanged: -r = f(\pi - \theta) is equivalent to the original.

About \theta = \pi/2: symmetric if either

f(\pi - \theta) = f(\theta) (primary), or
Replacing (r, \theta) by (-r, -\theta): -r = f(-\theta) is equivalent to the original.

About the pole: symmetric if either

f(\theta + \pi) = f(\theta) (primary), or
Replacing r by -r leaves the equation unchanged: -r = f(\theta) implies r = f(\theta).


6. Important Logical Consequence
Proposition. If a curve has any two of the three symmetries, it automatically has the third.
Proof. Let S_1 = symmetry about polar axis, S_2 = symmetry about \theta = \pi/2, S_3 = symmetry about pole.
S_3 = (rotation by \pi) = (reflection in x-axis) \circ (reflection in y-axis) = S_1 \circ S_2.
So: S_1 and S_2 \Rightarrow S_3. Similarly, S_1 and S_3 \Rightarrow S_2, and S_2 and S_3 \Rightarrow S_1. \square
Practical use. If you establish polar axis symmetry and \theta = \pi/2 symmetry, you get symmetry about the pole for free.

7. Symmetry and Integration: The Payoff
The real value of symmetry in calculus is halving (or quartering) integrals.
Theorem. If r = f(\theta) is symmetric about the polar axis, then the area enclosed is:
A = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\pi [f(\theta)]^2, d\theta = \int_0^\pi [f(\theta)]^2, d\theta
instead of integrating over [0, 2\pi].
General principle. If the curve has an n-fold rotational symmetry (e.g., a 2n-petal rose), integrate over 1/n-th of the full period and multiply by n.
7.1 Example: Area of r = \cos(2\theta) (4-petal rose)
The rose r = \cos(2\theta) has 4-fold symmetry (symmetric about both axes and the pole). Compute the area of one petal, then multiply by 4.
One petal exists for \theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4] (where r \geq 0):
A_{\text{petal}} = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \cos^2(2\theta), d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \frac{1 + \cos(4\theta)}{2}, d\theta
= \frac{1}{4}\left[\theta + \frac{\sin(4\theta)}{4}\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = \frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{\pi}{4} + 0 - \left(-\frac{\pi}{4} + 0\right)\right] = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{8}
Total area = 4 \cdot \frac{\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{2}.
Without symmetry, you would integrate over [0, 2\pi] and carefully subtract the r < 0 contributions — far more error-prone.
7.2 Example: Area of a Limaçon r = 2 + \cos\theta
Symmetric about polar axis (f(-\theta) = 2 + \cos(-\theta) = 2 + \cos\theta):
A = \int_0^\pi (2 + \cos\theta)^2, d\theta = \int_0^\pi (4 + 4\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta), d\theta
= \int_0^\pi \left(4 + 4\cos\theta + \frac{1 + \cos(2\theta)}{2}\right)d\theta = \left[4\theta + 4\sin\theta + \frac{\theta}{2} + \frac{\sin(2\theta)}{4}\right]_0^\pi
= 4\pi + 0 + \frac{\pi}{2} + 0 = \frac{9\pi}{2}

8. Symmetry in Named Curves: A Complete Table





































































































CurveEquationPolar Axis\theta = \pi/2PoleNotesCircler = a✓✓✓All symmetriesCardioid (right)r = a(1+\cos\theta)✓✗✗Opens rightCardioid (up)r = a(1+\sin\theta)✗✓✗Opens upLimaçonr = b + a\cos\theta✓✗✗3-petal roser = \cos(3\theta)✓✗✗3-fold, not 2-fold4-petal roser = \cos(2\theta)✓✓✓All three4-petal roser = \sin(2\theta)✓*✓*✓*Test fails but symmetry holdsLemniscater^2 = a^2\cos(2\theta)✓✗✓Lemniscater^2 = a^2\sin(2\theta)✗✓*✓Archimedean spiralr = a\theta✗✗✗No symmetryLog spiralr = ae^{b\theta}✗✗✗Self-similar only
*Symmetry present but not detected by primary sufficient test alone.

9. n-fold Rotational Symmetry of Rose Curves
This deserves special treatment. The curve r = \cos(n\theta) has a rotational symmetry of order n (if n is odd) or 2n (if n is even):
Odd n: r = \cos(n\theta) has n petals. It has n-fold symmetry (invariant under rotation by 2\pi/n). It passes through the pole n times (once per petal).
Even n: r = \cos(n\theta) has 2n petals. It has 2n-fold symmetry. The extra petals arise because when r < 0, the point plots on the opposite side.
Why does even n double the petals?
At \theta \in [0, 2\pi], the function \cos(n\theta) takes both positive and negative values. When \cos(n\theta) < 0, we have r < 0, which plots the point in the direction \theta + \pi. So the “negative” values of r trace petals that the “positive” values didn’t. For even n, these negative petals fall in the gaps between the positive petals, yielding 2n total. For odd n, the negative petals overlap with the positive petals (same directions), yielding only n total.
r = cos(2θ): 4 petals          r = cos(3θ): 3 petals

     ✿                               ❧
  (even n)                        (odd n)
  negative r fills the gaps      negative r overlaps


10. Visualization: Symmetry Tests at a Glance

 │  Full area = ½∫₀²π r² dθ (no symmetry known)           │

 │    A = 2∫₀^(π/2) r² dθ  (one quadrant, ×4... check!)  │

 │  n-fold rose:                                           │
 │    A = n × (area of one petal)                          │

11. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
Symmetry in polar curves is not merely an analytic convenience. It is a special case of the pervasive principle of equivariance and invariance that structures modern deep learning.
11.1 Symmetry as a Form of Prior Knowledge
When we observe that r = f(-\theta) = f(\theta) (polar axis symmetry), we are encoding that the function does not depend on the sign of the angle — only the magnitude. This is a constraint on the function space. In ML terms:
A model is invariant to a transformation T if f(T(x)) = f(x). A model is equivariant to T if f(T(x)) = T'(f(x)) for some related transformation T'.
The polar axis symmetry of a loss function \mathcal{L}(\theta) (say, as a function of a 2D parameter) means the loss has the same value at conjugate angles — the optimizer can exploit this to reduce search space.
11.2 Symmetry and Data Augmentation
If the true data-generating distribution has polar axis symmetry (e.g., a physical system that is symmetric about a fixed axis), then data augmentation by reflection is valid and provably optimal. The augmented training set is the orbit of the data under the symmetry group.
This is exactly what is done in image classification: horizontal flips (axis symmetry), 90° rotations (4-fold symmetry), etc. The theory is: if the distribution has symmetry G, a model that is G-invariant requires exponentially less data than a generic model (Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory with symmetry constraints).
11.3 Symmetric Kernels
A kernel k(x, x') that depends only on |x - x'| is radially symmetric — it is symmetric about every axis through the origin in the difference space. The Gram matrix K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j) inherits this symmetry: it is symmetric (K = K^T), which is why SVMs and Gaussian Processes are PSD (positive semidefinite) by construction.
In polar terms: a kernel k(r) that is a function of r = |x - x'| alone is invariant under all rotations — the maximal possible symmetry in polar coordinates.
11.4 Even/Odd Decomposition and Neural Activation Functions
Any function can be decomposed into its even and odd parts:
f(\theta) = \underbrace{\frac{f(\theta) + f(-\theta)}{2}}_{\text{even part}} + \underbrace{\frac{f(\theta) - f(-\theta)}{2}}_{\text{odd part}}
The even part has polar axis symmetry; the odd part is anti-symmetric.
This decomposition appears directly in activation function analysis:

ReLU: \text{ReLU}(x) = \frac{x + |x|}{2}. The even part is |x|/2, the odd part is x/2. ReLU is neither even nor odd.
Tanh: an odd function (\tanh(-x) = -\tanh(x)). This means networks with tanh activations can represent odd functions exactly with one layer, but need extra width for even functions.
GELU and Swish: approximately odd near zero, breaking symmetry away from origin.

The Fourier features \cos(n\theta) (even, polar axis symmetric) and \sin(n\theta) (odd, anti-symmetric) form the complete basis for L^2([0, 2\pi]) — and their even/odd nature is exactly why they are mutually orthogonal.
11.5 Equivariant Neural Networks for Molecular Data
In molecular property prediction (drug discovery, materials science), molecules are described by 3D atomic coordinates. The energy of a molecule is invariant under rotation and reflection — it has full SO(3) \times \mathbb{Z}_2 symmetry (the symmetry group of a sphere in polar coordinates).
Models like SchNet, DimeNet, and SE(3)-Transformers are architecturally constrained to respect this symmetry. In spherical coordinates (r, \theta, \phi), the angular part decomposes into spherical harmonics Y_\ell^m(\theta, \phi) — the 3D generalization of the polar rose curves r = \cos(n\theta). An equivariant network maps spherical harmonic features to spherical harmonic features, preserving the symmetry exactly.
11.6 Summary





































Polar Symmetry ConceptML / DL Analoguef(-\theta) = f(\theta) (even function)Even activation, symmetric kernelf(\pi - \theta) = f(\theta) (axis symmetry)Equivariant to reflectionf(\theta + \pi) = f(\theta) (pole symmetry)Invariant to 180° rotationn-fold rose symmetry\mathbb{Z}_n-equivariant networkSufficient test fails but symmetry holdsImplicit symmetry from representationSymmetry → halved integralSymmetry → halved sample complexitySpherical harmonics = 3D polar modesSE(3)-equivariant GNNs (SchNet, DimeNet)

12. Worked Problem Bank
Problem 1. Determine all symmetries of r = 3 - 3\sin\theta.
Polar axis: f(-\theta) = 3 - 3\sin(-\theta) = 3 + 3\sin\theta \neq f(\theta). Secondary: -r = f(\pi - \theta)? 3 - 3\sin(\pi - \theta) = 3 - 3\sin\theta = f(\theta). That’s not -r = f(\pi-\theta)… Let’s just test: is (r, \pi - \theta) on the curve when (r, \theta) is? We need r = 3 - 3\sin(\pi - \theta) = 3 - 3\sin\theta ✓. So symmetric about \theta = \pi/2.
\theta = \pi/2: f(\pi - \theta) = 3 - 3\sin(\pi - \theta) = 3 - 3\sin\theta = f(\theta). ✓ Symmetric about \theta = \pi/2.
Pole: f(\theta + \pi) = 3 - 3\sin(\theta + \pi) = 3 + 3\sin\theta \neq f(\theta). No.
Answer: Symmetric about \theta = \pi/2 only (it is the upward-opening cardioid).

Problem 2. r^2 = 4\sin(2\theta). Find all symmetries.
Polar axis: Replace \theta \to -\theta: r^2 = 4\sin(-2\theta) = -4\sin(2\theta). Since r^2 \geq 0 and -4\sin(2\theta) can be negative, this is not the same. Secondary: replace (r, \theta) \to (-r, \pi - \theta): (-r)^2 = 4\sin(2(\pi - \theta)) = 4\sin(2\pi - 2\theta) = -4\sin(2\theta). Still not the same. ✗
\theta = \pi/2: f(\pi - \theta): r^2 = 4\sin(2(\pi-\theta)) = 4\sin(2\pi - 2\theta) = -4\sin(2\theta). ✗ Primary fails. Secondary (-r, -\theta): r^2 = 4\sin(-2\theta) = -4\sin(2\theta). ✗
Pole: Replace r \to -r: (-r)^2 = r^2. Equation unchanged. ✓ Symmetric about pole.
Answer: Symmetric about the pole only. (This lemniscate is tilted 45° relative to the standard one.)

Problem 3. Compute the total area enclosed by r = \sin(3\theta) using symmetry.
The 3-petal rose. Check: f(-\theta) = \sin(-3\theta) = -\sin(3\theta) \neq f(\theta). Secondary: -r = f(\pi - \theta): -r = \sin(3\pi - 3\theta) = \sin(3\pi)\cos(3\theta) - \cos(3\pi)\sin(3\theta) = 0 + \sin(3\theta). So -r = \sin(3\theta), i.e., the reflected point (-r, \pi - \theta) satisfies the equation r = \sin(3\theta) ✓ (since (-r, \pi-\theta) means r' = -r = \sin(3\theta) when we rename r' \to r… this requires care).
Actually let’s just note: \sin(3\theta) = 0 at \theta = 0, \pi/3, 2\pi/3, \pi, \ldots. Petals lie on \theta = \pi/6, \pi/2, 5\pi/6. The curve is symmetric about the y-axis (the test via (-r, -\theta): r = \sin(3\theta) and the reflected point (-r, -\theta): does -r = \sin(-3\theta) = -\sin(3\theta), i.e., r = \sin(3\theta) ✓). So symmetric about polar axis via this secondary form.
By symmetry, all 3 petals have equal area. Compute one petal on [0, \pi/3] (where r \geq 0):
A_{\text{petal}} = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin^2(3\theta), d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\int_0^{\pi/3}(1 - \cos(6\theta)), d\theta
= \frac{1}{4}\left[\theta - \frac{\sin(6\theta)}{6}\right]_0^{\pi/3} = \frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{\pi}{3} - 0\right] = \frac{\pi}{12}
Total = 3 \cdot \frac{\pi}{12} = \frac{\pi}{4}.

13. Summary
THREE SYMMETRIES IN POLAR COORDINATES:

  1. About polar axis (x-axis):
       Primary test:    f(-θ) = f(θ)
       Secondary test:  replacing (r,θ) with (-r, π-θ) preserves equation

  2. About θ = π/2 (y-axis):
       Primary test:    f(π-θ) = f(θ)
       Secondary test:  replacing (r,θ) with (-r, -θ) preserves equation

  3. About pole (origin):
       Primary test:    f(θ+π) = f(θ)  OR  replacing r with -r preserves equation

  KEY LOGICAL FACTS:
    • Any 2 of the 3 symmetries imply the 3rd
    • Failing primary test ≠ no symmetry (non-uniqueness of polar representation)
    • Always try both primary and secondary tests before concluding

  INTEGRATION PAYOFF:
    • 1 symmetry  →  integrate over half the domain, ×2
    • 2 symmetries →  integrate over quarter domain, ×4
    • n-fold rose  →  integrate one petal, ×n


References

MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.02 Multivariable Calculus. Problem sets on polar integration and symmetry. ocw.mit.edu


Weiler, M. & Cesa, G. (2019). General E(2)-Equivariant Steerable CNNs. NeurIPS. — The algebraic theory of equivariance in neural networks.


Schütt, K. T. et al. (2017). SchNet: A continuous-filter convolutional neural network for modeling quantum interactions. NeurIPS. — Radial symmetry in molecular ML.


Cohen, T. & Welling, M. (2016). Group Equivariant Convolutional Networks. ICML. — Foundation of equivariant deep learning.

01.Maths/Calculus/10.Parametric-Equation.title: 12.Tangents to Polar Curves
01.Maths/Calculus/10.Parametric-Equation.content:
“The derivative in polar coordinates is not a polar object — it is a Cartesian slope computed via a parametric detour. Understanding this detour is understanding the geometry.”


0. The Central Idea
A polar curve r = f(\theta) is not given as y = g(x). So “the slope of the tangent” is not immediately meaningful in polar language. The strategy:

Reparametrize. Treat \theta as the parameter, writing x(\theta) = f(\theta)\cos\theta and y(\theta) = f(\theta)\sin\theta.
Apply parametric differentiation. The slope of the tangent is dy/dx = (dy/d\theta)/(dx/d\theta).
Interpret geometrically. Horizontal tangents, vertical tangents, and the behavior at the pole all have clean geometric meanings.

Everything reduces to parametric curve theory — which means every theorem you proved for parametric curves applies here immediately.

1. Derivation of the Slope Formula
Let r = f(\theta), where f is differentiable. The Cartesian parametrization is:
x(\theta) = f(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y(\theta) = f(\theta)\sin\theta
Differentiate both with respect to \theta using the product rule:
\frac{dx}{d\theta} = f'(\theta)\cos\theta - f(\theta)\sin\theta
\frac{dy}{d\theta} = f'(\theta)\sin\theta + f(\theta)\cos\theta
By the parametric chain rule \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta}:
\boxed{\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{f'(\theta)\sin\theta + f(\theta)\cos\theta}{f'(\theta)\cos\theta - f(\theta)\sin\theta}}
or equivalently, writing r for f(\theta) and r' for f'(\theta):
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}
This is valid whenever the denominator is nonzero. Points where both numerator and denominator vanish require separate analysis (they correspond to singular points or the pole).
1.1 Verification Against Cartesian
For the horizontal line \theta = \pi/4 (i.e., y = x), we can write r = C/(\cos\theta - \sin\theta)^{-1}… this is awkward. Instead verify on a circle: r = a (constant), so f'(\theta) = 0.
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{0 \cdot \sin\theta + a\cos\theta}{0 \cdot \cos\theta - a\sin\theta} = \frac{a\cos\theta}{-a\sin\theta} = -\cot\theta
For the circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2, implicit differentiation gives 2x + 2yy' = 0 \Rightarrow y' = -x/y = -(a\cos\theta)/(a\sin\theta) = -\cot\theta. ✓

2. Horizontal Tangents
A horizontal tangent occurs where dy/dx = 0, i.e., the numerator vanishes while the denominator does not.
\frac{dy}{d\theta} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{dx}{d\theta} \neq 0
\Updownarrow
r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta \neq 0
Geometric meaning. The tangent line is parallel to the x-axis (polar axis). The curve has a local extremum in the y-direction.

3. Vertical Tangents
A vertical tangent occurs where dy/dx is undefined with a nonzero numerator:
\frac{dx}{d\theta} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{dy}{d\theta} \neq 0
\Updownarrow
r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta \neq 0
Geometric meaning. The tangent line is parallel to the y-axis. The curve has a local extremum in the x-direction.

4. Worked Example: Cardioid r = 1 + \cos\theta
This is the central example. We find all horizontal and vertical tangents and determine the tangent at the pole.
f(\theta) = 1 + \cos\theta, \quad f'(\theta) = -\sin\theta.
\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -\sin\theta \cdot \sin\theta + (1 + \cos\theta)\cos\theta = -\sin^2\theta + \cos\theta + \cos^2\theta
= \cos(2\theta) + \cos\theta
Using \cos(2\theta) = 2\cos^2\theta - 1:
\frac{dy}{d\theta} = 2\cos^2\theta + \cos\theta - 1 = (2\cos\theta - 1)(\cos\theta + 1)
\frac{dx}{d\theta} = -\sin\theta\cos\theta - (1+\cos\theta)\sin\theta = -\sin\theta(\cos\theta + 1 + \cos\theta) = -\sin\theta(1 + 2\cos\theta)
4.1 Horizontal Tangents
Set \frac{dy}{d\theta} = 0: (2\cos\theta - 1)(\cos\theta + 1) = 0.
Case 1: \cos\theta = 1/2 \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/3 or \theta = 5\pi/3.

\theta = \pi/3: r = 1 + 1/2 = 3/2. Check dx/d\theta = -(\sqrt{3}/2)(1 + 1) = -\sqrt{3} \neq 0. ✓

Cartesian: x = (3/2)\cos(\pi/3) = 3/4, y = (3/2)\sin(\pi/3) = 3\sqrt{3}/4.


\theta = 5\pi/3: r = 3/2. By symmetry: (3/4, -3\sqrt{3}/4).

Case 2: \cos\theta = -1 \Rightarrow \theta = \pi.

r = 1 + (-1) = 0. The curve is at the pole. Check: dx/d\theta = -\sin(\pi)(1 + 2(-1)) = 0. Both vanish — this is a singular point at the pole. Handle separately (see §6).

Horizontal tangents: at (3/4, \pm 3\sqrt{3}/4).
4.2 Vertical Tangents
Set \frac{dx}{d\theta} = 0: -\sin\theta(1 + 2\cos\theta) = 0.
Case 1: \sin\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = 0 or \theta = \pi.

\theta = 0: r = 2. Check dy/d\theta = (2(1) - 1)(1 + 1) = 1 \cdot 2 = 2 \neq 0. ✓

Cartesian: (2, 0).


\theta = \pi: r = 0. Both dy/d\theta and dx/d\theta vanish — singular point again.

Case 2: 1 + 2\cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta = -1/2 \Rightarrow \theta = 2\pi/3 or \theta = 4\pi/3.

\theta = 2\pi/3: r = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2. Check dy/d\theta = (2(-1/2)-1)(-1/2+1) = (-2)(1/2) = -1 \neq 0. ✓

Cartesian: x = (1/2)(-1/2) = -1/4, y = (1/2)(\sqrt{3}/2) = \sqrt{3}/4.


\theta = 4\pi/3: r = 1/2. By symmetry: (-1/4, -\sqrt{3}/4).

Vertical tangents: at (2, 0) and (-1/4, \pm\sqrt{3}/4).
Cardioid r = 1 + cosθ with tangent points marked:

              (3/4, 3√3/4)  ← horizontal tangent
                   •
                  / \
    VT •─────── /   \ ─────• (2,0) ← vertical tangent
  (-1/4, √3/4)  \   /
                  \ /
                   • ← cusp at pole (θ = π)
              (3/4,-3√3/4) ← horizontal tangent


5. Worked Example: Rose Curve r = \cos(2\theta)
f(\theta) = \cos(2\theta), \quad f'(\theta) = -2\sin(2\theta).
\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -2\sin(2\theta)\sin\theta + \cos(2\theta)\cos\theta
\frac{dx}{d\theta} = -2\sin(2\theta)\cos\theta - \cos(2\theta)\sin\theta
Finding horizontal tangents on the first petal (\theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4]):
Use double-angle identities \sin(2\theta) = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta, \cos(2\theta) = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta:
\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -4\sin\theta\cos\theta\sin\theta + (1-2\sin^2\theta)\cos\theta = \cos\theta(-4\sin^2\theta + 1 - 2\sin^2\theta)
= \cos\theta(1 - 6\sin^2\theta)
Setting to zero on (-\pi/4, \pi/4): either \cos\theta = 0 (not in range) or \sin^2\theta = 1/6, so \sin\theta = \pm 1/\sqrt{6}, giving \theta = \pm\arcsin(1/\sqrt{6}).
At \theta = \arcsin(1/\sqrt{6}): r = \cos(2\theta) = 1 - 2/6 = 2/3.
The tip of the petal is at \theta = 0: r = 1, and dy/d\theta = \cos(0)(1 - 0) = 1 \neq 0, dx/d\theta = 0 - \sin(0) = 0. So the petal tip has a vertical tangent, as expected by symmetry.

6. Tangents at the Pole
The pole (r = 0) requires special treatment. When r = 0 and f'(\theta) \neq 0, both x(\theta) and y(\theta) equal zero, and the formula for dy/dx becomes 0/0.
However, we can evaluate the limit:
\lim_{\theta \to \theta_0} \frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta} = \lim_{\theta \to \theta_0} \frac{f'(\theta)\sin\theta + f(\theta)\cos\theta}{f'(\theta)\cos\theta - f(\theta)\sin\theta}
At \theta = \theta_0 where f(\theta_0) = 0 and f'(\theta_0) \neq 0:
= \frac{f'(\theta_0)\sin\theta_0 + 0}{f'(\theta_0)\cos\theta_0 - 0} = \frac{\sin\theta_0}{\cos\theta_0} = \tan\theta_0
Theorem. If f(\theta_0) = 0 and f'(\theta_0) \neq 0, then the curve r = f(\theta) passes through the pole with tangent direction \theta = \theta_0.
Geometric interpretation. The tangent line at the pole is simply the ray at angle \theta_0. The curve departs the pole along the ray \theta = \theta_0 and returns along \theta = \theta_0 + \pi (if it passes through the pole again).
Corollary. If f(\theta_0) = f(\theta_1) = 0 for two distinct values \theta_0, \theta_1 \in [0, 2\pi), and f'(\theta_0), f'(\theta_1) \neq 0, then the curve crosses itself at the pole and the two tangent directions are \theta_0 and \theta_1.
6.1 Example: Rose r = \sin(2\theta)
The curve passes through the pole at \theta = 0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2.
f'(\theta) = 2\cos(2\theta).

\theta = 0: f'(0) = 2 \neq 0. Tangent direction \theta = 0 (positive x-axis).
\theta = \pi/2: f'(\pi/2) = 2\cos(\pi) = -2 \neq 0. Tangent direction \theta = \pi/2 (positive y-axis).
\theta = \pi: tangent direction \theta = \pi.
\theta = 3\pi/2: tangent direction \theta = 3\pi/2.

The four tangent lines at the pole are the coordinate axes — and they are mutually perpendicular, reflecting the 4-fold symmetry of the rose. ✓
6.2 Example: Cardioid r = 1 + \cos\theta at the Pole
f(\pi) = 0, f'(\pi) = -\sin(\pi) = 0. Both vanish! The cardioid is not smooth at the pole — it has a cusp. This is the characteristic shape of the cardioid’s pointed bottom.
To analyze the cusp, higher-order terms are needed (expand f(\theta) around \theta = \pi).
Smooth crossing at pole:              Cusp at pole:
  r = sin(2θ)                           r = 1 + cosθ

    \  |  /                                  |
     \ | /                                  /|\
      \|/     ← four tangent lines          / | \
  ────●────                              ───●───   (pole)
      /|\                                   |
     / | \                              tangent undefined
    /  |  \


7. The Angle \psi Between the Radius Vector and the Tangent
This is an elegant result not always covered in introductory courses, but it appears naturally and is worth knowing.
Definition. Let \psi be the angle from the radius vector \overrightarrow{OP} (the ray at angle \theta) to the tangent line at P, measured counter-clockwise.
Theorem.
\tan\psi = \frac{r}{dr/d\theta} = \frac{r}{r'}
Proof. The radius vector makes angle \theta with the polar axis. The tangent makes angle \phi with the polar axis, where \tan\phi = dy/dx. So \psi = \phi - \theta.
\tan\psi = \tan(\phi - \theta) = \frac{\tan\phi - \tan\theta}{1 + \tan\phi\tan\theta}
Substituting \tan\phi = \frac{r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta} and \tan\theta = \sin\theta/\cos\theta, after simplification:
\tan\psi = \frac{r}{r'} \qquad \square
Geometric consequences:

If r' = 0 at a point, then \tan\psi \to \infty, i.e., \psi = \pi/2: the tangent is perpendicular to the radius. This occurs at the tip of a rose petal (where r is maximum).
If r = 0 (at the pole), \tan\psi = 0, i.e., \psi = 0: the tangent coincides with the radius vector — confirming the theorem of §6.
For the equiangular (logarithmic) spiral r = ae^{b\theta}: r' = abe^{b\theta} = br, so \tan\psi = r/(br) = 1/b = \text{const}. The angle \psi is constant for all points on the spiral — this is the defining property of the logarithmic spiral.

The angle ψ:

         tangent line
        /
       /  ← ψ (angle between radius and tangent)
      /ψ
─────●──────────────→ radius vector (angle θ)
     P

For log spiral r = ae^{bθ}: ψ = arctan(1/b) everywhere.
Self-similar: the spiral "looks the same" from every point.


8. Second Derivative and Concavity
For completeness: the second derivative d^2y/dx^2 in polar coordinates. Since dy/dx is itself a function of \theta:
\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = \frac{\frac{d}{d\theta}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{d\theta}}
Let Q(\theta) = dy/dx (computed by the formula in §1). Then:
\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{Q'(\theta)}{dx/d\theta} = \frac{Q'(\theta)}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}
This is rarely needed in introductory work but appears in curvature calculations.
Curvature formula in polar. The signed curvature of r = f(\theta) is:
\kappa = \frac{r^2 + 2(r')^2 - rr''}{[r^2 + (r')^2]^{3/2}}
This follows from the parametric curvature formula \kappa = (x'y'' - y'x'')/[(x')^2 + (y')^2]^{3/2} applied to the polar parametrization.

9. Complete Worked Example: Limaçon r = 1 + 2\sin\theta
This limaçon has an inner loop (since |2| > |1|). Let’s find all tangents and understand the inner loop geometrically.
f(\theta) = 1 + 2\sin\theta, \quad f'(\theta) = 2\cos\theta.
\frac{dy}{d\theta} = 2\cos\theta\sin\theta + (1+2\sin\theta)\cos\theta = \cos\theta(2\sin\theta + 1 + 2\sin\theta) = \cos\theta(1 + 4\sin\theta)
\frac{dx}{d\theta} = 2\cos\theta\cos\theta - (1+2\sin\theta)\sin\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - \sin\theta - 2\sin^2\theta
= 2(\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta) - \sin\theta = 2\cos(2\theta) - \sin\theta
Horizontal tangents: \cos\theta(1 + 4\sin\theta) = 0.

\cos\theta = 0: \theta = \pi/2 or 3\pi/2.

\theta = \pi/2: r = 1 + 2 = 3. Check dx/d\theta = 2(-1) - 1 = -3 \neq 0. ✓ Point: (0, 3).
\theta = 3\pi/2: r = 1 - 2 = -1. r < 0: actual point is at distance 1 in direction 3\pi/2 + \pi = \pi/2, so (0, 1). Check dx/d\theta = 2(-1) - (-1) = -1 \neq 0. ✓


\sin\theta = -1/4: \theta = \pi + \arcsin(1/4) or \theta = -\arcsin(1/4) (i.e., 2\pi - \arcsin(1/4)).

At \theta = -\arcsin(1/4): r = 1 + 2(-1/4) = 1/2.
At \theta = \pi + \arcsin(1/4): r = 1 + 2(-1/4) = 1/2.



Inner loop. The inner loop forms when r < 0, which occurs when 1 + 2\sin\theta < 0, i.e., \sin\theta < -1/2, i.e., \theta \in (7\pi/6, 11\pi/6).
The inner loop passes through the pole at \theta = 7\pi/6 and \theta = 11\pi/6.
Tangent at pole for \theta = 7\pi/6: direction 7\pi/6 (i.e., 210°). Tangent at pole for \theta = 11\pi/6: direction 11\pi/6 (i.e., 330°).
These two tangent lines cross at the pole at angle |330° - 210°| = 120° to each other — the inner loop self-intersects at the pole with a 120° crossing angle.
Limaçon r = 1 + 2sinθ:

      (0,3) ← horizontal tangent
        •
       / \       outer loop
      /   \
─────●─────● ← (r=0 crossings, pole)
      \   /
       \_/   ← inner loop
       
The inner loop lives where r < 0 (θ ∈ (7π/6, 11π/6))
Self-intersection at pole, crossing angle = 120°


10. Summary Table of Procedures













































GoalConditionFormulaSlope of tangent at (r,\theta)General\dfrac{r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}Horizontal tangentdy/d\theta = 0, dx/d\theta \neq 0r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta = 0Vertical tangentdx/d\theta = 0, dy/d\theta \neq 0r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta = 0Tangent at pole (r=0)f(\theta_0) = 0, f'(\theta_0)\neq 0Tangent direction is \theta = \theta_0Cusp at polef(\theta_0) = 0, f'(\theta_0) = 0Not smooth; cuspAngle \psi (radius to tangent)General\tan\psi = r/r'CurvatureGeneral\kappa = \dfrac{r^2 + 2(r')^2 - rr''}{[r^2+(r')^2]^{3/2}}

11. Visualization
TANGENT VECTOR GEOMETRY IN POLAR:

      y
      |       P = (r, θ)
      |      •  ← tangent direction (slope = dy/dx)
      |     /|
      |    / |         The slope dy/dx is a Cartesian quantity,
      |   /  |         computed via the parametric chain rule.
      |  / ψ |
      | /    |
      |/ θ   |
      O──────────────→ x
      
      ψ = angle from radius OP to tangent at P
      θ = angle of radius OP from polar axis
      φ = θ + ψ = angle of tangent from polar axis

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

TANGENT AT THE POLE:

  If r = f(θ₀) = 0, f'(θ₀) ≠ 0:
  
        tangent = ray at angle θ₀
       /
      /  θ₀
  ───O──────────────→ polar axis
  (pole)
  
  The curve ENTERS the pole along θ₀ and DEPARTS along θ₀ + π.
  
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

THREE SCENARIOS AT r = 0:

  f(θ₀) = 0, f'(θ₀) ≠ 0  →  smooth pass through pole
  f(θ₀) = 0, f'(θ₀) = 0  →  CUSP (e.g., cardioid tip)
  f(θ₀) = f(θ₁) = 0      →  SELF-INTERSECTION at pole


12. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
The mathematics of tangent lines in polar coordinates connects to ML in ways that are structural, not cosmetic.
12.1 Gradient as a Tangent Object
In machine learning, the gradient \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} is the tangent direction of steepest ascent of the loss \mathcal{L} as a function of model parameters \theta. When the parameter space is naturally polar (e.g., phase angles in complex-valued networks, or directions in weight space), the formula for dy/dx in polar coordinates is literally the expression for how the loss changes as you move tangentially along a polar curve in parameter space.
More precisely: if the loss landscape restricted to a 2D subspace of parameter space is described by a polar curve r = f(\phi) (level set or gradient flow curve), then:
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\phi}\bigg|_{\text{tangent}} = \frac{dy/d\phi}{dx/d\phi} \cdot \cos\alpha - \sin\alpha
where \alpha encodes the parameterization choice. This is exactly the polar tangent formula in a different notation.
12.2 Loss Surface Curvature and \kappa
The curvature formula \kappa = \frac{r^2 + 2(r')^2 - rr''}{[r^2+(r')^2]^{3/2}} measures how rapidly the tangent direction rotates. In the loss landscape:

High curvature = sharp minimum = poor generalization (the Hessian has large eigenvalues).
Low curvature = flat minimum = better generalization.

SAM (Sharpness-Aware Minimization) explicitly seeks minima with small \kappa along all directions — i.e., it minimizes the maximum curvature of the loss surface, exactly the quantity \kappa measures in polar parametrizations of 2D cross-sections.
12.3 Logarithmic Spiral and Adam Optimizer
The logarithmic spiral r = ae^{b\theta} has constant \psi = \arctan(1/b) — the tangent makes a fixed angle with the radius at every point. This self-similar structure means the spiral “looks the same” at every scale.
The Adam optimizer update has a similar self-similar property: by normalizing the gradient by its running second moment, Adam implicitly adapts the step length to be proportional to the “radius” in parameter space from the initialization. The effective trajectory of Adam in a quadratic loss is approximately a logarithmic spiral toward the minimum — the angle \psi is governed by the ratio of the learning rate to the second-moment estimate.
12.4 Tangents and Decision Boundaries
A classification decision boundary f(x) = 0 in 2D can often be expressed in polar coordinates, especially for radially-structured data. The tangent to the decision boundary at a point P determines the local geometry of the margin.
For an SVM with RBF kernel, the decision boundary in polar coordinates near the support vectors behaves like a smooth polar curve. The condition for a support vector is that the margin is exactly 1 — geometrically, the tangent to the decision boundary at the support vector is perpendicular to the weight vector \mathbf{w}. In polar terms: \psi = \pi/2, i.e., r' = 0 (a petal tip condition).
12.5 Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK)
The Neural Tangent Kernel \Theta(x, x') = \nabla_W f_W(x) \cdot \nabla_W f_W(x') measures the inner product of gradients (tangent vectors) in parameter space. In the infinite-width limit, training a neural network is equivalent to kernel regression with kernel \Theta.
The tangent vector \nabla_W f_W(x) at input x is precisely the derivative of the output with respect to parameters — the “tangent direction” of the output function as the network moves through parameter space. The polar tangent formula computes the same object in a 2D parametric setting.
12.6 Summary Table





































Polar Tangent ConceptML / DL Analoguedy/dx via parametric chain ruleGradient via chain rule (backprop)Horizontal tangent: dy/d\theta = 0Gradient zero in output directionVertical tangent: dx/d\theta = 0Gradient zero in input directionCusp at pole: f = f' = 0Non-smooth loss (ReLU kink)\tan\psi = r/r' (equiangular spiral)Adam’s self-similar parameter updatesCurvature \kappaSharpness of loss minimum (SAM)Neural Tangent KernelInner product of polar tangent vectors

13. Exercises


(Stewart §10.3) Find the slope of the tangent to r = 2\sin\theta at \theta = \pi/6. Verify by converting to Cartesian form and differentiating implicitly.


Find all horizontal and vertical tangents to r = 2 + 2\sin\theta (cardioid opening upward). Classify the tangent at the pole.


(Rose) For r = \cos(3\theta), find the tangent direction at the pole for each passage through the origin. How many distinct tangent directions are there, and what angles do they make?


(Angle \psi) Show that for the Archimedean spiral r = a\theta (a > 0), \tan\psi = \theta. Describe geometrically what happens to \psi as \theta \to \infty.


(Lemniscate) For r^2 = a^2\cos(2\theta), find dr/d\theta implicitly, then compute dy/dx at \theta = \pi/6. What happens as \theta \to \pi/4?


(Curvature) Compute the curvature \kappa of the circle r = 2a\cos\theta at an arbitrary point and verify it equals 1/(a) (radius of circle = a, curvature = 1/a).


(ML-flavored) A 2D loss landscape restricted to a ray from the origin is described by r = 1 - e^{-\theta^2} (a curve that starts at the pole and approaches r = 1). Compute \tan\psi as \theta \to 0^+ and \theta \to \infty. Interpret: is the gradient direction aligned with or transverse to the radial direction at initialization (\theta \approx 0)?

01.Maths/Calculus/10.Parametric-Equation.title: 13.Graphing Polar Curves
01.Maths/Calculus/10.Parametric-Equation.content:
“Before you integrate, before you differentiate — you must see. A polar curve that you cannot sketch from its equation is a curve you do not yet understand.”


0. The Philosophy of Polar Graphing
In Cartesian coordinates, graphing y = f(x) is mechanical: sweep x left to right, plot height f(x). The geometry is transparent because the axes are the geometry.
In polar coordinates, graphing r = f(\theta) is genuinely different. As \theta increases, you rotate around the origin, and the curve is traced by a point at distance r(\theta) from the pole. When r < 0, the point appears on the opposite side of the pole. The curve can cross itself, loop back, retrace, and produce far more intricate shapes than the equation suggests.
The discipline required: You must think simultaneously about angle (direction) and radius (distance), and you must track the sign of r carefully. The reward is that a one-line equation like r = \cos(2\theta) produces a four-petalled rose — and once you understand why, no memorization is needed.

1. The Systematic Graphing Procedure
Here is the procedure I always follow, in order. Do not skip steps.
Step 1 — Check symmetry. Apply the three symmetry tests. Every symmetry you establish halves (or quarters) the work. (See: Symmetry in Polar Curves)
Step 2 — Find zeros and maximum |r|. Solve f(\theta) = 0 — these are the angles where the curve passes through the pole. Find \theta where |f(\theta)| is maximum — these are the farthest points from the pole.
Step 3 — Find where r changes sign. Between consecutive zeros of f, determine the sign of r. When r > 0, the point is in the direction \theta. When r < 0, it is in the direction \theta + \pi.
Step 4 — Build a table of key values. Evaluate r at \theta = 0, \pi/6, \pi/4, \pi/3, \pi/2, 2\pi/3, 3\pi/4, 5\pi/6, \pi and by symmetry fill in the rest. Add any special angles from Steps 2–3.
Step 5 — Plot the key points in polar form. Mark them on a polar grid (concentric circles at r = 1, 2, 3, \ldots and rays at multiples of \pi/6 or \pi/4).
Step 6 — Connect smoothly. Join the points with a smooth curve, respecting the direction of increasing \theta. Note where the curve is approaching or leaving the pole.
Step 7 — Verify with Cartesian conversion (optional). Convert special points to (x, y) and check they lie in the expected position.

2. Polar Graph Paper: The Mental Model
POLAR GRID (mental reference — commit this to memory):

              π/2 (90°)
               |
         2π/3  |  π/3
              \|/
    5π/6  ────•────  π/6
              /|\
        π ──•─O─•── 0 = 2π   ← polar axis
              \|/
    7π/6  ────•────  11π/6
              /|\
         4π/3  |  5π/3
               |
             3π/2 (270°)

Concentric circles: r = 1, 2, 3, ...
Rays at multiples of π/6 (30°) and π/4 (45°).

KEY QUADRANT FACTS:
  θ ∈ [0, π/2]:      1st quadrant  (r > 0 → upper right)
  θ ∈ [π/2, π]:      2nd quadrant  (r > 0 → upper left)
  θ ∈ [π, 3π/2]:     3rd quadrant  (r > 0 → lower left)
  θ ∈ [3π/2, 2π]:    4th quadrant  (r > 0 → lower right)

  r < 0 at angle θ → plots in OPPOSITE quadrant


3. Graphing Circles and Lines
These are the base cases — understand them completely before moving to more complex curves.
3.1 Circle r = a
All points at distance |a| from the pole. This is the circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2.
r = 2:

      ╭───╮
     │  O  │   radius 2, centered at pole
      ╰───╯

3.2 Circle r = 2a\cos\theta
Convert: r^2 = 2ar\cos\theta \Rightarrow x^2 + y^2 = 2ax \Rightarrow (x-a)^2 + y^2 = a^2.
Circle of radius |a|, centered at (a, 0). Passes through the pole (since r = 0 when \theta = \pi/2).
r = 2cosθ  (a = 1):

       ╭──╮
      │    │
   ─O─╯    ╰   center at (1, 0), radius 1
            
Traced once as θ goes from -π/2 to π/2.
At θ = π/2 or -π/2: r = 0 (at the pole).
At θ = 0: r = 2 (rightmost point).

3.3 Circle r = 2a\sin\theta
Similarly: (x)^2 + (y-a)^2 = a^2. Circle centered at (0, a), passes through pole.
3.4 Line \theta = \alpha
All points at angle \alpha from the polar axis, for any r (including r < 0, giving the opposite ray). This is the full line through the pole at angle \alpha.
3.5 Line r = \frac{d}{\cos(\theta - \alpha)}
A line at perpendicular distance d from the pole, with the perpendicular foot in direction \alpha.

4. Graphing Limaçons: r = b \pm a\cos\theta or r = b \pm a\sin\theta
The limaçon family is controlled by the ratio k = a/b:

























ConditionShapek < 1 (i.e., a < b)Convex limaçon (no dimple, no loop)k = 1 (i.e., a = b)Cardioid1 < k < 2Limaçon with inner dimplek \geq 2 (i.e., a \geq 2b)Limaçon with inner loop
4.1 Full Analysis: Cardioid r = 1 + \cos\theta
Symmetry: f(-\theta) = 1 + \cos\theta = f(\theta) → symmetric about polar axis.
Zeros: r = 0 when \cos\theta = -1, i.e., \theta = \pi. Passes through pole once.
Maximum: r = 2 at \theta = 0.
Key values (upper half only, by symmetry):





















































\thetar = 1 + \cos\thetaApproxCartesian (x, y)022.00(2, 0)\pi/61 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}1.87(1.62, 0.93)\pi/33/21.50(0.75, 1.30)\pi/211.00(0, 1)2\pi/31/20.50(-0.25, 0.43)5\pi/61 - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}0.13(-0.11, 0.07)\pi00(0, 0) ← pole
Graphing narrative:

Start at \theta = 0: point (2, 0), the rightmost tip.
As \theta increases from 0 to \pi: r decreases from 2 to 0. The point spirals inward counter-clockwise, tracing the upper half of the cardioid.
At \theta = \pi: arrives at the pole, forming a cusp (since f'(\pi) = -\sin(\pi) = 0).
From \theta = \pi to 2\pi: by symmetry with the upper half, the lower half is traced.

Cardioid r = 1 + cosθ:

            (0,1)
             •
           /   \
         /       \
(-.25,.43)•      •(2,0)    ← maximum radius
         \       /
           \   /
             •
           (pole, cusp)
           
Shape: like a heart, cusp pointing LEFT,
       maximum extent to the RIGHT.

4.2 Full Analysis: Limaçon with Inner Loop r = 1 + 2\cos\theta
Here a/b = 2 > 1, so there is an inner loop.
Zeros: r = 0 when \cos\theta = -1/2, i.e., \theta = 2\pi/3 and \theta = 4\pi/3.
Sign of r:

\theta \in [0, 2\pi/3): \cos\theta > -1/2, so r > 0.
\theta \in (2\pi/3, 4\pi/3): \cos\theta < -1/2, so r < 0 → inner loop (points reflect through pole).
\theta \in (4\pi/3, 2\pi]: r > 0 again.

Maximum: r = 3 at \theta = 0. Inner loop maximum: |r| = 1 at \theta = \pi (r = -1, so |r| = 1).



























































\thetarSignDirection plotted03+\theta = 0\pi/32+\theta = \pi/3\pi/21+\theta = \pi/22\pi/30—pole5\pi/6-\sqrt{3}+1 \approx -0.73-\theta = 5\pi/6 + \pi = 11\pi/6\pi-1-\theta = 0 (inner loop on pos. x-axis)7\pi/6-\sqrt{3}+1-\theta = \pi/64\pi/30—pole
Inner loop narrative:
When \theta \in (2\pi/3, 4\pi/3), we have r < 0. The point plots at angle \theta + \pi, with distance |r| from the pole. So:

At \theta = \pi: r = -1, point at (-(-1), \pi + \pi) = (1, 0) in polar → the Cartesian point (1, 0). This is inside the outer loop.

The inner loop is traced as \theta sweeps from 2\pi/3 to 4\pi/3, but the actual point moves in the angular range [2\pi/3 + \pi, 4\pi/3 + \pi] = [5\pi/3, 7\pi/3], i.e., back around the right side of the plane.
Limaçon r = 1 + 2cosθ:

         outer loop
        ╭────────╮
       │           │
  ─────●─────────────●────  (r=3)
       │   ╭───╮   │
        ╰──│   │──╯
           ╰───╯
           inner loop
           (traced when r < 0)
           
Outer loop: r > 0, θ ∈ [0,2π/3] ∪ [4π/3, 2π]
Inner loop: r < 0, θ ∈ [2π/3, 4π/3]


5. Graphing Rose Curves: r = a\cos(n\theta) and r = a\sin(n\theta)
The petal count rule:

n odd: n petals.
n even: 2n petals.

Why? (See the rigorous argument in Symmetry in Polar Curves.)
For odd n: when r < 0 during \theta \in (\pi/(2n), 3\pi/(2n)) etc., the negative-r portions retrace petals that were already drawn with r > 0, just approached from the opposite direction.
For even n: the negative-r portions draw new petals in the gaps, doubling the count.
5.1 Full Analysis: 4-Petal Rose r = \cos(2\theta)
Symmetry: f(-\theta) = \cos(-2\theta) = \cos(2\theta) → about polar axis. f(\pi - \theta) = \cos(2\pi - 2\theta) = \cos(2\theta) → about \theta = \pi/2. By the proposition (any two → all three): also about the pole.
Zeros: \cos(2\theta) = 0 \Rightarrow 2\theta = \pi/2 + k\pi \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/4, 3\pi/4, 5\pi/4, 7\pi/4. Four zeros → four passages through the pole.
Maxima: r = \pm 1 at \theta = 0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2.
Sign analysis over [0, 2\pi]:















































\theta interval2\theta interval\cos(2\theta)r signPetal[0, \pi/4][0, \pi/2]++Petal 1 (right)[\pi/4, 3\pi/4][\pi/2, 3\pi/2]--Petal 2* (upper, via r<0)[3\pi/4, 5\pi/4][3\pi/2, 5\pi/2]++Petal 3 (left)[5\pi/4, 7\pi/4][5\pi/2, 7\pi/2]--Petal 4* (lower, via r<0)[7\pi/4, 2\pi][7\pi/2, 4\pi]++Returns to Petal 1
*Petals 2 and 4 are drawn with r < 0. At \theta = \pi/2, r = \cos(\pi) = -1, so the point is at distance 1 in direction \pi/2 + \pi = 3\pi/2 — the downward direction. But by the full sign table, the upper petal (r < 0, \theta \in [\pi/4, 3\pi/4]) actually traces upward since the reflected direction points upward.
Let me be explicit. At \theta = \pi/2: r = -1. Point: distance 1, direction \pi/2 + \pi = 3\pi/2. That is (0, -1) in Cartesian — downward, not upward. So the petal drawn during \theta \in [\pi/4, 3\pi/4] with r < 0 is actually the downward petal (Petal 4), not the upper one.
Wait — let’s redo this carefully.
At \theta = \pi/2: r = \cos(\pi) = -1 → point at (|r|, \theta + \pi) = (1, 3\pi/2) → Cartesian (0, -1).
So during \theta \in [\pi/4, 3\pi/4]: r < 0, actual direction = \theta + \pi \in [5\pi/4, 7\pi/4] — the lower half. This draws the bottom two petals.
The full tracing order:

\theta \in [0, \pi/4]: Right petal traced outward.
\theta \in [\pi/4, 3\pi/4]: r < 0 → bottom two petals partially traced.
\theta \in [3\pi/4, 5\pi/4]: Left petal.
\theta \in [5\pi/4, 7\pi/4]: r < 0 → top two petals partially traced.
\theta \in [7\pi/4, 2\pi]: Back to right petal start.

The standard description (right, top, left, bottom petals at \theta = 0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2) is correct; it’s the order of tracing that requires care.
4-petal rose r = cos(2θ):

         top petal
            •
            |
left  •──── O ────•  right
  petal     |      petal
            •
         bottom petal

Petal tips at θ = 0 (right), π/2 (top? — check!),
π (left), 3π/2 (bottom).

At θ = π/2: r = cos(π) = -1 → point at (1, 3π/2) = (0,-1).
So the petal at θ = π/2 is actually the BOTTOM petal (via r < 0).
The TOP petal is traced at θ = 3π/2: r = cos(3π) = -1 → (1, π/2) = (0,1). ✓

5.2 Full Analysis: 3-Petal Rose r = \cos(3\theta)
Zeros: 3\theta = \pi/2 + k\pi \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/6, \pi/2, 5\pi/6, 7\pi/6, 3\pi/2, 11\pi/6.
Six passages through the pole during [0, 2\pi].
Sign over [0, \pi] (then check if lower half retraces):






























\thetar = \cos(3\theta)Sign[0, \pi/6]positive+ → Petal 1 (right)[\pi/6, \pi/2]negative- → points in [\pi/6+\pi, \pi/2+\pi] = [7\pi/6, 3\pi/2][\pi/2, 5\pi/6]positive+ → Petal 2 (upper left)[5\pi/6, \pi]negative- → points in [5\pi/6+\pi, 2\pi] = [11\pi/6, 2\pi]
During \theta \in [\pi/6, \pi/2] with r < 0: actual direction \in [7\pi/6, 3\pi/2] (lower left to downward). This traces the lower left petal (Petal 3’s bottom half).
For odd n = 3: petals lie at \theta = 0, 2\pi/3, 4\pi/3 (where r = 1). The three petals are equally spaced at 120°. The r < 0 segments retrace each petal from the other side, not creating new petals.
3-petal rose r = cos(3θ):

      Petal 2 ↗
         •
        / \
       /   \
   ───O─────•──  Petal 1 (θ=0, r=1, point at (1,0))
       \   /
        \ /
         •
      Petal 3 ↘

Petals at angles 0°, 120°, 240°.
Each petal has length r = 1.
Odd n → n petals (the r<0 portions retrace existing petals).

5.3 The General Rose r = a\cos(n\theta): Key Facts Summary
ROSE CURVE FACTS:
                                                  
  r = a·cos(nθ):                                  
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  n odd:  n petals, each of length a         │
  │          Petals at θ = 0, 2π/n, 4π/n, ...  │
  │          Symmetric about polar axis         │
  │                                             │
  │  n even: 2n petals, each of length a        │
  │          Petals at θ = 0, π/n, 2π/n, ...   │
  │          Symmetric about BOTH axes + pole   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  r = a·sin(nθ):  same counts, but ROTATED by π/(2n)
  
  Area of ONE petal = πa²/(4n)   [derive via ½∫r²dθ]
  Total area:
    n odd:  n · πa²/(4n) = πa²/4
    n even: 2n · πa²/(4n) = πa²/2


6. Graphing the Lemniscate: r^2 = a^2\cos(2\theta)
This is qualitatively different — r^2 rather than r, so r is only defined where \cos(2\theta) \geq 0.
Domain: \cos(2\theta) \geq 0 \Leftrightarrow 2\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2] \cup [3\pi/2, 5\pi/2] \Leftrightarrow \theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4] \cup [3\pi/4, 5\pi/4].
The curve simply does not exist for \theta \in (\pi/4, 3\pi/4) \cup (5\pi/4, 7\pi/4).
Graphing:

At \theta = 0: r = a. Rightmost point (a, 0).
As \theta \to \pi/4: r \to 0. Arrives at pole.
The curve traces the right lobe for \theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4].
For \theta \in [3\pi/4, 5\pi/4]: traces the left lobe.

Lemniscate r² = a²cos(2θ):

        does not     does not
        exist here   exist here
          ↓               ↓
  ←──────── (π/4 to 3π/4: no curve) ────────→
  
Left lobe:  •────────────O────────────•  Right lobe
  (traced                             (traced
  θ∈[3π/4,5π/4])                    θ∈[-π/4, π/4])
  
Figure-eight shape. Each lobe is a closed curve
passing through the pole.
Resembles the symbol ∞.

Cartesian form: r^4 = a^2 r^2 \cos(2\theta) = a^2(r^2\cos^2\theta - r^2\sin^2\theta) = a^2(x^2 - y^2). Since r^2 = x^2 + y^2: (x^2 + y^2)^2 = a^2(x^2 - y^2).

7. Graphing Spirals
7.1 Archimedean Spiral r = a\theta, \theta \geq 0

r increases linearly with \theta. Each full revolution (\Delta\theta = 2\pi) increases r by 2\pi a.
The spacing between successive arms is constant: \Delta r = 2\pi a.

Archimedean spiral r = θ (a=1):

         r increases by 2π per revolution
         
         ╭──────╮
        ╱    ╭──╯
       │    ╱
       ╰───O──────→
       
Arms equally spaced: Δr = 2π between adjacent arms.
No symmetry (r ≠ f(-θ) since θ ≥ 0 changes domain).

7.2 Logarithmic Spiral r = ae^{b\theta}

For b > 0: expands outward.
For b < 0: contracts toward the pole.
Self-similar: \tan\psi = 1/b is constant — the curve cuts every ray at the same angle.
As \theta \to -\infty (for b > 0): r \to 0, spiraling into the pole infinitely.

Log spiral r = e^{0.1θ}:

Arms get farther apart exponentially.
Same shape at every scale (self-similar).
        
        ╭────────╮
       ╱    ╭───╯
      │   ╭─╯
      ╰──O
      
The golden spiral (nautilus shell) is a log spiral.


8. A Systematic Graphing Example: r = 2\sin(3\theta)
This is a 3-petal rose (odd n = 3), using sine instead of cosine, so it is rotated.
Step 1 — Symmetry.
f(\pi - \theta) = 2\sin(3\pi - 3\theta) = 2\sin(3\pi)\cos(3\theta) - 2\cos(3\pi)\sin(3\theta) = 0 + 2\sin(3\theta) = f(\theta). ✓ Symmetric about \theta = \pi/2.
Step 2 — Zeros. 2\sin(3\theta) = 0 \Rightarrow 3\theta = k\pi \Rightarrow \theta = 0, \pi/3, 2\pi/3, \pi, 4\pi/3, 5\pi/3.
Step 3 — Sign.















































\theta interval\sin(3\theta)rActual direction(0, \pi/3)+> 0Same as \theta(\pi/3, 2\pi/3)-< 0\theta + \pi(2\pi/3, \pi)+> 0Same as \theta(\pi, 4\pi/3)-< 0\theta + \pi(4\pi/3, 5\pi/3)+> 0Same as \theta(5\pi/3, 2\pi)-< 0\theta + \pi
For odd n: positive-r intervals trace petals; negative-r intervals retrace those same petals from the other direction. Only 3 distinct petals.
Step 4 — Maximum r = 2 at 3\theta = \pi/2, 5\pi/2, 9\pi/2, i.e., \theta = \pi/6, 5\pi/6, 3\pi/2.
Petal tips: (\pi/6, 2), (5\pi/6, 2), (3\pi/2, 2).
In Cartesian:

\theta = \pi/6: (2\cos(\pi/6), 2\sin(\pi/6)) = (\sqrt{3}, 1).
\theta = 5\pi/6: (-\sqrt{3}, 1).
\theta = 3\pi/2: (0, -2).

Step 5 — Key values table:





































\thetar00\pi/62\pi/30\pi/2-2 (i.e., actual point (0, 2) — wait: r = 2\sin(3\pi/2) = 2(-1) = -2; point at direction \pi/2 + \pi = 3\pi/2, distance 2 → (0, -2))2\pi/305\pi/62\pi0
Step 6 — Sketch:
3-petal rose r = 2sin(3θ):

         • (-√3, 1)    • (√3, 1)
          \           /
      petal 2       petal 1
            \       /
             ──O──
                |
             petal 3
                •
              (0, -2)

Symmetry: about θ = π/2 (y-axis). ✓
Petals are at 30°, 150°, 270° (tilted vs r = cos(3θ) which has petals at 0°, 120°, 240°).


9. Recognizing Curve Type from Equation: A Quick Reference
Before graphing, identify the curve type from the equation’s structure:
EQUATION RECOGNITION GUIDE:

  r = a                         → Circle (center at pole)
  r = 2a·cosθ or r = 2a·sinθ   → Circle (through pole)
  r = a ± b·cosθ (or sinθ)     → Limaçon family:
       a = b  →  Cardioid
       a > b  →  Convex/dimpled limaçon
       a < b  →  Limaçon with inner loop
  r = a·cos(nθ) or a·sin(nθ)   → Rose curve:
       n odd  →  n petals
       n even →  2n petals
  r² = a²·cos(2θ)               → Lemniscate (figure-eight)
  r² = a²·sin(2θ)               → Lemniscate (rotated 45°)
  r = aθ                        → Archimedean spiral
  r = ae^{bθ}                   → Logarithmic spiral
  r·cosθ = a  (i.e., x = a)    → Vertical line
  r·sinθ = b  (i.e., y = b)    → Horizontal line


10. Common Graphing Errors and How to Avoid Them
Error 1: Ignoring r < 0.
The most common mistake. When r < 0, the point is NOT at (\text{negative distance}, \theta) — it is at (|r|, \theta + \pi). Always check the sign of r in each interval.
Fix: In your sign table, explicitly write the “actual direction” column as in §8.
Error 2: Wrong petal count on rose curves.
Students often say ”r = \cos(4\theta) has 4 petals” when it has 8.
Fix: Memorize the rule — even n gives 2n petals. Alternatively, find all zeros of r in [0, 2\pi] and count: r = \cos(n\theta) = 0 at 2n values of \theta, and consecutive zeros bound one petal each.
Error 3: Conflating the parameter interval with the full curve.
For r = \cos(2\theta), the full curve is traced as \theta \in [0, 2\pi]. For r = \cos\theta, the full circle is traced in \theta \in [0, \pi] (the second half retraces).
Fix: Find the period of r = f(\theta). For f(\theta) = \cos(n\theta), the period is 2\pi/n. Trace over [0, 2\pi] but note when retracing begins.
Error 4: Missing the symmetry → overworking.
Students compute all of [0, 2\pi] when they could exploit symmetry to do half.
Fix: Always run the symmetry check first. Symmetric about polar axis → compute [0, \pi] and reflect.
Error 5: Incorrect orientation of rotated curves.
r = a\cos\theta → circle on the right of the pole. r = a\sin\theta → circle on top. r = a\cos(n\theta) → first petal along positive x-axis. r = a\sin(n\theta) → first petal rotated by \pi/(2n).
Fix: The cos-version always has a feature on the polar axis. The sin-version is the cos-version rotated by \pi/(2n) (for rose) or \pi/2 (for cardioid).

11. Visualization Gallery
POLAR CURVE GALLERY:

  r = 1 + cosθ          r = 1 + 2cosθ          r = 2 + cosθ
  (cardioid)            (inner loop limaçon)    (convex limaçon)
  
       ♥                   ⊃⊂                       ⊃
   cusp at               inner loop              no dimple
   θ = π                 on right                smooth
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  r = cos(2θ)           r = cos(3θ)            r = cos(4θ)
  (4-petal rose)        (3-petal rose)          (8-petal rose)

       ✿                    ❧                      ✾
   4 petals              3 petals               8 petals
   (n even → 2n)         (n odd → n)            (n even → 2n)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  r² = cos(2θ)          r = θ                  r = e^{0.1θ}
  (lemniscate)          (Archimedean)           (log spiral)

       ∞                    🌀                      🌀
   figure-eight          equal spacing           exp spacing
   two lobes              between arms            self-similar


12. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
12.1 Polar Graphs as Visualization Tools in ML
In ML model evaluation, radar charts (also called spider charts or polar charts) are direct applications of polar graphing: each metric (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC) is assigned an angular direction, and performance is plotted as a polar curve. Comparing two models is equivalent to asking which polar region is larger — the area formula A = \frac{1}{2}\int r^2, d\theta quantifies this.
12.2 Feature Map Visualization via Rose Patterns
In convolutional neural networks, filters in the first layer learn oriented features — edges at various angles. Visualizing the orientation tuning of a neuron as a polar plot (response r as a function of angle \theta of the input edge) produces a rose-like curve. A neuron tuned to a single orientation produces a 2-petal rose (r = \cos^2\theta roughly); a neuron with broader tuning produces a more circular plot.
This is not metaphor — it is literally how orientation tuning curves are displayed in computational neuroscience and CNN interpretability research.
12.3 Limaçon-Shaped Decision Boundaries
A linear classifier has a straight-line decision boundary. A kernel SVM or a neural network can produce curved boundaries. In polar coordinates centered at a cluster center, a smooth convex boundary looks like a limaçon (cardioid when the boundary passes through the origin; convex limaçon when it doesn’t). Classifiers that produce boundaries with inner loops effectively create “islands” of one class inside the other — the inner loop encloses a pocket of the positive class inside the negative class.
12.4 Lemniscate and Information Geometry
The lemniscate r^2 = a^2\cos(2\theta) satisfies (x^2 + y^2)^2 = a^2(x^2 - y^2). In information geometry, the Fisher information metric on a family of probability distributions can produce level curves with this shape near saddle points of the KL divergence. The lemniscate’s figure-eight form means there are two “basins” of nearby distributions, meeting at a point (the pole) — a geometric picture of bimodal model families.
12.5 Spiral Dynamics in Gradient Descent
The trajectory of gradient descent with momentum in a 2D quadratic loss \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{2}(\lambda_1 w_1^2 + \lambda_2 w_2^2) with \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2 is an inward spiral. In polar coordinates centered at the minimum, this trajectory approximates a logarithmic spiral r = ae^{-b\theta} (contracting, b > 0). The spiral’s winding is tighter when the condition number \lambda_2/\lambda_1 is large — an ill-conditioned loss makes the spiral oscillate widely before converging. This is precisely why ill-conditioned problems are hard: the log spiral has many turns before r \approx 0.
Preconditioning (used in Adam, AdaGrad, natural gradient) effectively makes \lambda_1 \approx \lambda_2, converting the tight spiral into a nearly radial path — the angle \psi \approx \pi/2 everywhere (perpendicular to the level curves), which is the steepest descent direction.
12.6 Sinusoidal Positional Encodings as Polar Plots
The positional encoding in the original Transformer (\text{PE}_{k,2i} = \sin(k/10000^{2i/d}), \text{PE}_{k,2i+1} = \cos(k/10000^{2i/d})) can be read as: for each frequency band i, the 2D vector (\cos(\omega_i k), \sin(\omega_i k)) traces a circle (the polar curve r = 1) as k increases. Different frequency bands trace this circle at different angular rates \omega_i. The full positional encoding is a stack of these circular traces — a multi-frequency polar representation of position.
RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) makes this exact: it applies a rotation by \omega_i k to each 2D subspace of the embedding, which is literally multiplication by the rotation matrix in polar form e^{i\omega_i k}. The polar curve r = 1 (unit circle) is the geometry underlying RoPE.
12.7 Summary Table





































Polar Graphing ConceptML / DL AnalogueRadar/polar chart of metricsModel evaluation across multiple axesRose curve = orientation tuningCNN filter visualization, V1 neuronsLimaçon with inner loopDecision boundary with interior pocketLemniscate (figure-eight)Bimodal information geometryLog spiral = grad. descent pathGD with momentum in ill-conditioned lossr = 1 (unit circle)Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)Petal count (odd/even n)Symmetry of learned representations

13. Exercises
Exercise 1. Sketch r = 3\cos\theta by identifying it as a circle. Find its center and radius. Verify: at what value of \theta does the curve pass through the pole?
Exercise 2. Sketch r = 2 - 2\sin\theta. Classify (cardioid/dimpled/inner loop), determine symmetry, find the maximum r, and identify where the cusp lies.
Exercise 3. (Stewart §10.3) For r = \cos(4\theta): how many petals? In which directions do the petal tips point? Compute the area of one petal.
Exercise 4. For r = 2 + 3\cos\theta: find the values of \theta where r = 0. Trace the inner loop carefully — what range of \theta produces the inner loop, and in what angular region of the plane does the inner loop lie?
Exercise 5. (Lemniscate) For r^2 = 9\sin(2\theta): determine the domain (which \theta give real r?), the symmetry, and sketch the curve.
Exercise 6. (MIT 18.02 flavored) A curve is defined by r = 1 - 2\sin(2\theta). This is NOT a standard limaçon. Analyze it: find all zeros and maxima of r, determine all symmetries, identify how many times the curve passes through the pole and with what tangent directions, and produce a careful sketch.
Exercise 7. (Comparison) Sketch both r = \sin(2\theta) and r = \cos(2\theta) on the same polar axes. By what angle is one the rotation of the other? Verify using the identity \cos(2\theta) = \sin(2\theta + \pi/2).
Exercise 8. (ML-flavored) Consider the radar chart of two models A and B:

Model A: accuracy = 0.9, precision = 0.8, recall = 0.7, F1 = 0.74 (metrics at \theta = 0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2).
Model B: accuracy = 0.7, precision = 0.9, recall = 0.95, F1 = 0.92.

Treating the metrics as r values at equally spaced angles and connecting them as a polar curve, estimate which model has greater enclosed area. Which model would you prefer for a medical diagnosis task (where recall matters most)?
