01.Maths/Calculus/12.Vectors-and-the-Geo.content:
Tags: calculus linearalgebra machinelearning deeplearning foundations References: Stewart §12.2, MIT 18.02 Lecture Notes


“To handle more than one number at a time without losing track of what belongs to what — that is the soul of a vector.” — Personal margin note


0. Why Vectors, Before Anything Else
In single-variable calculus we got comfortable with one number at a time: a position on a line, a temperature, a rate. But the real world is obstinately multi-dimensional. A weather system has pressure, temperature, humidity, and wind velocity at every point in space. A neural network maps an input image — hundreds of thousands of pixel intensities — to a probability distribution over classes. None of that fits in a single real number.
The vector is the minimal honest object for multidimensional data. It carries both magnitude (how much?) and direction (which way?), and it obeys a clean algebra that turns geometric intuition into machinery we can compute with.

1. The Definition — Two Complementary Views
1.1 Geometric View
A vector \mathbf{v} in \mathbb{R}^n is a directed line segment — an arrow — characterized entirely by its length (magnitude) and direction, not by where it starts. Two arrows that are parallel, point the same way, and have the same length are the same vector, regardless of their foot.

Personal note: This “position independence” is non-trivial. It is exactly what lets us add a displacement vector to a position point and get a new position — the vector lives in its own space, the point lives in affine space. MIT 18.02 is careful about this distinction when it introduces position vectors.

1.2 Algebraic / Component View
Fix an orthonormal basis {\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{e}_n} (the standard basis in \mathbb{R}^n). Every vector \mathbf{v} decomposes uniquely:
\mathbf{v} = v_1,\mathbf{e}_1 + v_2,\mathbf{e}_2 + \cdots + v_n,\mathbf{e}_n
We write \mathbf{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n \rangle or as a column matrix. The scalars v_i are the components of \mathbf{v} relative to that basis.

Warning: Components depend on the chosen basis. The vector itself does not. This subtlety matters enormously in ML when we talk about changing representation spaces.


2. Basic Operations — Definitions and Geometry
2.1 Vector Addition
\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \langle u_1 + v_1,; u_2 + v_2,; \ldots,; u_n + v_n \rangle
Geometric interpretation (Parallelogram Law): Place \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v} tail-to-tail; their sum is the diagonal of the parallelogram they span.
        u+v
       /   |
      /    |
     /     v
    u -----

Equivalently, Triangle Law: Place \mathbf{v}‘s tail at \mathbf{u}‘s head; the sum goes from \mathbf{u}‘s tail to \mathbf{v}‘s head.
2.2 Scalar Multiplication
c,\mathbf{v} = \langle c,v_1, c,v_2, \ldots, c,v_n \rangle
Stretches (or shrinks, or flips) the vector. c > 1 elongates, 0 < c < 1 shortens, c < 0 reverses direction.
2.3 The Zero Vector and Negation
\mathbf{0} = \langle 0, 0, \ldots, 0 \rangle is the additive identity. -\mathbf{v} = (-1)\mathbf{v}, so \mathbf{v} + (-\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}.

3. Magnitude (Norm)
|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \cdots + v_n^2}
This is just the Pythagorean theorem iterated. In \mathbb{R}^2 it is the familiar distance formula; in \mathbb{R}^3 Stewart derives it from two applications of Pythagoras (§12.2).
Unit vector: A vector of magnitude 1. Given any nonzero \mathbf{v}: \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|}
This is the operation of normalization — it preserves direction and discards magnitude. Standard basis vectors \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k} in \mathbb{R}^3 are unit vectors.

Example. Let \mathbf{v} = \langle 3, -4 \rangle. Then |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{9+16} = 5, and \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \langle \tfrac{3}{5}, -\tfrac{4}{5} \rangle.


4. The Dot Product — The Most Important Operation
4.1 Definition (Algebraic)
\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} u_i v_i = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + \cdots + u_n v_n
The result is a scalar (a single number), not a vector. Also called the inner product or scalar product.
4.2 The Geometric Formula (The Key Theorem)
Theorem. For any \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n: \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}|,|\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta where \theta \in [0, \pi] is the angle between the vectors.
Proof sketch (Stewart’s approach via Law of Cosines): Consider the triangle formed by \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, and \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}. By the Law of Cosines: |\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2 - 2|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta Expanding |\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}|^2 algebraically using components yields the identity. \square
4.3 Orthogonality
\mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v} \iff \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0
(Assuming neither is the zero vector.) This follows directly from \cos(90°) = 0.
4.4 Projection
The scalar projection of \mathbf{u} onto \mathbf{v} (how much of \mathbf{u} points along \hat{\mathbf{v}}): \text{comp}_{\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|}
The vector projection (the actual component vector along \mathbf{v}): \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2},\mathbf{v}
    u
   /|
  / |
 /  |  ← perpendicular component
/θ  |
----+--------> v
  proj_v u


Example. Find the projection of \mathbf{u} = \langle 2, 3 \rangle onto \mathbf{v} = \langle 4, 0 \rangle (the x-axis): \text{proj}_\mathbf{v},\mathbf{u} = \frac{8}{16}\langle 4,0\rangle = \langle 2, 0\rangle Geometrically obvious: the shadow of \langle 2,3 \rangle on the x-axis is \langle 2, 0 \rangle.


5. The Cross Product — Exclusive to \mathbb{R}^3
5.1 Definition
Given \mathbf{u} = \langle u_1, u_2, u_3 \rangle and \mathbf{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, v_3 \rangle: \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \end{vmatrix} = \langle u_2 v_3 - u_3 v_2,; u_3 v_1 - u_1 v_3,; u_1 v_2 - u_2 v_1 \rangle
The result is a vector (perpendicular to both \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v}).
5.2 Geometric Interpretation
|\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}| = |\mathbf{u}|,|\mathbf{v}|\sin\theta

Magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v}.
Direction is given by the right-hand rule: curl fingers from \mathbf{u} toward \mathbf{v}; thumb points in the direction of \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}.

Key property: \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = -(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{u}) — the cross product is anti-commutative.
5.3 Immediate Corollary
\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \iff \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v} are parallel (or one is zero).

Example. \mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{j} = \mathbf{k}, ;\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{k} = \mathbf{i}, ;\mathbf{k} \times \mathbf{i} = \mathbf{j}.


6. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Work Done by a Force
A force \mathbf{F} = \langle 3, 4, 0 \rangle Newtons moves a particle along displacement \mathbf{d} = \langle 2, 1, 5 \rangle meters. Work done: W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 6 + 4 + 0 = 10 \text{ Joules}
Only the component of force along the direction of motion does work — that’s the dot product.
Example 2 — Normal to a Plane
Find a normal vector to the plane containing A = (1,0,0), B = (0,1,0), C = (0,0,1).
\mathbf{u} = \overrightarrow{AB} = \langle -1, 1, 0 \rangle, \quad \mathbf{v} = \overrightarrow{AC} = \langle -1, 0, 1 \rangle
\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \langle 1\cdot1 - 0\cdot0,; 0\cdot(-1) - (-1)\cdot1,; (-1)\cdot0 - 1\cdot(-1) \rangle = \langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle
Plane equation: x + y + z = 1. ✓
Example 3 — Angle Between Vectors
Find the angle between \mathbf{a} = \langle 1, 2, 2 \rangle and \mathbf{b} = \langle 0, 1, -1 \rangle:
\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|} = \frac{0+2-2}{3\cdot\sqrt{2}} = 0
So \theta = 90°. These vectors are orthogonal.

7. Visualization
7.1 Vectors in \mathbb{R}^2 — Adding \langle 2,1 \rangle + \langle -1,2 \rangle
  ^
3 |       . (1,3)
  |      /|
2 |  v  / |
  |  /  / |
1 |./u /  |
  |  /   |
  +--+---+----->
  0  1   2

\mathbf{u} = \langle 2,1 \rangle (right 2, up 1), \mathbf{v} = \langle -1,2 \rangle (left 1, up 2).
Sum = \langle 1, 3 \rangle: the diagonal of the parallelogram.
7.2 Dot Product as Projection Meter
High alignment (θ small):        Orthogonal (θ = 90°):     Opposite (θ = 180°):
    u·v = large positive              u·v = 0                   u·v = negative
    →→→→→→                           →→→→→                     →→→→→
    ↗↗↗↗↗↗                           ↑↑↑↑↑                     ←←←←←

The dot product measures how much two vectors agree in direction.

8. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning

This is where the abstract machinery earns its keep.

8.1 Data as Vectors
In ML, every data point is a vector. An image of size 28 \times 28 pixels is flattened to \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{784}. A word in NLP is mapped to an embedding vector \mathbf{e} \in \mathbb{R}^{300} or \mathbb{R}^{768} (in BERT-style models). A patient’s medical record with 50 features is \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{50}.
The entire machinery of ML is vector algebra applied at scale.
8.2 Linear Layers Are Matrix-Vector Products
A linear (fully-connected) layer in a neural network computes: \mathbf{z} = W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b} where \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n is the input vector, W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} is the weight matrix, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^m is the bias vector, and \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^m is the output vector. Each row of W is a weight vector whose dot product with \mathbf{x} gives one output neuron’s pre-activation.
z_i = \mathbf{w}_i \cdot \mathbf{x} + b_i
A neuron fires strongly when its weight vector \mathbf{w}_i is aligned with the input \mathbf{x} — i.e., when the dot product (angle) is small. This is the dot product’s geometric meaning made computational.
8.3 Cosine Similarity — Measuring Semantic Closeness
The cosine similarity between two vectors: \text{cosim}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|} = \cos\theta
This is exactly the geometric formula from §4.2, normalized to [-1, 1].
In NLP: word embedding vectors for “king” and “queen” have high cosine similarity. “king” and “bicycle” have near-zero similarity. Recommendation systems use cosine similarity to find “most similar” items in embedding space.
In deep learning: attention mechanisms (e.g., Transformers) compute pairwise dot products between query and key vectors to determine which tokens “attend” to which: \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
The QK^\top term is a matrix of dot products — measuring alignment of every query vector with every key vector.
8.4 Gradient Vectors — The Direction of Steepest Ascent
The gradient \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} of the loss function \mathcal{L} with respect to parameters \theta is a vector in parameter space \mathbb{R}^p (where p can be billions). It points in the direction of steepest increase of the loss.
Gradient descent updates: \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta,\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}
This is vector subtraction — we move against the gradient vector to reduce loss. The learning rate \eta is scalar multiplication scaling the step size.
The entire training loop of a deep neural network is iterative vector subtraction in a very high-dimensional space. Understanding vectors is understanding why gradient descent works geometrically.
8.5 Normalization — Why Unit Vectors Matter in DL
In batch normalization and layer normalization, activations are normalized to have unit norm (or unit variance). This corresponds exactly to the unit vector operation \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{v}/|\mathbf{v}|. It stabilizes training by preventing activations from growing unboundedly across layers.
Similarly, weight normalization explicitly reparametrizes weights as \mathbf{w} = g \cdot \hat{\mathbf{v}}, separating magnitude g from direction \hat{\mathbf{v}}.
8.6 Cross Product — Normals in 3D Vision and Physics Simulations
The cross product appears in 3D computer graphics (computing surface normals for lighting), physics engines (computing torques \boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}), and robotics (computing angular velocities and Jacobians).
In NeRFs (Neural Radiance Fields) and 3D-aware deep learning models, the geometry of 3D scenes is represented using vector fields and surface normals, all built on cross product intuition.

9. Summary Table



























































ConceptFormulaOutputKey FactAddition\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}VectorParallelogram lawScalar mult.c\mathbf{v}VectorStretches/flipsMagnitude\|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{\sum v_i^2}ScalarPythagorasDot product\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \sum u_i v_iScalar= \|\mathbf{u}\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\thetaProjection\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2}\mathbf{v}VectorShadow of \mathbf{u} on \mathbf{v}Cross product\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}Vector (\mathbb{R}^3 only)\perp to both, area = \|\mathbf{u}\|\mathbf{v}\|\sin\thetaUnit vector\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{v}/\|\mathbf{v}\|VectorDirection only, \|\hat{\mathbf{v}}\|=1Cosine similarity\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|\mathbf{v}\|}Scalar \in[-1,1]Measures directional agreement

10. Things to Prove Yourself


Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality: |\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|. (Hint: Consider |\mathbf{u} - t\mathbf{v}|^2 \geq 0 as a quadratic in t, use the discriminant condition.)


Triangle Inequality: |\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}| + |\mathbf{v}|. (Follows from Cauchy-Schwarz.)


Lagrange’s Identity: |\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 - (\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2. (Verify componentwise in \mathbb{R}^3.)


Show that the dot product distributes over addition: \mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}.


Parallelogram Identity: |\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|^2 + |\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}|^2 = 2(|\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2). What does this say geometrically?



11. Looking Forward
From here we build immediately:

Lines and planes in \mathbb{R}^3 — parametric and normal forms, all using vectors (Stewart §12.5)
Vector-valued functions and curves — \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle x(t), y(t), z(t) \rangle, velocity, acceleration (Stewart §13)
Partial derivatives and the gradient — the gradient \nabla f is a vector field; the directional derivative is a dot product D_\mathbf{u}f = \nabla f \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} (MIT 18.02, Week 3)
Multiple integrals and flux — integrating vector fields over surfaces requires normals from cross products (MIT 18.02, Week 8–9)
Linear algebra proper — vector spaces, linear maps, eigenvalues: the full language of ML


12. References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §12.2 (Vectors), §12.3 (Dot Product), §12.4 (Cross Product).
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus. Lectures 1–3 (Vectors, Dot and Cross Products, Matrices). ocw.mit.edu
Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville. Deep Learning, Ch. 2 (Linear Algebra) — for the ML connections.
Jurafsky & Martin. Speech and Language Processing, Ch. 6 — for word embeddings and cosine similarity.

01.Maths/Calculus/12.Vectors-and-the-Geo.content:
Tags: calculus linearalgebra machinelearning deeplearning multivariable References: Stewart §12.3–12.4, MIT 18.02 Lectures 2–3 See also: Vectors


“The dot product asks: how much do these two arrows agree? The cross product asks: what is born from their disagreement?” — Personal margin note


0. Orientation — Two Products, Two Philosophies
The dot product and cross product are both ways to “multiply” vectors, but they answer fundamentally different geometric questions and produce fundamentally different outputs:








































Dot Product \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}Cross Product \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}OutputScalarVectorLives in\mathbb{R}^n, any dimension\mathbb{R}^3 onlyMeasuresAlignment / projectionArea & perpendicularityZero whenVectors are orthogonalVectors are parallelMax whenVectors are parallelVectors are orthogonalCommutative?Yes: \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u}No: \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{u}
Think of the dot product as measuring the shadow one vector casts on another. The cross product creates a new vector perpendicular to both, whose length encodes the area they sweep out.

Part I: The Dot Product
1. Definitions — Algebraic and Geometric
1.1 Algebraic Definition
Let \mathbf{u} = \langle u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_n \rangle and \mathbf{v} = \langle v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n \rangle in \mathbb{R}^n. Then:
\boxed{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} u_i v_i = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + \cdots + u_n v_n}
The output is a single real number — a scalar.

Note on notation. Some texts write \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle for the inner product, especially in functional analysis or quantum mechanics. In \mathbb{R}^n with the standard basis, these coincide. The dot product \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} is also written as the matrix product \mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{v} when vectors are column matrices.

1.2 The Geometric Formula — The Central Theorem
Theorem (Stewart §12.3). For any \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n: \boxed{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}|,|\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta} where \theta \in [0, \pi] is the angle between \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v}.
Proof. Place both vectors with their tails at the origin. The vector \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} forms the third side of the triangle. By the Law of Cosines:
|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2 - 2|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta
Now expand |\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}|^2 algebraically: |\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}|^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (u_i - v_i)^2 = \sum u_i^2 - 2\sum u_i v_i + \sum v_i^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 - 2(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + |\mathbf{v}|^2
Equating both expressions and canceling |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2 from both sides: -2(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) = -2|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta \implies \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta \qquad \square

This proof is beautiful. It is the bridge between pure computation (component-wise sum) and pure geometry (angle). Memorize the strategy: expand |\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}|^2 two ways and match.


2. Properties of the Dot Product
Let \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^n and c \in \mathbb{R}.

Commutativity: \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u} (clear from definition)
Distributivity: \mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}
Scalar pullout: (c,\mathbf{u})\cdot\mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{u}\cdot(c,\mathbf{v})
Self-dot = squared norm: \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{v}|^2
Zero vector: \mathbf{0}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0
Positive definiteness: \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v} \geq 0, with equality iff \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}

Properties 1–3 make the dot product a bilinear form. Properties 4–6, combined with 1, make it an inner product (on real vector spaces). These axioms generalize to infinite-dimensional spaces — the foundation of Hilbert spaces in functional analysis.

3. Reading \cos\theta — What the Dot Product Detects
From \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta, the sign of the dot product tells you the qualitative relationship between the vectors:
                  u
                 /
                / θ < 90°
               /____________ v
    u·v > 0: acute angle, vectors "lean toward each other"


       u __________ v
    u·v = 0: θ = 90°, orthogonal — no alignment at all


    u ____________
                  \
                   \ θ > 90°
                    v
    u·v < 0: obtuse angle, vectors "pull away from each other"

The extreme cases:

\mathbf{u} \parallel \mathbf{v}, same direction (\theta = 0): \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}| — maximum
\mathbf{u} \parallel \mathbf{v}, opposite direction (\theta = \pi): \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = -|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}| — minimum
\mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v} (\theta = \pi/2): \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0 — no projection


4. Projection — The Workhorse Application
4.1 Scalar Projection
The scalar projection (or component) of \mathbf{u} onto \mathbf{v} is the signed length of the shadow of \mathbf{u} along \hat{\mathbf{v}}:
\text{comp}_{\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|} = |\mathbf{u}|\cos\theta
4.2 Vector Projection
The vector projection is the actual shadow vector along \mathbf{v}:
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{u} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}\right)\mathbf{v} = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{v}
4.3 Orthogonal Decomposition
Every vector \mathbf{u} decomposes uniquely into a part along \mathbf{v} and a part perpendicular to \mathbf{v}:
\mathbf{u} = \underbrace{\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{u}}_{\text{parallel to } \mathbf{v}} + \underbrace{(\mathbf{u} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{u})}_{\perp, \text{to } \mathbf{v}}
Verify the perpendicular part is indeed orthogonal to \mathbf{v}: (\mathbf{u} - \text{proj}_\mathbf{v},\mathbf{u})\cdot\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} - \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0 \qquad \checkmark
         u
        /|
       / |
      /  |  ← perpendicular part (u - proj_v u)
     / θ |
    /    |
   +-----+-----------> v
         proj_v u


This decomposition is the root of the Gram-Schmidt process, which orthogonalizes a basis, which underlies QR decomposition, PCA, and essentially all of numerical linear algebra.


5. The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
Theorem. |\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}|,|\mathbf{v}|}
Proof (elegant algebraic method). Consider f(t) = |\mathbf{u} - t\mathbf{v}|^2 \geq 0 for all t \in \mathbb{R}.
Expanding: f(t) = |\mathbf{u}|^2 - 2t(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + t^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 \geq 0
This is a quadratic in t that is always non-negative, so its discriminant must be \leq 0: \Delta = 4(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2 - 4|\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 \leq 0 \implies (\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2 \leq |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 \implies |\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}| \qquad \square
Corollary. The geometric formula \cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|} is valid: Cauchy-Schwarz guarantees the right side lives in [-1,1], so \theta = \arccos(\cdots) is well-defined.
Corollary. The Triangle Inequality: |\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}| + |\mathbf{v}|.

Cauchy-Schwarz is one of the most used inequalities in all of mathematics. It appears in probability (correlation coefficients are bounded by 1), quantum mechanics (uncertainty principle), and optimization.


6. Worked Examples — Dot Product
Example 1 — Computing the Angle
Find the angle between \mathbf{a} = \langle 1, -2, 3 \rangle and \mathbf{b} = \langle 2, 1, 1 \rangle:
\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b} = 2 - 2 + 3 = 3 |\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{1+4+9} = \sqrt{14}, \quad |\mathbf{b}| = \sqrt{4+1+1} = \sqrt{6} \cos\theta = \frac{3}{\sqrt{14}\cdot\sqrt{6}} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{84}} = \frac{3}{2\sqrt{21}} \theta = \arccos!\left(\frac{3}{2\sqrt{21}}\right) \approx 70.9°
Example 2 — Projection and Decomposition
Project \mathbf{u} = \langle 4, 2, 0 \rangle onto \mathbf{v} = \langle 1, 1, 0 \rangle:
\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 4+2+0 = 6, \quad |\mathbf{v}|^2 = 2 \text{proj}_\mathbf{v},\mathbf{u} = \frac{6}{2}\langle 1,1,0\rangle = \langle 3,3,0\rangle \text{perpendicular part} = \langle 4,2,0\rangle - \langle 3,3,0\rangle = \langle 1,-1,0\rangle
Check: \langle 1,-1,0\rangle \cdot \langle 1,1,0\rangle = 1-1 = 0 ✓
Example 3 — Physical Work
A force \mathbf{F} = \langle 5, 3, -2 \rangle N displaces an object by \mathbf{d} = \langle 1, 0, 4 \rangle m. Work done:
W = \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{d} = 5 + 0 - 8 = -3 \text{ J}
Negative work means the force opposed the displacement (like friction doing negative work on a sliding object).

Part II: The Cross Product
7. Definition — Three Equivalent Forms
The cross product is defined only in \mathbb{R}^3. (A generalization exists in \mathbb{R}^7, but that’s exotic mathematics.)
7.1 Determinant Form (Most Practical)
\boxed{\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \end{vmatrix}}
Expanding along the first row:
\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{i}(u_2 v_3 - u_3 v_2) - \mathbf{j}(u_1 v_3 - u_3 v_1) + \mathbf{k}(u_1 v_2 - u_2 v_1)
= \langle u_2 v_3 - u_3 v_2,; u_3 v_1 - u_1 v_3,; u_1 v_2 - u_2 v_1 \rangle

Memory device. For the i-component, “cover” the first column and take the 2\times 2 determinant of what remains. Alternate signs: +, -, +.

7.2 Geometric Definition
\boxed{\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = (|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\sin\theta),\hat{\mathbf{n}}}
where \theta \in [0,\pi] is the angle between \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v}, and \hat{\mathbf{n}} is the unit vector perpendicular to both, determined by the right-hand rule.
Right-hand rule: Point fingers of right hand along \mathbf{u}, curl them toward \mathbf{v}. Thumb points in direction of \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}.
        ^ n = u × v (thumb)
        |
        |
   u ---+---> (fingers curl from u toward v)
         \
          v

7.3 Standard Basis Cross Products
\mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{j} = \mathbf{k}, \quad \mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{i}, \quad \mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{i} = \mathbf{j} \mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{i} = -\mathbf{k}, \quad \mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{j} = -\mathbf{i}, \quad \mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{k} = -\mathbf{j} \mathbf{i}\times\mathbf{i} = \mathbf{j}\times\mathbf{j} = \mathbf{k}\times\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{0}
Mnemonic (cyclic):
    i → j → k → i → j → k → ...
    Going forward: positive
    Going backward: negative


8. Properties of the Cross Product
Let \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and c \in \mathbb{R}.

Anti-commutativity: \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} = -(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{u})
Distributivity over addition: \mathbf{u}\times(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{w}
Scalar pullout: (c,\mathbf{u})\times\mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{u}\times(c,\mathbf{v})
Self-cross = zero: \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0} (since \sin 0 = 0)
Perpendicularity: (\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0 and (\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0
NOT associative: (\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\times\mathbf{w} \neq \mathbf{u}\times(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w}) in general


Property 1 is the critical one. The cross product is anti-commutative, not commutative. Reversing the order flips the direction of the result. This is why order matters in 3D geometry — and in physics (torque, angular momentum).

Proof of Property 5 (perpendicularity to \mathbf{u}): (\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{u} = (u_2 v_3 - u_3 v_2)u_1 + (u_3 v_1 - u_1 v_3)u_2 + (u_1 v_2 - u_2 v_1)u_3 Expanding: u_1 u_2 v_3 - u_1 u_3 v_2 + u_2 u_3 v_1 - u_1 u_2 v_3 + u_1 u_3 v_2 - u_2 u_3 v_1 = 0 \square

9. Geometric Content — Area and Volume
9.1 Area of a Parallelogram
\text{Area} = |\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}| = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\sin\theta
This is the area of the parallelogram with sides \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v}.
         v
        /----/
       /    /   Area = ||u × v||
      /----/
           u

Area of the triangle with sides \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v}: \frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}|.
9.2 Scalar Triple Product and Volume of a Parallelepiped
The scalar triple product (or box product):
[\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}] = \mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w}) = \begin{vmatrix} u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \ w_1 & w_2 & w_3 \end{vmatrix}
This gives the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}.
V = |\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w})|
Key property: \mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{v}\cdot(\mathbf{w}\times\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{w}\cdot(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}) — cyclic permutations preserve the value.
Coplanarity test: \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} are coplanar \iff \mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w}) = 0.

10. Lagrange’s Identity
Theorem. |\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 - (\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2
Proof (component-wise): Denote \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} = \langle a,b,c\rangle where a = u_2v_3-u_3v_2, etc. Compute a^2+b^2+c^2 and expand. Meanwhile: |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 - (\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2 = (u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2)(v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2) - (u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3)^2 Expanding both and matching terms confirms equality. \square
Geometric meaning: Using \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta:
|\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2(1 - \cos^2\theta) = |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2\sin^2\theta
So |\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}| = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\sin\theta. The geometric formula falls out of Lagrange’s identity — the two definitions (determinant and geometric) are equivalent.

11. The BAC-CAB Rule
A crucial identity for the vector triple product:
\boxed{\mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C}) = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B})}
Mnemonic: BAC minus CAB. The result is a linear combination of \mathbf{B} and \mathbf{C} — which makes sense, since \mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C} is perpendicular to both \mathbf{B} and \mathbf{C}, so \mathbf{A}\times(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{C}) lies in the plane spanned by \mathbf{B} and \mathbf{C}.

This identity appears constantly in electromagnetism (\nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{E})) and fluid mechanics.


12. Worked Examples — Cross Product
Example 1 — Computing a Cross Product
Let \mathbf{u} = \langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle and \mathbf{v} = \langle -1, 1, 0 \rangle:
\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 1 & 2 & 3 \ -1 & 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix}
= \mathbf{i}(2\cdot0 - 3\cdot1) - \mathbf{j}(1\cdot0 - 3\cdot(-1)) + \mathbf{k}(1\cdot1 - 2\cdot(-1))
= \mathbf{i}(-3) - \mathbf{j}(3) + \mathbf{k}(3) = \langle -3, -3, 3 \rangle
Verify perpendicularity: \langle -3,-3,3\rangle \cdot \langle 1,2,3\rangle = -3-6+9 = 0 ✓ \langle -3,-3,3\rangle \cdot \langle -1,1,0\rangle = 3-3+0 = 0 ✓
Example 2 — Area of a Triangle
Find the area of the triangle with vertices A = (1,0,0), B = (0,2,0), C = (0,0,3):
\overrightarrow{AB} = \langle -1,2,0\rangle, \quad \overrightarrow{AC} = \langle -1,0,3\rangle
\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\-1&2&0\-1&0&3\end{vmatrix} = \langle 6, 3, 2\rangle
\text{Area} = \tfrac{1}{2}|\langle 6,3,2\rangle| = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{36+9+4} = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{49} = \frac{7}{2}
Example 3 — Volume of a Parallelepiped
\mathbf{u} = \langle 1,0,0\rangle, \mathbf{v} = \langle 1,1,0\rangle, \mathbf{w} = \langle 1,1,1\rangle:
V = \left|,\det\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\1&1&0\1&1&1\end{pmatrix}\right| = |1\cdot(1\cdot1-0\cdot1)| = 1

13. Dot vs. Cross — Side-by-Side Comparison
SAME INPUT: u = <1, 0, 0>,  v = <0, 1, 0>  (perpendicular unit vectors)

DOT PRODUCT:                    CROSS PRODUCT:
u · v = 0                       u × v = k = <0, 0, 1>
→ Zero because θ = 90°          → Maximum magnitude (sin 90° = 1)
→ Captures: no alignment        → Captures: maximal area swept

SAME INPUT: u = <1, 0, 0>,  v = <2, 0, 0>  (parallel vectors)

DOT PRODUCT:                    CROSS PRODUCT:
u · v = 2                       u × v = <0, 0, 0>
→ Maximum (cos 0° = 1)          → Zero (sin 0° = 0)
→ Captures: perfect alignment   → Captures: no area, degenerate

The duality: the dot product maximizes when vectors agree, the cross product maximizes when they disagree. They are “complementary sensors.”

14. Connections to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
14.1 The Dot Product is Everywhere in Neural Networks
Every forward pass in a neural network is fundamentally repeated dot products. A single neuron computes: z = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} + b = \sum_{i} w_i x_i + b
The dot product measures how much the input vector \mathbf{x} aligns with the learned weight vector \mathbf{w}. A neuron activates strongly precisely when its weight vector points in nearly the same direction as the input — the geometric picture from §3.
Efficiency: Modern hardware (GPUs/TPUs) is physically optimized to compute dot products in parallel (matrix multiplication = batched dot products). The dot product’s simplicity is what makes deep learning computationally feasible at scale.
14.2 Cosine Similarity — Semantic Search and Embeddings
From the geometric formula, cosine similarity isolates direction and discards magnitude: \text{cosim}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|}
This is the dot product of the normalized vectors, i.e., unit vectors. It measures purely directional agreement.
Applications:

Word2Vec / GloVe: The famous king - man + woman ≈ queen result is vector addition/subtraction; nearness is measured by cosine similarity.
BERT embeddings: Sentences mapped to \mathbb{R}^{768} vectors; semantic similarity is cosine similarity.
Vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, Chroma): Store embeddings of documents; a user query is embedded and the top-k results are the k vectors with highest cosine similarity. The entire retrieval step in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines is a batched dot product search.

14.3 Self-Attention — Dot Products Scaled Up
The Transformer’s attention mechanism: \text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
QK^\top is a matrix of pairwise dot products: entry (i,j) is \mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{k}_j — how much query token i attends to key token j. This is exactly cosine-like: the higher the dot product, the more attention is paid.
The \sqrt{d_k} scaling prevents dot products from becoming too large in high dimensions (where even near-orthogonal vectors accumulate non-negligible dot products), which would saturate softmax and kill gradients. This is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality being respected in practice.
14.4 Gradient as a Dot Product — Directional Derivatives
The directional derivative of a scalar field f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} in direction \hat{\mathbf{u}}: D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} f = \nabla f \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}
This is a dot product. The gradient \nabla f (a vector in parameter space) is the direction of steepest ascent. The rate of change in any other direction \hat{\mathbf{u}} is the projection of \nabla f onto \hat{\mathbf{u}} — exactly |\nabla f|\cos\theta.
Gradient descent works because moving opposite to \nabla f (i.e., choosing \hat{\mathbf{u}} = -\hat{\nabla f}) maximizes the decrease in f: D_{-\hat{\nabla f}} f = \nabla f \cdot (-\hat{\nabla f}) = -|\nabla f| This is the minimum possible directional derivative (by Cauchy-Schwarz).

The entire theory of gradient descent is the statement: the dot product is minimized when the angle is \pi.

14.5 The Cross Product in 3D Deep Learning
Cross products appear when learning from or generating 3D geometric data:

Surface normals in 3D vision: Given two tangent vectors on a surface mesh, their cross product gives the normal — used in lighting models, physics simulations, and 3D generative models.
NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields): Ray marching through 3D scenes; computing intersections and normals uses cross product geometry.
Rotation representations: Angular velocity \boldsymbol{\omega} of a rotating body gives instantaneous linear velocity \mathbf{v} = \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}. Robot learning agents modeling 3D kinematics use this constantly.
Graph Neural Networks on point clouds: Local coordinate frames at each point are defined using cross products of estimated tangent vectors.

14.6 PCA — Projection via Eigenvectors and Dot Products
Principal Component Analysis (the most fundamental dimensionality reduction technique):

Center the data: subtract the mean from every data vector.
Compute the covariance matrix \Sigma = \frac{1}{n} X^\top X — every entry is a dot product.
Find eigenvectors \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots of \Sigma.
Project data onto the top eigenvectors: z_i = \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{v}_i — a dot product.

PCA is Gram-Schmidt (orthogonal decomposition, §4.3) applied to data, driven by dot products.

15. Summary
Dot Product
\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \sum u_i v_i = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta

Scalar output. Works in \mathbb{R}^n.
Zero \iff orthogonal. Measures alignment.
Powers: projections, angles, work, attention mechanisms, gradient descent, similarity search.

Cross Product
\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} = \det\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\u_1&u_2&u_3\v_1&v_2&v_3\end{pmatrix} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\sin\theta;\hat{\mathbf{n}}

Vector output. Only in \mathbb{R}^3.
Zero \iff parallel. Measures area, perpendicular axis.
Powers: surface normals, torques, plane equations, 3D vision.

The Deep Connection
|\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 = (\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2 + |\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}|^2
(Lagrange’s identity.) In words: the “total interaction” between two vectors splits into a scalar part (dot product — alignment) and a vector part (cross product — perpendicularity). They are complementary, and together they capture the complete relationship between \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v}.

16. Exercises


Prove that \mathbf{u}\times(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w}) + \mathbf{v}\times(\mathbf{w}\times\mathbf{u}) + \mathbf{w}\times(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0} (Jacobi identity). Use BAC-CAB.


Prove that (\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\cdot(\mathbf{w}\times\mathbf{z}) = (\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w})(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{z}) - (\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{z})(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w}).


Show that the distance from point P to the line through A with direction \hat{\mathbf{d}} is |\overrightarrow{AP} - (\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{d}})\hat{\mathbf{d}}|, or equivalently \frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\mathbf{d}|}{|\mathbf{d}|}.


ML connection: If \mathbf{w} and \mathbf{x} are both unit vectors (normalized), show that \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x} = \cos\theta. What is the maximum value of the dot product, and when is it achieved? What does this mean for a neuron with normalized weight and input vectors?


Prove the polarization identity: \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \frac{1}{4}(|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|^2 - |\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}|^2). (The dot product is determined by the norm — this is why knowing all distances in a vector space is equivalent to knowing the inner product.)



17. Looking Forward

Lines and Planes (Stewart §12.5): Normal vectors to planes are found via the cross product. The plane through P_0 with normal \mathbf{n} is \mathbf{n}\cdot(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0) = 0 — a dot product equation.
Calculus of Vector Fields (MIT 18.02, Week 8–9): Flux integrals \iint \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} are dot products integrated over surfaces. Curl uses the cross product: \nabla\times\mathbf{F}.
Linear Algebra: The dot product is the standard inner product; generalizing it yields Hilbert spaces, used in functional analysis and quantum mechanics.
Deep Learning Theory: Kernel methods generalize the dot product to nonlinear similarity. The kernel trick embeds data into a high-dimensional feature space and computes dot products there implicitly.


18. References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §12.3 (The Dot Product), §12.4 (The Cross Product).
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus. Lectures 2–3. ocw.mit.edu
Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville. Deep Learning, Ch. 2 — Linear Algebra review with ML context.
Vaswani et al. Attention is All You Need (2017) — the Transformer paper; §3.2 on scaled dot-product attention.
Axler, Sheldon. Linear Algebra Done Right, Ch. 6 — inner products done rigorously and abstractly.

01.Maths/Calculus/12.Vectors-and-the-Geo.title: 04.Direction Angles & Direction Cosines
01.Maths/Calculus/12.Vectors-and-the-Geo.content:
“The direction of a vector is the soul of its geometry. Angles make that soul legible.” — personal note, §12.3 philosophy


0. Motivation — Why Should We Care?
When you write \mathbf{v} = \langle 3, -1, 2 \rangle, you know the components. But what is its orientation in space? How does it tilt relative to each axis?
Direction angles answer this precisely. Direction cosines encode orientation in a form that is invariant under scaling, deeply connected to dot products, and — as we will see — absolutely central to how neural networks and SVMs work.

1. Setup & Notation
Let \mathbf{a} = \langle a_1, a_2, a_3 \rangle \in \mathbb{R}^3 be a nonzero vector.
|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}
Denote the standard basis vectors \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k} (i.e., \mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3).

2. Definition: Direction Angles

Definition. The direction angles \alpha, \beta, \gamma of \mathbf{a} are the angles it makes with the positive x-, y-, z-axes respectively:
\alpha = \angle(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{i}), \quad \beta = \angle(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{j}), \quad \gamma = \angle(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{k})
with each angle in [0, \pi].

These are not Euler angles — they are the three separate angles the vector makes with the coordinate axes, one at a time.
2.1 Derivation via the Dot Product
Recall the fundamental formula: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta.
Applying this to \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{i} = \langle 1,0,0 \rangle:
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{i} = a_1
|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{i}|\cos\alpha = |\mathbf{a}| \cdot 1 \cdot \cos\alpha
Therefore:
\boxed{\cos\alpha = \frac{a_1}{|\mathbf{a}|}, \quad \cos\beta = \frac{a_2}{|\mathbf{a}|}, \quad \cos\gamma = \frac{a_3}{|\mathbf{a}|}}

3. Definition: Direction Cosines

Definition. The three quantities \cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma are called the direction cosines of \mathbf{a}.

They are simply the components of the unit vector in the direction of \mathbf{a}:
\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{a}|} = \langle \cos\alpha,, \cos\beta,, \cos\gamma \rangle
This is both conceptually clean and computationally useful.

4. The Fundamental Identity
Theorem. For any nonzero \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^3:
\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1
Proof. Since \hat{\mathbf{a}} is a unit vector:
|\hat{\mathbf{a}}|^2 = \cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1 \qquad \square

⚠️ Key insight. Not every triple (\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma) is freely choosable — this identity is a constraint surface (a sphere of radius 1 in direction-cosine space). This is the 2-sphere S^2.


5. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Explicit Computation
Let \mathbf{a} = \langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle.
Step 1. Compute the magnitude: |\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{14}
Step 2. Direction cosines: \cos\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}, \quad \cos\beta = \frac{2}{\sqrt{14}}, \quad \cos\gamma = \frac{3}{\sqrt{14}}
Step 3. Direction angles (in radians, approx): \alpha \approx 1.301, \quad \beta \approx 1.006, \quad \gamma \approx 0.641
Verification: \frac{1}{14} + \frac{4}{14} + \frac{9}{14} = \frac{14}{14} = 1 \checkmark

Example 2 — Axis-aligned vector
Let \mathbf{a} = \langle 0, 0, 5 \rangle (pointing straight up).
|\mathbf{a}| = 5, \quad \cos\alpha = 0, \quad \cos\beta = 0, \quad \cos\gamma = 1
So \alpha = \beta = \frac{\pi}{2}, \gamma = 0.
This makes perfect sense: the vector is perpendicular to x and y, and perfectly aligned with z.

Example 3 — Symmetric direction
Let \mathbf{a} = \langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle.
|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{3}, \quad \cos\alpha = \cos\beta = \cos\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}
All direction angles are equal: \alpha = \beta = \gamma = \arccos!\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \approx 54.74°.
The “body diagonal” of the unit cube — a beautifully symmetric case.

6. Geometric Visualization
         z
         |   /  ← a
         |  /
  γ      | /
(angle)  |/________ y
        /|
       / |   β = angle to y-axis
      /  |
     x   α = angle to x-axis

Each direction angle is measured from its axis to the vector a.
The unit vector â = (cos α, cos β, cos γ) lies on the unit sphere S².

ASCII picture of direction cosine space:
All valid (cos α, cos β, cos γ) triples live on this sphere:

        cos γ
          |
    1 ----+---- 1
   /      |      \
  /       |       \
 cos α ---+------- cos β
          |
         -1

Constraint: cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1  (the unit sphere)


7. Extension to \mathbb{R}^n
The concept generalizes immediately. For \mathbf{v} = \langle v_1, \ldots, v_n \rangle \in \mathbb{R}^n:
\cos\theta_i = \frac{v_i}{|\mathbf{v}|}, \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} \cos^2\theta_i = 1
The direction cosines are still just the components of the unit vector \hat{\mathbf{v}}, now living on S^{n-1}.
This is the natural habitat of machine learning.

8. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning

This section is where the abstraction pays off. Direction cosines are not just geometry — they are the backbone of how modern ML models measure similarity, learn representations, and make decisions.


8.1 Cosine Similarity
The cosine similarity between two vectors \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n is:
\text{sim}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|} = \hat{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \cos\theta
where \theta is the angle between the two vectors.
This is precisely the dot product of their direction-cosine vectors. It measures angular proximity, ignoring magnitude.
Why this matters in NLP: Word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) represent words as high-dimensional vectors. “king” and “queen” have high cosine similarity. “cat” and “refrigerator” do not. The cosine of the direction angles between their respective unit vectors is what is being compared.
\text{king} - \text{man} + \text{woman} \approx \text{queen} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \text{direction angles tell the story}

8.2 Weight Vectors and Decision Boundaries in SVMs
A Support Vector Machine constructs a hyperplane
\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b = 0
The vector \mathbf{w} is the normal to this hyperplane. The direction cosines of \mathbf{w} determine the orientation of the decision boundary in feature space.
The signed distance from a point \mathbf{x}_0 to the hyperplane is:
d = \frac{\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_0 + b}{|\mathbf{w}|} = \hat{\mathbf{w}} \cdot \mathbf{x}_0 + \frac{b}{|\mathbf{w}|}
Here \hat{\mathbf{w}} = \langle \cos\alpha_1, \ldots, \cos\alpha_n \rangle — the direction cosines of the weight vector — directly project each feature onto the axis of decision.

8.3 Attention Mechanisms (Transformers)
In the scaled dot-product attention:
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
The raw score QK^\top computes q_i \cdot k_j = |q_i||k_j|\cos\theta_{ij}.
The direction of the query and key vectors — encoded in their direction cosines — determines which values get attended to. The \sqrt{d_k} normalization factor is precisely to control the magnitude effect, making the angular alignment (direction cosines) the dominant factor.

8.4 Normalized Embeddings and Contrastive Learning
In contrastive learning (e.g., SimCLR, CLIP), embeddings are typically L^2-normalized before computing loss:
\hat{\mathbf{z}}_i = \frac{\mathbf{z}_i}{|\mathbf{z}_i|}
After normalization, \hat{\mathbf{z}}_i is exactly the direction-cosine vector of \mathbf{z}_i. The loss function then works entirely on the unit sphere S^{n-1} — a space defined by the constraint we proved in §4.
The model learns to align directions, not magnitudes. The geometry is entirely in direction angles.

8.5 Gradient Descent and Direction Cosines
The gradient \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} points in the direction of steepest ascent. The direction cosines of the gradient tell you which parameters \theta_i the loss is most sensitive to:
\cos\alpha_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \theta_i}{|\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}|}
A large |\cos\alpha_i| means \theta_i is almost aligned with the gradient — a small nudge there produces the most change.

9. Summary Table



































QuantityFormulaGeometric MeaningDirection angle \alpha_i\arccos!\left(\tfrac{a_i}{\|\mathbf{a}\|}\right)Angle between \mathbf{a} and axis iDirection cosine \cos\alpha_i\tfrac{a_i}{\|\mathbf{a}\|}i-th component of \hat{\mathbf{a}}Unit vector \hat{\mathbf{a}}\tfrac{\mathbf{a}}{\|\mathbf{a}\|}Vector of all direction cosinesFundamental identity\sum \cos^2\alpha_i = 1\hat{\mathbf{a}} lives on S^{n-1}Cosine similarity\hat{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{v}}Angle between two directions

10. Exercises


(Warm-up) Find the direction angles of \mathbf{a} = \langle 2, -1, 2 \rangle. Verify the identity.


(Theoretical) Prove that there is no vector in \mathbb{R}^3 with all three direction angles equal to \frac{\pi}{3}. What is the minimum possible common value?


(Converse) Given that \cos\alpha = \frac{1}{2} and \cos\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, find all possible values of \cos\gamma.


(ML connection) Two word embeddings have \mathbf{u} = \langle 3, 1, -2, 0 \rangle and \mathbf{v} = \langle -1, 2, 1, 4 \rangle. Compute the cosine similarity. What does a value near 0 mean geometrically?


(Higher dimensions) A vector in \mathbb{R}^n makes equal angles with all coordinate axes. Show that \cos\alpha_i = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} for all i.



11. References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §12.3 — “The Dot Product.” The definition, dot product formula, and worked examples draw from this section.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (OCW). Lecture notes on vectors, dot product, and direction cosines. The geometric perspective and \mathbb{R}^3 setup follow this course’s treatment.

01.Maths/Calculus/12.Vectors-and-the-Geo.title: 05.Projections
01.Maths/Calculus/12.Vectors-and-the-Geo.content:
“Projection is the art of seeing one vector through the eyes of another.”


0. Motivation
You have two vectors \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b}. A natural question: how much of \mathbf{b} points in the direction of \mathbf{a}?
This is not a vague question — it has a precise, unique, geometric answer. The projection extracts the “shadow” of \mathbf{b} cast along \mathbf{a}, and the remainder is the part of \mathbf{b} that is purely perpendicular to \mathbf{a}.
Everything in applied mathematics — least squares, attention mechanisms, PCA, Gram-Schmidt — rests on this one idea.

1. Scalar Projection

Definition. The scalar projection (or component) of \mathbf{b} onto \mathbf{a} is:
\text{comp}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|}

Derivation. Drop a perpendicular from the tip of \mathbf{b} onto the line through \mathbf{a}. The foot of that perpendicular is at signed distance |\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta from the origin along \hat{\mathbf{a}}.
From the dot product formula \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta:
|\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|}
Note this is a signed scalar — negative when \theta > \frac{\pi}{2}.
Equivalently, using the unit vector \hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{a}|}:
\text{comp}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \mathbf{b}
The scalar projection is the dot product of \mathbf{b} with the unit vector in the target direction. Clean.

2. Vector Projection

Definition. The vector projection of \mathbf{b} onto \mathbf{a} is:
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2},\mathbf{a} = \left(\hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \mathbf{b}\right)\hat{\mathbf{a}}

Derivation. We want a vector parallel to \mathbf{a}, with signed length equal to \text{comp}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}:
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = (\text{comp}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}),\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{a}|} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2},\mathbf{a}
Write this more compactly using the outer product notation:
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \frac{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^\top}{|\mathbf{a}|^2},\mathbf{b} = \hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top,\mathbf{b}
The matrix P = \hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top is the projection matrix onto \text{span}{\mathbf{a}}.

3. The Orthogonal Decomposition

Theorem. Any vector \mathbf{b} decomposes uniquely as:
\mathbf{b} = \underbrace{\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}}_{\parallel,\mathbf{a}} + \underbrace{(\mathbf{b} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b})}_{\perp,\mathbf{a}}

Proof of orthogonality. Let \mathbf{b}_\perp = \mathbf{b} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}. Then:
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}_\perp = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} \cdot \left(\frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2},\mathbf{a}\right) = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} - \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2}|\mathbf{a}|^2 = 0 \quad \square
Proof of uniqueness. Suppose \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q} with \mathbf{p} \parallel \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{q} \perp \mathbf{a}. Then \mathbf{p} = c\mathbf{a} for some scalar c, and \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{q} = 0. Taking the dot product of \mathbf{b} = c\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{q} with \mathbf{a}:
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = c|\mathbf{a}|^2 \implies c = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2}
uniquely determined. \quad\square

4. Geometric Visualization
                  b
                 /|
                / |
               /  |  b_⊥  (perpendicular component)
              /   |
             / θ  |
            /_____|_________
           O   proj_a(b)    a →

  |proj_a(b)| = |b| cos θ  (the "shadow" of b on a)
  b_⊥ = b - proj_a(b)      (the "lift" off the line)
  b_⊥ ⊥ a  by construction

  Special cases:

  θ = 0:   b ∥ a  →  proj_a(b) = b,   b_⊥ = 0
  θ = π/2: b ⊥ a  →  proj_a(b) = 0,   b_⊥ = b
  θ = π:   b anti-∥ a → proj = -|b|â  (negative shadow)


5. Projection as a Linear Map — The Projection Matrix
Let \hat{\mathbf{a}} \in \mathbb{R}^n be a unit vector. Define:
P = \hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}
Then \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = P\mathbf{b} for all \mathbf{b}.
Properties:






























PropertyFormulaMeaningIdempotentP^2 = PProjecting twice = projecting onceSymmetricP^\top = POrthogonal projectionRank\text{rank}(P) = 1Projects onto a lineEigenvalues{0, 1}Vectors parallel: eigenvalue 1; perpendicular: eigenvalue 0
Proof of idempotency: P^2 = (\hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top)(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top) = \hat{\mathbf{a}}(\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top\hat{\mathbf{a}})\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top = \hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot 1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top = P \quad \square
The complementary projection (onto the orthogonal complement) is I - P.

6. Projection onto a Subspace
More generally, suppose W = \text{span}{\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_k} where \mathbf{u}_i are orthonormal. Then:
\text{proj}_W \mathbf{b} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} (\mathbf{u}_i \cdot \mathbf{b}),\mathbf{u}_i = UU^\top \mathbf{b}
where U = [\mathbf{u}_1 \mid \cdots \mid \mathbf{u}_k].
If the columns of A span W but are not orthonormal, the projection formula becomes:
\text{proj}_W \mathbf{b} = A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top \mathbf{b}
This is the normal equations formula — the exact solution to the least squares problem.

7. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Standard vector projection
Let \mathbf{b} = \langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle, \mathbf{a} = \langle 1, 1, 0 \rangle.
Step 1. Dot product: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 1 + 2 + 0 = 3
Step 2. |\mathbf{a}|^2 = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2
Step 3. Vector projection: \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \frac{3}{2}\langle 1,1,0 \rangle = \left\langle \frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2}, 0 \right\rangle
Step 4. Perpendicular component: \mathbf{b}_\perp = \langle 1,2,3 \rangle - \left\langle \frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2}, 0 \right\rangle = \left\langle -\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}, 3 \right\rangle
Verification: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}_\perp = 1\cdot(-\frac{1}{2}) + 1\cdot\frac{1}{2} + 0 = 0 \checkmark

Example 2 — Work done by a force
A force \mathbf{F} = \langle 3, 4, 0 \rangle is applied to move an object along \mathbf{d} = \langle 5, 0, 0 \rangle.
The work done is the force in the direction of motion, times the distance:
W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}} \cdot |\mathbf{d}| = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 15
The scalar projection \text{comp}_{\mathbf{d}},\mathbf{F} = \frac{15}{5} = 3 is the effective component of force. The component 4\hat{\mathbf{j}} does zero work — it is perpendicular to displacement.

Example 3 — Projection matrix explicitly
Let \hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\langle 1, 1 \rangle. Then:
P = \hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1\1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}
Apply to \mathbf{b} = \langle 3, 1 \rangle:
P\mathbf{b} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}4\4\end{pmatrix} = \langle 2, 2 \rangle
Check: \langle 2,2 \rangle is indeed parallel to \langle 1,1 \rangle. And P^2 = P:
P^2 = \frac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix}2&2\2&2\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\1&1\end{pmatrix} = P \checkmark

8. Connection to Direction Cosines
The scalar projection onto \mathbf{e}_i (the i-th standard basis vector) is simply:
\text{comp}_{\mathbf{e}_i},\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{e}_i|} = a_i
The direction cosine \cos\alpha_i = \frac{a_i}{|\mathbf{a}|} is the scalar projection of \hat{\mathbf{a}} onto \mathbf{e}_i.
In other words: the direction cosines are the projections of the unit vector onto the coordinate axes. The fundamental identity \sum \cos^2\alpha_i = 1 is just |\hat{\mathbf{a}}|^2 = 1 in disguise.

9. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
9.1 Least Squares — The Core of Linear Regression
Given data matrix X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p} and labels \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n, linear regression solves:
\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} |\mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}|^2
The solution is:
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top \mathbf{y}
and the fitted values are:
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = X\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \underbrace{X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top}_{\text{hat matrix } H},\mathbf{y} = \text{proj}_{\text{col}(X)},\mathbf{y}
Linear regression is exactly the orthogonal projection of \mathbf{y} onto the column space of X. The residual \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}} is perpendicular to every column of X — that is the normal equations.
X^\top(\mathbf{y} - X\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \mathbf{0}
This is the orthogonality condition from §3, generalized.

9.2 Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
PCA finds directions \mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k (principal components) that maximize variance. Each data point \mathbf{x}_i is projected onto these directions:
z_{ij} = \mathbf{v}_j \cdot \mathbf{x}_i = \text{scalar projection of } \mathbf{x}_i \text{ onto } \mathbf{v}_j
The matrix of projected coordinates Z = XV is exactly the projection of the data onto the subspace spanned by the principal components. The reconstruction \hat{X} = ZV^\top = XV V^\top uses the projection matrix P = VV^\top (since columns of V are orthonormal).
Dimensionality reduction is projection. The information discarded is \mathbf{x} - P\mathbf{x}, the part perpendicular to the subspace.

9.3 Gram-Schmidt and Orthogonalization in Neural Networks
The Gram-Schmidt process builds an orthonormal basis by iteratively removing projections:
\mathbf{u}_k = \mathbf{v}_k - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_j},\mathbf{v}_k
This is used in:

QR decomposition (backbone of many numerical solvers)
Orthogonal weight initialization in RNNs and deep nets, to preserve gradient norms
Spectral normalization layers, which project weight matrices to have unit spectral norm


9.4 Attention as Projection
In the Transformer, the query \mathbf{q} and key \mathbf{k} interact via:
\text{score}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}) = \frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{d_k}} = \frac{|\mathbf{q}||\mathbf{k}|}{\sqrt{d_k}}\cos\theta
The scalar projection of \mathbf{k} onto \mathbf{q} is \text{comp}_{\mathbf{q}},\mathbf{k} = \frac{\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}}{|\mathbf{q}|}. The attention score is a rescaled version of this. The softmax then selects values proportional to how much each key “projects” onto the current query.
The learned weight matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V are projection matrices into query/key/value subspaces.

9.5 Residual Connections and Orthogonal Decomposition
In ResNets, the residual block computes:
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} + \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})
Viewed through the lens of projection: \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) learns the component of the desired output that is not already captured by the identity map — the orthogonal complement of what \mathbf{x} already represents. This is the same spirit as \mathbf{b}_\perp = \mathbf{b} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}. The network learns the residual, not the full transformation.

10. Summary
\boxed{ \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2},\mathbf{a}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{b}_\perp, \qquad \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}_\perp = 0 }



































ConceptFormulaKey PropertyScalar projection\hat{\mathbf{a}}\cdot\mathbf{b}Signed lengthVector projection(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\cdot\mathbf{b})\hat{\mathbf{a}}Parallel to \mathbf{a}Projection matrixP = \hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\topP^2 = P, P^\top = POrthogonal complement\mathbf{b} - P\mathbf{b}Perpendicular to \mathbf{a}Subspace projectionA(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top\mathbf{b}Normal equations

11. Exercises


(Warm-up) Compute \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} and \mathbf{b}_\perp for \mathbf{a} = \langle 2, 1, -1 \rangle, \mathbf{b} = \langle 4, 0, 3 \rangle. Verify orthogonality.


(Projection matrix) Write out the 3\times 3 projection matrix P onto \hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\langle 1,1,1\rangle. Verify P^2 = P and find all eigenvalues.


(Theoretical) Show that |{}\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}| \leq |\mathbf{b}|, with equality iff \mathbf{b} \parallel \mathbf{a}. What classical inequality does this imply?


(Least squares) Three data points (1,2), (2,3), (3,5). Set up the matrix X and compute \hat{\mathbf{y}} = Hy explicitly. Verify the residual \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}} is orthogonal to the columns of X.


(ML connection) In PCA on centered data X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}, the first PC \mathbf{v}_1 is the eigenvector of X^\top X with the largest eigenvalue. Show that the projected variance along \mathbf{v}_1 equals \lambda_1/n, where \lambda_1 is that eigenvalue.



12. References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §12.3 — “The Dot Product.” Scalar and vector projections, worked examples, and the orthogonal decomposition.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (OCW). Lecture notes on dot products and projections. Geometric treatment and applications to physics (work).


See also: Direction Angles and Direction Cosines

01.Maths/Calculus/12.Vectors-and-the-Geo.title: 06.Triple Products
01.Maths/Calculus/12.Vectors-and-the-Geo.content:
“The scalar triple product is the determinant in geometric clothing. The vector triple product is the identity that separates the masters from the beginners.” — personal note, §12.4–12.5 philosophy


0. Motivation
We have the dot product \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} (scalar) and the cross product \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} (vector). What happens when we combine three vectors?
There are exactly two natural ways:




















NameExpressionOutputScalar triple product\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})scalarVector triple product\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})vector
Both appear constantly in physics, geometry, and ML. Let’s build them carefully.

1. The Scalar Triple Product
1.1 Definition

Definition. For \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, the scalar triple product is
\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) \in \mathbb{R}

1.2 Determinant Formula
Write \mathbf{a} = \langle a_1, a_2, a_3 \rangle, \mathbf{b} = \langle b_1, b_2, b_3 \rangle, \mathbf{c} = \langle c_1, c_2, c_3 \rangle.
Recall \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} = \langle b_2 c_3 - b_3 c_2,; b_3 c_1 - b_1 c_3,; b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1 \rangle.
Then:
\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = a_1(b_2 c_3 - b_3 c_2) - a_2(b_1 c_3 - b_3 c_1) + a_3(b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1)
This is exactly the expansion of a 3 \times 3 determinant along the first row:
\boxed{\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}}
The rows are \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} in that order. This is not a coincidence — it is the definition.

1.3 Geometric Meaning: Volume of a Parallelepiped

Theorem. |\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})| equals the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}.

Proof.

\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} is perpendicular to both \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{c}, with magnitude |\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}| =  area of base parallelogram.
Let \theta be the angle between \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}.
The height of the parallelepiped is h = |\mathbf{a}||\cos\theta|.

Therefore:
V = \text{base area} \times h = |\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}| \cdot |\mathbf{a}||\cos\theta| = |\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})| \qquad \square
ASCII diagram of the parallelepiped:

        a·(b×c) > 0: a is on the same side as b×c (right-hand orientation)
        a·(b×c) < 0: a is on the opposite side (left-hand orientation)
        a·(b×c) = 0: a lies in the plane of b and c  →  V = 0

              *---------*
             /|  ^      /|
            / |  | b×c / |  ← height = |a|cosθ
           *---------*   |
           |  |      |   |
       a → |  *------|---*
           | /  c    |  /
           |/        | /  ← base = parallelogram spanned by b, c
           *---------*
                b

Corollary. \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = 0 if and only if \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} are coplanar.

1.4 Cyclic Symmetry
Using determinant row-swap properties (each swap flips sign):
\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b} \cdot (\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{c} \cdot (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})
These are cyclic permutations — rotating (\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}) \to (\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a}) \to (\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}) preserves the determinant.
An anticyclic permutation flips the sign:
\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = -\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{b})
Compact notation: [\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}] or (\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}) for the scalar triple product.

1.5 Dot and Cross Are Interchangeable
\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{c}
Proof. Both equal the same determinant — this follows from the cyclic property above. Specifically, the right side is \mathbf{c} \cdot (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}), which is a cyclic permutation of the left side. \square
This is why the dot and cross in the scalar triple product are sometimes written interchangeably: the result is the same either way.

1.6 Worked Example
Let \mathbf{a} = \langle 1, 4, -7 \rangle, \mathbf{b} = \langle 2, -1, 4 \rangle, \mathbf{c} = \langle 0, -9, 18 \rangle.
\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 4 & -7 \ 2 & -1 & 4 \ 0 & -9 & 18 \end{vmatrix}
Expanding along the first row:
= 1\begin{vmatrix} -1 & 4 \ -9 & 18 \end{vmatrix} - 4\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 \ 0 & 18 \end{vmatrix} + (-7)\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1 \ 0 & -9 \end{vmatrix}
= 1(-18 + 36) - 4(36 - 0) - 7(-18 - 0)
= 18 - 144 + 126 = 0
So the three vectors are coplanar. (Indeed, one can verify \mathbf{c} = -\frac{9}{2}\mathbf{b} + \ldots — they lie in a common plane through the origin.)

2. The Vector Triple Product
2.1 Definition

Definition. The vector triple product of \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is
\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) \in \mathbb{R}^3

Note the parentheses matter: \mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) \neq (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \times \mathbf{c} in general.
2.2 The BAC–CAB Identity

Theorem (BAC–CAB rule).
\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b})

Mnemonic: \mathbf{A} \times (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{C}) = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}). Read: “BAC minus CAB.”
Proof (direct computation).
Let \mathbf{a} = \langle a_1, a_2, a_3 \rangle, etc. Compute \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} first:
\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} = \langle b_2 c_3 - b_3 c_2,; b_3 c_1 - b_1 c_3,; b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1 \rangle
Now compute \mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) — take the first component as representative:
[\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})]_1 = a_2(b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1) - a_3(b_3 c_1 - b_1 c_3)
= a_2 b_1 c_2 - a_2 b_2 c_1 - a_3 b_3 c_1 + a_3 b_1 c_3
= b_1(a_2 c_2 + a_3 c_3) - c_1(a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3)
Add and subtract b_1 a_1 c_1 - c_1 a_1 b_1 = 0:
= b_1(a_1 c_1 + a_2 c_2 + a_3 c_3) - c_1(a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3)
= b_1(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}) - c_1(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b})
This is exactly the first component of \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}). The other two components follow identically. \square

2.3 Geometric Meaning
Claim. \mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) lies in the plane spanned by \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{c}.
Proof. By BAC–CAB, the result is \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}), which is a linear combination of \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{c}. \square
This makes sense: \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} is perpendicular to the \mathbf{b}-\mathbf{c} plane; crossing anything with it brings you back into that plane.
        b×c  ↑  (perpendicular to the b-c plane)
              |
   ___________↑__________
  /           |          /   ← plane of b and c
 /  b         |   c     /
/__________________________/

  a × (b×c) lives inside this plane.
  It is a linear combination of b and c — the "projection" effect.


2.4 The Other Parenthesization
(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \times \mathbf{c} = -\mathbf{c} \times (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) = -[\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{b}) - \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{a})]
= \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c})
Compare with \mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}).
They differ unless \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}), confirming that the cross product is not associative.

2.5 Worked Example
Let \mathbf{a} = \langle 1,2,3 \rangle, \mathbf{b} = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle, \mathbf{c} = \langle 1,0,1 \rangle.
Via BAC–CAB:
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c} = 1 + 0 + 3 = 4, \qquad \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 0 + 2 + 0 = 2
\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = 4\mathbf{b} - 2\mathbf{c} = 4\langle 0,1,0 \rangle - 2\langle 1,0,1 \rangle = \langle -2, 4, -2 \rangle
Verify directly:
\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} = \langle 1\cdot1 - 0\cdot0,; 0\cdot1 - 0\cdot1,; 0\cdot0 - 1\cdot1 \rangle = \langle 1, 0, -1 \rangle
\mathbf{a} \times \langle 1,0,-1 \rangle = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 1 & 2 & 3 \ 1 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} = \langle (2)(-1)-(3)(0),; (3)(1)-(1)(-1),; (1)(0)-(2)(1) \rangle
= \langle -2, 4, -2 \rangle \checkmark

3. Summary of All Identities





































IdentityExpressionScalar triple product = determinant\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = \det[\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}]Volume of parallelepiped$V =Cyclic symmetry\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})Dot-cross swap\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = (\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{c}BAC–CAB\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})Non-associativity\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) \neq (\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{c} in generalCoplanarity test\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = 0 \iff \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c} coplanar

4. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
4.1 Volume Forms and Change of Variables in Generative Models
The scalar triple product is the 3 \times 3 determinant. In normalizing flows and variational autoencoders, transformations f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n preserve probability mass via the change-of-variables formula:
p_X(\mathbf{x}) = p_Z(f^{-1}(\mathbf{x})) \left|\det J_f(\mathbf{x})\right|^{-1}
The Jacobian determinant \det J_f is the n-dimensional generalization of the scalar triple product. For n = 3, the Jacobian determinant of a linear map f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} with rows \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} is exactly \mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}).
Understanding the triple product = understanding the volume scaling of a linear transformation = understanding how generative models warp probability distributions.

4.2 The BAC–CAB Rule in Backpropagation Through Cross Products
Certain physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and 3D geometry models (e.g., PointNet, mesh CNNs) compute cross products as part of the forward pass — to get surface normals, angular momentum, torque.
When backpropagating through \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}, the gradient with respect to \mathbf{b} involves:
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{b}}[\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})] = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c}
This uses exactly the dot-cross swap identity from §1.5. The BAC–CAB rule then appears in higher-order derivatives through cross product layers.

4.3 Coplanarity → Linear Dependence → Rank Deficiency
The condition \mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = 0 is coplanarity, which is exactly \det[\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}] = 0, i.e., linear dependence.
In ML:

A feature matrix with linearly dependent columns has a singular (rank-deficient) Gram matrix X^\top X. This breaks ordinary least squares and causes the normal equations to have no unique solution.
Regularization (Ridge, Lasso) is the practical fix — but the geometry is precisely the parallelepiped collapsing to zero volume.
A neural network with redundant neurons has weight vectors that are coplanar → the corresponding rows of the weight matrix are dependent → the layer is not full rank → information is being wasted.


4.4 Quaternions and 3D Rotation in Deep Learning
Quaternion multiplication for \mathbf{p} = (p_0, \mathbf{p}) and \mathbf{q} = (q_0, \mathbf{q}):
\mathbf{p}\mathbf{q} = (p_0 q_0 - \mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q},; p_0\mathbf{q} + q_0\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{p}\times\mathbf{q})
The vector part of the product involves \mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{q}. When composing rotations or computing the double cover SO(3) \cong S^3/{\pm 1}, the BAC–CAB identity underlies the Rodrigues’ rotation formula:
R_{\hat{n},\theta}(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{v}\cos\theta + (\hat{n}\times\mathbf{v})\sin\theta + \hat{n}(\hat{n}\cdot\mathbf{v})(1-\cos\theta)
Expanding \hat{n} \times (\hat{n} \times \mathbf{v}) via BAC–CAB gives \hat{n}(\hat{n}\cdot\mathbf{v}) - \mathbf{v}, which is exactly the third term.
This rotation formula is used in 3D pose estimation networks (e.g., in robotics, human pose, and NeRF-based models where camera orientations must be parameterized).

4.5 Geometric Algebra and Attention Over 3D Structures
In equivariant neural networks (e.g., SE(3)-Transformers, Equiformer), layers must be equivariant to rotations and reflections. The scalar triple product \mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) is a pseudoscalar — it is invariant under rotations but flips sign under reflections.
Networks that operate on molecular geometry (AlphaFold2, DiffDock) need to decide whether to use true scalars or pseudoscalars as features, because this determines how the model transforms under orientation reversal. Getting this wrong breaks equivariance.

5. Exercises


(Volume) Find the volume of the parallelepiped with edges \mathbf{a} = \langle 2,3,4 \rangle, \mathbf{b} = \langle 1,0,-1 \rangle, \mathbf{c} = \langle 0,1,2 \rangle.


(Coplanarity) For which value of k are \mathbf{a} = \langle 1,2,k \rangle, \mathbf{b} = \langle 3,1,0 \rangle, \mathbf{c} = \langle 1,-1,2 \rangle coplanar?


(BAC–CAB proof check) Verify the BAC–CAB identity for the second and third components of the example in §2.5.


(Non-associativity) With \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{k}, compute both \mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) and (\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{c} explicitly. Confirm they differ.


(Theoretical) Prove that \mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) + \mathbf{b}\times(\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a}) + \mathbf{c}\times(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{0}. (This is the Jacobi identity for the cross product.)


(ML) A 3 \times 3 weight matrix W in a neural network has rows \mathbf{w}_1, \mathbf{w}_2, \mathbf{w}_3. Show that \det(W) = \mathbf{w}_1 \cdot (\mathbf{w}_2 \times \mathbf{w}_3), and explain what \det(W) = 0 means for the network’s expressive power.



6. References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §12.4 “The Cross Product” and §12.5 extensions. The determinant formula, parallelepiped volume, and worked examples follow this treatment.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (OCW). Lecture notes §1–3 on vectors and determinants; the geometric interpretation of the scalar triple product as a signed volume is developed there.
