01.Maths/Calculus/12.Vectors-and-the-Geo.content:
The geometry we built in the previous note wasn’t just aesthetic. Every major domain — physics, engineering, computer vision, machine learning — quietly runs on quadric surfaces. This note is about seeing them everywhere.

Tags: multivariable-calculus applications machine-learning deep-learning physics engineering
References: Stewart §12.6, §14.7 · MIT 18.02 · Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (Bishop) · Goodfellow et al. Deep Learning
Prerequisite note: Quadratic Surfaces

0. The Organizing Principle
Every application in this note traces back to one of three fundamental facts:

Fact A. The level sets of any quadratic form \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x} = c are quadric surfaces.
Fact B. Any smooth function looks quadratic near a critical point (Taylor expansion).
Fact C. Physical laws written in terms of energy, distance, or intensity naturally produce degree-2 equations.

Keep these in mind. When you spot a quadric in the wild, ask: which fact brought it here?

1. Physics
1.1 Moment of Inertia Ellipsoid (Rigid Body Dynamics)
For a rigid body rotating about an axis \hat{\mathbf{n}}, the moment of inertia is:
I(\hat{\mathbf{n}}) = \hat{\mathbf{n}}^T \mathbf{I} \hat{\mathbf{n}}
where \mathbf{I} is the inertia tensor — a real symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix:
\mathbf{I} = \begin{pmatrix} I_{xx} & -I_{xy} & -I_{xz} \ -I_{xy} & I_{yy} & -I_{yz} \ -I_{xz} & -I_{yz} & I_{zz} \end{pmatrix}
The surface {(\hat{\mathbf{n}}) : I(\hat{\mathbf{n}}) = 1} traces out an ellipsoid called the Poinsot ellipsoid (or inertia ellipsoid). Its principal axes are the principal axes of inertia — the directions for which products of inertia vanish and the body rotates “cleanly.”
Why it matters: Euler’s equations of rigid body motion are simplest in the principal axis frame. Satellites, gyroscopes, and spacecraft attitude control all exploit this geometry. The famous “tennis racket theorem” (intermediate axis theorem) — a rigid body tumbling unstably about its intermediate-inertia axis — is a consequence of the saddle-like structure of energy on the angular momentum sphere intersected with the Poinsot ellipsoid.
\boxed{\text{The ellipsoid encodes ALL rotational inertia of a body.}}

1.2 Index Ellipsoid in Optics
In an anisotropic crystal, the refractive index depends on polarization direction. The optical indicatrix (index ellipsoid) is:
\frac{x^2}{n_x^2} + \frac{y^2}{n_y^2} + \frac{z^2}{n_z^2} = 1
where n_x, n_y, n_z are principal refractive indices. Given a wave propagating in direction \hat{\mathbf{k}}, the allowed polarizations and their speeds are found by intersecting the plane \hat{\mathbf{k}} \cdot \mathbf{r} = 0 with this ellipsoid — the two semi-axes of the resulting ellipse give the two refractive indices (birefringence).
Special cases:

n_x = n_y \neq n_z: uniaxial crystal (e.g., calcite) — ellipsoid of revolution. One optic axis.
n_x = n_y = n_z: isotropic (sphere). No birefringence.
All different: biaxial crystal — general ellipsoid. Two optic axes.

This is the foundational geometry of wave plates, polarizers, and electro-optic modulators.

1.3 Equipotential Surfaces
For a point charge q at the origin, the electric potential is V = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r}, and equipotentials are spheres x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = r^2 — the simplest quadric.
More interesting: for a quadrupole or in an external field, potentials become:
V = \alpha x^2 + \beta y^2 + \gamma z^2 + \text{linear terms}
and equipotential surfaces are general quadrics. Magnetic traps (e.g., Penning traps for electrons/ions) use quadrupole fields whose equipotentials are hyperboloids — the geometry determines which particles stay confined.

1.4 Stress and Strain Quadrics (Continuum Mechanics)
At any point in a deformed solid, the stress state is described by a symmetric tensor \boldsymbol{\sigma}. The stress quadric \mathbf{x}^T \boldsymbol{\sigma} \mathbf{x} = \pm 1 encodes the normal stress on every plane through that point: the normal stress on a plane with unit normal \hat{\mathbf{n}} is \hat{\mathbf{n}}^T \boldsymbol{\sigma} \hat{\mathbf{n}}.
Principal stresses = eigenvalues of \boldsymbol{\sigma} = semi-axes of the quadric. Engineering design requires these to stay within yield criteria — Mohr’s circle in 2D is a slice of this quadric.

2. Engineering & Architecture
2.1 Paraboloidal Reflectors — Satellite Dishes, Telescopes, Headlights
The elliptic paraboloid z = \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} (circular for a=b) has a miraculous reflective property:

Theorem. All rays parallel to the axis of a circular paraboloid z = \frac{x^2+y^2}{4f} reflect through the single focus F = (0,0,f).

Proof. A point on the paraboloid is P = (x_0, y_0, \frac{x_0^2+y_0^2}{4f}). The outward normal direction at P is \nabla(x^2+y^2-4fz) = (2x_0, 2y_0, -4f). An incoming ray \mathbf{d} = (0,0,-1) (downward) reflects as \mathbf{d} - 2(\mathbf{d}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}})\hat{\mathbf{n}}. After normalizing and computing, one verifies the reflected ray passes through (0,0,f). \blacksquare
Applications:

Radio telescopes (Arecibo, VLA): collect weak signals into a detector at the focus.
Satellite dishes: same geometry.
Automobile headlights: run backward — place a bulb at the focus, get a parallel beam.
Solar concentrators: focus sunlight to heat a fluid.

The key insight is purely geometric and follows from the quadric’s definition as the locus equidistant from a focus and a directrix plane.

2.2 Cooling Towers and Hyperboloidal Structures
The hyperboloid of one sheet \frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1 is a ruled surface — it can be generated by straight lines (two families of them). This means:

It can be built from straight steel rods or cables despite having a curved shape.
It is structurally efficient: the doubly-ruled structure distributes load well.

Nuclear cooling towers and many architectural landmarks (the Canton Tower in Guangzhou, the McDonnell Planetarium in St. Louis) use this geometry precisely because it combines structural strength, material efficiency, and aesthetic curvature — all from a single algebraic equation.

A contractor can build a hyperboloidal tower using only straight pieces of material. Every point on the surface lies on two straight lines entirely contained in the surface. That is a remarkable theorem.


2.3 Elliptic Reflectors in Acoustics and Medicine
The ellipsoid has two foci F_1, F_2 such that any ray from F_1 reflects to F_2. This is a direct consequence of the ellipse reflection property extended to 3D.
Applications:

Lithotripsy: Shock waves generated at F_1 of an ellipsoidal reflector converge at F_2 inside the patient, shattering kidney stones without surgery.
Whispering galleries: An elliptical (or ellipsoidal) room makes a whisper at one focus audible at the other — used in museum exhibits and architecturally in the Capitol building’s Statuary Hall.
Acoustic horns: Near-ellipsoidal designs optimize sound directivity.


2.4 Gear Teeth and Cam Profiles
Elliptic gears (cross-sections are ellipses) transmit variable angular velocity — useful in mechanical presses and looms where you need speed variation within a cycle. The 3D cams whose profiles produce prescribed motion profiles are often quadric sections. Not glamorous, but every time you use a variable-speed mechanism, there’s a conic or quadric hiding in the design.

3. Computer Graphics and Computer Vision
3.1 Ray–Quadric Intersection
In ray tracing (the algorithm behind physically-based rendering in films and games), a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is intersected with a quadric surface defined by \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{x} + c = 0.
Substituting:
(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d})^T A (\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) + \mathbf{b}^T(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) + c = 0
Expanding, this is a quadratic in t:
(\mathbf{d}^T A \mathbf{d}) t^2 + (2\mathbf{d}^T A \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{d}) t + (\mathbf{o}^T A \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{o} + c) = 0
i.e., \alpha t^2 + \beta t + \gamma = 0. The discriminant \Delta = \beta^2 - 4\alpha\gamma immediately tells you:

\Delta < 0: ray misses the surface.
\Delta = 0: tangent.
\Delta > 0: two intersection points; take the smaller positive t.

This is why spheres, ellipsoids, cylinders, and cones are primitive shapes in almost every ray tracer — their intersection test reduces to solving a single quadratic equation, which is analytically exact and computationally cheap.

3.2 Ellipsoid Fitting and Shape Estimation
Given a point cloud {p_1, \ldots, p_n} \subset \mathbb{R}^3 (from a 3D scanner, LiDAR, or depth camera), fitting an ellipsoid means finding A, \mathbf{b}, c minimizing:
\sum_{i=1}^n \left( p_i^T A p_i + \mathbf{b}^T p_i + c \right)^2
This is a least-squares problem on the coefficients of a quadric. Applications:

Medical imaging: Fitting an ellipsoid to a segmented organ (heart, kidney) provides compact shape descriptors for disease tracking.
Robotics: Fitting ellipsoids to object point clouds gives bounding volumes for collision detection.
Astronomy: Fitting ellipsoidal models to galaxy images to extract morphological parameters.


3.3 Quadrics in Projective Space — The Foundation of Geometric Computer Vision
In projective geometry, a quadric is defined by \mathbf{x}^T Q \mathbf{x} = 0 for homogeneous coordinates \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{P}^3. The absolute conic — a fundamental object in camera calibration — is the intersection of the quadric x^2+y^2+z^2=0 (complex, but projectively real) with the plane at infinity.
Camera calibration (recovering intrinsic parameters from images of known patterns) exploits the image of the absolute conic. Every time you scan a QR code or do AR on your phone, the camera calibration that makes it work has quadric geometry at its foundation.

4. Machine Learning — Deep Dive
4.1 The Loss Landscape Is Locally a Quadric
This deserves a careful statement.
Setup. Let L: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R} be a smooth loss function with a critical point at \theta^_ (i.e., \nabla L(\theta^_) = 0). Taylor expansion gives:
L(\theta) = L(\theta^_) + \frac{1}{2}(\theta - \theta^_)^T H (\theta - \theta^_) + O(|\theta - \theta^_|^3)
where H = \nabla^2 L(\theta^*) \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p} is the Hessian. The level sets of this local approximation are quadric hypersurfaces in \mathbb{R}^p.
Classification of critical points:






























Hessian signatureQuadric typeCritical point typeAll \lambda_i > 0Ellipsoid (bowl)Local minimumAll \lambda_i < 0Inverted ellipsoidLocal maximumMixed signsSaddle (hyperbolic)Saddle pointSome \lambda_i = 0Degenerate quadricNeeds higher-order analysis
Key result (Dauphin et al., 2014): For random matrix models of neural network loss surfaces, the fraction of critical points that are local minima (all \lambda_i > 0) decays exponentially with the number of negative eigenvalues. In high dimensions, almost all critical points are saddles. The loss value at a saddle is typically higher than at minima — but the very deepest saddles have loss close to the global minimum. This means finding a saddle with low loss value is almost as good as finding a local minimum.

4.2 Condition Number, Ellipsoids, and Gradient Descent Convergence
The geometry. For a quadratic loss L(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}\theta^T H \theta with H \succ 0 (positive definite), the level set L(\theta) = c is the ellipsoid:
\theta^T H \theta = 2c
whose principal axes are eigenvectors of H with lengths \sqrt{2c/\lambda_i}.
Gradient descent with step size \eta:
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla L(\theta_t) = \theta_t - \eta H \theta_t = (I - \eta H)\theta_t
In the eigenbasis of H, component i evolves as \theta_t^{(i)} = (1 - \eta \lambda_i)^t \theta_0^{(i)}.
For convergence: |1 - \eta \lambda_i| < 1 for all i, requiring \eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}.
The convergence rate of component i is |1 - \eta \lambda_i|. The worst-conditioned component dictates overall speed.
Condition number \kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}:

The optimal step size is \eta^* = 2/(\lambda_{\max} + \lambda_{\min}).
At this step size, the convergence factor is \frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}.
For \kappa = 1000 (highly elongated ellipsoid): factor \approx 0.998 — need \sim 3000 iterations to reduce error by e^{-6}.
For \kappa = 1 (sphere): factor = 0 — one step convergence.

\boxed{\text{Elongated ellipsoid} \Leftrightarrow \text{high condition number} \Leftrightarrow \text{slow gradient descent.}}
What fixes this:

Preconditioning / Newton’s method: Use H^{-1}\nabla L instead of \nabla L — transforms the ellipsoid back into a sphere in the new metric.
Batch normalization: Implicitly reduces condition number of the Fisher information matrix (related to the Hessian).
Adam / RMSProp: Maintain per-parameter step sizes, effectively approximating the diagonal of H^{-1}.


4.3 Gaussian Distributions and the Mahalanobis Ellipsoid
The density. For X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma) in \mathbb{R}^d:
p(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp!\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)\right)
The exponent is -\frac{1}{2} d_M^2(x, \mu) where d_M(x,\mu) = \sqrt{(x-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)} is the Mahalanobis distance.
Level sets {x : d_M(x,\mu) = r} are ellipsoids with:

Center: \mu.
Axes: eigenvectors of \Sigma.
Axis lengths: r\sqrt{\lambda_i(\Sigma)}.

The 68-95-99.7 rule in d dimensions. The fraction of probability within the ellipsoid d_M \leq r is:
P(\chi^2_d \leq r^2)
This depends on dimension d — in high dimensions, most probability mass concentrates in a thin shell near r = \sqrt{d}. The ellipsoid geometry is essential for understanding this concentration of measure phenomenon.
Applications:

Anomaly detection: Flag x as anomalous if d_M(x, \mu) > \tau for some threshold \tau. Geometrically: is x outside the “normal” ellipsoid?
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA): Classify by nearest class center in Mahalanobis distance — the decision boundary is a quadric surface (hyperplane when two classes have equal \Sigma, quadric in general).
Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM): The EM algorithm fits a mixture of Gaussians; each component’s “territory” is carved by quadric decision boundaries.
Kalman Filter: State uncertainty is an ellipsoid in state space; Kalman updates are ellipsoid-to-ellipsoid operations.


4.4 PCA — Eigendecomposition of the Covariance Ellipsoid
Setup. Given centered data X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}, the sample covariance is:
\hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{n} X^T X
The level set {x : x^T \hat{\Sigma}^{-1} x = 1} is an ellipsoid — the data ellipsoid — oriented along the principal directions of variation.
PCA finds the axes of this ellipsoid. The k-th principal component is the k-th largest eigenvector of \hat{\Sigma} — the direction of the k-th longest axis. Projecting onto the top k axes retains maximum variance.
Geometric interpretation: PCA whitens the data (transforms the covariance ellipsoid into a sphere) via z = \Lambda^{-1/2} P^T x where \hat{\Sigma} = P \Lambda P^T. After whitening, Euclidean distance equals Mahalanobis distance.
Connection to SVD: \hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{n} X^T X. If X = U S V^T (SVD), then \hat{\Sigma} = V \frac{S^2}{n} V^T — the eigenvectors of \hat{\Sigma} are the right singular vectors of X.

4.5 Kernel Methods — Quadric Decision Boundaries
A support vector machine with a degree-2 polynomial kernel K(x, x') = (x \cdot x' + 1)^2 implicitly maps \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^{d(d+3)/2 + 1} via:
\phi(x) = (x_1^2, \ldots, x_d^2, \sqrt{2}x_1 x_2, \ldots, \sqrt{2}x_{d-1}x_d, \sqrt{2}x_1, \ldots, \sqrt{2}x_d, 1)
A linear hyperplane in this feature space corresponds to a quadric surface in the original \mathbb{R}^d.
Concrete example. In \mathbb{R}^2, the decision function:
f(x) = w_1 x_1^2 + w_2 x_2^2 + w_3 x_1 x_2 + w_4 x_1 + w_5 x_2 + w_6 = 0
is a conic section (ellipse, hyperbola, or parabola). The XOR problem (not linearly separable) is separable by an ellipse — which is exactly a quadric decision boundary.

4.6 Quadratic Approximations in Bayesian Inference — The Laplace Approximation
In Bayesian ML, the posterior p(\theta | \mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D}|\theta)p(\theta) is often intractable. The Laplace approximation approximates it as a Gaussian:

Find the MAP estimate \theta^* = \arg\max_\theta \log p(\theta|\mathcal{D}).
Compute H = -\nabla^2 \log p(\theta|\mathcal{D})\big|_{\theta^*} (the Hessian of the negative log-posterior).
Approximate: p(\theta|\mathcal{D}) \approx \mathcal{N}(\theta^*,\ H^{-1}).

The uncertainty region {\theta : (\theta-\theta^_)^T H (\theta-\theta^_) \leq c} is an ellipsoid in parameter space — the local quadric geometry of the log-posterior encoded into a Gaussian approximation. This is the foundation of methods like KFAC, natural gradient, and Bayesian neural networks with Laplace approximations.

4.7 Second-Order Methods and the Newton Step
Newton’s method for minimizing L(\theta):
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - H_t^{-1} \nabla L(\theta_t)
Geometric interpretation. At each step, Newton locally approximates L by the quadratic \hat{L}(\theta) = L(\theta_t) + \nabla L^T(\theta-\theta_t) + \frac{1}{2}(\theta-\theta_t)^T H_t (\theta-\theta_t) and jumps to its minimum exactly. The level sets of \hat{L} are ellipsoids; Newton corrects for the elongation by applying H_t^{-1}, effectively working in the metric defined by the quadric.
Why not always use Newton? Computing and inverting H \in \mathbb{R}^{p\times p} costs O(p^3) — infeasible for p = 10^8 (modern neural nets). Quasi-Newton methods (L-BFGS) maintain a low-rank approximation of H^{-1} built from gradient differences.

5. Statistics
5.1 Confidence Ellipsoids
For a parameter estimate \hat{\theta} with asymptotic covariance \Sigma, the 1-\alpha confidence region is:
\left{\theta : (\theta - \hat{\theta})^T \Sigma^{-1} (\theta - \hat{\theta}) \leq \chi^2_{p,1-\alpha}\right}
This is an ellipsoid in parameter space. The chi-squared quantile determines its scale; \Sigma determines its shape and orientation. Visualizing this ellipsoid (or its 2D cross-sections) is standard practice in econometrics, biostatistics, and experimental physics.

5.2 Chi-Squared Distribution Geometry
If X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d), then |X|^2 = \sum_{i=1}^d X_i^2 \sim \chi^2_d.
The “sphere” |X|^2 = r^2 is where most probability concentrates. In general (correlated) Gaussians, this sphere becomes an ellipsoid. The chi-squared distribution is literally describing probability in the quadric level sets of the Gaussian density. Every p-value and hypothesis test at its core is asking: “is this observation inside or outside the ellipsoid?“

6. Differential Geometry and General Relativity (A Glimpse)
6.1 Curvature and the Dupin Indicatrix
At a point P on a smooth surface, the Dupin indicatrix is the conic section:
\kappa_1 u^2 + \kappa_2 v^2 = \pm 1
where \kappa_1, \kappa_2 are the principal curvatures (eigenvalues of the second fundamental form). Its type classifies P:






























IndicatrixGaussian curvature K = \kappa_1\kappa_2Point typeEllipseK > 0Elliptic — bowl-shaped (like a sphere)HyperbolaK < 0Hyperbolic — saddle-shapedParallel linesK = 0Parabolic — flat in one directionDegenerate\kappa_1 = \kappa_2 = 0Planar (umbilic or flat)
This connects quadric surfaces to the intrinsic geometry of general surfaces: every surface is locally classified by which quadric its curvature resembles.
6.2 Metric Tensors in General Relativity
The metric tensor g_{\mu\nu} defines the spacetime interval:
ds^2 = g_{\mu\nu} dx^\mu dx^\nu
This is a quadratic form in dx^\mu. The light cone ds^2 = 0 is a quadric (a cone in 4D spacetime). Near a massive body, the “ellipsoid of simultaneity” and the null cone geometry are quadrics in spacetime — and their deformation by gravity is literally what general relativity describes.

7. Geodesy and Earth Modeling
The Earth is not a sphere. It is more accurately modeled as an oblate spheroid — an ellipsoid of revolution:
\frac{x^2 + y^2}{a^2} + \frac{z^2}{b^2} = 1, \quad a > b
with a \approx 6{,}378{,}137 m (equatorial radius) and b \approx 6{,}356{,}752 m (polar radius). The flattening f = (a-b)/a \approx 1/298.257 is small but critical for GPS.
GPS and WGS84: The World Geodetic System 1984 defines coordinates relative to this reference ellipsoid. Every GPS receiver on the planet computes your latitude, longitude, and altitude by finding your position relative to this specific quadric surface embedded in 3D space. Your phone’s location is literally solving an ellipsoid problem billions of times per year.
Gravity and the geoid: The actual equipotential surface of Earth’s gravity field (the geoid) deviates from the reference ellipsoid by up to \pm 100 m. Geodesy is the science of measuring and modeling this deviation.

8. Summary — The Quadric Surface Zoo in Applications











































































SurfaceDomainApplicationEllipsoidPhysicsInertia tensor, stress quadric, optical indicatrixEllipsoidML/StatsGaussian level sets, PCA, confidence regions, Mahalanobis distanceEllipsoidGeodesyEarth reference model (WGS84), GPSEllipsoidMedicineLithotripsy reflectors, organ shape descriptorsElliptic paraboloidEngineeringSatellite dishes, telescopes, solar concentratorsElliptic paraboloidMLLocal model of a convex loss near a minimumHyperbolic paraboloidML/DLSaddle points in loss landscapesHyperbolic paraboloidArchitectureThin-shell roof structures (anticlastic shells)Hyperboloid (1 sheet)EngineeringCooling towers, ruled structural surfacesHyperboloid (1 sheet)PhysicsMagnetic trapping geometriesConeComputer graphicsRay tracing primitives, shadow volumesGeneral quadricComputer visionCamera calibration (absolute conic), quadric fittingGeneral quadricMLKernel SVM decision boundaries, Laplace approximation

9. A Unifying Perspective
Here is the thread connecting everything:
A quadric surface is the geometry of a symmetric bilinear form.
Every domain has a natural symmetric bilinear form:

Physics: kinetic energy T = \frac{1}{2}\omega^T \mathbf{I} \omega, potential energy, stress.
ML: loss curvature \theta^T H \theta, data covariance x^T \Sigma^{-1} x.
Statistics: chi-squared distances.
Geometry: the second fundamental form.
Relativity: the metric tensor g_{\mu\nu}.

In every case, the level sets of that form are quadric surfaces, and their geometry — the eigenvalues, condition number, positive/negative definiteness — tells you the qualitative behavior of the system.

This is why linear algebra is the language of modern science. Symmetric matrices produce quadric surfaces. Quadric surfaces encode geometry. Geometry governs behavior.


10. Practice Problems
Problem 1 (Physics). A uniform solid cylinder has moments of inertia I_1 = I_2 = \frac{1}{4}MR^2 + \frac{1}{12}ML^2 and I_3 = \frac{1}{2}MR^2 about its axes. Write the equation of the Poinsot inertia ellipsoid for a cylinder with M=1, R=1, L=2. What are its semi-axes?
Problem 2 (Ray tracing). A ray \mathbf{r}(t) = (1, 0, 0) + t(-1, 1, 1)/\sqrt{3} intersects the ellipsoid x^2 + \frac{y^2}{4} + \frac{z^2}{9} = 1. Find the intersection points.
Problem 3 (ML). A 2D loss has Hessian H = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 3 \ 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix} at a critical point. (a) Is this a minimum, maximum, or saddle?
(b) What is the condition number?
(c) Describe the geometry of the loss level sets.
(d) Find the principal axes of the corresponding quadric.
Problem 4 (Gaussian geometry). For X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma) with \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, find the equation of the 1\sigma confidence ellipse (d_M = 1). Find its principal axes and lengths.
Problem 5 (GPS). The WGS84 ellipsoid has a = 6378137 m and b = 6356752 m. Compute the eccentricity e = \sqrt{1 - b^2/a^2} and the flattening f = (a-b)/a. A point on the equator is at distance a from the center; a point at the pole is at distance b. How much closer to the center (in km) are you at the pole?
Problem 6 (Architecture). The cooling tower at a power plant has the equation \frac{x^2}{25} + \frac{y^2}{25} - \frac{z^2}{100} = 1 (meters). Find: (a) the radius at the waist (z=0), (b) the radius at height z = 20 m, (c) write explicitly one straight line lying entirely on this surface.

Last updated: 2026. Cross-reference: Quadratic Surfaces for the classification theory.

01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/01.title: 01.Vector Functions
01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/01.content:
“A vector function is simply a machine: feed it a number, and it hands back an arrow.” — personal note, inspired by Stewart §13.1 & MIT 18.02


0. Motivation — Why Not Just Use Scalars?
In single-variable calculus we tracked one number evolving over time. But the real world moves in space. A particle doesn’t just have a speed — it has a position, a velocity, and an acceleration, all of which are arrows pointing somewhere in \mathbb{R}^3.
Vector functions are the language for this. And, as we will see later, they are the hidden backbone of neural networks, where every forward pass is literally a composition of vector-valued maps.

1. Definition

Definition 1.1 (Vector Function / Vector-Valued Function). A vector function (or vector-valued function) is a map \mathbf{r} : D \subseteq \mathbb{R} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^n where D is the domain (a subset of real numbers) and n \geq 1.

For n = 3 — the most common case in Stewart and MIT 18.02 — we write:
\boxed{\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t),, g(t),, h(t) \rangle = f(t),\mathbf{i} + g(t),\mathbf{j} + h(t),\mathbf{k}}
where f, g, h : D \to \mathbb{R} are the component functions.
Remark. The two notations \langle f, g, h \rangle and f\mathbf{i} + g\mathbf{j} + h\mathbf{k} are identical. I prefer angle-bracket notation — it is cleaner and avoids confusion between the unit vector \mathbf{k} and a generic index.

2. Domain
The natural domain of \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t) \rangle is:
D = \mathrm{dom}(f) \cap \mathrm{dom}(g) \cap \mathrm{dom}(h)
Example 2.1. Find the domain of \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \sqrt{t-1},\ \ln(3-t),\ t^2 \rangle.

f(t) = \sqrt{t-1} requires t \geq 1.
g(t) = \ln(3-t) requires t < 3.
h(t) = t^2 is defined everywhere.

D = [1, 3)
This is exactly how you restrict inputs in a machine learning pipeline: each feature/component imposes its own constraint, and the valid input set is the intersection.

3. The Space Curve
As t varies over D, the tip of \mathbf{r}(t) traces out a space curve C in \mathbb{R}^3.
          z
          |
          |       • r(t₂)
          |      /
          |   • r(t₁)
          |  /
          | /   C (the curve)
          |/_________________ y
         /
        x

The curve C is the image (range) of \mathbf{r}, not the function itself. The function carries the parametrization — the speed and direction of traversal. Two different vector functions can trace the same curve at different speeds. This distinction matters enormously in physics and in optimization (gradient descent traces a curve in parameter space — the parametrization is what the learning rate controls).

4. Concrete Examples
4.1 The Helix
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t,\ \sin t,\ t \rangle, \quad t \in [0, 4\pi]

x(t) = \cos t,\ y(t) = \sin t traces a circle: x^2 + y^2 = 1.
z(t) = t climbs linearly.
Together: a circular helix — like a coil spring or a DNA strand.

Visualization (top view vs side view):
Top view (xy-plane):       Side view (xz-plane):

       y                         z
       |   * *                   |        *
       |  *   *              4π  |       *
       | *     *                 |      *
       |*       *            2π  |     *
       +----------x              |    *
        (circle)              0  |___*_______ x

4.2 A Line in \mathbb{R}^3
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 1,2,3 \rangle + t\langle 4,-1,2 \rangle = \langle 1+4t,\ 2-t,\ 3+2t \rangle
This is the line through (1,2,3) in direction (4,-1,2). Every line in \mathbb{R}^3 can be written this way.
Connection to ML: In linear regression, the prediction \hat{y} = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b defines a hyperplane. The weight vector \mathbf{w} is literally the direction vector of a linear map on input space. The parametric line is the 1D analogue.
4.3 Lissajous Curve (2D)
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \sin(2t),\ \sin(3t) \rangle, \quad t \in [0, 2\pi]
The component frequencies being incommensurate (2:3) produces a curve that almost-but-not-quite closes. This is used in signal processing and appears in the analysis of recurrent networks (the hidden state traces a curve in state space whose topology encodes memory).

5. Limits and Continuity
Definition 5.1 (Limit). Let \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t) \rangle. Then:
\lim_{t \to a} \mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle \lim_{t \to a} f(t),\ \lim_{t \to a} g(t),\ \lim_{t \to a} h(t) \right\rangle
provided each component limit exists.
Definition 5.2 (Continuity). \mathbf{r} is continuous at t = a if:
\lim_{t \to a} \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{r}(a)
This reduces, component by component, to continuity of f, g, and h at a.
Theorem 5.3. \mathbf{r} is continuous at a \iff f, g, and h are each continuous at a.
Proof. Follows immediately from the component-wise definition of the limit and the equivalence of the Euclidean norm with the \ell^\infty norm in finite dimensions. \blacksquare
Remark (AI context). Activation functions in neural networks are required to be continuous (and usually differentiable) precisely so that the output vector \mathbf{r}(t) — interpreting t as a parameter controlling the input — varies smoothly. ReLU is continuous but not differentiable at 0, which is why subdifferentials are needed in backprop.

6. The Derivative
6.1 Definition from First Principles
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \frac{d\mathbf{r}}{dt} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\mathbf{r}(t + \Delta t) - \mathbf{r}(t)}{\Delta t}
Geometrically: \mathbf{r}(t+\Delta t) - \mathbf{r}(t) is a secant vector. As \Delta t \to 0, this secant vector (after scaling) approaches the tangent vector to the curve at \mathbf{r}(t).
                   r(t + Δt)
                  *
                 /↑  ← secant vector
                / |
    r(t) →    *  |
              |   (as Δt → 0, secant → tangent)
              ↓ tangent r'(t)

6.2 Computation Rule
Theorem 6.1. If \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t) \rangle and f, g, h are differentiable, then:
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle f'(t),\ g'(t),\ h'(t) \rangle
Proof. By the component-wise definition of the limit: \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\mathbf{r}(t+\Delta t) - \mathbf{r}(t)}{\Delta t} = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \left\langle \frac{f(t+\Delta t)-f(t)}{\Delta t},\ \frac{g(t+\Delta t)-g(t)}{\Delta t},\ \frac{h(t+\Delta t)-h(t)}{\Delta t} \right\rangle = \langle f'(t),\ g'(t),\ h'(t) \rangle \qquad \blacksquare
Example 6.2. Differentiate \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t^3,\ e^{2t},\ \sin t \rangle:
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle 3t^2,\ 2e^{2t},\ \cos t \rangle
6.3 Differentiation Rules
Let \mathbf{u}(t) and \mathbf{v}(t) be differentiable vector functions, f(t) a scalar function.





























RuleFormulaSum\frac{d}{dt}[\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}] = \mathbf{u}' + \mathbf{v}'Scalar multiple\frac{d}{dt}[f,\mathbf{u}] = f'\mathbf{u} + f\mathbf{u}'Dot product\frac{d}{dt}[\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}] = \mathbf{u}' \cdot \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}'Cross product\frac{d}{dt}[\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}] = \mathbf{u}' \times \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}'Chain rule\frac{d}{dt}[\mathbf{u}(f(t))] = f'(t),\mathbf{u}'(f(t))
Warning (cross product). Order matters: \mathbf{u}' \times \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}', not the reverse. The cross product is anticommutative.
Key lemma — constant length implies orthogonal derivative:
Lemma 6.3. If |\mathbf{r}(t)| = c (constant) for all t, then \mathbf{r}(t) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) = 0.
Proof. \mathbf{r}(t) \cdot \mathbf{r}(t) = c^2. Differentiate both sides: \frac{d}{dt}[\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{r}] = 2\mathbf{r}(t) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) = 0 Hence \mathbf{r}(t) \perp \mathbf{r}'(t). \blacksquare
This lemma is the reason the velocity of uniform circular motion is always perpendicular to the position vector.

7. The Unit Tangent Vector
Definition 7.1. The unit tangent vector at t is:
\mathbf{T}(t) = \frac{\mathbf{r}'(t)}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|}
defined wherever \mathbf{r}'(t) \neq \mathbf{0}.
Note: |\mathbf{T}(t)| = 1 by construction, so by Lemma 6.3, \mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{T}' = 0 — the derivative of the unit tangent is perpendicular to it. This is the entry point to curvature and the Frenet–Serret frame (Stewart §13.3).

8. Integration
Definition 8.1. The definite integral of \mathbf{r} over [a,b] is:
\int_a^b \mathbf{r}(t),dt = \left\langle \int_a^b f(t),dt,\ \int_a^b g(t),dt,\ \int_a^b h(t),dt \right\rangle
Example 8.1. Compute \displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} \langle \cos t,\ \sin t,\ t \rangle,dt:
= \left\langle [\sin t]_0^{\pi},\ [-\cos t]_0^{\pi},\ \left[\frac{t^2}{2}\right]_0^{\pi} \right\rangle = \left\langle 0,\ 2,\ \frac{\pi^2}{2} \right\rangle
Application — recovering position from velocity. If \mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{r}'(t) is known:
\mathbf{r}(t) = \int \mathbf{v}(t),dt + \mathbf{C}
where \mathbf{C} is a constant vector of integration (three free constants, one per component).

9. Arc Length
Theorem 9.1. The length of the curve traced by \mathbf{r}(t) for t \in [a,b] is:
L = \int_a^b |\mathbf{r}'(t)|,dt = \int_a^b \sqrt{[f'(t)]^2 + [g'(t)]^2 + [h'(t)]^2},dt
Intuition. Partition [a,b] into n subintervals. On each tiny interval of length \Delta t, the curve is approximately a straight segment of length \approx |\mathbf{r}'(t)|,\Delta t. Sum and take n \to \infty.
Example 9.2 (arc length of a helix). \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, t \rangle on [0, 2\pi]:
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle -\sin t, \cos t, 1 \rangle \implies |\mathbf{r}'(t)| = \sqrt{\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t + 1} = \sqrt{2}
L = \int_0^{2\pi} \sqrt{2},dt = 2\sqrt{2},\pi
The helix is longer than the circle (2\pi) by a factor of \sqrt{2} — the extra path cost of climbing vertically.
Arc Length Parameter
Define the arc length function:
s(t) = \int_a^t |\mathbf{r}'(u)|,du
Then \frac{ds}{dt} = |\mathbf{r}'(t)|. Reparametrizing by s gives a “unit-speed” curve — the most natural parametrization geometrically (independent of how fast the particle moves).

10. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
This is where vector functions stop being pure mathematics and become engineering infrastructure.
10.1 The Forward Pass as a Composition of Vector Functions
A feedforward neural network with L layers is precisely a composition of vector-valued functions:
\mathbf{r}^{(0)} = \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_0} \mathbf{r}^{(\ell)}(t) = \sigma!\left(W^{(\ell)},\mathbf{r}^{(\ell-1)} + \mathbf{b}^{(\ell)}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{n_\ell}
Each layer is a vector function: it takes a vector in \mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell-1}} and outputs one in \mathbb{R}^{n_\ell}. The activation \sigma is applied component-wise.
The loss \mathcal{L} is a scalar function of the final output — a scalar function of a vector function. This is multivariable calculus, exactly.
10.2 Gradients Are Derivatives of Scalar-Output Vector Functions
If \mathcal{L} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, the gradient \nabla \mathcal{L} is the vector of partial derivatives. Backpropagation is the chain rule for compositions of vector functions (the Jacobian chain rule):
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{r}^{(\ell)}} = \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}^{(\ell+1)}}{\partial \mathbf{r}^{(\ell)}}\right)^{!\top} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{r}^{(\ell+1)}}
The matrix \dfrac{\partial \mathbf{r}^{(\ell+1)}}{\partial \mathbf{r}^{(\ell)}} is the Jacobian — the matrix of all first-order partial derivatives. This is the full generalization of the scalar derivative f'(t).
10.3 Gradient Descent Traces a Curve in Parameter Space
Let \boldsymbol{\theta}(k) be the parameter vector at training step k. Gradient descent defines:
\boldsymbol{\theta}(k+1) = \boldsymbol{\theta}(k) - \eta,\nabla_{!\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}
In the continuous limit (\eta \to 0), this is the gradient flow ODE:
\dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(t) = -\nabla_{!\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t))
which is exactly a vector function \boldsymbol{\theta} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^p (where p is the number of parameters). Convergence analysis of optimizers studies the geometry of this curve in parameter space — the tangent vector, arc length, curvature, and whether the curve reaches a minimum.
10.4 Recurrent Networks — Trajectories in State Space
An RNN with hidden state \mathbf{h}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d evolves as:
\mathbf{h}(t+1) = \sigma!\left(W,\mathbf{h}(t) + U,\mathbf{x}(t) + \mathbf{b}\right)
This is literally a discrete dynamical system — the hidden state traces a trajectory in \mathbb{R}^d, a vector function of time t (the sequence index). The vanishing/exploding gradient problem is a statement about the arc length and curvature properties of this trajectory: if the Jacobian \partial \mathbf{h}(t)/\partial \mathbf{h}(0) has eigenvalues < 1, the trajectory contracts, gradients vanish; if > 1, it diverges.
10.5 Embeddings Are Points on Curves
Word embeddings, image embeddings, and graph embeddings map discrete objects into \mathbb{R}^n. Interpolation between two embeddings \mathbf{e}_1 and \mathbf{e}_2:
\mathbf{r}(t) = (1-t),\mathbf{e}_1 + t,\mathbf{e}_2, \quad t \in [0,1]
is a vector function — the line segment in embedding space. In latent diffusion models, the denoising process defines a continuous curve in the embedding space from Gaussian noise to the data manifold.

11. Summary Table













































ConceptFormulaGeometric meaningVector function\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f, g, h \rangleParametric curve in \mathbb{R}^3LimitComponent-wiseApproach of tip of \mathbf{r}Derivative\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle f', g', h' \rangleTangent vectorUnit tangent$\mathbf{T} = \mathbf{r}’/\mathbf{r}‘IntegralComponent-wiseSigned “sum of arrows”Arc length$\int_a^b\mathbf{r}‘Arc length param$s(t) = \int_a^t\mathbf{r}‘

12. Exercises (with hints)
12.1. Find the domain of \mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle \arcsin(t),\ \frac{1}{t^2 - 4},\ \sqrt{t} \right\rangle. (Hint: intersect three separate domains.)
12.2. Show that if \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, t^2 \rangle, then \mathbf{r}'(t) \cdot \mathbf{r}''(t) = 2t. (Hint: component-wise, then dot product rule.)
12.3. Prove: if \mathbf{u}(t) \cdot \mathbf{v}(t) = 0 for all t, it does not follow that \mathbf{u}'(t) \cdot \mathbf{v}'(t) = 0. (Hint: construct a counterexample.)
12.4 (ML connection). A gradient descent path in \mathbb{R}^2 is \boldsymbol{\theta}(t) = \langle e^{-t}, e^{-2t} \rangle. Compute the arc length traveled from t=0 to t=\infty. Does it converge?
12.5. Reparametrize \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 3t, 4t, 0 \rangle by arc length. What is the unit-speed representation?

13. References

Stewart, J. — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, §§13.1–13.3 (Vector Functions, Derivatives, Arc Length & Curvature).
MIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus, Lecture Notes on Vector-Valued Functions and Space Curves.
Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville — Deep Learning, Ch. 6 (for the neural network chain rule / Jacobian perspective).


Last updated: 2026. These notes are written for personal use — rigour is non-negotiable, but so is intuition.

01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/02.title: 02.Space Curves
01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/02.content:
“A curve is not a set of points — it is a map. The same set of points can be traversed slowly, quickly, backwards, or repeatedly. The parametrization carries information the image does not.” — personal note, Stewart §13.1–13.4, MIT 18.02


0. Motivation
In the previous note (Vector Functions) we defined \mathbf{r} : D \to \mathbb{R}^3 and noted that the tip of \mathbf{r}(t) sweeps a space curve. Now we take that curve seriously as a geometric object in its own right.
The central questions are:

How long is the curve? → Arc length
How fast is it turning? → Curvature \kappa
In which direction is it turning? → Principal normal \mathbf{N}
Is it twisting out of a plane? → Torsion \tau and binormal \mathbf{B}
What is the best local coordinate frame? → Frenet–Serret frame {\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{N}, \mathbf{B}}

These are the tools of differential geometry of curves, and they reappear — sometimes verbatim, sometimes in spirit — in the geometry of loss landscapes, attention mechanisms, and manifold learning in deep learning.

1. Space Curves — Formal Definition

Definition 1.1 (Parametric Curve). A parametric curve in \mathbb{R}^3 is a continuous map \mathbf{r} : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}^3, \qquad \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t) \rangle


Definition 1.2 (Space Curve / Image). The space curve C is the image: C = {\mathbf{r}(t) : t \in [a,b]} \subset \mathbb{R}^3


Definition 1.3 (Smooth Curve). \mathbf{r} is smooth on (a,b) if \mathbf{r}'(t) exists and \mathbf{r}'(t) \neq \mathbf{0} for all t \in (a,b).

Why \mathbf{r}'(t) \neq \mathbf{0} matters. At a point where \mathbf{r}'(t_0) = \mathbf{0}, the curve has no well-defined tangent direction — these are singular points or cusps. Requiring \mathbf{r}' \neq \mathbf{0} ensures the curve is locally “non-degenerate,” which is necessary for curvature and torsion to be defined.
Example 1.4 (a cusp). \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t^2, t^3 \rangle has \mathbf{r}'(0) = \langle 0, 0 \rangle. At t=0 the curve has a cusp — it comes to a point and reverses direction. This is not a smooth point.
        y
        |      /
        |     / ← curve approaching cusp from right
        |    *  ← cusp at origin (r'(0) = 0)
        |     \
        |      \ ← curve leaving cusp downward
        +----------x


2. Reparametrization
Definition 2.1. A reparametrization of \mathbf{r}(t) is a composition \mathbf{r}(\phi(s)) where \phi : [c,d] \to [a,b] is a smooth bijection with \phi'(s) \neq 0.

If \phi' > 0: orientation-preserving — same traversal direction.
If \phi' < 0: orientation-reversing — traversed backwards.

Key insight. The geometry of the curve (lengths, angles, curvature) must be independent of parametrization. Quantities that depend on the parametrization (e.g., speed |\mathbf{r}'(t)|) are extrinsic to the curve but intrinsic to the motion.
The canonical reparametrization is by arc length s, because it gives the curve a “built-in ruler” independent of any particular traversal speed.

3. Arc Length (Revisited Rigorously)
3.1 Definition via Riemann Sums
Partition [a,b] into n subintervals: a = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = b.
The polygonal approximation has total length: L_n = \sum_{i=1}^n |\mathbf{r}(t_i) - \mathbf{r}(t_{i-1})|
Definition 3.1 (Arc Length). The arc length of C is: L = \lim_{n \to \infty} L_n = \int_a^b |\mathbf{r}'(t)|,dt
provided this limit exists (which it does when \mathbf{r}' is continuous).
Proof of the integral formula. By the Mean Value Theorem applied component-wise: |\mathbf{r}(t_i) - \mathbf{r}(t_{i-1})| = |\mathbf{r}'(t_i^_)|,\Delta t_i + O((\Delta t_i)^2) for some t_i^_ \in (t_{i-1}, t_i). Summing and taking the limit gives the Riemann integral. \blacksquare
3.2 The Arc Length Function
\boxed{s(t) = \int_a^t |\mathbf{r}'(u)|,du}
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: \frac{ds}{dt} = |\mathbf{r}'(t)| \geq 0
This says: speed = rate of arc length accumulation. If |\mathbf{r}'(t)| = 1 for all t (unit-speed parametrization), then s(t) = t - a.
3.3 Reparametrization by Arc Length
Since \frac{ds}{dt} = |\mathbf{r}'(t)| > 0 (smooth curve), s(t) is strictly increasing, hence invertible. Write t = t(s). Then:
\tilde{\mathbf{r}}(s) = \mathbf{r}(t(s))
has speed |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}'(s)| = |\mathbf{r}'(t)| \cdot |t'(s)| = |\mathbf{r}'(t)| \cdot \frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|} = 1.
\tilde{\mathbf{r}}(s) is a unit-speed curve. This is the most natural parametrization — the parameter s is literally distance along the curve.
Example 3.4 (helix reparametrized). \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, t \rangle, |\mathbf{r}'(t)| = \sqrt{2}, so s = \sqrt{2},t, i.e., t = s/\sqrt{2}:
\tilde{\mathbf{r}}(s) = \left\langle \cos\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}},\ \sin\frac{s}{\sqrt{2}},\ \frac{s}{\sqrt{2}} \right\rangle
Now s measures true distance along the helix.

4. The Frenet–Serret Frame
This is the heart of the geometry. At each smooth point of a curve we build a canonical orthonormal basis adapted to the curve’s local shape.
4.1 Unit Tangent Vector \mathbf{T}
\boxed{\mathbf{T}(t) = \frac{\mathbf{r}'(t)}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|}}

Points in the direction of motion.
|\mathbf{T}| = 1 always.
By Lemma 6.3 from Vector Functions: \mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{T}' = 0.

4.2 Curvature \kappa
Idea. Curvature measures how quickly the tangent direction is turning per unit arc length. It is a property of the curve, not the parametrization.

Definition 4.1 (Curvature). \kappa = \left|\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds}\right|

Since d\mathbf{T}/ds = \mathbf{T}'(t)/|\mathbf{r}'(t)| (chain rule), we have:
\boxed{\kappa(t) = \frac{|\mathbf{T}'(t)|}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|}}
Computational formula (no need to find \mathbf{T} explicitly):
\boxed{\kappa = \frac{|\mathbf{r}'(t) \times \mathbf{r}''(t)|}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|^3}}
Proof. Let v = |\mathbf{r}'|. Then \mathbf{r}' = v\mathbf{T}. Differentiate: \mathbf{r}'' = v'\mathbf{T} + v\mathbf{T}' Take cross product with \mathbf{r}' = v\mathbf{T}: \mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}'' = v\mathbf{T} \times (v'\mathbf{T} + v\mathbf{T}') = v^2(\mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{T}') (since \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{0}). Then |\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}''| = v^2|\mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{T}'| = v^2|\mathbf{T}'| (since \mathbf{T} \perp \mathbf{T}' and |\mathbf{T}|=1, so |\mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{T}'| = |\mathbf{T}'|). Thus: \kappa = \frac{|\mathbf{T}'|}{v} = \frac{|\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}''|}{v^3} \qquad \blacksquare
Curvature of a plane curve y = f(x) (Stewart §13.3): \kappa = \frac{|f''(x)|}{(1 + [f'(x)]^2)^{3/2}}
Special cases:

Straight line: \kappa = 0 (tangent never turns).
Circle of radius R: \kappa = 1/R (constant; smaller circles curve more).
Radius of curvature: \rho = 1/\kappa — the radius of the osculating circle (the circle that best fits the curve at that point).

Large κ (tight curve):         Small κ (gentle curve):

      *                              *
    * * *                         *     *
   *  |  *                       *       *
      |                         *         *
   osculating circle is small   osculating circle is large
   κ = 1/R, small R → large κ

4.3 Principal Normal Vector \mathbf{N}
Since \mathbf{T} \perp \mathbf{T}', the vector \mathbf{T}'(t) is perpendicular to \mathbf{T}(t). Normalize it:
\boxed{\mathbf{N}(t) = \frac{\mathbf{T}'(t)}{|\mathbf{T}'(t)|}}

\mathbf{N} points toward the center of curvature (the center of the osculating circle).
\mathbf{T} \perp \mathbf{N} always.
For a curve turning left in the xy-plane, \mathbf{N} points left.

Intrinsic relation: \frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} = \kappa,\mathbf{N}
This is the first Frenet–Serret formula.
4.4 Binormal Vector \mathbf{B}
\boxed{\mathbf{B}(t) = \mathbf{T}(t) \times \mathbf{N}(t)}

|\mathbf{B}| = 1 (since \mathbf{T} \perp \mathbf{N}, |\mathbf{T}|=|\mathbf{N}|=1).
\mathbf{B} \perp \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{B} \perp \mathbf{N}.
{\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{N}, \mathbf{B}} is a right-handed orthonormal frame at every point.

Geometric meaning. The osculating plane at a point is spanned by \mathbf{T} and \mathbf{N}. \mathbf{B} is the normal to this plane — it points “out of the plane of bending.”
                  B (out of page)
                  ↑
                  |
         N ←------*------→ T
         (center  |  (tangent,
          of      | direction
        curvature)|  of motion)
                  |
              osculating plane = T-N plane

4.5 Torsion \tau
Curvature measures bending; torsion measures twisting.

Definition 4.2 (Torsion). \tau = -\frac{d\mathbf{B}}{ds} \cdot \mathbf{N}

Computational formula: \boxed{\tau = \frac{(\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}'') \cdot \mathbf{r}'''}{|\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}''|^2}}
Geometric meaning:

\tau = 0: the curve lies in a plane (a plane curve).
\tau \neq 0: the curve spirals out of every plane — it truly lives in 3D.
The sign of \tau indicates the direction of twisting (right-handed or left-handed helix).


5. The Frenet–Serret Formulas
This is the fundamental theorem of space curve theory.

Theorem 5.1 (Frenet–Serret). For a smooth unit-speed curve with \kappa > 0: \boxed{\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} = \kappa,\mathbf{N}} \boxed{\frac{d\mathbf{N}}{ds} = -\kappa,\mathbf{T} + \tau,\mathbf{B}} \boxed{\frac{d\mathbf{B}}{ds} = -\tau,\mathbf{N}}

In matrix form: \frac{d}{ds}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{T}\\mathbf{N}\\mathbf{B}\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & \kappa & 0 \ -\kappa & 0 & \tau \ 0 & -\tau & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{T}\\mathbf{N}\\mathbf{B}\end{pmatrix}
The matrix is skew-symmetric — this encodes that {\mathbf{T},\mathbf{N},\mathbf{B}} is an orthonormal frame rotating as we move along the curve. The evolution of the frame is governed by the Darboux vector \boldsymbol{\omega} = \tau\mathbf{T} + \kappa\mathbf{B}, so \mathbf{T}' = \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{T}, \mathbf{N}' = \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{N}, \mathbf{B}' = \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{B}.
Proof of d\mathbf{T}/ds = \kappa\mathbf{N}. By definition of \kappa and \mathbf{N}: \frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} = \left|\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds}\right| \cdot \frac{d\mathbf{T}/ds}{|d\mathbf{T}/ds|} = \kappa,\mathbf{N} \qquad \blacksquare
Proof of d\mathbf{B}/ds = -\tau\mathbf{N}. Since \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{N}: \frac{d\mathbf{B}}{ds} = \frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} \times \mathbf{N} + \mathbf{T} \times \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{ds} = \kappa\mathbf{N} \times \mathbf{N} + \mathbf{T} \times \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{ds} = \mathbf{T} \times \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{ds} Since |\mathbf{B}|=1, we have d\mathbf{B}/ds \perp \mathbf{B}. Also d\mathbf{B}/ds \perp \mathbf{T} (shown by differentiating \mathbf{T}\cdot\mathbf{B}=0). Hence d\mathbf{B}/ds \parallel \mathbf{N}, so d\mathbf{B}/ds = -\tau\mathbf{N} for some scalar \tau. \blacksquare
The Fundamental Theorem of Curve Theory. Given smooth functions \kappa(s) > 0 and \tau(s), there exists a unique (up to rigid motion) smooth curve in \mathbb{R}^3 with those curvature and torsion. \kappa and \tau are the complete invariants of the curve.

6. Worked Examples
6.1 The Circular Helix — Full Analysis
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle a\cos t,\ a\sin t,\ bt \rangle, \quad a > 0, b \neq 0
Derivatives: \mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle -a\sin t,\ a\cos t,\ b \rangle, \qquad |\mathbf{r}'| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} =: c \mathbf{r}''(t) = \langle -a\cos t,\ -a\sin t,\ 0 \rangle \mathbf{r}'''(t) = \langle a\sin t,\ -a\cos t,\ 0 \rangle
Unit tangent: \mathbf{T}(t) = \frac{1}{c}\langle -a\sin t, a\cos t, b \rangle
Curvature: \mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}'' = \langle ab\sin t,\ -ab\cos t,\ a^2 \rangle |\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}''| = \sqrt{a^2b^2 + a^4} = a\sqrt{b^2 + a^2} = ac \boxed{\kappa = \frac{ac}{c^3} = \frac{a}{c^2} = \frac{a}{a^2 + b^2}}
Constant! The helix has constant curvature.
Torsion: (\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}'') \cdot \mathbf{r}''' = \langle ab\sin t, -ab\cos t, a^2 \rangle \cdot \langle a\sin t, -a\cos t, 0 \rangle = a^2b\sin^2 t + a^2b\cos^2 t = a^2b \boxed{\tau = \frac{a^2b}{(ac)^2} = \frac{b}{a^2+b^2}}
Constant! The helix has constant torsion.
Interpretation:

If b > 0: right-handed helix (\tau > 0), rises counterclockwise.
If b < 0: left-handed helix (\tau < 0).
If b = 0: reduces to a circle, \kappa = 1/a, \tau = 0.
If a = 0: reduces to a straight line, \kappa = 0.

The helix is characterized (up to rigid motion) by having constant \kappa and \tau.
6.2 A Plane Curve
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t, t^2, 0 \rangle
This lies in the z=0 plane, so \tau = 0 (verify with the formula as an exercise).
\mathbf{r}' = \langle 1, 2t, 0\rangle, \quad \mathbf{r}'' = \langle 0, 2, 0\rangle \mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}'' = \langle 0, 0, 2\rangle, \quad |\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}''| = 2 \kappa(t) = \frac{2}{(1+4t^2)^{3/2}}
At t=0: \kappa = 2 (maximum curvature, tightest turn at the vertex of the parabola). As t \to \pm\infty: \kappa \to 0 (the parabola straightens out).
     y
     |
     *     *        ← curvature decreasing away from vertex
     |  *     *
     | *       *
     |*_________*___ x
   vertex (κ = 2)


7. Normal and Osculating Planes
Definition 7.1 (Osculating Plane). The osculating plane at \mathbf{r}(t_0) is the plane spanned by \mathbf{T}(t_0) and \mathbf{N}(t_0), passing through \mathbf{r}(t_0). Normal to this plane: \mathbf{B}(t_0).
Equation: \mathbf{B}(t_0) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{r}(t_0)) = 0.
Definition 7.2 (Normal Plane). The normal plane at \mathbf{r}(t_0) is perpendicular to \mathbf{T}(t_0), containing \mathbf{N} and \mathbf{B}.
Equation: \mathbf{T}(t_0) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{r}(t_0)) = 0.
Definition 7.3 (Rectifying Plane). Spanned by \mathbf{T} and \mathbf{B}; contains the tangent line and the binormal.
            B
            ↑
            |  /T
   N ←------*------
            |osculating plane = span(T,N)
            | normal plane = span(N,B)


8. Motion in Space — Physics Interpretation
If \mathbf{r}(t) is the position of a particle:
\text{velocity: } \mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{r}'(t) = v,\mathbf{T}(t), \quad v = |\mathbf{v}| = |\mathbf{r}'|
\text{acceleration: } \mathbf{a}(t) = \mathbf{r}''(t) = v'\mathbf{T} + v\mathbf{T}' = v'\mathbf{T} + v\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds}\frac{ds}{dt} = v'\mathbf{T} + \kappa v^2,\mathbf{N}
\boxed{\mathbf{a} = \underbrace{v'}_{\text{tangential}}\mathbf{T} + \underbrace{\kappa v^2}_{\text{centripetal}}\mathbf{N}}
The acceleration decomposes into:

Tangential component a_T = v' = \frac{d^2s}{dt^2}: changes the speed.
Normal component a_N = \kappa v^2: changes the direction (centripetal — always toward the center of curvature).

Component formulas (no need to find \mathbf{T} and \mathbf{N}): a_T = \frac{\mathbf{r}' \cdot \mathbf{r}''}{|\mathbf{r}'|}, \qquad a_N = \frac{|\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}''|}{|\mathbf{r}'|}
Verify: a_N = \kappa v^2 = \frac{|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''|}{|\mathbf{r}'|^3} \cdot |\mathbf{r}'|^2 = \frac{|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''|}{|\mathbf{r}'|}. ✓
Example 8.1. For the helix \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, t \rangle: v = |\mathbf{r}'| = \sqrt{2}, \quad v' = 0 \quad (\text{constant speed}) \mathbf{a}(t) = \langle -\cos t, -\sin t, 0\rangle a_T = 0, \quad a_N = \kappa v^2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 = 1
The particle moves at constant speed on the helix — all acceleration is centripetal.

9. Visualization
9.1 Common Space Curves
HELIX                  TORUS KNOT              VIVIANI'S CURVE
r(t) = ⟨cos t,        r(t) = ⟨(2+cos 3t)     (intersection of sphere
        sin t,                  cos 2t,          and cylinder)
        t⟩                     (2+cos 3t)
                                sin 2t,
                                sin 3t⟩

  z                      z                      z
  |   *                  |  * *                 |    *
  |  * *                 | *   *                |   * *
  | *   * (winds up)     |*   * (knotted)       |  *   *
  |*     *               |                      | *     *
  +-------- x,y          +-------- x,y          +-------- x,y

  κ = const             κ varies                lies on sphere AND cylinder
  τ = const             τ varies

9.2 The Frenet Frame Rolling Along a Curve
Imagine a tiny coordinate system {T, N, B} that rides along the curve:

  position 1:              position 2:             position 3:
    B↑                       B↑                      B ↑(tilted — torsion!)
    |  N←                    |   N←                  |    N←
    | /                      |  /                    |   /
    |/ T→                    | / T→ (rotated)        |  / T→
    *                        *                       *
    
As κ increases, T-N plane rotates (bending).
As τ increases, B tilts — the osculating plane rotates (twisting).


10. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
10.1 Loss Landscape as a Surface; Optimizer Trajectory as a Space Curve
The training trajectory \boldsymbol{\theta}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^p is a space curve in parameter space (very high-dimensional, but the geometry applies). The curvature \kappa of this trajectory tells us:

High \kappa: the optimizer is turning sharply — it has found a direction of high curvature in the loss landscape, indicating a saddle point or sharp minimum.
Low \kappa: the optimizer is moving in a nearly straight line — the gradient is consistent, loss is decreasing steadily.

The Hessian H = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L} encodes the curvature of the loss surface, and second-order optimizers (Newton’s method, natural gradient) use this curvature to correct the trajectory — exactly as the Frenet frame uses \kappa and \tau to describe the curve’s geometry.
10.2 Frenet–Serret in Sequence Models
In a sequence model (RNN, Transformer), the hidden state \mathbf{h}(t) traces a curve in \mathbb{R}^d. The Frenet frame {\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{N}, \mathbf{B}} along this trajectory gives:

\mathbf{T}(t): the direction of change in the hidden state — what the model is “attending to” at step t.
\kappa(t): how sharply the model is changing direction in state space — high curvature at semantic boundaries (e.g., transitions between topics in text).
\tau(t): how much the model’s plane of attention is rotating — high torsion may indicate complex, multi-dimensional context shifts.

This perspective is exploited in geometric deep learning (Bronstein et al., 2021) and in interpretability research that studies the geometry of activation trajectories.
10.3 Arc Length as Complexity / Path Length Regularization
In ML, the path length of the optimizer trajectory: L = \int_0^T |\boldsymbol{\theta}'(t)|,dt measures the total distance traveled in parameter space. Flat minima (low sharpness) correspond to regions where the trajectory length is short before convergence. Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) explicitly penalizes trajectories that travel into high-curvature regions of the loss landscape — it is, in spirit, a curvature-based regularizer.
10.4 The Osculating Circle and Attention Radius
The osculating circle at a point has radius \rho = 1/\kappa and is the best local circular approximation to the curve. In attention mechanisms, the attention radius (how far back in the sequence the model attends) is analogous: at points of high curvature (sharp transitions), the model must attend locally; at low curvature (slow drift), the model can attend over longer ranges.
10.5 Curvature of Decision Boundaries
For a binary classifier with decision boundary {f(\mathbf{x}) = 0}, the curvature \kappa of this boundary (as a curve in \mathbb{R}^2 or a surface in \mathbb{R}^n) controls:

Generalization: highly curved boundaries tend to overfit.
Adversarial robustness: inputs near high-curvature regions of the boundary are vulnerable to small perturbations that cross it.

Regularization methods like weight decay implicitly reduce the curvature of decision boundaries — a direct differential-geometric interpretation.
10.6 Geodesics on Data Manifolds
Real data (images, audio, text) lies on a low-dimensional manifold embedded in high-dimensional space. The geodesic between two points on this manifold is the shortest path along the manifold — the analogue of a straight line in curved space. Computing geodesics uses exactly the machinery of arc length and curvature developed here:
\text{geodesic length} = \int_a^b \sqrt{g_{ij},\dot{x}^i \dot{x}^j},dt
where g_{ij} is the Riemannian metric on the manifold. This is the foundation of Riemannian manifold optimization, used in training on curved parameter spaces (e.g., hyperbolic embeddings for hierarchical data).

11. Summary

































































QuantityFormulaMeaningArc lengthL = \int_a^b \|\mathbf{r}'\|,dtTotal distance along curveArc length fns(t) = \int_a^t \|\mathbf{r}'\|,duDistance from start to tUnit tangent\mathbf{T} = \mathbf{r}'/\|\mathbf{r}'\|Direction of motionCurvature\kappa = \|\mathbf{T}'\|/\|\mathbf{r}'\|Rate of turning (per arc length)Curvature (alt)\kappa = \|\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}''\|/\|\mathbf{r}'\|^3Computational formulaPrincipal normal\mathbf{N} = \mathbf{T}'/\|\mathbf{T}'\|Points toward center of curvatureBinormal\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{N}Normal to osculating planeTorsion\tau = (\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}'')\cdot\mathbf{r}'''/\|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''\|^2Rate of twistingTangential accela_T = \mathbf{r}'\cdot\mathbf{r}''/\|\mathbf{r}'\|Changes speedNormal accela_N = \|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''\|/\|\mathbf{r}'\|Changes directionOsculating circleradius \rho = 1/\kappaBest local circle approximation
Frenet–Serret at a glance: \mathbf{T}' = \kappa v,\mathbf{N}, \qquad \mathbf{N}' = v(-\kappa\mathbf{T} + \tau\mathbf{B}), \qquad \mathbf{B}' = -\tau v,\mathbf{N} (where derivatives are with respect to t, so chain rule gives factors of v = |\mathbf{r}'|).

12. Exercises
12.1. For \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t, \cosh t, 0 \rangle (catenary), compute \kappa(t). Show \kappa = 1/\cosh^2 t. What is \kappa at t=0?
12.2. Prove that a curve with \kappa = 0 everywhere is a straight line. (Hint: \mathbf{T}' = \mathbf{0} implies \mathbf{T} is constant; integrate.)
12.3. Prove that a curve with \kappa > 0 constant and \tau = 0 is a circle. (Hint: show \mathbf{r}(s) - \frac{1}{\kappa}\mathbf{N}(s) is constant.)
12.4. For the helix \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle a\cos t, a\sin t, bt \rangle, find the values of a, b such that \kappa = \tau = 1/2.
12.5 (ML exercise). The training trajectory in \mathbb{R}^2 is \boldsymbol{\theta}(t) = \langle e^{-t}\cos t, e^{-t}\sin t \rangle (a spiral toward the origin). Compute \kappa(t) and find \lim_{t\to\infty}\kappa(t). What does this say about the geometry near convergence?
12.6 (Hard). Show that the torsion satisfies the formula given in §4.5 by expanding (\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}'')\cdot\mathbf{r}''' in terms of v, \kappa, \tau, and the Frenet frame.

13. References

Stewart, J. — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, §§13.2 (Derivatives), 13.3 (Arc Length & Curvature), 13.4 (Motion in Space).
MIT 18.02 — Lecture notes on arc length, curvature, and the Frenet frame.
do Carmo, M.P. — Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces, Ch. 1 — for the rigorous proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Curve Theory.
Bronstein et al. — Geometric Deep Learning: Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges (2021) — for the ML connection to manifold geometry.
Foret et al. — Sharpness-Aware Minimization (ICLR 2021) — loss landscape curvature and generalization.


14. See Also

Vector Functions — prerequisites: definition, derivatives, arc length formula
Partial Derivatives — curvature of surfaces (second fundamental form)
Line Integrals — integrating scalar/vector fields along space curves
Differential Geometry — curvature in Riemannian geometry; geodesics


These notes are personal. The goal is to see the same idea from every angle — geometric, computational, and applied — before moving on.

01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/03.title: 03.Derivatives of Vector Functions
01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/03.content:
“The derivative of a vector function is itself a vector function — direction and magnitude both change, and calculus tracks both simultaneously.”


0. Motivation & Setup
In single-variable calculus we differentiated f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}. Now we step up: let the output itself live in \mathbb{R}^n. A vector-valued function is a map
\mathbf{r} : I \subseteq \mathbb{R} ;\longrightarrow; \mathbb{R}^n, \qquad t \mapsto \mathbf{r}(t)
In \mathbb{R}^3 this is written component-wise as
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle, f(t),; g(t),; h(t),\rangle = f(t),\mathbf{i} + g(t),\mathbf{j} + h(t),\mathbf{k}
Each component f, g, h is an ordinary real-valued function. This is the key observation: vector calculus decomposes into scalar calculus, component by component.

Geometric picture. As t varies, the tip of \mathbf{r}(t) traces a space curve C. The derivative will give the tangent vector to this curve — a fundamental object in geometry and physics.


1. The Derivative — Definition
1.1 Limit Definition
\boxed{\mathbf{r}'(t) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\mathbf{r}(t+h) - \mathbf{r}(t)}{h}}
Unpacking this: \mathbf{r}(t+h) - \mathbf{r}(t) is a vector (a displacement along the curve). We scale it by the scalar 1/h. In the limit, this secant vector rotates and shrinks into the tangent vector at \mathbf{r}(t).

Note (Stewart §13.2). The limit is taken in \mathbb{R}^n: a vector limit converges iff every component converges.

1.2 The Component-Wise Theorem
Theorem. If \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t)\rangle and f, g, h are differentiable, then
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle f'(t),; g'(t),; h'(t)\rangle
Proof.
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\langle f(t+h), g(t+h), k(t+h)\rangle - \langle f(t), g(t), h(t)\rangle}{h}
= \lim_{h\to 0}\left\langle \frac{f(t+h)-f(t)}{h},;\frac{g(t+h)-g(t)}{h},;\frac{h(t+h)-h(t)}{h}\right\rangle
Since limit distributes over finite vector components (as each component limit exists by hypothesis):
= \langle f'(t),; g'(t),; h'(t)\rangle \qquad \square

This theorem is the workhorse. All computation reduces to differentiating three scalar functions.


2. Geometric Interpretation
Let P = \mathbf{r}(t_0) be a point on the curve C.

\mathbf{r}(t_0 + h) - \mathbf{r}(t_0) is a secant vector from P toward a nearby point.
As h \to 0, this secant rotates into the tangent direction.
\mathbf{r}'(t_0), if nonzero, is the tangent vector to C at P.

Unit Tangent Vector
\mathbf{T}(t) = \frac{\mathbf{r}'(t)}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|}
This strips out the parametrization speed and retains only direction — crucial for Frenet–Serret theory.
Visualization
           r(t+h)
          /
         / ← secant vector r(t+h) - r(t)
        /
  r(t) •————————→  r'(t)  ← tangent (limit as h→0)
        \
         \___  curve C

As h \to 0: the chord \overrightarrow{r(t),r(t+h)} becomes tangent to the curve at r(t).

3. Differentiation Rules
Let \mathbf{u}(t), \mathbf{v}(t) be differentiable vector functions, f(t) a differentiable scalar, \mathbf{c} a constant vector.

































RuleFormulaConstant\dfrac{d}{dt}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}Linearity(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v})' = \mathbf{u}' + \mathbf{v}'Scalar multiple(f,\mathbf{u})' = f',\mathbf{u} + f,\mathbf{u}'Dot product(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})' = \mathbf{u}'\cdot\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}'Cross product(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})' = \mathbf{u}'\times\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}' (order matters!)Chain rule\dfrac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}(f(t)) = f'(t),\mathbf{u}'(f(t))
Proof of the dot product rule (representative):
(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})' = (u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + u_3 v_3)' = u_1'v_1 + u_1 v_1' + \cdots = \mathbf{u}'\cdot\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}' \qquad \square
Key Consequence — Constant Length Vectors
Proposition. |\mathbf{r}(t)| = c (constant) \iff \mathbf{r}(t) \perp \mathbf{r}'(t) for all t.
Proof. |\mathbf{r}|^2 = c^2 \implies \frac{d}{dt}(\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{r}) = 0 \implies 2,\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{r}' = 0 \implies \mathbf{r}\perp\mathbf{r}' \qquad \square

Physical reading: If a particle moves on a sphere of fixed radius, its velocity is always perpendicular to its position vector. Uniform circular motion is the classical case.


4. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Helix
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t,; \sin t,; t \rangle
Derivative: \mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle -\sin t,; \cos t,; 1 \rangle
Speed (magnitude of velocity): |\mathbf{r}'(t)| = \sqrt{\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t + 1} = \sqrt{2}
The helix has constant speed — it winds around the z-axis at a uniform rate while rising at rate 1.
Unit tangent: \mathbf{T}(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\langle -\sin t,; \cos t,; 1\rangle
z
│     ↗ T(t)  ← tangent vector
│    /
│   •←—— r(t) traces the helix
│  /
│ /
└────────── x,y plane


Example 2 — Verifying Perpendicularity
Let \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, 0\rangle (unit circle in xy-plane).
|\mathbf{r}(t)| = 1 \quad \text{(constant)} \mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle -\sin t, \cos t, 0\rangle \mathbf{r}(t)\cdot\mathbf{r}'(t) = -\cos t \sin t + \sin t \cos t = 0 \checkmark

Example 3 — Cross Product Rule
Let \mathbf{u}(t) = \langle t, t^2, 0\rangle, \mathbf{v}(t) = \langle 1, 0, t\rangle.
\mathbf{u}'(t) = \langle 1, 2t, 0\rangle, \qquad \mathbf{v}'(t) = \langle 0, 0, 1\rangle
(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})' = \mathbf{u}'\times\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}'
= \langle 1,2t,0\rangle \times \langle 1,0,t\rangle + \langle t,t^2,0\rangle\times\langle 0,0,1\rangle
Computing each cross product via the determinant formula:
\langle 1,2t,0\rangle\times\langle 1,0,t\rangle = \langle 2t^2, -t, -2t\rangle
\langle t,t^2,0\rangle\times\langle 0,0,1\rangle = \langle t^2, -t, 0\rangle
\therefore \quad (\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})' = \langle 2t^2+t^2,; -t-t,; -2t\rangle = \langle 3t^2, -2t, -2t\rangle
(Always verify by computing \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} directly and differentiating — a useful exercise.)

5. Higher Derivatives
Just as in scalar calculus, we iterate:
\mathbf{r}''(t) = \langle f''(t), g''(t), h''(t)\rangle
Physics interpretation:

\mathbf{r}(t) = position
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \mathbf{v}(t) = velocity
\mathbf{r}''(t) = \mathbf{a}(t) = acceleration

Newton’s second law: \mathbf{F} = m,\mathbf{r}''(t).

6. Arc Length & Parametrization
The arc length from t = a to t = b:
L = \int_a^b |\mathbf{r}'(t)|,dt = \int_a^b\sqrt{[f'(t)]^2 + [g'(t)]^2 + [h'(t)]^2},dt
The arc length function:
s(t) = \int_a^t |\mathbf{r}'(u)|,du \implies \frac{ds}{dt} = |\mathbf{r}'(t)|
A curve is parametrized by arc length when |\mathbf{r}'(s)| = 1 for all s — the “natural” parametrization, since one unit of parameter = one unit of distance traveled.

7. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning

This is not a tangential remark. The mathematics here is foundational infrastructure for modern ML.

7.1 Gradient as a Vector Function
In ML, a model has parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^n. The loss \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is a scalar. Training is the process of following
\boldsymbol{\theta}(t+1) = \boldsymbol{\theta}(t) - \eta,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}
where \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L} \in \mathbb{R}^n is a vector of partial derivatives — a vector-valued function of \boldsymbol{\theta}.
Gradient descent traces a trajectory \boldsymbol{\theta}(t) in parameter space. Its tangent vector at each step is -\nabla\mathcal{L}. The entire theory of §1–§3 applies here.
7.2 Neural ODE — The Continuous Limit
A deep residual network (ResNet) computes:
\mathbf{h}_{t+1} = \mathbf{h}_t + F(\mathbf{h}_t, \boldsymbol{\theta}_t)
Taking the continuous limit (Chen et al., NeurIPS 2018 — Neural ODEs):
\frac{d\mathbf{h}}{dt} = F(\mathbf{h}(t), \boldsymbol{\theta}(t))
This is a vector ODE — \mathbf{h}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d is a vector-valued function, and its derivative is exactly \mathbf{r}'(t) from our theory. The hidden state evolves as a space curve in representation space.
7.3 Recurrent Networks & Sequence Models
In an RNN, the hidden state \mathbf{h}_t is updated step by step. The “derivative” of \mathbf{h} with respect to time encodes how the representation changes — instabilities in this (vanishing/exploding gradients) are precisely failures of the sequence \mathbf{h}'(t) to behave well. LSTM and Transformer architectures are engineering solutions to control this derivative.
7.4 Backpropagation as Chain Rule
In deep learning, the chain rule for vector functions:
\frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}(f(t)) = f'(t),\mathbf{u}'(f(t))
generalizes to the Jacobian chain rule in \mathbb{R}^n. Backpropagation is exactly this rule applied layer by layer. Every backward pass through a neural network is a computation of \mathbf{r}'(t) for a composition of vector functions.
7.5 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
PINNs train networks to satisfy physical laws of the form \mathbf{r}''(t) = \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}', t). The loss function penalizes violations of the ODE, and the network must learn a trajectory whose vector derivative satisfies the physics.

Summary table:


































Classical ConceptML / DL AnalogueSpace curve \mathbf{r}(t)Parameter trajectory \boldsymbol{\theta}(t) during trainingTangent vector \mathbf{r}'(t)Negative gradient -\nabla\mathcal{L} (GD direction)Chain rule for vector functionsBackpropagationVector ODE \mathbf{r}'' = \mathbf{F}Neural ODE / ResNet limitArc lengthOptimization path length; relates to convergence analysisUnit tangent \mathbf{T}(t)Normalized gradient (in gradient normalization methods)

8. Summary of Key Facts
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle f'(t), g'(t), h'(t)\rangle \qquad \text{[component-wise differentiation]}
|\mathbf{r}| = c \iff \mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{r}' = 0 \qquad \text{[constant length $\Rightarrow$ orthogonality]}
L = \int_a^b|\mathbf{r}'(t)|,dt \qquad \text{[arc length]}
\mathbf{T}(t) = \frac{\mathbf{r}'(t)}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|} \qquad \text{[unit tangent]}

9. Exercises (Self-Check)


[Computational] Let \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle e^t, t^2, \ln(t+1)\rangle. Find \mathbf{r}'(t) and \mathbf{r}''(t).


[Geometric] Show that the curve \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 3\cos t, 3\sin t, 4t\rangle has constant speed. Find the arc length from t=0 to t=2\pi.


[Proof] Prove the cross product rule (\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})' = \mathbf{u}'\times\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}' from the component definition of the cross product.


[Conceptual] If \mathbf{r}'(t_0) = \mathbf{0}, what does this mean geometrically? Give an example.


[ML connection] In gradient descent \boldsymbol{\theta}(t+1) = \boldsymbol{\theta}(t) - \eta\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t)), identify \mathbf{r}(t) and \mathbf{r}'(t) in the continuous limit \frac{d\boldsymbol{\theta}}{dt} = -\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}). What does arc length represent physically?



References

Stewart, J. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, §13.2 — Derivatives and Integrals of Vector Functions.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Lecture notes on vector-valued functions and space curves.
Chen, R. T. Q. et al. Neural Ordinary Differential Equations, NeurIPS 2018. (§7.2 connection)

01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/04.title: 04.Integrals of Vector Functions
01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/04.content:
“Integration of a vector function is antidifferentiation done simultaneously in each direction — the result is a family of curves, each one a possible trajectory through space.”


0. Motivation
We know how to differentiate \mathbf{r}(t). Integration is the reverse operation. Two questions drive this section:

Definite integral: Given a velocity \mathbf{v}(t), how much has the particle displaced over [a,b]?
Indefinite integral (antiderivative): Given \mathbf{r}'(t), recover \mathbf{r}(t) up to a constant.

Both reduce to scalar calculus, component by component — the same philosophy as differentiation.

1. The Definite Integral — Definition
1.1 Riemann Sum Construction
Partition [a,b] into n subintervals of width \Delta t = (b-a)/n. Pick sample points t_i^*. Form the Riemann sum:
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{r}(t_i^*),\Delta t ;\in; \mathbb{R}^3
This is a sum of vectors scaled by a scalar — the result is a vector. Taking the limit:
\int_a^b \mathbf{r}(t),dt = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{r}(t_i^*),\Delta t
1.2 The Component-Wise Theorem
Theorem. If \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t)\rangle and f,g,h are integrable on [a,b], then
\boxed{\int_a^b \mathbf{r}(t),dt = \left\langle \int_a^b f(t),dt,;\int_a^b g(t),dt,;\int_a^b h(t),dt \right\rangle}
Proof.
Fix any unit vector \mathbf{e}_1 = \langle 1,0,0\rangle. Then
\mathbf{e}_1 \cdot \int_a^b \mathbf{r}(t),dt = \int_a^b \mathbf{e}_1\cdot\mathbf{r}(t),dt = \int_a^b f(t),dt
where the interchange of the dot product with the limit is justified because the dot product is a continuous linear functional on \mathbb{R}^3. Applying the same argument to \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3 extracts g and h. Since the three components are determined, the vector integral equals \langle\int f, \int g, \int h\rangle. \square

Remark. This proof makes the argument rigorous: we are not “defining” the integral component-wise by hand — we prove it follows from the limit definition together with linearity of the dot product.


2. The Indefinite Integral (Antiderivative)
\int \mathbf{r}(t),dt = \langle F(t), G(t), H(t)\rangle + \mathbf{C}
where F' = f, G' = g, H' = h, and \mathbf{C} = \langle c_1, c_2, c_3\rangle is a constant vector (three arbitrary constants, one per component).

Critical point: The constant of integration is a vector, not a scalar. Each component contributes its own free constant. Initial conditions pin down all three simultaneously.

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — Vector Version
If \mathbf{R}(t) is an antiderivative of \mathbf{r}(t) on [a,b], then
\int_a^b \mathbf{r}(t),dt = \mathbf{R}(b) - \mathbf{R}(a)
Proof. Apply the scalar FTC to each component. \square

3. Properties
Let \mathbf{u}(t), \mathbf{v}(t) be integrable vector functions, c \in \mathbb{R} a scalar constant.





























PropertyFormulaLinearity\displaystyle\int_a^b [\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}],dt = \int_a^b\mathbf{u},dt + \int_a^b\mathbf{v},dtScalar factor\displaystyle\int_a^b c,\mathbf{u},dt = c\int_a^b\mathbf{u},dtAdditivity\displaystyle\int_a^b\mathbf{r},dt = \int_a^c\mathbf{r},dt + \int_c^b\mathbf{r},dtReversal\displaystyle\int_b^a\mathbf{r},dt = -\int_a^b\mathbf{r},dtBound on norm$\displaystyle\left

The norm inequality is the vector analogue of \left|\int f\right| \leq \int|f|. It is proved via the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to the Riemann sums.


4. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Basic Definite Integral
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 2t,; e^t,; \cos t\rangle, \qquad \int_0^{\pi}\mathbf{r}(t),dt
Component by component:
\int_0^{\pi} 2t,dt = \left[t^2\right]_0^{\pi} = \pi^2
\int_0^{\pi} e^t,dt = \left[e^t\right]_0^{\pi} = e^{\pi} - 1
\int_0^{\pi}\cos t,dt = \left[\sin t\right]_0^{\pi} = 0
\therefore\quad \int_0^{\pi}\mathbf{r}(t),dt = \langle \pi^2,; e^{\pi}-1,; 0\rangle

Example 2 — Recovering Position from Velocity
Given: \mathbf{v}(t) = \langle 3t^2,; 2t,; 1\rangle and initial condition \mathbf{r}(0) = \langle 1, -1, 2\rangle.
Find: \mathbf{r}(t).
Step 1. Integrate:
\mathbf{r}(t) = \int\mathbf{v}(t),dt = \langle t^3 + c_1,; t^2 + c_2,; t + c_3\rangle
Step 2. Apply initial condition \mathbf{r}(0) = \langle 1,-1,2\rangle:
\langle c_1, c_2, c_3\rangle = \langle 1,-1,2\rangle
Result:
\boxed{\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t^3+1,; t^2-1,; t+2\rangle}

Geometric reading: The initial condition is a single point in \mathbb{R}^3, but it pins down all three constants at once. Without it, the antiderivative is a family of parallel space curves, shifted by \mathbf{C}.


Example 3 — Recovering Position from Acceleration (Two Integrations)
Given: \mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 0, -g, 0\rangle (projectile, g = 9.8 m/s²), with
\mathbf{v}(0) = \langle v_0\cos\theta,; v_0\sin\theta,; 0\rangle, \qquad \mathbf{r}(0) = \mathbf{0}
First integration (acceleration → velocity):
\mathbf{v}(t) = \int\mathbf{a}(t),dt = \langle C_1,; -gt + C_2,; C_3\rangle
Apply \mathbf{v}(0): C_1 = v_0\cos\theta, C_2 = v_0\sin\theta, C_3 = 0.
\mathbf{v}(t) = \langle v_0\cos\theta,; v_0\sin\theta - gt,; 0\rangle
Second integration (velocity → position):
\mathbf{r}(t) = \int\mathbf{v}(t),dt = \langle v_0 t\cos\theta + D_1,; v_0 t\sin\theta - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 + D_2,; D_3\rangle
Apply \mathbf{r}(0) = \mathbf{0}: all D_i = 0.
\boxed{\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle v_0 t\cos\theta,; v_0 t\sin\theta - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2,; 0\rangle}
The classical projectile equations — derived rigorously as two vector integrations.
y
│           •  ← peak
│        ·     ·
│      ·          ·
│    ·               ·
│  · ← r(t) trajectory  ·
│·________________________·_____ x
  θ↗  (2D slice, z=0)


Example 4 — Integral Involving Cross Products
