Sometimes we need \int_a^b [\mathbf{u}(t)\times\mathbf{v}(t)],dt. Compute the cross product first (getting a vector function), then integrate component-wise.
Example: \mathbf{u}(t) = \langle 1,t,0\rangle, \mathbf{v}(t) = \langle 0,1,t\rangle.
\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k}\ 1 & t & 0\ 0 & 1 & t\end{vmatrix} = \langle t^2 - 0,; 0 - t,; 1-0\rangle = \langle t^2,; -t,; 1\rangle
\int_0^1 (\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}),dt = \left\langle \frac{t^3}{3}, -\frac{t^2}{2}, t\right\rangle_0^1 = \left\langle \frac{1}{3}, -\frac{1}{2}, 1\right\rangle

5. Arc Length Revisited — Via Integration
From the derivatives note, arc length is
L = \int_a^b |\mathbf{r}'(t)|,dt
This is a scalar integral of the magnitude of a vector function — not a vector integral itself. But it arises directly from the theory: |\mathbf{r}'(t)| is the speed, and integrating speed gives distance.
Arc Length Function
s(t) = \int_a^t |\mathbf{r}'(u)|,du \implies \frac{ds}{dt} = |\mathbf{r}'(t)|
To reparametrize by arc length: solve s = s(t) for t = t(s), then form \tilde{\mathbf{r}}(s) = \mathbf{r}(t(s)). One then verifies |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}'(s)| = 1.

6. The Displacement vs. Distance Distinction
This is a subtle point worth dwelling on.




















QuantityFormulaTypeDisplacement\displaystyle\int_a^b \mathbf{v}(t),dt = \mathbf{r}(b) - \mathbf{r}(a)VectorDistance traveled$\displaystyle\int_a^b\mathbf{v}(t)
A particle that returns to its start has zero displacement but nonzero distance traveled — both computed by integrals, but of different types.

Analogy with scalar calculus: \int_a^b f,dt vs \int_a^b|f|,dt — net signed area vs total area. The vector version is geometrically richer.


7. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
7.1 Gradient Flow as a Vector Integral
In continuous gradient descent, the parameter trajectory satisfies
\frac{d\boldsymbol{\theta}}{dt} = -\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t))
Integrating both sides from 0 to T:
\boldsymbol{\theta}(T) = \boldsymbol{\theta}(0) + \int_0^T \left(-\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t))\right)dt
This is exactly the vector antiderivative problem: given the “velocity” -\nabla\mathcal{L}, recover the trajectory \boldsymbol{\theta}(t). The initial condition \boldsymbol{\theta}(0) (random initialization) plays the role of the constant vector \mathbf{C}.
The displacement after training is \boldsymbol{\theta}(T) - \boldsymbol{\theta}(0) — a vector in parameter space measuring how far initialization moved during learning.
7.2 Neural ODEs — Forward Pass as Integration
A Neural ODE (Chen et al., 2018) defines the forward pass as:
\mathbf{h}(T) = \mathbf{h}(0) + \int_0^T F(\mathbf{h}(t), \boldsymbol{\theta}, t),dt
where F is a neural network. The output of the model is literally a vector integral. This is computed using an ODE solver (e.g., Runge–Kutta) at training time — numerical integration of a vector function is the entire forward pass.
h(0) ──→ [ODE Solver: ∫F dt] ──→ h(T) ──→ Output
         ↑
    F = neural network
    evaluates r'(t) at each step

The backward pass (adjoint method) also involves integrating a vector ODE — backwards in time.
7.3 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
A PINN solving Newton’s law \mathbf{r}''(t) = \mathbf{F}/m enforces:
\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{r}(0) + \mathbf{v}(0),t + \int_0^t\int_0^{s}\frac{\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u))}{m},du,ds
Two vector integrations, mirroring Example 3 exactly. The network must implicitly learn these integrals from data, and the loss function penalizes violations.
7.4 Displacement vs. Distance in Optimization
The distinction from §6 has a direct ML interpretation:

Displacement \int_0^T(-\nabla\mathcal{L}),dt = \boldsymbol{\theta}(T) - \boldsymbol{\theta}(0): the net change in parameters. Can be small even after long training if the optimizer oscillates.
Path length \int_0^T|\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t))|,dt: total distance traveled in parameter space. A diagnostic for optimizer efficiency — large path length with small displacement indicates oscillation or poor conditioning.


This is why adaptive optimizers (Adam, RMSProp) work well: they effectively normalize the gradient vector at each step, keeping |\mathbf{v}(t)| bounded and ensuring displacement ≈ path length.

7.5 Attention and Integral Transforms
The attention mechanism in Transformers can be written in continuous form as
\text{Attn}(\mathbf{q}) = \int K({\mathbf{q}}, \mathbf{k}),\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{k}),d\mathbf{k}
where K is a scalar kernel and \mathbf{v} is a vector-valued function of keys. This is a weighted vector integral — a continuous generalization of the discrete softmax attention sum. The “value” output is a vector obtained by integrating a vector function against a scalar weight.

Summary table:


































Classical ConceptML / DL Analogue\int\mathbf{r}'(t),dt = \mathbf{r}(t)+\mathbf{C}Integrating gradient flow to recover \boldsymbol{\theta}(t)Initial condition pins \mathbf{C}Random initialization \boldsymbol{\theta}(0)Two integrations: \mathbf{a}\to\mathbf{v}\to\mathbf{r}Neural ODE forward pass (nested integration)Displacement \neq distanceNet weight change vs total optimization path\int_a^b\mathbf{r}(t),dt as Riemann sum limitNumerical ODE solvers (Euler, RK4) in Neural ODEs\int K,\mathbf{v},d\mathbf{k}Continuous attention mechanism in Transformers

8. Summary of Key Formulas
\int_a^b\mathbf{r}(t),dt = \left\langle\int_a^b f,;\int_a^b g,;\int_a^b h\right\rangle \qquad \text{[component-wise]}
\int\mathbf{r}(t),dt = \mathbf{R}(t) + \mathbf{C}, \quad \mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^3 \qquad \text{[constant vector]}
\int_a^b\mathbf{r}(t),dt = \mathbf{R}(b) - \mathbf{R}(a) \qquad \text{[FTC — vector version]}
\left|\int_a^b\mathbf{r}(t),dt\right| \leq \int_a^b|\mathbf{r}(t)|,dt \qquad \text{[norm inequality]}
L = \int_a^b|\mathbf{r}'(t)|,dt \qquad \text{[arc length]}

9. Exercises (Self-Check)


[Computational] Evaluate \displaystyle\int_0^1\langle t e^{t^2},;\sin(\pi t),;\sqrt{1-t^2}\rangle,dt.


[Initial Value Problem] Given \mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 6t, 2, 0\rangle, \mathbf{v}(0) = \langle -1, 0, 3\rangle, \mathbf{r}(0) = \langle 0, 1, 0\rangle, find \mathbf{r}(t).


[Conceptual] A particle moves with \mathbf{v}(t) = \langle\cos t, \sin t, 0\rangle for t \in [0, 4\pi]. Compute the displacement and the distance traveled. Explain the discrepancy.


[Proof] Prove the norm inequality \left|\int_a^b\mathbf{r}(t),dt\right|\leq\int_a^b|\mathbf{r}(t)|,dt using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to the Riemann sums.


[ML connection] In the continuous gradient descent ODE \dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = -\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}), suppose \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{2}|\boldsymbol{\theta}|^2 (weight decay). Solve the IVP explicitly as a vector integral. What trajectory does \boldsymbol{\theta}(t) trace?



Related Notes

Derivatives of Vector Functions — differentiation, tangent vectors, chain rule
Arc Length and Curvature — Frenet–Serret frame, curvature \kappa, torsion \tau
Line Integrals — integrating along a curve (next step after parametric integrals)


References

Stewart, J. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, §13.3 — Arc Length and Curvature; §13.4 — Motion in Space.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Lecture notes on vector integrals and motion.
Chen, R. T. Q. et al. Neural Ordinary Differential Equations, NeurIPS 2018.

01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/05.title: 05.Arc Length and Curvature
01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/05.content:
“Curvature is the rate at which the curve turns — measured not against the clock, but against the road itself.”


0. Motivation
We already know \mathbf{r}'(t) is the tangent vector. But two natural questions remain:

How long is the curve? — this is arc length.
How sharply does the curve bend? — this is curvature.

Both questions demand we measure intrinsic properties of the curve — properties that don’t depend on how fast we happen to traverse it. This forces us to re-parametrize by arc length, the natural “ruler” on a curve.

1. Arc Length
1.1 Definition
Let \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t), h(t)\rangle be a smooth curve on [a, b]. Partition [a,b] into n subintervals. The k-th chord has length |\mathbf{r}(t_k) - \mathbf{r}(t_{k-1})|. Taking the limit of the sum of chord lengths:
\boxed{L = \int_a^b |\mathbf{r}'(t)|,dt = \int_a^b \sqrt{[f'(t)]^2 + [g'(t)]^2 + [h'(t)]^2};dt}
Why |\mathbf{r}'(t)|? By the Mean Value Theorem applied component-wise, |\mathbf{r}(t_k)-\mathbf{r}(t_{k-1})| \approx |\mathbf{r}'(t_k^*)|,\Delta t_k. Summing and passing to the limit gives the integral. This is a clean Riemann sum argument.

Key insight (MIT 18.02). |\mathbf{r}'(t)| is the speed of the parametrization — how fast the point moves. Arc length integrates speed over time to get distance. Same formula as d = \int v,dt from physics.

1.2 The Arc Length Function
Fix a basepoint a. Define:
s(t) = \int_a^t |\mathbf{r}'(u)|,du
By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus:
\frac{ds}{dt} = |\mathbf{r}'(t)|
So s measures how much curve has been traversed up to time t. The infinitesimal arc length element is:
ds = |\mathbf{r}'(t)|,dt
1.3 Worked Example — Helix
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t,; \sin t,; t\rangle, \qquad t \in [0, 2\pi]
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle -\sin t,; \cos t,; 1\rangle, \qquad |\mathbf{r}'(t)| = \sqrt{\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t + 1} = \sqrt{2}
L = \int_0^{2\pi} \sqrt{2},dt = 2\sqrt{2},\pi

The helix has constant speed \sqrt{2}, so its length is simply speed × time = \sqrt{2} \cdot 2\pi. One full turn rises by 2\pi in z while wrapping a circle of circumference 2\pi — Pythagoras gives \sqrt{(2\pi)^2 + (2\pi)^2} = 2\sqrt{2}\pi. ✓

1.4 Parametrization Invariance
Arc length is independent of parametrization. If \tilde{\mathbf{r}}(\tau) = \mathbf{r}(t(\tau)) with t'(\tau) > 0, then by the chain rule:
|\tilde{\mathbf{r}}'(\tau)| = |\mathbf{r}'(t(\tau))|\cdot t'(\tau)
\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}|\tilde{\mathbf{r}}'(\tau)|,d\tau = \int_a^b |\mathbf{r}'(t)|,dt
The curve length is a geometric fact — not an artifact of how we label points on it.

2. Parametrization by Arc Length
2.1 The Natural Parametrization
A curve is parametrized by arc length (or unit-speed) when:
|\mathbf{r}'(s)| = 1 \quad \text{for all } s
This is the parametrization where “parameter = distance traveled.” It strips away the arbitrary speed of any other parametrization and exposes the curve’s pure geometry.
How to find it: Given \mathbf{r}(t), compute s(t) = \int_a^t |\mathbf{r}'(u)|,du, invert to get t(s), then set \tilde{\mathbf{r}}(s) = \mathbf{r}(t(s)).
Verification: |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}'(s)| = |\mathbf{r}'(t(s))| \cdot |t'(s)| = |\mathbf{r}'(t)| \cdot \dfrac{1}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|} = 1. ✓
2.2 Example — Circle
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle R\cos t,; R\sin t\rangle, \qquad |\mathbf{r}'(t)| = R
s = Rt \implies t = \frac{s}{R}
\tilde{\mathbf{r}}(s) = \left\langle R\cos\frac{s}{R},; R\sin\frac{s}{R}\right\rangle
Check: |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}'(s)| = \left|\left\langle -\sin\frac{s}{R},; \cos\frac{s}{R}\right\rangle\right| = 1. ✓

3. Curvature
3.1 The Core Idea
The unit tangent vector \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{r}'/|\mathbf{r}'| always has magnitude 1, so it lives on the unit sphere. Curvature measures how rapidly \mathbf{T} turns as we move along the curve.
But “rapidly” must be measured per unit of arc length, not per unit of time — otherwise a fast-moving particle on a straight line would appear to have curvature.
3.2 Definition
\boxed{\kappa = \left|\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds}\right|}
where s is arc length. Equivalently, by the chain rule \dfrac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} = \dfrac{d\mathbf{T}/dt}{ds/dt}:
\kappa = \frac{|\mathbf{T}'(t)|}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|}
Geometric reading: \kappa is large where the curve bends sharply (tight corner); \kappa = 0 on a straight line; \kappa is constant on a circle.
Low curvature:              High curvature:
                                ╭──╮
────────────────             ───╯  ╰───
κ ≈ 0                           κ >> 0

3.3 Computational Formula (Stewart §13.3)
Computing \mathbf{T} and then \mathbf{T}' is often messy. The following formula is far more practical:
\boxed{\kappa = \frac{|\mathbf{r}'(t) \times \mathbf{r}''(t)|}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|^3}}
Proof. Let v = |\mathbf{r}'| = ds/dt. Then \mathbf{r}' = v\mathbf{T}. Differentiate:
\mathbf{r}'' = v'\mathbf{T} + v\mathbf{T}'
Take the cross product with \mathbf{r}' = v\mathbf{T}:
\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}'' = v\mathbf{T}\times(v'\mathbf{T} + v\mathbf{T}') = v^2(\mathbf{T}\times\mathbf{T}')
Since \mathbf{T}\perp\mathbf{T}' (constant length — recall §7 of the previous note) and |\mathbf{T}|=1:
|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''| = v^2|\mathbf{T}'|
But \kappa = |\mathbf{T}'|/v, so |\mathbf{T}'| = \kappa v, giving:
|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''| = v^2 \cdot \kappa v = \kappa v^3 = \kappa|\mathbf{r}'|^3
\therefore \quad \kappa = \frac{|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''|}{|\mathbf{r}'|^3} \qquad \square
3.4 Curvature of a Plane Curve y = f(x)
For \mathbf{r}(x) = \langle x, f(x)\rangle:
\mathbf{r}' = \langle 1, f'\rangle, \quad \mathbf{r}'' = \langle 0, f''\rangle
\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}'' = \langle 1,f',0\rangle\times\langle 0,f'',0\rangle = \langle 0, 0, f''\rangle \implies |\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''| = |f''|
|\mathbf{r}'|^3 = (1+[f']^2)^{3/2}
\boxed{\kappa = \frac{|f''(x)|}{(1+[f'(x)]^2)^{3/2}}}

At an inflection point f'' = 0, curvature is zero — the curve momentarily “straightens.” At a local max/min where f' = 0, curvature simplifies to |f''| — pure second derivative.


4. The Frenet–Serret Frame
Curvature is part of a richer structure — the moving frame attached to a curve.
4.1 The Three Vectors

























VectorDefinitionMeaning\mathbf{T}$\mathbf{r}’/\mathbf{r}’\mathbf{N}$\mathbf{T}’/\mathbf{T}‘\mathbf{B}\mathbf{T}\times\mathbf{N}Unit binormal — axis of the osculating plane
These three form an orthonormal basis at every point of the curve — a “local coordinate system” that travels with the curve.
Why \mathbf{N}\perp\mathbf{T}? Since |\mathbf{T}|=1, we have \mathbf{T}\cdot\mathbf{T}'=0, so \mathbf{T}' \perp \mathbf{T} always. \mathbf{N} is just \mathbf{T}' normalized.
4.2 The Frenet–Serret Equations
\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} = \kappa,\mathbf{N}
\frac{d\mathbf{N}}{ds} = -\kappa,\mathbf{T} + \tau,\mathbf{B}
\frac{d\mathbf{B}}{ds} = -\tau,\mathbf{N}
where \tau is the torsion — the rate at which the curve twists out of its osculating plane.

\kappa > 0: curve bends
\tau = 0: curve is planar
\tau \neq 0: curve twists in 3D (like a helix)

4.3 Geometric Picture
                B (binormal)
                ↑
                │
                │   osculating plane
     N ←────── • ──────→ T (tangent)
    (normal)   P
               
   The curve bends in the T-N plane.
   Torsion measures how fast B rotates.


5. The Osculating Circle
At each point P on a curve, the osculating circle (from Latin osculari, “to kiss”) is the circle that:

Passes through P
Has the same tangent as the curve at P
Has the same curvature \kappa as the curve at P

Its radius of curvature is:
\rho = \frac{1}{\kappa}
Its center lies at P + \rho,\mathbf{N} — a distance \rho along the normal direction.

Intuition. On a straight road, \kappa = 0, \rho = \infty: the “osculating circle” has infinite radius. On a sharp hairpin, \kappa is large, \rho is small. A circle of radius R has \kappa = 1/R everywhere.

5.1 Example — Parabola
y = x^2, \quad f'=2x, \quad f''=2
\kappa(x) = \frac{2}{(1+4x^2)^{3/2}}
At x = 0 (vertex): \kappa = 2, \rho = 1/2.
At x \to \infty: \kappa \to 0 — the parabola flattens out.
               ↑ y
          ─────┤─────
        ╱      │      ╲
       ╱   ⊙ ← osculating circle
      ╱    radius 1/2
     ╱─────┴─────╲
                   x


6. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Curvature of the Helix
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle a\cos t,; a\sin t,; bt\rangle \qquad (a,b > 0)
\mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle -a\sin t,; a\cos t,; b\rangle, \qquad |\mathbf{r}'| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}
\mathbf{r}''(t) = \langle -a\cos t,; -a\sin t,; 0\rangle
\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}'' = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ -a\sin t & a\cos t & b \ -a\cos t & -a\sin t & 0\end{vmatrix}
= \langle a\cdot 0 - b(-a\sin t),; b(-a\cos t) - (-a\sin t)\cdot 0,; (-a\sin t)(-a\sin t) - (a\cos t)(-a\cos t)\rangle
= \langle ab\sin t,; -ab\cos t,; a^2\rangle
|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''| = \sqrt{a^2b^2\sin^2 t + a^2b^2\cos^2 t + a^4} = \sqrt{a^2b^2+a^4} = a\sqrt{a^2+b^2}
\kappa = \frac{a\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}{(a^2+b^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{a}{a^2+b^2}
The curvature of a helix is constant. When b=0: circle with \kappa = 1/a. As b\to\infty (helix stretches vertically): \kappa\to 0. ✓
Example 2 — Curvature of y = \sin x
f' = \cos x, \quad f'' = -\sin x
\kappa(x) = \frac{|\sin x|}{(1+\cos^2 x)^{3/2}}

At x = \pi/2: \kappa = \dfrac{1}{(1+0)^{3/2}} = 1, \rho = 1.
At x = 0: \kappa = 0 (inflection point — straightening).
Maximum curvature occurs at the peaks and troughs, as expected.


7. Summary of Key Formulas
L = \int_a^b |\mathbf{r}'(t)|,dt \qquad \text{[arc length]}
\frac{ds}{dt} = |\mathbf{r}'(t)| \qquad \text{[speed = rate of arc length]}
\kappa = \left|\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds}\right| = \frac{|\mathbf{T}'(t)|}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|} = \frac{|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''|}{|\mathbf{r}'|^3} \qquad \text{[curvature]}
\kappa = \frac{|f''|}{(1+[f']^2)^{3/2}} \qquad \text{[for } y=f(x) \text{]}
\rho = \frac{1}{\kappa} \qquad \text{[radius of curvature]}
\mathbf{T} = \frac{\mathbf{r}'}{|\mathbf{r}'|}, \quad \mathbf{N} = \frac{\mathbf{T}'}{|\mathbf{T}'|}, \quad \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T}\times\mathbf{N}

8. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
8.1 Loss Landscape Geometry — Curvature of Optimization Paths
During gradient descent, the parameter trajectory \boldsymbol{\theta}(t) is a curve in \mathbb{R}^n. Its curvature \kappa measures how sharply the optimization path bends. High curvature near a saddle point means the optimizer is changing direction rapidly — a sign of instability.
The Hessian H = \nabla^2\mathcal{L} is the second derivative of the loss, encoding the curvature of the loss surface. Second-order optimizers (Newton’s method, L-BFGS) explicitly use H — they are computing the osculating paraboloid of \mathcal{L}, the surface analogue of the osculating circle.
8.2 Natural Gradient — Arc Length in Parameter Space
The ordinary gradient \nabla\mathcal{L} measures steepness in Euclidean parameter space. But the natural gradient (Amari, 1998) accounts for the Riemannian metric on the statistical manifold of model distributions:
\tilde{\nabla}\mathcal{L} = F^{-1}\nabla\mathcal{L}
where F is the Fisher information matrix. This corrects for the fact that equal Euclidean steps in \boldsymbol{\theta}-space do not correspond to equal arc lengths in distribution space. The natural gradient is precisely the gradient after re-parametrizing by the arc length of the information geometry.
8.3 Attention and Sequence Curvature
In Transformer models, the hidden states \mathbf{h}_1, \mathbf{h}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{h}_n form a discrete curve in representation space. Attention mechanisms can be interpreted as computing a weighted average of positions on this curve — a discretized integral operator analogous to \int \mathbf{r}(t),w(t),dt.
The curvature of the hidden-state trajectory correlates with how “surprising” or semantically complex the sequence is at that position.
8.4 Neural ODEs and Curvature Regularization
In a Neural ODE \frac{d\mathbf{h}}{dt} = F(\mathbf{h}, t), the trajectory \mathbf{h}(t) is a curve in latent space. A natural regularizer is:
\mathcal{R} = \int_0^T |\mathbf{h}''(t)|^2,dt
This penalizes large acceleration (equivalently, high curvature of the hidden-state trajectory), encouraging the network to learn smooth, gradual transformations. This is directly the squared curvature functional from differential geometry.
8.5 Geodesics and Shortest Path in Latent Space
In generative models (VAEs, diffusion models), the latent space has a geometry. Interpolating between two latent codes along the geodesic (the curve of minimal arc length) produces more natural interpolations than linear interpolation in Euclidean space. This requires computing:
L[\gamma] = \int_0^1 |\gamma'(t)|_g,dt
where |\cdot|_g is the Riemannian metric induced by the generative model — a direct application of our arc length formula.
8.6 Curvature of Decision Boundaries
In classification, the decision boundary is a surface (or curve in 2D). Its curvature measures how “wiggly” the boundary is:

High curvature → overfitting (the model memorized the training data with sharp twists)
Low curvature → smoother generalization

Regularization methods (weight decay, dropout, spectral normalization) implicitly reduce the curvature of decision boundaries.

Summary table:














































Classical ConceptML / DL AnalogueArc length $L = \int\mathbf{r}‘Curvature \kappa = \|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''\|/\|\mathbf{r}'\|^3Hessian eigenvalues; loss landscape curvatureRadius of curvature \rho = 1/\kappaInverse sharpness of a loss minimum (flat minima generalize better)Osculating circleLocal quadratic approximation used by 2nd-order optimizersArc-length parametrizationNatural gradient (reparametrize by Fisher information)Frenet–Serret frame {\mathbf{T,N,B}}Principal curvature directions of the loss surface (Hessian eigenvectors)GeodesicShortest-path interpolation in latent space (VAE/diffusion)Curvature of plane curveCurvature of decision boundary; high \kappa = overfittingCurvature regularization \int \|\mathbf{h}''\|^2Smoothness regularization in Neural ODEs

9. Exercises (Self-Check)


[Computational] Find the arc length of \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle t^2, \sin t - t\cos t, \cos t + t\sin t\rangle on [0, \pi]. (Hint: compute |\mathbf{r}'(t)| first — it simplifies.)


[Parametrization] Re-parametrize the line \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle 1+3t, 2-t, 4t\rangle by arc length starting at t=0.


[Curvature] Prove that \kappa = 0 everywhere on a line. What does this say about \mathbf{T}'?


[Formula] Use \kappa = |f''|/(1+[f']^2)^{3/2} to find the point of maximum curvature on y = e^x.


[Proof] Show that a circle of radius R has constant curvature \kappa = 1/R using the cross-product formula.


[Conceptual — ML] A model trained with early stopping has a decision boundary of lower curvature than one trained to convergence. Explain this in terms of \kappa and the bias-variance tradeoff.



References

Stewart, J. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, §13.3 — Arc Length and Curvature.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Lecture notes on arc length, curvature, and the TNB frame.
Amari, S. Natural Gradient Works Efficiently in Learning, Neural Computation, 1998. (§8.2)
Chen, R. T. Q. et al. Neural Ordinary Differential Equations, NeurIPS 2018. (§8.4)
Shao, H. et al. Riemannian Geometry of Deep Generative Models, CVPR 2018. (§8.5)

01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/06.title: 06.Normal and Binormal Vectors
01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/06.content:
“A curve in space carries its own coordinate system with it — one that breathes, twists, and tilts as we walk along it. This is the Frenet–Serret frame: the most natural house a curve can live in.”


0. Motivation & Setup
We already know the unit tangent vector \mathbf{T}(t), which points in the direction of motion along a curve \mathbf{r}(t). But motion in space is richer than a single direction. As you drive along a winding mountain road, three things happen simultaneously:

You move forward — direction of \mathbf{T}.
The road curves — some direction orthogonal to \mathbf{T}.
The road may bank or twist out of the plane — a third direction.

These three orthogonal directions form the Frenet–Serret frame {\mathbf{T},, \mathbf{N},, \mathbf{B}}, a moving orthonormal basis that travels with the curve.
Standing assumption throughout: \mathbf{r}(t) is a smooth curve with \mathbf{r}'(t) \neq \mathbf{0} everywhere, and \mathbf{r}''(t) \not\parallel \mathbf{r}'(t) (so the curve is not locally straight).

1. Recall: The Unit Tangent Vector
\mathbf{T}(t) = \frac{\mathbf{r}'(t)}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|}
Key property: Since \mathbf{T} is a unit vector, |\mathbf{T}(t)| = 1 for all t, which implies:
\mathbf{T}(t) \cdot \mathbf{T}(t) = 1 \implies \frac{d}{dt}[\mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{T}] = 0 \implies 2,\mathbf{T}(t)\cdot \mathbf{T}'(t) = 0
\boxed{\mathbf{T}'(t) \perp \mathbf{T}(t)}
This is the pivotal observation: the derivative of any unit vector is always perpendicular to that vector. We use this fact repeatedly.

2. The Principal Normal Vector \mathbf{N}
Definition
Since \mathbf{T}'(t) \perp \mathbf{T}(t), the vector \mathbf{T}'(t) (when nonzero) points in the direction the curve is turning. We normalize it to get the principal unit normal vector:
\boxed{\mathbf{N}(t) = \frac{\mathbf{T}'(t)}{|\mathbf{T}'(t)|}}
Geometric Meaning
\mathbf{N}(t) points toward the center of curvature — the center of the “best-fit circle” (osculating circle) at the point \mathbf{r}(t). It lives in the osculating plane (the plane that best fits the curve locally), orthogonal to \mathbf{T}.

On a circle traversed counterclockwise, \mathbf{N} points radially inward (toward the center).
On a straight line, \mathbf{T}' = \mathbf{0}, so \mathbf{N} is undefined — straight lines have no bending direction.

Connection to Curvature
Recall the curvature \kappa = \left|\dfrac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds}\right| where s is arc length. Since \dfrac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} = \dfrac{\mathbf{T}'(t)}{|\mathbf{r}'(t)|}, we have:
\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} = \kappa,\mathbf{N}
This is the first Frenet–Serret formula (derived below). It says: as you walk along the curve at unit speed, the tangent changes at rate \kappa in the direction \mathbf{N}.

3. The Binormal Vector \mathbf{B}
Definition
With \mathbf{T} and \mathbf{N} in hand — both unit vectors, mutually orthogonal — we complete the right-handed orthonormal frame by taking the cross product:
\boxed{\mathbf{B}(t) = \mathbf{T}(t) \times \mathbf{N}(t)}
\mathbf{B} is the unit binormal vector.
It is automatically a unit vector: Since \mathbf{T} and \mathbf{N} are unit vectors orthogonal to each other, |\mathbf{B}| = |\mathbf{T}||\mathbf{N}|\sin(90°) = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1. \checkmark
Geometric Meaning
\mathbf{B} is the normal to the osculating plane. As the curve evolves:

If \mathbf{B} stays constant, the curve lies entirely in a plane (zero torsion).
If \mathbf{B} is rotating, the curve is genuinely twisting through space.

The three planes defined by pairs of frame vectors have classical names:

























PlaneSpanned byContainsOsculating plane\mathbf{T},, \mathbf{N}The curve’s “bending”Normal plane\mathbf{N},, \mathbf{B}\perp to direction of motionRectifying plane\mathbf{T},, \mathbf{B}The curve’s “twisting”

4. The Full Frenet–Serret Apparatus
Torsion \tau
Since \mathbf{B} is a unit vector, \mathbf{B}' \perp \mathbf{B}. We claim \mathbf{B}' \perp \mathbf{T} as well:
Proof: \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{N}. Differentiate: \mathbf{B}' = \mathbf{T}' \times \mathbf{N} + \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{N}'
Now \mathbf{T}' = \kappa|\mathbf{r}'|,\mathbf{N} (from \frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} = \kappa\mathbf{N}, chain rule), so: \mathbf{T}' \times \mathbf{N} = \kappa|\mathbf{r}'|(\mathbf{N} \times \mathbf{N}) = \mathbf{0}
Thus \mathbf{B}' = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{N}', which is orthogonal to \mathbf{T}. Combined with \mathbf{B}' \perp \mathbf{B}, we conclude \mathbf{B}' is parallel to \mathbf{N}. We define torsion \tau by:
\frac{d\mathbf{B}}{ds} = -\tau,\mathbf{N}
The sign is conventional — positive \tau means a right-handed twist.
The Three Frenet–Serret Formulas
With respect to arc-length parameter s:
\boxed{\dfrac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} = \kappa,\mathbf{N}}
\boxed{\dfrac{d\mathbf{N}}{ds} = -\kappa,\mathbf{T} + \tau,\mathbf{B}}
\boxed{\dfrac{d\mathbf{B}}{ds} = -\tau,\mathbf{N}}
Proof of the middle formula: Since \mathbf{N} = \mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{T}, differentiate using the product rule and substitute the first and third formulas.
In matrix form (Frenet–Serret system):
\frac{d}{ds}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{T}\\mathbf{N}\\mathbf{B}\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \kappa & 0 \ -\kappa & 0 & \tau \ 0 & -\tau & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{T}\\mathbf{N}\\mathbf{B}\end{pmatrix}
Note the antisymmetry of the matrix — a signature of the fact that the frame evolves by rotation (no stretching, since all vectors remain unit vectors).

5. Worked Examples
Example 1: Circle of Radius r in the xy-Plane
\mathbf{r}(t) = (r\cos t,, r\sin t,, 0)
Tangent: \mathbf{r}'(t) = (-r\sin t,, r\cos t,, 0), \quad |\mathbf{r}'| = r \mathbf{T}(t) = (-\sin t,, \cos t,, 0)
Normal: \mathbf{T}'(t) = (-\cos t,, -\sin t,, 0), \quad |\mathbf{T}'| = 1 \mathbf{N}(t) = (-\cos t,, -\sin t,, 0)
Check: \mathbf{N} points from the curve toward the origin (0,0,0) — indeed the center of the circle. ✓
Binormal: \mathbf{B}(t) = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{N} = (-\sin t,\cos t,0)\times(-\cos t,-\sin t,0) = (0,0,\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t) = (0,0,1)
\mathbf{B} is constant — the curve lies in the xy-plane, so the osculating plane never changes. Torsion \tau = 0. ✓
Curvature: \kappa = 1/r. Tighter circles \Rightarrow larger curvature. ✓

Example 2: Helix
\mathbf{r}(t) = (a\cos t,, a\sin t,, bt)
This is the prototypical curve with both nonzero curvature and nonzero torsion.
Step 1: \mathbf{r}'(t) = (-a\sin t, a\cos t, b), \quad |\mathbf{r}'| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} =: c
\mathbf{T}(t) = \frac{1}{c}(-a\sin t,, a\cos t,, b)
Step 2: \mathbf{T}'(t) = \frac{1}{c}(-a\cos t,, -a\sin t,, 0), \quad |\mathbf{T}'| = \frac{a}{c}
\mathbf{N}(t) = (-\cos t,, -\sin t,, 0)
\mathbf{N} always points horizontally toward the z-axis — “inward,” as expected.
Step 3: \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T}\times\mathbf{N} = \frac{1}{c}(-a\sin t, a\cos t, b)\times(-\cos t,-\sin t,0)
Computing the cross product: \mathbf{B}(t) = \frac{1}{c}(b\sin t,, -b\cos t,, a)
Curvature and Torsion of the Helix: \kappa = \frac{a}{a^2+b^2}, \qquad \tau = \frac{b}{a^2+b^2}

When b = 0: helix degenerates to a circle, \kappa = 1/a, \tau = 0.
When a = 0: straight line, \kappa = 0.
Equal \kappa and \tau when a = b — a “balanced” helix.


Intuition check: The helix has constant \kappa and \tau — it’s the unique curve with this property (up to congruence). This reflects the helix’s translational symmetry along the z-axis.


6. Visualization: The Frenet Frame in Motion
          B (binormal)
          ↑
          |   ← osculating plane →
          |  /
          | /
          |/________→ N (principal normal)
         /|
        / |
       /  |
      ↗   
     T (tangent)

The frame {T, N, B} forms a right-handed coordinate system
that travels and rotates along the curve.

Helix visualization (schematic):
z
│     *←B (tilted out of page)
│    / \
│   *   N (pointing inward)
│  /|   ↓
│ * |  center axis
│/  ↑
*   T (tangent, going up and around)
────────── x

As we travel along the helix:

\mathbf{T} always points “up and around” at a fixed angle
\mathbf{N} always points straight inward toward the axis
\mathbf{B} rotates slowly — the signature of nonzero torsion


7. Computing \mathbf{N} and \mathbf{B} Without Arc-Length Parametrization
In practice, curves are rarely given in arc-length form. For a general parameter t:
\mathbf{T}(t) = \frac{\mathbf{r}'}{|\mathbf{r}'|}
\mathbf{N}(t) = \frac{\mathbf{T}'(t)}{|\mathbf{T}'(t)|}
\mathbf{B}(t) = \mathbf{T}(t) \times \mathbf{N}(t)
For curvature and torsion in terms of \mathbf{r}' and \mathbf{r}'':
\kappa = \frac{|\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}''|}{|\mathbf{r}'|^3}
\tau = \frac{(\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}'') \cdot \mathbf{r}'''}{|\mathbf{r}' \times \mathbf{r}''|^2}
These formulas are what you actually use in computation. The arc-length formulas are for theory.

8. The Fundamental Theorem of Space Curves

Theorem (Existence and Uniqueness): Given smooth functions \kappa(s) > 0 and \tau(s), there exists a unique space curve (up to rigid motion) with those curvature and torsion functions.

This is the analogue for curves of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — and it says: \kappa and \tau completely characterize a curve’s shape. The Frenet–Serret formulas are then an ODE system whose solution is the frame (and thus the curve).
Proof sketch: The system \frac{d}{ds}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{T}\\mathbf{N}\\mathbf{B}\end{pmatrix} = A(s)\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{T}\\mathbf{N}\\mathbf{B}\end{pmatrix} is a linear ODE with smooth coefficients — existence and uniqueness follow from the Picard–Lindelöf theorem. The antisymmetry of A ensures orthonormality is preserved. Uniqueness up to rigid motion follows from the initial condition {\mathbf{T}_0, \mathbf{N}_0, \mathbf{B}_0, \mathbf{r}(0)}.

9. Special Cases and Intuition



































Curve\kappa\tauMeaningStraight line0undefinedNo bending, no frameCircleconstant \neq 00Bends, stays in planeHelixconstant \neq 0constant \neq 0Bends and twists uniformlyPlanar curveany0\mathbf{B} =  const. normal to plane
A planar curve has \tau = 0 if and only if it lies in a plane. This is the geometric test: compute \tau and check.

10. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
The Frenet–Serret frame is not merely a classical geometry artifact — it surfaces throughout modern machine learning in deep and sometimes unexpected ways.
10.1 Curve Geometry in Latent Spaces
Deep neural networks map data into high-dimensional latent spaces (think of the hidden layers of a VAE or the embedding space of a transformer). Trajectories in these spaces — sequences of token embeddings, latent diffusion paths, optimization paths — are curves in \mathbb{R}^n.
The curvature \kappa of such a trajectory measures how sharply the latent representation is changing direction. A sudden spike in curvature during a language model’s generation trajectory can indicate:

A semantic shift (changing topic)
Hallucination onset (leaving the “manifold of plausible text”)
A difficult reasoning step

Researchers use curvature as a diagnostic tool for interpretability — analyzing the geometry of latent trajectories.
10.2 Riemannian Geometry of Neural Network Loss Landscapes
The loss landscape \mathcal{L}(\theta) of a neural network is a high-dimensional surface. The gradient descent trajectory \theta(t) is a curve on this surface. Its Frenet–Serret frame tells us:

\mathbf{T}: Direction of parameter update (steepest descent direction)
\mathbf{N}: Direction in which the gradient is rotating — connected to the Hessian of the loss
\kappa: How quickly the gradient direction changes — large \kappa near saddle points or sharp valleys

The Natural Gradient method (Amari, 1998) and K-FAC approximate the Fisher information matrix, which is intimately related to the curvature of the statistical manifold the model lives on — a direct application of differential geometry.
10.3 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and Trajectory Modeling
When neural networks learn to predict physical trajectories (robot arms, drone paths, molecular dynamics), the Frenet–Serret formulas appear explicitly in the loss function or constraints:

A robot arm following a smooth path minimizes torsion \tau (reduces mechanical stress).
Path planning algorithms enforce \kappa \leq \kappa_{\max} (curvature constraints for vehicle turning radius).
Neural ODEs that model particle trajectories must learn the geometry of phase-space curves, where \mathbf{N} and \mathbf{B} encode centripetal and gyroscopic forces.

10.4 Recurrent Neural Networks as Dynamical Systems
A trained RNN defines a vector field \mathbf{h}_{t+1} = f(\mathbf{h}_t, \mathbf{x}_t) on hidden state space. The trajectories of this dynamical system are curves. The Frenet frame of these hidden-state trajectories has been used to:

Identify fixed points (where \mathbf{T} \to 0) and saddle points in the RNN dynamics
Measure sensitivity of the RNN to inputs via changes in \kappa
Understand long-range dependencies: trajectories with large torsion indicate the RNN is “twisting” through state space — often correlated with forgetting

This connects to the vanishing/exploding gradient problem: in the Frenet frame language, gradients vanish when the loss trajectory has near-zero curvature (the optimization isn’t turning anywhere useful).
10.5 Curve Fitting and Shape Analysis (Computer Vision)
In computer vision and shape analysis, the Frenet frame is used directly:

3D shape descriptors: Curvature and torsion profiles (\kappa(s), \tau(s)) are used as rotation-invariant signatures of 3D curves (blood vessels, protein backbones, road networks)
Deep learning on point clouds (PointNet, DGCNN): These architectures implicitly learn local geometric features, including curvature and frame information
Protein structure prediction (AlphaFold2): The backbone of a protein is a space curve. The Frenet frame of the C_\alpha trace encodes secondary structure — helices have constant \kappa and \tau, strands have \tau \approx 0

10.6 Normalizing Flows and Manifold Learning
Normalizing flows learn diffeomorphic maps between distributions. The Jacobian of such a map encodes local geometric distortion. Along flow trajectories, \mathbf{N} and \mathbf{B} encode how the coordinate frame twists and bends — this is related to torsion of connections in the Riemannian geometry of the data manifold.
Summary table:

































ML ContextRole of Frenet–Serret ConceptsLatent space analysis\kappa diagnoses semantic changes in trajectoriesLoss landscape geometry\kappa near Hessian curvature; \mathbf{N} near gradient rotationPhysics-informed NNsExplicit \kappa, \tau constraints in lossRNN dynamicsFrame reveals fixed points, sensitivity, memoryProtein structure (AlphaFold)Helix ↔ constant \kappa,\tau; strand ↔ \tau \approx 0Shape learning (3D vision)(\kappa(s), \tau(s)) as rotation-invariant descriptors

11. Summary and Big Picture
The Frenet–Serret frame {\mathbf{T}, \mathbf{N}, \mathbf{B}} is the most natural coordinate system a curve carries with itself:
\mathbf{T} = \frac{\mathbf{r}'}{|\mathbf{r}'|}, \qquad \mathbf{N} = \frac{\mathbf{T}'}{|\mathbf{T}'|}, \qquad \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{T}\times\mathbf{N}
The three Frenet–Serret equations encode how this frame evolves:
\frac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds} = \kappa\mathbf{N}, \qquad \frac{d\mathbf{N}}{ds} = -\kappa\mathbf{T}+\tau\mathbf{B}, \qquad \frac{d\mathbf{B}}{ds} = -\tau\mathbf{N}
Curvature \kappa measures bending; torsion \tau measures twisting. Together, they completely characterize the shape of a space curve. This is a theorem — not merely a description.
In modern mathematics and its applications, this classical framework reappears whenever we study:

Paths in high-dimensional spaces (optimization, generative models)
Geometric structure of data manifolds
Physical trajectories constrained by curvature and torsion bounds
Biological structures like proteins, neurons, and DNA

The curve doesn’t just know where it’s going — it carries, at every point, a full description of how it’s going there. That’s the content of \mathbf{N} and \mathbf{B}.

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Sections 13.3–13.4. — Primary source for definitions, examples, and computational formulas.
MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02. Multivariable Calculus (Auroux). Lecture notes on space curves, curvature, and the Frenet frame. — The arc-length parametrization approach and Frenet–Serret ODE perspective.
do Carmo, M. Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces. — For the Fundamental Theorem and the full Riemannian generalization.
Amari, S. “Natural Gradient Works Efficiently in Learning.” Neural Computation (1998). — Curvature of statistical manifolds in ML.
Jumper, J. et al. “Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold.” Nature (2021). — Geometric structure of protein backbone curves.

01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/07.title: 07.Motion in Space
01.Maths/Calculus/13.Vector-Functions/07.content:
“Newton saw the planets and asked: what function \mathbf{r}(t) produces an ellipse under the force law \mathbf{F} = -GMm/r^2,\hat{\mathbf{r}}? The answer required him to invent calculus. We now have that calculus — let us use it properly.”


0. Setup and Philosophy
A particle moving through \mathbb{R}^3 is described by a smooth vector-valued function:
\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle x(t),, y(t),, z(t)\rangle, \qquad t \in I \subseteq \mathbb{R}
Everything — velocity, acceleration, speed, arc length, force — is derived from this single function by differentiation. The miracle of vector calculus is that all of Newton’s mechanics packages cleanly into vector equations, and the geometry of the Frenet–Serret frame (see Normal and Binormal Vectors) tells us why acceleration splits the way it does.
Convention throughout: t is time. Prime ' denotes d/dt. We assume \mathbf{r}(t) is at least twice continuously differentiable.

1. Velocity
Definition
The velocity vector is the derivative of the position vector:
\boxed{\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle x'(t),, y'(t),, z'(t)\rangle}
It is the instantaneous rate of change of position — both direction and magnitude carry meaning:

Direction of \mathbf{v}(t): Tangent to the curve at \mathbf{r}(t) — the direction of motion.
Magnitude |\mathbf{v}(t)|: The speed at time t.

Speed
v(t) := |\mathbf{v}(t)| = \sqrt{[x'(t)]^2 + [y'(t)]^2 + [z'(t)]^2}
Speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector. This distinction is not pedantry — it is the difference between “60 km/h” and “60 km/h due north.”
Relation to the Unit Tangent Vector
Recall \mathbf{T}(t) = \mathbf{r}'(t)/|\mathbf{r}'(t)|. Therefore:
\mathbf{v}(t) = |\mathbf{v}(t)|,\mathbf{T}(t) = v(t),\mathbf{T}(t)
Velocity is speed times the unit tangent. This is the canonical decomposition of velocity — speed tells you how fast, \mathbf{T} tells you which way.
Arc Length and Speed
Arc length satisfies \dfrac{ds}{dt} = |\mathbf{r}'(t)| = v(t). So:
s(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} |\mathbf{r}'(u)|,du = \int_{t_0}^{t} v(u),du
Speed is the rate of change of arc length. This is not a coincidence — it is the definition.

2. Acceleration
Definition
The acceleration vector is the derivative of velocity:
\boxed{\mathbf{a}(t) = \mathbf{v}'(t) = \mathbf{r}''(t) = \langle x''(t),, y''(t),, z''(t)\rangle}
Unlike velocity, acceleration does not generally point along \mathbf{T}. It can point in any direction — and decomposing it into the Frenet frame is the central result of this section.
Newton’s Second Law
For a particle of mass m:
\mathbf{F}(t) = m,\mathbf{a}(t) = m,\mathbf{r}''(t)
The vector equation encodes three scalar ODEs simultaneously. Knowing \mathbf{F} as a function of \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{v}, t gives a second-order ODE system — the equation of motion. The trajectory \mathbf{r}(t) is its solution.

3. The Tangential and Normal Components of Acceleration
This is the theorem that makes everything click. Acceleration splits into exactly two parts: one that changes your speed, and one that changes your direction.
Derivation
Start from \mathbf{v} = v,\mathbf{T}. Differentiate using the product rule:
\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{v}' = v',\mathbf{T} + v,\mathbf{T}'
Now use the first Frenet–Serret formula: \mathbf{T}' = \dfrac{d\mathbf{T}}{ds}\dfrac{ds}{dt} = \kappa,\mathbf{N}\cdot v. So:
\mathbf{a} = v',\mathbf{T} + \kappa v^2,\mathbf{N}
Define:
\boxed{a_T = v' = \frac{dv}{dt}, \qquad a_N = \kappa v^2}
Then:
\boxed{\mathbf{a} = a_T,\mathbf{T} + a_N,\mathbf{N}}
This is exact — no approximation. Acceleration has zero component along \mathbf{B}.
Geometric Interpretation




















ComponentFormulaPhysical Meaninga_T,\mathbf{T}v',\mathbf{T}Change in speed (speeding up or slowing down)a_N,\mathbf{N}\kappa v^2,\mathbf{N}Change in direction (centripetal, toward center of curvature)
Key observations:

If you drive at constant speed on a curved road: a_T = 0, but a_N = \kappa v^2 \neq 0. You are accelerating — your direction changes.
If you drive in a straight line and speed up: a_N = 0 (since \kappa = 0), only a_T \neq 0.
Acceleration is never along \mathbf{B}. Torsion (twisting) does not produce force directly — it produces a change in the osculating plane.

Why a_N = \kappa v^2?
Write it as a_N = v^2/\rho where \rho = 1/\kappa is the radius of curvature. This is the familiar centripetal acceleration formula a = v^2/r from circular motion — now generalized to any curve, using the instantaneous radius of the osculating circle. Beautiful.

4. Computing a_T and a_N Without the Frenet Frame
In practice you rarely know \kappa and \mathbf{N} explicitly. Here are computational formulas:
a_T = \frac{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{v}|} = \frac{\mathbf{r}'\cdot\mathbf{r}''}{|\mathbf{r}'|}
a_N = \frac{|\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{a}|}{|\mathbf{v}|} = \frac{|\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{r}''|}{|\mathbf{r}'|}
Proof of a_T: Project \mathbf{a} = a_T\mathbf{T} + a_N\mathbf{N} onto \mathbf{T}: \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{T} = a_T(\mathbf{T}\cdot\mathbf{T}) + a_N(\mathbf{N}\cdot\mathbf{T}) = a_T
Since \mathbf{v} = v\mathbf{T}, we get \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{v} = a_T v, hence a_T = \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{v}/v.
Proof of a_N: Compute \mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{a}: \mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{a} = v\mathbf{T}\times(a_T\mathbf{T}+a_N\mathbf{N}) = v,a_T(\mathbf{T}\times\mathbf{T}) + v,a_N(\mathbf{T}\times\mathbf{N}) = v,a_N,\mathbf{B}
So |\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{a}| = v,a_N (since |\mathbf{B}|=1), giving a_N = |\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{a}|/v.
Pythagoras check:
|\mathbf{a}|^2 = a_T^2 + a_N^2
since \mathbf{T} \perp \mathbf{N}. This gives a useful consistency check.

5. Worked Examples
Example 1: Circular Motion at Constant Speed
\mathbf{r}(t) = (R\cos\omega t,, R\sin\omega t,, 0)
where R > 0 is the radius and \omega > 0 is the angular frequency.
Velocity: \mathbf{v}(t) = (-R\omega\sin\omega t,, R\omega\cos\omega t,, 0), \qquad v = |\mathbf{v}| = R\omega
Constant speed — no speeding up or slowing down.
Acceleration: \mathbf{a}(t) = (-R\omega^2\cos\omega t,, -R\omega^2\sin\omega t,, 0) = -\omega^2(R\cos\omega t,, R\sin\omega t,, 0) = -\omega^2,\mathbf{r}(t)
The acceleration points toward the origin — centripetal. Its magnitude: |\mathbf{a}| = R\omega^2.
Decomposition: a_T = \frac{dv}{dt} = 0 \quad \checkmark \qquad a_N = \kappa v^2 = \frac{1}{R}(R\omega)^2 = R\omega^2 \quad \checkmark
The centripetal force required: F = m,a_N = mR\omega^2 = mv^2/R.

Example 2: Projectile Motion
A ball launched from the origin with initial velocity \mathbf{v}_0 = \langle v_0\cos\theta,, v_0\sin\theta,, 0\rangle, under gravity \mathbf{g} = \langle 0, -g, 0\rangle:
\mathbf{a}(t) = \langle 0,, -g,, 0\rangle
Integrate once (velocity): \mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{v}_0 + \mathbf{g}t = \langle v_0\cos\theta,; v_0\sin\theta - gt,; 0\rangle
Integrate again (position): \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{v}_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{g}t^2 = \langle v_0\cos\theta\cdot t,; v_0\sin\theta\cdot t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2,; 0\rangle
Speed at time t: v(t) = \sqrt{v_0^2\cos^2\theta + (v_0\sin\theta - gt)^2}
Tangential acceleration (rate of change of speed): a_T = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{(v_0\sin\theta - gt)(-g)}{v(t)} = \frac{-g(v_y)}{v}
At the apex (v_y = 0): a_T = 0 — speed is momentarily neither increasing nor decreasing. But a_N = g — the ball is still curving.
Normal acceleration at apex: a_N = \sqrt{|\mathbf{a}|^2 - a_T^2} = \sqrt{g^2 - 0} = g
At the apex, the full gravitational acceleration is centripetal — exactly as expected from the geometry.

Example 3: Helix with Increasing Speed
\mathbf{r}(t) = (\cos t^2,, \sin t^2,, t)
Velocity: \mathbf{v}(t) = (-2t\sin t^2,, 2t\cos t^2,, 1) v = |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{4t^2 + 1}
Acceleration: \mathbf{a}(t) = (-2\sin t^2 - 4t^2\cos t^2,; 2\cos t^2 - 4t^2\sin t^2,; 0)
a_T: a_T = \frac{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{a}}{v} = \frac{(-2t\sin t^2)(-2\sin t^2 - 4t^2\cos t^2) + (2t\cos t^2)(2\cos t^2 - 4t^2\sin t^2)}{\sqrt{4t^2+1}}
Expanding the numerator: = \frac{4t\sin^2 t^2 + 8t^3\sin t^2\cos t^2 + 4t\cos^2 t^2 - 8t^3\cos t^2\sin t^2}{\sqrt{4t^2+1}} = \frac{4t}{\sqrt{4t^2+1}}
Check: v = \sqrt{4t^2+1}, so v' = 4t/\sqrt{4t^2+1} = a_T. ✓
The speed is increasing (for t > 0) while the particle also curves — both a_T and a_N are nonzero.

6. Visualization
The Acceleration Decomposition
                 N (principal normal)
                 ↑
                 |  a_N·N (centripetal)
                 |  ↑
                 | /
  ───────────────*──────────→  T (tangent)
                /|
               / |
     a_T·T →  /  |
             /   |
            ↗    
           a (total acceleration)
           = a_T·T + a_N·N

  Note: a has NO component along B (binormal).

Speed vs. Curvature Trade-off
High speed, low curvature:        Low speed, high curvature:
  a_N = κv² → large               a_N = κv² → moderate

  ─────────────────────            ╭──────────────╮
  (fast, gently curving road)      (slow, sharp turn)

Both can produce the same |a_N| — the driver feels the same lateral force.
This is why speed limits decrease at sharp curves.

Phase Diagram: Speeding Up vs. Slowing Down
  a_T > 0  →  speeding up   (a has component in direction of motion)
  a_T < 0  →  slowing down  (a opposes direction of motion)
  a_T = 0  →  constant speed (a ⊥ T, purely centripetal)

  Example — car on a mountain road:
  Ascending curve:   a_T < 0 (engine fights gravity), a_N ≠ 0 (turning)
  Descending curve:  a_T > 0 (gravity aids motion), a_N ≠ 0 (turning)
  At apex (flat):    a_T ≈ 0 momentarily, a_N from curvature


7. Integration: Finding Position from Acceleration
Given \mathbf{a}(t) and initial conditions \mathbf{r}(t_0) = \mathbf{r}_0, \mathbf{v}(t_0) = \mathbf{v}_0:
\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{v}_0 + \int_{t_0}^{t}\mathbf{a}(u),du
\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{r}_0 + \int_{t_0}^{t}\mathbf{v}(u),du
Integration is componentwise: each equation is three scalar ODEs integrated independently.
Key point: The initial conditions (\mathbf{r}_0, \mathbf{v}_0) — six scalar values — completely determine the trajectory when \mathbf{a} is given. This is the vector form of the initial value problem, and uniqueness follows from Picard–Lindelöf applied componentwise.

8. Kepler’s First Law (A Taste of What the Formalism Buys)
Consider a planet of mass m orbiting a star of mass M at the origin. Newton’s law gives:
\mathbf{r}'' = -\frac{GM}{|\mathbf{r}|^3},\mathbf{r}
Claim: The angular momentum \mathbf{L} = m(\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{v}) is conserved.
Proof: \frac{d\mathbf{L}}{dt} = m(\mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{v}') = m(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{a}) = m\left(\mathbf{0} + \mathbf{r}\times\left(-\frac{GM}{|\mathbf{r}|^3}\mathbf{r}\right)\right) = \mathbf{0}
since \mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}. Therefore \mathbf{L} =  const., which means the motion is planar (confined to the plane perpendicular to \mathbf{L}). This is the first step in proving the orbit is a conic section — and it falls out of a two-line vector calculation.
This illustrates the power of the vector formalism: what would require pages of component algebra becomes transparent.

9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
The concepts of velocity and acceleration in vector calculus map directly onto some of the most important algorithms and ideas in modern machine learning.
9.1 Gradient Descent as Motion in Parameter Space
Training a neural network by gradient descent defines a trajectory \boldsymbol{\theta}(t) in parameter space \mathbb{R}^p (where p can be billions). The analog of Newton’s equations:

























PhysicsML OptimizationPosition \mathbf{r}(t)Parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}(t)Velocity \mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{r}'Rate of parameter change \boldsymbol{\theta}'Force / AccelerationNegative gradient -\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}MassLearning rate \eta (inverse analog)
Vanilla gradient descent is literally Euler’s method for the ODE: \frac{d\boldsymbol{\theta}}{dt} = -\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
The “velocity” in parameter space is -\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L} — you move in the direction of steepest descent.
9.2 Momentum Methods — Literally Acceleration
SGD with momentum (Polyak, 1964) introduces an auxiliary “velocity” variable:
\mathbf{m}_{t+1} = \beta,\mathbf{m}_t - \eta,\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t) \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t + \mathbf{m}_{t+1}
This is a discrete heavy-ball ODE: \boldsymbol{\theta}'' + (1-\beta)\boldsymbol{\theta}' = -\eta,\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}
where \boldsymbol{\theta}'' is the “acceleration” in parameter space. The momentum term \beta\mathbf{m}_t is literally carrying forward the previous velocity — inertia. This is why momentum helps:

In a long ravine (loss landscape), the tangential component a_T accumulates — you speed up in the ravine direction.
Noisy gradients partially cancel in the normal component a_N — you don’t oscillate wildly across the ravine.

Nesterov accelerated gradient looks ahead before computing the gradient — equivalent to a better ODE discretization with faster convergence. Sutskever et al. (2013) showed this achieves the optimal O(1/t^2) convergence rate for convex functions.
9.3 Adam and Adaptive Curvature
Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2014) maintains:

\mathbf{m}_t: exponential moving average of gradients (≈ velocity)
\mathbf{v}_t: exponential moving average of squared gradients (≈ estimate of local curvature / a_N)

The update normalizes the velocity by the estimated curvature: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \eta,\frac{\hat{\mathbf{m}}_t}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}_t}+\epsilon}
This is an adaptive normal acceleration correction — in directions of high curvature (oscillation), the effective step is reduced; in directions of low curvature (flat), it is increased. Adam is essentially adapting a_N to the local geometry.
9.4 Neural ODEs
Neural ODEs (Chen et al., NeurIPS 2018) explicitly model the hidden state as a particle trajectory:
\frac{d\mathbf{h}(t)}{dt} = f_\theta(\mathbf{h}(t), t)
Here f_\theta is a neural network that defines the velocity field — the analog of \mathbf{v}(t). The forward pass is an ODE solve, not a sequence of layer applications. The backward pass uses the adjoint method — a continuous analog of backpropagation derived from the calculus of variations.
The acceleration \mathbf{h}''(t) = \frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial \mathbf{h}}f_\theta + \frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial t} encodes how the hidden state changes direction in representation space — directly analogous to \mathbf{a} = a_T\mathbf{T}+a_N\mathbf{N}.
9.5 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
PINNs solve PDEs by embedding the equation of motion into the loss. For instance, learning the trajectory of a charged particle:
\mathbf{r}'' = \frac{q}{m}(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{r}'\times\mathbf{B})
The loss penalizes violation of this ODE: \mathcal{L} = \left|\mathbf{r}''_\theta(t) - \frac{q}{m}\left(\mathbf{E}(t) + \mathbf{r}'_\theta(t)\times\mathbf{B}(t)\right)\right|^2
where \mathbf{r}_\theta(t) is a neural network approximating the trajectory. The network must learn both the velocity and acceleration components correctly — a_T (along the trajectory) and a_N (centripetal, from the magnetic force q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}, which is always perpendicular to \mathbf{v}).
9.6 Robotics and Reinforcement Learning
In model-based RL, the agent learns a dynamics model: \mathbf{s}_{t+1} = f(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t)
which is a discrete version of \mathbf{r}'' = \mathbf{F}/m. For robotic arm control:

Joint velocities \mathbf{v} are the control inputs.
Joint accelerations \mathbf{a} are constrained (actuator torque limits).
The tangential component a_T changes the end-effector speed; the normal component a_N changes its direction.

Trajectory optimization explicitly minimizes \int_0^T |\mathbf{a}(t)|^2,dt subject to dynamics constraints — minimizing the total acceleration effort, decomposed into a_T^2 + a_N^2.
9.7 Attention and Transformer Dynamics
Recent theoretical work models the forward pass of a transformer as a continuous dynamical system (an ODE in layer depth). The residual stream update at each layer is:
\mathbf{x}_{l+1} = \mathbf{x}_l + F_l(\mathbf{x}_l)
as l \to \infty, this converges to \mathbf{x}' = F(\mathbf{x}) — a velocity field on the embedding manifold. The acceleration \mathbf{x}'' captures how attention heads curve the representation trajectory through token space. This framework (Continuous Depth Networks) enables analysis of representation stability using tools directly from this section.

10. Summary
Starting from position \mathbf{r}(t), differentiation gives:
\mathbf{r}(t) \xrightarrow{;d/dt;} \mathbf{v}(t) \xrightarrow{;d/dt;} \mathbf{a}(t)
The master decomposition of acceleration:
\mathbf{a} = \underbrace{v',\mathbf{T}}_{\text{tangential}} + \underbrace{\kappa v^2,\mathbf{N}}_{\text{normal}}
with computational formulas:
a_T = \frac{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{v}|}, \qquad a_N = \frac{|\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{a}|}{|\mathbf{v}|}, \qquad |\mathbf{a}|^2 = a_T^2 + a_N^2
The physical content:

a_T is what your speedometer feels — rate of speed change.
a_N is what presses you into your seat on a turn — centripetal, always toward center of curvature.
No acceleration ever has a binormal component — torsion is invisible to Newton’s \mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a} in 3D.

In machine learning, this framework reappears as: momentum in gradient descent (inertia in parameter space), adaptive curvature correction (Adam), continuous dynamics of neural networks (Neural ODEs), and constrained trajectory optimization in robotics.

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Section 13.4 — Motion in Space: Velocity and Acceleration. Primary source for definitions, examples, and the a_T, a_N decomposition.
MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02. Multivariable Calculus (Auroux). Lectures on vector differentiation, projectile motion, and Kepler’s laws. The approach to Kepler via angular momentum conservation.
Polyak, B.T. “Some methods of speeding up the convergence of iteration methods.” USSR Comp. Math. (1964). — Original momentum paper.
Kingma, D. & Ba, J. “Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization.” ICLR (2015). — Adaptive curvature estimation.
Chen, R.T.Q. et al. “Neural Ordinary Differential Equations.” NeurIPS (2018). — Hidden states as particle trajectories.
Sutskever, I. et al. “On the importance of initialization and momentum in deep learning.” ICML (2013). — Nesterov acceleration for deep networks.

01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.title: 01.Functions of Two Variables
01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.content:
“A function of one variable is a curve. A function of two variables is a landscape — it has hills, valleys, ridges, and saddle points. Learning to read that landscape is the entire project of multivariable calculus.”


0. Motivation
In single-variable calculus, we study f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}. But the real world is rarely one-dimensional:

Temperature in a room depends on position (x, y) on the floor.
The pressure of a gas depends on volume V and temperature T.
The loss of a neural network depends on millions of parameters (\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_p).

The step from one variable to two is not merely an added variable — it is a qualitative leap in richness. New phenomena appear: partial derivatives, mixed partials, level curves, saddle points, constrained extrema. Understanding the two-variable case deeply is the prerequisite for everything that follows.

1. Definition
Formal Definition
A function of two variables is a rule f that assigns to each ordered pair (x, y) in a set D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 a unique real number z = f(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}:
f: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad (x,y) \mapsto f(x,y)

D is the domain of f — the set of valid inputs.
The range is {f(x,y) : (x,y) \in D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}.
z = f(x,y) is the dependent variable; x, y are independent variables.

Natural Domain
Unless stated otherwise, the domain of f is the largest subset of \mathbb{R}^2 for which the expression f(x,y) makes sense (real-valued, defined). This requires excluding:

Points where denominators vanish.
Points where expressions under even roots are negative.
Points where logarithms receive non-positive arguments.

Example: f(x,y) = \dfrac{\sqrt{y - x^2}}{1 - x^2 - y^2}

Need y - x^2 \geq 0: above or on the parabola y = x^2.
Need 1 - x^2 - y^2 \neq 0: outside the unit circle.

Domain: {(x,y) : y \geq x^2} \setminus {(x,y): x^2+y^2 = 1}.

2. The Graph
Definition
The graph of f: D \to \mathbb{R} is the set of all points (x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 such that z = f(x,y) and (x,y) \in D:
\text{graph}(f) = {(x, y, f(x,y)) : (x,y) \in D} \subset \mathbb{R}^3
Geometrically: a surface in \mathbb{R}^3 lying above (or below) the xy-plane.
Visualization
Think of the xy-plane as a map. The value f(x,y) is the elevation at location (x,y). The graph is the terrain — the topographic surface.
        z
        │        *  surface z = f(x,y)
        │      * *  *
        │    *       *
        │  *           *
        │*               *
        └──────────────────── y
       /
      /
     x

For each (x,y) in the domain, there is exactly one height z = f(x,y).

Key Surfaces to Know

































FunctionSurfacez = ax + by + cPlanez = x^2 + y^2Circular paraboloid (bowl)z = x^2 - y^2Hyperbolic paraboloid (saddle)z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}Conez = \sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2}Upper hemisphere of unit spherez = e^{-(x^2+y^2)}Gaussian bell surface

3. Level Curves
Definition
The level curve (or contour) of f at height c \in \mathbb{R} is the set:
L_c = {(x,y) \in D : f(x,y) = c}
It is the horizontal cross-section of the graph at height z = c, projected down to the xy-plane.
Crucially: A point (x,y) lies on the level curve L_c if and only if the surface passes through height c directly above it.
The Contour Map
A contour map (contour plot) is the collection of level curves {L_c} for various values of c, drawn in the xy-plane. Every topographic map you have ever read is a contour map.
Reading a contour map:

Closely spaced contours: Steep terrain (rapid change in f).
Widely spaced contours: Gentle terrain (slow change in f).
Closed contours: Peaks, valleys, or saddle points.
Contours never cross: If L_c and L_{c'} crossed at a point (x_0, y_0), then f(x_0,y_0) = c and f(x_0,y_0) = c' simultaneously — impossible for c \neq c'.

Examples
f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2: Level curves c = x^2 + y^2 are circles of radius \sqrt{c} centered at the origin. The surface is a paraboloid. Contours are evenly spaced circles — but the paraboloid gets steeper as r increases, so equal spacing in c gives circles that pack closer together.
f(x,y) = x^2 - y^2: Level curves c = x^2 - y^2 are hyperbolas (for c \neq 0) and the two lines y = \pm x (for c = 0). This is the saddle surface — its contour map looks like a topographic pass between two mountains.
f(x,y) = xy: Level curves xy = c are rectangular hyperbolas with asymptotes along the axes.
Contour map of z = x² + y²:       Contour map of z = x² - y² (saddle):

    y                                   y
    │   (3)  (2)  (1)                   │
    │  ╭──╮╭──╮╭──╮                    │  ╲ ╱ ╲ ╱
    │  │  ││  ││  │                     │   ╳   ╳
    │  ╰──╯╰──╯╰──╯                    │  ╱ ╲ ╱ ╲
    └──────────────── x                 └──────────────── x

  circles = level curves               hyperbolas = level curves
  (bowl shape)                         (saddle shape)


4. Limits and Continuity
The Core Difficulty
In \mathbb{R}, approaching a point a means coming from the left or right — only two paths. In \mathbb{R}^2, approaching (a,b) means coming from infinitely many directions and along infinitely many curved paths. For a limit to exist, the function must approach the same value along every possible path.
Definition
\lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)} f(x,y) = L
means: for every \varepsilon > 0, there exists \delta > 0 such that:
0 < \sqrt{(x-a)^2 + (y-b)^2} < \delta \implies |f(x,y) - L| < \varepsilon
The Two-Path Test (Nonexistence)
To show a limit does not exist: find two paths to (a,b) along which f approaches different values.
Example: Show \displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{x^2 - y^2}{x^2 + y^2} does not exist.

Along y = 0: f(x,0) = x^2/x^2 = 1 \to 1.
Along x = 0: f(0,y) = -y^2/y^2 = -1 \to -1.

Since 1 \neq -1, the limit does not exist. \square
Example (subtler): Show \displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{xy^2}{x^2+y^4} does not exist.

Along y = 0: f \to 0.
Along x = y^2: f = \frac{y^2\cdot y^2}{y^4 + y^4} = \frac{1}{2} \to \frac{1}{2}.

Limit does not exist. Note: along any straight line y = mx, the limit is 0 — only a parabolic path reveals the failure. This shows why the two-path test must consider curves, not just lines.
Continuity
f is continuous at (a,b) if:

f(a,b) is defined.
\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)} f(x,y) exists.
\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)} f(x,y) = f(a,b).

Theorem: Polynomials in x,y are continuous on all of \mathbb{R}^2. Rational functions are continuous on their domains. Compositions of continuous functions are continuous.
Consequence: For nice functions (polynomials, rationals away from singularities, exponentials, trig), you can evaluate limits by direct substitution. The challenge is only at boundary points of the domain or suspected discontinuities.

5. Partial Derivatives (First Pass)
Full treatment in the next note. Here, the idea.
The partial derivative \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(a,b) is the derivative of f in the x-direction, holding y = b fixed:
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(a,b) = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h,b) - f(a,b)}{h}
Geometrically: it is the slope of the curve obtained by slicing the surface z = f(x,y) with the vertical plane y = b.
Similarly for \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}: hold x = a fixed, differentiate in y.
Rule: To compute \partial f/\partial x, treat y as a constant and differentiate in x using all single-variable rules.

6. Worked Examples
Example 1: Domain
Find the domain of f(x,y) = \ln(x + y - 1).
Need x + y - 1 > 0, i.e., x + y > 1.
Domain: the open half-plane above the line x + y = 1. The boundary line is excluded (log of zero is undefined).

Example 2: Level Curves of a Gaussian
Let f(x,y) = e^{-(x^2 + y^2)}.
Level curve at height c (where 0 < c \leq 1): e^{-(x^2+y^2)} = c \implies x^2 + y^2 = -\ln c
For 0 < c < 1: -\ln c > 0, so these are circles of radius \sqrt{-\ln c}. As c \to 1^-: radius \to 0 (peak at origin). As c \to 0^+: radius \to \infty (function decays to zero far from origin).
The contour map is a family of concentric circles — and the circles get farther apart as c decreases (the Gaussian decays rapidly near origin, then flattens out).

Example 3: A Subtle Limit
Show \displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{x^2 y}{x^2+y^2} = 0.
Use the Squeeze Theorem. Observe: \left|\frac{x^2 y}{x^2+y^2}\right| \leq \frac{x^2 |y|}{x^2+y^2} \leq |y|
since x^2 \leq x^2 + y^2. As (x,y) \to (0,0), |y| \to 0. By squeeze, the limit is 0.
Note: To confirm, convert to polar: x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta: \frac{r^2\cos^2\theta \cdot r\sin\theta}{r^2} = r\cos^2\theta\sin\theta \to 0 \text{ as } r\to 0
since |\cos^2\theta\sin\theta| \leq 1 for all \theta. The polar method works when the bound is independent of \theta.

Example 4: Discontinuity
Let f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{2xy}{x^2+y^2} & (x,y)\neq(0,0) \ 0 & (x,y) = (0,0)\end{cases}
Is f continuous at (0,0)?
Along y = mx: f(x,mx) = \dfrac{2mx^2}{x^2(1+m^2)} = \dfrac{2m}{1+m^2}, which depends on m.
For m = 1: limit is 1. For m = 0: limit is 0. The limit does not exist, so f is not continuous at (0,0), regardless of how we define f(0,0).

7. Visualization Toolkit
Reading a Surface from Its Contours
Close contours = steep         Sparse contours = gentle

  ════════════                   ══════════════════
  ══════════════                 ══════════════════
  ════════════════               ══════════════════

  Think: cliff face              Think: gentle meadow

Identifying Features from Contour Maps
Peak:              Valley:            Saddle:
  ╭───╮              ╭───╮             ╲   ╱
  │ ╭─╯              │ ╭─╯              ╲ ╱
  │ │                │ │                 ╳
  ╰─╯                ╰─╯                ╱╲
                                       ╱  ╲
  Concentric closed   Concentric closed   Hyperbolas;
  contours,           contours,           two "uphill"
  values increase     values decrease     and two "downhill"
  inward              inward              directions

The “Slicing” Interpretation
The surface z = f(x,y) is simultaneously:

The set of all level curves stacked at their respective heights.
The set of all “traces” — curves obtained by fixing x or y to a constant.

Fix y = b:  curve z = f(x, b) in the plane y = b  →  slope = ∂f/∂x
Fix x = a:  curve z = f(a, y) in the plane x = a  →  slope = ∂f/∂y


8. Functions of Three or More Variables
The definitions extend naturally:
f: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad (x_1, \ldots, x_n) \mapsto f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
We can no longer visualize the graph (it lives in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}). Instead, we study level sets:
L_c = {(x_1,\ldots,x_n) : f(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = c}
which are (n-1)-dimensional hypersurfaces in \mathbb{R}^n.
For n = 3: f(x,y,z) = c defines a level surface in \mathbb{R}^3 — e.g., x^2+y^2+z^2 = r^2 (sphere), x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2+z^2/c^2 = 1 (ellipsoid).
All the theory — limits, continuity, partial derivatives, gradients — extends verbatim to n variables. The geometry is harder to visualize but the algebra is identical.

9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
9.1 The Loss Function Is a Function of Millions of Variables
The most important function in all of machine learning is the loss function:
\mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\theta} \mapsto \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
where p is the number of parameters (GPT-4: p \sim 10^{12}). This is exactly a function of p variables — the direct generalization of f(x,y) to p dimensions.
Everything we study for f(x,y) has a direct ML analog:





























f(x,y) conceptML analogDomain D \subset \mathbb{R}^2Parameter space \mathbb{R}^pGraph z = f(x,y)Loss landscape (unvisualizable for p \gg 2)Level curve f(x,y) = cLoss contour \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\theta) = c — iso-loss surface in parameter spaceContinuitySmoothness of \mathcal{L} (required for gradient methods to work)Partial derivative \partial f/\partial xGradient component \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\theta_i — used in backpropagation
9.2 Level Curves as Decision Boundaries
For a binary classifier f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}, the decision boundary is the level curve f(x,y) = 0.5 (or f = 0 for logistic regression). The classifier outputs:

Class 1 if f(x,y) > 0.5
Class 0 if f(x,y) < 0.5

A linear classifier produces straight-line decision boundaries (level curves of a linear f). A neural network can produce arbitrarily complex level curves — this is the Universal Approximation Theorem in geometric form: a neural network can approximate any continuous function f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}, hence any level curve as a decision boundary.
9.3 Continuity and the Vanishing Gradient Problem
The continuity of the loss function near a region of parameter space is directly connected to gradient flow. At a discontinuity or near a point where the gradient is zero but the function is not at a minimum (a flat region or plateau), gradient descent stalls — the optimization analogue of a function with zero partial derivatives everywhere in a region.
The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation \text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0,x) makes networks that are continuous but not differentiable at x = 0. The composed function \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\theta) for a ReLU network is a piecewise linear function of \boldsymbol\theta — continuous everywhere, differentiable almost everywhere.
9.4 Gaussian Functions and Radial Basis Networks
The function f(x,y) = e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2\sigma^2} (Example 2 above) is the 2D Gaussian. Its level curves are concentric circles. In ML:

Kernel methods (SVMs with RBF kernel): The kernel K(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = e^{-|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'|^2/2\sigma^2} measures similarity as a Gaussian of distance.
Radial Basis Function (RBF) networks: Hidden units compute \phi(\mathbf{x}) = e^{-|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}_i|^2/2\sigma_i^2} — exactly the two-variable Gaussian, with centers \mathbf{c}_i.
Gaussian Processes: The covariance function is a Gaussian of the input distance — level curves of this covariance are ellipses in input space.

9.5 Latent Space and Feature Maps
In a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) or diffusion model, data is mapped to a 2D (or low-dimensional) latent space. The decoder then defines a function f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^d (going from 2 latent variables to a high-dimensional output — the reverse direction of what we study here, but the domain is \mathbb{R}^2).
The latent space interpolation — walking along a straight line or curve in the (z_1, z_2) plane — is exactly choosing a path in the domain D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 of the decoder function. The continuity of f ensures nearby latent points decode to nearby outputs.
9.6 Two-Variable Functions as Neural Network Layers
A single neuron with two inputs computes:
z = \sigma(w_1 x + w_2 y + b)
This is a function f(x,y) = \sigma(w_1 x + w_2 y + b). Its level curves are:
w_1 x + w_2 y + b = \sigma^{-1}(c) = \text{const}
which are straight lines (linear decision boundaries). Stacking neurons allows the level curves of the composed function to become arbitrarily curved — the geometric meaning of expressiveness.
9.7 Domain and Data Manifold
In practice, input data does not fill all of \mathbb{R}^n. Natural images, for instance, occupy a low-dimensional manifold \mathcal{M} \subset \mathbb{R}^n (the manifold hypothesis). The effective domain of the learned function f is this manifold — points off the manifold are out-of-distribution. This is the geometric basis for why neural networks hallucinate and fail on adversarial examples: the function is evaluated outside its meaningful domain D.

10. Summary
A function of two variables f: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R} is a surface in \mathbb{R}^3, studied through:
Domain: Largest set where f(x,y) makes sense — exclude division by zero, square roots of negatives, logs of non-positives.
Graph: The surface z = f(x,y) in \mathbb{R}^3 — the geometric object we analyze.
Level curves: f(x,y) = c — horizontal slices of the graph, contour lines on a map. They never cross; dense packing means steep terrain.
Limits: Must agree along every path to (a,b), not just along lines. Two-path test proves nonexistence; polar coordinates and squeeze theorem prove existence.
Continuity: Defined exactly as in one variable, but the limit condition is harder to verify due to the infinity of approach paths.
The entire theory extends to n variables. In machine learning, the loss landscape \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\theta) is a function of millions of variables — but every concept introduced here (domain, level sets, continuity, partial derivatives) applies directly, at scale.

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Sections 14.1–14.2. — Primary source: definitions, domain, level curves, limits, continuity, worked examples.
MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02. Multivariable Calculus (Auroux). Lectures on functions of several variables and their graphs. — The contour map perspective and polar coordinate limit technique.
Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., Courville, A. Deep Learning. MIT Press (2016). Ch. 4–6. — Loss landscapes, activation functions, and the geometric view of neural networks.
Kingma, D. & Welling, M. “Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes.” ICLR (2014). — Latent space as a two-variable domain.
