In full generality: let X, Y be normed vector spaces, f: X \to Y, \mathbf{a} \in X.
Definition. f is Fréchet differentiable at \mathbf{a} if there exists a bounded linear operator A: X \to Y such that:
\lim_{|\mathbf{h}|_X \to 0} \frac{|f(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) - f(\mathbf{a}) - A\mathbf{h}|_Y}{|\mathbf{h}|_X} = 0
A is called the Fréchet derivative Df(\mathbf{a}) of f at \mathbf{a}.
Special cases:

X = \mathbb{R}, Y = \mathbb{R}: A = f'(a) (scalar multiplication) — ordinary derivative
X = \mathbb{R}^n, Y = \mathbb{R}^m: A = J_\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{a}) (matrix multiplication) — Jacobian
X = C([0,1]), Y = \mathbb{R}: A is an integral operator — calculus of variations

The Fréchet derivative is the unique best linear approximation in the above sense. The chain rule still holds: D(f \circ g)(\mathbf{a}) = Df(g(\mathbf{a})) \circ Dg(\mathbf{a}) (composition of linear operators).
This framework applies to neural networks as maps between function spaces, and to the analysis of infinite-dimensional optimization problems.

§10. Summary — The Hierarchy of Approximations
f(\mathbf{x}) = \underbrace{f(\mathbf{a})}_{\text{0th order}} + \underbrace{\nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})}_{\text{1st order (linear)}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T H(\mathbf{a}) (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})}_{\text{2nd order (quadratic)}} + \cdots



































OrderNameErrorUse Case0Constant approx.O(\|\Delta\mathbf{x}\|)Crude estimate1Linear approx. (this note)O(\|\Delta\mathbf{x}\|^2)Gradient descent, error propagation, sensitivity2Quadratic approx.O(\|\Delta\mathbf{x}\|^3)Newton’s method, curvature analysiskTaylor polynomialO(\|\Delta\mathbf{x}\|^{k+1})Series solutions, numerical methods
The linear approximation is the sweet spot: cheap to compute (just first derivatives), error decays quadratically, and it captures directional information (which constant approximation misses).

§11. Things That Will Trip You Up

The linear approximation requires differentiability, not just partial derivatives. Existence of f_x and f_y is not sufficient. You need them to be continuous, or directly verify the o(|\Delta\mathbf{x}|) limit.


The total differential df is not the same as \Delta f. The differential is exact only for linear functions. For everything else, \Delta f = df + O(|\Delta\mathbf{x}|^2).


Error bounds require bounding the second derivative. The approximation "f(x) \approx L(x)" is qualitative. Quantitative error analysis always needs the Lagrange remainder.


Affine \neq linear. A linear approximation passing through (a, f(a)) with f(a) \neq 0 is not a linear function — it is affine. This distinction matters in algebra and optimization.


The Jacobian is a matrix, not a determinant. The Jacobian determinant \det(J) is a scalar used for change-of-variables; the Jacobian matrix is the derivative of a vector-valued map. Do not conflate them.


§12. Theorems to Know Cold
Theorem 1 (Linear Approximation, Scalar). If f is differentiable at a, then for x near a: f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + o(x-a)
Theorem 2 (Linear Approximation, Vector). If f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} is differentiable at \mathbf{a}, then: f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}) + o(|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}|)
Theorem 3 (Error Bound via Taylor). If |f''| \leq M on [a, x], then |f(x) - L(x)| \leq \frac{M}{2}(x-a)^2.
Theorem 4 (Jacobian Chain Rule). For differentiable \mathbf{g}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^n and \mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m: J_{\mathbf{f} \circ \mathbf{g}}(\mathbf{a}) = J_\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{a})), J_\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{a})
Theorem 5 (Fréchet Uniqueness). The Fréchet derivative, when it exists, is the unique bounded linear operator satisfying the o(|\mathbf{h}|) error condition.

References

James Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. — §3.10 (Linear Approximations and Differentials), §14.4 (Tangent Planes and Linear Approximations), §11.11 (Taylor Series).
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Notes on Linear Approximation and the Total Differential; Denis Auroux’s treatment of differentiability and the Jacobian.
Goodfellow, Shlens, Szegedy (2014), Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples — FGSM and the linear approximation of deep networks.
Jacot, Gabriel, Hongler (NeurIPS 2018), Neural Tangent Kernel — the NTK as a global linear approximation in parameter space.


See Also

Tangent Planes — the geometric side of linear approximation in \mathbb{R}^2
Taylor Series — higher-order extensions
Gradient and Directional Derivatives — the geometry of \nabla f
Optimization and Critical Points — where linear approximation is trivial and second order takes over

01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.title: 11.Differentials
01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.content:
“The derivative tells you the rate. The differential tells you the amount — infinitesimally. One is a number; the other is a linear map. Confusing them is the source of half the errors in applied mathematics.”


§1. Motivation — Why Differentials?
In single-variable calculus, the derivative f'(a) is a number. But the expression
dy = f'(x),dx
is something different: it is a linear approximation to the change in y given a small change dx in x. This object — a differential — carries more structural information than the derivative alone. It:

Lives in the dual space (acts on tangent vectors, returns scalars)
Transforms correctly under change of variables (chain rule becomes trivial)
Generalizes naturally to surfaces, manifolds, and high-dimensional parameter spaces
Is the building block of integration, differential forms, and the entire apparatus of modern geometry

The goal of this note is to understand differentials rigorously, compute with them fluently, and see exactly how they power machine learning.

§2. Differentials in One Variable
2.1 — The Setup
Let y = f(x), and suppose f is differentiable at x. Define:

dx — an independent variable representing an arbitrary increment in x
\Delta x = dx — the actual change (same thing here)
\Delta y = f(x + dx) - f(x) — the actual change in y

Definition. The differential of y is:
dy = f'(x),dx
Key point. dx is a free variable — it can be anything. dy is then determined by it. Together, (dx, dy) parameterize the tangent line at x.
2.2 — The Error
The relationship between \Delta y and dy:
\Delta y = f'(x),dx + \varepsilon \cdot dx, \quad \text{where } \varepsilon \to 0 \text{ as } dx \to 0
More precisely, by Taylor’s theorem:
\Delta y = dy + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}f''(x)(dx)^2 + \cdots}_{\text{higher-order terms}}
So dy approximates \Delta y with error O((dx)^2) — quadratically small. This is what makes differentials useful for estimation.
2.3 — Geometric Picture
  y
  |          * ← actual point (x+dx, f(x+dx))
  |        /·
  |      /  ← Δy (actual rise)
  |    /·· ← dy (tangent line rise)
  |  * ← (x, f(x))
  |________________________ x
       dx

dy is the rise along the tangent line; \Delta y is the rise along the curve. They agree to first order.

§3. Differentials in Several Variables
3.1 — Definition
Let z = f(x, y) be differentiable at (a, b). The total differential is:
\boxed{dz = f_x(x,y),dx + f_y(x,y),dy = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x},dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y},dy}
Here dx and dy are independent free variables (increments in x and y). dz is the resulting increment in z along the tangent plane.
Connection to tangent planes. This is exactly the tangent plane formula in differential form. If we set dx = x - a, dy = y - b:
z \approx f(a,b) + dz = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b),dx + f_y(a,b),dy
The total differential is the tangent plane, written infinitesimally.
3.2 — For n Variables
If w = f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n):
dw = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1},dx_1 + \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2},dx_2 + \cdots + \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n},dx_n = \nabla f \cdot d\mathbf{x}
This is a linear functional on the vector of increments d\mathbf{x} = (dx_1, \ldots, dx_n).
3.3 — Formal Properties (Differential Rules)
Differentials obey exactly the same rules as derivatives — because they are derivatives, just written in a different notation.

































RuleExpressionConstantd(c) = 0Sumd(f \pm g) = df \pm dgProductd(fg) = f,dg + g,dfQuotientd(f/g) = \frac{g,df - f,dg}{g^2}Chaind(f(g)) = f'(g),dgPowerd(x^n) = nx^{n-1},dx
These rules let you compute differentials algebraically, without restating the chain rule every time.
Example. w = x^2 \sin(xy). Compute dw.
dw = d(x^2)\sin(xy) + x^2,d(\sin(xy)) = 2x,dx \cdot \sin(xy) + x^2 \cos(xy),d(xy) = 2x\sin(xy),dx + x^2\cos(xy)(y,dx + x,dy) = \left[2x\sin(xy) + x^2 y\cos(xy)\right]dx + x^3\cos(xy),dy
Read off: \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} = 2x\sin(xy) + x^2 y\cos(xy), \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} = x^3\cos(xy).

§4. Error Estimation and Propagation
This is the most immediate application. Given a quantity Q = f(x_1, \ldots, x_n) where each x_i is measured with error |\Delta x_i| \leq \delta_i, the propagated error is estimated by:
|\Delta Q| \approx |dQ| \leq \left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}\right|\delta_1 + \cdots + \left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\right|\delta_n
The inequality uses the triangle inequality on the differential.
Relative error:
\frac{|dQ|}{|Q|} \approx \left|\frac{\partial \ln f}{\partial x_1}\right|\delta_1 + \cdots
For products and powers, logarithmic differentiation simplifies the relative error enormously.
Example — Resistance
Two resistors R_1 = 100,\Omega \pm 1% and R_2 = 200,\Omega \pm 1% in parallel. Find the error in total resistance R = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}.
Use logarithmic differentials. First,
\ln R = \ln R_1 + \ln R_2 - \ln(R_1 + R_2)
\frac{dR}{R} = \frac{dR_1}{R_1} + \frac{dR_2}{R_2} - \frac{dR_1 + dR_2}{R_1 + R_2}
= dR_1\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_1+R_2}\right) + dR_2\left(\frac{1}{R_2} - \frac{1}{R_1+R_2}\right)
= dR_1 \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1(R_1+R_2)} + dR_2 \cdot \frac{R_1}{R_2(R_1+R_2)}
With R_1 = 100, R_2 = 200, R_1 + R_2 = 300:
\frac{|dR|}{R} \leq \frac{200}{100 \cdot 300}(1) + \frac{100}{200 \cdot 300}(2) \approx 0.0067 + 0.0033 = 1%
So the parallel combination also has roughly 1% error.

§5. The Chain Rule, Written as Differentials
Suppose z = f(x,y), x = x(t), y = y(t). Then:
dz = f_x,dx + f_y,dy = f_x \frac{dx}{dt},dt + f_y \frac{dy}{dt},dt = \left(f_x\frac{dx}{dt} + f_y\frac{dy}{dt}\right)dt
So \frac{dz}{dt} = f_x\frac{dx}{dt} + f_y\frac{dy}{dt}. The chain rule is just division of the differential by dt.
This is why the notation dy/dx is more than notation — it genuinely behaves like a fraction when differentials are manipulated carefully.
Implicit Differentiation via Differentials
Given F(x,y) = 0, take the differential of both sides:
dF = F_x,dx + F_y,dy = 0 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{F_x}{F_y}
No quotient rule gymnastics. Just differentiate F, set dF = 0, solve for dy/dx.
Example. x^3 + y^3 = 6xy. Find dy/dx.
d(x^3 + y^3) = d(6xy) 3x^2,dx + 3y^2,dy = 6y,dx + 6x,dy (3y^2 - 6x),dy = (6y - 3x^2),dx \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{6y - 3x^2}{3y^2 - 6x} = \frac{2y - x^2}{y^2 - 2x}
One line of algebra, no chain rule bookkeeping.

§6. Differentials as Linear Maps — The Rigorous View
Here is the fully honest definition. Fix a point \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n.
Definition. If f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} is differentiable at \mathbf{a}, the differential of f at \mathbf{a} is the unique linear map df_\mathbf{a}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} such that:
\lim_{\mathbf{h} \to \mathbf{0}} \frac{f(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) - f(\mathbf{a}) - df_\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{h})}{|\mathbf{h}|} = 0
In coordinates: df_\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{h}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h} = \sum_i \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a}), h_i.
What is dx_i? The differential of the coordinate function x_i: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, (x_1, \ldots, x_n) \mapsto x_i. Evaluated on a vector \mathbf{h}: dx_i(\mathbf{h}) = h_i. So dx_i simply extracts the i-th component.
Then:
df = \sum_i \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i},dx_i
is an equation between linear maps: both sides, when applied to \mathbf{h}, give \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{h}.
For vector-valued f: the Jacobian. If \mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m, then d\mathbf{f}_\mathbf{a} is the linear map represented by the Jacobian matrix:
J = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_n} \ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ \frac{\partial f_m}{\partial x_1} & \cdots & \frac{\partial f_m}{\partial x_n} \end{pmatrix}
The differential is d\mathbf{f}_\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{h}) = J\mathbf{h}. This is the most general form.

§7. Second Differentials and Quadratic Approximation
The second differential of f at \mathbf{a} is:
d^2f = \sum_{i,j} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j},dx_i,dx_j
This is a quadratic form in dx_i. It encodes the curvature of f, and the associated matrix is the Hessian H_{ij} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}.
The second-order Taylor expansion:
f(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + df_\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{h}) + \frac{1}{2}d^2f_\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{h}) + O(|\mathbf{h}|^3)
= f(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{h} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^\top H, \mathbf{h} + \cdots
The differential df approximates f linearly; d^2f adds the curvature correction.

§8. Differential Forms (The Bigger Picture)
A differential k-form on \mathbb{R}^n is an antisymmetric multilinear map on k tangent vectors. The differentials dx, dy, dz are 1-forms. The exterior product dx \wedge dy is a 2-form that measures signed area.
The objects you integrate are differential forms:

\int_C f,dx + g,dy — line integral of a 1-form
\iint_S f,dA = \iint f,dx\wedge dy — surface integral of a 2-form

Stokes’ theorem (the grand unification) becomes:
\int_{\partial M} \omega = \int_M d\omega
where d is the exterior derivative — the coordinate-free generalization of df. Every theorem of vector calculus (Green’s, Divergence, classical Stokes’) is a special case.
The total differential df = f_x,dx + f_y,dy is a 1-form. It is exact (equals dg for some g) if and only if \frac{\partial f_x}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial f_y}{\partial x} — the condition for a conservative vector field. This is why the cross-partial condition appears everywhere.

§9. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Differential Computation
Let f(x,y,z) = x^2 e^{yz}. Compute df.
df = 2x e^{yz},dx + x^2 z e^{yz},dy + x^2 y e^{yz},dz
Example 2 — Approximation
Approximate \sqrt{(3.98)^2 + (3.02)^2 + (5.99)^2} using differentials.
Base point: (4, 3, 6). f(4,3,6) = \sqrt{16+9+36} = \sqrt{61}.
df = \frac{x,dx + y,dy + z,dz}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}}
With dx = -0.02, dy = 0.02, dz = -0.01:
df = \frac{4(-0.02) + 3(0.02) + 6(-0.01)}{\sqrt{61}} = \frac{-0.08 + 0.06 - 0.06}{\sqrt{61}} = \frac{-0.08}{\sqrt{61}}
f \approx \sqrt{61} - \frac{0.08}{\sqrt{61}} = \frac{61 - 0.08}{\sqrt{61}} = \frac{60.92}{\sqrt{61}} \approx 7.803
Example 3 — Implicit Surface
Find the tangent plane to x^2 + 2y^2 + 3z^2 = 6 at (1, 1, 1).
Let F = x^2 + 2y^2 + 3z^2 - 6. Then dF = 2x,dx + 4y,dy + 6z,dz.
At (1,1,1): \nabla F = \langle 2, 4, 6 \rangle. Tangent plane:
2(x-1) + 4(y-1) + 6(z-1) = 0 \implies x + 2y + 3z = 6
Example 4 — Change of Variables
Polar coordinates: x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta.
dx = \cos\theta,dr - r\sin\theta,d\theta dy = \sin\theta,dr + r\cos\theta,d\theta
The area element: dA = dx \wedge dy = (\cos\theta,dr - r\sin\theta,d\theta) \wedge (\sin\theta,dr + r\cos\theta,d\theta)
= \cos\theta \cdot r\cos\theta,(dr \wedge d\theta) + (-r\sin\theta)\cdot\sin\theta,(d\theta \wedge dr)
= r\cos^2\theta,(dr\wedge d\theta) + r\sin^2\theta,(dr \wedge d\theta) = r,dr\wedge d\theta
So dA = r,dr,d\theta — the Jacobian factor r emerges automatically from the differential calculus of forms. No determinant computation needed.

§10. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
10.1 — Differentials Are What Backpropagation Computes
Let \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) be the loss of a neural network. The total differential is:
d\mathcal{L} = \sum_i \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta_i},d\theta_i = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L} \cdot d\boldsymbol{\theta}
Backpropagation computes \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L} — i.e., it computes the coefficients of the total differential of the loss with respect to every parameter. The gradient is not a mysterious vector; it is the linear map d\mathcal{L}, written in coordinates.
10.2 — The Jacobian and Vector Differentials
A neural network layer \mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m computes \mathbf{y} = \sigma(W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}). Its differential at \mathbf{x}:
d\mathbf{y} = \text{diag}(\sigma'(W\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b})) \cdot W,d\mathbf{x}
This is the Jacobian acting on d\mathbf{x}. The forward pass evaluates \mathbf{y}; the backward pass evaluates the transpose Jacobian acting on upstream gradients (via the adjoint of the differential):
d\mathbf{x} \leftarrow W^\top \text{diag}(\sigma') \cdot d\mathbf{y}
The entire backpropagation algorithm is: compose differentials through the network, then adjoint them back.
10.3 — Automatic Differentiation (Autograd)
Modern frameworks (PyTorch, JAX) implement automatic differentiation, which is a computational implementation of the chain rule on differentials. Two modes:
Forward mode AD: propagates d\mathbf{x} forward through the computation graph, computing d\mathbf{y} at each node. Efficient when n \ll m (few inputs, many outputs).
Reverse mode AD (backprop): propagates d\mathcal{L} backward through the graph via adjoint differentials. Efficient when m \ll n (scalar loss, many parameters). This is why backprop is used in neural nets — m = 1 (scalar loss).
Every operation in the computation graph stores both its value and its differential rule. Backprop is just the chain rule d(f \circ g) = df \circ dg, applied in reverse.
10.4 — Gradient Descent as Differential Integration
Given d\mathcal{L} = \nabla \mathcal{L} \cdot d\boldsymbol{\theta}, gradient descent takes:
\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} - \eta,\nabla\mathcal{L}
This is a discretization of the differential equation \frac{d\boldsymbol{\theta}}{dt} = -\nabla\mathcal{L}, i.e., gradient flow. The continuous version is:
d\boldsymbol{\theta} = -\nabla\mathcal{L},dt
In the continuous limit, \mathcal{L} decreases at rate |\nabla\mathcal{L}|^2 per unit time. Adam, RMSProp, and other optimizers scale the differential by the inverse of historical gradient magnitudes — they are adaptive scalings of d\boldsymbol{\theta}.
10.5 — Second-Order Methods: the Hessian and d^2\mathcal{L}
The Newton step minimizes the second-order approximation:
\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta} + d\boldsymbol{\theta}) \approx \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \nabla\mathcal{L}^\top d\boldsymbol{\theta} + \frac{1}{2}d\boldsymbol{\theta}^\top H,d\boldsymbol{\theta}
Setting d(d\mathcal{L})/d(d\boldsymbol{\theta}) = 0 gives d\boldsymbol{\theta} = -H^{-1}\nabla\mathcal{L}. Computing H^{-1} costs O(n^3) — intractable for large networks. Quasi-Newton methods (L-BFGS) approximate H^{-1} from successive gradient differentials \Delta\nabla\mathcal{L} and parameter differentials \Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}, using the secant equation:
H,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta} \approx \Delta\nabla\mathcal{L}
This is a finite-difference approximation to the second differential d^2\mathcal{L}.
10.6 — Differentials in GANs and Score Matching
In generative models, score matching learns the score function \nabla_\mathbf{x} \log p(\mathbf{x}) — the differential of the log-density. Diffusion models (DDPM, Score SDE) define dynamics via stochastic differential equations:
d\mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_t, t),dt + g(t),d\mathbf{W}_t
Here d\mathbf{x}_t, dt, and d\mathbf{W}_t (Wiener differential, i.e., Brownian increment) are stochastic differentials — the Itô calculus extension of the framework we’ve been building. The score \nabla_\mathbf{x} \log p_t(\mathbf{x}) is a differential that the network learns to approximate at each noise level t. Reversing the SDE for generation requires the score — i.e., the differential of the log-density.

§11. Summary — The Differential at a Glance
\underbrace{dz}_{\text{linear approx}} = \underbrace{f_x,dx + f_y,dy}_{\text{gradient dotted with increment}}








































SituationWhat df isComputed asf: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}A 1-form on \mathbb{R}f'(x),dxf: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}A covector / 1-form\nabla f \cdot d\mathbf{x}\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^mA linear map \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^mJacobian J,d\mathbf{x}Neural network \mathcal{L}Gradient vectorComputed by backpropImplicit curve F = 0Constraint on dx, dydF = 0Coordinate changeJacobian of transformationdx\wedge dy = r,dr\wedge d\theta

§12. Theorems to Know Cold
Theorem 1 (Differentiability and the Differential). f is differentiable at \mathbf{a} iff there exists a linear map L such that f(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{h}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + L(\mathbf{h}) + o(|\mathbf{h}|). In that case, L = df_\mathbf{a}.
Theorem 2 (Chain Rule for Differentials). If \mathbf{g} is differentiable at \mathbf{a} and f is differentiable at \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{a}), then d(f \circ \mathbf{g})_\mathbf{a} = df_{\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{a})} \circ d\mathbf{g}_\mathbf{a}.
In matrix form: J_{f \circ g} = J_f \cdot J_g.
Theorem 3 (Exactness Condition). A 1-form P,dx + Q,dy is exact (equals df for some f) iff \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} on a simply connected domain.
Theorem 4 (Error Bound). If |f_{x_i}| \leq M_i on a region, then: |\Delta f - df| \leq \frac{1}{2}\max|f_{x_i x_j}| \cdot (|\Delta\mathbf{x}|)^2
Theorem 5 (Fundamental Theorem via Differentials). \int_{\mathbf{a}}^{\mathbf{b}} df = f(\mathbf{b}) - f(\mathbf{a}) for any path — the line integral of an exact form is path-independent.

§13. Common Errors

dx is not infinitesimally small. In the definition, dx is a free real variable. It only needs to be “small” when you use df as an approximation to \Delta f.


df \neq \Delta f. They differ by O((dx)^2). Writing df = \Delta f is an approximation, not an equality.


Partial derivatives are not the same as differentials. \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} is a number; df is a linear functional. The partial derivative is the coefficient of dx in df, not the same object.


Not every expression P,dx + Q,dy is a differential of some function. Exactness is not free — it requires P_y = Q_x.


In implicit differentiation, dF = 0 only holds because F is held constant on the curve/surface. Make this explicit in your reasoning.


References

James Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. — §3.10 (Linear Approximations), §14.4 (Tangent Planes and Differentials), §14.5 (Chain Rule).
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Notes on Total Differentials; Denis Auroux, Lectures 11–13 on differentials, chain rule, implicit differentiation.
Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds — Chapter 4 for differential forms and the exterior derivative.
Baydin et al. (2018), “Automatic Differentiation in Machine Learning: a Survey” — for the AD/backprop connection.
Song & Ermon (2020), “Score-Based Generative Modeling” — for stochastic differentials in diffusion models.

01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.title: 12.Chain Rule
01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.content:
“The chain rule is not a formula. It is a theorem about the composition of linear approximations. Everything else — backpropagation, automatic differentiation, implicit differentiation — is a corollary.”


§1. Motivation — Composition and Rate of Change
In single-variable calculus, if y = f(u) and u = g(x), then:
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}
This is almost too clean. The fractions “cancel.” But in multiple variables, the story is richer: a function can depend on many intermediate variables, each of which depends on many others. The chain rule tells us how to trace the influence of a change at the source through every path it takes to the output.
The multivariable chain rule is not one formula — it is a family of formulas, all instances of one underlying theorem: the derivative of a composition is the composition of the derivatives.

§2. The One-Variable Chain Rule — The Right Way to Think About It
Let f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} and g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, both differentiable. Define h = f \circ g, i.e., h(x) = f(g(x)).
Theorem (Chain Rule, 1D). h'(x) = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x).
Proof sketch. By differentiability of g at x: g(x+\Delta x) = g(x) + g'(x)\Delta x + \varepsilon_1 \Delta x, \quad \varepsilon_1 \to 0
By differentiability of f at u = g(x): f(u + \Delta u) = f(u) + f'(u)\Delta u + \varepsilon_2 \Delta u, \quad \varepsilon_2 \to 0
Setting \Delta u = g(x+\Delta x) - g(x) = g'(x)\Delta x + \varepsilon_1 \Delta x:
h(x+\Delta x) - h(x) = f'(g(x))\bigl[g'(x)\Delta x + \varepsilon_1\Delta x\bigr] + \varepsilon_2\bigl[g'(x)\Delta x + \varepsilon_1\Delta x\bigr]
Divide by \Delta x and let \Delta x \to 0. The error terms vanish: h'(x) = f'(g(x))g'(x). \blacksquare
The key insight. The chain rule says: the linear approximation of a composition is the composition of the linear approximations. Derivatives linearize; linear maps compose by multiplication. That is all.

§3. The Multivariable Chain Rule — General Statement
Let \mathbf{g}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m be differentiable at \mathbf{a}, and f: \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R} be differentiable at \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{a}). Define h = f \circ \mathbf{g}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}.
Theorem (Chain Rule, General). h is differentiable at \mathbf{a}, and:
dh_\mathbf{a} = df_{\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{a})} \circ d\mathbf{g}_\mathbf{a}
In matrix/coordinate form, if \mathbf{g} = (g_1, \ldots, g_m) and \mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n):
\frac{\partial h}{\partial x_j} = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{\partial f}{\partial u_i} \cdot \frac{\partial g_i}{\partial x_j}
or equivalently: J_h = J_f \cdot J_\mathbf{g} (Jacobian of composition = product of Jacobians).
In differential notation (the most elegant form):
dh = df = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{\partial f}{\partial u_i},du_i, \quad du_i = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\partial g_i}{\partial x_j},dx_j
Substitute du_i into dh: you get the chain rule automatically, by pure algebraic substitution.

§4. Case I — One Independent Variable
z = f(x, y), x = x(t), y = y(t). Then z is a function of t alone:
\frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}
Think of it as: every path from t to z must pass through either x or y. Sum the contributions along each path:
        t
       / \
      x   y
       \ /
        z

Each edge contributes a derivative; each path contributes a product; sum over all paths.
Example. z = x^2 + \sin(xy), x = e^t, y = t^2. Find \frac{dz}{dt}.
\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 2x + y\cos(xy), \quad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = x\cos(xy) \frac{dx}{dt} = e^t, \quad \frac{dy}{dt} = 2t
\frac{dz}{dt} = (2x + y\cos(xy))e^t + x\cos(xy) \cdot 2t
Substituting x = e^t, y = t^2 gives the explicit form if needed.

§5. Case II — Two Independent Variables
z = f(x, y), x = x(s, t), y = y(s, t). Now z is a function of s and t:
\frac{\partial z}{\partial s} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s}
\frac{\partial z}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial t}
Dependency diagram:
      s   t         s   t
       \ /           \ /
        x             y
         \           /
          \         /
               z

For \partial z/\partial s: trace all paths from s to z. Path s \to x \to z contributes \frac{\partial x}{\partial s} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}. Path s \to y \to z contributes \frac{\partial y}{\partial s} \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}. Sum them.
Example. z = e^{xy}, x = s^2 - t^2, y = s + 2t.
\frac{\partial z}{\partial s} = ye^{xy}(2s) + xe^{xy}(1) = (2sy + x)e^{xy} \frac{\partial z}{\partial t} = ye^{xy}(-2t) + xe^{xy}(2) = (-2ty + 2x)e^{xy}

§6. The Tree Diagram Rule — A Systematic Algorithm
For any composition, the chain rule is computed by the following algorithm:

Draw the dependency diagram. Each variable is a node. An arrow from u to v means ”v depends on u.”
For each path from an independent variable to the target, form the product of derivatives along that path.
Sum over all such paths.

This is not a heuristic — it is a direct consequence of the general formula \frac{\partial z}{\partial x_j} = \sum_i \frac{\partial z}{\partial u_i}\frac{\partial u_i}{\partial x_j}.
Example — Three layers. w = f(x, y, z), each of x, y, z depending on s and t:
\frac{\partial w}{\partial s} = \frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial y}\frac{\partial y}{\partial s} + \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial s}
Three paths from s to w; each contributes one term.

§7. Implicit Differentiation — The Chain Rule in Disguise
Suppose F(x, y) = 0 defines y implicitly as a function of x. Differentiate both sides with respect to x, treating y = y(x):
\frac{d}{dx}F(x, y(x)) = 0
Chain rule on the left:
F_x \cdot 1 + F_y \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = 0 \implies \boxed{\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{F_x}{F_y}}
For F(x, y, z) = 0 defining z = z(x,y):
\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\frac{F_x}{F_z}, \qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -\frac{F_y}{F_z}
Proof. Differentiate F(x, y, z(x,y)) = 0 with respect to x, holding y fixed:
F_x \cdot 1 + F_y \cdot 0 + F_z \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 0
Solve for \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}. The formula follows immediately. \blacksquare
Example. x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz = 1. Find \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}.
F = x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz. Then F_x = 3x^2 - 3yz, F_z = 3z^2 - 3xy.
\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\frac{3x^2 - 3yz}{3z^2 - 3xy} = \frac{yz - x^2}{z^2 - xy}

§8. The Chain Rule in Differential Notation
In differentials, the chain rule requires no separate statement — it is automatic substitution.
z = f(u, v), u = u(x, y), v = v(x,y):
dz = f_u,du + f_v,dv
Now substitute du = u_x,dx + u_y,dy and dv = v_x,dx + v_y,dy:
dz = f_u(u_x,dx + u_y,dy) + f_v(v_x,dx + v_y,dy) = (f_u u_x + f_v v_x),dx + (f_u u_y + f_v v_y),dy
Read off \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} and \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} as coefficients. The chain rule is invisible — it’s already encoded in the substitution.

§9. The Jacobian Formulation
For \mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m and \mathbf{g}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^n, the Jacobian of \mathbf{f} \circ \mathbf{g} is:
J_{\mathbf{f} \circ \mathbf{g}}(\mathbf{x}) = J_\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})) \cdot J_\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})
where J_\mathbf{f} is m \times n and J_\mathbf{g} is n \times p, so the product is m \times p. The chain rule is matrix multiplication of Jacobians.
Coordinate form:
(J_{\mathbf{f}\circ\mathbf{g}})_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^n (J_\mathbf{f})_{ik}(J_\mathbf{g})_{kj} = \sum_k \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial u_k}\frac{\partial g_k}{\partial x_j}
This is the master formula from which every special case follows.

§10. Special Cases Worth Knowing
10.1 — Gradient of a Composition
h(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})), f: \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}, \mathbf{g}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m:
\nabla h(\mathbf{x}) = J_\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})^\top \nabla f(\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}))
The gradient transforms by the transpose Jacobian. This is the adjoint, and it is exactly why backpropagation uses transposed weight matrices.
10.2 — Directional Derivative via Chain Rule
The directional derivative of f at \mathbf{a} in direction \hat{\mathbf{u}} is obtained by setting \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t\hat{\mathbf{u}} and differentiating at t = 0:
D_{\hat{u}} f = \frac{d}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0} f(\mathbf{a} + t\hat{\mathbf{u}}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}
The chain rule converts a directional derivative into a dot product with the gradient.
10.3 — Tangent Vector to a Curve on a Surface
If \mathbf{r}(t) is a curve on a level surface f(\mathbf{x}) = c, then f(\mathbf{r}(t)) = c for all t. Differentiate:
\nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) = 0
The gradient is perpendicular to every tangent vector on the surface — a purely chain-rule proof.
10.4 — Change of Variables in PDEs
Suppose u = u(x,t) satisfies a PDE, and we change variables: \xi = x - ct, \tau = t. Then:
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial \xi}\frac{\partial \xi}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau}\frac{\partial \tau}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial \xi} \cdot 1 + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau} \cdot 0 = \frac{\partial u}{\partial \xi}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial \xi}\frac{\partial \xi}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau}\frac{\partial \tau}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial u}{\partial \xi}(-c) + \frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau}
So \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + c\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0 becomes \frac{\partial u}{\partial \tau} = 0: the transport equation transforms to a trivial PDE. The chain rule is the engine of every change-of-variables in PDEs.

§11. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Polar Laplacian
Express \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} in polar coordinates x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta.
Step 1. Compute \frac{\partial f}{\partial r} and \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} by chain rule:
\frac{\partial f}{\partial r} = f_x \cos\theta + f_y \sin\theta \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} = -f_x r\sin\theta + f_y r\cos\theta
Step 2. Invert (solve for f_x, f_y):
f_x = \cos\theta,\frac{\partial f}{\partial r} - \frac{\sin\theta}{r}\frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} f_y = \sin\theta,\frac{\partial f}{\partial r} + \frac{\cos\theta}{r}\frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}
Step 3. Differentiate again (apply the operators \frac{\partial}{\partial x} and \frac{\partial}{\partial y} using the chain rule on the result). After careful computation:
\nabla^2 f = f_{xx} + f_{yy} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial r^2} + \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial f}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial\theta^2}
The Laplacian in polar coordinates, derived entirely by chain rule.
Example 2 — Sensitivity Analysis
Revenue R = p \cdot q(p, a) where p is price and a is advertising spend. Find \frac{dR}{dp} when p and a are both functions of a budget constraint parameter \lambda.
\frac{dR}{d\lambda} = \frac{\partial R}{\partial p}\frac{dp}{d\lambda} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial a}\frac{da}{d\lambda}
\frac{\partial R}{\partial p} = q + p\frac{\partial q}{\partial p}, \quad \frac{\partial R}{\partial a} = p\frac{\partial q}{\partial a}
The chain rule decomposes the total effect into direct and indirect channels — a standard tool in economics.
Example 3 — Second Derivative via Chain Rule
Let z = f(u), u = x^2 + y^2. Compute \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x^2}.
First derivative:
\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = f'(u) \cdot 2x
Second derivative (product rule + chain rule):
\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}[f'(u) \cdot 2x] = f''(u)\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} \cdot 2x + f'(u) \cdot 2 = f''(u)(2x)^2 + 2f'(u) = 4x^2 f''(u) + 2f'(u)
Similarly \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial y^2} = 4y^2 f''(u) + 2f'(u). So:
\nabla^2 z = 4(x^2 + y^2)f''(u) + 4f'(u) = 4u,f''(u) + 4f'(u)

§12. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
The chain rule is not merely related to machine learning. It is machine learning. The entire discipline of differentiable programming rests on one fact: you can differentiate a composition by multiplying Jacobians.
12.1 — Backpropagation Is the Chain Rule
A neural network is a composition:
\mathcal{L} = \ell \circ f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1
where f_k(\mathbf{x}) = \sigma_k(W_k \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_k) is the k-th layer. Define intermediate activations:
\mathbf{a}_0 = \mathbf{x}, \quad \mathbf{a}_k = f_k(\mathbf{a}_{k-1}), \quad \mathcal{L} = \ell(\mathbf{a}_L)
By the Jacobian chain rule:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{a}_k} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{a}_{k+1}} \cdot J_{f_{k+1}}(\mathbf{a}_k)
Backpropagation is this recursion, run from k = L down to k = 0. The “error signal” \boldsymbol{\delta}_k = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{a}_k} propagates backward through transposed Jacobians.
For a single layer \mathbf{z}_k = W_k \mathbf{a}_{k-1} + \mathbf{b}_k, \mathbf{a}_k = \sigma(\mathbf{z}_k):
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_k} = \boldsymbol{\delta}_k \cdot \mathbf{a}_{k-1}^\top, \quad \boldsymbol{\delta}_{k-1} = W_k^\top \boldsymbol{\delta}_k \odot \sigma'(\mathbf{z}_{k-1})
The transpose W_k^\top is the adjoint of the Jacobian J = W_k (since the layer is linear in \mathbf{a}_{k-1}). This is §10.1 above, instantiated for neural networks.
12.2 — Forward Mode vs Reverse Mode
The chain rule can be evaluated in two directions:
Forward mode (tangent computation). Start with d\mathbf{a}_0 = d\mathbf{x} and propagate forward:
d\mathbf{a}_k = J_{f_k}(\mathbf{a}_{k-1}) \cdot d\mathbf{a}_{k-1}
Cost per forward pass: O(n) Jacobian-vector products (one per input). Efficient when n \ll m (few inputs).
Reverse mode (cotangent computation, backprop). Start with \bar{\mathcal{L}} = 1 and propagate backward:
\bar{\mathbf{a}}_{k-1} = J_{f_k}(\mathbf{a}_{k-1})^\top \cdot \bar{\mathbf{a}}_k
Cost: O(m) vector-Jacobian products (one per output). Efficient when m \ll n. For neural networks: m = 1 (scalar loss), n =  billions of parameters. Reverse mode wins decisively.
This is why backpropagation is efficient: it is reverse-mode automatic differentiation, which is the chain rule evaluated right-to-left on the computation graph.
12.3 — Computation Graphs and the Chain Rule
Every computation in a neural network can be represented as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where:

Nodes are intermediate values
Edges encode dependencies
Each edge carries a local Jacobian

The chain rule says: the gradient at any node is the sum over all paths from that node to the output, of the product of edge Jacobians along each path.
Input x → [Layer 1] → a₁ → [Layer 2] → a₂ → ... → [Loss] → ℒ
              ↑                  ↑
           ∂a₁/∂x           ∂a₂/∂a₁

Backprop traverses this graph in reverse topological order, accumulating products. This is exactly the tree diagram rule from §6, instantiated for computation graphs.
12.4 — Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
For a deep network with L layers and activation \sigma, the gradient at layer k involves the product:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{a}_k} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{a}_L} \cdot \prod_{j=k}^{L-1} J_{f_{j+1}}
Each factor J_{f_j} = W_j^\top \text{diag}(\sigma'(\mathbf{z}_j)) has spectral radius (largest singular value) roughly |W_j| \cdot \max|\sigma'|.

If |J_j| < 1 for most j: the product \to 0 exponentially fast. Vanishing gradients. Early layers learn nothing.
If |J_j| > 1 for most j: the product \to \infty exponentially fast. Exploding gradients. Training diverges.

Both pathologies are pure consequences of the chain rule applied to a long product of matrices. Solutions: careful initialization (Xavier/He), batch normalization (controls |J_j|), residual connections (add identity to the Jacobian), gradient clipping.
ReLU activations have \sigma'(x) \in {0, 1}, which helps with vanishing gradients compared to sigmoid (\sigma' \leq 0.25). This is a chain rule argument.
12.5 — Recurrent Neural Networks and BPTT
In an RNN, the hidden state evolves as \mathbf{h}_t = f(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_t; W). The gradient of loss at time T with respect to parameters at time k involves:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_T}{\partial W}\bigg|_{\text{step } k} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_T}{\partial \mathbf{h}_T}\left(\prod_{j=k}^{T-1} \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_{j+1}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_j}\right)\frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_k}{\partial W}
The product of T - k Jacobians \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_{j+1}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_j} is the chain rule unrolled through time — called Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT). The vanishing/exploding gradient problem is especially severe here because T can be hundreds of steps. LSTMs and GRUs introduce gating mechanisms that approximately maintain \left|\prod \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_{j+1}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_j}\right| \approx 1.
12.6 — Residual Networks (ResNets) — The Chain Rule Fix
A residual block computes \mathbf{a}_{k+1} = \mathbf{a}_k + F(\mathbf{a}_k). Its Jacobian:
\frac{\partial \mathbf{a}_{k+1}}{\partial \mathbf{a}_k} = I + J_F(\mathbf{a}_k)
The identity I ensures that the product of Jacobians through L residual blocks always contains the identity term:
\prod_{k=1}^L \left(I + J_{F_k}\right)
This expands (like a polynomial) into a sum of 2^L terms, most of which contain fewer than L Jacobian factors. Some paths are short — gradients can flow through them without vanishing. This is the chain rule explanation of why ResNets can be trained to depth 1000+.

§13. Summary Table









































SettingChain Rule Formulay = f(g(x))\frac{dy}{dx} = f'(g),g'z = f(x(t), y(t))\frac{dz}{dt} = f_x x' + f_y y'z = f(x(s,t), y(s,t))\frac{\partial z}{\partial s} = f_x x_s + f_y y_sF(x,y) = 0 implicit\frac{dy}{dx} = -F_x / F_y\mathbf{f} \circ \mathbf{g}, generalJ_{f \circ g} = J_f \cdot J_gGradient of composition\nabla(f \circ \mathbf{g}) = J_\mathbf{g}^\top \nabla fNeural network layer\boldsymbol{\delta}_{k-1} = W_k^\top (\boldsymbol{\delta}_k \odot \sigma')BPTT (RNN)\prod_{j=k}^{T-1} \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_{j+1}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_j}

§14. Theorems to Know Cold
Theorem 1 (Chain Rule). If \mathbf{g} is differentiable at \mathbf{a} and f is differentiable at \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{a}), then f \circ \mathbf{g} is differentiable at \mathbf{a} and d(f \circ \mathbf{g})_\mathbf{a} = df_{\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{a})} \circ d\mathbf{g}_\mathbf{a}.
Theorem 2 (Implicit Function Theorem). If F(\mathbf{x}, y) is C^1 near (\mathbf{a}, b) with F(\mathbf{a}, b) = 0 and F_y(\mathbf{a}, b) \neq 0, then there exists a C^1 function y = g(\mathbf{x}) near \mathbf{a} with F(\mathbf{x}, g(\mathbf{x})) = 0, and \frac{\partial g}{\partial x_i} = -\frac{F_{x_i}}{F_y}.
Theorem 3 (Gradient Orthogonality). If \mathbf{r}(t) lies on the level set f = c, then \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \perp \mathbf{r}'(t) for all t.
Theorem 4 (Jacobian of Inverse). If \mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n is invertible and differentiable, then J_{\mathbf{f}^{-1}}(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})) = [J_\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})]^{-1}.

§15. Things That Will Trip You Up

\partial z/\partial x means different things depending on context. If z = f(x,y) and y depends on x, you must decide: are you holding y fixed (partial), or letting it vary (total derivative)? Sloppy notation kills you here.


The chain rule requires differentiability, not just existence of partial derivatives. If \mathbf{g} is merely continuous, the composition may not be differentiable.


Implicit differentiation is not magic. It is the chain rule + implicit function theorem. Always verify F_y \neq 0 before writing dy/dx = -F_x/F_y.


Second derivatives require the chain rule twice, and produce extra terms. \frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x^2} \neq \left(f''(u)\right)(u_x)^2 alone — you must also include f'(u) u_{xx}.


In backprop, the gradient of the loss with respect to a parameter W_k is not \boldsymbol{\delta}_k alone — it requires the outer product \boldsymbol{\delta}_k \mathbf{a}_{k-1}^\top. Confusing the upstream gradient with the parameter gradient is a common error in manual backprop derivations.


References

James Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. — §14.5 (The Chain Rule), §14.3, §14.4.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Denis Auroux, Lectures 11–14; Notes on chain rule, tree diagrams, implicit differentiation.
Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Chapter 9 — for the rigorous Jacobian chain rule theorem.
Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville, Deep Learning (MIT Press, 2016) — Chapter 6 for backpropagation as chain rule.
Baydin et al. (2018), “Automatic Differentiation in Machine Learning: a Survey”, JMLR.
He et al. (2016), “Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition” — the ResNet paper; chain rule motivation for skip connections.

01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.title: 13.Implicit Differentiation
01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.content:
“Explicit functions are a convenience. Most relationships in nature are implicit — a constraint that variables must satisfy. Implicit differentiation is how we extract rates of change from constraints, without ever solving for one variable in terms of the others.”


§1. Motivation — When You Cannot Solve Explicitly
Consider the curve x^3 + y^3 = 6xy (the folium of Descartes). Can you solve for y in terms of x? Technically yes — via the cubic formula — but the result is a nightmare. Yet we can ask: what is the slope of this curve at the point (3, 3)?
Or consider e^{xy} + \sin(x + y) = 2. Solving for y is impossible in closed form. But the curve exists, it has slopes at each point, and we can compute them.
Implicit differentiation extracts \frac{dy}{dx} (or \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}) directly from the defining equation F(x, y) = 0, without isolating the dependent variable. The theoretical guarantee that such a function even exists is the Implicit Function Theorem.

§2. The Core Idea — Differentiate the Constraint
Suppose y is implicitly defined as a function of x by F(x, y) = 0. This means there exists (locally) a function y = g(x) such that:
F(x,, g(x)) = 0 \quad \text{for all } x \text{ near } a
Differentiate both sides with respect to x. Left side: chain rule. Right side: zero.
\frac{d}{dx}F(x, g(x)) = F_x(x, y) \cdot 1 + F_y(x, y) \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = 0
Solve:
\boxed{\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{F_x}{F_y}}
That is the whole algorithm. The rest of this note is making it rigorous, generalizing it, and understanding when it works.

§3. The Implicit Function Theorem — The Guarantee
Before computing derivatives, we must ask: does F(x, y) = 0 actually define y as a function of x near a given point?
Theorem (Implicit Function Theorem, 2D). Let F: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R} be C^1 in a neighborhood of (a, b), with F(a, b) = 0. If:
F_y(a, b) \neq 0
then there exists an open interval I containing a and a unique C^1 function y = g(x) on I such that:

g(a) = b
F(x, g(x)) = 0 for all x \in I
g'(x) = -\dfrac{F_x(x, g(x))}{F_y(x, g(x))}

What the theorem says geometrically. Near (a, b), the level curve F = 0 looks like the graph of a function. The condition F_y \neq 0 ensures the curve is not “vertical” there — it has a well-defined slope.
What happens when F_y = 0? The theorem fails. The curve may have a vertical tangent, a self-intersection, a cusp, or a fold. These are exactly the singular points where implicit differentiation breaks down.
Example. F(x, y) = x^2 + y^2 - 1 (unit circle). F_y = 2y. The theorem fails at y = 0, i.e., at (1, 0) and (-1, 0) — exactly where the circle has vertical tangents.

§4. Algorithm — One Equation, Two Variables
Given F(x, y) = 0, to find \frac{dy}{dx}:
Method 1 — Direct chain rule: Differentiate F(x, y) = 0 with respect to x, treating y as a function of x. Apply the chain rule to every term involving y. Collect \frac{dy}{dx} terms on one side and solve.
Method 2 — Differential: Take dF = 0, i.e., F_x,dx + F_y,dy = 0. Divide by dx: \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{F_x}{F_y}.
Both methods are equivalent. Method 2 is faster for complex expressions.
Example 1 — Folium of Descartes
x^3 + y^3 = 6xy. Find \frac{dy}{dx}.
Set F = x^3 + y^3 - 6xy. Then:
F_x = 3x^2 - 6y, \quad F_y = 3y^2 - 6x
\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{3x^2 - 6y}{3y^2 - 6x} = \frac{2y - x^2}{y^2 - 2x}
At (3, 3): \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{6 - 9}{9 - 6} = \frac{-3}{3} = -1. The tangent line at (3,3) is y - 3 = -(x - 3), i.e., x + y = 6.
Example 2 — Transcendental Equation
e^{xy} + \sin(x + y) = 2. Find \frac{dy}{dx} at (0, 0).
F = e^{xy} + \sin(x+y) - 2.
F_x = ye^{xy} + \cos(x+y), \quad F_y = xe^{xy} + \cos(x+y)
At (0, 0): F_x = 0 + \cos(0) = 1, F_y = 0 + \cos(0) = 1.
\frac{dy}{dx}\bigg|_{(0,0)} = -\frac{1}{1} = -1
Example 3 — Second Derivative
x^2 + y^2 = r^2 (circle). Find \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}.
First derivative: 2x + 2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y}.
Second derivative. Differentiate \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y} with respect to x:
\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = -\frac{y \cdot 1 - x \cdot \frac{dy}{dx}}{y^2} = -\frac{y - x\left(-\frac{x}{y}\right)}{y^2} = -\frac{y + \frac{x^2}{y}}{y^2} = -\frac{y^2 + x^2}{y^3} = -\frac{r^2}{y^3}
Note: substitute \frac{dy}{dx} before simplifying — always.

§5. Three Variables — Implicit Surface
Now F(x, y, z) = 0 defines a surface. Suppose z = z(x, y) implicitly.
Differentiate F(x, y, z(x,y)) = 0 with respect to x (holding y constant):
F_x + F_z \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 0 \implies \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\frac{F_x}{F_z}
Differentiate with respect to y:
F_y + F_z \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = 0 \implies \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -\frac{F_y}{F_z}
Condition for validity: F_z \neq 0 at the point (Implicit Function Theorem in 3D).
The gradient of z = g(x,y) is:
\nabla g = \left(-\frac{F_x}{F_z},, -\frac{F_y}{F_z}\right)
and the tangent plane to the surface F = 0 at (a, b, c) is:
F_x(a,b,c)(x-a) + F_y(a,b,c)(y-b) + F_z(a,b,c)(z-c) = 0
Example — Ellipsoid
\frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{y^2}{9} + z^2 = 1. Find \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} and \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}.
F = \frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{y^2}{9} + z^2 - 1.
F_x = \frac{x}{2}, \quad F_y = \frac{2y}{9}, \quad F_z = 2z
\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\frac{x/2}{2z} = -\frac{x}{4z}, \qquad \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -\frac{2y/9}{2z} = -\frac{y}{9z}
At (2, 0, 0): F_z = 0 — the theorem fails. Indeed, (2, 0, 0) is a point with a vertical tangent plane (z is not differentiable there).

§6. The General Case — n Variables, m Constraints
Let \mathbf{F}: \mathbb{R}^{n+m} \to \mathbb{R}^m be C^1 near (\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^m with \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{0}.
Write the variables as (\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^m. The Jacobian of \mathbf{F} with respect to \mathbf{y}:
J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F} = \left(\frac{\partial F_i}{\partial y_j}\right)_{i,j=1}^{m}
Theorem (Implicit Function Theorem, General). If \det(J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})) \neq 0, then there exists a unique C^1 function \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}) near \mathbf{a} with \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})) = \mathbf{0}. Moreover:
J_\mathbf{x}\mathbf{g} = -(J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F})^{-1} \cdot J_\mathbf{x}\mathbf{F}
This is the matrix version of \frac{dy}{dx} = -F_x/F_y.
Proof sketch. Differentiate \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x})) = \mathbf{0} with respect to \mathbf{x} via the chain rule:
J_\mathbf{x}\mathbf{F} + J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F} \cdot J_\mathbf{x}\mathbf{g} = 0
Since J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F} is invertible (by hypothesis), solve: J_\mathbf{x}\mathbf{g} = -(J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F})^{-1} J_\mathbf{x}\mathbf{F}. \blacksquare
The existence of \mathbf{g} (not just its derivative) requires a deeper argument — the contraction mapping theorem or inverse function theorem.

§7. Implicit Differentiation via Differentials — The Slickest Method
For any equation F(x, y) = c, take the total differential:
dF = F_x,dx + F_y,dy = 0
Then \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{F_x}{F_y} immediately, by treating dF = 0 as a linear constraint on dx and dy.
For F(x, y, z) = c:
F_x,dx + F_y,dy + F_z,dz = 0

Hold y fixed (dy = 0): \quad\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = -\frac{F_x}{F_z}
Hold x fixed (dx = 0): \quad\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -\frac{F_y}{F_z}

No chain rule bookkeeping. Just algebra on differentials.
The Cyclic Identity (a Beautiful Consequence)
From F(x, y, z) = 0, we have three implicit partial derivatives:
\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\bigg|_y = -\frac{F_x}{F_z}, \quad \frac{\partial x}{\partial y}\bigg|_z = -\frac{F_y}{F_x}, \quad \frac{\partial y}{\partial z}\bigg|_x = -\frac{F_z}{F_y}
Multiply all three:
\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\bigg|_y \cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial y}\bigg|_z \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial z}\bigg|_x = \left(-\frac{F_x}{F_z}\right)\left(-\frac{F_y}{F_x}\right)\left(-\frac{F_z}{F_y}\right) = -1
\boxed{\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\bigg|_y \cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial y}\bigg|_z \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial z}\bigg|_x = -1}
This is the cyclic identity (or triple product rule, or Euler’s chain rule). It is not the chain rule — it produces -1, not +1. It appears everywhere in thermodynamics: (∂P/∂V)_T (∂V/∂T)_P (∂T/∂P)_V = -1 is the same identity for an ideal gas.
Warning. This is not \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial y} \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial z} in the chain rule sense. The subscripts matter — each partial holds a different variable fixed.

§8. Second-Order Implicit Differentiation
Given F(x, y) = 0, compute \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}.
Step 1. Compute y' = -\frac{F_x}{F_y}.
Step 2. Differentiate y' = -\frac{F_x(x,y)}{F_y(x,y)} with respect to x, using the quotient rule and chain rule (treating y = y(x)):
y'' = -\frac{(F_{xx} + F_{xy}y')F_y - F_x(F_{yx} + F_{yy}y')}{F_y^2}
Substitute y' = -F_x/F_y and simplify:
y'' = -\frac{F_{xx}F_y^2 - 2F_{xy}F_xF_y + F_{yy}F_x^2}{F_y^3}
This is the standard formula. In practice, substitute y' explicitly rather than memorizing this — the derivation is more reliable.
Example — Implicitly Defined Curve
x^2 + xy + y^2 = 3. Find y'' at (1, 1).
Differential: 2x,dx + y,dx + x,dy + 2y,dy = 0 \Rightarrow (2x+y),dx + (x+2y),dy = 0 y' = -\frac{2x+y}{x+2y}
At (1,1): y' = -\frac{3}{3} = -1.
Second derivative. Differentiate y'(x+2y) = -(2x+y):
(x + 2y)y'' + (1 + 2y')y' = -(2 + y')
At (1,1), y' = -1: (3)y'' + (1 - 2)(-1) = -(2 - 1) 3y'' + 1 = -1 \implies y'' = -\frac{2}{3}

§9. Logarithmic Differentiation — Implicit Differentiation’s Cousin
For y = f(x)^{g(x)} or products/quotients of many factors, take the log of both sides first, then differentiate implicitly.
y = f(x)^{g(x)}. Take \ln y = g(x)\ln f(x).
Differentiate both sides with respect to x:
\frac{y'}{y} = g'(x)\ln f(x) + g(x)\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}
y' = y\left[g'\ln f + \frac{gf'}{f}\right] = f(x)^{g(x)}\left[g'(x)\ln f(x) + \frac{g(x)f'(x)}{f(x)}\right]
Example. y = x^{\sin x}.
\ln y = \sin x \cdot \ln x \frac{y'}{y} = \cos x \ln x + \frac{\sin x}{x} y' = x^{\sin x}\left(\cos x \ln x + \frac{\sin x}{x}\right)

§10. Worked Examples — Gallery
Example A — Tangent Line to an Implicit Curve
Find the tangent line to y^2 = x^3(2 - x) (lemniscate-type) at (1, 1).
F = y^2 - x^3(2-x) = y^2 - 2x^3 + x^4.
F_x = -6x^2 + 4x^3, \quad F_y = 2y
At (1, 1): F_x = -6 + 4 = -2, F_y = 2.
\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{-2}{2} = 1
Tangent line: y - 1 = 1(x - 1), i.e., y = x.
Example B — Horizontal and Vertical Tangents
x^2 - xy + y^2 = 3.
F_x = 2x - y, \quad F_y = -x + 2y, \quad y' = -\frac{2x-y}{-x+2y} = \frac{2x-y}{x-2y}
Horizontal tangents (y' = 0): 2x - y = 0 \Rightarrow y = 2x. Substitute into the curve: x^2 - x(2x) + (2x)^2 = 3 \Rightarrow 3x^2 = 3 \Rightarrow x = \pm 1 Points: (1, 2) and (-1, -2).
Vertical tangents (y' = \infty, i.e., F_y = 0): x - 2y = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2y. Substitute: (2y)^2 - (2y)y + y^2 = 3 \Rightarrow 3y^2 = 3 \Rightarrow y = \pm 1 Points: (2, 1) and (-2, -1).
Example C — Partial Derivatives from an Implicit Surface
The ideal gas law PV = nRT defines any variable as a function of the others. Take F(P, V, T) = PV - nRT = 0.
\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\bigg|_P = -\frac{F_T}{F_V} = -\frac{-nR}{P} = \frac{nR}{P}
\frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\bigg|_T = -\frac{F_V}{F_P} = -\frac{P}{V}
\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\bigg|_V = -\frac{F_P}{F_T} = -\frac{V}{-nR} = \frac{V}{nR}
Check the cyclic identity:
\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\bigg|_P \cdot \frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\bigg|_V \cdot \frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\bigg|_T = \frac{nR}{P} \cdot \frac{V}{nR} \cdot \left(-\frac{P}{V}\right) = -1 \checkmark

§11. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
11.1 — Implicit Layers in Deep Learning
The standard neural network layer is explicit: given input \mathbf{x}, compute output \mathbf{y} = f(\mathbf{x}; \theta) in one forward pass.
An implicit layer is defined by a constraint:
F(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}; \theta) = 0
The output \mathbf{y} is the solution to this equation. Examples:

Fixed-point layers: \mathbf{y} = f(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}) (Deep Equilibrium Models)
Optimization layers: \mathbf{y} = \arg\min_\mathbf{z} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x}; \theta), which satisfies \nabla_\mathbf{z} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}; \theta) = 0

To train these by gradient descent, we need \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \theta} and \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} — but \mathbf{y} has no explicit formula. Enter implicit differentiation.
The Implicit Function Theorem applied. Differentiate F(\mathbf{y}(\theta), \mathbf{x}, \theta) = 0 with respect to \theta:
\underbrace{\frac{\partial F}{\partial \mathbf{y}}}_{\text{square matrix}} \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \theta} + \frac{\partial F}{\partial \theta} = 0
\frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \theta} = -\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial \mathbf{y}}\right)^{-1} \frac{\partial F}{\partial \theta}
This is the general IFT formula. We never need to unroll the iterative solver that finds \mathbf{y} — we only need the Jacobian \frac{\partial F}{\partial \mathbf{y}} at the solution. This is called implicit differentiation through fixed points.
11.2 — Deep Equilibrium Models (DEQ)
A DEQ (Bai et al., 2019) replaces all layers with:
\mathbf{z}^\star = f_\theta(\mathbf{z}^\star, \mathbf{x})
i.e., \mathbf{z}^\star is a fixed point. Forward pass: iterate f until convergence (Newton’s method, Anderson acceleration). Backward pass: never unroll the iterations. Instead, at convergence:
F(\mathbf{z}^\star, \mathbf{x}; \theta) = \mathbf{z}^\star - f_\theta(\mathbf{z}^\star, \mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}
Implicit differentiation gives:
\frac{\partial \mathbf{z}^\star}{\partial \theta} = -\left(I - \frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial \mathbf{z}}\bigg|_{\mathbf{z}^\star}\right)^{-1} \frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial \theta}\bigg|_{\mathbf{z}^\star}
The matrix \left(I - J_f\right) must be invertible — this is the IFT condition. At a stable fixed point (spectral radius of J_f < 1), the Neumann series guarantees invertibility:
(I - J_f)^{-1} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty J_f^k
Convergence of the fixed-point iteration and invertibility of (I - J_f) are two sides of the same contraction condition.
Memory advantage. An explicit L-layer network stores O(L) activations for backprop. A DEQ stores only the fixed point \mathbf{z}^\star — O(1) memory, regardless of how many iterations the forward pass took.
11.3 — Differentiable Optimization Layers (OptNet, cvxpylayers)
An optimization layer solves:
\mathbf{y}^\star(\mathbf{x}) = \arg\min_{\mathbf{y}} f(\mathbf{y}; \mathbf{x}) \quad \text{s.t. } g(\mathbf{y}; \mathbf{x}) \leq 0
At the optimum, the KKT conditions (necessary optimality conditions) give a system:
\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{y}^\star, \boldsymbol{\lambda}^\star, \mathbf{x}) = 0
where \boldsymbol{\lambda} are the dual variables. Implicit differentiation on \mathbf{F} = 0:
\frac{\partial(\mathbf{y}^\star, \boldsymbol{\lambda}^\star)}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = -\left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{F}}{\partial (\mathbf{y}, \boldsymbol{\lambda})}\right)^{-1} \frac{\partial \mathbf{F}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}
This is the foundation of differentiable convex optimization (Amos & Kolter, 2017). The optimization layer can be embedded anywhere in a neural network, and gradients flow through it via the IFT, not through the solver iterations.
11.4 — Neural ODEs
A Neural ODE (Chen et al., 2018) defines the hidden state dynamics by:
\frac{d\mathbf{h}}{dt} = f_\theta(\mathbf{h}(t), t)
with \mathbf{h}(t_0) = \mathbf{x}. The output \mathbf{h}(T) is the solution of this ODE at time T. The adjoint method for computing \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} is implicit differentiation applied to the ODE:
Define the adjoint \mathbf{a}(t) = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{h}(t)}. It satisfies the adjoint ODE:
\frac{d\mathbf{a}}{dt} = -\mathbf{a}(t)^\top \frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial \mathbf{h}}
The gradient with respect to parameters:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} = -\int_{t_0}^{T} \mathbf{a}(t)^\top \frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial \theta},dt
No backpropagation through the ODE solver. Memory is O(1) in depth. The adjoint ODE is derived by implicit differentiation of the optimality conditions — the IFT, applied continuously.
11.5 — The IFT and Meta-Learning
MAML (Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning, Finn et al., 2017) seeks parameters \theta such that one gradient step on a new task gives good performance. The inner-loop update:
\phi(\theta) = \theta - \alpha \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}(\theta)
The meta-objective requires \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial \theta}. For one gradient step this is explicit. For many steps, computing \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial \theta} via unrolling is expensive. iMAML (Rajeswaran et al., 2019) instead defines \phi as the solution to:
\phi^\star(\theta) = \arg\min_\phi \left[\mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}(\phi) + \frac{\lambda}{2}|\phi - \theta|^2\right]
which satisfies \nabla_\phi \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}(\phi^\star) + \lambda(\phi^\star - \theta) = 0. This is F(\phi^\star, \theta) = 0. Implicit differentiation:
\frac{\partial \phi^\star}{\partial \theta} = \left(\nabla^2_\phi \mathcal{L}_{\text{task}} + \lambda I\right)^{-1} \cdot \lambda I
The Hessian inverse appears — but it can be approximated by conjugate gradient, making iMAML practical. The IFT removes the need to store the full inner-loop computation graph.

§12. Summary — The Structure of Implicit Differentiation
F(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = 0 \xrightarrow{\text{differentiate}} J_\mathbf{x}F + J_\mathbf{y}F \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = 0 \xrightarrow{\text{solve}} \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = -(J_\mathbf{y}F)^{-1} J_\mathbf{x}F



































SettingFormulaConditionF(x,y)=0, find y'y' = -F_x/F_yF_y \neq 0F(x,y,z)=0, find z_xz_x = -F_x/F_zF_z \neq 0\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=0, find J_\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}-(J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F})^{-1}J_\mathbf{x}\mathbf{F}\det(J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F}) \neq 0Fixed point \mathbf{z}=f(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x})-(I-J_\mathbf{z}f)^{-1}J_\mathbf{x}f\rho(J_\mathbf{z}f) < 1Optimization layer-(J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F}_{\text{KKT}})^{-1}J_\mathbf{x}\mathbf{F}_{\text{KKT}}KKT nondegeneracy

§13. Theorems to Know Cold
Theorem 1 (Implicit Function Theorem, 2D). If F \in C^1 near (a,b), F(a,b) = 0, F_y(a,b) \neq 0: then y = g(x) exists locally, is C^1, and g' = -F_x/F_y.
Theorem 2 (IFT, nD). If \mathbf{F} \in C^1 near (\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}), \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{0}, \det(J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F}) \neq 0: then \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{x}) exists locally, is C^1, and J\mathbf{g} = -(J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F})^{-1}J_\mathbf{x}\mathbf{F}.
Theorem 3 (Cyclic Identity). If F(x,y,z)=0 defines each variable implicitly in terms of the other two: \frac{\partial x}{\partial y}\bigg|_z \cdot \frac{\partial y}{\partial z}\bigg|_x \cdot \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\bigg|_y = -1
Theorem 4 (Inverse Function Theorem — a Corollary of IFT). If \mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n is C^1 near \mathbf{a} and \det(J_\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{a})) \neq 0, then \mathbf{f} is locally invertible near \mathbf{a}, and J_{\mathbf{f}^{-1}}(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{a})) = (J_\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{a}))^{-1}.
Proof: Apply IFT to F(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y}) - \mathbf{x} = 0.

§14. Things That Will Trip You Up

F_y = 0 kills implicit differentiation at that point. The tangent may be vertical, or the curve may have a singularity. Always check.


The notation \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} is ambiguous without context. Is y being held fixed? Is z defined implicitly by one equation or two? Always state what is being held constant.


Second derivatives require substituting y' before simplifying. Never leave y' in the expression for y'' — substitute the formula you found and simplify.


The cyclic identity gives -1, not +1. This surprises everyone the first time. It is not the chain rule.


Implicit differentiation gives local information only. The IFT guarantees a function y = g(x) only near the point where F_y \neq 0. The function may not extend globally, and there may be multiple branches.


In the ML context: implicit differentiation through a solver assumes the solver has converged. The formula \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \theta} = -(J_\mathbf{y}\mathbf{F})^{-1}J_\theta\mathbf{F} is only valid at the exact solution \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{y}^\star, \theta) = 0. Approximate solutions give biased gradients.


References

James Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. — §3.5 (Implicit Differentiation), §14.3, §14.5.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Denis Auroux, Notes on Implicit Differentiation and the Implicit Function Theorem.
Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, Chapter 9 — rigorous proof of the Implicit and Inverse Function Theorems.
Bai, Kolter, Koltun (2019), “Deep Equilibrium Models” — implicit layers via fixed-point differentiation.
Amos & Kolter (2017), “OptNet: Differentiable Optimization as a Layer” — KKT-based implicit differentiation.
Chen et al. (2018), “Neural Ordinary Differential Equations” — adjoint method as implicit differentiation.
Rajeswaran et al. (2019), “Meta-Learning with Implicit Gradients” — iMAML and the IFT in meta-learning.

01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.title: 14.Directional Derivatives
01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.content:
“The partial derivative is a coward — it only moves along coordinate axes. The directional derivative is the full general.” — Professor’s notebook, MIT 18.02


§0. Motivation: Why Partial Derivatives Are Not Enough
Suppose you are standing on a mountain whose height is given by f(x,y). The partial derivatives \partial f/\partial x and \partial f/\partial y tell you the rate of change only along the east and north directions, respectively.
But you might want to hike northeast, or southwest, or in any arbitrary direction. The directional derivative is precisely the tool that answers: “How fast is f changing as I walk in direction \mathbf{u}?”
This is not a philosophical question — in machine learning, gradient descent asks exactly this, and the directional derivative is the engine underneath.

§1. Setup and Notation
Let:

f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} be a scalar field (a function of n real variables)
\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n be a point in the domain
\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^n be a unit vector (i.e., |\mathbf{u}| = 1) indicating a direction

We want to measure how f changes at \mathbf{a} in the direction \mathbf{u}.

Convention (Stewart & MIT 18.02): The direction vector \mathbf{u} must be a unit vector. If you are given a direction vector \mathbf{v} that is not normalized, compute \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}/|\mathbf{v}| first.


§2. The Formal Definition
Definition 2.1 (Directional Derivative)
The directional derivative of f at \mathbf{a} in the direction \mathbf{u} is defined as:
D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) := \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(\mathbf{a} + h\mathbf{u}) - f(\mathbf{a})}{h}
provided this limit exists.
Unpacking the definition:

\mathbf{a} + h\mathbf{u} is a point on the line through \mathbf{a} in direction \mathbf{u}, at signed distance h from \mathbf{a}
The numerator is the change in f over that displacement
Dividing by h and taking h \to 0 gives the instantaneous rate of change

Geometric picture (2D): Consider the vertical plane through \mathbf{a} in direction \mathbf{u}. This plane slices the surface z = f(x,y) in a curve. The directional derivative is the slope of this curve at the point above \mathbf{a}.
         z = f(x,y)
              |   /← slope here is D_u f(a)
              |  /
              | /
     ─────────●──────────────► direction u
              a

Remark: Partial Derivatives as Special Cases
The partial derivatives are directional derivatives in the coordinate directions: \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a}) = D_{\mathbf{e}_i} f(\mathbf{a}) where \mathbf{e}_i is the i-th standard basis vector. The directional derivative strictly generalizes this.

§3. The Computational Theorem
The limit definition is conceptually clean but computationally painful. The key theorem connects directional derivatives to the gradient.
Theorem 3.1 (Gradient Formula)
If f is differentiable at \mathbf{a}, then for any unit vector \mathbf{u}:
\boxed{D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u}}
where \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}, \ldots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\right) is the gradient of f at \mathbf{a}.
Proof (Full Rigorous Proof)
Setup: Let g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} be defined by: g(t) = f(\mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{u})
Then by definition: D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(\mathbf{a} + h\mathbf{u}) - f(\mathbf{a})}{h} = g'(0)
Applying the Chain Rule: Write \mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{u}, so \mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{u}. Then g(t) = f(\mathbf{x}(t)).
Since f is differentiable at \mathbf{a}, by the multivariable chain rule:
g'(t) = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{x}'(t) = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{u}
Evaluating at t = 0:
g'(0) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u}
Therefore D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u}. \blacksquare

Critical hypothesis: The theorem requires f to be differentiable at \mathbf{a}, not merely that partial derivatives exist. Existence of partials alone is insufficient (see §6 for a counterexample).


§4. Geometric Interpretation via the Dot Product
Write the dot product formula using the angle \theta between \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) and \mathbf{u}:
D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u} = |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| \cdot \underbrace{|\mathbf{u}|}_{=1} \cdot \cos\theta = |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| \cos\theta
This yields three fundamental facts:

























ConditionD_{\mathbf{u}} fMeaning\theta = 0 (u parallel to \nabla f)\|\nabla f\| (maximum)Steepest ascent\theta = \pi (u anti-parallel to \nabla f)-\|\nabla f\| (minimum)Steepest descent\theta = \pi/2 (u perpendicular to \nabla f)0No change — level curve direction
Corollaries
Corollary 4.1 (Direction of Steepest Ascent): The gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) points in the direction of maximum increase of f, and |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| is the maximum rate of change.
Corollary 4.2 (Level Sets): The gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) is perpendicular to the level curve (or level surface) f = c passing through \mathbf{a}.
Level curves of f(x,y):

        f = 3
      f = 2   ↑ ∇f  (perpendicular to level curves)
    f = 1   ╱
          ╱
        ●  ← point a
        
The gradient arrows always point "uphill", 
perpendicular to the contour lines.


§5. Worked Examples
Example 5.1 (Stewart-style)
Problem: Let f(x,y) = x^2 y + e^{xy}. Find D_{\mathbf{u}} f(1, 0) in the direction \mathbf{v} = \langle 3, 4 \rangle.
Step 1: Normalize. |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5, so \mathbf{u} = \langle 3/5, 4/5 \rangle.
Step 2: Compute the gradient. \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2xy + ye^{xy}, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = x^2 + xe^{xy}
At (1,0): \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(1,0) = 0 + 0 \cdot 1 = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(1,0) = 1 + 1 \cdot 1 = 2
So \nabla f(1,0) = \langle 0, 2 \rangle.
Step 3: Take the dot product. D_{\mathbf{u}} f(1,0) = \langle 0, 2 \rangle \cdot \langle 3/5, 4/5 \rangle = 0 \cdot \frac{3}{5} + 2 \cdot \frac{4}{5} = \frac{8}{5}
Answer: D_{\mathbf{u}} f(1,0) = 8/5.

Example 5.2 (3D — MIT 18.02 style)
Problem: Let f(x,y,z) = x^2 + 2y^2 - z^2. At the point P = (1, 1, 1):

Find the direction of steepest ascent.
Find the maximum rate of change.
Find a direction in which f does not change.

Gradient: \nabla f = \langle 2x, 4y, -2z \rangle \implies \nabla f(1,1,1) = \langle 2, 4, -2 \rangle


Steepest ascent direction: \mathbf{u} = \nabla f / |\nabla f|. |\nabla f| = \sqrt{4 + 16 + 4} = \sqrt{24} = 2\sqrt{6} \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}} \langle 2, 4, -2 \rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \langle 1, 2, -1 \rangle


Maximum rate of change: |\nabla f(1,1,1)| = 2\sqrt{6}.


Direction of zero change: Any \mathbf{u} with \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0, i.e., any vector perpendicular to \langle 2, 4, -2 \rangle. For example, \langle 2, 0, 2 \rangle (check: 2\cdot2 + 4\cdot0 + (-2)\cdot2 = 0 ✓). Normalize: \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \langle 1, 0, 1 \rangle.



Example 5.3 (Using the Definition Directly)
Problem: Verify the gradient formula using the definition for f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 at \mathbf{a} = (1,1) in direction \mathbf{u} = \langle 1/\sqrt{2}, 1/\sqrt{2} \rangle.
Via definition: D_{\mathbf{u}} f(1,1) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{(1 + h/\sqrt{2})^2 + (1 + h/\sqrt{2})^2 - 2}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{2(1 + h/\sqrt{2})^2 - 2}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{2[1 + 2h/\sqrt{2} + h^2/2] - 2}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{2h\sqrt{2} + h^2}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0} (2\sqrt{2} + h) = 2\sqrt{2}
Via gradient: \nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle \implies \nabla f(1,1) = \langle 2,2 \rangle. D_{\mathbf{u}} f(1,1) = \langle 2,2 \rangle \cdot \langle 1/\sqrt{2}, 1/\sqrt{2} \rangle = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} = 2\sqrt{2} \checkmark

§6. The Differentiability Hypothesis: A Cautionary Example
The gradient formula D_{\mathbf{u}} f = \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u} requires differentiability, not merely existence of partials. Here is the classic counterexample.
Example 6.1
Define: f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^2 y}{x^2 + y^2} & (x,y) \neq (0,0) \ 0 & (x,y) = (0,0) \end{cases}
Partial derivatives at origin exist: \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(0,0) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(h,0) - 0}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{0}{h} = 0 Similarly \partial f / \partial y (0,0) = 0, so \nabla f(0,0) = \langle 0,0 \rangle.
But directional derivative in direction \mathbf{u} = \langle \cos\theta, \sin\theta \rangle: D_{\mathbf{u}} f(0,0) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(h\cos\theta, h\sin\theta)}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{h^2\cos^2\theta \cdot h\sin\theta}{h(h^2\cos^2\theta + h^2\sin^2\theta)} = \cos^2\theta \sin\theta
Contradiction: The gradient formula would predict D_{\mathbf{u}} f = \langle 0,0 \rangle \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0 for all \mathbf{u}. But we computed D_{\mathbf{u}} f = \cos^2\theta \sin\theta, which is nonzero for \theta = \pi/4.
Conclusion: f is not differentiable at the origin (even though partials exist), so the formula fails. Differentiability is a strictly stronger condition than existence of partial derivatives.

§7. The General Case: f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m
For vector-valued functions \mathbf{F}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m, \mathbf{F} = (F_1, \ldots, F_m), the directional derivative is:
D_{\mathbf{u}} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{a}) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{a} + h\mathbf{u}) - \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{a})}{h} = J_{\mathbf{F}}(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u}
where J_{\mathbf{F}}(\mathbf{a}) is the Jacobian matrix (m \times n): (J_{\mathbf{F}})_{ij} = \frac{\partial F_i}{\partial x_j}
This is the full generalization: the scalar case has Jacobian = gradient (row vector), and the dot product collapses to a scalar.

§8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
This section is not decoration — directional derivatives are the mathematical spine of modern ML.
8.1 Gradient Descent is a Directional Derivative Statement
In supervised learning, we minimize a loss function \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) over parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^n.
The gradient descent update rule is: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \eta \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)
Why -\nabla \mathcal{L}?
By Corollary 4.1, the direction of steepest descent is \mathbf{u}^* = -\nabla \mathcal{L} / |\nabla \mathcal{L}|. The directional derivative in this direction equals -|\nabla \mathcal{L}|, the most negative possible value. Hence moving in -\nabla \mathcal{L} decreases \mathcal{L} as fast as possible.
In short: gradient descent is the algorithm that always moves in the direction of most negative directional derivative.
8.2 Directional Derivatives in Neural Network Analysis
Width of Loss Landscapes: Understanding a neural network’s behavior involves understanding D_{\mathbf{u}} \mathcal{L} for various directions \mathbf{u} in parameter space. Sharp minima have large |D_{\mathbf{u}} \mathcal{L}| in many directions; flat minima have small values. This is directly related to generalization.
Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM): The SAM optimizer (Foret et al., 2021) explicitly maximizes D_{\mathbf{u}} \mathcal{L} over a neighborhood to find flat minima. It solves: \max_{|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}| \leq \rho} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) \approx \mathcal{L}\left(\boldsymbol{\theta} + \rho \frac{\nabla \mathcal{L}}{|\nabla \mathcal{L}|}\right) This is exactly a directional derivative calculation.
8.3 Backpropagation is Directional Derivative Bookkeeping
During backpropagation, we compute \partial \mathcal{L} / \partial \theta_i for each parameter — these are partial derivatives. The full gradient \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L} is assembled from these partials. The gradient is then used as the “directional object” that gradient descent queries through a dot product.
The chain rule proof in §3 is precisely what backpropagation computes layer-by-layer. If the network is \mathbf{F} = f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1, then backprop computes \nabla \mathcal{L} by chaining Jacobians — the multivariable version of Theorem 3.1.
8.4 Natural Gradient Descent
Standard gradient descent measures steepness in Euclidean parameter space. But in probability model families (used in RL, variational inference), the natural geometry is not Euclidean — it is the Fisher information metric.
The natural gradient \tilde{\nabla} \mathcal{L} = F^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L} (where F is the Fisher matrix) is the gradient in this curved geometry. This is equivalent to taking directional derivatives with respect to the natural inner product \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle_F = \mathbf{u}^T F \mathbf{v} instead of the dot product. Amari’s natural gradient descent uses exactly this.
8.5 Directional Derivatives in Adversarial Robustness
In adversarial attacks (FGSM — Fast Gradient Sign Method), the adversarial perturbation is: \boldsymbol{\delta} = \epsilon \cdot \text{sign}(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \mathcal{L})
This perturbs the input \mathbf{x} in the direction that most increases the loss — again, the direction of maximum directional derivative. The gradient is the primary object, and the attack is literally “move in the direction of steepest ascent of the loss with respect to the input.”
Summary Table: ML Applications





































ML ConceptDirectional Derivative RoleGradient DescentMove in direction of steepest descent: \mathbf{u}^* = -\nabla \mathcal{L}/\|\nabla \mathcal{L}\|BackpropagationChain rule = Thm 3.1 applied layer-by-layerLoss Landscape AnalysisD_{\mathbf{u}} \mathcal{L} characterizes sharpness of minimaSAM OptimizerExplicitly maximizes D_{\mathbf{u}} \mathcal{L} to find flat minimaFGSM Adversarial AttackPerturbation = direction of max D_{\mathbf{u}} \mathcal{L} w.r.t. inputNatural GradientDirectional derivative under Fisher metricSecond-order methods (Newton)Use Hessian to understand curvature of D_{\mathbf{u}} \mathcal{L}

§9. Properties and Identities
Let f, g be differentiable scalar fields, c \in \mathbb{R}.
