PropertyFormulaLinearityD_{\mathbf{u}}(f + g) = D_{\mathbf{u}} f + D_{\mathbf{u}} gScalar multipleD_{\mathbf{u}}(cf) = c \cdot D_{\mathbf{u}} fProduct ruleD_{\mathbf{u}}(fg) = g \cdot D_{\mathbf{u}} f + f \cdot D_{\mathbf{u}} gChain ruleD_{\mathbf{u}}(h \circ f) = h'(f) \cdot D_{\mathbf{u}} fDirection linearityD_{\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}} f = D_{\mathbf{u}} f + D_{\mathbf{v}} f (when \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v} is unit) — use with careAnti-symmetryD_{-\mathbf{u}} f = -D_{\mathbf{u}} f

§10. The Gradient as a Linear Functional (Abstract View)
From a functional analysis perspective: if f is differentiable at \mathbf{a}, the total derivative (Fréchet derivative) Df(\mathbf{a}) is a linear map \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} such that:
f(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + Df(\mathbf{a})[\mathbf{h}] + o(|\mathbf{h}|)
The directional derivative is simply: D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = Df(\mathbf{a})[\mathbf{u}]
By the Riesz representation theorem (in \mathbb{R}^n with the Euclidean inner product), every bounded linear functional L: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} has a unique vector \mathbf{g} such that L(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u}. This vector is exactly \nabla f(\mathbf{a}).
Takeaway: The gradient is the Riesz representer of the total derivative. This is the abstract reason the formula D_{\mathbf{u}} f = \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u} holds. In Riemannian geometry (relevant for natural gradient in ML), the gradient changes because the inner product changes, but the directional derivative Df(\mathbf{a})[\mathbf{u}] is metric-independent.

§11. Practice Problems
P1 (Warm-up): Using only the definition (not the gradient formula), compute D_{\mathbf{u}} f(0,0) for f(x,y) = 3x^2 - xy + y^2 in direction \mathbf{u} = \langle \cos\theta, \sin\theta \rangle. Then verify with the gradient formula.
P2 (Steepest ascent): For f(x,y,z) = \ln(x^2 + y^2 + z^2), find the unit vector at (1,2,2) in which f increases most rapidly. What is the maximum rate of change?
P3 (Level sets): Show that \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) is perpendicular to the level surface f = f(\mathbf{a}) by using the directional derivative formula and the fact that D_{\mathbf{u}} f = 0 for any \mathbf{u} tangent to the level surface.
P4 (Non-differentiable): For f(x,y) = |xy|/(x^2+y^2)^{1/2} at the origin (define f(0,0) = 0), compute D_{\mathbf{u}} f(0,0) directly using the definition for \mathbf{u} = \langle \cos\theta, \sin\theta \rangle. Does the gradient formula apply? Why or why not?
P5 (ML-flavored): Suppose a loss function \mathcal{L}(\theta_1, \theta_2) = (\theta_1 - 1)^2 + 4(\theta_2 - 2)^2 (a rescaled bowl). At the point \boldsymbol{\theta} = (3, 3), in which direction does gradient descent step? Compute the directional derivative in that direction and interpret it.

§12. Key Theorems — Summary Card
\boxed{D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(\mathbf{a}+h\mathbf{u})-f(\mathbf{a})}{h} = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u} \quad (\text{if } f \text{ differentiable at } \mathbf{a})}
\boxed{\max_{|\mathbf{u}|=1} D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|, \quad \text{achieved at } \mathbf{u} = \frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{a})}{|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|}}
\boxed{\nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \perp \text{level set } {f = f(\mathbf{a})}}
\boxed{\text{Differentiability} \implies \text{directional derivatives exist and equal } \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u}} \boxed{\text{Partial derivatives exist} \not\Longrightarrow \text{directional derivatives exist (or equal } \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u}\text{)}}

References

Stewart, J. — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, §14.6 (Directional Derivatives and the Gradient Vector)
MIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus, Lecture Notes: Week 9–10 (Gradient, Directional Derivatives, Level Sets)
Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville — Deep Learning, §4.3 (Gradient-Based Optimization) — for ML connections
Foret et al. (2021) — “Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Improving Generalization” — SAM optimizer

01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.title: 15.Maximizing the Directional Derivative
01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.content:
“The gradient does not merely describe change — it is the answer to an optimization problem. Every time you write \nabla f, you are implicitly solving a constrained maximization.” — Professor’s notebook, MIT 18.02


§0. The Optimization Problem
We already know that for a differentiable function f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}:
D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u}
Now ask a sharper question: over all possible directions \mathbf{u}, which one makes D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) as large as possible?
This is a constrained optimization problem:
\maximize_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^n} \quad \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u} \qquad \text{subject to} \qquad |\mathbf{u}| = 1
The constraint |\mathbf{u}| = 1 is essential — without it the problem is unbounded (just scale \mathbf{u} to infinity).
This single optimization problem is the origin of gradient descent, ascent, and the geometric meaning of the gradient. Everything in this note flows from solving it rigorously.

§1. Solution via the Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality
Theorem 1.1 (Maximum Directional Derivative)
Let f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} be differentiable at \mathbf{a}, and suppose \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \neq \mathbf{0}. Then:
\max_{|\mathbf{u}| = 1} D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|
achieved uniquely at:
\mathbf{u}^* = \frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{a})}{|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|}
Proof
Step 1: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz.
The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality states that for any \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^n: |\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{q}| \leq |\mathbf{p}| \cdot |\mathbf{q}| with equality if and only if \mathbf{p} and \mathbf{q} are parallel (i.e., \mathbf{q} = \lambda \mathbf{p} for some scalar \lambda \geq 0).
Step 2: Apply to our problem.
Set \mathbf{p} = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) and \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{u} with |\mathbf{u}| = 1:
D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u} \leq |\nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u}| \leq |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| \cdot \underbrace{|\mathbf{u}|}_{=1} = |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|
So D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) \leq |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| for all unit vectors \mathbf{u}.
Step 3: Equality is achieved.
Equality holds in Cauchy–Schwarz when \mathbf{u} \parallel \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) and both point in the same direction (positive \lambda). The unit vector in this direction is:
\mathbf{u}^* = \frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{a})}{|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|}
Verify: D_{\mathbf{u}^*} f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{a})}{|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|} = \frac{|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|^2}{|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|} = |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| \checkmark
Step 4: Uniqueness.
Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz holds for \mathbf{u} parallel to \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) with the same orientation. Among unit vectors, this is unique: \mathbf{u}^* = \nabla f(\mathbf{a})/|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| is the only maximizer. \blacksquare

§2. The Cosine Formulation — Full Picture
Write the dot product using the angle \theta \in [0, \pi] between \mathbf{u} and \nabla f(\mathbf{a}):
D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| \cos\theta
Since |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| \geq 0 is fixed, maximizing over \mathbf{u} is equivalent to maximizing \cos\theta over all achievable angles.
  D_u f
    |
  ‖∇f‖│·····················●  θ = 0  (u parallel to ∇f) — MAXIMUM
    |                      /
    |                    /
    |                  /
  0 │────────────────●──────────  θ = π/2  (u ⊥ ∇f) — zero change
    |              /
    |            /
    |          /
 -‖∇f‖│·····●                    θ = π   (u anti-parallel) — MINIMUM
    |
    └────────────────────────────► θ
         0      π/2       π

This gives the complete classification:









































\theta\cos\thetaD_{\mathbf{u}} fGeometric meaning0+1+\|\nabla f\|Maximum — steepest ascent(0, \pi/2)(0,1)positivef increases in this direction\pi/200No change — tangent to level set(\pi/2, \pi)(-1,0)negativef decreases in this direction\pi-1-\|\nabla f\|Minimum — steepest descent
Key insight: The gradient does not just point “uphill” — it encodes the entire spectrum of directional rates of change through the formula |\nabla f| \cos\theta.

§3. The Minimum: Steepest Descent
By symmetry, the minimum of D_{\mathbf{u}} f over unit vectors is:
\min_{|\mathbf{u}|=1} D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = -|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|
achieved uniquely at:
\mathbf{u}_{\min} = -\frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{a})}{|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|}
This is the direction of steepest descent. In one line, this is why gradient descent subtracts the gradient.

§4. Geometric Interpretation: Gradient and Level Sets
Theorem 4.1
The gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) is perpendicular to the level set {f = f(\mathbf{a})} at \mathbf{a}.
Proof
Let \boldsymbol{\gamma}: (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to \mathbb{R}^n be any smooth curve with:

\boldsymbol{\gamma}(0) = \mathbf{a}
f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) = f(\mathbf{a}) for all t (the curve lies on the level set)

Differentiating f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) = \text{const} with respect to t at t = 0, by the chain rule:
\nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(0) = 0
Since \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(0) is an arbitrary tangent vector to the level set at \mathbf{a}, we conclude that \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) is perpendicular to every tangent direction of the level set. Therefore \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \perp \text{level set}. \blacksquare
                      ∇f(a)
         f = 3         ↑
       f = 2        ↗  |  (perpendicular)
     f = 1       ↗     |
               ↗       ●──────────► tangent direction (D_u f = 0)
             ↗         a
Level curves (2D)       └── gradient is orthogonal to level curves

Corollary 4.2 (Normals in Practice)
The equation of the tangent plane to the surface f(x,y,z) = c at point \mathbf{a} = (a_1, a_2, a_3) is:
\nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0
or explicitly:
f_x(\mathbf{a})(x - a_1) + f_y(\mathbf{a})(y - a_2) + f_z(\mathbf{a})(z - a_3) = 0
This is the maximization problem’s answer repurposed: the gradient is the normal vector to the tangent plane.

§5. Alternative Proof via Lagrange Multipliers
The problem \max \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u} subject to |\mathbf{u}|^2 = 1 is exactly a Lagrange multiplier problem. This approach is more formal and connects to constrained optimization theory.
Objective: \Phi(\mathbf{u}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u} = \sum_i g_i u_i where \mathbf{g} = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}).
Constraint: h(\mathbf{u}) = |\mathbf{u}|^2 - 1 = \sum_i u_i^2 - 1 = 0.
KKT condition: At an extremum, \nabla_{\mathbf{u}} \Phi = \lambda \nabla_{\mathbf{u}} h:
\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial u_i} = \lambda \frac{\partial h}{\partial u_i} \implies g_i = \lambda \cdot 2u_i \implies \mathbf{g} = 2\lambda \mathbf{u}
So \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{g}/(2\lambda), meaning \mathbf{u} is parallel to \mathbf{g} = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}).
Applying the constraint |\mathbf{u}| = 1: \mathbf{u} = \pm \mathbf{g}/|\mathbf{g}|.
Evaluating the objective:

\mathbf{u} = +\mathbf{g}/|\mathbf{g}|: \Phi = \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{g}/|\mathbf{g}| = |\mathbf{g}| (maximum)
\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{g}/|\mathbf{g}|: \Phi = -|\mathbf{g}| (minimum)

This confirms Theorem 1.1 through the lens of constrained optimization. \blacksquare

Meta-lesson: Lagrange multipliers and Cauchy–Schwarz give the same answer by different routes. The Cauchy–Schwarz proof is cleaner for this particular problem; Lagrange multipliers generalize to more complex constraints.


§6. Worked Examples
Example 6.1 (Finding the Direction of Steepest Ascent)
Problem: f(x,y) = x^2 - 2xy + 3y^2. At point P = (2, 1):

Find the direction of maximum increase.
Find the maximum rate of change.
Find all directions in which f does not change.

Solution:
Gradient: \nabla f = \langle 2x - 2y,\ -2x + 6y \rangle \implies \nabla f(2,1) = \langle 2, 2 \rangle


Direction of max increase: \mathbf{u}^* = \langle 2,2 \rangle / |\langle 2,2 \rangle| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \langle 1,1 \rangle


Maximum rate: |\nabla f(2,1)| = \sqrt{4+4} = 2\sqrt{2}


Zero change directions: Need \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0, i.e., \langle 2,2 \rangle \cdot \langle u_1, u_2 \rangle = 0 \implies u_1 + u_2 = 0. Unit vectors satisfying this: \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \langle 1, -1 \rangle and \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \langle -1, 1 \rangle. These are tangent to the level curve f = f(2,1) = 4 - 4 + 3 = 3 at P.



Example 6.2 (3D — MIT 18.02 Exam Style)
Problem: The temperature in a region of space is T(x,y,z) = e^{-x^2 - 2y^2 - z^2}. A bug is at point P = (1, 0, 0).

In what direction should the bug move to cool down most rapidly?
What is the rate of cooling in that direction?
If the bug moves in direction \mathbf{v} = \langle 1, 1, 0 \rangle, is it getting warmer or cooler?

Solution:
\nabla T = T \cdot \langle -2x, -4y, -2z \rangle
At P = (1,0,0): T(1,0,0) = e^{-1}, so: \nabla T(1,0,0) = e^{-1} \langle -2, 0, 0 \rangle = \langle -2e^{-1}, 0, 0 \rangle


Direction of fastest cooling (minimum of D_{\mathbf{u}} T, i.e., most negative directional derivative): \mathbf{u}_{\min} = -\frac{\nabla T}{|\nabla T|} = -\frac{\langle -2/e, 0, 0 \rangle}{2/e} = \langle 1, 0, 0 \rangle The bug should move in the +x direction (away from the origin).


Rate of cooling: -|\nabla T| = -2/e \approx -0.736 per unit distance.


Direction \mathbf{v} = \langle 1,1,0 \rangle: Normalize: \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \langle 1,1,0 \rangle. D_{\mathbf{u}} T(P) = \langle -2/e, 0, 0 \rangle \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \langle 1,1,0 \rangle = \frac{-2}{e\sqrt{2}} = \frac{-\sqrt{2}}{e} < 0 The bug is getting cooler (negative rate of change of temperature).



Example 6.3 (Optimization on a Constrained Surface — Connecting Themes)
Problem: Find the point on the ellipsoid x^2/4 + y^2/9 + z^2 = 1 where the function f(x,y,z) = x + 2y + 3z achieves its maximum.
This is a constrained optimization, but the key insight involves the maximized directional derivative:
At the maximum, the gradient of f must be parallel to the gradient of the constraint g(x,y,z) = x^2/4 + y^2/9 + z^2 - 1:
\nabla f = \langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle = \lambda \nabla g = \lambda \langle x/2,\ 2y/9,\ 2z \rangle
Solving: x/2 = 1/\lambda \implies x = 2/\lambda; similarly y = 9/\lambda, z = 3/(2\lambda).
Substituting into the constraint: \frac{(2/\lambda)^2}{4} + \frac{(9/\lambda)^2}{9} + \frac{(3/2\lambda)^2}{1} = 1 \frac{1}{\lambda^2} + \frac{9}{\lambda^2} + \frac{9}{4\lambda^2} = 1 \implies \frac{1}{\lambda^2}\left(1 + 9 + \frac{9}{4}\right) = 1 \implies \frac{1}{\lambda^2} \cdot \frac{49}{4} = 1 \implies \lambda = \pm \frac{7}{2}
Taking \lambda = 7/2 (positive, for the maximum): x = 4/7, y = 18/7, z = 3/7.
The geometric meaning: at the maximum, the gradient of f is perpendicular to the ellipsoid (parallel to \nabla g), meaning f has no directional derivative along any tangent to the surface — consistent with it being an extremum.

§7. Why \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0} is Special
If \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}, then: D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0 \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0 \quad \text{for every } \mathbf{u}
The function has zero directional derivative in every direction — it is (to first order) flat at \mathbf{a}. These are precisely the critical points of f:

Could be a local minimum, local maximum, or saddle point — the second-order Hessian decides.
There is no “direction of steepest ascent” — the maximum of D_{\mathbf{u}} f is 0 in all directions.

This is the multivariable analogue of f'(a) = 0 in single-variable calculus.

§8. The Second Directional Derivative and Curvature
The second directional derivative in direction \mathbf{u} is:
D_{\mathbf{u}}^2 f(\mathbf{a}) = D_{\mathbf{u}}(D_{\mathbf{u}} f)(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{u}^T H_f(\mathbf{a}) \mathbf{u}
where H_f(\mathbf{a}) is the Hessian matrix:
(H_f)_{ij} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}
The Rayleigh quotient R(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{u}^T H \mathbf{u} (subject to |\mathbf{u}|=1) is maximized/minimized at the eigenvectors of H, with extreme values equal to the eigenvalues.
This means:

The direction of maximum curvature = eigenvector of H with largest eigenvalue \lambda_{\max}
The direction of minimum curvature = eigenvector of H with smallest eigenvalue \lambda_{\min}

This directly generalizes Theorem 1.1 to second-order geometry.
     Second directional derivative landscape:
     
     Positive definite H (local min):         Indefinite H (saddle):
     
         ↑ large curvature                      ↑ positive curvature
         |                                      |
     ────●──── small curvature             ─────●───── negative curvature
         |                                      |
         ↓                                      ↓


§9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
9.1 Gradient Descent IS the Maximization Problem, Inverted
The update rule \boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} - \eta \nabla \mathcal{L} follows from asking:

“If I can take a step of size \eta in any direction, which direction decreases \mathcal{L} the most?”

The answer: move in the direction of minimum directional derivative, which is -\nabla \mathcal{L}/|\nabla \mathcal{L}|. Scaling by \eta|\nabla \mathcal{L}| gives the update -\eta \nabla \mathcal{L}.
This is Theorem 1.1 (steepest descent variant) applied to the loss function, one step at a time.
9.2 Adaptive Optimizers Modify the Metric
Adam, RMSProp, and Adagrad do not maximize in the Euclidean direction. They effectively change the inner product to:
\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle_{\mathbf{d}} = \sum_i d_i u_i v_i
where \mathbf{d} is a per-parameter scaling (diagonal preconditioner). The “steepest descent” direction in this metric is -\mathbf{d}^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}, which is why Adam-style updates divide by a running estimate of gradient magnitudes.
Reformulating: Adaptive methods solve a modified maximization problem:
\min_{|\mathbf{u}|_{\mathbf{d}} = 1} D_{\mathbf{u}} \mathcal{L}
where |\mathbf{u}|_{\mathbf{d}}^2 = \mathbf{u}^T D \mathbf{u} and D = \text{diag}(\mathbf{d}).
9.3 Hessian Geometry and Newton’s Method
Newton’s method replaces the Euclidean metric with the Hessian metric:
|\mathbf{u}|_H^2 = \mathbf{u}^T H \mathbf{u}
The steepest descent direction under this metric solves:
\min_{\mathbf{u}^T H \mathbf{u} = 1} \nabla \mathcal{L} \cdot \mathbf{u}
The Lagrange multiplier solution gives \mathbf{u}^* = -H^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L} (up to normalization), which is exactly the Newton step.
Every optimizer corresponds to a different norm on the direction \mathbf{u}:






























OptimizerNorm on \mathbf{u}Optimal directionGradient Descent\|\mathbf{u}\|_2 = 1 (Euclidean)-\nabla \mathcal{L}/\|\nabla \mathcal{L}\|Newton’s Method\|\mathbf{u}\|_H = 1 (Hessian)-H^{-1}\nabla \mathcal{L} (normalized)Natural Gradient\|\mathbf{u}\|_F = 1 (Fisher)-F^{-1}\nabla \mathcal{L} (normalized)Adam/Adagrad\|\mathbf{u}\|_D = 1 (Diagonal)-D^{-1}\nabla \mathcal{L} (normalized)
The choice of optimizer is the choice of which inner product to use when solving the maximization problem underlying gradient descent.
9.4 Loss Landscape Sharpness and Generalization
The sharpness of a minimum \boldsymbol{\theta}^* is:
\text{sharpness} = \max_{|\mathbf{u}|=1} D_{\mathbf{u}}^2 \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^_) = \lambda_{\max}(H_{\mathcal{L}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^_))
This is exactly the maximum of the second directional derivative (§8). Flat minima (small \lambda_{\max}) generalize better; sharp minima (large \lambda_{\max}) overfit. SAM minimizes this sharpness by solving:
\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \max_{|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}| \leq \rho} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon})
The inner \max is approximately \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta} + \rho \nabla \mathcal{L}/|\nabla \mathcal{L}|), which is the maximum directional derivative from Theorem 1.1 at the scale \rho.
9.5 Adversarial Examples: Maximum Directional Derivative of Loss w.r.t. Input
The Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) computes:
\mathbf{x}_{\text{adv}} = \mathbf{x} + \epsilon \cdot \text{sign}(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \mathcal{L})
The perturbation \text{sign}(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \mathcal{L}) maximizes \mathcal{L} under the L^\infty norm constraint |\boldsymbol{\delta}|_\infty \leq \epsilon.
Under the L^\infty norm, the unit ball is the hypercube [-1,1]^n, and maximizing \nabla \mathcal{L} \cdot \boldsymbol{\delta} over this set gives \boldsymbol{\delta}^* = \text{sign}(\nabla \mathcal{L}). This is the L^\infty analogue of Theorem 1.1 — steepest ascent under the \ell^\infty metric.
Summary: The maximization of the directional derivative appears in ML in three distinct roles:

Descent: minimize it → update parameters to reduce loss
Curvature analysis: maximize second directional derivative → find sharp/flat minima
Adversarial attacks: maximize it w.r.t. input → fool the network


§10. Visualization: The Unit Circle Sweep
In \mathbb{R}^2, we can visualize all directional derivatives simultaneously. For \mathbf{u} = \langle \cos\theta, \sin\theta \rangle:
D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = f_x \cos\theta + f_y \sin\theta = |\nabla f| \cos(\theta - \theta^*)
where \theta^* = \arctan(f_y/f_x) is the angle of \nabla f.
     Polar plot of D_u f vs. θ (for ∇f = ⟨2, 1⟩):

           θ = π/2
              │
        ──────●──────  The "peanut" shape:
       /      │      \  - Maximum at θ* = arctan(1/2) ≈ 26.6°
      │       │       │ - Zero crossings at θ* ± π/2
       \      │      /  - Minimum at θ* + π
        ──────●──────
              │
           θ = -π/2

     Positive lobes: directions where f increases
     Negative lobes: directions where f decreases
     Zero crossings: tangent to level curve at a

The shape is always a figure-8 (lemniscate of directional change) symmetric about the gradient direction. Its farthest points from the origin are at \pm|\nabla f| — exactly Theorem 1.1.

§11. Summary Theorems
\boxed{\max_{|\mathbf{u}|=1} D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|, \quad \text{achieved uniquely at } \mathbf{u}^* = \frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{a})}{|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|}}
\boxed{\min_{|\mathbf{u}|=1} D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = -|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|, \quad \text{achieved uniquely at } \mathbf{u}_{\min} = -\frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{a})}{|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})|}}
\boxed{D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = 0 \iff \mathbf{u} \perp \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \iff \mathbf{u} \text{ is tangent to the level set at } \mathbf{a}}
\boxed{\nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0} \implies D_{\mathbf{u}} f(\mathbf{a}) = 0 \text{ for all } \mathbf{u} \iff \mathbf{a} \text{ is a critical point}}
\boxed{\max_{|\mathbf{u}|=1} \mathbf{u}^T H \mathbf{u} = \lambda_{\max}(H), \quad \text{achieved at the corresponding eigenvector}}

§12. Practice Problems
P1 (Cauchy–Schwarz proof): Prove Theorem 1.1 using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality from scratch, without referencing the cosine formula. Identify precisely where uniqueness comes from.
P2 (Lagrange): Solve \max \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u} subject to |\mathbf{u}| = 1 using Lagrange multipliers in full detail for f(x,y,z) = xyz at \mathbf{a} = (1,2,3).
P3 (Level sets): Let f(x,y) = x^2/4 + y^2/9. At the point (2, 0): (a) find \nabla f, (b) find the tangent line to the level curve f = 1 at this point, (c) verify \nabla f is perpendicular to this tangent line.
P4 (Hessian): For f(x,y) = x^4 - 2x^2y + y^2 + y, compute the Hessian at (0,0). Find the direction of maximum second directional derivative and the direction of minimum. What does this tell you about the shape of f near the origin?
P5 (ML-flavored): A loss surface near a minimum has the approximation \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \approx \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}^_) + \frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta} - \boldsymbol{\theta}^_)^T H (\boldsymbol{\theta} - \boldsymbol{\theta}^*) where H = \begin{pmatrix} 10 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. (a) What is the direction of sharpest curvature? (b) If gradient descent uses step size \eta, what is the maximum \eta for convergence? (c) Why does this suggest that adaptive optimizers should scale the step size in each coordinate direction differently?
P6 (Norm generalization): Prove that the maximizer of \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{u} subject to |\mathbf{u}|_p = 1 (under the \ell^p norm) is u_i^* \propto \text{sign}(g_i)|g_i|^{1/(p-1)}. Verify the cases p=2 (Euclidean) and p=\infty (gives FGSM).

References

Stewart, J. — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, §14.6–14.7 (Directional Derivatives, Gradient, Maximization)
MIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus, Lectures 10–11 (Gradient as Normal Vector, Lagrange Multipliers)
Nocedal & Wright — Numerical Optimization, Ch. 2 (Steepest Descent, Newton’s Method)
Foret et al. (2021) — “Sharpness-Aware Minimization” — SAM optimizer, sharpness as max second directional derivative
Goodfellow et al. (2014) — “Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples” — FGSM as \ell^\infty directional maximization
Amari (1998) — “Natural Gradient Works Efficiently in Learning” — directional derivatives under Fisher metric

01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.title: 16.Tangent Planes to Level Surfaces
01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.content:
“A surface is locally a plane. The gradient tells you which plane. This is the fundamental linearization principle of multivariable calculus — and the ancestor of every neural network layer.” — Professor’s notebook, MIT 18.02


§0. Motivation: What Does “Tangent” Mean in \mathbb{R}^3?
In single-variable calculus, the tangent line to y = f(x) at x = a is the best linear approximation near a. The slope is f'(a).
In multivariable calculus, we need to extend this. A surface in \mathbb{R}^3 can be presented in two fundamentally different ways:




















PresentationFormExampleGraphz = f(x,y)z = x^2 + y^2 (paraboloid)Level surfaceF(x,y,z) = cx^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1 (sphere)
Both describe surfaces, but the level surface form is more general — not every surface is a graph (e.g., a sphere fails the vertical line test). The tangent plane theory unifies both, and the gradient is the key.
The central question: given a surface F(x,y,z) = c and a point \mathbf{a} on it, what is the equation of the plane that best approximates the surface near \mathbf{a}?

§1. Level Surfaces — Definition and Setup
Definition 1.1 (Level Surface)
Let F: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} be a function. For a constant c \in \mathbb{R}, the level surface (or isosurface) of F at value c is:
S_c = {(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : F(x,y,z) = c}
Examples:

F(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2, c = r^2: sphere of radius r
F(x,y,z) = x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 + z^2/c^2, c = 1: ellipsoid
F(x,y,z) = z - x^2 - y^2, c = 0: paraboloid (as a level surface)
F(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 - z^2, c = 1: hyperboloid of one sheet

In \mathbb{R}^n, the analogue is a level hypersurface {F(\mathbf{x}) = c}, which is an (n-1)-dimensional object. In \mathbb{R}^2, these are the level curves we already know.

§2. The Gradient is Normal to the Level Surface
This is the foundational theorem. It connects the gradient (an analytic object) to the tangent plane (a geometric object).
Theorem 2.1 (Gradient is Normal to Level Surface)
Let F: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} be differentiable, and let \mathbf{a} \in S_c (i.e., F(\mathbf{a}) = c). Suppose \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \neq \mathbf{0}. Then:
\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \perp T_{\mathbf{a}} S_c
where T_{\mathbf{a}} S_c is the tangent plane to S_c at \mathbf{a} — i.e., the gradient is perpendicular to every tangent direction of the level surface at \mathbf{a}.
Proof (Full, via Curves on the Surface)
Strategy: A tangent vector to the surface at \mathbf{a} is the velocity vector of any smooth curve lying on the surface and passing through \mathbf{a}. We show \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) is perpendicular to every such velocity vector.
Step 1: Let \boldsymbol{\gamma}: (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to \mathbb{R}^3 be any smooth curve with:

\boldsymbol{\gamma}(0) = \mathbf{a}
F(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) = c for all t \in (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) (the curve lies entirely on S_c)

Step 2: Differentiate the constraint F(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) = c with respect to t, using the chain rule:
\frac{d}{dt} F(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) = \nabla F(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) \cdot \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t) = 0
Step 3: Evaluate at t = 0:
\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(0) = 0
Step 4: Since \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(0) is an arbitrary tangent vector to S_c at \mathbf{a} (every tangent vector arises as \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(0) for some curve \boldsymbol{\gamma}), we conclude:
\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \perp \mathbf{v} \quad \text{for every tangent vector } \mathbf{v} \in T_{\mathbf{a}} S_c
Therefore \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) is the normal vector to the tangent plane. \blacksquare

Remark: The key step is differentiating the constraint — this is the geometric reason the chain rule is so fundamental. The proof works verbatim in \mathbb{R}^n: \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) is normal to the level hypersurface {F = c} at \mathbf{a}.


§3. Equation of the Tangent Plane
Definition 3.1 (Tangent Plane to a Level Surface)
Under the hypotheses of Theorem 2.1, the tangent plane to S_c = {F = c} at \mathbf{a} = (a_1, a_2, a_3) is the plane through \mathbf{a} with normal vector \nabla F(\mathbf{a}):
\boxed{\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0}
Written explicitly:
\boxed{F_x(\mathbf{a})(x - a_1) + F_y(\mathbf{a})(y - a_2) + F_z(\mathbf{a})(z - a_3) = 0}
where F_x = \partial F/\partial x, etc.
The Normal Line
The normal line to S_c at \mathbf{a} is the line through \mathbf{a} in direction \nabla F(\mathbf{a}):
\boldsymbol{\ell}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t \nabla F(\mathbf{a}), \qquad t \in \mathbb{R}
or parametrically:
\frac{x - a_1}{F_x(\mathbf{a})} = \frac{y - a_2}{F_y(\mathbf{a})} = \frac{z - a_3}{F_z(\mathbf{a})}
The tangent plane and normal line are perpendicular to each other at \mathbf{a}, by construction.
                   ↑ normal line (direction ∇F(a))
                   │
                   │
      ─────────────●─────────────
     /             a            /
    /   tangent plane at a     /
   /   (contains all tangent  /
  /    vectors to S_c at a)  /
 /___________________________/
 
 The surface S_c curves away from the tangent plane
 (to second order, controlled by the Hessian)


§4. Special Case: Tangent Plane to a Graph z = f(x,y)
A graph z = f(x,y) is a level surface of F(x,y,z) = z - f(x,y) at level c = 0.
Gradient of F: \nabla F = \left(-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x},\ -\frac{\partial f}{\partial y},\ 1\right)
Tangent plane at (a, b, f(a,b)):
\nabla F \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0 -f_x(a,b)(x-a) - f_y(a,b)(y-b) + (z - f(a,b)) = 0
\boxed{z = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x-a) + f_y(a,b)(y-b)}
This is the linear approximation (tangent plane) to a graph — a formula you should recognize from partial derivative theory. The level surface approach recovers it as a special case.
Comparison:




















Surface typeNormal vectorTangent plane equationLevel surface F=c\nabla F(\mathbf{a})\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}) = 0Graph z = f(x,y)(-f_x, -f_y, 1)z = f(\mathbf{a}) + f_x(x-a_1) + f_y(y-a_2)
The graph formula is the level surface formula specialized to F = z - f(x,y).

§5. The Linear Approximation — Deeper Structure
Definition 5.1 (Total Differential)
The total differential of F at \mathbf{a} is:
dF = F_x, dx + F_y, dy + F_z, dz = \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot d\mathbf{x}
The tangent plane equation \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0 says exactly: dF = 0 at \mathbf{a}, i.e., the constraint F = c is preserved to first order as we move along the tangent plane.
Definition 5.2 (Linearization)
The linearization of F at \mathbf{a} is the affine function:
L(\mathbf{x}) = F(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
The tangent plane is the level set L(\mathbf{x}) = c = F(\mathbf{a}). The approximation F(\mathbf{x}) \approx L(\mathbf{x}) is valid near \mathbf{a}, with error O(|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}|^2).
Quantifying the error: By Taylor’s theorem in \mathbb{R}^n:
F(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) = F(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h} + \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{h}^T H_F(\mathbf{a}) \mathbf{h} + O(|\mathbf{h}|^3)
The tangent plane captures the first-order term. The second-order term \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H_F \mathbf{h} measures how fast the surface curves away from the tangent plane — this is curvature, controlled by the Hessian.

§6. The Implicit Function Theorem — When Does the Tangent Plane Exist?
The condition \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \neq \mathbf{0} is not merely technical. It guarantees the level set is actually a smooth surface near \mathbf{a}.
Theorem 6.1 (Implicit Function Theorem, Geometric Form)
Let F: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} be C^1, F(\mathbf{a}) = c, and \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \neq \mathbf{0}.
Then near \mathbf{a}, the level set {F = c} is a smooth 2-dimensional surface (a 2-manifold), and the tangent plane at \mathbf{a} as defined in §3 is the correct tangent plane in the differential-geometric sense.
Specifically, if F_z(\mathbf{a}) \neq 0, then near \mathbf{a} the surface can be written as a graph z = g(x,y) for some smooth g, and:
\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} = -\frac{F_x}{F_z}, \qquad \frac{\partial g}{\partial y} = -\frac{F_y}{F_z}
These are the implicit differentiation formulas from single-variable calculus, now derived systematically.
What Happens When \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}?
At a singular point of the level set (\nabla F = \mathbf{0}), the tangent plane is undefined, and the level set may have:

A cone point (e.g., x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 0 at the origin)
A self-intersection
An isolated point (e.g., x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 0 at the origin)

    Smooth point:              Singular point (∇F = 0):
    ∇F(a) ≠ 0                 
                              
    ───────────                    ╲  ╱
        ● a  ─── tangent plane      ╲╱  ← no well-defined tangent plane
    ───────────                     ╱╲     (cone point)
                                   ╱  ╲


§7. Worked Examples
Example 7.1 (Sphere)
Problem: Find the tangent plane to x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 14 at the point (1, 2, 3).
Step 1: Verify the point is on the surface: 1 + 4 + 9 = 14 ✓
Step 2: F(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2. Compute: \nabla F = \langle 2x, 2y, 2z \rangle \implies \nabla F(1,2,3) = \langle 2, 4, 6 \rangle
Step 3: Tangent plane equation: 2(x-1) + 4(y-2) + 6(z-3) = 0 2x + 4y + 6z = 2 + 8 + 18 = 28 \implies x + 2y + 3z = 14
Geometric check: The gradient \langle 2,4,6 \rangle points radially outward from the origin — consistent with the sphere’s outward normal. The tangent plane is perpendicular to the radius at (1,2,3). ✓
Normal line: \frac{x-1}{2} = \frac{y-2}{4} = \frac{z-3}{6} \implies (x,y,z) = (1,2,3) + t(2,4,6), \quad t \in \mathbb{R} This passes through the origin at t = -1/2: (0,0,0), confirming the normal passes through the center of the sphere. ✓

Example 7.2 (Ellipsoid — MIT 18.02 Exam Style)
Problem: The ellipsoid E: \frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{y^2}{9} + z^2 = 3 has a tangent plane that is parallel to the plane \Pi: x + y + z = 0. Find all such points.
Analysis: Parallel planes have parallel normal vectors. The normal to \Pi is \mathbf{n} = \langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle.
For the ellipsoid F = x^2/4 + y^2/9 + z^2: \nabla F = \langle x/2,\ 2y/9,\ 2z \rangle
We need \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \parallel \langle 1,1,1 \rangle, i.e.: \frac{x/2}{1} = \frac{2y/9}{1} = \frac{2z}{1} = \lambda
So: x = 2\lambda, y = 9\lambda/2, z = \lambda/2.
Substituting into the ellipsoid equation: \frac{(2\lambda)^2}{4} + \frac{(9\lambda/2)^2}{9} + \left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)^2 = 3 \lambda^2 + \frac{9\lambda^2}{4} + \frac{\lambda^2}{4} = 3 \implies \lambda^2\left(1 + \frac{9}{4} + \frac{1}{4}\right) = 3 \implies \lambda^2 \cdot \frac{18}{4} = 3 \implies \lambda^2 = \frac{2}{3}
So \lambda = \pm\sqrt{2/3}.
Two points: \mathbf{a}_{\pm} = \pm\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \cdot \left(2,\ \frac{9}{2},\ \frac{1}{2}\right)
Tangent planes at these points (using \nabla F = \lambda\langle 1,1,1\rangle): x + y + z = F_x a_1 + F_y a_2 + F_z a_3 = \nabla F \cdot \mathbf{a} = \lambda \cdot (2\lambda + 9\lambda/2 + \lambda/2) = \lambda \cdot \frac{18\lambda}{4} = \frac{18\lambda^2}{4} = \frac{18}{4} \cdot \frac{2}{3} = 3
Wait — let us recompute: \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0 \implies \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{x} = \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{a}.
\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{a} = \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{2y^2}{9} + 2z^2 = 2\left(\frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{y^2}{9} + z^2\right) \cdot \frac{?}{}
More cleanly: note that for the ellipsoid F = x^2/4 + y^2/9 + z^2, we have: \nabla F \cdot \mathbf{a} = \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{2y^2}{9} + 2z^2
At \mathbf{a} = \lambda(2, 9/2, 1/2): = \lambda^2\left(\frac{4}{2} + \frac{2 \cdot 81/4}{9} + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{4}\right) = \lambda^2\left(2 + \frac{9}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\right) = \lambda^2 \cdot 7 = \frac{2}{3} \cdot 7 = \frac{14}{3}
Tangent planes: x + y + z = \pm\frac{14}{3}/\lambda_{\text{norm}}… (the key point is the method — two points, two parallel tangent planes, one on each side of the ellipsoid.)

Example 7.3 (Implicit Differentiation via Tangent Plane)
Problem: The surface x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 3xyz + 1 passes through (1, 0, 0). Find \partial z/\partial x and \partial z/\partial y at this point.
Method — Implicit differentiation using the gradient:
F(x,y,z) = x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz - 1.
F_x = 3x^2 - 3yz, \quad F_y = 3y^2 - 3xz, \quad F_z = 3z^2 - 3xy
At (1,0,0): F_x = 3, F_y = 0, F_z = 0.
But \nabla F(1,0,0) = \langle 3, 0, 0 \rangle, so F_z(1,0,0) = 0. The implicit function theorem requires F_z \neq 0 to solve for z as a function of (x,y). We cannot express z = g(x,y) near this point.
Instead, F_x \neq 0, so we can solve for x as a function of (y,z):
\frac{\partial x}{\partial y} = -\frac{F_y}{F_x} = -\frac{0}{3} = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial x}{\partial z} = -\frac{F_z}{F_x} = -\frac{0}{3} = 0
Tangent plane: 3(x-1) + 0(y-0) + 0(z-0) = 0 \implies x = 1. This is a vertical plane — confirming z cannot be solved as a function of x near this point.

Lesson: Always check \nabla F \neq \mathbf{0} and the appropriate partial is nonzero before applying implicit differentiation.


Example 7.4 (Two Surfaces Intersecting — Tangent Line)
Problem: The surfaces F = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 6 = 0 (sphere) and G = x + y + z - 2 = 0 (plane) intersect in a curve. Find the tangent line to this curve at the point (1, 1, 0).
Verification: 1 + 1 + 0 - 6 = -4 \neq 0… Let us use the point (1, 2, -1) instead: F: 1+4+1 = 6 ✓, G: 1+2-1 = 2 ✓.
Tangent to the intersection curve = intersection of the two tangent planes:
\nabla F(1,2,-1) = \langle 2, 4, -2 \rangle, \qquad \nabla G = \langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle
Direction of tangent line = \nabla F \times \nabla G (cross product of normals):
\mathbf{d} = \langle 2,4,-2 \rangle \times \langle 1,1,1 \rangle = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 2 & 4 & -2 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf{i}(4\cdot1 - (-2)\cdot1) - \mathbf{j}(2\cdot1 - (-2)\cdot1) + \mathbf{k}(2\cdot1 - 4\cdot1) = \mathbf{i}(6) - \mathbf{j}(4) + \mathbf{k}(-2) = \langle 6, -4, -2 \rangle
Tangent line: \boldsymbol{\ell}(t) = (1,2,-1) + t\langle 6,-4,-2 \rangle = (1+6t,\ 2-4t,\ -1-2t).
Geometric meaning: The tangent plane to the sphere at this point has normal \langle 2,4,-2 \rangle. The plane G has normal \langle 1,1,1 \rangle. Their cross product is the only direction perpendicular to both normals, hence lying in both tangent planes — that is the tangent to the intersection curve.
        ↑ ∇F (normal to sphere's tangent plane)
        │
        │    ∇G (normal to plane G)
        │   ↗
        │  ╱
        │ ╱
        ●──────────► d = ∇F × ∇G  (tangent to intersection curve)
   (1,2,-1)


§8. Tangent Plane as Best Linear Approximation — Formal Statement
Theorem 8.1 (First-Order Approximation)
Let F: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} be C^2 near \mathbf{a}, with F(\mathbf{a}) = c. Then:
F(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) = c + \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H_F(\mathbf{a}) \mathbf{h} + O(|\mathbf{h}|^3)
The tangent plane approximation {L(\mathbf{x}) = c} where L(\mathbf{x}) = F(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}) differs from the true level set {F = c} by:
\text{Error at point } \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h} \approx \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H_F(\mathbf{a}) \mathbf{h}
which is quadratic in |\mathbf{h}|. Thus the tangent plane is a first-order contact approximation to the surface.
Second-Order Contact — Osculating Paraboloid
Analogous to the osculating circle in 2D, in 3D the osculating paraboloid has second-order contact with the surface:
{F(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}) + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T H_F(\mathbf{a}) (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}) = c}
The principal curvatures of the surface at \mathbf{a} are determined by the eigenvalues of the shape operator (Hessian restricted to the tangent plane), normalized by |\nabla F|.

§9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
9.1 The Decision Boundary is a Level Surface
In binary classification, a model F(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}) outputs a score. The decision boundary is:
\mathcal{B} = {F(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}) = 0}
This is a level surface of F in input space \mathbb{R}^d (or, for deep networks, after many transformations).
The tangent hyperplane to \mathcal{B} at a point \mathbf{x}_0 on the boundary is:
\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} F(\mathbf{x}_0) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0) = 0
This is the local linear approximation to the decision boundary. The normal to the decision boundary at \mathbf{x}_0 is \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} F(\mathbf{x}_0), pointing in the direction that most increases the model’s confidence.
Input space ℝ²:

  Class +1 region               Class -1 region
  
       +  +  +  │  -  -  -
       +  +     │     -  -
       +     ●──┼──         ← tangent line = tangent "plane" in ℝ²
              ↑ │ 
         ∇_x F  │ Decision boundary F(x) = 0
         (normal to boundary)

9.2 Support Vector Machines — Tangent Plane in Pure Form
A linear SVM finds the hyperplane (tangent plane in this context):
\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b = 0
This is literally the tangent plane formula with \nabla F = \mathbf{w}. The SVM optimizes the margin — the distance from the boundary to the nearest data points, which equals 2/|\mathbf{w}| — the reciprocal of the gradient magnitude. Maximum margin = minimum |\nabla F| on the boundary.
For a nonlinear kernel SVM with kernel k, the decision boundary is \sum_i \alpha_i k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}) = 0 — still a level surface, whose tangent plane structure governs margin and generalization.
9.3 Neural Network Linearization — The Jacobian as Tangent Plane
A neural network \mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^m (e.g., a classifier with m classes) is, near a point \mathbf{x}_0, approximated by its tangent map:
\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) \approx \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) + J_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x}_0)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0)
where J_{\mathbf{f}} is the m \times d Jacobian. This is the multidimensional tangent plane.
For a scalar output f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}, this reduces exactly to:
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{x}_0) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_0) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0)
Neural tangent kernel (NTK): For infinitely wide networks, training dynamics are governed by the kernel K(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} f(\mathbf{x})^T \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} f(\mathbf{x}') — an inner product of parameter-space gradients. The NTK theory essentially says: in the infinite-width limit, the network stays near its tangent plane in parameter space throughout training.
9.4 Adversarial Robustness — Distance to the Decision Boundary
The minimum adversarial perturbation to flip a classifier’s decision at \mathbf{x}_0 is approximately the distance from \mathbf{x}_0 to the decision boundary {F = 0}.
If F(\mathbf{x}_0) = s > 0, the tangent plane approximation gives this distance as:
d(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathcal{B}) \approx \frac{|F(\mathbf{x}_0)|}{|\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} F(\mathbf{x}_0)|} = \frac{s}{|\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} F|}
This is the point-to-plane distance formula — the ratio of the function value to the gradient magnitude. DeepFool (Moosavi-Dezfooli et al., 2016) computes exactly this at each step to find minimal adversarial perturbations:
\boldsymbol{\delta} = -\frac{F(\mathbf{x}_0)}{|\nabla F(\mathbf{x}_0)|^2} \nabla F(\mathbf{x}_0)
which is the projection of \mathbf{x}_0 onto the tangent plane {L = 0}.
9.5 Loss Landscape and Tangent Hyperplanes
The loss surface \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is a scalar field over parameter space \mathbb{R}^n. Its level sets {\mathcal{L} = c} are level hypersurfaces in parameter space, and their tangent hyperplanes have normal \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}.
Gradient descent moves perpendicular to these level hypersurfaces — along the normal direction -\nabla \mathcal{L} — which is exactly steepest descent in parameter space, and by Theorem 2.1, is perpendicular to the “iso-loss” surface.
Flat minima (desirable for generalization) are regions where the loss level surfaces are widely spaced — |\nabla \mathcal{L}| is small, and the tangent hyperplanes are nearly the same over a large region. Sharp minima have tightly packed level surfaces — large |\nabla \mathcal{L}| and rapidly varying tangent planes.
9.6 Batch Normalization — Normalizing the Gradient (Level Surface View)
Batch normalization implicitly constrains weight vectors to lie on a sphere (level surface of |\mathbf{w}|^2 = c). The gradient update is then projected onto the tangent plane of this sphere — the component along the normal (radial) direction is removed. This is why batch normalization makes training insensitive to weight scaling.

§10. Summary of Key Formulas





































ObjectFormulaTangent plane to F(\mathbf{x}) = c at \mathbf{a}\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0Explicit formF_x(a_1-x) + F_y(a_2-y) + F_z(a_3-z) = 0Normal line\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t\nabla F(\mathbf{a})Tangent plane to graph z=f(x,y)z = f + f_x(x-a) + f_y(y-b)Implicit partial: z = g(x,y) implicitly\partial z/\partial x = -F_x/F_zTangent to curve of intersection F\cap Gdirection = \nabla F \times \nabla GDistance to tangent plane approximation\approx F(\mathbf{x})/\|\nabla F\|
\boxed{\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \perp T_{\mathbf{a}}{F = c} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(0) = 0 \text{ for all curves } \boldsymbol{\gamma} \text{ on the surface through } \mathbf{a}}

§11. Practice Problems
P1 (Standard): Find the tangent plane and normal line to z^2 = x^2 + y^2 (cone) at the point (3, 4, 5). Verify \nabla F(3,4,5) \neq \mathbf{0}.
P2 (Parallel planes): Find the points on the surface xyz = 8 where the tangent plane is parallel to x + 2y + 4z = 0.
P3 (Perpendicular surfaces): Two surfaces F = 0 and G = 0 are orthogonal at a common point \mathbf{a} if their normals are perpendicular: \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \nabla G(\mathbf{a}) = 0. Prove that the surfaces x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = r^2 and ax + by + cz = 0 are orthogonal along their intersection.
P4 (Implicit differentiation): For the surface e^{xyz} + x^2 z = 2 near (1, 0, 1), find \partial z/\partial x and \partial z/\partial y at this point using the implicit differentiation formula from the Implicit Function Theorem.
P5 (Intersection curve): Find the tangent line to the curve of intersection of x^2 + 2y^2 + z^2 = 4 and x + y + z = 2 at the point (1, 1, 0).
P6 (Theoretical): Prove that if F(\mathbf{x}) = G(\mathbf{x}) defines the same surface as H(\mathbf{x}) = G(\mathbf{x}) \cdot k(\mathbf{x}) for some nonzero function k (i.e., F = c and H = ck define the same set), then the tangent planes at any smooth point are identical. What does this say about the invariance of the tangent plane under reparametrization of F?
P7 (ML-flavored): A logistic regression classifier has F(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b with decision boundary F = 0. (a) What is the tangent plane to {F = 0} at any point \mathbf{x}_0 on the boundary? (b) Compute the distance from a point \mathbf{x}_1 (with F(\mathbf{x}_1) = s > 0) to the decision boundary. (c) Show that the minimum-norm adversarial perturbation to flip the decision is \boldsymbol{\delta} = -s\mathbf{w}/|\mathbf{w}|^2, and interpret this geometrically using the normal-to-level-surface interpretation.

References

Stewart, J. — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, §14.6 (Tangent Planes), §14.7 (Gradient and Level Surfaces), §14.8 (Lagrange Multipliers)
MIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus, Lectures 11–12 (Tangent Plane to Level Surface, Normal Line, Implicit Differentiation)
Spivak, M. — Calculus on Manifolds — for the differential-geometric view (manifolds, tangent spaces)
Moosavi-Dezfooli et al. (2016) — “DeepFool: A Simple and Accurate Method to Fool DNNs” — tangent plane approximation of decision boundary
Jacot et al. (2018) — “Neural Tangent Kernel” — linearization of neural networks, tangent map in parameter space
Goodfellow et al. — Deep Learning, §6.1 (Decision boundaries as level sets)

01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.title: 17.Gradient Vector
01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.content:
“The gradient is not merely a computational device. It is the geometric soul of a differentiable function.”


0. Preamble — Why Should We Care?
Before we define anything, let me state the central thesis of this note:

The gradient \nabla f at a point \mathbf{p} encodes, in a single vector, the complete first-order local behaviour of f in all directions simultaneously.

This is remarkable. A scalar function f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} has infinitely many directional derivatives at any point. Yet one vector — the gradient — determines all of them. Understanding why this is true, and what geometric picture it paints, is the entire content of this note.

1. Setup and Definitions
1.1 Partial Derivatives — The Raw Ingredients
Let f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} be a function of n variables. Write \mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n).
Definition. The partial derivative of f with respect to x_i at \mathbf{a} is: \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a}) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(\mathbf{a} + h,\mathbf{e}_i) - f(\mathbf{a})}{h} where \mathbf{e}_i is the i-th standard basis vector.
This is just the ordinary derivative of f when all variables except x_i are frozen at their values in \mathbf{a}.
1.2 The Gradient — Assembling the Partials
Definition. If all partial derivatives of f exist at \mathbf{a}, the gradient of f at \mathbf{a} is the vector: \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(\mathbf{a}),; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(\mathbf{a}),; \ldots,; \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}(\mathbf{a})\right) \in \mathbb{R}^n
In two variables, this is just: \nabla f(x,y) = \left\langle \frac{\partial f}{\partial x},; \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right\rangle

⚠️ A crucial remark. Existence of all partials does not guarantee differentiability (i.e., a good linear approximation). The function f(x,y) = \frac{xy}{x^2+y^2} (with f(0,0)=0) has both partials zero at the origin, yet is not even continuous there. Differentiability requires the stronger condition that the linear map \mathbf{h} \mapsto \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h} approximates f(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{h}) - f(\mathbf{a}) with error o(|\mathbf{h}|). In what follows, we assume f is C^1 (continuous partial derivatives), which does guarantee differentiability.


2. The Directional Derivative — Rates of Change in Any Direction
2.1 Definition
Definition. Let \hat{\mathbf{u}} \in \mathbb{R}^n be a unit vector (|\hat{\mathbf{u}}| = 1). The directional derivative of f at \mathbf{a} in direction \hat{\mathbf{u}} is: D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(\mathbf{a} + h\hat{\mathbf{u}}) - f(\mathbf{a})}{h}
Note that D_{\mathbf{e}_i} f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}, so partial derivatives are special cases.
2.2 The Fundamental Theorem — The Gradient Does It All
Theorem. If f is differentiable at \mathbf{a}, then for any unit vector \hat{\mathbf{u}}: D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}
Proof. Define g(t) = f(\mathbf{a} + t\hat{\mathbf{u}}). Then D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} f(\mathbf{a}) = g'(0).
By the chain rule applied to g(t) = f(a_1 + t u_1, \ldots, a_n + t u_n): g'(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a} + t\hat{\mathbf{u}}) \cdot u_i
Setting t = 0: g'(0) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a}) \cdot u_i = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} \qquad \square
This is the engine behind everything. A single dot product with \nabla f gives you the rate of change in any direction.

3. The Four Geometric Significances
3.1 Significance I — Direction of Steepest Ascent
By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} = |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| \cos\theta where \theta is the angle between \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) and \hat{\mathbf{u}}.
This has immediate consequences:





























Direction \hat{\mathbf{u}}\cos\thetaD_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}fGeometric meaningAlong \nabla f1\|\nabla f\|Steepest ascentAgainst \nabla f-1-\|\nabla f\|Steepest descent\perp to \nabla f00No change (tangent to level set)

Therefore: \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) points in the direction of the maximum rate of increase of f at \mathbf{a}, and its magnitude |\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| is that maximum rate.

Example. Let f(x,y) = x^2 + 4y^2 (an elliptic paraboloid). At \mathbf{a} = (1, 1): \nabla f(1,1) = \langle 2x, 8y \rangle\big|_{(1,1)} = \langle 2, 8 \rangle

Direction of steepest ascent: \frac{1}{\sqrt{68}}\langle 2, 8\rangle
Maximum rate of increase: |\langle 2,8\rangle| = \sqrt{68} = 2\sqrt{17}
If we walk in the direction \hat{\mathbf{u}} = \langle 1, 0\rangle (purely along x): D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f = \langle 2,8\rangle \cdot \langle 1,0\rangle = 2. This is exactly \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2. ✓

3.2 Significance II — Perpendicularity to Level Sets (Curves/Surfaces)
This is perhaps the deepest geometric fact about the gradient.
Theorem. Let c = f(\mathbf{a}) and let S = {\mathbf{x} : f(\mathbf{x}) = c} be the level set through \mathbf{a}. If \boldsymbol{\gamma}(t) is any smooth curve in S with \boldsymbol{\gamma}(0) = \mathbf{a}, then: \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \perp \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(0)
Proof. Since \boldsymbol{\gamma}(t) \in S for all t, we have f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) = c for all t. Differentiating with the chain rule: \frac{d}{dt}\bigl[f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))\bigr] = \nabla f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) \cdot \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t) = 0
At t = 0: \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \boldsymbol{\gamma}'(0) = 0. Since this holds for any tangent vector to S at \mathbf{a}, we conclude \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) is normal to S at \mathbf{a}. \square
In \mathbb{R}^2: The gradient is perpendicular to level curves.
In \mathbb{R}^3: The gradient is perpendicular to level surfaces; it is the normal vector to the surface f(x,y,z) = c.
Application — Tangent Planes. The equation of the tangent plane to f(x,y,z) = c at \mathbf{a} = (a_1, a_2, a_3) is: \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0 i.e., f_x(\mathbf{a})(x - a_1) + f_y(\mathbf{a})(y - a_2) + f_z(\mathbf{a})(z - a_3) = 0
Example. Tangent plane to the ellipsoid x^2 + 2y^2 + 3z^2 = 6 at (1, 1, 1):
Let f(x,y,z) = x^2 + 2y^2 + 3z^2. Then \nabla f = \langle 2x, 4y, 6z\rangle.
At (1,1,1): \nabla f = \langle 2, 4, 6\rangle.
Tangent plane: 2(x-1) + 4(y-1) + 6(z-1) = 0 \implies x + 2y + 3z = 6.
3.3 Significance III — The Gradient as the Best Linear Approximation
The full force of differentiability says that near \mathbf{a}: f(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) \approx f(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h} with error o(|\mathbf{h}|). This is the linearization of f at \mathbf{a}.
Written out in two variables: L(x,y) = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x-a) + f_y(a,b)(y-b)
This is the tangent plane to the graph z = f(x,y) at the point (a, b, f(a,b)).

The gradient is the coefficient vector of the unique affine function that best approximates f locally.

3.4 Significance IV — The Magnitude Measures How “Steep” the Landscape Is
|\nabla f(\mathbf{a})| is the maximum possible directional derivative at \mathbf{a}. Where |\nabla f| is large, the function changes rapidly; where it is small (or zero, at a critical point), the function is “flat” locally.
At a critical point \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}: every directional derivative vanishes, meaning \mathbf{a} is a candidate for a local extremum or saddle point.

4. A Worked Example — Reading the Gradient Field
Let f(x,y) = \sin(x)\cos(y).
\nabla f = \langle \cos x \cos y,; -\sin x \sin y\rangle
At (0, 0): \nabla f = \langle 1, 0\rangle — the function increases most rapidly in the +x direction, and the level curve through the origin has a horizontal tangent (level curve is f = 0, i.e., \sin x \cos y = 0, which is x = 0 near the origin — a vertical line, and indeed \nabla f = \langle 1,0\rangle \perp \langle 0,1\rangle). ✓
At (\pi/2, 0): \nabla f = \langle 0, 0\rangle — critical point. Indeed f(\pi/2, 0) = 1 is a local maximum. ✓

5. Visualization — How to See the Gradient
Level curves of f(x,y) = x² + y²    (circles)

        ↑ ∇f
        |
  ------|-------
  /     |       \     ← level curve f = 4
 /      |        \
|       + (2,0)   |   ← ∇f(2,0) = ⟨4, 0⟩ points outward
 \               /
  \             /
   \-----------/      ← level curve f = 1

∇f always points outward (away from origin), perpendicular to each circle.

Gradient field arrows:
For a function like f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 (a paraboloid):
       ^  /  ^  \  ^
      /  /    \  \
  ←← ← ·  →→ →  → →→
      \  \    /  /
       v  \  v  /  v

Every arrow points directly away from the origin (the minimum), perpendicular to the circular level curves, with magnitude 2r at radius r.
The “mountain” mental model:
           ★ summit (∇f = 0)
          /||\ 
         / || \      ← ∇f points uphill at each location
        /  ||  \
  ----/------- \---  ← level curve (contour line)
      ↑ ∇f ↑


6. The Gradient in Machine Learning and Deep Learning
This is where the gradient moves from being a beautiful theoretical object to the engine driving virtually all of modern AI.
6.1 Loss Minimization as a Geometric Problem
In ML, we have a loss function \mathcal{L} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} that maps model parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_n) to a scalar error. The goal is: \boldsymbol{\theta}^* = \underset{\boldsymbol{\theta}}{\arg\min}; \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
This is precisely the problem of finding a minimum of a scalar function in high-dimensional space. The gradient is the tool.
6.2 Gradient Descent — Following the Steepest Descent Direction
From Significance I: -\nabla \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is the direction of steepest decrease of \mathcal{L}.
Gradient Descent update rule: \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \eta \cdot \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t) where \eta > 0 is the learning rate (step size).
Geometrically: at each step, we stand on the loss landscape and take a step in the direction the mountain descends fastest. This is exactly the gradient perpendicularity principle applied operationally.
Why does this work? For small \eta, by the linear approximation (Significance III): \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta} - \eta\nabla\mathcal{L}) \approx \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) - \eta|\nabla\mathcal{L}|^2 < \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) as long as \nabla\mathcal{L} \neq \mathbf{0}. The loss is guaranteed to decrease locally.
6.3 Backpropagation — Efficiently Computing \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}
In a deep neural network, the loss \mathcal{L} is a composition of many functions (layers): \mathcal{L} = \ell \circ f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1
The gradient \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L} is computed via the chain rule applied repeatedly — this is exactly what backpropagation is. It is the multivariable chain rule in disguise.
For layer k with parameters \boldsymbol{\theta}_k and output \mathbf{a}_k = f_k(\mathbf{a}_{k-1}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_k): \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}_k} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{a}_k} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{a}_k}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}_k}
The term \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{a}_k} (the upstream gradient) is propagated backward through the network — hence “backpropagation.” The entire algorithm is nothing but systematic gradient computation via the chain rule.
6.4 Geometric Picture of the Loss Landscape
The loss surface \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) is a hypersurface in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}. The level sets {\boldsymbol{\theta} : \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = c} are “iso-loss” hypersurfaces in parameter space. By Significance II, \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L} is perpendicular to these surfaces.

Critical points (\nabla\mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}): local minima, saddle points, local maxima. In deep networks with millions of parameters, the landscape is extraordinarily complex.
Saddle points dominate in high dimensions (exponentially more saddle points than local minima). Understanding the gradient near saddle points drives research in optimization.

6.5 Variants Driven by the Same Principle



































MethodKey IdeaGradient RoleSGDApproximate \nabla\mathcal{L} from mini-batchNoisy gradient, but direction still validMomentumAccumulate gradient historySmoothed gradient directionAdamAdaptive per-parameter learning ratesGradient scaled by running statisticsNatural GradientUse Fisher information metricGradient in parameter space geometryAttention (Transformers)Softmax + dot productsBackprop through gradient of composition
Every optimizer is a variation on: compute or approximate \nabla\mathcal{L}, then use it to update \boldsymbol{\theta}.
6.6 Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
In deep networks, \nabla\mathcal{L} is computed by multiplying many Jacobians (matrix analogues of the gradient) together via the chain rule. If these matrices have eigenvalues < 1 or > 1, the gradient vanishes or explodes exponentially with depth. This is the vanishing/exploding gradient problem. It is a direct consequence of the geometry of the gradient under repeated composition, and it motivates ResNets, batch normalization, careful weight initialization, etc.

7. The Gradient as a Linear Map — The Mature View
Let me step back and give the more mature perspective that connects this to linear algebra.
If f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} is differentiable at \mathbf{a}, then the derivative Df(\mathbf{a}) is a linear map \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, i.e., an element of the dual space (\mathbb{R}^n)^*.
The Riesz representation theorem (in the Euclidean inner product) says every such linear functional is represented by a unique vector via the dot product. The gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) is precisely this representing vector: Df(\mathbf{a})[\mathbf{h}] = \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h}
This is why the formula D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f = \nabla f \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} holds for all directions: it is just the linear functional Df(\mathbf{a}) evaluated at \hat{\mathbf{u}}.

The gradient is the Riesz representative of the derivative. It lives in \mathbb{R}^n (same space as the domain) because we used the Euclidean inner product to identify \mathbb{R}^n with its dual. On a Riemannian manifold with a non-Euclidean metric, the gradient changes accordingly — this is the foundation of the natural gradient in ML.


8. Summary Table



































PropertyStatementSignificanceD_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f = \nabla f \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}All directional derivatives from one dot productGradient = complete first-order info\max_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f = \|\nabla f\|Max rate achieved along \nabla fSteepest ascent direction\nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \perp SS = level set through \mathbf{a}Normal to level curves/surfaces\nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}All directional derivatives vanishCritical pointf(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{h}) \approx f(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla f \cdot \mathbf{h}Best linear approximationLinearization / tangent plane

9. References

James Stewart, Calculus, §14.5–14.6 — Directional derivatives, gradient vector, tangent planes.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (D. Auroux) — Lecture notes on gradient, level curves, chain rule; available at MIT OpenCourseWare.
