01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.title: 18.Minimum and Maximum Values
01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.content:
“Finding extrema is the central problem of optimization. Everything else — Lagrange multipliers, second derivative tests, convexity — is commentary.”


0. Preamble — The Problem
Given a function f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, we want to find where f is largest or smallest. This question has two flavors:

Unconstrained: optimize f over all of \mathbb{R}^n (or an open domain)
Constrained: optimize f subject to g(\mathbf{x}) = c (on a curve, surface, etc.)

Both cases reduce to a single geometric idea: at an extremum, the gradient must vanish — or be parallel to the constraint.

1. Absolute vs. Local Extrema
Definition. Let f : D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}.

f has an absolute (global) maximum at \mathbf{a} \in D if f(\mathbf{a}) \geq f(\mathbf{x}) for all \mathbf{x} \in D.
f has an absolute (global) minimum at \mathbf{a} \in D if f(\mathbf{a}) \leq f(\mathbf{x}) for all \mathbf{x} \in D.
f has a local maximum at \mathbf{a} if f(\mathbf{a}) \geq f(\mathbf{x}) for all \mathbf{x} in some open ball around \mathbf{a}.
f has a local minimum at \mathbf{a} if f(\mathbf{a}) \leq f(\mathbf{x}) for all \mathbf{x} in some open ball around \mathbf{a}.

Existence — Extreme Value Theorem (multivariable). If f is continuous on a closed and bounded set D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n, then f attains both its absolute maximum and minimum on D.

⚠️ Closed and bounded is essential. On an open domain f(x) = x has no maximum on (0,1). On an unbounded domain f(x,y) = x has no maximum on \mathbb{R}^2. Both conditions are required.


2. Critical Points — Fermat’s Theorem in \mathbb{R}^n
Theorem (Fermat). If f has a local extremum at an interior point \mathbf{a} of its domain, and f is differentiable at \mathbf{a}, then: \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}
Proof. Fix any direction \hat{\mathbf{e}}_i. Define g(t) = f(\mathbf{a} + t\hat{\mathbf{e}}_i). Then g has a local extremum at t = 0, so by the single-variable Fermat theorem: g'(0) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a}) = 0 Since i was arbitrary, all partial derivatives vanish, so \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}. \square
Definition. A point \mathbf{a} where \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0} (or \nabla f does not exist) is called a critical point of f.

⚠️ The converse is false. A critical point need not be a local extremum — it could be a saddle point. The gradient vanishing is necessary but not sufficient.

Example of a saddle point. f(x,y) = x^2 - y^2 at the origin.
\nabla f = \langle 2x, -2y\rangle = \mathbf{0} at (0,0). But f(t, 0) = t^2 > 0 and f(0, t) = -t^2 < 0 for t \neq 0, so (0,0) is neither a local max nor a local min — it is a saddle point (a mountain pass).

3. The Second Derivative Test — Classifying Critical Points
3.1 The Hessian Matrix
At a critical point \mathbf{a}, the second-order behavior of f is encoded by the Hessian matrix: H_f(\mathbf{a}) = \begin{pmatrix} f_{xx} & f_{xy} \ f_{xy} & f_{yy} \end{pmatrix}\Bigg|_{\mathbf{a}}
(assuming f \in C^2, so f_{xy} = f_{yx} by Clairaut’s theorem).
The Hessian is a real symmetric matrix, so by the spectral theorem all its eigenvalues are real. The signs of these eigenvalues determine the local shape of f.
3.2 The Discriminant (in \mathbb{R}^2)
Define the discriminant: D(\mathbf{a}) = \det H_f(\mathbf{a}) = f_{xx} f_{yy} - (f_{xy})^2
Theorem (Second Derivative Test). Let \mathbf{a} be a critical point of f \in C^2.

























ConditionClassificationD(\mathbf{a}) > 0 and f_{xx}(\mathbf{a}) > 0Local minimumD(\mathbf{a}) > 0 and f_{xx}(\mathbf{a}) < 0Local maximumD(\mathbf{a}) < 0Saddle pointD(\mathbf{a}) = 0Inconclusive (higher-order analysis needed)
Why this works. Near \mathbf{a}, by Taylor’s theorem with the gradient zero: f(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) \approx f(\mathbf{a}) + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H_f(\mathbf{a}), \mathbf{h}
The sign of the quadratic form Q(\mathbf{h}) = \mathbf{h}^T H \mathbf{h} determines everything:

Q > 0 for all \mathbf{h} \neq \mathbf{0} (H is positive definite, eigenvalues both positive) \implies local min
Q < 0 for all \mathbf{h} \neq \mathbf{0} (H is negative definite, eigenvalues both negative) \implies local max
Q takes both signs (H is indefinite, eigenvalues have mixed signs) \implies saddle

The discriminant D = \lambda_1 \lambda_2 (product of eigenvalues = determinant) and f_{xx} = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 \cdot (\text{rotation terms}) encode exactly this.
3.3 Full Worked Example
Let f(x,y) = x^3 - 3x + y^2 - 2y.
Step 1 — Find critical points. \nabla f = \langle 3x^2 - 3,; 2y - 2\rangle = \mathbf{0} 3x^2 - 3 = 0 \implies x = \pm 1, \qquad 2y - 2 = 0 \implies y = 1
Critical points: (-1, 1) and (1, 1).
Step 2 — Compute the Hessian. f_{xx} = 6x, \quad f_{xy} = 0, \quad f_{yy} = 2 H_f = \begin{pmatrix} 6x & 0 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
Step 3 — Apply the test.
At (-1, 1): D = (6(-1))(2) - 0 = -12 < 0 → saddle point.
At (1, 1): D = (6)(2) - 0 = 12 > 0, f_{xx} = 6 > 0 → local minimum.
f(1, 1) = 1 - 3 + 1 - 2 = -3.

4. Absolute Extrema on a Closed Bounded Domain
By the Extreme Value Theorem, absolute extrema exist on a closed bounded domain D. The strategy is:

Closed Domain Method

Find all interior critical points (solve \nabla f = \mathbf{0})
Examine f on the boundary of D
Compare all values — the largest is the absolute max, the smallest is the absolute min


The boundary examination in step 2 typically reduces to a single-variable optimization problem on each boundary piece.
Example. Find the absolute extrema of f(x,y) = x^2 - 2xy + 2y on the square D = [0,3] \times [0,2].
Interior critical points: \nabla f = \langle 2x - 2y,; -2x + 2\rangle = \mathbf{0} \implies x = 1,; y = 1 f(1,1) = 1 - 2 + 2 = 1.
Boundary analysis (four edges):

y = 0,; x \in [0,3]: f = x^2. Max at x=3: f=9. Min at x=0: f=0.
y = 2,; x \in [0,3]: f = x^2 - 4x + 4 = (x-2)^2. Max at x=0 or x=3: f=4. Min at x=2: f=0.
x = 0,; y \in [0,2]: f = 2y. Max at y=2: f=4. Min at y=0: f=0.
x = 3,; y \in [0,2]: f = 9 - 6y + 2y = 9 - 4y. Max at y=0: f=9. Min at y=2: f=1.

Comparing all values: {1, 9, 0, 4, 0, 4, 0, 9, 1}
Absolute maximum: 9 at (3, 0). Absolute minimum: 0 at (0,0), (3/2, 0)… let me refine — at (0,0) and (2,2).

5. Constrained Optimization — Lagrange Multipliers
5.1 The Geometric Idea
Suppose we want to maximize f(x,y) subject to g(x,y) = c.
Geometrically: we are moving along the constraint curve g = c and asking where f is largest. At the constrained maximum, the level curve of f through that point must be tangent to the constraint curve — otherwise we could slide along the constraint and increase f further.
Two curves are tangent \iff they have the same tangent line \iff they have parallel normal vectors.
Their normals are \nabla f and \nabla g. So the condition is: \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \lambda, \nabla g(\mathbf{a}) for some scalar \lambda (the Lagrange multiplier).
5.2 The Formal Theorem
Theorem (Lagrange). Suppose f, g \in C^1 and f has a local extremum at \mathbf{a} subject to the constraint g(\mathbf{a}) = c. If \nabla g(\mathbf{a}) \neq \mathbf{0}, then there exists \lambda \in \mathbb{R} such that: \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \lambda, \nabla g(\mathbf{a})
Proof sketch. Since \nabla g(\mathbf{a}) \neq \mathbf{0}, the constraint surface g = c is a smooth (n-1)-manifold near \mathbf{a}. Any tangent vector \mathbf{v} to this surface satisfies \nabla g(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0.
Since \mathbf{a} is a constrained extremum of f, the directional derivative of f along any direction tangent to the constraint must vanish: \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0 for all such \mathbf{v}.
Therefore \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) is perpendicular to the entire tangent space of the constraint surface — meaning \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) is parallel to the normal \nabla g(\mathbf{a}), i.e., \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \lambda \nabla g(\mathbf{a}). \square
5.3 The Lagrange System
To find constrained extrema of f subject to g = c, solve the system: \begin{cases} \nabla f = \lambda, \nabla g \ g(\mathbf{x}) = c \end{cases}
In two variables (x,y), this is three equations in three unknowns (x, y, \lambda): f_x = \lambda g_x, \quad f_y = \lambda g_y, \quad g(x,y) = c
5.4 Worked Example
Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 on the ellipse \frac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1.
Wait — this is just distance squared from the origin on an ellipse, so we want the closest and farthest points. Let g(x,y) = \frac{x^2}{4} + y^2.
Lagrange system: f_x = 2x = \lambda \cdot \frac{x}{2}, \quad f_y = 2y = \lambda \cdot 2y, \quad \frac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1
Case 1: y \neq 0. From the second equation: 2 = 2\lambda \implies \lambda = 1. Substituting: 2x = \frac{x}{2} \implies \frac{3x}{2} = 0 \implies x = 0. Constraint: y^2 = 1 \implies y = \pm 1. Points: (0, \pm 1), f = 1.
Case 2: y = 0. Constraint: \frac{x^2}{4} = 1 \implies x = \pm 2. From first eq: 2x = \frac{\lambda x}{2} \implies \lambda = 4. Points: (\pm 2, 0), f = 4.
Conclusion: Maximum value 4 at (\pm 2, 0); minimum value 1 at (0, \pm 1). ✓ (These are the semi-axes of the ellipse.)
5.5 Two Constraints
For f(\mathbf{x}) subject to g(\mathbf{x}) = c_1 and h(\mathbf{x}) = c_2: \nabla f = \lambda, \nabla g + \mu, \nabla h

6. Global Picture — Visualization
6.1 Topographic Map View (unconstrained, \mathbb{R}^2)
Level curves of f (topographic map):

           ·  ·  ·
        ·   ( MAX )   ·       ← closed loops around local max
           ·  ·  ·
    ↘                ↗        ← open curves near saddle
          ×  SADDLE           ← curves cross at saddle point
    ↗                ↘
           ·  ·  ·
        ·   ( MIN )   ·       ← closed loops around local min
           ·  ·  ·

∇f ⊥ each level curve, pointing toward max.
|∇f| is large where curves are dense (steep).
∇f = 0 at max, min, and saddle.

6.2 Lagrange Geometry (constrained)
  Level curves of f:          Constraint g = c:

  f = 5  ·····················
  f = 4  ···  (tangency pt) ··\··· ← optimal point
  f = 3  ··       ∗           \
  f = 2  ··                    \
                                \  ← constraint curve

  At ∗: ∇f ∥ ∇g (same direction or opposite)
        they share the same tangent line

6.3 Saddle Point Geometry
  f(x,y) = x² - y²    (hyperbolic paraboloid / Pringle shape)

        z
        |   ↗ increases along x-axis
        |  /
  ------+------  ← saddle at origin
       /|
      ↙ |  ↘ decreases along y-axis

  Level curves: x² - y² = c → hyperbolas (for c ≠ 0), asymptotes (c = 0)
  ∇f(0,0) = ⟨0,0⟩ yet not an extremum.


7. The Hessian — General \mathbb{R}^n Version
In \mathbb{R}^n, the Hessian at a critical point \mathbf{a} is the n \times n symmetric matrix: [H_f(\mathbf{a})]_{ij} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(\mathbf{a})
The classification is by definiteness of H_f(\mathbf{a}):






























Hessian HAll eigenvaluesConclusionPositive definite> 0Local minimumNegative definite< 0Local maximumIndefiniteMixed signsSaddle pointPositive/Negative semidefinite\geq 0 or \leq 0Inconclusive
The determinant test in \mathbb{R}^2 is just the 2 \times 2 case of checking definiteness via eigenvalue signs (D = \lambda_1\lambda_2 > 0 means same sign; f_{xx} > 0 means both positive).

8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
8.1 The Entire Goal of Training is Minimization
Every supervised learning model minimizes a loss function \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) over parameters \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^n (where n can be 10^9 or more). The theory of min/max is the mathematical foundation.
Critical points of \mathcal{L}: \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}. These are where gradient descent stalls. Understanding whether a critical point is a minimum, maximum, or saddle is the central problem of deep learning optimization theory.
8.2 The Loss Landscape — What Are We Minimizing Into?
The loss surface \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) of a deep neural network is a hypersurface in billions of dimensions. Its landscape looks nothing like the neat single-variable pictures:

Local minima are rare. In high dimensions, a local minimum requires all eigenvalues of the Hessian to be positive — exponentially unlikely if eigenvalues are random.
Saddle points dominate. Most critical points have Hessians with some positive and some negative eigenvalues. The network gets stuck near saddles, not local minima.
Global structure: Surprisingly, for overparameterized networks (more parameters than data), many local minima have similar loss values — the landscape has many “flat valleys” at the bottom.

Empirical insight (Dauphin et al., 2014): The difficulty in training deep networks is escaping saddle points, not getting stuck in bad local minima.
8.3 Second-Order Methods — Using the Hessian
Gradient descent uses only \nabla\mathcal{L} (first-order). Newton’s method uses H_\mathcal{L} (second-order): \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \eta, [H_{\mathcal{L}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)]^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)
At a local minimum, H_{\mathcal{L}} is positive definite (second derivative test!), so H^{-1} scales the gradient step to take into account the local curvature — taking large steps in flat directions, small steps in sharp directions. This is exactly the second derivative test applied operationally.
Why not always use Newton’s method? Inverting H_{\mathcal{L}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} costs O(n^3) — infeasible for n = 10^9. This motivates quasi-Newton methods (BFGS, L-BFGS) and natural gradient methods that approximate H^{-1}.
8.4 Convexity — When Local = Global
Definition. f is convex if for all \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} and t \in [0,1]: f(t\mathbf{x} + (1-t)\mathbf{y}) \leq t f(\mathbf{x}) + (1-t)f(\mathbf{y})
Theorem. If f is convex and \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}, then \mathbf{a} is a global minimum.
This is the key property. For convex loss functions (logistic regression, SVMs, linear regression), every critical point is a global minimum — the optimization is “safe.” For non-convex losses (deep networks), there is no such guarantee.
The Hessian connection: f is convex \iff H_f is positive semidefinite everywhere (\iff all eigenvalues \geq 0). This is the global version of the local minimum condition from the second derivative test.
8.5 Lagrange Multipliers in ML — Constrained Learning
Lagrange multipliers appear explicitly in:
Support Vector Machines (SVM). Maximize the margin subject to classification constraints. The Lagrangian is: \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}, b, \boldsymbol{\alpha}) = \frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{w}|^2 - \sum_i \alpha_i [y_i(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_i + b) - 1] The KKT conditions (generalized Lagrange conditions for inequalities) completely characterize the optimal \mathbf{w}.
Regularization as a Lagrange problem. Minimize \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) subject to |\boldsymbol{\theta}|^2 \leq C is equivalent (by Lagrange) to minimizing \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \lambda|\boldsymbol{\theta}|^2 (ridge regression / L^2 regularization). The multiplier \lambda is the regularization coefficient.
Variational autoencoders (VAE). The ELBO objective is a constrained optimization (maximize likelihood subject to KL divergence constraint), handled via Lagrange-style relaxation.
8.6 Summary — Min/Max Theory in the ML Pipeline





































Calculus ConceptML ManifestationCritical point \nabla f = \mathbf{0}Trained model (gradient descent converges)Second derivative test (Hessian)Diagnosing minima vs saddle pointsSaddle pointGradient descent stall; motivates Adam, momentumAbsolute minimum on closed domainConstrained parameter spacesLagrange multipliersSVMs, regularization, constrained decodingConvexity (positive definite Hessian)Loss functions with guaranteed global minNewton’s methodSecond-order optimizers (L-BFGS, K-FAC)

9. The Procedure — A Decision Tree
Given f on domain D, find extrema
│
├─ Is D closed and bounded?
│   ├─ YES → Extreme Value Theorem guarantees extrema exist
│   │         → Find interior critical points (∇f = 0)
│   │         → Analyze boundary (parameterize, or use Lagrange)
│   │         → Compare all values
│   │
│   └─ NO  → Only local extrema may exist
│             → Find critical points (∇f = 0)
│             → Apply Second Derivative Test (Hessian)
│
└─ Is there a constraint g(x) = c?
    └─ YES → Lagrange: solve ∇f = λ∇g, g = c
             → Evaluate f at solutions
             → Compare values (no 2nd derivative test needed
               if only finitely many solutions and domain compact)


10. A Subtle Point — When the Test Fails (D = 0)
When D(\mathbf{a}) = 0, the Hessian is singular (one eigenvalue is zero). The quadratic approximation \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H \mathbf{h} is neither positive nor negative definite, and higher-order terms determine the behavior.
Example. f(x,y) = x^4 + y^4. At (0,0): \nabla f = \mathbf{0}, H = 0, D = 0. Test is inconclusive. But clearly f \geq 0 with equality only at origin, so (0,0) is a global minimum.
Example. f(x,y) = x^3. At (0,0): \nabla f = \mathbf{0}, D = 0. But f takes both signs near the origin, so (0,0) is a saddle-like point.
When D = 0: compute f along various paths through \mathbf{a} directly.

11. Summary


















































ConceptKey EquationMeaningCritical point\nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}Necessary condition for interior extremumSecond derivative testD = f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2Classifies critical point via curvatureD > 0, f_{xx} > 0—Local minimumD > 0, f_{xx} < 0—Local maximumD < 0—Saddle pointAbsolute extremaClosed domain methodInterior crits + boundaryLagrange condition\nabla f = \lambda \nabla gConstrained extremum ↔ parallel gradientsConvexityH \succeq 0 everywhereLocal min = global min

12. References

James Stewart, Calculus, §14.7 — Maximum and Minimum Values; §14.8 — Lagrange Multipliers.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (D. Auroux) — Lecture notes on second derivative test, Lagrange multipliers; available at MIT OpenCourseWare.

01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.title: 19.Absolute Minimum and Maximum Values
01.Maths/Calculus/14.Partial-Derivatives.content:
“Local extrema tell you about the neighborhood. Absolute extrema tell you about the whole kingdom.”


0. Preamble — What Question Are We Really Asking?
A local extremum answers: “Is this the best point nearby?”
An absolute extremum answers: “Is this the best point anywhere in the domain?”
These are fundamentally different questions. A mountain range may have many local peaks, but only one highest summit. The theory of absolute extrema tells us: under what conditions does a highest summit exist, and how do we find it?
The answer rests on three pillars:

Existence — the Extreme Value Theorem
Interior candidates — critical points (\nabla f = \mathbf{0})
Boundary candidates — the boundary of the domain

Miss any pillar, and you will miss the answer.

1. Definitions
Definition. Let f : D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}.


f attains an absolute maximum at \mathbf{a} \in D if: f(\mathbf{a}) \geq f(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x} \in D The value f(\mathbf{a}) is called the absolute maximum value.


f attains an absolute minimum at \mathbf{a} \in D if: f(\mathbf{a}) \leq f(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x} \in D The value f(\mathbf{a}) is called the absolute minimum value.



Distinction from local extrema. A local maximum satisfies f(\mathbf{a}) \geq f(\mathbf{x}) only for \mathbf{x} near \mathbf{a}. An absolute maximum satisfies it for all \mathbf{x} \in D. Every absolute extremum is a local extremum (on the interior), but not vice versa.


2. Existence — The Extreme Value Theorem
Before hunting for extrema, we must know they exist. The following theorem guarantees this.
Theorem (Extreme Value Theorem — EVT). If f : D \to \mathbb{R} is continuous on a closed and bounded set D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n, then f attains both its absolute maximum and absolute minimum on D. That is, there exist \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in D such that: f(\mathbf{a}) \leq f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{b}) \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x} \in D
This is the multivariable generalization of the single-variable theorem from Stewart §4.1. The proof relies on:

Continuity \implies f(D) is a connected, bounded subset of \mathbb{R}
Closed and bounded \implies D is compact (Heine–Borel)
Continuous image of compact set is compact \implies f(D) is closed and bounded \implies f(D) contains its supremum and infimum

2.1 Why Both Conditions Are Necessary
“Closed” cannot be dropped.
Let f(x) = x on the open interval (0, 1) \subset \mathbb{R}.

f is continuous, domain is bounded.
\sup f = 1, but f(x) = 1 has no solution in (0,1).
No absolute maximum exists.

In \mathbb{R}^2: f(x,y) = x on the open disk x^2 + y^2 < 1. Again, no maximum attained.
“Bounded” cannot be dropped.
Let f(x) = x on the closed interval [1, \infty) \subset \mathbb{R}.

f is continuous, domain is closed.
f is unbounded above — no absolute maximum exists.

In \mathbb{R}^2: f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 on the closed set \mathbb{R}^2. No absolute maximum.
“Continuous” cannot be dropped.
Let f : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R} be f(x) = 1/x for x \in (0,1] and f(0) = 0.

Domain is closed and bounded.
f is not continuous at 0.
f is unbounded — no absolute maximum exists.


The EVT is an existence theorem — it guarantees a maximum and minimum exist but says nothing about where they are or how many there are. Finding them requires the method below.


3. The Closed Domain Method
This is the algorithm for finding absolute extrema of f on a closed bounded domain D.
\boxed{\text{Absolute extrema} = \max/\min \text{ of } {f \text{ at interior critical points}} \cup {f \text{ on } \partial D}}
Algorithm:

Step 1. Find all interior critical points: solve \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0} for \mathbf{x} \in \text{int}(D).
Step 2. Find the extreme values of f restricted to the boundary \partial D. This is itself an optimization problem (on a lower-dimensional set), solved by parameterization or Lagrange multipliers.
Step 3. Evaluate f at all candidates from Steps 1 and 2. The largest value is the absolute maximum; the smallest is the absolute minimum.

Why this is complete. By the EVT, absolute extrema exist. Each one is either:

In the interior of D: then by Fermat’s theorem it is a critical point → found in Step 1.
On the boundary \partial D: found in Step 2.

No candidates are missed.

4. Worked Example I — Triangular Domain
Problem. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of f(x,y) = x^2 - xy + y^2 - y on the closed triangular region D with vertices (0,0), (2,0), (0,2).
Step 1 — Interior Critical Points
\nabla f = \langle 2x - y,; -x + 2y - 1 \rangle = \mathbf{0}
From the first equation: y = 2x. Substituting into the second: -x + 4x - 1 = 0 \implies x = \frac{1}{3}, y = \frac{2}{3}.
Check: is \left(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\right) in the interior of D? The triangle has edges x \geq 0, y \geq 0, x + y \leq 2. Check: \frac{1}{3} + \frac{2}{3} = 1 \leq 2. ✓
f!\left(\tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}\right) = \tfrac{1}{9} - \tfrac{2}{9} + \tfrac{4}{9} - \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{3}{9} - \tfrac{6}{9} = -\tfrac{1}{3}
Step 2 — Boundary Analysis
The triangle D has three edges:
Edge 1: y = 0, x \in [0, 2]. f(x, 0) = x^2 Single-variable: increasing on [0,2]. Min at x=0: f=0. Max at x=2: f=4.
Edge 2: x = 0, y \in [0, 2]. f(0, y) = y^2 - y = y(y-1) Derivative: 2y - 1 = 0 \implies y = \frac{1}{2} (interior of this edge). f!\left(0, \frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2} = -\frac{1}{4}. At endpoints: f(0,0) = 0, f(0,2) = 2.
Edge 3: x + y = 2, so x = 2 - y, y \in [0, 2]. f(2-y, y) = (2-y)^2 - (2-y)y + y^2 - y = 4 - 4y + y^2 - 2y + y^2 + y^2 - y = 3y^2 - 7y + 4 Derivative: 6y - 7 = 0 \implies y = \frac{7}{6}, x = 2 - \frac{7}{6} = \frac{5}{6}. f!\left(\tfrac{5}{6}, \tfrac{7}{6}\right) = 3 \cdot \tfrac{49}{36} - 7 \cdot \tfrac{7}{6} + 4 = \tfrac{49}{12} - \tfrac{49}{6} + 4 = -\tfrac{49}{12} + 4 = -\tfrac{1}{12} At endpoints: f(2,0) = 4, f(0,2) = 2.
Step 3 — Compare All Candidates

































LocationValue\left(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\right) — interior critical point-\frac{1}{3} \approx -0.333(0, 0) — vertex0(2, 0) — vertex4(0, 2) — vertex2\left(0, \frac{1}{2}\right) — Edge 2 critical-\frac{1}{4} = -0.25\left(\frac{5}{6}, \frac{7}{6}\right) — Edge 3 critical-\frac{1}{12} \approx -0.083
\text{Absolute maximum: } 4 \text{ at } (2, 0) \text{Absolute minimum: } -\tfrac{1}{3} \text{ at } \left(\tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}\right)

5. Worked Example II — Rectangular Domain
Problem. Find the absolute extrema of f(x,y) = 4x^2 + 9y^2 - 8x - 12y + 4 on the rectangle D = {(x,y) : 0 \leq x \leq 2,; 0 \leq y \leq 2}.
Step 1 — Interior Critical Points
\nabla f = \langle 8x - 8,; 18y - 12 \rangle = \mathbf{0} x = 1, \quad y = \frac{2}{3}
Point \left(1, \frac{2}{3}\right) is interior to D. ✓
f!\left(1, \tfrac{2}{3}\right) = 4 - 8 + 4 - 8 + 4 = -4
Let me recompute carefully: = 4(1) + 9(\frac{4}{9}) - 8(1) - 12(\frac{2}{3}) + 4 = 4 + 4 - 8 - 8 + 4 = -4.
Step 2 — Boundary (Four Edges)
Bottom: y = 0, x \in [0,2]: f = 4x^2 - 8x + 4 = 4(x-1)^2. Critical: x = 1, f = 0. Endpoints: f(0,0) = 4, f(2,0) = 0.
Top: y = 2, x \in [0,2]: f = 4x^2 - 8x + 4 + 36 - 24 = 4(x-1)^2 + 16. Min at x=1: f = 16. Endpoints: f(0,2) = 20, f(2,2) = 16.
Left: x = 0, y \in [0,2]: f = 9y^2 - 12y + 4 = (3y-2)^2. Critical: y = \frac{2}{3}, f = 0. Endpoints: f(0,0) = 4, f(0,2) = 16.
Right: x = 2, y \in [0,2]: f = 16 + 9y^2 - 16 - 12y + 4 = 9y^2 - 12y + 4 = (3y-2)^2. Critical: y = \frac{2}{3}, f = 0. Endpoints: f(2,0) = 0, f(2,2) = 16.
Step 3 — Compare
All candidate values: {-4, 0, 4, 16, 20}.
\text{Absolute maximum: } 20 \text{ at } (0, 2) \text{Absolute minimum: } -4 \text{ at } \left(1, \frac{2}{3}\right)

6. Worked Example III — Disk Domain
Problem. Find the absolute extrema of f(x,y) = x^2 + 2y^2 - 2x on the closed disk D = {(x,y) : x^2 + y^2 \leq 4}.
Step 1 — Interior Critical Points
\nabla f = \langle 2x - 2,; 4y \rangle = \mathbf{0} \implies x = 1,; y = 0
Check: 1^2 + 0^2 = 1 \leq 4, so (1,0) is interior. ✓
f(1, 0) = 1 + 0 - 2 = -1
Step 2 — Boundary: Circle x^2 + y^2 = 4
Parameterize: x = 2\cos t, y = 2\sin t, t \in [0, 2\pi].
f(2\cos t, 2\sin t) = 4\cos^2 t + 8\sin^2 t - 4\cos t = 4\cos^2 t + 8(1 - \cos^2 t) - 4\cos t = 8 - 4\cos^2 t - 4\cos t
Let u = \cos t \in [-1, 1]. Minimize/maximize h(u) = -4u^2 - 4u + 8.
h'(u) = -8u - 4 = 0 \implies u = -\frac{1}{2}
h!\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -4 \cdot \frac{1}{4} + 2 + 8 = 9.
At endpoints: h(1) = -4 - 4 + 8 = 0 and h(-1) = -4 + 4 + 8 = 8.
So on the boundary:

Max: f = 9 at \cos t = -\frac{1}{2}, i.e., t = \frac{2\pi}{3} or \frac{4\pi}{3}, giving points \left(-1, \pm\sqrt{3}\right).
Min: f = 0 at t = 0, i.e., point (2, 0).

Step 3 — Compare





















CandidateValue(1,0) — interior-1(-1, \pm\sqrt{3}) — boundary9(2, 0) — boundary0
\text{Absolute maximum: } 9 \text{ at } (-1, \pm\sqrt{3}) \text{Absolute minimum: } -1 \text{ at } (1, 0)

7. Visualization
7.1 Why Boundary Matters — A Schematic
     Domain D (closed rectangle):

     ┌──────────────────────┐  ← boundary ∂D
     │                      │
     │   ×  local max       │
     │                      │
     │         ★ abs. max   │  ← abs max ON boundary
     │                      │
     │   ·  local min       │
     │                      │
     └──────────────────────┘
          ↑
          abs. min (interior critical point here)

  The absolute max lives on the boundary, NOT at any interior
  critical point. If you only check ∇f = 0, you miss it entirely.

7.2 Level Curve View
  f(x,y) = x² + y²    on disk x² + y² ≤ 4

        f = 4  ← boundary circle
      f = 3
    f = 2
   f = 1
  f = 0  ← absolute minimum at origin

  Level curves are concentric circles.
  Absolute min: origin (interior critical point ∇f = 0).
  Absolute max: entire boundary circle x²+y² = 4.
  The max is attained everywhere on ∂D — not unique.

7.3 Cross-Section Intuition
  z = f(x, y) viewed as a surface:

         z
         │        ·  ·  ·   ← high values at boundary
         │      ·           (absolute max somewhere on ∂D)
         │    ·
  ───────┼──·──────·──────── D (projection onto xy-plane)
         │·               ↑
         ·                boundary ∂D
    absolute min
    (interior dip)

  The surface may dip lowest in the interior (interior min)
  or rise highest at the boundary (boundary max).
  We must check BOTH regions to be sure.


8. Special Case — Absolute Extrema on a Curve (1D Constraint)
Sometimes the domain D is itself a curve g(x,y) = c (a 1D set). This arises naturally as the boundary problem in Step 2. Two methods:
Method A — Parameterization
Parameterize the curve \boldsymbol{\gamma}(t) and optimize the single-variable function f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)).
Best when the curve has a clean parameterization (circle → (\cos t, \sin t), line segment → (1-t)\mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}).
Method B — Lagrange Multipliers
Solve \nabla f = \lambda \nabla g, g = c.
Best when parameterization is messy. Gives the same candidates.

Both methods must be used with care: neither automatically delivers the absolute max/min. You still need to evaluate f at all candidates and compare.


9. Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them








































MistakeWhy It FailsCorrectionOnly solving \nabla f = \mathbf{0}Misses absolute extrema on \partial DAlways analyze the boundaryForgetting to check if critical point is in DA point outside D is not a candidateVerify each critical point lies in DNot checking all boundary piecesA rectangular domain has 4 edges and 4 cornersBe systematic; list every pieceAssuming interior min/max is absoluteA local extremum need not be globalCompare against all boundary valuesForgetting corner points of boundaryCorners are endpoints of edge sub-problemsAlways evaluate f at all vertices/cornersApplying EVT on open domainEVT requires closed and boundedVerify domain before applying EVT

10. Connection to Machine Learning and Deep Learning
10.1 Absolute Minimum = The Goal of Training
When training a neural network, we seek the absolute minimum of the loss function \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) over the parameter space. This is the global optimum — the parameter setting that makes the model best on training data.
The EVT guarantees: if we restrict to a closed bounded parameter region and \mathcal{L} is continuous, the absolute minimum exists. In practice, \boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^n (unbounded), so the EVT does not directly apply — existence of a global minimum is a non-trivial property of the loss function.
10.2 Why Absolute Minima Are Hard to Find in Deep Learning
In \mathbb{R}^n with n \sim 10^9 (modern LLMs):

There are exponentially many critical points.
Most critical points are saddle points (Hessian is indefinite), not local minima.
The boundary of parameter space is at |\boldsymbol{\theta}| \to \infty, where loss typically blows up — so boundary analysis is trivial (exclude).
Local minima exist, but the absolute minimum is essentially unreachable by gradient descent.

Strikingly, this turns out to be fine in practice: overparameterized networks have many local minima with nearly identical (and very low) loss values. The “absolute” minimum vs a “good local” minimum distinction becomes irrelevant — gradient descent finds solutions that generalize well even without reaching the true global minimum.
10.3 Constrained Absolute Optimization in ML
Weight constraints. Regularization imposes effective constraints: minimizing \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \lambda|\boldsymbol{\theta}|^2 is equivalent to minimizing \mathcal{L} on the closed ball |\boldsymbol{\theta}| \leq R. On this closed bounded set, the EVT applies — the absolute minimum exists.
Projection methods. Some algorithms explicitly project \boldsymbol{\theta} back to a feasible closed set after each gradient step, enforcing constraints. This is a direct application of the closed domain method: minimize over interior (unconstrained gradient step) then handle boundary (projection).
Hyperparameter tuning. When searching for optimal hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size) over a closed bounded grid, the EVT guarantees the absolute best hyperparameter combination exists within the grid — then we search for it systematically, exactly analogous to the closed domain method.
10.4 The Closed Domain Method as a Template for Search
The three-step method — (1) interior candidates, (2) boundary candidates, (3) compare — is the template for any complete optimization procedure:






























ML Setting”Interior” candidates”Boundary” candidatesGradient descent trainingConverged parameter (approx \nabla\mathcal{L} = 0)Constrained region boundary (clipping, projection)Architecture searchInterior model configsEdge cases (depth = 1, width = 1)Hyperparameter searchOptima found by Bayesian optGrid boundary valuesReinforcement learningStationary policyTerminal states / boundary of state space
The mathematical structure is identical: complete search requires covering both the interior and the boundary.

11. Summary
The method to find absolute extrema of a continuous f on a closed bounded domain D:
\underbrace{\nabla f = \mathbf{0} \text{ in int}(D)}_{\text{Step 1: interior}} \quad \cup \quad \underbrace{f\big|_{\partial D}}_{\text{Step 2: boundary}} \quad \xrightarrow{\text{evaluate and compare}} \quad \text{absolute max and min}
The EVT guarantees they exist. The closed domain method guarantees you find them. Together they are complete.

12. References

James Stewart, Calculus, §14.7 — Maximum and Minimum Values (Closed Domain Method, worked examples on rectangles and disks).
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (D. Auroux) — Lecture notes on finding absolute extrema; boundary analysis via parameterization and Lagrange multipliers; available at MIT OpenCourseWare.

01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.title: 01.Volumes and Double Integrals
01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.content:
“The single integral measures length swept into area. The double integral measures area swept into volume. The pattern continues — and so does the wonder.”


0. Preamble — Motivation
The definite integral \int_a^b f(x),dx computes the signed area between y = f(x) and the x-axis. Now we have a function f(x,y) of two variables — its graph is a surface z = f(x,y) floating above the xy-plane.
The question: What is the volume of the solid between this surface and the xy-plane, over a region D?
The answer is the double integral \iint_D f(x,y),dA, and building it from scratch — through the same limiting process as the single integral — is what this note is about.

1. The Riemann Sum Construction
1.1 Setting Up the Approximation
Let f : D \to \mathbb{R} be defined on a closed rectangle R = [a,b] \times [c,d]. Divide:

[a,b] into m subintervals of width \Delta x = \frac{b-a}{m}, with partition points x_0 = a < x_1 < \cdots < x_m = b
[c,d] into n subintervals of width \Delta y = \frac{d-c}{n}, with partition points y_0 = c < y_1 < \cdots < y_n = d

This creates mn sub-rectangles R_{ij} = [x_{i-1}, x_i] \times [y_{j-1}, y_j], each with area: \Delta A = \Delta x \cdot \Delta y
1.2 The Sample Points
In each R_{ij}, choose a sample point (x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_). The value f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_) is the height of the surface at that point. The volume of the thin box (column) over R_{ij} is approximately: \text{Volume of box}_{ij} \approx f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_) \cdot \Delta A
1.3 The Double Riemann Sum
Summing over all sub-rectangles: V \approx \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A
This is the double Riemann sum. As m, n \to \infty (boxes get thinner), the approximation becomes exact.
1.4 The Double Integral — Definition
Definition. If the limit exists and is the same regardless of choice of sample points, then f is integrable over R and: \iint_R f(x,y),dA = \lim_{m,n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A
Theorem. If f is continuous on R, then f is integrable over R.

Geometric meaning when f \geq 0: \iint_R f(x,y),dA is the volume of the solid between the surface z = f(x,y) and the rectangle R in the xy-plane.
When f takes negative values: Like the single integral, the double integral computes signed volume — regions where f < 0 contribute negatively.


2. Fubini’s Theorem — How to Actually Compute
The definition via limits is impractical. Fubini’s theorem converts a double integral into two successive single integrals.
2.1 The Theorem
Theorem (Fubini). If f is continuous on the rectangle R = [a,b] \times [c,d], then: \iint_R f(x,y),dA = \int_a^b \int_c^d f(x,y),dy,dx = \int_c^d \int_a^b f(x,y),dx,dy
Both iterated integrals give the same answer. The order of integration can be swapped freely (when f is continuous).
2.2 The Idea Behind Fubini — Cavalieri’s Principle
Fix x \in [a,b]. The cross-sectional area of the solid at position x is: A(x) = \int_c^d f(x,y),dy (treat x as a constant, integrate over y).
The volume is then: V = \int_a^b A(x),dx = \int_a^b \left[\int_c^d f(x,y),dy\right] dx
This is Cavalieri’s principle: volume = integral of cross-sectional areas. Fubini’s theorem is the rigorous version.
2.3 Notation
The iterated integral is written: \int_a^b \int_c^d f(x,y),dy,dx
Read from the inside out:

Inner integral: \int_c^d f(x,y),dy — integrate with respect to y, treating x as a constant. Result is a function of x.
Outer integral: \int_a^b [\cdots],dx — integrate the result with respect to x.

2.4 Worked Example — Rectangle
Compute \iint_R (x^2 + 2xy),dA where R = [0,2] \times [1,3].
Method (integrate y first, then x):
\int_0^2 \int_1^3 (x^2 + 2xy),dy,dx
Inner integral (x fixed): \int_1^3 (x^2 + 2xy),dy = \left[x^2 y + xy^2\right]_1^3 = (3x^2 + 9x) - (x^2 + x) = 2x^2 + 8x
Outer integral: \int_0^2 (2x^2 + 8x),dx = \left[\frac{2x^3}{3} + 4x^2\right]_0^2 = \frac{16}{3} + 16 = \frac{64}{3}
Verify by reversing order (integrate x first, then y):
\int_1^3 \int_0^2 (x^2 + 2xy),dx,dy
Inner integral (y fixed): \int_0^2 (x^2 + 2xy),dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3} + x^2 y\right]_0^2 = \frac{8}{3} + 4y
Outer integral: \int_1^3 \left(\frac{8}{3} + 4y\right)dy = \left[\frac{8y}{3} + 2y^2\right]_1^3 = \left(8 + 18\right) - \left(\frac{8}{3} + 2\right) = 26 - \frac{14}{3} = \frac{64}{3} \checkmark

3. Double Integrals Over General Regions
Most domains of interest are not rectangles. We integrate over general regions by describing the boundary carefully.
3.1 Type I Regions (vertical slices)
Definition. D is a Type I region if: D = {(x,y) : a \leq x \leq b,; g_1(x) \leq y \leq g_2(x)}
The y-limits depend on x — the region lies between two curves y = g_1(x) (bottom) and y = g_2(x) (top).
\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y),dy,dx
Example. The region bounded by y = x^2 and y = 2x is Type I with a = 0, b = 2 (intersection points: x^2 = 2x \implies x = 0, 2), g_1(x) = x^2, g_2(x) = 2x.
\iint_D f,dA = \int_0^2 \int_{x^2}^{2x} f(x,y),dy,dx
3.2 Type II Regions (horizontal slices)
Definition. D is a Type II region if: D = {(x,y) : c \leq y \leq d,; h_1(y) \leq x \leq h_2(y)}
The x-limits depend on y — the region lies between x = h_1(y) (left) and x = h_2(y) (right).
\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x,y),dx,dy
3.3 Choosing the Order of Integration
Some integrals are impossible (or very hard) in one order but elementary in the other. The strategy is:

Sketch the region D. Identify which description (Type I or Type II) produces integrable limits. Try the other order if the inner integral cannot be evaluated in closed form.

Example of switching order. Consider \int_0^1 \int_x^1 e^{y^2},dy,dx.
e^{y^2} has no elementary antiderivative in y — we cannot evaluate the inner integral directly.
Switch order. The region is {0 \leq x \leq y,; 0 \leq y \leq 1}. As a Type II region: 0 \leq y \leq 1, 0 \leq x \leq y.
\int_0^1 \int_0^y e^{y^2},dx,dy = \int_0^1 \left[xe^{y^2}\right]_0^y dy = \int_0^1 y e^{y^2},dy = \left[\frac{e^{y^2}}{2}\right]_0^1 = \frac{e-1}{2}

4. Volume as a Double Integral
The volume of the solid bounded above by z = f(x,y) \geq 0 and below by the region D in the xy-plane is:
V = \iint_D f(x,y),dA
This is the defining geometric interpretation.
4.1 Volume Between Two Surfaces
If f(x,y) \geq g(x,y) on D, the volume between the two surfaces z = f(x,y) (top) and z = g(x,y) (bottom) is: V = \iint_D [f(x,y) - g(x,y)],dA
4.2 Full Worked Example — Volume Under a Paraboloid
Problem. Find the volume of the solid bounded above by z = 4 - x^2 - y^2 and below by the xy-plane, over the region where z \geq 0.
The surface meets the xy-plane where 4 - x^2 - y^2 = 0, i.e., on the circle x^2 + y^2 = 4. So D = {x^2 + y^2 \leq 4}.
V = \iint_D (4 - x^2 - y^2),dA
Describe D as Type I: -2 \leq x \leq 2, -\sqrt{4-x^2} \leq y \leq \sqrt{4-x^2}.
V = \int_{-2}^{2} \int_{-\sqrt{4-x^2}}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}} (4 - x^2 - y^2),dy,dx
Inner integral: \int_{-\sqrt{4-x^2}}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}} (4 - x^2 - y^2),dy = \left[(4-x^2)y - \frac{y^3}{3}\right]_{-\sqrt{4-x^2}}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}}
Let r^2 = 4 - x^2. By symmetry in y: = 2\left[(4-x^2)\sqrt{4-x^2} - \frac{(4-x^2)^{3/2}}{3}\right] = 2(4-x^2)^{3/2}\left[1 - \frac{1}{3}\right] = \frac{4}{3}(4-x^2)^{3/2}
Outer integral: V = \int_{-2}^{2} \frac{4}{3}(4-x^2)^{3/2},dx
Substitute x = 2\sin\theta, dx = 2\cos\theta,d\theta, \sqrt{4-x^2} = 2\cos\theta, limits \theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]:
V = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \frac{4}{3}(2\cos\theta)^3 \cdot 2\cos\theta,d\theta = \frac{4}{3} \cdot 16 \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos^4\theta,d\theta
Using \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^4\theta,d\theta = \frac{3\pi}{8}:
V = \frac{64}{3} \cdot \frac{3\pi}{8} = 8\pi
(This result is more elegantly obtained using polar coordinates — see §6.)

5. Properties of the Double Integral
These mirror the single-variable properties exactly:
Linearity: \iint_D [f + g],dA = \iint_D f,dA + \iint_D g,dA, \qquad \iint_D cf,dA = c\iint_D f,dA
Additivity over regions: If D = D_1 \cup D_2 with D_1 \cap D_2 having zero area: \iint_D f,dA = \iint_{D_1} f,dA + \iint_{D_2} f,dA
Monotonicity: If f \geq g on D, then \iint_D f,dA \geq \iint_D g,dA.
Area formula: If f \equiv 1: \iint_D 1,dA = \text{Area}(D)
Average value: \bar{f} = \frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\iint_D f(x,y),dA

6. Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates
When D is a disk, annulus, or sector — or when f involves x^2 + y^2 — polar coordinates simplify the integral dramatically.
Transformation: x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta, with the crucial factor: dA = r,dr,d\theta

⚠️ The factor r is not optional. It arises from the Jacobian of the transformation: \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = r. A polar area element is a thin wedge of area r,dr,d\theta, not dr,d\theta.

Formula: \iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_\alpha^\beta \int_{r_1(\theta)}^{r_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\cdot r,dr,d\theta
6.1 Common Polar Regions

























RegionPolar DescriptionDisk x^2+y^2 \leq a^20 \leq r \leq a, 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\piUpper half-disk0 \leq r \leq a, 0 \leq \theta \leq \piAnnulus a^2 \leq x^2+y^2 \leq b^2a \leq r \leq b, 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\piSector, angle \alpha to \beta0 \leq r \leq a, \alpha \leq \theta \leq \beta
6.2 Revisiting the Paraboloid Volume
V = \iint_{x^2+y^2 \leq 4} (4 - x^2 - y^2),dA = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2 (4 - r^2),r,dr,d\theta
= \int_0^{2\pi}d\theta \cdot \int_0^2 (4r - r^3),dr = 2\pi \left[2r^2 - \frac{r^4}{4}\right]_0^2 = 2\pi\left(8 - 4\right) = 8\pi \checkmark
Far cleaner than Cartesian.
6.3 The Gaussian Integral — A Famous Application
Double integrals in polar coordinates give one of the most celebrated results in all of mathematics:
\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2},dx\right)^2 = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)},dA = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2} r,dr,d\theta = 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \pi
Therefore: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi}
This integral is the backbone of probability theory (it normalizes the Gaussian distribution) and appears throughout physics and ML.

7. Visualization
7.1 Riemann Sum Geometry
  z = f(x,y) surface
       ↑ z
       │    . . . . 
       │  .  ╔══╗  .
       │ .   ║  ║   .    ← thin rectangular column
       │.    ║  ║    .      height = f(xᵢⱼ*, yᵢⱼ*)
       │     ╚══╝           base area = Δx · Δy
       └─────────────── x
      /
     / y
    
    Volume ≈ Σᵢ Σⱼ f(xᵢⱼ*, yᵢⱼ*) · Δx · Δy

  As mesh → 0: columns become infinitely thin,
  sum → exact volume ∬_R f dA

7.2 Iterated Integral as Cross-Sections (Cavalieri)
                           Cross-section at fixed x:
  ↑ z                      A(x) = ∫_{g₁(x)}^{g₂(x)} f(x,y) dy
  │  /‾‾‾‾‾‾‾\
  │ /    ↑    \
  │/   A(x)   \            Volume = ∫_a^b A(x) dx
  └────┼────────── x
  a   x   b                "Stacking" cross-sections like bread slices

7.3 Type I vs Type II Regions
  Type I (vertical slices):      Type II (horizontal slices):
  
  y = g₂(x) ─╮                  d ──╮
              │  D                   │  D
  y = g₁(x) ─╯                  c ──╯
              a     b           x=h₁(y)  x=h₂(y)

  Fix x, sweep y from            Fix y, sweep x from
  g₁(x) to g₂(x).               h₁(y) to h₂(y).

7.4 Polar Area Element
  Polar area element dA = r dr dθ:

       θ + dθ
      /
     / ← arc length r·dθ
    /______
   |  dA  |  ← width dr
    \______/
     \
      θ

  dA ≈ (r dθ)(dr) = r dr dθ

  NOT dr dθ — the extra r accounts for
  the "stretching" as r grows.


8. Changing the Order of Integration — Strategy Guide
Step 1. Identify the region D from the given limits:

Inner limits of y: y goes from \phi_1(x) to \phi_2(x)
Outer limits of x: x goes from a to b
Sketch the region D.

Step 2. Re-describe D with the roles of x and y swapped:

New y range (outer): read off the global y extent from the sketch
New x range (inner): express x bounds as functions of y

Step 3. Write the new iterated integral and evaluate.
Example. Reverse the order: \int_0^1 \int_{y}^{1} \frac{\sin x}{x},dx,dy.
Region: {0 \leq y \leq x,; 0 \leq x \leq 1} (triangle below y=x).
As Type I: 0 \leq x \leq 1, 0 \leq y \leq x.
\int_0^1 \int_0^x \frac{\sin x}{x},dy,dx = \int_0^1 \frac{\sin x}{x} \cdot x,dx = \int_0^1 \sin x,dx = [-\cos x]_0^1 = 1 - \cos 1

9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
9.1 Probability Distributions — The Core Application
In ML, every probabilistic model involves a probability density function (pdf) p(\mathbf{x}), which satisfies p \geq 0 and: \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} p(x,y),dx,dy = 1
This normalization condition is a double integral. The Gaussian (normal) distribution in 2D is: p(x,y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_1\sigma_2} \exp!\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma_1^2} - \frac{y^2}{2\sigma_2^2}\right)
That this integrates to 1 is precisely a consequence of the Gaussian integral \int e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi} proved via polar coordinates in §6.3.
Expected values. If X, Y are continuous random variables with joint density p(x,y): \mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)] = \iint f(x,y),p(x,y),dx,dy
Every expectation in probabilistic ML — expected loss, expected reward in RL, variational lower bound in VAEs — is a (high-dimensional) integral of this form.
9.2 The Loss Function as an Expected Double Integral
In supervised learning, the population risk (expected loss over the true data distribution p(x,y)) is: \mathcal{R}(f) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim p},[\ell(f(x), y)] = \iint \ell(f(x), y),p(x,y),dx,dy
Training minimizes the empirical version (a Riemann sum approximation!): \hat{\mathcal{R}}(f) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f(x_i), y_i) \approx \mathcal{R}(f)
The law of large numbers says the empirical risk converges to the true integral as n \to \infty. The double Riemann sum is not just an approximation scheme for volumes — it is the mathematical model for how a training set approximates the underlying data distribution.
9.3 Monte Carlo Integration — The ML Workhorse
In high dimensions (n \gg 2), iterated integrals are computationally infeasible — the cost grows as N^n for a grid of N points per dimension. ML uses Monte Carlo integration instead:
\iint f(x,y),p(x,y),dx,dy \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i), \quad (x_i, y_i) \sim p
This is a stochastic Riemann sum: sample points from p, evaluate f, average. Error scales as 1/\sqrt{N} regardless of dimension — this dimension-independence is why Monte Carlo is used universally in ML (MCMC, variational inference, policy gradient in RL).
The whole theory — why MC works, its variance, importance sampling — rests on the definition of the integral as a limit of Riemann sums.
9.4 Convolutional Neural Networks — Convolution as an Integral
The convolution operation (which gives CNNs their name) is, in continuous form: (f * g)(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x - t),g(t),dt
In 2D (image processing): (f * g)(x,y) = \iint f(x - s,, y - t),g(s,t),ds,dt
A convolutional layer computes a discrete approximation of this — a double Riemann sum. Every convolution in deep learning is a double integral in disguise.
9.5 The Marginal Distribution — Integrating Out Variables
Given a joint distribution p(x,y), the marginal over x is: p(x) = \int p(x,y),dy
This is the fundamental operation in latent variable models (VAEs, GMMs, hidden Markov models): to compute the probability of observed data x, integrate out the latent variables y. The integral is usually intractable in closed form — approximating it is the central challenge of variational inference, which replaces the integral with an optimization problem.
9.6 Summary Table









































Calculus ConceptML ManifestationDouble integral \iint f,dAExpected value \mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)]Normalization \iint p = 1Valid probability densityRiemann sum approximationEmpirical risk / mini-batch gradientMonte Carlo = stochastic Riemann sumMCMC, variational inference, policy gradient2D convolution integralConvolutional layer in CNNMarginal \int p(x,y),dyLatent variable integration in generative modelsGaussian integral via polarNormalization of the Gaussian distributionChange of variables / JacobianNormalizing flows, change of representation

10. Summary of Techniques

































SituationMethodRectangular domain, continuous fFubini: either order, pick simplerGeneral domain, vertical slicesType I: \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f,dy,dxGeneral domain, horizontal slicesType II: \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f,dx,dyInner integral has no antiderivativeSwitch order of integrationD is a disk/annulus/sector, or f = f(x^2+y^2)Polar: \iint f,dA = \int!\int f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\cdot r,dr,d\thetaVolume between two surfacesV = \iint_D [f_\text{top} - f_\text{bottom}],dA

11. References

James Stewart, Calculus, §15.1–15.4 — Double integrals over rectangles, general regions, polar coordinates, applications.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (D. Auroux) — Lecture notes on double integrals, Fubini’s theorem, polar coordinates, change of variables; available at MIT OpenCourseWare.

01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.title: 02.Midpoint Rule for Double Integrals
01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.content:
“When the exact integral is out of reach, the midpoint rule gives you the best possible rectangular approximation — and tells you precisely how wrong you are.”


0. Preamble — Why Approximate?
The machinery of Fubini’s theorem computes \iint_D f(x,y),dA exactly — but only when f has a closed-form antiderivative. In practice:

f(x,y) may be given only as tabular data (sensor readings, simulation outputs)
The antiderivative of f may not exist in closed form (e.g., f = e^{-x^2 - y^2} over a square)
The domain D may be geometrically irregular

In all these cases, we need a numerical method. The midpoint rule is the simplest and most natural — it is the double Riemann sum with a specific, optimal choice of sample points.

1. Recall — The Single-Variable Midpoint Rule
For \int_a^b f(x),dx, divide [a,b] into n subintervals of width \Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}, with midpoints \bar{x}_i = a + \left(i - \frac{1}{2}\right)\Delta x:
M_n = \sum_{i=1}^n f(\bar{x}_i),\Delta x \approx \int_a^b f(x),dx
The midpoint is the optimal sample point for a rectangle because it cancels the leading error term (the linear part of f over the subinterval integrates to zero when sampled at the center).

2. The Midpoint Rule for Double Integrals — Setup
2.1 Partition the Rectangle
Let R = [a,b] \times [c,d]. Divide:

[a,b] into m equal subintervals of width \Delta x = \frac{b-a}{m}
[c,d] into n equal subintervals of width \Delta y = \frac{d-c}{n}

This produces mn sub-rectangles R_{ij} = [x_{i-1}, x_i] \times [y_{j-1}, y_j], each with area: \Delta A = \Delta x \cdot \Delta y
2.2 The Midpoints
The midpoint of the subinterval [x_{i-1}, x_i] is: \bar{x}_i = \frac{x_{i-1} + x_i}{2} = a + \left(i - \frac{1}{2}\right)\Delta x, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, m
The midpoint of the subinterval [y_{j-1}, y_j] is: \bar{y}_j = \frac{y_{j-1} + y_j}{2} = c + \left(j - \frac{1}{2}\right)\Delta y, \qquad j = 1, \ldots, n
The center of the sub-rectangle R_{ij} is (\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j).
2.3 The Midpoint Rule
Definition (Midpoint Rule for Double Integrals). The midpoint rule approximation is:
\boxed{M_{mn} = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} f(\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j),\Delta A}
where \Delta A = \Delta x \cdot \Delta y, and (\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j) is the center of the sub-rectangle R_{ij}.
Geometric meaning. Over each sub-rectangle R_{ij}, we build a rectangular column (box) whose height is the value of f at the center of the base. The midpoint rule sums the volumes of all these columns.
  z
  │       ┌─────┐   ← height = f(x̄ᵢ, ȳⱼ)
  │       │     │
  │       │     │
  └───────┴─────┴────── xy-plane
          R_{ij}
          ↑ center = (x̄ᵢ, ȳⱼ)


3. Why Midpoints? — The Error Analysis
3.1 Intuition from 1D
Over a single subinterval [x_{i-1}, x_i], expand f in a Taylor series about the midpoint \bar{x}_i: f(x) = f(\bar{x}_i) + f'(\bar{x}_i)(x - \bar{x}_i) + \frac{f''(\bar{x}_i)}{2}(x - \bar{x}_i)^2 + \cdots
Integrating over [x_{i-1}, x_i]: \int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i} f(x),dx = f(\bar{x}_i)\Delta x + f'(\bar{x}_i)\underbrace{\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i}(x - \bar{x}_i),dx}_{=,0\text{ (odd, symmetric)}} + O((\Delta x)^3)
The linear error term vanishes because (x - \bar{x}_i) is an odd function on [x_{i-1}, x_i] centered at \bar{x}_i. This is why the midpoint is better than an endpoint: it kills the O((\Delta x)^2) error per interval, leaving only O((\Delta x)^3) per interval.
The same cancellation happens in 2D over each R_{ij}.
3.2 Error Bound for the Midpoint Rule
Theorem. If |f_{xx}|, |f_{yy}| \leq K on R = [a,b]\times[c,d], then the error in the midpoint rule satisfies: |E_M| = \left|\iint_R f,dA - M_{mn}\right| \leq \frac{K(b-a)^3(d-c)}{24m^2} + \frac{K(b-a)(d-c)^3}{24n^2}
Key observations:

Error \sim O!\left(\frac{1}{m^2}\right) + O!\left(\frac{1}{n^2}\right) — doubling m and n reduces error by factor of 4.
Error \to 0 as m, n \to \infty — the rule is consistent.
The bound depends on second derivatives of f, not first — confirming the cancellation of linear error.


Compare with the naive left/right endpoint rule, whose error is O(1/m) + O(1/n) — the midpoint rule converges an order faster.


4. Worked Example I — Direct Computation
Problem. Use the midpoint rule with m = 2, n = 2 to approximate \iint_R \sqrt{x + 2y},dA where R = [0,2]\times[0,1].
Step 1 — Partition
\Delta x = \frac{2-0}{2} = 1, \qquad \Delta y = \frac{1-0}{2} = 0.5, \qquad \Delta A = 1 \times 0.5 = 0.5
Sub-rectangles (2×2 = 4 total):






























(i,j)x-intervaly-interval(1,1)[0,1][0, 0.5](1,2)[0,1][0.5, 1](2,1)[1,2][0, 0.5](2,2)[1,2][0.5, 1]
Step 2 — Midpoints
\bar{x}_1 = 0.5, \quad \bar{x}_2 = 1.5 \bar{y}_1 = 0.25, \quad \bar{y}_2 = 0.75
Step 3 — Evaluate f at Centers






























(i,j)(\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j)f = \sqrt{x + 2y}(1,1)(0.5,; 0.25)\sqrt{0.5 + 0.5} = \sqrt{1} = 1(1,2)(0.5,; 0.75)\sqrt{0.5 + 1.5} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.4142(2,1)(1.5,; 0.25)\sqrt{1.5 + 0.5} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.4142(2,2)(1.5,; 0.75)\sqrt{1.5 + 1.5} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.7321
Step 4 — Sum
M_{22} = (1 + \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}) \times 0.5 = (1 + 2\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}) \times 0.5 = (1 + 2(1.4142) + 1.7321) \times 0.5 = (1 + 2.8284 + 1.7321) \times 0.5 = 5.5605 \times 0.5 \approx 2.780
Step 5 — Compare with Exact Value
\iint_R \sqrt{x+2y},dA = \int_0^2\int_0^1 \sqrt{x+2y},dy,dx
Inner: \int_0^1 \sqrt{x+2y},dy = \left[\frac{(x+2y)^{3/2}}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{(x+2)^{3/2} - x^{3/2}}{3}
Outer: \int_0^2 \frac{(x+2)^{3/2} - x^{3/2}}{3},dx = \frac{1}{3}\left[\frac{2(x+2)^{5/2}}{5} - \frac{2x^{5/2}}{5}\right]_0^2
= \frac{2}{15}\left[(4^{5/2} - 2^{5/2}) - (2^{5/2} - 0)\right] = \frac{2}{15}\left[32 - 2\cdot 2^{5/2}\right] = \frac{2}{15}(32 - 8\sqrt{2})
= \frac{64 - 16\sqrt{2}}{15} \approx \frac{64 - 22.627}{15} \approx \frac{41.373}{15} \approx 2.758
Error: |2.780 - 2.758| = 0.022 with only a 2\times 2 grid. Already less than 1% error.

5. Worked Example II — Function Given as a Table
This is the scenario where the midpoint rule is indispensable: f is known only at discrete points.
Problem. The temperature T(x,y) (in °C) at the center of each sub-rectangle in the grid [0,4]\times[0,2] (with m=2, n=2, so \Delta x = 2, \Delta y = 1, \Delta A = 2) is measured as:




















\bar{y}_1 = 0.5\bar{y}_2 = 1.5\bar{x}_1 = 1T = 12T = 18\bar{x}_2 = 3T = 20T = 25
Estimate the total heat content \iint_R T(x,y),dA.
M_{22} = (12 + 18 + 20 + 25) \times 2 = 75 \times 2 = 150
The average temperature over R is \bar{T} = \frac{150}{8} = 18.75,^\circ\text{C} (area of R is 4 \times 2 = 8).

6. Visualization
6.1 The 2×2 Grid
  y
  1 ┤  ┌─────┬─────┐
    │  │(1,2)│(2,2)│
0.5 ┤  │  ·  │  ·  │   · = midpoint (x̄ᵢ, ȳⱼ)
    │  │(1,1)│(2,1)│
  0 ┤  └─────┴─────┘
    └──┬─────┬─────┬─ x
       0    0.5    1

(For R = [0,1]×[0,1] with m=n=2)
6.2 Why Midpoint Beats Endpoints (1D Analogy Extended to 2D)
  Over one sub-rectangle R_{ij}:

  Exact integral:        f   f + f_y·Δy + ...
                        ┌───────────────────┐
                    f + │   (curved surface) │
                  f_y·Δ │                   │
                        └───────────────────┘

  Left corner approx:   f(x_{i-1}, y_{j-1}) ← systematically low if f increasing
  Right corner approx:  f(x_i, y_j)         ← systematically high if f increasing
  Midpoint approx:      f(x̄_i, ȳ_j)        ← linear errors cancel (symmetric)

6.3 Convergence as Grid Refines
  m = n = 1:     m = n = 2:     m = n = 4:
  ┌───────┐      ┌───┬───┐      ┌─┬─┬─┬─┐
  │       │      │ · │ · │      │·│·│·│·│
  │   ·   │      ├───┼───┤      ├─┼─┼─┼─┤
  │       │      │ · │ · │      │·│·│·│·│
  └───────┘      └───┴───┘      └─┴─┴─┴─┘
   1 column      4 columns      16 columns
   Error ~ O(1)  Error ~ O(1/4)  Error ~ O(1/16)

  Each doubling of m AND n reduces error by factor 4.


7. The Midpoint Rule on General Regions
If D is not a rectangle, a standard approach is:

Enclose D in a rectangle R.
Extend f to R by setting f = 0 outside D.
Apply the midpoint rule to R.

The sub-rectangles R_{ij} that lie entirely outside D contribute zero. Sub-rectangles that straddle the boundary contribute an approximation error, but this boundary error \to 0 as the grid refines (assuming D has a reasonable boundary).
Alternative: Use the midpoint rule over each boundary-aligned sub-region after decomposing D into Type I or Type II strips.

8. Comparison with Other Rules









































RuleSample point in R_{ij}Error order (per dimension)NotesLeft endpoint(x_{i-1}, y_{j-1})O(1/m) + O(1/n)Simplest; systematic errorRight endpoint(x_i, y_j)O(1/m) + O(1/n)Systematic error (opposite sign)Midpoint(\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j)O(1/m^2) + O(1/n^2)Best among 1-point rulesTrapezoidal (2D)Average of 4 cornersO(1/m^2) + O(1/n^2)Same order as midpointSimpson’s (2D)Weighted comboO(1/m^4) + O(1/n^4)Higher order; needs even subdivisions

Key takeaway. The midpoint rule achieves the same asymptotic error order as the trapezoidal rule (both O(h^2)), but with half the function evaluations — one per sub-rectangle instead of four corner evaluations.


9. Connection to Machine Learning and Deep Learning
9.1 Mini-Batch SGD as a Midpoint Rule
In machine learning, the true objective is the expected loss: \mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \iint \ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}; x, y),p(x,y),dx,dy
This integral is approximated by sampling. When we use a mini-batch of B samples drawn uniformly from the dataset: \hat{\mathcal{R}}_B(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}; x_b, y_b)
If the data space is partitioned into B equal cells and one sample is drawn from near the center of each cell, this is structurally identical to the midpoint rule. The “midpoint” philosophy — sample the center of each region — is why stratified sampling (a structured variant of this) reduces variance in Monte Carlo integration.
The key analogy:

























Midpoint RuleMini-batch SGDPartition R into mn sub-rectanglesPartition dataset into B mini-batchesSample f at center (\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j)Evaluate loss at batch samples\frac{1}{mn}\sum_{ij} f(\bar{x}_i,\bar{y}_j)\frac{1}{B}\sum_b \ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}; x_b, y_b)Error \to 0 as mn \to \inftyGradient estimate improves as B \to \infty
9.2 Numerical Integration in Bayesian ML
Bayesian inference requires computing integrals of the form: p(y \mid x) = \int p(y \mid x, \boldsymbol{\theta}),p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathcal{D}),d\boldsymbol{\theta}
For low-dimensional \boldsymbol{\theta}, the midpoint rule (or more sophisticated quadrature) is applied directly. For high-dimensional \boldsymbol{\theta}, Monte Carlo methods (MCMC, variational inference) take over — but they are conceptually grid-free versions of the same Riemann sum philosophy.
9.3 Quadrature in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
Physics-Informed Neural Networks minimize residuals of PDEs over a domain: \mathcal{L} = \iint_D \left[\mathcal{N}[u](claude.ai/chat/x,y)\right]^2 dA
where \mathcal{N}[u] is a PDE operator applied to the network output u. This integral is approximated by the midpoint rule (or Gaussian quadrature) over a set of collocation points — the midpoints of a partition of D. The quality of the approximation directly controls training quality.
9.4 Gaussian Quadrature — The “Optimal Midpoint” Generalization
The midpoint rule uses one evaluation at the center of each sub-rectangle. Gaussian quadrature asks: what are the optimal evaluation points and weights for a given number of function evaluations? The answer (Gauss–Legendre points) generalizes the midpoint idea — place sample points where they eliminate the most error. This is used in high-performance numerical integration throughout scientific ML and finite element methods.

10. Full Procedure Summary
Given \iint_R f(x,y),dA over R = [a,b]\times[c,d], approximate with m \times n grid:
\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{m}, \quad \Delta y = \frac{d-c}{n}, \quad \Delta A = \Delta x \cdot \Delta y
\bar{x}_i = a + \left(i - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\Delta x \quad (i = 1,\ldots,m)
\bar{y}_j = c + \left(j - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\Delta y \quad (j = 1,\ldots,n)
M_{mn} = \Delta A \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} f(\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j)
To improve accuracy: increase m and n. Error decreases as O(1/m^2) + O(1/n^2).

11. References

James Stewart, Calculus, §15.1 — Double integrals over rectangles; midpoint rule approximation and examples.
MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (D. Auroux) — Lecture notes on Riemann sums, numerical approximation of double integrals; available at MIT OpenCourseWare.

01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.title: 04.Fubini's Theorem
01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.content:
“The ability to switch the order of integration is one of the most quietly powerful facts in all of analysis. Use it without ceremony — but never without understanding.”


§ 0 — Why This Theorem Exists
Before we state anything, let us ask: what problem does Fubini solve?
Suppose you want to compute
\iint_R f(x,y), dA
over some rectangle R = [a,b] \times [c,d]. The double integral is defined as a limit of Riemann sums over 2D partitions — conceptually clean, computationally brutal. What we want to do is reduce this to two ordinary 1D integrals, nested inside each other:
\int_a^b \left( \int_c^d f(x,y), dy \right) dx \quad \text{or} \quad \int_c^d \left( \int_a^b f(x,y), dx \right) dy
These are called iterated integrals. But why should they equal the double integral? And why should the two orderings give the same answer?
That is precisely what Fubini’s Theorem guarantees — under the right conditions.

§ 1 — Setup and Notation
Definition (Double Integral over a Rectangle). Let R = [a,b] \times [c,d] \subset \mathbb{R}^2. Partition [a,b] into m subintervals and [c,d] into n subintervals, forming mn subrectangles R_{ij} each of area \Delta A_{ij} = \Delta x_i \cdot \Delta y_j. Pick sample points (x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_) in each. The double integral is:
\iint_R f(x,y), dA = \lim_{|P| \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_), \Delta A_{ij}
where |P| is the norm of the partition (diameter of the largest subrectangle).
Definition (Iterated Integral). For fixed x, define g(x) = \int_c^d f(x,y), dy (integrate in y first). The iterated integral integrating y first is:
\int_a^b \int_c^d f(x,y), dy, dx = \int_a^b g(x), dx
Similarly, integrating x first:
\int_c^d \int_a^b f(x,y), dx, dy

§ 2 — The Theorem
Theorem (Fubini, rectangle version)

Let f be continuous on the rectangle R = [a,b] \times [c,d]. Then:
\iint_R f(x,y), dA = \int_a^b \int_c^d f(x,y), dy, dx = \int_c^d \int_a^b f(x,y), dx, dy

Two things are being asserted simultaneously:

The double integral equals each iterated integral (reducing 2D to nested 1D)
The two orderings are equal (order of integration can be swapped freely)


Remark (continuity is sufficient, not necessary). Continuity is the condition Stewart emphasizes, and it is the right condition for a first encounter. The theorem holds under weaker hypotheses (Fubini’s full theorem in measure theory requires only that f be integrable in the Lebesgue sense — see § 6 for the general statement). Continuity on a closed rectangle is more than enough.


§ 3 — Proof Sketch (the honest version)
A full measure-theoretic proof belongs to a real analysis course. But let us trace the argument to see why it is true.
Step 1: Continuity implies uniform continuity. Since f is continuous on the compact set R, it is uniformly continuous. This ensures that for any \varepsilon > 0, the iterated integrals are well-approximated by Riemann sums simultaneously in both variables.
Step 2: The inner integral defines a continuous function. Define
A(x) = \int_c^d f(x,y), dy
Since f is continuous jointly in (x,y), for fixed x the function y \mapsto f(x,y) is continuous (hence integrable), and A(x) is well-defined. Moreover, uniform continuity of f implies A(x) is continuous in x.
Step 3: Both equal the double integral. We use the uniform continuity to show that the Riemann sum approximations for \int_a^b A(x), dx and for \iint_R f, dA can be made to agree within \varepsilon. The key identity is:
\sum_i \sum_j f(x_i^_, y_j^_), \Delta x_i, \Delta y_j \approx \sum_i \left( \int_c^d f(x_i^*, y), dy \right) \Delta x_i \approx \int_a^b A(x), dx
Both approximation steps use uniform continuity. Taking |P| \to 0 gives the result. \blacksquare

§ 4 — Examples
Example 1 — Polynomial integrand (warm-up)
\iint_R (x^2 + 2xy), dA, \quad R = [0,1] \times [1,2]
Integrating y first:
\int_0^1 \int_1^2 (x^2 + 2xy), dy, dx
Inner integral (treat x as constant):
\int_1^2 (x^2 + 2xy), dy = \left[ x^2 y + xy^2 \right]_1^2 = (2x^2 + 4x) - (x^2 + x) = x^2 + 3x
Outer integral:
\int_0^1 (x^2 + 3x), dx = \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{3x^2}{2} \right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{3}{2} = \frac{11}{6}
Verify by switching order:
\int_1^2 \int_0^1 (x^2 + 2xy), dx, dy
Inner integral:
\int_0^1 (x^2 + 2xy), dx = \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} + x^2 y \right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3} + y
Outer integral:
\int_1^2 \left( \frac{1}{3} + y \right) dy = \left[ \frac{y}{3} + \frac{y^2}{2} \right]_1^2 = \left(\frac{2}{3} + 2\right) - \left(\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{3}{2} = \frac{11}{6} \checkmark

Example 2 — Separable functions (the cleanest case)
Suppose f(x,y) = g(x)\cdot h(y) on R = [a,b]\times[c,d]. Then:
\iint_R g(x)h(y), dA = \left(\int_a^b g(x), dx\right)\left(\int_c^d h(y), dy\right)
Proof:
\int_a^b \int_c^d g(x)h(y), dy, dx = \int_a^b g(x) \left(\int_c^d h(y), dy\right) dx = \left(\int_c^d h(y), dy\right)\int_a^b g(x), dx
The inner integral is a constant with respect to x, so it factors out. This is an extremely useful pattern — memorize it.
Concrete instance: \iint_{[0,\pi]\times[0,1]} \sin(x) \cdot e^y, dA = \int_0^\pi \sin x, dx \cdot \int_0^1 e^y, dy = 2 \cdot (e-1).

Example 3 — Switching order rescues a computation
Sometimes one iterated order is tractable and the other is not.
\int_0^1 \int_x^1 e^{y^2}, dy, dx
Integrating y first (as written) requires evaluating \int e^{y^2}, dy — a non-elementary integral. Stuck.
Switch the order. The region of integration is {(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1,, x \le y \le 1}, i.e., the triangle below the diagonal y = x in [0,1]^2.
Describing this region with y as the outer variable: 0 \le y \le 1, 0 \le x \le y.
\int_0^1 \int_0^y e^{y^2}, dx, dy = \int_0^1 e^{y^2} \cdot y, dy
Now substitute u = y^2, du = 2y, dy:
= \frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 e^u, du = \frac{1}{2}(e - 1)

Lesson: Fubini does not just tell you that you can switch order — it gives you the freedom to switch when one order makes the problem tractable.


§ 5 — Extension to General Regions
The theorem extends beyond rectangles. For a Type I region D = {(x,y) : a \le x \le b,, g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)}:
\iint_D f(x,y), dA = \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y), dy, dx
For a Type II region D = {(x,y) : c \le y \le d,, h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)}:
\iint_D f(x,y), dA = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x,y), dx, dy
The strategy is always: describe the region, identify which variable has fixed limits (the outer integral), and determine how the other variable’s bounds depend on the outer.

§ 6 — The Full Theorem (Measure-Theoretic Statement)

Fubini’s Theorem (general). Let (X, \mathcal{M}, \mu) and (Y, \mathcal{N}, \nu) be \sigma-finite measure spaces, and let f : X \times Y \to \mathbb{R} be measurable. If
\int_{X \times Y} |f|, d(\mu \times \nu) < \infty
(i.e., f \in L^1(\mu \times \nu)), then:
\int_{X \times Y} f, d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f(x,y), d\nu(y)\right) d\mu(x) = \int_Y \left(\int_X f(x,y), d\mu(x)\right) d\nu(y)

The Tonelli variant (for non-negative measurable f, no integrability hypothesis needed — equality holds though both sides may be +\infty) is often used to check the integrability hypothesis before invoking Fubini.
The Classic Counterexample
Without the absolute integrability condition, Fubini fails. Consider [0,1]^2 with:
f(x,y) = \frac{x^2 - y^2}{(x^2 + y^2)^2}
One can verify: \int_0^1 \int_0^1 f, dy, dx = \frac{\pi}{4} but \int_0^1 \int_0^1 f, dx, dy = -\frac{\pi}{4}.
The two iterated integrals disagree because \int \int |f|, dA = \infty. Fubini’s hypothesis is violated, and it shows.

§ 7 — Visualization
7.1 — The Geometric Interpretation
y
|
d |-----+-----+-----+
  |  f  |  f  |  f  |   ← fix y = y₀: integrate across x  →  A(y₀)
c |-----+-----+-----+
  a           b        x

∫_c^d A(y) dy  =  ∫_a^b B(x) dx  =  Volume under surface z = f(x,y)

The double integral computes the volume under the surface z = f(x,y) above the region R. Fubini says: slice the volume with planes x = \text{const} to get cross-sectional area A(y) (or B(x)), then integrate those areas.
7.2 — Cross-Section Mental Model
Imagine the solid {(x,y,z) : (x,y) \in R,, 0 \le z \le f(x,y)}.

Fix x = x_0. The cross-section is a 2D region in the yz-plane with area \int_c^d f(x_0, y), dy.
Slide x_0 from a to b. Integrating those cross-sectional areas gives the volume.

This is Cavalieri’s Principle in disguise. Fubini is the analytic rigorous version of: the volume is the integral of the cross-sectional areas.
z                      z = f(x,y)
|    /~~~~~\
|   /       \
|  /  cross  \
| /  section  \
|/_______________\ y
x = x₀  (fixed)

Area of slice = ∫_c^d f(x₀, y) dy


§ 8 — Fubini in AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
This is not a digression. Fubini is everywhere in modern ML.
8.1 — Expectation and Joint Distributions
The expected value of a function \phi(X, Y) under a joint distribution p(x,y) is:
\mathbb{E}[\phi(X,Y)] = \iint \phi(x,y), p(x,y), dx, dy
Fubini lets us marginalize in any order:
= \int \left(\int \phi(x,y), p(x|y), dx\right) p(y), dy = \int \left(\int \phi(x,y), p(y|x), dy\right) p(x), dx
Every time you condition on a variable and integrate out another, you are invoking Fubini.
8.2 — The ELBO in Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
The Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) involves:
\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}\left[\log p(x|z)\right] - \text{KL}(q(z|x) | p(z))
The KL divergence term requires switching integration and differentiation in a way that is only valid because the integrands are sufficiently well-behaved — Fubini-type arguments underlie the interchange.
8.3 — Gradient of Expectations (REINFORCE, Score Function Estimator)
In reinforcement learning and variational inference, one needs:
\nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta(x)}[f(x)] = \nabla_\theta \int f(x), p_\theta(x), dx = \int f(x), \nabla_\theta p_\theta(x), dx
Interchanging the gradient and the integral is justified by the Leibniz integral rule — a direct corollary of Fubini applied to a product measure (treating \theta as one coordinate, x as another). The score function trick \nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(x) = \frac{\nabla_\theta p_\theta(x)}{p_\theta(x)} is the payoff.
8.4 — Kernel Methods and Integral Operators
In kernel machines and Gaussian Processes, the kernel matrix entry is:
K(x, x') = \int \phi(x, \omega), \phi(x', \omega), p(\omega), d\omega
(Random Fourier Features, Bochner’s theorem). Manipulating such integrals — bounding generalization error, computing posterior means — routinely requires switching integration order.
8.5 — Convolutional Neural Networks
The convolution operation at layer l:
(f * g)(x) = \int f(x - y), g(y), dy
is itself an integral transform. Properties like associativity of convolution — essential to understanding deep network composition — follow from Fubini:
\int \int f(x - y), g(y - z), h(z), dy, dz = \int h(z) \left(\int f(x-y), g(y-z), dy\right) dz
The inner integral is a convolution; rearranging the order is Fubini.
8.6 — Normalizing Flows and Change of Variables
In normalizing flows, one models a complex distribution by a sequence of invertible transformations. The change of variables formula in multiple dimensions:
p_X(x) = p_Z(f^{-1}(x)) \left|\det J_{f^{-1}}(x)\right|
requires that the Jacobian determinant integrates correctly under the joint distribution — which is again a Fubini-type argument ensuring the integral of p_X over \mathbb{R}^n equals 1.

§ 9 — Summary and Working Rules





























SituationWhat to doRectangle, f continuousApply Fubini freely in either orderNon-rectangular regionSketch the region; decide Type I or Type II; set up limits carefullyOne order leads to non-elementary integralSwitch the order of integrationVerifying integrability (general f)Check \iint \|f\| < \infty first (Tonelli), then invoke FubiniCounterexample riskRemember: switching order without absolute integrability can give wrong answers
The working habit: Always sketch the region before setting up any iterated integral. Getting the limits wrong is far more common than misapplying the theorem itself.

§ 10 — References


Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §§ 15.2–15.3. — The standard presentation; excellent for building computational fluency and geometric intuition.


MIT 18.02: Multivariable Calculus (Auroux et al.) — Lecture notes on double integrals and iterated integrals; particularly clear on region description and switching order.


Rudin, Walter. Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed. Chapter 8. — The definitive rigorous treatment of Fubini–Tonelli in the Lebesgue setting.


Folland, Gerald. Real Analysis, 2nd ed. §2.5. — Careful proof with full measure-theoretic detail; the counterexample is treated explicitly.
