01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.title: 05.Average Values via Double Integrals
01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.content:
“The average is the single number that, spread uniformly over the region, produces the same total. Everything else is bookkeeping.”


§ 0 — Motivation: From 1D to 2D
Recall the average value of a function f(x) on [a,b] from single-variable calculus:
f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{b-a} \int_a^b f(x), dx
The denominator b-a is the measure (length) of the domain. The integral is the total accumulation. Their ratio is the average.
In two dimensions, nothing changes philosophically. The domain now has area instead of length, and we integrate over a region D \subset \mathbb{R}^2 instead of an interval. The formula becomes:
\boxed{f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{A(D)} \iint_D f(x,y), dA}
where A(D) = \iint_D dA is the area of D.

Intuition: Imagine pouring water whose depth at (x,y) is f(x,y) into a flat-bottomed container of the same footprint D. The water redistributes to a uniform depth f_{\text{avg}}. The total volume is conserved:
f_{\text{avg}} \cdot A(D) = \iint_D f(x,y), dA


§ 1 — Formal Definition
Definition. Let f be integrable on a bounded region D \subset \mathbb{R}^2 with area A(D) > 0. The average value of f over D is:
f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{A(D)} \iint_D f(x,y), dA
Remarks:

A(D) is itself a double integral: A(D) = \iint_D 1, dA.
If f is continuous and D is connected, the Mean Value Theorem for Double Integrals guarantees existence of a point (x_0, y_0) \in D with f(x_0, y_0) = f_{\text{avg}} (see § 4).
The definition extends immediately to \mathbb{R}^n: replace area with n-dimensional volume.


§ 2 — Mean Value Theorem for Double Integrals
Theorem

Let f be continuous on a closed, bounded, connected region D. Then there exists at least one point (x_0, y_0) \in D such that:
f(x_0, y_0) = \frac{1}{A(D)} \iint_D f(x,y), dA = f_{\text{avg}}

Proof
Since f is continuous on compact D, it attains its minimum m and maximum M:
m \le f(x,y) \le M \quad \forall, (x,y) \in D
Integrating over D:
m \cdot A(D) \le \iint_D f, dA \le M \cdot A(D)
Dividing by A(D):
m \le \underbrace{\frac{1}{A(D)} \iint_D f, dA}_{f_{\text{avg}}} \le M
So f_{\text{avg}} \in [m, M]. Since f is continuous on connected D, by the Intermediate Value Theorem, f takes every value between m and M. In particular, there exists (x_0, y_0) \in D with f(x_0, y_0) = f_{\text{avg}}. \blacksquare

Note: The MVT guarantees existence of such a point, but not uniqueness. There may be many such points, or (for non-connected D) none at all.


§ 3 — Computing Average Values: Full Examples
Example 1 — Average of a polynomial over a rectangle
Problem. Find the average value of f(x,y) = x^2 y + 3y^2 over R = [0,2] \times [0,1].
Step 1: Area.
A(R) = (2-0)(1-0) = 2
Step 2: Double integral.
\iint_R (x^2 y + 3y^2), dA = \int_0^2 \int_0^1 (x^2 y + 3y^2), dy, dx
Inner integral (x fixed):
\int_0^1 (x^2 y + 3y^2), dy = \left[\frac{x^2 y^2}{2} + y^3\right]_0^1 = \frac{x^2}{2} + 1
Outer integral:
\int_0^2 \left(\frac{x^2}{2} + 1\right) dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{6} + x\right]_0^2 = \frac{8}{6} + 2 = \frac{4}{3} + 2 = \frac{10}{3}
Step 3: Average.
f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{10}{3} = \frac{5}{3}

Example 2 — Average temperature over a triangular region
Problem. The temperature at (x,y) is T(x,y) = 4x + 2y (in °C). Find the average temperature over the triangle D with vertices (0,0), (2,0), (0,4).
Step 1: Describe D.
The hypotenuse has equation \frac{x}{2} + \frac{y}{4} = 1, i.e., y = 4 - 2x. So:
D = {(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 2,; 0 \le y \le 4 - 2x}
Step 2: Area.
A(D) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \text{base} \cdot \text{height} = \frac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4
(Or via integration: \int_0^2 (4-2x), dx = [4x - x^2]_0^2 = 4.)
Step 3: Double integral.
\iint_D (4x + 2y), dA = \int_0^2 \int_0^{4-2x} (4x + 2y), dy, dx
Inner integral:
\int_0^{4-2x} (4x + 2y), dy = \left[4xy + y^2\right]_0^{4-2x} = 4x(4-2x) + (4-2x)^2
= (4-2x)\left[4x + (4-2x)\right] = (4-2x)(4+2x) = 16 - 4x^2
Outer integral:
\int_0^2 (16 - 4x^2), dx = \left[16x - \frac{4x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = 32 - \frac{32}{3} = \frac{64}{3}
Step 4: Average.
T_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{64}{3} = \frac{16}{3} \approx 5.33^\circ\text{C}

Example 3 — Average over a disk (polar coordinates)
Problem. Find the average value of f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 over the disk D: x^2 + y^2 \le R^2.
Step 1: Area.
A(D) = \pi R^2
Step 2: Switch to polar. x^2 + y^2 = r^2, dA = r, dr, d\theta.
\iint_D (x^2 + y^2), dA = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^R r^2 \cdot r, dr, d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi} d\theta \int_0^R r^3, dr
= 2\pi \cdot \frac{R^4}{4} = \frac{\pi R^4}{2}
Step 3: Average.
f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{\pi R^2} \cdot \frac{\pi R^4}{2} = \frac{R^2}{2}

Sanity check: f = r^2 ranges from 0 (center) to R^2 (boundary). The average R^2/2 lies strictly between them. ✓
Geometric insight: The average is NOT R^2/2 because of a naive “midpoint” argument — it is R^2/2 because points near the boundary carry more area weight (circumference 2\pi r grows with r), pulling the average above the naive midpoint R^2/2… wait, here the naive midpoint is R^2/2. But in general, the area-weighted average shifts the answer. For f = r over the disk: f_{\text{avg}} = 2R/3 \ne R/2 — the boundary-heavy weighting pulls the average toward the rim.


§ 4 — Visualization
4.1 — The “Flatten the Water” Picture
  z                             z = f_avg (flat surface)
  |    /\      /\              |‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾|
  |   /  \    /  \     →→→    |                     |
  |  /    \  /    \           |   same total volume  |
  | /      \/      \          |_____________________|
  |________________________ x
       f(x,y) varies            f_avg is uniform

  ∫∫ f dA  =  f_avg × A(D)

4.2 — Locating the Mean Value Point
For Example 2 (T = 4x + 2y over the triangle), the average was 16/3. The MVT guarantees a point with 4x_0 + 2y_0 = 16/3 inside D. This is a line segment; any point on it inside D works. The theorem asserts existence — it does not pinpoint a unique location.
4.3 — Effect of Region Shape on the Average
For f(x,y) = x (temperature increasing left-to-right):





























Region DA(D)\iint x, dAf_{\text{avg}}Square [0,1]^211/21/2Triangle: vertices (0,0),(1,0),(0,1)1/21/61/3Triangle: vertices (0,0),(1,0),(1,1)1/25/125/6
The shape of D shifts the average by changing how much area lies near large vs. small values of f — the geometric analogue of a weighted average.

§ 5 — Weighted Average and Probability Density
When the region carries a weight function w(x,y) \ge 0 (a probability density, mass density, etc.), the weighted average is:
\langle f \rangle_w = \frac{\iint_D f(x,y), w(x,y), dA}{\iint_D w(x,y), dA}
The standard average is the special case w \equiv 1.
Center of mass is a weighted average of position:
\bar{x} = \frac{\iint_D x, \rho(x,y), dA}{\iint_D \rho(x,y), dA}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{\iint_D y, \rho(x,y), dA}{\iint_D \rho(x,y), dA}
where \rho is the surface mass density.

§ 6 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
6.1 — Expected Value IS a Weighted Average Integral
The expected value of a function \phi(x,y) under a joint density p(x,y):
\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y) \sim p}[\phi(X,Y)] = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} \phi(x,y), p(x,y), dx, dy
is precisely a weighted average with weight w = p. The denominator \iint p, dA = 1 (probability axiom). Every time you compute an expectation in ML, you are computing the weighted average value of a function over its domain.
6.2 — Loss Function as Average Loss
The empirical risk (training loss) in ML is a discrete average:
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \ell(\hat{y}_i, y_i)
Its continuous population analogue is exactly the average value integral:
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \iint \ell(f_\theta(x), y), p(x, y), dx, dy
The difference between training loss (sample average) and population loss (integral average) is generalization error — and bounding it requires understanding how well discrete sums approximate double integrals (uniform laws of large numbers, VC theory).
6.3 — Batch Normalization
Batch normalization computes the mean and variance of activations over the spatial dimensions of a feature map. For a H \times W feature map F:
\mu = \frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i=1}^H \sum_{j=1}^W F_{ij}
This is a discrete double average — the exact discretization of \frac{1}{A} \iint F(x,y), dA over the spatial domain. The continuous formulation is used when deriving the theory of spatial statistics and analyzing convolutional architectures.
6.4 — Gaussian Process Posterior Mean
In a Gaussian Process, the posterior mean function is:
\mu^*(x) = \int k(x, x'), \alpha(x'), dx'
where k is the kernel and \alpha encodes the training data. Over a 2D input space (x_1, x_2), this is a weighted average value of \alpha with weight kernel k — a double integral of exactly the form § 5 above.
6.5 — Spatial Pooling in CNNs
Global Average Pooling (GAP) — common in modern architectures (ResNet, GoogLeNet) — replaces the final fully-connected layer with:
\text{GAP}(F^{(c)}) = \frac{1}{H \cdot W} \sum_{i,j} F^{(c)}_{ij}
for channel c. This is literally the discrete average value of the feature map over the spatial domain. The motivation: compute the average activation of each feature detector across the entire image. The continuous limit is f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{A} \iint F^{(c)}(x,y), dA.
GAP reduces a 3D tensor to a vector while being translation-invariant — a property that follows from the invariance of the average value under rearrangement of the domain (Fubini + change of variables).
6.6 — Monte Carlo Integration
The average value formula is the basis of Monte Carlo integration. To compute \iint_D f, dA:

Sample N points (x_i, y_i) uniformly from D.
Estimate: \iint_D f, dA \approx A(D) \cdot \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i)

Because the sample mean \frac{1}{N}\sum f(x_i, y_i) is an unbiased estimator of f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{A(D)}\iint f, dA, by the Law of Large Numbers.
Monte Carlo integration is the workhorse of:

Bayesian posterior approximation (MCMC sampling)
Policy gradient methods in RL (estimating \mathbb{E}_\pi[R])
Training diffusion models (DDPM, score matching objectives)
Dropout (averaging over random subnetworks at test time)

The error scales as O(1/\sqrt{N}) regardless of dimension — this dimension-independence is why MC dominates for high-dimensional integrals, while deterministic quadrature degrades exponentially (the curse of dimensionality).

§ 7 — Summary





























ConceptFormulaAverage value over Df_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{1}{A(D)} \iint_D f, dAArea of DA(D) = \iint_D 1, dAReconstruction identity\iint_D f, dA = f_{\text{avg}} \cdot A(D)Weighted average\langle f \rangle_w = \dfrac{\iint f, w, dA}{\iint w, dA}MVT guarantee\exists,(x_0,y_0)\in D s.t. f(x_0,y_0) = f_{\text{avg}} (f cts, D connected)
The workflow for every problem:
1. Sketch D
2. Compute A(D)  [geometry or integration]
3. Set up ∬_D f dA  [choose order, set variable limits]
4. Evaluate the iterated integral
5. Divide by A(D)


§ 8 — References


Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. § 15.3 — Average Value of a Function. The worked examples and the MVT statement follow Stewart’s treatment closely.


MIT 18.02: Multivariable Calculus (Auroux) — Lecture notes on double integrals; the “flatten the solid” geometric interpretation is developed there.


Bishop, Christopher. Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, § 1.2 — Probability densities and expectations as weighted averages.

01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.title: 06.Double Integrals Over General Regions
01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.content:
“The art of integration is the art of finding the right order.” — a recurring theme in 18.02


§0 — Personal Preamble
When we first define \iint_R f,dA over a rectangle, life is pleasant: both limits are constants and Fubini’s theorem is almost a triviality. The interesting mathematics begins the moment the region D stops being a box. This note develops the full rigorous theory, catalogues the practical techniques, supplies worked examples, and — because it cannot be avoided — explains why this machinery is exactly what gradient descent and the study of probability distributions secretly rely on.
All references are to Stewart, Calculus (8e) (§§15.2–15.3) and MIT 18.02 lecture notes.

§1 — Motivation: Why Leave the Rectangle?
In applications the domain of integration is almost never a rectangle.

A probability density p(x,y) is integrated over the region {(x,y): x^2 + y^2 \le 1}.
A neural network’s weight space carries a prior supported on a simplex.
A fluid-dynamics calculation integrates pressure over the cross-section of a pipe.

We need a definition of \iint_D f,dA that handles arbitrary bounded regions D \subset \mathbb{R}^2.

§2 — The Rigorous Definition (Extension by Zero)
Setup. Let D \subset \mathbb{R}^2 be a bounded region and f : D \to \mathbb{R} bounded. Enclose D in a rectangle R = [a,b]\times[c,d].
Define the extended function:
F(x,y) = \begin{cases} f(x,y) & \text{if } (x,y) \in D \ 0 & \text{if } (x,y) \in R \setminus D \end{cases}
Definition (Stewart §15.2). If F is integrable over R, we set
\boxed{\iint_D f,dA ;:=; \iint_R F,dA}
Remark. The value is independent of which rectangle R we choose (since F = 0 outside D). The non-trivial part is proving F is integrable — this requires the boundary \partial D to have measure zero (e.g., \partial D is a piecewise-smooth curve), which covers every region we encounter in practice.

§3 — Type I and Type II Regions
The payoff of the abstract definition is the following concrete evaluation theorem. We isolate two archetypal shapes.
3.1 Type I Region
D = {(x,y) : a \le x \le b,; g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)}
y
│      g₂(x)
│    ╭──────╮
│   /        \
│  /  D       \
│  \          /
│   ╰──────╯
│      g₁(x)
│
└───────────────── x
    a           b

Theorem (Fubini, Type I). If f is continuous on D:
\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y),dy,dx
Proof sketch. The extension-by-zero F equals f when g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x) and 0 elsewhere. By Fubini on the rectangle:
\iint_R F,dA = \int_a^b \left[\int_c^d F(x,y),dy\right]dx = \int_a^b \left[\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y),dy\right]dx \qquad \square
3.2 Type II Region
D = {(x,y) : c \le y \le d,; h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)}
y
d ─────────────────╮
│                   │
│      D            │
│                   │
c ─────────────────╯
│  h₁(y)      h₂(y)
└──────────────────── x

Theorem (Fubini, Type II). If f is continuous on D:
\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x,y),dx,dy

§4 — Properties (The Algebra of Double Integrals)
Let D, D_1, D_2 be regions and f, g integrable.





























PropertyStatementLinearity\iint_D (\alpha f + \beta g),dA = \alpha\iint_D f,dA + \beta\iint_D g,dAAdditivityIf D = D_1 \cup D_2, D_1 \cap D_2 has area 0: \iint_D f,dA = \iint_{D_1} f,dA + \iint_{D_2} f,dAMonotonicityf \le g on D \Rightarrow \iint_D f,dA \le \iint_D g,dAArea formula\iint_D 1,dA = \text{Area}(D)Estimationm\cdot\text{Area}(D) \le \iint_D f,dA \le M\cdot\text{Area}(D) when m \le f \le M

§5 — Worked Examples
Example 1 — Triangle (Type I)
Compute \displaystyle\iint_D x,dA where D is the triangle with vertices (0,0), (1,0), (1,1).
Setting up the region. The boundary lines are x=1, y=0, and y=x. As a Type I region:
D = {(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1,; 0 \le y \le x}
y
1 ─        ╱│
│         ╱ │
│        ╱  │
│       ╱ D │
│      ╱    │
0 ────╱─────┤── x
     0      1

Evaluation.
\iint_D x,dA = \int_0^1 \int_0^x x,dy,dx = \int_0^1 x\cdot[y]_0^x,dx = \int_0^1 x^2,dx = \frac{1}{3}
Check via Type II. Rewrite as D = {0 \le y \le 1,; y \le x \le 1}:
\int_0^1 \int_y^1 x,dx,dy = \int_0^1 \frac{1-y^2}{2},dy = \frac{1}{2}\left[y - \frac{y^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3} \checkmark

Example 2 — Reversing the Order of Integration
Compute \displaystyle\int_0^1 \int_x^1 e^{y^2},dy,dx.
The inner integral \int_x^1 e^{y^2},dy has no closed form in this order. Reverse order.
The region. The original order (Type I) describes:
D = {(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1,; x \le y \le 1}
As Type II:
D = {(x,y) : 0 \le y \le 1,; 0 \le x \le y}
y
1 ─╮
│╲ │
│ ╲│ D
│  ╲
│   ╲
0 ───╲─── x
0     1

Evaluation.
\int_0^1 \int_0^y e^{y^2},dx,dy = \int_0^1 y,e^{y^2},dy = \frac{1}{2}\left[e^{y^2}\right]_0^1 = \frac{e-1}{2}

Key lesson. Switching the order of integration is not a trick — it is a rigorous operation guaranteed by Fubini’s theorem. The limits change precisely because the same region D is described in two different orders.


Example 3 — Parabolic Region
Compute \displaystyle\iint_D (x+y),dA where D = {(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1,; x^2 \le y \le \sqrt{x}}.
Note y = x^2 and y = \sqrt{x} intersect at (0,0) and (1,1), and x^2 \le \sqrt{x} on [0,1].
y
1 ─────────────────╮  ← y = √x
│          ╭───╯
│       ╭──╯   D
│    ╭──╯
│ ╭──╯  ← y = x²
0 ─────────────────── x
  0                 1

\iint_D (x+y),dA = \int_0^1\int_{x^2}^{\sqrt{x}}(x+y),dy,dx
Inner integral:
\int_{x^2}^{\sqrt{x}}(x+y),dy = \left[xy + \frac{y^2}{2}\right]_{x^2}^{\sqrt{x}} = \left(x^{3/2} + \frac{x}{2}\right) - \left(x^3 + \frac{x^4}{2}\right)
Outer integral:
\int_0^1\left(x^{3/2} + \frac{x}{2} - x^3 - \frac{x^4}{2}\right)dx = \frac{2}{5} + \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{10} = \frac{3}{10}

Example 4 — Non-elementary Region via Additivity
Compute the area of the region enclosed between y = \sin x and y = \cos x on [0, \pi].
The curves cross at x = \pi/4. Split D = D_1 \cup D_2:
\text{Area} = \int_0^{\pi/4}(\cos x - \sin x),dx + \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi}(\sin x - \cos x),dx
= [\sin x + \cos x]_0^{\pi/4} + [-\cos x - \sin x]_{\pi/4}^\pi = (\sqrt{2}-1) + (1+\sqrt{2}) = 2\sqrt{2}

§6 — The Non-Obvious Subtlety: When Fubini Fails
Fubini’s theorem requires absolute integrability: \iint_D |f|,dA < \infty.
Counterexample (Sierpiński-type). Define
f(x,y) = \frac{x^2 - y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}, \quad D = [0,1]^2
One can verify:
\int_0^1\left(\int_0^1 f,dy\right)dx = \frac{\pi}{4}, \qquad \int_0^1\left(\int_0^1 f,dx\right)dy = -\frac{\pi}{4}
The iterated integrals are unequal because \iint_D |f|,dA = \infty. This is the canonical warning that order cannot be swapped carelessly.

§7 — Connection to Probability Theory
Let (X, Y) be a jointly continuous random vector with density p(x,y) \ge 0.
The marginal density of X is:
p_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty p(x,y),dy
This is precisely the inner integral of a double integral over the strip {X = x}. Computing \mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)] is:
\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)] = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} g(x,y),p(x,y),dA
Fubini’s theorem is invoked every time we compute a marginal or compute an expectation by iterated integration.

§8 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
This is not decorative. Double integrals over general regions are structurally embedded in modern ML.
8.1 Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs)
A normalizing flow maps a simple distribution p_Z to a complex distribution p_X via an invertible map \phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d. The probability of X \in D is:
\Pr(X \in D) = \iint_D p_X(x,y),dA = \iint_{\phi^{-1}(D)} p_Z(z_1,z_2),|\det J_\phi|,dA
The change of variables — a multivariable generalization of substitution in double integrals — is the mathematical core of this technique. The region \phi^{-1}(D) is typically not a rectangle: it is a general region determined by the geometry of the flow.
8.2 Gaussian Processes and Kernel Machines
The covariance operator in a Gaussian Process is:
(Kf)(x) = \int_D k(x, x') f(x'),dx'
For 2D spatial data (images, spatial predictions), this becomes:
(Kf)(x_1, x_2) = \iint_D k!\left((x_1,x_2),(x_1',x_2')\right) f(x_1',x_2'),dx_1',dx_2'
The domain D is the support of the data — often a non-rectangular region like a geographic boundary or an image mask.
8.3 Variational Inference and the ELBO
The Evidence Lower Bound in variational autoencoders is:
\mathcal{L}(q) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}!\left[\log p(x \mid z)\right] - \mathrm{KL}(q(z) | p(z))
Both terms involve integrals of the form \iint q(z) \log[\cdot],dz. In practice, the variational family q is a Gaussian, and the reparameterisation trick converts this into a double integral over a rectangle in the (\mu, \sigma) parameter space — but the original problem lives over a general latent region.
8.4 Monte Carlo Integration: Numerical Double Integrals
When the region D is complex (e.g., the feasible region of a constrained optimisation), double integrals are estimated by:
\iint_D f,dA \approx \frac{\text{Area}(D)}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i), \quad (x_i, y_i) \sim \text{Uniform}(D)
Sampling uniformly from a general region D — not a rectangle — is a non-trivial computational geometry problem, and the correctness of the estimator rests on the theory of this section.
8.5 Convolutional Neural Networks (CNFs) — Continuous Limit
A 2D convolution is:
(f * g)(x, y) = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x - x', y - y'),g(x', y'),dA
In the continuous limit of a CNN, the “receptive field” of a neuron is a bounded, possibly non-rectangular region D, and the activation is \iint_D f(x-x', y-y'),g(x',y'),dA. Understanding how varying D changes the integral is precisely the theory developed here.

§9 — Visualization Gallery
9.1 The Key Mantra for Setting Limits
For a Type I integral ∫∫_D f dA:

STEP 1:  Sketch D.
STEP 2:  Draw a vertical strip at position x.
          ─ Its bottom is y = g₁(x)
          ─ Its top    is y = g₂(x)
          These become the y-limits.
STEP 3:  The strip sweeps from x = a to x = b.
          These become the x-limits.

∫_a^b  ∫_{g₁(x)}^{g₂(x)}  f(x,y) dy dx
outer  ←────────────────────────────────
        inner

For Type II: draw a horizontal strip, read off x-limits as functions of y.
9.2 Region Classification Flowchart
            Is D a rectangle?
                   │
         ┌─── Yes ──┘── No ───┐
         │                    │
    Use constant         Can D be described as
    limits directly.     x ∈ [a,b], g₁(x) ≤ y ≤ g₂(x)?
                                │
                     ┌─── Yes ──┘── No ───┐
                     │                    │
                Type I            y ∈ [c,d], h₁(y) ≤ x ≤ h₂(y)?
                                          │
                               ┌─── Yes ──┘── No ────────────┐
                               │                              │
                           Type II              Split into Type I + Type II
                                                  or use change of variables
                                                  (polar, etc.)

9.3 Switching Order — The Geometric Key
Original (dy dx):              Reversed (dx dy):

y                              y
│    ┌────┐ ← y = g₂(x)       d ──────────────╮
│    │    │                    │               │
│    │ D  │                    │     D         │
│    │    │                    │               │
│    └────┘ ← y = g₁(x)       c ──────────────╯
└────┴────┴──── x              └──┬────────────── x
     a    b                       h₁(y)    h₂(y)

Fix x, sweep y.                Fix y, sweep x.
Outer integral: x.             Outer integral: y.


§10 — Theoretical Depth: Measure-Theoretic Footnotes
(For the reader who wants the full story.)
Why does \partial D having measure zero matter? The Riemann integral on R exists iff the set of discontinuities of F has Lebesgue measure zero (Lebesgue’s theorem on Riemann integrability). The discontinuities of F are precisely the points of \partial D where f \ne 0, so if \partial D has measure zero, F is Riemann integrable.
Lebesgue’s criterion. F : R \to \mathbb{R} is Riemann integrable \iff F is bounded and the set of its discontinuities has Lebesgue measure zero.
This is why any region bounded by finitely many smooth curves is legal: a smooth curve in \mathbb{R}^2 has 2D Lebesgue measure zero.
Fubini–Tonelli. In Lebesgue theory, for f \ge 0 measurable (Tonelli) or \int\int |f|,dA < \infty (Fubini):
\int_D f,d(m_1 \times m_2) = \int_a^b \left[\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y),dm_1(y)\right]dm_1(x)
The Riemann version we use is a special case.

§11 — Common Mistakes and Pathologies



































MistakeWhat Goes WrongRemedySwapping limits without re-drawingDescribes a different region or the empty setAlways re-derive limits from a fresh sketchForgetting to check g_1 \le g_2Negative area contributionVerify inequality holds on the entire x-intervalSplitting at the wrong x-valueRegion mis-describedFind intersections of boundary curves firstApplying Fubini when $\int\intf= \infty$Treating a non-Type-I region as Type IVariable limits depend on y, not xCheck: are the top/bottom bounds functions of x only?

§12 — Summary Theorem Sheet
Theorem 1 (Fubini, Type I). If f is continuous on D = {a \le x \le b,; g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)}: \iint_D f,dA = \int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y),dy,dx
Theorem 2 (Fubini, Type II). If f is continuous on D = {c \le y \le d,; h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)}: \iint_D f,dA = \int_c^d\int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x,y),dx,dy
Theorem 3 (Additivity). If D = D_1 \cup D_2 and D_1 \cap D_2 has area zero: \iint_D f,dA = \iint_{D_1} f,dA + \iint_{D_2} f,dA
Theorem 4 (Area). \text{Area}(D) = \iint_D 1,dA

§13 — References

Stewart, J. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Cengage, 2016. §§15.2–15.3.
MIT OpenCourseWare. 18.02 Multivariable Calculus, Lecture Notes on Double Integrals. Available at: ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/
Apostol, T. Mathematical Analysis, 2nd ed. Addison-Wesley, 1974. §Ch. 14 (for the Lebesgue criterion).
Bishop, C.M. Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer, 2006. §§2.3, 10.1 (for the ML connections).
Kingma, D. & Welling, M. “Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes.” ICLR 2014. (ELBO and reparameterisation.)

01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.title: 07.Properties of Double Integrals
01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.content:
“Properties are not bureaucratic formalities — each one is a theorem that earns its proof.”


§0 — Preamble
Single-variable integration has a clean list of properties: linearity, additivity, monotonicity, the triangle inequality. Double integrals inherit every one of these, and add a few of their own born from the two-dimensional domain. This note proves each property rigorously from the definition, supplies geometric intuition, catalogues the failure modes, and traces the properties into their machine learning incarnations — because every identity here gets used implicitly in probabilistic modelling and numerical integration.
Convention throughout. D \subset \mathbb{R}^2 is a bounded region whose boundary has measure zero. All functions are assumed bounded and continuous unless otherwise stated, ensuring Riemann integrability.

§1 — The Definition We Are Working From
Recall: enclose D in a rectangle R. Partition R into sub-rectangles R_{ij} of area \Delta A_{ij} = \Delta x_i \Delta y_j. Choose sample points (x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_). The double integral is the limit of the Riemann sum:
\iint_D f,dA := \lim_{|P| \to 0} \sum_{i,j} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A_{ij}
where the sum ranges only over sub-rectangles that intersect D, and |P| is the mesh (largest diagonal of any sub-rectangle).
Every property below follows from manipulating this sum and taking limits.

§2 — Property I: Linearity
2.1 Homogeneity
\boxed{\iint_D c,f(x,y),dA = c\iint_D f(x,y),dA, \quad c \in \mathbb{R}}
Proof. At the level of Riemann sums:
\sum_{i,j} [c,f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_)],\Delta A_{ij} = c\sum_{i,j} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A_{ij}
Taking |P| \to 0 and using the linearity of limits gives the result. \square
2.2 Additivity of Integrand
\boxed{\iint_D [f(x,y) + g(x,y)],dA = \iint_D f(x,y),dA + \iint_D g(x,y),dA}
Proof. Identical: the Riemann sum of a sum is the sum of Riemann sums, and limits distribute over finite sums. \square
2.3 Combined Linearity
Combining 2.1 and 2.2: for \alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R},
\iint_D [\alpha f + \beta g],dA = \alpha\iint_D f,dA + \beta\iint_D g,dA
Geometric reading. \iint_D f,dA is the signed volume under z = f(x,y) over D. Scaling f by c scales the volume by c; stacking two surfaces f and g yields the sum of their volumes.
z
│       f+g
│      ╱╲
│     ╱  ╲   ← volume under f+g = vol(f) + vol(g)
│    ╱  f  ╲
│   ╱────────╲
│  ╱    g     ╲
└──────────────── xy-plane (D)

ML connection. The expected value operator \mathbb{E} is a double integral (when the state space is \mathbb{R}^2):
\mathbb{E}[\alpha f(X,Y) + \beta g(X,Y)] = \alpha,\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)] + \beta,\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)]
This is exactly linearity of the double integral against the density p(x,y). Every linearity argument in a derivation involving expected values — loss function decomposition, bias-variance tradeoff, ELBO manipulation — is an invocation of this property.

§3 — Property II: Domain Additivity
\boxed{\iint_D f,dA = \iint_{D_1} f,dA + \iint_{D_2} f,dA}
whenever D = D_1 \cup D_2 and D_1 \cap D_2 has area zero (e.g., they share only a boundary curve).
Proof. The extension-by-zero functions F_1, F_2 (of f onto a common rectangle R) satisfy F_1 + F_2 = F pointwise a.e. (they agree except on the shared boundary, which has measure zero). Linearity of the integral over R gives the result. \square
Geometric reading.
         D₁        │        D₂
  ╭───────────╮    │    ╭───────────╮
  │           │    │    │           │
  │  ∫∫f dA  │ ───┼─── │  ∫∫f dA  │
  │   D₁      │    │    │   D₂      │
  ╰───────────╯    │    ╰───────────╯
                   ↑ shared boundary = measure zero

Corollary. For any finite decomposition D = D_1 \cup \cdots \cup D_n (pairwise overlapping only on boundaries):
\iint_D f,dA = \sum_{k=1}^n \iint_{D_k} f,dA
ML connection. In mixture models, the joint density is p(x,y) = \sum_k \pi_k p_k(x,y) with \sum_k \pi_k = 1. Computing the marginal:
p_X(x) = \int p(x,y),dy = \sum_k \pi_k \int p_k(x,y),dy = \sum_k \pi_k p_{k,X}(x)
The interchange of sum and integral is domain additivity (plus linearity) applied to the decomposition of the support into mixture components.

§4 — Property III: Monotonicity
\boxed{f(x,y) \le g(x,y) \text{ on } D \implies \iint_D f,dA \le \iint_D g,dA}
Proof. Since f \le g on D, for every partition and every sample point:
\sum_{i,j} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A_{ij} \le \sum_{i,j} g(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A_{ij}
Taking limits preserves the inequality. \square
Corollary (Positivity). f \ge 0 on D \implies \iint_D f,dA \ge 0.
Proof. Apply monotonicity with g \equiv 0. \square
Geometric reading. If the surface z = f lies entirely below z = g over D, then the volume under f cannot exceed the volume under g.
z
│    z = g(x,y)  ←  upper surface
│   ╭──────────╮
│  ╭╯          ╰╮  z = f(x,y)  ← lower surface
│  │     D      │
└──┴────────────┴── xy
    vol(f) ≤ vol(g)


§5 — Property IV: Estimation (Bounding)
Let m \le f(x,y) \le M for all (x,y) \in D. Then:
\boxed{m \cdot \text{Area}(D) \le \iint_D f(x,y),dA \le M \cdot \text{Area}(D)}
Proof. Apply monotonicity to the chain m \le f \le M and use:
\iint_D m,dA = m\cdot\text{Area}(D), \qquad \iint_D M,dA = M\cdot\text{Area}(D) \qquad \square
Geometric reading.
z = M ─────────────────────  ← top slab, volume = M · Area(D)
         ╭──────╮
z = f ───╯  D   ╰────────    ← actual surface, volume in between
z = m ─────────────────────  ← bottom slab, volume = m · Area(D)

The integral is “sandwiched” between two box-volumes.
ML connection. In Bayesian inference, when the likelihood \mathcal{L}(\theta \mid x,y) \le M is bounded, the normalising constant (evidence) satisfies:
m \cdot \text{Vol}(\Theta) \le \int_\Theta \mathcal{L}(\theta),\pi(\theta),d\theta \le M \cdot \text{Vol}(\Theta)
These bounds are used to check the sanity of variational approximations and to set hyperparameters in variational inference without computing the evidence exactly.

§6 — Property V: The Area Formula
\boxed{\iint_D 1,dA = \text{Area}(D)}
Proof. The Riemann sum for f \equiv 1 is \sum_{i,j} 1 \cdot \Delta A_{ij}, which is the total area of all sub-rectangles intersecting D. In the limit |P| \to 0 this converges to \text{Area}(D) (since \partial D has measure zero). \square
This is not a definition — it is a theorem that the double integral recovers area, validating the geometric interpretation.
Example. Area of the unit disk D = {x^2 + y^2 \le 1}:
\iint_D 1,dA = \pi(1)^2 = \pi
(verified directly via polar coordinates: \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r,dr,d\theta = \pi).

§7 — Property VI: Absolute Value Inequality (Triangle Inequality)
\boxed{\left|\iint_D f,dA\right| \le \iint_D |f|,dA}
Proof. Since -|f| \le f \le |f|, monotonicity gives:
-\iint_D |f|,dA \le \iint_D f,dA \le \iint_D |f|,dA
which is the two-sided inequality. \square
Why it matters. This is the 2D analogue of |\int f| \le \int |f|. In functional analysis it is the key estimate for showing that integration defines a bounded linear functional on L^1(D).
ML connection. In generalisation bounds (e.g., PAC learning theory), the difference in expected risk between two models f and g is bounded:
\left|\mathbb{E}[\ell(f)] - \mathbb{E}[\ell(g)]\right| = \left|\iint [\ell(f) - \ell(g)],p,dA\right| \le \iint |\ell(f) - \ell(g)|,p,dA
This is precisely the triangle inequality for double integrals. Rademacher complexity bounds and uniform convergence arguments all rely on it.

§8 — Property VII: Mean Value Theorem for Double Integrals
\boxed{\iint_D f,dA = f(x_0, y_0)\cdot\text{Area}(D)}
for some (x_0, y_0) \in D, provided f is continuous and D is connected and compact.
Proof. Since D is compact and f continuous, f attains its minimum m and maximum M on D. By the estimation property:
m \le \frac{\iint_D f,dA}{\text{Area}(D)} \le M
By the Intermediate Value Theorem (since D is connected and f is continuous), f takes every value between m and M. In particular, there exists (x_0, y_0) \in D such that:
f(x_0, y_0) = \frac{\iint_D f,dA}{\text{Area}(D)} \qquad \square
The point (x_0, y_0) is called the mean value point — it is the spatial location at which the function exactly equals its average value over D.
Geometric reading. The volume under z = f over D equals the volume of a flat box of height f(x_0, y_0) and base D.
z
│   ┌─────────────────┐  ← z = f(x₀,y₀)  (the average height)
│   │                 │
│   │  same volume!   │
│   │                 │
└───┴─────────────────┴── D
    Area(D) × f(x₀,y₀) = ∫∫f dA

ML connection. The average activation of a feature map in a CNN over a spatial region D (Global Average Pooling) is:
\bar{f} = \frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\iint_D f(x,y),dA = f(x_0, y_0)
The MVT guarantees that this average is attained somewhere — it is not merely an abstract number but a realised value of the function.

§9 — Property VIII: Comparison with Integral Over Subdomain
If D_1 \subseteq D_2 and f \ge 0 on D_2:
\boxed{\iint_{D_1} f,dA \le \iint_{D_2} f,dA}
Proof. Write D_2 = D_1 \cup (D_2 \setminus D_1) (essentially disjoint). By domain additivity and positivity:
\iint_{D_2} f,dA = \iint_{D_1} f,dA + \underbrace{\iint_{D_2 \setminus D_1} f,dA}_{\ge 0} \ge \iint_{D_1} f,dA \qquad \square
Remark. The hypothesis f \ge 0 is essential. For signed f, enlarging the domain can decrease the integral.

§10 — Property IX: Symmetry Reduction
These properties dramatically simplify computation when the domain has geometric symmetry.
10.1 Odd Function on Symmetric Domain
If D is symmetric about the y-axis (i.e., (x,y) \in D \Rightarrow (-x,y) \in D) and f is odd in x (f(-x,y) = -f(x,y)):
\boxed{\iint_D f(x,y),dA = 0}
Proof. Split D = D^+ \cup D^- where D^+ = D \cap {x \ge 0}. Map D^+ to D^- via (x,y) \mapsto (-x,y):
\iint_{D^-} f,dA = \iint_{D^+} f(-x,y),dA = -\iint_{D^+} f(x,y),dA
So \iint_D f,dA = \iint_{D^+} f,dA + \iint_{D^-} f,dA = 0. \square
10.2 Even Function on Symmetric Domain
If D is symmetric about the y-axis and f is even in x (f(-x,y) = f(x,y)):
\boxed{\iint_D f(x,y),dA = 2\iint_{D^+} f(x,y),dA}
Analogues. Replace “y-axis / odd in x” with “x-axis / odd in y”, ”x=y / odd under swap”, etc. Full symmetry (both axes) and odd function \Rightarrow integral is zero.
Example. \iint_D xy,dA where D = {x^2 + y^2 \le 1}.
D is symmetric about both axes. f(x,y) = xy is odd in x (and in y). Immediate conclusion: \iint_D xy,dA = 0.
ML connection. In neural network weight initialisation, symmetry arguments like this explain why certain initialisations (e.g., all-zeros) cause symmetry breaking failure: the gradient \nabla_W \mathcal{L} — an integral over the data distribution — vanishes by a symmetry argument analogous to the above, trapping all neurons in identical states.

§11 — Property X: Separability
If f(x,y) = g(x)\cdot h(y) and D = [a,b]\times[c,d] is a rectangle:
\boxed{\iint_D g(x),h(y),dA = \left(\int_a^b g(x),dx\right)!\left(\int_c^d h(y),dy\right)}
Proof. By Fubini:
\iint_D g(x),h(y),dA = \int_a^b g(x)\left[\int_c^d h(y),dy\right]dx = \left(\int_c^d h(y),dy\right)\int_a^b g(x),dx \qquad \square
Warning. Separability requires D to be a rectangle. On a general domain, \iint_D g(x)h(y),dA does not factor, because the limits of the inner integral depend on x.
ML connection. In probabilistic graphical models, if X \perp Y (independence), then p(x,y) = p_X(x),p_Y(y). The joint expectation factors:
\mathbb{E}[g(X)h(Y)] = \iint g(x)h(y),p_X(x),p_Y(y),dA = \mathbb{E}[g(X)]\cdot\mathbb{E}[h(Y)]
This is separability of the double integral. The breakdown of separability when X \not\perp Y is precisely the reason correlation matters.

§12 — The Symmetry of the Properties: A Summary Table







































































#PropertyHypothesisStatementILinearityf, g integrable\iint_D (\alpha f + \beta g),dA = \alpha\iint f + \beta\iint gIIDomain AdditivityD = D_1 \cup D_2, overlap measure 0\iint_D f = \iint_{D_1} f + \iint_{D_2} fIIIMonotonicityf \le g on D\iint_D f \le \iint_D gIVEstimationm \le f \le M on Dm\cdot A(D) \le \iint_D f \le M\cdot A(D)VAreaf \equiv 1\iint_D 1,dA = \text{Area}(D)VITriangle Ineq.f integrable$VIIMean Value Thmf continuous, D compact connected\exists(x_0,y_0)\in D: \iint_D f = f(x_0,y_0)\cdot A(D)VIIISubdomainD_1 \subseteq D_2, f \ge 0\iint_{D_1} f \le \iint_{D_2} fIXSymmetrySymmetric D, odd/even f\iint_D f = 0 or = 2\iint_{D^+} fXSeparabilityf = g(x)h(y), D rectangle\iint_D f = (\int g)(\int h)

§13 — Worked Examples Using the Properties
Example 1 — Symmetry Kills the Integral
Compute \displaystyle\iint_D (x^3 + \sin y + 4),dA where D = {(x,y): x^2 + y^2 \le 9}.
Strategy. Use linearity to split, then symmetry.
\iint_D (x^3 + \sin y + 4),dA = \underbrace{\iint_D x^3,dA}_{=0,\ \text{odd in }x} + \underbrace{\iint_D \sin y,dA}_{=0,\ \text{odd in }y} + \iint_D 4,dA
D is a disk of radius 3: \text{Area}(D) = 9\pi. Therefore:
= 0 + 0 + 4\cdot 9\pi = 36\pi
Example 2 — Estimation Without Computing
Show that \displaystyle\iint_D e^{x^2 + y^2},dA \le e^2\pi where D = {x^2 + y^2 \le 1}.
On D: 0 \le x^2 + y^2 \le 1, so e^0 \le e^{x^2+y^2} \le e^1.
By estimation:
\iint_D e^{x^2+y^2},dA \le e\cdot\text{Area}(D) = e\cdot\pi \lt e^2\pi \qquad \checkmark
In fact the sharp upper bound is e\pi, but e^2\pi follows immediately from the estimation property.
Example 3 — Separability
Compute \displaystyle\iint_{[0,1]^2} e^x \cos y,dA.
f(x,y) = e^x \cos y = g(x)h(y) and D is a rectangle. By separability:
= \left(\int_0^1 e^x,dx\right)!\left(\int_0^1 \cos y,dy\right) = (e - 1)(\sin 1)
Example 4 — Mean Value Theorem Applied
Find a point (x_0, y_0) in D = [0,1]^2 such that \iint_D (x + y),dA = (x_0 + y_0)\cdot\text{Area}(D).
Compute:
\iint_D (x+y),dA = \int_0^1\int_0^1(x+y),dy,dx = \int_0^1\left(x + \frac{1}{2}\right)dx = 1
\text{Area}(D) = 1, so we need x_0 + y_0 = 1. Any point on the segment {x + y = 1} \cap [0,1]^2 works — e.g., (x_0, y_0) = (1/2, 1/2). (The MVT guarantees existence; it does not specify uniqueness.)

§14 — Failure Modes and Pathological Cases
14.1 Linearity Does Not Extend to Infinite Sums
\iint_D \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x,y),dA \ne \sum_{n=1}^\infty \iint_D f_n(x,y),dA \quad \text{in general}
Swapping infinite sums and integrals requires uniform convergence (or dominated convergence in the Lebesgue sense). This failure is the core obstruction in many analysis problems.
14.2 Domain Additivity Requires Measure-Zero Overlap
If D_1 \cap D_2 has positive area, the formula \iint_D f = \iint_{D_1} f + \iint_{D_2} f overcounts the overlap region. The correct formula is inclusion-exclusion:
\iint_{D_1 \cup D_2} f = \iint_{D_1} f + \iint_{D_2} f - \iint_{D_1 \cap D_2} f
14.3 Symmetry Requires the Domain to Be Symmetric
\iint_D x,dA = 0 only if D is symmetric about the y-axis. If D = [0,1]^2 (not symmetric), then:
\iint_D x,dA = \int_0^1\int_0^1 x,dy,dx = \frac{1}{2} \ne 0
14.4 Separability Fails on Non-Rectangular Domains
On the triangle D = {0 \le x \le 1, 0 \le y \le x}:
\iint_D xy,dA = \int_0^1 x\int_0^x y,dy,dx = \int_0^1 x\cdot\frac{x^2}{2},dx = \frac{1}{8}
But \left(\int_0^1 x,dx\right)!\left(\int_0^1 y,dy\right) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4} \ne \frac{1}{8}.

§15 — Measure-Theoretic Perspective
(For the reader who wants to see behind the curtain.)
In Lebesgue theory, the double integral is \int_D f,d(m_1 \times m_2) where m_1 \times m_2 is the product measure on \mathbb{R}^2. The properties become:

































Riemann PropertyMeasure-Theoretic BasisLinearityLinearity of the Lebesgue integralDomain AdditivityCountable additivity of measureMonotonicityMonotonicity of the Lebesgue integralEstimationm \cdot \mu(D) \le \int_D f \le M \cdot \mu(D)Area formulam_1 \times m_2(D) = \text{Area}(D)Triangle inequalityL^1 norm satisfies $|f|_1 = \int
The MVT is a theorem about continuous functions on compact connected sets — it is not a purely measure-theoretic statement (it uses topology).
Why this matters for ML. Deep learning theory increasingly uses measure theory directly:

The Wasserstein distance (used in Wasserstein GANs) is defined via an infimum of integrals over coupling measures.
Neural ODEs and continuous normalizing flows work with push-forward measures.
The Neural Tangent Kernel convergence proofs use dominated convergence (the measure-theoretic version of swapping limits and integrals).

All of these require the properties above, in their full Lebesgue generality.

§16 — Summary: The Dependency Graph of Properties
Definition (Riemann Sum)
        │
        ├──→ Linearity (I)
        │         │
        │         ├──→ Domain Additivity (II)
        │         │         │
        │         │         └──→ Subdomain Monotonicity (VIII)
        │         │
        │         └──→ Separability (X)
        │
        ├──→ Monotonicity (III)
        │         │
        │         ├──→ Estimation (IV)
        │         │         │
        │         │         └──→ Mean Value Theorem (VII)
        │         │
        │         └──→ Triangle Inequality (VI)
        │
        └──→ Area Formula (V)
                  │
                  └──→ Estimation (IV) [via m·Area, M·Area]

        Symmetry (IX) ← Linearity + Domain Additivity + Change of Variables


§17 — References

MIT OpenCourseWare. 18.02SC Multivariable Calculus, Fall 2010. Session 54: Double Integrals and Properties. ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/

Folland, G.B. Real Analysis: Modern Techniques and Their Applications, 2nd ed. Wiley, 1999. Ch. 2 — Product measures and Fubini–Tonelli.
Bishop, C.M. Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer, 2006. §2.3 — Gaussian distributions; §10.1 — Variational inference.

01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.title: 08.Applications of Double Integrals
01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.content:
“The integral does not care whether you are weighing a lamina, locating a centroid, or training a neural network. It is always the same operation — accumulate, then normalize.”


§ 0 — The Unifying Idea
Every application in this note follows the same template:
\text{Global quantity} = \iint_D (\text{local density of that quantity}), dA
The “local density” changes — mass density, charge density, probability density, squared-distance density — but the machinery is identical. Master the pattern once; apply it everywhere.

§ 1 — Mass and Density
Setup
A lamina is a thin flat plate occupying region D \subset \mathbb{R}^2. Its surface mass density \rho(x,y) (units: kg/m²) describes how mass is distributed: a small patch dA near (x,y) has mass \approx \rho(x,y), dA.
Definition
M = \iint_D \rho(x,y), dA
If \rho is constant (uniform lamina), then M = \rho \cdot A(D) — consistent with the elementary formula.
Example 1 — Variable density lamina
A triangular lamina occupies D = {(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1,, 0 \le y \le x} with density \rho(x,y) = x + y.
Sketch of D: the region below the line y = x in the unit square; a right triangle with legs along the axes.
Mass:
M = \int_0^1 \int_0^x (x+y), dy, dx
Inner integral:
\int_0^x (x+y), dy = \left[xy + \frac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^x = x^2 + \frac{x^2}{2} = \frac{3x^2}{2}
Outer integral:
M = \int_0^1 \frac{3x^2}{2}, dx = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{2}

§ 2 — Moments and Center of Mass
Motivation
The center of mass (\bar{x}, \bar{y}) is the point at which the lamina would balance on a pin. It is the density-weighted average position.
Definitions
The first moments about the coordinate axes:
M_y = \iint_D x, \rho(x,y), dA \qquad \text{(moment about the } y\text{-axis)}
M_x = \iint_D y, \rho(x,y), dA \qquad \text{(moment about the } x\text{-axis)}
The center of mass:
\bar{x} = \frac{M_y}{M} = \frac{\iint_D x, \rho, dA}{\iint_D \rho, dA}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{M_x}{M} = \frac{\iint_D y, \rho, dA}{\iint_D \rho, dA}

Why M_y uses x? The moment about the y-axis measures tendency to rotate around the y-axis — driven by perpendicular distance, which is the x-coordinate.

Special case: uniform density
When \rho =  const, it cancels:
\bar{x} = \frac{\iint_D x, dA}{A(D)}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{\iint_D y, dA}{A(D)}
This is the centroid — purely geometric, depending only on the shape of D.
Example 2 — Center of mass of Example 1’s lamina
Continuing with D = {0 \le x \le 1, 0 \le y \le x}, \rho = x+y, M = 1/2.
Compute M_y:
M_y = \int_0^1 \int_0^x x(x+y), dy, dx
Inner: \int_0^x (x^2 + xy), dy = x^2 y + \frac{xy^2}{2}\Big|_0^x = x^3 + \frac{x^3}{2} = \frac{3x^3}{2}
Outer: \int_0^1 \frac{3x^3}{2}, dx = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{8}
Compute M_x:
M_x = \int_0^1 \int_0^x y(x+y), dy, dx
Inner: \int_0^x (xy + y^2), dy = \frac{xy^2}{2} + \frac{y^3}{3}\Big|_0^x = \frac{x^3}{2} + \frac{x^3}{3} = \frac{5x^3}{6}
Outer: \int_0^1 \frac{5x^3}{6}, dx = \frac{5}{6} \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{5}{24}
Center of mass:
\bar{x} = \frac{M_y}{M} = \frac{3/8}{1/2} = \frac{3}{4}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{M_x}{M} = \frac{5/24}{1/2} = \frac{5}{12}

Sanity check: The lamina lives in 0 \le y \le x \le 1. The density \rho = x+y is heavier toward the corner (1,1). So \bar{x} should be above 1/2, and \bar{y} should be above the geometric centroid y = 1/3 of the region. Both are: \bar{x} = 3/4 ✓, \bar{y} = 5/12 > 1/3 ✓.


§ 3 — Moments of Inertia
Motivation
While the center of mass governs translational balance, the moment of inertia governs rotational inertia — resistance to angular acceleration. It is the rotational analogue of mass.
For a point mass m at distance r from the axis: I = mr^2. For a distributed mass, integrate.
Definitions
Second moments (moments of inertia):
I_x = \iint_D y^2, \rho(x,y), dA \qquad \text{(about the }x\text{-axis, distance = }|y|\text{)}
I_y = \iint_D x^2, \rho(x,y), dA \qquad \text{(about the }y\text{-axis, distance = }|x|\text{)}
I_0 = \iint_D (x^2 + y^2), \rho(x,y), dA \qquad \text{(about the origin/}z\text{-axis)}
Note: I_0 = I_x + I_y (the perpendicular axis theorem).
Radius of gyration \tilde{x} about the y-axis:
\tilde{x} = \sqrt{\frac{I_y}{M}}
\tilde{x} is the distance from the axis at which all the mass, if concentrated, would give the same I_y.
Example 3 — Disk with uniform density
Disk D: x^2 + y^2 \le R^2, uniform density \rho.
By symmetry I_x = I_y, so compute I_0 = \iint_D r^2 \rho, dA in polar:
I_0 = \rho \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^R r^2 \cdot r, dr, d\theta = \rho \cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{R^4}{4} = \frac{\pi \rho R^4}{2}
Since M = \rho \pi R^2:
I_0 = \frac{MR^2}{2}, \qquad I_x = I_y = \frac{MR^2}{4}
These are the standard formulas used throughout engineering mechanics.
Example 4 — Rectangle, uniform density
Rectangle [0,a] \times [0,b], uniform \rho. Mass M = \rho ab.
I_x = \rho \int_0^a \int_0^b y^2, dy, dx = \rho \cdot a \cdot \frac{b^3}{3} = \frac{\rho a b^3}{3} = \frac{M b^2}{3}
I_y = \frac{M a^2}{3}

Why engineers care: I appears in \tau = I\alpha (torque = moment of inertia × angular acceleration) and in the deflection of beams under load. A wide, flat beam resists bending better — that is I_x \propto b^3: doubling height multiplies bending resistance by 8.


§ 4 — Probability
Setup
A function f(x,y) \ge 0 is a joint probability density function (PDF) for continuous random variables X, Y if:
\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x,y), dA = 1
The probability that (X,Y) falls in a region D:
P\big((X,Y) \in D\big) = \iint_D f(x,y), dA
Marginal Densities
Integrate out one variable to get the marginal:
f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y), dy, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y), dx
Independence
X and Y are independent if and only if f(x,y) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y) — the joint PDF factors.
Example 5 — Verifying a PDF and computing probability
Let f(x,y) = 6xy^2 on D = {0 \le x \le 1,, 0 \le y \le 1}, zero elsewhere.
Verify: \int_0^1 \int_0^1 6xy^2, dy, dx = 6 \int_0^1 x, dx \int_0^1 y^2, dy = 6 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 1 ✓
Compute P(X > Y): the region is {0 \le y \le x \le 1}.
P(X > Y) = \int_0^1 \int_0^x 6xy^2, dy, dx = \int_0^1 6x \cdot \frac{x^3}{3}, dx = \int_0^1 2x^4, dx = \frac{2}{5}
Example 6 — Bivariate normal (the fundamental distribution in ML)
The bivariate normal with independent components \sigma_X = \sigma_Y = \sigma, means \mu_X = \mu_Y = 0:
f(x,y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2} \exp!\left(-\frac{x^2+y^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
This factors as f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y) — confirming independence. To verify \iint f = 1, switch to polar:
\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2} e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2} r, dr, d\theta = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\int_0^\infty r, e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}, dr
Substitute u = r^2/2\sigma^2: integral = \sigma^2 \int_0^\infty e^{-u}, du = \sigma^2. So \frac{1}{\sigma^2} \cdot \sigma^2 = 1 ✓

§ 5 — Expected Values
Definitions
For random variables (X,Y) with joint PDF f:
\mathbb{E}[X] = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} x, f(x,y), dA = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x, f_X(x), dx
\mathbb{E}[Y] = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} y, f(x,y), dA
\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)] = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} g(x,y), f(x,y), dA
Variance:
\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] = \iint (x - \mu_X)^2 f(x,y), dA
Covariance:
\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)] = \iint (x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y), f(x,y), dA

Structural observation: Compare with § 2.





























PhysicsProbabilityMass density \rho(x,y)Probability density f(x,y)Total mass M = \iint \rho, dATotal probability = 1First moment M_y = \iint x\rho, dA\mathbb{E}[X] = \iint xf, dAMoment of inertia I_y = \iint x^2\rho, dA\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \iint x^2 f, dAI_y/M = \tilde{x}^2\mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu_X^2 = \text{Var}(X)
The physics and probability are the same mathematical structure with different interpretations of the weight function.

Example 7 — Expected value and variance
Using f(x,y) = 6xy^2 from Example 5:
\mathbb{E}[X]: (use marginal f_X(x) = \int_0^1 6xy^2, dy = 2x)
\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^1 x \cdot 2x, dx = 2\int_0^1 x^2, dx = \frac{2}{3}
\mathbb{E}[Y]: (marginal f_Y(y) = \int_0^1 6xy^2, dx = 3y^2)
\mathbb{E}[Y] = \int_0^1 y \cdot 3y^2, dy = 3\int_0^1 y^3, dy = \frac{3}{4}
\text{Var}(X): \mathbb{E}[X^2] = \int_0^1 x^2 \cdot 2x, dx = \frac{1}{2}, so \text{Var}(X) = \frac{1}{2} - \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{4}{9} = \frac{1}{18}

§ 6 — Visualization
6.1 — The Master Diagram
Physical interpretation        Mathematical object
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

f(x,y) = height of surface     z = ρ(x,y) or z = p(x,y)

∬_D f dA  =  "signed volume" under the surface above D
           =  total mass / total probability / ...

6.2 — Center of Mass vs. Centroid
Uniform ρ (centroid):           Non-uniform ρ (center of mass):

████████                        ░░░▒▒▒███
████████     ★ centroid         ░░░▒▒▒███    ★ shifts right
████████     at geometric       ░░░▒▒▒███    toward heavy side
████████     center

★ = (x̄, ȳ) = geometric center  ★ = weighted average position

6.3 — Moment of Inertia: Why Distance Squared?
Axis of rotation (y-axis)
       |
       |    •  mass dm at distance x
       |

Contribution to I_y = x² dm

Doubling x quadruples resistance to rotation.
This is why mass near the rim of a flywheel matters more.

6.4 — Probability Region

§ 7 — Applications in AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
7.1 — The Loss Function is a Moment Integral
The population risk (true loss) is:
\mathcal{R}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim p}[\ell(f_\theta(x), y)] = \iint \ell(f_\theta(x), y), p(x,y), dx, dy
This is the first moment of the loss function under the data distribution. Minimizing \mathcal{R}(\theta) is the theoretical objective; empirical risk minimization (ERM) approximates this integral by a sample mean — a Monte Carlo estimate of the double integral.
7.2 — Variance and Bias-Variance Tradeoff
The bias-variance decomposition involves:
\mathbb{E}[(f_\theta(x) - y)^2] = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \sigma^2_{\text{noise}}
Each term is an integral of the form \iint (\cdot)^2, p(x,y), dx, dy — a second moment, exactly as I_y = \iint x^2 \rho, dA. The parallel is not a metaphor; the mathematics is identical.
7.3 — Covariance and Feature Correlation
The covariance matrix \Sigma of a feature vector (X_1, \ldots, X_d) has entries:
\Sigma_{ij} = \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = \iint (x_i - \mu_i)(x_j - \mu_j), p(\mathbf{x}), d\mathbf{x}
In 2D: \text{Cov}(X,Y) = \iint (x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y), f(x,y), dA.
PCA finds the eigenvectors of \Sigma, which requires computing these double (or higher-dimensional) integrals from data. The empirical covariance matrix \hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(x_i - \bar{x})^T is the Monte Carlo estimate of this integral.
7.4 — Gaussian Distributions are Everywhere
The multivariate Gaussian \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma) with density:
f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp!\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\mu)\right)
is defined by the condition \iint \cdots \int f, d\mathbf{x} = 1. Verifying this uses the polar-coordinates trick from Example 6, generalized to d dimensions. Every forward pass through a Bayesian neural network, every Gaussian Process prediction, and every VAE latent space manipulation involves this integral implicitly.
7.5 — Center of Mass in Attention Mechanisms
The attention mechanism in Transformers computes:
\text{Attn}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V
The softmax produces a probability distribution (the weights), and the output is their weighted average of the values V. In the continuous limit (over a sequence modeled as a density), this is:
\text{output}(q) = \int \alpha(q, k), v(k), dk, \qquad \int \alpha(q,k), dk = 1
This is precisely a center of mass computation: the output is the \alpha-weighted average of the values v — the continuous analogue of \bar{x} = \frac{1}{M}\iint x\rho, dA.
7.6 — Moment of Inertia and Regularization
Weight regularization (L2/ridge) adds \lambda |\theta|^2 to the loss:
\mathcal{L}(\theta) + \lambda \sum_i \theta_i^2
The sum \sum \theta_i^2 is a discrete second moment — the analogue of moment of inertia I = \sum m_i r_i^2. Regularization is the assertion: keep the parameter “mass” close to the origin. The continuous limit is \lambda \int \theta^2, p(\theta), d\theta — a 1D (or higher) moment of inertia.
7.7 — Probability Density Estimation
Kernel Density Estimation (KDE):
\hat{f}(x,y) = \frac{1}{Nh^2} \sum_{i=1}^N K!\left(\frac{x-x_i}{h}, \frac{y-y_i}{h}\right)
estimates f(x,y) from data. The kernel K must satisfy \iint K = 1 — a double integral normalization condition. Evaluating probabilities under \hat{f} over regions requires \iint_D \hat{f}, dA, switching the double integral and the sum via Fubini.
7.8 — Score-Based Diffusion Models
Modern diffusion models (DDPM, score matching) learn \nabla_x \log p(x), the score function of the data density. The training objective involves:
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}}\left[|s_\theta(x + \sigma\epsilon) - \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x)|^2\right]
Every expectation here is a double (or higher-dimensional) integral. The entire theoretical foundation — existence of scores, denoising score matching equivalence, probability flow ODEs — rests on properties of these integrals: their existence, Fubini-type interchanges, and moments of the Gaussian kernel.

§ 8 — Summary Table




























































QuantityFormulaAnalogue in ProbabilityMassM = \iint \rho, dATotal probability = 1First moment (about y-axis)M_y = \iint x\rho, dA\mathbb{E}[X] = \iint xf, dAFirst moment (about x-axis)M_x = \iint y\rho, dA\mathbb{E}[Y] = \iint yf, dACenter of mass\bar{x} = M_y/M\mu_X = \mathbb{E}[X]Moment of inertia (y-axis)I_y = \iint x^2\rho, dA\mathbb{E}[X^2]Moment of inertia (x-axis)I_x = \iint y^2\rho, dA\mathbb{E}[Y^2]Polar momentI_0 = I_x + I_y\mathbb{E}[X^2 + Y^2] = \mathbb{E}[r^2]Radius of gyration\tilde{x} = \sqrt{I_y/M}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]} =  RMS of X——\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu_X^2——\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)]

01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.title: 09.Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates
01.Maths/Calculus/15.Multiple-Integrals/.content:
“Cartesian coordinates are honest but often unkind. Polar coordinates reward those who see the geometry.”


§0 — Preamble
There is a class of double integrals that is technically legitimate in Cartesian form but computationally brutal — integrands involving x^2 + y^2, domains that are disks or sectors or annuli. Forcing these into the dx,dy framework is like trying to describe a circle with a ruler: possible in principle, ugly in practice.
Polar coordinates exist precisely for this class of problems. The passage from (x,y) to (r,\theta) is not merely a substitution — it is a change of measure, and the appearance of the Jacobian factor r is the theorem’s most important output. This note proves the transformation rigorously, develops the geometric intuition, catalogues the standard domain types, supplies worked examples (including the famous Gaussian integral), and traces polar integration into deep learning and probability.
References: Stewart §15.3; MIT 18.02 Sessions 55–56.

§1 — Motivation: When Cartesian Coordinates Fail
1.1 The Archetypal Hard Integral
\iint_D e^{-(x^2+y^2)},dA, \quad D = {x^2 + y^2 \le R^2}
In Cartesian form:
\int_{-R}^{R}\int_{-\sqrt{R^2-x^2}}^{\sqrt{R^2-x^2}} e^{-(x^2+y^2)},dy,dx
The inner integral \int e^{-(x^2+y^2)},dy has no closed form in elementary functions. The limits involve square roots. This is a disaster.
In polar form, the same integral becomes \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R e^{-r^2},r,dr,d\theta — a product of two elementary integrals.
1.2 The Diagnostic Test
Use polar coordinates when:

The integrand contains x^2 + y^2, \sqrt{x^2+y^2}, x^2 - y^2, \arctan(y/x), or xy/(x^2+y^2)
The domain is a disk, annulus, sector, or wedge
The domain boundary is described by r = f(\theta)


§2 — The Polar Coordinate System
2.1 The Transformation
The polar coordinate map \Phi: (r,\theta) \mapsto (x,y) is:
x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta
with inverse (on \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus {(0,0)}):
r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}, \qquad \theta = \arctan!\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \quad \text{(with quadrant correction)}
Convention. We always take r \ge 0 and \theta \in [0, 2\pi) (or (-\pi, \pi] when convenient). Negative r is defined by (-r, \theta) = (r, \theta + \pi), but we never need it here.
2.2 Polar Grid Geometry
The two families of coordinate curves are:

Circles r = c: centred at the origin
Rays \theta = \alpha: emanating from the origin

θ = π/2
      │
      │
      │    r = 2
      │  ╭───╮
      │ ╭╯   ╰╮   r = 1
      │╭╯ ╭──╮╰╮
      ││  │  │  │
──────┼╯  │  │  ╰┼──── θ = 0
      │╰╮ ╰──╯ ╭╯│
      │ ╰╮   ╭╯  │
      │  ╰───╯   │
      │
θ = 3π/2

A “polar rectangle” [r_1, r_2] \times [\theta_1, \theta_2] is a curved wedge — an annular sector.

§3 — The Jacobian: The Central Theorem
This is the heart of the matter. The change-of-variables formula for double integrals says:
\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \iint_{D^*} f(r\cos\theta,, r\sin\theta),|\det J_\Phi|,dr,d\theta
where D^* is the pre-image of D in the (r,\theta)-plane, and J_\Phi is the Jacobian matrix of \Phi.
3.1 Computing the Jacobian
J_\Phi = \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = \begin{pmatrix} \partial x/\partial r & \partial x/\partial\theta \ \partial y/\partial r & \partial y/\partial\theta \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta \end{pmatrix}
\det J_\Phi = \cos\theta \cdot r\cos\theta - (-r\sin\theta)\cdot\sin\theta = r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = r
Since r \ge 0: |\det J_\Phi| = r.
3.2 The Main Formula
\boxed{\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \iint_{D^*} f(r\cos\theta,, r\sin\theta);r;dr,d\theta}
The r is not optional. It is the Jacobian determinant, encoding the geometric fact that a polar area element is not dr,d\theta but r,dr,d\theta.
3.3 Geometric Proof of the r Factor
Consider a small polar rectangle: r \in [r, r+\Delta r], \theta \in [\theta, \theta + \Delta\theta].
           ╭────╮  ← arc of radius r + Δr, length (r+Δr)Δθ
          ╱      ╲
    Δr   ╱  ΔA    ╲
        ╱    ≈ r   ╲
       ╰────╯        ← arc of radius r, length rΔθ
       ←  rΔθ  →

The area of this curved wedge is:
\Delta A = \frac{1}{2}(r+\Delta r)^2\Delta\theta - \frac{1}{2}r^2\Delta\theta = r,\Delta r,\Delta\theta + \frac{1}{2}(\Delta r)^2\Delta\theta
In the limit \Delta r, \Delta\theta \to 0:
dA = r,dr,d\theta
The r factor is the ratio of arc length to radius — it compensates for the fact that arcs at larger r subtend more area per unit angle than arcs near the origin.

§4 — Standard Polar Domains
4.1 Type I Polar Region (Fixed r-bounds)
D^* = {(\theta, r) : \alpha \le \theta \le \beta,; 0 \le r \le R}
Examples: Full disk (\alpha=0, \beta=2\pi), half-disk, sector.
\iint_D f,dA = \int_\alpha^\beta \int_0^R f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta),r,dr,d\theta
4.2 Type II Polar Region (r-bounds depend on \theta)
D^* = {(\theta, r) : \alpha \le \theta \le \beta,; r_1(\theta) \le r \le r_2(\theta)}
Examples: Regions bounded by polar curves like r = 1 + \cos\theta (cardioid), r = \cos(2\theta) (rose).
\iint_D f,dA = \int_\alpha^\beta \int_{r_1(\theta)}^{r_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta),r,dr,d\theta
4.3 Common Polar Domains Illustrated
DISK                ANNULUS             SECTOR
r ∈ [0, R]          r ∈ [a, b]          r ∈ [0, R]
θ ∈ [0, 2π]         θ ∈ [0, 2π]         θ ∈ [α, β]

   ╭───╮               ╭───╮            ╭──╮
  ╱     ╲            ╱╭───╮╲          ╱ ╲ β╲
 │   •   │          │ │ • │ │        │  •  ╲│
  ╲     ╱            ╲╰───╯╱          ╲  α  ╱
   ╰───╯               ╰───╯            ╰──╯

CARDIOID (r = 1+cosθ)   LEMNISCATE (r² = cos2θ)
      ╭──╮                    ╭──╮ ╭──╮
     ╱    ╲                  ╱    X    ╲
    │   •  │                │  •     •  │
     ╲    ╱                  ╲    X    ╱
      ╰──╯                    ╰──╯ ╰──╯


§5 — Worked Examples
Example 1 — Area of a Disk (Verification)
Compute \text{Area}(D) where D = {x^2 + y^2 \le R^2}.
\text{Area}(D) = \iint_D 1,dA = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R r,dr,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}\frac{R^2}{2},d\theta = \pi R^2 \checkmark

Example 2 — The Gaussian Integral (The Most Important Integral in Probability)
Compute I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx.
The trick. Consider I^2:
I^2 = \left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx\right)!\left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-y^2},dy\right) = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)},dA
The second equality uses separability (the domain is all of \mathbb{R}^2, a “rectangle” in the extended sense).
Switch to polar. Let D_R = {r \le R}. By exhaustion (D_R \nearrow \mathbb{R}^2 as R \to \infty):
I^2 = \lim_{R\to\infty}\iint_{D_R} e^{-r^2},r,dr,d\theta = \lim_{R\to\infty}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R e^{-r^2},r,dr,d\theta
Inner integral: let u = r^2, du = 2r,dr:
\int_0^R e^{-r^2},r,dr = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{R^2}e^{-u},du = \frac{1}{2}(1-e^{-R^2})
Therefore:
I^2 = \lim_{R\to\infty}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{1}{2}(1-e^{-R^2}),d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\pi\cdot 1 = \pi
\boxed{I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi}}
This is the most elegant application of polar integration. Every Gaussian in probability and deep learning traces back to this computation.

Example 3 — Integrand with x^2 + y^2
Compute \displaystyle\iint_D (x^2 + y^2)^{3/2},dA where D = {1 \le x^2 + y^2 \le 4} (annulus).
In polar: x^2 + y^2 = r^2, so (x^2+y^2)^{3/2} = r^3. Domain: r \in [1,2], \theta \in [0,2\pi].
= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_1^2 r^3 \cdot r,dr,d\theta = 2\pi\int_1^2 r^4,dr = 2\pi\cdot\frac{r^5}{5}\Bigg|_1^2 = 2\pi\cdot\frac{31}{5} = \frac{62\pi}{5}

Example 4 — Sector Region
Compute \displaystyle\iint_D xy,dA where D is the region in the first quadrant between the circles r=1 and r=3.
D: r \in [1,3], \theta \in [0,\pi/2]. In polar: xy = r\cos\theta \cdot r\sin\theta = r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{r^2}{2}\sin(2\theta).
= \int_0^{\pi/2}\int_1^3 \frac{r^2}{2}\sin(2\theta)\cdot r,dr,d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left(\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin(2\theta),d\theta\right)!\left(\int_1^3 r^3,dr\right)
= \frac{1}{2}\cdot\left[-\frac{\cos(2\theta)}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2}\cdot\frac{r^4}{4}\Bigg|_1^3 = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1 \cdot 20 = 10

Example 5 — Non-standard Limits: Region Described by a Polar Curve
Compute the area enclosed by one petal of the rose r = \cos(2\theta).
One petal lies in \theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4] (where \cos(2\theta) \ge 0).
\text{Area} = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\int_0^{\cos(2\theta)} r,dr,d\theta = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{\cos^2(2\theta)}{2},d\theta
Using \cos^2(u) = \frac{1+\cos(2u)}{2}:
= \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{1+\cos(4\theta)}{2},d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\left[\theta + \frac{\sin(4\theta)}{4}\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{8}

Example 6 — Converting a Cartesian Integral to Polar
Evaluate \displaystyle\int_0^1\int_0^{\sqrt{1-x^2}} e^{x^2+y^2},dy,dx.
Identify the region. This is the quarter-disk in the first quadrant: x^2 + y^2 \le 1, x \ge 0, y \ge 0.
Polar translation: r \in [0,1], \theta \in [0, \pi/2]. Integrand: e^{r^2}.
= \int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^1 e^{r^2},r,dr,d\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\left[e^{r^2}\right]_0^1 = \frac{\pi}{4}(e-1)

§6 — The Change of Variables Theorem (Full Generality)
The polar substitution is a special case of the general Change of Variables theorem. This section states the general theorem so that polar is properly contextualised.
Theorem (Change of Variables). Let \Phi: D^* \to D be a C^1 bijection (except possibly on a set of measure zero), where D^*, D \subset \mathbb{R}^2. Then:
\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \iint_{D^*} f(\Phi(u,v)),\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|,du,dv
where \left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right| = |\det J_\Phi| is the absolute Jacobian determinant.
For polar coordinates: \Phi(r,\theta) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta), |\det J_\Phi| = r.
Geometric meaning of the Jacobian. |\det J_\Phi| measures the local area magnification of \Phi: a small region near (u,v) of area \delta A in the (u,v)-plane maps to a region of area \approx |\det J_\Phi|\cdot\delta A in the (x,y)-plane. The Jacobian is the correction factor ensuring areas are correctly accounted for.
(r,θ)-plane                    (x,y)-plane
                    Φ
  ┌──────┐   ─────────────→   ╭──────╮
  │ Δr Δθ│                   ╱  r·Δr·Δθ ╲
  └──────┘                  ╱            ╲
  area = ΔrΔθ               ╰────────────╯
                              area = r·ΔrΔθ

  magnification factor = r = |det J_Φ|


§7 — Common Errors and Pathologies
Error 1 — Forgetting the r Factor
\iint_D f,dA \ne \int_\alpha^\beta\int_{r_1}^{r_2} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta),dr,d\theta
The correct formula always has r,dr,d\theta. Forgetting r produces a systematically wrong answer with no warning sign.
Mnemonic. dA = dx,dy = r,dr,d\theta. The area element on the left is the same object expressed in two coordinate systems.
Error 2 — Wrong \theta-Range for a Full Circle
A full circle requires \theta \in [0, 2\pi], not [0, \pi]. The interval [0,\pi] gives a half-disk.
Error 3 — Origin Included When r_1 = 0
When r_1 = 0, \Phi is not injective at the origin (every \theta maps to (0,0)). This is legal because {r=0} has measure zero in the (r,\theta)-plane — the change-of-variables theorem allows failures on measure-zero sets.
Error 4 — Applying Polar to a Non-Circular Domain
Polar coordinates are optimal for circular geometry. For ellipses \frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}\le 1, use the elliptic substitution x = ar\cos\theta, y = br\sin\theta (Jacobian: abr), not standard polar.
Error 5 — Sign of r
Always r \ge 0 in our convention. If a polar curve formula gives r < 0 for some \theta, the curve traces a reflected point — handle by restricting \theta or using |r|.

§8 — Symmetry in Polar Coordinates
Symmetry is easier to exploit in polar form.






























SymmetryConditionSimplificationAbout x-axisf(r,-\theta) = f(r,\theta) and D symmetric\int_0^{2\pi} \to 2\int_0^\piAbout y-axisf(r,\pi-\theta) = f(r,\theta) and D symmetric\int_0^{2\pi} \to 2\int_0^\piFull rotationalf depends only on r\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta = 2\pi factors outn-fold rotationalf(r,\theta+2\pi/n) = f(r,\theta)\int_0^{2\pi} = n\int_0^{2\pi/n}
Key example. If f(x,y) = g(r) depends only on r (radially symmetric):
\iint_D g(r),dA = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R g(r),r,dr,d\theta = 2\pi\int_0^R g(r),r,dr

§9 — The Polar Coordinate Machine: Step-by-Step Protocol
GIVEN: ∫∫_D f(x,y) dA

STEP 1.  Does the domain D have circular/radial structure?
         └── No → stay Cartesian (or use other substitution)
         └── Yes → proceed

STEP 2.  Describe D in polar:
         Find α, β (θ-range) and r₁(θ), r₂(θ) (r-bounds at each θ).
         Draw the region. Label all boundary curves in polar form.

STEP 3.  Substitute:
         x = r cosθ,  y = r sinθ
         Replace all occurrences of x²+y² with r².

STEP 4.  Write the integral:
         ∫_α^β ∫_{r₁(θ)}^{r₂(θ)}  f(rcosθ, rsinθ) · r  dr dθ
                                                        ↑
                                               NEVER FORGET THIS

STEP 5.  Evaluate inner integral (in r), then outer (in θ).

STEP 6.  Check dimensional sanity: Area integrals should give [length]².


§10 — Connection to Probability and Machine Learning
10.1 The Gaussian Distribution — Its Very Existence Depends on This
The univariate normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0,1) has density \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}. The normalisation constant \sqrt{2\pi} comes from:
\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2},dx = \sqrt{2\pi}
Proof: Substitute x = t/\sqrt{2} to get \sqrt{2}\int e^{-t^2/2},dt… which reduces to our Gaussian integral. So the very fact that the standard normal density integrates to 1 is a consequence of polar coordinates applied to a double integral. Without this calculation, the Gaussian distribution is not well-defined.
10.2 Multivariate Gaussian
For \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2 with covariance \Sigma = \sigma^2 I:
p(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}e^{-|\mathbf{x}|^2/(2\sigma^2)}
Normalisation check:
\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} p(x,y),dA = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)},r,dr,d\theta = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}\cdot 2\pi\cdot\sigma^2 = 1
This is exactly the polar double integral computation, and it must equal 1 for p to be a valid density.
10.3 Reparameterisation Trick in VAEs (Radial Decomposition)
In Variational Autoencoders, the latent space prior is \mathcal{N}(0, I). Sampling from this prior and computing expectations uses the identity:
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)}[f(\mathbf{z})] = \iint f(x,y),\frac{e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}}{2\pi},dA = \int_0^\infty\int_0^{2\pi} f(r,\theta),\frac{e^{-r^2/2}}{2\pi},r,d\theta,dr
Decomposing into radial and angular components (polar coordinates) underlies the radial basis function interpretation of the latent space and the geometry of the latent manifold.
10.4 Attention Mechanisms — Radial Decay
In some spatial attention architectures (e.g., for point clouds or 2D feature maps), attention weights decay radially:
\alpha(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}) = \exp!\left(-\frac{|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k}|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
Computing the total attention mass over a spatial region D is:
\int_D \alpha(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}),dA = \iint_D e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)},r,dr,d\theta
(centring at \mathbf{q}). This is a polar integral, and its closed form informs how to set \sigma for a desired effective receptive field size.
10.5 Score-Based Generative Models (Diffusion)
The score function \nabla_\mathbf{x}\log p(\mathbf{x}) for a radially symmetric density p(\mathbf{x}) \propto e^{-V(r)} is:
\nabla_\mathbf{x}\log p = -V'(r),\hat{r} = -V'(r),\frac{\mathbf{x}}{r}
Computing normalisation constants and partition functions for such densities requires polar integration. Diffusion model theory (DDPM, Score SDE) extensively uses radially-symmetric reference distributions whose analysis is pure polar calculus.

§11 — Extended Example: Normalising an Unnormalised Density
Problem. The function f(x,y) = C e^{-(x^2+y^2)}(1 + x^2 + y^2) is a probability density on \mathbb{R}^2. Find C.
We need \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} f,dA = 1, so C^{-1} = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)}(1+x^2+y^2),dA.
Polar form. r \in [0,\infty), \theta \in [0,2\pi], integrand = e^{-r^2}(1+r^2):
C^{-1} = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}(1+r^2),r,dr,d\theta = 2\pi\int_0^\infty (re^{-r^2} + r^3 e^{-r^2}),dr
Compute each piece using \int_0^\infty r^{2k+1}e^{-r^2},dr = \frac{k!}{2}:

\int_0^\infty re^{-r^2},dr = \frac{0!}{2} = \frac{1}{2}
\int_0^\infty r^3 e^{-r^2},dr = \frac{1!}{2} = \frac{1}{2}

C^{-1} = 2\pi\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right) = 2\pi \implies \boxed{C = \frac{1}{2\pi}}
This is a non-trivial unnormalised density that arises in practice (it is related to the Chi-squared distribution), and polar coordinates make the normalisation tractable.

§12 — Connections to Other Coordinate Systems
Polar coordinates in 2D are the first member of a family:



































DimensionCoordinatesJacobianArea/Volume Element2DPolar (r, \theta)rr,dr,d\theta3D (cylinder)Cylindrical (r,\theta,z)rr,dr,d\theta,dz3D (sphere)Spherical (\rho,\phi,\theta)\rho^2\sin\phi\rho^2\sin\phi,d\rho,d\phi,d\thetaGeneral(u_1,\ldots,u_n)$\det J
The Jacobian r (polar) generalises to r (cylindrical) and \rho^2\sin\phi (spherical). In all cases, it is the determinant of the coordinate transformation’s Jacobian matrix.

§13 — Summary Theorem Sheet
Main Formula:
\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_\alpha^\beta\int_{r_1(\theta)}^{r_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta);r;dr,d\theta
Key substitutions:
x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad x^2+y^2 = r^2, \quad dA = r,dr,d\theta
Jacobian: \det\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = r
Gaussian integral (consequence): \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi}
Radially symmetric integrand: \displaystyle\iint_D g(r),dA = 2\pi\int_0^R g(r),r,dr (for full disk of radius R)

§14 — References

Stewart, J. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Cengage, 2016. §15.3 — Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates; §15.9 — Change of Variables.
MIT OpenCourseWare. 18.02SC Multivariable Calculus, Fall 2010. Sessions 55–56. ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/
Apostol, T. Mathematical Analysis, 2nd ed. Addison-Wesley, 1974. §11.7 — Change of Variables.
Bishop, C.M. Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer, 2006. §2.3 — Gaussian distribution and normalisation.
Song, Y. & Ermon, S. “Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution.” NeurIPS 2019. (Score-based models using Gaussian reference densities.)
Kingma, D. & Welling, M. “Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes.” ICLR 2014. (VAE latent space geometry.)
