01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/10..title: 10.Curl
01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/10..content:
“The divergence asks how much a field spreads out. The curl asks how much it spins. Together they are the complete local description of a vector field — the two numbers that determine everything about its infinitesimal behavior.”


§1. Motivation — Measuring Rotation in a Vector Field
Imagine dropping a small paddle wheel into a flowing fluid. If the fluid rotates the wheel, the field has curl at that point. If the wheel translates without spinning, the curl is zero there. The curl captures the local rotational tendency of a vector field — how much, and in which direction, the field tends to rotate nearby matter.
This is not the same as the field itself being circular in shape. A field can look perfectly straight and still have nonzero curl; a field can look circular and have zero curl. Curl is an infinitesimal, local measurement — not a global geometric description.
The deepest reason to care: curl is the object that appears on the right side of Stokes’ theorem and the left side of Maxwell’s equations. It is the bridge between local field behavior and global flux through surfaces. In physics it governs electromagnetism, fluid mechanics, and elasticity. In mathematics it governs the cohomology of differential forms.

§2. Definition
2.1 The Curl in \mathbb{R}^3
Let \mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R\rangle: U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3 be a C^1 vector field. The curl of \mathbf{F} is the vector field:
\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \text{curl},\mathbf{F} = \left\langle \frac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial z},; \frac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial R}{\partial x},; \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right\rangle
Mnemonic — the formal determinant:
\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z} \[6pt] P & Q & R \end{vmatrix}
Expand along the first row: = \mathbf{i}\left(\frac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}\right) - \mathbf{j}\left(\frac{\partial R}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial z}\right) + \mathbf{k}\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)

Warning. This determinant is a mnemonic, not a true determinant — its entries are not numbers but operators and functions. Treat the expansion mechanically: operator acts on function below it.

2.2 Components and Their Meaning
Each component of \nabla \times \mathbf{F} measures rotation in a coordinate plane:





























ComponentFormulaMeasures rotation in…About axis…(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})_xR_y - Q_zyz-planex-axis(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})_yP_z - R_xxz-planey-axis(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})_zQ_x - P_yxy-planez-axis
The direction of \nabla\times\mathbf{F} is the axis of rotation (by the right-hand rule). The magnitude |\nabla\times\mathbf{F}| is the rate of rotation.
2.3 The Scalar Curl in \mathbb{R}^2
For a planar field \mathbf{F} = \langle P(x,y), Q(x,y), 0\rangle, the curl has only a z-component:
\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \left\langle 0, 0, \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right\rangle
We call the scalar \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} the scalar curl or 2D curl of \mathbf{F}. This is the quantity appearing in Green’s theorem.

§3. Intrinsic (Coordinate-Free) Definition
The determinant formula is convenient for computation but hides the geometric meaning. The coordinate-free definition is more fundamental.

Definition (Curl via Stokes’ theorem). For a C^1 vector field \mathbf{F} on U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3, the curl \nabla\times\mathbf{F} at a point p is the unique vector field such that for every unit vector \hat{\mathbf{n}}:
(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})(p) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \lim_{A(D_\varepsilon)\to 0} \frac{1}{A(D_\varepsilon)} \oint_{\partial D_\varepsilon} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}
where D_\varepsilon is a disk of area A(D_\varepsilon) centered at p with normal \hat{\mathbf{n}}, and the boundary is oriented by the right-hand rule with respect to \hat{\mathbf{n}}.

In words: The component of curl in direction \hat{\mathbf{n}} is the circulation per unit area around infinitesimally small loops perpendicular to \hat{\mathbf{n}}.
This is the paddle-wheel interpretation made precise:

Orient the paddle wheel with its axis pointing in direction \hat{\mathbf{n}}
(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}} is proportional to the angular velocity of the wheel
Maximize over all \hat{\mathbf{n}}: the direction that maximizes spin is the direction of \nabla\times\mathbf{F}


§4. Full Proof: Coordinate Formula from Intrinsic Definition
We verify that the coordinate formula arises from the intrinsic definition. We derive the z-component; the others follow by symmetry.
Setup. Take \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{k} (the z-axis). Let D_\varepsilon be the disk of radius \varepsilon centered at (a,b,c) in the plane z = c, with boundary C_\varepsilon oriented counterclockwise (viewed from above).
Apply Green’s theorem to C_\varepsilon:
\oint_{C_\varepsilon} P,dx + Q,dy = \iint_{D_\varepsilon} \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dA
Divide by the area A(D_\varepsilon) = \pi\varepsilon^2 and take \varepsilon \to 0:
By the Mean Value Theorem for integrals, there exists a point (x_\varepsilon, y_\varepsilon) \in D_\varepsilon such that:
\frac{1}{\pi\varepsilon^2}\iint_{D_\varepsilon}\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dA = \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)(x_\varepsilon, y_\varepsilon, c)
As \varepsilon \to 0, (x_\varepsilon, y_\varepsilon) \to (a,b), so by continuity:
\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{A(D_\varepsilon)}\oint_{C_\varepsilon} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)(a,b,c) = (\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot\mathbf{k} \quad\square
Repeating with \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{i} and \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{j} gives the other components.

§5. Fundamental Identities
These identities should be internalized, not just memorized.
5.1 Curl of a Gradient is Zero
\nabla \times (\nabla f) = \mathbf{0}
Proof. Compute the z-component: (\nabla\times\nabla f)_z = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(f_y) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(f_x) = f_{yx} - f_{xy} = 0
by Clairaut’s theorem (assuming f \in C^2). Similarly for all components. \square
Meaning: Gradient fields have no rotation. Conservative fields are irrotational. This is the analytical content of the FTLI: a gradient field can do no net work around a closed loop.
5.2 Divergence of a Curl is Zero
\nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) = 0
Proof. Direct computation (for \mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R\rangle):
\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{F}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(R_y - Q_z) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(P_z - R_x) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(Q_x - P_y)
= R_{xy} - Q_{xz} + P_{yz} - R_{yx} + Q_{zx} - P_{zy}
= (R_{xy} - R_{yx}) + (P_{yz} - P_{zy}) + (Q_{zx} - Q_{xz}) = 0
by Clairaut’s theorem (assuming \mathbf{F} \in C^2). \square
Meaning: Curl fields have no sources or sinks. A magnetic field \mathbf{B} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A} satisfies \nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0 automatically — there are no magnetic monopoles, as a mathematical consequence.
5.3 Vector Laplacian Identity
\nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{F}) = \nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}) - \nabla^2\mathbf{F}
where \nabla^2\mathbf{F} = \langle \nabla^2 P, \nabla^2 Q, \nabla^2 R\rangle is the componentwise Laplacian. This identity is central to electromagnetic wave equations.
5.4 Curl of a Cross Product
\nabla\times(\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{G}) = \mathbf{F}(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{G}) - \mathbf{G}(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}) + (\mathbf{G}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{F} - (\mathbf{F}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{G}
5.5 Curl of f\mathbf{F}
\nabla\times(f\mathbf{F}) = f(\nabla\times\mathbf{F}) + (\nabla f)\times\mathbf{F}

§7. Stokes’ Theorem — The Curl’s Global Theorem
The intrinsic definition of curl was:
(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{A(D_\varepsilon)}\oint_{\partial D_\varepsilon}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}
Integrate this over a surface S with unit normal \hat{\mathbf{n}} — you get Stokes’ theorem:
\boxed{\iint_S (\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \oint_{\partial S}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}}
The flux of the curl through a surface equals the circulation of \mathbf{F} around its boundary. Green’s theorem is the special case where S is a flat planar region and \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{k}.
Key observation: The boundary \partial S on the right depends only on the boundary of S, not the interior. So for any two surfaces S_1, S_2 with the same boundary C:
\iint_{S_1}(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_{S_2}(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \oint_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}
The flux of curl is independent of the surface, depending only on the boundary curve.

§8. Irrotational Fields and Conservative Fields

Theorem. Let U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 be simply connected. For a C^1 vector field \mathbf{F} on U, the following are equivalent:

\mathbf{F} = \nabla f for some f \in C^2(U) (conservative)
\nabla\times\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0} on U (irrotational)
\oint_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = 0 for every closed curve C in U
\int_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} is path-independent in U


(1)\Rightarrow(2): Identity \nabla\times\nabla f = \mathbf{0}.
(2)\Rightarrow(3): By Stokes’ theorem on any surface bounded by C.
(3)\Rightarrow(4): Take two paths C_1, C_2 with same endpoints; C_1 - C_2 is closed.
(4)\Rightarrow(1): Define f(\mathbf{r}) = \int_{p_0}^{\mathbf{r}}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} (well-defined by path-independence); then \nabla f = \mathbf{F}.
On non-simply connected domains: (1)\Rightarrow(2) always; (2)\not\Rightarrow(1) in general. The obstruction lives in H^1_{\text{dR}}(U).

§9. Worked Examples
Example A — Basic Computation
\mathbf{F} = \langle xz, xyz, -y^2\rangle. Find \nabla\times\mathbf{F}.
(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})_x = \frac{\partial(-y^2)}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial(xyz)}{\partial z} = -2y - xy
(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})_y = \frac{\partial(xz)}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial(-y^2)}{\partial x} = x - 0 = x
(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})_z = \frac{\partial(xyz)}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial(xz)}{\partial y} = yz - 0 = yz
\nabla\times\mathbf{F} = \langle -2y - xy,; x,; yz\rangle

Example B — Testing for Conservative Field
Is \mathbf{F} = \langle 2xy + z^3,; x^2,; 3xz^2\rangle conservative?
Compute curl:
(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})_x = \frac{\partial(3xz^2)}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial(x^2)}{\partial z} = 0 - 0 = 0 \checkmark
(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})_y = \frac{\partial(2xy+z^3)}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial(3xz^2)}{\partial x} = 3z^2 - 3z^2 = 0 \checkmark
(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})_z = \frac{\partial(x^2)}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial(2xy+z^3)}{\partial y} = 2x - 2x = 0 \checkmark
\nabla\times\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}. Conservative on \mathbb{R}^3 (simply connected).
Find the potential: f_x = 2xy + z^3 \Rightarrow f = x^2y + xz^3 + g(y,z). f_y = x^2 + g_y = x^2 \Rightarrow g_y = 0 \Rightarrow g = h(z). f_z = 3xz^2 + h'(z) = 3xz^2 \Rightarrow h'(z) = 0.
\boxed{f(x,y,z) = x^2 y + xz^3 + C}

Example C — Rotational Fields
\mathbf{F} = \langle -y, x, 0\rangle (rigid rotation about z-axis).
\nabla\times\mathbf{F} = \left\langle 0 - 0,; 0 - 0,; \frac{\partial x}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial(-y)}{\partial y}\right\rangle = \langle 0, 0, 1-(-1)\rangle = \langle 0, 0, 2\rangle
The curl is 2\mathbf{k} — a constant vector pointing in the z-direction. This makes sense: \mathbf{F} rotates everything about the z-axis with angular velocity \omega, and the relation between curl and angular velocity is \nabla\times\mathbf{F} = 2\boldsymbol{\omega} (see §11).

Example D — Nonzero Curl, Non-Obvious Example
\mathbf{F} = \langle 0, 0, y\rangle (field pointing in z-direction, magnitude varying with y).
\nabla\times\mathbf{F} = \left\langle \frac{\partial y}{\partial y} - 0,; 0 - \frac{\partial y}{\partial z},; 0 - 0\right\rangle = \langle 1, 0, 0\rangle
The curl is \mathbf{i}. The field looks like it just points in the z-direction — no obvious rotation — yet the curl is nonzero. Why? Because the field is stronger at large y than at small y: a paddle wheel with its axis pointing in the x-direction would indeed spin (the high-y face gets pushed harder in the z-direction than the low-y face).
This is the crucial lesson: curl measures velocity shear, not just vortical geometry.

Example E — Verifying \text{div}(\text{curl}) = 0
For \mathbf{F} = \langle xy, yz, xz\rangle:
\nabla\times\mathbf{F} = \langle z_y - yz_z,; xy_z - xz_x,; yz_x - xy_y\rangle = \langle 0-y,; 0-x,; 0-x\rangle = \langle -y, -x, -x\rangle
\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{F}) = \frac{\partial(-y)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial(-x)}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial(-x)}{\partial z} = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0 \checkmark

§11. Curl in Physics
11.1 Rigid Body Rotation
A rigid body rotating with angular velocity vector \boldsymbol{\omega} = \omega,\mathbf{k} has velocity field: \mathbf{v} = \boldsymbol{\omega}\times\mathbf{r} = \omega\mathbf{k}\times\langle x,y,z\rangle = \langle -\omega y, \omega x, 0\rangle
Compute: \nabla\times\mathbf{v} = \langle 0, 0, \omega - (-\omega)\rangle = \langle 0, 0, 2\omega\rangle = 2\boldsymbol{\omega}.
\boxed{\nabla\times\mathbf{v} = 2\boldsymbol{\omega}}
The curl of the velocity field is twice the angular velocity. This is the precise relationship between local rotation (curl) and macroscopic spin. It is why curl is also called the vorticity in fluid mechanics.
11.2 Maxwell’s Equations
Curl appears in two of Maxwell’s four equations:
Faraday’s Law (Induction): \nabla\times\mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}
A time-varying magnetic field \mathbf{B} generates a rotating electric field \mathbf{E}. The curl of \mathbf{E} is the rate of change of \mathbf{B}. This is the principle behind electric generators.
Ampère-Maxwell Law: \nabla\times\mathbf{B} = \mu_0\mathbf{J} + \mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t}
Electric current \mathbf{J} and a time-varying electric field generate a rotating magnetic field \mathbf{B}. Maxwell’s addition of the \partial\mathbf{E}/\partial t term (displacement current) was the key insight that predicted electromagnetic waves.
Electromagnetic wave equation (derived from the two curl equations): \nabla^2\mathbf{E} = \mu_0\varepsilon_0\frac{\partial^2\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^2}
using the identity \nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{E}) = \nabla(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}) - \nabla^2\mathbf{E}. The wave speed is c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}.
11.3 Fluid Mechanics — Vorticity
In fluid mechanics, the vorticity of a velocity field \mathbf{u} is: \boldsymbol{\xi} = \nabla\times\mathbf{u}

Irrotational flow (\boldsymbol{\xi} = \mathbf{0}): no local spinning; typical of potential flows far from boundaries
Vortex filaments: thin tubes where |\boldsymbol{\xi}| is large — like tornadoes or wingtip vortices
Vorticity equation (from Navier-Stokes): \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\boldsymbol{\xi} = (\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u} + \nu\nabla^2\boldsymbol{\xi}

The term (\boldsymbol{\xi}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u} is vortex stretching — the mechanism by which turbulence cascades to smaller scales.

§12. The Helmholtz Decomposition
Theorem (Helmholtz). Every C^2 vector field \mathbf{F} on \mathbb{R}^3 (decaying sufficiently at infinity) decomposes uniquely as:
\mathbf{F} = -\nabla\phi + \nabla\times\mathbf{A}
where:

\phi is a scalar potential: -\nabla\phi is the irrotational part (curl-free)
\mathbf{A} is a vector potential: \nabla\times\mathbf{A} is the solenoidal part (divergence-free)

Explicitly: \phi(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac{\nabla'\cdot\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}')}{|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'|},dV', \qquad \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac{\nabla'\times\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}')}{|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'|},dV'
Consequence: \mathbf{F} is completely determined by its divergence and curl:

\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} determines the irrotational part
\nabla\times\mathbf{F} determines the solenoidal part

This is why Maxwell’s equations use both div and curl — together they fully specify the electromagnetic field from its sources (charges and currents).

§13. Curl in Curvilinear Coordinates
For completeness — these arise in physics and numerical ML (e.g., polar grids).
13.1 Cylindrical Coordinates (r, \theta, z)
\nabla\times\mathbf{F} = \left\langle \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial F_z}{\partial\theta} - \frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial z},; \frac{\partial F_r}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial F_z}{\partial r},; \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial(rF_\theta)}{\partial r} - \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial F_r}{\partial\theta}\right\rangle
13.2 Spherical Coordinates (r, \theta, \phi)
\nabla\times\mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\left\langle \frac{\partial(\sin\theta, F_\phi)}{\partial\theta} - \frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial\phi},; \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial F_r}{\partial\phi} - \frac{\partial(rF_\phi)}{\partial r},; \frac{\partial(rF_\theta)}{\partial r} - \frac{\partial F_r}{\partial\theta}\right\rangle

Honestly: always look these up. The Cartesian formula is the one to internalize. The curvilinear versions follow from the metric tensor; derive them from first principles if needed rather than memorizing.


§14. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning

Curl — as a measure of local rotation and antisymmetric structure — appears throughout modern ML in ways that are only recently being made explicit. The keyword to watch for: antisymmetry, rotation, non-conservative dynamics.

14.1 GAN Training Dynamics — Curl is the Problem
As discussed in the extended Green’s theorem note, GAN training in the joint parameter space (\theta_G, \theta_D) has a gradient vector field: \mathbf{v} = (-\nabla_G\mathcal{L},; \nabla_D\mathcal{L})
The curl of \mathbf{v} is the antisymmetric part of the Jacobian J_\mathbf{v}: (\nabla\times\mathbf{v})_{ij} = \frac{\partial v_j}{\partial \theta_i} - \frac{\partial v_i}{\partial \theta_j} = J_{ij} - J_{ji}
When \nabla\times\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}, gradient descent cycles around the equilibrium. The magnitude of the curl quantifies how badly the training cycles.
Symplectic Gradient Adjustment (SGA) (Balduzzi et al. 2018) explicitly subtracts the curl component: \mathbf{v}_{\text{SGA}} = \mathbf{v} - \lambda,(\text{antisymmetric part of }J_\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{v}
This is, literally, computing the discrete curl of the training dynamics and correcting for it.
14.2 Second-Order Optimization — The Hessian and Its Antisymmetric Part
The Jacobian of the gradient \nabla\mathcal{L} is the Hessian H. By Clairaut’s theorem, H is symmetric for smooth loss functions. But in multi-player games (GANs, multi-agent RL), the effective “Hessian” of the joint dynamics is not the Hessian of a single function — it has an antisymmetric part that represents the curl.
The Competitive Gradient Descent algorithm (Schäfer & Anandkumar 2019) computes: \text{symmetric part of } J = \frac{J + J^T}{2} \quad (\text{gradient component}) \text{antisymmetric part of } J = \frac{J - J^T}{2} \quad (\text{curl component})
The second-order update uses both, correctly accounting for both descent and rotation.
14.3 Neural Network Weight Space — Curl-Free Flows
Normalizing flows (RealNVP, Glow, Neural ODE flows) require computing the Jacobian determinant of a learned map \mathbf{g}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n. For volume-preserving flows (important for sampling and density estimation), one constraint is \nabla\cdot\mathbf{g} = 0 (divergence-free). But there is a complementary condition: flows can be decomposed (Helmholtz) into gradient (curl-free) and solenoidal (div-free) components, and the two components contribute differently to the Jacobian determinant.
FFJORD (Chen et al. 2018) and Neural ODEs define a continuous flow: \frac{d\mathbf{z}}{dt} = f_\theta(\mathbf{z}, t)
The log-likelihood change is: \frac{d\log p(\mathbf{z})}{dt} = -\nabla\cdot f_\theta
Note: the divergence of the flow controls log-likelihood. The curl of the flow is “free” — it doesn’t affect the density. This means curl-free and solenoidal flows have entirely different roles in normalizing flows.
14.4 Attention Mechanisms — Antisymmetric Interactions
In self-attention, the attention matrix A_{ij} = \text{softmax}(q_i \cdot k_j / \sqrt{d}) is generally not symmetric — A_{ij} \neq A_{ji}. The antisymmetric part of the attention matrix: A^{\text{anti}}_{ij} = \frac{A_{ij} - A_{ji}}{2}
is the discrete analog of curl — it measures asymmetric, rotational information flow between tokens. Recent work on Antisymmetric Transformers and Directional Graph Attention explicitly constructs attention mechanisms whose antisymmetric part encodes directed information flow, exploiting the curl structure.
14.5 Hamiltonian Neural Networks and Symplectic Structure
Hamiltonian Neural Networks (Greydanus et al. 2019) learn energy-conserving dynamics. A Hamiltonian system satisfies: \dot{q} = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p}, \qquad \dot{p} = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}
The vector field \mathbf{v} = (\dot{q}, \dot{p}) is:

Divergence-free: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{v} = H_{qp} - H_{pq} = 0 (by Clairaut)
Not curl-free: the dynamics are inherently rotational

In 2D phase space, the “curl” of \mathbf{v} is: \frac{\partial\dot{p}}{\partial q} - \frac{\partial\dot{q}}{\partial p} = -H_{qq} - H_{pp} = -\nabla^2 H
Hamiltonian systems preserve phase space volume (Liouville’s theorem) and have canonical symplectic structure — the 2D analog of being divergence-free while having specific curl structure. HNNs enforce this by parameterizing \mathbf{v} = J\nabla H where J = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix} is the symplectic matrix.
14.6 Physics-Informed Neural Networks — Learning Curl-Free and Solenoidal Fields
PINNs for fluid dynamics must learn velocity fields satisfying:

\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0 (incompressibility — divergence-free)
\nabla\times\boldsymbol{\xi} = \nabla\times(\nabla\times\mathbf{u}) (vorticity transport)

The Helmholtz decomposition is used to enforce incompressibility: parameterize \mathbf{u} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A} for a learned vector potential \mathbf{A}. Since \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{A}) = 0 always, incompressibility is automatically satisfied — the PINN only needs to learn \mathbf{A}.
This is curl as a constraint mechanism: by writing the field as a curl, you enforce the divergence-free condition by construction, reducing the learning problem.
14.7 Graph Neural Networks — Discrete Curl and Hodge Theory
On a simplicial complex (graph with triangles), the discrete curl is the coboundary operator \delta_1:
(\delta_1 \mathbf{f})_{ijk} = f_{ij} + f_{jk} + f_{ki}
for edge flow \mathbf{f}, where (ijk) is an oriented triangle. This measures the “circulation” around each triangle — the discrete curl.
The Hodge decomposition of edge flows: \mathbf{f} = \underbrace{\nabla\phi}_{\text{gradient/irrotational}} + \underbrace{\nabla\times\mathbf{A}}_{\text{curl/solenoidal}} + \underbrace{\mathbf{h}}_{\text{harmonic}}
Hodge-aware GNNs (Ebli et al. 2020; Yang et al. 2021) decompose signals into these three components, processing each separately. The curl component captures cyclic flow patterns (e.g., loops in citation networks, cycles in traffic flow), which traditional GNNs miss entirely because they only process node features.
Applications:

Traffic prediction: \mathbf{f} = traffic flow on road edges; curl detects congestion loops
Ranking from pairwise comparisons: gradient component = consistent global ranking; curl component = cyclic inconsistencies (A beats B, B beats C, C beats A)
Signal processing on meshes: curl-free and solenoidal components of 3D surface flows

14.8 Equivariant Neural Networks — SO(3) and Curl
Equivariant networks (e3nn, SE(3)-Transformers, NequIP) process 3D data (molecules, point clouds) in a way that respects rotational symmetry. Their features are irreducible representations of SO(3): scalars (invariant), vectors (equivariant), and higher-order tensors.
The curl is a key operation in these networks:

The cross product \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} (related to curl) maps two vectors to a pseudovector
Tensor products of vector features are decomposed into irreps, and the antisymmetric part (the curl-like component) is separated from the symmetric part

The mathematical backbone — that curl transforms as a pseudovector under rotations — is what allows equivariant networks to correctly handle chirality (left- vs right-handedness) in molecular property prediction.

§16. Personal Notes

The determinant mnemonic is essential for computation; the intrinsic definition (circulation per unit area) is essential for understanding. Know both. When you forget the formula on an exam, derive it from the intrinsic definition using Green’s theorem — you can reconstruct the z-component in two lines.
The shear flow example (\mathbf{F} = \langle y, 0, 0\rangle, curl = -\mathbf{k}) is the most important conceptual example. It demolishes the naive intuition that “curl means the field goes in circles.” It does not. Curl is about velocity gradients perpendicular to the flow direction.
\nabla\times\nabla f = 0 and \nabla\cdot\nabla\times\mathbf{F} = 0 are both consequences of Clairaut’s theorem. They are not independent theorems — they are the same algebraic identity d\circ d = 0 in the language of differential forms.
The Helmholtz decomposition is the vector calculus version of the fact that any matrix decomposes into symmetric + antisymmetric parts. The symmetric part = irrotational (gradient), antisymmetric part = solenoidal (curl). This analogy is exact and worth meditating on.
In ML: every time you see an antisymmetric matrix, an antisymmetric update rule, or non-conservative dynamics, you are seeing the discrete fingerprint of curl. The recent surge of interest in Hamiltonian networks, symplectic integrators, and Hodge GNNs is the field finally taking curl seriously as a computational object, not just a physics concept.
The four Maxwell’s equations are the most beautiful application of the divergence and curl. Two of the four are \nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0 (div of curl = 0, automatic) and \nabla\times\mathbf{E} = -\partial_t\mathbf{B} (curl = rate of change). The whole structure of electromagnetism is organized around div and curl.

01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/11..title: 11.Divergence
01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/11..content:
“The divergence asks a single, precise question at every point: is this a source, a sink, or neither? It is the scalar that measures how much the field breathes — expanding or contracting — at infinitesimal scale. Curl tells you about spin. Divergence tells you about expansion. Together they are the complete local portrait of a vector field.”


§1. Motivation — Sources, Sinks, and the Idea of Flux Density
Picture a vector field as a fluid flow. Drop an infinitesimally small sphere into the flow at a point p. Three things can happen:

More fluid flows out of the sphere than in — p is a source. Net outward flux > 0.
More fluid flows in than out — p is a sink. Net outward flux < 0.
The inflow exactly balances the outflow — p is neither. Net outward flux = 0.

The divergence \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}(p) is the net outward flux per unit volume, in the limit as the volume shrinks to p. It is a scalar field — at each point, a single number that tells you the local source/sink strength.
This is not the same as the field being large or small in magnitude. A field can be enormous and have zero divergence. A field can be tiny and have a huge divergence. Divergence is an infinitesimal, local measurement of expansion/contraction, not field strength.
The deepest reason to care: divergence appears on the right side of Gauss’s theorem (the Divergence theorem), in \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} = \rho/\varepsilon_0 (Gauss’s law for electricity), and in \nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0 (no magnetic monopoles). It is the bridge between local source density and global flux through closed surfaces. Understanding divergence is prerequisite to understanding electromagnetism, fluid mechanics, heat flow, and — as we will see — deep learning.

§2. Definition
2.1 The Divergence in \mathbb{R}^3
Let \mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangle : U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3 be a C^1 vector field. The divergence of \mathbf{F} is the scalar field:
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \text{div},\mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}
The notation \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} is read “del dot \mathbf{F},” treating \nabla = \langle \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z \rangle as a formal vector and taking the dot product with \mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangle:
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \langle \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z \rangle \cdot \langle P, Q, R \rangle = \partial_x P + \partial_y Q + \partial_z R

Warning. As with the curl determinant, this is a mnemonic — \nabla is a differential operator, not a vector. Treat the dot product mechanically: each component of \nabla differentiates the corresponding component of \mathbf{F}.

2.2 Components and Their Meaning
Each term \partial P / \partial x, \partial Q / \partial y, \partial R / \partial z measures how much the field spreads out in a single coordinate direction:





















TermMeasures\partial P / \partial xHow much \mathbf{F} accelerates in the x-direction as you move in x\partial Q / \partial yHow much \mathbf{F} accelerates in the y-direction as you move in y\partial R / \partial zHow much \mathbf{F} accelerates in the z-direction as you move in z
Their sum captures total volumetric expansion: if all three are positive, the field is diverging away from p in all three coordinate directions simultaneously — a pure source. The sign of \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} tells you the net tendency.
2.3 Divergence in \mathbb{R}^2
For a planar field \mathbf{F} = \langle P(x,y), Q(x,y) \rangle:
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}
This is the quantity appearing in Green’s theorem (normal form) and in 2D fluid mechanics.

§3. Intrinsic (Coordinate-Free) Definition
The formula \partial_x P + \partial_y Q + \partial_z R is useful computationally. The geometric definition is more fundamental.

Definition (Divergence via Gauss’s theorem). For a C^1 vector field \mathbf{F} on U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3, the divergence \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} at a point p is:
(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F})(p) = \lim_{V(B_\varepsilon) \to 0} \frac{1}{V(B_\varepsilon)} \oiint_{\partial B_\varepsilon} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
where B_\varepsilon is a ball of volume V(B_\varepsilon) centered at p, and the surface integral is over its boundary with outward-pointing normals.

In words: The divergence is the net outward flux per unit volume, in the limit as the volume shrinks to the point. It is independent of coordinates — which is why the formula looks the same after any rotation of axes.
This definition makes the physics transparent:

\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}(p) > 0: p is a source — the field pushes outward on net.
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}(p) < 0: p is a sink — the field pulls inward on net.
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}(p) = 0: p is neither — the field is divergence-free (solenoidal) at p.


§4. Full Proof: Coordinate Formula from Intrinsic Definition
We derive \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \partial_x P + \partial_y Q + \partial_z R from the limit definition, using the small-box argument.
Setup. Fix a point (a, b, c). Consider a small rectangular box B_\varepsilon with sides \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z centered at (a,b,c), with faces perpendicular to the coordinate axes. The total outward flux through \partial B_\varepsilon is the sum of fluxes through the six faces.
Flux through the x-faces.
The right face (at x = a + \Delta x/2) has outward normal \mathbf{i}, area \Delta y,\Delta z. The left face (at x = a - \Delta x/2) has outward normal -\mathbf{i}, area \Delta y,\Delta z. The net flux in the x-direction:
\Phi_x \approx P!\left(a + \frac{\Delta x}{2}, b, c\right)\Delta y,\Delta z - P!\left(a - \frac{\Delta x}{2}, b, c\right)\Delta y,\Delta z
By the Mean Value Theorem applied to P in x:
P!\left(a + \tfrac{\Delta x}{2}, b, c\right) - P!\left(a - \tfrac{\Delta x}{2}, b, c\right) \approx \frac{\partial P}{\partial x}(a,b,c),\Delta x
So \Phi_x \approx \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x},\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z.
Same argument for the y- and z-faces:
\Phi_y \approx \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y},\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z, \qquad \Phi_z \approx \frac{\partial R}{\partial z},\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z
Total flux and the limit:
\oiint_{\partial B_\varepsilon} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} \approx \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}\right)\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z
Dividing by V(B_\varepsilon) = \Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z and taking \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z \to 0:
\lim_{V \to 0}\frac{1}{V}\oiint_{\partial B_\varepsilon}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z} \quad \square
The formula is coordinate-free in the sense that the limit is independent of coordinates; it is a coincidence of Cartesian geometry that the formula takes the symmetric sum-of-partial-derivatives form in this basis.

§5. The Divergence Theorem
The intrinsic definition was:
(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F})(p) = \lim_{V \to 0} \frac{1}{V}\oiint_{\partial B} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S}
Integrate both sides over a solid region E — you get the Divergence Theorem (Gauss’s theorem):
\boxed{\iiint_E (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}),dV = \oiint_{\partial E}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S}}
The total source strength inside E equals the net outward flux through its boundary. This is one of the deepest theorems in vector calculus.
Key consequences:

If \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = 0 everywhere inside E, then \oiint_{\partial E}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0 — the field has no net flux through any closed surface enclosing a divergence-free region.
For a field with a point source at the origin (e.g., gravitational or Coulomb field), the integral \oiint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} equals the same constant for any surface surrounding the origin — the flux depends only on the enclosed sources, not the surface shape.
Green’s theorem (normal form) is the 2D special case: \iint_D (\partial_x P + \partial_y Q),dA = \oint_{\partial D} \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}},ds.


§6. Fundamental Identities
6.1 Divergence of a Curl is Zero
\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{F}) = 0
Proof. For \mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R\rangle, expand:
\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{F}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(R_y - Q_z) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(P_z - R_x) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(Q_x - P_y)
= R_{xy} - Q_{xz} + P_{yz} - R_{yx} + Q_{zx} - P_{zy}
= (R_{xy} - R_{yx}) + (P_{yz} - P_{zy}) + (Q_{zx} - Q_{xz}) = 0
by Clairaut’s theorem. \square
Meaning: Curl fields are automatically divergence-free — a curl field has no sources or sinks. The magnetic field \mathbf{B} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A} satisfies \nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0 identically — there are no magnetic monopoles, as a mathematical necessity.
6.2 Divergence of a Gradient is the Laplacian
\nabla\cdot(\nabla f) = \nabla^2 f = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2}
The Laplacian \nabla^2 f is arguably the most important operator in mathematical physics. It measures how much f(p) differs from the average of f over small spheres around p:
\nabla^2 f(p) = \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\left(\frac{1}{|S^2_\varepsilon|}\oiint_{S^2_\varepsilon} f,dS - f(p)\right) \cdot C
for a dimensional constant C. A harmonic function (\nabla^2 f = 0) takes no value larger or smaller than its surrounding average — this is the mean value property, which implies the maximum principle.
6.3 Product Rule for Divergence
\nabla\cdot(f\mathbf{F}) = f(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}) + \mathbf{F}\cdot(\nabla f)
Proof. Compute directly: \nabla\cdot(f\mathbf{F}) = \partial_x(fP) + \partial_y(fQ) + \partial_z(fR) = (f_x P + f P_x) + (f_y Q + f Q_y) + (f_z R + f R_z) = f(\partial_x P + \partial_y Q + \partial_z R) + (f_x P + f_y Q + f_z R) = f,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} + \nabla f\cdot\mathbf{F} \quad\square
This is the integration by parts formula for divergence. It yields Green’s first identity: \iiint_E f,\nabla^2 g,dV = \oiint_{\partial E} f,\nabla g\cdot d\mathbf{S} - \iiint_E \nabla f\cdot\nabla g,dV
and Green’s second identity (symmetric version). These are the fundamental tools for PDE theory.
6.4 Divergence of r^n\hat{\mathbf{r}} — The Key Physics Example
For the radial field \mathbf{F} = r^n\hat{\mathbf{r}} = r^{n-1}\langle x, y, z\rangle (where r = |\mathbf{r}|):
\nabla\cdot(r^n\hat{\mathbf{r}}) = (n+2)r^{n-1}
Special case n = -2 (the Coulomb/Newton field \mathbf{F} = \hat{\mathbf{r}}/r^2):
\nabla\cdot\left(\frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}}}{r^2}\right) = 0 \quad \text{for } r \neq 0
Yet \oiint_S \frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}}}{r^2}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = 4\pi for any sphere surrounding the origin. The resolution: the divergence is zero everywhere except the origin, where it is a Dirac delta:
\nabla\cdot\left(\frac{\hat{\mathbf{r}}}{r^2}\right) = 4\pi,\delta^3(\mathbf{r})
This is the mathematical content of Gauss’s law: the point charge at the origin is the source of the Coulomb field.

§7. The Logical Chain
              f ∈ C²
               │
               │ ∇ (gradient)
               ▼
         F = ∇f (conservative)
               │
               │ ∇· (divergence)
               ▼
         ∇·∇f = ∇²f (Laplacian)
         ∇²f = 0 ↔ harmonic function

Also:
         G = ∇ × F (curl field)
               │
               │ ∇· (divergence)
               ▼
         ∇·G = 0 always (solenoidal / divergence-free)

And the full de Rham chain:

  Ω⁰ ──grad──▶ Ω¹ ──curl──▶ Ω² ──div──▶ Ω³
           d             d            d

  d∘d = 0 at every step:
    curl(grad f) = 0
    div(curl F)  = 0

In differential forms, the divergence is the exterior derivative d acting on 2-forms. The identity \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{F}) = 0 is the single statement d\circ d = 0, which encodes all these identities simultaneously.

§8. Solenoidal Fields and Vector Potentials

Theorem. Let U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 be simply connected (in fact, contractible suffices). For a C^1 vector field \mathbf{F} on U, the following are equivalent:

\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = 0 on U (divergence-free / solenoidal)
\mathbf{F} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A} for some \mathbf{A} \in C^2(U) (vector potential exists)
\oiint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0 for every closed surface S in U
\iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} depends only on \partial S, not on the surface itself


(1)\Rightarrow(2): Construction via integration (analogous to finding a scalar potential for curl-free fields).
(2)\Rightarrow(1): Identity \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{A}) = 0.
(1)\Rightarrow(3): Divergence theorem on any region bounded by S.
(3)\Rightarrow(4): Two surfaces with the same boundary form a closed surface.
Physical meaning: A solenoidal field has no sources or sinks anywhere — the field lines are either closed loops or extend to infinity without termination. The magnetic field \mathbf{B} is always solenoidal (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0) because there are no magnetic monopoles.
Gauge freedom: The vector potential \mathbf{A} is not unique — \mathbf{A}' = \mathbf{A} + \nabla\phi gives the same \mathbf{B} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A}' = \nabla\times\mathbf{A} for any scalar \phi. This is gauge invariance — the fundamental symmetry of electromagnetism and Yang-Mills theory.

§9. Worked Examples
Example A — Basic Computation
\mathbf{F} = \langle x^2 y,; y^2 z,; z^2 x \rangle. Find \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}.
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial(x^2 y)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial(y^2 z)}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial(z^2 x)}{\partial z} = 2xy + 2yz + 2zx

Example B — Verifying the Divergence Theorem
\mathbf{F} = \langle x, y, z\rangle, E the unit ball x^2+y^2+z^2 \leq 1.
Via divergence theorem: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = 1+1+1 = 3.
\iiint_E 3,dV = 3\cdot\frac{4\pi}{3} = 4\pi
Direct check: On the unit sphere \mathbf{F} = \hat{\mathbf{r}} (outward radial), \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}} = 1.
\oiint_{S^2}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \oiint_{S^2} 1,dS = 4\pi \quad\checkmark

Example C — Physically Motivated: Electric Field
\mathbf{E} = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{\hat{\mathbf{r}}}{r^2} (Coulomb field of charge q at origin). Compute \nabla\cdot\mathbf{E}.
For r \neq 0: we showed \nabla\cdot(\hat{\mathbf{r}}/r^2) = 0.
So \nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = 0 away from the origin. But:
\oiint_{S^2_R}\mathbf{E}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\frac{1}{R^2}\cdot 4\pi R^2 = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}
for any sphere of radius R around the origin. By the divergence theorem:
\iiint_{B_R}\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E},dV = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \implies \nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta^3(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}
This is Gauss’s law in differential form: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = \rho/\varepsilon_0.

Example D — Counterintuitive: Radially Symmetric Field with Nonzero Divergence
\mathbf{F} = \langle x, y, 0\rangle (2D radial field, constant in z). Compute \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}.
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2
The divergence is positive everywhere, uniformly. The field arrows point outward from the z-axis — this is a source everywhere, not just at the origin. Any tiny sphere in this field will have more fluid leaving it than entering.
Contrast with the Coulomb field: 1/r^2 decay is precisely the rate needed to make \nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = 0 away from the source.

Example E — Testing for Solenoidal
Is \mathbf{F} = \langle yz,; xz,; xy\rangle solenoidal?
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial(yz)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial(xz)}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial(xy)}{\partial z} = 0 + 0 + 0 = 0 \quad\checkmark
Yes. Find the vector potential \mathbf{A} such that \nabla\times\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{F}: this requires solving a system of PDEs and is more involved (the construction parallels finding a scalar potential for curl-free fields, but one dimension higher).

Example F — Applying Green’s First Identity
Prove that if \nabla^2 f = 0 in E and f = 0 on \partial E, then f \equiv 0.
Set \mathbf{F} = f,\nabla f in the product rule \nabla\cdot(f\nabla f) = f\nabla^2 f + |\nabla f|^2. Apply the divergence theorem:
\oiint_{\partial E} f,\nabla f\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_E (f\nabla^2 f + |\nabla f|^2),dV
Left side: f = 0 on \partial E, so the left side is zero. Right side: \nabla^2 f = 0 in E, so:
0 = \iiint_E |\nabla f|^2,dV
Since |\nabla f|^2 \geq 0 and its integral is zero, |\nabla f|^2 = 0 everywhere in E. Thus \nabla f = \mathbf{0}, so f is constant. Since f = 0 on \partial E, f \equiv 0. \square
This is the uniqueness of Laplace’s equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions — derived purely from the divergence theorem and the product rule.

§10. Visualization
10.1 Source, Sink, and Neutral
  SOURCE (div > 0):        SINK (div < 0):          NEUTRAL (div = 0):
  
     ↗  ↑  ↖                  ↘  ↓  ↙                →  →  →  →
     ←  ·  →                  →  ·  ←                →  →  →  →
     ↙  ↓  ↘                  ↗  ↑  ↖                →  →  →  →
  
  F = ⟨x, y, z⟩             F = ⟨-x, -y, -z⟩       F = ⟨1, 0, 0⟩
  div F = 3                  div F = -3              div F = 0
  
  Fluid expands outward.     Fluid collapses inward. Parallel flow, no source.
  Net flux out of any ball.  Net flux into any ball. Zero net flux, any ball.

10.2 Divergence as Flux Density
  Small box at point p:
  
       ╔═══════════╗
       ║           ║
  ──▶  ║     p     ║  ──▶▶   (more exits than enters → div > 0)
       ║           ║
       ╚═══════════╝
  
  div F(p) = lim   (net outward flux through ∂B)
             V→0   ─────────────────────────────
                          volume of B
  
  This is the "breathing rate" of the field at p.

10.3 Divergence Theorem Geometrically
  ∭_E (∇·F) dV = ∯_{∂E} F·dS
  
  Microscopic sources           Macroscopic flux
  summed over the volume   =   through the boundary
  
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  + + -   + + +                            │
  │    +   + - +   +                         ──▶ Total flux
  │  - + + +   + -   +                       ──▶ out through
  │    +   +   + + +                         ──▶ the boundary
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘
       Individual source/sink strengths
       cancel internally; only boundary
       contribution survives.

10.4 Solenoidal vs. Irrotational Fields
  SOLENOIDAL (div F = 0):        IRROTATIONAL (curl F = 0):
  No sources/sinks anywhere.     No local rotation anywhere.
  
  Field lines are closed loops   Field lines are not closed;
  or extend to ±∞:               they have a potential:
  
       ←────────                  ↗  ↗  ↗  ↗
      ↓          ↑               ↗  ↗  ↗  ↗
       ────────→                ↗  ↗  ↗  ↗
  
  Example: magnetic field B     Example: gradient field ∇f
  ∇·B = 0, no monopoles         ∇×∇f = 0, no vortices
  
  Paddle wheel: may spin.       Paddle wheel: never spins.
  Tiny sphere: zero net flux.   Tiny sphere: may have net flux.

10.5 The Laplacian as Local Average Deviation
  Harmonic function (∇²f = 0):   Sub-harmonic (∇²f > 0):

  f(p) = avg of f on nearby       f(p) < avg of f on nearby
         spheres                          spheres
  
  ─────●─────   f(p) = average    ────────●─
  f    p    f                     f      p    f+ε
  
  No hills, no valleys.           p is a local "valley".
  Max principle: max on boundary. Min principle violated.

10.6 Helmholtz: Every Field Decomposes
  Any F = irrotational part + solenoidal part
  
  F   =  -∇φ       +    ∇×A
  
       (curl-free)      (div-free)
       
  ↗↗↗↗↗         ←────────
  ↗↗↗↗↗     +  ↓        ↑   =   complicated F
  ↗↗↗↗↗          ────────→
  
  div(-∇φ) = -∇²φ = ∇·F   ← determines the gradient part
  curl(∇×A) = ∇×F          ← determines the solenoidal part
  
  F is completely determined by its divergence AND its curl.


§11. Divergence in Physics
11.1 Maxwell’s Equations — Gauss’s Laws
Divergence appears in two of Maxwell’s four equations:
Gauss’s Law for Electricity: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}
The divergence of the electric field at a point equals the local charge density divided by \varepsilon_0. Where there is charge, the electric field diverges (or converges). Where there is no charge, \nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = 0 — the electric field is solenoidal. This is the differential form of Coulomb’s law generalized to arbitrary charge distributions.
Gauss’s Law for Magnetism: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0
The magnetic field is always divergence-free — everywhere, always. This means: there are no magnetic monopoles. Every magnetic field line that enters a region must leave it. The mathematical reason: \mathbf{B} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A}, and \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{A}) = 0 identically. The absence of magnetic monopoles is a theorem, given the vector potential.
11.2 Fluid Mechanics — Incompressibility and Continuity
The continuity equation in fluid mechanics: \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf{u}) = 0
This says: the rate of change of density at a point equals minus the divergence of the mass flux \rho\mathbf{u}. If mass flux diverges away from a point (positive divergence), the density there decreases.
For an incompressible fluid (\rho = \text{const}): \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0
The velocity field of an incompressible fluid is solenoidal. Every fluid element preserves its volume — the fluid neither compresses nor expands. This is the cornerstone assumption of most CFD (computational fluid dynamics): the Navier-Stokes equations for incompressible flow include \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0 as a constraint.
11.3 Heat Equation and Poisson’s Equation
The heat equation in \mathbb{R}^3: \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = k,\nabla^2 u = k,\nabla\cdot(\nabla u)
Temperature changes at a point when the temperature is above or below the local average — measured by \nabla^2 u = \nabla\cdot(\nabla u).
Poisson’s equation (electrostatics, gravity, diffusion): \nabla^2 \phi = f
where f is a given source function. When f = 0, this is Laplace’s equation \nabla^2\phi = 0. Solutions are harmonic functions — the most regular functions in analysis.
11.4 General Relativity — The Einstein Tensor
In general relativity, the divergence-free condition appears at the deepest level. The Einstein field equations: G_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = \frac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu\nu}
require the Bianchi identity \nabla^\mu G_{\mu\nu} = 0 — the covariant divergence of the Einstein tensor is zero. This is the GR analog of \nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0: it encodes energy-momentum conservation as a geometric identity.

§12. The Helmholtz Decomposition

Theorem (Helmholtz). Every sufficiently smooth \mathbf{F}: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3 decaying at infinity decomposes uniquely as:
\mathbf{F} = \underbrace{-\nabla\phi}_{\text{irrotational}} + \underbrace{\nabla\times\mathbf{A}}_{\text{solenoidal}}

The scalar potential \phi and vector potential \mathbf{A} are determined by: \phi(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac{\nabla'\cdot\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}')}{|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'|},dV', \qquad \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}^3}\frac{\nabla'\times\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}')}{|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'|},dV'
What this means in words: \mathbf{F} is completely and uniquely determined by specifying two scalar/vector functions:

its divergence \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} (which determines the irrotational part)
its curl \nabla\times\mathbf{F} (which determines the solenoidal part)

The analogy with matrices: Any matrix M decomposes into symmetric + antisymmetric parts: M = \frac{M+M^T}{2} + \frac{M-M^T}{2}. The Helmholtz decomposition is the continuous analog: the gradient (irrotational) part is the “symmetric” component of the field’s local behavior; the curl (solenoidal) part is the “antisymmetric” component. This analogy is exact in the language of differential forms.
Why Maxwell’s equations use both div and curl: The four equations are exactly the specification of \mathbf{E} and \mathbf{B} via their divergences (Gauss’s laws) and their curls (Faraday and Ampère). By Helmholtz, this completely determines the fields from the sources \rho and \mathbf{J}.

§13. Divergence in Curvilinear Coordinates
13.1 Cylindrical Coordinates (r, \theta, z)
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial(r F_r)}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial F_\theta}{\partial\theta} + \frac{\partial F_z}{\partial z}
The factor 1/r in the first term reflects the geometry: the area element at radius r is r,dr,d\theta, not dr,d\theta.
13.2 Spherical Coordinates (r, \theta, \phi)
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial(r^2 F_r)}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial(\sin\theta, F_\theta)}{\partial\theta} + \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial F_\phi}{\partial\phi}
For a purely radial field \mathbf{F} = F_r(r)\hat{\mathbf{r}}: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{d(r^2 F_r)}{dr}
Check: for F_r = r (i.e., \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{r}): \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{d(r^3)}{dr} = \frac{3r^2}{r^2} = 3. Consistent with Cartesian result.
For F_r = 1/r^2 (Coulomb): \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{d(1)}{dr} = 0. Consistent. \checkmark

As with the curl formulas: look these up rather than memorizing. Derive them from the intrinsic definition using the appropriate volume element if needed.


§14. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning

The divergence — as a measure of local expansion/contraction, a detector of sources and sinks, and the key ingredient in the Helmholtz decomposition — is woven into modern ML in ways that are increasingly recognized as fundamental. The keyword to watch: volume, flow, density, incompressibility, information.

14.1 Normalizing Flows — The Central Role of Divergence
Normalizing flows learn a diffeomorphism \mathbf{g}_\theta: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d that maps a simple distribution (Gaussian) to a complex data distribution. The change-of-variables formula:
\log p_X(\mathbf{x}) = \log p_Z(\mathbf{g}_\theta^{-1}(\mathbf{x})) + \log\left|\det J_{\mathbf{g}_\theta^{-1}}(\mathbf{x})\right|
requires computing \log|\det J| — the log of the Jacobian determinant. For a d\times d Jacobian, this is O(d^3) — prohibitive for large d.
FFJORD (Neural ODEs) (Chen et al. 2018) defines the flow as a continuous ODE: \frac{d\mathbf{z}}{dt} = f_\theta(\mathbf{z}, t)
By the instantaneous change-of-variables formula (Liouville’s theorem in continuous time):
\frac{d\log p(\mathbf{z}(t))}{dt} = -\nabla\cdot f_\theta(\mathbf{z}(t), t) = -\text{tr}(J_{f_\theta})
The log-density evolves at rate equal to minus the divergence of the flow field. Instead of computing \det J (O(d^3)), you only need \text{tr}(J_{f_\theta}) — the divergence — which is O(d) via the Hutchinson estimator:
\text{tr}(J_{f_\theta}) \approx \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)}\left[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^T J_{f_\theta}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right]
This is divergence as the computational bottleneck and solution in generative modeling. The entire FFJORD framework rests on the fact that the Jacobian determinant of a flow is controlled by its divergence (trace of the Jacobian).
Key insight: The divergence-free condition (\nabla\cdot f = 0) means the flow preserves volume in latent space — log-density does not change. Volume-preserving flows are “free” in terms of log-likelihood cost. This is why symplectic flows (volume-preserving by construction) are computationally attractive.
14.2 Score-Based Diffusion Models — Divergence and the Score Function
Score-based generative models (Song & Ermon 2019; DDPM, DDIM, Score-SDE) learn the score function \mathbf{s}_\theta(\mathbf{x}, t) \approx \nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\log p_t(\mathbf{x}) — the gradient of the log-density.
The training objective via score matching involves the divergence:
\mathcal{L}_{\text{SM}} = \mathbb{E}_{p(\mathbf{x})}\left[\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{s}_\theta(\mathbf{x})|^2 + \nabla\cdot\mathbf{s}_\theta(\mathbf{x})\right] + \text{const}
Here \nabla\cdot\mathbf{s}_\theta is the divergence of the score network — it appears directly in the loss. Computing the exact divergence is O(d^2) (all Jacobian diagonal entries), so in practice:

Denoising score matching avoids computing divergence explicitly by using a surrogate loss.
Sliced score matching uses random projections: \mathbf{v}^T\nabla(\mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{s}_\theta) — a directional derivative, related to a projected divergence.

The Fokker-Planck equation for the density evolution under the diffusion SDE: \frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} = -\nabla\cdot(f(\mathbf{x},t)p_t) + \frac{g(t)^2}{2}\nabla^2 p_t
is a divergence equation — the right side is -\nabla\cdot(\text{probability flux}). The probability flux \mathbf{J} = f p_t - \frac{g^2}{2}\nabla p_t has divergence equal to minus the time derivative of the density. The entire theoretical framework of diffusion models rests on this divergence equation.
14.3 GAN Training — Divergences Between Distributions
This is a different but related usage of “divergence” — statistical divergences between distributions:

KL divergence: D_{KL}(p|q) = \int p\log(p/q),d\mathbf{x} (not a symmetric metric, but related to information theory)
Jensen-Shannon divergence: D_{JS}(p|q) = \frac{1}{2}D_{KL}(p|m) + \frac{1}{2}D_{KL}(q|m), where m = (p+q)/2. The original GAN minimizes D_{JS}.
Wasserstein distance (Wasserstein GAN): W_1(p, q) = \sup_{|\phi|_L \leq 1}\mathbb{E}_p[\phi] - \mathbb{E}_q[\phi]. More stable training.
f-divergences: D_f(p|q) = \int q,f(p/q),d\mathbf{x}. A general family containing KL and JS.

These “divergences” are not the vector-field divergence \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} — they are measures of dissimilarity between distributions. However, the connection runs deep: in optimal transport theory, the Wasserstein distance is related to the divergence of a vector field via:
W_2^2(p, q) = \min_{\mathbf{v}: \frac{\partial p}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot(p\mathbf{v}) = 0} \int_0^1\int |\mathbf{v}|^2 p,d\mathbf{x},dt
The continuity equation \partial_t p + \nabla\cdot(p\mathbf{v}) = 0 — a divergence equation — is the constraint that defines geodesics in the space of probability distributions (Benamou-Brenier formula). The field-theoretic divergence and the probabilistic divergence are genuinely connected via fluid mechanics.
14.4 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) — Divergence as a Hard Constraint
PINNs for fluid dynamics enforce: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0 \quad\text{(incompressibility)}
Two approaches:
Soft constraint: Add a penalty \lambda|\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u}|^2 to the loss. This requires computing \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} at collocation points — automatic differentiation gives \partial u_1/\partial x_1 + \cdots + \partial u_d/\partial x_d, which is just the divergence. The network is penalized for having nonzero divergence.
Hard constraint (divergence-free by construction): Parameterize the velocity as: \mathbf{u} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A}
for a learned vector potential \mathbf{A}. Since \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{A}) = 0 always, the incompressibility condition is automatically satisfied — no penalty needed, no error in the constraint. The network only needs to learn \mathbf{A}, which has one fewer degree of freedom.
This is a direct application of the theorem: solenoidal fields are exactly curls. The divergence theorem, used backwards, gives you a parameterization that enforces the physics exactly.
14.5 Equivariant Networks — Divergence-Free Feature Fields
SE(3)-equivariant networks (e3nn, NequIP, SEGNN) process 3D molecular data. Their internal representations include vector fields on point clouds. When modeling physical quantities:

Velocity fields must be divergence-free (incompressible fluid).
Force fields are gradients of potentials — irrotational, with \nabla\times\mathbf{F} = 0.
Electromagnetic fields satisfy specific divergence and curl conditions.

Incorporating these constraints into the network architecture — by parameterizing features as \nabla f (automatically irrotational) or \nabla\times\mathbf{A} (automatically solenoidal) — drastically reduces the hypothesis space and improves data efficiency for physical property prediction.
14.6 Optimal Transport and the Wasserstein Geometry of ML
The Benamou-Brenier formula (mentioned above) casts optimal transport as a fluid mechanics problem. The probability density evolves via:
\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf{v}) = 0
This is the continuity equation — a divergence equation. The velocity field \mathbf{v} that minimizes \int_0^1\int|\mathbf{v}|^2\rho,d\mathbf{x},dt subject to this constraint is the optimal transport map.
In practice, this framework underlies:

Wasserstein gradient flows — the training dynamics of many generative models, viewed as gradient descent in the space of probability measures with the Wasserstein metric.
JKO scheme — an implicit time-stepping scheme for diffusion equations: \rho_{n+1} = \arg\min_\rho \frac{1}{2\tau}W_2^2(\rho, \rho_n) + \mathcal{F}(\rho).
Distribution shift in domain adaptation — measuring and correcting for covariate shift using Wasserstein distances.

The divergence equation is the thread connecting all of these: the conservation of probability mass.
14.7 Information Geometry — Fisher Information and Divergence
The Fisher information matrix I(\theta) defines a Riemannian metric on the space of parameterized distributions p_\theta. The natural gradient \tilde{\nabla}\mathcal{L} = I(\theta)^{-1}\nabla\theta\mathcal{L} adjusts for the curvature of the distribution space.
The KL divergence D_{KL}(p_\theta|p_{\theta+d\theta}) \approx \frac{1}{2}d\theta^T I(\theta),d\theta — the infinitesimal KL divergence is exactly the Fisher-Riemannian metric. This means:

Gradient descent on parameters \theta = steepest descent in Euclidean parameter space.
Natural gradient descent = steepest descent in the space of distributions, with distance measured by KL divergence.

The Laplace-Beltrami operator (the curved-space generalization of \nabla^2 = \nabla\cdot\nabla) governs how information “diffuses” on the statistical manifold. Divergence on statistical manifolds = the generalized \nabla\cdot with respect to the Fisher metric — this is the arena of information geometry.
14.8 Hodge Theory on Graphs — Discrete Divergence
On a graph G = (V, E), the discrete divergence of an edge flow \mathbf{f}: E \to \mathbb{R} is the boundary operator \partial_1:
(\partial_1\mathbf{f})_v = \sum_{e: v = \text{head}(e)} f_e - \sum_{e: v = \text{tail}(e)} f_e
This is exactly the net flow out of each node — the discrete analog of \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}.
The Hodge decomposition of edge flows: \mathbf{f} = \underbrace{\partial_0^T\phi}_{\text{gradient (irrotational)}} + \underbrace{\partial_2^T \mathbf{g}}_{\text{curl (solenoidal)}} + \underbrace{\mathbf{h}}_{\text{harmonic}}
where:

\partial_0^T is the gradient operator (node values to edge differences)
\partial_2^T is the curl operator (triangle flows to edge curls)
\mathbf{h} is in the kernel of both — harmonic flows

The discrete divergence \partial_1 is the transpose of the gradient: \partial_1 = \partial_0^T‘s adjoint. In graph ML:

Message passing in GNNs is effectively computing (a learned version of) the discrete Laplacian L = \partial_0^T\partial_0 — related to \nabla\cdot\nabla = \nabla^2.
Hodge-aware GNNs decompose edge features using the full Hodge decomposition, capturing divergence-free (cyclic) flow separately from gradient (acyclic) flow.
Traffic flow prediction: the divergence-free component captures circular traffic patterns; the gradient component captures source-to-sink flow (e.g., from suburbs to city center).

The graph Laplacian L = D - A (degree minus adjacency matrix) is the discrete Laplacian. The normalized version L_{sym} = I - D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2} is used in spectral GNNs. Both are discrete versions of \nabla^2 = \nabla\cdot\nabla.

§15. Summary
\boxed{\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}}

































































PropertyStatementGeometric meaningNet outward flux per unit volume; local source/sink strengthSign> 0: source; < 0: sink; = 0: solenoidal (divergence-free)Div of curl\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{F}) = 0 always (C^2)Div of gradient\nabla\cdot\nabla f = \nabla^2 f (Laplacian)Solenoidal\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = 0 \iff \mathbf{F} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A} (on contractible domains)Divergence theorem\iiint_E\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F},dV = \oiint_{\partial E}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S}Maxwell\nabla\cdot\mathbf{E} = \rho/\varepsilon_0; \nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0FluidIncompressible flow: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0Laplacian\nabla^2 f = 0: harmonic; = f: Poisson equationHelmholtz\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} determines the irrotational part of \mathbf{F}ML: FlowsFFJORD: d\log p/dt = -\nabla\cdot f_\theta; volume-preserving = div-freeML: Score modelsScore matching loss contains \nabla\cdot\mathbf{s}_\theta; Fokker-Planck = divergence eqML: PINNsHard incompressibility: \mathbf{u} = \nabla\times\mathbf{A} by constructionML: GraphsGraph Laplacian = discrete \nabla\cdot\nabla; Hodge decomp = discrete Helmholtz

§16. Personal Notes


The product rule \nabla\cdot(f\mathbf{F}) = f,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} + \nabla f\cdot\mathbf{F} is more useful than it looks. It is the engine behind Green’s first identity, integration by parts for PDEs, and the derivation of the wave equation energy. Memorize it.


The Coulomb/Newton field \hat{\mathbf{r}}/r^2 is the canonical example: zero divergence everywhere except the origin, nonzero flux through any enclosing surface. The resolution requires the Dirac delta. Every physics student must work this out at least once by hand. The dimensional analysis is also illuminating: in \mathbb{R}^3, the field decaying as 1/r^2 has zero divergence; in \mathbb{R}^2, it would be 1/r; in \mathbb{R}^n, it would be r^{-(n-1)}. This is why the Newtonian potential is \log r in 2D and 1/r in 3D.


The Helmholtz decomposition is the most important structural theorem in vector calculus. It says: to know a vector field, know its sources (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}) and its vortices (\nabla\times\mathbf{F}). Maxwell’s equations are literally a specification of these two quantities for \mathbf{E} and \mathbf{B}. The whole of electromagnetism is encoded in this decomposition.


In ML, “divergence” appears in two senses: the vector-calculus divergence (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}, measuring field expansion) and the information-theoretic divergence (D_{KL}, D_{JS}, measuring distribution dissimilarity). The two are connected by the Benamou-Brenier formula through the continuity equation. When you see \nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf{v}) = 0, you are seeing the bridge between them.


The score function in diffusion models is \nabla_\mathbf{x}\log p(\mathbf{x}) — the gradient of the log-density. The divergence of the score is \nabla^2\log p(\mathbf{x}) — the Laplacian of the log-density. This appears in the score matching objective and in the Stein operator. The Laplacian is the divergence of a gradient; it measures the “concavity” of the log-density, i.e., how much the probability mass concentrates.


The graph Laplacian L = D - A is the discrete version of -\nabla^2 (note the sign: -\nabla^2 is positive semi-definite for a connected graph, as is L). The spectral decomposition of L is the graph analog of Fourier analysis. GNNs that use L are essentially performing a discrete version of the heat equation \partial_t f = \nabla^2 f = -Lf — diffusion on the graph. Understanding divergence is understanding why this works.


\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0 is probably the most consequential consequence of the identity \nabla\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf{A}) = 0. The non-existence of magnetic monopoles — a fundamental experimental fact — is in this one algebraic identity. Whether monopoles exist is still an open question in physics, but Maxwell’s equations as formulated require \nabla\cdot\mathbf{B} = 0 rigorously.



References

MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus. Sessions 33–36: “Divergence; Divergence Theorem.” ocw.mit.edu


Griffiths, David J. Introduction to Electrodynamics, 4th ed. Ch. 1–2: for Gauss’s law, Helmholtz theorem, and the Dirac delta.


Evans, Lawrence C. Partial Differential Equations, 2nd ed. AMS. Ch. 2: for Green’s identities, harmonic functions, and the Laplacian.


Chen, R. T. Q. et al. (2018). Neural Ordinary Differential Equations. NeurIPS — for FFJORD and the divergence trace formula.


Song, Y. & Ermon, S. (2019). Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution. NeurIPS — for score matching and the divergence in the loss.


Benamou, J.-D. & Brenier, Y. (2000). A computational fluid mechanics solution to the Monge-Kantorovich mass transfer problem. Numerische Mathematik — for the optimal transport / continuity equation connection.

01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/12..title: 12.Green's Theorem - Vector Forms
01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/12..content:
“Green’s theorem is not one theorem. It is two theorems wearing the same coat. The tangential form says: circulation around a boundary equals the curl through the interior. The normal form says: flux through a boundary equals the divergence of the interior. They are the same algebraic identity, rotated ninety degrees, and both are special cases of Stokes’ theorem in disguise.”


§1. Motivation — Two Questions About a Planar Field
Let \mathbf{F} = \langle P(x,y), Q(x,y) \rangle be a C^1 vector field on a simply connected region D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2, with boundary C = \partial D oriented counterclockwise (positive orientation).
There are exactly two natural scalar quantities you can form from \mathbf{F} and a boundary curve C:

Circulation: \oint_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \oint_C P,dx + Q,dy — how much does \mathbf{F} flow along C?
Flux: \oint_C \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}},ds — how much does \mathbf{F} flow through C, outward?

Green’s theorem in its two vector forms answers both questions in terms of interior integrals:

Circulation = \iint_D (curl of \mathbf{F}) — the tangential / circulation form
Flux = \iint_D (divergence of \mathbf{F}) — the normal / flux form

These are not two separate theorems — they are the same identity applied to the same field \mathbf{F}, or equivalently, applied to the rotated field \mathbf{F}^\perp. Understanding why they are the same identity, written twice, is the conceptual key to the whole subject.

§2. Setup and Notation
Throughout: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 is a bounded, simply connected region with piecewise C^1 boundary C = \partial D. The boundary is oriented counterclockwise (the interior is to the left as you traverse C).
Parametrize C by arc length s or by a parameter t. The two natural unit vectors on C:
\hat{\mathbf{T}} = \frac{d\mathbf{r}}{ds} = \langle \dot{x}, \dot{y}\rangle \quad\text{(unit tangent, counterclockwise)}
\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \langle \dot{y}, -\dot{x}\rangle \quad\text{(outward unit normal, obtained by rotating $\hat{\mathbf{T}}$ clockwise by $90°$)}

Why \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \langle \dot{y}, -\dot{x}\rangle? If \hat{\mathbf{T}} = \langle \dot{x}, \dot{y}\rangle, rotating 90° clockwise gives \langle \dot{y}, -\dot{x}\rangle. For counterclockwise orientation of C, this rotation points outward from D. Check: on the right side of a rectangle (traversed upward, \dot{x} = 0, \dot{y} = 1), \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \langle 1, 0\rangle — pointing right, i.e., outward. \checkmark


§3. The Scalar Statement (Reference)
The classical statement of Green’s theorem:
\oint_{\partial D} P,dx + Q,dy = \iint_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dA
This is the starting point. Both vector forms are obtained by choosing P, Q appropriately or by rewriting the line integral in terms of \mathbf{F}, \hat{\mathbf{T}}, and \hat{\mathbf{n}}.

§4. Form I — The Tangential (Circulation / Curl) Form
4.1 Statement
\boxed{\oint_{\partial D} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_D (\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot\mathbf{k},dA = \iint_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dA}
The circulation of \mathbf{F} around the boundary equals the integral of the (scalar) 2D curl over the interior.
4.2 Proof
The line integral \oint_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} uses the tangent vector:
\oint_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \oint_C \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{T}},ds = \oint_C \langle P, Q\rangle\cdot\langle dx, dy\rangle = \oint_C P,dx + Q,dy
Apply the scalar Green’s theorem:
\oint_C P,dx + Q,dy = \iint_D\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dA
The integrand \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} is precisely the z-component of \nabla\times\mathbf{F} for the planar field \mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, 0\rangle:
(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot\mathbf{k} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}
So:
\oint_{\partial D}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_D(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot\mathbf{k},dA \quad\square
4.3 Geometric Meaning
The curl (\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot\mathbf{k} measures the local counterclockwise rotation of \mathbf{F} at each point. Integrating it over D accumulates all the local rotation. The theorem says this total local rotation equals the global circulation around the boundary.
Intuition via tiling: Tile D with tiny squares. The circulation around each tiny square contributes (\nabla\times\mathbf{F}),\Delta A (by the intrinsic definition of curl). When adjacent squares share an edge, the contribution from that shared edge cancels — adjacent squares are traversed in opposite directions. Only the boundary edges survive. Summing over all tiles gives the total boundary circulation. This is Green’s theorem in its most transparent form.
  ┌──┬──┬──┐
  │→↑│→↑│→↑│   Each tiny square contributes
  ├──┼──┼──┤   curl · ΔA to the sum.
  │→↑│→↑│→↑│   Interior edges cancel pairwise.
  ├──┼──┼──┤   Only the outer boundary survives.
  │→↑│→↑│→↑│
  └──┴──┴──┘
  
  ∮_C F·dr = ∑_tiles (curl F) ΔA = ∬_D curl F dA

4.4 Special Case: Irrotational Fields
If \nabla\times\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0} on D (irrotational / conservative), then: \oint_{\partial D}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = 0
Zero curl everywhere \Rightarrow zero circulation around every simple closed curve. This is the analytical content of path-independence for conservative fields.

§5. Form II — The Normal (Flux / Divergence) Form
5.1 Statement
\boxed{\oint_{\partial D}\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}},ds = \iint_D \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F},dA = \iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)dA}
The outward flux of \mathbf{F} through the boundary equals the integral of the divergence over the interior.
5.2 Proof
Express the flux integral in coordinates. With C parametrized as (x(t), y(t)), dt from a to b, and \hat{\mathbf{n}},ds = \langle \dot{y}, -\dot{x}\rangle,dt:
\oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}},ds = \oint_C\langle P, Q\rangle\cdot\langle \dot{y}, -\dot{x}\rangle,dt = \oint_C P,dy - Q,dx
Apply the scalar Green’s theorem with the substitution P \leftarrow -Q and Q \leftarrow P:
\oint_C P,dy - Q,dx = \oint_C (-Q),dx + P,dy = \iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial(-Q)}{\partial y}\right)dA = \iint_D\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)dA
The integrand \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} is exactly \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}. So:
\oint_{\partial D}\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}},ds = \iint_D\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F},dA \quad\square
5.3 Geometric Meaning
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} measures the local outward expansion of \mathbf{F} at each point. Integrating it over D accumulates all local source/sink strength. The theorem says this total source strength equals the net outward flux through the boundary.
This is the 2D Divergence Theorem — the 2D special case of the full 3D Divergence theorem, restricted to planar fields.
Intuition via tiling: Same tiling argument. Each tiny square contributes (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}),\Delta A net outward flux. Interior edges cancel. Only boundary flux survives.
  ┌──┬──┬──┐
  │↗·│↗·│↗·│   Each tiny square contributes
  ├──┼──┼──┤   div F · ΔA net outward flux.
  │↗·│↗·│↗·│   Interior face fluxes cancel.
  ├──┼──┼──┤   Boundary face fluxes survive.
  │↗·│↗·│↗·│
  └──┴──┴──┘
  
  ∮_C F·n̂ ds = ∑_tiles (div F) ΔA = ∬_D div F dA

5.4 Special Case: Divergence-Free Fields
If \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = 0 on D (solenoidal), then: \oint_{\partial D}\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}},ds = 0
Zero divergence everywhere \Rightarrow zero net outward flux through every simple closed curve. The field has no sources or sinks — every line that enters the region must exit it.

§6. The Unifying Symmetry — One Identity, Rotated
The two forms are not coincidentally similar. They are the same identity, applied to \mathbf{F} and its 90°-rotation.
Define the clockwise rotation of \mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q\rangle: \mathbf{F}^\perp = \langle Q, -P\rangle
(Rotate each vector 90° clockwise.)
Claim: The normal form for \mathbf{F} equals the tangential form for \mathbf{F}^\perp.
Proof.
Tangential form for \mathbf{F}^\perp = \langle Q, -P\rangle:
\oint_C \mathbf{F}^\perp\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \oint_C Q,dx + (-P),dy = -\oint_C P,dy - Q,dx = -\oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}},ds
(using the relation \oint_C P,dy - Q,dx = \oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}},ds from §5.2.)
The curl of \mathbf{F}^\perp: \frac{\partial(-P)}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} = -\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}
So the tangential form for \mathbf{F}^\perp gives: -\oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}},ds = \iint_D(-\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}),dA
Multiply by -1: \oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}},ds = \iint_D\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F},dA \quad\square
