01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/16..title: 16.Surface Area
01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/16..content:
“To measure is to know.” — Lord Kelvin


§0. Prefatory Remarks
Surface area is one of those concepts that feels intuitively obvious — and is analytically subtle. The naive approach (approximate by rectangles, take a limit) fails catastrophically: there exist continuous surfaces whose “rectangular” approximations diverge to infinity while the true area is finite. This is the Schwarz lantern paradox, and it forces us to be precise about what “area” means.
The correct approach: approximate by flat triangular patches (tangent plane pieces), not by rectangles. This leads to the integral \iint |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|, du, dv, which is the formula we derive and prove here.
Surface area appears throughout:

Physics: heat transfer, fluid drag, electrostatics (Gauss’s law)
Differential geometry: minimal surfaces, isoperimetric inequalities
Computer graphics: texture mapping, mesh parameterization
Machine learning / deep learning: kernel methods, Gaussian process priors on manifolds, surface-loss functions in neural geometry processing

This note builds the theory from scratch, connects it to the previous notes on Surfaces_of_Revolution and Tangent_Planes, and proves everything.

§1. The Problem — Why Rectangles Fail
1.1 Arc Length as a Warm-Up
Recall how we measure arc length. For a curve \boldsymbol{\gamma}: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^3, we approximate by straight-line segments:
L \approx \sum_{i} |\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_{i+1}) - \boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_i)|.
As the partition refines, this converges to \int_a^b |\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t)|,dt. The key: we approximate by line segments tangent to the curve. This works.
1.2 The Schwarz Lantern Paradox
Inscribe a cylinder of radius 1 and height 1 with a triangular mesh: divide the height into n horizontal strips and rotate by \pi/m between strips, placing m triangles per strip. The true lateral area of the cylinder is 2\pi.
As n, m \to \infty, what does the mesh area converge to?
If n = m (balanced refinement): the area converges to 2\pi. ✓
If n = m^2 (height refined faster than circumference): the area diverges to \infty. ✗
Moral. The limit depends on how you refine, not just that you refine. Rectangular subdivisions of a surface — unlike line-segment subdivisions of a curve — do not automatically converge to the correct area. We must use a definition that is independent of parameterization and robust to this issue.
The fix: use the tangent plane at each point. The correct area element is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the tangent vectors \mathbf{r}_u , du and \mathbf{r}_v , dv.

§2. The Setup — Parameterized Surfaces
Definition 2.1. A smooth parameterized surface is a map \mathbf{r}: D \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3, (u,v) \mapsto \mathbf{r}(u,v), where D is a bounded region, \mathbf{r} \in C^1(D), and the cross product \mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v \neq \mathbf{0} everywhere on D (the regular condition).
The tangent vectors at (u_0, v_0): \mathbf{r}_u = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial u}, \quad \mathbf{r}_v = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial v}.
These span the tangent plane at \mathbf{r}(u_0,v_0) (as established in Tangent_Planes, §4).
The area element. For a small rectangle [u_0, u_0+\Delta u] \times [v_0, v_0+\Delta v] in parameter space, the image on the surface is approximated by the parallelogram with sides \mathbf{r}_u \Delta u and \mathbf{r}_v \Delta v. The area of this parallelogram is
|\mathbf{r}_u \Delta u \times \mathbf{r}_v \Delta v| = |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|, \Delta u, \Delta v.
Summing over all such patches and taking the limit gives the definition.

§3. The Surface Area Formula
Definition / Theorem 3.1 (Surface Area). The surface area of a smooth parameterized surface \mathbf{r}: D \to \mathbb{R}^3 is
\boxed{A = \iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|, dA,}
where dA = du, dv is the area element in parameter space.
Proof (rigorous sketch). Partition D into small rectangles R_{ij} = [u_i, u_{i+1}] \times [v_j, v_{j+1}] with \Delta u = u_{i+1}-u_i, \Delta v = v_{j+1}-v_j. At each rectangle, approximate the surface patch \mathbf{r}(R_{ij}) by the parallelogram with sides
\mathbf{r}_u(u_i, v_j),\Delta u \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{r}_v(u_i,v_j),\Delta v.
The area of this parallelogram is |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|(u_i,v_j),\Delta u,\Delta v. Summing:
A \approx \sum_{i,j} |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|(u_i,v_j),\Delta u,\Delta v.
This is a Riemann sum for \iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,dA. Since |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v| is continuous on the compact set D (as \mathbf{r} \in C^1), the Riemann sums converge as \Delta u, \Delta v \to 0. This limit is the definition of surface area (independent of parameterization — proved in §5). \blacksquare
The Three Representations
Depending on how the surface is given, the formula takes three forms.
Case 1 — Explicit: z = f(x,y).
Parameterize by (x,y) itself: \mathbf{r}(x,y) = (x, y, f(x,y)).
\mathbf{r}_x = (1, 0, f_x), \quad \mathbf{r}_y = (0, 1, f_y).
\mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_y = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 1 & 0 & f_x \ 0 & 1 & f_y\end{vmatrix} = (-f_x,, -f_y,, 1).
|\mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_y| = \sqrt{f_x^2 + f_y^2 + 1}.
\boxed{A = \iint_D \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right)^2}; dA.}
Case 2 — Parametric: \mathbf{r}(u,v).
\boxed{A = \iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|; du, dv.}
Case 3 — Implicit: G(x,y,z) = 0, solved as z = f(x,y).
Use Case 1 with f_x = -G_x/G_z and f_y = -G_y/G_z:
\sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2} = \frac{\sqrt{G_x^2 + G_y^2 + G_z^2}}{|G_z|} = \frac{|\nabla G|}{|G_z|}.
\boxed{A = \iint_D \frac{|\nabla G|}{|G_z|}; dA.}

§4. The First Fundamental Form
The quantity |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v| can be expressed in terms of the first fundamental form (metric tensor) of the surface. Define:
E = \mathbf{r}_u \cdot \mathbf{r}_u, \quad F = \mathbf{r}_u \cdot \mathbf{r}_v, \quad G = \mathbf{r}_v \cdot \mathbf{r}_v.
These are the coefficients of the metric g_{ij}, and we have the classical identity:
|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|^2 = |\mathbf{r}_u|^2|\mathbf{r}_v|^2 - (\mathbf{r}_u \cdot \mathbf{r}_v)^2 = EG - F^2 = \det[g_{ij}].
Proof of the identity. By the Lagrange identity: |\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|^2 = |\mathbf{a}|^2|\mathbf{b}|^2 - (\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})^2. \blacksquare
So the area formula becomes:
A = \iint_D \sqrt{EG - F^2}; du, dv.
This is the intrinsic formula — it depends only on the metric, not on the embedding in \mathbb{R}^3. From the Tangent_Planes note, for a surface of revolution \mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = (x, f\cos\theta, f\sin\theta):
E = 1+(f')^2, \quad F = 0, \quad G = f^2 \implies \sqrt{EG-F^2} = f\sqrt{1+(f')^2},
recovering the formula from Surfaces_of_Revolution, §3. ✓

§5. Independence of Parameterization
A critical property: the area should not depend on how we parameterize the surface. This is non-obvious — the formula \iint |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv explicitly involves u, v.
Theorem 5.1 (Reparameterization Invariance). Let \mathbf{r}: D \to S and \tilde{\mathbf{r}}: \tilde{D} \to S be two regular parameterizations of the same surface, related by \mathbf{r}(u,v) = \tilde{\mathbf{r}}(\phi(u,v), \psi(u,v)) where (u,v) \mapsto (\phi,\psi) is a C^1 diffeomorphism with Jacobian J. Then
\iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv = \iint_{\tilde{D}} |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \times \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi|,d\phi,d\psi.
Proof. By the chain rule: \mathbf{r}_u = \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \phi_u + \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi \psi_u and \mathbf{r}_v = \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \phi_v + \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi \psi_v. The cross product:
\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v = (\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \phi_u + \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi\psi_u) \times (\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi\phi_v + \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi\psi_v).
Expanding using bilinearity and \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}:
= (\phi_u\psi_v - \phi_v\psi_u)(\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \times \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi) = J \cdot (\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \times \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi),
where J = \frac{\partial(\phi,\psi)}{\partial(u,v)} is the Jacobian determinant. So:
\iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv = \iint_D |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \times \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi| \cdot |J|,du,dv = \iint_{\tilde{D}} |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \times \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi|,d\phi,d\psi,
by the change-of-variables formula. \blacksquare

This is the multivariable analogue of the substitution rule for integrals. The Jacobian of the change of coordinates exactly cancels the change in |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|.


§6. Worked Examples
Example 6.1 — Sphere of Radius R
Method 1: Explicit parameterization. Use \mathbf{r}(\phi,\theta) = (R\sin\phi\cos\theta, R\sin\phi\sin\theta, R\cos\phi) for (\phi,\theta) \in [0,\pi]\times[0,2\pi].
\mathbf{r}_\phi = R(\cos\phi\cos\theta, \cos\phi\sin\theta, -\sin\phi), \mathbf{r}_\theta = R(-\sin\phi\sin\theta, \sin\phi\cos\theta, 0).
Computing the cross product and its magnitude:
E = R^2, \quad F = 0, \quad G = R^2\sin^2\phi, |\mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta| = R^2\sin\phi.
A = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi R^2\sin\phi, d\phi, d\theta = 2\pi R^2 \int_0^\pi \sin\phi, d\phi = 2\pi R^2 \cdot 2 = 4\pi R^2. \checkmark
Method 2: Explicit surface z = f(x,y). Use upper hemisphere z = \sqrt{R^2 - x^2 - y^2} over D: x^2+y^2 \leq R^2 and double.
f_x = \frac{-x}{\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}}, \quad f_y = \frac{-y}{\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}}.
1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2 = 1 + \frac{x^2+y^2}{R^2-x^2-y^2} = \frac{R^2}{R^2-x^2-y^2}.
A = 2\iint_{x^2+y^2\leq R^2} \frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}}, dA.
Switch to polar x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta:
A = 2\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R \frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2-r^2}}, r, dr, d\theta = 4\pi R \int_0^R \frac{r, dr}{\sqrt{R^2-r^2}}.
Let u = R^2 - r^2, du = -2r,dr:
= 4\pi R \int_{R^2}^0 \frac{-du/2}{\sqrt{u}} = 2\pi R \int_0^{R^2} u^{-1/2},du = 2\pi R \cdot 2R = 4\pi R^2. \checkmark
Example 6.2 — Paraboloid z = x^2 + y^2 over x^2+y^2 \leq 1
f_x = 2x, \quad f_y = 2y, \quad \sqrt{1 + 4x^2 + 4y^2} = \sqrt{1+4r^2}.
A = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 \sqrt{1+4r^2}, r, dr, d\theta = 2\pi \int_0^1 r\sqrt{1+4r^2}, dr.
Let u = 1 + 4r^2, du = 8r,dr:
A = 2\pi \int_1^5 \sqrt{u}\cdot\frac{du}{8} = \frac{\pi}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\left[u^{3/2}\right]_1^5 = \frac{\pi}{6}(5^{3/2} - 1) = \frac{\pi}{6}(5\sqrt{5}-1).
Example 6.3 — Cone z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} over x^2+y^2 \leq R^2
f_x = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}, \quad f_y = \frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}, \quad 1+f_x^2+f_y^2 = 2.
A = \iint_{x^2+y^2\leq R^2} \sqrt{2}, dA = \sqrt{2}\cdot \pi R^2.
Sanity check: A cone of base radius R and height R (so z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} has slope 1, height R at radius R) has slant height \ell = R\sqrt{2}, lateral area \pi R\ell = \pi R^2\sqrt{2}. ✓
Example 6.4 — Torus
\mathbf{r}(\phi,\theta) = ((R+r\cos\phi)\cos\theta, (R+r\cos\phi)\sin\theta, r\sin\phi).
E = r^2, \quad F = 0, \quad G = (R+r\cos\phi)^2, |\mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta| = r(R+r\cos\phi).
A = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} r(R+r\cos\phi), d\phi, d\theta = 2\pi r \int_0^{2\pi}(R + r\cos\phi), d\phi = 2\pi r \cdot 2\pi R = 4\pi^2 Rr.
(The \int_0^{2\pi}\cos\phi,d\phi = 0 term vanishes.) This is Pappus’s theorem: A = 2\pi R \cdot 2\pi r. ✓

§8. Surface Integrals — Integrating over the Surface
Once we have dA = |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv, we can integrate any function over the surface.
Definition 8.1 (Surface Integral of a Scalar). For a continuous function g: S \to \mathbb{R}:
\iint_S g, dA = \iint_D g(\mathbf{r}(u,v)), |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|, du, dv.
Setting g \equiv 1 recovers surface area.
Example 8.2. Compute the average z-coordinate on the upper unit hemisphere z = \sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}.
From Example 6.1 (with R=1): |\mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta| = \sin\phi, and z = \cos\phi on the sphere.
\bar{z} = \frac{1}{A}\iint_S z, dA = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos\phi\sin\phi,d\phi,d\theta = \frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot 2\pi\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos\phi\sin\phi,d\phi.
= \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin 2\phi}{2},d\phi = \frac{1}{2}\left[-\frac{\cos 2\phi}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1 = \frac{1}{2}.
So the average height on the upper hemisphere is \frac{1}{2} — exactly halfway up. Geometric sanity check: the centroid of a hemisphere is at height R/2. ✓

§9. Special Cases and Classical Formulas
9.1 Surface Area of Revolution (Revisited)
From Surfaces_of_Revolution, \mathbf{r}(x,\theta), |\mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_\theta| = f(x)\sqrt{1+(f')^2}:
A = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_a^b f(x)\sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx,d\theta = 2\pi\int_a^b f(x)\sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx.
This is now seen as a special case of the general parametric formula.
9.2 Flat Surface (Plane)
Plane z = ax + by + c over domain D:
f_x = a, \quad f_y = b, \quad A = \sqrt{1+a^2+b^2}\cdot \text{Area}(D).
The factor \sqrt{1+a^2+b^2} is the secant of the angle between the plane and the horizontal — the area stretching factor.
9.3 Cylinder x^2 + y^2 = R^2, 0 \leq z \leq h
Parameterize: \mathbf{r}(\theta, z) = (R\cos\theta, R\sin\theta, z).
\mathbf{r}_\theta = (-R\sin\theta, R\cos\theta, 0), \quad \mathbf{r}_z = (0,0,1).
\mathbf{r}_\theta \times \mathbf{r}_z = (R\cos\theta, R\sin\theta, 0), \quad |\cdot| = R.
A = \int_0^h\int_0^{2\pi} R,d\theta, dz = 2\pi R h. \checkmark

§10. Minimal Surfaces
A minimal surface is one whose mean curvature H = \frac{1}{2}(\kappa_1+\kappa_2) = 0 vanishes everywhere. Equivalently — and this is the variational characterization — minimal surfaces are critical points of the area functional.
Variational Setup. Fix the boundary \partial S. Among all surfaces with this boundary, which has smallest area? The Euler-Lagrange equation for the area functional A[\mathbf{r}] = \iint |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv is exactly H = 0.
Theorem 10.1 (Euler-Lagrange for Area). A smooth surface is a critical point of A[\mathbf{r}] under fixed-boundary perturbations if and only if its mean curvature H = 0 everywhere.
Proof sketch. Perturb: \mathbf{r}_\epsilon = \mathbf{r} + \epsilon\phi\hat{n} for a compactly supported function \phi and unit normal \hat{n}. Compute \frac{d}{d\epsilon}A[\mathbf{r}_\epsilon]\big|_{\epsilon=0} and integrate by parts. The vanishing of this for all \phi forces H = 0 (the first variation of area formula). \blacksquare

Plateau’s problem (1760, solved 1930–31 by Douglas and Radó): Given any closed curve in \mathbb{R}^3, does there exist a minimal surface bounded by it? Answer: yes (for rectifiable curves). Douglas won the first Fields Medal partly for this.

§11. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
11.1 Surface Area as a Regularizer in Neural Geometry Processing
In neural implicit surface representations (NeRF, NeuralRBF, DeepSDF), a network F_\theta: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} defines a surface S = {F_\theta = 0}. To prevent over-fitting and encourage smooth, minimal surfaces, practitioners add a surface area regularizer to the training loss:
\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} = \iint_S dA = \iint \frac{|\nabla F_\theta|}{|F_{\theta,z}|}, dA,
using the implicit surface formula of §3. Minimizing this term biases the learned surface toward smaller area — towards minimal surface solutions. This is Plateau’s problem implemented as gradient descent.
11.2 Riemannian Metric Learning
The surface area formula A = \iint \sqrt{EG-F^2},du,dv depends only on the first fundamental form g = {E, F, G} — the intrinsic metric. In metric learning, one directly learns a metric g on the data manifold \mathcal{M} such that geodesic distances reflect semantic similarity. The “volume” of data space (generalized area) is then \int \sqrt{\det g}, du, dv — exactly the Riemannian volume form. Controlling this volume controls the density of the learned representation.
11.3 Information Geometry and the Fisher Metric
In a statistical model {p_\theta}, the Fisher information metric
g_{ij}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial \log p_\theta}{\partial\theta_i}\frac{\partial \log p_\theta}{\partial\theta_j}\right]
defines a Riemannian metric on the manifold of probability distributions. The volume of parameter space under this metric is \int\sqrt{\det g},d\theta — a generalized surface area. Natural gradient descent replaces the Euclidean gradient with the Riemannian gradient under g (exactly the Riemannian optimization from Tangent_Planes, §10.6):
\Delta\theta = -\eta, g^{-1}\nabla\mathcal{L}.
This is the mathematical foundation of K-FAC and other second-order optimizers. The Fisher metric quantifies how much the distribution changes per unit parameter change — it measures the “area” of the statistical manifold that a gradient step traverses.
11.4 Gaussian Processes on Manifolds
A Gaussian process prior on a manifold \mathcal{M} requires a kernel k: \mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}. The heat kernel on a surface (the fundamental solution to the heat equation \partial_t u = \Delta_{\mathcal{M}} u) is intrinsic to the surface geometry and depends on the metric \sqrt{EG-F^2}. Stationary kernels on surfaces generalize the RBF kernel, with the geodesic distance replacing Euclidean distance. Their spectral density (Mercer expansion via eigenfunctions of \Delta_\mathcal{M}) depends on the Riemannian volume form — our area element.
11.5 Score Matching and Diffusion on Surfaces
Diffusion models (DDPM, score matching) are increasingly generalized to data on manifolds — e.g., proteins (data on SO(3)), molecular conformations (data on S^2), or any geometry-aware generative model. The score function \nabla_x \log p_t(x) on a manifold is the Riemannian gradient, and the forward/reverse diffusion processes use the Laplace-Beltrami operator \Delta_\mathcal{M} — which is defined via the metric \sqrt{EG-F^2}. Without surface area theory, none of this makes sense.
11.6 Mesh-Based Deep Learning and Surface Discretization
In graph neural networks on meshes (MeshCNN, DiffusionNet, PoinTr), the surface is discretized into triangles. Each triangle’s area is \frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{e}_1 \times \mathbf{e}_2| where \mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2 are edge vectors — a discrete version of our cross-product formula. The cotangent Laplacian used in spectral mesh processing weights edges by \cot\alpha + \cot\beta (angles opposite the edge), which is exactly the discretization of \sqrt{EG-F^2}. Every convolution on a mesh implicitly uses surface area.

§12. Exercises
12.1. Compute the surface area of z = xy over the unit square [0,1]^2.
12.2. Find the area of the part of the plane x + 2y + 3z = 6 that lies inside the cylinder x^2+y^2=4.
12.3. [Implicit surface] Use the formula A = \iint |\nabla G|/|G_z|,dA to find the area of the ellipsoid \frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}+\frac{z^2}{c^2}=1 in the special case a=b (oblate spheroid). You should obtain an integral that can be evaluated by trigonometric substitution.
12.4. Show directly (by computing E, F, G) that a sphere of radius R in spherical coordinates has \sqrt{EG-F^2} = R^2\sin\phi, and verify the area is 4\pi R^2.
12.5. [Pappus verification] A circle of radius r centered at (R, 0, 0) (with R > r) is revolved about the z-axis. Use the parametric surface area formula to verify Pappus’s theorem: A = 4\pi^2 Rr.
12.6. [Minimal surfaces] Show that the helicoid \mathbf{r}(u,v) = (u\cos v, u\sin v, v) has E = 1+v^2 — wait, recheck. Actually compute E, F, G for the helicoid and find H.
12.7. [ML connection] A neural network defines a surface S = {F_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = 0} where F_\theta(x,y,z) = z - \sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y). Write the surface area integral explicitly and discuss why adding \lambda A to the training loss encourages “flatter” surfaces.

§13. Summary
| Surface | |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v| | Area | |---|---|---| | z = f(x,y) | \sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2} | \iint_D \sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2},dA | | General parametric | \sqrt{EG-F^2} | \iint_D \sqrt{EG-F^2},du,dv | | Surface of revolution | f(x)\sqrt{1+(f')^2} | 2\pi\int_a^b f\sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx | | Sphere radius R | R^2\sin\phi | 4\pi R^2 | | Cylinder radius R, height h | R | 2\pi Rh | | Cone, base R, slant \ell | \sqrt{2}R (for 45° cone) | \pi R\ell | | Torus (R,r) | r(R+r\cos\phi) | 4\pi^2 Rr |
The conceptual hierarchy:
\text{tangent vectors } \mathbf{r}_u, \mathbf{r}_v \xrightarrow{\text{cross product}} \text{area element } |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v| \xrightarrow{\text{integrate}} \text{surface area}
\text{metric tensor } g_{ij} \xrightarrow{\det} \sqrt{EG-F^2} \xrightarrow{\text{integrate}} \text{intrinsic area}
The deep point: both routes give the same answer, and neither depends on how you parameterize the surface. This invariance — under reparameterization — is the geometric content of the change-of-variables theorem.

01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/17..title: 17.Surface Integrals
01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/17..content:
“Integration is the act of adding up infinitely many infinitely small things. On a surface, each infinitely small thing is a tiny parallelogram.”


§0. Prefatory Remarks
A surface integral is the generalization of a line integral to two dimensions: instead of integrating along a curve, we integrate over a surface. There are two fundamentally different kinds:

Surface integrals of scalar fields \iint_S f, dS — integrate a function over the surface, weighted by area
Surface integrals of vector fields \iint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} — integrate the flux of a vector field through the surface

The second type requires the surface to be oriented — it must have a consistent notion of “inside” and “outside,” or “up” and “down.” This orientation is the new conceptual ingredient.
These integrals are the backbone of:

Physics: Electric flux (Gauss’s law), magnetic flux, fluid flow, heat transfer
Differential geometry: Integration of differential forms on manifolds
Deep learning: Information geometry, Fisher information matrix as a surface integral
PDEs: Green’s theorem, divergence theorem, Stokes’ theorem

Everything in this note builds from the parametric surface machinery developed in Surfaces_of_Revolution and Tangent_Planes.

§1. Parametric Surfaces — Recollection and Setup
Recall from Tangent_Planes §4: a parametric surface is a map
\mathbf{r}: D \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^3, \quad \mathbf{r}(u,v) = \bigl(x(u,v),; y(u,v),; z(u,v)\bigr),
where D is a domain in the uv-plane (usually a rectangle or region with piecewise smooth boundary).
The tangent vectors: \mathbf{r}_u = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial u} = \left(\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}, \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}, \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\right), \qquad \mathbf{r}_v = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial v} = \left(\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}, \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}, \frac{\partial z}{\partial v}\right).
The surface element. At a point (u_0, v_0), the small patch of surface corresponding to [u_0, u_0+du] \times [v_0, v_0+dv] is approximated by the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf{r}_u, du and \mathbf{r}_v, dv. Its area is:
dS = |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|; du, dv.
Definition 1.1 (Regular Surface). The parametrization \mathbf{r} is regular at (u_0,v_0) if
\mathbf{r}_u(u_0,v_0) \times \mathbf{r}_v(u_0,v_0) \neq \mathbf{0}.
At regular points, the cross product gives a well-defined normal direction, and the tangent plane exists.
Standard Examples of Parametric Surfaces
Sphere x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = a^2: \mathbf{r}(\phi,\theta) = (a\sin\phi\cos\theta,; a\sin\phi\sin\theta,; a\cos\phi), \quad \phi \in [0,\pi],; \theta \in [0,2\pi].
Graph z = f(x,y) over region D: \mathbf{r}(x,y) = (x,; y,; f(x,y)), \quad (x,y) \in D.
Cylinder x^2 + y^2 = R^2, 0 \leq z \leq h: \mathbf{r}(\theta,z) = (R\cos\theta,; R\sin\theta,; z), \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi],; z \in [0,h].
Surface of revolution (from Surfaces_of_Revolution): \mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = (x,; f(x)\cos\theta,; f(x)\sin\theta), \quad x \in [a,b],; \theta \in [0,2\pi].

§2. Surface Integrals of Scalar Fields
Definition 2.1 (Surface Integral of a Scalar Field). Let f: S \subset \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} be continuous and \mathbf{r}: D \to S a regular parametrization. The surface integral of f over S is
\boxed{\iint_S f, dS = \iint_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)), |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|; du, dv.}
Motivation. Partition D into small rectangles \Delta u_i \times \Delta v_j. Each maps to a small surface patch of area \approx |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,\Delta u_i,\Delta v_j. The Riemann sum \sum_{i,j} f(\mathbf{r}(u_i,v_j)),|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,\Delta u_i,\Delta v_j converges to the integral in the limit.
Special case: f \equiv 1. Then \iint_S 1, dS = \iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|, du, dv is the surface area — consistent with Surfaces_of_Revolution §3.
For a graph z = g(x,y): use \mathbf{r}(x,y) = (x,y,g(x,y)).
\mathbf{r}_x = (1, 0, g_x), \quad \mathbf{r}_y = (0, 1, g_y), \quad \mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_y = (-g_x, -g_y, 1).
|\mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_y| = \sqrt{1 + g_x^2 + g_y^2}.
So for a graph: \iint_S f, dS = \iint_D f(x, y, g(x,y))\sqrt{1 + g_x^2 + g_y^2}; dx, dy.
Example 2.1 — Mass of a Surface
A thin metallic sheet has the shape of the hemisphere x^2+y^2+z^2 = 1, z \geq 0, with surface density \rho(x,y,z) = z. Find its total mass.
Parametrize: \mathbf{r}(\phi,\theta) = (\sin\phi\cos\theta, \sin\phi\sin\theta, \cos\phi), \phi \in [0,\pi/2], \theta \in [0,2\pi].
Compute cross product: \mathbf{r}_\phi = (\cos\phi\cos\theta, \cos\phi\sin\theta, -\sin\phi), \quad \mathbf{r}_\theta = (-\sin\phi\sin\theta, \sin\phi\cos\theta, 0).
\mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta = (\sin^2\phi\cos\theta,; \sin^2\phi\sin\theta,; \sin\phi\cos\phi).
|\mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta| = \sin\phi\sqrt{\sin^2\phi + \cos^2\phi} = \sin\phi.
Integrate: z = \cos\phi on the sphere, so
M = \iint_S z, dS = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos\phi \cdot \sin\phi; d\phi, d\theta = 2\pi \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin\phi\cos\phi; d\phi = 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \pi. \quad \checkmark
Example 2.2 — Surface Integral over a Graph
Compute \iint_S (x^2+y^2), dS where S is the surface z = 1 + 2x + 3y over D = [0,1]\times[0,1].
g_x = 2, ; g_y = 3, \quad \sqrt{1+4+9} = \sqrt{14}.
\iint_S (x^2+y^2), dS = \sqrt{14}\int_0^1\int_0^1 (x^2+y^2), dx, dy = \sqrt{14} \cdot \frac{2}{3}.

§3. Oriented Surfaces
This is where the new geometry enters. To integrate a vector field over a surface, we need to know which side is “positive” — i.e., which way the normal vector points.
Definition 3.1 (Orientation). An orientation of a smooth surface S is a continuous choice of unit normal vector \hat{\mathbf{n}}(P) at each regular point P \in S.
A surface is orientable if such a continuous choice exists globally. Most familiar surfaces are orientable: spheres, planes, graphs z = f(x,y), cylinders (if we specify inner or outer). The famous exception is the Möbius band — it has only one side.
Two orientations always exist on an orientable connected surface: \hat{\mathbf{n}} and -\hat{\mathbf{n}}. Choosing one is called orienting the surface.
Standard Conventions:





















SurfacePositive normalClosed surface (sphere, box)Outward-pointingGraph z = f(x,y)Upward: \hat{\mathbf{n}} has positive z-componentParametric surface$\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v}{
Reversing orientation: Swapping u \leftrightarrow v reverses the sign of \mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v, hence reverses the orientation. Swapping the parameters is how you change which side is “positive.”
Definition 3.2 (Oriented Surface Element). Given orientation \hat{\mathbf{n}}, define the vector area element:
d\mathbf{S} = \hat{\mathbf{n}}, dS = \frac{\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v}{|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|} \cdot |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|; du, dv = (\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v); du, dv.
The vector d\mathbf{S} encodes both the area element dS and the direction \hat{\mathbf{n}} simultaneously.

§4. Surface Integrals of Vector Fields (Flux Integrals)
Definition 4.1 (Flux Integral). Let \mathbf{F}: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3 be a continuous vector field and S an oriented surface with unit normal \hat{\mathbf{n}}. The flux of \mathbf{F} through S is
\boxed{\iint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_S (\mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}), dS.}
In terms of parametrization \mathbf{r}(u,v) with the induced orientation \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v}{|\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v|}:
\iint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v); du, dv.
Physical interpretation. \mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = |\mathbf{F}|\cos\theta where \theta is the angle between \mathbf{F} and \hat{\mathbf{n}}. This is the component of \mathbf{F} through the surface (not tangent to it).

If \mathbf{F} is a fluid velocity field: flux = net volume flow rate per unit time through S
If \mathbf{F} is electric field: flux = total electric charge enclosed (Gauss’s law)
If \mathbf{F} is magnetic field: flux = magnetic flux (Faraday’s law involves its time derivative)

For a graph z = g(x,y), \hat{\mathbf{n}} upward:
\mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_y = (-g_x, -g_y, 1), \quad d\mathbf{S} = (-g_x, -g_y, 1), dx, dy.
If \mathbf{F} = (P, Q, R):
\iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_D \bigl(-Pg_x - Qg_y + R\bigr)\big|_{z=g(x,y)}; dx, dy.

§5. Computing the Cross Product Systematically
Given \mathbf{r}(u,v), the key computational step is always \mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v. Here is the systematic approach:
\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ \partial_u x & \partial_u y & \partial_u z \ \partial_v x & \partial_v y & \partial_v z \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} \partial_u y & \partial_u z \ \partial_v y & \partial_v z \end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} - \begin{vmatrix} \partial_u x & \partial_u z \ \partial_v x & \partial_v z \end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j} + \begin{vmatrix} \partial_u x & \partial_u y \ \partial_v x & \partial_v y \end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k}.
In shorthand using the Jacobian notation:
\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v = \left(\frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)},; \frac{\partial(z,x)}{\partial(u,v)},; \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right),
where \frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)} = \begin{vmatrix} y_u & y_v \ z_u & z_v \end{vmatrix} = y_u z_v - y_v z_u, etc.
This Jacobian notation reveals the deep structure: each component of \mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v is the area of the projected parallelogram onto one coordinate plane. More on this in §8.

§6. Worked Examples — Flux Integrals
Example 6.1 — Flux Through a Sphere
Let \mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = (x, y, z) (radial field). Compute the flux outward through the sphere S: x^2+y^2+z^2 = a^2.
Method 1 (geometric shortcut). On the sphere, \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{(x,y,z)}{a} (outward unit normal). So
\mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{x^2+y^2+z^2}{a} = \frac{a^2}{a} = a.
The integrand is constant! So
\iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = a \cdot \text{Area}(S) = a \cdot 4\pi a^2 = 4\pi a^3.
(Preview: by the Divergence Theorem, \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 3, and \iiint_{B} 3, dV = 3 \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi a^3 = 4\pi a^3. ✓)
Example 6.2 — Flux Through a Cylinder (with caps)
Let \mathbf{F} = (x, y, 0). Compute the outward flux through the closed cylinder x^2+y^2 \leq 1, 0 \leq z \leq 1.
The surface has three pieces: lateral side S_1, top cap S_2 (z=1), bottom cap S_3 (z=0).
Lateral side S_1: \mathbf{r}(\theta,z) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, z). \mathbf{r}_\theta = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0), \quad \mathbf{r}_z = (0,0,1). \mathbf{r}_\theta \times \mathbf{r}_z = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0) \quad \text{(outward, since } x\text{-component positive when }\theta\in[0,\pi/2]\text{)}. \mathbf{F}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_\theta \times \mathbf{r}_z) = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1. \iint_{S_1} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 1; dz, d\theta = 2\pi.
Top cap S_2 (z = 1, upward normal \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{k}): \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}} = (x,y,0)\cdot(0,0,1) = 0. \quad \iint_{S_2} = 0.
Bottom cap S_3 (z = 0, downward normal \hat{\mathbf{n}} = -\mathbf{k}): \mathbf{F}\cdot(-\mathbf{k}) = 0. \quad \iint_{S_3} = 0.
Total flux: 2\pi + 0 + 0 = 2\pi.
(Check via Divergence Theorem: \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = 2, volume = \pi. 2\pi \cdot 1 = 2\pi. ✓)
Example 6.3 — Flux Through a Graph
Let \mathbf{F} = (0, 0, z) and S: z = x^2 + y^2, 0 \leq z \leq 1 (paraboloid), upward orientation.
\mathbf{r}(x,y) = (x, y, x^2+y^2), \quad D = {x^2+y^2 \leq 1}. g_x = 2x, \quad g_y = 2y, \quad d\mathbf{S} = (-2x, -2y, 1), dx, dy. \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = (0,0, x^2+y^2)\cdot(-2x,-2y,1) = x^2+y^2. \iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_D (x^2+y^2), dx, dy = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r^2 \cdot r; dr, d\theta = 2\pi\cdot\frac{1}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2}.
Example 6.4 — Flux Through the Torus (Conceptual)
The torus has outward normal pointing away from the central circle (see Surfaces_of_Revolution §4 for parameterization). For a constant field \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{k}, the flux through the torus is zero by symmetry: for every patch where \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}} > 0, there is a symmetric patch where \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}} < 0. This is an instance of the general principle: \iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0 for any closed surface when \mathbf{F} is constant and the surface is closed (by the Divergence Theorem, \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = 0).

§8. The Differential Form Perspective
The surface integral of a vector field has a beautiful rewriting. If \mathbf{F} = (P, Q, R), then
\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{F}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v), du, dv = P,\frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)} + Q,\frac{\partial(z,x)}{\partial(u,v)} + R,\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}; du, dv.
This is the 2-form: \iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_S P, dy\wedge dz + Q, dz\wedge dx + R, dx\wedge dy.
This notation is not mere decoration — it is the language of differential geometry and Stokes’ theorem on manifolds.
The exterior derivative of the 1-form \omega = P,dx + Q,dy + R,dz gives a 2-form d\omega, and Stokes’ theorem says \int_{\partial \Sigma} \omega = \iint_\Sigma d\omega for any oriented 2-manifold \Sigma with boundary \partial\Sigma. This unifies:

























Classical theoremDifferential formsFundamental theorem of calculus\int_a^b f',dx = f(b) - f(a)Green’s theorem\oint_C P,dx + Q,dy = \iint_D (Q_x - P_y),dAStokes’ theorem\oint_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S}Divergence theorem\oiint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_V (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}),dV
All are special cases of \int_{\partial M} \omega = \int_M d\omega.

§9. Stokes’ Theorem and the Divergence Theorem — Statement
We state these without proof, as they deserve their own notes, but place them here for context.
Theorem 9.1 (Stokes’ Theorem). Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple closed curve \partial S, oriented consistently (right-hand rule). Let \mathbf{F} be C^1 on an open set containing S. Then:
\oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S}.
Theorem 9.2 (Divergence Theorem / Gauss’s Theorem). Let E be a simple solid region with outward-oriented boundary surface \partial E = S. Let \mathbf{F} be C^1 on an open set containing E. Then:
\oiint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_E (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}), dV.
Mnemonic. Both theorems say: the integral of a derivative over a domain equals the integral of the original function over the boundary. Stokes: 2D → 1D. Divergence: 3D → 2D.

§10. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
10.1 Fisher Information Matrix as a Surface Integral
The Fisher information matrix I(\theta) for a statistical model p(x;\theta) is
I(\theta)_{ij} = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(\cdot;\theta)}\left[\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_i}\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_j}\right].
In geometric terms, I(\theta) is the Riemannian metric on the manifold of probability distributions (Fisher-Rao metric). For a continuous model with density p(x;\theta) over a domain \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2:
I(\theta)_{ij} = \iint_\Omega \frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_i}\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_j}, p(x;\theta); dx_1, dx_2.
This is a surface integral of a scalar field — integrating \frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_i}\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_j} weighted by the probability measure p,dA. Natural gradient descent (used in KFAC, Shampoo, and other second-order optimizers) replaces the Euclidean gradient with the Riemannian gradient I(\theta)^{-1}\nabla\mathcal{L}, which is coordinate-invariant.
10.2 Flux and Information Flow in Neural Networks
Consider a neural network layer as a map \mathbf{z} = \sigma(W\mathbf{x}). The Jacobian J = \frac{\partial \mathbf{z}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} maps the input tangent space to the output tangent space. The singular values of J measure how much “information flux” passes through the layer.
For a 2D intermediate representation (e.g., a 2D convolutional feature map), the information flux through a surface S in feature space is:
\Phi = \iint_S \mathbf{J}\cdot d\mathbf{S},
where \mathbf{J} is the Jacobian field. Vanishing gradients correspond to \Phi \to 0 — the “flux” of gradient information through the network collapses. Exploding gradients correspond to \Phi \to \infty.
10.3 Gauss’s Law and Implicit Neural Surfaces
Implicit neural representations (e.g., Neural Unsigned Distance Functions) represent surfaces as {F_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = 0}. Gauss’s law applied to the learned signed distance function F_\theta:
\oiint_{\partial V} \nabla F_\theta \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_V \Delta F_\theta; dV,
where \Delta = \nabla^2 is the Laplacian. For a true signed distance function, |\nabla F| = 1 everywhere (Eikonal equation), so \Delta F =  (mean curvature of level sets). Eikonal loss in training NeRF and NeuS models enforces this constraint:
\mathcal{L}_\text{eikonal} = \mathbb{E}_\mathbf{x}\left[(|\nabla F_\theta(\mathbf{x})| - 1)^2\right].
This is precisely requiring the flux of the gradient field through every surface to be controlled.
10.4 Normalizing Flows and Change of Variables on Surfaces
A normalizing flow T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n transforms a base density p_Z to a target density p_X. The log-likelihood involves \log|\det J_T|. Geometrically:
\log|\det J_T(\mathbf{z})| = \log|\text{volume element distortion at } \mathbf{z}|.
For a 2D flow (e.g., a planar flow representing a 2D surface), |\det J_T| is the ratio of area elements — exactly the |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v| factor in our surface integral formula! Training a normalizing flow to maximize likelihood is equivalent to learning a parametrization of a surface in probability space that minimizes area distortion.
10.5 Stokes’ Theorem in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
PINNs solve PDEs by minimizing residuals. For Maxwell’s equations (governing electromagnetic fields in physics simulators and neural hardware models):
\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{J} + \mu_0\epsilon_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}.
Stokes’ theorem converts this: \oint_C \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla\times\mathbf{B})\cdot d\mathbf{S}. A PINN enforces this integral form as a loss:
\mathcal{L}_\text{Stokes} = \left|\oint_C \mathbf{B}_\theta \cdot d\mathbf{r} - \iint_S (\nabla\times\mathbf{B}_\theta)\cdot d\mathbf{S}\right|^2.
The surface integral directly appears in the training objective.
10.6 Orientation and Signed vs. Unsigned Surfaces in 3D Deep Learning
In 3D point cloud networks (PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN), surface orientation matters. A mesh-based network must consistently orient faces to define outward normals — exactly the orientation problem of §3. Learning orientation from unoriented point clouds is an active research area (2023–2025), and fails precisely on non-orientable surfaces — a topological obstruction, not a learning failure.
Watertight meshes (closed, orientable, consistently oriented) allow the Divergence Theorem to compute volumes from surface integrals:
\text{Vol} = \frac{1}{3}\oiint_S \mathbf{r}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{3}\oiint_S (x,y,z)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}, dS.
This formula is used in computational geometry and 3D printing quality checks.

§11. Exercises
11.1. Compute \iint_S z, dS where S is the cone z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}, 0 \leq z \leq 1.
11.2. Let \mathbf{F} = (y, -x, z^2). Compute the flux of \mathbf{F} upward through the paraboloid z = 4 - x^2 - y^2, z \geq 0.
11.3. Verify the Divergence Theorem for \mathbf{F} = (x^3, y^3, z^3) and the unit ball x^2+y^2+z^2 \leq 1. Compute both sides.
11.4. Show that the Möbius band is non-orientable by explicit construction: parametrize it and show that \mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v cannot be made continuous and nonzero globally.
(Parametrization hint: \mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left((1 + v\cos\frac{u}{2})\cos u,; (1+v\cos\frac{u}{2})\sin u,; v\sin\frac{u}{2}\right), u \in [0,2\pi], v \in [-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}].)
11.5. Let S be the surface of the unit cube [0,1]^3. Compute the outward flux of \mathbf{F} = (x^2, y^2, z^2) directly (six faces) and verify using the Divergence Theorem.
11.6. [Differential forms] Express the surface integral \iint_S xy, dz\wedge dx + z, dx\wedge dy in terms of a parametrization \mathbf{r}(u,v) and identify it as a flux integral of some \mathbf{F}.
11.7. [Deep learning connection] For a 2-layer neural network with weight matrices W_1, W_2 and scalar output y = \sigma(W_2\sigma(W_1\mathbf{x})), interpret the gradient \frac{\partial y}{\partial \mathbf{x}} as a flux through the “parameter surface” and explain what vanishing gradient means geometrically in terms of d\mathbf{S}.

§12. Summary


















































ObjectFormulaKey pointScalar surface integral\iint_S f, dS = \iint_D f(\mathbf{r}),\|\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v\|,du,dvArea-weightedArea elementdS = \|\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v\|,du,dvJacobian of parametrizationOrientationContinuous choice of \hat{\mathbf{n}}Required for flux integralsVector area elementd\mathbf{S} = (\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v),du,dvEncodes area + directionFlux integral\iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r})\cdot(\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v),du,dvOnly normal component contributesGraph z=g(x,y)d\mathbf{S} = (-g_x, -g_y, 1),dx,dy (upward)Standard formStokes’ theorem\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S}Boundary ↔ interiorDivergence theorem\oiint_{\partial E}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_E(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}),dVSurface ↔ volume
The conceptual hierarchy:
\underbrace{\int_a^b f,dx}_{\text{1D}} \longrightarrow \underbrace{\int_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}}_{\text{line integral}} \longrightarrow \underbrace{\iint_S f,dS}_{\text{scalar surface}} \longrightarrow \underbrace{\iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S}}_{\text{flux / vector surface}}
Each arrow adds one dimension and one new idea: parameterization, area distortion, orientation. The flux integral is the culmination — it integrates a vector field’s interaction with an oriented surface, and it is the object that Gauss, Stokes, and the entire theory of differential forms is built around.

References

Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §16.6–16.7 (Parametric Surfaces, Surface Integrals).
MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02. Multivariable Calculus — Lectures 33–35: surface integrals, flux, Stokes’ and divergence theorems.
do Carmo, Manfredo P. Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces. §2.3 for oriented surfaces.
Spivak, Michael. Calculus on Manifolds. For differential forms and the generalized Stokes’ theorem.
Amari, Shun-ichi. Information Geometry and Its Applications. Springer, 2016. For Fisher information as a Riemannian metric.
Wang et al. NeuS: Learning Neural Implicit Surfaces. NeurIPS 2021. For Eikonal loss and surface integrals in neural rendering.

01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/18..title: 18.Stokes' Theorem
01.Maths/Calculus/16.Vector-Calculus/18..content:
“In mathematics you don’t understand things. You just get used to them.” — von Neumann (But we’re going to understand this one.)


§ 0 — The Philosophy Before the Formula
Before writing a single symbol, let me tell you what Stokes’ theorem really is.
Every major theorem in vector calculus — Green’s theorem, the Divergence theorem, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — is secretly the same theorem. They all say:
\boxed{\int_{\partial \Omega} \omega = \int_{\Omega} d\omega}
The integral of a “derivative” over a region equals the integral of the original object over the boundary of that region. Stokes’ theorem is the 3-dimensional surface version of this idea.
This is not just aesthetics. It is a profound structural fact about the universe. And it shows up everywhere — from fluid dynamics to Maxwell’s equations to backpropagation.

§ 1 — Setting the Stage: What Are We Integrating Over?
1.1 Oriented Surfaces
Let S be a smooth, oriented surface in \mathbb{R}^3. Oriented means we have chosen a consistent normal vector field \mathbf{n} on S — think of it as choosing which side of the surface is “up.”
Examples of oriented surfaces:

The upper hemisphere z = \sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2}, with outward normal pointing up.
A saddle surface z = x^2 - y^2 over some domain, with \mathbf{n} pointing upward.
Any graph z = f(x,y) over a region D in the xy-plane.


Personal note: The word “oriented” is doing enormous work here. The theorem is false without it. You must commit to a side.

1.2 The Boundary Curve and the Right-Hand Rule
The boundary \partial S of S is a closed curve (or a union of closed curves). The orientation of \partial S is determined by the right-hand rule:

If the thumb of your right hand points in the direction of \mathbf{n}, your fingers curl in the positive direction of \partial S.

Visualization:
        ↑ n (normal)
        |
    ____↑____
   /         \
  /     S     \
 /             \
 ←——— ∂S ———→   (boundary traversed counterclockwise when viewed from above)

This is not a convention chosen arbitrarily. It is the one that makes the algebra consistent.

§ 2 — The Theorem
2.1 Statement

Theorem (Stokes). Let S be an oriented, piecewise-smooth surface in \mathbb{R}^3, bounded by a piecewise-smooth, positively oriented closed curve C = \partial S. Let \mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangle be a vector field whose components have continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing S. Then:
\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S}

Left side: A line integral of \mathbf{F} around the boundary curve C.
Right side: A surface integral of the curl of \mathbf{F} over S.
The curl is: \nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ \partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z \ P & Q & R \end{vmatrix} = \left\langle R_y - Q_z,\ P_z - R_x,\ Q_x - P_y \right\rangle
And the surface integral is: \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot \mathbf{n} , dS

§ 3 — Proof (The Real Thing)
We will prove Stokes’ theorem for a surface that is a graph: S: z = g(x,y), (x,y) \in D, with upward normal.
Step 1: Parameterize Everything
The surface is parameterized by \mathbf{r}(x, y) = \langle x, y, g(x,y) \rangle.
The boundary C = \partial S is the image of \partial D under this parameterization.
Step 2: Expand the Line Integral
\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \oint_C P,dx + Q,dy + R,dz
On C, we have z = g(x,y), so dz = g_x,dx + g_y,dy. Substituting:
= \oint_{\partial D} (P + R g_x),dx + (Q + R g_y),dy
Step 3: Apply Green’s Theorem to the Plane
Green’s theorem on D gives:
\oint_{\partial D} M,dx + N,dy = \iint_D \left(\frac{\partial N}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial M}{\partial y}\right) dA
with M = P + Rg_x and N = Q + Rg_y. Computing \partial N/\partial x - \partial M/\partial y (using the chain rule carefully):
\frac{\partial N}{\partial x} = Q_x + Q_z g_x + R_x g_y + R g_{yx} + R_z g_x g_y
\frac{\partial M}{\partial y} = P_y + P_z g_y + R_y g_x + R g_{xy} + R_z g_x g_y
Subtracting (and noting g_{xy} = g_{yx}, R_z g_x g_y cancels):
\frac{\partial N}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial M}{\partial y} = (Q_x - P_y) + (R_y - Q_z)(-g_x)(-1)^{-1}\cdot(-g_x)\ \ldots
Let me collect terms cleanly:
= (R_y - Q_z)(-g_x) + (P_z - R_x)(-g_y) + (Q_x - P_y)
Step 4: Recognize the Curl
The outward normal for z = g(x,y) with upward orientation is:
d\mathbf{S} = \langle -g_x, -g_y, 1 \rangle , dA
And \nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \langle R_y - Q_z,\ P_z - R_x,\ Q_x - P_y \rangle.
So:
(\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \left[(R_y - Q_z)(-g_x) + (P_z - R_x)(-g_y) + (Q_x - P_y)\right] dA
This is exactly what we computed in Step 3. Therefore:
\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_D (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} \qquad \blacksquare

Note: The general proof (for non-graph surfaces) follows by partitioning S into graph-like pieces and patching together. Interior boundary curves cancel in pairs because they are traversed in opposite directions — a beautiful combinatorial argument.


§ 4 — Geometric Interpretation
What is the curl measuring?
(\nabla \times \mathbf{F})(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \mathbf{n} measures the circulation density of \mathbf{F} at the point \mathbf{p} around the axis \mathbf{n}.
More precisely: if you place a tiny paddle wheel at \mathbf{p} with axis \mathbf{n}, the curl tells you how fast it spins and in which direction.
Stokes’ theorem then says:

The total circulation around the boundary of S equals the sum of all the local spin contributions over the interior of S.

This is the 3D version of how a river’s global swirl is built up from local eddies.
The “Telescope” Intuition
Divide S into infinitesimal parallelogram patches \delta S_i. Around each patch, the circulation of \mathbf{F} is approximately (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot \mathbf{n} , \delta A_i. When we sum all these tiny loops, the interior edges cancel (each shared edge is traversed once in each direction), leaving only the outer boundary C. This is Stokes’ theorem.
  +→→→→→→→→→→→+
  ↑  ↑→+  ↑→+ ↑
  ↑  ↑ ↓  ↑ ↓ ↑
  ↑  +-←+  +-←+↑
  ↑  ↑→+  ↑→+ ↑
  ↑  ↑ ↓  ↑ ↓ ↑
  +←←←←←←←←←←+
  (Interior arrows cancel; only the outer loop remains)


§ 5 — Worked Examples
Example 1: Verifying Stokes’ theorem directly
Setup: Let \mathbf{F} = \langle -y, x, 0 \rangle, and let S be the upper hemisphere x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1, z \geq 0, with upward normal. The boundary C is the unit circle x^2 + y^2 = 1, z = 0.
Left side (line integral):
Parameterize C: \mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, 0 \rangle, t \in [0, 2\pi].
\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_0^{2\pi} \langle -\sin t, \cos t, 0 \rangle \cdot \langle -\sin t, \cos t, 0 \rangle , dt = \int_0^{2\pi} (\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t) , dt = 2\pi
Right side (surface integral):
Compute the curl: \nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \langle 0 - 0,\ 0 - 0,\ 1 - (-1) \rangle = \langle 0, 0, 2 \rangle
On the hemisphere, d\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{n} , dS where \mathbf{n} is the outward unit normal. The curl dotted with \mathbf{n} integrates nicely:
\iint_S \langle 0, 0, 2 \rangle \cdot \mathbf{n} , dS = \iint_S 2 \cdot \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{n} , dS = 2 \iint_S \cos\phi , dS
where \phi is the polar angle. In spherical coordinates, dS = \sin\phi , d\phi , d\theta:
= 2 \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos\phi \sin\phi , d\phi , d\theta = 2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot \left[\frac{\sin^2\phi}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2} = 2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 2\pi \checkmark

Example 2: Choosing a Simpler Surface (The Key Trick)
Problem: Compute \oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} where \mathbf{F} = \langle y^2, z, x \rangle and C is the triangle with vertices (1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1), traversed counterclockwise when viewed from above.
Key insight from Stokes: The surface integral depends only on \partial S = C, not on which surface S we choose.
So we pick the flat triangular surface S lying in the plane x + y + z = 1, x,y,z \geq 0.
The normal to this plane (outward, consistent with the given orientation): \mathbf{n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle, and dS = \sqrt{3} , dA where dA is the area element in the xy-plane projection.
Compute the curl:
\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \langle R_y - Q_z, P_z - R_x, Q_x - P_y \rangle = \langle 0 - 1,\ 0 - 1,\ 0 - 2y \rangle = \langle -1, -1, -2y \rangle
Surface integral:
The projection of S onto the xy-plane is D: x \geq 0, y \geq 0, x + y \leq 1.
\iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot \mathbf{n} , dS = \iint_D \langle -1,-1,-2y \rangle \cdot \langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle , dA = \iint_D (-2 - 2y) , dA
= \int_0^1 \int_0^{1-x} (-2 - 2y) , dy , dx = \int_0^1 \left[-2y - y^2\right]_0^{1-x} dx
= \int_0^1 \left[-2(1-x) - (1-x)^2\right] dx = \int_0^1 \left[-(1-x)(2 + 1 - x)\right] dx
= \int_0^1 -(1-x)(3-x), dx = -\int_0^1 (3 - 4x + x^2), dx = -\left[3x - 2x^2 + \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = -\frac{4}{3}

Example 3: When the Curl Vanishes — Conservative Fields
If \mathbf{F} = \nabla f for some scalar f (a conservative field), then:
\nabla \times (\nabla f) = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{(always)}
Stokes’ theorem immediately gives:
\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S \mathbf{0} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0
for any closed curve C. This is the vector calculus proof that conservative fields do zero work around closed loops — a fundamental law in physics and a building block for understanding energy conservation.

§ 6 — Special Cases and Connections
6.1 Green’s Theorem as a Special Case
Take S to be a flat region D in the xy-plane, \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{k}. Then:
\iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot \mathbf{k} , dA = \iint_D (Q_x - P_y) , dA
And \oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \oint_{\partial D} P,dx + Q,dy.
This is exactly Green’s theorem. So Green’s theorem is Stokes’ theorem for flat surfaces. The hierarchy:
\underbrace{\text{FTC}}_{\text{1D}} \subset \underbrace{\text{Green}}_{\text{2D, flat}} \subset \underbrace{\text{Stokes}}_{\text{2D, curved}} \subset \underbrace{\text{Generalized Stokes}}_{\text{any } n\text{-manifold}}
6.2 Stokes’ Theorem in Physics: Maxwell’s Equations
Maxwell’s equations in integral form use Stokes’ theorem directly.
Faraday’s Law:
\oint_C \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = -\frac{d}{dt} \iint_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
The left side is the EMF around a closed loop. The right side involves the flux of the magnetic field. The differential form \nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\partial \mathbf{B}/\partial t is exactly Stokes applied locally.
Ampere’s Law:
\oint_C \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \mu_0 \iint_S \mathbf{J} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
Without Stokes’ theorem, these laws would be harder to state, let alone manipulate.

§ 7 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning

This is where a lot of courses stop. We will not.

7.1 Geometry of Loss Landscapes
In deep learning, we optimize a loss function \mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} over parameter space (the weights \theta). Stokes’ theorem underpins several key ideas here:
Gradient flow as a vector field. The gradient \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} is a vector field on parameter space. When we ask “does the optimizer get trapped in a loop?” — that is, can the gradient field have circulation? — the answer is: a pure gradient field is conservative, so \nabla \times (\nabla \mathcal{L}) = 0. This means gradient descent on a smooth loss cannot cycle: any closed path has zero net “work” done by the gradient.
But stochastic and adaptive optimizers (Adam, RMSProp) modify the effective gradient field, potentially introducing non-conservative components. The study of when these methods cycle or converge is partly a question about the curl of the effective update field.
7.2 Differential Geometry and Neural Manifolds
Modern deep learning theory models the data manifold — the submanifold of \mathbb{R}^d that the data lies on. When analyzing how neural networks learn or generalize, one asks:

What is the curvature of the data manifold?
How does a network’s representation of the data change across layers?

Stokes’ theorem (in its full generality on manifolds) is used in:

Topological Data Analysis (TDA): Persistent homology, which characterizes the topology of data (loops, voids, connected components), is built on the machinery of differential forms and their boundaries — the same framework as the generalized Stokes theorem.
Information geometry: The Fisher information metric makes parameter space into a Riemannian manifold. Curvature quantities (like the Riemann tensor) arise from the same algebraic structure as curl and circulation.

7.3 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
PINNs train neural networks to satisfy PDEs (like Maxwell’s equations or Navier–Stokes). Many of the PDEs they enforce are divergence/curl conditions:
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0, \quad \nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}
Stokes’ theorem is used to convert between the PDE (differential form) and its integral form when setting up training losses or evaluating conservation properties. A PINN that does not respect the Stokes structure will fail to conserve physical invariants.
7.4 Normalizing Flows and Generative Models
Normalizing flows are generative models that learn a diffeomorphism (a smooth, invertible map) f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d transforming a simple distribution into a complex one. The change-of-variables formula involves the Jacobian determinant |\det Df|.
Computing this determinant is expensive. One approach uses the instantaneous change of variables (continuous normalizing flows), where f is the flow of a vector field \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}, t). The trace of the Jacobian \text{tr}(D\mathbf{v}) is the divergence \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}. Stokes / Divergence theorem guarantees that the integral of this divergence over a region equals the flux through the boundary — a key identity for deriving the log-likelihood update rule.
7.5 Equivariant Neural Networks and Symmetry
Modern architectures (e.g., for molecular property prediction, physics simulation) enforce equivariance to rotation and reflection. The mathematical framework — group representations, differential forms on Lie groups — is the same framework that Stokes’ theorem lives in. The general Stokes theorem on Lie groups is used to derive conservation laws that equivariant networks must respect by construction.

§ 8 — Common Mistakes and Pitfalls






























MistakeWhy it’s wrongFixIgnoring orientation of CStokes’ theorem requires a specific orientation of C relative to \mathbf{n}; reversing C negates the answerApply the right-hand rule explicitlyUsing the wrong surfaceAny surface with \partial S = C works — but pick the simplest oneChoose a flat disk or obvious surfaceForgetting that \mathbf{F} must be C^1 on an open set containing SIf \mathbf{F} has a singularity inside S, the theorem failsCheck the domain of \mathbf{F} firstConfusing Stokes with the Divergence theoremStokes: curl integrated over a surface. Divergence: divergence over a volumeRemember: Stokes = boundary is a curve, Divergence = boundary is a surface

§ 9 — Summary Card
\boxed{\oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S}}





























ObjectWhat it isSOriented, piecewise-smooth surface\partial S = CBoundary curve, positively oriented via right-hand rule\mathbf{F}C^1 vector field on open set \supseteq S\nabla \times \mathbf{F}Curl: measures local rotation of \mathbf{F}d\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{n},dSOriented surface area element
The theorem says: Global circulation around the boundary = Total local spin over the interior.

References


James Stewart — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, §16.8 (Stokes’ Theorem). The standard worked examples and computational techniques follow Stewart’s treatment closely.


MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Lecture notes and problem sets on vector calculus, surface integrals, and Stokes’ theorem. The proof strategy via Green’s theorem on the projected region follows the 18.02 approach.


Spivak, M. — Calculus on Manifolds — For the generalized Stokes theorem in the language of differential forms (the \int_{\partial \Omega} \omega = \int_\Omega d\omega framework sketched in §0).


Bronstein et al. — Geometric Deep Learning: Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges (2021) — For the connection between differential geometry, Stokes’ theorem, and equivariant neural networks.
