>  The transformation is _linear_ — straight lines stay straight, parallel lines stay parallel, and the origin stays fixed. The grid warps but never curves.

When I see a $3 \times 3$ matrix, I should first ask: what kind of transformation is this? Does it rotate? Does it collapse a dimension? The entries encode the answer.

### 2) The Column Picture
_Where do the axes go after the transformation?_
Regroup the same system by columns:
$$ x \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}-y \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
- z \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} $$
Let me name these:
$$ \mathbf{a}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{a}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{a}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} $$
The question is now purely geometric in $\mathbb{R}^3$: can I find scalars $x, y, z$ such that
$$x\mathbf{a}_1 + y\mathbf{a}_2 + z\mathbf{a}_3 = \mathbf{b}$$
Think of it as: I am standing at the origin with three moves available — I can go $x$ units in the direction of $\mathbf{a}_1$, $y$ units in the direction of $\mathbf{a}_2$, $z$ units in the direction of $\mathbf{a}_3$. Can I reach $\mathbf{b}$?

Write the matrix as three column vectors:
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} | & | & | \\ \mathbf{a}_1 & \mathbf{a}_2 & \mathbf{a}_3 \\ | & | & | \end{bmatrix}$$
These columns tell me exactly where the standard basis vectors land:
- $\mathbf{a}_1$ = where $(1,0,0)$ — the $x$-axis — lands after the transformation
- $\mathbf{a}_2$ = where $(0,1,0)$ — the $y$-axis — lands after the transformation
- $\mathbf{a}_3$ = where $(0,0,1)$ — the $z$-axis — lands after the transformation
The three columns together form a **parallelepiped** — the image of the unit cube under $A$.

>  Are the columns **linearly independent**?
> - **Yes** → parallelepiped has real 3D volume → transformation is invertible
> - **No** → columns are coplanar → space **collapses** into a plane or line → not invertible

If the three columns span all of $\mathbb{R}^3$ (linearly independent, $A$ invertible), then I can reach every $\mathbf{b}$. If the columns are coplanar (linearly dependent), I can only reach vectors in that plane — most $\mathbf{b}$ are unreachable. The column picture makes the existence question about $\mathbf{b}$ and the column space completely transparent.

### 3) The Row Picture
Each row of $A$ gives one equation. Each equation $\mathbf{a}_i^T \mathbf{x} = b_i$ defines a **plane** in $\mathbb{R}^3$ — the set of all points $(x, y, z)$ whose dot product with the normal vector $\mathbf{a}_i$ equals $b_i$.
When I solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, I am asking: where do these three planes intersect?
For my system:
**Plane 1:** $2x - y + z = 3$, normal vector $\mathbf{n}_1 = (2, -1, 1)$
**Plane 2:** $x + 3y - z = 5$, normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2 = (1, 3, -1)$
**Plane 3:** $-x + y + 4z = 2$, normal vector $\mathbf{n}_3 = (-1, 1, 4)$
The plane is perpendicular to its normal vector, sitting at signed distance $b_i / |\mathbf{n}_i|$ from the origin.
![[Pasted image 20260413095222.png]]
**The solution is the point where all three planes intersect.** Generically in $\mathbb{R}^3$: two planes intersect in a line; three planes intersect in a point.

When things go wrong:
- Two planes parallel → no intersection → no solution
- Three planes sharing a common line → infinitely many solutions
- All three planes parallel → no solution
- Three planes reducing to the same plane → infinitely many solutions
The row picture makes the geometry of failure completely clear. But it tells me nothing efficient about how to _find_ the solution.


## Determinant — The Volume Story

The determinant is the single most important scalar attached to a matrix. It answers:

> By what factor does this transformation scale volume?

$$\det(A) = \text{signed volume of the parallelepiped formed by the columns}$$
![[Pasted image 20260413095454.png]]

| $\det(A)$ | Volume | Orientation | Invertible? |
| --------- | ------ | ----------- | ----------- |
| $> 0$     | Scaled | Preserved   | Yes         |
| $= 0$     | Zero   | Lost        | No          |
| $< 0$     | Scaled | Flipped     | Yes         |

If $\det(A) = 0$, the matrix is not invertible. 3D space has been squashed into a 2D plane (or worse, a line or a point). Information is irreversibly lost. There is no way to undo the transformation.


| -                  | Row Picture                     | Column Picture                                                      |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Objects            | Three planes in $\mathbb{R}^3$  | Three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$                                     |
| Solution           | Point where all planes meet     | Weights $x, y, z$ combining columns to give $\mathbf{b}$            |
| Unique solution    | Planes meet at one point        | Columns span all of $\mathbb{R}^3$, $\mathbf{b}$ reachable uniquely |
| No solution        | Some planes are parallel        | $\mathbf{b}$ outside column space                                   |
| $\infty$ solutions | Planes share a line or coincide | $\mathbf{b}$ in column space, columns dependent                     |
| Test               | Pivots all nonzero?             | $\det(A) \neq 0$?                                                   |

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 03.Elimination
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
Elimination is the systematic algorithm for solving A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.
The core idea: apply a sequence of row operations to A that preserve the solution set of A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}, and drive the system into upper triangular form. Once the system is triangular, back-substitution solves it immediately.
The deeper idea: elimination is actually computing the LU factorization of A. The row operations I apply are being recorded as elementary matrices, and their product is the lower triangular matrix L. The end result of elimination is U — the upper triangular matrix. So A = LU. Every step of elimination is a step toward this factorization.
Three Legal Row Operations:
These are the only operations I am allowed to perform. Each one preserves the solution set of A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.
1. Row swap: interchange two rows. R_i \leftrightarrow R_j
2. Scalar multiplication: multiply a row by a nonzero constant c \neq 0. R_i \leftarrow c \cdot R_i
3. Row replacement: replace a row by itself plus a multiple of another row. R_i \leftarrow R_i - \ell \cdot R_j, \quad j < i
Gaussian elimination uses almost exclusively the third operation. The multiplier \ell is chosen to kill an entry below a pivot.
Why do these preserve the solution set? Each operation corresponds to multiplying both sides of A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} by an invertible elementary matrix E on the left: EA\mathbf{x} = E\mathbf{b}. Since E is invertible, the new system has exactly the same solutions.
The Pivot
The pivot is the first nonzero entry in a row after elimination has cleared everything below and to the left of it. Concretely: after I have eliminated all entries in column j below row i, the entry a_{ii} that was used to do the eliminating is the pivot for that step.
Pivots must be nonzero. This is not optional — the multiplier \ell_{ij} = a_{ij} / a_{jj} requires dividing by the pivot. A zero pivot means I need to swap rows (a row exchange) to bring a nonzero entry into the pivot position. If no nonzero entry exists in that column, the matrix is singular and I cannot get a pivot there.
The pivots are the diagonal entries of U after all row operations are complete. Their product is the determinant:
\det(A) = \prod_i u_{ii} \cdot (\pm 1)
where the \pm 1 accounts for any row swaps.
Algorithm:
let, The input is A and \mathbf{b}; I work on the augmented matrix [A \mid \mathbf{b}].

Step 1. Use the (1,1) entry as the first pivot. For each row i > 1, compute the multiplier: \ell_{i1} = \frac{a_{i1}}{a_{11}} and replace R_i \leftarrow R_i - \ell_{i1} \cdot R_1. This kills every entry in column 1 below the pivot.
Step 2. Move to the (2,2) entry (or whatever is now in the second pivot position). Repeat: compute multipliers, eliminate below.
Step k. At stage k, the pivot is the (k,k) entry. Eliminate all entries in column k below row k using multipliers \ell_{ik} = a_{ik}^{(k)} / a_{kk}^{(k)}, where the superscript (k) denotes the matrix after k-1 stages of elimination.
Continue until the matrix is upper triangular.

3 \times 3 Example
Solve the following system:
2x + y - z = 8
-3x - y + 2z = -11
-2x + y + 2z = -3
Write the augmented matrix:
\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} 2 & 1 & -1 & 8 \\ -3 & -1 & 2 & -11 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -3 \end{array}\right)
Stage 1: Pivot is a_{11} = 2.
Multipliers: \ell_{21} = \frac{-3}{2}, \qquad \ell_{31} = \frac{-2}{2} = -1

R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - \left(-\tfrac{3}{2}\right) R_1 = R_2 + \tfrac{3}{2} R_1:
-3 + \tfrac{3}{2}(2) = 0, \quad -1 + \tfrac{3}{2}(1) = \tfrac{1}{2}, \quad 2 + \tfrac{3}{2}(-1) = \tfrac{1}{2}, \quad -11 + \tfrac{3}{2}(8) = 1
R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - (-1) R_1 = R_3 + R_1:
-2 + 2 = 0, \quad 1 + 1 = 2, \quad 2 + (-1) = 1, \quad -3 + 8 = 5

After Stage 1:
\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} 2 & 1 & -1 & 8 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 5 \end{array}\right)
Stage 2: Pivot is a_{22} = \tfrac{1}{2}.
Multiplier: \ell_{32} = \frac{2}{1/2} = 4

R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 4 R_2:
0, \quad 2 - 4\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = 0, \quad 1 - 4\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = -1, \quad 5 - 4(1) = 1

After Stage 2 — the upper triangular system U:
\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} 2 & 1 & -1 & 8 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 1 \end{array}\right)
Three pivots: 2, \tfrac{1}{2}, -1. All nonzero — A is invertible.
Back-substitution:
From row 3: -z = 1 \Rightarrow z = -1.
From row 2: \tfrac{1}{2}y + \tfrac{1}{2}(-1) = 1 \Rightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}y = \tfrac{3}{2} \Rightarrow y = 3.
From row 1: 2x + 3 - (-1) = 8 \Rightarrow 2x = 4 \Rightarrow x = 2.
Solution: (x, y, z) = (2, 3, -1).
Elimination as Matrix Multiplication: The E Matrices
Each row operation “replace R_i by R_i - \ell R_j” corresponds to left-multiplying by an elementary matrix E_{ij}. For a 3 \times 3 system, the matrix that subtracts \ell times row 1 from row 2 is:
E_{21} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\ell_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
Left-multiplying A by E_{21} does exactly the row operation. The full elimination is:
E_{32} E_{31} E_{21} A = U
(applying operations right to left). So:
A = E_{21}^{-1} E_{31}^{-1} E_{32}^{-1} U = LU
The matrix L = E_{21}^{-1} E_{31}^{-1} E_{32}^{-1} is lower triangular. And crucially, inverting each E_{ij} is trivial: just flip the sign of the multiplier.
E_{21}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \ell_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
The multipliers \ell_{ij} drop directly into L without any additional computation.
LU Factorization:
This is the payoff of the elimination viewpoint. Once I have run elimination (with no row swaps), the result is:
A = LU
where:
L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \ell_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ \ell_{31} & \ell_{32} & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad U = \begin{pmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12} & u_{13} \\ 0 & u_{22} & u_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & u_{33} \end{pmatrix}
L → unit lower triangular (ones on the diagonal; the multipliers fill the lower triangle).
U → upper triangular (the result of elimination; the pivots are on the diagonal).
For the example above, reading off the multipliers \ell_{21} = -3/2, \ell_{31} = -1, \ell_{32} = 4:
L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\tfrac{3}{2} & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 4 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad U = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}
Verification: LU should recover A. I trust the algebra but should check this at least once for a worked example.
Why LU and Not Just Elimination?
Once I have A = LU, solving A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} splits into two triangular systems:
L\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{b} \quad \text{(forward substitution)} U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{c} \quad \text{(back substitution)}
Both are O(n^2) to solve. The factorization itself costs O(n^3) — and I only do it once. If I need to solve A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} for many different right-hand sides \mathbf{b}, I factor A once and then solve each new \mathbf{b} in O(n^2) time. This is the practical reason LU matters.
see more10. A = LU

When Elimination Breaks Down — Row Exchanges
If during elimination a zero appears in the pivot position, but nonzero entries exist below it in the same column, I can fix this with a row swap. The corrected algorithm that incorporates row swaps is PA = LU factorization, where P is a permutation matrix.
PA = LU
P records which row swaps were performed. It is an orthogonal matrix (P^T = P^{-1}) with exactly one 1 per row and per column.
If no nonzero entry exists below a zero pivot position, then the matrix is singular — no row swap can save it. Elimination produces a row of zeros, and the rank is less than n.
A zero pivot is a warning. No possible pivot is a verdict.
see more:16.PA = LU

Failure: The Singular Case
Suppose after all row operations, the final matrix looks like:
\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} 2 & 1 & -1 & 8 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & c \end{array}\right)
If c \neq 0: the third equation says 0 = c. No solution. The right-hand side \mathbf{b} is not in the column space of A.
If c = 0: the third equation says 0 = 0. Infinitely many solutions. The variable corresponding to the missing third pivot is free — it can take any value, and the other variables adjust accordingly.
The number of pivots equals the rank r. The number of free variables is n - r.

The Cost of Elimination
For an n \times n matrix, how many operations does elimination require?
At stage k, I eliminate entries in column k below the pivot. There are n - k rows to update, and each row requires n - k + 1 multiplications and subtractions (updating the remaining n - k + 1 entries in that row, including the augmented column).
Total operations:
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} (n-k)(n-k+1) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{n} k^2 \approx \frac{n^3}{3}
So elimination costs O(n^3) — roughly n^3/3 multiplications. For n = 1000, that is roughly 3 \times 10^8 operations. For n = 10^6, elimination becomes impractical — this is why iterative methods exist.
Back-substitution costs O(n^2), which is negligible compared to n^3/3.
see more12.The Cost of Elimination

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 04.Permutation Matrices
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
A permutation matrix P is a square matrix obtained by reordering the rows of the identity matrix I.
Equivalently: P has exactly one entry equal to 1 in each row and exactly one entry equal to 1 in each column, with all other entries 0.
For n = 3, the identity permutation is I itself:
I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
The permutation matrix that swaps rows 1 and 2:
P_{12} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
Left-multiplying any 3 \times n matrix A by P_{12} swaps its first and second rows.
The permutation matrix that cycles rows 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1:
P_{\text{cyc}} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
All Permutation Matrices for n = 3

There are 3! = 6 permutations of three rows, so exactly 6 permutation matrices of size 3 \times 3. Let me write them all out explicitly.

The six permutations of (1, 2, 3) — written as: row 1 goes to position \sigma(1), row 2 to \sigma(2), row 3 to \sigma(3):
\sigma = (1,2,3) — identity: P_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\sigma = (2,1,3) — swap rows 1 and 2: P_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\sigma = (1,3,2) — swap rows 2 and 3: P_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\sigma = (3,2,1) — swap rows 1 and 3: P_4 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\sigma = (2,3,1) — cycle 1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 1: P_5 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\sigma = (3,1,2) — cycle 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1: P_6 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
For n \times n matrices there are n! permutation matrices total: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, 720, \ldots

What P Does: Left vs. Right Multiplication
This is worth being precise about because the two directions do completely different things.
Left multiplication PA: permutes the rows of A.Row i of PA is row \sigma(i) of A, where \sigma is the permutation encoded by P.
Right multiplication AP: permutes the columns of A.Column j of AP is column \sigma(j) of A.
In elimination I always left-multiply — I am rearranging rows, not columns. Right-multiplying A by P would rearrange the unknowns, which is a different operation entirely.
Algebraic Properties
1. Orthogonality:
P^T P = I \qquad$$$$ \Longrightarrow \qquad P^{-1} = P^T
This is the most important property. The inverse of a permutation matrix is its transpose.
Proof: the (i,j) entry of P^T P is the dot product of column i of P^T (which is row i of P) with column j of P. Row i of P has a single 1 in some position k; column j of P has a single 1 in some position \ell. The dot product is 1 iff k = \ell, which happens iff i = j (since each column has exactly one 1). So P^T P = I.
2. The inverse permutation:
If P sends row i to position \sigma(i), then P^{-1} = P^T sends row \sigma(i) back to position i. The transpose undoes the permutation.
For the swap matrix P_{12}:
P_{12}^T = P_{12}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = P_{12}
Swapping rows 1 and 2 twice returns to the original. So P_{12} is its own inverse: P_{12}^2 = I. This is true of any single-swap permutation matrix.
3. Determinant:
\det(P) = +1 \text{ or } -1


                  
                  Important
                  
                

\det(P) = +1 if P is an even permutation (achievable by an even number of swaps).
\det(P) = -1 if P is an odd permutation (achievable by an odd number of swaps).


The identity has \det = +1. Each row swap flips the sign. So:

P_1: \det = +1 (zero swaps)
P_2, P_3, P_4: \det = -1 (one swap each)
P_5, P_6: \det = +1 (two swaps each, or equivalently they are 3-cycles)

4. Closure under multiplication.
The product of two permutation matrices is a permutation matrix. The composition of two row rearrangements is another row rearrangement. The set of all n \times n permutation matrices forms a group under multiplication — the symmetric group S_n.

Permutation Matrices Are Orthogonal Matrices
P^{-1} = P^T is exactly the definition of an orthogonal matrix. So every permutation matrix is orthogonal.
What does this mean geometrically? Orthogonal matrices preserve lengths and angles:
|P\mathbf{x}| = |\mathbf{x}|, \qquad (P\mathbf{x}) \cdot (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}
Permuting the components of a vector does not change its length — this is obvious, since I am just reordering the squared terms in |\mathbf{x}|^2 = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2.
Permutation matrices are a special subclass of orthogonal matrices. In general, orthogonal matrices can rotate and reflect; permutation matrices can only permute coordinates. They are the “discrete” orthogonal matrices.
see more09.Orthogonal Matrix

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 05.The Augmented Matrix
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
When I solve A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}, I am performing row operations on A — but every row operation on A must be simultaneously applied to \mathbf{b}. If I manipulate A and forget to carry \mathbf{b} along, the right-hand side no longer corresponds to the transformed system and the solution is wrong.
The augmented matrix is the bookkeeping device that prevents this mistake. I attach \mathbf{b} as an extra column to A, separated by a vertical bar to remind me it plays a different role:
[A \mid \mathbf{b}] = \left(\begin{array}{cccc|c} a_{11} & a_{12} & \cdots & a_{1n} & b_1 \\ a_{21} & a_{22} & \cdots & a_{2n} & b_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ a_{m1} & a_{m2} & \cdots & a_{mn} & b_m \end{array}\right)
Now every row operation I perform on the left automatically carries through to the right. The vertical bar is a reminder — not a mathematical boundary — that the last column is \mathbf{b}, not a column of A.

row operations on [A \mid \mathbf{b}] produce [A' \mid \mathbf{b}'] where A'\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}' has exactly the same solution set as A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.

Row Operations
Each legal row operation corresponds to left-multiplying by an elementary matrix E:
E[A \mid \mathbf{b}] = [EA \mid E\mathbf{b}]
Since E is invertible, the systems A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} and (EA)\mathbf{x} = E\mathbf{b} have identical solution sets. The augmented matrix packages both sides so this simultaneous transformation is automatic.
After the full sequence of elimination steps E_k \cdots E_2 E_1, I arrive at:
[U \mid \mathbf{c}]
where U is upper triangular and \mathbf{c} = E_k \cdots E_1 \mathbf{b} is the transformed right-hand side. Then back-substitution on U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{c} gives the solution.
Anatomy of the Augmented Matrix After Elimination
After row reduction to row echelon form, the augmented matrix [U \mid \mathbf{c}] for an m \times n system of rank r looks like this:
\left(\begin{array}{ccccccc|c} \mathbf{p}_1 & * & * & * & * & * & * & c_1 \\ 0 & 0 & \mathbf{p}_2 & * & * & * & * & c_2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \mathbf{p}_3 & * & * & c_3 \\ \vdots & & & & & \ddots & & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \mathbf{p}_r & c_r \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & c_{r+1} \\ \vdots & & & & & & & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & c_m \end{array}\right)
The bold entries \mathbf{p}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{p}_r are the pivots. Everything below each pivot in its column is zero.
The rows r+1 through m (if any) are all-zero rows on the left side. Whether the system is consistent or inconsistent is determined entirely by the corresponding entries c_{r+1}, \ldots, c_m on the right.
Reading the Three Cases Directly from [U \mid \mathbf{c}]
Case 1 : Unique solution: r = n = m.
\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} p_1 & * & * & c_1 \\ 0 & p_2 & * & c_2 \\ 0 & 0 & p_3 & c_3 \end{array}\right)
Every column has a pivot, every row has a pivot. No free variables, no zero rows. Back-substitution gives a unique (x_1, x_2, x_3).
Case 2 — No solution: r < m and some c_i \neq 0 for i > r.
\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} p_1 & * & * & c_1 \\ 0 & p_2 & * & c_2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & c_3 \end{array}\right) \quad \text{with } c_3 \neq 0
The third row says 0 \cdot x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2 + 0 \cdot x_3 = c_3 \neq 0. This is 0 = c_3, a contradiction. The system is inconsistent. No solution exists. Geometrically: \mathbf{b} is not in the column space of A.
Case 3 — Infinitely many solutions: r < n and all c_i = 0 for i > r.
\left(\begin{array}{ccc|c} p_1 & * & * & c_1 \\ 0 & 0 & p_2 & c_2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right)
Column 2 has no pivot — it is a free column. The variable x_2 is free: it can take any value t \in \mathbb{R}, and x_1, x_3 are expressed in terms of t via back-substitution. The solution set is a line (or affine subspace of dimension n - r) in \mathbb{R}^n.
Example: 3 \times 4 System
I want to see an underdetermined system explicitly. For example:
x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 + x_4 = 7
2x_1 + 4x_2 + 7x_3 - x_4 = 9
x_1 + 2x_2 + 5x_3 - 3x_4 = 6
Augmented matrix:
\left(\begin{array}{cccc|c} 1 & 2 & 3 & 1 & 7 \\ 2 & 4 & 7 & -1 & 9 \\ 1 & 2 & 5 & -3 & 6 \end{array}\right)
Stage 1: Pivot = 1 in position (1,1).
R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1: (2-2,\\ 4-4,\\ 7-6,\\ -1-2,\\ 9-14) = (0,\\ 0,\\ 1,\\ -3,\\ -5)
R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - R_1: (1-1,\ 2-2,\ 5-3,\ -3-1,\ 6-7) = (0,\ 0,\ 2,\ -4,\ -1)
After Stage 1:
\left(\begin{array}{cccc|c} 1 & 2 & 3 & 1 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -4 & -1 \end{array}\right)
Column 2 has no pivot below row 1 — x_2 is a free variable.
Stage 2: Pivot = 1 in position (2,3).
R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 2R_2: (0,\ 0,\ 2-2,\ -4+6,\ -1+10) = (0,\ 0,\ 0,\ 2,\ 9)
After Stage 2:
\left(\begin{array}{cccc|c} 1 & 2 & 3 & 1 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 9 \end{array}\right)
Stage 3: Pivot = 2 in position (3,4).
No rows below. Elimination complete.
Three pivots: 1, 1, 2 in columns 1, 3, 4. Column 2 is free. Rank r = 3, free variables = n - r = 4 - 3 = 1.
Back-substitution:
From row 3: 2x_4 = 9 \Rightarrow x_4 = \tfrac{9}{2}.
From row 2: x_3 - 3x_4 = -5 \Rightarrow x_3 = -5 + 3\cdot\tfrac{9}{2} = -5 + \tfrac{27}{2} = \tfrac{17}{2}.
From row 1: x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 + x_4 = 7.
Let x_2 = t (free). Then: x_1 = 7 - 2t - 3\cdot\tfrac{17}{2} - \tfrac{9}{2} = 7 - 2t - \tfrac{51}{2} - \tfrac{9}{2} = 7 - 2t - 30 = -23 - 2t
Complete solution:
\mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix} -23 \\ 0 \\ \tfrac{17}{2} \\ \tfrac{9}{2} \end{pmatrix} + t \begin{pmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad t \in \mathbb{R}
The first vector is the particular solution \mathbf{x}_p (setting t = 0). The second vector is the special solution in the nullspace, corresponding to the free variable x_2 = 1.
This is precisely the structure \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{x}_n from before. The augmented matrix made every step of this visible and automatic.

The Augmented Matrix for Finding A^{-1}
There is a second major use of the augmented matrix: computing the inverse. If A is square and invertible, I augment with the identity:
[A \mid I]
Then I row reduce all the way to 04.Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF) — not just echelon form, but with zeros above the pivots as well, and pivots scaled to 1. The result is:
[I \mid A^{-1}]
Why this works: I am applying the same sequence of row operations to both A and I. The operations turn A into I, meaning I applied E_k \cdots E_1 A = I, so E_k \cdots E_1 = A^{-1}. The same operations applied to I give E_k \cdots E_1 I = A^{-1}.
This is Gauss-Jordan elimination. The cost is O(n^3), same as LU factorization, but now I get the full inverse rather than just a factorization.
When to use A^{-1} vs LU: If I need to solve A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} for one or a few \mathbf{b}, use LU. If I genuinely need A^{-1} itself (e.g., to form the matrix A^{-1}B for some other matrix B), use Gauss-Jordan.
see more: 06.Gauss–Jordan Elimination

A 2 \times 2 Inverse by Gauss-Jordan
A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
Augmented with identity:
\left(\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 3 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right)


R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - \tfrac{5}{2} R_1: \left(\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{5}{2} & 1 \end{array}\right)


R_2 \leftarrow 2 R_2 (scale pivot to 1):\left(\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 2 \end{array}\right)


R_1 \leftarrow R_1 - R_2 (eliminate above pivot in column 2): \left(\begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 0 & 6 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 2 \end{array}\right)


R_1 \leftarrow \tfrac{1}{2} R_1 (scale pivot to 1): \left(\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 2 \end{array}\right)


Therefore: A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
Check: AA^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 5 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \ -5 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 6-5 & -2+2 \ 15-15 & -5+6 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \checkmark

Reduced Row Echelon Form
The echelon form U has pivots in staircase position with zeros below each pivot. The reduced row echelon form (RREF) goes further:

Zeros above each pivot as well as below.
Each pivot scaled to exactly 1.

RREF is unique — every matrix has exactly one RREF. Echelon form is not unique (the operations used to reach it can vary). RREF is the canonical form.
For solving A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}: either echelon form followed by back-substitution, or RREF with the answer readable directly. For finding A^{-1}: RREF is required (Gauss-Jordan).
The RREF of A is often written R:
R = \text{rref}(A)
For an invertible n \times n matrix: R = I.
For a singular matrix: R has at least one all-zero row, and the pivot columns of R are standard basis vectors.
see more04.Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF)
What the Augmented Matrix Encodes — A Summary

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 06.Laws of Matrix Operations
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
Matrix Addition
Let A, B, C be m \times n matrices. Addition is defined componentwise: (A + B)_{ij} = a_{ij} + b_{ij}.

Commutativity: A + B = B + A
Associativity: (A + B) + C = A + (B + C)
Additive identity: The zero matrix 0 (all entries zero) satisfies A + 0 = A.
Additive inverse: A + (-A) = 0 where (-A)_{ij} = -a_{ij}.

These all hold componentwise and carry over directly from \mathbb{R}. Nothing interesting happens with addition — it is multiplication where the structure changes.
Scalar Multiplication
For scalar c \in \mathbb{R} and matrices A, B of compatible sizes:

c(A + B) = cA + cB
(c + d)A = cA + dA
(cd)A = c(dA)
1 \cdot A = A

Matrix Multiplication
For A of size m \times n and B of size n \times p, the product AB is m \times p with entries:
(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{ik} b_{kj}
Row i of A dotted with column j of B. The inner dimensions must match: A is m \times \mathbf{n} and B is \mathbf{n} \times p.
There are four ways to think about this product, and each illuminates something different:

** Entry by entry:** (AB)_{ij} = \mathbf{a}_i^T \mathbf{b}_j — dot product of row i of A with column j of B.
** Column by column:** each column of AB is A times the corresponding column of B. AB = A \begin{pmatrix} | & & | \\ \mathbf{b}_1 & \cdots & \mathbf{b}_p \\ | & & | \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} | & & | \\ A\mathbf{b}_1 & \cdots & A\mathbf{b}_p \\ | & & | \end{pmatrix}
Row by row: each row of AB is the corresponding row of A times B.
** Sum of outer products:** AB = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathbf{a}_k \mathbf{b}_k^T, where \mathbf{a}_k is the k-th column of A and \mathbf{b}_k^T is the k-th row of B. Each term is a rank-1 matrix.

The outer product view (4) is underrated. It shows that AB is a sum of n rank-1 matrices — useful for understanding rank and for thinking about low-rank approximations.
The Laws That Hold

Associativity: A(BC) = (AB)C
Proof: Both sides have the same size. The (i,j) entry of A(BC) is:
\sum_k a_{ik} (BC)_{kj} = \sum_k a_{ik} \sum_\ell b_{k\ell} c_{\ell j} = \sum_k \sum_\ell a_{ik} b_{k\ell} c_{\ell j}
The (i,j) entry of (AB)C is:
\sum_\ell (AB)_{i\ell} c_{\ell j} = \sum_\ell \left(\sum_k a_{ik} b_{k\ell}\right) c_{\ell j} = \sum_k \sum_\ell a_{ik} b_{k\ell} c_{\ell j}
Identical. So associativity holds. The proof is just rearranging a finite sum — no trick needed.
Consequence: I can write ABC without parentheses and it is unambiguous.

Left distributivity: A(B + C) = AB + AC
Right distributivity: (A + B)C = AC + BC
Both follow from expanding the sums entry by entry.
Powers of a square matrix: A^p = \underbrace{A \cdot A \cdots A}_{p \text{ times}}
Well-defined by associativity. A^0 = I by convention.
The Law That Fails: Commutativity
AB \neq BA \quad \text{in general}
This is not just “sometimes false” ; it is almost always false. Let me be explicit.
Dimension obstruction: if A is m \times n and B is n \times p, then AB is m \times p but BA requires B to be p \times m — a completely different size condition. So BA may not even be defined when AB is.
Even when both are defined: take A and B both 2 \times 2:
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
AB = \begin{pmatrix} 1\cdot1 + 1\cdot1 & 1\cdot0 + 1\cdot0 \\ 0\cdot1 + 0\cdot1 & 0\cdot0 + 0\cdot0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
BA = \begin{pmatrix} 1\cdot1 + 0\cdot0 & 1\cdot1 + 0\cdot0 \\ 1\cdot1 + 0\cdot0 & 1\cdot1 + 0\cdot0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
AB \neq BA. Not even close.
The cancellation law also fails. In ordinary algebra, AB = AC and A \neq 0 implies B = C. Not so for matrices:
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
AB = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = AC
but B \neq C. Left-cancellation fails because A is singular — it has a nontrivial nullspace.
Also: AB = 0 does not imply A = 0 or B = 0.
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
Two nonzero matrices multiply to zero. This is impossible for nonzero real numbers.
Transpose Laws
The transpose of A is the matrix A^T with (A^T)_{ij} = a_{ji} — rows and columns are swapped.
For A of size m \times n: A^T is n \times m.

(A^T)^T = ATransposing twice returns the original. Obvious from the definition.
(A + B)^T = A^T + B^TComponent wise: (A + B)_{ij} = a_{ij} + b_{ij}, so (A+B)^T_{ij} = a_{ji} + b_{ji} = (A^T)_{ij} + (B^T)_{ij}. Done.
the reversal law: (AB)^T = B^T A^TThis is the nontrivial one. The order reverses.

Proof: The (i,j) entry of (AB)^T is the (j,i) entry of AB: (AB)^T_{ij} = (AB)_{ji} = \sum_k a_{jk} b_{ki}
The (i,j) entry of B^T A^T is: (B^T A^T)_{ij} = \sum_k (B^T)_{ik} (A^T)_{kj} = \sum_k b_{ki} a_{jk}
These are equal (multiplication of scalars commutes). So (AB)^T = B^T A^T..
Generalizing: for a product of any number of matrices: (ABC \cdots Z)^T = Z^T \cdots C^T B^T A^T
The entire product reverses. I think of this as: “transpose reverses the order.” The same reversal appears in inverse laws.
Symmetric matrices: A is symmetric if A^T = A. For any matrix A, the product A^T A is always symmetric: (A^T A)^T = A^T (A^T)^T = A^T A \checkmark
This is used constantly in least squares and in the definition of positive definiteness. see more15.Symmetric Matrices
Inverse Laws
For a square invertible matrix A:
A^{-1} A = I \qquad \text{and} \qquad A A^{-1} = I
Both must hold — a one-sided inverse of a square matrix is automatically a two-sided inverse.

(A^{-1})^{-1} = A The inverse of A^{-1} is A itself.
(cA)^{-1} = \frac{1}{c} A^{-1} for scalar c \neq 0.
the reversal law: (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}
Order reverses, just like for the transpose.
Proof: I need to check that B^{-1} A^{-1} is indeed the inverse of AB:
(AB)(B^{-1} A^{-1}) = A(B B^{-1}) A^{-1} = A I A^{-1} = A A^{-1} = I
(B^{-1} A^{-1})(AB) = B^{-1}(A^{-1} A)B = B^{-1} I B = B^{-1} B = I
Both sides give I, so B^{-1} A^{-1} is the inverse of AB.
Generalizing: (ABC)^{-1} = C^{-1} B^{-1} A^{-1}
transpose of inverse:** (A^{-1})^T = (A^T)^{-1}
Proof: Start from AA^{-1} = I. Transpose both sides:
(AA^{-1})^T = I^T = I
(A^{-1})^T A^T = I
So (A^{-1})^T is the left inverse of A^T. Similarly from A^{-1} A = I: A^T (A^{-1})^T = I
So (A^{-1})^T is also the right inverse of A^T, meaning (A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T.

Consequence: for orthogonal matrices where A^{-1} = A^T, this law says (A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T = (A^T)^T = A. Consistent.
What Commutes With Everything — Scalar Matrices
The only n \times n matrices that commute with every n \times n matrix are the scalar matrices cI for c \in \mathbb{R}:
(cI)A = cA = A(cI)
This is a theorem, not just an observation. The center of the matrix algebra is {cI : c \in \mathbb{R}}.
So if someone hands me a matrix B and tells me BA = AB for all A, I can immediately conclude B = cI for some scalar c. That is a strong constraint.

































































LawStatementHolds?Addition commutativityA + B = B + AYesAddition associativity(A+B)+C = A+(B+C)YesMultiplication associativity(AB)C = A(BC)YesLeft distributivityA(B+C) = AB + ACYesRight distributivity(A+B)C = AC + BCYesMultiplication commutativityAB = BANoLeft cancellationAB = AC \Rightarrow B = CNo (if A singular)Zero productAB = 0 \Rightarrow A = 0 or B = 0NoTranspose reversal(AB)^T = B^T A^TYesInverse reversal(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1} A^{-1}Yes (if invertible)Transpose of inverse(A^{-1})^T = (A^T)^{-1}Yes (if invertible)
