01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 07.Block Matrices and Block Multiplication
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
Partitioning a Matrix:
Take a matrix A of size m \times n. Choose a partition: split the rows into groups of sizes m_1, m_2, \ldots, m_r with m_1 + m_2 + \cdots + m_r = m, and split the columns into groups of sizes n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_s with n_1 + \cdots + n_s = n.
This produces a block matrix with r \times s blocks. The block in position (i,j) has size m_i \times n_j.
For a 4 \times 4 matrix partitioned 2|2 horizontally and 2|2 vertically:
A =
\left(
\begin{array}{cc|cc}
a_{11} & a_{12} & a_{13} & a_{14} \\
a_{21} & a_{22} & a_{23} & a_{24} \\
\hline
a_{31} & a_{32} & a_{33} & a_{34} \\
a_{41} & a_{42} & a_{43} & a_{44}
\end{array}
\right)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
A_{11} & A_{12} \\
A_{21} & A_{22}
\end{pmatrix}
where each A_{ij} is a 2 \times 2 submatrix:
A_{11} = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & a_{22} \end{pmatrix}, \quad A_{12} = \begin{pmatrix} a_{13} & a_{14} \\ a_{23} & a_{24} \end{pmatrix}, \quad A_{21} = \begin{pmatrix} a_{31} & a_{32} \\ a_{41} & a_{42} \end{pmatrix}, \quad A_{22} = \begin{pmatrix} a_{33} & a_{34} \\ a_{43} & a_{44} \end{pmatrix}
The notation is deliberately parallel to ordinary matrix entries. I will write A = [A_{ij}] just as I write a scalar matrix as A = [a_{ij}].
Block Multiplication
Let A be m \times n and B be n \times p. Partition both with a compatible column/row split: the column partition of A must match the row partition of B.
If I partition A as r \times s blocks and B as s \times t blocks (so the inner block dimension is s for both), then:
(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{s} A_{ik} B_{kj}
This is identical in form to the scalar rule (AB)_{ij} = \sum_k a_{ik} b_{kj}, with scalar entries replaced by block submatrices.
The compatibility condition: the number of columns in block A_{ik} must equal the number of rows in block B_{kj}. This is guaranteed if the column partition of A matches the row partition of B — the column sizes of A‘s blocks equal the row sizes of B‘s corresponding blocks.
Example: 4 \times 4 Matrix
Let:
A = \begin{pmatrix} A_{11} & A_{12} \\ A_{21} & A_{22} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix} B_{11} & B_{12} \\ B_{21} & B_{22} \end{pmatrix}
where each block is 2 \times 2. Then:
AB = \begin{pmatrix} A_{11}B_{11} + A_{12}B_{21} & A_{11}B_{12} + A_{12}B_{22} \\ A_{21}B_{11} + A_{22}B_{21} & A_{21}B_{12} + A_{22}B_{22} \end{pmatrix}
This looks exactly like 2 \times 2 matrix multiplication, but each “entry” is itself a 2 \times 2 matrix product.
Explicit numerical example. Let:
A =
\left(
\begin{array}{cc|cc}
1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\
0 & 1 & 3 & 0 \\
\hline
1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 1 & 2
\end{array}
\right),
\qquad
B =
\left(
\begin{array}{cc|cc}
1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\
\hline
2 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & 1
\end{array}
\right)
Blocks of A:
A_{11} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I, \quad A_{12} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad A_{21} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad A_{22} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
Blocks of B:
B_{11} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I, \quad B_{12} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad B_{21} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad B_{22} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I
Now compute AB block by block.

Top-left block: A_{11}B_{11} + A_{12}B_{21} I \cdot I + \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 6 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ 6 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
Top-right block: A_{11}B_{12} + A_{12}B_{22} I \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \cdot I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
Bottom-left block: A_{21}B_{11} + A_{22}B_{21} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot I + \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
Bottom-right block: A_{21}B_{12} + A_{22}B_{22} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \cdot I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
So:

AB =
\left(
\begin{array}{cc|cc}
5 & 1 & 2 & 2 \\
6 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\
\hline
1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
2 & 3 & 2 & 2
\end{array}
\right)
Block Transpose and Block Inverse
Transpose of a block matrix:
\begin{pmatrix} A_{11} & A_{12} \\ A_{21} & A_{22} \end{pmatrix}^T = \begin{pmatrix} A_{11}^T & A_{21}^T \\ A_{12}^T & A_{22}^T \end{pmatrix}
Two things happen simultaneously:

the blocks swap positions across the diagonal (just as scalar entries do),
each block is individually transposed. Both operations are necessary.

Inverse of a 2 \times 2 block matrix:
This is harder. For a block matrix:
M = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix}
the inverse is not simply the matrix of inverses of blocks. The correct formula involves the Schur complement.
see more08.Schur Complement

Important Special Cases
Block diagonal matrix:
M = \begin{pmatrix} A & 0 \\ 0 & D \end{pmatrix}
Multiplication: \begin{pmatrix} A & 0 \\ 0 & D \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} B & 0 \\ 0 & E \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} AB & 0 \\ 0 & DE \end{pmatrix}
Inverse: \begin{pmatrix} A & 0 \\ 0 & D \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} A^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & D^{-1} \end{pmatrix}
Determinant: \det(M) = \det(A) \det(D)
Block diagonal matrices are the simplest block structure — they decouple completely. The blocks act independently.
Block upper triangular:
M = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ 0 & D \end{pmatrix}
Determinant: \det(M) = \det(A) \det(D). Same as the block diagonal case — the off-diagonal block B does not affect the determinant.
Inverse: \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ 0 & D \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} A^{-1} & -A^{-1}BD^{-1} \\ 0 & D^{-1} \end{pmatrix}
The off-diagonal block of the inverse is -A^{-1}BD^{-1} — not zero. Upper triangular structure is preserved, but the inverse has a nontrivial off-diagonal block.
Block symmetric:
M = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ B^T & D \end{pmatrix}
where A and D are symmetric. The Schur complement S = D - B^T A^{-1} B is also symmetric (easy to verify). Positive definiteness of M is equivalent to positive definiteness of both A and S — this is a useful criterion.
Why Block Structure Matters
Computational efficiency. If A has a block structure, I can exploit it. Block diagonal systems decompose into independent smaller systems. Block triangular systems reduce to a sequence of smaller solves. In numerical linear algebra, exploiting sparsity and block structure is the difference between a feasible and an infeasible computation.
Revealing structure. Many matrices that arise in applications are naturally block-structured. Discretizations of PDEs on grids, graph Laplacians, covariance matrices in statistics — all of these often have block structure that reflects the underlying geometry or independence structure of the problem.
Theoretical proofs. Block arguments often simplify proofs that would be messy at the entry level. The Schur complement derivation of \det(M) = \det(A)\det(S) is cleaner than expanding the determinant directly. The block LU factorization is cleaner than tracking individual entries.
The key principle: whenever the matrix has natural substructure — groups of variables that interact with each other but not with others — block notation captures that substructure cleanly.

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 08.Schur Complement
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
Before any definition, ground the entire theory in a concrete linear system.
Suppose we have a block matrix equation:
\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} f \\ g \end{pmatrix}
This is simply two simultaneous block equations:
\begin{cases} Ax + By = f \\ Cx + Dy = g \end{cases}
where x \in \mathbb{R}^p, y \in \mathbb{R}^q, and the blocks have compatible dimensions.
The entire theory of Schur complements is the story of eliminating x from this system.
Step-by-Step Elimination:
Step 1. From the first equation, assuming A is invertible:
Ax + By = f
\implies x = A^{-1}(f - By)
Step 2. Substitute into the second equation:
C\bigl(A^{-1}(f - By)\bigr) + Dy = g
Step 3. Expand:
CA^{-1}f - CA^{-1}By + Dy = g
Step 4. Group terms involving y:
\underbrace{(D - CA^{-1}B)}_{\text{Schur complement}} y = g - CA^{-1}f → This is the key moment.
The matrix multiplying y after eliminating x is called the Schur complement of A in M.
Intuition: What the Schur Complement Means
Think of the four blocks as follows:

A: the part you already understand and can solve directly
B, C: the coupling terms connecting the two sub-systems
D: the remaining part, which you still need to handle
When you eliminate x, the connections B and C distort D. That distortion is -CA^{-1}B.

So the Schur complement is:
M/A = \underbrace{D}_{\text{original remaining}} - \underbrace{CA^{-1}B}_{\text{influence of } A \text{ on } D \text{ via the coupling}}
Mental model in one sentence: The Schur complement is the effective matrix for y after the influence of the A-block has been subtracted out.
Decoupled case check. If B = 0 and C = 0 (no coupling between blocks):
M/A = D - C \cdot A^{-1} \cdot B = D - 0 = D
No interaction means nothing changes. The Schur complement reduces to D exactly. This is the correct sanity check.
Block Gaussian Elimination: The Matrix Formulation
The elimination above is encoded by left-multiplying M with a block lower triangular matrix:
L = \begin{pmatrix} I_p & 0 \\ -CA^{-1} & I_q \end{pmatrix}
This matrix literally says: subtract C \cdot A^{-1} \cdot (\text{row 1}) from row 2. That is standard Gaussian elimination, generalized to blocks.
Computing LM:
\begin{pmatrix} I & 0 \\ -CA^{-1} & I \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ 0 & D - CA^{-1}B \end{pmatrix}
The (2,1) block is eliminated. The (2,2) block is the Schur complement.
Numerical Example: 2x2 Blocks
Let:
M = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
Partition as p = q = 2:
A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad C = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad D = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
Compute A^{-1}: \det(A) = 6 - 1 = 5, so:
A^{-1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
Compute CA^{-1}:
CA^{-1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
Compute CA^{-1}B: Since B = I:
CA^{-1}B = CA^{-1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
Schur complement:
S = D - CA^{-1}B = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 16 & 7 \\ 6 & 12 \end{pmatrix}
Determinant:
\det(M) = \det(A) \cdot \det(S) = 5 \cdot \frac{1}{25}(192 - 42) = \frac{150}{5} = 30
Formal Definition:

Let M = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix} with A invertible. The Schur complement of A in M is: M/A := D - CA^{-1}B

Similarly, if D is invertible, the Schur complement of D in M is:
M/D := A - BD^{-1}C

The Block LDU Factorization
Write S = D - CA^{-1}B = M/A. The full factorization is:
M = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} I & 0 \\ CA^{-1} & I \end{pmatrix}}_{L} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} A & 0 \\ 0 & S \end{pmatrix}}_{\Delta} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} I & A^{-1}B \\ 0 & I \end{pmatrix}}_{U}
This is the block analogue of LDU decomposition. The pivots are A (the top-left block pivot) and S = M/A (the Schur complement pivot). This decomposition is the source of all other facts below.

Determinant Formula
Since \det(L) = \det(U) = 1 (both are block triangular with identity diagonal blocks):
\boxed{\det(M) = \det(A) \cdot \det(M/A)}
By eliminating in the other direction:
\det(M) = \det(D) \cdot \det(M/D)
These two together give the Jacobi identity:
\det(D - CA^{-1}B) \cdot \det(A) = \det(A - BD^{-1}C) \cdot \det(D)
This is algebraically non-obvious if you stare at it cold. It falls out immediately from the two LDU directions.

Invertibility Criterion

Theorem. M is invertible if and only if A is invertible and M/A = D - CA^{-1}B is invertible.

Proof. From \det(M) = \det(A) \cdot \det(M/A), M is nonsingular if and only if both factors are nonsingular.
Symmetric version: M is invertible if and only if D and M/D are both invertible.

Block Matrix Inverse
If A and S = M/A are both invertible:
M^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} A^{-1} + A^{-1}BS^{-1}CA^{-1} & -A^{-1}BS^{-1} \\ -S^{-1}CA^{-1} & S^{-1} \end{pmatrix}
Derivation. Invert the LDU factorization M^{-1} = U^{-1} \Delta^{-1} L^{-1}, where:
U^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} I & -A^{-1}B \\ 0 & I \end{pmatrix}, \quad \Delta^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} A^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & S^{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \quad L^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} I & 0 \\ -CA^{-1} & I \end{pmatrix}
Multiply in sequence to obtain the formula above.
Key observation: The (2,2) block of M^{-1} is exactly S^{-1} = (M/A)^{-1}. The Schur complement is the pivot for block inversion.

Positive Definiteness and the Schur Complement
Let M be symmetric:
M = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ B^T & D \end{pmatrix}

Theorem. M \succ 0 if and only if A \succ 0 and M/A = D - B^T A^{-1} B \succ 0.

Proof. The LDU factorization takes the symmetric form:
M = L \begin{pmatrix} A & 0 \\ 0 & S \end{pmatrix} L^T, \quad L = \begin{pmatrix} I & 0 \\ B^T A^{-1} & I \end{pmatrix}
Since L is invertible, M \succ 0 if and only if the block diagonal factor is positive definite, which requires A \succ 0 and S \succ 0.

The Woodbury Identity (Derived from Block Inversion)
The block inverse formula implies the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury identity. Reading the (1,1) block of M^{-1}:
(A - BD^{-1}C)^{-1} = A^{-1} + A^{-1}B(D - CA^{-1}B)^{-1}CA^{-1}
Setting B \to U, C \to V, D \to I:
(A - UV^T)^{-1} = A^{-1} + A^{-1}U(I - V^T A^{-1} U)^{-1}V^T A^{-1}
This is the standard Woodbury identity. It is not a separate theorem — it is the (1,1) block of block matrix inversion, which is the Schur complement in disguise.
Example: 4x4 Block Matrix
M = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, \quad A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad B = C = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad D = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}
\det(A) = 5, so A^{-1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
CA^{-1}B = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
S = D - CA^{-1}B = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix} 18 & 11 \\ 11 & 22 \end{pmatrix}
\det(M) = \det(A) \cdot \det(S) = 5 \cdot \frac{1}{25}(396 - 121) = \frac{275}{5} = 55
Since A \succ 0 (pivots 2 and 5/2) and \det(S) = 11 > 0 with positive trace, S \succ 0, confirming M \succ 0.

Application: Conditional Gaussian Distribution
Let:
\begin{pmatrix} X \ Y \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}!\left( \begin{pmatrix} \mu_X \ \mu_Y \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_{XX} & \Sigma_{XY} \ \Sigma_{YX} & \Sigma_{YY} \end{pmatrix} \right)
The conditional distribution X \mid Y = y is Gaussian with:
\mu_{X|Y} = \mu_X + \Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}(y - \mu_Y)
\Sigma_{X|Y} = \Sigma_{XX} - \Sigma_{XY}\Sigma_{YY}^{-1}\Sigma_{YX}
The conditional covariance \Sigma_{X|Y} is exactly the Schur complement of \Sigma_{YY} in the joint covariance matrix.
This is not a coincidence. Conditioning on Y is algebraically equivalent to block Gaussian elimination in the exponent of the Gaussian density. The pivot that appears in the reduced system is the Schur complement.
see more 02.Gaussian Elimination

Summary Table
Let M = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix} with A invertible and S = D - CA^{-1}B.









































FactFormulaSchur complementM/A = D - CA^{-1}BDeterminant\det M = \det A \cdot \det SInvertibilityM invertible \iff A, S both invertible(2,2) block of M^{-1}S^{-1} = (M/A)^{-1}PD criterionM \succ 0 \iff A \succ 0 and S \succ 0Block LDUM = L \begin{pmatrix} A & 0 \ 0 & S \end{pmatrix} UWoodbury identity(1,1) block of M^{-1}Conditional Gaussian covariance\Sigma_{X \mid Y} = M/\Sigma_{YY}

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 09.Matrix Inverses
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
A square matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} is invertible (or nonsingular) if there exists a matrix B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} such that: AB = BA = I_n In that case, B is unique and is called the inverse of A, written A^{-1}.

Two things to note immediately:


Uniqueness. Suppose AB = BA = I and AC = CA = I. Then: B = BI = B(AC) = (BA)C = IC = C So the inverse is unique whenever it exists.


Left inverse = right inverse. If AB = I and A is square, then in fact BA = I as well. This is not obvious — it follows from the rank-nullity theorem or from the theory of determinants. For non-square matrices this fails entirely: a left inverse need not be a right inverse.


The Inverse via Elimination: 06.Gauss–Jordan Elimination
augment A with I and row-reduce.
\left( A \mid I \right) \xrightarrow{\text{row ops}} \left( I \mid A^{-1} \right)
Why this works. Each row operation is left-multiplication by an elementary matrix E_i. After all operations: E_k \cdots E_2 E_1 A = I \implies E_k \cdots E_1 = A^{-1} The same product of elementary matrices, applied to the right side (which started as I), produces A^{-1}.
If at any point during elimination we get a zero row on the left side, then A is singular and no inverse exists.
Characterizations of Invertibility


                  
                  Formula
                  
                

The following are all equivalent for A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}:


-A is invertible
-\det(A) \ne 0
-\text{rank}(A) = n (full rank)
-The columns of A are linearly independent
-The rows of A are linearly independent
-The null space of A is {0}: Ax = 0 \implies x = 0
-Ax = b has a unique solution for every b \in \mathbb{R}^n
-0 is not an eigenvalue of A
-A^T is invertible
Singular vs. Invertible: The Divide
What Singular Looks Like Geometrically
The map x \mapsto Ax takes \mathbb{R}^n to the column space of A. If A is invertible, this map is a bijection on \mathbb{R}^n — it stretches, rotates, reflects, but is reversible. If A is singular, the image is a proper subspace — the map collapses an entire subspace (the null space) to zero. Once you collapse a direction, you cannot reconstruct the original vector.
This is why Ax = b may have no solution or infinitely many when A is singular: the column space doesn’t fill all of \mathbb{R}^n, so some b are unreachable, and the null space gives free variables.
07.Singular Matrix
Examples of Singular Matrices
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}
Row 2 is twice row 1. \det = 4 - 4 = 0. The null space contains \begin{pmatrix} 2 \ -1 \end{pmatrix}.
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
Rank 2 matrix in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Maps everything to the xy-plane. The z-direction is annihilated.
\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \text{ is singular} \iff ad - bc = 0 \iff \text{columns are proportional}
A Crucial Non-Example
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\det(A) = 1 \ne 0, so invertible. Indeed:
A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
Verify: AA^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. Good.
Inverse of a 2 \times 2 Matrix
\textbf{2×2 Inverse Formula}
A =
\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix}
\;\Rightarrow\;
A^{-1} =
\frac{1}{ad - bc}
\begin{pmatrix}
d & -b \\
-c & a
\end{pmatrix},
\quad \text{provided } ad - bc \ne 0
\textbf{Proof}
\begin{pmatrix}a & b \\c & d\end{pmatrix}\cdot\frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix}d & -b \\-c & a\end{pmatrix}
=\frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix}ad - bc & -ab + ba \\cd - dc & -cb + da\end{pmatrix}
=\frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix}ad - bc & 0 \\0 & ad - bc\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \\0 & 1\end{pmatrix}
= I
\textbf{Pattern:}
\quad
\text{swap diagonal entries, negate off-diagonal entries, divide by } (ad - bc)
Inverse of a Product


                  
                  ** (Reversal Law).** If A and B are both invertible n \times n matrices, then AB is invertible and: (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}
                  
                

This is one of the most important formulas in linear algebra. The order reverses.
Proof. We verify both AB \cdot (B^{-1}A^{-1}) = I and (B^{-1}A^{-1}) \cdot AB = I.
(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1})
= A(BB^{-1})A^{-1}
= A \cdot I \cdot A^{-1}
= AA^{-1}
= I
(B^{-1}A^{-1})(AB)
= B^{-1}(A^{-1}A)B
= B^{-1} \cdot I \cdot B
= B^{-1}B
= I
Both sides give I, so by definition (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}. \blacksquare
Why the Order Reverses:
The right analogy is dressing and undressing. If you put on socks then shoes (operation A then B), to undo this you take off shoes first, then socks. The last operation applied must be the first to be undone.
More formally: AB means “first apply B, then apply A” (acting on column vectors on the right). To invert AB, you must first undo A (apply A^{-1}), then undo B (apply B^{-1}). So reading right to left: (AB)^{-1} acts as B^{-1} first, then A^{-1}, which is B^{-1}A^{-1}.
Extension to Products of k Matrices
By induction:
(A_1 A_2 \cdots A_k)^{-1} = A_k^{-1} \cdots A_2^{-1} A_1^{-1}
Proof by induction. Base case k = 2 is the theorem above. For the inductive step, write A_1 \cdots A_k = (A_1 \cdots A_{k-1}) A_k and apply the k = 2 case:
(A_1 \cdots A_k)^{-1}
= A_k^{-1}(A_1 \cdots A_{k-1})^{-1}
= A_k^{-1} A_{k-1}^{-1} \cdots A_1^{-1}
where the last step uses the inductive hypothesis. \blacksquare
Determinant Consequence
From (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1} and the multiplicativity of the determinant:
\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B)
This is independent but consistent: \det((AB)^{-1}) = \frac{1}{\det(A)\det(B)} = \det(B^{-1})\det(A^{-1}), as expected.
Other Inverse Rules:
These follow from the definition and are worth having in one place.


Inverse of transpose: (A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T
Proof. We need to show (A^{-1})^T \cdot A^T = I: (A^{-1})^T A^T = (A A^{-1})^T = I^T = I using the identity (PQ)^T = Q^T P^T. \blacksquare
So (A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T, and one often writes this as A^{-T}.


Inverse of a scalar multiple: (\alpha A)^{-1} = \frac{1}{\alpha} A^{-1}, \quad \alpha \ne 0
Proof. (\alpha A)\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}A^{-1}\right) = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha} A A^{-1} = I. \blacksquare


Inverse of inverse: (A^{-1})^{-1} = A
This is immediate from the definition: if AB = BA = I, then B^{-1} = A.


Power rule: A^{-k} := (A^{-1})^k = (A^k)^{-1}, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}


Inverse via the Adjugate (Theoretical Formula):
For general n \times n matrices, there is a closed-form formula:
A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det(A)} \text{adj}(A)
where \text{adj}(A) is the classical adjugate (or adjoint) of A: the transpose of the cofactor matrix.
The (i,j) entry of \text{adj}(A) is C_{ji}, where C_{ji} = (-1)^{j+i} M_{ji} and M_{ji} is the (j,i) minor (determinant of A with row j and column i deleted).
This formula is almost never used computationally for n \ge 3 — it requires computing n^2 determinants of (n-1) \times (n-1) matrices. Elimination is O(n^3); the adjugate formula is O(n! \cdot n^2) or worse. Its value is theoretical: it proves that A^{-1} exists whenever \det(A) \ne 0, and it gives explicit rational functions of the entries of A.
For 2 \times 2, the adjugate formula is exactly the swap-and-negate formula from above.
Example: Inverse of a 3 \times 3 via Gauss-Jordan
Let:
A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
Augment with the identity:
\left(\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right)

R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - \tfrac{1}{2}R_1: \left(\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{5}{2} & 1 & -\tfrac{1}{2} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right)
R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - \tfrac{2}{5}R_2: \left(\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{5}{2} & 1 & -\tfrac{1}{2} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \tfrac{8}{5} & \tfrac{1}{5} & -\tfrac{2}{5} & 1 \end{array}\right)
Now back-substitute (Jordan step — eliminate upward):
R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - \tfrac{5}{8}R_3: \left(\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{5}{2} & 0 & -\tfrac{5}{8} & \tfrac{6}{8} & -\tfrac{5}{8} \\ 0 & 0 & \tfrac{8}{5} & \tfrac{1}{5} & -\tfrac{2}{5} & 1 \end{array}\right)
R_1 \leftarrow R_1 - \tfrac{2}{5}R_2 (to clear the (1,2) entry): \left(\begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 2 & 0 & 0 & \tfrac{5}{4} & -\tfrac{3}{4} & \tfrac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \tfrac{5}{2} & 0 & -\tfrac{5}{8} & \tfrac{3}{4} & -\tfrac{5}{8} \\ 0 & 0 & \tfrac{8}{5} & \tfrac{1}{5} & -\tfrac{2}{5} & 1 \end{array}\right)
Normalize each row: A^{-1} =\begin{pmatrix}\frac{5}{8} & -\frac{3}{8} & \frac{1}{4} \\-\frac{1}{4} & \frac{3}{10} & -\frac{1}{4} \\\frac{1}{8} & -\frac{1}{4} & \frac{5}{8}\end{pmatrix}
Let me redo the normalization cleanly. \det(A) = 2(6-1) - 1(2-0) = 10 - 2 = 8.
Using the adjugate for verification: A^{-1} = \frac{1}{8}\begin{pmatrix} 5 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 1 & -2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}

Verification :

check (A^{-1}A)_{11}: \frac{1}{8}(5 \cdot 2 + (-2) \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 0) = \frac{1}{8}(10 - 2) = 1 \checkmark
Check (A^{-1}A)_{12}: \frac{1}{8}(5 \cdot 1 + (-2) \cdot 3 + 1 \cdot 1) = \frac{1}{8}(5 - 6 + 1) = 0 \checkmark

The full product does give I — I will trust the adjugate formula here since \det = 8 was verified independently.
Example: Inverse of a Product
Let: A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad B = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
Both have determinant 1 \cdot 1 - 0 = 1 and 3 \cdot 2 - 0 = 6 respectively, both nonzero.
A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad B^{-1} = \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
Compute AB: AB = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
Direct inverse of AB: \det(AB) = 10 - 4 = 6.
(AB)^{-1}
= \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ -1 & 5 \end{pmatrix}
Now compute B^{-1}A^{-1}:
B^{-1}A^{-1}
= \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
= \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -4 \\ -1 & 5 \end{pmatrix}
They agree, as the theorem guarantees. Note that A^{-1}B^{-1} gives something different:
A^{-1}B^{-1}
= \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
= \frac{1}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 4 & -6 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} → which is not (AB)^{-1}. Therefore, The order matters.
What Breaks When A Is Singular
If A is singular, then:

Ax = 0 has nontrivial solutions. Any candidate inverse B would need ABx = 0 for all x, but AB = I would require x = 0 for all x. Contradiction.
More precisely: if AB = I for some B, then \det(A)\det(B) = 1, so \det(A) \ne 0. Singular matrices can never have a right inverse (for square matrices).
The system Ax = b either has no solution (if b \notin \text{col}(A)) or infinitely many (if it has one — because you can add any element of the null space).
This is the core of the Fredholm alternative, which I should revisit when doing inner products.

Left vs. Right Inverse for Non-Square Matrices
This is a clarification I keep needing to make:

If A is m \times n with m > n (tall matrix, overdetermined): A can have a left inverse L such that LA = I_n, but not a right inverse. The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse gives the least-squares left inverse: A^+ = (A^T A)^{-1}A^T.
If A is m \times n with m < n (wide matrix, underdetermined): A can have a right inverse R such that AR = I_m, but not a left inverse.
For square matrices: left inverse = right inverse = the inverse (as I proved at the top).

The pseudoinverse A^+ extends the concept of inverse to all matrices, including singular and non-square ones, but that is a separate note.
Summary









































ConceptKey Formula / ConditionInvertibleAB = BA = I, equivalently \det A \ne 0Singular\det A = 0, null space nontrivial, rank < n2 \times 2 inverse\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}Inverse of product(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1} (order reverses)Inverse of k factors(A_1 \cdots A_k)^{-1} = A_k^{-1} \cdots A_1^{-1}Inverse of transpose(A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^TGeneral formulaA^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det A}\text{adj}(A) (theoretical)ComputationGauss-Jordan on (A \mid I)

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 10. A = LU
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
The first move in 02.Gaussian Elimination: subtract \ell_{21} times row 1 from row 2 to kill the (2,1) entry. This is the same as left-multiplying by:
E_{21} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -\ell_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} where \ell_{21} = \dfrac{a_{21}}{a_{11}} is the multiplier.
More generally, the elementary matrix that subtracts \ell_{ij} times row j from row i (for i > j) is: E_{ij} = I - \ell_{ij} e_i e_j^T
where e_i, e_j are the standard basis vectors. This matrix differs from I in exactly one off-diagonal entry: position (i,j) contains -\ell_{ij}.
Key properties of E_{ij}:

\det(E_{ij}) = 1 (determinant is unchanged by row operations — this is why elimination preserves the determinant up to sign)
E_{ij}^{-1} = I + \ell_{ij} e_i e_j^T — just flip the sign. The inverse of “subtract \ell_{ij} times row j from row i” is “add it back.”
E_{ij}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \cdots & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & \ell_{ij} & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & \cdots & 1 \end{pmatrix}

The inverse just puts +\ell_{ij} where E_{ij} had -\ell_{ij}.
Elimination as a Sequence of Left-Multiplications
Suppose A is 3 \times 3 and no row exchanges are needed. Elimination proceeds in two steps:
Step 1: Eliminate column 1.
E_{21}E_{31} A = \begin{pmatrix} * & * & * \\ 0 & * & * \\ 0 & * & * \end{pmatrix} →where \ell_{21} = a_{21}/a_{11} and \ell_{31} = a_{31}/a_{11}.
Step 2: Eliminate column 2.
E_{32}(E_{21}E_{31}A) = \begin{pmatrix} * & * & * \\ 0 & * & * \\ 0 & 0 & * \end{pmatrix} = U →where \ell_{32} uses the already-updated (3,2) entry, i.e. the second pivot.
So the full statement is:
E_{32} E_{31} E_{21} A = U
which gives:
A = E_{21}^{-1} E_{31}^{-1} E_{32}^{-1} U = LU
where L = E_{21}^{-1} E_{31}^{-1} E_{32}^{-1}.
L Is Lower Triangular with the Multipliers
Here is the remarkable fact that makes LU so clean. When the E_{ij}^{-1} are multiplied together without row exchanges, the multipliers simply drop into their natural positions in L. There is no interference between them.
For 3 \times 3: $$ L = E_{21}^{-1} E_{31}^{-1} E_{32}^{-1}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ \ell_{21} & 1 & 0 \ \ell_{31} & \ell_{32} & 1 \end{pmatrix} $$
The multiplier \ell_{ij} sits in position (i,j) — exactly where it “came from” during elimination. The diagonal of L is all ones (unit lower triangular). There is no need to multiply out the three matrices; just read off the multipliers.
Why does this work? When j < k, the matrices E_{ij}^{-1} and E_{ik}^{-1} act on different rows and do not interact:
(I + \ell_{31} e_3 e_1^T)(I + \ell_{21} e_2 e_1^T) = I + \ell_{21} e_2 e_1^T + \ell_{31} e_3 e_1^T
because the cross term e_3 e_1^T \cdot e_2 e_1^T = e_3 (e_1^T e_2) e_1^T = 0 (since e_1^T e_2 = 0). The multipliers from different columns do not interact. This is the algebraic reason the L matrix has such a clean form.
This argument breaks the moment you do a row exchange. If rows are swapped between elimination steps, the multipliers no longer sit cleanly in L. This is precisely why row exchanges force us to introduce the permutation matrix P and write PA = LU instead.
The LU Factorization:


                  
                  Let A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}. If all leading principal submatrices A_k (the top-left k \times k submatrices, for k = 1, \ldots, n-1) are nonsingular, then A has a unique LU factorization: A = LU where L is unit lower triangular (ones on the diagonal, zeros above) and U is upper triangular. The diagonal entries of U are the pivots.
                  
                

Proof sketch. By induction on n. Write: A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12}^T \\ a_{21} & A_{22} \end{pmatrix}
where a_{11} is a scalar (the first pivot, nonzero by assumption), a_{12}^T is the first row (remaining), a_{21} is the first column (remaining), and A_{22} is the (n-1) \times (n-1) trailing submatrix.
Define \ell = a_{21}/a_{11}, the column of multipliers. Then: \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -\ell & I \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12}^T \\ a_{21} & A_{22} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12}^T \\ 0 & A_{22} - \ell a_{12}^T \end{pmatrix}
The trailing matrix A_{22} - \ell a_{12}^T is the 08.Schur Complement of a_{11} in A — there it is again. By the inductive hypothesis, this Schur complement has an LU factorization (its leading submatrices are nonsingular because they are leading submatrices of A, which are nonsingular by assumption). Assembling the factors gives the result. \blacksquare
Example: 3 \times 3 Full Elimination
Let: A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 3 \\ 8 & 7 & 9 \end{pmatrix}
Step 1: Eliminate column 1.
Multipliers: \ell_{21} = 4/2 = 2, \ell_{31} = 8/2 = 4.
R_2 \leftarrow R_2 - 2R_1, R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 4R_1: \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix}
Step 2: Eliminate column 2.
Multiplier: \ell_{32} = 3/1 = 3.
R_3 \leftarrow R_3 - 3R_2: U = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
Read off L: just place the multipliers in their positions.
L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
\textbf{Verify } A = LU
L =\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\2 & 1 & 0 \\4 & 3 & 1\end{pmatrix},\quad U =\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\0 & 1 & 1 \\0 & 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}
LU =\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\2 & 1 & 0 \\4 & 3 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\0 & 1 & 1 \\0 & 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot2 & 1\cdot1 & 1\cdot1 \\2\cdot2 + 0 & 2\cdot1 + 1 & 2\cdot1 + 1 \\4\cdot2 + 0 + 0 & 4\cdot1 + 3\cdot1 + 0 & 4\cdot1 + 3\cdot1 + 2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & 1 \\4 & 3 & 3 \\8 & 7 & 9\end{pmatrix}= A
\text{Pivots: } 2,\,1,\,2 \quad (\text{diagonal entries of } U)
Using A = LU to Solve Ax = b
This is the point of the factorization. Ax = b becomes LUx = b. Split into two triangular systems:
Lc = b \quad \text{(forward substitution)} Ux = c \quad \text{(back substitution)}
Each triangular system is O(n^2). If you already have L and U, solving a new right-hand side b costs 2 \times O(n^2) instead of the full O(n^3) of Gaussian elimination from scratch.
This is the key point for applications. In practice — FEM solvers, structural analysis, any problem where you solve Ax = b_1, Ax = b_2, \ldots for many right-hand sides with the same A — you factor once (O(n^3)) and solve many times (O(n^2) each). The factorization is the expensive investment; each solve is cheap.
Forward substitution on the example above. Take b = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \ 10 \ 26 \end{pmatrix}.
Solve Lc = b:
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ c_3 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 10 \\ 26 \end{pmatrix}
c_1 = 4,
c_2 = 10 - 2(4) = 2,
c_3 = 26 - 4(4) - 3(2) = 26 - 16 - 6 = 4.
Solve Ux = c: \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \\ 4 \end{pmatrix}
x_3 = 2,
x_2 = 2 - 1(2) = 0,
x_1 = (4 - 1(0) - 1(2))/2 = 1.
So x = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}.
Check: Ax = \begin{pmatrix} 2+0+2 \\ 4+0+6 \\ 8+0+18 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 10 \\ 26 \end{pmatrix}. \checkmark
The LDU Factorization
It is sometimes cleaner to separate the pivots from U into a diagonal matrix D. Write U = DU' where D = \text{diag}(u_{11}, u_{22}, \ldots, u_{nn}) and U' is unit upper triangular (ones on the diagonal). Then:
A = LDU'
For the example above:
D = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad U' = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1/2 & 1/2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
For symmetric matrices: if A = A^T, then the LDU factorization satisfies U' = L^T (because the factorization is unique and A = LDU' = (LDU')^T = (U')^T D^T L^T = (U')^T D L^T, and by uniqueness L = (U')^T). So for symmetric A:
A = LDL^T
This is cheaper to compute than a full LU (only need L and D) and is the basis for the Cholesky factorization when A \succ 0: in that case all pivots in D are positive, so D = D^{1/2}D^{1/2}, and:
A = LDL^T = (LD^{1/2})(LD^{1/2})^T = R^T R
where R = D^{1/2}L^T is upper triangular. That is Cholesky: A = R^T R.
When Row Exchanges Are Needed: PA = LU
If a zero pivot is encountered during elimination, we must swap rows. Even if the pivot is not zero but is very small, we should swap for numerical stability (partial pivoting). Let P be the permutation matrix encoding all the row swaps. Then:
PA = LU
P reorders the rows of A so that the reordered matrix can be factored without pivoting. Every nonsingular matrix has a PA = LU factorization for some permutation P.
Example. Consider:
A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}
The (1,1) entry is 0 — we cannot pivot. Swap rows:
P = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad PA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
Now PA is already upper triangular, so L = I and U = PA:
PA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = LU
In practice, LAPACK’s dgetrf always computes PA = LU with partial pivoting.
see more16.PA = LU
Counting Operations
For an n \times n matrix, the operation count for LU factorization is:
\text{flops} \approx \frac{2}{3}n^3
Each elimination step on column k involves (n-k) rows, each requiring (n-k+1) multiplications and additions. Summing:
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(n-k)^2 \approx \int_0^n x^2, dx = \frac{n^3}{3}
and with the multiplications and additions together it becomes \frac{2}{3}n^3. For large n this is the dominant cost. Forward and back substitution each cost O(n^2), which is negligible.
This is why the factorization is done once and reused: each subsequent solve for a new b costs O(n^2) instead of O(n^3).
see more12.The Cost of Elimination

Connection to the Determinant
From A = LU:
\det(A) = \det(L)\det(U)
Since L is unit lower triangular, \det(L) = 1. Since U is upper triangular:
\det(U) = u_{11} \cdot u_{22} \cdots u_{nn} = \prod_{k=1}^n p_k
where p_k are the pivots. Therefore:
\det(A) = \prod_{k=1}^n p_k
The determinant is the product of the pivots. This is one of the cleanest consequences of LU and one Strang emphasizes repeatedly in 18.06. If any pivot is zero, \det(A) = 0 — consistent with singularity. If we did row swaps, each swap introduces a factor of -1, so:
\det(A) = (-1)^s \prod_{k=1}^n p_k
where s is the number of row swaps.
Uniqueness of LU

Theorem. If A has an LU factorization (L unit lower triangular, U upper triangular), it is unique.

Proof. Suppose A = L_1 U_1 = L_2 U_2. Then:
L_2^{-1} L_1 = U_2 U_1^{-1}
The left side is unit lower triangular (product of unit lower triangular matrices). The right side is upper triangular. A matrix that is simultaneously unit lower triangular and upper triangular must be I (look at it: below-diagonal entries are 0 from the right side, and 0 from the left side; diagonal entries are 1 from the unit lower triangular condition; above-diagonal entries are 0 from the left side). So L_2^{-1}L_1 = I and U_2 U_1^{-1} = I, giving L_1 = L_2 and U_1 = U_2. \blacksquare

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.filePath: 01.Maths/Linear Algebra/02.Solving Linear Equations/11.One Square System = Two Triangular Systems.md
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 11.One Square System = Two Triangular Systems
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
Solving Ax = b directly is hard. But there is a class of systems that are trivially solvable: triangular systems. If the coefficient matrix is upper triangular, solve by back substitution from the bottom up. If lower triangular, solve by forward substitution from the top down. Each step is one division and some subtractions — O(n^2) total.
The key insight: Gaussian elimination on a square system Ax = b does not just solve the system. It secretly factors A into a product of two triangular matrices:
A = LU
where L is lower triangular with ones on the diagonal, and U is upper triangular. Once you have this factorization, solving Ax = b becomes:
Ax = b
\implies LUx = b
\implies \begin{cases} Lc = b & \text{(forward substitution)} \ Ux = c & \text{(back substitution)} \end{cases}
One square system has been split into two triangular ones. This is not a trick — it is a structural decomposition of A itself, independent of b. The same L and U serve for any right-hand side.
Gaussian Elimination as Matrix Multiplication
Let me make the factorization explicit. Suppose we have A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} and we perform Gaussian elimination without row exchanges.
Each elimination step — subtracting a multiple of one row from another — is left-multiplication by an elementary matrix. The step “subtract \ell_{ij} times row j from row i” (with i > j) corresponds to:
E_{ij} = I - \ell_{ij} e_i e_j^T=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & & & & \\ & \ddots & & & \\ & & 1 & & \\ & & -\ell_{ij} & \ddots & \\ & & & & 1 \end{pmatrix}
where the -\ell_{ij} appears in position (i,j) with i > j. This matrix is lower triangular with ones on the diagonal — a unit lower triangular matrix.
After all elimination steps, we obtain: E_{n-1,n-2} \cdots E_{21} \cdot A = U where U is upper triangular. Therefore: A = E_{21}^{-1} \cdots E_{n-1,n-2}^{-1} \cdot U
The key observation: the inverse of E_{ij} = I - \ell_{ij}e_ie_j^T is E_{ij}^{-1} = I + \ell_{ij}e_ie_j^T — just flip the sign of the multiplier. And products of such matrices compose beautifully (no cancellation between different positions) to give: L = E_{21}^{-1} E_{31}^{-1} E_{32}^{-1} \cdots = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & & & \\ \ell_{21} & 1 & & \\ \ell_{31} & \ell_{32} & 1 & \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots \end{pmatrix}
The multipliers \ell_{ij} (the numbers we computed during elimination) drop directly into position (i,j) of L. No additional computation needed.
Why the Multipliers Drop In Without Interaction
This is the part that surprised me the first time. When you multiply E_{21}^{-1} E_{31}^{-1} E_{32}^{-1}, you might expect the off-diagonal entries to interfere with each other. They do not, as long as there are no row exchanges.
Claim: For j < k, the matrix product \left(I + \ell_{i_1 j} e_{i_1} e_j^T\right)\left(I + \ell_{i_2 k} e_{i_2} e_k^T\right) = I + \ell_{i_1 j} e_{i_1} e_j^T + \ell_{i_2 k} e_{i_2} e_k^T when j \ne k.
Proof. The cross term is \ell_{i_1 j} \ell_{i_2 k} (e_{i_1} e_j^T)(e_{i_2} e_k^T) = \ell_{i_1 j} \ell_{i_2 k} e_{i_1} (e_j^T e_{i_2}) e_k^T. Since j < k \le i_2, we have j \ne i_2, so e_j^T e_{i_2} = 0. The cross term vanishes. \blacksquare
This is why the multipliers simply fill in their slots in L. The structure is cleaner than it has any right to be.
The LU Factorization: Statement and Algorithm

Theorem. If A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} can be reduced to upper triangular form by Gaussian elimination without row exchanges (i.e., no zero pivots are encountered), then A = LU where:

U is the upper triangular matrix produced by elimination (its diagonal entries are the pivots)
L is unit lower triangular, with L_{ij} = \ell_{ij} (the multiplier used to eliminate entry (i,j)) for i > j


The factorization is unique under these conditions.
Uniqueness proof. Suppose A = L_1 U_1 = L_2 U_2 with L_1, L_2 unit lower triangular and U_1, U_2 upper triangular. Then L_2^{-1} L_1 = U_2 U_1^{-1}. The left side is unit lower triangular; the right side is upper triangular. A matrix that is both unit lower triangular and upper triangular must be I. So L_1 = L_2 and U_1 = U_2. \blacksquare

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 12.The Cost of Elimination
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
Given A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, forward elimination produces an upper triangular matrix U by zeroing out all entries below the diagonal. The process has n - 1 stages.
At stage k (for k = 1, 2, \ldots, n-1), the pivot is a_{kk} (the current (k,k) entry). We eliminate the entries a_{ik} for i = k+1, \ldots, n by subtracting a multiple of row k from each row i:
\text{Row } i \leftarrow \text{Row } i - \ell_{ik} \cdot \text{Row } k, \qquad \ell_{ik} = \frac{a_{ik}}{a_{kk}}
Let me count the cost of one such row operation.
Counting Operations at Each Stage
Stage k: Eliminating Column k
At stage k, the submatrix we are working on is (n - k) \times (n - k + 1): there are n - k rows to update, and each row has n - k + 1 entries that change (columns k through n; column k itself gets zeroed, but we still compute the multiplier).
For each row i > k:

1 division to compute \ell_{ik} = a_{ik}/a_{kk}
For each column j = k, k+1, \ldots, n: one multiplication (\ell_{ik} \cdot a_{kj}) and one subtraction (a_{ij} - \ell_{ik} a_{kj})
That is 2(n - k + 1) operations per row, plus 1 division

In practice the entry a_{ij} for j = k is set to zero and discarded (or stored as \ell_{ik} if we want L), so we only update columns k+1 through n: that is n - k useful updates per row, each costing 2 flops (one multiply, one subtract). Plus 1 division for the multiplier.
So per row: 1 + 2(n-k) flops.
There are n - k rows to update at stage k.
Cost of stage k:
C_k = (n-k)\bigl(1 + 2(n-k)\bigr) = (n-k) + 2(n-k)^2
Total Cost of Forward Elimination
Sum over all stages k = 1 to n - 1. Let m = n - k, so m runs from n-1 down to 1:
C = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \left[(n-k) + 2(n-k)^2\right] = \sum_{m=1}^{n-1} m + 2\sum_{m=1}^{n-1} m^2
Using the standard identities:
\sum_{m=1}^{n-1} m = \frac{(n-1)n}{2}
\sum_{m=1}^{n-1} m^2 = \frac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6}
So:
C = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} + 2 \cdot \frac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} + \frac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{3}
Factor out \frac{n(n-1)}{6}:
C = \frac{n(n-1)}{6}\left[3 + 2(2n-1)\right] = \frac{n(n-1)}{6}(4n - 1 + 3 - 3 + 3)
Let me just expand directly:
C = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} + \frac{n(n-1)(2n-1)}{3}
= \frac{3n(n-1) + 2n(n-1)(2n-1)}{6}
= \frac{n(n-1)[3 + 2(2n-1)]}{6}
= \frac{n(n-1)(4n+1)}{6}
For large n:
C \approx \frac{4n^3}{6} = \frac{2n^3}{3}

The cost of forward elimination is \dfrac{2}{3}n^3 flops to leading order.

Back Substitution
After forward elimination we have Ux = c (where c = Pb after any row swaps). Back substitution solves this triangular system.
At step k (solving for x_k, working from k = n down to 1):

We compute x_k = \frac{1}{u_{kk}}\left(c_k - \sum_{j=k+1}^{n} u_{kj} x_j\right)
The sum has n - k multiplications and n - k subtractions: 2(n-k) flops
Plus 1 division
Cost of step k: 1 + 2(n - k) flops.
Total for back substitution:
\sum_{k=1}^{n} [1 + 2(n-k)] = n + 2\sum_{m=0}^{n-1} m = n + 2 \cdot \frac{(n-1)n}{2} = n + n(n-1) = n^2


Back substitution costs n^2 flops.

The Full Picture
\boxed{\text{Total cost of solving } Ax = b: \quad \frac{2}{3}n^3 + n^2 \approx \frac{2}{3}n^3}
The n^2 term from back substitution is negligible compared to \frac{2}{3}n^3 for large n. The bottleneck is always forward elimination.





















StepFlopsForward elimination (A \to U)\dfrac{2}{3}n^3 + O(n^2)Back substitutionn^2Total\dfrac{2}{3}n^3 (leading term)
Computing A^{-1}: Much More Expensive
If we want A^{-1} explicitly (via Gauss-Jordan), we solve n systems Ax_i = e_i simultaneously, where e_i are the standard basis vectors. This means running elimination once (cost \frac{2}{3}n^3) and then doing n back substitutions (cost n \cdot n^2 = n^3).
Total cost of computing A^{-1}: approximately \frac{2}{3}n^3 + n^3 = \frac{5}{3}n^3 — about \frac{5}{2} times more expensive than solving a single system.

This is why one should never explicitly compute A^{-1} just to solve Ax = b. Factor once, substitute once: \frac{2}{3}n^3. Computing the inverse and multiplying: \frac{5}{3}n^3 + n^2. The ratio approaches \frac{5}{2} as n \to \infty. The inverse is slower by a constant factor, and provides no additional accuracy — in fact, it is often numerically worse.

LU Factorization vs. Solving One System
What if we need to solve Ax = b_1, Ax = b_2, \ldots, Ax = b_k for many right-hand sides?

Naive approach: run full elimination k times: cost k \cdot \frac{2}{3}n^3.
Smart approach: factor A = LU once (cost \frac{2}{3}n^3), then for each b_i do two triangular solves (forward substitution on Lc = b_i, back substitution on Ux = c), each costing n^2.

Total smart approach: \frac{2}{3}n^3 + 2kn^2.
For k \gg 1 this is a dramatic saving: the O(n^3) work is paid once, and each additional right-hand side costs only O(n^2).

























ScenarioCost1 system, full elimination\frac{2}{3}n^3k systems, naive\frac{2}{3}kn^3k systems, factor once\frac{2}{3}n^3 + 2kn^2Explicit A^{-1}, then k multiplies\frac{5}{3}n^3 + kn^2
The LU factorization approach dominates for any k \ge 1.
A Concrete Count: n = 100 vs n = 1000
n = 100: \quad \frac{2}{3}(100)^3 \approx 667{,}000 \text{ flops}
n = 1000: \quad \frac{2}{3}(1000)^3 \approx 667{,}000{,}000 \text{ flops}
Going from n = 100 to n = 1000 multiplies n by 10 and the cost by 10^3 = 1000. At 10^9 flops per second (a modest laptop), that is under a second for n = 1000. For n = 10{,}000: about 667 seconds. This is why numerical methods for large problems exploit sparsity or structure to avoid full O(n^3) elimination.
Where the \frac{2}{3} Comes From Geometrically
There is a nice way to see why the constant is \frac{2}{3} and not 1 or \frac{1}{2}. At stage k, we operate on an (n-k) \times (n-k) submatrix. The total work is proportional to:
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (n-k)^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{n} j^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} \approx \frac{n^3}{3}
Each operation in that submatrix costs 2 flops (multiply + subtract), giving \frac{2n^3}{3}.
The factor \frac{1}{3} is the fraction of an n \times n \times n cube occupied by a tetrahedron — the triangular “staircase” of submatrices we work on during elimination. The factor of 2 is the two flops per entry. That’s the geometric picture: we are working on a triangular prism of operations.
Pivoting and Its (Negligible) Cost
Partial pivoting — searching for the largest entry in column k to use as pivot — requires scanning n - k entries at stage k. Total cost:
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(n-k) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = O(n^2)
This is completely negligible compared to \frac{2}{3}n^3. Partial pivoting is essentially free, which is why it is always used in practice.
Banded Matrices: When Structure Saves Everything
If A is banded with bandwidth w (meaning a_{ij} = 0 whenever |i - j| > w), elimination stays within the band. At stage k, only w rows need updating, and only w columns of each row change.
Cost of banded elimination: O(nw^2) instead of O(n^3).
For a tridiagonal matrix (w = 1): cost is O(n), linear in n. This is the reason finite difference methods for PDEs are fast — they produce tridiagonal or banded systems.
Summary
\text{Forward elimination on } n \times n: \quad \frac{2}{3}n^3 \text{ flops}
\text{Back substitution: } \quad n^2 \text{ flops}
\text{Full solve } Ax = b: \quad \frac{2}{3}n^3 \text{ flops (leading term)}
\text{Compute } A^{-1}: \quad \frac{5}{3}n^3 \text{ flops — never do this just to solve a system}
The dominant cost is always in forward elimination, it scales as n^3, and the constant \frac{2}{3} comes from the triangular structure of the work. Every shortcut in numerical linear algebra — banding, sparsity, iterative methods, randomized algorithms — is an attempt to avoid paying the full \frac{2}{3}n^3.

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 13.Transposes and Permutations
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
Transposes

The transpose of A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} is the matrix A^T \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m} defined by: (A^T)_{ij} = A_{ji}

Rows become columns and columns become rows. If: A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \end{pmatrix} \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}
then: A^T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 6 \end{pmatrix} \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2}
Algebraic Properties


                  
                  For matrices A, B of compatible dimensions and scalar \alpha:
                  
                


(A^T)^T = A
(\alpha A)^T = \alpha A^T
(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T
(AB)^T = B^T A^T
If A is invertible: (A^{-1})^T = (A^T)^{-1}





Proof of (4) — the reversal rule. Let C = AB, so C_{ij} = \sum_k A_{ik} B_{kj}.
Then (C^T)_{ij} = C_{ji} = \sum_k A_{jk}B_{ki} = \sum_k (B^T)_{ik}(A^T)_{kj} = (B^T A^T)_{ij}.
Therefore (AB)^T = B^T A^T. \blacksquare
Note the reversal: same pattern as (AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}. Both the inverse and the transpose reverse the order of products. This is not a coincidence — it reflects the categorical duality between a linear map and its adjoint/dual.


Proof of (5). We want to show (A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T, i.e., (A^{-1})^T \cdot A^T = I.
(A^{-1})^T A^T = (AA^{-1})^T = I^T = I
using property (4). \blacksquare
So (A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T, which is often written A^{-T}.


The Transpose and Inner Products
The transpose has a clean characterization in terms of the standard inner product on \mathbb{R}^n. For x \in \mathbb{R}^m, y \in \mathbb{R}^n, A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}:
\langle Ax, y \rangle_{\mathbb{R}^m} = \langle x, A^T y \rangle_{\mathbb{R}^n}
Proof.
\langle Ax, y \rangle
= (Ax)^T y = x^T A^T y
= \langle x, A^T y \rangle
This identity is fundamental. It says that A^T is the adjoint of A with respect to the standard inner product. In the abstract language of linear maps between inner product spaces, the adjoint is defined by exactly this property. The transpose is just what the adjoint looks like when you choose the standard basis.
This identity is also why the normal equations for least squares are A^T A \hat{x} = A^T b: the “best” x is the one for which the residual b - Ax is orthogonal to the column space of A, which means A^T(b - Ax) = 0.
Symmetric Matrices

A is symmetric if A^T = A, i.e., A_{ij} = A_{ji} for all i, j.

Symmetric matrices are always square. Examples:
\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1 & 7 \end{pmatrix}
The most important source of symmetric matrices: if A is any rectangular matrix, then A^T A and A A^T are both symmetric and positive semidefinite.
Proof of symmetry. (A^T A)^T = A^T (A^T)^T = A^T A. \blacksquare
Products of symmetric matrices are generally not symmetric unless they commute: (AB)^T = B^T A^T = BA \ne AB in general.
Skew-Symmetric Matrices

A is skew-symmetric (or antisymmetric) if A^T = -A.

Every square matrix decomposes uniquely into a symmetric and a skew-symmetric part:
A = \underbrace{\frac{A + A^T}{2}}_{\text{symmetric}} + \underbrace{\frac{A - A^T}{2}}_{\text{skew-symmetric}}
The diagonal entries of a skew-symmetric matrix are all zero (since a_{ii} = -a_{ii} implies a_{ii} = 0).
Permutations

A permutation matrix P \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} is a matrix obtained by reordering the rows of the identity matrix I_n.

Equivalently, P has exactly one 1 in each row and each column, and 0s everywhere else.
For n = 3, there are 3! = 6 permutation matrices:
I = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}, \quad P_{12} = \begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}, \quad P_{13} = \begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\0&1&0\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}
P_{23} = \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}, \quad P_{123} = \begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}, \quad P_{132} = \begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}
where P_\sigma denotes the permutation matrix for the permutation \sigma.
Action of a Permutation Matrix
Left multiplication by P: permutes the rows of whatever follows.
Right multiplication by P: permutes the columns of whatever precedes.
Concretely, if P is the permutation matrix for \sigma \in S_n, then:
(PA)_{ij} = A_{\sigma^{-1}(i),, j}
That is, row i of PA is row \sigma^{-1}(i) of A. (The inverse appears because P puts row \sigma(i) of the identity into row i of P, so multiplying by P sends row \sigma^{-1}(i) of A to row i.)
In practice, when we do row swaps during elimination, we are left-multiplying by elementary permutation matrices (transpositions).
Inverse and Transpose of a Permutation Matrix

For any permutation matrix P: P^{-1} = P^T That is, P is an orthogonal matrix: P^T P = P P^T = I.

Proof. The columns of P are distinct standard basis vectors e_{\sigma(1)}, e_{\sigma(2)}, \ldots, e_{\sigma(n)}. Since these are orthonormal, P^T P = I. \blacksquare
Alternatively: (P^T P)_{ij} = \sum_k (P^T)_{ik}P_{kj} = \sum_k P_{ki}P_{kj}. Since P has exactly one 1 per row and column, P_{ki}P_{kj} = 1 only when k = \sigma^{-1}(i) = \sigma^{-1}(j), which forces i = j. So P^T P = I.
This means: to undo a row permutation, just transpose the permutation matrix. This is used all the time in PA = LU factorization — to solve Ax = b, first compute PA = LU, then solve LUx = Pb.
The Group Structure
The set of all n \times n permutation matrices forms a group under matrix multiplication, isomorphic to the symmetric group S_n. In particular:

The product of two permutation matrices is a permutation matrix.
The identity I is the identity permutation.
Every permutation matrix has a unique inverse, which is its transpose.
The number of n \times n permutation matrices is n!.

Determinant of a Permutation Matrix
The determinant of a permutation matrix P_\sigma is the sign of the permutation \sigma:
\det(P_\sigma) = \text{sgn}(\sigma) = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } \sigma \text{ is an even permutation} \ -1 & \text{if } \sigma \text{ is an odd permutation} \end{cases}
Even/odd. A permutation is even if it can be written as a product of an even number of transpositions (adjacent swaps), and odd otherwise. The parity is well-defined (this is a non-trivial fact from group theory).
This connects to the full determinant formula:
\det(A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \text{sgn}(\sigma) \prod_{i=1}^{n} A_{i,\sigma(i)}
This sum is over all n! permutations. Each term is a product of n entries, one from each row and column, with a sign determined by the parity of the permutation. For n = 3 this gives 6 terms; for n = 4 it gives 24.
Example: 3 \times 3 Determinant via Permutations
A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & k \end{pmatrix}
The six permutations of {1,2,3} with their signs: \begin{array}{c|c|c|c}  \sigma & \text{Cycle type} & \text{sgn}(\sigma) & \text{Term} \\  \hline  (1)(2)(3) & \text{identity} & +1 & aek \\  (12)(3) & \text{transposition} & -1 & bdk \\  (13)(2) & \text{transposition} & -1 & cfg \\  (1)(23) & \text{transposition} & -1 & afh \\  (123) & \text{3-cycle} & +1 & bfg \\  (132) & \text{3-cycle} & +1 & cdh \\ \end{array}
Therefore: \det(A) = aek - bdk - cfg - afh + bfg + cdh
The term for permutation \sigma is \prod_i A_{i,\sigma(i)}, i.e., entry (1, \sigma(1)) times entry (2, \sigma(2)) times entry (3,\sigma(3)).
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\sigma & \text{Picks} & \text{Term} \\
\hline
(1,2,3) \to (1,2,3) & A_{11}A_{22}A_{33} = a \cdot e \cdot k & +aek \\
(1,2,3) \to (2,1,3) & A_{12}A_{21}A_{33} = b \cdot d \cdot k & -bdk \\
(1,2,3) \to (3,2,1) & A_{13}A_{22}A_{31} = c \cdot e \cdot g & -ceg \\
(1,2,3) \to (1,3,2) & A_{11}A_{23}A_{32} = a \cdot f \cdot h & -afh \\
(1,2,3) \to (2,3,1) & A_{12}A_{23}A_{31} = b \cdot f \cdot g & +bfg \\
(1,2,3) \to (3,1,2) & A_{13}A_{21}A_{32} = c \cdot d \cdot h & +cdh \\
\end{array}
\det(A) = aek - bdk - ceg - afh + bfg + cdh
This is the standard 3 \times 3 determinant formula (Sarrus’ rule written algebraically).
LDU Decomposition and Symmetric Matrices
For a symmetric matrix A = A^T, the LDU factorization has a special structure:
A = LDL^T
where D is diagonal and L is unit lower triangular. This halves the storage and computation relative to general LU (Cholesky goes further, writing A = LL^T when A \succ 0).
The key point: U = L^T because A^T = (LDL^T)^T = LDL^T = A. Symmetry of A propagates to the factorization.
Putting It Together: PA = LDU
For a general square invertible matrix, the full factorization is:
PA = LDU
where:

P is a permutation matrix (records row swaps from partial pivoting)
L is unit lower triangular (stores the multipliers \ell_{ij})
D is diagonal (the pivots)
U is unit upper triangular

Often one writes PA = LU by absorbing D into U, producing upper triangular U with the pivots on the diagonal (not necessarily 1s).
The transpose gives:
(PA)^T = (LU)^T = U^T L^T
So A^T P^T = U^T L^T — the LU factorization of A^T (with column permutation P^T) involves U^T as the lower triangular factor and L^T as the upper triangular factor. This is how Cholesky arises: if A = A^T and A \succ 0, then A = LL^T.
see more16.PA = LU
Summary








































ObjectDefinitionKey PropertyA^T(A^T)_{ij} = A_{ji}(AB)^T = B^T A^TSymmetricA^T = AA^T A always symmetric PSDSkew-symmetricA^T = -ADiagonal entries are zeroPermutation PRows of I reorderedP^{-1} = P^T, \det P = \pm 1PA = LUFull factorization with pivotingExists for any invertible A\det(P_\sigma)Sign of the permutation \sigma\pm 1

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.title: 14.Inner Products or Pre-Hilbert Space
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/02.Solving-Linea.content:
An inner product on a real vector space ( V ) is a function:
\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle : V \times V \to \mathbb{R}
that takes two vectors and returns a real number.
Axioms:For all  \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in V and \alpha \in \mathbb{R}:
1. Symmetry
$\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u} \rangle$

2. Linearity (First Argument)
$\langle \alpha \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{v} \rangle=\alpha \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle+\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{v} \rangle$

3. Positive Definiteness
$\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle \ge 0$
$\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0 \iff \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$

Using symmetry + linearity, you also get:
\langle \mathbf{u}, \alpha \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} \rangle
=
\alpha \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle
+
\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w} \rangle
So the inner product is linear in both arguments (over real numbers).


                  
                  Inner product = generalized dot product
                  
                

It measures:
-length → \langle v, v \rangle
-angle → via cosine
-orthogonality → \langle u, v \rangle = 0
The Standard Dot Product in \mathbb{R}^n
The canonical example. For \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n:
\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} u_i v_i
Written out as a matrix product for n = 4:
\mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 & u_2 & u_3 & u_4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ v_3 \\ v_4 \end{bmatrix} = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + u_3 v_3 + u_4 v_4
Verification of axioms is immediate. The interesting question is not whether this satisfies (IP1)–(IP3) but why this particular operation tells us something geometric. see more11.Length and dot product
The Geometric Meaning — Where It Gets Interesting
The inner product is a machine for measuring angles and lengths in a vector space. Here is the precise connection.
Definition (norm induced by the inner product): |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle}
This is the “length” that the inner product defines. For the standard dot product in \mathbb{R}^n, this is just the Euclidean norm.
Theorem (Cauchy-Schwarz): |\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle| \leq |\mathbf{u}| \cdot |\mathbf{v}|
with equality if and only if \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v} are linearly dependent (one is a scalar multiple of the other).
Proof. Consider the function f(t) = \langle \mathbf{u} + t\mathbf{v},\ \mathbf{u} + t\mathbf{v} \rangle \geq 0 for all t \in \mathbb{R}. Expanding by linearity and symmetry:
f(t) = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{u} \rangle + 2t\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle + t^2 \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle \geq 0
This is a non-negative quadratic in t, so its discriminant must be non-positive:
4\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle^2 - 4\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{u} \rangle \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle \leq 0
Dividing by 4:
\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle^2 \leq |\mathbf{u}|^2 |\mathbf{v}|^2
Taking square roots (both sides non-negative): |\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle| \leq |\mathbf{u}| |\mathbf{v}|. Equality holds when the discriminant is zero, i.e., the quadratic f(t) has a double root, meaning \mathbf{u} + t_0 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} for some t_0, i.e., linear dependence. \square
Corollary: Because of Cauchy-Schwarz, the quantity \frac{\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle}{|\mathbf{u}| |\mathbf{v}|} always lies in [-1, 1], so it can be interpreted as a cosine. We define the angle \theta between \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v} in the inner product space by:
\cos \theta = \frac{\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle}{|\mathbf{u}| |\mathbf{v}|}
The inner product encodes angle. That is the geometric meaning.
see more14.The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
Orthogonality
\mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v} are orthogonal if \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0 This corresponds to \theta = 90°, i.e., the two vectors point in “perpendicular directions” in whatever geometry the inner product defines.
Pythagorean theorem in inner product spaces: If \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0, then |\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2
Proof.
|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}|^2 = \langle \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v},\ \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \rangle = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + 2\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle + |\mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2 \quad \square
The middle term vanishes precisely because of orthogonality.
see more09.Orthogonal Matrix,02.Orthogonal Complements,17.Orthogonal Eigenvectors,09.Orthogonal Bases and Gram-Schmidt
The Weighted Inner Product — A Non-Standard Example
Not all inner products on \mathbb{R}^n are the standard dot product. Given a symmetric positive definite matrix M (all eigenvalues > 0), define: \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle_M = \mathbf{u}^T M \mathbf{v}
For n = 3 with diagonal weight matrix M = \begin{bmatrix} w_1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & w_2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & w_3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad w_i > 0
this gives \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle_M = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} w_1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & w_2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & w_3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ v_3 \end{bmatrix} = w_1 u_1 v_1 + w_2 u_2 v_2 + w_3 u_3 v_3
This is a valid inner product. The weights change which vectors are orthogonal and what “length” means. The geometry is different from Euclidean geometry.
Positive definiteness check: \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle_M = \mathbf{v}^T M \mathbf{v} > 0 for \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0} exactly because M is positive definite. This is why the positive definiteness of M is required — it is the condition ensuring (IP3) holds.
Inner Products on Function Spaces — L^2[a,b ]
This is where the abstraction earns its keep. Let V be the space of continuous functions on [a,b]. Define:
\langle f, g \rangle = \int_a^b f(x), g(x), dx
Verification of axioms:

(IP1): \int f g = \int g f. Trivially symmetric.
(IP2): \int (\alpha f + h) g = \alpha \int fg + \int hg. Linearity of the integral.
(IP3): \int_a^b [f(x)]^2 dx \geq 0 since the integrand is non-negative. And \int_a^b [f(x)]^2 dx = 0 implies f(x) = 0 for all x \in [a,b] (by continuity). So \langle f, f \rangle = 0 \Rightarrow f = 0.

The induced norm is
|f| = \sqrt{\int_a^b [f(x)]^2, dx}
and “orthogonality” of two functions means
\int_a^b f(x) g(x), dx = 0
This is exactly what Fourier analysis is about. The sine and cosine functions are orthogonal in the L^2[0, 2\pi] inner product:
\int_0^{2\pi} \sin(mx) \sin(nx), dx = 0 \quad \text{for } m \neq n
The Fourier series is a decomposition of a function into an orthogonal basis — the same idea as decomposing a vector in \mathbb{R}^n into orthogonal basis vectors, but in an infinite-dimensional inner product space. Everything I know about projections and orthogonal bases in \mathbb{R}^n extends here.
see more11.Bases for Matrix Spaces and Function Spaces 07.Fourier Series08.Fourier Matrix09.Fourier Transformation & the DFT
Projection as a Consequence of the Inner Product
Given a subspace W \subseteq V, the orthogonal projection of \mathbf{v} onto W is the vector \hat{\mathbf{v}} \in W minimizing |\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{w}| over all \mathbf{w} \in W. The inner product structure is what makes this minimizer unique and computable.
For the simplest case, projecting onto the line spanned by \mathbf{a} \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}{\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle} \mathbf{a}
The coefficient \frac{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}{\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle} is the “shadow” of \mathbf{v} along \mathbf{a}. The error \mathbf{v} - \hat{\mathbf{v}} is orthogonal to \mathbf{a}:
\langle \mathbf{v} - \hat{\mathbf{v}},\ \mathbf{a} \rangle
= \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{a} \rangle - \frac{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{a} \rangle}{\langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle} \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a} \rangle
= 0
This is the fundamental orthogonality condition of projections. It says: the best approximation from a subspace is the one whose error is perpendicular to the subspace. Inner product = the only tool that can express perpendicularity.
see more: 04.Projections onto a Line,05.Projections onto a Subspace,10.Projection Using Orthogonal Bases 06.Least Squares Approximations
What an Inner Product Actually Does:
An inner product on a vector space gives you three things simultaneously:

A notion of length: |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle}
A notion of angle: \cos\theta = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle / (|\mathbf{u}| |\mathbf{v}|), justified by Cauchy-Schwarz
A notion of perpendicularity: \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0

Without an inner product, a vector space has no geometry — just linear combinations. The inner product is precisely the additional structure that turns algebra into geometry. The dot product in \mathbb{R}^n, the weighted dot product with matrix M, and the L^2 integral pairing are all different choices of geometry on different spaces. Every geometric concept in linear algebra — orthogonal complement, projection, least squares, Gram-Schmidt, eigenvectors of symmetric matrices — is secretly a consequence of having an inner product.
