01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 14.The Matrix Exponential
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
Why This Object Exists
The scalar ODE u' = au has solution u(t) = e^{at}u_0. The matrix ODE \mathbf{u}' = A\mathbf{u} has solution \mathbf{u}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{u}_0. The second equation is a definition: it defines e^{At} to be whatever operator solves the matrix ODE. The question is whether this definition is consistent, computable, and well-behaved.
The answer is yes to all three, and the proof runs through the power series.

Definition via the Power Series
e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(At)^k}{k!} = I + At + \frac{A^2 t^2}{2!} + \frac{A^3 t^3}{3!} + \cdots
This is a series of n \times n matrices. It converges absolutely for every matrix A and every t \in \mathbb{R} (or \mathbb{C}). The proof uses the submultiplicativity of any matrix norm: |A^k| \leq |A|^k, so
\left|\sum_{k=0}^N \frac{(At)^k}{k!}\right| \leq \sum_{k=0}^N \frac{|A|^k |t|^k}{k!} \leq e^{|A||t|} < \infty
The series converges faster than the scalar exponential e^{|A||t|}. No issues with convergence, ever.
This definition immediately gives e^{A \cdot 0} = I and \frac{d}{dt}e^{At} = Ae^{At}:
\frac{d}{dt}e^{At} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{k A^k t^{k-1}}{k!} = A\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{A^{k-1}t^{k-1}}{(k-1)!} = Ae^{At}
So e^{At} satisfies the matrix ODE \frac{d}{dt}e^{At} = Ae^{At} with initial condition e^{A\cdot 0} = I. This is the justification: the power series definition produces exactly the solution operator we need.

The Four Fundamental Properties
Let A and B be n \times n matrices. Then:
1. e^{A \cdot 0} = I
2. \dfrac{d}{dt}e^{At} = Ae^{At} = e^{At}A
3. (e^{At})^{-1} = e^{-At}
4. If AB = BA, then e^{(A+B)t} = e^{At}e^{Bt}
Property 3 follows from property 4: e^{At}e^{-At} = e^{(A-A)t} = e^{0} = I. So e^{At} is always invertible, for every A and every t. This is not obvious from the definition but is an immediate consequence of property 4 when commutativity holds (and A commutes with -A).
Property 4 is the dangerous one. The scalar identity e^{a+b} = e^ae^b holds for all a, b \in \mathbb{R}. The matrix version requires AB = BA. Without commutativity, e^{A+B} \neq e^Ae^B in general. The correction is given by the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula, which involves commutators [A,B] = AB - BA and is almost never a closed form.
Counterexample for property 4 without commutativity. Let
A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
Then AB = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\0&0\end{pmatrix} and BA = \begin{pmatrix}0&0\0&1\end{pmatrix}, so AB \neq BA. One can verify that e^{A+B} \neq e^Ae^B directly. The failure of commutativity is the only obstruction.

Computing e^{At}: The Four Methods
Method 1: Diagonalization
If A = PDP^{-1} with D = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n), then A^k = PD^kP^{-1}, so
e^{At} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(PDP^{-1})^k t^k}{k!} = P\left(\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{D^k t^k}{k!}\right)P^{-1} = Pe^{Dt}P^{-1}
where
e^{Dt} = \begin{pmatrix} e^{\lambda_1 t} & & & \ & e^{\lambda_2 t} & & \ & & \ddots & \ & & & e^{\lambda_n t} \end{pmatrix}
This is the main method. It reduces the matrix exponential to scalar exponentials applied to the eigenvalues. From Matrix Powers, A^k = PD^kP^{-1}; replace \lambda_i^k with e^{\lambda_i t}.
Full worked example. Let
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & -1 \end{pmatrix}
Eigenvalues: \lambda_1 = 1, \lambda_2 = -1 (upper triangular, read the diagonal).
For \lambda_1 = 1: (A - I) = \begin{pmatrix}0&2\0&-2\end{pmatrix}. Eigenvector \mathbf{x}_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1\0\end{pmatrix}.
For \lambda_2 = -1: (A + I) = \begin{pmatrix}2&2\0&0\end{pmatrix}. Eigenvector \mathbf{x}_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1\-1\end{pmatrix}.
P = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\0 & -1\end{pmatrix}, \quad P^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\0 & -1\end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\0 & -1\end{pmatrix}
(In this case P^{-1} = P, a coincidence. Verify: PP^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\0&-1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\0&1\end{pmatrix}. Yes.)
e^{At} = P\begin{pmatrix}e^t & 0\0 & e^{-t}\end{pmatrix}P^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}e^t & 0\0 & e^{-t}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\0&-1\end{pmatrix}
Multiply left two:
\begin{pmatrix}e^t & e^{-t}\0 & -e^{-t}\end{pmatrix}
Multiply by P^{-1}:
e^{At} = \begin{pmatrix}e^t & e^{-t}\0 & -e^{-t}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\0&-1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}e^t & e^t - e^{-t}\0 & e^{-t}\end{pmatrix}
Check at t=0: \begin{pmatrix}1&0\0&1\end{pmatrix} = I. Good. Check \frac{d}{dt}e^{At}\big|_{t=0} = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\0&-1\end{pmatrix} = A. Good.

Method 2: Jordan Form (Non-Diagonalizable Case)
When A is defective, write A = PJP^{-1} where J is the Jordan normal form. Then e^{At} = Pe^{Jt}P^{-1}, and e^{Jt} is block diagonal with one block per Jordan block.
For a Jordan block of size m with eigenvalue \lambda_0:
J_m(\lambda_0) = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ 0 & \lambda_0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \ 0 & 0 & \lambda_0 & \cdots & 0 \ \vdots & & & \ddots & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & \lambda_0 \end{pmatrix}
Write J_m(\lambda_0) = \lambda_0 I + N where N is the nilpotent shift matrix with 1s on the superdiagonal and N^m = 0. Since \lambda_0 I and N commute:
e^{J_m(\lambda_0)t} = e^{\lambda_0 t}e^{Nt} = e^{\lambda_0 t}\left(I + Nt + \frac{N^2 t^2}{2!} + \cdots + \frac{N^{m-1}t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\right)
Explicitly:
e^{J_m(\lambda_0)t} = e^{\lambda_0 t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & t & \dfrac{t^2}{2!} & \cdots & \dfrac{t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!} \[6pt] 0 & 1 & t & \cdots & \dfrac{t^{m-2}}{(m-2)!} \[6pt] 0 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & \vdots \ \vdots & & & \ddots & t \ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \end{pmatrix}
The polynomial factors 1, t, t^2/2!, \ldots in the superdiagonals are the signature of a defective eigenvalue. This is exactly the Jordan block computation from Nondiagonalizable Matrices Jordan Form, now applied to e^{At} instead of A^k.
The 2\times 2 case explicitly. A = \begin{pmatrix}\lambda_0 & 1 \ 0 & \lambda_0\end{pmatrix}:
e^{At} = e^{\lambda_0 t}\begin{pmatrix}1 & t \ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}
This is the formula used in Second-Order ODEs to prove the te^{\lambda_0 t} solution for repeated roots, and in Euler Spirals for the rotation generator.

Method 3: Cayley-Hamilton
Every n\times n matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I). By Cayley-Hamilton, p(A) = 0.
For a 2\times 2 matrix with characteristic polynomial \lambda^2 - T\lambda + D = 0, this gives A^2 = TA - DI. Every power A^k for k \geq 2 can be reduced to a linear combination of I and A. Therefore e^{At} is also a linear combination of I and A:
e^{At} = \alpha(t)I + \beta(t)A
for scalar functions \alpha(t) and \beta(t) to be determined. Since e^{\lambda t} must satisfy the same scalar recurrence when \lambda is an eigenvalue, impose:
e^{\lambda_1 t} = \alpha(t) + \beta(t)\lambda_1 e^{\lambda_2 t} = \alpha(t) + \beta(t)\lambda_2
This is a 2\times 2 linear system for \alpha(t) and \beta(t), solvable when \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2.
Example. A = \begin{pmatrix}1&2\0&-1\end{pmatrix}, eigenvalues \lambda_1 = 1, \lambda_2 = -1.
e^t = \alpha + \beta, \qquad e^{-t} = \alpha - \beta
Solving: \alpha = \frac{e^t + e^{-t}}{2} = \cosh t, \beta = \frac{e^t - e^{-t}}{2} = \sinh t.
e^{At} = \cosh(t),I + \sinh(t),A = \begin{pmatrix}\cosh t & 0\,0 & \cosh t\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}\sinh t & 2\sinh t \ 0 & -\sinh t\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}e^t & 2\sinh t \ 0 & e^{-t}\end{pmatrix}
This matches Method 1 since e^t - e^{-t} = 2\sinh t. Good.
For the repeated eigenvalue case (\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \lambda_0), differentiate the condition with respect to \lambda:
e^{\lambda_0 t} = \alpha + \beta\lambda_0, \qquad te^{\lambda_0 t} = \beta
giving \beta = te^{\lambda_0 t} and \alpha = (1 - \lambda_0 t)e^{\lambda_0 t}.

Method 4: Putzer’s Algorithm
An alternative to Cayley-Hamilton that avoids solving systems. Write
e^{At} = r_1(t)I + r_2(t)(A - \lambda_1 I)
for 2\times 2 matrices, where r_1 and r_2 satisfy
r_1' = \lambda_1 r_1, \quad r_1(0) = 1 \implies r_1(t) = e^{\lambda_1 t} r_2' = \lambda_2 r_2 + r_1, \quad r_2(0) = 0
The second ODE is a first-order linear scalar ODE, solvable directly. This avoids matrix inversion entirely and generalizes cleanly to n\times n matrices. It is particularly useful when eigenvalues are repeated.

Geometric Interpretation
The matrix e^{At} is the flow map of the vector field \mathbf{u}' = A\mathbf{u}. It takes any initial condition \mathbf{u}_0 and returns the position \mathbf{u}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{u}_0 at time t. So:

e^{At} is a linear map from \mathbb{R}^n to \mathbb{R}^n for each fixed t.
The family {e^{At}}_{t \in \mathbb{R}} is a one-parameter group of linear maps: e^{As}e^{At} = e^{A(s+t)}.
The determinant satisfies \det(e^{At}) = e^{(\text{tr},A)t} (Jacobi’s formula / Liouville’s theorem).

The last identity is remarkable. It says the volume of any region in \mathbb{R}^n expands or contracts at rate e^{Tt} where T = \text{tr}(A). From Stability of 2x2 Systems, T < 0 means volume contracts, T > 0 means volume expands, T = 0 means volume is preserved (the center case).
Proof of \det(e^{At}) = e^{Tt}. For diagonalizable A:
\det(e^{At}) = \det(Pe^{Dt}P^{-1}) = \det(e^{Dt}) = \prod_{i=1}^n e^{\lambda_i t} = e^{(\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n)t} = e^{(\text{tr},A)t}
The general case follows by density of diagonalizable matrices.

Special Cases Worth Knowing
Nilpotent matrix (A^m = 0)
The series terminates:
e^{At} = I + At + \frac{A^2t^2}{2!} + \cdots + \frac{A^{m-1}t^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}
Polynomial in t, no exponentials. This is exactly the structure of a pure Jordan block with \lambda_0 = 0.
Skew-symmetric matrix (A^T = -A)
The eigenvalues of a real skew-symmetric matrix are purely imaginary (or zero). The matrix exponential e^{At} is orthogonal: (e^{At})^T = e^{A^Tt} = e^{-At} = (e^{At})^{-1}.
The rotation matrices e^{\Omega t} from Euler Spirals are the prime example. \Omega = \begin{pmatrix}0&-1\1&0\end{pmatrix} is skew-symmetric, and e^{\Omega t} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos t & -\sin t\\sin t & \cos t\end{pmatrix} is a rotation matrix.
More generally, e^{At} \in SO(n) whenever A is skew-symmetric. The skew-symmetric matrices are the Lie algebra \mathfrak{so}(n), and e^{At} maps into the Lie group SO(n). The matrix exponential is the exponential map of the Lie group.
Symmetric matrix (A^T = A)
Eigenvalues are real (spectral theorem). e^{At} is symmetric: (e^{At})^T = e^{A^Tt} = e^{At}. If A is negative definite (all eigenvalues negative), then e^{At} \to 0 exponentially and |e^{At}| \leq e^{\lambda_{\max}(A)t}.
Scalar multiple of identity (A = cI)
e^{cIt} = e^{ct}I
Obvious from the series. Every matrix exponential reduces to this in each eigenspace.

The Cayley-Hamilton Theorem and Polynomial Reduction
For an n\times n matrix with characteristic polynomial p(\lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^n(\lambda - \lambda_i), Cayley-Hamilton gives p(A) = 0. This means A^n is a linear combination of I, A, \ldots, A^{n-1}, and so is every higher power. Therefore e^{At} is an n\times n matrix whose entries are linear combinations of {e^{\lambda_i t}, te^{\lambda_i t}, \ldots, t^{m_i-1}e^{\lambda_i t}} where m_i is the size of the largest Jordan block for \lambda_i.
This is the definitive statement: the entries of e^{At} are linear combinations of the functions t^j e^{\lambda_i t} where \lambda_i ranges over eigenvalues and j ranges from 0 to one less than the size of the corresponding Jordan block. No other functions appear. The eigenvalues of A are exactly the exponential rates in e^{At}.

Connection to Everything Else in These Notes

































ObjectConnection to e^{At}Matrix Powers A^kReplace \lambda_i^k with e^{\lambda_i t}; same PDP^{-1} structureDifferential Equations and e^Ate^{At} is the solution operator; this note gives the computationSecond-Order ODEste^{\lambda_0 t} solutions come from 2\times 2 Jordan blocks in e^{Jt}Stability of 2x2 Systemse^{At}\to 0 iff all \text{Re}(\lambda_i) < 0 iff T<0 and D>0Euler Spiralse^{\Omega s^2/2} is the rotation matrix generating the spiral; \Omega skew-symmetricNondiagonalizable Matrices Jordan FormJordan form gives e^{Jt}; polynomial corrections from nilpotent part

The One Formula to Remember
\boxed{e^{At} = Pe^{Dt}P^{-1}, \qquad e^{Dt} = \begin{pmatrix}e^{\lambda_1 t} & & \ & \ddots & \ & & e^{\lambda_n t}\end{pmatrix}}
When A is not diagonalizable, replace D with J (Jordan form) and each diagonal block e^{\lambda_i t} with the full Jordan block exponential.
The entries of e^{At} are exactly the functions you need to solve \mathbf{u}' = A\mathbf{u}: linear combinations of t^j e^{\lambda_i t}, one for each Jordan block. Everything else --- stability, oscillation, growth, decay --- is a consequence of which \lambda_i appear and what their real parts are.

References: Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (Ch. 6.3); MIT 18.06 Lectures 23-24

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 15.Symmetric Matrices
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
The Object
A matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} is symmetric if A^T = A, meaning a_{ij} = a_{ji} for all i, j. Written out for n = 3:
A = \begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} & a_{13} \ a_{12} & a_{22} & a_{23} \ a_{13} & a_{23} & a_{33} \end{pmatrix}
The entries below the diagonal are the mirror image of the entries above it. There are \frac{n(n+1)}{2} free parameters, not n^2.
Symmetric matrices are everywhere: covariance matrices in statistics, stiffness matrices in mechanics, Laplacians in graph theory, Hessians in optimization, and the kernel of every least-squares problem A^TA. The reason they dominate applications is the spectral theorem: symmetric matrices are the matrices that are perfectly diagonalizable, with orthogonal eigenvectors and real eigenvalues. No defective eigenvalues, no complex numbers, no Jordan blocks. Everything is clean.

The Spectral Theorem
Theorem (Spectral Theorem for Real Symmetric Matrices). If A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is symmetric, then:

All eigenvalues of A are real.
Eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
There exists an orthonormal basis of \mathbb{R}^n consisting entirely of eigenvectors of A.

Equivalently: A can be orthogonally diagonalized,
A = Q\Lambda Q^T
where Q is orthogonal (Q^TQ = I, columns are orthonormal eigenvectors) and \Lambda = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n) with all \lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}.
This is the most important theorem in applied linear algebra. Every structured matrix decomposition in data science --- PCA, SVD, spectral clustering --- runs through this theorem.

Proof of the Spectral Theorem
I want to prove all three parts carefully. This is worth doing once, completely.
Part 1: Eigenvalues are real
Let \lambda \in \mathbb{C} be an eigenvalue with eigenvector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{C}^n, \mathbf{x} \neq 0.
Take the inner product of A\mathbf{x} = \lambda\mathbf{x} with \mathbf{x} over \mathbb{C}:
\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T A\mathbf{x} = \lambda \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T\mathbf{x} = \lambda|\mathbf{x}|^2
Now take the conjugate transpose of the left side. Since A is real and symmetric, A^T = A and \bar{A} = A, so A^* = \bar{A}^T = A:
\overline{\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T A\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}^T A^* \bar{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}^T A\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \overline{\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T A\mathbf{x}}
More directly: \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T A\mathbf{x} is a 1\times 1 matrix (a scalar). Its conjugate is (\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T A\mathbf{x})^* = \mathbf{x}^T A^T \bar{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}^T A\bar{\mathbf{x}}.
But also \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T A\mathbf{x} = \overline{\mathbf{x}^T A\bar{\mathbf{x}}}… let me be cleaner.
Write s = \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T A\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{C}. Take its complex conjugate:
\bar{s} = \overline{\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T A\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}^T\overline{A\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}^T A\bar{\mathbf{x}} = (A\mathbf{x})^T\bar{\mathbf{x}} \cdot \text{[wrong direction]}
Let me use the cleaner route. Since A = A^T and A is real:
\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T(A\mathbf{x}) = \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T(\lambda\mathbf{x}) = \lambda|\mathbf{x}|^2
(A\mathbf{x})^T\bar{\mathbf{x}} = (A^T\mathbf{x})^T\bar{\mathbf{x}} = (A\mathbf{x})^T\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \lambda(\mathbf{x})^T\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \lambda|\mathbf{x}|^2
But (A\mathbf{x})^T\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}^TA^T\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}^TA\bar{\mathbf{x}}. And \overline{\bar{\mathbf{x}}^TA\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}^T\overline{A},\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}^TA\bar{\mathbf{x}} (since A is real). So \bar{s} = s, meaning s is real. But s = \lambda|\mathbf{x}|^2 and |\mathbf{x}|^2 > 0, so \lambda is real. \square
Part 2: Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal
Let A\mathbf{x} = \lambda\mathbf{x} and A\mathbf{y} = \mu\mathbf{y} with \lambda \neq \mu, both real.
\lambda(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}) = (A\mathbf{x})\cdot\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^TA^T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}\cdot(A\mathbf{y}) = \mu(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y})
So (\lambda - \mu)(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y}) = 0. Since \lambda \neq \mu, we get \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{y} = 0. \square
The key step was the symmetry of A: it allows us to move A from acting on \mathbf{x} to acting on \mathbf{y}, picking up the other eigenvalue. Symmetry is the algebraic reason eigenvectors are orthogonal.
Part 3: Orthonormal basis of eigenvectors
This requires showing that even repeated eigenvalues have a full set of orthonormal eigenvectors, i.e., no Jordan blocks occur. The proof is by induction on n.
Base case: n = 1. Trivial.
Inductive step: Assume every (n-1)\times(n-1) symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Let \lambda_1 be any eigenvalue of A (real by Part 1) and \mathbf{q}_1 a unit eigenvector. Extend to an orthonormal basis {\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n} of \mathbb{R}^n.
In this basis, A becomes Q_1^TAQ_1 where Q_1 = [\mathbf{q}_1;\mathbf{v}_2;\cdots;\mathbf{v}_n]. Compute the first column:
Q_1^TAQ_1\mathbf{e}_1 = Q_1^TA\mathbf{q}_1 = Q_1^T(\lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1) = \lambda_1\mathbf{e}_1
So the first column of Q_1^TAQ_1 is \lambda_1\mathbf{e}_1. Since Q_1^TAQ_1 is still symmetric ((Q_1^TAQ_1)^T = Q_1^TA^TQ_1 = Q_1^TAQ_1), the first row must also be \lambda_1\mathbf{e}_1^T. Therefore:
Q_1^TAQ_1 = \begin{pmatrix}\lambda_1 & \mathbf{0}^T \ \mathbf{0} & B\end{pmatrix}
where B is an (n-1)\times(n-1) symmetric matrix. By induction, B has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Lifting back to \mathbb{R}^n gives the full orthonormal eigenbasis of A. \square
The crucial point: symmetric matrices are never defective. A repeated eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix always has a full geometric eigenspace equal to its algebraic multiplicity. Jordan blocks of size \geq 2 cannot occur. This is what makes symmetric matrices the nicest matrices in existence.

The Spectral Decomposition
From A = Q\Lambda Q^T with Q = [\mathbf{q}_1 \cdots \mathbf{q}_n]:
A = \lambda_1\mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^T + \lambda_2\mathbf{q}_2\mathbf{q}_2^T + \cdots + \lambda_n\mathbf{q}_n\mathbf{q}_n^T = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T
Each term \mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T is a rank-1 orthogonal projection onto the span of \mathbf{q}_i. The identity \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T = QQ^T = I says these projections partition the identity: every vector in \mathbb{R}^n is decomposed into n orthogonal components, each scaled by the corresponding eigenvalue.
This is the spectral decomposition. It is the most explicit possible statement of what A does: it stretches along \mathbf{q}_1 by \lambda_1, along \mathbf{q}_2 by \lambda_2, and so on, in n mutually orthogonal directions.
Applying a function to A. Since A = Q\Lambda Q^T:
f(A) = Qf(\Lambda)Q^T = \sum_{i=1}^n f(\lambda_i)\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T
for any function f applied to the eigenvalues. For example:
A^k = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i^k,\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T, \qquad e^{At} = \sum_{i=1}^n e^{\lambda_i t},\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T
A^{-1} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\lambda_i},\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T \quad (\text{if all } \lambda_i \neq 0), \qquad A^{1/2} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sqrt{\lambda_i},\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T \quad (\text{if all } \lambda_i \geq 0)
The last formula is the square root of a positive semidefinite matrix, well-defined and unique. The spectral decomposition makes every matrix function trivial to write down for symmetric matrices.

Quadratic Forms
Every symmetric matrix defines a quadratic form
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}x_ix_j
Since a_{ij} = a_{ji}, the cross terms a_{ij}x_ix_j + a_{ji}x_jx_i = 2a_{ij}x_ix_j combine cleanly. The quadratic form is a real-valued function on \mathbb{R}^n that is homogeneous of degree 2.
In the eigenvector basis \mathbf{x} = \sum_i c_i\mathbf{q}_i:
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} = \left(\sum_i c_i\mathbf{q}_i\right)^T A\left(\sum_j c_j\mathbf{q}_j\right) = \sum_{i,j}c_ic_j\mathbf{q}_i^TA\mathbf{q}_j = \sum_{i,j}c_ic_j\lambda_j\mathbf{q}_i^T\mathbf{q}_j = \sum_i \lambda_i c_i^2
The quadratic form is a sum of squares \sum\lambda_i c_i^2 in the eigenvector basis. The eigenvalues are the coefficients. This is the principal axis theorem: every quadratic form can be written as a weighted sum of squares by rotating to the eigenvector basis.
The sign pattern of the eigenvalues determines the shape of the level sets {\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} = 1}:

All \lambda_i > 0: ellipsoid (stretched in eigenvector directions by 1/\sqrt{\lambda_i})
All \lambda_i < 0: imaginary ellipsoid (no real solutions)
Mixed signs: hyperboloid (saddle surface)


Positive Definite Matrices
A symmetric matrix A is positive definite (written A \succ 0) if
\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} > 0 \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x} \neq 0
From the spectral decomposition Q(\mathbf{x}) = \sum\lambda_i c_i^2, this holds if and only if all \lambda_i > 0.
Five equivalent conditions for a symmetric matrix A to be positive definite:

All eigenvalues are positive: \lambda_i > 0 for all i.
\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} > 0 for all \mathbf{x} \neq 0.
All n leading principal minors are positive (Sylvester’s criterion):

a_{11} > 0, \quad \det\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}\a_{12}&a_{22}\end{pmatrix} > 0, \quad \ldots, \quad \det(A) > 0

A = R^TR for some matrix R with independent columns (Cholesky factorization: R can be taken upper triangular).
All pivots in Gaussian elimination are positive.

These five conditions are all equivalent. Condition 2 is the definition. Condition 1 is the spectral characterization. Condition 3 is the computational test. Condition 4 is the factorization. Condition 5 is the algorithm.
The Cholesky factorization A = R^TR is the symmetric analogue of LU decomposition, and it is twice as efficient: since A is symmetric, only the upper triangular part needs to be stored, and the factorization exploits this to halve the work. It is the standard method for solving A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} when A is known to be positive definite.
Positive semidefinite (A \succeq 0): replace strict inequalities with \geq 0. Allows zero eigenvalues.

The 2\times 2 Case in Full Detail
A = \begin{pmatrix}a & b \ b & d\end{pmatrix}
Characteristic polynomial: \lambda^2 - (a+d)\lambda + (ad - b^2) = 0.
Eigenvalues:
\lambda = \frac{(a+d) \pm \sqrt{(a+d)^2 - 4(ad-b^2)}}{2} = \frac{(a+d) \pm \sqrt{(a-d)^2 + 4b^2}}{2}
The discriminant (a-d)^2 + 4b^2 \geq 0 always. So the eigenvalues are always real, as the spectral theorem guarantees. They are equal if and only if a = d and b = 0, i.e., A = aI.
Eigenvectors. For eigenvalue \lambda_1 = \frac{(a+d) + \sqrt{(a-d)^2+4b^2}}{2}:
(A - \lambda_1 I)\mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix}a-\lambda_1 & b \ b & d - \lambda_1\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{x} = 0
The eigenvector is \mathbf{x}_1 = \begin{pmatrix}b \ \lambda_1 - a\end{pmatrix} (or any scalar multiple). Similarly for \lambda_2.
These eigenvectors are automatically orthogonal: \mathbf{x}_1\cdot\mathbf{x}_2 = b\cdot b + (\lambda_1 - a)(\lambda_2 - a) = b^2 + \lambda_1\lambda_2 - a(\lambda_1+\lambda_2) + a^2.
Using Vieta: \lambda_1\lambda_2 = ad - b^2 and \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = a + d:
\mathbf{x}_1\cdot\mathbf{x}_2 = b^2 + (ad-b^2) - a(a+d) + a^2 = ad - a^2 - ad + a^2 = 0 \checkmark
Positive definiteness test. A \succ 0 iff \lambda_1, \lambda_2 > 0 iff T = a + d > 0 and D = ad - b^2 > 0.
Compare with Stability of 2x2 Systems: the stability condition T < 0, D > 0 is the negative definite condition A \prec 0 (all eigenvalues negative). A symmetric A gives a stable system iff A is negative definite.

Worked Example: Full Diagonalization
A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 \ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}
T = 6, D = 9 - 1 = 8. Positive definite (both positive). Eigenvalues:
\lambda = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 32}}{2} = \frac{6\pm 2}{2} = 4 \text{ or } 2
For \lambda_1 = 4: (A - 4I) = \begin{pmatrix}-1&1\1&-1\end{pmatrix}. Null space: \mathbf{x}_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1\1\end{pmatrix}. Unit vector: \mathbf{q}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\1\end{pmatrix}.
For \lambda_2 = 2: (A - 2I) = \begin{pmatrix}1&1\1&1\end{pmatrix}. Null space: \mathbf{x}_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1\-1\end{pmatrix}. Unit vector: \mathbf{q}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\-1\end{pmatrix}.
Check orthogonality: \mathbf{q}_1\cdot\mathbf{q}_2 = \frac{1}{2}(1\cdot1 + 1\cdot(-1)) = 0. Good.
Q = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\1&-1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Lambda = \begin{pmatrix}4&0\0&2\end{pmatrix}
Verify A = Q\Lambda Q^T:
Q\Lambda Q^T = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}4&0\0&2\end{pmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\1&-1\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}4&2\4&-2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\1&-1\end{pmatrix}
= \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}4+2&4-2\4-2&4+2\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}6&2\2&6\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3&1\1&3\end{pmatrix} = A \checkmark
Spectral decomposition:
A = 4\cdot\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1\1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix} + 2\cdot\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1\-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\end{pmatrix} = 2\begin{pmatrix}1&1\1&1\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}1&-1\-1&1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3&1\1&3\end{pmatrix} \checkmark
The matrix stretches by 4 along the diagonal direction (1,1)/\sqrt{2} and by 2 along the anti-diagonal direction (1,-1)/\sqrt{2}. The level curves of \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} = 1 are an ellipse with semi-axes 1/\sqrt{4} = 1/2 and 1/\sqrt{2} along these directions.

Rayleigh Quotient
The Rayleigh quotient of a symmetric matrix A at \mathbf{x} \neq 0 is
R(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{x}}
From the spectral decomposition with \mathbf{x} = \sum c_i\mathbf{q}_i:
R(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\sum\lambda_i c_i^2}{\sum c_i^2}
This is a weighted average of eigenvalues, with weights c_i^2/\sum c_j^2 \geq 0 summing to 1. Therefore:
\lambda_{\min} \leq R(\mathbf{x}) \leq \lambda_{\max} \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x} \neq 0
with equality: R(\mathbf{q}_{\min}) = \lambda_{\min} and R(\mathbf{q}_{\max}) = \lambda_{\max}.
This gives a variational characterization of eigenvalues:
\lambda_{\max} = \max_{\mathbf{x}\neq 0} \frac{\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{x}}, \qquad \lambda_{\min} = \min_{\mathbf{x}\neq 0}\frac{\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{x}}
This is the min-max theorem (Courant-Fischer). It is foundational in numerical linear algebra: eigenvalues of symmetric matrices are extrema of the Rayleigh quotient, which means gradient-based methods can find them.
Practical implication. For any unit vector \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} is sandwiched between the smallest and largest eigenvalues. If you want a lower bound on \lambda_{\min}, exhibit any \mathbf{x} and compute R(\mathbf{x}). If you want to know \lambda_{\max}, the power method converges to it because A^k\mathbf{x} = \sum \lambda_i^k c_i\mathbf{q}_i is dominated by the largest |\lambda_i|.

The Matrix Exponential of a Symmetric Matrix
From The Matrix Exponential and the spectral decomposition:
e^{At} = \sum_{i=1}^n e^{\lambda_i t},\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T
Since all \lambda_i are real:

If A \prec 0 (negative definite, all \lambda_i < 0): e^{At} \to 0 exponentially. The system \mathbf{u}' = A\mathbf{u} is asymptotically stable.
If A \succ 0 (positive definite, all \lambda_i > 0): e^{At} \to \infty. Unstable.
If A is indefinite: mixed growth and decay.

No Jordan blocks, no te^{\lambda t} terms. The matrix exponential of a symmetric matrix is always \sum e^{\lambda_i t}\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T, clean and diagonal in the eigenvector basis.
The norm satisfies |e^{At}| = e^{\lambda_{\max}(A)t} (operator norm), since e^{At} stretches most in the direction of the largest eigenvalue.

A^TA Is Always Positive Semidefinite
For any matrix A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, the product A^TA is an n\times n symmetric, positive semidefinite matrix.
Proof. Symmetric: (A^TA)^T = A^T(A^T)^T = A^TA. Positive semidefinite: \mathbf{x}^T(A^TA)\mathbf{x} = (A\mathbf{x})^T(A\mathbf{x}) = |A\mathbf{x}|^2 \geq 0. \square
The eigenvalues of A^TA are non-negative. Their square roots are the singular values of A. This is the connection between the spectral theorem and the singular value decomposition: SVD is the spectral theorem applied to A^TA and AA^T.
The null space of A^TA equals the null space of A: A^TA\mathbf{x} = 0 \iff |A\mathbf{x}|^2 = 0 \iff A\mathbf{x} = 0. So A^TA is positive definite iff A has independent columns.
This is why A^TA appears in the normal equations for least squares: A^TA\hat{\mathbf{x}} = A^T\mathbf{b}. The matrix A^TA is always symmetric, and positive definite when A has independent columns, so the normal equations have a unique solution in that case.

Summary
A real symmetric matrix A = A^T has:
\boxed{A = Q\Lambda Q^T = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i,\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T}
with Q orthogonal, all \lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}, eigenvectors \mathbf{q}_i mutually orthogonal.

































PropertyConditionAll \lambda_i > 0Positive definite: \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} > 0 for all \mathbf{x} \neq 0All \lambda_i \geq 0Positive semidefiniteAll \lambda_i < 0Negative definite: stable ODEMixed signsIndefinite: saddle surface, unstable ODESmallest \lambda\min_{\mathbf{x}\neq 0} R(\mathbf{x}), Rayleigh quotientLargest \lambda\max_{\mathbf{x}\neq 0} R(\mathbf{x}), power method converges to this
No Jordan blocks ever. No complex eigenvalues ever. No defective eigenvalues ever. The spectral theorem is the guarantee that symmetric matrices are always perfectly diagonalizable in an orthonormal basis.

References: Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (Ch. 6.4, 6.5); MIT 18.06 Lectures 25-26

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 16.The Spectral Theorem
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
The Statement Worth Knowing Cold
There are several versions of the spectral theorem. I want to state them in increasing generality, because the progression reveals what the theorem is actually about.
Version 1 (Real symmetric). If A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and A^T = A, then there exists an orthogonal matrix Q and a real diagonal matrix \Lambda such that
A = Q\Lambda Q^T
Version 2 (Complex Hermitian). If A \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times n} and A^* = A (where A^* = \bar{A}^T), then there exists a unitary matrix U (U^*U = I) and a real diagonal matrix \Lambda such that
A = U\Lambda U^*
Version 3 (Normal matrices). A \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times n} is unitarily diagonalizable if and only if A^_A = AA^_ (i.e., A is normal). In this case A = U\Lambda U^* with U unitary and \Lambda diagonal (possibly complex).
The real symmetric case is the most important for applications. The normal matrix case is the most general. The Hermitian case sits between them.
The theorem is saying something deep: symmetry (of the right kind) forces perfect diagonalizability with orthogonal eigenvectors. No Jordan blocks, no complex eigenvalues for the real symmetric case, no missing eigenvectors anywhere. The algebraic structure of A^T = A completely controls the spectral structure.

What the Theorem Is Really Saying
Every n\times n matrix acts on \mathbb{R}^n as a linear map. For a general matrix, this action can twist, shear, and stretch space in complicated ways --- the eigenvectors need not be orthogonal, and repeated eigenvalues may not have enough eigenvectors.
For a symmetric matrix, none of that happens. The action is pure stretching: there exist n mutually perpendicular directions (the eigenvectors \mathbf{q}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{q}_n) such that A simply scales each direction by a real factor \lambda_i. In coordinates aligned with the eigenvectors, A looks like
A\mathbf{x} = \lambda_1(\mathbf{q}_1^T\mathbf{x})\mathbf{q}_1 + \lambda_2(\mathbf{q}_2^T\mathbf{x})\mathbf{q}_2 + \cdots + \lambda_n(\mathbf{q}_n^T\mathbf{x})\mathbf{q}_n
This is the spectral decomposition A = \sum_i\lambda_i\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T in a more geometric form. The coefficient \mathbf{q}_i^T\mathbf{x} is the component of \mathbf{x} in the direction \mathbf{q}_i, and A scales that component by \lambda_i.
A symmetric matrix does not rotate. It only stretches and reflects. This geometric fact is equivalent to A^T = A.

The Proof, Done Properly
The proof I want here is the one by induction that also explains why Jordan blocks cannot appear. Symmetric Matrices has the three-part proof; I want to go deeper on the key step here and think about what the proof is actually using.
What the proof needs from symmetry. The key identity is: for any \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n,
\mathbf{y}^T(A\mathbf{x}) = (A\mathbf{y})^T\mathbf{x}
This is just \mathbf{y}^TA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}^TA^T\mathbf{x} rearranged using A = A^T. In words: A is self-adjoint with respect to the standard inner product. The inner product sees no difference between A acting on the left or the right.
This one identity implies everything:
Real eigenvalues. Suppose A\mathbf{x} = \lambda\mathbf{x} over \mathbb{C}. Apply self-adjointness to \mathbf{y} = \bar{\mathbf{x}}:
\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T(A\mathbf{x}) = (A\bar{\mathbf{x}})^T\mathbf{x} = \overline{(A\mathbf{x})}^T\mathbf{x} = \overline{\lambda\mathbf{x}}^T\mathbf{x} = \bar{\lambda}|\mathbf{x}|^2
But also \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T(A\mathbf{x}) = \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T(\lambda\mathbf{x}) = \lambda|\mathbf{x}|^2. So \lambda = \bar{\lambda}, meaning \lambda \in \mathbb{R}.
Orthogonality. Suppose A\mathbf{x} = \lambda\mathbf{x} and A\mathbf{y} = \mu\mathbf{y} with \lambda\neq\mu. Then:
\lambda(\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}) = (A\mathbf{x})^T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^T(A\mathbf{y}) = \mu(\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y})
So (\lambda-\mu)(\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}) = 0, giving \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y} = 0.
No Jordan blocks. This is the step that is usually skipped. Suppose \lambda_0 is an eigenvalue and (A - \lambda_0 I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{x} where \mathbf{x} is the eigenvector (A\mathbf{x} = \lambda_0\mathbf{x}). This would mean \mathbf{v} is a generalized eigenvector of order 2, i.e., a Jordan block of size \geq 2 exists.
Compute \mathbf{x}^T(A-\lambda_0 I)\mathbf{v} in two ways:
Way 1: \mathbf{x}^T(A-\lambda_0 I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{x} = |\mathbf{x}|^2 > 0.
Way 2: By self-adjointness of A - \lambda_0 I (which is also symmetric):
\mathbf{x}^T(A-\lambda_0 I)\mathbf{v} = ((A-\lambda_0 I)\mathbf{x})^T\mathbf{v} = (A\mathbf{x} - \lambda_0\mathbf{x})^T\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}^T\mathbf{v} = 0
Contradiction: |\mathbf{x}|^2 > 0 but also = 0. So no generalized eigenvectors of order 2 can exist. By induction, no Jordan block of size \geq 2 exists for any eigenvalue. \square
This is the clean proof that Jordan blocks are impossible for symmetric matrices. The self-adjoint property forces (A-\lambda_0 I) to be orthogonal to its own image on the eigenspace, which is impossible if the image is nonzero. Defectiveness is self-contradictory for symmetric matrices.

The Three Spectral Theorems Side by Side



































Real symmetricComplex HermitianNormalConditionA = A^TA = A^*AA^* = A^*ADiagonalizing matrixOrthogonal QUnitary UUnitary UEigenvaluesRealRealComplexKey propertySelf-adjoint over \mathbb{R}Self-adjoint over \mathbb{C}Commutes with adjoint
Normal matrices include: Hermitian (A^* = A), skew-Hermitian (A^* = -A), and unitary (A^*A = I) matrices, plus products and sums thereof. All are unitarily diagonalizable.
The rotation matrix \Omega = \begin{pmatrix}0&-1\1&0\end{pmatrix} from The Matrix Exponential and Euler Spirals is skew-symmetric (\Omega^T = -\Omega), hence normal, hence unitarily diagonalizable with eigenvalues \pm i. It is not orthogonally diagonalizable over \mathbb{R} since its eigenvalues are not real --- you need the complex eigenvectors \begin{pmatrix}1\\pm i\end{pmatrix}.

The Spectral Decomposition as a Projection Sum
The decomposition A = Q\Lambda Q^T = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T deserves its own analysis because each term P_i = \mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T is a projection.
Properties of P_i = \mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T:

P_i^2 = \mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T = \mathbf{q}_i(1)\mathbf{q}_i^T = P_i: idempotent (a projection).
P_i^T = P_i: symmetric (an orthogonal projection).
P_i\mathbf{q}_i = \mathbf{q}_i: fixes \mathbf{q}_i.
P_i\mathbf{q}_j = \mathbf{0} for j\neq i: kills all other eigenvectors.
\sum_{i=1}^n P_i = QQ^T = I: resolution of the identity.
P_iP_j = \mathbf{0} for i\neq j: projections onto orthogonal subspaces are disjoint.

The spectral theorem says A decomposes into n orthogonal rank-1 projections, each scaled by the corresponding eigenvalue:
A = \lambda_1 P_1 + \lambda_2 P_2 + \cdots + \lambda_n P_n
This is the most explicit form of the theorem. It says A acts on any vector \mathbf{x} by:

Project \mathbf{x} onto each eigendirection.
Scale each projection by the eigenvalue.
Sum.

When some eigenvalues are repeated, the corresponding projections can be grouped into a higher-rank orthogonal projection onto the full eigenspace.

Applying Functions via the Spectral Decomposition
For any function f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}, define
f(A) = \sum_{i=1}^n f(\lambda_i)P_i = Qf(\Lambda)Q^T
where f(\Lambda) = \text{diag}(f(\lambda_1),\ldots,f(\lambda_n)).
This is well-defined whenever f is defined on the spectrum of A. The examples:
A^k = \sum \lambda_i^k P_i \qquad \text{(connects to [[Matrix Powers]])}
e^{At} = \sum e^{\lambda_i t} P_i \qquad \text{(connects to [[The Matrix Exponential]])}
A^{-1} = \sum \frac{1}{\lambda_i} P_i \qquad (\text{requires all } \lambda_i \neq 0)
\log A = \sum \log(\lambda_i) P_i \qquad (\text{requires all } \lambda_i > 0)
A^{1/2} = \sum \sqrt{\lambda_i}, P_i \qquad (\text{requires all } \lambda_i \geq 0)
\sin(At) = \sum \sin(\lambda_i t) P_i
\cos(At) = \sum \cos(\lambda_i t) P_i
The last two are the solution operators for the wave equation \mathbf{u}'' = A\mathbf{u} (with A negative definite so that -A is positive definite and \sqrt{-A} makes sense):
\mathbf{u}(t) = \cos(\sqrt{-A},t),\mathbf{u}_0 + \sin(\sqrt{-A},t)(\sqrt{-A})^{-1}\mathbf{u}'_0
Every matrix function of a symmetric matrix is defined by applying the scalar function to the eigenvalues. The eigenvectors do not change, only the scaling factors. This is the power of the spectral decomposition.
Consistency check. Since f(A) = Qf(\Lambda)Q^T, we have f(A) = A when f(\lambda) = \lambda (trivial), f(A) = I when f(\lambda) = 1 (gives QIQ^T = I), and f(A)g(A) = (fg)(A) (composition of functions). The algebra of functions of A is commutative: f(A)g(A) = g(A)f(A). This is because all such matrices are simultaneously diagonalized by Q.

The Spectral Theorem and Quadratic Forms
From Symmetric Matrices, the quadratic form Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} becomes \sum_i\lambda_i c_i^2 in the eigenvector basis where c_i = \mathbf{q}_i^T\mathbf{x}.
The spectral theorem is the algebraic core of the principal axis theorem for quadratic forms: every real quadratic form can be brought to the sum-of-squares form \sum\lambda_i y_i^2 by an orthogonal change of variables \mathbf{y} = Q^T\mathbf{x}.
The sign pattern of the \lambda_i determines the geometry:
All \lambda_i > 0 (positive definite). Level set {\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} = 1} is an ellipsoid with semi-axes 1/\sqrt{\lambda_i} along \mathbf{q}_i. The largest eigenvalue corresponds to the shortest axis (most strongly constrained direction), the smallest eigenvalue to the longest axis (least constrained direction).
All \lambda_i < 0 (negative definite). Level set {\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} = -1} is an ellipsoid. No real solutions to \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} = 1.
Mixed signs (indefinite). Level set is a hyperboloid. There exist directions where \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} > 0 and directions where \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} < 0. The origin is a saddle point of the quadratic form.
Some \lambda_i = 0 (positive semidefinite or indefinite). The quadratic form is zero in those directions; the level set is unbounded along the null space of A.
This geometry is the foundation of the second-derivative test in multivariable calculus. If f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} has a critical point at \mathbf{x}^_, the Hessian H = D^2f(\mathbf{x}^_) is symmetric, and:

H \succ 0: local minimum (level sets are ellipsoids)
H \prec 0: local maximum
H indefinite: saddle point

The spectral theorem for the Hessian is the second-derivative test.

The Condition Number
For a positive definite symmetric matrix, the condition number is
\kappa(A) = \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}}
This measures how close A is to singular and how much the solution A^{-1}\mathbf{b} is amplified by perturbations in \mathbf{b}.
Specifically, if A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} and A(\mathbf{x}+\delta\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b}+\delta\mathbf{b}, then
\frac{|\delta\mathbf{x}|}{|\mathbf{x}|} \leq \kappa(A)\frac{|\delta\mathbf{b}|}{|\mathbf{b}|}
A large condition number means small perturbations in \mathbf{b} cause large changes in \mathbf{x}: the system is ill-conditioned. From the spectral decomposition:
|A| = \lambda_{\max}, \qquad |A^{-1}| = \frac{1}{\lambda_{\min}}, \qquad \kappa(A) = |A|\cdot|A^{-1}| = \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}}
The spectral theorem gives exact formulas for the norms. For a general matrix, |A| = \sigma_{\max} (largest singular value), but for symmetric positive definite matrices, singular values equal eigenvalues, so \kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}.
The Rayleigh quotient bounds from Symmetric Matrices make this concrete: A\mathbf{x} can be at most \lambda_{\max}|\mathbf{x}| and at least \lambda_{\min}|\mathbf{x}| in norm. The ratio \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min} is exactly how much the geometry of A distorts lengths.

The Courant-Fischer Min-Max Theorem
The eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix have a variational characterization that goes beyond the Rayleigh quotient for extreme eigenvalues.
Theorem (Courant-Fischer). Order the eigenvalues \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_n. Then:
\lambda_k = \min_{\dim(V)=k};\max_{\mathbf{x}\in V,,\mathbf{x}\neq 0} \frac{\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{x}} = \max_{\dim(V)=n-k+1};\min_{\mathbf{x}\in V,,\mathbf{x}\neq 0}\frac{\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{x}}
where the outer min (or max) is over all subspaces V of the given dimension.
Special cases: \lambda_1 = \min_{\mathbf{x}\neq 0} R(\mathbf{x}) and \lambda_n = \max_{\mathbf{x}\neq 0} R(\mathbf{x}), the Rayleigh quotient bounds from Symmetric Matrices.
The full theorem is the foundation for:

Interlacing theorems: if B is a principal submatrix of A, the eigenvalues of B interlace those of A.
Perturbation theory: |\lambda_k(A+E) - \lambda_k(A)| \leq |E| (Weyl’s inequality). Eigenvalues of symmetric matrices are Lipschitz continuous in the matrix.
Numerical methods: the Lanczos algorithm, conjugate gradient, and other Krylov methods converge at rates determined by the eigenvalue distribution and the condition number.


Why Symmetry Is the Right Condition
It is worth asking: what is special about A = A^T that makes all of this work?
The answer is that A = A^T is exactly the condition for A to be self-adjoint with respect to the standard inner product. Self-adjointness means
\langle A\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\rangle = \langle\mathbf{x}, A\mathbf{y}\rangle \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}
where \langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}. This is \mathbf{y}^TA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{y}, i.e., (A\mathbf{x})^T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^T(A\mathbf{y}), which is \mathbf{x}^TA^T\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{y}, i.e., A = A^T.
Self-adjointness is the algebraic condition that makes eigenvectors orthogonal (as proved above). The standard proof of the spectral theorem in functional analysis --- for compact self-adjoint operators on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces --- is the same inductive structure, just with compactness replacing finite-dimensionality to guarantee that eigenvalues exist.
The infinite-dimensional version: the Laplacian -d^2/dx^2 on [0,\pi] with Dirichlet boundary conditions is self-adjoint with respect to the L^2 inner product. Its eigenfunctions are \sin(nx) with eigenvalues n^2. The spectral theorem says these eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis of L^2([0,\pi]) --- this is exactly the Fourier sine series. The spectral theorem for symmetric matrices and the completeness of the Fourier basis are the same theorem in finite and infinite dimensions.

Summary
\boxed{A = A^T \implies A = Q\Lambda Q^T = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i,\mathbf{q}_i\mathbf{q}_i^T}
with all \lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}, all \mathbf{q}_i orthonormal. No exceptions, no Jordan blocks, no complex eigenvalues.
The spectral theorem is not just a computational tool. It is the statement that symmetric matrices are, in a precise sense, the nicest matrices: they are exactly the linear maps that are pure stretching in n orthogonal directions, with no rotation, no shearing, no defectiveness.
Everything in the theory of symmetric matrices --- quadratic forms, positive definiteness, the condition number, the Rayleigh quotient, Courant-Fischer, matrix functions, the connection to Fourier series --- follows from this one decomposition and the self-adjointness that produces it.

References: Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (Ch. 6.4); MIT 18.06 Lectures 25-26

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 17.Orthogonal Eigenvectors
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
The Central Question
Why do symmetric matrices have orthogonal eigenvectors? Not just “they do” — I want to feel why the symmetry condition forces eigenvectors from different eigenspaces to land perpendicular to each other. This is the question that actually matters here.

Setup: What We Already Know
Recall that if A\mathbf{x} = \lambda \mathbf{x}, then \mathbf{x} is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \lambda. Nothing about orthogonality yet — we are just finding directions that A stretches or flips without rotating.
Two eigenvectors \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2 corresponding to different eigenvalues \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2 need not be orthogonal in general. For a random matrix, there is no reason to expect \mathbf{x}_1 \cdot \mathbf{x}_2 = 0.
Symmetry changes everything.

The Key Theorem
Theorem (Spectral Theorem, real case). Let A be a real symmetric matrix (A = A^T). Then:

All eigenvalues of A are real.
Eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
There exists an orthonormal basis of \mathbb{R}^n consisting entirely of eigenvectors of A.

Point 3 is the full spectral theorem — it requires handling repeated eigenvalues too. I will prove points 1 and 2 here, and note what extra work point 3 needs.

Proof that Eigenvalues are Real
This always trips me up when I first see it, because it requires going to \mathbb{C}^n even though A is a real matrix.
Suppose A\mathbf{x} = \lambda \mathbf{x} with \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{C}^n, \mathbf{x} \neq 0. Take the conjugate transpose of both sides:
\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T A^T = \bar{\lambda} \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T
Since A = A^T (and A is real, so \bar{A} = A):
\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T A = \bar{\lambda} \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T
Now multiply both sides on the right by \mathbf{x}:
\bar{\mathbf{x}}^T A \mathbf{x} = \bar{\lambda} \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T \mathbf{x}
But A\mathbf{x} = \lambda \mathbf{x}, so the left side is also \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T (\lambda \mathbf{x}) = \lambda \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T \mathbf{x}.
Therefore:
\lambda \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T \mathbf{x} = \bar{\lambda} \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T \mathbf{x}
Now \bar{\mathbf{x}}^T \mathbf{x} = |\mathbf{x}|^2 > 0 (since \mathbf{x} \neq 0), so we can divide both sides by it:
\lambda = \bar{\lambda}
This means \lambda is real. Done.
The same argument works for complex Hermitian matrices (A = \bar{A}^T), which is the general version of this. Symmetric real matrices are just Hermitian matrices whose entries happen to be real.

Proof that Eigenvectors for Distinct Eigenvalues are Orthogonal
This is the one I want to really nail. Let A\mathbf{x}_1 = \lambda_1 \mathbf{x}_1 and A\mathbf{x}_2 = \lambda_2 \mathbf{x}_2 with \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2.
Step 1. Compute \mathbf{x}_2^T A \mathbf{x}_1 in two different ways using symmetry.
Using the first eigenvector equation:
\mathbf{x}_2^T A \mathbf{x}_1 = \mathbf{x}_2^T (\lambda_1 \mathbf{x}_1) = \lambda_1 (\mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{x}_1)
Using the transpose and symmetry:
\mathbf{x}_2^T A \mathbf{x}_1 = \mathbf{x}_2^T A^T \mathbf{x}_1 = (A\mathbf{x}_2)^T \mathbf{x}_1 = (\lambda_2 \mathbf{x}_2)^T \mathbf{x}_1 = \lambda_2 (\mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{x}_1)
Step 2. Set the two expressions equal:
\lambda_1 (\mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{x}_1) = \lambda_2 (\mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{x}_1)
(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)(\mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{x}_1) = 0
Step 3. Since \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2, we have \lambda_1 - \lambda_2 \neq 0, so:
\mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{x}_1 = 0
The eigenvectors are orthogonal. \square
The elegance here is in step 1: symmetry lets us “move A to the other side” — \mathbf{x}_2^T A = (A^T \mathbf{x}_2)^T = (A\mathbf{x}_2)^T — which extracts the second eigenvalue from what started as an expression involving the first. Symmetry is exactly the condition that lets you do this.

What About Repeated Eigenvalues?
The proof above only works when \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2. If a symmetric matrix has a repeated eigenvalue, the corresponding eigenspace might be multi-dimensional — but one can still choose an orthonormal basis within that eigenspace (by Gram-Schmidt). The full spectral theorem guarantees the eigenspace has the right dimension to fill out \mathbb{R}^n, but that requires a separate argument (usually the inductive proof via the fact that A restricted to the orthogonal complement of an eigenvector is again symmetric).
For now, the case of distinct eigenvalues is the heart of it. The repeated case is a technicality.

A Concrete Example
Take a 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix and watch the orthogonality fall out explicitly.
A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 2 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
The characteristic polynomial:
\det(A - \lambda I) = \det \begin{bmatrix} 2-\lambda & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 2-\lambda & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 3-\lambda \end{bmatrix}
Expanding along the third column:
= (3 - \lambda)\det\begin{bmatrix} 2-\lambda & 1 \ 1 & 2-\lambda \end{bmatrix} = (3 - \lambda)\left[(2-\lambda)^2 - 1\right]
= (3-\lambda)(4 - 4\lambda + \lambda^2 - 1) = (3-\lambda)(\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3) = (3-\lambda)(\lambda-1)(\lambda-3)
So the eigenvalues are \lambda_1 = 1, \lambda_2 = 3 (repeated).
Eigenvector for \lambda = 1:
A - I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
Row reduce: x_1 + x_2 = 0, x_3 = 0. So \mathbf{x}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ -1 \ 0 \end{bmatrix}.
Eigenvectors for \lambda = 3:
A - 3I = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & -1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
Row reduce: -x_1 + x_2 = 0 (i.e. x_1 = x_2), x_3 free. Two free variables: \mathbf{x}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 1 \ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{x}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 0 \ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
Checking orthogonality:
\mathbf{x}_1 \cdot \mathbf{x}_2 = (1)(1) + (-1)(1) + (0)(0) = 0 \checkmark \mathbf{x}_1 \cdot \mathbf{x}_3 = (1)(0) + (-1)(0) + (0)(1) = 0 \checkmark \mathbf{x}_2 \cdot \mathbf{x}_3 = (1)(0) + (1)(0) + (0)(1) = 0 \checkmark
Three mutually orthogonal eigenvectors, as the theorem demands. The repeated eigenvalue \lambda = 3 happened to give an eigenspace with an orthogonal basis directly — in general I would need Gram-Schmidt inside the eigenspace.

The Diagonalization Picture: A = Q\Lambda Q^T
Once I have an orthonormal set of eigenvectors \mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_n, I can form the orthogonal matrix:
Q = \begin{bmatrix} | & | & & | \ \mathbf{q}_1 & \mathbf{q}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{q}_n \ | & | & & | \end{bmatrix}
Since the columns are orthonormal: Q^T Q = I, so Q^{-1} = Q^T.
The diagonalization A = Q \Lambda Q^T where:
\Lambda = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ 0 & \lambda_2 & \cdots & 0 \ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \ 0 & 0 & \cdots & \lambda_n \end{bmatrix}
This is more than just diagonalization — it is a decomposition of A into a sum of rank-one projections:
A = \lambda_1 \mathbf{q}_1 \mathbf{q}_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf{q}_2 \mathbf{q}_2^T + \cdots + \lambda_n \mathbf{q}_n \mathbf{q}_n^T
Each term \mathbf{q}_i \mathbf{q}_i^T is the projection matrix onto the i-th eigenspace. This is the spectral decomposition, and it is the payoff for all of this orthogonality work. It says A acts on any vector by projecting it onto each eigenspace and scaling by the corresponding eigenvalue.

Why This Matters: Quadratic Forms
A symmetric matrix A defines a quadratic form Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}. The spectral decomposition tells us that in the eigenvector basis, this simplifies to:
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \lambda_1 y_1^2 + \lambda_2 y_2^2 + \cdots + \lambda_n y_n^2
where \mathbf{y} = Q^T \mathbf{x} are the coordinates in the eigenvector basis. The cross terms vanish precisely because the eigenvectors are orthogonal. This is the principal axis theorem. Every quadratic form is a pure sum of squares in the right coordinate system — and the right coordinate system is exactly the eigenvectors of A.
Positive definiteness is then just the condition that all \lambda_i > 0.

Things I Should Come Back To

Gram-Schmidt and how it modifies eigenvectors within a repeated eigenspace without breaking anything
The full inductive proof of the spectral theorem (Strang sketches it, Axler does it properly in Linear Algebra Done Right Ch. 9)
Connection to singular value decomposition: for a non-square matrix A, the matrices A^T A and A A^T are symmetric positive semidefinite — their eigenvectors are the right and left singular vectors of A
The complex case: Hermitian matrices and unitary diagonalization


Summary in One Line
Symmetry (A = A^T) forces eigenvectors from different eigenspaces to be orthogonal because it lets you compute \mathbf{x}_2^T A \mathbf{x}_1 in two ways — once extracting \lambda_1, once extracting \lambda_2 — and if \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2, the inner product must be zero.

References: Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th ed.), Ch. 6.4–6.5; MIT 18.06 Lectures 21–24.

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 18.Complex Eigenvalues of Real Matrices
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
Why This Topic Exists
Last note I proved that symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues. That proof implicitly acknowledged that a general real matrix might not — and that is what I want to understand now. The characteristic polynomial of an n \times n real matrix has real coefficients, but its roots can be complex. When they are, what is actually happening geometrically? And what structure do those complex eigenvalues have to obey?

The Basic Fact: Complex Roots Come in Conjugate Pairs
If A is a real matrix and \lambda = a + bi is an eigenvalue (with b \neq 0), then \bar{\lambda} = a - bi is also an eigenvalue.
Proof. Suppose A\mathbf{x} = \lambda \mathbf{x} with \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{C}^n, \mathbf{x} \neq 0. Take the complex conjugate of both sides:
\overline{A\mathbf{x}} = \overline{\lambda \mathbf{x}}
\bar{A}\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \bar{\lambda}\bar{\mathbf{x}}
But A is a real matrix, so \bar{A} = A:
A\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \bar{\lambda}\bar{\mathbf{x}}
So \bar{\mathbf{x}} is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue \bar{\lambda}. \square
Two immediate consequences:

A real matrix of odd dimension must have at least one real eigenvalue (complex roots of a real polynomial come in pairs, so an odd-degree polynomial must have at least one real root).
The complex eigenvalues appear in conjugate pairs a \pm bi, and the corresponding eigenvectors also come as conjugate pairs \mathbf{x} and \bar{\mathbf{x}}.


The Canonical Example: Rotation
The 2 \times 2 rotation matrix is the clearest place to see all of this.
A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}
This rotates every vector in \mathbb{R}^2 by angle \theta. Over \mathbb{R}, no nonzero vector is sent to a scalar multiple of itself (unless \theta = 0 or \theta = \pi), so there are no real eigenvectors. The geometry is telling you something: real eigenvectors require a direction that is preserved by the transformation, and pure rotation preserves no direction.
Computing the eigenvalues:
\det(A - \lambda I) = \det\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta - \lambda & -\sin\theta \ \sin\theta & \cos\theta - \lambda \end{bmatrix}
= (\cos\theta - \lambda)^2 + \sin^2\theta = \lambda^2 - 2\cos\theta \cdot \lambda + 1
Using the quadratic formula:
\lambda = \frac{2\cos\theta \pm \sqrt{4\cos^2\theta - 4}}{2} = \cos\theta \pm \sqrt{\cos^2\theta - 1} = \cos\theta \pm i\sin\theta
So:
\lambda_1 = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta = e^{i\theta}, \qquad \lambda_2 = \cos\theta - i\sin\theta = e^{-i\theta}
Conjugate pair, as expected. Both lie on the unit circle in \mathbb{C}. The modulus |\lambda| = 1 reflects the fact that rotation preserves lengths — the eigenvalues encode this in their absolute value.
The eigenvectors:
For \lambda_1 = e^{i\theta}, solve (A - \lambda_1 I)\mathbf{x} = 0:
\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta - e^{i\theta} & -\sin\theta \ \sin\theta & \cos\theta - e^{i\theta} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 0 \end{bmatrix}
Since \cos\theta - e^{i\theta} = -i\sin\theta, the first row gives:
-i\sin\theta \cdot x_1 - \sin\theta \cdot x_2 = 0 \implies x_2 = -ix_1
So the eigenvector is \mathbf{x}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ -i \end{bmatrix}, and by conjugation \mathbf{x}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ i \end{bmatrix} for \lambda_2.
These are complex vectors — there is no real direction in \mathbb{R}^2 that rotation fixes. The eigenvectors live in \mathbb{C}^2 and have no direct geometric interpretation in the original real plane.

What the Complex Eigenvalue a + bi Encodes
For a general 2 \times 2 real matrix with complex eigenvalues \lambda = a \pm bi, write \lambda in polar form:
\lambda = r e^{i\theta}, \qquad r = |\lambda| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}, \qquad \theta = \arctan(b/a)

r is the scaling factor: how much the transformation stretches or contracts.
\theta is the rotation angle: the amount of rotation mixed in.

The pure rotation matrix above had r = 1. A matrix that both scales and rotates would have r \neq 1. This is the geometric content: complex eigenvalues signal that the transformation acts like a rotation-scaling in some 2D invariant subspace.

The Real Canonical Form (Block Diagonalization)
Over \mathbb{C}, a matrix with eigenvalues \lambda = a \pm bi diagonalizes to:
\begin{bmatrix} a + bi & 0 \ 0 & a - bi \end{bmatrix}
But I am working over \mathbb{R} and I want a real form. The trick: instead of diagonalizing, block-diagonalize using the real and imaginary parts.
Let \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{u} + i\mathbf{v} be the eigenvector for \lambda = a + bi (where \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n). Then from A\mathbf{x} = \lambda \mathbf{x}:
A(\mathbf{u} + i\mathbf{v}) = (a + bi)(\mathbf{u} + i\mathbf{v})
Expand the right side:
(a + bi)(\mathbf{u} + i\mathbf{v}) = a\mathbf{u} - b\mathbf{v} + i(b\mathbf{u} + a\mathbf{v})
Matching real and imaginary parts:
A\mathbf{u} = a\mathbf{u} - b\mathbf{v} A\mathbf{v} = b\mathbf{u} + a\mathbf{v}
This says that A acts on the real subspace \text{span}{\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}} and, in the basis {\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}}, the matrix of this action is:
\begin{bmatrix} a & b \ -b & a \end{bmatrix}
This is the real 2 \times 2 block corresponding to the complex conjugate pair a \pm bi. It is a rotation-scaling matrix: factor out r = \sqrt{a^2+b^2},
r\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}
So in the basis of real and imaginary parts of the eigenvector, A genuinely rotates and scales. The complex eigenvalue is not an artifact — it is capturing real geometric behavior that just cannot be seen from a single real eigenvector.

Full Real Block Diagonal Form
For an n \times n real matrix with eigenvalues:

Real eigenvalues \lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_k
Complex conjugate pairs a_j \pm b_j i for j = 1, \ldots, m (so k + 2m = n)

There exists a real invertible matrix M such that A = M B M^{-1} where B is block diagonal:
B = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & & & & & \ & \ddots & & & & \ & & \lambda_k & & & \ & & & \begin{bmatrix} a_1 & b_1 \ -b_1 & a_1 \end{bmatrix} & & \ & & & & \ddots & \ & & & & & \begin{bmatrix} a_m & b_m \ -b_m & a_m \end{bmatrix} \end{bmatrix}
Real eigenvalues give 1 \times 1 blocks; complex conjugate pairs give 2 \times 2 rotation-scaling blocks. No complex numbers appear anywhere in B or M.

A Worked Example
A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
This is rotation by 90° (i.e. \theta = \pi/2, so \cos\theta = 0, \sin\theta = 1).
Characteristic polynomial:
\det(A - \lambda I) = \det\begin{bmatrix} -\lambda & -1 \ 1 & -\lambda \end{bmatrix} = \lambda^2 + 1
Eigenvalues: \lambda = \pm i (i.e. a = 0, b = 1, r = 1, \theta = \pi/2).
Eigenvector for \lambda = i:
(A - iI)\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} -i & -1 \ 1 & -i \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = 0
First row: -ix_1 - x_2 = 0 \implies x_2 = -ix_1. Take x_1 = 1:
\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ -i \end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{u}} + i\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \ -1 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{v}}
Verify the real block form. With a = 0, b = 1:
A\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 1 \end{bmatrix} = a\mathbf{u} - b\mathbf{v} = 0\cdot\begin{bmatrix}1\0\end{bmatrix} - 1\cdot\begin{bmatrix}0\-1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0\1\end{bmatrix} \checkmark
A\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \ -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 0 \end{bmatrix} = b\mathbf{u} + a\mathbf{v} = 1\cdot\begin{bmatrix}1\0\end{bmatrix} + 0\cdot\begin{bmatrix}0\-1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1\0\end{bmatrix} \checkmark
The block is \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, which is rotation by -\pi/2… wait, that seems off by a sign. Let me recheck.
The matrix of A in the basis {\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}} is found by writing A\mathbf{u} and A\mathbf{v} in that basis:
A\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 1 \end{bmatrix} = 0 \cdot \mathbf{u} + (-1) \cdot \mathbf{v}, since \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix}0\-1\end{bmatrix}.
A\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix}1\0\end{bmatrix} = 1 \cdot \mathbf{u} + 0 \cdot \mathbf{v}.
So the block is \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. This matches \begin{bmatrix} a & b \ -b & a \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. The sign convention in the formula is consistent — the off-diagonal entries are b and -b, which here are 1 and -1. Good.

Connection to Powers and Exponentials
If A has eigenvalues re^{\pm i\theta}, then A^k has eigenvalues r^k e^{\pm ik\theta}. In the real block picture, A^k corresponds to a block
r^k \begin{bmatrix} \cos(k\theta) & \sin(k\theta) \ -\sin(k\theta) & \cos(k\theta) \end{bmatrix}
This is exactly what you expect: applying a rotation-scaling k times scales by r^k and rotates by k\theta.
For the matrix exponential e^{At}, the complex eigenvalue a + bi contributes e^{(a+bi)t} = e^{at}(\cos bt + i\sin bt). In real block form the corresponding block of e^{At} is:
e^{at}\begin{bmatrix} \cos(bt) & \sin(bt) \ -\sin(bt) & \cos(bt) \end{bmatrix}
This is the oscillatory behavior you see in solutions to systems of ODEs with complex eigenvalues: e^{at} is the envelope (growing if a > 0, decaying if a < 0, constant if a = 0), and \cos bt, \sin bt are the oscillations. The real part of the eigenvalue governs stability; the imaginary part governs frequency.

Why Symmetric Matrices Avoid This
Pulling the thread from the last note: symmetric matrices have \lambda = \bar{\lambda} for every eigenvalue, which forces b = 0. The imaginary part is zero. No rotation blocks — only real 1 \times 1 blocks. Symmetry is the condition that kills all the oscillatory behavior. A symmetric matrix only stretches and reflects, never rotates.
Antisymmetric matrices (A = -A^T), on the other hand, have purely imaginary eigenvalues (a = 0), giving pure rotation with r = 1 — no growth, no decay, just oscillation.

Things to Come Back To

The Jordan form over \mathbb{C} when eigenvalues repeat — the block diagonal picture breaks down and you get Jordan blocks instead of diagonal entries.
Stability of linear ODE systems: eigenvalue real parts determine whether solutions blow up, decay, or oscillate at constant amplitude.
Normal matrices: the class of matrices (including symmetric, antisymmetric, and orthogonal) that diagonalize over \mathbb{C} with an orthonormal basis. Symmetric is the real special case.


Summary
A real matrix with complex eigenvalues a \pm bi cannot be diagonalized over \mathbb{R}, but it can be block-diagonalized with 2 \times 2 rotation-scaling blocks \begin{bmatrix} a & b \ -b & a \end{bmatrix}. The complex eigenvalue is not a failure of the real picture — it is the fingerprint of genuine rotational behavior in a 2D invariant subspace. The modulus r = \sqrt{a^2+b^2} measures scaling; the argument \theta = \arctan(b/a) measures rotation. Complex roots of a real characteristic polynomial always come in conjugate pairs because taking the complex conjugate of an eigenvector equation produces the conjugate eigenvector equation — and nothing about the real matrix breaks that symmetry.

References: Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th ed.), Ch. 6.3; MIT 18.06 Lecture 21.

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 19.Eigenvalues versus Pivots
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
Why Compare These at All?
Pivots come from elimination. Eigenvalues come from the characteristic polynomial. On the surface they feel like they belong to completely different parts of the subject — one is a computational procedure, the other is a spectral property. But for symmetric matrices they are measuring the same underlying thing from two different angles, and the signs of the two sets of numbers agree in a precise sense.
This is not a coincidence. It is a theorem, and understanding it properly ties together the two biggest threads of 18.06.

Quick Recall: What Each One Is
Pivots are the diagonal entries that appear during Gaussian elimination, after all row operations that use rows above the current row. For a symmetric positive definite matrix, elimination can always be done without row exchanges, and the pivots are the numbers d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_n in the factorization A = LDL^T.
Eigenvalues are the roots of \det(A - \lambda I) = 0. For a real symmetric matrix they are all real, and they are the diagonal entries of \Lambda in A = Q\Lambda Q^T.
Two very different procedures. Same matrix. What do they have in common?

The Connection: Signs Agree
Theorem. Let A be a real symmetric matrix. Then the number of positive pivots equals the number of positive eigenvalues, and the number of negative pivots equals the number of negative eigenvalues.
In particular:

A is positive definite \iff all pivots > 0 \iff all eigenvalues > 0.
A is negative definite \iff all pivots < 0 \iff all eigenvalues < 0.
A is indefinite \iff pivots (or eigenvalues) have mixed signs.

This is the Law of Inertia (Sylvester’s law of inertia, to be precise): the number of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues is an invariant of the matrix — it does not change under any congruence transformation A \mapsto S^T A S for invertible S.

The Product Relationship
Before proving the sign-count, notice a simpler relationship that holds for any square matrix:
Product of pivots = determinant of A.
This is immediate from A = LDL^T: since \det(L) = \det(L^T) = 1 (triangular with 1s on diagonal), \det(A) = \det(D) = d_1 d_2 \cdots d_n.
Product of eigenvalues = determinant of A.
This follows from the characteristic polynomial: \det(A - \lambda I) = (\lambda_1 - \lambda)(\lambda_2 - \lambda)\cdots(\lambda_n - \lambda), so setting \lambda = 0 gives \det(A) = \lambda_1 \lambda_2 \cdots \lambda_n.
So both products equal \det(A). But they are generally not equal entry-by-entry — individual pivots and eigenvalues are different numbers. What is preserved is only the count of signs.
Trace relationship as well:
Sum of pivots is generally not \text{tr}(A).
Sum of eigenvalues = \text{tr}(A).
(The trace equals the sum of diagonal entries, and also equals the sum of eigenvalues — immediate from the characteristic polynomial by comparing the coefficient of \lambda^{n-1}.)
So eigenvalues own the trace; both own the determinant (via product).

Why the Sign Counts Agree: The Congruence Argument
This is the part worth understanding carefully.
The LDL^T factorization of a symmetric matrix A is a congruence: A = L D L^T where L is lower triangular with 1s on the diagonal. Congruence means A = S^T D S for S = L^T (invertible). The diagonal matrix D has the pivots on its diagonal.
Sylvester’s law of inertia says: two symmetric matrices that are congruent have the same number of positive, negative, and zero diagonal entries when diagonalized. More precisely, the number of positive eigenvalues is preserved under congruence — it is an invariant of the congruence class.
Now, D = \text{diag}(d_1, \ldots, d_n) is already diagonal, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, which are the pivots. And A is congruent to D. So the number of positive eigenvalues of A equals the number of positive eigenvalues of D, which equals the number of positive pivots.
Proof of Sylvester’s law of inertia (sketch). Suppose A and B = S^T A S are congruent with S invertible. Suppose for contradiction that A has p positive eigenvalues but B has fewer. Then B has a subspace of dimension > n - p on which \mathbf{x}^T B \mathbf{x} \leq 0. Pulling back through S (which is a bijection on \mathbb{R}^n) gives a subspace of the same dimension on which \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x} \leq 0. But by the spectral theorem, A with p positive eigenvalues has a p-dimensional subspace on which \mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x} > 0. A dimension count shows these two subspaces must intersect nontrivially — contradiction. \square
The formal version of this argument uses the min-max characterization of eigenvalues (Courant-Fischer), which I have not covered yet. But the idea is dimension counting: you cannot have a large subspace of positivity and a large subspace of non-positivity coexist in \mathbb{R}^n without overlapping.

A Concrete Example
A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}
Finding the pivots via elimination:
First pivot: d_1 = 2 (the (1,1) entry).
Eliminate: subtract \frac{2}{2} = 1 times row 1 from row 2:
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 - 1\cdot 2 & 5 - 1\cdot 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
Second pivot: d_2 = 3.
Pivots: d_1 = 2, d_2 = 3. Both positive.
Finding the eigenvalues:
\det(A - \lambda I) = (2-\lambda)(5-\lambda) - 4 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 6 = (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 6)
Eigenvalues: \lambda_1 = 1, \lambda_2 = 6. Both positive.
Checking the relationships:
Product: d_1 d_2 = 6 = \lambda_1 \lambda_2 = \det(A). \checkmark
Sum: d_1 + d_2 = 5 \neq 7 = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \text{tr}(A).
Sign count: both pivots positive, both eigenvalues positive. \checkmark

Another Example: Indefinite Matrix
A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
Pivots:
First pivot: d_1 = 1.
Eliminate: subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2:
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & 1 - 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}
Second pivot: d_2 = -3.
Pivots: 1 and -3. One positive, one negative.
Eigenvalues:
\det(A - \lambda I) = (1-\lambda)^2 - 4 = \lambda^2 - 2\lambda - 3 = (\lambda - 3)(\lambda + 1)
Eigenvalues: \lambda_1 = 3, \lambda_2 = -1. One positive, one negative.
Sign count: one positive pivot, one positive eigenvalue; one negative pivot, one negative eigenvalue. \checkmark
Product: d_1 d_2 = -3 = \lambda_1 \lambda_2 = \det(A). \checkmark
The individual numbers 1, -3 (pivots) and 3, -1 (eigenvalues) are completely different. But the sign pattern +, - is the same.

The Subdeterminant Test: A Third Characterization
For positive definiteness, there is a third equivalent condition involving the upper-left submatrices (also called leading principal submatrices).
Define A_k as the k \times k upper-left submatrix of A:
A_1 = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} \end{bmatrix}, \quad A_2 = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} \ a_{21} & a_{22} \end{bmatrix}, \quad \ldots, \quad A_n = A
Theorem. A is positive definite \iff \det(A_k) > 0 for all k = 1, \ldots, n.
The connection to pivots: the pivots are the ratios of consecutive subdeterminants:
d_k = \frac{\det(A_k)}{\det(A_{k-1})}
(with \det(A_0) = 1 by convention). So the pivots are all positive iff all the subdeterminants are positive, iff all the eigenvalues are positive. Three equivalent tests for the same thing.
For the example A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \ 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}: \det(A_1) = 2 > 0, \det(A_2) = 10 - 4 = 6 > 0. Positive definite. \checkmark

The Full Picture for Symmetric Matrices



































PropertyPivotsEigenvaluesSubdeterminantsPositive definiteall d_k > 0all \lambda_k > 0all \det(A_k) > 0Positive semidefiniteall d_k \geq 0all \lambda_k \geq 0all \det(A_k) \geq 0Negative definiteall d_k < 0all \lambda_k < 0alternating signsIndefinitemixed signsmixed signs—
The alternating sign condition for negative definiteness: \det(A_1) < 0, \det(A_2) > 0, \det(A_3) < 0, etc. This follows because \det(A_k) = d_1 d_2 \cdots d_k, and if all d_k < 0 then d_1 d_2 \cdots d_k has sign (-1)^k.

Why Pivots Are Often More Useful Computationally
Eigenvalues require solving \det(A - \lambda I) = 0, which for large n is a degree-n polynomial — completely impractical. Pivots come from elimination, which costs O(n^3) and is stable. So in practice, if I want to check positive definiteness of a large matrix, I run Cholesky factorization (the symmetric positive definite version of LU) and check whether it succeeds without encountering a zero or negative pivot. No eigenvalue computation needed.
Eigenvalues win theoretically — they give more information (actual values, not just signs) and they are basis-independent (trace, determinant). Pivots win computationally.

Connection to A = LDL^T More Explicitly
Write out the LDL^T factorization for a 3\times 3 case to make it concrete. Suppose:
A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \ b & d & e \ c & e & f \end{bmatrix}
After elimination:
L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ b/a & 1 & 0 \ c/a & \ell_{32} & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad D = \begin{bmatrix} d_1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & d_2 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & d_3 \end{bmatrix}
where d_1 = a, d_2 = d - b^2/a, d_3 = f - c^2/a - (e - bc/a)^2/d_2. Each pivot depends on all the entries above it — which is why pivots and eigenvalues are individually different numbers even though their sign patterns match.
The factorization A = L D L^T says A is congruent to D. Sylvester’s law then guarantees the sign counts of D‘s diagonal (the pivots) match the sign counts of A‘s eigenvalues.

Things to Come Back To

The min-max (Courant-Fischer) theorem: it characterizes eigenvalues as solutions to variational problems over subspaces, and gives the cleanest proof of Sylvester’s law.
Cholesky factorization: for positive definite A, D has all positive entries so we can write D = \sqrt{D}\sqrt{D} and absorb the square roots into L, giving A = R^T R for upper triangular R. This is Cholesky.
Semidefinite case: when a pivot is zero, elimination stalls. The rank of A equals the number of nonzero pivots, which also equals the number of nonzero eigenvalues.


Summary
Pivots and eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are not the same numbers, but they carry the same sign information. This follows from Sylvester’s law of inertia: congruence (A \mapsto S^T A S) preserves the count of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues, and the LDL^T factorization is exactly a congruence that transforms A into the diagonal matrix of its pivots. Three tests — signs of pivots, signs of eigenvalues, and signs of leading subdeterminants — are all equivalent for symmetric matrices. The practical upshot is that positive definiteness can be checked by elimination alone, without ever computing a single eigenvalue.

References: Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (5th ed.), Ch. 6.4–6.5; MIT 18.06 Lectures 21, 27.
