01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 27.Eigenvalues of Large Matrices
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
For a 2 \times 2 or 3 \times 3 matrix, computing eigenvalues by hand via \det(A - \lambda I) = 0 is painful but feasible. For a 100 \times 100 matrix it is completely out of the question. The characteristic polynomial has degree 100, and there is no general algebraic formula for roots of polynomials of degree 5 or higher (Abel-Ruffini). Even numerically, forming the characteristic polynomial and then finding its roots is a terrible algorithm — the polynomial’s coefficients are catastrophically sensitive to perturbations.
This note is about what you do instead: how to locate, estimate, and compute eigenvalues of large matrices without touching the characteristic polynomial.

What We Can and Cannot Do
Cannot do (for large n):

Compute \det(A - \lambda I) symbolically
Find all eigenvalues exactly in finitely many arithmetic steps (Abel-Ruffini)
Diagonalize explicitly by solving n coupled equations

Can do:

Locate eigenvalues in regions of the complex plane (Gershgorin)
Bound the spectral radius
Compute the largest eigenvalue iteratively (Power Method)
Compute all eigenvalues numerically to machine precision (QR Algorithm)
Exploit structure (symmetry, sparsity, tridiagonal form) heavily

The shift from “solve” to “iterate” is the fundamental move in large-scale linear algebra.

Gershgorin Circle Theorem
This is the first and most elegant tool: a completely non-iterative way to locate all eigenvalues using only the matrix entries.
Theorem (Gershgorin, 1931). Let A be an n \times n complex matrix. For each i = 1, \ldots, n, define the Gershgorin disc
D_i = \left{ z \in \mathbb{C} : |z - a_{ii}| \leq R_i \right}, \qquad R_i = \sum_{j \neq i} |a_{ij}|
That is: center at the diagonal entry a_{ii}, radius equal to the sum of absolute values of the off-diagonal entries in row i.
Then every eigenvalue of A lies in the union \bigcup_{i=1}^n D_i.
Proof. Let \lambda be an eigenvalue with eigenvector x \neq 0. Let k be the index where |x_k| = |x|_\infty (the component of largest absolute value). From Ax = \lambda x, the k-th row gives
\sum_{j=1}^n a_{kj} x_j = \lambda x_k
(\lambda - a_{kk}) x_k = \sum_{j \neq k} a_{kj} x_j
Taking absolute values:
|\lambda - a_{kk}| |x_k| \leq \sum_{j \neq k} |a_{kj}| |x_j| \leq |x_k| \sum_{j \neq k} |a_{kj}| = R_k |x_k|
Since |x_k| > 0, divide through:
|\lambda - a_{kk}| \leq R_k
So \lambda \in D_k \subseteq \bigcup_i D_i. \square
Example. Take
A = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 1 & 0 \ 2 & 8 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}
Gershgorin discs:

Row 1: center 10, radius |1| + |0| = 1. Disc: |z - 10| \leq 1, so \lambda \in [9, 11].
Row 2: center 8, radius |2| + |1| = 3. Disc: |z - 8| \leq 3, so \lambda \in [5, 11].
Row 3: center 5, radius |1| + |0| = 1. Disc: |z - 5| \leq 1, so \lambda \in [4, 6].

All eigenvalues lie in [4, 6] \cup [5, 11]. Since the matrix is symmetric with positive diagonal, they are all real and positive — so the matrix is positive definite, confirmed without computing a single eigenvalue.
Refinement. If a connected component of \bigcup_i D_i consists of exactly k discs, then it contains exactly k eigenvalues (counted with multiplicity). This follows from a continuity argument — perturb A to a diagonal matrix and track where eigenvalues go.

Diagonal Dominance and the Gershgorin Corollary
A matrix is strictly diagonally dominant if |a_{ii}| > R_i for every i. By Gershgorin, all eigenvalues lie in discs that do not contain 0, so 0 is not an eigenvalue, so A is invertible.
Moreover, if A is strictly diagonally dominant with positive diagonal entries, then every Gershgorin disc lies in the right half-plane, so all eigenvalues have positive real part. If A is also symmetric, all eigenvalues are real and positive: A is positive definite.
This is a completely elementary sufficient condition for positive definiteness that requires no computation.

The Power Method
The Power Method computes the dominant eigenvalue — the eigenvalue of largest absolute value, assuming it is unique.
Setup. Assume A has eigenvalues |\lambda_1| > |\lambda_2| \geq \cdots \geq |\lambda_n|. We want \lambda_1.
Algorithm. Start with an arbitrary vector b_0 (not orthogonal to the eigenvector v_1 — almost any random vector works). Iterate:
b_{k+1} = \frac{Ab_k}{|Ab_k|}
At each step, multiply by A and renormalize. The Rayleigh quotient
\mu_k = \frac{b_k^T A b_k}{b_k^T b_k}
converges to \lambda_1.
Why it works. Expand b_0 in the eigenvector basis:
b_0 = c_1 v_1 + c_2 v_2 + \cdots + c_n v_n
Then (ignoring renormalization for clarity):
A^k b_0 = c_1 \lambda_1^k v_1 + c_2 \lambda_2^k v_2 + \cdots + c_n \lambda_n^k v_n = \lambda_1^k \left( c_1 v_1 + c_2 \left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right)^k v_2 + \cdots \right)
Since |\lambda_2 / \lambda_1| < 1, all terms except the first decay geometrically. The direction of A^k b_0 converges to v_1 at rate |\lambda_2 / \lambda_1|^k.
Rate of convergence. The error after k steps is O\left(\left|\dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right|^k\right). If \lambda_2 is close to \lambda_1, convergence is slow. This is the key weakness.
Shift to accelerate. If you know \lambda_1 \approx \mu, apply the power method to (A - \mu I)^{-1} instead. Its dominant eigenvalue is (\lambda_j - \mu)^{-1} where \lambda_j is the eigenvalue closest to \mu. By shifting close to a target eigenvalue, you can make the ratio arbitrarily favorable. This is inverse iteration.

Inverse Iteration and the Rayleigh Quotient Iteration
Inverse iteration. Fix a shift \sigma near a target eigenvalue \lambda_j. Solve
(A - \sigma I) b_{k+1} = b_k, \qquad \text{then normalize}
at each step. This converges to the eigenvector for the eigenvalue closest to \sigma, at rate \left|\dfrac{\lambda_j - \sigma}{\lambda_\ell - \sigma}\right|^k where \lambda_\ell is the second-closest eigenvalue to \sigma.
Rayleigh quotient iteration. Update the shift at each step using the current Rayleigh quotient:
\sigma_k = \frac{b_k^T A b_k}{b_k^T b_k}
then solve (A - \sigma_k I)b_{k+1} = b_k. For symmetric matrices, this converges cubically once close to an eigenvector. Practically instantaneous near convergence.
The cost per step is solving a linear system with the shifted matrix — for dense matrices this is O(n^3) once (via LU factorization) then O(n^2) per step.

Reduction to Hessenberg Form
Before running any iterative algorithm on a large dense matrix, reduce it to upper Hessenberg form (for general matrices) or tridiagonal form (for symmetric matrices). A Hessenberg matrix has zeros below the first subdiagonal:
H = \begin{bmatrix} * & * & * & * & * \ * & * & * & * & * \ 0 & * & * & * & * \ 0 & 0 & * & * & * \ 0 & 0 & 0 & * & * \end{bmatrix}
For symmetric A, the Hessenberg reduction produces a symmetric tridiagonal matrix:
T = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha_1 & \beta_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ \beta_1 & \alpha_2 & \beta_2 & \cdots & 0 \ 0 & \beta_2 & \alpha_3 & \cdots & 0 \ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \ 0 & 0 & \cdots & \beta_{n-1} & \alpha_n \end{bmatrix}
This reduction is exact (not iterative), accomplished via n-2 Householder reflections in O(n^3) time. The resulting H (or T) is similar to A, so has the same eigenvalues. Every subsequent step of the QR algorithm costs only O(n^2) for Hessenberg matrices (versus O(n^3) for full matrices), making the reduction a one-time investment that pays off over many iterations.

The QR Algorithm
This is the algorithm actually used to compute all eigenvalues of a dense matrix to machine precision. It is one of the ten greatest algorithms of the 20th century.
Basic QR iteration. Start with A_0 = A.
At step k:

Factor A_k = Q_k R_k (QR decomposition: Q_k orthogonal, R_k upper triangular)
Set A_{k+1} = R_k Q_k

Note: A_{k+1} = R_k Q_k = Q_k^T (Q_k R_k) Q_k = Q_k^T A_k Q_k, so each A_{k+1} is orthogonally similar to A_k, hence similar to A. All eigenvalues are preserved exactly.
Convergence. Under mild conditions, A_k converges to a block upper triangular matrix (Schur form) whose diagonal blocks are 1 \times 1 (real eigenvalues) or 2 \times 2 (complex conjugate pairs). The subdiagonal entries decay to zero.
The convergence rate of the (i,i+1) subdiagonal entry is O\left(\left|\dfrac{\lambda_{i+1}}{\lambda_i}\right|^k\right) — the same ratio as the power method, which makes sense: QR iteration is essentially running the power method simultaneously for all eigenvalues.
Practical QR algorithm (what LAPACK actually does):

Reduce A to Hessenberg form H = Q_0^T A Q_0 via Householder reflections. One-time cost O(n^3).
Apply QR iteration with shifts: at each step, choose a shift \sigma_k (e.g., the bottom-right entry of A_k, or a Wilkinson shift) and factor A_k - \sigma_k I = Q_k R_k, then set A_{k+1} = R_k Q_k + \sigma_k I.
Deflate: once a subdiagonal entry is negligible, split the matrix and work on smaller pieces.

With Wilkinson shifts, the convergence is typically cubic for the last subdiagonal entry. In practice, for a symmetric tridiagonal n \times n matrix, the full eigendecomposition takes O(n^2) iterations total.

Special Structure: Sparse and Symmetric Matrices
For very large matrices (think n = 10^6) arising in PDE discretizations, finite element methods, or graph problems, even storing the full matrix is impossible. These matrices are sparse: most entries are zero. The algorithms of choice are Krylov subspace methods.
Lanczos algorithm (symmetric case). The key observation: A, Ab_0, A^2 b_0, \ldots span a Krylov subspace. Instead of iterating randomly, build an orthonormal basis for \mathcal{K}_k = \text{span}{b_0, Ab_0, \ldots, A^{k-1}b_0} via a three-term recurrence (for symmetric A):
\beta_{j+1} q_{j+1} = Aq_j - \alpha_j q_j - \beta_j q_{j-1}
where \alpha_j = q_j^T A q_j and \beta_{j+1} = |Aq_j - \alpha_j q_j - \beta_j q_{j-1}|.
After k steps, you have a k \times k tridiagonal matrix T_k with diagonal \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_k and off-diagonal \beta_2, \ldots, \beta_k. Its eigenvalues (Ritz values) approximate the extreme eigenvalues of A.
Key property. The Lanczos algorithm only requires matrix-vector products Aq. For a sparse matrix stored in compressed format, each product costs O(\text{nnz}) where nnz is the number of nonzero entries. You never form A explicitly or do anything that costs more than a matrix-vector multiply per step.
For a matrix with n = 10^6 and nnz = 10^7, you might need k = 100 Lanczos steps to get good approximations of the 10 largest eigenvalues — a total cost of 10^9 operations, entirely feasible.
Arnoldi algorithm (non-symmetric case). Generalization of Lanczos to non-symmetric matrices. Produces an upper Hessenberg projection of A onto the Krylov subspace. Eigenvalues of the Hessenberg projection approximate eigenvalues of A.

Bounding the Spectral Radius
The spectral radius of A is \rho(A) = \max_i |\lambda_i|. Several elementary bounds:
From matrix norms. For any induced matrix norm |\cdot|:
\rho(A) \leq |A|
The spectral radius is the infimum of |A| over all consistent matrix norms. In particular:
\rho(A) \leq |A|_1 = \max_j \sum_i |a_{ij}| \qquad \text{(max column sum)} \rho(A) \leq |A|_\infty = \max_i \sum_j |a_{ij}| \qquad \text{(max row sum)} \rho(A) \leq |A|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j} a_{ij}^2} \qquad \text{(Frobenius norm)}
From Gershgorin. \rho(A) \leq \max_i (|a_{ii}| + R_i), the radius of the outermost Gershgorin disc.
Perron-Frobenius (for non-negative matrices). If A has all non-negative entries and is irreducible, then the spectral radius is a simple eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector. This is fundamental in Markov chains, PageRank, and network analysis — the dominant eigenvalue of a transition matrix is 1, and the corresponding eigenvector is the stationary distribution.

Why the Characteristic Polynomial is a Bad Algorithm
Worth making this explicit. Suppose you form p(\lambda) = \det(A - \lambda I) for a 20 \times 20 matrix and try to find its roots numerically. The coefficients of p involve sums of products of up to 20 entries of A. These coefficients can be astronomically large or small. A tiny perturbation in a coefficient (say, due to floating point) can shift a root by a huge amount.
The classic demonstration: Wilkinson’s polynomial \prod_{k=1}^{20}(\lambda - k) has roots 1, 2, \ldots, 20. Perturbing the coefficient of \lambda^{19} by 2^{-23} moves one root from the real axis to a complex value far from any integer. The roots are wildly sensitive to the coefficients.
The QR algorithm avoids this entirely by working with the matrix directly, using orthogonal transformations that are perfectly conditioned (orthogonal matrices have condition number 1).

Summary: Which Algorithm for Which Problem


















































ProblemMatrix TypeAlgorithmAll eigenvalues, dense, small (n \lesssim 10^3)GeneralQR algorithm (after Hessenberg reduction)All eigenvalues, dense, symmetricSymmetricTridiagonalize, then QR or divide-and-conquerLargest eigenvalueAnyPower MethodEigenvalue near a target \sigmaAnyInverse iteration with shiftFew extreme eigenvalues, large sparseSymmetricLanczos algorithmFew eigenvalues, large sparse, non-symmetricGeneralArnoldi / GMRESLocate eigenvalues without computingAnyGershgorin circlesPositive definiteness checkSymmetricGershgorin + diagonal dominance

A Personal Remark
The gap between “find eigenvalues of a 3 \times 3 matrix” and “find eigenvalues of a 1000 \times 1000 matrix” is not just computational — it is conceptual. The characteristic polynomial approach, which feels so clean theoretically, becomes completely useless. You are forced to think differently: iteratively, approximately, exploiting structure.
The QR algorithm is the right way to think about this. It does not solve an equation; it deforms the matrix continuously, step by step, toward a form where eigenvalues are readable. The eigenvalues were always there in the diagonal entries — you just needed to conjugate away the off-diagonal noise. That is a very different philosophy from “find roots of a polynomial.”
Strang’s 18.06 touches on the Power Method and mentions QR, but the real depth here is in numerical linear algebra (Trefethen and Bau is the reference to eventually read).

Previous: Jordan Normal Form Related: Similar Matrices, Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors, Positive Definite Matrices, QR Decomposition Future: Krylov subspaces in depth, Lanczos in depth, preconditioning

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 28.Singular Value Decomposition
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
The singular value decomposition is the decomposition. Not the most elegant, not the most specialized — the most universally useful factorization in all of applied linear algebra. Every matrix has one, rectangular or square, singular or invertible, real or complex. It reveals the complete geometric action of a linear map, and it underlies an enormous range of applications: least squares, low-rank approximation, PCA, image compression, pseudoinverse, numerical rank detection.
If eigendecomposition answers “what does A do to its own eigenvectors,” SVD answers “what does A do to any vector, in a geometrically clean way.” The two questions are different, and SVD is the deeper answer.

The Statement
Theorem (SVD). Let A be an m \times n real matrix. Then there exist:

U: an m \times m orthogonal matrix
\Sigma: an m \times n matrix with non-negative entries \sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_r > 0 on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, where r = \text{rank}(A)
V: an n \times n orthogonal matrix

such that
A = U \Sigma V^T
The diagonal entries \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r are the singular values of A. The columns of U are the left singular vectors, the columns of V are the right singular vectors.
Written out in full, \Sigma looks like this for m > n with rank r < n:
\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ 0 & \sigma_2 & \cdots & 0 \ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \ 0 & 0 & \cdots & \sigma_r \ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ \vdots & & & \vdots \ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \end{bmatrix}
r nonzero diagonal entries, everything else zero.

The Geometric Picture
This is the insight that makes SVD worth understanding deeply, not just as a formula.
Every linear map A: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m acts on the unit sphere S^{n-1} \subset \mathbb{R}^n and maps it to an ellipsoid in \mathbb{R}^m. The SVD makes this precise:
A = U \Sigma V^T
Read right to left:


V^T rotates (and possibly reflects) the unit sphere in \mathbb{R}^n. Since V is orthogonal, V^T is a rigid motion — it maps the sphere to itself, just reorienting it. Specifically, V^T aligns the right singular vectors v_1, \ldots, v_n with the coordinate axes.


\Sigma stretches along the coordinate axes by factors \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r (and collapses the last n - r directions to zero). The unit sphere becomes an ellipsoid with semi-axes of length \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r.


U rotates the resulting ellipsoid in \mathbb{R}^m, aligning its axes with the left singular vectors u_1, \ldots, u_m.


So: rotation, then stretching, then rotation. The singular values are the lengths of the semi-axes of the image ellipsoid. This is the complete description of what A does.
The eigendecomposition A = S \Lambda S^{-1} uses the same basis twice (eigenvectors for both input and output) and requires A to be square and diagonalizable. The SVD uses two separate orthonormal bases — one for the input space \mathbb{R}^n, one for the output space \mathbb{R}^m — and works for every matrix without exception.

Existence: The Proof
Proof. We construct U, \Sigma, V explicitly.
Consider the symmetric positive semidefinite matrix A^T A (size n \times n). By the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices, it has a full orthonormal eigenvector basis v_1, \ldots, v_n with eigenvalues \lambda_1 \geq \cdots \geq \lambda_n \geq 0.
Define \sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i} for i = 1, \ldots, n. These are non-negative. Let r be the number of nonzero \sigma_i.
For i = 1, \ldots, r, define
u_i = \frac{Av_i}{\sigma_i}
Claim: {u_1, \ldots, u_r} is an orthonormal set in \mathbb{R}^m.
Proof of claim: u_i^T u_j = \frac{(Av_i)^T(Av_j)}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} = \frac{v_i^T A^T A v_j}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} = \frac{v_i^T (\lambda_j v_j)}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} = \frac{\lambda_j}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} v_i^T v_j = \frac{\sigma_j^2}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} \delta_{ij} = \sigma_j / \sigma_i \cdot \delta_{ij}
For i = j: u_i^T u_i = \sigma_i / \sigma_i = 1. For i \neq j: u_i^T u_j = 0. Orthonormal. \checkmark
Extend {u_1, \ldots, u_r} to a full orthonormal basis {u_1, \ldots, u_m} of \mathbb{R}^m (by Gram-Schmidt, say). Let U = [u_1 \cdots u_m] and V = [v_1 \cdots v_n].
Now check AV = U\Sigma:

For i \leq r: Av_i = \sigma_i u_i by definition.
For i > r: \sigma_i = 0, so A^T A v_i = 0, which gives |Av_i|^2 = v_i^T A^T A v_i = 0, so Av_i = 0.

In both cases, Av_i = \sigma_i u_i (with \sigma_i = 0 for i > r). Since V is orthogonal, A = AV V^T = U\Sigma V^T. \square

Connection to Eigenvalues
The singular values of A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of A^T A (equivalently, of AA^T, which has the same nonzero eigenvalues).
A^T A = (U\Sigma V^T)^T (U\Sigma V^T) = V\Sigma^T U^T U \Sigma V^T = V(\Sigma^T \Sigma)V^T
So V diagonalizes A^T A with eigenvalues \sigma_1^2, \ldots, \sigma_r^2, 0, \ldots, 0.
AA^T = U\Sigma V^T V \Sigma^T U^T = U(\Sigma \Sigma^T) U^T
So U diagonalizes AA^T with the same nonzero eigenvalues.
This is the computational entry point: to find the SVD of A, diagonalize A^T A.
Warning. Forming A^T A explicitly and diagonalizing it is numerically unstable for ill-conditioned matrices — squaring the matrix squares the condition number. Production SVD algorithms (e.g., in LAPACK) work with A directly via bidiagonalization and do not form A^T A.

The Four Fundamental Subspaces via SVD
SVD makes the four fundamental subspaces completely explicit.
Let A = U\Sigma V^T with rank r.

Column space C(A) = \text{span}{u_1, \ldots, u_r}: the first r columns of U.
Left null space N(A^T) = \text{span}{u_{r+1}, \ldots, u_m}: the last m - r columns of U.
Row space C(A^T) = \text{span}{v_1, \ldots, v_r}: the first r columns of V.
Null space N(A) = \text{span}{v_{r+1}, \ldots, v_n}: the last n - r columns of V.

And crucially: A maps v_i \mapsto \sigma_i u_i for i \leq r, and v_i \mapsto 0 for i > r. The SVD is the four fundamental subspaces theorem given explicit, orthonormal bases. Strang’s “big picture” of linear algebra — the two orthogonal complements, the map between them — is exactly what \Sigma encodes.

Reduced (Thin) SVD
For an m \times n matrix with m \geq n, the full SVD has U of size m \times m, which is large. The reduced SVD (also called economy or thin SVD) keeps only the first r columns:
A = U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T
where:

U_r is m \times r (first r columns of U, orthonormal but not square)
\Sigma_r is r \times r diagonal with \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r
V_r is n \times r (first r columns of V)

This contains all the information. The remaining columns of U span the left null space and multiply zero columns of \Sigma — they contribute nothing to A.

Outer Product Form and Low-Rank Approximation
The most powerful way to write the SVD:
A = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i u_i v_i^T
Each term \sigma_i u_i v_i^T is a rank-one matrix — an outer product. The SVD expresses A as a sum of r rank-one matrices, weighted by the singular values.
This is the foundation of low-rank approximation.
Eckart-Young Theorem. The best rank-k approximation to A in both the spectral norm and the Frobenius norm is
A_k = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i u_i v_i^T
obtained by keeping only the first k terms. The approximation error is:
|A - A_k|_2 = \sigma_{k+1} |A - A_k|_F = \sqrt{\sigma_{k+1}^2 + \cdots + \sigma_r^2}
No rank-k matrix is closer to A (in either norm) than A_k. This is a non-trivial theorem — the proof uses the minimax characterization of singular values.
Example: image compression. An m \times n grayscale image is a matrix of pixel values. Its SVD gives a hierarchy of rank-one images, each capturing a coarser or finer feature. Keeping the top k terms requires storing k(m + n + 1) numbers instead of mn. For a 1000 \times 1000 image with rank k = 50, you store 100{,}050 numbers instead of 1{,}000{,}000 — a 10\times compression — with the truncation error controlled by \sigma_{51}.

A Worked Example
Let
A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
This is 3 \times 2, rank 2. Compute A^T A:
A^T A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 0 \ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
Eigenvalues of A^T A: \lambda_1 = 9, \lambda_2 = 4. Eigenvectors: v_1 = e_1, v_2 = e_2. So
\sigma_1 = 3, \quad \sigma_2 = 2, \qquad V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I_2
Compute u_1 = Av_1 / \sigma_1 = (3, 0, 0)^T / 3 = (1, 0, 0)^T and u_2 = Av_2 / \sigma_2 = (0, 2, 0)^T / 2 = (0, 1, 0)^T.
Extend to a basis of \mathbb{R}^3: u_3 = (0, 0, 1)^T.
U = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 1 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I_3, \qquad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 0 & 2 \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
So A = I_3 \cdot \Sigma \cdot I_2^T = \Sigma. Trivially correct. A slightly more interesting example:
A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
A^T A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
Eigenvalues of \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}: characteristic polynomial (2-\lambda)^2 - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = 3 or \lambda = 1.
\sigma_1 = \sqrt{3}, \quad \sigma_2 = 1
Eigenvectors:


\lambda = 3: (A^T A - 3I)v = 0 \Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}v = 0 \Rightarrow v_1 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1\1\end{bmatrix}


\lambda = 1: (A^T A - I)v = 0 \Rightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}v = 0 \Rightarrow v_2 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}1\-1\end{bmatrix}


V = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
Now compute u_1 = Av_1 / \sigma_1:
Av_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\1\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}2\1\1\end{bmatrix}
u_1 = \frac{Av_1}{\sigma_1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \begin{bmatrix}2\1\1\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{bmatrix}2\1\1\end{bmatrix}
Av_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0\-1\1\end{bmatrix}, \quad u_2 = \frac{Av_2}{\sigma_2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix}0\-1\1\end{bmatrix}
Find u_3 orthogonal to u_1, u_2 (e.g., via cross product or Gram-Schmidt):
u_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}-1\1\1\end{bmatrix}
(Verify: u_3^T u_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}(-2 + 1 + 1) = 0, u_3^T u_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(0 - 1 + 1) = 0. Good.)
U = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{6}} & 0 & \dfrac{-1}{\sqrt{3}} \[8pt] \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \dfrac{-1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \[8pt] \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{3} & 0 \ 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad V = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}

The Pseudoinverse
For an invertible square matrix, A^{-1} = V\Sigma^{-1}U^T. The SVD makes this obvious: (U\Sigma V^T)^{-1} = V\Sigma^{-1}U^T.
For a rectangular or rank-deficient matrix, this formula still makes sense if we replace \Sigma^{-1} with \Sigma^+: invert the nonzero singular values and leave zeros as zeros.
\Sigma^+ = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sigma_1 & & & \ & \ddots & & \ & & 1/\sigma_r & \ & & & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{(transposed shape: } n \times m \text{)}
The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse is
A^+ = V\Sigma^+ U^T
Properties:

AA^+ A = A
A^+ A A^+ = A^+
(AA^+)^T = AA^+
(A^+ A)^T = A^+ A

Least squares. The least squares solution to Ax = b (minimizing |Ax - b|_2) with minimum norm is \hat{x} = A^+ b. This is the solution that lies entirely in the row space of A.
Explicitly:
\hat{x} = A^+ b = V\Sigma^+ U^T b = \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{u_i^T b}{\sigma_i} v_i
Each term projects b onto u_i, scales by 1/\sigma_i, and contributes v_i to the solution. Small singular values amplify noise in b — this is the source of ill-conditioning in least squares.

Condition Number
The condition number of A (for linear systems or least squares) is
\kappa(A) = \frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_r}
the ratio of largest to smallest singular value. It measures how much a relative perturbation in b can be amplified in the solution x. A large condition number means the problem is ill-conditioned: small errors in data can produce large errors in the answer.
For a square invertible matrix: \kappa(A) = |A|_2 |A^{-1}|_2 = \sigma_1 / \sigma_n.
The matrix is effectively rank-deficient (numerically singular) if \sigma_r / \sigma_1 is smaller than machine epsilon \approx 10^{-16}. This is how production software determines numerical rank — not by checking whether entries are exactly zero, but by thresholding singular values.

Spectral Norm and Frobenius Norm
SVD gives clean expressions for two important matrix norms:
|A|_2 = \sigma_1 \qquad \text{(spectral norm = largest singular value)}
|A|_F = \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \cdots + \sigma_r^2} \qquad \text{(Frobenius norm)}
The spectral norm is the maximum stretching factor: |A|_2 = \max_{|x|=1} |Ax|, achieved when x = v_1.
The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of all matrix entries: |A|_F^2 = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}^2 = \text{tr}(A^T A).

Principal Component Analysis
PCA is applied SVD. Given a data matrix X of size m \times n (m observations, n features), center the data so columns have mean zero. Then compute the SVD:
X = U\Sigma V^T
The columns of V (right singular vectors) are the principal components — the orthogonal directions of maximum variance in the data. The i-th principal component v_i captures variance proportional to \sigma_i^2. The low-rank approximation X_k is the best rank-k summary of the data in the least-squares sense.
Equivalently, PCA diagonalizes the sample covariance matrix X^T X / (m-1). The eigenvectors of X^T X are the columns of V. SVD gives you PCA without ever forming the covariance matrix — numerically preferable for high-dimensional data.

Comparison: SVD vs Eigendecomposition













































PropertyEigendecomposition A = S\Lambda S^{-1}SVD A = U\Sigma V^TExists forSquare, diagonalizable matricesEvery matrixShapen \times n onlym \times n, any shapeBasis matricesS, S^{-1} (not necessarily orthogonal)U, V (orthogonal)Diagonal entriesEigenvalues (complex in general)Singular values (real, non-negative, always)Same basis input/outputYesNo (different bases for domain and codomain)Geometric meaningScaling along eigenvectorsRotation, stretch, rotationNumerical stabilityPoor if S is ill-conditionedExcellent (U, V orthogonal, condition number 1)
For a symmetric positive definite matrix A, the two coincide: A = Q\Lambda Q^T where Q is orthogonal (spectral theorem), and this is simultaneously the eigendecomposition and the SVD with \sigma_i = \lambda_i.

A Personal Remark
The first time you see SVD, it looks like a more complicated eigendecomposition for rectangular matrices. That undersells it completely.
The eigendecomposition is about invariant directions — vectors the matrix does not rotate, only scales. It is a special property of specific vectors. SVD is about the geometry of the map itself, for every input, without exception. The singular values are not a property of special vectors; they are a property of the transformation.
The Eckart-Young theorem is the moment where SVD reveals its depth. The fact that truncating the SVD gives the best low-rank approximation — not just a good one, the best possible one — in a strong norm sense, is genuinely non-obvious. It says that the information in a matrix is stratified: \sigma_1 captures the most, \sigma_2 the next most, and so on, in a precise quantitative sense. That is why SVD is at the heart of data science, signal processing, and numerical linear algebra simultaneously.
Strang calls it the most important factorization in applied linear algebra. He is right.

Previous: Eigenvalues of Large Matrices Next: Pseudoinverse and Least Squares, Principal Component Analysis Related: Similar Matrices, Four Fundamental Subspaces, Positive Definite Matrices, QR Decomposition

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 29.Image Compression via SVD
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
This note is the concrete payoff of Singular Value Decomposition. We established the Eckart-Young theorem abstractly — the rank-k truncation A_k = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i u_i v_i^T is the best rank-k approximation to A in both the spectral and Frobenius norms. Here we make that statement visible and quantitative in the context of images.
A grayscale image is a matrix. Compressing the image is approximating that matrix with a low-rank one. Everything else is bookkeeping.

The Setup
A grayscale image of resolution m \times n is exactly an m \times n matrix A where entry A_{ij} \in [0, 255] (or [0,1] after normalization) is the pixel intensity at row i, column j.
Storing A naively requires mn numbers.
The SVD gives
A = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i u_i v_i^T
where r = \text{rank}(A), u_i \in \mathbb{R}^m, v_i \in \mathbb{R}^n, and \sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_r > 0.
The rank-k approximation is
A_k = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i u_i v_i^T
Storing A_k requires: k values of \sigma_i, k vectors u_i of length m, k vectors v_i of length n. Total:
k(1 + m + n) \approx k(m + n) \text{ numbers}
Compression ratio:
\frac{\text{storage of } A_k}{\text{storage of } A} = \frac{k(m + n)}{mn}
For this to be less than 1 (i.e., to actually compress), we need
k < \frac{mn}{m+n}
For a square n \times n image, this means k < n/2. For a 1000 \times 1000 image:

k = 10: store 20{,}000 numbers instead of 1{,}000{,}000. Compression ratio 0.02.
k = 50: store 100{,}000 numbers. Ratio 0.10.
k = 100: store 200{,}000 numbers. Ratio 0.20.

The question is always: how large does k need to be before A_k is visually indistinguishable from A?

What Makes an Image Compressible
Not all matrices are equally compressible. The SVD always exists, but the compression is only good if the singular values decay fast — if most of the “energy” of the image is concentrated in the first few singular values.
Define the energy of the full image and the rank-k approximation:
|A|_F^2 = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i^2, \qquad |A_k|_F^2 = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i^2
The fraction of energy captured by the rank-k approximation:
\frac{|A_k|_F^2}{|A|_F^2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i^2}
The approximation error in Frobenius norm:
|A - A_k|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i=k+1}^r \sigma_i^2}
Natural images (photographs, portraits, landscapes) tend to have rapidly decaying singular values — the image has spatial coherence, so nearby pixels are correlated, and most variation lives in low-frequency structure. Text, random noise, and fine-grained textures compress poorly.
Structured images — smooth gradients, faces, skies — compress extremely well. A photograph of a blue sky is nearly rank-1: almost every row is the same vector.

The Rank-One Term
It is worth understanding what a single term \sigma_i u_i v_i^T looks like visually.
u_i v_i^T is a rank-one matrix. Every row is a scalar multiple of v_i^T, and the scalar for row j is (u_i)_j. So the image encoded by u_i v_i^T has a single “pattern” v_i repeated across rows, modulated by the weights in u_i.

v_i captures a horizontal pattern (a spatial frequency or shape across columns).
u_i captures how that pattern varies across rows.
\sigma_i scales how strongly that pattern contributes.

The first term \sigma_1 u_1 v_1^T captures the dominant pattern: typically the overall brightness distribution of the image. Subsequent terms add finer and finer corrections.
This is not coincidence — it is the content of the Eckart-Young theorem. The greedy decomposition into rank-one terms, ordered by \sigma_i, is provably optimal. You cannot do better by choosing a different set of rank-one matrices.

Color Images
A color image is three matrices stacked: one each for the red, green, and blue channels. Compress each channel separately:
R = U_R \Sigma_R V_R^T, \quad G = U_G \Sigma_G V_G^T, \quad B = U_B \Sigma_B V_B^T
Storage for rank-k approximation of a color image:
3k(m + n) \text{ numbers vs. } 3mn
Compression ratio is the same as the grayscale case, just with a factor of 3 throughout. Alternatively, convert to a color space like YCbCr (luminance + two chrominance channels) and compress the chrominance channels more aggressively, since the human eye is more sensitive to luminance variation — this is what JPEG does in spirit.

SVD vs. JPEG: What’s Actually Used
It is worth being honest about where SVD image compression sits relative to production formats.
JPEG does not use SVD. It uses the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT): divide the image into 8 \times 8 blocks, apply the DCT to each block (a fixed orthogonal transform, not data-dependent), then quantize and entropy-code the coefficients. The DCT basis functions are fixed sinusoids, not the data-adapted singular vectors.
Why JPEG uses DCT instead of SVD:

DCT basis is fixed and universal — encoder and decoder both know it, no need to transmit U and V.
SVD is data-adaptive — you must transmit the singular vectors along with the singular values, which costs storage. For small k, the overhead of transmitting U and V may dominate.
DCT on 8 \times 8 blocks is O(n^2 \log n) via the Fast Fourier Transform; SVD on the full image is O(mn \cdot \min(m,n)), which is expensive.

Where SVD compression wins:

When the image has strong global structure (the singular vectors capture global patterns, not just 8 \times 8 local ones).
As a teaching and analysis tool — SVD compression is a clean, mathematically transparent demonstration of what low-rank approximation means.
In applications like video compression, where the matrix is a difference frame (highly low-rank), or in hyperspectral imaging.

JPEG 2000 uses wavelet transforms instead of DCT — closer in spirit to SVD (multiresolution, globally supported basis functions) but still with a fixed basis.
The honest summary: SVD gives the optimal low-rank approximation in the Frobenius sense, but “optimal” in that algebraic sense is not the same as “best for human visual perception.” Perceptual image quality is not measured by Frobenius norm. JPEG’s quantization tables are tuned to human visual sensitivity, not matrix norms.

The Numerical Experiment You Should Run
If you have access to Python:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image
 
# Load image and convert to grayscale float matrix
img = np.array(Image.open("photo.jpg").convert("L"), dtype=float)
m, n = img.shape
 
# Compute SVD
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(img, full_matrices=False)
 
# Plot singular value decay
plt.semilogy(s)
plt.xlabel("index $i$")
plt.ylabel("$\\sigma_i$")
plt.title("Singular value decay")
plt.show()
 
# Rank-k approximations
for k in [5, 20, 50, 100]:
    Ak = U[:, :k] @ np.diag(s[:k]) @ Vt[:k, :]
    energy = np.sum(s[:k]**2) / np.sum(s**2)
    ratio = k * (m + n) / (m * n)
    print(f"k={k}: energy={energy:.4f}, compression ratio={ratio:.4f}")
    plt.imshow(Ak, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255)
    plt.title(f"Rank-{k} approximation")
    plt.axis("off")
    plt.show()
What to look for:

The singular value plot on a log scale. For a natural photograph, you typically see a rapid initial decay followed by a long, slowly decaying tail. The “knee” of the curve is roughly where truncation becomes visually acceptable.
At k = 5, the image should be recognizable but blurry. At k = 50, often near-indistinguishable from the original at normal viewing distance.
Compare a photograph (smooth, compressible) against a random noise image (flat singular value spectrum, incompressible). The noise image requires k \approx r to look right.

The singular value spectrum is a fingerprint of the image’s complexity. A nearly flat spectrum means the image has no low-rank structure. A steeply decaying spectrum means the image is well-approximated by a few rank-one matrices.

Quantifying the Error Precisely
Let E_k = |A - A_k|_F / |A|_F be the relative approximation error. Then:
E_k = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=k+1}^r \sigma_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i^2}} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i^2}}
This is computable from the singular values alone, without looking at the image. Given a target error tolerance \varepsilon, the minimum k needed is the smallest integer such that
\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i^2 \geq (1 - \varepsilon^2) \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i^2
This is the principled way to choose k: decide on an acceptable error level, then read off k from the singular value spectrum. It is completely determined by the data.

Connection to Randomized SVD
For very large images or matrices, computing the full SVD is expensive: O(mn \cdot \min(m,n)). If you only need the top-k singular vectors/values, you do not need the full decomposition.
Randomized SVD (Halko, Martinsson, Tropp 2011) computes an approximate rank-k SVD in O(mn \log k) time:

Draw a random n \times (k + p) Gaussian matrix \Omega (with p a small oversampling parameter, e.g. p = 10).
Form Y = A\Omega (size m \times (k+p)): k+p random linear combinations of columns of A.
Compute Q: orthonormal basis for the columns of Y (via QR).
Form B = Q^T A (size (k+p) \times n).
Compute the SVD of the small matrix B = \hat{U}\hat{\Sigma}\hat{V}^T.
Set U = Q\hat{U}.

The output U\hat{\Sigma}\hat{V}^T is a near-optimal rank-k approximation to A with high probability. The key insight: Y = A\Omega captures the dominant column space of A because the random matrix is unlikely to miss directions with large singular values. The subsequent steps are just cleaning up the approximation.
For a 10^4 \times 10^4 image, full SVD costs \sim 10^{12} operations. Randomized SVD for top-50 components costs \sim 10^7. This is why randomized linear algebra has become central to large-scale data science.

Summary

































QuantityFormulaFull storagemnRank-k storagek(m + n) (plus k singular values)Compression ratiok(m+n) / mnApproximation error (Frobenius)\sqrt{\sum_{i > k} \sigma_i^2}Energy captured\sum_{i \leq k} \sigma_i^2 ,/, \sum_i \sigma_i^2Optimal rank-k approxA_k = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i u_i v_i^T (Eckart-Young)
The deeper point: image compression is not special. The same mathematics applies to any matrix you want to approximate with a low-rank one — recommender systems (user-item rating matrices), genomics (gene expression matrices), natural language (word co-occurrence matrices). SVD finds the low-dimensional structure hiding in high-dimensional data. Images are just the most visually intuitive instance of this.

Previous: Singular Value Decomposition Related: Eckart-Young Theorem, Principal Component Analysis, Pseudoinverse and Least Squares See also: Halko, Martinsson, Tropp — “Finding Structure with Randomness” (2011)

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 30.The Bases and SVD
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
This note is about what the SVD actually is at the level of bases — not the formula A = U\Sigma V^T, which is a computational object, but the statement that every linear map A: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m has a pair of orthonormal bases, one for the input space and one for the output space, in which A acts by pure scaling.
That sentence is the theorem. Everything else is unpacking it.

The Central Question
Eigendecomposition asks: is there a single basis {v_1, \ldots, v_n} for \mathbb{R}^n such that A maps each v_i to a scalar multiple of itself? If yes, A = S\Lambda S^{-1}.
This requires A to be square, and it fails when A is defective. Even when it succeeds, the basis S is generally not orthonormal — the eigenvectors of a non-symmetric matrix are not perpendicular.
SVD asks a different and more natural question: is there an orthonormal basis {v_1, \ldots, v_n} for \mathbb{R}^n (the input space) and an orthonormal basis {u_1, \ldots, u_m} for \mathbb{R}^m (the output space) such that
Av_i = \sigma_i u_i
for every i? The answer is always yes, for every matrix A, rectangular or square, any rank.
This is the content of SVD. Not a factorization formula — a statement about the existence of good bases.

Why Two Bases, Not One
For a square matrix A: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n, input and output live in the same space. So it is meaningful to ask for a single basis that works for both — this is eigendecomposition.
For a rectangular matrix A: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m with m \neq n, input and output live in different spaces. There is no such thing as a single basis. You must choose a basis for \mathbb{R}^n and a separate basis for \mathbb{R}^m. The question becomes: can these two bases be chosen so that A acts diagonally between them?
SVD says yes, and more: they can be chosen to be orthonormal.
Even for square A, this is a stronger and cleaner statement than eigendecomposition. Eigendecomposition demands that A maps v_i to a multiple of v_i — the same vector. SVD only demands that A maps v_i to a multiple of u_i, a potentially different vector. The relaxation is what makes it universal.

The Diagram
Write the action of A as a commutative diagram:
\mathbb{R}^n \xrightarrow{A} \mathbb{R}^m
In the V-basis for \mathbb{R}^n and the U-basis for \mathbb{R}^m, the map A becomes \Sigma:
\begin{array}{ccc} \mathbb{R}^n & \xrightarrow{A} & \mathbb{R}^m \ !!!!!!!!!!!!!{}_{V}\uparrow\phantom{V} & & \phantom{U}\uparrow{}_{U}!!!!!!!!!!!! \ \mathbb{R}^n & \xrightarrow{\Sigma} & \mathbb{R}^m \end{array}
More precisely: in coordinates relative to the standard basis, the map is A. Change to the V-basis in the domain and the U-basis in the codomain, and the map becomes \Sigma — diagonal, pure scaling.
The formula A = U\Sigma V^T says exactly this: V^T is the change-of-basis matrix from standard to V-coordinates in \mathbb{R}^n, \Sigma is the map in those coordinates, and U is the change-of-basis matrix from U-coordinates back to standard in \mathbb{R}^m.
A = \underbrace{U}_{\text{change basis back}} \underbrace{\Sigma}_{\text{scale}} \underbrace{V^T}_{\text{change basis}}

The Four Subspaces, Revisited
The bases U and V do not treat all of \mathbb{R}^n and \mathbb{R}^m symmetrically. Let r = \text{rank}(A).
Partition the columns of V into two groups:
V = \begin{bmatrix} \underbrace{v_1 \cdots v_r}_{\text{row space of }A} & \underbrace{v_{r+1} \cdots v_n}_{\text{null space of }A} \end{bmatrix}
Partition the columns of U into two groups:
U = \begin{bmatrix} \underbrace{u_1 \cdots u_r}_{\text{column space of }A} & \underbrace{u_{r+1} \cdots u_m}_{\text{left null space of }A} \end{bmatrix}
The action of A:

Av_i = \sigma_i u_i for i = 1, \ldots, r — the row space maps isomorphically onto the column space, with scaling by \sigma_i.
Av_i = 0 for i = r+1, \ldots, n — the null space maps to zero.
u_{r+1}, \ldots, u_m span the left null space: A^T u_i = 0 for i > r.

The four fundamental subspaces are not just described by the SVD — they are given by it, with explicit orthonormal bases. The abstract orthogonality relations (row space \perp null space, column space \perp left null space) become visible: they hold because V and U are orthogonal matrices, so their columns are automatically perpendicular.
Strang’s “big picture” is:
\underbrace{C(A^T)}_{\text{row space}} \xrightarrow{A,\ \text{invertible}} \underbrace{C(A)}_{\text{column space}} \underbrace{N(A)}_{\text{null space}} \xrightarrow{A} \underbrace{{0}}
SVD gives this picture with explicit orthonormal bases: {v_1,\ldots,v_r} for the row space, {v_{r+1},\ldots,v_n} for the null space, {u_1,\ldots,u_r} for the column space, {u_{r+1},\ldots,u_m} for the left null space. And the map from row space to column space is not just “invertible” — it is diagonal with factors \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r.

Choosing Bases: A Sequence of Decisions
It is illuminating to think about how much freedom you have at each step in constructing the SVD bases, and where the constraints come from.
Step 1. Diagonalize A^T A (symmetric, positive semidefinite). By the spectral theorem, this can always be done with an orthonormal eigenvector basis. The eigenvectors are the right singular vectors v_1, \ldots, v_n, the columns of V.
The eigenvalues \sigma_i^2 \geq 0 are uniquely determined (if all distinct). The eigenvectors v_i are determined up to sign (if eigenvalues are distinct) or up to an orthogonal transformation within each eigenspace (if there are repeated eigenvalues).
Step 2. For i \leq r, define u_i = Av_i / \sigma_i. These are forced — no choice. Given the choice of v_i, the u_i are determined (up to the sign of v_i, which propagates to u_i).
Step 3. Extend {u_1, \ldots, u_r} to a full orthonormal basis of \mathbb{R}^m. The vectors u_{r+1}, \ldots, u_m spanning the left null space can be chosen freely (any orthonormal basis for the left null space works). They do not affect A at all, since \Sigma has zeros in those rows.
Conclusion. The singular values \sigma_1 \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_r are uniquely determined by A — they are invariants of the linear map, independent of any basis choice. The singular vectors have freedom only in degenerate cases (repeated singular values) or in the null space parts. In the generic case (all singular values distinct), U and V are determined up to signing of columns.

What Changes Between Eigendecomposition and SVD
Let A be a symmetric positive definite n \times n matrix. Then:

Spectral theorem: A = Q\Lambda Q^T, with Q orthogonal and \Lambda diagonal with positive entries.
SVD: A = U\Sigma V^T.

For a symmetric positive definite matrix, these coincide: U = V = Q and \Sigma = \Lambda. The input and output bases are the same because A maps its own eigenvectors to multiples of themselves — input and output are in the same space and the eigenvectors are orthogonal.
Now break symmetry. Take a non-symmetric square matrix A with real eigenvalues. Eigendecomposition gives A = S\Lambda S^{-1}, but S is generally not orthogonal — the eigenvectors are not perpendicular. SVD gives A = U\Sigma V^T with U \neq V (the input and output bases differ) and both orthogonal.
The eigendecomposition is asking: in what basis does A look diagonal? SVD is asking: in what pair of bases does A look diagonal? The extra freedom of choosing two separate bases (rather than one) is exactly what makes SVD universally possible and orthonormal.

The Basis Interpretation of Low-Rank Approximation
The outer product form A = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i u_i v_i^T now has a clear basis interpretation.
Each pair (u_i, v_i) is a “mode”: v_i is a direction in input space, u_i is the corresponding direction in output space, and \sigma_i is how strongly A couples them. The rank-k approximation
A_k = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i u_i v_i^T
keeps only the k most strongly coupled input-output direction pairs. It discards all modes with coupling strength \sigma_{k+1}, \ldots, \sigma_r.
The Eckart-Young theorem says this is the best you can do with rank k: no other choice of k input-output pairs (not necessarily orthonormal, not necessarily from the SVD) can give a smaller Frobenius or spectral norm error. The SVD modes are sorted in descending order of importance, and truncation from the bottom is optimal.
This is why the SVD basis is special. Any orthonormal basis {w_1, \ldots, w_n} for \mathbb{R}^n and {z_1, \ldots, z_m} for \mathbb{R}^m would let you write
A = \sum_{i,j} c_{ij} z_i w_j^T
for some coefficients c_{ij} — but this expansion is not diagonal in general (c_{ij} \neq 0 for i \neq j). Only the SVD bases produce a diagonal expansion: c_{ij} = \sigma_i \delta_{ij}. The input directions v_i and output directions u_i are matched one-to-one by A with no cross-coupling.

Change of Basis: Putting It All Together
Let me write this out pedantically once, because I want to be completely clear about what V^T and U are doing.
Let x \in \mathbb{R}^n be a vector. Write x in the V-basis:
x = \sum_{i=1}^n \hat{x}_i v_i, \qquad \hat{x}_i = v_i^T x
In coordinates: \hat{x} = V^T x. Now apply A:
Ax = A\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{x}_i v_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^r \hat{x}_i \sigma_i u_i
(Terms i > r vanish since Av_i = 0.) Write this in the U-basis: the i-th coordinate in the U-basis of Ax is u_i^T(Ax) = \hat{x}_i \sigma_i. So in coordinates:
\widehat{Ax} = \Sigma \hat{x}
where \widehat{Ax} = U^T(Ax) is the U-coordinate representation of Ax and \hat{x} = V^T x is the V-coordinate representation of x.
The diagram in coordinates:
\hat{x} = V^T x \xrightarrow{\Sigma} \widehat{Ax} = \Sigma \hat{x} \xrightarrow{U} Ax = U\widehat{Ax}
Composing: Ax = U\Sigma V^T x = Ax. Consistent.
The change of basis from standard to V-coordinates is V^T (because V is orthogonal: (V^T)^{-1} = V). In the V-basis, A acts as \Sigma. Then U converts back from U-coordinates to standard coordinates.

Why Orthonormality of the Bases Matters
The bases U and V are not just any two bases that diagonalize A. They are orthonormal. This has consequences everywhere:
Inverse is transpose. U^{-1} = U^T and V^{-1} = V^T. The change-of-basis computation costs a matrix-vector multiply, not a solve.
Norms are preserved. |Vx| = |x| for any x. Rotating a vector does not change its length. So all the stretching done by A is encoded entirely in \Sigma, not distributed across U and V.
Numerical stability. Orthogonal matrices have condition number 1 — they are perfectly conditioned. Computing U^T b or V^T x in floating point introduces no amplification of errors. This is why SVD-based algorithms (least squares via SVD, pseudoinverse computation, PCA) are numerically stable even when A is ill-conditioned.
Geometric cleanliness. The singular values \sigma_i = |Av_i| are the lengths of the images of the right singular vectors. This is a geometric quantity — the amount of stretching in direction v_i. It is well-defined and does not depend on how we scale v_i (since v_i is a unit vector).
If U and V were not orthonormal, the singular values would depend on the normalization of the basis vectors and would lose their geometric meaning.

The Closest Orthogonal Matrix Problem
A beautiful application of the SVD basis interpretation: given a square matrix A, find the orthogonal matrix Q closest to A in Frobenius norm.
Solution. Let A = U\Sigma V^T be the SVD. The closest orthogonal matrix is
Q = UV^T
Proof sketch. We want to minimize |A - Q|_F over orthogonal Q. Write
|A - Q|_F^2 = |U\Sigma V^T - Q|_F^2 = |\Sigma - U^T Q V|_F^2
(using the fact that Frobenius norm is invariant under orthogonal multiplication). Since U^T Q V is orthogonal (product of orthogonal matrices), the problem reduces to finding the orthogonal matrix P = U^T Q V closest to \Sigma in Frobenius norm. Since \Sigma is diagonal with non-negative entries, the closest orthogonal matrix to \Sigma is I (set each diagonal of P to +1). So P = I, giving Q = UV^T. \square
This is the orthogonal Procrustes problem and it arises in computer vision (aligning point clouds), robotics (finding the best rotation), and structural biology (aligning protein structures).

Summary: The Three Levels of Understanding SVD
Level 1 — Formula. A = U\Sigma V^T with U, V orthogonal and \Sigma diagonal with non-negative entries. This is what you write on an exam.
Level 2 — Factorization. A^T A = V\Sigma^2 V^T, so V diagonalizes A^T A, and u_i = Av_i/\sigma_i. This is how you compute it.
Level 3 — Bases. There exist orthonormal bases {v_i} for \mathbb{R}^n and {u_i} for \mathbb{R}^m such that Av_i = \sigma_i u_i. In these coordinates, A acts as pure scaling. This is what it means.
Level 3 is the right way to think about it. The SVD is the statement that every linear map, no matter how complicated, becomes a diagonal map in the right pair of orthonormal coordinates. The singular values are the diagonal entries — the intrinsic scaling factors of the map, independent of any coordinate choice.

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 31.SVD of a Singular Matrix
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
A singular matrix is one where \det(A) = 0, equivalently where \text{rank}(A) < n for an n \times n matrix. The eigendecomposition breaks down badly here — \lambda = 0 is an eigenvalue with a non-trivial null space, and if the geometric multiplicity is less than the algebraic multiplicity, there is not even a full set of eigenvectors. Diagonalization fails.
SVD does not break down. It does not even flinch. A singular matrix has an SVD just like any other matrix — the only difference is that some singular values are exactly zero, and those zeros encode the singularity precisely.
This note is about what the SVD of a singular matrix looks like, what the zero singular values mean geometrically, and how SVD is the right language for understanding rank, null spaces, and near-singularity.

What Singularity Means for the SVD
Let A be n \times n with \text{rank}(A) = r < n. The SVD is
A = U\Sigma V^T = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i u_i v_i^T
where \sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_r > 0 and \sigma_{r+1} = \cdots = \sigma_n = 0.
Written out fully, \Sigma is:
\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ 0 & \sigma_2 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ \vdots & & \ddots & & & & \vdots \ 0 & 0 & \cdots & \sigma_r & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ \vdots & & & & & \ddots & \vdots \ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \end{bmatrix}
with r nonzero diagonal entries and n - r zeros. \det(\Sigma) = 0. Since \det(A) = \det(U)\det(\Sigma)\det(V^T) = (\pm 1) \cdot 0 \cdot (\pm 1) = 0, the singularity of A is entirely carried by \Sigma.
The subspaces:

{v_1, \ldots, v_r}: orthonormal basis for the row space C(A^T)
{v_{r+1}, \ldots, v_n}: orthonormal basis for the null space N(A)
{u_1, \ldots, u_r}: orthonormal basis for the column space C(A)
{u_{r+1}, \ldots, u_n}: orthonormal basis for the left null space N(A^T)

The null space has dimension n - r > 0 — this is the content of singularity. A collapses the directions v_{r+1}, \ldots, v_n entirely to zero.

A Worked Example: Rank-1 Matrix
Let
A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}
Immediately: row 2 is twice row 1. \text{rank}(A) = 1. \det(A) = 4 - 4 = 0.
Step 1: Compute A^T A.
A^T A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 10 \ 10 & 20 \end{bmatrix}
Step 2: Eigenvalues of A^T A.
\det(A^T A - \lambda I) = (5 - \lambda)(20 - \lambda) - 100 = \lambda^2 - 25\lambda = \lambda(\lambda - 25) = 0
\lambda_1 = 25, \lambda_2 = 0.
So \sigma_1 = 5, \sigma_2 = 0. One nonzero singular value. Rank 1 confirmed.
Step 3: Eigenvectors of A^T A.
For \lambda_1 = 25:
A^T A - 25I = \begin{bmatrix} -20 & 10 \ 10 & -5 \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow v_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 2 \end{bmatrix}
For \lambda_2 = 0:
A^T A - 0 \cdot I = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 10 \ 10 & 20 \end{bmatrix} \rightarrow v_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \ -1 \end{bmatrix}
Check: v_1^T v_2 = \frac{1}{5}(2 - 2) = 0. Orthogonal. \checkmark
V = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
Step 4: Left singular vectors.
For i = 1 (only nonzero \sigma):
Av_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 5 \ 10 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \sqrt{5}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}
u_1 = \frac{Av_1}{\sigma_1} = \frac{1}{5} \cdot \sqrt{5}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 2 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \sqrt{5}^{-1} \cdot \sqrt{5} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 2 \end{bmatrix}
Wait — let me recompute cleanly.
Av_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 1\cdot1 + 2\cdot2 \ 2\cdot1 + 4\cdot2 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 5 \ 10 \end{bmatrix}
u_1 = \frac{Av_1}{\sigma_1} = \frac{1}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 5 \ 10 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 2 \end{bmatrix}
For u_2: need a unit vector in \mathbb{R}^2 orthogonal to u_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(1,2)^T:
u_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \ -1 \end{bmatrix}
Step 5: Assemble.
U = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad V = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
Notice U = V here. This happens because A is symmetric: A = A^T, so A^T A = A^2 and the left and right singular vectors coincide with the eigenvectors of A.
Verify: U\Sigma V^T = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1&2\2&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5&0\0&0\end{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}1&2\2&-1\end{bmatrix}^T
= \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}5&0\10&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&2\2&-1\end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}5&10\10&20\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\2&4\end{bmatrix} = A \quad \checkmark
Reading the geometry: v_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(1,2)^T spans the row space. v_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2,-1)^T spans the null space — check: Av_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2 - 2, 4 - 4)^T = 0. \checkmark
The map A annihilates the entire direction (2,-1)^T and stretches the direction (1,2)^T by factor 5, sending it to a multiple of u_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(1,2)^T in the column space.

A Rank-Deficient 3 \times 3 Example
Let
A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
Row 3 = row 1 + row 2. So \text{rank}(A) = 2 and \dim N(A) = 1.
A^T A:
A^T A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}^T \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \ 1 & 2 & 3 \ 3 & 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}
Null space of A: Solve Ax = 0.
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \ x_3 \end{bmatrix} = 0 \implies x_1 = -x_3,\ x_2 = -x_3
Null space: \text{span}\left{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{bmatrix}-1\-1\1\end{bmatrix}\right}
This is v_3 — the right singular vector for \sigma_3 = 0. It is the direction A collapses.
The characteristic polynomial of A^T A has \lambda = 0 as a root (since \text{rank}(A^T A) = \text{rank}(A) = 2). The nonzero eigenvalues \lambda_1, \lambda_2 satisfy:
\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \text{tr}(A^T A) = 2 + 2 + 6 = 10 \lambda_1 \lambda_2 = \frac{1}{2}\left[(\text{tr}(A^T A))^2 - \text{tr}((A^T A)^2)\right] / 1
Actually, easier: \text{tr}(A^T A) = |A|_F^2 = 1+0+1+0+1+1+1+1+4 = 10 and from the characteristic polynomial constrained to the 2D nonzero eigenspace, the nonzero eigenvalues satisfy \lambda^2 - 10\lambda + c = 0 where c can be read from the 2\times 2 principal minors. But the exact values matter less than the structure:
\sigma_3 = 0, \quad \sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 > 0
The null space direction v_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-1,-1,1)^T is already determined without computing \sigma_1, \sigma_2 — it is just the null space of A.

Zero Singular Values and the Null Space
This is the key structural fact.
Claim. \sigma_i = 0 if and only if v_i \in N(A).
Proof. \sigma_i = 0 \iff A^T A v_i = \sigma_i^2 v_i = 0 \iff |Av_i|^2 = v_i^T A^T A v_i = 0 \iff Av_i = 0 \iff v_i \in N(A). \square
So the right singular vectors for zero singular values are the null space. Not just related to it — they are an orthonormal basis for it. The SVD automatically finds the null space.
Symmetrically, the left singular vectors u_{r+1}, \ldots, u_n for the “zero rows” of \Sigma form an orthonormal basis for N(A^T) — the left null space.
The number of zero singular values equals the nullity: \dim N(A) = n - r.

Numerical Rank and Near-Singularity
This is where SVD is indispensable and no other tool competes.
In exact arithmetic, the distinction between \sigma_r > 0 and \sigma_{r+1} = 0 is sharp. In floating point, it never is. Every computed singular value is perturbed by rounding errors of order \epsilon_{\text{machine}} |A|. The “zero” singular values become small but nonzero. How small? That depends on the matrix and the problem.
Numerical rank is determined by thresholding:
r_{\text{num}} = #{i : \sigma_i > \tau}
where \tau is a tolerance, typically \tau = \epsilon_{\text{machine}} \cdot \sigma_1 \cdot n (scaled to the size of the matrix and the machine precision).
This is the only reliable way to determine rank in floating point. The alternatives:

Gaussian elimination with pivoting can diagnose rank, but it is sensitive to the pivot threshold choice and can fail for nearly singular matrices.
Determinant is completely useless: \det(A) can be astronomically small for a matrix that is far from singular (large n, large entries), or can be non-negligible for a nearly singular matrix due to cancellation.
Checking if Ax = 0 has a solution requires knowing A exactly.

SVD does not have these problems. \sigma_i is a geometric quantity — the length of Av_i for a unit vector v_i. It is computable to machine precision via the QR-based bidiagonalization algorithm. The gap between “large” and “small” singular values, when it exists, is unambiguous.

The Condition Number Revisited
For a singular matrix, \sigma_n = 0 and the condition number
\kappa(A) = \frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_n} = \frac{\sigma_1}{0} = \infty
An infinite condition number means the linear system Ax = b is either inconsistent (no solution) or has infinitely many solutions. The SVD diagnoses which:

Inconsistent (b \notin C(A)): b has a nonzero component in the left null space. Specifically, u_i^T b \neq 0 for some i > r.
Infinitely many solutions (b \in C(A)): the system is consistent but the null space has dimension > 0, so you can add any multiple of v_{r+1}, \ldots, v_n to any particular solution.

The pseudoinverse A^+ = V\Sigma^+ U^T handles both cases cleanly: it gives the minimum-norm least-squares solution, projecting b onto C(A) and finding the solution with no component in N(A).

Near-Singular Matrices and the Gap
The most practically important case: A is invertible but nearly singular. \sigma_n is small but nonzero.
Example. The Hilbert matrix H_n with H_{ij} = 1/(i+j-1):
H_5 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1/2 & 1/3 & 1/4 & 1/5 \ 1/2 & 1/3 & 1/4 & 1/5 & 1/6 \ 1/3 & 1/4 & 1/5 & 1/6 & 1/7 \ 1/4 & 1/5 & 1/6 & 1/7 & 1/8 \ 1/5 & 1/6 & 1/7 & 1/8 & 1/9 \end{bmatrix}
H_5 is symmetric positive definite — all eigenvalues strictly positive, no zero singular values. But \sigma_1 \approx 1.57 and \sigma_5 \approx 3.3 \times 10^{-6}. Condition number \approx 4.8 \times 10^5.
For H_{10}, the condition number exceeds 10^{13} — beyond double precision’s \sim 10^{16} limit, the matrix is numerically singular.
The SVD reveals this: you see \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_k of reasonable size, then a cliff, then \sigma_{k+1}, \ldots, \sigma_n near or below machine epsilon times \sigma_1. The “numerical rank” is k, and the corresponding right singular vectors v_{k+1}, \ldots, v_n span the “numerical null space” — directions along which A is effectively zero.
The singular matrix is the limiting case: the cliff reaches exactly zero. The near-singular matrix is approaching that limit. SVD makes the continuum visible.

Regularization via SVD
When A is (nearly) singular, the least-squares problem \min |Ax - b| can have solutions that are enormous — the pseudoinverse amplifies the components of b in directions where \sigma_i is tiny, by a factor 1/\sigma_i.
Tikhonov regularization replaces the pseudoinverse with a damped version. Instead of \hat{x} = A^+ b = \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{u_i^T b}{\sigma_i} v_i, use:
\hat{x}_\delta = \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2 + \delta^2} (u_i^T b) v_i
The factor \frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2 + \delta^2} replaces \frac{1}{\sigma_i}. For large \sigma_i (relative to \delta): \frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2 + \delta^2} \approx \frac{1}{\sigma_i}, unchanged. For small \sigma_i (relative to \delta): \frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2 + \delta^2} \approx \frac{\sigma_i}{\delta^2} \approx 0, suppressed.
The regularization parameter \delta smoothly interpolates between “trust small singular values” (\delta \to 0, pseudoinverse) and “ignore everything” (\delta \to \infty, \hat{x} = 0). Choosing \delta well is the art of regularization — it depends on the noise level in b and the desired fidelity of the solution.
This is a direct consequence of the singular structure. Without SVD, regularization is a black box. With SVD, you can see exactly which directions are being damped and by how much.

What the Zero Singular Values “Look Like”
A mental model worth having. Take any n \times n matrix of rank r. It acts on the unit sphere S^{n-1} and maps it to an ellipsoid in \mathbb{R}^n. The semi-axes of the ellipsoid have lengths \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_n.
For a singular matrix: n - r of those semi-axes have length zero. The ellipsoid degenerates — it is actually an ellipsoid living in a proper subspace of \mathbb{R}^n, an (r)-dimensional “pancake.” The entire unit sphere gets squashed: the n - r directions v_{r+1}, \ldots, v_n get crushed to zero, and only the r directions v_1, \ldots, v_r survive and get stretched.
This is the geometric content of singularity. A matrix is singular if and only if its geometric image of the unit sphere is lower-dimensional than the sphere itself. The rank is the dimension of that image. The null space is the set of directions that get crushed.

Summary


















































PropertyNonsingular ASingular A (rank r < n)Singular values\sigma_1 \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_n > 0\sigma_1 \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_r > 0, \sigma_{r+1} = \cdots = \sigma_n = 0\det(A)\prod \sigma_i \neq 00\kappa(A)\sigma_1 / \sigma_n < \infty\inftyNull space N(A){0}\text{span}{v_{r+1}, \ldots, v_n}Left null space N(A^T){0}\text{span}{u_{r+1}, \ldots, u_n}Ax = bUnique solutionNo solution or \infty manyPseudoinverse A^+= A^{-1}Min-norm least-squares solutionImage of unit sphereNon-degenerate ellipsoidDegenerate ellipsoid in r-dim subspace
The SVD does not treat singular matrices as a special case. It handles them with the same formula, the same algorithm, the same geometric picture. The zero singular values are not a failure — they are the most informative part of the decomposition for understanding the structure of the map.

01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.title: 32.eigshow
01.Maths/Linear-Algebra/06.Eigenvalues-a.content:
eigshow is a MATLAB demonstration written by Strang (and used throughout 18.06) that makes the geometry of eigenvalues and singular values visible. The idea is simple: draw the unit circle in \mathbb{R}^2, apply a 2 \times 2 matrix A to every point on it, and watch what happens to the image vector Ax as x rotates around the circle.
Two separate things are being shown, and it is worth being precise about which is which.

What eigshow Actually Does
Let x be a unit vector in \mathbb{R}^2. As x sweeps around the unit circle, eigshow plots both x and Ax simultaneously. Two vectors rotate together on screen — one tracing the circle, the other tracing the image ellipse.
The demonstration has two modes:
Eigenvalue mode. Look for the moments when x and Ax are parallel — pointing in the same direction or exactly opposite directions. At those moments, Ax = \lambda x for some scalar \lambda. You have found an eigenvector. The ratio |Ax| / |x| at that moment is |\lambda|.
Singular value mode. Look for the moments when x and Ax are perpendicular to each other in a specific sense — not x \perp Ax, but rather when Ax reaches its maximum and minimum length. At those moments, x = v_i and Ax = \sigma_i u_i. The right singular vectors v_1, v_2 are the input positions where |Ax| is maximized and minimized. The singular values \sigma_1, \sigma_2 are those maximum and minimum lengths.

The Geometry of the Two Modes
Eigenvalue Mode
For a 2 \times 2 matrix with real eigenvalues, there are exactly two directions where Ax \parallel x. You see them in eigshow as the two positions where both vectors align along the same line through the origin.
If \lambda > 0: x and Ax point the same direction. The matrix stretches along x.
If \lambda < 0: x and Ax point opposite directions. The matrix stretches and flips.
If the eigenvalues are complex (which happens for rotation-like matrices), there are no such positions — Ax is never parallel to x for any real unit vector x, and you see the two vectors perpetually chasing each other around without aligning.
This is eigshow making complex eigenvalues visceral: you watch and watch for the alignment and it never comes.
Singular Value Mode
The image of the unit circle under A is always an ellipse (or a degenerate ellipse — a line segment — if A is rank 1). The semi-axes of that ellipse are \sigma_1 u_1 and \sigma_2 u_2.
In singular value mode, eigshow finds the two input positions v_1 and v_2 where:

|Av| is maximized: this is v_1, and the maximum value is \sigma_1.
|Av| is minimized: this is v_2, and the minimum value is \sigma_2.

And it shows that Av_1 \perp Av_2 — the images of the right singular vectors are perpendicular. The input directions v_1, v_2 need not be perpendicular to each other in general — but they are, because the v_i are eigenvectors of the symmetric matrix A^T A, which always has orthogonal eigenvectors.
So eigshow is making the following visible all at once:
v_1 \perp v_2, \quad Av_1 \perp Av_2, \quad |Av_1| = \sigma_1, \quad |Av_2| = \sigma_2
This is the SVD in 2 \times 2, drawn on screen.

A Specific Example to Run in Your Head
Take
A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
What you see in eigenvalue mode.
Compute the eigenvalues: \lambda_1 = 3, \lambda_2 = 2. There are two positions where Ax \parallel x. As x rotates around the circle, at two moments the two vectors on screen lock into alignment — one when x points near the e_1 direction (eigenvector for \lambda = 3), once when x is near (1, -1)/\sqrt{2} direction (eigenvector for \lambda = 2, found by solving (A - 2I)v = 0: v = (1, -1)^T / \sqrt{2}). At the first alignment, Ax is 3 times as long as x. At the second, 2 times.
What you see in singular value mode.
Compute A^T A:
A^T A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 3 \ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}
Eigenvalues of A^T A: characteristic polynomial \lambda^2 - 14\lambda + 36 = 0, so \lambda = 7 \pm \sqrt{13}.
\sigma_1 = \sqrt{7 + \sqrt{13}} \approx 3.30, \qquad \sigma_2 = \sqrt{7 - \sqrt{13}} \approx 1.82
In eigshow singular value mode, the two vectors align orthogonally (in the right sense) twice as x rotates. The image ellipse has semi-axes of length \approx 3.30 and \approx 1.82. The eigenvectors of A^T A give the directions v_1 and v_2 where these extremes are achieved.
Notice: the eigenvalues of A are 3 and 2, but the singular values are approximately 3.30 and 1.82. They are not the same — the eigenvalues are the scaling factors for the eigenvectors, while the singular values are the maximum and minimum stretching over all unit vectors. For a symmetric positive definite matrix, the two would coincide. For a non-symmetric matrix like this one, they differ.

What eigshow Teaches About SVD vs Eigenvalues
The clearest thing eigshow does is force you to see that eigenvalues and singular values are answers to different questions.
Eigenvalue question: for which input directions x is the output Ax parallel to x?
Singular value question: for which input directions x is the output Ax as long as possible (or as short as possible)?
These are genuinely different geometric questions. They happen to have the same answer for symmetric matrices — but for non-symmetric matrices they diverge, and eigshow lets you see the divergence by running both modes on the same matrix.
A rotation matrix R_\theta = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} has:

Eigenvalues e^{i\theta} and e^{-i\theta} — complex, no real eigenvectors. In eigenvalue mode: the two vectors never align. They perpetually rotate relative to each other.
Singular values both equal to 1 — a rotation maps the unit circle to itself. In singular value mode: |Ax| = 1 for every x, so every direction is simultaneously a maximizer and minimizer. Singular values are 1 in every direction.

eigshow makes both of these facts immediately visible without computation.

The Key Observation for SVD
Here is the observation that eigshow is really set up to deliver, stated precisely:
As x rotates around the unit circle, Ax traces an ellipse. At the moment |Ax| is maximized, the output Ax is perpendicular to the direction of motion of Ax — that is, Ax is perpendicular to \frac{d}{d\theta}(Ax).
\frac{d}{d\theta}(Ax) = A\frac{dx}{d\theta}. If x = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)^T, then dx/d\theta = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)^T, which is perpendicular to x.
So the condition ”Ax is perpendicular to A(dx/d\theta)” becomes (Ax)^T A(dx/d\theta) = 0, i.e., x^T A^T A (dx/d\theta) = 0.
This says x and dx/d\theta are orthogonal with respect to the inner product defined by A^T A. Since dx/d\theta \perp x in the standard sense, the condition reduces to x being an eigenvector of A^T A.
Conclusion. The input directions that maximize or minimize |Ax| are exactly the eigenvectors of A^T A — the right singular vectors. This is not just a computation; it is a calculus argument that eigshow visualizes. The extremes of the output length, as you sweep through all input directions, occur precisely at the right singular vectors. The SVD is the answer to an optimization problem, and eigshow shows you the optimization happening in real time.

Running eigshow
In MATLAB:
eigshow          % opens the demo with a default matrix
eigshow(A)       % runs with your own 2x2 matrix A
Click to toggle between eigenvalue mode and singular value mode. Use the arrow keys or drag to rotate x around the circle. Watch when the vectors align (eigenvalue mode) or when the output reaches its extreme length (singular value mode).
If you do not have MATLAB: the same demonstration can be reproduced in Python with matplotlib animations. The key is to plot x(\theta) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)^T and Ax(\theta) simultaneously as \theta varies, and mark the special angles.
A minimal Python version:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 
A = np.array([[3, 1], [0, 2]])
theta = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 500)
x = np.array([np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)])   # unit circle, shape (2, 500)
Ax = A @ x                                      # image ellipse, shape (2, 500)
 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6))
ax.plot(x[0], x[1], 'b--', label='unit circle')
ax.plot(Ax[0], Ax[1], 'r-', label='image ellipse $Ax$')
ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.5)
ax.axvline(0, color='k', lw=0.5)
ax.legend()
ax.set_title('eigshow: image of unit circle under $A$')
plt.show()
To find and mark the singular vectors:
# Right singular vectors: eigenvectors of A^T A
AtA = A.T @ A
eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(AtA)       # sorted ascending
sigma = np.sqrt(eigvals[::-1])               # descending singular values
V = eigvecs[:, ::-1]                         # right singular vectors as columns
 
for i in range(2):
    vi = V[:, i]
    Avi = A @ vi
    ax.annotate('', xy=vi, xytext=(0,0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='blue', lw=2))
    ax.annotate('', xy=Avi, xytext=(0,0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='red', lw=2))

What to Take Away
eigshow is not a gimmick. It is a way of building geometric intuition that the algebra alone does not give you. After running it on a few matrices, the following become obvious rather than just true:

Eigenvectors are the input directions where A does not rotate — only stretches or flips. They are special and rare (only n of them for a diagonalizable n \times n matrix).
Right singular vectors are the input directions where the output is extremal in length. They always exist, they are always orthogonal, and there are always n of them.
The image of the unit circle is always an ellipse. The semi-axes of that ellipse are the singular values.
For a symmetric positive definite matrix, the eigenvectors and right singular vectors coincide, and the eigenvalues equal the singular values. eigshow looks the same in both modes.
For a rotation matrix, eigenvalue mode shows no alignment ever; singular value mode shows all directions are equivalent.

These are the pictures that should be in your head when you read a theorem about eigenvalues or singular values. eigshow puts them there.

Related: Singular Value Decomposition, The Bases and SVD, Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors, Similar Matrices See: MIT 18.06 lecture notes, Strang — eigshow MATLAB demo
