                   Is Bayes' rule the rule for updating beliefs, or just a rule?
                  
                

The answer — and this is the thing that should keep you up at night — is that it is the rule. Any agent that updates beliefs differently is incoherent in a precise, exploitable sense. You can be Dutch-booked: forced to accept a combination of bets that guarantees a loss regardless of outcomes.
This note builds up to that result carefully. No hand-waving.

What Does “Coherent” Even Mean?
The classical answer is the Dutch book argument (de Finetti, Ramsey). Operationalise a belief P(A) = p as a willingness to buy or sell a ticket that pays 1 if A$ occurs, for price p. An agent is coherent if no finite collection of such bets guarantees a loss for them in all possible worlds.


                  
                   Theorem (de Finetti). An agent is coherent if and only if their beliefs satisfy the Kolmogorov axioms:
                  
                


P(A) \geq 0 for all events A
P(\Omega) = 1
If A \cap B = \emptyset, then P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)




Proof sketch. Any violation of these axioms admits a Dutch book. Conversely, if they hold, you can show via the minimax theorem that no finite book beats you. \square
This is the static coherence story. Now: what about updating?

Conditional Probability from First Principles
Definition. For events A, B with \\P(B) > 0:
P(A \mid B) \ = \ \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}
This is not an axiom — it is a definition. But it is forced on us. Here is the argument.
Suppose we learn that B occurred. We want a new belief function \Pr(,\cdot \mid B) satisfying:

Kolmogorov internally on B: P(,\cdot \mid B) should be a valid probability measure on the restricted space B (i.e., renormalize to B).
Ratio preservation: For any A_1, A_2 \subseteq B, learning B should not change the relative odds of A_1 versus A_2.

Condition (1) forces \P(B \mid B) = 1. Condition (2) forces:
\frac{P(A_1 \mid B)}{P(A_2 \mid B)} = \frac{P(A_1)}{P(A_2)} \quad \text{for } A_1, A_2 \subseteq B
The unique function satisfying both is P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B). So the definition is not arbitrary — it is the unique answer to a natural set of desiderata.

Bayes’ Rule: The Derivation
From the definition of conditional probability, symmetrically:
P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)P(B) = P(B \mid A)P(A)
Solving for P(A \mid B):
\boxed{P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}}
That’s it. One line. The depth is entirely in what the pieces mean and why no other formula could work.


The Coherence Theorem (The Real Point of This Note)
Here is the result that justifies everything.
Theorem (Coherence of Bayesian Updating). Suppose an agent has prior beliefs \Pr satisfying the Kolmogorov axioms, and updates to posterior beliefs \Pr' after observing event B. If \Pr' is coherent (no Dutch book can be constructed against the agent using bets made before and after observing B), then:
P'(A) = P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}
Proof. (I’ll sketch the Dutch book argument.)
Step 1. Consider a conditional bet: a ticket that pays 1 if Aoccurs, _given that the bet is called off ifBdoesn't occur_. By pre-update coherence, the fair price for this ticket isP(A \cap B)/P(B) = P(A \mid B)$.
Step 2. Now suppose the agent updates to P'(A) \neq P(A \mid B). WLOG say P'(A) > P(A \mid B).
Step 3. Construct the book: before observing B:

Buy the conditional bet at price P(A \mid B).

After observing B:

Sell a ticket on A at price P'(A) (the agent’s new “fair” price).

Step 4. Net payoff analysis. If A occurs: gain 1 - P'(A) from the sell, and 1 - P(A \mid B) from the buy. Oh wait — these are the same ticket. The point is: the agent is inconsistent in their pricing before and after. Specifically, they would accept a combination of bets that nets them P'(A) - P(A \mid B) > 0 up front but loses money in all states of the world (worked out carefully using the calloff structure).
Therefore: any P' \neq P(\cdot \mid B) is incoherent. \square
Remark. This is genuinely important. It says Bayesian updating is not a modelling choice. It is forced on any rational agent with probabilistic beliefs. Other “update rules” (e.g., Jeffrey conditioning, maximum entropy methods) arise only when the evidence is not a clean “event observed with certainty.”

01.Maths/Probability/02.Conditional-Prob.title: 10.The Monty Hall Problem
01.Maths/Probability/02.Conditional-Prob.content:
You’re on a game show. There are 3 doors. Behind one is a car. Behind the other two are goats. You pick door 1. The host, Monty Hall, who knows where the car is, opens one of the other two doors to reveal a goat — say he opens door 3. He then offers you the choice: stick with door 1, or switch to door 2.
Should you switch?

The instinctive answer is: it doesn’t matter, it’s 50-50 now. This is wrong. You should switch. Switching wins with probability \mathbf{2/3}.
This result is so counterintuitive that when Marilyn vos Savant published it in 1990, she received roughly 10,000 letters — many from professional mathematicians — telling her she was wrong. She was right. They were not.
Let’s understand exactly why, from multiple angles, until it becomes obvious.

Solution 1 — Sample Space (Naive Probability, Direct)
Enumerate. The car is equally likely behind any door, probability 1/3 each. You pick door 1. Three cases:





























Car behindMonty opensStick wins?Switch wins?Door 1Door 2 or 3 (his choice)✓✗Door 2Door 3 (forced)✗✓Door 3Door 2 (forced)✗✓
Each row has probability 1/3. Stick wins in 1 out of 3 cases. Switch wins in 2 out of 3.
P(\text{win} \mid \text{switch}) = \frac{2}{3}, \qquad P(\text{win} \mid \text{stick}) = \frac{1}{3}

The key observation: when you initially pick the wrong door (probability 2/3), Monty is forced to open the only other goat door, so the car is guaranteed to be behind the door you’d switch to. You only lose by switching when you picked correctly from the start, which happens with probability 1/3.


Solution 2 — Conditional Probability (The Full Bayes Treatment)
Let’s be rigorous. Define events:

C_i = car is behind door i, for i = 1, 2, 3
M_3 = Monty opens door 3

We want P(C_1 \mid M_3) (probability car is behind door 1, given Monty opened door 3) — this is the probability that sticking wins.
Prior: P(C_1) = P(C_2) = P(C_3) = 1/3.
Likelihoods — this is where Monty’s behavior matters:
P(M_3 \mid C_1) = \frac{1}{2} Monty can open either door 2 or door 3 (both goats). By symmetry, 1/2.
P(M_3 \mid C_2) = 1 Monty cannot open door 2 (car there), cannot open door 1 (your pick). He must open door 3.
P(M_3 \mid C_3) = 0 Monty cannot open door 3 — that would reveal the car.
LOTP to get the marginal: P(M_3) = P(M_3 \mid C_1)P(C_1) + P(M_3 \mid C_2)P(C_2) + P(M_3 \mid C_3)P(C_3) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} + 1 \cdot \frac{1}{3} + 0 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{2}
Bayes’ theorem:
P(C_1 \mid M_3) = \frac{P(M_3 \mid C_1) P(C_1)}{P(M_3)} = \frac{\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3}}{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{3}
P(C_2 \mid M_3) = \frac{P(M_3 \mid C_2) P(C_2)}{P(M_3)} = \frac{1 \cdot \frac{1}{3}}{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{2}{3}
So:
\boxed{P(\text{win} \mid \text{switch}) = P(C_2 \mid M_3) = \frac{2}{3}}

What Bayes tells us that the table argument doesn’t: The update is entirely driven by the likelihood ratio P(M_3 \mid C_1) / P(M_3 \mid C_2) = \frac{1/2}{1} = \frac{1}{2}. Door 2 is twice as likely to have the car as door 1 after Monty opens door 3, because Monty was twice as likely to open door 3 if the car were behind door 2 (he had no choice) than if it were behind door 1 (he had a choice). The information in Monty’s action is asymmetric.


The Crux: Why Intuition Fails
The wrong reasoning: “There are two doors left, one has the car, so each has probability 1/2.”
This would be correct if Monty picked a door uniformly at random and happened to reveal a goat. That is a different problem. In that version, the answer genuinely is 1/2.
The error is ignoring the dependence between Monty’s action and the car’s location. Monty is not choosing randomly — he is choosing with full knowledge. His action carries information. Specifically:

If you picked wrong (prob 2/3), Monty’s hand is forced — he must open the one remaining goat door. The switch door is the car with certainty.
If you picked right (prob 1/3), Monty has a free choice. The switch door is a goat with certainty.

Monty’s opening of door 3 is not a symmetric event. It is more likely to occur when the car is behind door 2 than when it’s behind door 1. That asymmetry is the entire content of the problem.

The “Random Monty” Variant — Why it Actually is 50-50
It’s worth solving this explicitly to make the contrast sharp.
Variant: Monty picks one of the two remaining doors uniformly at random. He opens it and it happens to show a goat. Now should you switch?
Likelihoods now: P(M_3 \mid C_1) = \frac{1}{2}, \quad P(M_3 \mid C_2) = \frac{1}{2}, \quad P(M_3 \mid C_3) = \frac{1}{2}
Wait — P(M_3 \mid C_3) = 1/2? Yes, because Monty picks randomly, so he might open door 3 even if the car is there. But we’re conditioning on him opening door 3 and revealing a goat, so we need to be more careful.
Let G_3 = door 3 is opened and shows a goat.
P(G_3 \mid C_1) = \frac{1}{2}, \quad P(G_3 \mid C_2) = \frac{1}{2}, \quad P(G_3 \mid C_3) = 0
Now Bayes: P(C_1 \mid G_3) = \frac{\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3}}{\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} + 0} = \frac{1/6}{1/3} = \frac{1}{2}
P(C_2 \mid G_3) = \frac{1}{2}
In this version, it genuinely is 50-50. Switching doesn’t help. The difference: Monty’s equal likelihood of opening door 3 regardless of whether the car is behind door 1 or door 2 means his action contains no asymmetric information. There’s nothing to update on.

This is the cleanest demonstration that the answer to Monty Hall depends critically on the host’s strategy, not just on what you observe. Two scenarios with identical observations (k=3 opened, goat revealed) yield completely different posterior probabilities because the data-generating process differs.


Generalization: n Doors
There are n doors, car behind one, you pick door 1, Monty opens n-2 goat doors (all of the other goat doors except one), leaving your door and one other.
P(\text{win} \mid \text{switch}) = \frac{n-1}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{n-2} \cdot (n-2) = \frac{n-1}{n}
More cleanly: you win by switching iff your initial pick was wrong, which has probability \frac{n-1}{n}. When your initial pick is wrong, Monty is forced to leave the car door closed — switching always wins in that case. So:
P(\text{win} \mid \text{switch}) = \frac{n-1}{n}
For n=3: 2/3. For n=100: 99/100. As n \to \infty, switching is essentially certain to win.

With 100 doors, you pick one, Monty opens 98 goat doors, leaving yours and one other. The remaining door is almost surely the car. The original problem scaled up until the answer is impossible to get wrong.


Simulation Argument (for the skeptic in me)
If I still felt uneasy, here’s how I’d think about running this:
Play the game N times, always switching.

Fraction of games where initial pick was correct: \approx 1/3. In these, switching loses.
Fraction where initial pick was wrong: \approx 2/3. In these, Monty’s forced, switching wins.

Win rate by switching \approx 2/3. This is not a proof but it’s the sanity check that the answer isn’t absurd.

What This Problem Is Really About
Monty Hall is a lesson in three things:
1. Conditional probability changes the sample space. After Monty opens door 3, we don’t have a uniform distribution over {C_1, C_2}. We have a posterior, and the posterior is not uniform because the prior wasn’t updated symmetrically.
2. The data-generating process is part of the model. The probability of an observation depends not just on what you see but on how it was generated. Monty’s knowledge and strategy are part of the probability model. Change the strategy, change the answer — even with identical observations.
3. Information is asymmetric when the agent has knowledge. Monty’s action is a function of the car’s location. That functional dependence is exactly what Bayes captures through the likelihood. When P(\text{observation} \mid \text{hypothesis}) differs across hypotheses, the observation has discriminatory power. That’s what posterior updating means.
_

01.Maths/Probability/02.Conditional-Prob.title: 11.Gambler's ruin
01.Maths/Probability/02.Conditional-Prob.content:
A gambler starts with k\k k dollars. At each round, they win 1$1 1 with probability pp p and lose 1$1 1 with probability q=1−pq = 1-p q=1−p. The game ends when they either reach N$N N (target — they win) or hit 0$0 $0 (ruin — they go broke). What is the probability of ruin?
                  
                


1) Setting Up the Model Precisely
The state space. Two players, A and B, share a fixed total of N dollars. At any moment, let the state be i =  A’s current fortune, so i \in {0, 1, 2, \ldots, N}.
The dynamics. At each round, independently of all previous rounds: X_{n+1} = \begin{cases} X_n + 1 & \text{with probability } p \ X_n - 1 & \text{with probability } q := 1 - p \end{cases}
The absorbing states. States 0 and N are absorbing: once reached, the process stays there. State 0 = A is ruined. State N = A has won everything.
The question. Starting from X_0 = i, define
P_i := \mathbb{P}(\text{A wins} \mid X_0 = i) = \mathbb{P}(\text{process hits } N \text{ before } 0 \mid X_0 = i)
We want a closed-form expression for P_i for every i \in {0, 1, \ldots, N}.


                  
                  This is a finite-state Markov chain. The transient states are {1, 2, \ldots, N-1} and the two absorbing states are {0, N}. Absorption is guaranteed because the chain is irreducible on the transient states and those states are all transient — the process must eventually leave them. I'll take this for granted here; the proof uses the fact that from any transient state, there's a positive probability path to an absorbing state in finitely many steps.
                  
                

2) First-Step Analysis: Deriving the Recurrence
This is the key technique. Instead of thinking about the whole trajectory at once, we condition on just the first step and use the Markov property.
For 1 \leq i \leq N-1:
P_i = \mathbb{P}(\text{hit } N \text{ before } 0 \mid X_0 = i)
Condition on X_1:
P_i = \mathbb{P}(X_1 = i+1) \cdot \mathbb{P}(\text{hit } N \text{ before } 0 \mid X_1 = i+1) + \mathbb{P}(X_1 = i-1) \cdot \mathbb{P}(\text{hit } N \text{ before } 0 \mid X_1 = i-1)
By the Markov property, the future evolution depends only on the current state, not on how we got there. So \mathbb{P}(\text{hit } N \text{ before } 0 \mid X_1 = j) = P_j. Therefore:
\boxed{P_i = p \cdot P_{i+1} + q \cdot P_{i-1}} \qquad \text{for } i = 1, 2, \ldots, N-1
with boundary conditions:
P_0 = 0 \qquad P_N = 1
This is a second-order linear recurrence — the discrete analogue of a second-order ODE. Since it’s linear with constant coefficients, we solve it exactly as we would an ODE: find the characteristic equation, get the general solution, then apply boundary conditions to pin down the constants.
3) Solving the Recurrence: Full Algebra
Step 1 — Rewrite in standard form
The recurrence is: P_i = p \cdot P_{i+1} + q \cdot P_{i-1}
Since p + q = 1, multiply the left side by (p + q) = 1: p \cdot P_i + q \cdot P_i = p \cdot P_{i+1} + q \cdot P_{i-1}
Rearrange: p(P_{i+1} - P_i) = q(P_i - P_{i-1})
Step 2 — Introduce the differences
Define d_i := P_i - P_{i-1} for i = 1, 2, \ldots, N. Then the relation above becomes:
p \cdot d_{i+1} = q \cdot d_i
\therefore \quad d_{i+1} = \frac{q}{p} \cdot d_i
This says the sequence (d_i) is geometric with common ratio r := q/p.
Step 3 — Write out the geometric sequence
d_1 = d_1 d_2 = r \cdot d_1 d_3 = r^2 \cdot d_1 \vdots d_i = r^{i-1} \cdot d_1
Step 4 — Telescope to get P_i
Since P_0 = 0, we can recover P_i by summing the differences:
P_i = P_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{i} d_k = \sum_{k=1}^{i} r^{k-1} \cdot d_1 = d_1 \sum_{k=0}^{i-1} r^k
Now we split into two cases depending on whether r = 1.
4) Case 1: Fair Game (p = q = \tfrac{1}{2}, so r = 1)
When r = 1, all differences are equal: d_k = d_1 for all k.
The sum becomes:
P_i = d_1 \cdot \sum_{k=0}^{i-1} 1 = i \cdot d_1
Apply the boundary condition P_N = 1:
1 = N \cdot d_1 \implies d_1 = \frac{1}{N}
Therefore:
\boxed{P_i = \frac{i}{N}} \qquad \text{(Fair game)}
What this is saying. Your probability of winning is exactly your share of the total wealth. If you bring 30 to a table where the total money in play is 100, you will — on average — win with probability 30%. This is a beautiful result: no matter how the game plays out round by round, the long-run probability reduces to a simple ratio.


                  
                  Notice the asymmetry baked into this formula. Even though the game is fair round-by-round (zero expected gain per step), the outcome is not symmetric in terms of survival. If you have 1 and your opponent has 99, you win with probability only 1%. Fairness in each step does not mean fairness in the long run when players have unequal resources. This is the core message of the whole theorem.
                  
                

5) Case 2: Biased Game
When r \neq 1, the sum is a standard finite geometric series:
\sum_{k=0}^{i-1} r^k = \frac{1 - r^i}{1 - r}
So:
P_i = d_1 \cdot \frac{1 - r^i}{1 - r}
Now apply P_N = 1:
1 = d_1 \cdot \frac{1 - r^N}{1 - r} \implies d_1 = \frac{1 - r}{1 - r^N}
Substitute back:
P_i = \frac{1-r}{1-r^N} \cdot \frac{1-r^i}{1-r}
\boxed{P_i = \frac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N}} \qquad r = \frac{q}{p}, \quad r \neq 1
Sanity checks
Let me verify this actually satisfies what it should:

P_0: \frac{1 - r^0}{1 - r^N} = \frac{0}{1-r^N} = 0 ✓
P_N: \frac{1 - r^N}{1 - r^N} = 1 ✓
Limit as r \to 1: Apply L’Hôpital (or Taylor expand): \frac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N} \to \frac{i}{N} as r \to 1 ✓ — recovers the fair game case continuously.



                  
                  The continuity at r = 1 is reassuring. There's no discontinuous "phase transition" between fair and biased games — the biased formula smoothly collapses to the fair formula as p \to \frac{1}{2}.
                  
                

The exponential effect of small biases
This is the part that always surprises me. Let’s be concrete. Set N = 100, so total wealth is 100. You start with i = 50$ — exactly half the money. Seems fair, right?



































Win prob pr = q/pP_{50} (your win probability)0.501.0000.5000.510.9610.8800.491.0410.1190.550.8180.9990.451.2220.001
Starting with half the money, a 1% disadvantage per round drops your survival probability from 50% to about 12%. A 5% disadvantage makes ruin near-certain. The exponential structure of r^i is brutal.
6) Expected Duration of the Game
While we’re here, let’s also derive the expected duration. This requires the same first-step analysis, applied to a different function.
Let D_i = \mathbb{E}[\text{number of rounds} \mid X_0 = i], with D_0 = D_N = 0.
Step 1 — Write the recurrence
Conditioning on the first step:
D_i = 1 + p \cdot D_{i+1} + q \cdot D_{i-1} \qquad \text{for } 1 \leq i \leq N-1
The “1” accounts for the current round. This is an inhomogeneous second-order recurrence (the +1 on the right is the forcing term).
Step 2 — Find the particular solution
We need a particular solution to D_i - p \cdot D_{i+1} - q \cdot D_{i-1} = 1.
For the fair game (p = q = \frac{1}{2}): The homogeneous part has general solution A + Bi (since r=1 gives a repeated root). Try a particular solution of the form D_i^{(p)} = Ci^2.
Substituting: Ci^2 = 1 + \frac{1}{2}C(i+1)^2 + \frac{1}{2}C(i-1)^2 Ci^2 = 1 + \frac{C}{2}(i^2 + 2i + 1) + \frac{C}{2}(i^2 - 2i + 1) Ci^2 = 1 + Ci^2 + C
This gives 0 = 1 + C, so C = -1.
Particular solution: D_i^{(p)} = -i^2.
Step 3 — General solution
D_i = A + Bi + (-i^2) = A + Bi - i^2
Step 4 — Apply boundary conditions
D_0 = 0: \quad A = 0
D_N = 0: \quad BN - N^2 = 0 \implies B = N
Therefore:
\boxed{D_i = i(N - i)} \qquad \text{(Fair game)}
This is a downward parabola in i, symmetric about i = N/2, with maximum value N^2/4 at i = N/2.
Interpretation. The longest games happen when the players start with equal wealth. If one player is much richer, the game ends quickly — the poor player gets wiped out fast. Equal wealth maximises the duration because neither absorbing state is “nearby.” The maximum expected duration scales as N^2, which grows much faster than N — doubling the total wealth quadruples the expected game length.


                  
                  If you want the biased-game formula for D_i, the algebra is similar but messier. The particular solution in that case is D_i^{(p)} = \frac{i}{q - p} (when p \neq q), giving after boundary conditions: D_i = \frac{1}{q-p}\left[i - N \cdot \frac{1-r^i}{1-r^N}\right] \qquad r = \frac{q}{p} I'll leave verifying the boundary conditions as an exercise. The key thing to notice is that when p < q (unfavorable game), this grows much faster — the game can still take a very long time even when ruin is nearly certain, because the walk wanders around a lot before hitting 0.
                  
                

7) The Martingale Proof (The “Right” Way to See It)
Once you know martingales, this whole problem has a cleaner proof that’s also more illuminating.
7a — Fair game via X_n
Claim. When p = q = \frac{1}{2}, the wealth process (X_n) is a martingale with respect to \mathcal{F}_n = \sigma(X_0, X_1, \ldots, X_n).
Proof. \mathbb{E}[X_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = X_n \cdot \mathbb{P}(\text{no change}) + (X_n + 1) \cdot p + (X_n - 1) \cdot q = X_n + (p - q) = X_n
since p = q. ✓
Now let T = \min{n : X_n \in {0, N}} be the stopping time. Since the process is bounded (0 \leq X_n \leq N) and T is finite almost surely (the process must eventually absorb), the Optional Stopping Theorem applies:
\mathbb{E}[X_T] = \mathbb{E}[X_0] = i
But at time T, we know X_T \in {0, N}:
\mathbb{E}[X_T] = N \cdot \mathbb{P}(X_T = N) + 0 \cdot \mathbb{P}(X_T = 0) = N \cdot P_i
Therefore N \cdot P_i = i, giving P_i = i/N. \blacksquare


                  
                  Notice what we just did: we derived Gambler's Ruin without solving any recurrence. The whole proof is: "wealth is a martingale → OST → done." This is why martingales are so powerful. The recurrence proof works from the bottom up; the martingale proof works from the top down, using structure.
                  
                


7b — Biased game via (q/p)^{X_n}
For the biased case, X_n itself is not a martingale (it has a drift of p - q per step). But we can find a function of X_n that is a martingale.
Claim. When p \neq q, the process Y_n = \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{X_n} is a martingale.
Proof. Let r = q/p. Then:
\mathbb{E}[Y_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = p \cdot r^{X_n + 1} + q \cdot r^{X_n - 1}
= r^{X_n} \left[ p \cdot r + q \cdot r^{-1} \right]
= r^{X_n} \left[ p \cdot \frac{q}{p} + q \cdot \frac{p}{q} \right]
= r^{X_n} \left[ q + p \right] = r^{X_n} = Y_n
So Y_n is a martingale. ✓
Apply the Optional Stopping Theorem to Y_n (same conditions apply — bounded, finite stopping time):
\mathbb{E}[Y_T] = \mathbb{E}[Y_0] = r^i
But X_T \in {0, N}:
r^i = r^N \cdot P_i + r^0 \cdot (1 - P_i) = r^N \cdot P_i + 1 - P_i
r^i - 1 = P_i(r^N - 1)
\boxed{P_i = \frac{r^i - 1}{r^N - 1} = \frac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N}} \quad \checkmark
Same formula. The two proofs are completely consistent — but the martingale proof reveals why the formula has the form it does. It’s because (q/p)^{X_n} is the natural “harmonic function” for this walk.
7c — What about the duration? (Optional Stopping, again)
For the fair game, the process M_n = X_n^2 - n is a martingale (you can verify this directly). Apply OST:
\mathbb{E}[X_T^2 - T] = \mathbb{E}[X_0^2 - 0] = i^2
So:
\mathbb{E}[X_T^2] - \mathbb{E}[T] = i^2
Now \mathbb{E}[X_T^2] = N^2 \cdot P_i + 0 \cdot (1-P_i) = N^2 \cdot \frac{i}{N} = Ni.
Therefore:
Ni - \mathbb{E}[T] = i^2 \implies \mathbb{E}[T] = Ni - i^2 = i(N - i) \quad \checkmark
Again, same formula — derived in two lines using the right martingale.


                  
                   The general pattern. For a random walk with a drift, there's a systematic way to find martingales. If f is "harmonic" for the generator of the walk — meaning \mathbb{E}[f(X_1) \mid X_0 = i] = f(i) — then f(X_n) is a martingale. For the fair walk, the harmonic functions are f(i) = 1 (trivial) and f(i) = i (gives the win probability). For the biased walk, they are f(i) = 1 and f(i) = (q/p)^i. This is deeply connected to the theory of harmonic functions for Markov chains, which generalises to continuous-time diffusions and Brownian motion.
                  
                

8) What “Ruin is Certain” Means as N \to \infty
A natural question: what happens if we remove the upper boundary and let the opponent have infinite wealth? This models a gambler vs. an infinitely rich casino.
Take the formula P_i = \frac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N} (biased case) and let N \to \infty.
If r > 1 (i.e. p < q, unfavorable game):
r^N \to \infty \implies P_i = \frac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N} \to \frac{1 - r^i}{-r^N} \to 0
Ruin is certain.
If r < 1 (i.e. p > q, favorable game):
r^N \to 0 \implies P_i = \frac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N} \to \frac{1 - r^i}{1} = 1 - r^i = 1 - \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^i
There is a positive probability of never being ruined — specifically, P(\text{survive forever}) = 1 - (q/p)^i.
If r = 1 (fair game):
P_i = \frac{i}{N} \to 0 \text{ as } N \to \infty
Ruin is certain even in a fair game against an infinitely rich opponent.


                  
                  This last point is the gut-punch result. A fair game against a casino with infinite resources = certain ruin. There is no strategy that changes this. The only variable is when you go broke, not whether. This is the mathematical reason why "systems" like Martingale betting or any other strategy fail in the long run — against an infinite house, the absorbing state 0 is unavoidable.
                  
                

9) The Casino Calculation (Made Concrete)
You walk into a casino with 100. The house edge per bet is p_{\text{house}} = 0.51, so p_{\text{you}} = 0.49$.
Assume for simplicity the casino has M dollars and total wealth is N = 100 + M.
r = \frac{q}{p} = \frac{0.51}{0.49} \approx 1.0408
P_{100} = \frac{1 - (1.0408)^{100}}{1 - (1.0408)^{N}}
For M = 10{,}000 (total N = 10{,}100):
(1.0408)^{100} \approx 56.9 \qquad (1.0408)^{10{,}100} \approx \text{astronomically large}
P_{100} \approx \frac{1 - 56.9}{1 - \infty} \approx \frac{-55.9}{-\infty} \approx 0
In practice, with N large: P(\text{win}) \approx 1 - r^i = 1 - (1.0408)^{100}… wait, that’s the infinite-wealth limit, which gives a negative number — confirming ruin is certain.
The exact formula gives approximately P(\text{ruin}) > 99.8.
10) Connection to the Big Picture
Here’s the chain of ideas this feeds into, and what to study next:
Gambler's Ruin
     ↓
First-step analysis (recurrence relations for Markov chains)
     ↓
Harmonic functions for Markov chains
     ↓
Optional Stopping Theorem (discrete time)
     ↓
Doob's martingale convergence theorems
     ↓
Brownian motion as the limit of scaled random walks
     ↓
Dirichlet problem (harmonic analysis / PDEs)
     ↓
Itô calculus and stochastic differential equations

The Gambler’s Ruin is literally the first step in this entire tower. The “first-step analysis” recurrence is the discrete analogue of solving a boundary value ODE. The martingale proof is the discrete analogue of the maximum principle for harmonic functions. When you later see Brownian motion hit a boundary, or an SDE absorbed at zero, you’ll recognise the same structure.
Quick Reference






























QuantityFair (p = q = \frac{1}{2})Biased (p \neq q, r = q/p)Win probability P_i\dfrac{i}{N}\dfrac{1 - r^i}{1 - r^N}Ruin probability\dfrac{N-i}{N}1 - P_iExpected duration D_ii(N-i)\dfrac{1}{q-p}!\left[i - N\cdot\dfrac{1-r^i}{1-r^N}\right]Win prob vs. \infty-rich opponent00 if p < \frac{1}{2}; ;1-(q/p)^i if p > \frac{1}{2}

01.Maths/Probability/02.Conditional-Prob.title: 12.The Prosecutor's Fallacy
01.Maths/Probability/02.Conditional-Prob.content:
In a criminal trial, the prosecutor presents DNA evidence and states: "The probability of this DNA match occurring by chance in an innocent person is 1 in 1,000,000. Therefore, there is only a 1 in 1,000,000 chance the defendant is innocent."
                  
                

What is wrong with this reasoning?
The Core Confusion
The prosecutor’s fallacy is a specific, named instance of conflating a conditional with its transpose. In court, it goes like this:

The prosecution presents evidence E (say, a DNA match).
The expert witness states: “The probability of this match if the defendant is innocent is 1 in a million.”
The jury hears: “The probability that the defendant is innocent is 1 in a million.”

Formally, the fallacy is:
P(E \mid \text{innocent}) \approx 0 \implies P(\text{innocent} \mid E) \approx 0
This inference is not valid. It ignores the prior. It is exactly the error Bayes’ rule exists to correct.

The Fallacy in Symbols
Let I = “defendant is innocent”, E = “evidence observed (e.g. DNA match)“.
What the expert gives us: P(E \mid I) = \varepsilon \quad \text{(very small)}
What Bayes’ rule says we actually need: P(I \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid I)P(I)}{P(E)}
Expanding the denominator by LOTP: P(I \mid E) = \frac{\varepsilon \cdot P(I)}{\varepsilon \cdot P(I) + P(E \mid I^c)\cdot P(I^c)}
The fallacy amounts to treating P(I \mid E) as though P(I) and P(E \mid I^c) don’t exist — as if the prior were uniform and the likelihood ratio were the whole story.

Why the Error is So Easy to Make
The statement P(E \mid I) = 10^{-6} sounds like it says something about guilt. It doesn’t. It says something about the generative model under innocence — how surprising the evidence would be in a world where the defendant didn’t do it.
The question a jury must answer is the posterior: given everything we know, how probable is guilt? That requires:

A prior P(I) — before seeing the DNA, how likely was this specific person to be the perpetrator?
The likelihood under guilt P(E \mid I^c) — how probable is the evidence if they did do it?

Both are typically left out of expert testimony, and both matter enormously.

A Worked Example: The DNA Database Trawl
This is the case that makes students genuinely uncomfortable.
Setup. A crime occurs. Police have a DNA sample from the scene. They trawl a database of N = 1{,}000{,}000 people. The DNA test has a false positive rate of \Pr(\text{match} \mid \text{innocent}) = 10^{-6}.
One person — call him X — matches. He is arrested. The prosecutor argues: “The probability of a false match is 1 in a million. He must be guilty.”
Let’s actually compute P(X \text{ is innocent} \mid X \text{ matched}).
Assume the true perpetrator is in the database (worst case for the defendant). So exactly one person is guilty. The prior probability that X specifically is guilty, before seeing any match:
P(X \text{ is guilty}) = \frac{1}{N} = 10^{-6}
Now apply LOTP. There are N = 10^6 people. Expected number of matches:

From the guilty person: 1 (they always match, assume \Pr(\text{match} \mid \text{guilty}) = 1)
From the innocent N-1 people: (N-1) \times 10^{-6} \approx 1 false positive

So we expect roughly 2 matches total. X is one of approximately 2 people who matched. Therefore:
P(X \text{ is innocent} \mid X \text{ matched}) \approx \frac{1}{2}
The probability of innocence is approximately 50% — not 1 in a million. The prosecutor was off by a factor of 500{,}000.
The lesson. When you trawl a large database, the false positive rate must be multiplied by the database size. The prior probability of guilt for any single person is 1/N, which exactly cancels the small false-positive rate when N \sim 1/\varepsilon. This is sometimes called the database trawl problem or the birthday-problem cousin — rare events become likely when you look at enough trials.

The Formal Theorem: What the Fallacy Ignores
State it cleanly. We always have:
\frac{P(I \mid E)}{P(I^c \mid E)} = \underbrace{\frac{P(E \mid I)}{P(E \mid I^c)}}_{\Lambda\text{ (Bayes factor)}} \times \underbrace{\frac{P(I)}{P(I^c)}}_{\text{prior odds}}
The prosecutor’s fallacy is equivalent to claiming that \Lambda alone determines P(I \mid E). But:

If P(I) \approx 1 (the person was chosen from a huge population with no other evidence), \Lambda = 10^6 might still leave posterior odds roughly 1:1.
If P(I) \approx 0 (caught at the scene, fingerprints everywhere), even a weak \Lambda = 10 makes \Pr(I \mid E) very small.

The Bayes factor is not the posterior. It is the update multiplicative factor. These are very different things.

The Transposed Conditional: A Taxonomy
The prosecutor’s fallacy is the most famous instance of a general error. Worth cataloguing:






























ContextFallacyCorrect statementCriminal trial\Pr(E \mid I) \small implies guiltNeed \Pr(I \mid E) via BayesMedical testingPositive test \Rightarrow disease\Pr(D \mid T^+) depends on prevalenceHypothesis testingp < 0.05 \Rightarrow H_0 falsep-value is \Pr(\text{data} \mid H_0), not \Pr(H_0 \mid \text{data})Machine learningHigh accuracy \Rightarrow reliable on minority classAccuracy ignores class imbalance
The third row is particularly painful: the entire frequentist p-value framework is vulnerable to exactly this confusion. A p-value of 0.01 does not mean there is a 1% probability the null hypothesis is true. It means: if the null were true, data this extreme would occur 1% of the time. These are different.

Real Cases
Sally Clark (UK, 1999). Convicted of murdering her two infant sons. Expert witness Sir Roy Meadow claimed the probability of two cot deaths in one family was 1/73{,}000{,}000. He obtained this by squaring 1/8500 (the rate of a single cot death in affluent families) — treating the deaths as independent. But:

The events are not independent (genetic and environmental factors are shared).
More importantly, he gave \Pr(\text{two cot deaths} \mid \text{innocent}) and the jury treated it as \Pr(\text{innocent} \mid \text{two cot deaths}).
The correct computation must also account for the prior probability of a mother murdering two children, which is also extremely rare.

Sally Clark was convicted, spent three years in prison, was eventually acquitted, and died of acute alcohol poisoning four years later. The Royal Statistical Society issued a public statement condemning the use of statistics in her trial.
R v. Adams (UK, 1996). A Bayesian defence. The defence actually tried to walk the jury through Bayes’ rule. The Court of Appeal rejected it, ruling that Bayesian reasoning was “inappropriate” for juries to use when assessing non-statistical evidence. This remains controversial.

The Defence Fallacy (The Other Side)
There is a symmetric error made by defence attorneys, sometimes called the defence attorney’s fallacy:

“One in a million people match this DNA profile. There are 60 million people in this country. Therefore there are 60 other potential suspects. My client is just one of 61.”

This ignores all other evidence. If the defendant was also found at the crime scene, knew the victim, had motive, and left fingerprints, the prior \Pr(I) is already very low. Bayes’ rule accounts for all evidence jointly, not just the DNA.
Both fallacies are failures to properly compute the posterior. One ignores the prior (prosecutor), one ignores the likelihood of other evidence (defence).

Connection to p-Values and Why This Matters for You
When you encounter a paper that says ”p = 0.03, therefore the effect is real,” that is a soft version of the prosecutor’s fallacy. The p-value is:
p = P(\text{test statistic} \geq t_{\text{obs}} \mid H_0 \text{ true})
To get P(H_0 \text{ true} \mid \text{data}), you need:

A prior on H_0
The likelihood under H_1

This is exactly what Bayesian hypothesis testing provides. The frequentist framework deliberately avoids specifying a prior — which is philosophically motivated but means the p-value literally cannot tell you the probability that your null is false. Every time someone interprets it that way, they are committing a version of the prosecutor’s fallacy.

Summary



































AspectProsecutor’s ClaimCorrect CalculationQuantity statedP(E \mid I)Need P(I \mid E)What’s missingPrior P(I), base ratesFull Bayes’ ruleDirection of errorAlways overstates guiltDepends on priorFixApply Bayes’ rule with explicit priorPosterior = likelihood × prior / evidenceThe fallacy is seductive because P(E \mid I) is easy to compute and easy to state. The posterior P(I \mid E) requires committing to a prior, which feels subjective. But refusing to specify a prior doesn’t make it go away — it just means you’re implicitly using a flat prior and pretending otherwise.
see also: 14.The Defense Attorney’s Fallacy

01.Maths/Probability/02.Conditional-Prob.title: 13.Simpson's Paradox
01.Maths/Probability/02.Conditional-Prob.content:
Simpson’s Paradox: A trend or association that appears in several subgroups of data can disappear or reverse when the subgroups are combined into a single aggregate.
This is not a statistical error. It is not a rounding artifact. It is a mathematically exact phenomenon, and it happens because the subgroups are not sampled in equal proportions.

A Concrete Example — The Classic Drug Trial
Two treatments for kidney stones: Treatment A and Treatment B.
Small stones:























TreatmentRecoveredTotalSuccess rateTreatment A818793%Treatment B23427087%
A beats B for small stones.
Large stones:























TreatmentRecoveredTotalSuccess rateTreatment A19226373%Treatment B558069%
A beats B for large stones.
Combined (ignoring stone size):























TreatmentRecoveredTotalSuccess rateTreatment A27335078%Treatment B28935083%
B beats A overall.
A is better for small stones. A is better for large stones. B is better overall. This is not a trick — these are real numbers from a real 1986 medical study (Charig et al.).

Why Does This Happen? — The Weighted Average Argument
The key: the mixing proportions differ between groups.
Treatment A was predominantly given to patients with large stones (the harder cases) — 263 out of 350. Treatment B was predominantly given to patients with small stones (the easier cases) — 270 out of 350.
The overall success rate is a weighted average of the subgroup rates, where the weights are the group sizes:
P(\text{success} \mid A) = P(\text{success} \mid A, \text{small}) \cdot P(\text{small} \mid A) + P(\text{success} \mid A, \text{large}) \cdot P(\text{large} \mid A)
= 0.93 \cdot \frac{87}{350} + 0.73 \cdot \frac{263}{350} = 0.93 \cdot 0.249 + 0.73 \cdot 0.751 \approx 0.78
P(\text{success} \mid B) = 0.87 \cdot \frac{270}{350} + 0.69 \cdot \frac{80}{350} = 0.87 \cdot 0.771 + 0.69 \cdot 0.229 \approx 0.83
Treatment A is dragged down by being applied to harder cases. Treatment B is buoyed by being applied to easier cases. The aggregate hides this entirely.

This is just LOTP in action — total probability as a weighted average over a partition. The paradox is what happens when those weights differ systematically between the two groups being compared.


The Mathematical Skeleton
Strip away the story. The paradox says: it is possible to have
\frac{a_1}{b_1} > \frac{c_1}{d_1} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{a_2}{b_2} > \frac{c_2}{d_2}
and yet
\frac{a_1 + a_2}{b_1 + b_2} < \frac{c_1 + c_2}{d_1 + d_2}
A minimal numerical example:
\frac{1}{2} > \frac{0}{1} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{3}{5} > \frac{3}{10}
but
\frac{1+3}{2+5} = \frac{4}{7} \approx 0.571 < \frac{0+3}{1+10} = \frac{3}{11} \approx 0.273
Wait — let me construct it properly.
\frac{3}{4} > \frac{1}{2} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{1}{5} > \frac{0}{4}
but
\frac{3+1}{4+5} = \frac{4}{9} \approx 0.44 < \frac{1+0}{2+4} = \frac{1}{6} \approx 0.17
Hmm, that doesn’t flip. The point is that the flip requires the group with the lower rate to have much larger weight in one arm. Let me just keep the kidney stone numbers — they are the cleanest real example.
The algebraic condition for the reversal: let w_A^S = P(\text{small} \mid A) and w_B^S = P(\text{small} \mid B). The reversal occurs when w_B^S \gg w_A^S — i.e., when the group with the higher subgroup rate (small stones, where both treatments do well) is heavily overrepresented in arm B. The confound tilts the aggregate.

The Causal Lens — When Should You Condition?
This is where Simpson’s Paradox stops being just a math curiosity and becomes a question about causal inference.
There are two different questions:

“Which treatment has a better success rate in this dataset?” — descriptive/associational
“Which treatment should I prescribe to a new patient?” — causal/interventional

For question 2, the answer is Treatment A, despite its lower aggregate rate. Here’s why: stone size is a confounder — it affects both which treatment doctors chose to give and the probability of recovery. When you condition on stone size, you remove the confounding and see the true treatment effect.
The aggregate rate mixes two effects:

The effect of treatment on recovery (what we want)
The effect of doctor selection bias on who gets which treatment (noise we don’t want)

Conditioning on stone size blocks the back-door path: \text{Treatment} \leftarrow \text{Stone Size} \rightarrow \text{Recovery}. The subgroup analysis is causally correct. The aggregate is causally misleading.

Pearl’s language: The aggregate comparison is an associational quantity, P(\text{recovery} \mid \text{treatment} = A). What we actually want for a decision is the interventional quantity, P(\text{recovery} \mid \text{do}(\text{treatment} = A)). These coincide only when there is no confounding. Simpson’s Paradox is precisely the failure of the associational quantity to track the interventional one.


But Sometimes You Should NOT Condition — The Reversal Trap
Here is the dangerous flip side. Not every variable you could condition on is a confounder. Sometimes conditioning creates a spurious reversal rather than fixing one.
Example: Collider Bias
Suppose you study the relationship between talent and hard work among professional athletes. You find that among pros, talent and hard work are negatively correlated — the most talented athletes tend to work out less.
Does this mean talent makes you lazy?
No. The population of professional athletes is a selected subset — you’ve conditioned on “made it to the pros,” which is a collider: both talent and hard work independently cause someone to become a pro. Conditioning on a collider induces a spurious negative correlation between its causes, even if talent and hard work are independent in the general population.
The causal graph:
\text{Talent} \rightarrow \text{Pro} \leftarrow \text{Hard Work}
Conditioning on \text{Pro} opens a path between Talent and Hard Work that didn’t exist before. This is the Berkson’s Paradox — conditioning on a collider introduces association between independent causes.

The lesson: Whether to condition on a variable is a causal question, not a statistical one. Conditioning on a confounder (like stone size) fixes Simpson’s Paradox. Conditioning on a collider (like “being a pro”) creates a new spurious association. The data alone cannot tell you which is which — you need a causal model (a DAG).


The LOTP Connection
Every instance of Simpson’s Paradox is just LOTP with adversarially chosen weights.
P(B \mid A) = \sum_i P(B \mid A, C_i) P(C_i \mid A) P(B \mid A^c) = \sum_i P(B \mid A^c, C_i) P(C_i \mid A^c)
It is entirely possible that:
P(B \mid A, C_i) > P(B \mid A^c, C_i) \quad \forall i
and yet:
P(B \mid A) < P(B \mid A^c)
if the weights P(C_i \mid A) and P(C_i \mid A^c) differ enough in the wrong direction.
The aggregate comparison P(B \mid A) vs P(B \mid A^c) is a weighted average of the conditional comparisons, and the weights depend on the conditional distribution of C given A — which differs between the two arms. That’s the whole mechanism, full stop.

Another Classic Example — UC Berkeley Admissions (1973)
UC Berkeley was sued for gender bias in graduate admissions. The aggregate data showed men were admitted at a higher rate than women.























GroupAppliedAdmittedRateMen8442373844%Women4321149435%
Looks like bias. But when broken down by department, most individual departments showed either no bias or a slight bias in favor of women.
What happened? Women applied disproportionately to more competitive departments (English, History) with low admission rates for everyone. Men applied more to less competitive departments (Engineering, Chemistry) with high admission rates. The aggregate masked completely different application patterns.
The confound: department choice, which is correlated with both gender and admission probability.
Here the causal question is subtle — is department choice itself affected by gender discrimination (e.g., women steered away from engineering)? If so, conditioning on department might over-correct. This is exactly the Pearl point: the right answer depends on the causal graph, not just the numbers.

How to Detect It in Practice
Simpson’s Paradox lurks whenever:

You have a confounding variable C that is correlated with both the treatment A and the outcome B
The distribution of C differs between the groups being compared
You are looking at an aggregate comparison without conditioning on C

Red flags in data:

Unequal group sizes across subgroups
Known or suspected confounders that weren’t controlled for
Results that seem “too good” or “too bad” in one direction


Summary of the Key Distinctions

























SituationVariable typeShould you condition?Stone size in drug trialConfounder (causes both treatment assignment and outcome)Yes — conditioning removes bias”Being a pro” in talent/work studyCollider (caused by both variables)No — conditioning introduces spurious associationDepartment in BerkeleyMediator or confounder?Depends on the causal graph
The statistics cannot answer this question. The causal graph can.

01.Maths/Probability/02.Conditional-Prob.title: 14.The Defense Attorney's Fallacy
01.Maths/Probability/02.Conditional-Prob.content:
You’re sitting in a courtroom. The prosecution presents DNA evidence:

“The probability of a random innocent person matching this DNA profile is 1 in a million.”

The defense attorney stands up and says:

“There are 8 million people in this city. That means roughly 8 people share this DNA. My client is just one of those 8. The probability he’s guilty given the match is only 1 in 8 — that’s just 12.5%! Reasonable doubt!”

Sounds reasonable. It is wrong. Here’s why.


The Formal Setup
Let me define the events cleanly:
M = \text{"the defendant's DNA matches the sample"} G = \text{"the defendant is guilty"}
The prosecutor told us: P(M \mid G^c) = 10^{-6}
What we actually care about — what the jury needs — is: P(G \mid M) = ;?
These are not the same thing. Confusing them is the Prosecutor’s Fallacy (its own entry). But the defense attorney is making a different — and subtler — mistake.

The Defense Attorney’s Error
The defense attorney’s argument implicitly computes:
P(G \mid M) = \frac{1}{8}
by reasoning: “8 people match, so each has equal probability \frac{1}{8}.”
This would be valid only if the prior probability of guilt is uniform over all 8 million people, i.e., if the defendant was chosen uniformly at random from the city with no other evidence.
But that’s not what happened.
The defendant wasn’t plucked randomly from the population. He was already a suspect — perhaps identified through witnesses, security footage, motive, opportunity. The prior P(G) is not \frac{1}{8{,}000{,}000}.

The Correct Framework — Bayes’ Theorem
Let’s use Bayes properly. By LOTP (Law of Total Probability):
P(G \mid M) = \frac{P(M \mid G), P(G)}{P(M \mid G), P(G) + P(M \mid G^c), P(G^c)}
Now plug in what we know:

P(M \mid G) = 1 — if guilty, their DNA certainly matches
P(M \mid G^c) = 10^{-6} — given innocent, the chance of matching is 1 in a million
P(G) — this is the key variable the defense attorney ignores

Let’s see what happens under different priors:
Scenario A: Weak Prior — Defendant was selected nearly randomly
P(G) = \frac{1}{8{,}000{,}000}
P(G \mid M) = \frac{1 \cdot \frac{1}{8{,}000{,}000}}{1 \cdot \frac{1}{8{,}000{,}000} + 10^{-6} \cdot \frac{8{,}000{,}000 - 1}{8{,}000{,}000}}
\approx \frac{10^{-6}/8}{10^{-6}/8 + 10^{-6}} = \frac{1/8}{1/8 + 1} = \frac{1}{9} \approx 11
Here the defense attorney’s estimate is roughly right — but only because the prior is uniform, which is an unrealistic assumption.
Scenario B: Strong Prior — Defendant was identified via other evidence
Suppose P(G) = 0.6 before the DNA match (based on witness testimony, security footage, etc.)
P(G \mid M) = \frac{1 \cdot 0.6}{1 \cdot 0.6 + 10^{-6} \cdot 0.4} = \frac{0.6}{0.6 + 0.0000004} \approx 0.9999993
The DNA match, on top of other evidence, makes guilt nearly certain. The defense attorney’s “1 in 8” argument evaporates completely.

What the Fallacy Actually Is
The defense attorney’s fallacy is the error of ignoring the prior — treating P(G \mid M) as if the defendant were a randomly selected member of the population, when in fact the act of being a defendant already carries significant prior information.
More precisely:

The defense attorney implicitly assumes P(G) = P(\text{random person is guilty}) when computing P(G \mid M), ignoring all evidence that led to the suspect being identified in the first place.

This is a failure to respect the full posterior, not just the likelihood ratio.

The Symmetry with the Prosecutor’s Fallacy
These two fallacies form a pair — each is the mirror image of the other:




















FallacyThe ErrorDirection of BiasProsecutor’sP(M \mid G^c) is small, therefore P(G^c \mid M) is smallOverstates guiltDefense Attorney’sIgnores prior; treats match as one-of-many in populationUnderstates guilt
The prosecutor transposes the conditional. The defense attorney ignores what made this person a defendant.
Neither is doing Bayes correctly.

A Cleaner Way to See It — Likelihood Ratios
The Bayes factor (likelihood ratio) approach is often cleaner for courtroom reasoning:
\underbrace{\frac{P(G \mid M)}{P(G^c \mid M)}}_{\text{posterior odds}} = \underbrace{\frac{P(M \mid G)}{P(M \mid G^c)}}_{\text{likelihood ratio}} \times \underbrace{\frac{P(G)}{P(G^c)}}_{\text{prior odds}}
The DNA evidence gives a likelihood ratio of:
\frac{1}{10^{-6}} = 1{,}000{,}000
So the DNA evidence multiplies the prior odds by one million. Whether that makes the posterior odds compelling depends entirely on what the prior odds were.
The defense attorney wants you to use prior odds of \frac{1}{8{,}000{,}000}, giving posterior odds of about \frac{1}{8}. The prosecutor might reasonably argue for a much higher prior based on other evidence, making the posterior odds enormous.
The DNA evidence itself doesn’t determine guilt — it updates whatever prior the jury should already have.

The Deeper Lesson
This fallacy appears everywhere outside courtrooms:

Medical testing: “Only 1 in 10,000 people have this disease, so even with a positive test result, the patient is probably fine” — this ignores what made the doctor order the test.
Rare event detection: Treating a rare match as uninformative by comparing to the population, when the prior for the specific case is much stronger.

The key takeaway from Blitzstein’s framing (STAT 110, Lecture 5-ish):

Conditional probabilities are not symmetric. The event you condition on matters enormously. Before you flip P(A \mid B) to P(B \mid A), ask yourself whether you have any justification whatsoever for that transposition.


Summary:

The defense attorney’s fallacy uses a population-level base rate as the prior for a specific defendant, ignoring all evidence that elevated that individual to suspect status in the first place.

01.Maths/Probability/03.Random-Variable/.title: 01.Random Variable (RV)
01.Maths/Probability/03.Random-Variable/.content:
A Random Variable (RV) is a function that assigns a numerical value to each outcome of a random experiment.

Formal:

X: \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}
where \Omega is the sample space.
Random Variables are of 2 types:

1. Discrete Random Variable

Takes countable values.
Examples: number of heads in 10 coin flips, number of cars passing a checkpoint.
Associated with a PMF (Probability Mass Function).

p_X(x) = P(X = x)
2. Continuous Random Variable

Takes uncountable values (any real number in an interval).
Examples: height of a person, time to complete a task.
Associated with a PDF (Probability Density Function).

f_X(x) \ge 0, \quad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x) dx = 1

Probabilities computed as area under the curve:

P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f_X(x) dx

Support
The support of a random variable (X) is the set of values with non-zero probability (discrete) or non-zero density (continuous):
\text{Support}(X) = \{ x : p_X(x) > 0 \} \quad \text{or} \quad \{ x : f_X(x) > 0 \}

You use it whenever you want to identify the domain of possible outcomes with non-zero probability or density.

Side-by-Side Comparison






























PropertyDiscreteContinuousDefined byP(X = x) > 0f_X(x) > 0Support typeCountable setInterval (or union of intervals)Example{1,2,3,4,5,6}[0, 1]Outside supportProbability = 0Density = 0
Why Support Matters


                  
                  Strategic Insight The support is foundational to everything that follows in probability: 
                  
                


Expectations \mathbb{E}[X]: Sum/integrate only over the support
Normalization: The total probability over the support must equal 1
Conditioning: When conditioning on events, the support can shrink
Distributions: Many named distributions (Binomial, Poisson, Exponential, Normal) are partially characterized by their support



see more: 09.Support of a Random Variable

Examples
Example 1: Discrete RV

Toss a coin 3 times; let (X) = number of heads.
Support: ({0,1,2,3})
PMF:

p_X(x) = \binom{3}{x} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3
Example 2: Continuous RV

Let (X) = height of students in a class (in cm), modeled as continuous.
PDF: Normal distribution with mean 170 cm, SD 10 cm.

f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi 10^2}} e^{-(x-170)^2/(2\cdot10^2)}

Probability of a student being 160–180 cm tall:

P(160 \le X \le 180) = \int_{160}^{180} f_X(x) dx

Relation to PMF / PDF / CDF

Discrete RV: PMF → CDF

F_X(x) = \sum_{t \le x} p_X(t)
more detailed in 11.CDF vs PMF

Continuous RV: PDF → CDF

F_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(t) dt
see more: 08.Probability Mass Function (PMF)
