01.Maths/Probability/05.Continuous-Rando.title: 05.Independence — Events vs. Random Variables
01.Maths/Probability/05.Continuous-Rando.content:
Independence is one of those words that feels intuitive until you try to prove something with it. Then you realize the intuition was doing a lot of hidden work, and you need the definition to take over.


Two Notions, One Word
The word “independent” appears in two distinct but related contexts in probability:

Independence of events: A and B are independent if knowing A occurred gives no information about whether B occurred.
Independence of random variables: X and Y are independent if knowing the value of X gives no information about the distribution of Y.

These are not the same definition. The second generalizes the first in a precise way. I want to understand both from the ground up, understand the relationship between them, and understand the common errors that come from conflating them.

Part I — Independence of Events
The Definition
Events A and B are independent if:
P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)
That is the definition. Not P(A \mid B) = P(A), at least not as the primary definition. The conditional form is equivalent when P(B) > 0, but the product form is primary because it does not require conditioning to be defined.
Why the product form is primary: Conditional probability P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B) / P(B) is undefined when P(B) = 0. But two events can be independent even when one of them has probability zero — the product form handles this without issue. Defining independence via the product form avoids the degenerate case cleanly.
The conditional restatement: When P(B) > 0:
P(A \cap B) = P(A) P(B) \iff P(A \mid B) = P(A)
This is the intuitive version: conditioning on B does not change the probability of A. By symmetry, it also equals P(B \mid A) = P(B) when P(A) > 0. Independence is symmetric.
Mutual Independence of Multiple Events
For three events A, B, C, mutual independence requires all of the following:
P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B) P(A \cap C) = P(A)P(C) P(B \cap C) = P(B)P(C) P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(A)P(B)P(C)
All four conditions. The first three say the events are pairwise independent. The fourth is an additional condition. Pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence.
The canonical counterexample — Pairwise but not mutually independent:
Toss two fair coins. Let:

A = first coin is Heads
B = second coin is Heads
C = the two coins match (both H or both T)

Then P(A) = P(B) = P(C) = 1/2.
Check pairwise independence: P(A \cap B) = P(\text{HH}) = 1/4 = P(A)P(B) \quad \checkmark P(A \cap C) = P(\text{HH}) = 1/4 = P(A)P(C) \quad \checkmark P(B \cap C) = P(\text{HH}) = 1/4 = P(B)P(C) \quad \checkmark
Check mutual independence: P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(\text{HH}) = 1/4 \neq \frac{1}{8} = P(A)P(B)P(C) \quad \times
So A, B, C are pairwise independent but not mutually independent. Knowing A and B both occurred tells you C occurred with certainty — so A and B together are not independent of C.

This example should be internalized. It shows that independence is not just a pairwise property. For n events to be mutually independent, all 2^n - n - 1 subset conditions must hold. This is a genuinely stronger requirement.

For n events A_1, \ldots, A_n to be mutually independent:
P!\left(\bigcap_{i \in S} A_i\right) = \prod_{i \in S} P(A_i) \quad \text{for every subset } S \subseteq {1, \ldots, n}
Independence vs. Disjointness — The Most Common Confusion
If A and B are disjoint (A \cap B = \emptyset) and both have positive probability, then:
P(A \cap B) = 0 \neq P(A)P(B) > 0
So disjoint events with positive probability are never independent. In fact, they are maximally dependent: knowing A occurred tells you with certainty that B did not.
Independence says the events have no information about each other. Disjointness says one rules out the other completely. These are opposite extremes on the spectrum of dependence.

I remind myself of this whenever I am tempted to say “these events don’t overlap so they should be independent.” That is exactly backwards.


Part II — Independence of Random Variables
The Definition
Random variables X and Y are independent if for all sets A and B:
P(X \in A, Y \in B) = P(X \in A) \cdot P(Y \in B)
Equivalently — and this is the version I use most in practice — X and Y are independent if and only if their joint CDF factors:
F_{X,Y}(x, y) = F_X(x) \cdot F_Y(y) \quad \text{for all } x, y
For discrete random variables, this becomes: the joint PMF factors into the marginals:
P(X = x, Y = y) = P(X = x) \cdot P(Y = y) \quad \text{for all } x, y
For continuous random variables: the joint PDF factors:
f_{X,Y}(x, y) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y) \quad \text{for all } x, y
The factorization condition is both necessary and sufficient.
The Relationship to Event Independence
Let A \in \sigma(X) be any event defined in terms of X (i.e., any event of the form {X \in B}), and similarly C \in \sigma(Y). Then:
X \perp Y \implies A \text{ and } C \text{ are independent events}
Random variable independence implies event independence for all events generated by those random variables. This is why random variable independence is strictly stronger than any particular pair of events being independent.
Conversely, if every event generated by X is independent of every event generated by Y, then X and Y are independent as random variables. The random variable definition is exactly the requirement that the event independence holds simultaneously and universally.
Checking Independence via Joint Density Factorization
In practice, for continuous random variables, the most direct method is:

Write down f_{X,Y}(x,y).
Check whether it factors as g(x) \cdot h(y) for some functions g and h.
If it does, then X \perp Y (and g and h are proportional to the marginals).

Crucial subtlety — the support must factor too. If the support of (X,Y) is a region that cannot be written as a Cartesian product S_X \times S_Y, then X and Y cannot be independent, regardless of whether the density formula factors.
Counterexample: Suppose (X,Y) is uniform on the triangle {(x,y) : x > 0, y > 0, x + y < 1}. The joint density is f(x,y) = 2 on this region. The density formula is a constant, which trivially factors. But X and Y are not independent — knowing X = 0.9 forces Y < 0.1. The support is not a rectangle, so independence fails.
The correct factorization condition is:
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = g(x) h(y) \quad \text{for all } (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2
not just on the support. When the support is a non-rectangular region, f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 0 for points outside it but f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y) > 0 for those same points, so the product form fails globally.

Part III — What Independence Buys You
Independence is not just a philosophical statement. It is a computational engine. Here are the key consequences, each with its justification.
1. Expectation of a Product
X \perp Y \implies E[XY] = E[X] \cdot E[Y]
Proof (continuous):
E[XY] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty xy \cdot f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty xy \cdot f_X(x) f_Y(y), dx, dy
= \left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty x f_X(x), dx\right)!\left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty y f_Y(y), dy\right) = E[X] \cdot E[Y]
The factorization of the joint density is what allows the double integral to split into a product of single integrals.
The converse is false. E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] — called uncorrelatedness — does not imply independence. This is one of the most important non-implications in probability.
Counterexample: Let Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) and X = Z, Y = Z^2. Then:
E[XY] = E[Z^3] = 0 = E[Z] \cdot E[Z^2] = 0 \cdot 1
So E[XY] = E[X]E[Y], but X and Y are clearly dependent — knowing X = z tells you Y = z^2 with certainty.
2. Variance of a Sum
X \perp Y \implies \text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)
Proof:
\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\text{Cov}(X,Y)
Independence implies \text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] = 0. So the cross-term vanishes.
Note: \text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0 (uncorrelated) does not imply independence, as shown above. But independence does imply zero covariance.
3. MGF of a Sum
X \perp Y \implies M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t) \cdot M_Y(t)
Proof:
M_{X+Y}(t) = E[e^{t(X+Y)}] = E[e^{tX} e^{tY}] = E[e^{tX}] \cdot E[e^{tY}] = M_X(t) \cdot M_Y(t)
The second equality uses independence via the product expectation rule. This is how I prove that sums of independent Poissons are Poisson, sums of independent Normals are Normal, sums of independent Gammas are Gamma.
4. LOTUS for Independent Variables
X \perp Y \implies E[g(X) h(Y)] = E[g(X)] \cdot E[h(Y)]
for any functions g and h. This follows from the same splitting argument as the expectation of a product, applied to g(X) and h(Y) which are themselves independent (functions of independent r.v.s are independent).

Part IV — Functions of Independent Random Variables
Theorem. If X \perp Y and g, h are measurable functions, then g(X) \perp h(Y).
Proof sketch. Any event defined in terms of g(X) is of the form {g(X) \in A} = {X \in g^{-1}(A)}, which is an event in \sigma(X). Similarly for h(Y). Since X \perp Y, all events in \sigma(X) are independent of all events in \sigma(Y). \square
This is used constantly without comment. When I write the MGF factorization E[e^{tX} e^{tY}] = E[e^{tX}]E[e^{tY}], I am applying this theorem to g(x) = e^{tx} and h(y) = e^{ty}.

Part V — Conditional Independence
Events A and B are conditionally independent given C if:
P(A \cap B \mid C) = P(A \mid C) \cdot P(B \mid C)
Random variables X and Y are conditionally independent given Z if, for all x, y, z:
f_{X,Y \mid Z}(x, y \mid z) = f_{X \mid Z}(x \mid z) \cdot f_{Y \mid Z}(y \mid z)
Conditional independence does not imply marginal independence, and vice versa.
Example (conditional independence, not marginal): X and Y are the results of two different tests for the same disease. Marginally, they are correlated — both depend on whether the person has the disease. But conditionally on the disease status Z, the tests are independent (each test is a noisy independent measurement given the true state).
Example (marginal independence, not conditional): Two fair coins X and Y are independent. But condition on C = {X + Y = 1} (exactly one Head). Then given C, knowing X tells you Y exactly. Marginally independent, conditionally dependent.

Part VI — The Hierarchy of Dependence Concepts
It is worth placing all the concepts in order:
\text{Mutual independence} \implies \text{Pairwise independence} \text{Independence of r.v.s} \implies \text{Zero covariance (uncorrelated)} \text{Independence of r.v.s} \implies \text{Every pair of generated events is independent}
None of these arrows reverse in general. The failure modes are:



































ClaimTrue?CounterexamplePairwise ind. \Rightarrow mutual ind.NoCoins A, B, C example aboveUncorrelated \Rightarrow independentNoX = Z, Y = Z^2, Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)Disjoint \Rightarrow independentNoDisjoint events are maximally dependentCond. ind. \Rightarrow marginal ind.NoDisease-test exampleMarginal ind. \Rightarrow cond. ind.NoTwo coins conditioned on sum
For jointly Normal random variables, uncorrelated does imply independent. This is a special property of the Normal, not a general fact.
Proof: If (X,Y) is jointly Normal and \text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0, the joint density is:
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_X\sigma_Y}\exp!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu_X)^2}{2\sigma_X^2} - \frac{(y-\mu_Y)^2}{2\sigma_Y^2}\right) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y)
The joint density factors because the covariance term in the bivariate Normal exponent vanishes when \rho = 0. This factorization is exactly the independence condition.

What I Should Be Able to Do Without Notes

State the definition of independence for events and explain why the product form is primary over the conditional form.
Construct the pairwise-but-not-mutually-independent counterexample from scratch.
State the definition of independence for random variables in terms of joint CDF, joint PMF, and joint PDF factorization.
Explain why non-rectangular support prevents independence even if the density formula factors.
Prove E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] under independence.
Give the X = Z, Y = Z^2 counterexample to “uncorrelated implies independent.”
State the one case where uncorrelated does imply independent, and prove it.
State both directions of conditional vs. marginal independence failure with examples.

01.Maths/Probability/05.Continuous-Rando.title: 06.Normal Distribution
01.Maths/Probability/05.Continuous-Rando.content:
Every distribution, pushed far enough, wants to be Normal. That is not a metaphor — it is a theorem. The Central Limit Theorem is the reason the Normal is everywhere, and until you understand that theorem deeply, the Normal feels like a lucky coincidence rather than an inevitability.


Definition
X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) has PDF:
f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp!\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \quad x \in \mathbb{R}
Two parameters: \mu \in \mathbb{R} is the mean (location), \sigma^2 > 0 is the variance (spread). The distribution is symmetric about \mu, bell-shaped, and supported on all of \mathbb{R}.
The standard Normal is the special case \mu = 0, \sigma^2 = 1:
Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), \quad \varphi(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}
Everything about the general Normal reduces to the standard one via standardization: if X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), then Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1).

The Normalization Constant — Why \sqrt{2\pi}
The fact that \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2}, dx = \sqrt{2\pi} is not obvious. It is one of those results that every analyst knows and everyone should derive at least once. The trick is to square the integral and convert to polar coordinates.
Let I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2}, dx. Then:
I^2 = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2}, dx, dy
Convert to polar: x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta, dx,dy = r,dr,d\theta, x^2 + y^2 = r^2:
I^2 = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/2} \cdot r, dr, d\theta = 2\pi \int_0^\infty r e^{-r^2/2}, dr
Let u = r^2/2, du = r,dr:
I^2 = 2\pi \int_0^\infty e^{-u}, du = 2\pi \cdot 1 = 2\pi
Therefore I = \sqrt{2\pi}. \square
This is clean. The Gaussian integral does not yield to direct computation — it requires lifting to two dimensions, exploiting rotational symmetry, and collapsing back down. The appearance of \pi is a consequence of that symmetry, not a numerical accident.

Mean, Variance, and MGF
Mean
By symmetry of \varphi about 0, E[Z] = 0 for the standard Normal. For the general case, if X = \mu + \sigma Z:
E[X] = \mu + \sigma E[Z] = \mu
I can also compute it directly. Since \varphi is symmetric, the integrand z \cdot \varphi(z) is odd, and the integral over \mathbb{R} is zero.
Variance
\text{Var}(Z) = E[Z^2] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty z^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}, dz
Integrate by parts: let u = z, dv = z e^{-z^2/2}, dz, so v = -e^{-z^2/2}:
E[Z^2] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\left[-z e^{-z^2/2}\Big|_{-\infty}^\infty + \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz\right] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\left[0 + \sqrt{2\pi}\right] = 1
So \text{Var}(Z) = 1, and \text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2 \text{Var}(Z) = \sigma^2.
MGF
M_Z(t) = E[e^{tZ}] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{tz} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}, dz = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{tz - z^2/2}, dz
Complete the square in the exponent:
tz - \frac{z^2}{2} = -\frac{1}{2}(z^2 - 2tz) = -\frac{1}{2}(z-t)^2 + \frac{t^2}{2}
So:
M_Z(t) = \frac{e^{t^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(z-t)^2/2}, dz = e^{t^2/2} \cdot 1 = e^{t^2/2}
The integral equals 1 because e^{-(z-t)^2/2} is (up to the \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} normalizer) a \mathcal{N}(t,1) PDF integrating to 1, and we already pulled that normalizer out.
For the general \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2):
M_X(t) = E[e^{t(\mu + \sigma Z)}] = e^{\mu t} M_Z(\sigma t) = e^{\mu t} \cdot e^{\sigma^2 t^2 / 2} = \exp!\left(\mu t + \frac{\sigma^2 t^2}{2}\right)
This is the MGF I need to know cold. The completing-the-square trick is the move that makes it tractable — I use it in so many other Normal calculations that it should become reflexive.

Moments via the MGF
From M_Z(t) = e^{t^2/2}, expand as a power series:
e^{t^2/2} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(t^2/2)^n}{n!} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^{2n}}{2^n \cdot n!}
The coefficient of t^k / k! in the MGF is E[Z^k]. From the expansion, odd powers of t have zero coefficient, confirming all odd moments are zero (by symmetry). For even moments, the coefficient of t^{2n} is \frac{1}{2^n \cdot n!}, so:
E[Z^{2n}] = \frac{(2n)!}{2^n \cdot n!} = (2n-1)!! = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2n-1)
where (2n-1)!! is the double factorial. So:
E[Z^2] = 1, \quad E[Z^4] = 3, \quad E[Z^6] = 15, \quad E[Z^8] = 105, \ldots
The fourth standardized moment (kurtosis) of the Normal is E[Z^4] = 3. This is why excess kurtosis is defined as E[Z^4] - 3 — it measures departure from Normality.

Linear Transformations
If X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) and Y = aX + b with a \neq 0, then:
Y \sim \mathcal{N}(a\mu + b,\ a^2 \sigma^2)
Proof via MGF:
M_Y(t) = E[e^{t(aX+b)}] = e^{bt} M_X(at) = e^{bt} \exp!\left(\mu(at) + \frac{\sigma^2(at)^2}{2}\right) = \exp!\left((a\mu+b)t + \frac{a^2\sigma^2 t^2}{2}\right)
This is the MGF of \mathcal{N}(a\mu + b, a^2\sigma^2). \square
The Normal family is closed under linear transformations. This is not true of most distributions. It is the reason the Normal is analytically tractable.

Sums of Independent Normals
If X_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2) and X_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2) independently, then:
X_1 + X_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1 + \mu_2,\ \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)
Proof via MGF:
M_{X_1+X_2}(t) = M_{X_1}(t) \cdot M_{X_2}(t) = \exp!\left(\mu_1 t + \frac{\sigma_1^2 t^2}{2}\right)\exp!\left(\mu_2 t + \frac{\sigma_2^2 t^2}{2}\right) = \exp!\left((\mu_1+\mu_2)t + \frac{(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)t^2}{2}\right)
Done. This generalizes: the sum of any finite number of independent Normals is Normal. Variances add (assuming independence). Means always add.

The means adding is just linearity of expectation — no independence needed. The variances adding requires independence. I should never confuse these two facts.


The CDF and \Phi
There is no closed-form expression for the CDF of the standard Normal:
\Phi(z) = \int_{-\infty}^z \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-t^2/2}, dt
This integral cannot be expressed in terms of elementary functions. It is a special function, tabulated and computed numerically.
Symmetry: \Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z). This follows from the symmetry of \varphi.
Useful values to know:













































z\Phi(z)Interpretation00.5Median equals mean1\approx 0.8413One standard deviation above mean1.645\approx 0.9595th percentile1.96\approx 0.975Used in 95% confidence intervals2\approx 0.9772Two standard deviations2.576\approx 0.99599th percentile3\approx 0.9987Three standard deviations
The 68-95-99.7 rule: P(|X - \mu| \leq \sigma) \approx 0.6827 P(|X - \mu| \leq 2\sigma) \approx 0.9545 P(|X - \mu| \leq 3\sigma) \approx 0.9973
These come from 2\Phi(k) - 1 for k = 1, 2, 3. Memorize them — they are used constantly.

The Log-Normal Distribution
If X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), then Y = e^X is log-Normal — its logarithm is Normal.
E[Y] = E[e^X] = M_X(1) = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}
\text{Var}(Y) = E[Y^2] - (E[Y])^2 = e^{2\mu + 2\sigma^2} - e^{2\mu + \sigma^2} = e^{2\mu + \sigma^2}(e^{\sigma^2} - 1)
The mean of the log-Normal is e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}, not e^\mu. The \sigma^2/2 correction comes from the MGF evaluated at t=1, and it matters. Stock prices, income distributions, and biological measurements are often modeled as log-Normal precisely because their logarithms are approximately Normal.

The Normal as a Limit — The Central Limit Theorem
This is the theorem that makes the Normal unavoidable.
Theorem (CLT). Let X_1, X_2, \ldots be i.i.d. with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2 < \infty. Define the standardized sample mean:
Z_n = \frac{\bar{X}_n - \mu}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu)}{\sigma}
Then Z_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1) as n \to \infty.
Proof via MGFs (under the additional assumption that the MGF of X_i exists in a neighborhood of 0):
Let Y_i = (X_i - \mu)/\sigma, so E[Y_i] = 0, \text{Var}(Y_i) = 1. Then Z_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i.
The MGF of Z_n:
M_{Z_n}(t) = \left[M_Y!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right]^n
Now expand M_Y(s) around s = 0:
M_Y(s) = 1 + E[Y]s + \frac{E[Y^2]}{2}s^2 + O(s^3) = 1 + 0 + \frac{s^2}{2} + O(s^3)
Setting s = t/\sqrt{n}:
M_Y!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 1 + \frac{t^2}{2n} + O(n^{-3/2})
Therefore:
M_{Z_n}(t) = \left(1 + \frac{t^2}{2n} + O(n^{-3/2})\right)^n \to e^{t^2/2} \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
The limit \left(1 + \frac{x}{n}\right)^n \to e^x is the standard exponential limit. The result e^{t^2/2} is exactly M_Z(t) for Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1). By the continuity theorem for MGFs, Z_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1). \square
What the CLT is actually saying:
The CLT is a statement about the shape of the distribution of \bar{X}_n, after standardization. It says that regardless of the original distribution of the X_i (as long as finite variance exists), the aggregate behavior of the sum normalizes to Gaussian. The Gaussian is the fixed point of this normalization procedure.
The finite-variance condition is essential. The CLT fails for Cauchy-distributed X_i because \text{Var}(X_i) = \infty. The sample mean of Cauchy r.v.s has the same Cauchy distribution regardless of n — there is no normalization and no convergence to Gaussian.

The Normal and the Poisson — A Connection Worth Knowing
For large \lambda, \text{Pois}(\lambda) \approx \mathcal{N}(\lambda, \lambda). This follows from the CLT: \text{Pois}(\lambda) is the sum of \lambda i.i.d. \text{Pois}(1) random variables (each with mean 1 and variance 1), so by the CLT:
\frac{X - \lambda}{\sqrt{\lambda}} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1)
Similarly, \text{Bin}(n, p) \approx \mathcal{N}(np, np(1-p)) for large n. Same argument: the Binomial is a sum of n i.i.d. Bernoulli(p) r.v.s.
These approximations are the pre-computer method for computing Binomial and Poisson probabilities. They are less important now computationally, but they reveal the structural unity underlying all three distributions.

Gaussian Tail Bounds — Why Tails Matter
The Normal has light tails — exponentially decaying, in fact. For large z > 0:
P(Z > z) = 1 - \Phi(z) \approx \frac{\varphi(z)}{z} = \frac{1}{z\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}
This is the Mills ratio approximation. More precisely:
\frac{\varphi(z)}{z}\left(1 - \frac{1}{z^2}\right) \leq P(Z > z) \leq \frac{\varphi(z)}{z}
The upper bound is easy to prove: integrate by parts on \int_z^\infty \varphi(t),dt, bounding 1/t \leq 1/z for t \geq z. This bound is useful for showing that Normal tail probabilities decay extremely fast — much faster than, say, the Cauchy or t-distribution tails.

Characterizations of the Normal
The Normal is not just a convenient distribution — it is characterized by several deep properties.
Characterization 1 (Rotational invariance). If X and Y are i.i.d. with the property that (X,Y) is rotationally symmetric (i.e., the distribution of (X,Y) depends only on X^2 + Y^2), then X and Y are Normal. This is essentially how Maxwell derived the velocity distribution of gas particles.
Characterization 2 (Maximum entropy). Among all distributions on \mathbb{R} with fixed mean \mu and variance \sigma^2, the Normal maximizes differential entropy h(X) = -\int f \log f. The Normal is the most spread-out, least-informative distribution consistent with knowing only the mean and variance.
Characterization 3 (Stability). The Normal is a stable distribution: the sum of independent Normals is Normal (after rescaling). More precisely, if X_1, X_2 \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1), then \frac{X_1 + X_2}{\sqrt{2}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1). The shape is preserved under convolution and rescaling.
These three characterizations — rotational symmetry, maximum entropy, stability — are independent reasons the Normal appears in physics, information theory, and probability. It is not an arbitrary choice.

What I Should Be Able to Do Without Notes

Derive the Gaussian integral \int e^{-x^2/2},dx = \sqrt{2\pi} via the polar coordinate trick.
Derive the MGF by completing the square, for both standard and general Normal.
Prove that linear transformations of Normals are Normal via the MGF.
Prove that sums of independent Normals are Normal via the MGF.
State the CLT precisely and prove it via the MGF Taylor expansion argument.
Explain why the CLT fails for Cauchy-distributed variables.
State the three characterizations and know what each one means.
Compute E[e^X] for X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) using the MGF (log-Normal mean).

01.Maths/Probability/05.Continuous-Rando.title: 07.The Central Limit Theorem
01.Maths/Probability/05.Continuous-Rando.content:
The CLT is the reason probability is useful. It says that the universe, on aggregate, is Normal — not because individual components are Normal, but because addition, done enough times, forces Normality regardless of what you started with. That is a miracle that deserves a proof.

The Statement — Precisely
Theorem (Central Limit Theorem). Let X_1, X_2, \ldots be i.i.d. random variables with mean \mu = E[X_i] and variance \sigma^2 = \text{Var}(X_i), where \sigma^2 \in (0, \infty). Define the standardized sum:
Z_n = \frac{S_n - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} = \frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu)}{\sigma}
where S_n = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i and \bar{X}_n = S_n / n. Then:
Z_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1) \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
That is, for every x \in \mathbb{R}:
\lim_{n \to \infty} P(Z_n \leq x) = \Phi(x)
Three conditions that must all hold: the X_i are identically distributed, they are independent, and the variance is finite and positive. Each condition is doing real work.

What the CLT Is and Is Not Saying
The CLT is a statement about convergence in distribution of a sequence of standardized partial sums. It is not saying:

That S_n is approximately Normal. It is not — S_n has mean n\mu and variance n\sigma^2, both growing without bound.
That \bar{X}_n is approximately Normal. It is not — \bar{X}_n has mean \mu and variance \sigma^2/n, collapsing to a point.
That the distribution of X_i is approximately Normal.

It is saying that after the specific standardization Z_n = (\bar{X}_n - \mu) / (\sigma/\sqrt{n}), the distribution of the result converges to \mathcal{N}(0,1).
Practically, this means: for large n,
\bar{X}_n \overset{\text{approx}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}!\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
and
S_n \overset{\text{approx}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(n\mu, n\sigma^2)
These are approximations whose quality depends on n and on how far the X_i are from Normal. The CLT says they become exact in the limit.

Proof via MGFs
This is the proof I want to own completely. It requires that the MGF of X_i exists in a neighborhood of zero — a condition slightly stronger than finite variance, but satisfied by all the named distributions I work with.
Setup. Without loss of generality, standardize each X_i first. Let:
Y_i = \frac{X_i - \mu}{\sigma}
Then the Y_i are i.i.d. with E[Y_i] = 0, E[Y_i^2] = 1. And:
Z_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i
Step 1: MGF of Z_n.
By independence:
M_{Z_n}(t) = E!\left[e^{t Z_n}\right] = E!\left[\exp!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\right)\right] = \prod_{i=1}^n E!\left[e^{(t/\sqrt{n}) Y_i}\right] = \left[M_Y!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right]^n
The factorization uses independence of the Y_i: M_{Y_1 + \cdots + Y_n}(t) = \prod_i M_{Y_i}(t).
Step 2: Taylor expand M_Y around 0.
Since M_Y exists in a neighborhood of 0, it is infinitely differentiable there. Expand:
M_Y(s) = M_Y(0) + M_Y'(0) s + \frac{M_Y''(0)}{2} s^2 + O(s^3)
Now: M_Y(0) = 1, M_Y'(0) = E[Y] = 0, M_Y''(0) = E[Y^2] = 1. So:
M_Y(s) = 1 + \frac{s^2}{2} + O(s^3)
Step 3: Substitute s = t/\sqrt{n}.
M_Y!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 1 + \frac{t^2}{2n} + O(n^{-3/2})
Step 4: Raise to the n-th power and take n \to \infty.
M_{Z_n}(t) = \left(1 + \frac{t^2}{2n} + O(n^{-3/2})\right)^n
Use the fundamental limit \left(1 + \frac{x}{n} + o(1/n)\right)^n \to e^x:
M_{Z_n}(t) \to e^{t^2/2}
Step 5: Identify the limit.
e^{t^2/2} is the MGF of \mathcal{N}(0,1). By the continuity theorem for MGFs — if M_{Z_n}(t) \to M(t) for all t in a neighborhood of 0, and M is the MGF of some distribution, then Z_n \xrightarrow{d} that distribution — we conclude Z_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1). \square

The Continuity Theorem — Why the Proof Is Complete
The continuity theorem for MGFs is doing real work in the last step. It says MGF convergence implies distributional convergence. I am using it as a black box here, but I should know what it asserts:

If M_{X_n}(t) \to M_X(t) for all t in a neighborhood of zero, then X_n \xrightarrow{d} X.

The converse also holds. This theorem is the MGF analogue of the continuity theorem for characteristic functions (Fourier transforms of distributions), which is the version used in the fully general proof of the CLT that does not require the MGF to exist. The characteristic function proof covers, for instance, X_i \sim \text{Cauchy} — but wait, the CLT fails there. Let me be precise about why.

Where the CLT Fails — The Conditions Are Not Decorative
Finite variance is necessary
The CLT requires \sigma^2 < \infty. For X_i \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1), the variance is infinite. The standardized sum Z_n does not converge to \mathcal{N}(0,1). In fact, \bar{X}_n \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1) for every n — the distribution does not shrink at all. Averaging Cauchy random variables accomplishes nothing because heavy-tailed outliers dominate the sum regardless of sample size.
More precisely: \text{Cauchy} is a stable distribution with index \alpha = 1. Stable distributions with \alpha < 2 have infinite variance, and their normalized sums converge to a non-Gaussian stable distribution rather than the Normal. The Normal is the \alpha = 2 stable distribution.
Independence is necessary
If the X_i are identically distributed but dependent, the CLT can fail. The simplest example: let X_i = X for all i, where X is a fixed random variable with mean 0 and variance 1. Then S_n = nX and Z_n = \sqrt{n} X. The distribution of Z_n does not converge — it just scales X by \sqrt{n}, blowing up.
Less pathologically, for stationary time series with strong positive serial correlation, the variance of S_n grows faster than n, and the CLT fails in the standard form. Modified versions (the CLT for mixing processes) exist under weaker dependence conditions, but they require the dependence to decay fast enough.
Identical distribution — the Lindeberg condition
The i.i.d. assumption can be relaxed. The Lindeberg CLT covers independent but not identically distributed random variables, replacing the i.i.d. assumption with a condition that no single summand dominates the sum. Precisely, the Lindeberg condition is:
For every \varepsilon > 0:
\frac{1}{s_n^2} \sum_{i=1}^n E!\left[(X_i - \mu_i)^2 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{|X_i - \mu_i| > \varepsilon s_n}\right] \to 0
where s_n^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i^2. This says: the contribution to the total variance from any individual term with large deviation goes to zero. Under this condition, the CLT holds without identical distribution.
The i.i.d. CLT I proved above is a special case of the Lindeberg CLT, where all \mu_i = \mu, \sigma_i = \sigma, and the Lindeberg condition reduces to the finiteness of the second moment.

Rates of Convergence — The Berry-Esseen Theorem
The CLT tells me the limit but not the rate. The Berry-Esseen theorem gives a quantitative bound:
\sup_x \left|P(Z_n \leq x) - \Phi(x)\right| \leq \frac{C \cdot E[|Y|^3]}{\sqrt{n}}
where C is a universal constant (best known value C \approx 0.4748) and Y = (X - \mu)/\sigma.
What this means: The error in the Normal approximation is O(1/\sqrt{n}) uniformly in x, controlled by the third absolute moment of the standardized variable. Distributions with heavier tails (larger third moment) converge more slowly. Symmetric distributions (odd third moment = 0) often converge faster in practice.
Practical implication: For the Bernoulli(p) case, E[|Y|^3] = (p^2(1-p) + (1-p)^2 p) / (p(1-p))^{3/2}, which blows up as p \to 0 or p \to 1. This explains why the Normal approximation to the Binomial is poor when p is close to 0 or 1 — and why the Poisson approximation is preferred in that regime.

The CLT in Action — Applications
Binomial approximation
\text{Bin}(n,p) \approx \mathcal{N}(np, np(1-p)) for large n. More precisely:
P(a \leq X \leq b) \approx \Phi!\left(\frac{b + \frac{1}{2} - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right) - \Phi!\left(\frac{a - \frac{1}{2} - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right)
The \pm 1/2 terms are the continuity correction, which accounts for approximating a discrete distribution by a continuous one. Without it, P(X = k) \approx 0 (since a single point has zero Normal probability). With it, P(X = k) \approx P(k - 1/2 \leq Y \leq k + 1/2) for Y \sim \mathcal{N}(np, np(1-p)).
Poisson approximation
\text{Pois}(n) \approx \mathcal{N}(n, n) for large n, by the same argument: \text{Pois}(n) is the sum of n i.i.d. \text{Pois}(1) variables.
Sample mean and confidence intervals
The core statistical application: if X_1, \ldots, X_n are i.i.d. with unknown mean \mu and variance \sigma^2, then for large n:
P!\left(\left|\bar{X}_n - \mu\right| \leq z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \approx 1 - \alpha
where z_{\alpha/2} = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha/2). For \alpha = 0.05: z_{0.025} = 1.96. This is the 95% confidence interval for \mu:
\bar{X}_n \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
The entire frequentist theory of estimation and hypothesis testing for means rests on the CLT. Without it, this interval would have no justification for non-Normal data.

The CLT vs. the Law of Large Numbers
These two theorems are often conflated. They are different statements about different things.
Law of Large Numbers (LLN): \bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{P} \mu. The sample mean converges in probability to the true mean. This is about where \bar{X}_n ends up — it concentrates at \mu.
CLT: \frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu)}{\sigma} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1). After zooming in by a factor of \sqrt{n}, the fluctuations of \bar{X}_n around \mu are Normally distributed.
The LLN describes the first-order behavior: \bar{X}_n \approx \mu. The CLT describes the second-order behavior: the fluctuations around \mu have size \sigma/\sqrt{n} and a Normal shape.
To remember the distinction: the LLN says the error goes to zero. The CLT says, right before it reaches zero, what shape it had.

The Delta Method — CLT for Nonlinear Functions
If g is differentiable at \mu with g'(\mu) \neq 0, and \sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2), then:
\sqrt{n}(g(\bar{X}_n) - g(\mu)) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,\ [g'(\mu)]^2 \sigma^2)
Proof sketch. Taylor expand g around \mu:
g(\bar{X}_n) \approx g(\mu) + g'(\mu)(\bar{X}_n - \mu)
Multiply both sides by \sqrt{n}:
\sqrt{n}(g(\bar{X}_n) - g(\mu)) \approx g'(\mu) \cdot \sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,\ [g'(\mu)]^2 \sigma^2)
The delta method is the CLT for smooth transformations of sample means. It is used constantly in statistics — for confidence intervals of proportions, odds ratios, log-transformed means — anywhere you want to apply the CLT to a quantity that is a function of \bar{X}_n rather than \bar{X}_n itself.

A Personal Summary of Why This Theorem Is Deep
The CLT is deep for three reasons that I try to hold simultaneously.
First, it is universal. The distribution of X_i is irrelevant — Bernoulli, Poisson, Exponential, uniform, anything — as long as it has finite variance. The limiting distribution is always the same. The Normal is not a special case; it is a fixed point. All finite-variance distributions, under summation and rescaling, flow toward the Normal.
Second, it explains a pattern in nature. Heights, measurement errors, test scores, and countless other natural quantities are approximately Normal not because the underlying mechanism is Gaussian, but because these quantities are the aggregate of many small independent contributions. The CLT is the mathematical explanation for why bell curves appear everywhere.
Third, the proof reveals something structural. The key step is the Taylor expansion M_Y(s) = 1 + s^2/2 + O(s^3). The constant and linear terms are fixed for all standardized variables: M_Y(0) = 1 always, M_Y'(0) = E[Y] = 0 by construction. The first term that distinguishes distributions is the quadratic term, E[Y^2]/2 = 1/2, which is also fixed by the standardization. Everything that distinguishes the original distribution is in the O(s^3) remainder, which gets killed by raising to the n-th power as n \to \infty. The Normal emerges because standardization pins down the first two terms of the MGF expansion, and those two terms are enough to determine the limit.

What I Should Be Able to Do Without Notes

State the CLT precisely: i.i.d., finite positive variance, convergence in distribution of the standardized sum.
Prove it via MGF Taylor expansion, identifying exactly where independence, zero mean, and unit variance are each used.
Explain why the CLT fails for Cauchy-distributed variables.
State the Lindeberg condition and explain what it relaxes.
State the Berry-Esseen theorem and explain what it says about the rate of convergence.
Explain the continuity correction and when it matters.
State the LLN and distinguish it precisely from the CLT.
Derive the delta method from a first-order Taylor expansion.

01.Maths/Probability/05.Continuous-Rando.title: 08.The Normal Normalizing Constant
01.Maths/Probability/05.Continuous-Rando.content:
Why c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}

The Gaussian integral cannot be solved by any standard technique. It requires leaving the real line entirely, going to \mathbb{R}^2, exploiting rotational symmetry, and coming back down. The fact that \pi appears in a probability distribution is a direct consequence of that geometry.

The Setup
The standard Normal PDF is claimed to be:
f(z) = c \cdot e^{-z^2/2}, \quad z \in \mathbb{R}
for some constant c > 0. For f to be a valid PDF, it must integrate to 1:
c \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz = 1 \implies c = \frac{1}{\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz}
So everything reduces to computing I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz.

Why Direct Antidifferentiation Fails
The function e^{-z^2/2} has no elementary antiderivative. This is not a gap in technique — it is a theorem (Liouville’s theorem on elementary integrals) that no composition of polynomials, exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometric functions equals \int e^{-z^2/2}, dz. The antiderivative exists as a function (by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus) but cannot be written in closed form.
This means every standard single-variable technique — substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions — will fail. The definite integral over all of \mathbb{R} must be computed by a different route entirely.

The Double Integral Trick
The key insight: if I cannot compute I directly, compute I^2 instead and take a square root.
I^2 = \left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2}, dx\right)!\left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-y^2/2}, dy\right)
I have written the same integral twice, using different dummy variables x and y. Since these are independent integrals, I can combine them into a double integral over \mathbb{R}^2:
I^2 = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2} \cdot e^{-y^2/2}, dx, dy = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2}, dx, dy
The exponents add because the integrand factors. Now I have converted a one-dimensional problem I cannot solve into a two-dimensional problem I can — because x^2 + y^2 is the squared distance from the origin in \mathbb{R}^2, which is naturally expressed in polar coordinates.

Polar Coordinate Transformation
Substitute x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta, where r \in [0, \infty) and \theta \in [0, 2\pi).
The key facts:

x^2 + y^2 = r^2 (Pythagorean theorem)
The area element transforms as dx, dy = r, dr, d\theta (the factor r is the Jacobian of the polar coordinate transformation)

The Jacobian r is not optional — it accounts for the fact that at radius r, a small angular slice d\theta sweeps out an arc of length r, d\theta, so the area element grows with r.
The integral becomes:
I^2 = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/2} \cdot r, dr, d\theta
The limits change: r runs from 0 to \infty (all distances from origin), \theta runs from 0 to 2\pi (full rotation). Together these cover all of \mathbb{R}^2 exactly once.

Evaluating the Transformed Integral
The double integral separates into a product because the integrand factors as a function of r alone times a function of \theta alone:
I^2 = \left(\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta\right)!\left(\int_0^\infty r e^{-r^2/2}, dr\right)
Outer integral:
\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta = 2\pi
This is where \pi enters. The full rotation around the origin contributes exactly 2\pi.
Inner integral:
\int_0^\infty r e^{-r^2/2}, dr
Substitute u = r^2/2, so du = r, dr. When r = 0, u = 0; when r \to \infty, u \to \infty:
\int_0^\infty e^{-u}, du = \Big[-e^{-u}\Big]_0^\infty = 0 - (-1) = 1
The factor r in the integrand is precisely the du from the substitution. Without it — if the integrand were just e^{-r^2/2} — this substitution would not work. The Jacobian r is what makes the inner integral tractable.

Final Result
I^2 = 2\pi \cdot 1 = 2\pi
I = \sqrt{2\pi}
Therefore:
c = \frac{1}{I} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
And the standard Normal PDF is confirmed:
f(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}

Why \pi Appears Here
This is worth pausing on. \pi appears in the Normal distribution not because of anything circular in the probability setup, but because:

The trick requires going to \mathbb{R}^2.
In \mathbb{R}^2, the natural coordinate system for e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2} is polar.
The angular integration over a full rotation produces 2\pi.

The circle is hiding inside the Gaussian. The rotational symmetry of e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2} — it depends only on the distance r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} from the origin, not on the angle — is the property that makes the polar transformation so powerful. This same rotational symmetry is one of the characterizations of the Normal distribution: it is the only spherically symmetric distribution with independent components.

Derivation of the Mean — E[Z] = 0
With the PDF established, compute the mean:
E[Z] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty z \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}, dz
By symmetry. The integrand is z \cdot f(z). Since f(z) = f(-z) (even function) and z is odd, the product z \cdot f(z) is an odd function. The integral of any odd function over a symmetric interval is zero:
\int_{-\infty}^\infty (\text{odd function}), dz = 0
provided the integral converges absolutely, which it does here since z \cdot e^{-z^2/2} decays faster than any polynomial.
Therefore E[Z] = 0.

Derivation of the Variance — \text{Var}(Z) = 1
Since E[Z] = 0:
\text{Var}(Z) = E[Z^2] - (E[Z])^2 = E[Z^2]
By LOTUS:
E[Z^2] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty z^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}, dz = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty z^2 e^{-z^2/2}, dz
Integration by parts. Write z^2 e^{-z^2/2} = z \cdot \left(z e^{-z^2/2}\right) and set:
u = z \implies du = dz dv = z e^{-z^2/2}, dz \implies v = -e^{-z^2/2}
where v is found by the substitution w = z^2/2, dw = z, dz, giving \int z e^{-z^2/2}, dz = -e^{-z^2/2}.
Apply integration by parts \int u, dv = uv - \int v, du:
\int_{-\infty}^\infty z^2 e^{-z^2/2}, dz = \Big[-z e^{-z^2/2}\Big]_{-\infty}^\infty + \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz
Boundary term. Evaluate \lim_{z \to \pm\infty} z e^{-z^2/2}. The exponential decay dominates the linear growth:
\lim_{z \to \infty} z e^{-z^2/2} = 0, \quad \lim_{z \to -\infty} z e^{-z^2/2} = 0
So the boundary term \Big[-z e^{-z^2/2}\Big]_{-\infty}^\infty = 0 - 0 = 0.
Remaining integral. What is left is:
\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz = I = \sqrt{2\pi}
exactly the Gaussian integral already computed.
Therefore:
E[Z^2] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot \sqrt{2\pi} = 1
\text{Var}(Z) = 1 \quad \square

The Structural Elegance
The variance derivation has a loop in it that is worth appreciating:
\int z^2 e^{-z^2/2}, dz \xrightarrow{\text{IBP}} \int e^{-z^2/2}, dz
Integration by parts converts the z^2 moment integral back into the normalizing integral. The variance equals 1 because the normalizing integral equals \sqrt{2\pi}, and the \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} in front of the PDF cancels it exactly. The normalizing constant and the variance are not independent — the same integral I determines both.
This self-referential structure is not a coincidence. For any distribution in the exponential family, the moments are derivatives of the log-normalizing constant. For the Normal, this becomes the observation that differentiating \log Z(\theta) with respect to the natural parameter recovers the moments — and the variance being 1 for the standard Normal is the simplest instance of this.

Summary of What Was Derived
