Kurtosis undefined when E[X^4] = \infty. The Cauchy distribution has no finite moments at all — kurtosis undefined. The t_3 distribution has finite variance but no fourth moment — kurtosis undefined. Always check existence first.


Confusing “leptokurtic” and “platykurtic.” Mnemonic: lepto = thin (the tails are thin in the center, fat at the extremes) — so leptokurtic = heavy tails. Platy = flat (the distribution is flatter, more spread, lighter tails). Actually I just remember: \widetilde{\kappa} > 0 is leptokurtic. That’s enough.

01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/04.Sampl.title: 04.Sample Variance and Sample Standard Deviation
01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/04.Sampl.content:
This is one of those topics where the formula is deceptively simple and the justification is genuinely subtle. The n-1 denominator is not a correction pulled from thin air — it comes from a real calculation, and understanding why is worth every minute. I’ve seen people use this formula for years without knowing where it comes from. Don’t be that person.

Setup and Motivation
We have a population with some unknown mean \mu and unknown variance \sigma^2. We observe a random sample X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n — i.i.d. draws from this population. We want to estimate \sigma^2 from the data.
The natural first instinct: just compute the average squared deviation from the mean. But we don’t know \mu. So we substitute the sample mean:
\bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
This substitution has a cost, and the n-1 is the price we pay for it.

Definitions
Sample mean: \bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
Sample variance: S_n^2 = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2
Sample standard deviation: S_n = \sqrt{S_n^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2}

The n-1 in the denominator is called Bessel’s correction. The quantity with n in the denominator — \frac{1}{n}\sum(X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2 — is sometimes called the biased sample variance or the MLE of \sigma^2 under Normality. We will see exactly why n is wrong and n-1 is right.


The Central Theorem: Unbiasedness of S_n^2
Theorem. E[S_n^2] = \sigma^2.
That is, S_n^2 is an unbiased estimator of the population variance \sigma^2.
Proof.
We compute E!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2\right] by a standard algebraic trick — adding and subtracting \mu:
X_i - \bar{X}_n = (X_i - \mu) - (\bar{X}_n - \mu)
Let Z_i = X_i - \mu (centered observations) and \bar{Z} = \bar{X}_n - \mu. Then:
\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (Z_i - \bar{Z})^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2 - n\bar{Z}^2
Justification of the last step: \sum_{i=1}^n (Z_i - \bar{Z})^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2 - 2\bar{Z}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i + n\bar{Z}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2 - 2n\bar{Z}^2 + n\bar{Z}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2 - n\bar{Z}^2
Now take expectations:
E!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2\right] = n \cdot E[Z_i^2] = n \cdot E[(X_i - \mu)^2] = n\sigma^2
E!\left[n\bar{Z}^2\right] = n \cdot E!\left[(\bar{X}_n - \mu)^2\right] = n \cdot \text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = n \cdot \frac{\sigma^2}{n} = \sigma^2
Therefore:
E!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2\right] = n\sigma^2 - \sigma^2 = (n-1)\sigma^2
Dividing by n-1:
E[S_n^2] = \frac{(n-1)\sigma^2}{n-1} = \sigma^2 \quad \square

Why the Biased Version Is Biased
Define the biased sample variance: \widetilde{S}_n^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2
From the proof above: E[\widetilde{S}_n^2] = \frac{(n-1)\sigma^2}{n} = \sigma^2 - \frac{\sigma^2}{n} < \sigma^2
So \widetilde{S}_n^2 systematically underestimates \sigma^2. The bias is -\sigma^2/n, which vanishes as n \to \infty but is real for finite samples.
Intuition for why it underestimates:
We are computing deviations from the sample mean \bar{X}_n, not from the true mean \mu. The sample mean is the point that minimizes the sum of squared deviations from the data — it is by definition closer to the data than \mu is (unless \bar{X}_n = \mu, which happens with probability zero for continuous distributions). So deviations from \bar{X}_n are systematically smaller than deviations from \mu, and we are underestimating \sigma^2.
Dividing by n-1 instead of n inflates the estimate just enough to correct for this.

Degrees of Freedom: The Right Way to Think About n-1
The most conceptually satisfying explanation of n-1 is through degrees of freedom.
The n residuals X_1 - \bar{X}_n, X_2 - \bar{X}_n, \ldots, X_n - \bar{X}_n satisfy the constraint: \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n) = 0
This is an identity — always true, for any data. So the n residuals lie in an (n-1)-dimensional subspace of \mathbb{R}^n. They have only n-1 degrees of freedom — only n-1 of them can vary freely; the last is determined by the constraint.
We estimated one parameter (\mu, replaced by \bar{X}_n) from n observations, consuming one degree of freedom. We have n-1 left. The sample variance divides by the remaining degrees of freedom.

This generalizes. In linear regression with p predictors (including intercept), the residual variance is \frac{1}{n-p}\sum \hat{\varepsilon}_i^2, dividing by n-p degrees of freedom — one lost per estimated parameter. The n-1 here is the special case p=1 (just the mean).


Properties of \bar{X}_n and S_n^2
Proposition 1. E[\bar{X}_n] = \mu and \text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \sigma^2/n.
Proof. By linearity of expectation and independence: E[\bar{X}_n] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i] = \mu \text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \text{Var}(X_i) = \frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} \quad \square
Proposition 2. \bar{X}_n and S_n^2 are uncorrelated for any population. They are independent when the population is Normal.
Proof of independence under Normality (sketch).
Write \mathbf{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_n)^T \sim N(\mu\mathbf{1}, \sigma^2 I). The sample mean is \bar{X}_n = \mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{X} for \mathbf{a} = \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}. The residual vector (X_i - \bar{X}_n) lives in the orthogonal complement of \mathbf{1} in \mathbb{R}^n. Since jointly Normal, orthogonality implies independence. And S_n^2 is a function of the residuals alone, so S_n^2 \perp \bar{X}_n. \square

This independence is far from obvious and is special to the Normal. It underlies the validity of the t-test: the test statistic \frac{\bar{X}_n - \mu}{S_n/\sqrt{n}} has a t-distribution precisely because numerator and denominator are independent.

Proposition 3. Under Normality: \frac{(n-1)S_n^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-1}.
Proof (sketch).
The residual vector (X_i - \bar{X}_n) is a Normal vector of dimension n constrained to a (n-1)-dimensional subspace. Its squared norm, scaled by 1/\sigma^2, is a sum of n-1 squared independent standard Normals — i.e., \chi^2_{n-1}.
More precisely: \frac{(n-1)S_n^2}{\sigma^2} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{X_i - \bar{X}_n}{\sigma}\right)^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1} \quad \square
This immediately gives: E!\left[\frac{(n-1)S_n^2}{\sigma^2}\right] = n-1 \implies E[S_n^2] = \sigma^2 \quad \checkmark
and: \text{Var}!\left(\frac{(n-1)S_n^2}{\sigma^2}\right) = 2(n-1) \implies \text{Var}(S_n^2) = \frac{2\sigma^4}{n-1}

Sample Standard Deviation Is Biased
Here is a subtle and frequently overlooked point:

S_n is not an unbiased estimator of \sigma, even though S_n^2 is unbiased for \sigma^2.

By Jensen’s inequality, since x \mapsto \sqrt{x} is concave for x > 0: E[S_n] = E[\sqrt{S_n^2}] < \sqrt{E[S_n^2]} = \sqrt{\sigma^2} = \sigma
So S_n systematically underestimates \sigma. The bias is of order 1/n and vanishes asymptotically, but it is real.
Under Normality, the exact correction factor is known. Since (n-1)S_n^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}, we can compute E[S_n] exactly using the moments of the \chi distribution:
E[S_n] = \sigma \cdot c_n, \quad \text{where } c_n = \sqrt{\frac{2}{n-1}} \cdot \frac{\Gamma(n/2)}{\Gamma((n-1)/2)}
An unbiased estimator of \sigma under Normality is therefore S_n / c_n. In practice nobody uses this — S_n is consistent and the bias is negligible for moderate n. But it’s good to know that unbiasedness of S_n^2 does not pass through the square root.

Consistency
Both estimators are consistent: they converge in probability to the true parameter as n \to \infty.
Proposition. S_n^2 \xrightarrow{p} \sigma^2 as n \to \infty.
Proof.
By the Law of Large Numbers: \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 \xrightarrow{p} E[X^2] = \sigma^2 + \mu^2 \bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{p} \mu \implies \bar{X}_n^2 \xrightarrow{p} \mu^2
Now use the computational formula: S_n^2 = \frac{n}{n-1}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 - \bar{X}_n^2\right) \xrightarrow{p} 1 \cdot \left((\sigma^2 + \mu^2) - \mu^2\right) = \sigma^2 \quad \square
Similarly S_n \xrightarrow{p} \sigma.

The Computational Formula
For hand calculation (less numerically stable but instructive):
\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 - n\bar{X}_n^2
Proof. \sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2 = \sum X_i^2 - 2\bar{X}\sum X_i + n\bar{X}^2 = \sum X_i^2 - 2n\bar{X}^2 + n\bar{X}^2 = \sum X_i^2 - n\bar{X}^2 \quad \square
So: S_n^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2 - n\bar{X}_n^2\right)

⚠️ Numerical warning. This formula is algebraically correct but numerically dangerous for floating-point arithmetic when \sum X_i^2 and n\bar{X}^2 are both large numbers that nearly cancel. Always use the definition \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2 in code, or Welford’s online algorithm.


The t-Statistic
The canonical application of sample variance: constructing a pivot for inference on \mu when \sigma is unknown.
Under Normality, define the one-sample t-statistic: T = \frac{\bar{X}_n - \mu}{S_n / \sqrt{n}}
Theorem. T \sim t_{n-1}.
Proof.
Write: T = \frac{\bar{X}_n - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \cdot \frac{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}{S_n/\sqrt{n}} = Z \cdot \frac{\sigma}{S_n} = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/(n-1)}}
where:

Z = \frac{\bar{X}_n - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0,1)
V = \frac{(n-1)S_n^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-1}
Z \perp V (by Proposition 2 — independence of \bar{X}_n and S_n^2 under Normality)

The ratio Z / \sqrt{V/(n-1)} is the definition of a t_{n-1} random variable. \square

This is the reason the t-distribution exists. Without the n-1 in Bessel’s correction — without S_n^2 being built the right way — this pivot would not have a clean distribution and t-tests would not work.


Things I Keep Getting Confused

Honest accounting.



Dividing by n instead of n-1 “just because it’s the sample size.” No. The n-1 is the whole point. The biased version is fine asymptotically but conceptually wrong for finite samples.


Thinking S_n is unbiased for \sigma because S_n^2 is unbiased for \sigma^2. Jensen kills this. Concavity of \sqrt{\cdot} means E[S_n] < \sigma always.


Forgetting that \bar{X}_n \perp S_n^2 is special to the Normal. For a general population they are uncorrelated but not independent. The t-test technically requires Normality for exact validity.


The degrees of freedom story sounding like a hand-wave. It’s not — it’s a precise statement about the dimension of the subspace in which the residual vector lives. The constraint \sum(X_i - \bar{X}_n) = 0 is exact, not approximate.


Using the computational formula in floating-point without thinking. Catastrophic cancellation is real. Use the two-pass formula or Welford’s algorithm when implementing.

01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/05.Momen.title: 05.Moment Generating Function (MGF)
01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/05.Momen.content:
The MGF is one of those objects that seems like a clever trick the first time you see it — “oh, derivatives give moments, cute.” But the deeper reason to care is the uniqueness theorem and what it implies for convergence. That’s where the MGF earns its name as one of the most powerful tools in probability. Write this the right way.

We want a single object that encodes all the moments of a distribution — mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, everything — in a way that is algebraically tractable. The natural candidate is a generating function.
The idea: if we can write E[e^{tX}] as a power series in t, then the coefficient of t^n/n! will be E[X^n], because:
e^{tX} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(tX)^n}{n!} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n}{n!} X^n
E[e^{tX}] = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n}{n!} E[X^n]
Differentiating n times with respect to t and setting t = 0 recovers E[X^n]. This is the MGF.

Definition
Let X be a random variable. The moment generating function (MGF) of X is:
\boxed{M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]}, \quad t \in \mathbb{R}
whenever this expectation is finite. Explicitly:
M_X(t) = \begin{cases} \displaystyle\sum_x e^{tx} P(X = x) & X \text{ discrete} \[10pt] \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{tx} f_X(x), dx & X \text{ continuous} \end{cases}
The MGF exists at t if E[e^{tX}] < \infty. We say the MGF exists (in the useful sense) if it is finite on an open interval (-\delta, \delta) containing 0 for some \delta > 0.

Existence on an open interval around 0 is crucial — it’s what makes the power series argument work and what gives us the uniqueness theorem. A MGF that only exists at t = 0 (where M(0) = 1 trivially for any distribution) is useless.


The Moment Extraction Property
Theorem. If M_X(t) exists on (-\delta, \delta) for some \delta > 0, then for all n \geq 1:
E[X^n] = M_X^{(n)}(0) = \left.\frac{d^n}{dt^n} M_X(t)\right|_{t=0}
Proof.
Since M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] and the MGF exists on an open interval around 0, we can interchange differentiation and expectation (justified by dominated convergence — the existence assumption is precisely what provides the dominating integrable function):
\frac{d}{dt} M_X(t) = \frac{d}{dt} E[e^{tX}] = E!\left[\frac{d}{dt} e^{tX}\right] = E[X e^{tX}]
At t = 0: M_X'(0) = E[X]. Iterating:
M_X^{(n)}(t) = E[X^n e^{tX}]
At t = 0: M_X^{(n)}(0) = E[X^n \cdot 1] = E[X^n]. \square
Alternatively, via the power series: M_X(t) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{E[X^n]}{n!} t^n = 1 + E[X]t + \frac{E[X^2]}{2!}t^2 + \frac{E[X^3]}{3!}t^3 + \cdots
Reading off coefficients: E[X^n] = n! \cdot [t^n] M_X(t).

The Uniqueness Theorem
This is the theorem that makes the MGF worth caring about deeply.
Theorem (Uniqueness). If M_X(t) = M_Y(t) for all t in some open interval (-\delta, \delta), then X and Y have the same distribution.
That is: the MGF, when it exists, uniquely determines the distribution.
Proof idea. The MGF is essentially the bilateral Laplace transform of the distribution. Two distinct probability measures cannot have the same Laplace transform on an open set — this follows from the injectivity of the Laplace transform, which in turn follows from the uniqueness of analytic continuation (the MGF, when it exists on an open interval, extends to an analytic function on a strip of the complex plane). The formal proof requires complex analysis beyond this course, but the statement is exact. \square

This theorem is the real reason we care about MGFs. It means: to prove X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda), it suffices to show M_X(t) = e^{\lambda(e^t - 1)}. To prove a sum of independent Normals is Normal, compute its MGF and identify it. This is often dramatically easier than working with densities or CDFs directly.

Warning: The converse direction — all moments equal does not imply same distribution — is true in general only when the MGF exists. There exist distinct distributions with identical moments of all orders (the lognormal family provides counterexamples). Existence of the MGF on an open interval rules this out.

Properties
Proposition 1 (Normalization). M_X(0) = 1 always.
Proof. M_X(0) = E[e^0] = E[1] = 1. \square
Proposition 2 (Affine transformations).
M_{aX+b}(t) = e^{bt} M_X(at)
Proof. M_{aX+b}(t) = E[e^{t(aX+b)}] = e^{bt} E[e^{(at)X}] = e^{bt} M_X(at) \quad \square
Corollary. For the standardized variable Z = (X - \mu)/\sigma: M_Z(t) = e^{-\mu t/\sigma} M_X(t/\sigma)
Proposition 3 (Independence and products).
If X \perp Y, then: M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t) \cdot M_Y(t)
Proof. M_{X+Y}(t) = E[e^{t(X+Y)}] = E[e^{tX} e^{tY}] = E[e^{tX}] \cdot E[e^{tY}] = M_X(t) M_Y(t)
where the third equality uses independence. \square

This is the MGF’s killer feature for sums of independent random variables. Computing the distribution of X + Y via convolution of densities is painful. Multiplying MGFs is instant.

Proposition 4 (Extension to n variables).
If X_1, \ldots, X_n are independent, then: M_{X_1 + \cdots + X_n}(t) = \prod_{i=1}^n M_{X_i}(t)
If additionally X_1, \ldots, X_n are i.i.d.: M_{S_n}(t) = \left(M_X(t)\right)^n

MGFs of Named Distributions
Bernoulli X \sim \text{Bern}(p)
M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] = e^{t \cdot 0}(1-p) + e^{t \cdot 1} p = (1-p) + pe^t = q + pe^t
where q = 1-p. Exists for all t \in \mathbb{R}.
Moments: M'(t) = pe^t, so E[X] = M'(0) = p. M''(t) = pe^t, so E[X^2] = p. Then \text{Var}(X) = p - p^2 = p(1-p). ✓

Binomial X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)
By independence (X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i, i.i.d. Bern(p)): M_X(t) = (q + pe^t)^n
Exists for all t \in \mathbb{R}.
Moment extraction: M'(t) = n(q + pe^t)^{n-1} \cdot pe^t E[X] = M'(0) = n(q+p)^{n-1} \cdot p = np \quad \checkmark

Poisson X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)
M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty e^{tk} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!} = e^{-\lambda} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(\lambda e^t)^k}{k!} = e^{-\lambda} e^{\lambda e^t}
\boxed{M_X(t) = e^{\lambda(e^t - 1)}}
Exists for all t \in \mathbb{R}.
Verification via Binomial convergence:
Since Pois(\lambda) is the limit of Bin(n, \lambda/n) as n \to \infty: \left(1 - \frac{\lambda}{n} + \frac{\lambda}{n}e^t\right)^n = \left(1 + \frac{\lambda(e^t-1)}{n}\right)^n \to e^{\lambda(e^t-1)} \quad \checkmark
Additivity:
If X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda) and Y \sim \text{Pois}(\mu) independent, then: M_{X+Y}(t) = e^{\lambda(e^t-1)} \cdot e^{\mu(e^t-1)} = e^{(\lambda+\mu)(e^t-1)} So X + Y \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda + \mu). The uniqueness theorem does the work. \square

Geometric X \sim \text{Geom}(p) (number of trials until first success)
M_X(t) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty e^{tk}(1-p)^{k-1}p = \frac{pe^t}{1-(1-p)e^t}, \quad t < -\log(1-p)
Exists only for t < -\log(1-p) — the MGF has a finite radius of existence.

Exponential X \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)
M_X(t) = \int_0^\infty e^{tx} \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx = \lambda \int_0^\infty e^{-({\lambda - t})x}, dx = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}, \quad t < \lambda
\boxed{M_X(t) = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t} = \left(1 - \frac{t}{\lambda}\right)^{-1}}
Moment extraction: M'(t) = \frac{\lambda}{(\lambda-t)^2} \implies E[X] = \frac{1}{\lambda} \quad \checkmark M''(t) = \frac{2\lambda}{(\lambda-t)^3} \implies E[X^2] = \frac{2}{\lambda^2} \implies \text{Var}(X) = \frac{1}{\lambda^2} \quad \checkmark

Gamma X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, \lambda)
By independence (X = \sum_{i=1}^a X_i, i.i.d. Expo(\lambda) when a is a positive integer): M_X(t) = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-t}\right)^a = \left(1 - \frac{t}{\lambda}\right)^{-a}, \quad t < \lambda
This holds for all a > 0 by analytic continuation.

Normal X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)
The fundamental computation. Take Z \sim N(0,1) first:
M_Z(t) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{tz} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}, dz = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-\frac{1}{2}(z^2 - 2tz)}, dz
Complete the square: z^2 - 2tz = (z-t)^2 - t^2. So:
M_Z(t) = \frac{e^{t^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-\frac{(z-t)^2}{2}}, dz = e^{t^2/2}
since the integral is \sqrt{2\pi} (it’s a Normal density integrating to 1).
\boxed{M_Z(t) = e^{t^2/2}}
For X = \mu + \sigma Z \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), by the affine transformation property: M_X(t) = e^{\mu t} M_Z(\sigma t) = e^{\mu t} e^{\sigma^2 t^2/2}
\boxed{M_X(t) = \exp!\left(\mu t + \frac{\sigma^2 t^2}{2}\right)}
Exists for all t \in \mathbb{R}.
Moment extraction from M_Z(t) = e^{t^2/2}:
M_Z(t) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(t^2/2)^n}{n!} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^{2n}}{2^n n!}
The coefficient of t^{2n}/(2n)! is E[Z^{2n}], so: E[Z^{2n}] = \frac{(2n)!}{2^n n!} = (2n-1)!! = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2n-1)
All odd moments are 0 (by symmetry). So E[Z^4] = 3, giving \text{Kurt}(Z) = 3. ✓
Additivity of independent Normals:
If X \sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2) and Y \sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2) independent: M_{X+Y}(t) = e^{\mu_1 t + \sigma_1^2 t^2/2} \cdot e^{\mu_2 t + \sigma_2^2 t^2/2} = e^{(\mu_1+\mu_2)t + (\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)t^2/2}
So X + Y \sim N(\mu_1+\mu_2,, \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2). \square

Summary Table













































DistributionMGF M_X(t)Domain\text{Bern}(p)q + pe^t\mathbb{R}\text{Bin}(n,p)(q+pe^t)^n\mathbb{R}\text{Pois}(\lambda)e^{\lambda(e^t-1)}\mathbb{R}\text{Expo}(\lambda)\lambda/(\lambda-t)t < \lambda\text{Gamma}(a,\lambda)(\lambda/(\lambda-t))^at < \lambdaN(\mu,\sigma^2)e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}\mathbb{R}\text{Geom}(p)pe^t/(1-qe^t)t < -\log q

When the MGF Does Not Exist
Not every distribution has an MGF on an open interval around 0.
Example: Log-Normal.
If X = e^Z with Z \sim N(0,1), then: M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] = E[e^{te^Z}] For any t > 0, e^{te^Z} grows faster than any exponential as Z \to \infty, so E[e^{te^Z}] = \infty. The MGF of the lognormal does not exist for any t > 0.
Example: Cauchy.
The Cauchy distribution has no finite moments at all. E[e^{tX}] = \infty for all t \neq 0.
Example: Pareto, t-distribution with small \nu.
Heavy-tailed distributions whose moments fail to exist beyond some finite order will have MGFs that fail to exist on any open interval around 0.

When the MGF does not exist, we use the characteristic function \varphi_X(t) = E[e^{itX}] instead — it always exists since |e^{itX}| = 1. This requires complex analysis but works universally. The MGF is the real-line version; the characteristic function is the full story.


The MGF and the CLT
The MGF gives one of the cleanest proofs of the CLT (under the assumption that the MGF exists).
Setup. Let X_1, X_2, \ldots be i.i.d. with mean 0, variance \sigma^2, and MGF M(t) existing on (-\delta, \delta). Let S_n = (X_1 + \cdots + X_n)/(\sigma\sqrt{n}).
Claim. M_{S_n}(t) \to e^{t^2/2} for each fixed t, which is the MGF of N(0,1).
Proof.
M_{S_n}(t) = E!\left[e^{t S_n}\right] = \left(M!\left(\frac{t}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\right)\right)^n
Let u = t/(\sigma\sqrt{n}). As n \to \infty, u \to 0. Taylor expand M(u) around 0:
M(u) = 1 + E[X]\cdot u + \frac{E[X^2]}{2}u^2 + O(u^3) = 1 + 0 + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}u^2 + O(u^3)
since E[X] = 0 and E[X^2] = \sigma^2. Substituting u = t/(\sigma\sqrt{n}):
M!\left(\frac{t}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\right) = 1 + \frac{t^2}{2n} + O(n^{-3/2})
Therefore:
M_{S_n}(t) = \left(1 + \frac{t^2}{2n} + O(n^{-3/2})\right)^n \to e^{t^2/2}
by the standard limit (1 + x/n)^n \to e^x. By the uniqueness theorem (extended to convergence of distributions), S_n \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1). \square

This proof shows exactly why the CLT is true: the first two cumulants of S_n are fixed at 0 and 1, and all higher-order terms in the Taylor expansion vanish as n \to \infty. The 1/n and 1/\sqrt{n} decay of excess kurtosis and skewness from 02.Skewness and 03.Kurtosis is the same phenomenon, seen through cumulants.


Things I Keep Getting Confused

Honest accounting.



Thinking the MGF always exists. It doesn’t. Heavy-tailed distributions (lognormal, Cauchy, Pareto) may have no MGF. Always check existence before using.


Differentiating inside the expectation without justification. The interchange \frac{d}{dt}E[\cdot] = E!\left[\frac{d}{dt}\cdot\right] requires dominated convergence, which is guaranteed by existence of the MGF on an open interval. This is why the open interval condition matters.


Confusing MGF with probability generating function (PGF). The PGF is G_X(z) = E[z^X] for non-negative integer X. The MGF is M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]. They are related by M_X(t) = G_X(e^t), but they are different objects used in different contexts.


Using the uniqueness theorem sloppily. The uniqueness theorem requires the MGF to exist on an open interval around 0, not just at 0. Two distributions with the same MGF at a single point tell us nothing.


Forgetting that M_{X+Y} = M_X M_Y requires independence. For dependent X, Y: E[e^{t(X+Y)}] = E[e^{tX}e^{tY}] \neq E[e^{tX}]E[e^{tY}] in general.

01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/06.Gener.title: 06.Generating Moments with the MGF
01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/06.Gener.content:
This is the computational heart of the MGF — the part where you actually sit down and grind out E[X^n] without doing a single integral by brute force. Once you have the MGF of a distribution, you own all its moments. The skill is knowing which method — differentiation or series expansion — is cleaner for a given distribution. I keep a mental ranking. Write that down here.

The Core Principle
If M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] exists on an open interval around 0, then the n-th moment of X is recovered by:
\boxed{E[X^n] = M_X^{(n)}(0)}
Two methods to extract E[X^n] from M_X(t):

Differentiate directly — take n derivatives, evaluate at t = 0.
Expand as a power series — read off the coefficient of t^n/n!.

Both are always valid. The question is which is less painful for the distribution at hand. Method 1 is better when M(t) has a clean closed form that differentiates nicely. Method 2 is better when M(t) is already a known series or has a form that expands cleanly.

Method 1: Direct Differentiation
Setup
M_X'(t) = E[Xe^{tX}] \implies M_X'(0) = E[X] M_X''(t) = E[X^2 e^{tX}] \implies M_X''(0) = E[X^2] M_X^{(n)}(t) = E[X^n e^{tX}] \implies M_X^{(n)}(0) = E[X^n]
The variance then follows from: \text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = M''(0) - (M'(0))^2

Example 1: Exponential X \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)
M_X(t) = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t} = \lambda(\lambda - t)^{-1}, \quad t < \lambda
Differentiate: M'(t) = \lambda(\lambda-t)^{-2} M''(t) = 2\lambda(\lambda-t)^{-3} M^{(n)}(t) = n!,\lambda(\lambda-t)^{-(n+1)}
At t = 0:
\boxed{E[X^n] = \frac{n!}{\lambda^n}}
Verification: E[X] = 1/\lambda ✓, E[X^2] = 2/\lambda^2 ✓, \text{Var}(X) = 2/\lambda^2 - 1/\lambda^2 = 1/\lambda^2 ✓.
The pattern E[X^n] = n!/\lambda^n is worth knowing. It follows from the MGF with almost no effort. Doing this integral directly — E[X^n] = \int_0^\infty x^n \lambda e^{-\lambda x},dx — requires integration by parts n times or the Gamma function. The MGF does it in one line.

Example 2: Normal Z \sim N(0,1)
M_Z(t) = e^{t^2/2}
Differentiating this repeatedly is annoying because of the chain rule compounding. Better to use Method 2 here — but let’s do the first few to see the pattern:
M'(t) = te^{t^2/2} M''(t) = e^{t^2/2} + t^2 e^{t^2/2} = (1 + t^2)e^{t^2/2} M'''(t) = (3t + t^3)e^{t^2/2} M^{(4)}(t) = (3 + 6t^2 + t^4)e^{t^2/2}
At t = 0: E[Z] = 0, \quad E[Z^2] = 1, \quad E[Z^3] = 0, \quad E[Z^4] = 3
This quickly becomes messy. The series method is far cleaner for the Normal.

Example 3: Binomial X \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)
M_X(t) = (q + pe^t)^n, \quad q = 1-p
M'(t) = n(q+pe^t)^{n-1} \cdot pe^t
At t = 0, using q + p = 1: E[X] = n \cdot 1^{n-1} \cdot p = np \quad \checkmark
For E[X^2], differentiate M'(t): M''(t) = n(n-1)(q+pe^t)^{n-2}(pe^t)^2 + n(q+pe^t)^{n-1}pe^t
At t = 0: E[X^2] = n(n-1)p^2 + np
Therefore: \text{Var}(X) = n(n-1)p^2 + np - n^2p^2 = np - np^2 = np(1-p) = npq \quad \checkmark

The trick here: always simplify q + pe^t\big|_{t=0} = q + p = 1 first, then collect terms. This avoids carrying unnecessary algebra.


Method 2: Power Series Expansion
The MGF has the power series: M_X(t) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{E[X^n]}{n!}, t^n
So if we can expand M_X(t) as a power series around t = 0, we read off E[X^n] = n! \cdot [t^n]M_X(t) directly. No differentiation needed.

Example 4: Normal Z \sim N(0,1)
M_Z(t) = e^{t^2/2} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(t^2/2)^k}{k!} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{t^{2k}}{2^k k!}
This is a power series in t^2 only — all odd powers of t are absent, confirming E[Z^{2k+1}] = 0 for all k \geq 0.
For even moments, the coefficient of t^{2k} is \frac{1}{2^k k!}, so:
E[Z^{2k}] = (2k)! \cdot \frac{1}{2^k k!} = \frac{(2k)!}{2^k k!}
\boxed{E[Z^{2k}] = (2k-1)!! = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2k-1)}
where (2k-1)!!  is the double factorial. Explicitly:



































kE[Z^{2k}]Value01111123!! = 1\cdot 3335!! = 1\cdot 3\cdot 51547!! = 1\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7105
This is the cleanest derivation of the Normal moments. No integrals, no Hermite polynomials, no recursion. Just expand e^{t^2/2} and read off the answer.
The kurtosis check: E[Z^4] = 3 ✓, so \text{Kurt}(Z) = 3 ✓.

Example 5: Poisson X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)
M_X(t) = e^{\lambda(e^t - 1)}
To expand, first expand e^t - 1: e^t - 1 = t + \frac{t^2}{2!} + \frac{t^3}{3!} + \cdots
So: M_X(t) = e^{\lambda\left(t + \frac{t^2}{2} + \frac{t^3}{6} + \cdots\right)}
For the first two moments, we only need terms up to t^2: M_X(t) = \exp!\left(\lambda t + \frac{\lambda t^2}{2} + O(t^3)\right)
Use e^{a+b} \approx 1 + (a+b) + \frac{(a+b)^2}{2} + \cdots with a = \lambda t and b = \lambda t^2/2:
M_X(t) = 1 + \lambda t + \frac{\lambda t^2}{2} + \frac{\lambda^2 t^2}{2} + O(t^3) = 1 + \lambda t + \frac{\lambda + \lambda^2}{2}t^2 + O(t^3)
Reading off: E[X] = \lambda \quad \checkmark E[X^2] = \lambda + \lambda^2 \implies \text{Var}(X) = \lambda + \lambda^2 - \lambda^2 = \lambda \quad \checkmark

For Poisson, the cleaner path to E[X] and \text{Var}(X) is differentiation. But for higher moments like E[X^3], the series expansion keeps all the bookkeeping in one place.


Example 6: Gamma X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, \lambda)
M_X(t) = \left(1 - \frac{t}{\lambda}\right)^{-a}, \quad t < \lambda
Use the generalized binomial series (1 - u)^{-a} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \binom{a+n-1}{n} u^n with u = t/\lambda:
M_X(t) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \binom{a+n-1}{n} \frac{t^n}{\lambda^n}
Reading off the coefficient of t^n/n!:
E[X^n] = \frac{n!}{\lambda^n}\binom{a+n-1}{n} = \frac{n!}{\lambda^n} \cdot \frac{(a+n-1)!}{n!(a-1)!} = \frac{(a+n-1)!}{\lambda^n (a-1)!}
For integer a, using the rising factorial (Pochhammer symbol) a^{(n)} = a(a+1)\cdots(a+n-1):
\boxed{E[X^n] = \frac{a(a+1)\cdots(a+n-1)}{\lambda^n} = \frac{a^{(n)}}{\lambda^n}}
Check for n=1: E[X] = a/\lambda ✓
Check for n=2: E[X^2] = a(a+1)/\lambda^2, so \text{Var}(X) = a(a+1)/\lambda^2 - a^2/\lambda^2 = a/\lambda^2 ✓

Combining Both Methods: A Worked Example
Problem. Let X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2). Find E[X^3] and E[X^4].
Step 1. Write X = \mu + \sigma Z where Z \sim N(0,1). By the binomial theorem:
E[X^3] = E[(\mu + \sigma Z)^3] = \mu^3 + 3\mu^2\sigma E[Z] + 3\mu\sigma^2 E[Z^2] + \sigma^3 E[Z^3] = \mu^3 + 0 + 3\mu\sigma^2 + 0 = \mu^3 + 3\mu\sigma^2
E[X^4] = E[(\mu + \sigma Z)^4] = \mu^4 + 4\mu^3\sigma E[Z] + 6\mu^2\sigma^2 E[Z^2] + 4\mu\sigma^3 E[Z^3] + \sigma^4 E[Z^4] = \mu^4 + 0 + 6\mu^2\sigma^2 + 0 + 3\sigma^4 = \mu^4 + 6\mu^2\sigma^2 + 3\sigma^4
Step 2. The Normal moments E[Z^k] come from the series expansion of e^{t^2/2} computed above. No integrals needed at any stage.

The strategy: reduce general N(\mu, \sigma^2) moments to standard N(0,1) moments via the affine transformation, then use the MGF series to read off E[Z^k]. This is almost always the cleanest path.


The Log-Trick for Variance
For any distribution, there is a slick way to extract the variance directly from the MGF without computing E[X^2] and E[X] separately. Define:
K(t) = \log M_X(t) \quad \text{(the CGF)}
Then: K'(t) = \frac{M'(t)}{M(t)} \implies K'(0) = \frac{M'(0)}{M(0)} = \frac{E[X]}{1} = E[X]
K''(t) = \frac{M''(t)M(t) - (M'(t))^2}{M(t)^2} \implies K''(0) = M''(0) - (M'(0))^2 = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = \text{Var}(X)
\boxed{K'(0) = E[X], \qquad K''(0) = \text{Var}(X)}
This is the CGF doing what it does best — the second derivative gives the variance directly, without the subtraction step. For distributions where \log M(t) is simpler than M(t) (e.g., Normal, where K(t) = \mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2 is a polynomial), this is far more efficient.

Practical Decision Tree
\text{Need } E[X^n] \text{ from } M_X(t)?
Is M(t) a rational function?        → Differentiate directly (Expo, Gamma with integer a)
  e.g. λ/(λ-t), (λ/(λ-t))^a

Is M(t) an exponential of a         → Series expand the exponent (Pois, Normal)  
  simple function?
  e.g. e^{t²/2}, e^{λ(eᵗ-1)}

Is M(t) a polynomial/power?         → Differentiate (Bern, Bin)
  e.g. (q+peᵗ)ⁿ

Do you only need E[X] and Var(X)?   → Use K(t) = log M(t), take 1st and 2nd derivatives


Things I Keep Getting Confused

Honest accounting.



Evaluating derivatives at t = 0 before simplifying. Always simplify the derivative expression first, then set t = 0. Setting t = 0 mid-differentiation loses terms.


Series expansion bookkeeping for the Poisson. The composition e^{\lambda(e^t - 1)} requires expanding e^t - 1 first, then re-exponentiating. Don’t try to expand e^{\lambda e^t} directly without the -\lambda adjustment — you’ll get the raw moments of the wrong distribution.


Forgetting that the coefficient of t^n in M(t) is E[X^n]/n!, not E[X^n]. The factorial is there because of the Taylor series structure. Off by n! is a common and painful error.


Trying to compute E[X^3] and E[X^4] for N(\mu, \sigma^2) by differentiating e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2} directly. Painful. Always reduce to Z \sim N(0,1) first using the affine transformation, then use the series expansion of e^{t^2/2}.


Using the MGF to compute moments when the MGF doesn’t exist. If X is lognormal or Cauchy, you can’t use this method. Check existence first.

01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/07.Weibu.title: 07.Weibull Distribution
01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/07.Weibu.content:
The Weibull is one of those distributions that doesn’t show up in the first half of a probability course and then suddenly appears everywhere in applications — reliability engineering, survival analysis, extreme value theory. The reason it’s so useful is that its hazard rate is not constant: it can increase, decrease, or stay flat depending on a single shape parameter. That flexibility is the whole story. Understand the hazard rate and you understand the Weibull.

Motivation
The Exponential distribution models waiting times under the memoryless assumption — the hazard rate (instantaneous failure rate) is constant. In reality:

A new lightbulb is no more likely to fail in the next hour than it was an hour ago. ← Exponential is fine.
A machine that has been running for 10 years is more likely to fail than a brand new one. ← Increasing hazard. Exponential fails.
Infant mortality: a product is less likely to fail as it survives longer (early defects weed themselves out). ← Decreasing hazard. Exponential fails.

The Weibull is the minimal generalization that handles all three cases through a single shape parameter k.

Definition
A random variable X has the Weibull distribution with shape k > 0 and scale \lambda > 0, written X \sim \text{Weibull}(k, \lambda), if its PDF is:
\boxed{f_X(x) = \frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1} e^{-(x/\lambda)^k}, \quad x > 0}
and f_X(x) = 0 for x \leq 0.
The corresponding CDF is:
\boxed{F_X(x) = 1 - e^{-(x/\lambda)^k}, \quad x > 0}
Proof that the CDF is correct: F_X(x) = \int_0^x \frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{t}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1} e^{-(t/\lambda)^k}, dt
Substitute u = (t/\lambda)^k, so du = \frac{k}{\lambda}(t/\lambda)^{k-1}, dt:
F_X(x) = \int_0^{(x/\lambda)^k} e^{-u}, du = 1 - e^{-(x/\lambda)^k} \quad \square

The substitution u = (t/\lambda)^k is the key move that makes Weibull integrals tractable. Memorize this substitution — it appears in every Weibull calculation.


The Fundamental Connection to Exponential
This is the most important structural fact about the Weibull.
Theorem. X \sim \text{Weibull}(k, \lambda) if and only if X^k \sim \text{Expo}(1/\lambda^k).
Equivalently: if Y \sim \text{Expo}(1), then X = \lambda Y^{1/k} \sim \text{Weibull}(k, \lambda).
Proof (\Rightarrow). Let X \sim \text{Weibull}(k, \lambda). Then: P(X^k \leq y) = P(X \leq y^{1/k}) = 1 - e^{-(y^{1/k}/\lambda)^k} = 1 - e^{-y/\lambda^k}
This is the CDF of \text{Expo}(1/\lambda^k). \square
Proof (\Leftarrow). Let Y \sim \text{Expo}(1), X = \lambda Y^{1/k}. Then: P(X \leq x) = P!\left(Y \leq \left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^k\right) = 1 - e^{-(x/\lambda)^k} \quad \square

This is the right way to think about the Weibull: it is a power transformation of an Exponential. Every property of the Weibull can be derived by applying this transformation to the corresponding Exponential property. This is how I remember the moments — transform, compute for Expo, transform back.

Simulation corollary. To simulate X \sim \text{Weibull}(k, \lambda):

Generate U \sim \text{Unif}(0,1).
Set X = \lambda(-\log U)^{1/k}.

This follows from the inverse CDF method: F_X^{-1}(u) = \lambda(-\log(1-u))^{1/k}, and 1 - U \overset{d}{=} U.

Special Cases





















ParametersDistributionk = 1\text{Expo}(1/\lambda) — constant hazardk = 2Rayleigh distribution — arises in signal processingk \approx 3.6Approximates N(\mu, \sigma^2) in shape
When k = 1: f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\lambda}e^{-x/\lambda} \quad \checkmark This is exactly \text{Expo}(1/\lambda) in the parameterization where \lambda is the mean. Perfect.

Hazard Rate
The hazard rate (or failure rate) of a continuous distribution is:
h(x) = \frac{f_X(x)}{1 - F_X(x)} = \frac{f_X(x)}{S(x)}
where S(x) = P(X > x) is the survival function. Intuitively, h(x),dx \approx P(X \in (x, x+dx) \mid X > x) — the instantaneous probability of failure given survival to time x.
For the Weibull: h(x) = \frac{\frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1} e^{-(x/\lambda)^k}}{e^{-(x/\lambda)^k}} = \frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}
\boxed{h(x) = \frac{k}{\lambda^k} x^{k-1}}
This is a power law in x. The behavior depends entirely on k:

k < 1: h(x) is decreasing in x — infant mortality, early failures. The longer it has survived, the less likely it is to fail now.
k = 1: h(x) = 1/\lambda is constant — memoryless Exponential.
k > 1: h(x) is increasing in x — wear and tear, aging. The longer it has survived, the more likely it is to fail now.


This is the Weibull’s entire raison d’être. It is the parametric family that interpolates between decreasing, constant, and increasing hazard with a single parameter. In reliability engineering, fitting a Weibull to data and estimating k immediately tells you which failure regime you’re in.

The cumulative hazard function is: H(x) = \int_0^x h(t), dt = \left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^k
And note S(x) = e^{-H(x)} = e^{-(x/\lambda)^k} — the survival function is the exponential of the negative cumulative hazard. This is a general identity, not special to the Weibull.

Moments
All moments of the Weibull are expressed using the Gamma function \Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}, dt.
General n-th moment:
\boxed{E[X^n] = \lambda^n ,\Gamma!\left(1 + \frac{n}{k}\right)}
Proof. Use the Exponential connection: X \overset{d}{=} \lambda Y^{1/k} where Y \sim \text{Expo}(1).
E[X^n] = E[\lambda^n Y^{n/k}] = \lambda^n E[Y^{n/k}]
For Y \sim \text{Expo}(1), using LOTUS: E[Y^{n/k}] = \int_0^\infty y^{n/k} e^{-y}, dy = \Gamma!\left(\frac{n}{k} + 1\right) \quad \square
where the last step is the definition of the Gamma function.
Mean: E[X] = \lambda,\Gamma!\left(1 + \frac{1}{k}\right)
Second moment: E[X^2] = \lambda^2,\Gamma!\left(1 + \frac{2}{k}\right)
Variance: \text{Var}(X) = \lambda^2\left[\Gamma!\left(1 + \frac{2}{k}\right) - \left(\Gamma!\left(1 + \frac{1}{k}\right)\right)^2\right]
Verification for k = 1 (Exponential):
E[X] = \lambda,\Gamma(2) = \lambda \cdot 1! = \lambda \quad \checkmark E[X^2] = \lambda^2,\Gamma(3) = \lambda^2 \cdot 2! = 2\lambda^2 \quad \checkmark \text{Var}(X) = \lambda^2(2 - 1) = \lambda^2 \quad \checkmark

In practice, Gamma function values at 1 + n/k for non-integer n/k require a table or software. The key special values: \Gamma(1) = 1, \Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}, \Gamma(n) = (n-1)! for positive integers n, and the recursion \Gamma(z+1) = z\Gamma(z).


MGF: Why It Doesn’t Have a Closed Form
Unlike the Exponential and Normal, the Weibull does not have a closed-form MGF in general.
M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n}{n!} E[X^n] = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(t\lambda)^n}{n!},\Gamma!\left(1 + \frac{n}{k}\right)
For k = 1 (Exponential), \Gamma(1 + n) = n! and the series collapses to \sum (t\lambda)^n = 1/(1-t\lambda) — the Exponential MGF. For general k, no closed form exists.
Consequence: We cannot use the MGF to compute Weibull moments. Instead, we use LOTUS directly (as in the proof above) with the Gamma function. This is the correct tool when the MGF fails.

Median and Mode
Median. Solve F_X(m) = 1/2: 1 - e^{-(m/\lambda)^k} = \frac{1}{2} \implies (m/\lambda)^k = \log 2 \implies \boxed{m = \lambda(\log 2)^{1/k}}
Mode. For k > 1, the PDF has an interior maximum. Set f_X'(x) = 0:
f_X'(x) = 0 \implies \frac{k-1}{x} = \frac{k}{\lambda^k}x^{k-1} \implies x^k = \frac{(k-1)\lambda^k}{k}
\boxed{x_{\text{mode}} = \lambda\left(\frac{k-1}{k}\right)^{1/k}, \quad k > 1}
For k \leq 1: the PDF is decreasing on (0, \infty), so the mode is at x = 0 (or +\infty if you count the boundary).

Skewness and Kurtosis
Using the general moment formula E[X^n] = \lambda^n \Gamma(1 + n/k), define for brevity: \gamma_n = \Gamma!\left(1 + \frac{n}{k}\right)
Then: \mu = \lambda\gamma_1, \quad \sigma^2 = \lambda^2(\gamma_2 - \gamma_1^2)
Skewness: \text{Skew}(X) = \frac{\lambda^3(\gamma_3 - 3\gamma_1\gamma_2 + 2\gamma_1^3)}{(\lambda^2(\gamma_2 - \gamma_1^2))^{3/2}} = \frac{\gamma_3 - 3\gamma_1\gamma_2 + 2\gamma_1^3}{(\gamma_2 - \gamma_1^2)^{3/2}}
For k = 1: \gamma_n = n!, giving numerator 6 - 6 + 2 = 2 and denominator 1, so \text{Skew} = 2 ✓ (Exponential skewness).
The Weibull skewness is always positive for k < 3.6 approximately, and approaches zero as k \to \infty (the distribution concentrates and symmetrizes).
Key qualitative fact: the Weibull is right-skewed for most practical values of k, becoming less skewed as k increases.

Fitting the Weibull: The Log-Transform
A useful practical fact. Taking logs of X \sim \text{Weibull}(k, \lambda):
P(\log X \leq y) = P(X \leq e^y) = 1 - e^{-(e^y/\lambda)^k} = 1 - e^{-e^{k(y - \log\lambda)}}
This is the CDF of a Gumbel distribution (minimum extreme value distribution) with location \log\lambda and scale 1/k. So:
\log X \sim \text{Gumbel}!\left(\log\lambda,, \frac{1}{k}\right)
Practical consequence: to fit a Weibull to data, take logs of the observations and fit a Gumbel (or equivalently, use a Weibull probability plot — plot \log(-\log(1 - \hat{F}(x))) against \log x, which should be linear with slope k and intercept -k\log\lambda).

The Weibull in Extreme Value Theory
The Weibull arises naturally in the theory of extremes. The Weibull distribution (in the extreme value parameterization) describes the limiting distribution of the minimum of many i.i.d. random variables under appropriate conditions — just as the Gumbel describes the maximum.
Specifically: if X_1, \ldots, X_n are i.i.d. with a distribution whose left tail behaves like a power law, then \min(X_1, \ldots, X_n), properly normalized, converges in distribution to a Weibull. This is the Fisher-Tippett-Gnedenko theorem for minima.

This is why the Weibull appears in reliability: we are often interested in the time until the first failure in a system of many components — i.e., the minimum of many component lifetimes.


Summary of Key Facts

















































PropertyValuePDF\frac{k}{\lambda}\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)^{k-1}e^{-(x/\lambda)^k}CDF1 - e^{-(x/\lambda)^k}Survival S(x)e^{-(x/\lambda)^k}Hazard h(x)\frac{k}{\lambda^k}x^{k-1}Mean\lambda,\Gamma(1 + 1/k)Variance\lambda^2\left[\Gamma(1+2/k) - \Gamma(1+1/k)^2\right]Median\lambda(\log 2)^{1/k}Mode (k>1)\lambda\left(\frac{k-1}{k}\right)^{1/k}MGFNo closed form (series only)Special case k=1\text{Expo}(1/\lambda)

Things I Keep Getting Confused

Honest accounting.



Parameterization inconsistency. There are two common parameterizations of the Weibull. Some sources write f(x) = \frac{k}{\lambda}(x/\lambda)^{k-1}e^{-(x/\lambda)^k} (as above, where \lambda is the scale). Others write f(x) = kx^{k-1}e^{-x^k} (absorbing \lambda into a unit-scale version). And some engineering texts use \lambda as a rate, not a scale. Always check which convention is in use before computing moments.


Forgetting the Gamma function for moments. There is no MGF shortcut here. The moments require \Gamma(1 + n/k), which for non-integer k and n is a transcendental number. Numerical computation is the norm.


Confusing the Weibull CDF with the Exponential CDF. The Exponential CDF is 1 - e^{-\lambda x}. The Weibull CDF is 1 - e^{-(x/\lambda)^k}. The k-th power inside the exponent is the entire difference.


The hazard rate interpretation. h(x) is not a probability. It’s a rate — it can exceed 1. The probability of failure in (x, x+dx) given survival to x is approximately h(x),dx, not h(x).


Assuming the Weibull MGF exists in closed form. It doesn’t, for general k. Don’t try to differentiate a closed-form MGF that isn’t there.

01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/08.Sum-o.title: 08.Sum of Independent RVs via MGFs
01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/08.Sum-o.content:
The MGF is one of those tools that seems like overkill until the day you need it — and then it becomes indispensable. The key insight here is almost embarrassingly clean: independence turns convolution into multiplication.


Why MGFs at all?
Computing the distribution of X + Y directly means convolving the densities (or PMFs). That’s painful. The MGF converts this convolution problem into an algebraic one: independence means the joint factors, and the expectation of a product becomes a product of expectations.
This is the same philosophical move as using Fourier transforms for convolution in signal processing. The MGF is (essentially) a two-sided Laplace transform of the distribution.

The Main Theorem
Theorem. Let X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n be independent random variables with MGFs M_{X_1}(t), \ldots, M_{X_n}(t), each finite in some open interval (-h, h) around 0. Define S_n = X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n. Then:
\boxed{M_{S_n}(t) = \prod_{i=1}^n M_{X_i}(t)}
Proof
This is one of those proofs where, once you see it, you wonder why anyone writes it out. But let’s be careful.
M_{S_n}(t) = \mathbb{E}\left[e^{t S_n}\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[e^{t(X_1 + \cdots + X_n)}\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=1}^n e^{t X_i}\right]
Now I use the key step: for independent random variables, the expectation of a product equals the product of expectations. This is not obvious — it requires independence, not just uncorrelatedness.

Lemma. If X_1, \ldots, X_n are independent, then for any Borel functions g_1, \ldots, g_n (with finite expectations): \mathbb{E}\left[\prod_{i=1}^n g_i(X_i)\right] = \prod_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[g_i(X_i)]
Proof sketch. For n=2: independence means the joint density (or PMF) factors as f_{X_1, X_2}(x_1, x_2) = f_{X_1}(x_1) f_{X_2}(x_2). Then: \mathbb{E}[g_1(X_1)g_2(X_2)] = \int \int g_1(x_1)g_2(x_2) f_{X_1}(x_1)f_{X_2}(x_2), dx_1, dx_2 = \left(\int g_1(x_1) f_{X_1}(x_1), dx_1\right)\left(\int g_2(x_2) f_{X_2}(x_2), dx_2\right) = \mathbb{E}[g_1(X_1)] \cdot \mathbb{E}[g_2(X_2)] Induction handles n > 2. \square

Applying the lemma with g_i(x) = e^{tx}:
M_{S_n}(t) = \prod_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}\left[e^{t X_i}\right] = \prod_{i=1}^n M_{X_i}(t) \qquad \square

The Uniqueness Theorem (Critical!)
The above theorem would be useless without this:
Theorem (Uniqueness of MGFs). If two distributions have MGFs that are equal and finite on some open interval (-h, h), then the two distributions are identical.
This is the theorem that lets you “read off” the distribution from the MGF. Without uniqueness, knowing M_{S_n} tells you nothing about the law of S_n.

I always need to remind myself: the uniqueness theorem is non-trivial and its proof goes through the theory of moment problems / analytic functions. Blitzstein & Hwang sketch this; the full proof lives in Billingsley or Durrett. Accept it as a black box for now unless you want to go down that rabbit hole.


Working Examples
1. Sum of Independent Poissons
Let X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i), independent. Recall: M_X(t) = e^{\lambda(e^t - 1)}
Then: M_{S_n}(t) = \prod_{i=1}^n e^{\lambda_i(e^t - 1)} = e^{(\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i)(e^t - 1)}
This is the MGF of a \text{Poisson}(\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n). By uniqueness:
\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \text{Poisson}!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\right)
This is the reproductive property of the Poisson. Makes sense intuitively: merging independent Poisson processes (with rates \lambda_i) gives a Poisson process with rate \sum \lambda_i.

2. Sum of Independent Normals
Let X_i \sim N(\mu_i, \sigma_i^2), independent. Recall: M_X(t) = e^{\mu t + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 t^2}
Then: M_{S_n}(t) = \prod_{i=1}^n e^{\mu_i t + \frac{1}{2}\sigma_i^2 t^2} = e^{(\sum \mu_i)t + \frac{1}{2}(\sum \sigma_i^2)t^2}
By uniqueness:
\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim N!\left(\sum \mu_i,, \sum \sigma_i^2\right)
This is the most important special case. The MGF proof is far cleaner than the density convolution approach.

3. Sum of n i.i.d. Exponentials → Gamma
Let X_i \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda) (rate \lambda), i.i.d. Recall: M_X(t) = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}, \quad t < \lambda
Then: M_{S_n}(t) = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}\right)^n
This is exactly the MGF of a \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda) distribution. So:
X_1 + \cdots + X_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)
This is how you prove that a Gamma is the sum of i.i.d. Exponentials — the “waiting time for the n-th arrival in a Poisson process” interpretation made rigorous.

4. Sum of Independent Gammas (same rate)
More generally: X_i \sim \text{Gamma}(a_i, \lambda), independent, same rate \lambda. Then:
M_{S_n}(t) = \prod_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}\right)^{a_i} = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}\right)^{\sum a_i}
So S_n \sim \text{Gamma}(\sum a_i, \lambda). The Gamma is also reproductive — in its shape parameter, holding rate fixed.

⚠️ Watch out: This breaks down if the rates differ. \text{Gamma}(a_1, \lambda_1) + \text{Gamma}(a_2, \lambda_2) with \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2 does not have a closed-form Gamma distribution. The MGF is \left(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1-t}\right)^{a_1}\left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_2-t}\right)^{a_2}, which doesn’t simplify to a standard family.


Cumulant Generating Function (a cleaner object)
Define the CGF: K_X(t) = \log M_X(t).
Then independence gives:
K_{S_n}(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n K_{X_i}(t)
The CGF turns products into sums, and its derivatives at 0 give the cumulants: \kappa_1 = \mathbb{E}[X], \kappa_2 = \text{Var}(X), \kappa_3 = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^3], etc.
So the fact that \text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) (for independent X, Y) is just K''_{X+Y}(0) = K''_X(0) + K''_Y(0), which is obvious from the sum formula.

Common MGF Reference













































DistributionMGF M_X(t)Domain\text{Bernoulli}(p)1 - p + pe^tall t\text{Binomial}(n,p)(1-p+pe^t)^nall t\text{Poisson}(\lambda)e^{\lambda(e^t-1)}all t\text{Expo}(\lambda)\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}t < \lambda\text{Gamma}(a, \lambda)\left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-t}\right)^at < \lambdaN(\mu, \sigma^2)e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2}all t\chi^2_n(1-2t)^{-n/2}t < 1/2

The \chi^2_n row: since \chi^2_n = Z_1^2 + \cdots + Z_n^2 with Z_i \sim N(0,1) i.i.d., and Z_i^2 \sim \text{Gamma}(1/2, 1/2), you get M_{\chi^2_n}(t) = (1-2t)^{-n/2} by the Gamma reproductive property. Clean.


Pitfalls and Subtleties
1. MGF may not exist.
The MGF M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] can be infinite. For example, the log-normal distribution has no finite MGF at any t > 0. In those cases, the characteristic function \varphi_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{itX}] always exists (since |e^{itX}| = 1), and the same product formula holds for sums of independent RVs. This is the basis of the proof of the CLT.
2. Independence is essential.
The product formula M_{X+Y}(t) = M_X(t) M_Y(t) requires independence. For general X, Y: M_{X+Y}(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{t(X+Y)}], and this does not factor unless X \perp Y.
3. Domain must overlap.
Each M_{X_i}(t) must be finite in a common open interval containing 0. If the domains don’t overlap, the product isn’t valid.

Connection to the CLT
The MGF/CF approach is the clean path to the Central Limit Theorem. If X_i are i.i.d. with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2, standardize:
Z_n = \frac{S_n - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}
Then M_{Z_n}(t) \to e^{t^2/2} as n \to \infty — the MGF of N(0,1). The machinery behind this is a Taylor expansion of \log M_X(t/\sigma\sqrt{n}) around 0. See the CLT note.

01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/09.Lapla.title: 09.Laplace's Rule of Succession
01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/09.Lapla.content:
Laplace asked: the sun has risen every day for 5000 years — what’s the probability it rises tomorrow? The answer he derived is one of the most elegant pieces of Bayesian reasoning ever written down. The mathematics is simple. The philosophy it encodes is deep enough that people still argue about it.


The Problem
You observe a sequence of trials. The first n are all successes. What is the probability the (n+1)-th trial is also a success?
The frequentist answer is \hat{p} = 1, which is absurd — we’ve never seen a failure, so we just declare certainty? Laplace’s answer avoids this by placing a prior on the unknown success probability.
Laplace’s Rule of Succession: After observing n successes in n trials:
P(\text{next trial is a success} \mid \text{$n$ successes in $n$ trials}) = \frac{n+1}{n+2}
More generally, after s successes in n trials:
P(\text{next is success} \mid s \text{ successes in } n \text{ trials}) = \frac{s+1}{n+2}

Setup and Proof
Model. Suppose the trials are i.i.d. \text{Bernoulli}(p), but p is unknown. We model our uncertainty about p with a prior distribution.
Laplace’s prior: p \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1), i.e. f(p) = 1 on [0,1].
This is the principle of indifference — with no prior knowledge, treat all values of p as equally likely. (We’ll discuss whether this is reasonable.)
Let X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Bern}(p), and let S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n be the number of successes.
We want P(X_{n+1} = 1 \mid S_n = s).
Step 1: Likelihood.
P(S_n = s \mid p) = \binom{n}{s} p^s (1-p)^{n-s}
Step 2: Posterior via Bayes.
f(p \mid S_n = s) = \frac{P(S_n = s \mid p), f(p)}{P(S_n = s)} = \frac{\binom{n}{s} p^s (1-p)^{n-s} \cdot 1}{\int_0^1 \binom{n}{s} p^s (1-p)^{n-s}, dp}
The normalising constant is:
\int_0^1 p^s (1-p)^{n-s}, dp = B(s+1,, n-s+1) = \frac{s!,(n-s)!}{(n+1)!}
using the Beta function identity B(a,b) = \frac{(a-1)!(b-1)!}{(a+b-1)!} (for integer arguments). So:
f(p \mid S_n = s) = \frac{p^s(1-p)^{n-s}}{B(s+1, n-s+1)} = \frac{(n+1)!}{s!,(n-s)!}, p^s(1-p)^{n-s}
This is exactly a \text{Beta}(s+1,, n-s+1) density. So:
p \mid S_n = s \sim \text{Beta}(s+1,, n-s+1)
Step 3: Posterior predictive.
P(X_{n+1} = 1 \mid S_n = s) = \mathbb{E}[p \mid S_n = s]
The last equality holds because, given p, X_{n+1} \sim \text{Bern}(p), so P(X_{n+1}=1 \mid p) = p, and:
P(X_{n+1} = 1 \mid S_n = s) = \int_0^1 P(X_{n+1}=1 \mid p), f(p \mid S_n = s), dp = \mathbb{E}[p \mid S_n = s]
The mean of \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta) is \frac{\alpha}{\alpha + \beta}, so:
\mathbb{E}[p \mid S_n = s] = \frac{s+1}{(s+1)+(n-s+1)} = \frac{s+1}{n+2}
Therefore:
\boxed{P(X_{n+1} = 1 \mid S_n = s) = \frac{s+1}{n+2}}
\square
For the all-successes case s = n: P = \frac{n+1}{n+2}. For n = 5000 years of sunrises, this gives \frac{5001}{5002} \approx 0.9998. Not certain, but very close — and the answer is finite, unlike the frequentist estimate of 1. \square

The Beta-Binomial Conjugate Pair
The proof above reveals something more important than just the formula: the Beta-Binomial conjugacy.
Definition. A prior family \mathcal{F} is conjugate to a likelihood if the posterior is also in \mathcal{F}.
Theorem. The \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta) prior is conjugate to the Binomial likelihood. Specifically:
p \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta), \quad S_n \mid p \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)
\implies p \mid S_n = s \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha + s,, \beta + n - s)
Proof.
f(p \mid S_n = s) \propto f(p) \cdot P(S_n = s \mid p) \propto p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1} \cdot p^s(1-p)^{n-s} = p^{(\alpha+s)-1}(1-p)^{(\beta+n-s)-1}
This is proportional to a \text{Beta}(\alpha+s, \beta+n-s) density. Since it must normalise to 1, it is that density. \square
Interpretation. \alpha and \beta act like “prior pseudo-counts”: \alpha = prior successes, \beta = prior failures. Each observed success increments \alpha by 1; each failure increments \beta by 1.
Laplace’s uniform prior is \text{Beta}(1, 1) — one phantom success and one phantom failure, encoding total ignorance.
The posterior predictive mean is:
\frac{\alpha + s}{\alpha + \beta + n}
which interpolates between the prior mean \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta} and the MLE \frac{s}{n}, with the balance determined by how much data you have relative to the strength of the prior (\alpha + \beta).

What the Formula Is Really Saying
Rewrite:
\frac{s+1}{n+2} = \frac{n}{n+2} \cdot \frac{s}{n} + \frac{2}{n+2} \cdot \frac{1}{2}
The prediction is a weighted average of the MLE s/n and the prior mean 1/2, with weights proportional to n and 2 (the “strength” of the uniform prior = \alpha + \beta = 2).
As n \to \infty, the data overwhelms the prior and the formula converges to s/n — exactly what you’d expect from any reasonable Bayesian procedure.

A More General Version
Theorem. Suppose p \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta) and we observe s successes in n trials. Then the probability of m successes in the next k trials is:
P(S_k^{\text{new}} = m \mid S_n = s) = \binom{k}{m} \frac{B(\alpha + s + m,, \beta + n - s + k - m)}{B(\alpha + s,, \beta + n - s)}
This is the Beta-Binomial distribution. Laplace’s rule is the special case k = 1, m = 1, \alpha = \beta = 1.

Philosophical Caveats

I feel obligated to record these, because a result this clean always conceals some philosophical debt.

1. The uniform prior is not “assumption-free.”
The principle of indifference — assigning equal probability to each value of p — is not a neutral act. Under a change of variables \theta = p^2, the uniform prior on p becomes a non-uniform prior on \theta. There is no such thing as an objective ignorance prior in general. This is Bertrand’s paradox applied to priors.
Jeffreys proposed a prior that is invariant under reparametrisation: for the Binomial, the Jeffreys prior is \text{Beta}(1/2, 1/2), giving the prediction:
P(X_{n+1} = 1 \mid S_n = s) = \frac{s + 1/2}{n+1}
which is slightly different from Laplace’s formula.
2. The exchangeability assumption.
The model assumes the trials are i.i.d. given p, and that the data is exchangeable. This is reasonable for coin flips; less so for sunrises (the sun doesn’t flip a coin each morning).
de Finetti’s theorem makes this precise: a sequence is exchangeable if and only if it can be represented as i.i.d. given some latent parameter with some prior. So the Beta-Binomial model is the most general exchangeable model for binary sequences.
3. The rule handles zero observations correctly.
Classic problem: you’ve never seen a nuclear war. Does that mean P(\text{nuclear war tomorrow}) = 0? The frequentist says yes. Laplace says \frac{0+1}{n+2} = \frac{1}{n+2}, which is small but positive — a much saner answer.

Summary Table

























PriorPosteriorPredictive probability\text{Beta}(1,1) (Laplace)\text{Beta}(s+1, n-s+1)\frac{s+1}{n+2}\text{Beta}(1/2,1/2) (Jeffreys)\text{Beta}(s+\frac{1}{2}, n-s+\frac{1}{2})\frac{s+1/2}{n+1}\text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta) (general)\text{Beta}(\alpha+s, \beta+n-s)\frac{\alpha+s}{\alpha+\beta+n}

01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/10.Proba.title: 10.Probability Generating Functions
01.Maths/Probability/06.Moments/10.Proba.content:
The PGF is the MGF’s more elegant sibling, tailor-made for non-negative integer-valued RVs. Where the MGF encodes moments, the PGF encodes the entire probability sequence — and you can literally read off P(X = k) by differentiating k times. That’s not a trick; it’s the point.


Motivation
Suppose X takes values in {0, 1, 2, \ldots}. We could use the MGF M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]. But for integer-valued RVs there’s a more natural object: substitute z = e^t, and instead of expanding in powers of e^t, expand in powers of z. The PGF is a power series whose coefficients are exactly the probabilities.
This makes it a generating function in the combinatorial sense — the same object that appears in enumerative combinatorics, which is no coincidence.

Definition
Definition. Let X be a non-negative integer-valued RV. The probability generating function (PGF) of X is:
G_X(z) = \mathbb{E}[z^X] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty P(X = k), z^k
defined for all z \in \mathbb{C} for which the series converges. It always converges for |z| \leq 1 (since \sum P(X=k) = 1), and often in a larger disk.
Relation to MGF: G_X(z) = M_X(\log z), or equivalently M_X(t) = G_X(e^t). They carry the same information; the PGF is just a reparametrisation optimised for discrete distributions.

Recovery of Probabilities
This is the key property that justifies the name. Since G_X(z) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty P(X=k), z^k is a power series, we can recover each probability by differentiating:
P(X = k) = \frac{G_X^{(k)}(0)}{k!}
where G_X^{(k)} denotes the k-th derivative. This is just the standard formula for Taylor coefficients.
Proof. Differentiate G_X(z) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty P(X=k), z^k term by term (justified by uniform convergence on |z| < R where R is the radius of convergence):
G_X^{(k)}(z) = \sum_{n=k}^\infty P(X=n), \frac{n!}{(n-k)!}, z^{n-k}
Evaluating at z = 0 kills every term except n = k:
G_X^{(k)}(0) = k!, P(X = k) \implies P(X = k) = \frac{G_X^{(k)}(0)}{k!} \qquad \square

Moments from the PGF
Define the factorial moments: \mathbb{E}[X(X-1)\cdots(X-k+1)] = \mathbb{E}[(X)_k], the k-th falling factorial moment.
Theorem. G_X^{(k)}(1) = \mathbb{E}[(X)_k].
Proof. Differentiate G_X(z) = \mathbb{E}[z^X] under the expectation k times:
G_X^{(k)}(z) = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{d^k}{dz^k} z^X\right] = \mathbb{E}[X(X-1)\cdots(X-k+1), z^{X-k}]
Set z = 1: G_X^{(k)}(1) = \mathbb{E}[X(X-1)\cdots(X-k+1)]. \square
Extracting ordinary moments:
\mathbb{E}[X] = G_X'(1) \mathbb{E}[X^2] = G_X''(1) + G_X'(1) \text{Var}(X) = G_X''(1) + G_X'(1) - [G_X'(1)]^2

The variance formula is worth memorising. \text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X(X-1)] + \mathbb{E}[X] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 = G''(1) + G'(1) - (G'(1))^2.


Sum of Independent RVs
The same product formula from 08.Sum of Independent RVs via MGFs carries over:
Theorem. If X_1, \ldots, X_n are independent non-negative integer-valued RVs, then:
G_{X_1 + \cdots + X_n}(z) = \prod_{i=1}^n G_{X_i}(z)
Proof. Identical to the MGF proof: \mathbb{E}[z^{X_1 + \cdots + X_n}] = \mathbb{E}[\prod z^{X_i}] = \prod \mathbb{E}[z^{X_i}] by independence. \square

Standard PGFs
Bernoulli(p)
G_X(z) = (1-p) + pz = q + pz
Binomial(n, p)
X = \sum_{i=1}^n B_i, B_i \sim \text{Bern}(p) i.i.d. By the product formula:
G_X(z) = (q + pz)^n
This is the reproductive property of the Binomial: \text{Bin}(m,p) + \text{Bin}(n,p) \sim \text{Bin}(m+n, p).
Geometric(p) (number of trials until first success, supported on {1, 2, \ldots})
P(X = k) = q^{k-1}p for k \geq 1:
G_X(z) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty q^{k-1}p, z^k = pz \sum_{k=0}^\infty (qz)^k = \frac{pz}{1-qz}, \quad |z| < 1/q
Negative Binomial,(r, p) (number of trials until r-th success)
X = \sum_{i=1}^r G_i, G_i \sim \text{Geom}(p) i.i.d.:
G_X(z) = \left(\frac{pz}{1-qz}\right)^r
Poisson(\lambda)
P(X = k) = e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!:
G_X(z) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}z^k = e^{-\lambda}\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(\lambda z)^k}{k!} = e^{\lambda(z-1)}
Check: G_X'(1) = \lambda e^{\lambda(z-1)}\big|_{z=1} = \lambda = \mathbb{E}[X]. ✓
Reproductive property: \text{Poisson}(\lambda_1) + \text{Poisson}(\lambda_2) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2), since: e^{\lambda_1(z-1)} \cdot e^{\lambda_2(z-1)} = e^{(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)(z-1)}

Compound Distributions (The Real Payoff)
This is where PGFs earn their keep. A compound distribution is S = X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_N, where N itself is a random variable, independent of the i.i.d. X_i.
Think: N is the number of customers today, X_i is what customer i spends. What’s G_S(z)?
Theorem (Compound PGF). If N \perp (X_1, X_2, \ldots) with X_i i.i.d. copies of X, then:
\boxed{G_S(z) = G_N(G_X(z))}
That’s the PGF of N, evaluated at G_X(z). Composition, not multiplication.
Proof
Condition on N:
G_S(z) = \mathbb{E}[z^S] = \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}[z^S \mid N]\right]
Given N = n: S = X_1 + \cdots + X_n, so \mathbb{E}[z^S \mid N = n] = G_X(z)^n (by independence and the product formula). Therefore:
G_S(z) = \mathbb{E}\left[G_X(z)^N\right] = G_N(G_X(z))
where the last step uses the definition of G_N: G_N(w) = \mathbb{E}[w^N], with w = G_X(z). \square
Example: Compound Poisson
Let N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda), X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu). Then:
G_S(z) = G_N(G_X(z)) = e^{\lambda(G_X(z) - 1)} = e^{\lambda(e^{\mu(z-1)} - 1)}
This is the PGF of a compound Poisson distribution (relevant in insurance risk theory, queueing, etc.).

The compound PGF formula G_S = G_N \circ G_X is one of my favourite results in all of probability. It’s the kind of thing where the notation is doing serious mathematical work — iteration of functions as a model of randomness built on randomness.


Branching Processes
The most beautiful application of compound PGFs. A Galton–Watson branching process models population growth:

Generation 0: one individual (the ancestor).
Each individual independently produces k offspring with probability p_k, k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots
Z_n = population in generation n.

Let G(z) = G_{Z_1}(z) = \sum_k p_k z^k be the offspring PGF.
Claim: The PGF of Z_n is the n-fold iterate of G:
G_{Z_n}(z) = \underbrace{G \circ G \circ \cdots \circ G}_{n \text{ times}}(z) =: G^{(n)}(z)
Proof by induction. Base: G_{Z_1} = G. ✓
Inductive step: Z_{n+1} = \sum_{i=1}^{Z_n} X_i, where X_i are i.i.d. offspring counts. By the compound PGF theorem:
G_{Z_{n+1}}(z) = G_{Z_n}(G(z)) = G^{(n)}(G(z)) = G^{(n+1)}(z) \qquad \square
Extinction probability. Let q = P(\text{extinction}) = P(Z_n = 0 \text{ for some } n) = \lim_{n\to\infty} P(Z_n = 0).
Since P(Z_n = 0) = G^{(n)}(0) and extinction is an increasing event:
q = \lim_{n \to \infty} G^{(n)}(0)
One can show q satisfies the fixed-point equation:
q = G(q)
and is the smallest non-negative fixed point of G.
Theorem. Let \mu = G'(1) = \mathbb{E}[Z_1] be the mean offspring number. Then:

If \mu \leq 1: q = 1 (certain extinction).
If \mu > 1: q < 1 (positive probability of survival), and q is the unique fixed point of G in [0, 1).


I find the fixed-point characterisation of the extinction probability beautiful. The equation q = G(q) is saying: to go extinct, either the first individual has no children (p_0), or it has some children, each of whose lineages independently go extinct. That’s just conditioning on the first generation. The PGF encodes this recursion automatically.


PGF vs MGF: When to Use Which








































PGF G_X(z) = \mathbb{E}[z^X]MGF M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]Best forNon-negative integer-valued RVsAny RV (continuous, discrete, mixed)ProbabilitiesDirectly: P(X=k) = G^{(k)}(0)/k!Not directly readableMomentsFactorial moments from G^{(k)}(1)Ordinary moments from M^{(k)}(0)Compound distributionsClean: G_S = G_N \circ G_XMessierBranching processesNatural (iterated composition)UnnaturalCLT / continuity theoremNot the right toolYes (or use characteristic functions)

Uniqueness
Just as with MGFs: the PGF uniquely determines the distribution. Since G_X(z) = \sum_{k \geq 0} P(X=k), z^k is a power series, and power series have unique coefficients, knowing G_X is equivalent to knowing all of P(X=0), P(X=1), \ldots — i.e., the entire distribution.

Worked Problem (Stat 110 Style)
Problem. N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda) light bulbs, each independently survives one day with probability p. Let S = number of bulbs surviving. Find the distribution of S.
Solution via PGF. Each bulb survives \sim \text{Bern}(p), so G_{\text{Bern}}(z) = q + pz. By the compound formula:
G_S(z) = G_N(G_{\text{Bern}}(z)) = e^{\lambda(q+pz - 1)} = e^{\lambda p(z-1)}
This is the PGF of \text{Poisson}(\lambda p). So S \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda p).
This is the Poisson thinning result: thin a Poisson by independent p-coin flips, get a Poisson with rate \lambda p. Proved in one line with PGFs.

01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.title: 01.Joint, Marginal, and Conditional Distributions
01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.content:
Most of probability is about one random variable at a time. Real problems involve many. The moment you have two RVs living on the same probability space, you need the joint distribution — and everything else (marginals, conditionals, independence) is derived from it. The joint is the ground truth; everything else is a projection or a slice.


The Joint Distribution
Definition (discrete). For RVs X and Y on the same probability space, the joint PMF is:
p_{X,Y}(x, y) = P(X = x,, Y = y)
defined for all (x, y) in the support. It satisfies: \sum_x \sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1, \qquad p_{X,Y}(x,y) \geq 0
Definition (continuous). The joint PDF f_{X,Y}(x,y) satisfies:
P((X,Y) \in A) = \iint_A f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy
for all Borel sets A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2. Normalisation: \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy = 1
Definition (joint CDF). For any (X, Y) (discrete, continuous, or mixed):
F_{X,Y}(x,y) = P(X \leq x,, Y \leq y)
The joint CDF always exists and uniquely determines the joint distribution. The PDF/PMF may not exist (e.g. if there’s a point mass).

Marginal Distributions
The marginal distribution of X is simply the distribution of X alone, recovered by summing/integrating out Y.
Discrete: p_X(x) = \sum_y p_{X,Y}(x, y), \qquad p_Y(y) = \sum_x p_{X,Y}(x,y)
Continuous: f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx

Crucial point: you can always recover the marginals from the joint, but not vice versa. The joint contains strictly more information. Two distributions can have identical marginals but completely different joint distributions — independence is a special additional structure.

Example
Joint PMF of (X, Y):





























Y=0Y=1p_XX=01/41/41/2X=11/41/41/2p_Y1/21/21
Marginals: X \sim \text{Bern}(1/2), Y \sim \text{Bern}(1/2).
But the same marginals are consistent with many different joints. For instance:





























Y=0Y=1p_XX=01/201/2X=101/21/2p_Y1/21/21
Here X = Y with probability 1 — as far from independent as possible — yet the marginals are identical.

Conditional Distributions
Discrete Case
Definition. The conditional PMF of Y given X = x is:
p_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) = P(Y = y \mid X = x) = \frac{P(X = x, Y = y)}{P(X = x)} = \frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_X(x)}
defined for all x with p_X(x) > 0.
This is just Bayes’ rule / the definition of conditional probability, applied to events {Y = y} and {X = x}.
For each fixed x, the function y \mapsto p_{Y|X}(y \mid x) is a valid PMF: it sums to 1 over y.
Continuous Case
Here we must be careful. The event {X = x} has probability zero, so we can’t naively write P(Y \leq y \mid X = x) = P(Y \leq y, X = x)/P(X = x) — that’s 0/0.
Definition. If f_{X,Y}(x,y) is the joint PDF and f_X(x) > 0, the conditional PDF of Y given X = x is:
f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}
Why is this the right definition? It’s the density version of the limit:
P(Y \leq y \mid x < X \leq x + dx) = \frac{P(Y \leq y,, x < X \leq x+dx)}{P(x < X \leq x+dx)} \xrightarrow{dx \to 0} \frac{\int_{-\infty}^y f_{X,Y}(x,t),dt}{f_X(x)}
Differentiating in y gives f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_X(x).

The Fundamental Factorisation
The definitions immediately give:
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x), f_X(x) = f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y), f_Y(y)
This is the chain rule for joint distributions. It extends to n variables:
f_{X_1, \ldots, X_n}(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = f_{X_1}(x_1), f_{X_2 \mid X_1}(x_2 \mid x_1), f_{X_3 \mid X_1, X_2}(x_3 \mid x_1, x_2) \cdots

This factorisation is the backbone of graphical models, Bayesian networks, and HMMs. Every time you specify a generative model by saying “sample X_1, then sample X_2 \mid X_1, then sample X_3 \mid X_1, X_2…”, you are implicitly specifying a joint via this chain rule.


Independence
Definition. X and Y are independent if:
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x), f_Y(y) \quad \text{for all } (x,y)
(or p_{X,Y}(x,y) = p_X(x), p_Y(y) in the discrete case).
Equivalent characterisations:

f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) = f_Y(y) for all x, y — knowing X tells you nothing about Y.
F_{X,Y}(x,y) = F_X(x), F_Y(y) for all x, y.
\mathbb{E}[g(X)h(Y)] = \mathbb{E}[g(X)], \mathbb{E}[h(Y)] for all bounded Borel g, h.
The joint factors as a function of x alone times a function of y alone.

Characterisation 4 is a practical test: if you can write f_{X,Y}(x,y) = g(x)h(y) with the support a product set, then X \perp Y.
LOTUS and Independence
A fact used constantly: if X \perp Y, then \mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y], so \text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0. But the converse fails: uncorrelated does not imply independent in general.
Standard counterexample. X \sim \text{Uniform}(-1, 1), Y = X^2. Then \text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[X^3] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[X^2] = 0 - 0 = 0, yet Y is a deterministic function of X — they are as dependent as possible.

Conditional Expectation
Definition. The conditional expectation \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x] is:
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x] = \begin{cases} \sum_y y, p_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) & \text{(discrete)} \ \int_{-\infty}^\infty y, f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x), dy & \text{(continuous)} \end{cases}
This is a function of x. When we write \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X], we mean this function evaluated at the random variable X — so \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] is itself a random variable.
Adam’s Law (Law of Total Expectation)
\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\right]
Proof (continuous). \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]] = \int \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x], f_X(x), dx = \int \left(\int y, f_{Y|X}(y|x), dy\right) f_X(x), dx = \int\int y, f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy, dx = \int y, f_Y(y), dy = \mathbb{E}[Y] \qquad \square
Eve’s Law (Law of Total Variance)
\text{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(Y \mid X)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X])
Unexplained variance + variance of explained mean.
Proof. Write \text{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[Y^2] - (\mathbb{E}[Y])^2. Apply Adam’s law to each term:
\mathbb{E}[Y^2] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y^2 \mid X]] = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(Y|X) + (\mathbb{E}[Y|X])^2]
(\mathbb{E}[Y])^2 = (\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y|X]])^2
So: \text{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(Y|X)] + \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[Y|X])^2] - (\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y|X]])^2 = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(Y|X)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y|X]) \qquad \square

Eve’s law decomposes variance into two parts: the average residual variance after conditioning (unexplained noise), and the variance of the conditional mean (signal). This shows up constantly — in ANOVA, mixed models, random effects, and any time you’re partitioning variability.


Covariance and Correlation
Definition. \text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}X)(Y - \mathbb{E}Y)] = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]
\rho(X,Y) = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)\text{Var}(Y)}} \in [-1, 1]
Properties:

\text{Cov}(X,X) = \text{Var}(X)
\text{Cov}(aX + b, cY + d) = ac,\text{Cov}(X,Y)
\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\text{Cov}(X,Y)
More generally: \text{Var}!\left(\sum_i X_i\right) = \sum_i \text{Var}(X_i) + 2\sum_{i < j} \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)

The covariance matrix. For a random vector \mathbf{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_n)^T:
\Sigma = \text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X} - \mathbb{E}\mathbf{X})(\mathbf{X} - \mathbb{E}\mathbf{X})^T]
with \Sigma_{ij} = \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j). This matrix is always positive semi-definite: for any \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n:
\mathbf{v}^T \Sigma \mathbf{v} = \text{Var}(\mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{X}) \geq 0

The Bivariate Normal
The most important joint continuous distribution. (X, Y) is bivariate normal with parameters \mu_X, \mu_Y, \sigma_X^2, \sigma_Y^2, \rho if:
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_X\sigma_Y\sqrt{1-\rho^2}} \exp!\left(-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}\left[\frac{(x-\mu_X)^2}{\sigma_X^2} - \frac{2\rho(x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y} + \frac{(y-\mu_Y)^2}{\sigma_Y^2}\right]\right)
Key properties:


Marginals are normal: X \sim N(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2), Y \sim N(\mu_Y, \sigma_Y^2).


Conditionals are normal: Y \mid X = x \sim N!\left(\mu_Y + \rho\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(x - \mu_X),; \sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2)\right)


For bivariate normal, uncorrelated \iff independent. This is the one case where the converse of \text{Cov} = 0 \implies uncorrelated holds.


Linear combinations are normal: aX + bY \sim N(a\mu_X + b\mu_Y,; a^2\sigma_X^2 + b^2\sigma_Y^2 + 2ab\rho\sigma_X\sigma_Y).



The conditional mean formula \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x] = \mu_Y + \rho\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(x-\mu_X) is exactly the linear regression of Y on X. The bivariate normal is the distribution where the regression function is linear — and the conditional variance \sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2) is constant (homoskedastic). That’s not a coincidence; it’s a theorem.


Computing Joint Distributions: Worked Examples
Example 1: Discrete joint to conditional
X \sim \text{Uniform}{1,2,3}, and Y \mid X = x \sim \text{Uniform}{1, \ldots, x}. Find P(Y = 1).
By Adam’s law: P(Y=1) = \mathbb{E}[P(Y=1 \mid X)] = \sum_{x=1}^3 P(Y=1 \mid X=x) P(X=x) = \frac{1}{3}\left(1 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{11}{18}
Example 2: Continuous — finding the marginal
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = e^{-y} for 0 < x < y < \infty. Find f_X(x).
f_X(x) = \int_x^\infty e^{-y}, dy = e^{-x}, \quad x > 0
So X \sim \text{Expo}(1).
Example 3: Independence check via factorisation
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 6e^{-2x-3y} for x, y > 0. Does X \perp Y?
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = (2e^{-2x})(3e^{-3y}), which factors as g(x)h(y) on the product support (0,\infty)^2. So yes, X \perp Y, with X \sim \text{Expo}(2) and Y \sim \text{Expo}(3).

Pitfalls
1. Marginals don’t determine the joint.
Already emphasised, but worth repeating: specifying f_X and f_Y separately does not specify f_{X,Y}. You need either the joint directly, the factorisation (if independent), or one marginal plus the conditional.
2. The support matters for independence.
Even if f_{X,Y}(x,y) = g(x)h(y) algebraically, if the support is not a product set (i.e. the region where f > 0 depends on both x and y), then X and Y are not independent.
Example: f_{X,Y}(x,y) \propto 1 on the triangle {0 < x < y < 1}. The support is not [0,1]^2; it depends on both variables jointly. X and Y are dependent even though the density is “constant.”
3. \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] is a random variable, not a number.
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x] is a number for fixed x. \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] is a function of X, hence random. Adam’s law says \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]] = \mathbb{E}[Y] — the outer expectation is over X.

Summary








































ObjectDiscreteContinuousJointp_{X,Y}(x,y)f_{X,Y}(x,y)Marginal of X\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y)\int f_{X,Y}(x,y),dyConditional Y \mid X=xp_{X,Y}(x,y)/p_X(x)f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_X(x)Independencep_{X,Y} = p_X p_Yf_{X,Y} = f_X f_YAdam’s law\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]]sameEve’s law\text{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(Y \mid X)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X])same

01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.title: 02.Joint CDF and Joint PMF
01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.content:
The joint PMF is conceptually simple — it’s just a table of probabilities. The joint CDF is the object that unifies discrete, continuous, and mixed distributions under one roof. Understanding both, and the exact relationship between them, is what separates someone who “knows probability” from someone who actually understands its foundations.


Joint PMF (Discrete Case)
Definition
Let X and Y be discrete RVs on the same probability space. Their joint PMF is the function:
p_{X,Y}(x, y) = P(X = x,, Y = y)
defined for all (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2. It is zero outside the (countable) support.
Validity conditions: p_{X,Y}(x,y) \geq 0 \quad \text{for all } (x,y) \sum_{x} \sum_{y} p_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1
where the sums are over the support.
Computing Probabilities from the Joint PMF
For any event A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2:
P((X,Y) \in A) = \sum_{(x,y) \in A} p_{X,Y}(x,y)
