This is the fundamental usage. Every probability question about (X,Y) reduces to summing the joint PMF over the relevant region.
The Joint PMF Table
For finite-support discrete RVs, the joint PMF is most naturally represented as a table. If X \in {x_1, \ldots, x_m} and Y \in {y_1, \ldots, y_n}:
\begin{array}{c|cccc|c} & y_1 & y_2 & \cdots & y_n & p_X \ \hline x_1 & p_{11} & p_{12} & \cdots & p_{1n} & \sum_j p_{1j} \ x_2 & p_{21} & p_{22} & \cdots & p_{2n} & \sum_j p_{2j} \ \vdots & \vdots & & & \vdots & \vdots \ x_m & p_{m1} & p_{m2} & \cdots & p_{mn} & \sum_j p_{mj} \ \hline p_Y & \sum_i p_{i1} & \sum_i p_{i2} & \cdots & \sum_i p_{in} & 1 \end{array}
Row sums give p_X; column sums give p_Y. The grand total is 1. This is why it’s called a marginalisation — you sum across the margins of the table.
Worked Example: Two Dice
Roll two fair dice. Let X = value of die 1, Y = value of die 2. Then:
p_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{1}{36}, \quad x,y \in {1,2,3,4,5,6}
This is a uniform joint PMF on a 6 \times 6 grid. Every cell has mass 1/36.
What is P(X + Y = 7)? Sum over all cells where x + y = 7: P(X+Y=7) = \sum_{\substack{x,y \ x+y=7}} \frac{1}{36} = \frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}
(The six pairs: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1).)
What is P(X > Y)? Sum over the lower triangle: P(X > Y) = \sum_{x=1}^6 \sum_{y=1}^{x-1} \frac{1}{36} = \frac{1}{36}\sum_{x=1}^6 (x-1) = \frac{0+1+2+3+4+5}{36} = \frac{15}{36} = \frac{5}{12}
Worked Example: Dependent Discrete Joint
Let N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda) and X \mid N = n \sim \text{Bin}(n, p). Find the joint PMF of (N, X).
p_{N,X}(n, x) = P(N=n), P(X=x \mid N=n) = e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!} \cdot \binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x}
for n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots and x = 0, 1, \ldots, n. (Zero otherwise.)
This joint is the starting point for deriving that X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda p) — you marginalise over n:
p_X(x) = \sum_{n=x}^\infty e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}\binom{n}{x}p^x(1-p)^{n-x}
which, after algebra (factor out e^{-\lambda p}(\lambda p)^x/x! and recognise the remaining sum as e^{\lambda(1-p)}), gives p_X(x) = e^{-\lambda p}(\lambda p)^x / x!. This is Poisson thinning done at the PMF level rather than via PGFs.

Joint CDF
Definition
The joint CDF of (X,Y) — whether discrete, continuous, or mixed — is:
F_{X,Y}(x,y) = P(X \leq x,, Y \leq y)
for all (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2.
The joint CDF is the universal representation: it exists for every joint distribution without exception, regardless of whether the joint PMF or joint PDF exists.
Properties of the Joint CDF
P1. Monotonicity. F_{X,Y}(x,y) is non-decreasing in each argument separately: x_1 \leq x_2 \implies F_{X,Y}(x_1, y) \leq F_{X,Y}(x_2, y) and similarly in y.
P2. Right-continuity. F_{X,Y} is right-continuous in each argument: \lim_{x' \downarrow x} F_{X,Y}(x', y) = F_{X,Y}(x,y), \quad \lim_{y' \downarrow y} F_{X,Y}(x, y') = F_{X,Y}(x,y)
P3. Boundary limits. \lim_{x \to -\infty} F_{X,Y}(x,y) = 0, \qquad \lim_{y \to -\infty} F_{X,Y}(x,y) = 0 \lim_{x \to \infty,, y \to \infty} F_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1
P4. Marginal recovery. Sending one argument to +\infty: \lim_{y \to \infty} F_{X,Y}(x,y) = F_X(x), \qquad \lim_{x \to \infty} F_{X,Y}(x,y) = F_Y(y)
P5. Rectangle probability formula (crucial). For x_1 < x_2, y_1 < y_2:
P(x_1 < X \leq x_2,, y_1 < Y \leq y_2) = F(x_2, y_2) - F(x_1, y_2) - F(x_2, y_1) + F(x_1, y_1)

This is the inclusion-exclusion for rectangles. Draw the four corners: you want the probability in the rectangle. You add the top-right CDF value, subtract the two “side” values (which over-subtract the bottom-left), and add back the bottom-left. Get this formula tattooed. It’s used constantly, and it’s easy to get the signs wrong under pressure.

Proof. Write {x_1 < X \leq x_2, y_1 < Y \leq y_2} as a set difference:
= {X \leq x_2, Y \leq y_2} \setminus \left[{X \leq x_1, Y \leq y_2} \cup {X \leq x_2, Y \leq y_1}\right]
By inclusion-exclusion: P = F(x_2,y_2) - P(X \leq x_1, Y \leq y_2) - P(X \leq x_2, Y \leq y_1) + P(X \leq x_1, Y \leq y_1) = F(x_2,y_2) - F(x_1,y_2) - F(x_2,y_1) + F(x_1,y_1) \qquad \square
P6. 2-increasing (supermodularity condition). The above formula must always be \geq 0: F(x_2,y_2) - F(x_1,y_2) - F(x_2,y_1) + F(x_1,y_1) \geq 0
for all x_1 \leq x_2, y_1 \leq y_2. This is necessary and sufficient for F to be a valid joint CDF. A function satisfying this is called 2-increasing (or supermodular in this context).
This is the property that separates a valid joint CDF from just any function satisfying P1–P4. Marginal CDFs can be chosen freely; their “coupling” must satisfy the rectangle inequality.
Recovering the Joint PMF from the CDF (Discrete Case)
For a discrete (X,Y), the joint PMF is recovered by:
p_{X,Y}(x,y) = P(X = x, Y = y) = F(x,y) - F(x^-,y) - F(x,y^-) + F(x^-,y^-)
where F(x^-, y) = \lim_{x' \uparrow x} F(x',y) is the left limit. In the discrete case with integer-valued support this simplifies to:
p_{X,Y}(x,y) = F(x,y) - F(x-1,y) - F(x,y-1) + F(x-1,y-1)
This is the 2D analogue of P(X = k) = F(k) - F(k-1) for the univariate discrete case.
Proof. By the rectangle formula with x_1 = x-1, x_2 = x, y_1 = y-1, y_2 = y: P(X = x, Y = y) = F(x,y) - F(x-1,y) - F(x,y-1) + F(x-1,y-1) \qquad \square
Recovering the Joint PDF from the CDF (Continuous Case)
If F_{X,Y} is sufficiently smooth (mixed partial derivative exists and is continuous):
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{\partial^2 F_{X,Y}}{\partial x, \partial y}(x,y)
Proof. By the fundamental theorem of calculus applied twice: F_{X,Y}(x,y) = \int_{-\infty}^x \int_{-\infty}^y f_{X,Y}(s,t), dt, ds
Differentiating in x then y (justified by continuity of f) gives f_{X,Y}(x,y). \square

The formula f = \partial^2 F / \partial x \partial y is the 2D version of f = F'. In one dimension you take one derivative to get the density. In two dimensions you take the mixed partial. The rectangle formula for probabilities is the 2D version of P(a < X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a).


Relationship Between Joint PMF and Joint CDF
For a discrete (X,Y) with support {(x_i, y_j)}:
F_{X,Y}(x,y) = \sum_{x_i \leq x} \sum_{y_j \leq y} p_{X,Y}(x_i, y_j)
It’s a cumulative sum over all mass points in the lower-left quadrant (-\infty, x] \times (-\infty, y].
The joint CDF of a discrete distribution is a step function in each variable — flat everywhere except at the support points, where it jumps by the mass p_{X,Y}(x_i, y_j).
Schematic for (X,Y) \in {0,1}^2 with joint PMF:




















Y=0Y=1X=0abX=1cd
Then: F(0,0) = a, \quad F(0,1) = a+b, \quad F(1,0) = a+c, \quad F(1,1) = a+b+c+d = 1
And recovering the PMF: p(1,1) = F(1,1) - F(0,1) - F(1,0) + F(0,0) = 1 - (a+b) - (a+c) + a = d \checkmark

Independence in Terms of the Joint CDF
X and Y are independent if and only if:
F_{X,Y}(x,y) = F_X(x), F_Y(y) \quad \text{for all } (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2
This is the CDF version of the factorisation condition. It holds for all distributions — discrete, continuous, mixed — without requiring the existence of a density or PMF.
For the PMF version: if F factors, then so does the PMF: p_{X,Y}(x,y) = \Delta_{xx}\Delta_{yy} F(x,y) = \Delta_{xx} F_X(x) \cdot \Delta_{yy} F_Y(y) = p_X(x), p_Y(y)
where \Delta_{xx} f(x) = f(x) - f(x^-) denotes the jump at x.

Marginal CDFs from the Joint CDF
F_X(x) = \lim_{y \to \infty} F_{X,Y}(x,y), \qquad F_Y(y) = \lim_{x \to \infty} F_{X,Y}(x,y)
These limits always exist (since F is bounded and monotone) and give valid univariate CDFs. This is property P4 above — sending the other variable to +\infty collapses the constraint on it.

Sklar’s Theorem (Copulas) — A Glimpse
The factorisation issue — that marginals don’t determine the joint — has a complete theoretical resolution:
Theorem (Sklar, 1959). For any joint CDF F_{X,Y} with marginals F_X and F_Y, there exists a function C: [0,1]^2 \to [0,1] (called a copula) such that:
F_{X,Y}(x,y) = C(F_X(x), F_Y(y))
If F_X and F_Y are continuous, C is unique. Conversely, for any copula C and any marginal CDFs F_X, F_Y, the above formula defines a valid joint CDF.
The copula C encodes all the dependence structure of (X,Y), completely separated from the marginals. Independence corresponds to C(u,v) = uv (the product copula). The upper Fréchet–Hoeffding bound C(u,v) = \min(u,v) corresponds to X = T(Y) a.s. for some increasing T (comonotonicity).

I’m recording this because it’s the right way to think about why marginals don’t determine the joint. The joint CDF = copula + marginals. Specifying both marginals only pins down the margins of the table; the copula is the free parameter that controls the interior.


Pitfalls
1. The rectangle formula has four terms, not two.
P(x_1 < X \leq x_2, y_1 < Y \leq y_2) \neq F(x_2,y_2) - F(x_1,y_1). That’s wrong — it misses the two off-diagonal terms. Always write all four.
2. Strict vs non-strict inequalities matter in the discrete case.
P(X < x) \neq P(X \leq x) when X has a point mass at x. Specifically P(X \leq x) - P(X < x) = P(X = x). In the continuous case they’re equal, which is why this pitfall only bites in the discrete/mixed setting.
3. The joint CDF is right-continuous, not left-continuous.
F_{X,Y}(x,y) = P(X \leq x, Y \leq y) uses \leq, not <. So jumps happen at the support points, and F is right-continuous with left limits. This is a convention, but it’s universal.
4. Not every function satisfying P1–P4 is a valid joint CDF.
You also need the 2-increasing condition (P6). Example: F(x,y) = F_X(x) for all y \geq 0 and 0 otherwise is monotone in each argument and has the right limits — but the rectangle probability F(x_2,y_2) - F(x_1,y_2) - F(x_2,y_1) + F(x_1,y_1) can be negative, so it’s invalid.

Summary








































Joint PMFJoint CDFExists forDiscrete (X,Y) onlyAll (X,Y)Definitionp(x,y) = P(X=x, Y=y)F(x,y) = P(X \leq x, Y \leq y)Recover probabilitiesSum over regionRectangle formulaRecover marginalsSum over other variableSend other variable to +\inftyIndependencep_{X,Y} = p_X p_YF_{X,Y} = F_X F_YFrom the otherp = \Delta_x \Delta_y F (difference operator)F(x,y) = \sum_{x_i \leq x}\sum_{y_j \leq y} p(x_i,y_j)

01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.title: 03.Marginal PMF
01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.content:
The whole point of the marginal distribution is to forget. You have a joint law on (X, Y) and you want to think about just one of them — so you sum the other out of existence.


The Setup
Say we have two discrete r.v.’s X and Y defined on the same probability space. Their joint PMF is
p_{X,Y}(x,y) = P(X = x,, Y = y).
Everything about the pair lives here. But sometimes I only care about X alone — not because Y is unimportant, but because I want to study X unconditionally. To recover the law of X alone, I need to marginalize out Y.

Definition
\boxed{p_X(x) = P(X = x) = \sum_{y} p_{X,Y}(x,y)}
where the sum ranges over all values y in the support of Y.
Symmetrically,
p_Y(y) = \sum_{x} p_{X,Y}(x,y).
These are called the marginal PMFs of X and Y respectively.

Proof That It’s Actually a PMF
This always trips me up on first glance — let me make sure it checks out.
Claim: p_X defined above is a valid PMF.
Nonnegativity: For any fixed x, p_{X,Y}(x,y) \geq 0 for all y, so a sum of them is \geq 0. ✓
Sums to 1:
\sum_x p_X(x) = \sum_x \sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y) = \sum_{x,y} p_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1.
The interchange of the double sum is valid since all terms are nonneg (Tonelli, or just finite support in the discrete case). ✓
That’s it. The marginal is a genuine PMF.

The “Summing Over Rows/Columns” Picture
If I write the joint PMF as a table with x indexing rows and y indexing columns, then:

p_X(x) = the row sum for row x
p_Y(y) = the column sum for column y

This is literally why they’re called marginal — historically, you’d write the row totals in the margin of the table. The name is a relic of hand computation and I find it kind of charming.

Worked Example: Dice Sum
Let X =  first die, Y =  second die, both fair, independent. The joint PMF is
p_{X,Y}(i,j) = \frac{1}{36}, \quad i,j \in {1,\ldots,6}.
The marginal:
p_X(i) = \sum_{j=1}^{6} \frac{1}{36} = \frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}.
Unsurprising — marginalization recovers the Uniform{1,\ldots,6} distribution, as it should.
Now let S = X + Y and D = X - Y. These are not independent — knowing S tells me something about D. The joint PMF of (S,D) is more interesting. Its marginal on S gives the distribution of the sum of two dice:
p_S(k) = \frac{6 - |k - 7|}{36}, \quad k \in {2,\ldots,12}.
(Derivation: count the number of (i,j) pairs with i + j = k. For k \leq 7 there are k-1 such pairs; for k > 7 there are 13 - k.)

The Law of Total Probability Connection
Notice:
p_X(x) = \sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y) = \sum_y P(X = x \mid Y = y), P(Y = y) = \sum_y p_{X|Y}(x|y), p_Y(y).
This is just LOTP in disguise, conditioning on the partition {Y = y}.
Mnemonic I keep coming back to: marginalization = LOTP on the joint.

What Marginals Don’t Tell You
The marginals do not determine the joint. This is one of the most important things to internalize early.
Example. Let (X,Y) be uniform on {(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)}. Then X \sim \text{Bern}(1/2) and Y \sim \text{Bern}(1/2).
But now let (X', Y') be such that X' \sim \text{Bern}(1/2) and Y' = X' always. Then Y' \sim \text{Bern}(1/2) too. But the joints are completely different: the first puts mass 1/4 on each of the four corners; the second puts mass 1/2 on (0,0) and 1/2 on (1,1).
Same marginals. Totally different dependence structure.
This is why joint distributions exist in the first place — marginals lose dependence information. Copulas (later) are precisely the machinery for isolating what the joint tells you beyond the marginals.

Independence Criterion
(X, Y) are independent iff
p_{X,Y}(x,y) = p_X(x), p_Y(y) \quad \text{for all } (x,y).
In words: the joint factors into the product of the marginals. This is the definition.
A useful sanity check: if I compute the marginals and their product doesn’t give me back the joint everywhere, I know they’re dependent. If it does, they’re independent.

Extension to More Variables
For a random vector (X_1, \ldots, X_n) with joint PMF p_{X_1,\ldots,X_n}, the marginal of (X_1, \ldots, X_k) for k < n is
p_{X_1,\ldots,X_k}(x_1,\ldots,x_k) = \sum_{x_{k+1}} \cdots \sum_{x_n} p_{X_1,\ldots,X_n}(x_1,\ldots,x_n).
Example — Multinomial. If (X_1,\ldots,X_k) \sim \text{Mult}_k(n, \mathbf{p}), then the marginal of X_i alone is \text{Bin}(n, p_i). The proof is just marginalization: summing out the other components collapses the multinomial to a binomial. I spent longer convincing myself of this than I should have — eventually I just wrote out the generating function and it fell out immediately.

Common Mistake to Avoid
When computing p_X(x), the sum is over all possible values of Y, not just the values that appear “next to” x in some table. If the support of Y depends on x (a non-rectangular support), be careful:
Example. (X, Y) uniform on {(x,y) : 1 \leq x \leq y \leq 3,, x,y \in \mathbb{Z}}, which has 6 points: (1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,2),(2,3),(3,3).
Then p_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1/6 on those six points and 0 elsewhere. To get p_X(1):
p_X(1) = p_{X,Y}(1,1) + p_{X,Y}(1,2) + p_{X,Y}(1,3) = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}.
The support of Y given X = 1 is {1,2,3}, but given X = 3 it’s just {3}. This kind of asymmetry makes things like E[Y|X] interesting — worth revisiting in Conditional Expectation.

01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.title: 04.Conditional PDF
01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.content:
The conditional PDF is where the continuous theory gets genuinely subtle. In the discrete case, conditioning on X = x is unambiguous — it’s an event with positive probability. In the continuous case, P(X = x) = 0 for every x, so you can’t condition the usual way. The definition that saves us is elegant, but you should understand why it’s forced on us, not just accept it as a decree.


The Problem with Continuous Conditioning
Recall: for discrete RVs, the conditional PMF is just Bayes’ rule applied to point events:
p_{Y|X}(y \mid x) = \frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_X(x)}
This works because P(X = x) = p_X(x) > 0 (assuming x is in the support).
For continuous RVs, P(X = x) = 0 for every x. So writing
P(Y \leq y \mid X = x) = \frac{P(Y \leq y,; X = x)}{P(X = x)} = \frac{0}{0}
is meaningless. We need a different approach.

The Right Definition, Derived
The idea: replace the zero-probability event {X = x} with a thin strip {x < X \leq x + \varepsilon}, which has positive probability, do ordinary conditioning there, and take \varepsilon \to 0.
For fixed y, define the conditional CDF we want as:
P(Y \leq y \mid X = x) := \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} P(Y \leq y \mid x < X \leq x + \varepsilon)
Expanding the right side:
P(Y \leq y \mid x < X \leq x + \varepsilon) = \frac{P(Y \leq y,; x < X \leq x + \varepsilon)}{P(x < X \leq x + \varepsilon)}
Numerator: P(Y \leq y,; x < X \leq x+\varepsilon) = \int_x^{x+\varepsilon} \int_{-\infty}^y f_{X,Y}(s,t), dt, ds \approx \varepsilon \int_{-\infty}^y f_{X,Y}(x,t), dt
Denominator: P(x < X \leq x + \varepsilon) = \int_x^{x+\varepsilon} f_X(s), ds \approx \varepsilon, f_X(x)
Dividing and taking \varepsilon \to 0:
P(Y \leq y \mid X = x) = \frac{\int_{-\infty}^y f_{X,Y}(x,t), dt}{f_X(x)}
Differentiating in y gives the conditional density:
\boxed{f_{Y|X}(y \mid x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}}
defined for all x with f_X(x) > 0.

The formula looks identical to the discrete case, with densities in place of PMFs. That’s not a coincidence — the derivation above shows it’s the natural limit of ordinary conditioning. The notation hides the limiting argument that justifies it.


Verification: It’s a Valid PDF
For each fixed x with f_X(x) > 0, the function y \mapsto f_{Y|X}(y \mid x) is a genuine PDF:
Non-negativity: f_{X,Y}(x,y) \geq 0 and f_X(x) > 0, so f_{Y|X}(y \mid x) \geq 0. ✓
Normalisation: \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{Y|X}(y \mid x), dy = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}, dy = \frac{1}{f_X(x)} \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy = \frac{f_X(x)}{f_X(x)} = 1 \checkmark

The Factorisation Identity
Rearranging the definition gives the chain rule for densities:
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_{Y|X}(y \mid x), f_X(x) = f_{X|Y}(x \mid y), f_Y(y)
This is the continuous analogue of P(A \cap B) = P(A|B)P(B). Both factorisations are valid; choosing which to use depends on what’s natural to specify first.
Bayes’ rule for densities falls out immediately by equating the two factorisations:
f_{X|Y}(x \mid y) = \frac{f_{Y|X}(y \mid x), f_X(x)}{f_Y(y)}
This is exactly 09.Laplace’s Rule of Succession’s mechanism, now stated for general densities. The denominator f_Y(y) = \int f_{Y|X}(y|x) f_X(x), dx is the normalising constant (total probability).

Conditional Expectation from the Conditional PDF
Given the conditional PDF, the conditional expectation is just the expected value under that density:
\mathbb{E}[g(Y) \mid X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty g(y), f_{Y|X}(y \mid x), dy
As x varies, this is a function of x. Setting h(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x], we get the random variable \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] = h(X).
Adam’s Law then says \mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}[h(X)], which in integral form is:
\mathbb{E}[Y] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x], f_X(x), dx = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty y, f_{Y|X}(y|x), f_X(x), dy, dx
which reduces to \int\int y, f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy, dx = \mathbb{E}[Y] by Fubini. Consistent. ✓

Worked Examples
Example 1: Uniform on a Triangle
Let (X, Y) be uniform on the triangle \mathcal{T} = {(x,y) : 0 < x < 1,; 0 < y < x}.
The area of \mathcal{T} is \frac{1}{2}, so f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 2 on \mathcal{T}.
Marginal of X: f_X(x) = \int_0^x 2, dy = 2x, \quad 0 < x < 1
Conditional PDF of Y given X = x: f_{Y|X}(y \mid x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)} = \frac{2}{2x} = \frac{1}{x}, \quad 0 < y < x
So Y \mid X = x \sim \text{Uniform}(0, x). This makes sense: given the “width” of the triangle at height x, the y-value is uniform over [0,x].
Conditional mean: \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x] = x/2, so \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] = X/2.
Marginal mean via Adam’s law: \mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}[X/2] = \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{3}
(using \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^1 x \cdot 2x, dx = 2/3 since X \sim \text{Beta}(2,1).)

Example 2: Exponential Conditioning
Let X \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda) and Y \mid X = x \sim \text{Uniform}(0, x).
Joint PDF: f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_{Y|X}(y|x), f_X(x) = \frac{1}{x} \cdot \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \quad 0 < y < x
Marginal of Y: integrate out x over {x > y}: f_Y(y) = \int_y^\infty \frac{\lambda e^{-\lambda x}}{x}, dx
This integral doesn’t have a closed form in elementary functions (it involves the exponential integral \text{Ei}). That’s fine — the marginal of Y need not be a standard distribution.
Conditional mean of Y: \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x] = \frac{x}{2}
Marginal mean via Adam’s law: \mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}!\left[\frac{X}{2}\right] = \frac{1}{2\lambda}
using \mathbb{E}[X] = 1/\lambda.

Notice: we computed \mathbb{E}[Y] without ever writing down f_Y(y). Adam’s law lets you short-circuit the marginalisation entirely. This is one of the most useful computational tricks in the subject.


Example 3: Recovering a Known Distribution
Let f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \lambda^2 e^{-\lambda y} for 0 < x < y.
Marginal of X: f_X(x) = \int_x^\infty \lambda^2 e^{-\lambda y}, dy = \lambda^2 \cdot \frac{e^{-\lambda x}}{\lambda} = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}
So X \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda).
Conditional PDF of Y given X = x: f_{Y|X}(y \mid x) = \frac{\lambda^2 e^{-\lambda y}}{\lambda e^{-\lambda x}} = \lambda e^{-\lambda(y-x)}, \quad y > x
This is \text{Expo}(\lambda) shifted to start at x: Y \mid X = x \sim x + \text{Expo}(\lambda).
Interpretation: Y is the time of the second arrival in a Poisson process, and X is the first. Given the first arrival at time x, the second arrival is x plus an independent \text{Expo}(\lambda) waiting time — exactly the memoryless property.

The Continuous Bayes’ Rule in Practice
The factorisation f_{X|Y}(x|y) \propto f_{Y|X}(y|x), f_X(x) is the engine of Bayesian inference:

f_X(x) is the prior on parameter x.
f_{Y|X}(y|x) is the likelihood of data y given parameter x.
f_{X|Y}(x|y) is the posterior — what we believe about x after seeing y.

The denominator f_Y(y) = \int f_{Y|X}(y|x), f_X(x), dx is the marginal likelihood (or evidence), which is just the normalising constant ensuring the posterior integrates to 1.
In the Beta-Binomial model from 09.Laplace’s Rule of Succession], x = p plays the role of the parameter, y = s (observed successes) is the data, and the prior f_X = \text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta) is conjugate to the Binomial likelihood — making the posterior analytically tractable.

Conditional PDF vs Conditional Probability of an Event
A point of notation that causes confusion: f_{Y|X}(y|x) is a density, not a probability. To get a probability, integrate:
P(Y \in B \mid X = x) = \int_B f_{Y|X}(y \mid x), dy
In particular, f_{Y|X}(y|x) can exceed 1 — it’s a density, not a probability mass. What must integrate to 1 over y is the conditional density, not its pointwise values.

Independence Restated
X and Y are independent if and only if the conditional PDF equals the marginal:
f_{Y|X}(y \mid x) = f_Y(y) \quad \text{for all } x, y
This says: conditioning on X = x gives you no information about Y — the distribution of Y is the same regardless of what X is. Formally:
f_{Y|X}(y|x) = f_Y(y) \iff \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)} = f_Y(y) \iff f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)
which is exactly the definition of independence. Full circle. ✓

Pitfalls
1. The conditioning value must be in the support.
f_{Y|X}(y \mid x) is only defined where f_X(x) > 0. Conditioning on a value outside the support of X is undefined.
2. Non-product supports break independence even when the formula “looks” factored.
If f_{X,Y}(x,y) = c on {0 < x < y < 1}, the density is constant — but the support is triangular, not a product set. The conditional f_{Y|X}(y|x) = 1/(1-x) on (x,1) depends on x, confirming dependence.
3. Conditional densities are defined pointwise in x, but the conditional expectation \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] is defined up to a.e. equivalence.
At a single point x with f_X(x) = 0, the conditional density is undefined. This rarely matters in calculations but matters in the measure-theoretic treatment (where \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] is defined as a Radon-Nikodym derivative — see Billingsley if you want the full story).

Summary of Key Formulas
f_{Y|X}(y \mid x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_{Y|X}(y \mid x), f_X(x)
f_{X|Y}(x \mid y) = \frac{f_{Y|X}(y \mid x), f_X(x)}{\int f_{Y|X}(y \mid x'), f_X(x'), dx'} \quad \text{(Bayes)}
\mathbb{E}[g(Y) \mid X = x] = \int g(y), f_{Y|X}(y \mid x), dy
\mathbb{E}[Y] = \int \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x], f_X(x), dx \quad \text{(Adam's law)}

01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.title: 05.Joint PDF
01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.content:
The joint PDF is not a probability — it’s a density. The probability lives in the volume under the surface, and that’s everything. Internalize this and the rest follows.

Motivation
In the discrete case, the joint PMF assigns actual probabilities to individual points: P(X = x, Y = y). In the continuous case, individual points have probability zero. The right object is instead a function f_{X,Y} such that probabilities of regions are computed by integrating f_{X,Y} over those regions.
The passage from discrete to continuous is just: sums become integrals, PMF becomes PDF. The conceptual structure is identical.

Definition
A pair of continuous random variables (X, Y) has joint PDF f_{X,Y} : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R} if for every (reasonable) region A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2,
P\bigl((X,Y) \in A\bigr) = \iint_A f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy.
In particular, for a rectangle:
P(a \leq X \leq b,; c \leq Y \leq d) = \int_a^b \int_c^d f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy, dx.

Valid Joint PDF: The Two Conditions
f_{X,Y} is a valid joint PDF if and only if:


Nonnegativity: f_{X,Y}(x,y) \geq 0 for all (x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2.


Normalisation: \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy = 1.


That’s it. The “probability” of any event is then recovered by integrating over the corresponding region. Note that f_{X,Y}(x,y) itself can exceed 1 — it’s a density, not a probability. What matters is that it integrates to 1.

Marginal PDFs
Exactly parallel to the discrete case, marginalizing means integrating out the unwanted variable:
\boxed{f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy}
f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx.
The proof that f_X is a valid PDF: nonnegativity is clear, and
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x), dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy, dx = 1
by Fubini (all terms nonneg, so interchange is justified). Exactly the same argument as in the discrete case, just with Fubini instead of Tonelli.

Independence
(X,Y) are independent (as continuous r.v.’s) iff
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x), f_Y(y) \quad \text{for all } (x,y).
Practical check: can you write f_{X,Y}(x,y) = g(x) \cdot h(y) for some functions g,h, and the support is a rectangle (does not depend on x or y jointly)? If yes, X \perp Y, and then g and h are automatically proportional to f_X and f_Y.
The support condition is easy to forget. If the support is a triangle like {0 < x < y < 1}, the joint does not factor no matter what f looks like — knowing Y tells you something about the range of X, so they cannot be independent.

Worked Example 1: Uniform on the Unit Square
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1, \quad 0 < x < 1,; 0 < y < 1.
Marginals:
f_X(x) = \int_0^1 1, dy = 1, \quad 0 < x < 1.
So X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1), and by symmetry Y \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1).
Independence: f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1 = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y), and the support is the square (rectangular). So X \perp Y. ✓

Worked Example 2: Uniform on the Triangle
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 2, \quad 0 < x < y < 1.
(The factor of 2 ensures normalisation: the triangle has area 1/2, so 2 \cdot 1/2 = 1.)
Marginals: For 0 < x < 1:
f_X(x) = \int_x^1 2, dy = 2(1-x).
For 0 < y < 1:
f_Y(y) = \int_0^y 2, dx = 2y.
Check: \int_0^1 2(1-x),dx = 2[x - x^2/2]_0^1 = 1. ✓
Independence? f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y) = 4y(1-x) \neq 2 = f_{X,Y}(x,y) in general. Also the support is a triangle, not a rectangle. So X and Y are dependent.
Intuition: If I tell you Y = 0.1, then X must be less than 0.1. Knowing Y constrains X. Of course they’re dependent.

Worked Example 3: Exponential Joint
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = e^{-x-y}, \quad x > 0,; y > 0.
This factors immediately: e^{-x-y} = e^{-x} \cdot e^{-y}, and the support is the first quadrant (a rectangle). So X \sim \text{Expo}(1), Y \sim \text{Expo}(1), and X \perp Y. No integration needed — the factorisation is the proof.

Computing Probabilities: The Region Matters
Example. With (X,Y) uniform on [0,1]^2, find P(X + Y \leq 1).
The region is a right triangle with vertices (0,0),(1,0),(0,1), area 1/2.
P(X+Y \leq 1) = \int_0^1 \int_0^{1-x} 1, dy, dx = \int_0^1 (1-x), dx = \frac{1}{2}.
Or just: area of region times constant density = 1/2 \cdot 1 = 1/2. Always draw the region first.
Example. With (X,Y) uniform on the triangle {0 < x < y < 1}, find P(Y - X > 1/2).
P(Y - X > 1/2) = \int_0^{1/2}\int_{x+1/2}^{1} 2, dy, dx = \int_0^{1/2} 2!\left(\tfrac{1}{2} - x\right)dx = \bigl[x - x^2\bigr]_0^{1/2} = \frac{1}{4}.

The Joint CDF
F_{X,Y}(x,y) = P(X \leq x, Y \leq y) = \int_{-\infty}^x \int_{-\infty}^y f_{X,Y}(s,t), dt, ds.
Recovering the PDF: if F_{X,Y} is sufficiently smooth,
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x, \partial y} F_{X,Y}(x,y).
I rarely need to go through the CDF directly — setting up the double integral over the region is usually more transparent. But the mixed partial formula is worth knowing cold.

Non-Rectangular Supports: The Dangerous Case
When the support of (X,Y) is not a rectangle, the limits of integration in the marginals depend on the other variable, and the order of integration matters.
General strategy: draw the support region. For f_X(x): fix x, ask “what values can y take?” → those are the inner limits. Then integrate x over its full marginal range.
Example. f_{X,Y}(x,y) = c \cdot x on {0 < x < 1, 0 < y < x}.
Find c:
1 = \int_0^1 \int_0^x cx, dy, dx = \int_0^1 cx^2, dx = \frac{c}{3} \implies c = 3.
Marginal of X:
f_X(x) = \int_0^x 3x, dy = 3x^2, \quad 0 < x < 1. \qquad [\text{Beta}(3,1)]
Marginal of Y: Fix y \in (0,1); x ranges from y to 1 (since we need x > y):
f_Y(y) = \int_y^1 3x, dx = \frac{3}{2}(1-y^2), \quad 0 < y < 1.
The critical step: when switching to f_Y, the lower limit of the x-integral is y, not 0. Getting this wrong is the single most common mistake on these problems.

A Note on Existence
Not every pair of random variables admits a joint PDF. It is possible for both marginals to be continuous yet the joint to be singular. The canonical example: X \sim N(0,1) and Y = X. Then (X,Y) is concentrated on the line y = x in \mathbb{R}^2, which has 2D Lebesgue measure zero, so no joint density exists. The formal statement is that a joint PDF exists iff the joint distribution is absolutely continuous with respect to 2D Lebesgue measure.
The Bivariate Normal is the canonical well-behaved example:
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_X\sigma_Y\sqrt{1-\rho^2}} \exp!\left(-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}\left[\frac{(x-\mu_X)^2}{\sigma_X^2} - \frac{2\rho(x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y} + \frac{(y-\mu_Y)^2}{\sigma_Y^2}\right]\right).
Takeaway for now: both marginals are normal, and X \perp Y \iff \rho = 0. The bivariate normal is the unique distribution where uncorrelated implies independent — this is special to the Gaussian family and fails in general.

01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.title: 06.Marginal PDF
01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.content:
Marginalizing a joint PDF is the continuous act of forgetting. You integrate out the variable you don’t care about, and what’s left is the unconditional law of the one you do. The logic is identical to the discrete case — sums just became integrals.

Let (X, Y) have joint PDF f_{X,Y}. The marginal PDF of X is
\boxed{f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy,}
and symmetrically the marginal PDF of Y is
f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx.
This is the continuous analogue of summing over rows (or columns) in the discrete joint PMF table. The name marginal is a literal relic — you’d write the row totals in the margin of a hand-computed table.

Proof That It’s a Valid PDF
Claim: f_X defined above is a valid PDF.
Nonnegativity: For each fixed x, f_{X,Y}(x,y) \geq 0 for all y, so the integral is \geq 0. ✓
Normalisation:
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x), dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy, dx = 1.
The interchange of the two integrals is justified by Tonelli’s theorem: since f_{X,Y} \geq 0, we can swap the order of integration freely, and the double integral equals 1 by normalisation of the joint PDF. ✓
(Tonelli applies here — not Fubini — because Tonelli only requires nonnegativity, whereas Fubini requires absolute integrability. For PDFs nonnegativity is always given, so Tonelli is the right citation. In practice everyone just swaps and doesn’t mention it, but I want to know why I’m allowed to.)

The LOTP Connection
The marginal PDF is the continuous version of the Law of Total Probability. Using the definition of the conditional PDF:
f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y), f_Y(y), dy.
This is LOTP in density form: to get the unconditional density of X at x, average the conditional density f_{X|Y}(x|y) over all possible values of Y, weighted by f_Y.
Mnemonic: marginalization = LOTP on the joint, regardless of discrete or continuous.

Setting Up the Limits: The Only Hard Part
Computing a marginal PDF is conceptually trivial — the entire difficulty is setting the limits of integration correctly when the support is not a rectangle.
The procedure, always:

Draw the support of (X,Y) in the xy-plane.
To compute f_X(x): fix x at an arbitrary value in its marginal range. Draw the vertical slice x = \text{const} through the support. The endpoints of that slice are the limits of the inner integral over y.
To compute f_Y(y): fix y and draw the horizontal slice. The endpoints give the limits of the inner integral over x.

The limits depend on which variable is the outer one — this is the single step where errors happen.

Worked Example 1: Rectangular Support (Easy)
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = e^{-x-y}, \quad x > 0,; y > 0.
Support is the first quadrant — a rectangle (in the sense that the support of Y does not depend on x, and vice versa).
f_X(x) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-x-y}, dy = e^{-x} \int_0^{\infty} e^{-y}, dy = e^{-x} \cdot 1 = e^{-x}, \quad x > 0.
So X \sim \text{Expo}(1). By symmetry Y \sim \text{Expo}(1).
No geometric thinking needed here — rectangular support means the limits are constants.

Worked Example 2: Triangular Support (The Real Test)
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 2, \quad 0 < x < y < 1.
The support is the triangle {(x,y) : 0 < x < y < 1} — above the diagonal y = x in the unit square.
Marginal of X: Fix x \in (0,1). The vertical slice x = \text{const} hits the support for y \in (x, 1) — y must be above x (from the constraint x < y) and below 1.
f_X(x) = \int_x^1 2, dy = 2(1-x), \quad 0 < x < 1.
Marginal of Y: Fix y \in (0,1). The horizontal slice y = \text{const} hits the support for x \in (0, y) — x must be positive and below y.
f_Y(y) = \int_0^y 2, dx = 2y, \quad 0 < y < 1.
Verification:
\int_0^1 2(1-x), dx = 2!\left[x - \frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^1 = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 1. \checkmark
\int_0^1 2y, dy = \left[y^2\right]_0^1 = 1. \checkmark
Named distributions: f_X(x) = 2(1-x) is \text{Beta}(1,2). f_Y(y) = 2y is \text{Beta}(2,1). Both are Beta distributions, which makes sense — the uniform distribution on the ordered simplex {0 < x < y < 1} has Beta marginals.

Worked Example 3: Support Boundary Depending on x
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 3x, \quad 0 < y < x < 1.
(Same support as before but with x and y swapped — now y < x, so the support is the triangle below the diagonal.)
Verify normalisation first: \int_0^1 \int_0^x 3x, dy, dx = \int_0^1 3x^2, dx = 1. ✓
Marginal of X: Fix x \in (0,1); y ranges from 0 to x.
f_X(x) = \int_0^x 3x, dy = 3x^2, \quad 0 < x < 1. \qquad [\text{Beta}(3,1)]
Marginal of Y: Fix y \in (0,1); x ranges from y to 1 (we need x > y).
f_Y(y) = \int_y^1 3x, dx = 3 \cdot \frac{1 - y^2}{2} = \frac{3}{2}(1-y^2), \quad 0 < y < 1.
The trap: when computing f_Y, the lower limit of the x-integral is y, not 0. The natural instinct is to write \int_0^1, but that would include the region above the diagonal where the density is zero. Drawing the support and slicing horizontally makes the correct limits obvious.

Worked Example 4: A Genuinely Interesting One
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{1}{\pi}, \quad x^2 + y^2 < 1.
(X,Y) is uniform on the unit disk. The normalising constant 1/\pi is correct since the disk has area \pi.
Marginal of X: Fix x \in (-1,1). The vertical slice at x intersects the disk for y \in (-\sqrt{1-x^2},, \sqrt{1-x^2}).
f_X(x) = \int_{-\sqrt{1-x^2}}^{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \frac{1}{\pi}, dy = \frac{2\sqrt{1-x^2}}{\pi}, \quad -1 < x < 1.
This is the arcsine-adjacent distribution — or more precisely, \frac{2}{\pi}\sqrt{1-x^2}, which is the PDF of \cos(\Theta) where \Theta \sim \text{Uniform}(0,\pi). It’s also related to the semicircle law in random matrix theory.
By symmetry f_Y(y) = \frac{2\sqrt{1-y^2}}{\pi}.
Are X and Y independent? No: the support is a disk, not a rectangle. Knowing |X| is close to 1 forces Y \approx 0. The marginals being identical doesn’t make them independent.

What Marginals Don’t Carry: Dependence
This deserves repeating in the continuous setting.
The marginal PDFs f_X and f_Y together do not determine the joint f_{X,Y}. Two pairs of random variables can have identical marginals but completely different dependence structures.
Example. Let f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1 on the unit square (independent uniforms). Now let U = V = W where W \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1), so f_{U,V} is concentrated on the diagonal and doesn’t even have a density. Both have \text{Uniform}(0,1) marginals. The joints are as different as they can be.
This is precisely the problem that copulas solve: they separate the marginal structure from the dependence structure. Sklar’s theorem says every joint distribution can be written as a copula applied to its marginals. Worth a dedicated note eventually.

The Marginal CDF from the Joint CDF
If I have the joint CDF F_{X,Y}(x,y) = P(X \leq x, Y \leq y), the marginal CDFs are recovered by taking limits:
F_X(x) = P(X \leq x) = P(X \leq x, Y < \infty) = \lim_{y \to \infty} F_{X,Y}(x,y).
F_Y(y) = \lim_{x \to \infty} F_{X,Y}(x,y).
Then differentiating gives the marginal PDFs in the usual way. I almost never use this route — differentiating F_{X,Y} and then taking limits is more painful than just integrating f_{X,Y} directly — but it’s good to know the connection.

Extension to n Variables
For a random vector (X_1, \ldots, X_n) with joint density f_{X_1,\ldots,X_n}, the marginal density of (X_1, \ldots, X_k) for k < n is
f_{X_1,\ldots,X_k}(x_1,\ldots,x_k) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \cdots \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X_1,\ldots,X_n}(x_1,\ldots,x_n), dx_{k+1} \cdots dx_n.
Example — Multivariate Normal. If (X_1,\ldots,X_n) \sim N(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma), then any marginal (X_1,\ldots,X_k) is also multivariate normal with the corresponding subvector of \boldsymbol{\mu} and the top-left k \times k submatrix of \Sigma. This is one of the defining nice properties of the multivariate normal — marginals stay in the same family.

01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.title: 07.Fubini's Theorem
01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.content:
Fubini is the theorem that lets you stop worrying about order. The moment you swap dx,dy to dy,dx without thinking, you’re invoking it. The point of this note is to know exactly when you’re allowed to, and what goes wrong when you’re not.

The Core Question
Given a double integral
\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x,y), dx, dy,
when can I evaluate it as an iterated integral, and when does the order of integration not matter?
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y), dy, dx \stackrel{?}{=} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y), dx, dy.
The answer is: always, if f \geq 0 (Tonelli); and if f is integrable (Fubini). These are different theorems with different hypotheses, and conflating them is the source of every “illegal swap” in probability.

Tonelli’s Theorem
Theorem (Tonelli). Let f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to [0, \infty] be measurable. Then:
\int!!\int f(x,y), d(x,y) = \int!\left(\int f(x,y), dy\right) dx = \int!\left(\int f(x,y), dx\right) dy.
All three expressions are equal (possibly +\infty), and the inner integrals are measurable functions of the outer variable.
Hypotheses: f \geq 0 and measurable. That’s it. No finiteness required.
What it gives: You can freely interchange the order of integration for nonneg functions. The common value might be +\infty, which is allowed.
Why this is the right theorem for PDFs. Joint PDFs are nonneg by definition. So every marginalisation step — every \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy — is justified by Tonelli, not Fubini. This is why the 06.Marginal PDF proof works without any integrability assumption beyond what the PDF already satisfies.

Fubini’s Theorem
Theorem (Fubini). Let f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R} be measurable. Suppose
\int!!\int |f(x,y)|, d(x,y) < \infty,
i.e., f is integrable (equivalently, \int!\int f^+, d(x,y) < \infty and \int!\int f^-, d(x,y) < \infty separately). Then:

For a.e. x, the function y \mapsto f(x,y) is integrable.
The function x \mapsto \int f(x,y), dy is integrable.
The iterated integrals equal the double integral:

\int!!\int f(x,y), d(x,y) = \int!\left(\int f(x,y), dy\right) dx = \int!\left(\int f(x,y), dx\right) dy.
Hypotheses: f integrable — meaning \int!\int |f| < \infty.
What it gives: Order of integration is interchangeable for integrable functions (which may change sign).
The key difference from Tonelli: Fubini requires absolute integrability. If f takes both positive and negative values and \int!\int |f| = \infty, the iterated integrals may exist but give different values — the double integral doesn’t exist in the Lebesgue sense.

The Unified Statement
In practice, the two theorems are often stated together as:

Fubini-Tonelli. If either (a) f \geq 0, or (b) \int!\int |f| < \infty, then all iterated integrals and the double integral coincide.

When in doubt about which applies: if f \geq 0, cite Tonelli. If f changes sign, first use Tonelli on |f| to check \int!\int|f| < \infty, then apply Fubini.

The Counterexample: Why Fubini Can Fail
This is the example that justifies the hypotheses. Let
f(x,y) = \frac{x^2 - y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}, \quad (x,y) \neq (0,0).
Iterated integral in one order:
\int_0^1!\left(\int_0^1 \frac{x^2-y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}, dy\right) dx.
The inner integral \int_0^1 \frac{x^2-y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}, dy = \left[\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{x^2+1}.
So the outer integral is \int_0^1 \frac{1}{x^2+1}, dx = \arctan(1) - \arctan(0) = \frac{\pi}{4}.
Iterated integral in the other order:
By antisymmetry (f(x,y) = -f(y,x)), swapping gives -\pi/4.
Conclusion: \frac{\pi}{4} \neq -\frac{\pi}{4}. The two iterated integrals disagree.
Why did this happen? Because \int_0^1!\int_0^1 |f(x,y)|, dx, dy = \infty — f is not integrable on [0,1]^2. Fubini’s hypothesis fails, and the conclusion fails too.
Moral: Never swap integration order for a sign-changing function without first verifying absolute integrability.

How This Appears in Probability
Marginalisation
f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy.
Tonelli applies (PDFs are nonneg). The interchange in the normalisation proof:
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x), dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy, dx \stackrel{\text{Tonelli}}{=} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy = 1.
Expected Value of a Function
E[g(X,Y)] = \int!!\int g(x,y), f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy.
If g \geq 0: Tonelli. If g changes sign: need E[|g(X,Y)|] < \infty before swapping.
This is why E[X] exists requires E[|X|] < \infty — the same logic one dimension down.
Independence and Product Expectations
If X \perp Y and g, h are measurable:
E[g(X)h(Y)] = \int!!\int g(x)h(y), f_X(x), f_Y(y), dx, dy = \int g(x), f_X(x), dx \int h(y), f_Y(y), dy = E[g(X)], E[h(Y)].
The factorisation of the double integral into a product requires swapping, which requires Fubini (if g \cdot h changes sign). If g, h \geq 0, Tonelli suffices.
Convolutions
If X \perp Y and Z = X + Y:
f_Z(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(z-y), f_Y(y), dy.
This is derived by marginalising the joint of (Z,Y), which involves swapping the order of integration. Tonelli applies (all factors are nonneg PDFs).
Moment Generating Functions
M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{tx} f_X(x), dx.
When exchanging expectation and differentiation: \frac{d}{dt} M_X(t) = E[X e^{tX}]. Justifying the swap of \frac{d}{dt} and \int uses the dominated convergence theorem or Fubini (depending on how you set it up). For t in the interior of the MGF’s domain, this is fine.

The Discrete Analogue
For double sums over nonneg terms (i.e., PMFs):
\sum_x \sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y) = \sum_y \sum_x p_{X,Y}(x,y).
This is Tonelli for sums — also called the “nonneg interchange” or just “obvious by absolute convergence.” The same counterexample logic applies: for sums of sign-changing terms, you need absolute convergence (\sum_x \sum_y |a_{xy}| < \infty) to interchange freely. The discrete analogue of the Fubini counterexample is a conditionally convergent double series whose iterated sums disagree.

Practical Decision Tree
When I want to swap \int dx, dy to \int dy, dx:
Is the integrand f ≥ 0 everywhere?
    YES → Tonelli applies. Swap freely. (Citation: Tonelli)
    NO  → Compute ∬|f| dx dy (use Tonelli on |f|, which is nonneg)
              Is ∬|f| < ∞?
                  YES → Fubini applies. Swap freely. (Citation: Fubini)
                  NO  → DO NOT SWAP. The iterated integrals may disagree.

In probability: almost everything uses Tonelli (PDFs are nonneg). Fubini enters when computing E[g(X,Y)] for g that may be negative — e.g. covariance computations, characteristic functions (which are complex-valued), or when proving the tower property of conditional expectation rigorously.

A Subtlety: “Almost Everywhere”
Fubini’s conclusion says the inner integral exists “for a.e. x” — not necessarily for every x. The set of x where the inner integral is undefined has Lebesgue measure zero and doesn’t affect the outer integral. In practice this is never an issue for the integrands that arise in probability, but it’s worth knowing the theorem says a.e., not everywhere.

Statement in Measure-Theoretic Language (for Later)
The full theorem lives in the language of product measures. If (X, \mathcal{A}, \mu) and (Y, \mathcal{B}, \nu) are \sigma-finite measure spaces, then there exists a unique product measure \mu \otimes \nu on (X \times Y, \mathcal{A} \otimes \mathcal{B}) such that (\mu \otimes \nu)(A \times B) = \mu(A)\nu(B).
Tonelli: For f \geq 0 measurable,
\int_{X \times Y} f, d(\mu \otimes \nu) = \int_X \int_Y f(x,y), d\nu(y), d\mu(x) = \int_Y \int_X f(x,y), d\mu(x), d\nu(y).
Fubini: If additionally \int_{X \times Y} |f|, d(\mu \otimes \nu) < \infty, the same equalities hold for f (not just |f|).
The \sigma-finiteness condition on the measure spaces is necessary — the theorem can fail for non-\sigma-finite spaces. For probability, \mu = \nu =  Lebesgue measure on \mathbb{R}, which is \sigma-finite. Never a concern in this course.

01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.title: 08.Continuous Bayes' Rule and LOTP
01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.content:
The continuous forms aren’t new theorems — they’re the same theorems wearing different clothes. Once you see that the conditional PDF is just a ratio of joint to marginal, Bayes and LOTP fall out immediately. The hard part was always the discrete case; this is just calculus on top of it.

Setup: The Conditional PDF
Before writing down Bayes or LOTP, I need the conditional PDF. The definition is:
f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}, \quad \text{provided } f_Y(y) > 0.
This is defined pointwise in y and is a valid PDF in x for each fixed y:

Nonnegativity: clear.
Integrates to 1: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}, dx = \frac{1}{f_Y(y)} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx = \frac{f_Y(y)}{f_Y(y)} = 1.

Think of f_{X|Y}(x|y) as: given that Y has landed at the value y, what does the density of X look like? We’re slicing the joint surface at height y and renormalising.

The Continuous LOTP
The Law of Total Probability says: to get the marginal of X, average the conditional density of X given Y over all values of Y, weighted by f_Y.
\boxed{f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y), f_Y(y), dy}
Proof. Just substitute the definition f_{X|Y}(x|y) = f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_Y(y):
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y), f_Y(y), dy = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)} \cdot f_Y(y), dy = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy = f_X(x). \quad \square
The last step is exactly the definition of the marginal PDF. So LOTP is just marginalisation written in conditional language.
Compare with discrete LOTP:
P(X = x) = \sum_y P(X = x \mid Y = y), P(Y = y).
Structurally identical — sum replaced by integral, PMF replaced by PDF.

The Continuous Bayes’ Rule
Starting from the symmetry of the joint PDF:
f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y), f_Y(y) = f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x), f_X(x).
Solving for f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y):
\boxed{f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y) = \frac{f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x), f_X(x)}{f_Y(y)}}
Substituting LOTP for the denominator:
f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y) = \frac{f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x), f_X(x)}{\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x'), f_X(x'), dx'}
This is the form that actually gets used in Bayesian inference — the denominator is the normalising constant, often written just as C or “proportional to” signs swallow it entirely.
The Bayesian reading:

























ObjectRolef_X(x)Prior: what I believe about X before seeing dataf_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x)Likelihood: probability of observing Y = y if X = xf_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)Posterior: updated belief about X after observing Y = yf_Y(y)Marginal likelihood: normalising constant, often ignored
The formula says: posterior \propto likelihood \times prior.

Mixed Forms
This is where it gets interesting — and where the continuous Bayes’ rule reveals its full generality. X and Y don’t have to be the same type.
Case 1: Continuous X, Discrete Y
X is continuous (e.g. an unknown parameter), Y is discrete (e.g. a count or a coin flip outcome).
LOTP:
P(Y = k) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} P(Y = k \mid X = x), f_X(x), dx.
Bayes:
f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid Y = k) = \frac{P(Y = k \mid X = x), f_X(x)}{P(Y = k)}.
This is the fundamental setup for Bayesian parameter estimation: X = \theta is an unknown continuous parameter, Y is discrete data. The prior f_\theta is a PDF; the likelihood P(Y = k \mid \theta) is a PMF evaluated at the data.
Case 2: Discrete X, Continuous Y
X is discrete (e.g. a hypothesis label), Y is continuous (e.g. a measurement).
LOTP:
f_Y(y) = \sum_x f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x), P(X = x).
Bayes:
P(X = x \mid Y = y) = \frac{f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x), P(X = x)}{f_Y(y)}.
This is the setup for continuous-data classification or hypothesis testing with continuous observations: which discrete hypothesis X is most probable given continuous evidence Y?

Worked Example 1: Beta-Binomial (The Canonical Bayesian Example)
This is the example Blitzstein builds the whole Bayesian chapter around, and rightly so.
Setup. A coin has unknown bias p. I place a prior p \sim \text{Beta}(a, b) — a continuous distribution on (0,1) encoding my prior belief. I flip the coin n times and observe k heads. What is the posterior distribution of p?
Here X = p (continuous), Y = k (discrete).
Prior: f_p(p) = \frac{1}{B(a,b)} p^{a-1}(1-p)^{b-1}, p \in (0,1).
Likelihood: P(Y = k \mid p) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}.
Posterior via Bayes:
f_{p \mid Y}(p \mid k) = \frac{P(Y = k \mid p), f_p(p)}{P(Y = k)} \propto p^k(1-p)^{n-k} \cdot p^{a-1}(1-p)^{b-1} = p^{a+k-1}(1-p)^{b+n-k-1}.
I recognise this as the kernel of a \text{Beta}(a+k,, b+n-k) distribution. So:
p \mid Y = k ;\sim; \text{Beta}(a+k,, b+n-k).
What just happened: I never computed the normalising constant P(Y = k) explicitly. The proportionality argument — recognise the kernel, read off the distribution — is the standard technique in Bayesian inference. The Beta prior is conjugate to the Binomial likelihood precisely because this works out.
Intuition: The prior \text{Beta}(a,b) acts like we already observed a heads and b tails in pseudo-data. After seeing k real heads and n-k real tails, we update to \text{Beta}(a+k, b+n-k). Bayesian updating is just adding counts.

Worked Example 2: Normal-Normal (The Other Canonical Example)
Setup. An unknown signal \theta \sim N(\mu_0, \tau^2) (prior). I observe a noisy measurement X \mid \theta \sim N(\theta, \sigma^2). What is the posterior \theta \mid X = x?
Posterior via Bayes (dropping normalising constants):
f_{\theta \mid X}(\theta \mid x) \propto f_{X \mid \theta}(x \mid \theta), f_\theta(\theta)
\propto \exp!\left(-\frac{(x-\theta)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \cdot \exp!\left(-\frac{(\theta - \mu_0)^2}{2\tau^2}\right).
Combine the exponents — both are quadratic in \theta — and complete the square:
-\frac{(x-\theta)^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{(\theta-\mu_0)^2}{2\tau^2} = -\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\tau^2}\right)!\left(\theta - \mu_1\right)^2 + \text{const in } \theta,
where
\mu_1 = \frac{\frac{x}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu_0}{\tau^2}}{\frac{1}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\tau^2}}, \qquad \frac{1}{\tau_1^2} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\tau^2}.
The posterior is \theta \mid X = x \sim N(\mu_1, \tau_1^2). The Normal is conjugate to itself.
What to notice:

The posterior mean \mu_1 is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean \mu_0 and the observation x. Precision = 1/\text{variance}.
As \sigma^2 \to 0 (very clean measurement), \mu_1 \to x: the data overwhelms the prior.
As \tau^2 \to 0 (very strong prior), \mu_1 \to \mu_0: the prior overwhelms the data.
The posterior precision 1/\tau_1^2 = prior precision + data precision. Precisions add. This is the right way to think about combining information.


Worked Example 3: LOTP for a Marginal
Setup. X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1) and Y \mid X = x \sim \text{Uniform}(0, x). Find the marginal PDF of Y.
f_Y(y) = \int_0^1 f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x), f_X(x), dx.
For fixed y, the condition Y \mid X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,x) requires x > y (otherwise y is outside the support of the conditional). So:
f_Y(y) = \int_y^1 \frac{1}{x} \cdot 1, dx = \left[\ln x\right]_y^1 = -\ln y, \quad 0 < y < 1.
Check: \int_0^1 (-\ln y), dy = \left[-y\ln y + y\right]_0^1 = 1. ✓ (Using \lim_{y\to 0^+} y\ln y = 0.)
The marginal of Y is f_Y(y) = -\ln y — not a named distribution you’d recognise immediately, but it’s a valid PDF and the derivation via continuous LOTP is clean.

The Proportionality Shortcut
In practice, the denominator f_Y(y) in Bayes’ rule is a constant with respect to x (it’s an integral over x', so x has been integrated out). So:
f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y) \propto f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x), f_X(x)
where "\propto" means “proportional to, as a function of x.” The normalising constant is determined by the requirement that the posterior integrate to 1.
Workflow:

Write f_{Y|X}(y|x) \cdot f_X(x) and simplify, treating y as fixed.
Recognise the kernel — the functional form in x.
Read off the distribution; the normalising constant comes for free.

If you can’t recognise the kernel, you compute the integral explicitly. But recognising it is almost always faster and is the expected method in Stat 110.

Summary: All Four Forms at Once
Let X be the unknown, Y be the observed. Suppressing arguments for clarity:




















Y discreteY continuousX discreteP(X \mid Y) = \frac{P(Y \mid X),P(X)}{P(Y)}P(X \mid Y) = \frac{f_{Y\mid X},P(X)}{f_Y}X continuousf_{X\mid Y} = \frac{P(Y \mid X),f_X}{P(Y)}f_{X\mid Y} = \frac{f_{Y\mid X},f_X}{f_Y}
Every cell has the same structure: likelihood times prior, divided by normalising constant. The types of the objects differ; the formula does not.

01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.title: 09.Cauchy Distribution
01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.content:
The Cauchy is probability’s most wanted counterexample. It looks like a Normal — symmetric, unimodal, bell-shaped — but it has no mean, no variance, no MGF. It is the distribution that breaks every theorem you thought was unconditional. Keep it close.

Definition
A random variable X has the standard Cauchy distribution if its PDF is
\boxed{f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}.}
The corresponding CDF is
F_X(x) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\pi}\arctan(x).
The general Cauchy with location \mu \in \mathbb{R} and scale \gamma > 0 has PDF
f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi\gamma\left[1 + \left(\frac{x-\mu}{\gamma}\right)^2\right]}.
We write X \sim \text{Cauchy}(\mu, \gamma). The standard Cauchy is \text{Cauchy}(0,1).

Verifying It’s a Valid PDF
Nonnegativity: 1 + x^2 > 0 for all x, so f_X(x) > 0. ✓
Normalisation: We need \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}, dx = 1.
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}, dx = \frac{1}{\pi}\left[\arctan(x)\right]_{-\infty}^{\infty} = \frac{1}{\pi}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) = \frac{1}{\pi} \cdot \pi = 1. \quad \checkmark

The Canonical Construction: Ratio of Two Normals
This is the result Stat 110 leads with, and it’s the right way to first encounter the Cauchy.
Theorem. If X, Y \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0,1), then T = X/Y \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1).
Proof. We derive the PDF of T = X/Y by conditioning on Y.
For Y = y \neq 0, the conditional distribution of T given Y = y is T \mid Y = y \sim N(0, 1/y^2) \cdot \text{sign}(y)… actually, let me be careful and go through the CDF directly.
Fix t \in \mathbb{R}. By LOTP:
f_T(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{T \mid Y}(t \mid y), f_Y(y), dy.
Given Y = y, we have T = X/y, so T \mid Y = y has the distribution of X/y where X \sim N(0,1). The PDF of X/y at t is |y| \cdot \phi(ty) where \phi is the standard normal PDF:
f_{T \mid Y}(t \mid y) = |y|,\phi(ty) = |y| \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-t^2 y^2/2}.
Therefore:
f_T(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |y| \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-t^2 y^2/2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-y^2/2}, dy = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |y|, e^{-y^2(1+t^2)/2}, dy.
Since the integrand is even in y:
= \frac{1}{2\pi} \cdot 2\int_0^{\infty} y, e^{-y^2(1+t^2)/2}, dy.
Substitute u = y^2(1+t^2)/2, so du = y(1+t^2), dy:
= \frac{1}{\pi} \int_0^{\infty} \frac{1}{1+t^2} e^{-u}, du = \frac{1}{\pi(1+t^2)} \cdot \left[-e^{-u}\right]_0^{\infty} = \frac{1}{\pi(1+t^2)}.
This is exactly the Cauchy PDF. \square
Geometric intuition. Throw a dart uniformly at the unit circle — equivalently, choose \theta \sim \text{Uniform}(-\pi/2, \pi/2) and draw the line through the origin at angle \theta. Where it hits the line y = 1 has x-coordinate \tan(\theta) \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1).
This is a second construction: X \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1) iff X \stackrel{d}{=} \tan(\theta) where \theta \sim \text{Uniform}(-\pi/2, \pi/2).
Verification: F_X(x) = P(\tan\theta \leq x) = P(\theta \leq \arctan x) = \frac{\arctan x - (-\pi/2)}{\pi} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\arctan x}{\pi}. Differentiate: f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}. ✓

The Mean Does Not Exist
This is the theorem. Not “the mean is infinite” — the mean does not exist.
Claim. E[X] is undefined for X \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1).
Proof. For E[X] to exist in the Lebesgue sense, we need E[|X|] < \infty. Compute:
E[|X|] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x| \cdot \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}, dx = \frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\infty} \frac{x}{1+x^2}, dx = \frac{2}{\pi}\left[\frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2)\right]_0^{\infty} = +\infty.
Since E[|X|] = \infty, the expectation E[X] is not defined — neither +\infty nor -\infty nor any real number. \square
The naive objection: “But surely by symmetry E[X] = 0?” This is the subtle point. Symmetry alone is not sufficient to conclude E[X] = 0. The correct statement is: if E[|X|] < \infty and f_X is symmetric about 0, then E[X] = 0. Without integrability, you cannot invoke symmetry to assign a value.
The rigorous statement: the improper Riemann integral \lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{-R}^R x \cdot f_X(x), dx = 0 by symmetry. But this is the principal value of the integral, not the Lebesgue integral. The Lebesgue integral requires the positive and negative parts to be separately finite, which fails here. The Lebesgue integral of X does not exist; the Cauchy principal value is 0.
This distinction — Lebesgue integral vs Cauchy principal value — is one of the places where the formalism is doing real work.

No Variance, No MGF
Since the mean doesn’t exist, variance (E[X^2] - (E[X])^2) is not even a meaningful quantity. But we can verify E[X^2] = \infty directly:
E[X^2] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{x^2}{\pi(1+x^2)}, dx = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{x^2}{1+x^2}, dx = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(1 - \frac{1}{1+x^2}\right)dx = \infty.
The MGF is M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}]. For t \neq 0:
E[e^{tX}] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{tx}}{\pi(1+x^2)}, dx.
For t > 0, as x \to +\infty: e^{tx}/(\pi(1+x^2)) \to \infty faster than any polynomial, and the integral diverges. So M_X(t) = \infty for all t \neq 0. The MGF does not exist anywhere except t = 0.
This is catastrophic for the standard toolkit — all MGF-based proofs of the CLT, moment calculations, etc., fail completely for the Cauchy.

The Characteristic Function Exists
The one analytic tool that works is the characteristic function:
\varphi_X(t) = E[e^{itX}] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{itx}}{\pi(1+x^2)}, dx = e^{-|t|}.
Since |e^{itx}| = 1, the integrand is bounded in absolute value by f_X(x), which is integrable. So Fubini applies and \varphi_X(t) is well-defined for all t \in \mathbb{R}.
The evaluation \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{itx}}{\pi(1+x^2)}, dx = e^{-|t|} follows from contour integration (residue theorem — close in the upper or lower half-plane depending on the sign of t). The result e^{-|t|} is the characteristic function of the standard Cauchy.
This is the right object. The characteristic function always exists for any distribution. The Cauchy’s characteristic function has the form e^{-|t|}, which is not differentiable at t = 0 — consistent with the non-existence of moments (\varphi_X'(0) = iE[X], which doesn’t exist).

The CLT Fails — Badly
If X_1, X_2, \ldots \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Cauchy}(0,1), then the sample mean
\bar{X}_n = \frac{X_1 + \cdots + X_n}{n} \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1)
for every n. The distribution of \bar{X}_n does not converge to a normal — it stays Cauchy forever, with exactly the same spread as a single observation. Averaging does nothing.
Proof. By the ratio-of-normals construction: if X_i = U_i / V_i with U_i, V_i \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0,1), then
\bar{X}_n = \frac{\sum U_i}{\sum V_i} \cdot \frac{1}{n} \cdot n = \frac{U_1 + \cdots + U_n}{V_1 + \cdots + V_n}.
But U_1 + \cdots + U_n \sim N(0,n) and V_1 + \cdots + V_n \sim N(0,n), so their ratio is N(0,n)/N(0,n) \stackrel{d}{=} N(0,1)/N(0,1) \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1). \square
Alternatively via characteristic functions: \varphi_{\bar{X}_n}(t) = \left(\varphi_X(t/n)\right)^n = \left(e^{-|t|/n}\right)^n = e^{-|t|}. So \bar{X}_n has the same characteristic function as X_1, hence the same distribution.
Why does the CLT fail? Because the CLT requires finite variance (E[X^2] < \infty). The Cauchy has no finite moments at all. The CLT is not wrong — its hypotheses are just not met.

The Cauchy Is a Stable Distribution
The calculation \bar{X}_n \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1) is a special case of stability: a distribution is stable if a sum of independent copies, when scaled, has the same distribution.
More precisely, X is stable if for X_1, X_2 \stackrel{iid}{\sim} X, there exist a, b > 0 such that X_1 + X_2 \stackrel{d}{=} aX + b.
The Cauchy is a stable distribution with index \alpha = 1. The Normal is stable with index \alpha = 2 (the only stable distribution with finite variance). The Lévy distribution is stable with index \alpha = 1/2.
The generalised CLT says: for i.i.d. variables in the domain of attraction of a stable distribution with index \alpha, appropriately scaled sums converge to that stable distribution. The classical CLT is the \alpha = 2 case.

Median and Mode Exist
Even though moments don’t exist, the median and mode are perfectly well-defined.
Median: By symmetry of f_X around 0, P(X \leq 0) = 1/2, so the median is 0.
Mode: f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)} is maximised at x = 0, so the mode is 0.
Interquartile range: F_X^{-1}(3/4) - F_X^{-1}(1/4) = \tan(\pi/4) - \tan(-\pi/4) = 1 - (-1) = 2.
The IQR is a sensible measure of spread for the Cauchy; variance is not. This is a general lesson: for heavy-tailed distributions, quantile-based summaries (median, IQR) are more appropriate than moment-based ones.

Connection to the t-Distribution
The Student t-distribution with \nu degrees of freedom has PDF
f(x) = \frac{\Gamma!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\nu\pi},\Gamma!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)}\left(1 + \frac{x^2}{\nu}\right)^{-(\nu+1)/2}.
At \nu = 1: the t_1 distribution is exactly the standard Cauchy. The Cauchy is the t-distribution with one degree of freedom.
As \nu \to \infty: the t_\nu distribution converges to N(0,1). The Cauchy (\nu = 1) sits at the heavy-tailed extreme.
For \nu \geq 2: E[X] = 0. For \nu \geq 3: \text{Var}(X) = \nu/(\nu-2). At \nu = 1 (Cauchy): neither exists.

Summary of What Exists and What Doesn’t























































PropertyExists?ValuePDF✓\frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}CDF✓\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\pi}\arctan(x)Median✓0Mode✓0Characteristic function✓e^{-\vert t \vert}Mean E[X]✗Undefined (principal value = 0)Variance✗UndefinedE[X^k] for any k \geq 1✗+\inftyMGF M_X(t) for t \neq 0✗+\infty

01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.title: 10.Hybrid or Mixed Distributions
01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.content:
Reality does not respect the discrete/continuous divide. Insurance payouts, option prices, rainfall totals — these are neither purely discrete nor purely continuous. The hybrid is not a pathology. It is the generic case, and discrete and continuous are the special ones.

The Problem with the Discrete/Continuous Dichotomy
Every introductory probability course splits random variables into discrete (PMF) and continuous (PDF). But what about:

Insurance: a payout that is exactly 0 with probability 1/2 (no accident), and otherwise exponentially distributed.
Censored data: a survival time that is observed exactly if death occurred, but recorded as T > C (a point mass at C) if the subject was censored.
Option pricing: a call option worth exactly 0 (with positive probability) if it expires out of the money, and continuously distributed otherwise.

These are hybrid (or mixed) random variables — they have both a discrete component (point masses) and a continuous component (a density). Neither a PMF alone nor a PDF alone describes them.
The CDF is the object that handles all cases uniformly.

The CDF Is Always Well-Defined
For any random variable X — discrete, continuous, or hybrid — the CDF
F_X(x) = P(X \leq x)
is well-defined, right-continuous, nondecreasing, with F_X(-\infty) = 0 and F_X(\infty) = 1.
A hybrid X has a CDF that is:

Flat on intervals where there is no mass (neither discrete nor continuous),
Jumps at points with positive probability (the discrete atoms),
Rises smoothly on intervals where X has a density.

The Lebesgue decomposition theorem says every CDF decomposes uniquely into a discrete part, an absolutely continuous part, and a singular continuous part. For all distributions we encounter in probability courses, the singular part is zero — so every mixed distribution is a convex combination of a purely discrete and purely continuous distribution.

The Decomposition
Write the CDF of a hybrid X as:
F_X(x) = p \cdot F_{\text{disc}}(x) + (1-p) \cdot F_{\text{cont}}(x), \quad p \in [0,1],
where:

F_{\text{disc}} is the CDF of a purely discrete distribution (a step function),
F_{\text{cont}} is the CDF of a purely continuous distribution (a continuous function),
p is the total probability mass sitting on discrete atoms.

Equivalently, there exist:

A set of atoms {x_1, x_2, \ldots} with point masses p_i = P(X = x_i) > 0 summing to p,
A density f_{\text{cont}}(x) for the continuous part, integrating to 1-p.

The full “density” of X — in the sense of a measure — is:
\mu_X = p_{\text{disc}} + (1-p), f_{\text{cont}}(x), dx,
where p_{\text{disc}} = \sum_i p_i \delta_{x_i} is a sum of Dirac delta masses.
I won’t use measure theory throughout — the CDF and the case-by-case approach is cleaner for computation.

Computing Probabilities: Always Go Through the CDF
For a hybrid X, probabilities of intervals are:
P(a < X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a).
P(a \leq X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a^-) = F_X(b) - \lim_{x \nearrow a} F_X(x).
The distinction between F_X(a) and F_X(a^-) matters when a is an atom:
P(X = a) = F_X(a) - F_X(a^-).
For continuous points, F_X(a) = F_X(a^-) and P(X = a) = 0.

The Canonical Example: Zero-Inflated Exponential
X = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{with probability } p \ Y & \text{with probability } 1-p \end{cases}
where Y \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda), independent of the Bernoulli trial.
CDF:
F_X(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \ p + (1-p)(1 - e^{-\lambda x}) & x \geq 0. \end{cases}
At x = 0: F_X(0) = p. So there’s a jump of size p at 0, corresponding to P(X = 0) = p. For x > 0, F_X rises smoothly.
Expected value:
E[X] = p \cdot 0 + (1-p) \cdot E[Y] = \frac{1-p}{\lambda}.
This is LOTP for expectations: E[X] = E[X \mid \text{atom}]\cdot p + E[X \mid \text{continuous}]\cdot (1-p).
General formula for E[X]: For any hybrid X =  discrete atoms + continuous density:
E[X] = \sum_i x_i , p_i + \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x, f_{\text{cont}}(x), dx.
This is just linearity of expectation applied to the decomposition.

Worked Example 1: Insurance Payout
A policy pays 0 if there is no claim (probability 3/4), and pays an amount \text{Expo}(1/1000) (mean payout 1000) if there is a claim (probability 1/4$).
Let X be the payout.
CDF: For x < 0: F_X(x) = 0. For x \geq 0:
F_X(x) = \frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{4}(1 - e^{-x/1000}) = 1 - \frac{1}{4}e^{-x/1000}.
Jump of 3/4 at x = 0. Smooth rise for x > 0.
Mean payout:
E[X] = \frac{3}{4} \cdot 0 + \frac{1}{4} \cdot 1000 = 250.
P(X > 500):
P(X > 500) = 1 - F_X(500) = \frac{1}{4}e^{-1/2} \approx \frac{1}{4}(0.6065) \approx 0.1516.

Worked Example 2: The Censored Random Variable
In survival analysis, a subject either dies (event time T \sim f_T) or is censored at time C (still alive at end of study). The observed time is:
X = \min(T, C), \quad \Delta = \mathbf{1}[T \leq C].
If T \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda) and C is a fixed constant:
P(X = C) = P(T > C) = e^{-\lambda C}.
P(X \leq x) = P(T \leq x),\mathbf{1}[x < C] + 1 \cdot \mathbf{1}[x \geq C] = (1 - e^{-\lambda x}),\mathbf{1}[x < C] + \mathbf{1}[x \geq C].
So X has:

A continuous density \lambda e^{-\lambda x} on [0, C),
A point mass e^{-\lambda C} at x = C.

This is a hybrid distribution — it is impossible to describe X with either a PMF or a PDF alone.

Worked Example 3: Mixed Bayes (The Key Probability Example)
This is the Stat 110 use case. A continuous prior, discrete likelihood — or vice versa.
Setup. A coin has bias p \sim \text{Beta}(1,1) = \text{Uniform}(0,1) (continuous prior). I flip it once and observe X \in {0,1} (discrete).
The joint distribution of (p, X) is hybrid: p is continuous, X is discrete. The marginal of X is discrete; the marginal of p is continuous; the joint has no single representation as either a PMF or a PDF.
The joint “density” is:
f_{p, X}(p, x) = P(X = x \mid p), f_p(p) = p^x(1-p)^{1-x} \cdot 1, \quad p \in (0,1),; x \in {0,1}.
Marginal of X:
P(X = 1) = \int_0^1 p \cdot 1, dp = \frac{1}{2}.
Posterior of p given X = 1:
f_{p \mid X}(p \mid 1) = \frac{P(X=1 \mid p), f_p(p)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{p \cdot 1}{1/2} = 2p, \quad p \in (0,1).
So p \mid X = 1 \sim \text{Beta}(2,1). ✓
This is mixed Bayes: the prior is a continuous PDF, the likelihood is a discrete PMF, the posterior is a continuous PDF. The formula structure is identical to pure continuous Bayes — you just mix the object types appropriately.

Expectation via LOTP: The General Tool
For a hybrid X and any event A, LOTP gives:
E[X] = E[X \mid A], P(A) + E[X \mid A^c], P(A^c).
This always works regardless of whether X is discrete, continuous, or hybrid. The conditioning splits X into pieces that may each be easier to handle.
Example. X is zero-inflated Exponential as above. Let A = {X = 0}.
E[X] = E[X \mid X = 0], P(X=0) + E[X \mid X > 0], P(X > 0) = 0 \cdot p + \frac{1}{\lambda}\cdot(1-p) = \frac{1-p}{\lambda}.
Here E[X \mid X > 0] = E[\text{Expo}(\lambda)] = 1/\lambda because given the continuous part is realised, X \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda).

The CDF Characterises Everything
For a hybrid X, the CDF F_X completely characterises the distribution. From F_X:

Identify atoms: points where F_X jumps. The jump size at x_0 is P(X = x_0) = F_X(x_0) - F_X(x_0^-).
Identify continuous density: wherever F_X is differentiable, f_{\text{cont}}(x) = F_X'(x).
Recover all probabilities: P(X \in B) = \int_B dF_X (Lebesgue-Stieltjes integral — the unified notation that handles both sums over atoms and integrals over densities).

The Lebesgue-Stieltjes integral \int g(x), dF_X(x) is the right way to write E[g(X)] for any distribution:

Discrete: \sum_i g(x_i), p_i.
Continuous: \int g(x), f_X(x), dx.
Hybrid: both terms summed.

This is the formalism that unifies everything. I don’t need it for computation — LOTP does the work — but it’s the reason there’s no separate theory for each case.

Common Mistake: Forgetting Point Masses in the CDF
For a hybrid X with an atom at x_0:
P(X < x_0) = F_X(x_0^-) \neq F_X(x_0) = P(X \leq x_0).
The difference is P(X = x_0) > 0.
When computing P(a \leq X \leq b), always be explicit about whether endpoints are included:
P(a \leq X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a^-).
If a is an atom and you write F_X(b) - F_X(a) instead, you lose the mass at a. This is a silent error — the formula looks right and the answer is just slightly off.

Why This Matters Beyond Probability Theory
The hybrid framework is not an abstract curiosity. It appears everywhere:

Econometrics: Tobit models — a continuous outcome censored at zero (wages, consumption). The observed variable is hybrid.
Biostatistics: Survival data with administrative censoring — the exact structure of Worked Example 2.
Finance: Digital options, barrier options — positive probability of ending at exactly zero or exactly at the barrier.
Mixture models: Latent variable models where a hidden discrete variable selects which continuous component generates the data. The marginal over the hidden variable is hybrid.
Renewal theory: The age of a renewal process at a fixed time has a point mass at zero (if a renewal just occurred) plus a continuous component.

In all these cases, the right tool is the CDF, LOTP conditioning on the discrete/continuous split, and the Lebesgue-Stieltjes expectation formula.

01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.title: 11.2D LOTUS
01.Maths/Probability/07.Joint-Distributi.content:
07.LOTUSsays you don’t need to find the distribution of g(X,Y) to compute its expectation. You just integrate g against the joint density you already have. This sounds obvious — it is not. It is a theorem, and a useful one.

Motivation
Suppose (X, Y) has joint PDF f_{X,Y} and I want to compute E[g(X,Y)] for some function g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}.
The naive approach: find the distribution of Z = g(X,Y) — its PDF or CDF — then compute E[Z] = \int z, f_Z(z), dz.
The LOTUS approach: skip finding f_Z entirely and compute directly.
Finding the distribution of Z = g(X,Y) is often painful. It requires a change of variables, setting up inequalities, differentiating CDFs. LOTUS bypasses all of this.

The Theorem
Theorem (2D LOTUS). Let (X,Y) be a continuous random vector with joint PDF f_{X,Y}, and let g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R} be a measurable function. Then:
\boxed{E[g(X,Y)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x,y), f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy,}
provided the integral converges absolutely (i.e., E[|g(X,Y)|] < \infty).
For the discrete case, with joint PMF p_{X,Y}:
E[g(X,Y)] = \sum_x \sum_y g(x,y), p_{X,Y}(x,y).
What the theorem says: the expectation of a function of (X,Y) is computed by integrating that function against the joint density. You do not need to know the distribution of g(X,Y).

Why It’s a Theorem, Not a Definition
E[Z] is defined as \int z, f_Z(z), dz for a random variable Z with PDF f_Z. The statement that this equals \int!\int g(x,y) f_{X,Y}(x,y),dx,dy when Z = g(X,Y) is a genuine result — it requires proof.
Proof sketch (continuous case). By definition, E[g(X,Y)] = \int z, f_{g(X,Y)}(z), dz. The PDF f_{g(X,Y)} is obtained by pushing forward the joint measure (X,Y) through g. The change-of-variables formula for measures gives exactly the right-hand side. More concretely, for g \geq 0:
E[g(X,Y)] = \int_0^{\infty} P(g(X,Y) > t), dt = \int_0^{\infty} \iint_{{g(x,y)>t}} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy, dt.
Swapping the order of integration (Tonelli — all terms are nonneg):
= \iint \left(\int_0^{g(x,y)} dt\right) f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy = \iint g(x,y), f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy. \quad \square
For general g: decompose g = g^+ - g^- and apply the nonneg result to each part, assuming absolute integrability.

Special Cases Worth Naming
Linearity. E[aX + bY + c] = a,E[X] + b,E[Y] + c.
Proof via 2D LOTUS with g(x,y) = ax+by+c and f_{X,Y} arbitrary:
E[aX+bY+c] = \iint (ax+by+c), f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy = a\iint x, f_{X,Y}, dx, dy + b\iint y, f_{X,Y}, dx, dy + c.
The first double integral equals \int x, f_X(x), dx = E[X] (marginalise out y). Similarly for E[Y]. Linearity of expectation follows — and note it holds regardless of whether X and Y are independent.
Product of independent r.v.’s. If X \perp Y, then f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y), so:
E[g(X)h(Y)] = \iint g(x)h(y), f_X(x), f_Y(y), dx, dy = \int g(x) f_X(x), dx \cdot \int h(y) f_Y(y), dy = E[g(X)], E[h(Y)].
This is the factorisation identity for independent r.v.’s, proved directly from 2D LOTUS + independence.
Covariance. \text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]. By 2D LOTUS:
\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \iint (x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y), f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy.
Expanding and using linearity: \text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X],E[Y], where E[XY] = \iint xy, f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy by 2D LOTUS with g(x,y) = xy.

Worked Example 1: E[XY] for a Triangular Joint
(X,Y) uniform on the triangle {0 < x < y < 1}, so f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 2.
E[XY] = \int_0^1\int_0^y xy \cdot 2, dx, dy = \int_0^1 2y \cdot \frac{y^2}{2}, dy = \int_0^1 y^3, dy = \frac{1}{4}.
Compare: E[X] = \int_0^1 2x(1-x), dx = 2\left[\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3}.
E[Y] = \int_0^1 2y \cdot y, dy = \int_0^1 2y^2, dy = \frac{2}{3}.
So \text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{2}{9} = \frac{9-8}{36} = \frac{1}{36} > 0.
Positive covariance makes sense: large X forces large Y (since Y > X).

Worked Example 2: E[X^2 + Y^2] for Uniform on the Disk
(X,Y) uniform on the unit disk, f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1/\pi for x^2 + y^2 < 1.
E[X^2 + Y^2] = \iint_{x^2+y^2 < 1} \frac{x^2+y^2}{\pi}, dx, dy.
Switch to polar coordinates: x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta, Jacobian = r.
= \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r^2 \cdot r, dr, d\theta = \frac{1}{\pi} \cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}.
By symmetry E[X^2] = E[Y^2], so E[X^2] = \frac{1}{4}.
Also E[X] = 0 by symmetry, so \text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = \frac{1}{4}.

Worked Example 3: E[\max(X,Y)]
(X,Y) i.i.d. \text{Uniform}(0,1), so f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1 on [0,1]^2. Let M = \max(X,Y).
