01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.title: 01.Conditional Expectation
01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.content:
This is the note I wish I had at the start of the course. Conditional expectation appears in two completely different-looking forms — conditioning on an event vs. conditioning on a random variable — and if you don’t clearly separate them in your head, everything downstream (Adam’s Law, martingales, Bayesian updating) becomes a blur. Write this down carefully once, and refer back to it.


0. Motivation
We already know \mathbb{E}[X] — the average of X over all randomness. But often we have partial information: we know the value of some other variable Y, or we know that some event A occurred. Conditional expectation is the right tool to update our estimate of X given that information.
The two cases:

Conditioning on an event A: gives a number \mathbb{E}[X \mid A]
Conditioning on a random variable Y: gives a random variable \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]

This distinction is the entire conceptual core of the note.

1. Conditioning on an Event
1.1 Definition
For an event A with P(A) > 0:
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X \mid A] = \frac{\mathbb{E}[X \cdot \mathbf{1}_A]}{P(A)}}
Equivalently, in the discrete case:
\mathbb{E}[X \mid A] = \sum_x x, P(X = x \mid A) = \sum_x x, \frac{P(X=x,, A)}{P(A)}
and in the continuous case:
\mathbb{E}[X \mid A] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x, f_{X\mid A}(x), dx
where f_{X\mid A}(x) = f_X(x \cdot \mathbf{1}_A) / P(A) — i.e., the density of X restricted to A and renormalised.

Think of it as: throw away all outcomes where A didn’t happen, renormalise what’s left, then compute the ordinary expectation. It’s just a weighted average over a restricted universe.

1.2 The Law of Total Expectation (LTE) — Event Version
If A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n partition \Omega (disjoint, exhaustive) with P(A_i) > 0:
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[X \mid A_i], P(A_i)}
Proof. \sum_i \mathbb{E}[X \mid A_i] P(A_i) = \sum_i \mathbb{E}[X \cdot \mathbf{1}_{A_i}] = \mathbb{E}!\left[X \sum_i \mathbf{1}_{A_i}\right] = \mathbb{E}[X \cdot 1] = \mathbb{E}[X] \qquad \blacksquare
The last step uses \sum_i \mathbf{1}_{A_i} = 1 since the A_i partition \Omega.
1.3 Example: Geometric from First Principles
Let X \sim \text{Geom}(p) — number of trials until first success. Compute \mathbb{E}[X] by conditioning on the first trial.
Let A = {\text{first trial is success}}, A^c = {\text{first trial is failure}}.
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid A], p + \mathbb{E}[X \mid A^c],(1-p)

\mathbb{E}[X \mid A] = 1 (done in one trial)
\mathbb{E}[X \mid A^c] = 1 + \mathbb{E}[X] (wasted one trial, back to start by memorylessness)

\mathbb{E}[X] = p + (1-p)(1 + \mathbb{E}[X]) = 1 + (1-p)\mathbb{E}[X]
p,\mathbb{E}[X] = 1 \implies \mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{1}{p}

This is the first-step analysis / recursive expectation trick. Conditioning on an event, setting up the recurrence, solving. Memorise this pattern — it appears everywhere: random walks, branching processes, Markov chains.


2. Conditioning on a Random Variable
2.1 Definition
For a random variable Y, \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] is not a number — it is a function of Y, hence itself a random variable.
Discrete Y: For each possible value y of Y:
\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y] = \sum_x x, P(X = x \mid Y = y)
Then \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] is the random variable obtained by plugging in: wherever Y = y, the value is \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=y]. Formally:
\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] = g(Y) \quad \text{where} \quad g(y) = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y]
Continuous Y: Use the conditional density f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y) = f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_Y(y):
\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x, f_{X\mid Y}(x \mid y), dx
Again, \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] = g(Y) is a random variable.

This is the part that trips people up. \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = 3] is a number. \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] is a random variable — it’s uncertain because Y is uncertain. Once Y is observed to be 3, \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] becomes \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=3], which is then a number. The randomness in \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] comes entirely from the randomness of Y.

2.2 The Law of Total Expectation (Adam’s Law)
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]] = \mathbb{E}[X]}
Proof (discrete case).
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]] = \sum_y \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=y], P(Y=y) = \sum_y \sum_x x, P(X=x \mid Y=y), P(Y=y)
= \sum_x x \sum_y P(X=x, Y=y) = \sum_x x, P(X=x) = \mathbb{E}[X] \qquad \blacksquare
In words: average the conditional expectation over the randomness in Y, and you recover the unconditional expectation. The inner expectation uses the randomness of X given Y; the outer expectation averages over Y.

This is sometimes called the Tower Property or iterated expectation. It’s one of the most-used tools in all of probability. Every time you see a complex expectation, ask: “what should I condition on to make X easy?” Then Adam’s Law collapses the conditioning.

2.3 Key Properties
Let g be any (measurable) function. Then:
(i) Linearity: \mathbb{E}[aX + bZ \mid Y] = a,\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y] + b,\mathbb{E}[Z \mid Y]
(ii) Taking out what is known: If h(Y) is a function of Y alone: \mathbb{E}[h(Y)\cdot X \mid Y] = h(Y)\cdot \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]
Proof. Given Y=y, h(Y) = h(y) is a constant, so it factors out of the expectation. \blacksquare
(iii) Independence: If X \perp Y: \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] = \mathbb{E}[X]
Proof. P(X = x \mid Y = y) = P(X=x) by independence, so conditioning gives nothing. \blacksquare
(iv) Tower property (iterated conditioning): \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z] \mid Y] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]
The coarser conditioning wins: conditioning on less information on the outside collapses the finer conditioning inside.

3. The Law of Total Variance (Eve’s Law)
\boxed{\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X \mid Y)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y])}
Proof.
Start from \text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 and apply Adam’s Law to each piece.
By Adam’s Law: \mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]], so (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 = (\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]])^2.
Also: \mathbb{E}[X^2] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X^2 \mid Y]].
Now write \mathbb{E}[X^2 \mid Y] = \text{Var}(X\mid Y) + (\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])^2. So:
\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)] + \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])^2]
Therefore:
\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)] + \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])^2] - (\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]])^2
= \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]) \qquad \blacksquare
Naming the two pieces:




















TermNameWhat it captures\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X \mid Y)]Unexplained varianceAverage spread of X within each value of Y — the noise that Y cannot explain\text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y])Explained varianceSpread of the conditional mean as Y varies — the variation that Y explains

Eve’s Law is Adam’s Law for variance. If you understand the decomposition “total = unexplained + explained,” you understand ANOVA, linear regression R^2, and the bias-variance tradeoff at their core. That’s not a coincidence — it’s all the same identity.

3.1 Example: Beta-Binomial Variance
W \sim \text{Beta}(a,b), X \mid W \sim \text{Binomial}(n, W).
From Beta Expectations §6:

\text{Var}(X \mid W) = nW(1-W) — Binomial variance given p = W
\mathbb{E}[X \mid W] = nW — Binomial mean given p = W

Unexplained variance: \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid W)] = n(\mathbb{E}[W] - \mathbb{E}[W^2]) = n\left(\frac{a}{s} - \frac{a(a+1)}{s(s+1)}\right) = \frac{nab}{s(s+1)}
where s = a+b.
Explained variance: \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid W]) = \text{Var}(nW) = n^2,\text{Var}(W) = \frac{n^2 ab}{s^2(s+1)}
Total: \text{Var}(X) = \frac{nab}{s(s+1)} + \frac{n^2 ab}{s^2(s+1)} = \frac{nab}{s^2(s+1)}(s + n)
Consistent with Beta Expectations §6. ✓

4. Conditional Expectation as Projection
This is the graduate-level view, but it’s worth planting the seed now.
\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] is the best predictor of X given Y, in the sense of minimising mean squared error:
\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] = \underset{g(Y)}{\arg\min}; \mathbb{E}[(X - g(Y))^2]
Proof. For any function g:
\mathbb{E}[(X - g(Y))^2] = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y] + \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y] - g(Y))^2]
The cross term vanishes (by the property \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])h(Y)] = 0 for any h — a consequence of “taking out what is known”). So:
= \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])^2] + \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y] - g(Y))^2]
The first term doesn’t depend on g; the second is \geq 0 and equals 0 iff g(Y) = \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y] a.s. \blacksquare

In Hilbert space language: \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] is the orthogonal projection of X onto the subspace of Y-measurable random variables, with inner product \langle X, Z \rangle = \mathbb{E}[XZ]. Eve’s Law is the Pythagorean theorem in this space. This is where the theory is going — keep it in mind.


5. Common Patterns and Pitfalls
Pattern 1: First-Step / Recursive Conditioning
Set up \mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid A],P(A) + \mathbb{E}[X \mid A^c],P(A^c), express \mathbb{E}[X \mid A^c] in terms of \mathbb{E}[X] using structure of the problem, solve. Seen in: Geometric mean, random walk hitting times, Gambler’s ruin.
Pattern 2: Condition on the “Random Parameter”
Hierarchical model: \Theta \sim \text{prior}, X \mid \Theta \sim \text{likelihood}.

\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid \Theta]] by Adam’s Law
\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid\Theta)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid\Theta]) by Eve’s Law

Seen in: Beta-Binomial, Poisson-Gamma (negative binomial), any mixture model.
Pattern 3: Simplify \mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)] by conditioning on Y
\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)\mid Y]] = \mathbb{E}[h(Y)]
where h(y) = \mathbb{E}[g(X,y) \mid Y=y]. The inner expectation treats Y=y as fixed and integrates over X.
Pitfall: \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] \neq \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y]
The left side is a random variable. The right side (for fixed y) is a number. Don’t write one when you mean the other.
Pitfall: \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] \neq \mathbb{E}[X] unless X \perp Y
Conditioning changes expectations unless independence holds. This sounds obvious but gets misapplied under pressure.

6. Summary






























Conditioning on event AConditioning on RV YResult typeNumberRandom variableDefinition\mathbb{E}[X\cdot\mathbf{1}_A]/P(A)g(Y) where g(y) = \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]Total expectation\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_i \mathbb{E}[X\mid A_i]P(A_i)\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]]Total variance—\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])

References

Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, Ch. 9 (Conditional expectation — both definitions, Adam’s Law, Eve’s Law, projection interpretation)
Harvard Stat 110, Lectures 19–20 — the “taking out what is known” property and the projection view are emphasised heavily; the Beta-Binomial Eve’s Law calculation is a worked example


Links

Beta-Gamma Connections — foundation for Beta distribution used throughout
Beta Expectations — \mathbb{E}[W], \mathbb{E}[W^2], \text{Var}(W) used in Beta-Binomial example
Order Statistics — Adam’s Law used to compute \mathbb{E}[U_{(k)}] via spacing exchangeability

Open Questions

 Prove the projection characterisation rigorously in Hilbert space language — what is the \sigma-algebra generated by Y?
 Show that \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])h(Y)] = 0 for all h — this is the orthogonality condition, prove it from “taking out what is known”
 Martingales: if M_n = \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{F}_n], show (M_n) is a martingale — this is the tower property in disguise
 Conditional variance: is \text{Var}(X \mid Y=y) always \leq \text{Var}(X)? (Yes — conditioning reduces variance on average, but not necessarily for a fixed y)

01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.title: 02.Adam's Law (Law of Total Expectation)
01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.content:
Adam’s Law is deceptively simple to state and endlessly useful in practice. The whole skill is learning to ask the right question: “what should I condition on to make this expectation tractable?” Once you pick the right conditioning variable, the law does the rest. This note is about building that instinct.


0. Statement
Let X and Y be random variables on the same probability space with \mathbb{E}|X| < \infty. Then:
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]] = \mathbb{E}[X]}
Or equivalently, if Y takes values y_1, y_2, \ldots:
\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_i \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y_i], P(Y = y_i)
In the continuous case:
\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y], f_Y(y), dy

Recall from Conditional Expectation: \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] is a random variable — a function of Y. Adam’s Law says: take the expectation of that random variable (averaging over the randomness of Y), and you recover \mathbb{E}[X] unconditionally. The two layers of randomness — X given Y, then Y itself — collapse back into one.


1. Proof
Discrete case. Let X, Y be jointly discrete.
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]] = \sum_y \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y], P(Y = y)
= \sum_y \left(\sum_x x, P(X = x \mid Y = y)\right) P(Y = y)
= \sum_y \sum_x x, \frac{P(X=x,, Y=y)}{P(Y=y)} \cdot P(Y=y)
= \sum_x x \sum_y P(X=x,, Y=y)
= \sum_x x, P(X = x) = \mathbb{E}[X] \qquad \blacksquare
The key step is swapping the order of summation and recognising \sum_y P(X=x,Y=y) = P(X=x) (marginalisation).
Continuous case. Replace sums with integrals and P(Y=y) with f_Y(y),dy; the argument is identical. \blacksquare

2. The More General Form
Adam’s Law holds with more conditioning on both sides:
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z] \mid Z] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z]
Reading this: condition on Z throughout. Given Z, the inner expectation conditions additionally on Y; the outer expectation averages over Y. The net effect: conditioning on Z alone.
This is the Tower Property: the coarser conditioning always wins.
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \mid \mathcal{H}] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{H}] \quad \text{whenever } \mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathcal{G}
(in the \sigma-algebra language of Stat 210 — file this away for later).

3. The Instinct: What to Condition On
Adam’s Law is a tool. The skill is choosing Y to condition on. Two heuristics:
Heuristic 1: Condition on the “random parameter.”
If the problem has a hierarchical structure — some latent variable \Theta that governs the distribution of X — condition on \Theta. Given \Theta, X is usually a standard distribution with known mean.
Heuristic 2: Condition on the “first step” or “first outcome.”
In sequential problems (games, random walks, waiting times), condition on the first thing that happens. Express the conditional expectation in terms of the unconditional one, then solve the equation.
Both patterns appear below.

4. Examples
4.1 Geometric Mean (First-Step Analysis)
X \sim \text{Geom}(p). Condition on A = {\text{first trial success}}.
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid A], p + \mathbb{E}[X \mid A^c],(1-p) = 1 \cdot p + (1 + \mathbb{E}[X])(1-p)
Solve: \mathbb{E}[X] = 1/p. ✓
Pattern: memorylessness makes \mathbb{E}[X \mid A^c] = 1 + \mathbb{E}[X] (start over after one wasted trial). Set up the equation, solve.
4.2 Negative Binomial Mean
X =  number of trials until r-th success, p = success probability. Think of X = X_1 + \cdots + X_r where X_i \sim \text{Geom}(p) i.i.d. (waiting times between consecutive successes).
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[X_1 + \cdots + X_r] = r \cdot \frac{1}{p} = \frac{r}{p}
No conditioning needed here — linearity of expectation does it. But the same first-step argument works if you condition on the first trial.
4.3 Poisson-Gamma (Negative Binomial) Model
\Lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(r, \beta), X \mid \Lambda \sim \text{Poisson}(\Lambda).
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid \Lambda]] = \mathbb{E}[\Lambda] = \frac{r}{\beta}
Because \mathbb{E}[X \mid \Lambda = \lambda] = \lambda (Poisson mean), so \mathbb{E}[X \mid \Lambda] = \Lambda.
4.4 Beta-Binomial Mean
W \sim \text{Beta}(a,b), X \mid W \sim \text{Binomial}(n, W).
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid W]] = \mathbb{E}[nW] = n \cdot \frac{a}{a+b}
Because \mathbb{E}[X \mid W = w] = nw, so \mathbb{E}[X \mid W] = nW, then Adam’s Law applies.
4.5 Random Sum
N is a non-negative integer-valued RV, X_1, X_2, \ldots are i.i.d. with mean \mu, independent of N. Let S = X_1 + \cdots + X_N (Wald’s Identity setup).
\mathbb{E}[S] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[S \mid N]] = \mathbb{E}[N\mu] = \mu, \mathbb{E}[N]
Proof of the inner step: \mathbb{E}[S \mid N = n] = \mathbb{E}[X_1 + \cdots + X_n] = n\mu so \mathbb{E}[S \mid N] = N\mu, then Adam’s Law gives \mathbb{E}[S] = \mu,\mathbb{E}[N]. \blacksquare

This is Wald’s Identity. It’s used constantly in sequential analysis and insurance models. The key move: given N=n, the sum has n terms each with mean \mu. Linearity finishes it.

4.6 Order Statistics Mean (Quick)
U_{(k)} is the k-th order statistic of n i.i.d. \text{Uniform}(0,1). From Order Statistics, U_{(k)} \sim \text{Beta}(k, n-k+1), so \mathbb{E}[U_{(k)}] = k/(n+1).
Alternatively: by symmetry of spacings (which itself uses Adam’s Law on the Poisson process representation), all n+1 gaps are exchangeable with mean 1/(n+1), so \mathbb{E}[U_{(k)}] = k/(n+1). Two routes, same answer.

5. Adam’s Law and Variance: The Connection to Eve’s Law
Adam’s Law computes \mathbb{E}[X]. Eve’s Law decomposes \text{Var}(X). They are companions:
\text{Var}(X) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X \mid Y)]}_{\text{unexplained}} + \underbrace{\text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y])}_{\text{explained}}
Adam’s Law is hidden inside Eve’s Law twice:

\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X^2 \mid Y]] (Adam’s Law)
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]] (Adam’s Law)

Eve’s Law is what you get when you apply Adam’s Law to the variance decomposition. See Conditional Expectation §3 for the full proof.

6. A Subtlety: Iterated Conditioning
A common mistake is thinking Adam’s Law means you can always “peel off” conditioning layers freely. The tower property is precise:
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z] \mid Z] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z] \qquad \checkmark
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Z] \mid Y, Z] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z] \qquad \checkmark
The second line: if you already know Z, adding Y to the outer conditioning doesn’t change a function of Z alone — “taking out what is known.”
What fails:
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] \mid Z] \neq \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z] \quad \text{in general}
Unless Y and Z are related in a special way (e.g., Z is a function of Y, or X \perp Z \mid Y).

The tower property requires the conditioning on the outside to be a subset of the conditioning on the inside. When that nesting condition fails, you can’t simplify.


7. Summary of Key Computations



































SettingCondition onResultX \sim \text{Geom}(p)First trial outcome\mathbb{E}[X] = 1/p via recurrenceX\mid\Lambda \sim \text{Pois}(\Lambda)\Lambda\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[\Lambda]X\mid W \sim \text{Bin}(n,W)W\mathbb{E}[X] = n\mathbb{E}[W]Random sum S = \sum_{i=1}^N X_iN\mathbb{E}[S] = \mathbb{E}[N],\mathbb{E}[X_1]Any hierarchical modelLatent parameterReduces to known mean

References

Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, §9.3 (Adam’s Law), §9.4 (Eve’s Law and applications)
Harvard Stat 110, Lecture 19 — the “what to condition on” instinct is the whole point of the lecture; Blitzstein calls it the most important tool in the course


Links

Conditional Expectation — definitions of \mathbb{E}[X\mid A] and \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]; proof infrastructure
Beta Expectations — Beta-Binomial mean computed via Adam’s Law in §6
Order Statistics — \mathbb{E}[U_{(k)}] = k/(n+1) via spacings argument using symmetry
Eve’s Law — the variance companion; proof uses Adam’s Law twice

Open Questions

 Wald’s second identity: \text{Var}(S) = \mathbb{E}[N],\text{Var}(X_1) + (\mathbb{E}[X_1])^2,\text{Var}(N) — prove via Eve’s Law
 Martingale connection: if M_n = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_n], then (M_n) is a martingale. The tower property is exactly the martingale property \mathbb{E}[M_n \mid M_1,\ldots,M_{n-1}] = M_{n-1}
 When does \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]\mid Z] = \mathbb{E}[X\mid Z]? Characterise the conditions precisely

01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.title: 03.Properties of Expectation
01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.content:
These are the load-bearing axioms of probability calculations. None of them are surprising in isolation, but together they are the entire toolkit. Every complex expectation computation I’ve ever done reduces to some combination of linearity, non-negativity, and a clever conditioning argument. Prove each one carefully at least once — after that, use them without guilt.


0. Setup
X, Y, X_1, \ldots, X_n are random variables on a common probability space. All expectations are assumed to exist (i.e. \mathbb{E}|X| < \infty) unless stated otherwise.

1. Linearity
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a,\mathbb{E}[X] + b,\mathbb{E}[Y]}
for all constants a, b \in \mathbb{R}.
This holds regardless of whether X and Y are independent.
Proof (discrete case).
\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = \sum_{x}\sum_{y}(ax + by),P(X=x,, Y=y)
= a\sum_x x \underbrace{\sum_y P(X=x,Y=y)}_{P(X=x)} + b\sum_y y\underbrace{\sum_x P(X=x,Y=y)}_{P(Y=y)}
= a,\mathbb{E}[X] + b,\mathbb{E}[Y] \qquad \blacksquare
The proof is just marginalisation. Independence played no role.
Extension to n variables:
\mathbb{E}!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i\right] = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i, \mathbb{E}[X_i]
by induction. And for countably infinite sums, linearity holds provided \sum_i \mathbb{E}|X_i| < \infty (dominated convergence).

Linearity is the single most-used property in the entire course. Whenever you see a sum of random variables, your first instinct should be to push \mathbb{E} inside. The fact that independence is not required is what makes this powerful — you can always decompose.

1.1 Indicator Trick (Fundamental Consequence)
For any event A, define \mathbf{1}_A = 1 if A occurs, 0 otherwise. Then:
\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_A] = P(A)
Combined with linearity, this gives a powerful method for computing expectations of counts.
Example. X =  number of heads in n fair coin flips. Write X = \mathbf{1}_{A_1} + \cdots + \mathbf{1}_{A_n} where A_i = {i\text{-th flip is heads}}. Then:
\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_{A_i}] = \sum_{i=1}^n P(A_i) = \frac{n}{2}
No need to use the Binomial PMF at all.
Example. Number of fixed points of a random permutation of {1,\ldots,n}. Let X_i = \mathbf{1}_{{\sigma(i) = i}}. Then \mathbb{E}[X_i] = 1/n (by symmetry: each element is equally likely to be fixed). So:
\mathbb{E}!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right] = n \cdot \frac{1}{n} = 1
The expected number of fixed points is always 1, regardless of n.

2. Non-Negativity and Monotonicity
\boxed{X \geq 0 \text{ a.s.} \implies \mathbb{E}[X] \geq 0}
\boxed{X \geq Y \text{ a.s.} \implies \mathbb{E}[X] \geq \mathbb{E}[Y]}
The second follows from the first applied to X - Y \geq 0.
Proof (discrete). If X \geq 0 a.s., then every term x \cdot P(X=x) in \sum_x x,P(X=x) is non-negative. \blacksquare
2.1 Consequence: Bounding Expectations
If a \leq X \leq b a.s., then a \leq \mathbb{E}[X] \leq b.
If |X| \leq Y a.s. and \mathbb{E}[Y] < \infty, then \mathbb{E}|X| \leq \mathbb{E}[Y] < \infty — so \mathbb{E}[X] exists.

3. Expectation of a Function: LOTUS
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \sum_x g(x),P(X=x) \quad \text{(discrete)}}
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty g(x),f_X(x), dx \quad \text{(continuous)}}
This is the Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS). You do not need to find the distribution of g(X) first — just apply g inside the sum/integral over the distribution of X.
Proof (discrete). Let Y = g(X). Then:
\mathbb{E}[Y] = \sum_y y, P(Y = y) = \sum_y y \sum_{x:, g(x)=y} P(X=x) = \sum_x g(x),P(X=x) \qquad \blacksquare
The last step collects all x with the same g-value.

LOTUS is why we can compute \mathbb{E}[X^2], \mathbb{E}[1/X], \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] (the MGF) — all without deriving a new distribution. It’s implicit in every moment calculation I’ve written in these notes.

Example. X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1). Compute \mathbb{E}[X^2].
\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \int_0^1 x^2 \cdot 1, dx = \frac{1}{3}
No need to find the distribution of X^2.
Example. X \sim \text{Geom}(p) on {1,2,\ldots}. Compute \mathbb{E}[X(X-1)] (the second factorial moment).
\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)] = \sum_{k=1}^\infty k(k-1)(1-p)^{k-1}p
Differentiate the generating function \sum_{k=0}^\infty r^k = 1/(1-r) twice with respect to r to evaluate. Result: \mathbb{E}[X(X-1)] = 2(1-p)/p^2, from which \text{Var}(X) = (1-p)/p^2.

4. Independence and Expectation of Products
\boxed{X \perp Y \implies \mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X],\mathbb{E}[Y]}
Proof (discrete).
\mathbb{E}[XY] = \sum_x\sum_y xy, P(X=x,, Y=y) \overset{\perp}{=} \sum_x\sum_y xy, P(X=x)P(Y=y)
= \left(\sum_x x,P(X=x)\right)\left(\sum_y y,P(Y=y)\right) = \mathbb{E}[X],\mathbb{E}[Y] \qquad \blacksquare
The converse is false. \mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] (i.e. \text{Cov}(X,Y)=0) does not imply independence. Uncorrelated \not\Rightarrow independent. Standard counterexample: X \sim \text{Uniform}(-1,1), Y = X^2. Then \text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[X^3] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[X^2] = 0 - 0 = 0, but Y is a deterministic function of X.
Extension. For X_1, \ldots, X_n mutually independent:
\mathbb{E}!\left[\prod_{i=1}^n g_i(X_i)\right] = \prod_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[g_i(X_i)]
by the same factorisation argument applied to the joint PMF/PDF.

5. Jensen’s Inequality
\boxed{g \text{ convex} \implies \mathbb{E}[g(X)] \geq g(\mathbb{E}[X])}
\boxed{g \text{ concave} \implies \mathbb{E}[g(X)] \leq g(\mathbb{E}[X])}
Proof. Since g is convex, for any \mu = \mathbb{E}[X] there exists a supporting hyperplane: a linear function \ell(x) = g(\mu) + c(x - \mu) such that g(x) \geq \ell(x) for all x. Then:
\mathbb{E}[g(X)] \geq \mathbb{E}[\ell(X)] = g(\mu) + c(\mathbb{E}[X] - \mu) = g(\mu) \qquad \blacksquare

The supporting hyperplane is the tangent line at \mu (when g is differentiable). Jensen says: convexity curves upward, so the function evaluated at the average is below the average of the function. Draw this — it’s obvious geometrically, and the proof just formalises the picture.

Common applications:



































Function gConvex/ConcaveJensen givese^xConvex\mathbb{E}[e^X] \geq e^{\mathbb{E}[X]}x^2Convex\mathbb{E}[X^2] \geq (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 — i.e. \text{Var}(X) \geq 0\log xConcave\mathbb{E}[\log X] \leq \log\mathbb{E}[X]\sqrt{x}Concave\mathbb{E}[\sqrt{X}] \leq \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X]}1/xConvex (x>0)\mathbb{E}[1/X] \geq 1/\mathbb{E}[X]
The second row is particularly important: Jensen applied to g(x) = x^2 immediately gives \text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 \geq 0. Variance non-negativity is just Jensen.
When does equality hold? \mathbb{E}[g(X)] = g(\mathbb{E}[X]) iff X is a.s. constant, or g is linear on the support of X.

6. Markov’s Inequality
\boxed{X \geq 0 \text{ a.s.},; a > 0 \implies P(X \geq a) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[X]}{a}}
Proof.
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[X \cdot \mathbf{1}_{X \geq a}] + \mathbb{E}[X \cdot \mathbf{1}_{X < a}] \geq \mathbb{E}[X \cdot \mathbf{1}_{X \geq a}] \geq a, P(X \geq a) \qquad \blacksquare
The first inequality drops a non-negative term; the second uses X \geq a on the event {X \geq a}.

Markov’s inequality is weak but universal — it needs only non-negativity and a finite mean. Every other tail bound (Chebyshev, Chernoff) is Markov applied to a smarter function of X.

Chebyshev from Markov. Apply Markov to Y = (X - \mu)^2 \geq 0 with a = \varepsilon^2:
P(|X - \mu| \geq \varepsilon) = P((X-\mu)^2 \geq \varepsilon^2) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]}{\varepsilon^2} = \frac{\text{Var}(X)}{\varepsilon^2}
Chernoff from Markov. Apply Markov to Y = e^{tX} with a = e^{ta}:
P(X \geq a) = P(e^{tX} \geq e^{ta}) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]}{e^{ta}} = e^{-ta} M_X(t)
Optimise over t > 0 to get the sharpest bound. This is the MGF method.

7. Tail Sum Formula
For a non-negative integer-valued RV X:
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty P(X > k) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty P(X \geq k)}
For a non-negative continuous RV X:
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^\infty P(X > t), dt}
Proof (continuous). Switch the order of integration:
\int_0^\infty P(X > t), dt = \int_0^\infty \int_t^\infty f_X(x), dx, dt = \int_0^\infty \int_0^x dt, f_X(x), dx = \int_0^\infty x, f_X(x), dx = \mathbb{E}[X]
The region {(t,x) : 0 \leq t \leq x} is integrated two ways: first x then t, or first t then x. \blacksquare
Proof (discrete). Write X = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \mathbf{1}_{X \geq k}, take expectations, apply linearity. \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_{X \geq k}] = P(X \geq k). \blacksquare

This formula converts a sum/integral over the distribution of X into a sum/integral over the survival function P(X > t). It’s often easier to compute P(X > t) than the full distribution, so this is a genuine computational tool — not just a curiosity.

Example. X \sim \text{Geom}(p) on {0, 1, 2, \ldots} (number of failures before first success). Then P(X > k) = (1-p)^{k+1}.
\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty (1-p)^{k+1} = \frac{1-p}{1-(1-p)} = \frac{1-p}{p}
No need for the standard \mathbb{E}[X] = \sum k(1-p)^k p computation.

8. Symmetry
If X is symmetric about 0 (i.e. X \overset{d}{=} -X) and \mathbb{E}|X| < \infty:
\mathbb{E}[X] = 0
Proof. \mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[-X] = -\mathbb{E}[X], so \mathbb{E}[X] = 0. \blacksquare
More generally, if X is symmetric about \mu (i.e. X - \mu \overset{d}{=} \mu - X), then \mathbb{E}[X] = \mu.

9. Summary


















































PropertyStatementKey conditionLinearity\mathbb{E}[aX+bY] = a\mathbb{E}[X]+b\mathbb{E}[Y]None — always holdsNon-negativityX \geq 0 \Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[X] \geq 0X \geq 0 a.s.LOTUS\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int g(x)f(x)dxg measurableProduct rule\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]X \perp YJensen\mathbb{E}[g(X)] \geq g(\mathbb{E}[X])g convexMarkovP(X\geq a) \leq \mathbb{E}[X]/aX \geq 0, a > 0Tail sum\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^\infty P(X>t)dtX \geq 0SymmetryX \overset{d}{=} -X \Rightarrow \mathbb{E}[X] = 0Symmetric about 0

References

Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, §4.1–4.3 (expectation, LOTUS, linearity), §10.1 (inequalities)
Harvard Stat 110, Lectures 7–8 (linearity and indicators), Lecture 15 (Jensen, Markov, Chebyshev) — the indicator decomposition approach to computing means is a theme throughout


Links

Conditional Expectation — all properties extend conditionally: \mathbb{E}[aX+bY\mid Z] = a\mathbb{E}[X\mid Z]+b\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z], conditional Jensen, etc.
Adams Law — the deepest property of conditional expectation; uses linearity at its core
Beta Expectations — every computation there is LOTUS + Beta integral recognition
Order Statistics — indicator trick used to get \mathbb{E}[U_{(k)}] = k/(n+1) via spacing symmetry

Open Questions

 Prove the continuous version of the tail sum formula by Fubini’s theorem stated precisely — what integrability condition is needed to swap the order?
 Reverse Jensen: when is \mathbb{E}[g(X)] \leq g(\mathbb{E}[X]) + C for some controlled C? (Connects to concentration inequalities)
 When does \mathbb{E}[g(X)] = g(\mathbb{E}[X]) characterise X being degenerate? Make this precise.
 Cauchy-Schwarz: (\mathbb{E}[XY])^2 \leq \mathbb{E}[X^2]\mathbb{E}[Y^2] — prove via non-negativity of \mathbb{E}[(X - tY)^2] as a quadratic in t

01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.title: 04.Adam's Law with Extra Conditioning
01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.content:
This is the version of Adam’s Law that trips people up on exams and in proofs. The basic form \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]] = \mathbb{E}[X] is intuitive. But what happens when there’s already some conditioning in the background — when everything is happening conditional on Z? The answer is clean, but you have to see it clearly at least once to trust it.


0. The Statement
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z] \mid Z] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z]}
Reading it: inside, we condition on both Y and Z. Outside, we average over Y — but Z is held fixed throughout. The result: the Y-conditioning disappears, and we’re left with conditioning on Z alone.
This is the Tower Property in full generality. The basic Adam’s Law \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]] = \mathbb{E}[X] is the special case Z = \emptyset (no background conditioning).

1. Proof
Work conditional on Z = z throughout. For fixed z, apply ordinary Adam’s Law in the conditional universe where Z = z:
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z] \mid Z = z] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z=z] \mid Z=z]
Now Z = z is fixed — so \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z=z] is a function of Y alone (call it g(Y) where g(y) = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=y, Z=z]). Adam’s Law in the Z=z universe says:
\mathbb{E}[g(Y) \mid Z = z] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z = z]
Since this holds for every z, we conclude:
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z] \mid Z] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z] \qquad \blacksquare

The proof is just: freeze Z, apply ordinary Adam’s Law in the reduced universe, unfreeze. Every property of conditional expectation works this way — condition on Z and you’re back in familiar territory.


2. The Nesting Condition
The Tower Property requires that the inner conditioning is finer than the outer. Precisely:
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}] \mid \mathcal{H}] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{H}] \quad \text{when } \mathcal{H} \subseteq \mathcal{G}
In variable terms: the outer conditioning must involve less information than the inner. Examples of valid nestings:






























InnerOuterValid?\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z]condition on Z✓ — Z alone is less than (Y,Z)\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z]condition on Y✓ — Y alone is less than (Y,Z)\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]condition on g(Y) for some function g✓ — g(Y) is coarser than Y\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]condition on Z (unrelated)✗ — no nesting, cannot simplify
The last row is the common mistake. \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]\mid Z] does not generally simplify unless Z and Y are related (e.g. Z is a function of Y, or X \perp Z \mid Y).

3. Two Directions of the Tower
There are two useful forms, both valid:
Form 1 (average out the finer): \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z] \mid Z] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z] Conditioning on Y additionally inside, then averaging Y away outside, leaves Z.
Form 2 (adding coarser conditioning outside does nothing): \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Z] \mid Y, Z] = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z] \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z] is already a function of Z. Conditioning additionally on Y outside cannot change a quantity that depends only on Z — “taking out what is known.”

Form 2 is the “taking out what is known” property in disguise. If you already have Z in the outer conditioning, anything that depends only on Z passes through unchanged.


4. Worked Examples
4.1 Three-Level Hierarchy
\Theta \sim \text{prior}, \Lambda \mid \Theta \sim \text{something}, X \mid \Lambda, \Theta \sim \text{Poisson}(\Lambda).
Suppose \mathbb{E}[X \mid \Lambda, \Theta] = \Lambda (Poisson mean). What is \mathbb{E}[X \mid \Theta]?
\mathbb{E}[X \mid \Theta] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid \Lambda, \Theta] \mid \Theta] = \mathbb{E}[\Lambda \mid \Theta]
The tower collapses one level: X-given-(\Lambda,\Theta) averaged over \Lambda becomes X-given-\Theta. To go all the way:
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid \Theta]] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[\Lambda \mid \Theta]] = \mathbb{E}[\Lambda]
Each application of Adam’s Law strips one layer of conditioning.
4.2 Order Statistics Conditional Mean
Let U_{(1)} \leq \cdots \leq U_{(n)} be order statistics of n i.i.d. \text{Uniform}(0,1). What is \mathbb{E}[U_{(k)} \mid U_{(j)}] for j < k?
Given U_{(j)} = u, the variables U_{(j+1)}, \ldots, U_{(n)} are the order statistics of n - j i.i.d. Uniforms on (u, 1) (by the memoryless-like property of order statistics given an intermediate value). So:
\mathbb{E}[U_{(k)} \mid U_{(j)} = u] = u + (1-u)\cdot \frac{k-j}{n-j+1}
The k-th order statistic among the upper n-j uniforms on (u,1) sits at position (k-j)/(n-j+1) of the remaining interval (u,1).
Now verify Adam’s Law: \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[U_{(k)}\mid U_{(j)}]] = \mathbb{E}[U_{(k)}]?
\mathbb{E}!\left[U_{(j)} + (1-U_{(j)})\frac{k-j}{n-j+1}\right] = \frac{j}{n+1} + \left(1 - \frac{j}{n+1}\right)\frac{k-j}{n-j+1}
= \frac{j}{n+1} + \frac{n-j+1}{n+1}\cdot\frac{k-j}{n-j+1} = \frac{j}{n+1} + \frac{k-j}{n+1} = \frac{k}{n+1} = \mathbb{E}[U_{(k)}] \qquad \checkmark

A nice sanity check: the tower collapses correctly, and the answer k/(n+1) from Order Statistics comes out.

4.3 Conditional Variance via Eve’s Law with Extra Conditioning
Eve’s Law also has an extra-conditioning version:
\text{Var}(X \mid Z) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X \mid Y, Z) \mid Z] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z] \mid Z)
Proof. Apply Eve’s Law in the conditional universe given Z = z, then unfreeze z. \blacksquare
Reading it:

\text{Var}(X \mid Z) = total conditional variance given Z
\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X \mid Y, Z) \mid Z] = unexplained variance (noise within Y-groups, averaged over Y)
\text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z] \mid Z) = explained variance (spread of conditional means across Y-values)

Same decomposition as ordinary Eve’s Law, but everything lives in the Z-conditional universe.

5. The Martingale in Disguise
Plant this seed now — it will matter in Stat 212.
Define M_n = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y_1, \ldots, Y_n] for a sequence Y_1, Y_2, \ldots of observed variables. Then (M_n) is a martingale:
\mathbb{E}[M_n \mid M_1, \ldots, M_{n-1}] = M_{n-1}
Why? M_{n-1} = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_{n-1}]. By the tower property:
\mathbb{E}[M_n \mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_{n-1}] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]\mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_{n-1}] = \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y_1,\ldots,Y_{n-1}] = M_{n-1}
The Tower Property is the martingale property. Every time you update a Bayesian posterior as new data arrives, you’re running a martingale. The sequence of posterior means is a martingale with respect to the data filtration.

6. Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Collapsing without nesting.
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y] \mid Z] \neq \mathbb{E}[X \mid Z] \quad \text{in general}
This would require Z to be “coarser” than Y, i.e. Z = g(Y) for some g. If Z is independent of Y, the left side is \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]]= \mathbb{E}[X], not \mathbb{E}[X\mid Z] (unless X \perp Z).
Mistake 2: Forgetting the background Z in the inner expectation.
Writing \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]\mid Z] when you mean \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y,Z]\mid Z] is a different object. In hierarchical models where Z affects the distribution of X directly, you must include Z in the inner conditioning.
Mistake 3: Applying tower to variance directly.
\text{Var}(X) \neq \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)]
This ignores the explained variance term. The correct statement is Eve’s Law. Variance does not telescope the way expectation does.

7. Summary






























FormStatementWhen to useBasic Adam\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]] = \mathbb{E}[X]No background conditioningTower (strip outer)\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y,Z]\mid Z] = \mathbb{E}[X\mid Z]Average away finer conditioning YTower (add coarser)\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Z]\mid Y,Z] = \mathbb{E}[X\mid Z]Known function of Z is unchangedEve’s with Z\text{Var}(X\mid Z) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y,Z)\mid Z] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y,Z]\mid Z)Variance decomposition in Z-universe
The one-line rule: The tower collapses the inner conditioning to match the outer, provided the outer is coarser. Coarser wins.

References

Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, §9.3 (Tower property), §9.4 (Eve’s Law)
Harvard Stat 110, Lecture 20 — the extra conditioning form is used implicitly in every hierarchical model; the martingale connection is mentioned briefly and developed in Stat 212


Links

Adams Law — the basic form; this note is the strict generalisation
Conditional Expectation — definitions, “taking out what is known,” projection interpretation
Beta Expectations — §6 uses Eve’s Law; the extra-conditioning version applies in multi-level Beta hierarchies
Order Statistics — §4.2 above is an extended example using tower on order statistics

Open Questions

 Make the \sigma-algebra version precise: \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]\mid\mathcal{H}] = \mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{H}] for \mathcal{H}\subseteq\mathcal{G} — this is Stat 210 territory but worth stating cleanly
 Prove that (M_n) defined in §5 is a uniformly integrable martingale when \mathbb{E}|X| < \infty — this is what guarantees M_n \to X a.s. (Lévy’s upward theorem)
 What is \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]\mid Z] explicitly when X,Y,Z are jointly Gaussian? (Gaussian conditioning is linear — the answer is computable in closed form)

01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.title: 05.Linear Regression
01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.content:
Linear regression sits at the intersection of everything we’ve built. It’s not just a fitting procedure — it’s a statement about conditional expectation, a consequence of the projection interpretation of \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y], and a direct application of Eve’s Law. The moment I saw that the regression line minimises MSE by the same argument as the projection theorem, the whole thing clicked into place.


0. The Setup and the Question
We have two random variables X and Y on the same probability space. We want to predict Y from X — find a function g(X) that is “close” to Y in some sense.
The best predictor (minimising mean squared error) is \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] — this is the projection theorem from Conditional Expectation §4. But \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] can be any function of X: nonlinear, discontinuous, anything.
Restriction: What if we constrain g to be linear — g(X) = a + bX? What are the optimal a and b?
This is simple linear regression: find a, b \in \mathbb{R} minimising:
\text{MSE}(a,b) = \mathbb{E}[(Y - a - bX)^2]

1. Solving for the Optimal Coefficients
1.1 Finding b: The Slope
Expand \text{MSE}(a,b):
\mathbb{E}[(Y - a - bX)^2] = \mathbb{E}[Y^2] + a^2 + b^2\mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2a\mathbb{E}[Y] - 2b\mathbb{E}[XY] + 2ab\mathbb{E}[X]
Differentiate with respect to a and b and set to zero:
\frac{\partial}{\partial a}\text{MSE} = 2a - 2\mathbb{E}[Y] + 2b\mathbb{E}[X] = 0 \implies a = \mathbb{E}[Y] - b\mathbb{E}[X] \tag{1}
\frac{\partial}{\partial b}\text{MSE} = 2b\mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2\mathbb{E}[XY] + 2a\mathbb{E}[X] = 0 \tag{2}
Substitute (1) into (2):
b\mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mathbb{E}[XY] + (\mathbb{E}[Y] - b\mathbb{E}[X])\mathbb{E}[X] = 0
b(\mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]
\boxed{b = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\text{Var}(X)}}
1.2 Finding a: The Intercept
From (1):
\boxed{a = \mathbb{E}[Y] - b,\mathbb{E}[X]}
1.3 The Regression Line
The optimal linear predictor is:
\hat{Y} = \mathbb{E}[Y] + \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\text{Var}(X)}(X - \mathbb{E}[X])
Written symmetrically: the line passes through (\mathbb{E}[X], \mathbb{E}[Y]) — the centre of mass of the joint distribution — with slope \text{Cov}(X,Y)/\text{Var}(X).

The intercept formula a = \mathbb{E}[Y] - b\mathbb{E}[X] tells you something immediately: the regression line always passes through the point of means. This is not a coincidence — it’s forced by the first-order condition on a. The mean is the anchor; the slope tells you the direction.


2. The Correlation Coefficient
Define the correlation:
\boxed{\rho = \text{Corr}(X,Y) = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\text{SD}(X),\text{SD}(Y)}}
where \text{SD}(X) = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}. Then \rho \in [-1, 1] (proved below) and the slope becomes:
b = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\text{Var}(X)} = \rho \cdot \frac{\text{SD}(Y)}{\text{SD}(X)}
So the regression line is:
\frac{\hat{Y} - \mathbb{E}[Y]}{\text{SD}(Y)} = \rho \cdot \frac{X - \mathbb{E}[X]}{\text{SD}(X)}
In standardised units: a 1 standard deviation move in X corresponds to a \rho standard deviation move in \hat{Y}. The correlation is exactly the slope in standardised coordinates.
Proof that |\rho| \leq 1. Apply Cauchy-Schwarz:
|\text{Cov}(X,Y)| = |\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)]| \leq \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)^2]}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mu_Y)^2]} = \text{SD}(X),\text{SD}(Y)
Divide both sides by \text{SD}(X),\text{SD}(Y): |\rho| \leq 1. \blacksquare
Equality |\rho| = 1 iff Y - \mu_Y = c(X-\mu_X) a.s. for some constant c — i.e. Y is a.s. a linear function of X.
Alternatively via non-negativity. For all t \in \mathbb{R}:
0 \leq \text{Var}(tX + Y) = t^2\text{Var}(X) + 2t,\text{Cov}(X,Y) + \text{Var}(Y)
This quadratic in t is non-negative, so its discriminant is \leq 0:
4,\text{Cov}(X,Y)^2 - 4,\text{Var}(X),\text{Var}(Y) \leq 0 \implies \rho^2 \leq 1 \qquad \blacksquare

3. The Minimum MSE and R^2
What is the MSE achieved by the optimal linear predictor?
\text{MSE}^* = \mathbb{E}[(Y - \hat{Y})^2]
Claim:
\boxed{\text{MSE}^* = \text{Var}(Y)(1 - \rho^2)}
Proof. Write the residual Y - \hat{Y} = Y - \mathbb{E}[Y] - b(X - \mathbb{E}[X]). Let \tilde{Y} = Y - \mathbb{E}[Y], \tilde{X} = X - \mathbb{E}[X] (centred variables). Then:
\text{MSE}^* = \mathbb{E}[(\tilde{Y} - b\tilde{X})^2] = \text{Var}(Y) - 2b,\text{Cov}(X,Y) + b^2\text{Var}(X)
Substitute b = \text{Cov}(X,Y)/\text{Var}(X):
= \text{Var}(Y) - 2\frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\text{Var}(X)} + \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\text{Var}(X)} = \text{Var}(Y) - \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\text{Var}(X)}
= \text{Var}(Y)\left(1 - \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\text{Var}(X)\text{Var}(Y)}\right) = \text{Var}(Y)(1 - \rho^2) \qquad \blacksquare
Reading the formula:

\rho^2 = 0: no linear relationship, \text{MSE}^* = \text{Var}(Y) — predicting \hat{Y} = \mathbb{E}[Y] (the constant predictor) is optimal
\rho^2 = 1: perfect linear relationship, \text{MSE}^* = 0 — we can predict Y from X without error
\rho^2 \in (0,1): partial predictability; \rho^2 is the proportion of variance explained

This is R^2 from regression: R^2 = \rho^2 = 1 - \text{MSE}^*/\text{Var}(Y).

4. Connection to Eve’s Law
This is the punchline I promised at the top.
Eve’s Law (Conditional Expectation §3) says:
\text{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(Y\mid X)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])
Now if \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] is linear in X — i.e. \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] = a + bX — then:
\text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]) = b^2\text{Var}(X) = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\text{Var}(X)} = \rho^2,\text{Var}(Y)
\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(Y\mid X)] = \text{Var}(Y) - \rho^2,\text{Var}(Y) = (1-\rho^2),\text{Var}(Y)
So:

Explained variance = \rho^2,\text{Var}(Y) = variance of the fitted values
Unexplained variance = (1-\rho^2),\text{Var}(Y) = variance of the residuals = MSE^*

Eve’s Law is exactly the ANOVA decomposition: \text{SS}_\text{total} = \text{SS}_\text{regression} + \text{SS}_\text{residual}.

When \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] is truly linear — e.g. in the bivariate normal — this isn’t an approximation. The linear predictor IS the conditional expectation. When \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] is nonlinear, the regression line is the best linear approximation to it, and R^2 = \rho^2 understates the true predictive power of X.


5. The Bivariate Normal: When Linearity is Exact
(X,Y) jointly bivariate normal with means \mu_X, \mu_Y, variances \sigma_X^2, \sigma_Y^2, correlation \rho. Then:
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] = \mu_Y + \rho\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(X - \mu_X)
\text{Var}(Y \mid X) = \sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2)
This is exact — not an approximation. For bivariate normals, the conditional expectation \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] is linear in X. So the linear regression IS the optimal predictor, not merely the best linear one.
Note also: \text{Var}(Y\mid X) = \sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2) is constant in X (homoskedasticity). The residual variance does not depend on where you are on the X-axis. This is a special property of the normal.
Proof sketch. Write Y = \mu_Y + \rho\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(X-\mu_X) + \varepsilon where \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2)) and \varepsilon \perp X (verify by computing \text{Cov}(\varepsilon, X) = 0 and using joint normality implies independence). Then \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] = \mu_Y + \rho\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(X-\mu_X) and \text{Var}(Y\mid X) = \text{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2). \blacksquare

6. Regression to the Mean
This is the phenomenon Galton discovered and named “regression.” It’s worth understanding precisely.
In standardised units, the regression prediction is \hat{Z}_Y = \rho Z_X where Z_X = (X-\mu_X)/\sigma_X, Z_Y = (Y-\mu_Y)/\sigma_Y.
If |\rho| < 1, then |\hat{Z}_Y| < |Z_X| — the predicted Y is closer to the mean (in standard deviations) than X is. An extreme observation of X predicts a less extreme Y.
Why? Because extreme X values arise partly from the linear relationship with Y and partly from noise. The noise doesn’t persist into Y. The factor \rho attenuates the signal.
The Galton paradox. Tall parents tend to have tall children, but children of the tallest parents are on average shorter than their parents (though still taller than average). This is not biology — it’s mathematics. \rho < 1 for any two non-perfectly-correlated variables.

Regression to the mean is responsible for an enormous number of misattributed causal stories. Intervention after an extreme outcome looks effective simply because of this phenomenon. Keep this in the back of your head whenever someone claims “it worked” after treating an outlier.


7. Summary of Key Formulas





































QuantityFormulaSlopeb = \text{Cov}(X,Y)/\text{Var}(X) = \rho,\sigma_Y/\sigma_XIntercepta = \mathbb{E}[Y] - b,\mathbb{E}[X]Correlation\rho = \text{Cov}(X,Y)/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y) \in [-1,1]Minimum MSE\text{Var}(Y)(1-\rho^2)R^2\rho^2 = proportion of variance explainedBivariate normal \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]\mu_Y + \rho(\sigma_Y/\sigma_X)(X-\mu_X) — exact, not approximateBivariate normal \text{Var}(Y\mid X)\sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2) — constant in X

References

Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, §7.5 (correlation), §9.5 (linear regression as conditional expectation, R^2), §7.6 (bivariate normal)
Harvard Stat 110, Lecture 21 — regression is introduced directly from the MSE minimisation perspective; the Eve’s Law connection to ANOVA is the payoff of the lecture


Links

Conditional Expectation — projection theorem: \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] is the best predictor; linear regression is the best linear predictor
Adams Law — used in §4 to connect regression to Eve’s Law
Properties of Expectation — Cauchy-Schwarz and variance non-negativity used to prove |\rho| \leq 1
Beta Expectations — R^2 interpretation mirrors the explained/unexplained split in Eve’s Law

Open Questions

 Multiple regression: generalise to \hat{Y} = a + b_1X_1 + \cdots + b_pX_p. The normal equations become a matrix system \mathbf{b} = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y} — derive this as the multivariate projection
 When \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] is nonlinear, is the linear regression slope still \text{Cov}(X,Y)/\text{Var}(X)? (Yes — the formula is always optimal among linear predictors regardless of the true conditional expectation)
 Prove that in the bivariate normal, \varepsilon = Y - \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] is independent of X — not just uncorrelated. This uses the fact that joint normality plus uncorrelated implies independent
 What is \text{Corr}(X, Y-\hat{Y})? (It’s 0 — the residual is uncorrelated with the predictor by the first-order condition. Verify this directly from the formula for a.)

01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.title: 06.Geometric Interpretation of Conditional Expectation
01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.content:
This is the note that reframes everything. Once you see conditional expectation as orthogonal projection in a Hilbert space, every identity we’ve proved — Adam’s Law, Eve’s Law, the regression formula, the Tower Property — becomes a geometric theorem. The algebra didn’t lie, but the geometry explains why it had to come out that way. I wish I had this picture from day one.


0. The Space
Define the space:
L^2 = {X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R} \mid \mathbb{E}[X^2] < \infty}
Elements of L^2 are random variables with finite second moment. We give this space an inner product:
\langle X, Y \rangle = \mathbb{E}[XY]
Verification that this is an inner product:

Symmetry: \langle X, Y\rangle = \mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[YX] = \langle Y,X\rangle ✓
Linearity: \langle aX + bZ, Y\rangle = \mathbb{E}[(aX+bZ)Y] = a\mathbb{E}[XY] + b\mathbb{E}[ZY] ✓
Non-negativity: \langle X,X\rangle = \mathbb{E}[X^2] \geq 0 ✓
Definiteness: \langle X,X\rangle = 0 \iff \mathbb{E}[X^2] = 0 \iff X = 0 a.s. ✓

(Technically we work with equivalence classes of a.s.-equal RVs to make definiteness exact — but don’t lose sleep over this.)
The induced norm is:
|X| = \sqrt{\langle X,X\rangle} = \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]}
This is the L^2 norm, or the root mean square. With this structure, L^2 is a Hilbert space — a complete inner product space. Infinite-dimensional, but all the Euclidean geometry you know works here.

1. Orthogonality
Two random variables X, Y \in L^2 are orthogonal if:
X \perp_2 Y \iff \langle X, Y\rangle = 0 \iff \mathbb{E}[XY] = 0
This is a statement about second moments — not the same as independence (X \perp Y). Independence implies orthogonality of centred variables, but not conversely.
Centering and orthogonality. It is often more natural to work with centred variables. Define:
\tilde{X} = X - \mathbb{E}[X], \quad \tilde{Y} = Y - \mathbb{E}[Y]
Then:
\langle \tilde{X}, \tilde{Y}\rangle = \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}\tilde{Y}] = \text{Cov}(X,Y)
So \text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0 (uncorrelatedness) is orthogonality of the centred versions in L^2.
The norm of a centred variable:
|\tilde{X}|^2 = \mathbb{E}[\tilde{X}^2] = \text{Var}(X)
Standard deviation is the L^2 norm of the centred variable. Correlation is the cosine of the angle between the centred variables:
\rho(X,Y) = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\text{SD}(X),\text{SD}(Y)} = \frac{\langle \tilde{X},\tilde{Y}\rangle}{|\tilde{X}||\tilde{Y}|} = \cos\theta
where \theta is the angle between \tilde{X} and \tilde{Y} in L^2. This is exactly the formula for cosine in Euclidean geometry. Correlation is cosine.

\rho = 1: vectors point the same direction (Y is a positive linear function of X). \rho = -1: opposite directions. \rho = 0: right angle — uncorrelated, orthogonal centred variables. The |\rho| \leq 1 bound is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality: |\cos\theta| \leq 1.


2. Projection
Let V \subseteq L^2 be a closed subspace — think of it as a “flat” (a hyperplane, a line, a plane through the origin) inside the Hilbert space.
Theorem (Projection). For any Y \in L^2, there exists a unique element \hat{Y} \in V such that:
|Y - \hat{Y}| = \min_{Z \in V} |Y - Z|
This \hat{Y} is the orthogonal projection of Y onto V. It is characterised by the orthogonality condition:
Y - \hat{Y} \perp_2 Z \quad \text{for all } Z \in V
i.e. \mathbb{E}[(Y - \hat{Y})Z] = 0 for all Z \in V.
Why this characterises it. For any Z \in V:
|Y - Z|^2 = |Y - \hat{Y} + \hat{Y} - Z|^2 = |Y - \hat{Y}|^2 + |\hat{Y} - Z|^2 + 2\langle Y - \hat{Y}, \hat{Y} - Z\rangle
The cross term vanishes by the orthogonality condition (Y - \hat{Y} \perp_2 \hat{Y} - Z since \hat{Y} - Z \in V). So:
|Y - Z|^2 = |Y - \hat{Y}|^2 + |\hat{Y} - Z|^2 \geq |Y - \hat{Y}|^2
with equality iff Z = \hat{Y}. This is the Pythagorean theorem in L^2. \blacksquare

3. Conditional Expectation IS Projection
Theorem. \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] is the orthogonal projection of Y onto:
V_X = {g(X) : g \text{ measurable}, \mathbb{E}[g(X)^2] < \infty}
the subspace of all (square-integrable) functions of X.
Proof. We need to show \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] \in V_X and Y - \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] \perp_2 Z for all Z \in V_X.
The first part is clear: \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] = g(X) for g(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x], so it’s in V_X.
For the second: take any Z = h(X) \in V_X. Then:
\mathbb{E}[(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])h(X)] = \mathbb{E}[Yh(X)] - \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]h(X)]
For the second term, use “taking out what is known”:
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]h(X)] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Yh(X)\mid X]] = \mathbb{E}[Yh(X)]
So \mathbb{E}[(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])h(X)] = 0 for all h(X) \in V_X — the residual is orthogonal to the subspace. \blacksquare

The “taking out what is known” property from Conditional Expectation is doing all the work. Geometrically it’s saying: projections are self-adjoint. The projection of Y onto V_X, dotted against anything in V_X, equals Y dotted against that thing.


4. Every Identity as Geometry
4.1 Adam’s Law: Projection Preserves Mass
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]] = \mathbb{E}[Y]
Geometrically. The constant random variable \mathbf{1} \in V_X (since \mathbf{1} = g(X) with g \equiv 1). Take h(X) = 1 in the orthogonality condition:
\mathbb{E}[(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]) \cdot 1] = 0 \implies \mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]
Adam’s Law is orthogonality with respect to the constant vector \mathbf{1}. \blacksquare
4.2 Eve’s Law: The Pythagorean Theorem
\text{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(Y\mid X)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])
Geometrically. Work with centred \tilde{Y} = Y - \mathbb{E}[Y]. Its projection onto \widetilde{V}_X (centred functions of X) is \widetilde{\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]} = \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] - \mathbb{E}[Y].
The Pythagorean theorem in L^2 says:
|\tilde{Y}|^2 = |\tilde{Y} - \text{proj}|^2 + |\text{proj}|^2
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\tilde{Y}^2]}_{\text{Var}(Y)} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])^2]}_{\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(Y\mid X)]} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] - \mathbb{E}[Y])^2]}_{\text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])}
Eve’s Law is the Pythagorean theorem. \blacksquare
        Y
       /|
      / |
     /  |  ← residual Y - Ŷ (orthogonal to V_X)
    /   |
   /    |
  Ŷ----+-------- V_X
  ↑
  E[Y|X] = projection

The hypotenuse is \tilde{Y} (total variation). The leg along V_X is \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X] - \mathbb{E}[Y] (explained variation). The leg perpendicular to V_X is the residual (unexplained variation).
4.3 Tower Property: Projection of a Projection
\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X, Z] \mid Z] = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid Z]
Geometrically. Let V_{X,Z} be functions of (X,Z) and V_Z be functions of Z alone. Clearly V_Z \subseteq V_{X,Z}.
Projecting Y onto the larger subspace V_{X,Z} gives \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X,Z]. Now project that onto the smaller subspace V_Z. The result is the same as projecting Y directly onto V_Z:
\text{proj}_{V_Z}(\text{proj}_{V_{X,Z}}(Y)) = \text{proj}_{V_Z}(Y)
This is the idempotency of nested projections — a standard theorem in Hilbert spaces. The Tower Property is exactly this. \blacksquare

In \mathbb{R}^3: projecting a vector onto a plane, then projecting that result onto a line within the plane, gives the same answer as projecting the original vector directly onto the line. Draw this. It’s obvious in 3D, and the same fact holds in L^2.

4.4 Linear Regression: Projection onto a Line
From 01.Linear Regression, the optimal linear predictor \hat{Y} = a + bX minimises \mathbb{E}[(Y - a - bX)^2].
Geometrically: restrict the projection to the subspace V_\text{lin} = {a + bX : a, b \in \mathbb{R}} \subset V_X, a two-dimensional subspace (spanned by \mathbf{1} and X).
The slope formula b = \text{Cov}(X,Y)/\text{Var}(X) = \langle \tilde{Y}, \tilde{X}\rangle / |\tilde{X}|^2 is exactly the formula for the projection coefficient onto \tilde{X} in L^2 — just like projecting a vector \mathbf{v} onto a vector \mathbf{u} gives coefficient \langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u}\rangle / |\mathbf{u}|^2.
The minimum \text{MSE}^* = \text{Var}(Y)(1 - \rho^2) is the squared length of the residual after projection — by the Pythagorean theorem in V_\text{lin}.
|\tilde{Y}|^2 = |\hat{\tilde{Y}}|^2 + |\tilde{Y} - \hat{\tilde{Y}}|^2 \text{Var}(Y) = \rho^2,\text{Var}(Y) + (1-\rho^2),\text{Var}(Y)
R^2 = \rho^2 = \cos^2\theta where \theta is the angle between \tilde{Y} and \tilde{X}.

5. Cauchy-Schwarz is the Cosine Bound
In Euclidean space: |\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}| because |\cos\theta| \leq 1.
In L^2: exactly the same.
|\langle X, Y\rangle| \leq |X||Y| \iff |\mathbb{E}[XY]| \leq \sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[Y^2]}
Applied to centred variables: |\text{Cov}(X,Y)| \leq \text{SD}(X),\text{SD}(Y), i.e. |\rho| \leq 1.
Proof in L^2. For any t \in \mathbb{R}:
0 \leq |X - tY|^2 = |X|^2 - 2t\langle X,Y\rangle + t^2|Y|^2
This is a non-negative quadratic in t, so its discriminant is \leq 0:
4\langle X,Y\rangle^2 - 4|X|^2|Y|^2 \leq 0 \qquad \blacksquare
Equality holds iff X = tY a.s. — i.e. one is a scalar multiple of the other, meaning \rho = \pm 1.

6. The Full Dictionary





























































Euclidean \mathbb{R}^nL^2 probabilityVector \mathbf{v}Random variable XInner product \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\mathbb{E}[XY]Norm \|\mathbf{v}\|\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]} (RMS)Length of centred vector\text{SD}(X)\mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v}\mathbb{E}[XY] = 0 (orthogonal)Cosine of angle\text{Corr}(X,Y) = \rhoSubspace spanned by \mathbf{u}V_X = {g(X)}Projection of \mathbf{v} onto subspace\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]Projection coefficientb = \langle \tilde{Y},\tilde{X}\rangle/\|\tilde{X}\|^2 = \text{Cov}/\text{Var}Pythagorean theoremEve’s LawCauchy-Schwarz$Nested projection idempotencyTower PropertyProjection onto 1D subspaceLinear regression

7. What the Geometry Cannot Tell You
The L^2 geometry captures second-moment information: means, variances, covariances, correlations, linear regression. It does not capture:

Higher moments (skewness, kurtosis)
Tail behaviour
The actual conditional distribution f_{Y\mid X} (only its mean \mathbb{E}[Y\mid X])
Independence (only uncorrelatedness / orthogonality)

For the bivariate normal, the second-moment picture is the whole picture — because the normal is entirely characterised by its first two moments. That’s why the bivariate normal is the natural home for all of this geometry.

References

Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, §9.5 (projection interpretation), §7.5 (correlation as cosine)
Harvard Stat 110, Lecture 21 — the projection picture is introduced here; Blitzstein draws the right-angle diagram explicitly
Luenberger, Optimization by Vector Space Methods, Ch. 3 — the Hilbert space projection theorem in full generality, if you want the functional analysis underneath


Links

Conditional Expectation — the projection theorem is stated in §4; this note provides the full geometric development

Adams Law — proved geometrically in §4.1: orthogonality with respect to \mathbf{1}
Adams Law with Extra Conditioning — Tower Property proved geometrically in §4.3: nested projection idempotency
Properties of Expectation — Cauchy-Schwarz proved geometrically in §5

Open Questions

 Make the subspace V_X precise as a closed subspace of L^2 — why is it closed? (Completeness of L^2 + measurability)
 The projection theorem requires V to be a closed subspace. Why does V_X = {g(X)} qualify? What goes wrong if it isn’t closed?
 Gram-Schmidt in L^2: orthogonalise {1, X, X^2, \ldots} to get orthogonal polynomials (Hermite polynomials for the Gaussian measure). This is the beginning of polynomial regression and spectral methods
 For (X,Y) bivariate normal: the projection of Y onto V_X equals the projection onto V_\text{lin} — they coincide because the conditional expectation is exactly linear. Characterise all distributions where this holds
 Martingales revisited: (M_n) = (\mathbb{E}[Y\mid \mathcal{F}_n]) is a sequence of nested projections converging to Y. The L^2 convergence M_n \to Y in norm is Lévy’s theorem — prove it using the completeness of L^2

01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.title: 07.Conditional Variance
01.Maths/Probability/09.Conditional-Expe.content:
Conditional variance is the quantity that Eve’s Law decomposes. But before you can use Eve’s Law fluently, you have to be comfortable with what \text{Var}(X \mid Y) actually is — because it has the same type ambiguity as conditional expectation: sometimes a number, sometimes a random variable, and conflating the two is the source of most mistakes.

0. Definition
Conditioning on an Event
For an event A with P(A) > 0, the conditional variance of X given A is just the ordinary variance computed under the conditional distribution:
\text{Var}(X \mid A) = \mathbb{E}[X^2 \mid A] - (\mathbb{E}[X \mid A])^2
This is a number.
Conditioning on a Random Variable
For a random variable Y, define:
\text{Var}(X \mid Y) = \mathbb{E}[X^2 \mid Y] - (\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y])^2 = \mathbb{E}!\left[(X - \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])^2 ,\Big|, Y\right]
This is a random variable — a function of Y, just like \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]. More explicitly: for each value Y = y, compute the conditional variance of X given Y = y as a number, then let Y vary. The result is \text{Var}(X\mid Y) = h(Y) where h(y) = \text{Var}(X \mid Y=y).


                  
                  Type Ambiguity The type ambiguity here is identical to what we saw for \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y] in Conditional Expectation.
                  
                


\text{Var}(X\mid Y=y) is a number.
\text{Var}(X\mid Y) is a random variable.

In Eve’s Law, \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)] takes the expectation of that random variable — averaging the conditional variance over the randomness of Y.



1. Eve’s Law (Law of Total Variance)
\boxed{\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X \mid Y)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y])}
This was proved in Conditional Expectation §3. The two terms:
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X \mid Y)]}_{\text{average within-group variance}} + \underbrace{\text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y])}_{\text{variance of group means}}

First term: on average (over Y), how spread out is X within each Y-group? This is the noise Y cannot explain.
Second term: how much do the group means themselves vary as Y changes? This is the variation Y does explain.

\text{Total variance} = \text{unexplained} + \text{explained}


                  
                  Big Picture This is ANOVA. This is R^2. This is the bias-variance tradeoff. It's all the same identity.
                  
                

1.1 Proof
Start from \text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 and apply Adam’s Law to each piece:
\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X^2 \mid Y]]
Write \mathbb{E}[X^2 \mid Y] = \text{Var}(X\mid Y) + (\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])^2:
\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)] + \mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])^2]
Also (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 = (\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]])^2 by Adam’s Law. Subtracting:
\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)] + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])^2] - (\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]])^2}_{\text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])} \qquad \blacksquare

2. Key Properties
2.1 Non-Negativity
\text{Var}(X \mid Y) \geq 0 \text{ a.s.}
since it’s defined as a conditional expectation of a squared quantity. Therefore both terms in Eve’s Law are non-negative, giving the bound:
\text{Var}(X) \geq \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])
Conditioning on average reduces variance. The conditional mean has less variance than X itself.
2.2 When Does Conditioning Eliminate All Variance?
\text{Var}(X\mid Y) = 0 \text{ a.s.} \iff X \text{ is a.s. a function of } Y
If X = g(Y) for some g, then given Y = y, X = g(y) is deterministic — zero conditional variance. Then Eve’s Law gives:
\text{Var}(X) = 0 + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]) = \text{Var}(g(Y)) = \text{Var}(X) \qquad \checkmark
2.3 When Does Y Explain Nothing?
X \perp Y \implies \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]) = \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X]) = 0
because \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y] = \mathbb{E}[X] (constant) when X \perp Y. Eve’s Law then gives:
\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)] + 0 = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X)] = \text{Var}(X) \qquad \checkmark
Independence means Y explains zero variance in X.
2.4 Linearity of Conditional Variance (Fails in General)


                  
                  Unlike conditional expectation, conditional variance is not linear: \text{Var}(X + Z \mid Y) \neq \text{Var}(X\mid Y) + \text{Var}(Z\mid Y) \quad \text{in general}
                  
                

The correct formula includes a covariance term:
\text{Var}(X + Z \mid Y) = \text{Var}(X\mid Y) + \text{Var}(Z\mid Y) + 2,\text{Cov}(X, Z\mid Y)
where \text{Cov}(X,Z\mid Y) = \mathbb{E}[XZ\mid Y] - \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]\mathbb{E}[Z\mid Y].
If X \perp Z \mid Y (conditional independence given Y), then \text{Cov}(X,Z\mid Y) = 0 and variances add. But unconditional independence is not enough.

3. Eve’s Law with Extra Conditioning
The version with background conditioning on Z:
\text{Var}(X \mid Z) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X \mid Y, Z) \mid Z] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y, Z] \mid Z)
Proof. Apply Eve’s Law in the conditional universe given Z = z, then let z vary. \blacksquare
This is the version used in multi-level models — see §4.3 below.

4. Worked Examples
4.1 Beta-Binomial
W \sim \text{Beta}(a,b), X\mid W \sim \text{Binomial}(n,W), s = a+b.
\text{Var}(X\mid W) = nW(1-W) \quad \text{(random variable, function of } W\text{)} \mathbb{E}[X\mid W] = nW \quad \text{(random variable)}
Unexplained variance:
\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid W)] = n(\mathbb{E}[W] - \mathbb{E}[W^2]) = n!\left(\frac{a}{s} - \frac{a(a+1)}{s(s+1)}\right) = \frac{nab}{s(s+1)}
Explained variance:
\text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid W]) = \text{Var}(nW) = n^2,\text{Var}(W) = \frac{n^2 ab}{s^2(s+1)}
Total:
\text{Var}(X) = \frac{nab}{s(s+1)} + \frac{n^2 ab}{s^2(s+1)} = \frac{nab(s+n)}{s^2(s+1)}
As s = a+b \to \infty (strong prior, W concentrates at p = a/s), \text{Var}(X) \to np(1-p) — recovering the Binomial variance. ✓
4.2 Random Sum (Wald’s Second Identity)
N non-negative integer-valued; X_1, X_2, \ldots i.i.d. with mean \mu, variance \sigma^2, independent of N; S = X_1 + \cdots + X_N.
Conditional on N = n: S = X_1 + \cdots + X_n is a sum of n i.i.d. terms, so:
\mathbb{E}[S\mid N] = N\mu, \qquad \text{Var}(S\mid N) = N\sigma^2
Unexplained variance: \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(S\mid N)] = \sigma^2,\mathbb{E}[N]
Explained variance: \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[S\mid N]) = \text{Var}(N\mu) = \mu^2,\text{Var}(N)
Total (Wald’s second identity):
\boxed{\text{Var}(S) = \sigma^2,\mathbb{E}[N] + \mu^2,\text{Var}(N)}
Reading it:

If N is deterministic (\text{Var}(N) = 0): \text{Var}(S) = n\sigma^2 — standard variance of a fixed sum.
If \mu = 0: \text{Var}(S) = \sigma^2,\mathbb{E}[N] — variance grows with expected number of terms, regardless of how random N is.
Extra variance from random N is \mu^2,\text{Var}(N) — each extra term contributes mean \mu, so uncertainty in the count propagates as \mu^2,\text{Var}(N).

4.3 Three-Level Hierarchy
\Theta \sim \text{prior}, \Lambda \mid \Theta \sim p(\lambda\mid\theta), X\mid\Lambda \sim \text{Pois}(\Lambda).
Step 1. Apply Eve’s Law conditioning on \Lambda:
\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid\Lambda)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid\Lambda]) = \mathbb{E}[\Lambda] + \text{Var}(\Lambda)
since \mathbb{E}[X\mid\Lambda] = \Lambda and \text{Var}(X\mid\Lambda) = \Lambda (Poisson).
Step 2. To get \text{Var}(\Lambda), apply Eve’s Law again conditioning on \Theta:
\text{Var}(\Lambda) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(\Lambda\mid\Theta)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[\Lambda\mid\Theta])
Each application of Eve’s Law strips one level of the hierarchy — the Tower Property for variance, applied recursively.
4.4 Bivariate Normal
(X,Y) bivariate normal with parameters \mu_X, \mu_Y, \sigma_X, \sigma_Y, \rho. From 01.Linear Regression §5:
\text{Var}(Y\mid X) = \sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2)
This is constant — does not depend on X. Homoskedasticity is automatic for bivariate normals.
Verify Eve’s Law:
\text{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(Y\mid X)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]) \sigma_Y^2 = \sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2) + \text{Var}!\left(\mu_Y + \rho\frac{\sigma_Y}{\sigma_X}(X-\mu_X)\right) = \sigma_Y^2(1-\rho^2) + \rho^2\sigma_Y^2 \qquad \checkmark

5. Common Confusions


                  
                   \text{Var}(X\mid Y) \neq \text{Var}(Y) The left side is the variance of X given Y — a function of Y. The right side is the unconditional variance of Y — a number. These are completely different objects.
                  
                



                  
                   \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)] \neq \text{Var}(X) The left side is the unexplained variance — only part of \text{Var}(X). You must add the explained variance \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]) to recover \text{Var}(X).
                  
                


6. Geometric Interpretation
From Geometric Interpretation of Conditional Expectation, Eve’s Law is the Pythagorean theorem in L^2:
|\tilde{X}|^2 = |\tilde{X} - \text{proj}_{V_Y}(\tilde{X})|^2 + |\text{proj}_{V_Y}(\tilde{X})|^2
where \tilde{X} = X - \mathbb{E}[X] and the projection is \mathbb{E}[X\mid Y] - \mathbb{E}[X].





















TermMeaning\|\tilde{X}\|^2 = \text{Var}(X)Total length squared\|\text{proj}\|^2 = \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])Explained: length of the projection\|\tilde{X} - \text{proj}\|^2 = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)]Unexplained: length of the residual
\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)] is the squared distance from \tilde{X} to the subspace V_Y. The conditional variance, averaged over Y, measures how far X is from being a function of Y.

7. Summary



































QuantityTypeMeaning\text{Var}(X\mid Y=y)NumberVariance of X in the slice Y=y\text{Var}(X\mid Y)Random variable (function of Y)Variance of X as a function of the slice\mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid Y)]NumberAverage conditional variance — unexplained\text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y])NumberVariance of conditional mean — explained\text{Var}(X)NumberSum of the above two — Eve’s Law

References
