01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.title: 05.Entropy
01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.content:
Entropy is one of those definitions that feels arbitrary until suddenly it doesn’t. Why -\sum p_i \log p_i? Why not something else? The answer is that Shannon essentially proved this is the only function satisfying a small list of properties any reasonable measure of uncertainty should have. Once you accept those axioms, entropy is forced on you. And then it starts appearing everywhere — in coding theory, in statistical mechanics, in hypothesis testing, in the geometry of exponential families. This note is my attempt to understand entropy deeply, not just compute it.


Tags
#probability #information-theory #entropy #KL-divergence #jensen #stat110 #blitzstein

Prerequisites

Discrete distributions, PMFs
\log — base 2 for information-theoretic interpretations (bits), natural log for analytic ones. The choice rescales entropy by a constant; all inequalities hold regardless.
Jensen’s Inequality: g convex \Rightarrow g(\mathbb{E}[X]) \leq \mathbb{E}[g(X)]; concave flips it
KL Divergence — defined here, but appears in the Jensen note too


1. Definition
1.1 Entropy of a Discrete Distribution
Let X be a discrete r.v. with PMF p(x) = \mathbb{P}(X = x) on a finite or countable support \mathcal{X}. The entropy of X is:
H(X) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x)\log p(x) = \mathbb{E}[-\log p(X)]
with the convention 0 \log 0 = 0 (since x\log x \to 0 as x \to 0^+).


                  
                  The Right Way to Remember This The form H(X) = \mathbb{E}[-\log p(X)] is the one to remember. Entropy is the expected surprise or self-information -\log p(X). When X = x is rare (p(x) small), -\log p(x) is large — you're surprised. When X = x is certain (p(x) = 1), -\log p(x) = 0 — no surprise at all. Entropy averages this surprise over all outcomes.
                  
                

1.2 Units

























BaseUnitNote2bitsH(X) = 1 bit means X is a fair coin flipenatsUsed in analysis; cleaner formulas10ditsRare
The relationship: H_2(X) = H_e(X) / \ln 2. Everything scales by \log_2 e = 1/\ln 2 \approx 1.443.

2. The Axiomatic Derivation (Why This Formula?)
Shannon (1948) showed entropy is the unique function satisfying:

Continuity: H(p_1,\ldots,p_n) is continuous in the p_i.
Symmetry: H is invariant under permutation of outcomes.
Maximality: H is maximized when p_i = 1/n for all i (uniform).
Additivity / Recursion: H(p_1,\ldots,p_n) = H(p_1+p_2, p_3,\ldots,p_n) + (p_1+p_2),H!\left(\tfrac{p_1}{p_1+p_2}, \tfrac{p_2}{p_1+p_2}\right)

The fourth axiom says: coarsening and then refining gives the same total entropy. Under these axioms, entropy must be -C\sum p_i \log p_i for some constant C > 0. Setting C fixes the base of the logarithm.


                  
                  Why This is Satisfying The formula is not pulled from thin air — it is forced by requirements that any sane measure of uncertainty must satisfy. This is analogous to how the normal distribution is forced by the CLT, or how the Poisson is forced by the limit of rare events. 
                  
                


3. Basic Properties
3.1 Non-Negativity
H(X) \geq 0
Proof. Since p(x) \in [0,1], we have \log p(x) \leq 0, so -p(x)\log p(x) \geq 0 for each term. \square
Equality iff X is constant a.s. (one p(x) = 1, rest 0): zero uncertainty means zero entropy.
3.2 Maximum Entropy: the Uniform Distribution
For X supported on n outcomes:
H(X) \leq \log n
with equality iff X \sim \text{Uniform}{1,\ldots,n}.
Proof. Let u(x) = 1/n be the uniform PMF. Then:
H(X) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x) = -\sum_x p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{u(x)} + \sum_x p(x)\log\frac{1}{u(x)}
= -D_{\text{KL}}(p|u) + \log n \leq \log n
since D_{\text{KL}}(p|u) \geq 0 (by Jensen). Equality iff p = u. \square


                  
                  This proof shows the gap between H(X) and \log n is exactly D_{\text{KL}}(p|u) — the KL divergence to the uniform. Maximum entropy distributions are those closest to uniform in the KL sense. This perspective generalizes: the max-entropy distribution subject to constraints is the one minimizing KL to the unconstrained maximum, which leads to exponential families.
                  
                

3.3 Deterministic Transformation Loses Entropy
If Y = f(X) for a deterministic function f:
H(Y) \leq H(X)
with equality iff f is injective on the support of X. Applying a function can only lose information, never gain it.

4. Joint Entropy and Conditional Entropy
4.1 Joint Entropy
For a pair (X, Y):
H(X, Y) = -\sum_{x,y} p(x,y)\log p(x,y) = \mathbb{E}[-\log p(X,Y)]
4.2 Conditional Entropy
H(Y \mid X) = \sum_x p(x),H(Y \mid X = x) = -\sum_{x,y} p(x,y)\log p(y\mid x) = \mathbb{E}[-\log p(Y\mid X)]
Conditional entropy is the average uncertainty in Y after observing X. It’s an expectation of a log-probability of the conditional distribution — the symmetry with the unconditional definition is exact.
4.3 Chain Rule for Entropy
H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y \mid X)
Proof.
H(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[-\log p(X,Y)] = \mathbb{E}[-\log(p(X)p(Y\mid X))] = \mathbb{E}[-\log p(X)] + \mathbb{E}[-\log p(Y\mid X)]
= H(X) + H(Y\mid X) \qquad \square
Extends to any number of variables:
H(X_1,\ldots,X_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n H(X_i \mid X_1,\ldots,X_{i-1})
4.4 Conditioning Reduces Entropy
H(Y \mid X) \leq H(Y)
with equality iff X and Y are independent.
Proof. H(Y) - H(Y\mid X) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) =: I(X;Y) \geq 0 (mutual information, proved below). \square
Observing X can only reduce (or maintain) uncertainty about Y, never increase it — the information-theoretic formalization of “data never hurts.”

5. Mutual Information
5.1 Definition
The mutual information between X and Y:
I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) = H(X) - H(X\mid Y) = H(Y) - H(Y\mid X)
Equivalently:
I(X;Y) = \sum_{x,y} p(x,y)\log\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)} = D_{\text{KL}}(p_{XY} ,|, p_X \otimes p_Y)


                  
                  Mutual information is the KL divergence between the joint distribution and the product of marginals. It measures how far (X,Y) is from being independent — KL divergence to the "independence model."
                  
                

5.2 Non-Negativity of Mutual Information
I(X;Y) \geq 0
with equality iff X \perp Y.
Proof. I(X;Y) = D_{\text{KL}}(p_{XY}|p_X p_Y) \geq 0 by the non-negativity of KL divergence (Jensen applied to -\log). \square
This simultaneously proves H(Y\mid X) \leq H(Y) and gives the equality condition.
5.3 The Entropy Venn Diagram
H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - I(X;Y)
Draw a Venn diagram: two circles for H(X) and H(Y), their overlap is I(X;Y), their union is H(X,Y). For two variables, the picture is exact.


                  
                  Unlike set Venn diagrams, conditional entropy can behave oddly with three or more variables — conditional entropy can exceed joint entropy in some extended senses. The diagram is exact for two variables only. 
                  
                


6. KL Divergence — The Parent of Everything
6.1 Definition
For two PMFs p, q on the same support \mathcal{X}:
D_{\text{KL}}(p | q) = \sum_{x} p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = \mathbb{E}_p!\left[\log\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\right]
with 0\log(0/0) = 0 and p(x)\log(p(x)/0) = +\infty if p(x) > 0.


                  
                  KL divergence is not a metric — it's not symmetric and doesn't satisfy the triangle inequality. But it is always non-negative.
                  
                

6.2 Non-Negativity via Jensen
Proof. Apply Jensen to g(t) = -\log t (convex) and the r.v. q(X)/p(X) under \mathbb{P} = p:
D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) = \mathbb{E}_p!\left[-\log\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\right] \geq -\log\mathbb{E}_p!\left[\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\right] = -\log\sum_x p(x)\frac{q(x)}{p(x)} = -\log 1 = 0
Equality iff q(X)/p(X) is constant p-a.s., i.e., p = q. \square
6.3 Entropy as KL to the Uniform
H(X) = \log|\mathcal{X}| - D_{\text{KL}}(p | u)
where u is uniform on \mathcal{X}. So H(X) \leq \log|\mathcal{X}| with equality iff p = u.


                  
                  Entropy is not a standalone object — it's always secretly a KL divergence to the uniform. The "amount of information" in X is the distance from p to maximum ignorance.
                  
                


7. Cross-Entropy
7.1 Definition
The cross-entropy of q relative to p:
H(p, q) = -\sum_x p(x)\log q(x) = \mathbb{E}_p[-\log q(X)]
7.2 Relation to KL and Entropy
H(p, q) = H(p) + D_{\text{KL}}(p|q)
Proof.
H(p,q) = -\mathbb{E}_p[\log q(X)] = -\mathbb{E}_p[\log p(X)] + \mathbb{E}_p!\left[\log\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\right] = H(p) + D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) \qquad\square
Since D_{\text{KL}} \geq 0: cross-entropy is always at least the true entropy, H(p,q) \geq H(p).


                  
                  Machine Learning Connection Cross-entropy is what you minimize in ML classification. Minimizing H(p,q) over q (with p fixed as the true distribution) is equivalent to minimizing D_{\text{KL}}(p|q), since H(p) doesn't depend on q. So training a classifier by minimizing cross-entropy loss is the same as minimizing KL divergence to the true distribution. Jensen is quietly inside every neural network training loop.
                  
                


8. Maximum Entropy Principle
8.1 The Unconstrained Case
Maximize H(X) over all distributions on n outcomes: the maximum is \log n, achieved uniquely by the uniform. Proved in §3.2.
8.2 Constrained Case — Exponential Families Emerge
Maximize H(X) subject to \mathbb{E}[f_k(X)] = \alpha_k for k = 1,\ldots,m (given moment constraints). By Lagrange multipliers, the solution has the form:
p^*(x) = \frac{1}{Z(\lambda)}\exp!\left(\sum_{k=1}^m \lambda_k f_k(x)\right)
where Z(\lambda) = \sum_x \exp(\sum_k \lambda_k f_k(x)) is the partition function and \lambda_k are Lagrange multipliers chosen to satisfy the constraints.
This is an exponential family:

























ConstraintMaxEnt DistributionSupport {0,1,\ldots}, mean = \muGeometricSupport {1,\ldots,n}, no constraintUniformSupport \mathbb{R}, mean = \mu, variance = \sigma^2NormalSupport [0,\infty), mean = \muExponential


                  
                  This is why the normal distribution is everywhere: it is the maximum entropy distribution given only a mean and variance constraint — pure maximum ignorance subject to those two numbers. Maximum entropy gives a principled reason these distributions are "natural." 
                  
                


9. Data Compression — Why Entropy Matters
9.1 Shannon’s Source Coding Theorem
If X_1, X_2, \ldots \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} p, then the minimum expected number of bits per symbol needed to encode the sequence is exactly H(X) bits. Formally: for any uniquely decodable code, the expected code length \bar L satisfies:
\bar L \geq H(X)
and there exist codes with \bar L < H(X) + 1.
Entropy is the fundamental limit of lossless compression. If H(X) = 3 bits, no compression scheme can do better than 3 bits per symbol on average. Huffman coding nearly achieves this.
9.2 The Surprise Interpretation
The optimal code assigns -\log_2 p(x) bits to outcome x. Rare events get long codes; common events get short codes. Entropy is the expected code length under the optimal code. This makes H(X) = \mathbb{E}[-\log_2 p(X)] completely natural — it’s the expected optimal code length.

10. Examples
10.1 Bernoulli(p) — Binary Entropy Function
X \sim \text{Bern}(p):
H(X) = -p\log p - (1-p)\log(1-p) =: h(p)

h(0) = h(1) = 0: no uncertainty when outcome is deterministic
h(1/2) = \log 2 = 1 bit: maximum uncertainty for a binary variable
h is concave on [0,1], symmetric around p = 1/2

10.2 Uniform on {1,\ldots,n}
H(X) = -\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{n}\log\frac{1}{n} = \log n
Maximum entropy on n outcomes, as expected.
10.3 Geometric(p) on {1, 2, 3, \ldots}
\mathbb{P}(X = k) = (1-p)^{k-1}p.
H(X) = -\sum_{k=1}^\infty (1-p)^{k-1}p\log((1-p)^{k-1}p) = \frac{h(p)}{p}
where h(p) is the binary entropy function. (Derivation: separate the log, use geometric series formulas for \sum k (1-p)^{k-1}.)

11. The Relationship Map
H(X) = \log|\mathcal{X}| - D_{\text{KL}}(p|u)
H(p,q) = H(p) + D_{\text{KL}}(p|q)
I(X;Y) = D_{\text{KL}}(p_{XY}|p_X p_Y)
H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y\mid X) \quad\text{(chain rule)}
I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X\mid Y) = H(Y) - H(Y\mid X)


                  
                  Every information-theoretic quantity is either an entropy or a KL divergence in disguise. The KL divergence is the atom. Everything else is built from it and from \log|\mathcal{X}|.
                  
                


12. Things I Should Be Able to Do Cold

 Write the definition two ways: sum form and expectation form
 Prove H(X) \leq \log n using D_{\text{KL}}(p|u) \geq 0
 State and prove the chain rule H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y\mid X)
 Define mutual information three ways (chain rule, KL divergence, symmetrized)
 Prove D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) \geq 0 using Jensen in three lines
 State Shannon’s source coding theorem and explain why -\log_2 p(x) is the optimal code length
 Write the MaxEnt distribution for given moment constraints and recognize it as an exponential family
 Compute H(X) for Bernoulli, Uniform, Geometric


13. Open Questions / Things to Sit With

 Continuous entropy (differential entropy): For continuous X with PDF f, define h(X) = -\int f(x)\log f(x),dx. This is NOT the limit of the discrete entropy as the partition gets finer (that limit is -\infty). Differential entropy can be negative, and many discrete entropy properties break. Worth a separate note.
 Rényi entropy: H_\alpha(X) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\log\sum_x p(x)^\alpha. This is a one-parameter family: H_1 = H (Shannon), H_0 = \log|\text{support}|, H_\infty = -\log\max_x p(x) (min-entropy). Appears in cryptography.
 The geometry of exponential families: The MaxEnt distributions form an exponential family, and KL divergence is the Bregman divergence associated to the negative entropy. The geometry here (information geometry) is beautiful — geodesics in KL are e-geodesics and m-geodesics, Pythagoras theorem holds for KL projections.
 Connection to statistical mechanics: The Boltzmann entropy S = k_B\log W is entropy of the uniform distribution over microstates. The Gibbs entropy -k_B\sum p_i \log p_i is Shannon entropy. They coincide at equilibrium because equilibrium is maximum entropy. The partition function Z(\beta) in statistical mechanics is the same object as the MGF of the energy.


14. References

Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability — entropy appears in the context of information and the Jensen/KL divergence discussion; the surprise interpretation is developed carefully
Harvard Stat 110 — the lecture connecting Jensen → KL ≥ 0 → entropy ≤ log n is the cleanest pedagogical path
Shannon (1948), A Mathematical Theory of Communication — the original paper is actually readable; the axiomatic derivation is in the appendix


Links

Jensen’s Inequality — the analytic engine behind KL ≥ 0 and every entropy inequality
KL Divergence — defined here; non-negativity proved via Jensen
Exponential Families — MaxEnt distributions subject to moment constraints
Conditional Expectation — conditional entropy parallels conditional expectation exactly

01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.title: 06.Kullback-Leibler Divergence
01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.content:
KL divergence is the central object of information theory, and once you see it clearly, you realize it was already hiding inside everything you knew. The non-negativity of KL is Jensen applied to -\log. Entropy is KL to the uniform. Mutual information is KL to the independence model. The maximum likelihood estimator minimizes KL to the true distribution. The exponential family is the solution to a KL projection. Fisher information is the second derivative of KL at zero. Every time I think I’ve found the boundary of where KL appears, it turns out to be further out. This note is about understanding KL as a geometric object — a way of measuring distance between distributions — and tracing all the threads that lead out from it.


Tags
#probability #information-theory #KL-divergence #entropy #jensen #MLE #exponential-families #stat110 #blitzstein

Prerequisites

Entropy: H(X) = \mathbb{E}[-\log p(X)]
Jensen’s inequality — the proof of D_{\text{KL}} \geq 0 is one application
Likelihood and MLE — the connection to KL is the deepest reason MLE works
Exponential families (at least the definition) — KL projections land there


1. Definition
1.1 Discrete case
Let p and q be PMFs on the same finite or countable support \mathcal{X}. The Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL divergence, relative entropy) of p from q is:
D_{\text{KL}}(p | q) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}
with the conventions:

0 \log(0/0) = 0
0 \log(0/q(x)) = 0 for q(x) > 0
p(x)\log(p(x)/0) = +\infty if p(x) > 0 — so D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) = +\infty if p is not absolutely continuous with respect to q

1.2 Continuous case
For PDFs f, g on \mathbb{R}:
D_{\text{KL}}(f | g) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\log\frac{f(x)}{g(x)},dx
Same conventions apply. Requires f \ll g (absolute continuity: g(x) = 0 \Rightarrow f(x) = 0).
1.3 The expectation form
D_{\text{KL}}(p | q) = \mathbb{E}_p!\left[\log\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\right] = \mathbb{E}_p[-\log q(X)] - \mathbb{E}_p[-\log p(X)] = H(p,q) - H(p)
where H(p,q) = \mathbb{E}_p[-\log q(X)] is the cross-entropy. So:
\boxed{D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) = H(p,q) - H(p)}

KL divergence is the excess surprise you experience when you use q to encode data that actually comes from p. If you use the wrong distribution q, you pay H(p,q) bits per symbol on average. The true minimum cost is H(p). The excess is D_{\text{KL}}(p|q). This is why KL appears in coding theory, and why minimizing KL is the right objective for learning.


2. Non-Negativity — The Fundamental Theorem
2.1 Statement
D_{\text{KL}}(p | q) \geq 0
with equality iff p = q (i.e., p(x) = q(x) for all x with p(x) > 0).
2.2 Proof via Jensen
Let X \sim p. Consider the random variable Z = q(X)/p(X) (the likelihood ratio viewed under p). Apply Jensen to g(t) = -\log t (convex on t > 0):
D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) = \mathbb{E}_p!\left[-\log\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\right] = \mathbb{E}_p[-\log Z] \geq -\log\mathbb{E}_p[Z]
Now compute \mathbb{E}_p[Z]:
\mathbb{E}_p[Z] = \mathbb{E}_p!\left[\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}\right] = \sum_x p(x)\cdot\frac{q(x)}{p(x)} = \sum_x q(x) = 1
Therefore:
D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) \geq -\log 1 = 0 \qquad \square
Equality iff Z = q(X)/p(X) is constant p-a.s. Since \mathbb{E}_p[Z] = 1, that constant must be 1, i.e., q(x) = p(x) for all x in the support of p.

Three lines. The key identity is \mathbb{E}_p[q(X)/p(X)] = 1 — this is always true because it is just \sum_x q(x) = 1 rewritten. The quantity q(X)/p(X) is the likelihood ratio (Radon-Nikodym derivative of q w.r.t. p), and its expectation under p is always 1. This normalization identity is doing all the work; Jensen gives the direction.

2.3 Alternative: the log-sum inequality
For a_x, b_x > 0:
\sum_x a_x \log\frac{a_x}{b_x} \geq \left(\sum_x a_x\right)\log\frac{\sum_x a_x}{\sum_x b_x}
Setting a_x = p(x), b_x = q(x): \sum p(x) = \sum q(x) = 1, so the RHS is 0. This gives D_{\text{KL}} \geq 0 directly. The log-sum inequality itself follows from convexity of t\log t.

3. KL is Not a Metric
3.1 Asymmetry
D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) \neq D_{\text{KL}}(q|p) \quad \text{in general}
Example: p = \text{Bern}(0.01), q = \text{Bern}(0.5):
D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) \approx 0.645 \text{ nats}, \qquad D_{\text{KL}}(q|p) \approx 1.972 \text{ nats}
D_{\text{KL}}(q|p) is larger because q puts substantial mass (0.5) where p has almost none (0.01) — the term 0.5\log(0.5/0.01) is large.
3.2 The meaning of direction
Forward KL, D_{\text{KL}}(p|q): p is truth, q is approximation. Penalizes q for having zero mass where p has mass. Forces q to cover all of p‘s support. Minimizing forward KL gives mean-seeking behavior — q spreads to cover all modes.
Reverse KL, D_{\text{KL}}(q|p): Penalizes q for putting mass where p has none. Forces q to stay inside p‘s support. Minimizing reverse KL gives mode-seeking behavior — q concentrates on one mode.

This distinction is not academic. Variational inference minimizes D_{\text{KL}}(q|p_{\text{posterior}}) (reverse KL) because the forward KL requires integrating against the intractable posterior. The consequence: variational posteriors underestimate uncertainty and collapse to modes. Understanding why this happens is understanding the geometry of KL.

3.3 A symmetric alternative
The Jensen-Shannon divergence:
\text{JSD}(p, q) = \frac{1}{2}D_{\text{KL}}!\left(p,\Big|,\frac{p+q}{2}\right) + \frac{1}{2}D_{\text{KL}}!\left(q,\Big|,\frac{p+q}{2}\right)
is symmetric, bounded in [0, \log 2], and \sqrt{\text{JSD}} is a true metric. It appears in the theory of GANs (the original GAN objective is equivalent to minimizing JSD between the data distribution and the generator).

4. KL and All the Entropy Quantities
4.1 The full dictionary
H(p) = \log|\mathcal{X}| - D_{\text{KL}}(p|u) \quad (u \text{ uniform})
H(p,q) = H(p) + D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) \quad \text{(cross-entropy)}
I(X;Y) = D_{\text{KL}}(p_{XY} | p_X \otimes p_Y) \quad \text{(mutual information)}
Every information-theoretic quantity is a KL divergence or differs from one by a constant that doesn’t depend on what you’re optimizing.
4.2 Non-negativity cascade
D_{\text{KL}} \geq 0 \implies I(X;Y) \geq 0 \implies H(Y\mid X) \leq H(Y) \implies H(X) \leq \log|\mathcal{X}|
One inequality (Jensen on -\log), four consequences in a chain.

5. KL and Maximum Likelihood
5.1 MLE minimizes KL
Let X_1,\ldots,X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} p^* (true, unknown). Fit parametric model {q_\theta} by MLE:
\hat\theta = \arg\max_\theta \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log q_\theta(X_i) \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} \arg\max_\theta \mathbb{E}_{p^*}[\log q_\theta(X)]
Now:
\mathbb{E}_{p^*}[\log q_\theta(X)] = \underbrace{-H(p^_)}_{\text{const in }\theta} - D_{\text{KL}}(p^_|q_\theta)
So:
\hat\theta \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} \arg\min_\theta D_{\text{KL}}(p^*|q_\theta)
MLE is the KL projection of the true distribution onto the model family.

This is why MLE is the right thing to do. It’s not a heuristic — it is the procedure that finds the closest distribution to the truth (in the forward KL sense) within your model. If p^_ \in {q_\theta}, KL is zero at the optimum and MLE recovers p^_. If not, MLE finds the best approximation the model can offer.

5.2 Moment matching in exponential families
If {q_\theta} is an exponential family with sufficient statistic T(x):
q_\theta(x) \propto \exp(\theta^\top T(x))
then the KL projection condition \nabla_\theta D_{\text{KL}}(p^*|q_\theta) = 0 reduces to:
\mathbb{E}_{q_\theta}[T(X)] = \mathbb{E}_{p^*}[T(X)]
The MLE matches the model’s expected sufficient statistics to the empirical ones. This is the general form of moment matching, and it’s why MLE in exponential families always reduces to matching moments.

6. Fisher Information as the Curvature of KL
6.1 The second-order expansion
For a smooth parametric family {p_\theta}, expand KL between nearby parameters:
D_{\text{KL}}(p_\theta | p_{\theta + \epsilon}) = \frac{\epsilon^2}{2},\mathcal{I}(\theta) + O(\epsilon^3)
where the Fisher information is:
\mathcal{I}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}!\left[\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log p_\theta(X)\right)^2\right] = -\mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}!\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\log p_\theta(X)\right]
Derivation sketch. Let \ell_\theta(x) = \log p_\theta(x). Expand:
D_{\text{KL}}(p_\theta|p_{\theta+\epsilon}) = \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[\ell_\theta(X) - \ell_{\theta+\epsilon}(X)] \approx -\epsilon,\mathbb{E}[\ell'_\theta] - \frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\mathbb{E}[\ell''_\theta]
The first term: \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[\ell'_\theta(X)] = \partial_\theta \sum_x p_\theta(x) = \partial_\theta 1 = 0 (score function has mean zero). The second term gives \frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\mathcal{I}(\theta).

Fisher information is the local curvature of KL divergence. It measures how fast distributions separate as you move in parameter space. Large \mathcal{I}(\theta) means parameters are easy to distinguish (nearby distributions are far in KL); small \mathcal{I}(\theta) means they’re hard to distinguish. The Cramér-Rao bound \text{Var}(\hat\theta) \geq 1/\mathcal{I}(\theta) then says: the harder distributions are to distinguish, the harder the parameter is to estimate. This is the right intuition.


7. The Data-Processing Inequality
Theorem. If X \to Y \to Z is a Markov chain, then:
D_{\text{KL}}(p_X | q_X) \geq D_{\text{KL}}(p_Y | q_Y) \geq D_{\text{KL}}(p_Z | q_Z)
Processing data can only decrease KL divergence — information cannot be created.
For mutual information: In the Markov chain X \to Y \to Z:
I(X;Y) \geq I(X;Z)
Any function of Y contains at most as much information about X as Y itself.

Sufficient statistics are exactly those for which equality holds: T(X) is sufficient for \theta iff I(\theta; T(X)) = I(\theta; X), i.e., no information about \theta is lost by passing from X to T(X). The data-processing inequality makes “sufficiency” into an information-theoretic statement, not just a conditional independence statement.


8. Worked Examples
8.1 Two Bernoullis
p = \text{Bern}(p_0), q = \text{Bern}(q_0):
D_{\text{KL}}(\text{Bern}(p_0)|\text{Bern}(q_0)) = p_0\log\frac{p_0}{q_0} + (1-p_0)\log\frac{1-p_0}{1-q_0}
Check: equals 0 when p_0 = q_0 ✓. Blows up as q_0 \to 0 with p_0 > 0 ✓.
8.2 Two Gaussians
p = N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2), q = N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2):
D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) = \log\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1} + \frac{\sigma_1^2 + (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2} - \frac{1}{2}
Equal variances \sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma:
D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) = \frac{(\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma^2}
This is the squared Mahalanobis distance. KL between equal-variance Gaussians is proportional to squared mean difference — KL is literally a distance here.
Derivation. Write \log(p/q) = \log(\sigma_2/\sigma_1) - \frac{(x-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2} + \frac{(x-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2}. Take \mathbb{E}_p, use \mathbb{E}_p[X] = \mu_1, \mathbb{E}_p[X^2] = \sigma_1^2 + \mu_1^2.
8.3 Two Poissons
p = \text{Pois}(\lambda), q = \text{Pois}(\mu):
D_{\text{KL}}(\text{Pois}(\lambda)|\text{Pois}(\mu)) = \lambda\log\frac{\lambda}{\mu} - \lambda + \mu
Check: at \lambda = \mu: \lambda\log 1 - \lambda + \lambda = 0 ✓.

9. Summary Table





























QuantityIn terms of KLH(p)\log\|\mathcal{X}\| - D_{\text{KL}}(p\|u)H(p,q)H(p) + D_{\text{KL}}(p\|q)I(X;Y)D_{\text{KL}}(p_{XY}\|p_X p_Y)MLE limit\arg\min_\theta D_{\text{KL}}(p^*\|q_\theta)Fisher info\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\epsilon^2}D_{\text{KL}}(p_\theta\|p_{\theta+\epsilon})\big\|_{\epsilon=0}

10. Things I Should Be Able to Do Cold

 Write the definition in sum form and expectation form, and as H(p,q) - H(p)
 Prove D_{\text{KL}}(p|q) \geq 0 via Jensen in three lines, citing the key identity \mathbb{E}_p[q(X)/p(X)] = 1
 Explain the asymmetry and what each direction penalizes
 Derive the MLE-KL connection from the LLN
 State that Fisher information is \partial^2_\epsilon D_{\text{KL}}(p_\theta|p_{\theta+\epsilon})|_{\epsilon=0} and sketch the derivation
 Compute KL for Bernoulli, Gaussian, and Poisson pairs
 State the data-processing inequality and connect it to sufficiency


11. Open Questions / Things to Sit With

Sanov’s theorem: The probability that the empirical distribution of n iid samples falls in a set \mathcal{Q} decays like \exp(-n \cdot \inf_{q\in\mathcal{Q}} D_{\text{KL}}(q|p)). KL is the rate function of large deviations for empirical measures. This is the deepest appearance of KL — not just a measure of closeness, but the exponential rate of distinguishability. When I study large deviations, this is the first theorem.
Information geometry: The parameter space of a smooth model carries a Riemannian metric given by the Fisher information matrix. KL is the squared “distance” in this geometry to second order. Geodesics split into e-geodesics and m-geodesics (exponential and mixture), and a Pythagorean theorem holds for KL projections. Amari’s work. Far future, but the seed is in §6.
f-divergences: KL is D_f with f(t) = t\log t. The family D_f(p|q) = \sum_x q(x)f(p(x)/q(x)) includes total variation (f(t) = |t-1|/2), \chi^2 (f(t) = (t-1)^2), Hellinger. All non-negative by convexity of f (Jensen again). The Csiszár-Morimoto theorem unifies them.
GANs and JSD: The original GAN minimax objective is equivalent to minimizing JSD between the data distribution and the generator. Later GANs (Wasserstein GAN) replace JSD with the Wasserstein distance, which has better gradient properties. The evolution of GAN objectives is a story about which divergence to minimize and why.


12. References

Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability — Jensen to KL to entropy chain; the information inequality
Harvard Stat 110 — the D_{\text{KL}} \geq 0 proof and its consequences
Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, Ch. 2 — the canonical reference; Chapter 11 for Sanov and large deviations
Self-note: when I see variational inference, come back to §3.2 on forward vs reverse KL. When I see exponential families, come back to §5.2 on moment matching. When I see large deviations, come back for Sanov. Fisher information connects this note to the estimation theory notes I haven’t written yet.


Last updated: self-study session, rigorous probability sequence.

01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.title: 07.Concentration Bounds- Markov, Chebyshev, Chernoff
01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.content:
The central question: how likely is a random variable to be far from its mean? The three bounds here — Markov, Chebyshev, Chernoff — form a hierarchy. Each uses more information about the distribution and buys you a sharper bound in return. Markov needs only a mean. Chebyshev needs a variance. Chernoff needs the full moment generating function. The cost of ignorance is exponential: Markov and Chebyshev give polynomial decay in the tail; Chernoff gives exponential decay. In repeated trials, exponential is the one that matters.


Tags
#probability #concentration-inequalities #markov #chebyshev #chernoff #tail-bounds #stat110

Prerequisites

Expectation, variance, MGF
Moment Generating Functions — Chernoff is entirely MGF-based
Jensen’s Inequality — used in the Chernoff proof
Law of Large Numbers — these bounds are the quantitative version of LLN


0. The Setup
We have a random variable X (or a sum S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n of i.i.d. trials) and we want to bound:
\mathbb{P}(X \geq t) \quad \text{or} \quad \mathbb{P}(|X - \mu| \geq t)
for large t. The three bounds give progressively sharper answers at progressively higher cost.





























BoundInput RequiredTail DecayTightnessMarkovMean \muO(1/t)WeakChebyshevMean \mu, variance \sigma^2O(1/t^2)ModerateChernoffFull MGF M(s) = \mathbb{E}[e^{sX}]e^{-\Theta(t)}Strong

1. Markov’s Inequality
1.1 Statement
For any non-negative random variable X and a > 0:
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(X \geq a) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[X]}{a}}
1.2 Proof
Since X \geq 0:
\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[X \cdot \mathbf{1}_{X \geq a}] + \mathbb{E}[X \cdot \mathbf{1}_{X < a}] \geq \mathbb{E}[X \cdot \mathbf{1}_{X \geq a}] \geq a \cdot \mathbb{P}(X \geq a)
Divide both sides by a. \square
1.3 Intuition
If the mean is \mu, then the probability of exceeding k\mu is at most 1/k. You can’t have too much mass far above the mean without pulling the mean up with it.
1.4 Tightness
Markov is tight: the bound is achieved by a two-point distribution X = 0 with prob 1 - \mu/a, X = a with prob \mu/a.
1.5 Applying to Functions
Markov applies to any non-negative function of X. This is the key trick: for any increasing \phi \geq 0:
\mathbb{P}(X \geq a) = \mathbb{P}(\phi(X) \geq \phi(a)) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[\phi(X)]}{\phi(a)}
Chebyshev uses \phi(x) = (x - \mu)^2. Chernoff uses \phi(x) = e^{sx}. Both are Markov in disguise.

2. Chebyshev’s Inequality
2.1 Statement
For any random variable X with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2, and any k > 0:
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(|X - \mu| \geq k) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{k^2}}
Equivalently, writing k = t\sigma:
\mathbb{P}(|X - \mu| \geq t\sigma) \leq \frac{1}{t^2}
2.2 Proof
Apply Markov to the non-negative r.v. (X - \mu)^2 with threshold k^2:
\mathbb{P}(|X - \mu| \geq k) = \mathbb{P}((X-\mu)^2 \geq k^2) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]}{k^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{k^2} \qquad \square
2.3 Intuition
Chebyshev gives O(1/t^2) decay. The LLN follows immediately: if \bar{X}_n = (X_1 + \cdots + X_n)/n with \text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \sigma^2/n, then for any \varepsilon > 0:
\mathbb{P}(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| \geq \varepsilon) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2} \to 0
This is a proof of the Weak Law of Large Numbers.
2.4 One-Sided Version (Cantelli’s Inequality)
For the one-sided tail:
\mathbb{P}(X - \mu \geq k) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + k^2}
This is tighter than \sigma^2/k^2 for one-sided deviations and doesn’t require symmetry.
2.5 Tightness
Chebyshev is tight: achieved by a three-point distribution putting mass 1/(2t^2) at \mu \pm t\sigma and 1 - 1/t^2 at \mu. So for a general distribution, the 1/t^2 decay cannot be improved — but for specific distributions (e.g. normal, Binomial) you can do much better.

3. Chernoff Bounds
3.1 The Core Idea
Apply Markov to e^{sX} for s > 0:
\mathbb{P}(X \geq a) = \mathbb{P}(e^{sX} \geq e^{sa}) \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{sX}]}{e^{sa}} = \frac{M_X(s)}{e^{sa}}
where M_X(s) = \mathbb{E}[e^{sX}] is the MGF. This holds for every s > 0, so optimize over s:
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(X \geq a) \leq \min_{s > 0} , e^{-sa} M_X(s)}
Taking logs, the bound is e^{-\sup_{s>0}(sa - \log M_X(s))}. The function \Lambda^*(a) = \sup_{s>0}(sa - \log M_X(s)) is the Legendre-Fenchel transform of the log-MGF — the object at the heart of large deviations theory.
3.2 Why Exponential Decay?
For i.i.d. X_1, \ldots, X_n with S_n = \sum X_i:
M_{S_n}(s) = M_X(s)^n
So the Chernoff bound on S_n \geq na (i.e., sample mean \geq a) becomes:
\mathbb{P}(S_n \geq na) \leq e^{-n \sup_{s>0}(sa - \log M_X(s))} = e^{-n\Lambda^*(a)}
The exponent grows linearly in n. This is exponential decay in the sample size — the Markov/Chebyshev bounds give O(1/n) or O(1/n^2); Chernoff gives e^{-cn}.

4. Chernoff Bounds for Binomial / Bernoulli Trials
This is the most important special case. Let X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Bern}(p), S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n \sim \text{Bin}(n,p), \mu = np.
4.1 MGF of a Bernoulli
M_{X_i}(s) = \mathbb{E}[e^{sX_i}] = pe^s + (1-p) = 1 + p(e^s - 1)
4.2 MGF of the Binomial Sum
M_{S_n}(s) = (pe^s + 1 - p)^n
4.3 Upper Tail Bound
For \delta > 0 (i.e., threshold (1+\delta)\mu above the mean), applying Markov to e^{sS_n} and optimizing over s:
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(S_n \geq (1+\delta)\mu) \leq \left(\frac{e^\delta}{(1+\delta)^{(1+\delta)}}\right)^\mu}
This is the exact Chernoff bound. It is derived by setting s = \log(1+\delta) (the optimal s).
Cleaner forms (weaker but simpler):
\mathbb{P}(S_n \geq (1+\delta)\mu) \leq e^{-\mu\delta^2/3} \quad \text{for } 0 < \delta \leq 1
\mathbb{P}(S_n \geq (1+\delta)\mu) \leq e^{-\mu\delta/3} \quad \text{for } \delta > 1
4.4 Lower Tail Bound
For 0 < \delta < 1 (threshold below the mean):
\boxed{\mathbb{P}(S_n \leq (1-\delta)\mu) \leq \left(\frac{e^{-\delta}}{(1-\delta)^{(1-\delta)}}\right)^\mu}
Simpler form:
\mathbb{P}(S_n \leq (1-\delta)\mu) \leq e^{-\mu\delta^2/2} \quad \text{for } 0 < \delta < 1
4.5 Two-Sided Bound
Combining upper and lower:
\mathbb{P}(|S_n - \mu| \geq \delta\mu) \leq 2e^{-\mu\delta^2/3} \quad \text{for } 0 < \delta \leq 1
4.6 Derivation of the Simple Upper Bound
Starting from the exact bound, we want to show \frac{e^\delta}{(1+\delta)^{1+\delta}} \leq e^{-\delta^2/3} for \delta \in (0,1].
Take logs: need \delta - (1+\delta)\log(1+\delta) \leq -\delta^2/3.
Use the Taylor bound \log(1+\delta) \geq \delta - \delta^2/2 + \delta^3/3 - \cdots. For \delta \in (0,1], one can verify (1+\delta)\log(1+\delta) \geq \delta + \delta^2/3, giving the result. \square

5. Worked Examples
5.1 Fair Coin Flips
S_n \sim \text{Bin}(n, 1/2), \mu = n/2. What is \mathbb{P}(S_n \geq 3n/4)?
Here (1+\delta)\mu = 3n/4 gives \delta = 1/2.
Markov: \mathbb{P}(S_n \geq 3n/4) \leq \frac{n/2}{3n/4} = \frac{2}{3}. Useless.
Chebyshev: \text{Var}(S_n) = n/4. \mathbb{P}(S_n \geq 3n/4) \leq \mathbb{P}(|S_n - n/2| \geq n/4) \leq \frac{n/4}{(n/4)^2} = \frac{4}{n}. Polynomial decay.
Chernoff: \mathbb{P}(S_n \geq 3n/4) \leq e^{-\mu\delta^2/3} = e^{-(n/2)(1/4)/3} = e^{-n/24}. Exponential decay.


                  
                  For n = 100: Chebyshev gives \leq 0.04; Chernoff gives \leq e^{-100/24} \approx 0.015. For n = 1000: Chebyshev gives \leq 0.004; Chernoff gives \leq e^{-1000/24} \approx 5 \times 10^{-19}. The gap is catastrophic at large n — Chernoff is the only bound that matters in asymptotics.
                  
                

5.2 Polling
n people polled, true fraction p = 0.5, want \mathbb{P}(|\hat{p} - 0.5| \geq 0.03) \leq 0.05.
Let S_n =  number of yes votes, \mu = 0.5n, threshold \delta = 0.06 (since 0.03 = \delta \cdot 0.5).
Two-sided Chernoff: 2e^{-\mu\delta^2/3} = 2e^{-(0.5n)(0.0036)/3} = 2e^{-0.0006n} \leq 0.05.
Solve: n \geq \frac{\ln(40)}{0.0006} \approx 6109.


                  
                  Standard polling uses n \approx 1000 for \pm 3% at 95% confidence — this comes from the CLT/normal approximation, which is tighter than Chernoff. Chernoff gives a rigorous but conservative bound; the CLT gives the asymptotically correct answer.
                  
                

5.3 Load Balancing
n jobs, each assigned uniformly to one of n machines. Let X = number of jobs on machine 1, X \sim \text{Bin}(n, 1/n), \mu = 1.
\mathbb{P}(X \geq c\log n / \log\log n) for large c? Chernoff with \mu = 1 gives:
\mathbb{P}(X \geq t) \leq \left(\frac{e}{t}\right)^t
for t = c\log n / \log\log n, this is \leq 1/n^2 for large enough c. Union bound over n machines: maximum load is O(\log n / \log\log n) with high probability. This is the classical balls-into-bins result.

6. The Hierarchy in One Picture
For S_n \sim \text{Bin}(n, p) and threshold a = (1+\delta)\mu:
\underbrace{\frac{\mu}{a}}_{\text{Markov}} \geq \underbrace{\frac{\sigma^2}{(a-\mu)^2}}_{\text{Chebyshev}} \geq \underbrace{e^{-\mu \delta^2/3}}_{\text{Chernoff}}
Each bound is a refinement of the previous. The Chernoff bound can be exponentially smaller.


                  
                  Why Does Exponential Decay Win? Markov uses \mathbb{E}[X]. Chebyshev uses \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2]. Chernoff uses \mathbb{E}[e^{sX}] — which encodes all moments simultaneously via the Taylor series e^{sX} = \sum_k (sX)^k/k!. Using all moments simultaneously is what buys exponential tails.
                  
                


7. Mill’s Inequality (Normal Tail Bound)
For Z \sim N(0,1), the tail satisfies:
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\left(\frac{1}{t} - \frac{1}{t^3}\right)e^{-t^2/2} \leq \mathbb{P}(Z \geq t) \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot \frac{1}{t} \cdot e^{-t^2/2}
The upper bound is the Mill’s inequality (or Mills ratio bound):
\mathbb{P}(Z \geq t) \leq \frac{\phi(t)}{t}
where \phi is the standard normal PDF. This is exponential in t^2/2 — the Chernoff bound applied to the Gaussian MGF.

8. Hoeffding’s Inequality
A generalization of Chernoff for bounded random variables that doesn’t require the Bernoulli structure.
If X_1, \ldots, X_n are independent with a_i \leq X_i \leq b_i and S_n = \sum X_i, \mu = \mathbb{E}[S_n]:
\mathbb{P}(S_n - \mu \geq t) \leq \exp!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (b_i - a_i)^2}\right)
For Bernoulli with [0,1] range, \sum(b_i - a_i)^2 = n, giving \mathbb{P}(S_n - \mu \geq t) \leq e^{-2t^2/n} — similar flavor to Chernoff but derived without needing the exact MGF.

9. Summary Table















































InequalityAssumptionBound on \mathbb{P}(X \geq a)Decay RateMarkovX \geq 0, know \mu\mu / a1/aChebyshevKnow \mu, \sigma^2\sigma^2 / (a - \mu)^21/(a-\mu)^2Chernoff (general)Know MGF M(s)\min_{s>0} e^{-sa}M(s)e^{-\Lambda^*(a)}Chernoff (Binomial, upper)S_n \sim \text{Bin}(n,p)e^{-\mu\delta^2/3} for \delta \leq 1e^{-\Theta(\mu\delta^2)}Chernoff (Binomial, lower)S_n \sim \text{Bin}(n,p)e^{-\mu\delta^2/2} for \delta < 1e^{-\Theta(\mu\delta^2)}HoeffdingBounded: X_i \in [a_i, b_i]e^{-2t^2/\sum(b_i-a_i)^2}e^{-\Theta(t^2/n)}

10. Things I Should Be Able to Do Cold

 State and prove Markov’s inequality in two lines
 Derive Chebyshev from Markov by applying it to (X - \mu)^2
 Explain why both are special cases of: apply Markov to \phi(X) for increasing \phi \geq 0
 Derive the Chernoff bound: apply Markov to e^{sX}, optimize over s
 Write the MGF of \text{Bern}(p) and \text{Bin}(n,p)
 State the simple Chernoff bounds (e^{-\mu\delta^2/3} upper, e^{-\mu\delta^2/2} lower)
 Explain why Chernoff beats Chebyshev exponentially for sums of i.i.d. trials
 Do a polling / load balancing calculation end to end


11. Open Questions / Things to Sit With

 Large deviations: The Legendre transform \Lambda^_(a) = \sup_s(sa - \log M(s)) is the rate function. The full Cramér theorem says \mathbb{P}(\bar{X}_n \geq a) = e^{-n\Lambda^_(a) + o(n)} — Chernoff gives the exponent exactly. How does the sub-exponential prefactor behave?
 Sub-Gaussian and Sub-Exponential: A random variable is sub-Gaussian if its MGF is bounded by a Gaussian MGF — equivalently, if Chernoff-style tails hold with Gaussian rate. Extend Hoeffding to the sub-Gaussian setting.
 Matrix Chernoff: For sums of random PSD matrices, there are matrix analogues of the scalar Chernoff bound using the matrix MGF. Used in randomized linear algebra.
 Second moment method: The first moment method is Markov (\mathbb{P}(X \geq 1) \leq \mathbb{E}[X]). The second moment method bounds \mathbb{P}(X = 0) \leq \text{Var}(X)/(\mathbb{E}[X])^2 — useful in the probabilistic method. Chebyshev in disguise.
 Paley-Zygmund: The reverse of Markov: \mathbb{P}(X \geq \theta\mathbb{E}[X]) \geq (1-\theta)^2 (\mathbb{E}[X])^2/\mathbb{E}[X^2]. Gives lower bounds on tail probabilities.


12. References

Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, Ch. 10 — Markov, Chebyshev, the LLN proof via Chebyshev
Harvard Stat 110, Lecture 22-23 — Chernoff bounds and applications to Binomial trials
Mitzenmacher & Upfal, Probability and Computing, Ch. 4 — definitive treatment of Chernoff for algorithms and randomized computation; load balancing example
Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, Ch. 2 — sub-Gaussian variables, Hoeffding, the modern framework


Links

Moment Generating Functions — the MGF is the input to Chernoff; know M_{Bern}(s) cold
Jensen’s Inequality — the analytic engine behind all three bounds (Markov uses it implicitly; Chernoff uses it explicitly)
Law of Large Numbers — Chebyshev proves the weak LLN; Chernoff gives the exponential rate of convergence
Central Limit Theorem — CLT gives the distributional limit; Chernoff gives non-asymptotic tail bounds valid for finite n
Entropy — the rate function \Lambda^*(a) equals the KL divergence D_{\text{KL}}(\text{Bern}(a)|\text{Bern}(p)) for Binomial trials; large deviations and entropy are the same thing

01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.title: 08.Law of Large Numbers
01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.content:
Tags: probability convergence theorems foundations
References: Blitzstein & Hwang — Introduction to Probability; Stat 110 (Harvard)
Status: 🟡 fleshing out


“The LLN is the theorem that makes probability empirically meaningful. Without it, the whole frequentist interpretation of probability would collapse.”
— something Joe Blitzstein basically said, paraphrased in my head


The Big Picture (before any formulas)
I keep thinking of this theorem as the bridge. On one side you have the abstract, measure-theoretic definition of probability — a number P(A) \in [0,1] attached to an event. On the other side you have the real world: you flip a coin a thousand times and observe a frequency. The LLN is the thing that justifies why those two sides correspond.
Without LLN, saying “a fair coin has probability 1/2 of heads” is just a mathematical assertion with no empirical content. LLN says: run the experiment enough times, and the observed frequency will converge to that number. That’s not obvious — it’s a theorem.
There are two versions, and they are genuinely different animals. I need to keep them straight.

Setup
Let X_1, X_2, \ldots be i.i.d. random variables with mean \mu = E[X_i] (and for the strong version, we’ll need this to exist finitely).
Define the sample mean: \bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i
The question is: in what sense does \bar{X}_n \to \mu?

Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN)
Statement
\bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{p} \mu \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
i.e., for every \varepsilon > 0: P!\left(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| > \varepsilon\right) \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
This is convergence in probability.
Proof (assuming finite variance)
Assume \text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty. This is a stronger assumption than strictly necessary, but the proof is clean and worth knowing cold.
Step 1: Compute the mean and variance of \bar{X}_n.
E[\bar{X}_n] = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i] = \mu
\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \text{Var}(X_i) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}
(Independence is used here — variance of a sum of independent r.v.’s is the sum of variances.)
Step 2: Apply Chebyshev’s inequality.
For any \varepsilon > 0: P!\left(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| > \varepsilon\right) \leq \frac{\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n)}{\varepsilon^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}
Step 3: Take the limit.
\frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2} \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
Therefore P(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| > \varepsilon) \to 0. \blacksquare

Personal note: this proof is genuinely beautiful in its economy. Chebyshev does all the heavy lifting, and variance shrinking like 1/n is the whole game. The proof is so short I sometimes distrust it — but it’s airtight.

What if \sigma^2 = \infty?
The WLLN still holds under weaker conditions — just finite mean is enough. But the proof then requires the characteristic function (Fourier transform of the distribution) rather than Chebyshev. The key identity is:
E[e^{it\bar{X}_n}] = \left(\varphi_X!\left(\frac{t}{n}\right)\right)^n
and a Taylor expansion around t=0 shows this converges to e^{i\mu t}, the characteristic function of the point mass at \mu. I’ll write that up separately when I cover characteristic functions properly.

Strong Law of Large Numbers (SLLN)
Statement
\bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{a.s.} \mu \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
i.e.: P!\left(\lim_{n\to\infty} \bar{X}_n = \mu\right) = 1
This is almost sure convergence (= convergence with probability 1).
Why this is genuinely stronger
The WLLN says: for any fixed \varepsilon, the probability of being far from \mu goes to zero. It does not say that a single infinite sequence of trials will settle down.
More precisely: convergence in probability does not imply almost sure convergence. A classic counterexample is the “typewriter sequence” — a sequence of r.v.’s that converge in probability to 0 but oscillate forever almost surely.
The SLLN says the stronger thing: with probability 1, the actual infinite sequence \bar{X}_1(\omega), \bar{X}_2(\omega), \bar{X}_3(\omega), \ldots converges to \mu. This is a statement about paths, not about probabilities of events at individual times.
\underbrace{P(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| > \varepsilon) \to 0}_{\text{WLLN}} \quad \text{vs.} \quad \underbrace{P!\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\bar{X}_n = \mu\right) = 1}_{\text{SLLN}}
Proof sketch (the L^4 moment approach — cleanest elementary proof)
A clean proof under the stronger assumption E[X_i^4] < \infty uses the fourth moment of \bar{X}_n - \mu and Borel-Cantelli.
Step 1: Let Y_i = X_i - \mu (center the r.v.’s). So E[Y_i] = 0, E[Y_i^4] = \mu_4 < \infty.
Step 2: Expand \left(\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\right)^4 and take expectations. By independence, cross terms with an unpaired index vanish:
E!\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\right)^4\right] = \sum_i E[Y_i^4] + 3\sum_{i \neq j} E[Y_i^2]E[Y_j^2] = O(n^2)
More precisely, this equals n\mu_4 + 3n(n-1)\sigma^4 \leq Cn^2 for some constant C.
Step 3: By Markov’s inequality applied to the fourth power:
P(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| > \varepsilon) = P!\left(\left|\sum Y_i\right|^4 > (n\varepsilon)^4\right) \leq \frac{E[(\sum Y_i)^4]}{n^4\varepsilon^4} \leq \frac{Cn^2}{n^4\varepsilon^4} = \frac{C}{n^2\varepsilon^4}
Step 4: Since \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{C}{n^2\varepsilon^4} < \infty, by the Borel-Cantelli Lemma, the event {|\bar{X}_n - \mu| > \varepsilon} occurs only finitely often almost surely.
Since this holds for every rational \varepsilon > 0, we get \bar{X}_n \to \mu almost surely. \blacksquare

The full SLLN proof (requiring only E|X| < \infty) is significantly harder — it’s one of those theorems where I feel like I understand the ideas but the bookkeeping is genuinely painful. The truncation argument (replacing X_i with X_i \mathbf{1}_{|X_i| \leq i}) is the key trick. Kolmogorov’s inequality replaces Chebyshev in that version.


The Hierarchy of Convergence Modes
Worth drawing this out for myself:
\text{a.s. convergence} \implies \text{convergence in probability} \implies \text{convergence in distribution}
None of these arrows reverse in general. The SLLN \implies WLLN direction follows from this hierarchy.

Applications & Intuition Building
Monte Carlo integration
If g is a function and I want \int_0^1 g(x),dx, I can draw U_1, \ldots, U_n \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1) and compute:
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n g(U_i) \xrightarrow{a.s.} E[g(U)] = \int_0^1 g(x),dx
The LLN is literally why Monte Carlo works. Beautiful.
Consistent estimators
In statistics, an estimator \hat{\theta}_n is consistent for \theta if \hat{\theta}_n \xrightarrow{p} \theta. The LLN immediately gives us that the sample mean is a consistent estimator for the population mean.
Law of Averages (the wrong version)
People often say “after 10 heads in a row, a tail is ‘due’.” This is not what LLN says. LLN says the frequency converges — not that future outcomes compensate for past outcomes. Each flip is independent. The coin has no memory. The sequence “HHHHHHHHHH” followed by i.i.d. flips will eventually see frequency \to 1/2 not because tails “catch up” in a causal sense, but because 10 heads gets diluted by millions of subsequent flips.

This misconception (the Gambler’s Fallacy) is worth understanding deeply because it shows up everywhere — roulette, hot streaks in sports, etc.


Things I Want to Prove Later / Open Threads

 WLLN via characteristic functions (no finite variance assumption)
 Full SLLN via Kolmogorov’s inequality + truncation
 Rate of convergence → this is the Central Limit Theorem (the next major theorem in the sequence)
 Almost sure convergence vs. convergence in probability: write out the typewriter sequence example explicitly
 Ergodic theorem: the “dynamical systems” generalization of SLLN


One-Line Summary for Future Me

WLLN: The probability of the sample mean being far from \mu vanishes. Proved by Chebyshev + variance shrinking like 1/n.
SLLN: With probability 1, the sample mean actually converges to \mu. Proved by Borel-Cantelli + fourth moment bound. Strictly stronger.

Next note: Central Limit Theorem

01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.title: 09.Central Limit Theorem
01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.content:
Tags: probability convergence theorems CLT foundations
References: Blitzstein & Hwang — Introduction to Probability; Stat 110 (Harvard)
Status: 🟡 fleshing out
Prerequisite notes: Law of Large Numbers, Moment Generating Functions, Characteristic Functions


“The LLN tells you where the sample mean goes. The CLT tells you how it gets there — and the answer is shockingly universal.”


The Big Picture
The LLN said \bar{X}_n \to \mu. Fine. But \bar{X}_n - \mu \to 0 is a degenerate statement — it converges to a point. If I zoom in at exactly the right rate, something non-trivial is sitting there. That’s the CLT.
The miracle is this: no matter what distribution you start with (subject to finite variance), if you standardize the sample mean, you always get the same limiting object — the standard normal. The Gaussian isn’t just one distribution among many. It’s an attractor in the space of distributions under convolution and scaling.
This is genuinely shocking. Sum a thousand Bernoullis, sum a thousand Exponentials, sum a thousand Uniforms — zoom in at scale \sqrt{n}, and you see the same bell curve every time. The proof reveals why.

Setup
Let X_1, X_2, \ldots be i.i.d. with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2 \in (0, \infty).
Define the standardized sample mean:
Z_n = \frac{\bar{X}_n - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}
The CLT says Z_n converges in distribution to Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1).

Statement
\frac{\bar{X}_n - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1)
Equivalently, for all x \in \mathbb{R}:
P(Z_n \leq x) \to \Phi(x) \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
Or in the most practically useful form:
\sum_{i=1}^n X_i ;\dot{\sim}; \mathcal{N}(n\mu,; n\sigma^2) \quad \text{for large } n

Proof via Moment Generating Functions
This is the Stat 110 proof. It’s clean, memorable, and illuminates why the normal appears.
Assume M(t) = E[e^{tX}] exists in a neighborhood of 0.
Step 1: Center and normalize.
Let Y_i = (X_i - \mu)/\sigma, so E[Y_i] = 0, \mathrm{Var}(Y_i) = 1, MGF is M_Y. Then:
Z_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i
Step 2: MGF of Z_n.
By independence and the i.i.d. structure:
M_{Z_n}(t) = E!\left[e^{tZ_n}\right] = \left[M_Y!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right]^n
Step 3: Taylor expand M_Y around 0.
Since E[Y] = 0 and E[Y^2] = 1:
M_Y(s) = 1 + s\underbrace{E[Y]}_{=,0} + \frac{s^2}{2}\underbrace{E[Y^2]}_{=,1} + O(s^3) = 1 + \frac{s^2}{2} + O(s^3)
Substituting s = t/\sqrt{n}:
M_Y!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 1 + \frac{t^2}{2n} + O!\left(n^{-3/2}\right)
Step 4: Raise to the n-th power.
M_{Z_n}(t) = \left[1 + \frac{t^2}{2n} + O!\left(n^{-3/2}\right)\right]^n \xrightarrow{n\to\infty} e^{t^2/2}
using the standard limit (1 + a/n + o(1/n))^n \to e^a.
Step 5: Recognize the limit.
e^{t^2/2} is exactly the MGF of \mathcal{N}(0,1). Since MGFs uniquely determine distributions and convergence of MGFs implies convergence in distribution:
Z_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1) \qquad \blacksquare

The hinge of this proof is Step 3. The Taylor expansion kills the first-order term because the mean is zero. The s^2/2 term — the variance term — is what survives. Everything of order s^3 and above vanishes faster than 1/n when raised to the n-th power. The normal is “selected” because it’s the distribution whose MGF is e^{t^2/2}, i.e., the one whose log-MGF is purely quadratic. The CLT is the statement that all the higher-order terms get annihilated by the scaling.


Proof via Characteristic Functions (the correct general proof)
The MGF proof requires the MGF to exist, which fails for heavy-tailed distributions. The right proof uses characteristic functions:
\varphi_X(t) = E[e^{itX}]
which always exists. The structure is identical: let Y_i = (X_i - \mu)/\sigma, then
\varphi_{Z_n}(t) = \left[\varphi_Y!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\right]^n
Taylor expand (using E[Y]=0, E[Y^2]=1, noting the i^2 = -1 sign):
\varphi_Y(s) = 1 + isE[Y] - \frac{s^2}{2}E[Y^2] + O(s^3) = 1 - \frac{s^2}{2} + O(s^3)
So:
\varphi_{Z_n}(t) = \left[1 - \frac{t^2}{2n} + O(n^{-3/2})\right]^n \to e^{-t^2/2}
And e^{-t^2/2} is the characteristic function of \mathcal{N}(0,1). The conclusion follows from Lévy’s continuity theorem: if characteristic functions converge pointwise to a function continuous at 0, the distributions converge in distribution.

This version works for all distributions with finite variance — no MGF assumption. The Cauchy distribution has neither finite mean nor variance, and indeed the CLT fails for it. Characteristic functions are the natural language here, not MGFs. I should think of the MGF proof as the “training wheels” version.


What \xrightarrow{d} Really Means
Convergence in distribution is the weakest mode:
\text{a.s.} \implies \text{in probability} \implies \text{in distribution}
It does not say the random variables Z_n themselves get close to Z in any pathwise sense — only that their laws converge. The CDFs converge at every continuity point of the limit CDF. The CLT lives at the bottom of this hierarchy, and that’s appropriate: what’s universal is the shape of the limiting distribution, not the realizations.

Rate of Convergence: Berry-Esseen
The CLT gives no rate. The Berry-Esseen theorem does:
\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \left|P(Z_n \leq x) - \Phi(x)\right| \leq \frac{C \cdot E|Y_i|^3}{\sqrt{n}}
for absolute constant C \leq 0.4748 (sharpest known). The rate is O(1/\sqrt{n}), controlled by the third absolute moment — a measure of skewness.

Symmetric distributions (zero skewness) converge faster.
Skewed distributions need larger n.

The folk theorem “n = 30 is enough” is a rough proxy for when O(1/\sqrt{n}) error becomes negligible. For skewed distributions — say, Exponential — you need much larger n.

Why the Normal? The Cumulant Explanation
This is the deep reason, not just the mechanical proof.
Cumulants are the coefficients of the cumulant generating function \log M_X(t):
\log M_X(t) = \kappa_1 t + \frac{\kappa_2}{2!}t^2 + \frac{\kappa_3}{3!}t^3 + \cdots
where \kappa_1 = \mu, \kappa_2 = \sigma^2, \kappa_3 = third cumulant (related to skewness), etc. Cumulants are additive for independent r.v.’s.
Now track what happens to Z_n = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\sum(X_i - \mu):

Centering kills \kappa_1
Scaling by 1/\sigma\sqrt{n} scales the k-th cumulant by (\sigma\sqrt{n})^{-k}, so \kappa_k(Z_n) = \frac{n \cdot \kappa_k(X)}{\sigma^k n^{k/2}} = \frac{\kappa_k(X)}{\sigma^k n^{k/2-1}}

For k \geq 3: \kappa_k(Z_n) \to 0 as n \to \infty (since k/2 - 1 > 0).
The only distribution with \kappa_1 = 0, \kappa_2 = 1, and all higher cumulants zero is \mathcal{N}(0,1). Convolution + scaling drives all cumulants of order \geq 3 to zero. The Gaussian is the unique fixed point of this operation.

This is the most satisfying answer to “why normal?” that I know. The proof shows how; the cumulant argument shows why. Both are worth internalizing. The Gaussian isn’t special because someone decided it was — it’s the unique distribution that survives the annihilation of all higher-order structure.


Applications
Normal approximation to Binomial
S_n \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p) — write it as a sum of i.i.d. \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p), so \mu = p, \sigma^2 = p(1-p):
\frac{S_n - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1)
Continuity correction (since S_n is discrete): use k + \tfrac{1}{2} as the cutoff when approximating P(S_n \leq k).
Normal approximation to Poisson
S_n \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda) with large \lambda: \mu = \sigma^2 = \lambda, so
\frac{S_n - \lambda}{\sqrt{\lambda}} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1)
The Delta Method
If \sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) and g is differentiable at \mu with g'(\mu) \neq 0:
\sqrt{n}\bigl(g(\bar{X}_n) - g(\mu)\bigr) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}!\left(0,; [g'(\mu)]^2\sigma^2\right)
Proof idea: Taylor expand g(\bar{X}_n) \approx g(\mu) + g'(\mu)(\bar{X}_n - \mu) and apply CLT to the linear term. This is one of the most practically powerful consequences of the CLT — it gives asymptotic distributions for any smooth transformation of the sample mean. Variance-stabilizing transformations (like \log, \arcsin\sqrt{\cdot}) are built by choosing g so that [g'(\mu)]^2\sigma^2(\mu) = \text{const}.

Multivariate CLT
Let \mathbf{X}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{X}_n be i.i.d. random vectors in \mathbb{R}^k with mean \boldsymbol{\mu} and covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}.
\sqrt{n}\left(\bar{\mathbf{X}}_n - \boldsymbol{\mu}\right) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}_k(\mathbf{0}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})
The proof uses the Cramér-Wold device: a sequence of random vectors converges in distribution iff every linear combination of its components converges. So check \mathbf{t}^\top \mathbf{Z}_n \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{t}) for all \mathbf{t} via the univariate CLT, and you’re done.

Failure Modes

Infinite variance: Cauchy has no finite mean or variance. The correct framework is stable distributions and the generalized CLT (Gnedenko). The scaling is n^{1/\alpha} for \alpha \in (0,2] instead of \sqrt{n}.
Dependence: For dependent sequences, extensions exist (CLT for martingales, m-dependent sequences, mixing processes) but require additional conditions controlling how fast dependence decays.
Non-identical distributions: The Lindeberg-Feller theorem gives the necessary and sufficient condition for CLT when the X_i are independent but not identically distributed. The condition (Lindeberg condition) says no single term dominates the sum.


Connection Back to LLN



































LLNCLTObject\bar{X}_n(\bar{X}_n - \mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})Limit\mu — a constant\mathcal{N}(0,1) — a distributionZoom scaleNone needed1/\sqrt{n}Mode of convergencea.s. / in probabilityin distributionAssumptionFinite meanFinite variance
LLN is first-order. CLT is second-order. Large deviation theory is the next layer — it asks about the probability of events far outside the \sqrt{n} window, i.e., exponentially unlikely deviations.

Open Threads

 Lévy’s continuity theorem — the tool that closes the characteristic function proof rigorously
 Berry-Esseen — work through the actual proof, not just the statement
 Delta method examples — \log transform, \arcsin\sqrt{\cdot}, variance-stabilizing transforms in full
 Lindeberg-Feller — necessary and sufficient conditions, understand why the condition is natural
 Stable distributions — what replaces normal when variance is infinite?
 Martingale CLT — the dependent-sequence version
 Large deviations — Cramér’s theorem as the “third act” after LLN and CLT


One-Line Summary for Future Me

CLT: Standardize the sample mean — whatever the original distribution, you get \mathcal{N}(0,1) in the limit. Proved via MGF/characteristic function Taylor expansion. The deep reason: convolution + 1/\sqrt{n} scaling annihilates all cumulants above the second, and the Gaussian is the unique distribution with only the first two cumulants nonzero.
