01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.title: 10.Convergence to Normal- Poisson, Gamma, Binomial
01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.content:
The Central Limit Theorem says sums of i.i.d. finite-variance random variables converge to normal. But three specific families — Binomial, Poisson, Gamma — converge to normal in their own natural parameter limits, and each convergence has its own flavor, its own rate, and its own practical lesson. Understanding why each one converges, not just that it does, is the goal of this note.


Tags
#probability #CLT #normal-approximation #poisson #gamma #binomial #stat110

Prerequisites

Central Limit Theorem — the engine behind all three results
Moment Generating Functions — MGF proofs of convergence
Poisson Distribution, Gamma Distribution, Binomial Distribution
Standardization: if X has mean \mu and variance \sigma^2, then \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)


0. The Unifying Idea
All three families are sums of i.i.d. random variables in disguise:
\text{Bin}(n,p) = \sum_{i=1}^n \text{Bern}(p) \qquad \text{Pois}(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^n \text{Pois}(\lambda/n) \qquad \text{Gamma}(n,\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^n \text{Expo}(\lambda)
The CLT applies to each. The only question is: which parameter grows, how fast, and what does the error look like?

































FamilyGrowing ParameterMeanVarianceRate of Convergence\text{Bin}(n,p)n \to \infty, p fixednpnp(1-p)O(1/\sqrt{n})\text{Pois}(\lambda)\lambda \to \infty\lambda\lambdaO(1/\sqrt{\lambda})\text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)n \to \infty, \lambda fixedn/\lambdan/\lambda^2O(1/\sqrt{n})

1. Binomial \to Normal
1.1 Statement
Let S_n \sim \text{Bin}(n, p) with p \in (0,1) fixed, \mu = np, \sigma^2 = np(1-p). Then:
\frac{S_n - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1) \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
That is, for fixed a < b:
\mathbb{P}!\left(a \leq \frac{S_n - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}} \leq b\right) \to \Phi(b) - \Phi(a)
where \Phi is the standard normal CDF.
1.2 Why: The CLT Applied Directly
S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n where X_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Bern}(p). Each X_i has mean p and variance p(1-p). The CLT applies immediately. This is the de Moivre–Laplace theorem, historically the first CLT (proved for p = 1/2 by de Moivre in 1733, generalized by Laplace).
1.3 MGF Proof Sketch
The MGF of \text{Bern}(p) is M(s) = 1 - p + pe^s. The standardized sum has MGF:
M_{Z_n}(s) = \left[M!\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right)\right]^n \cdot e^{-nps/\sqrt{np(1-p)}}
Taylor-expanding \log M(s/\sqrt{n}) around s = 0:
\log M_{Z_n}(s) \to \frac{s^2}{2}
which is the log-MGF of N(0,1). \square
1.4 Continuity Correction
Since S_n is integer-valued and N(\mu, \sigma^2) is continuous, replace:
\mathbb{P}(S_n = k) \approx \mathbb{P}!\left(k - \tfrac{1}{2} \leq N \leq k + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)
More generally:
\mathbb{P}(S_n \leq k) \approx \Phi!\left(\frac{k + \frac{1}{2} - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right)
The \frac{1}{2} correction is the continuity correction. It materially improves accuracy, especially for small n or extreme p.


                  
                  When to Use Continuity Correction Always apply it when approximating point probabilities \mathbb{P}(S_n = k) or when n is moderate. For large n the correction becomes negligible relative to \sqrt{n}, but it costs nothing to include it.
                  
                

1.5 Berry-Esseen Bound
The error in the normal approximation is controlled quantitatively. For X_i i.i.d. with mean \mu, variance \sigma^2, and \rho = \mathbb{E}[|X_i - \mu|^3] < \infty:
\sup_x \left|\mathbb{P}!\left(\frac{S_n - n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}} \leq x\right) - \Phi(x)\right| \leq \frac{C\rho}{\sigma^3 \sqrt{n}}
where C \leq 0.4748 (best known constant). For Binomial:
\text{Error} \leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}
The approximation is good when np(1-p) is large — i.e., when neither p nor 1-p is too small and n is large.
1.6 When Not to Use the Normal Approximation

p close to 0 or 1 with moderate n: use Poisson Approximation instead (\lambda = np)
p close to 1 with moderate n: flip and use Poisson on failures
Rule of thumb: normal approximation is good when np \geq 5 and n(1-p) \geq 5

1.7 Numerical Example
S_{100} \sim \text{Bin}(100, 0.4). Compute \mathbb{P}(S_{100} \leq 35).
\mu = 40, \sigma = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.899.
Without continuity correction: \Phi!\left(\frac{35 - 40}{4.899}\right) = \Phi(-1.021) \approx 0.1537.
With continuity correction: \Phi!\left(\frac{35.5 - 40}{4.899}\right) = \Phi(-0.918) \approx 0.1793.
Exact (by direct computation): \approx 0.1795. The correction is nearly exact.

2. Poisson \to Normal
2.1 Statement
Let X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda). Then as \lambda \to \infty:
\frac{X - \lambda}{\sqrt{\lambda}} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)
2.2 Why: Poisson as a Sum
The key representation: if X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Pois}(\lambda/n), then X_1 + \cdots + X_n \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda). As \lambda \to \infty, take n = \lambda and each summand is \text{Pois}(1) with mean 1 and variance 1. The CLT gives:
\frac{\text{Pois}(\lambda) - \lambda}{\sqrt{\lambda}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^\lambda \text{Pois}(1) - \lambda}{\sqrt{\lambda}} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)
2.3 MGF Proof
The MGF of \text{Pois}(\lambda) is M(s) = e^{\lambda(e^s - 1)}. The log-MGF of the standardized variable Z = (X - \lambda)/\sqrt{\lambda} is:
\log M_Z(s) = \lambda!\left(e^{s/\sqrt{\lambda}} - 1\right) - s\sqrt{\lambda}
Taylor-expand e^{s/\sqrt{\lambda}} = 1 + s/\sqrt{\lambda} + s^2/(2\lambda) + s^3/(6\lambda^{3/2}) + \cdots:
\log M_Z(s) = \lambda!\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{\lambda}} + \frac{s^2}{2\lambda} + O(\lambda^{-3/2})\right) - s\sqrt{\lambda} = \frac{s^2}{2} + O(\lambda^{-1/2}) \to \frac{s^2}{2}
The log-MGF converges to s^2/2, the log-MGF of N(0,1). \square
2.4 The Poisson–Binomial–Normal Triangle
\text{Bin}(n,p) \xrightarrow{n\to\infty,, np \to \lambda} \text{Pois}(\lambda) \xrightarrow{\lambda \to \infty} N(\lambda, \lambda)
Going directly: \text{Bin}(n,p) \xrightarrow{n\to\infty,, p\text{ fixed}} N(np, np(1-p)).
The Poisson is an intermediate stop between Binomial and Normal in parameter space. When p is small and \lambda = np is moderate, Poisson is better. When \lambda is large, Normal is good. The triangle tells you which approximation to reach for.
2.5 Continuity Correction
Same logic as for the Binomial — \text{Pois}(\lambda) is integer-valued:
\mathbb{P}(X \leq k) \approx \Phi!\left(\frac{k + \frac{1}{2} - \lambda}{\sqrt{\lambda}}\right)
2.6 Rule of Thumb
The normal approximation to the Poisson is good when \lambda \geq 20 or so. For \lambda < 20, work with the Poisson directly.
2.7 Numerical Example
X \sim \text{Pois}(25). Compute \mathbb{P}(X \leq 20).
\mu = \sigma^2 = 25, \sigma = 5.
Without correction: \Phi!\left(\frac{20 - 25}{5}\right) = \Phi(-1) \approx 0.1587.
With correction: \Phi!\left(\frac{20.5 - 25}{5}\right) = \Phi(-0.9) \approx 0.1841.
Exact: \approx 0.1827. Again the correction wins substantially.

3. Gamma \to Normal
3.1 Statement
Let X \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda) (shape n, rate \lambda), so \mathbb{E}[X] = n/\lambda and \text{Var}(X) = n/\lambda^2. Then as n \to \infty:
\frac{X - n/\lambda}{\sqrt{n}/\lambda} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)
3.2 Why: Gamma as a Sum of Exponentials
The fundamental representation: if T_1, \ldots, T_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Expo}(\lambda), then:
T_1 + \cdots + T_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)
Each T_i has mean 1/\lambda and variance 1/\lambda^2. The CLT gives:
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n T_i - n/\lambda}{\sqrt{n}/\lambda} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1) \qquad \square
No MGF argument needed — this is just the CLT applied to Exponential summands.
3.3 MGF Verification
The MGF of \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda) is M(s) = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - s}\right)^n for s < \lambda. The log-MGF of the standardized variable Z = (X - n/\lambda)/(\sqrt{n}/\lambda):
\log M_Z(s) = n\log!\left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - s\lambda/\sqrt{n}}\right) - \frac{s\sqrt{n}}{\lambda} \cdot \frac{n}{\lambda}
Let u = s/\sqrt{n}. Taylor-expand -\log(1 - u) = u + u^2/2 + u^3/3 + \cdots:
\log M_Z(s) = n\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} + \frac{s^2}{2n} + O(n^{-3/2})\right) - s\sqrt{n} = \frac{s^2}{2} + O(n^{-1/2}) \to \frac{s^2}{2} \qquad \square
3.4 The Chi-Squared Special Case
\chi^2_n = \text{Gamma}(n/2, 1/2) (shape n/2, rate 1/2). Mean = n, variance = 2n. By the same result:
\frac{\chi^2_n - n}{\sqrt{2n}} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)
Equivalently (Fisher’s approximation, sharper):
\sqrt{2\chi^2_n} - \sqrt{2n-1} \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)
The Fisher form converges faster because it removes skewness to first order.
3.5 Connection: Poisson Arrival Times
If arrivals are Poisson(\lambda) and T_n =  time of the n-th arrival, then T_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda). The normal approximation to T_n says: for large n, the n-th arrival time is approximately N(n/\lambda, n/\lambda^2). This is the CLT for renewal processes.
3.6 Numerical Example
X \sim \text{Gamma}(30, 2). Compute \mathbb{P}(X \leq 18).
\mu = 30/2 = 15, \sigma^2 = 30/4 = 7.5, \sigma \approx 2.739.
\mathbb{P}(X \leq 18) \approx \Phi!\left(\frac{18 - 15}{2.739}\right) = \Phi(1.095) \approx 0.8633.


                  
                  No continuity correction for Gamma — it is already a continuous distribution. The normal approximation applies directly without adjustment. 
                  
                


4. Rates of Convergence and the Berry-Esseen Perspective
For all three families, the Berry-Esseen theorem quantifies the error:
\sup_x \left|\mathbb{P}(Z_n \leq x) - \Phi(x)\right| \leq \frac{C \cdot \mathbb{E}[|X_i - \mu|^3]}{\sigma^3 \sqrt{n}}
The third absolute moment controls the rate. For each family:

























FamilyThird Central Moment \rhoError Bound\text{Bern}(p)(1-p)^3 p + p^3(1-p)\frac{C(1 - 2p(1-p))}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\text{Pois}(\lambda/n) (each summand)\lambda/nC/\sqrt{\lambda}\text{Expo}(\lambda)2/\lambda^3C \cdot 2/\sqrt{n}
The approximation degrades when:

p \to 0 or p \to 1 in the Binomial (skewness increases)
\lambda is small for the Poisson (heavy right tail)
n is small for the Gamma (Exponential is very skewed: skewness = 2)


5. Skewness: Why the Convergence Has Direction
All three families are right-skewed for finite parameters. The skewness of each:
\text{Skew}(\text{Bin}(n,p)) = \frac{1 - 2p}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}} \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
\text{Skew}(\text{Pois}(\lambda)) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda}} \to 0 \quad \text{as } \lambda \to \infty
\text{Skew}(\text{Gamma}(n,\lambda)) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{n}} \to 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
Convergence to normal is equivalent to skewness going to zero at rate 1/\sqrt{n} or 1/\sqrt{\lambda}. The normal approximation is most accurate in the center of the distribution and least accurate in the tails, where skewness persists longest.


                  
                  For fixed n or \lambda, the right tail of each distribution is heavier than the normal approximation predicts, and the left tail is lighter. This is why the Chernoff bound (which uses the exact MGF) beats the normal approximation for tail probabilities — the normal misses the asymmetry.
                  
                


6. The Square Root Trick (Variance-Stabilizing Transformations)
Sometimes instead of standardizing X directly, we transform it to make the variance constant (independent of the mean), then apply the normal approximation to the transformed variable.
6.1 Poisson: Square Root Transform
If X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda), then \sqrt{X} has approximately constant variance:
\sqrt{X} \approx N!\left(\sqrt{\lambda} - \frac{1}{8\sqrt{\lambda}},; \frac{1}{4}\right)
So 2\sqrt{X} \approx N(2\sqrt{\lambda}, 1) and the variance is approximately 1/4 regardless of \lambda. This is the Anscombe transform. Used in statistics to stabilize Poisson data before applying normal-based tests.
6.2 Binomial: Arcsin Transform
If \hat{p} = S_n/n \sim \text{Bin}(n,p)/n, the variance p(1-p)/n depends on p. The variance-stabilizing transform is:
\arcsin!\left(\sqrt{\hat{p}}\right) \approx N!\left(\arcsin!\left(\sqrt{p}\right),; \frac{1}{4n}\right)
Variance 1/(4n) is now independent of p.
6.3 Gamma: Log Transform
If X \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda), then \log X has approximately constant variance:
\log X \approx N!\left(\psi(n) - \log\lambda,; \psi'(n)\right) \approx N!\left(\log(n/\lambda),; \frac{1}{n}\right)
where \psi is the digamma function and \psi'(n) \approx 1/n for large n.

7. Summary: Which Approximation When?
Binomial \text{Bin}(n,p):

























RegimeBest Approximationn large, p fixed, np(1-p) \geq 10Normal with continuity correctionn large, p small, np = \lambda moderatePoisson(\lambda)n large, p small, np largeNormaln small, any pExact
Poisson(\lambda):

















RegimeBest Approximation\lambda \geq 20Normal with continuity correction\lambda < 20Exact Poisson
Gamma(n, \lambda):

















RegimeBest Approximationn \geq 30Normal (no continuity correction needed)n < 30Exact Gamma / use software

8. Things I Should Be Able to Do Cold

 State the normal limit for Bin(n,p), Pois(\lambda), Gamma(n,\lambda) — mean, variance, standardized form
 Explain why all three work: each is a sum of i.i.d. terms — name the summands
 Compute the MGF of Pois(\lambda) and show the log-MGF of the standardized version converges to s^2/2
 Apply continuity correction to Binomial and Poisson problems
 State the Berry-Esseen error bound and explain what controls the rate
 Explain the Poisson–Binomial–Normal triangle and when to use each
 State the chi-squared normal approximation (\chi^2_n - n)/\sqrt{2n} \to N(0,1)
 Explain why the normal approximation understimates tail probabilities (skewness)


9. Open Questions / Things to Sit With

 Edgeworth expansions: The normal approximation is the zeroth-order term. The Edgeworth expansion adds corrections: f_{Z_n}(x) \approx \phi(x)\left[1 + \frac{\kappa_3}{6\sqrt{n}}H_3(x) + \cdots\right] where H_3 is the third Hermite polynomial and \kappa_3 is the third cumulant. This explains why skewed distributions have predictable errors in the normal approximation.
 Local CLT: The CLT gives CDF convergence. The local CLT says the PMF/PDF itself converges: \sqrt{n},p_{S_n}(np + x\sqrt{n}) \to \phi(x) uniformly. This is needed for things like local limit theorems for random walks.
 Poisson CLT vs Binomial CLT: The Poisson is the limit of Bin(n, \lambda/n) as n \to \infty. The normal is the limit of Bin(n,p) as n \to \infty with p fixed. These are different limits (rare events vs common events). The transition between them is at p \sim 1/\sqrt{n}.
 Multivariate normal convergence: The Multinomial(n, p_1, \ldots, p_k) converges to a multivariate normal. The covariance matrix has \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = -np_ip_j for i \neq j. The singular covariance (since \sum X_i = n) means the limit lives on a hyperplane.
 Rate of convergence for the Gamma: The Gamma has skewness 2/\sqrt{n}, larger than the Binomial (\sim 1/\sqrt{n}) for comparable parameters. Does this mean the Gamma converges slower? Quantify using Berry-Esseen.


10. References

Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, Ch. 10 — normal approximation to the Binomial; continuity correction; Berry-Esseen stated
Harvard Stat 110, Lectures 29–30 — all three convergences; MGF proofs; the triangle diagram
Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 2, Ch. 8 — local and global CLT for the Binomial; definitive classical treatment
Ferguson, A Course in Large Sample Theory, Ch. 5 — Berry-Esseen proof; Edgeworth expansions


Links

Central Limit Theorem — the theorem behind all three; review the MGF proof
Moment Generating Functions — the analytic tool for all three convergence proofs
Poisson Distribution — Poisson as a sum of i.i.d. Pois(1) is the key representation
Gamma Distribution — Gamma as a sum of i.i.d. Expo(\lambda) is the key representation
Binomial Distribution — Binomial as a sum of i.i.d. Bern(p)
Concentration Bounds — Chernoff uses the exact MGF and beats the normal in the tails; read alongside this note
Entropy — the KL divergence between the true distribution and the normal approximation controls the error; large deviations and CLT are complementary perspectives

01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.title: 11.The Cauchy Distribution
01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.content:
The Cauchy distribution is probability’s most important pathology. It looks like a normal distribution — symmetric, bell-shaped, unimodal — but it has no mean, no variance, no moment generating function. The sample mean of Cauchy random variables has the same distribution as a single observation. The Law of Large Numbers fails completely. The CLT fails completely. It is the canonical example of a heavy-tailed distribution, and understanding why it breaks everything is as important as understanding why the normal distribution fixes everything.


Tags
#probability #cauchy #heavy-tails #pathology #CLT-failure #stable-distributions #stat110

Prerequisites

Normal Distribution — Cauchy is what happens when normality fails
Moment Generating Functions — the MGF does not exist for Cauchy
Central Limit Theorem — the CLT fails for Cauchy; understand why
Law of Large Numbers — also fails; understand why
Basic complex analysis / characteristic functions — the right tool for Cauchy


1. Definition
1.1 Standard Cauchy
The standard Cauchy distribution X \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1) has PDF:
f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1 + x^2)}, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}
CDF:
F(x) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\pi}\arctan(x)
Quantile function:
F^{-1}(u) = \tan!\left(\pi!\left(u - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)
1.2 General Cauchy
X \sim \text{Cauchy}(\mu, \gamma) with location \mu \in \mathbb{R} and scale \gamma > 0 has PDF:
f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi\gamma\left[1 + \left(\frac{x-\mu}{\gamma}\right)^2\right]}
The standard Cauchy is \text{Cauchy}(0, 1).
1.3 The t_1 Connection
\text{Cauchy}(0,1) = t_1
The Cauchy is the Student’s t-distribution with 1 degree of freedom. More generally, t_\nu has finite moments only up to order \nu - 1. The Cauchy (\nu = 1) has no finite moments at all — not even the mean.

2. The Ratio Representation
2.1 Statement
If X, Y \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1), then:
\frac{X}{Y} \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1)
2.2 Proof
Let Z = X/Y. Condition on Y = y: given Y = y, Z = X/y \sim N(0, 1/y^2), so Z \mid Y = y has PDF f_{Z|Y}(z|y) = \frac{|y|}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-y^2z^2/2}.
Marginalize over Y:
f_Z(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{|y|}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-y^2z^2/2} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-y^2/2},dy = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\infty y,e^{-y^2(1+z^2)/2},dy
Let u = y^2(1+z^2)/2, du = y(1+z^2),dy:
f_Z(z) = \frac{1}{\pi(1+z^2)}\int_0^\infty e^{-u},du = \frac{1}{\pi(1+z^2)} \qquad \square


                  
                  This representation explains intuitively why the Cauchy has no mean: it is a ratio of two mean-zero normals. The denominator can be arbitrarily close to zero, producing arbitrarily large values — and the tails are heavy enough that the expectation diverges. 
                  
                

2.3 Alternative Representation: Tangent of Uniform
If U \sim \text{Uniform}(-\pi/2, \pi/2), then:
\tan(U) \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1)
Proof. The CDF of \tan(U) at x is \mathbb{P}(\tan(U) \leq x) = \mathbb{P}(U \leq \arctan(x)) = \frac{\arctan(x) + \pi/2}{\pi} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\arctan(x)}{\pi}, which is the Cauchy CDF. \square
This representation gives an easy simulation method: generate U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1), return \tan(\pi(U - 1/2)).

3. No Mean, No Variance, No MGF
3.1 The Mean Does Not Exist
\mathbb{E}[|X|] = \frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\infty \frac{x}{1+x^2},dx = \frac{1}{\pi}\left[\log(1+x^2)\right]_0^\infty = +\infty
The absolute expectation is infinite, so \mathbb{E}[X] does not exist (the integral \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{x}{\pi(1+x^2)},dx is not absolutely convergent — it is \infty - \infty in a precise sense, though the symmetric principal value is 0).


                  
                  The Principal Value Trap \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{x}{\pi(1+x^2)},dx is sometimes written as 0 by symmetry. This is the Cauchy principal value \lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{-R}^{R}, not the actual expectation. The actual expectation requires absolute convergence, which fails. The "mean = 0 by symmetry" argument is wrong: the integral is \infty - \infty, which is undefined, not 0 - 0.
                  
                

3.2 All Moments Are Infinite
\mathbb{E}[|X|^k] = +\infty \quad \text{for all } k \geq 1
Since \frac{|x|^k}{1+x^2} \sim |x|^{k-2} for large x, the integral diverges for all k \geq 1. The Cauchy has no finite moments of any order.
3.3 The MGF Does Not Exist
M(s) = \mathbb{E}[e^{sX}] = +\infty \quad \text{for all } s \neq 0
Since e^{sx}/(1+x^2) \sim e^{sx}/x^2 grows faster than any power, the integral diverges for every s \neq 0. The MGF is identically +\infty on (-\infty, 0) \cup (0, \infty).


                  
                  This makes the MGF proof technique entirely useless for Cauchy. The right tool is the characteristic function \varphi(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{itX}], which always exists since |e^{itX}| = 1.
                  
                

3.4 The Characteristic Function
For X \sim \text{Cauchy}(\mu, \gamma):
\varphi(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{itX}] = e^{i\mu t - \gamma|t|}
For the standard Cauchy (\mu = 0, \gamma = 1):
\varphi(t) = e^{-|t|}
Proof sketch. Compute \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{e^{itx}}{\pi(1+x^2)},dx by contour integration (residue at x = i for t > 0): residue = e^{-t}/(2i), giving 2\pi i \cdot e^{-t}/(2\pi i) = e^{-t}. \square


                  
                  The characteristic function e^{-|t|} is not differentiable at t = 0. This is directly related to the non-existence of the mean: differentiating the characteristic function at 0 gives the mean, so if the characteristic function is not differentiable at 0, the mean does not exist.
                  
                


4. Stability: The LLN and CLT Both Fail
4.1 The Sample Mean Has the Same Distribution
Let X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Cauchy}(0,1). Then:
\bar{X}_n = \frac{X_1 + \cdots + X_n}{n} \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1)
The sample mean has exactly the same distribution as a single observation, for every n.
Proof via characteristic functions. The characteristic function of X_1 + \cdots + X_n is \varphi(t)^n = e^{-n|t|}. The characteristic function of \bar{X}_n = (X_1 + \cdots + X_n)/n is:
\varphi_{\bar{X}_n}(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{it\bar{X}_n}] = \varphi(t/n)^n = e^{-n|t/n|} = e^{-|t|}
which is the characteristic function of Cauchy(0,1). \square
4.2 The LLN Fails
The WLLN states \bar{X}_n \xrightarrow{p} \mathbb{E}[X] when \mathbb{E}[X] is finite. For Cauchy:

\mathbb{E}[X] does not exist → LLN does not apply
\bar{X}_n \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1) for all n → \bar{X}_n does not converge in probability to anything

No matter how many observations you take, the sample mean does not stabilize. Averaging Cauchy data is completely futile.
4.3 The CLT Fails
The CLT requires finite variance. The Cauchy has infinite variance (in fact infinite mean). The conclusion (\bar{X}_n - \mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n}) \to N(0,1) requires \sigma < \infty, which fails.
More precisely: the correct normalization for Cauchy sums is not \sqrt{n} but n itself. S_n/n \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1) — the sum grows linearly, not like \sqrt{n}.


                  
                  What Replaces the CLT? For heavy-tailed distributions, the CLT is replaced by the Generalized CLT: properly normalized sums converge to a stable distribution. The Cauchy is itself stable (see §5). The normal distribution is the stable distribution with index \alpha = 2; the Cauchy is stable with index \alpha = 1.
                  
                


5. Stability
5.1 Definition
A distribution is stable if sums of i.i.d. copies have the same distribution type (up to location and scale). Formally, X is stable if for any n, there exist a_n > 0 and b_n such that:
X_1 + \cdots + X_n \overset{d}{=} a_n X + b_n
5.2 Cauchy is Stable with Index 1
For X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Cauchy}(0,1):
X_1 + \cdots + X_n \overset{d}{=} n \cdot \text{Cauchy}(0,1) \overset{d}{=} \text{Cauchy}(0, n)
So a_n = n, b_n = 0. The scaling is linear in n, not \sqrt{n} as for the normal.
5.3 The Stable Family
The family of stable distributions is parametrized by the stability index \alpha \in (0, 2]:

\alpha = 2: Normal distribution (CLT limit for finite-variance variables)
\alpha = 1: Cauchy distribution
\alpha \in (1,2): Lévy alpha-stable distributions with infinite variance but finite mean
\alpha \in (0,1]: Infinite mean and infinite variance

The Cauchy sits at the boundary \alpha = 1 between distributions with finite mean (\alpha > 1) and no mean (\alpha \leq 1).

6. Tail Behavior
6.1 Power Law Tails
For large |x|:
f(x) \sim \frac{1}{\pi x^2}, \quad \mathbb{P}(X > x) \sim \frac{1}{\pi x}
The tails decay as 1/x^2 for the PDF and 1/x for the survival function. This is a power law with exponent 1 — the slowest possible decay that still integrates to 1.
Compare with the normal: f_N(x) \sim e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi} — exponentially faster decay.
6.2 Why the Mean Diverges: A Direct Argument
\mathbb{E}[X^+] = \int_0^\infty \frac{x}{\pi(1+x^2)},dx \approx \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{\pi x},dx = \frac{1}{\pi}\log x\Big|_1^\infty = +\infty
The 1/x tail is exactly at the boundary of integrability — \int_1^\infty x^{-p},dx converges iff p > 1, and the Cauchy tail \sim 1/(\pi x) has p = 1.
6.3 Contrast: Pareto and Other Power Laws
The Pareto distribution \mathbb{P}(X > x) = (x_m/x)^\alpha for x \geq x_m has:

Finite mean iff \alpha > 1
Finite variance iff \alpha > 2

The Cauchy corresponds to \alpha = 1 in the Pareto family — right at the boundary of finite mean. This is not a coincidence: both have 1/x survival functions.

7. Why the Cauchy Looks Normal but Isn’t
7.1 Visual Deception
The Cauchy PDF \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)} and the standard normal PDF \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2} are both:

Symmetric about 0
Unimodal with mode at 0
Bell-shaped

Near the center, they look similar. The difference is entirely in the tails: the Cauchy decays as 1/x^2 while the normal decays as e^{-x^2/2}. In a histogram, rare but enormous values will eventually reveal the Cauchy’s heavy tail — but it may take a very large sample.
7.2 The Empirical Mean Oscillates
For Cauchy data, the running sample mean \bar{X}_n does not converge. It oscillates indefinitely, occasionally jumping to large values when an extreme observation occurs. The histogram of \bar{X}_n for large n looks like a Cauchy — because it is one.
7.3 Median and Interquartile Range Work Fine
The Cauchy has a well-defined median (= 0 for standard Cauchy) and interquartile range (= 2 for standard Cauchy, since F^{-1}(3/4) - F^{-1}(1/4) = \tan(\pi/4) - \tan(-\pi/4) = 2). Robust statistics — median, IQR, quantiles — work correctly for Cauchy. Only moment-based statistics (mean, variance, standard deviation) break.

8. Practical Appearances of the Cauchy
8.1 Ratio of Normals
Any time you divide two independent zero-mean normals, you get a Cauchy. Ratios appear in:

Signal-to-noise estimates when the signal mean is uncertain
Regression coefficient divided by standard error under misspecification
Finance: ratio of two asset returns

8.2 Physics: Lorentzian / Breit-Wigner
The Cauchy distribution appears in physics as the Lorentzian line shape and the Breit-Wigner distribution for resonance peaks in particle physics. The parameter \gamma is the half-width at half-maximum of the resonance.
8.3 Electrical Engineering: Shot Noise
Certain shot noise processes have Cauchy-distributed outputs. The heavy tails correspond to rare but large voltage spikes.
8.4 Counterexample Generator
The Cauchy is the standard counterexample for:

LLN (fails: mean doesn’t exist)
CLT (fails: variance doesn’t exist)
MGF techniques (fails: MGF doesn’t exist)
Consistency of the sample mean (fails: \bar{X}_n \sim \text{Cauchy} for all n)


9. The Characteristic Function as the Right Tool
Since the MGF is useless, everything about the Cauchy must be done with the characteristic function \varphi(t) = e^{-|t|}.
Key facts derivable from the characteristic function:





























PropertyVia Characteristic Function\bar{X}_n \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1)$\varphi(t/n)^n = e^{-n\cdotCauchy is stable$\varphi(t)^n = e^{-nNo mean\varphi'(0) does not exist ($No variance\varphi''(0) does not existSum of Cauchys is Cauchy$e^{-
The characteristic function e^{-|t|} is the Fourier transform of \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)} — this is the one computation worth doing by hand (via residues) to see the whole picture.

10. Summary






































































PropertyNormal N(0,1)Cauchy(0,1)PDF\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}\frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}Mean0Does not existVariance1Does not existMGFe^{s^2/2}Does not exist (s \neq 0)Char. functione^{-t^2/2}e^{-\lvert t\rvert}Tail decaye^{-x^2/2} (super-exponential)1/(\pi x^2) (power law)\bar{X}_n distributionN(0, 1/n) — concentratesCauchy(0,1) — does not concentrateLLNHoldsFailsCLTHolds (trivially)FailsStable index\alpha = 2\alpha = 1Median00IQR\approx 1.352

11. Things I Should Be Able to Do Cold

 Write the Cauchy PDF and CDF from memory
 Prove X/Y \sim \text{Cauchy} when X, Y \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1) — by conditioning on Y
 Prove \tan(U) \sim \text{Cauchy} when U \sim \text{Uniform}(-\pi/2, \pi/2)
 Prove the mean does not exist (show \mathbb{E}[|X|] = \infty) and explain the principal value trap
 State the characteristic function \varphi(t) = e^{-|t|} and explain why it’s not differentiable at 0
 Prove \bar{X}_n \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1) for all n using characteristic functions in two lines
 Explain why the LLN and CLT both fail and what the correct scaling is (S_n/n, not S_n/\sqrt{n})
 Place Cauchy in the stable distribution family: \alpha = 1, Normal is \alpha = 2


12. Open Questions / Things to Sit With

 Truncated Cauchy: If you truncate the Cauchy to [-M, M], all moments exist. How does the sample mean of the truncated Cauchy behave? The truncation removes the heavy tails — does the LLN recover?
 Median as estimator: Since the sample mean fails for Cauchy, use the sample median. The sample median of n Cauchy(0,1) observations is approximately N(0, \pi^2/(4n)) by the delta method applied to the quantile function. This is a striking result — the median is consistent and asymptotically normal even when the mean is not.
 Stable distributions: What is the full parametrization of the stable family? What are the characteristic functions for general \alpha \in (0,2]? The Lévy distribution (\alpha = 1/2, one-sided) is another closed-form special case.
 Cauchy and Brownian motion: The Cauchy distribution appears as the distribution of the first hitting time of a level by Brownian motion and as the distribution of Brownian motion at a random exponential time. Understand this connection.
 Financial returns: Mandelbrot argued empirical asset returns have power-law tails inconsistent with normality — possibly \alpha \approx 1.5 to 1.8. The Cauchy (\alpha = 1) is too heavy-tailed, but the intuition is right. What is the right stable model for financial returns?


13. References

Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, Ch. 6 — the ratio representation; Student’s t connection
Harvard Stat 110, Lecture 28 — Cauchy as counterexample; characteristic function proof of \bar{X}_n \sim \text{Cauchy}
Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 2, Ch. 6 — stable distributions; characteristic functions; the full theory
Taleb, The Black Swan — popular treatment of why heavy tails matter and why Gaussian models fail in practice


Links

Central Limit Theorem — the CLT fails for Cauchy; this note is the canonical counterexample
Law of Large Numbers — also fails; the sample mean of Cauchys has the same distribution for all n
Moment Generating Functions — the MGF does not exist; characteristic functions are the replacement
Characteristic Functions — the right tool for all Cauchy calculations; \varphi(t) = e^{-|t|}
Normal Distribution — the Cauchy looks like the normal but breaks every normal-based theorem
Stable Distributions — Cauchy is the \alpha = 1 stable distribution; Normal is \alpha = 2
Concentration Bounds — Chernoff bounds require a finite MGF; none of the standard bounds apply to Cauchy
Student’s t Distribution — Cauchy = t_1; the t_\nu family interpolates between Cauchy and Normal as \nu \to \infty

01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.title: 12.Chi-Squared Distribution
01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.content:
Tags: probability distributions statistics chi-squared
References: Blitzstein & Hwang — Introduction to Probability; Stat 110 (Harvard)
Status: 🟡 fleshing out
Prerequisite notes: Normal Distribution, Central Limit Theorem, Gamma Distribution, Moment Generating Functions


“The chi-squared isn’t some arbitrary distribution someone cooked up for hypothesis testing. It falls out of the normal completely naturally — it’s what happens when you square standard normals and add them. Everything else follows from that one fact.”


The Big Picture
I used to think of \chi^2 as a statistical tool — something you invoke for goodness-of-fit tests. That framing puts the cart before the horse. The chi-squared distribution is a derived distribution: it’s the answer to the question “what is the distribution of a sum of squared standard normals?” That question arises constantly — estimating variance, testing independence, understanding quadratic forms in linear models. The distribution is just answering something natural.
Four facts to internalize before anything else:

\chi^2_1 = Z^2 where Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) — the entire family starts here.
\chi^2_n is the sum of n independent \chi^2_1‘s — the parameter literally counts squared normals.
\chi^2_n = \mathrm{Gamma}(n/2,, 1/2) — all Gamma machinery applies directly.
By CLT, \chi^2_n looks increasingly normal as n \to \infty — it’s a living demonstration of CLT.


Definition
The Right Way to Think About It
Let Z_1, \ldots, Z_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1). Define:
X = \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2
Then X \sim \chi^2_n, the chi-squared distribution with n degrees of freedom.
The parameter n is called degrees of freedom because here it literally is one: the number of unconstrained squared standard normals being summed. Later in regression and contingency tables the terminology gets murkier, but the root meaning is always “rank of the quadratic form.”
The Analytical Handle
\chi^2_n ;=; \mathrm{Gamma}!\left(\frac{n}{2},; \frac{1}{2}\right)
using the shape-rate parameterization: X \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta) has PDF \propto x^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta x} on (0,\infty).

The PDF
For x > 0:
f_n(x) = \frac{1}{2^{n/2},\Gamma(n/2)}; x^{n/2 - 1}; e^{-x/2}
This is Gamma(n/2, 1/2) written out explicitly.
Special cases worth memorizing:

n=1: f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi x}},e^{-x/2} — there’s a singularity at 0, because squaring a \mathcal{N}(0,1) concentrates mass near zero.
n=2: f(x) = \frac{1}{2}e^{-x/2} — this is \mathrm{Expo}(1/2). The chi-squared with 2 degrees of freedom is exponential. Clean and worth knowing cold.


Deriving \chi^2_1: The Base Case
Claim: If Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), then Z^2 \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(1/2,, 1/2).
Proof via CDF:
For x > 0: F_{Z^2}(x) = P(Z^2 \leq x) = P(-\sqrt{x} \leq Z \leq \sqrt{x}) = 2\Phi(\sqrt{x}) - 1
Differentiate with respect to x: f_{Z^2}(x) = 2\phi(\sqrt{x}) \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} = \frac{\phi(\sqrt{x})}{\sqrt{x}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi x}},e^{-x/2}
Rewrite to match the Gamma form: f_{Z^2}(x) = \frac{1}{2^{1/2},\Gamma(1/2)},x^{1/2-1},e^{-x/2}
using \Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}.
This is exactly \mathrm{Gamma}(1/2,, 1/2). \blacksquare

The appearance of \Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi} is the same \sqrt{\pi} that normalizes the Gaussian integral \int e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi}. The normalization constants are the same constant in different clothes. I find this genuinely satisfying — squaring a normal and integrating brings you right back to the same transcendental constant.


Building \chi^2_n: The Additive Property
Claim: If X_1 \sim \chi^2_{n_1} and X_2 \sim \chi^2_{n_2} are independent, then X_1 + X_2 \sim \chi^2_{n_1 + n_2}.
Proof via MGFs:
The MGF of \chi^2_n (derived below) is: M_{\chi^2_n}(t) = (1 - 2t)^{-n/2}, \qquad t < \tfrac{1}{2}
By independence: M_{X_1+X_2}(t) = (1-2t)^{-n_1/2} \cdot (1-2t)^{-n_2/2} = (1-2t)^{-(n_1+n_2)/2}
This is the MGF of \chi^2_{n_1+n_2}, and MGFs uniquely determine distributions. \blacksquare
The \chi^2_n being a sum of n independent \chi^2_1‘s is just Gamma additivity: \mathrm{Gamma}!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\right) * \cdots * \mathrm{Gamma}!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \mathrm{Gamma}!\left(\tfrac{n}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\right)

The MGF
M_X(t) = (1 - 2t)^{-n/2}, \qquad t < \tfrac{1}{2}
Proof (start from \chi^2_1):
M_{Z^2}(t) = E[e^{tZ^2}] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{tz^2},\frac{e^{-z^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}},dz = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2(1-2t)/2},dz
This is a Gaussian integral with variance 1/(1-2t), valid for t < 1/2. It evaluates to:
M_{Z^2}(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2t}} = (1-2t)^{-1/2}
By independence and i.i.d.: M_{\chi^2_n}(t) = \left[(1-2t)^{-1/2}\right]^n = (1-2t)^{-n/2} \qquad \blacksquare

The key step is recognizing that e^{tz^2} \cdot e^{-z^2/2} = e^{-z^2(1-2t)/2} is just another Gaussian, with variance 1/(1-2t). The MGF is doing a change of variance. This trick — completing the Gaussian integral by reading off the normalizing constant — comes up constantly.


Moments
From the Gamma moments E[\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\beta)] = \alpha/\beta and \mathrm{Var} = \alpha/\beta^2:
E[\chi^2_n] = \frac{n/2}{1/2} = n \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\chi^2_n) = \frac{n/2}{(1/2)^2} = 2n
Or directly: since E[Z_i^2] = 1 and \mathrm{Var}(Z_i^2) = E[Z^4] - (E[Z^2])^2 = 3 - 1 = 2, linearity gives the same answer. (The fourth moment E[Z^4] = 3 comes from the general formula E[Z^{2k}] = (2k-1)!! = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2k-1).)
The ratio \mathrm{Var}/E = 2 is constant in n — a useful sanity check.

Asymptotics: CLT for \chi^2_n
Since \chi^2_n = \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2 is a sum of i.i.d. r.v.’s with mean 1 and variance 2, the CLT gives immediately:
\frac{\chi^2_n - n}{\sqrt{2n}} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1)
The chi-squared distribution is itself a demonstration of what CLT does. For large n, using a normal table for chi-squared critical values is justified.
A sharper approximation (Wilson-Hilferty, 1931): (\chi^2_n/n)^{1/3} is approximately \mathcal{N}(1 - 2/(9n),; 2/(9n)). The cube-root transformation stabilizes the skewness. Worth knowing the approximation exists even if I won’t derive it now.

Key Relationships
Sample Variance
If X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) and S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i - \bar{X})^2, then:
\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-1}
and moreover \bar{X} \perp S^2 (independent!). This is Cochran’s theorem — one of the foundational results of classical statistics. The degrees of freedom drop from n to n-1 because one degree of freedom is consumed estimating \mu with \bar{X}.
The proof runs through the spectral decomposition of the quadratic form \sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2/\sigma^2 = \mathbf{Z}^\top(I - \tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top)\mathbf{Z} where \mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{0}, I). The matrix I - \tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top is idempotent with rank n-1. Deserves its own note.
t-Distribution
If Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) and V \sim \chi^2_n are independent:
T = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/n}} \sim t_n
This is why a t-test has n-1 degrees of freedom: the Z in the numerator is the standardized \bar{X}, and the V \sim \chi^2_{n-1} in the denominator is (proportional to) S^2, the estimated variance. Dividing by the estimated rather than known \sigma inflates the tails — t_n \to \mathcal{N}(0,1) as n \to \infty by LLN (the denominator \to 1).
F-Distribution
If U \sim \chi^2_m and V \sim \chi^2_n are independent:
F = \frac{U/m}{V/n} \sim F_{m,n}
A ratio of scaled chi-squareds. Appears in ANOVA (ratio of between-group to within-group variance) and in comparing two sample variances.
Quadratic Forms in Normal Vectors (the general picture)
If \mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}_n(\mathbf{0}, I) and A is an n \times n idempotent matrix with \mathrm{rank}(A) = r, then:
\mathbf{Z}^\top A,\mathbf{Z} \sim \chi^2_r
Every chi-squared that appears in statistics is secretly a quadratic form in a normal vector, and its degrees of freedom is the rank of the projection matrix. The sample variance case, the goodness-of-fit statistic, the residual sum of squares in regression — all of them.

Why Chi-Squared Appears in Tests
Goodness-of-Fit
Observed counts O_i vs. expected counts E_i = np_i across k categories:
\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i} \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{k-1}
Mechanically why: Each (O_i - E_i)/\sqrt{E_i} is approximately \mathcal{N}(0,1) by CLT (it’s a standardized count). Squaring and summing gives approximately \chi^2_k. The constraint \sum O_i = n reduces rank by 1, giving \chi^2_{k-1}. The precise derivation goes through the multivariate CLT applied to the multinomial.
Independence in Contingency Tables
r \times c table, observed O_{ij}, expected under independence E_{ij} = R_i C_j / n:
\chi^2 = \sum_{i,j}\frac{(O_{ij} - E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}} \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_{(r-1)(c-1)}
Degrees of freedom: (r-1)(c-1) — the number of cells that are “free” after fixing all marginals.
Likelihood Ratio Tests (Wilks’ Theorem)
For a null hypothesis that reduces a p-parameter model by d constraints:
-2\log\Lambda \xrightarrow{d} \chi^2_d
The \chi^2_d arises because the log-likelihood is locally quadratic near the MLE (Taylor expansion), so the likelihood ratio statistic is asymptotically a quadratic form in d approximately normal quantities. This is the most general justification — essentially every chi-squared test in statistics is a special case of Wilks’ theorem.

Wilks’ theorem is the reason chi-squared tests are so ubiquitous. It says: any likelihood ratio test, for any model, asymptotically distributes as chi-squared with degrees of freedom equal to the number of constraints tested. That’s a breathtaking level of generality.


Summary Table













































PropertyFormulaDefinition\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2, Z_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1)Gamma equivalent\mathrm{Gamma}(n/2,; 1/2)Support(0, \infty)MeannVariance2nMGF(1-2t)^{-n/2}, ;; t < 1/2Additive\chi^2_m + \chi^2_n \overset{d}{=} \chi^2_{m+n} (indep.)CLT(\chi^2_n - n)/\sqrt{2n} \to \mathcal{N}(0,1)Special case\chi^2_2 = \mathrm{Expo}(1/2)

Open Threads

 Cochran’s theorem — full proof via spectral decomposition; independence of \bar{X} and S^2
 Quadratic forms in normals — general \mathbf{Z}^\top A\mathbf{Z} \sim \chi^2_{\mathrm{rank}(A)} for idempotent A
 Wilks’ theorem — understand the Taylor expansion of the log-likelihood that produces \chi^2_d
 t-distribution — derive it from \mathcal{N}(0,1)/\sqrt{\chi^2_n/n}; show t_n \to \mathcal{N}(0,1)
 F-distribution — connection to ANOVA; note t_n^2 \sim F_{1,n}
 Wilson-Hilferty cube-root approximation — why does (\chi^2_n/n)^{1/3} stabilize skewness?


One-Line Summary for Future Me

\chi^2_n is \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2 for i.i.d. standard normals — equivalently \mathrm{Gamma}(n/2, 1/2), with mean n, variance 2n, and MGF (1-2t)^{-n/2}. It appears wherever quadratic forms in normal vectors appear, with degrees of freedom = rank of the underlying projection matrix. Every chi-squared test in statistics is either directly this or a consequence of Wilks’ theorem.

01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.title: 13.Student's t-Distribution
01.Maths/Probability/10.Inequalities-and.content:
Tags: probability distributions statistics t-distribution
References: Blitzstein & Hwang — Introduction to Probability; Stat 110 (Harvard)
Status: 🟡 fleshing out
Prerequisite notes: Normal Distribution, Chi-Squared Distribution, Gamma Distribution, Moment Generating Functions


“The t-distribution is what honesty looks like. When you don’t know \sigma and have to estimate it, your uncertainty about that estimate inflates the tails. The t quantifies exactly how much inflation.”


The Big Picture
Here is the situation the t-distribution was invented to resolve.
You have X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) and you want to make inference about \mu. If \sigma were known, you’d use the z-statistic:
Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)
exactly. But \sigma is never known. You replace it with the sample standard deviation S:
T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt{n}}
and now T is not \mathcal{N}(0,1). The randomness of S inflates the tails — T is more spread out than a standard normal, and the degree of inflation depends on how well-estimated S is, i.e., on n. The t-distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom captures this exactly.
William Gosset figured this out in 1908 while working at the Guinness brewery. He published under the pseudonym “Student” because Guinness didn’t allow employees to publish. Hence: Student’s t-distribution.

Definition
The Constructive Definition
If Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) and V \sim \chi^2_\nu are independent, then:
T = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/\nu}} \sim t_\nu
The parameter \nu is the degrees of freedom.
This is the definition that reveals what the t-distribution is: a normal divided by an independent (scaled) chi. The denominator is random, and that randomness is what fattens the tails.
Why This Is the Right Definition for Inference
In the one-sample setting: X_1,\ldots,X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2).

Numerator: \bar{X} - \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2/n), so Z = (\bar{X}-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n}) \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1).
Denominator: by Cochran’s theorem, (n-1)S^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}, and S^2 \perp \bar{X}.

So: T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{\frac{(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2}{n-1}}} = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/(n-1)}} \sim t_{n-1}
The \sigma^2 cancels exactly — that’s the point. You don’t need to know \sigma.

The independence of \bar{X} and S^2 is doing serious work here. Without Cochran’s theorem guaranteeing Z \perp V, the ratio wouldn’t have a t-distribution. This is a deeply non-obvious fact — in non-normal populations, \bar{X} and S^2 are generally dependent.


The PDF
Claim: T \sim t_\nu has PDF:
f_\nu(t) = \frac{\Gamma!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\nu\pi};\Gamma!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)} \left(1 + \frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)^{-(\nu+1)/2}, \qquad t \in \mathbb{R}
Proof: Use the constructive definition T = Z/\sqrt{V/\nu} with Z \perp V.
Condition on V = v. Given V=v, we have T | V=v \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \nu/v), so:
f_{T|V}(t|v) = \sqrt{\frac{v}{\nu}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp!\left(-\frac{vt^2}{2\nu}\right)
The marginal PDF of T is:
f_T(t) = \int_0^\infty f_{T|V}(t|v), f_V(v),dv
where f_V(v) = \frac{v^{\nu/2-1}e^{-v/2}}{2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)} is the \chi^2_\nu PDF. Substituting:
f_T(t) = \int_0^\infty \sqrt{\frac{v}{\nu}} \cdot \frac{e^{-vt^2/(2\nu)}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot \frac{v^{\nu/2-1}e^{-v/2}}{2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)},dv
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\nu},2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)} \int_0^\infty v^{(\nu+1)/2 - 1} \exp!\left(-\frac{v}{2}\left(1 + \frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)\right)dv
The integral is a Gamma integral. Let \lambda = \frac{1}{2}!\left(1 + \frac{t^2}{\nu}\right), so the integral = \Gamma!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)/\lambda^{(\nu+1)/2}:
f_T(t) = \frac{\Gamma!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{2\pi\nu},2^{\nu/2}\Gamma(\nu/2)} \cdot \frac{2^{(\nu+1)/2}}{\left(1 + t^2/\nu\right)^{(\nu+1)/2}}
Simplify the powers of 2: 2^{(\nu+1)/2}/2^{\nu/2} = 2^{1/2} = \sqrt{2}. Then \sqrt{2}/\sqrt{2\pi} = 1/\sqrt{\pi}:
\boxed{f_\nu(t) = \frac{\Gamma!\left(\frac{\nu+1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\nu\pi};\Gamma!\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)} \left(1 + \frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)^{-(\nu+1)/2}} \qquad \blacksquare

The key move is conditioning on V and recognizing the resulting integral as a Gamma function. This is a standard trick: when a distribution is defined as a ratio involving a \chi^2, condition on the denominator, do the integral, and you get a closed form. The same strategy proves the F-distribution PDF.


The Heavy Tails, Made Precise
The t_\nu PDF has polynomial tails: for large |t|,
f_\nu(t) \sim C_\nu \cdot |t|^{-(\nu+1)}
Compare this to the Gaussian, whose tails are \sim e^{-t^2/2} — exponential decay. The t-distribution tails decay polynomially, which is why they’re called heavy tails.
Consequence for moments: E[|T|^k] < \infty if and only if k < \nu.

\nu = 1 (Cauchy): no finite moments at all — not even E[|T|].
\nu = 2: finite mean (E[T] = 0 by symmetry) but infinite variance.
\nu \geq 3: finite variance = \nu/(\nu-2).
\nu \geq 5: finite kurtosis.

For \nu \geq 2:
E[T] = 0 \qquad \text{(by symmetry, when it exists)}
\mathrm{Var}(T) = \frac{\nu}{\nu - 2}, \qquad \nu > 2
The variance exceeds 1 for all finite \nu, reflecting the extra uncertainty from estimating \sigma. As \nu \to \infty, \mathrm{Var}(T) \to 1, consistent with convergence to \mathcal{N}(0,1).

t_\nu \to \mathcal{N}(0,1) as \nu \to \infty
Claim: As \nu \to \infty, t_\nu \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,1).
Proof via the constructive definition:
T = Z/\sqrt{V/\nu} where V \sim \chi^2_\nu.
By the LLN applied to V = \sum_{i=1}^\nu W_i^2 (i.i.d. \chi^2_1 terms):
\frac{V}{\nu} = \frac{1}{\nu}\sum_{i=1}^\nu W_i^2 \xrightarrow{a.s.} E[W_1^2] = 1
Therefore \sqrt{V/\nu} \xrightarrow{a.s.} 1, and by Slutsky’s theorem:
T = \frac{Z}{\sqrt{V/\nu}} \xrightarrow{d} \frac{Z}{1} = Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) \qquad \blacksquare
Alternatively, via the PDF directly:
\left(1 + \frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)^{-(\nu+1)/2} = \exp!\left(-\frac{\nu+1}{2}\log!\left(1 + \frac{t^2}{\nu}\right)\right) \to \exp!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2}\right)
using \log(1 + x/\nu) \approx x/\nu for large \nu. And the normalizing constant \frac{\Gamma((\nu+1)/2)}{\sqrt{\nu\pi},\Gamma(\nu/2)} \to \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} by Stirling’s approximation. So the PDF converges pointwise to \phi(t).

The Slutsky proof is the one I think of first — it’s the most conceptually direct. LLN kills the randomness in the denominator as \nu \to \infty, and what’s left is just Z. The heavy tails of t_\nu exist precisely because V/\nu fluctuates when \nu is small.


Special Cases
\nu = 1: The Cauchy Distribution
f_1(t) = \frac{1}{\pi(1 + t^2)}
This is the Cauchy distribution. It has:

No finite mean (the integral \int |t|/(1+t^2),dt diverges).
No finite variance.
Tails decaying as t^{-2} — the heaviest possible for a t-distribution.

The Cauchy is Z_1/|Z_2| for independent standard normals Z_1, Z_2, equivalently \tan(\theta) for \theta \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(-\pi/2, \pi/2).
It’s the canonical example of a distribution where the LLN fails — the sample mean of i.i.d. Cauchy r.v.’s does not converge to anything, because there is no population mean to converge to.
\nu = 2
f_2(t) = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{t^2}{2}\right)^{-3/2}
Finite mean (zero), infinite variance.
\nu \geq 30 (practical rule of thumb)
At \nu = 30, the t-distribution is so close to \mathcal{N}(0,1) that the difference is negligible in most applications. But for small \nu — say, \nu = 5 or \nu = 10 — the tails are meaningfully heavier and using a z-table instead of a t-table would give anti-conservative confidence intervals.

No MGF (and why that matters)
The t_\nu distribution has no moment generating function for any \nu. This is because the polynomial tail decay means E[e^{tT}] = \infty for all t \neq 0: the exponential function grows faster than any polynomial tail can suppress.
This is a substantive limitation: MGF-based proofs don’t apply to t. The characteristic function \varphi_T(t) = E[e^{itT}] does exist (it’s bounded), but it doesn’t have a clean closed form for general \nu.
For \nu = 1 (Cauchy): \varphi(t) = e^{-|t|}.

The absence of an MGF is a direct consequence of the heavy tails. Every moment E[|T|^k] eventually blows up as k exceeds \nu, and the MGF — which would require all moments to be finite and well-behaved — can’t exist. This is a good example of why MGFs are a tool of convenience, not universality; characteristic functions are always there when MGFs aren’t.


Connection to the F-Distribution
T^2 \sim F_{1,\nu}
Proof: T^2 = Z^2/(V/\nu). Now Z^2 \sim \chi^2_1 and V \sim \chi^2_\nu independently. So:
T^2 = \frac{Z^2/1}{V/\nu} = \frac{\chi^2_1/1}{\chi^2_\nu/\nu} \sim F_{1,\nu}
by definition of the F-distribution. \blacksquare
This is why a two-sided t-test at level \alpha is equivalent to an F-test at level \alpha — squaring the t-statistic gives an F_{1,\nu} statistic, and the rejection regions correspond exactly.

The t-Distribution as a Scale Mixture of Normals
There is a beautiful representation: T \sim t_\nu can be written as:
T \mid W \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1/W), \qquad W \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\nu/2,, \nu/2)
i.e., T is a normal distribution with a random variance, where the precision W follows a Gamma distribution. Marginalizing over W gives the t-distribution.
Why this matters:

It explains the heavy tails intuitively: some draws of W are very small (large variance), making extreme values of T plausible.
It connects to Bayesian statistics: under a Gaussian likelihood with a Gamma prior on the precision, the marginal distribution of the data is t-distributed.
It’s the basis of robust regression algorithms: by treating each observation’s variance as a latent variable drawn from a Gamma, you get t-distributed errors, which downweight outliers automatically (the EM algorithm for this is the basis of IRLS with t-errors).

The representation also makes the PDF derivation feel less magical: you’re just marginalizing a Gaussian with a random variance, and that integral is the Gamma integral that appeared in the proof.

This is the representation I keep coming back to. The t-distribution isn’t just a quirky thing that happens when you don’t know \sigma — it’s the natural distribution for a Gaussian model where you’re uncertain about the scale. That’s a deep structural fact with implications throughout Bayesian inference.


Applications in Classical Statistics
One-Sample t-Test
H_0: \mu = \mu_0 vs. H_1: \mu \neq \mu_0.
Test statistic: T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu_0}{S/\sqrt{n}} \sim t_{n-1} under H_0.
Reject at level \alpha if |T| > t_{n-1,,\alpha/2} (the upper \alpha/2 quantile of t_{n-1}).
Two-Sample t-Test (equal variances)
X_1,\ldots,X_m \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma^2) and Y_1,\ldots,Y_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma^2), both groups with the same \sigma^2.
Pooled variance: S_p^2 = \frac{(m-1)S_X^2 + (n-1)S_Y^2}{m+n-2} \sim \frac{\sigma^2}{m+n-2}\chi^2_{m+n-2}
Test statistic: T = \frac{\bar{X} - \bar{Y}}{S_p\sqrt{1/m + 1/n}} \sim t_{m+n-2}
Confidence Interval for \mu
\bar{X} \pm t_{n-1,,\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{S}{\sqrt{n}}
As n \to \infty, t_{n-1,\alpha/2} \to z_{\alpha/2} and this reduces to the standard z-interval.
Regression Coefficients
In a linear model \mathbf{Y} = X\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} with \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2), the OLS estimator satisfies:
\frac{\hat{\beta}_j - \beta_j}{\hat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat{\beta}_j)} \sim t_{n-p}
where p is the number of predictors. Every standard error and p-value in a regression table comes from this t-distribution. Degrees of freedom = n - p because p parameters are estimated, consuming p degrees of freedom from n.

Summary Table





















































Propertyt_\nuDefinitionZ/\sqrt{V/\nu}, Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1), V \sim \chi^2_\nu, independentSupport\mathbb{R}SymmetrySymmetric about 0Mean0 (for \nu > 1; undefined for \nu = 1)Variance\nu/(\nu-2) (for \nu > 2; infinite for 1 < \nu \leq 2)MGFDoes not existTail behaviorPolynomial: f(t) \sim \|t\|^{-(\nu+1)}MomentsE[\|T\|^k] < \infty \iff k < \nuSpecial case \nu=1Cauchy distributionLimit \nu \to \infty\mathcal{N}(0,1)Relation to FT^2 \sim F_{1,\nu}

Open Threads

 Slutsky’s theorem — state and prove it properly; it’s the tool used in the t \to \mathcal{N} limit
 Cochran’s theorem — independence of \bar{X} and S^2; the proof that makes the t-test valid
 F-distribution — derive its PDF via the same conditioning argument; understand ANOVA
 Scale mixture of normals — work through the marginalization integral explicitly; connect to Bayesian conjugate analysis
 Welch’s t-test — what happens when we don’t assume equal variances? The degrees of freedom become fractional (Welch-Satterthwaite approximation)
 Non-central t-distribution — what is the distribution of T under the alternative? Needed for power calculations


One-Line Summary for Future Me

t_\nu = \mathcal{N}(0,1)/\sqrt{\chi^2_\nu/\nu} (independent). Heavy polynomial tails because the denominator is random; variance = \nu/(\nu-2); no MGF. Converges to \mathcal{N}(0,1) by LLN killing the denominator. Arises in inference whenever \sigma is unknown and estimated from data, with degrees of freedom counting the observations minus the parameters estimated.

01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/01.title: 01.Markov Property & Transition Matrices
01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/01.content:
Tags: probability stochastic-processes markov-chains foundations
References: Blitzstein & Hwang — Introduction to Probability; Stat 110 (Harvard)
Status: 🟡 fleshing out
Prerequisite notes: Conditional Probability, Independence, Law of Total Probability


“The Markov property is the art of forgetting strategically. The entire past is irrelevant — all that matters is where you are right now. That’s not an approximation. For a Markov chain, it’s exact.”


The Big Picture
Most stochastic processes are intractable because the future depends on the entire history. To predict where you’ll be tomorrow, you need to know everything that happened before today. The Markov property is the assumption that cuts this Gordian knot: the future depends on the past only through the present state.
This is both a modeling assumption and a structural property. When it holds, an enormous amount of theory becomes available — stationary distributions, convergence, hitting times, all of it. When it’s a modeling assumption, it’s often a simplification, but frequently a good one: if the state space is rich enough, the present state really does encode all the relevant history.
The two objects that define a (discrete, time-homogeneous) Markov chain are:

The initial distribution — where you start.
The transition matrix Q — where you go from each state.

Everything else — n-step distributions, stationary distributions, long-run behavior — is derived from these two.

Setup
Let X_0, X_1, X_2, \ldots be a sequence of random variables taking values in a state space \mathcal{S}.
For now: \mathcal{S} is finite or countably infinite, and time is discrete (n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots). This is the setting of Stat 110 and B&H Chapter 11.

The Markov Property
Definition
The sequence (X_n)_{n \geq 0} is a Markov chain if for all n \geq 0 and all states i_0, i_1, \ldots, i_{n-1}, i, j \in \mathcal{S}:
P(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i,, X_{n-1} = i_{n-1},, \ldots,, X_0 = i_0) = P(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i)
whenever the conditioning event has positive probability.
In words: given the present, the future is independent of the past.
Time Homogeneity
The chain is time-homogeneous if P(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i) does not depend on n. We then write:
q_{ij} = P(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i)
and call q_{ij} the transition probability from state i to state j.
Almost everything in Stat 110 and B&H assumes time homogeneity. I’ll assume it throughout.
An Equivalent Formulation
The Markov property can be stated symmetrically: past and future are conditionally independent given the present:
X_0, \ldots, X_{n-1} \perp X_{n+1}, X_{n+2}, \ldots \mid X_n
This is the version that reveals the deep structure. The chain “screens off” its past from its future. Knowing X_n makes the past irrelevant for predicting the future, and makes the future irrelevant for retrodicting the past.

The symmetry of this formulation surprised me when I first saw it. You might expect that “future is independent of past given present” is an asymmetric statement — but it’s actually symmetric in past and future. Running a time-reversible Markov chain backwards gives another Markov chain.


The Transition Matrix
Definition
For a finite state space \mathcal{S} = {1, 2, \ldots, M}, the transition matrix is the M \times M matrix:
Q = (q_{ij})_{i,j \in \mathcal{S}}, \qquad q_{ij} = P(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i)
Row i of Q is the conditional distribution of X_{n+1} given X_n = i.
Two Properties That Must Hold
1. Non-negativity: q_{ij} \geq 0 \quad \text{for all } i, j
2. Row sums equal 1: \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} q_{ij} = 1 \quad \text{for all } i
because the conditional distribution of X_{n+1} given X_n = i must be a valid probability distribution. A matrix satisfying both properties is called a stochastic matrix (or row-stochastic matrix).

Columns do not need to sum to 1 in general. If both rows and columns sum to 1, the matrix is called doubly stochastic — that’s a special property with important consequences (it implies the uniform distribution is stationary).

Example: Two-State Chain
Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1-\alpha & \alpha \ \beta & 1-\beta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \alpha, \beta \in (0,1)
From state 1: stay with probability 1-\alpha, jump to state 2 with probability \alpha. From state 2: jump to state 1 with probability \beta, stay with probability 1-\beta.
Check: each row sums to 1. ✓
Example: Random Walk on {0, 1, \ldots, M}
q_{i,i+1} = p, \quad q_{i,i-1} = 1-p = q, \quad q_{i,j} = 0 \text{ otherwise}
with reflecting or absorbing boundaries at 0 and M. The transition matrix is tridiagonal.

The Joint Distribution of a Markov Chain
This is where the Markov property earns its keep. For any finite path i_0, i_1, \ldots, i_n:
P(X_0 = i_0, X_1 = i_1, \ldots, X_n = i_n) = P(X_0 = i_0)\prod_{k=0}^{n-1} q_{i_k, i_{k+1}}
Proof: Apply the chain rule of probability and then the Markov property repeatedly:
P(X_0 = i_0, \ldots, X_n = i_n) = P(X_0 = i_0),P(X_1=i_1|X_0=i_0),P(X_2=i_2|X_1=i_1,X_0=i_0)\cdots = P(X_0=i_0),q_{i_0 i_1},q_{i_1 i_2}\cdots q_{i_{n-1}i_n}
where each conditional simplifies to a single transition probability by the Markov property. \blacksquare
This factorization is the fundamental computational tool. The entire joint distribution of the chain is determined by the initial distribution and the transition matrix.

The n-Step Transition Matrix
Definition
The n-step transition probability is:
q_{ij}^{(n)} = P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i)
and the n-step transition matrix is Q^{(n)} = (q_{ij}^{(n)}).
The Chapman-Kolmogorov Equations
q_{ij}^{(m+n)} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{S}} q_{ik}^{(m)}, q_{kj}^{(n)}
In matrix form: Q^{(m+n)} = Q^{(m)} Q^{(n)}.
Proof: Condition on the intermediate state at time m:
P(X_{m+n} = j \mid X_0 = i) = \sum_k P(X_{m+n}=j \mid X_m=k),P(X_m=k \mid X_0=i) = \sum_k q_{kj}^{(n)},q_{ik}^{(m)}
This is the (i,j) entry of Q^{(m)} Q^{(n)}. \blacksquare
The Key Consequence: Q^{(n)} = Q^n
Setting m = 1 repeatedly: Q^{(n)} = Q^n.
The n-step transition matrix is the n-th matrix power of Q.
This is the central computational result of Markov chain theory. To find where the chain is after n steps, raise Q to the n-th power:
P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i) = (Q^n)_{ij}

This feels obvious once you know it, but it’s genuinely powerful. It means all the spectral theory of matrices — eigenvalues, diagonalization, Jordan forms — applies to Markov chains. The long-run behavior of the chain is controlled by the eigenvalues of Q. That’s a remarkable bridge between probability and linear algebra.


The Distribution at Time n
Let \mathbf{t}^{(0)} be the initial distribution: a row vector where t^{(0)}_i = P(X_0 = i).
Then the distribution at time n is:
\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n
where \mathbf{t}^{(n)}_j = P(X_n = j).
Proof: By the law of total probability:
P(X_n = j) = \sum_i P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i),P(X_0 = i) = \sum_i t^{(0)}_i,(Q^n)_{ij}
which is the j-th entry of the row vector \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n. \blacksquare
One-step update:
\mathbf{t}^{(n+1)} = \mathbf{t}^{(n)} Q
Row vectors left-multiply Q. This is a notational convention — some books use column vectors and right-multiply by Q^\top, but B&H and Stat 110 use row vectors.

Stationary Distributions (Preview)
A distribution \mathbf{s} (row vector) is stationary for Q if:
\mathbf{s} Q = \mathbf{s}
i.e., \mathbf{s} is a left eigenvector of Q with eigenvalue 1.
Equivalently, if X_0 \sim \mathbf{s}, then X_n \sim \mathbf{s} for all n — the distribution doesn’t change over time.
Why eigenvalue 1 always exists: Since Q is row-stochastic, Q\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1} (the all-ones vector is a right eigenvector with eigenvalue 1). By the left-right symmetry of eigenvalues, there must also be a left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. Under mild conditions (irreducibility, aperiodicity), this stationary distribution is unique and the chain converges to it from any starting point.
The full theory of stationary distributions and convergence deserves its own note — but the transition matrix is the object that everything is defined in terms of.

The Spectral Picture
For a finite state space, Q is an M \times M matrix with eigenvalues \lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_M.
Facts about eigenvalues of a stochastic matrix:

\lambda_1 = 1 always (Perron-Frobenius; Q\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}).
All eigenvalues satisfy |\lambda_k| \leq 1 — they lie in the unit disk.
For an irreducible aperiodic chain: \lambda_1 = 1 is the unique eigenvalue with |\lambda| = 1.

If Q is diagonalizable with eigenvalues 1 = \lambda_1 > |\lambda_2| \geq \cdots \geq |\lambda_M|:
Q^n = \sum_{k=1}^M \lambda_k^n \mathbf{u}_k \mathbf{v}_k^\top
where \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{v}_k are right and left eigenvectors. As n \to \infty, all terms with |\lambda_k| < 1 vanish, leaving only the k=1 term:
Q^n \to \mathbf{1}\mathbf{s}
where \mathbf{s} is the stationary distribution. The spectral gap 1 - |\lambda_2| controls the rate of convergence — a large gap means fast mixing.

This is the eigenvalue story of Markov chains. It’s the rigorous content behind the intuition that “chains forget their initial state.” The speed of forgetting is |\lambda_2|^n, and maximizing the spectral gap is a core problem in the theory of mixing times.


Constructing the Transition Matrix: A Checklist
When modeling a system as a Markov chain, I ask:

What is the state space \mathcal{S}? Make it rich enough that the Markov property is plausible — if the future depends on history, encode the relevant history into the state.
What are the transition probabilities q_{ij}? Specify how the system moves from each state.
Verify row sums equal 1. Every row must define a valid probability distribution.
What is the initial distribution? Where does the chain start?

The Markov property is a modeling choice. If I define my state space to include, say, both current position and the last k positions, the resulting process is still Markov — it just has a larger state space. The tradeoff is always state-space size vs. Markovian validity.

Examples Worth Knowing Cold
Gambler’s Ruin
States {0, 1, \ldots, N}. From state i \in {1,\ldots,N-1}: go to i+1 with probability p, go to i-1 with probability 1-p. States 0 and N are absorbing: q_{00} = q_{NN} = 1.
The transition matrix is tridiagonal with absorbing boundaries. The gambler’s ruin probabilities are derived from this chain.
Ehrenfest Urn Model
M balls distributed between two urns, total d balls. State = number in urn 1. From state i: a ball chosen uniformly at random is moved to the other urn — so go to i+1 with probability (d-i)/d and to i-1 with probability i/d.
This chain is reversible and has a Binomial stationary distribution. It models diffusion and approaches equilibrium — a classic example of a physically motivated Markov chain.
PageRank (Google)
The web is a directed graph. State = webpage. At each step, follow a random outgoing link with probability \alpha, or jump to a uniformly random page with probability 1-\alpha (the “teleportation” term). The stationary distribution of this Markov chain is the PageRank vector.

I keep this example in mind because it shows the transition matrix doesn’t have to come from a physical process — it can be engineered. PageRank is the stationary distribution of a deliberately constructed Markov chain on a 50-billion-state space.


Open Threads

 Stationary distributions — existence, uniqueness under irreducibility; the balance equations \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}
 Detailed balance / reversibility — when does s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji}? Connection to physical systems
 Convergence theorem — irreducible + aperiodic \Rightarrow convergence to unique stationary distribution
 Hitting times — T_j = \min{n \geq 1 : X_n = j}; expected hitting times from the transition matrix
 Absorbing chains — classification of states, absorption probabilities, expected absorption time
 Mixing times — formal definition; connection to spectral gap 1 - |\lambda_2|
 Continuous-time Markov chains — replace Q with the generator matrix \mathcal{G}; Q(t) = e^{t\mathcal{G}}


Summary Table








































ObjectDefinitionKey PropertyMarkov propertyP(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i, \text{past}) = P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)Future \perp Past \mid PresentTransition matrix Qq_{ij} = P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)Row-stochastic: q_{ij}\geq 0, \sum_j q_{ij}=1n-step transitionsQ^{(n)} = Q^nChapman-KolmogorovDistribution at time n\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)}Q^nLeft-multiply by row vectorStationary distribution\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}Left eigenvector of Q with eigenvalue 1Spectral gap1 - \|\lambda_2\|Controls rate of convergence to stationarity

One-Line Summary for Future Me

A Markov chain is defined by its transition matrix Q (row-stochastic, entries q_{ij} = P(\text{go to }j \mid \text{at }i)) and initial distribution \mathbf{t}^{(0)}. The Markov property says future \perp past \mid present. The n-step distribution is \mathbf{t}^{(0)}Q^n — raise Q to the n-th power. The eigenvalues of Q live in the unit disk; the spectral gap controls how fast the chain forgets where it started.
