01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/08.title: 08.Existance and uniqueness
01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/08.content:
“Existence says there is somewhere for the chain to settle. Uniqueness says it can only settle in one place. Both feel obvious for well-behaved chains — and both fail in precisely the ways you’d expect when the chain misbehaves. The proofs make the intuition rigorous, and the counterexamples sharpen it.”


The Question
From Stationary Distributions, I know what a stationary distribution is: a row vector \mathbf{s} with \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}, s_i \geq 0, \sum_i s_i = 1. The natural questions are:

Does one exist? Is the system \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}, \sum_i s_i = 1 always solvable?
Is it unique? Could there be multiple solutions?

The answer to both, under the right conditions, is yes — and those conditions are exactly irreducibility and positive recurrence. This note is the full proof.

The Main Theorem
Theorem (Existence and Uniqueness). Let (X_n) be a Markov chain on a countable state space \mathcal{S} with transition matrix Q.


(Existence) A stationary distribution exists if and only if the chain has at least one positive recurrent state.


(Uniqueness) If the chain is irreducible and positive recurrent, then the stationary distribution is unique, and is given by:


s_i = \frac{1}{m_i}, \qquad m_i = E[T_i \mid X_0 = i]
where T_i = \min{n \geq 1 : X_n = i} is the first return time to i.

(Finite chains) If \mathcal{S} is finite and the chain is irreducible, then all states are automatically positive recurrent, so a unique stationary distribution exists.


Part I: Existence
The Construction
Fix any positive recurrent state i \in \mathcal{S}. Since i is positive recurrent, m_i = E[T_i \mid X_0 = i] < \infty.
Define, for each j \in \mathcal{S}:
\pi_j = E!\left[\sum_{n=0}^{T_i - 1} \mathbf{1}[X_n = j] ,\Bigg|, X_0 = i\right]
This is the expected number of visits to state j in one excursion from i — counting time steps 0, 1, \ldots, T_i - 1, i.e., starting at i and running until just before the first return to i.
Step 1: \boldsymbol{\pi} sums to m_i.
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} \pi_j = E!\left[\sum_{n=0}^{T_i - 1} \sum_{j} \mathbf{1}[X_n = j],\Bigg|, X_0 = i\right] = E!\left[\sum_{n=0}^{T_i - 1} 1 ,\Bigg|, X_0 = i\right] = E[T_i \mid X_0 = i] = m_i
So define \mathbf{s} := \boldsymbol{\pi} / m_i. This is a probability vector: s_j \geq 0 and \sum_j s_j = 1.
Step 2: \mathbf{s} satisfies \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}.
I need to show \sum_j \pi_j q_{jk} = \pi_k for all k. Compute:
\sum_{j} \pi_j q_{jk} = \sum_j q_{jk} , E!\left[\sum_{n=0}^{T_i-1} \mathbf{1}[X_n = j],\Bigg|,X_0 = i\right]
Swap expectation and sum (Fubini, since everything is non-negative):
= E!\left[\sum_{n=0}^{T_i - 1} \sum_j q_{jk}, \mathbf{1}[X_n = j],\Bigg|,X_0=i\right] = E!\left[\sum_{n=0}^{T_i-1} P(X_{n+1}=k\mid X_n),\Bigg|,X_0=i\right]
= E!\left[\sum_{n=0}^{T_i-1} \mathbf{1}[X_{n+1}=k],\Bigg|,X_0=i\right] = E!\left[\sum_{n=1}^{T_i} \mathbf{1}[X_n=k],\Bigg|,X_0=i\right]
Now compare with \pi_k = E\bigl[\sum_{n=0}^{T_i-1} \mathbf{1}[X_n=k] \mid X_0=i\bigr]. The difference is:
\sum_j \pi_j q_{jk} - \pi_k = E!\left[\mathbf{1}[X_{T_i}=k] - \mathbf{1}[X_0=k],\Bigg|,X_0=i\right]
Since X_0 = i and X_{T_i} = i, both indicator functions equal \mathbf{1}[k=i]. They cancel:
\sum_j \pi_j q_{jk} - \pi_k = \mathbf{1}[k=i] - \mathbf{1}[k=i] = 0
So \boldsymbol{\pi} Q = \boldsymbol{\pi}, and dividing by m_i: \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}. \blacksquare

The index-shift \sum_{n=0}^{T_i-1} \to \sum_{n=1}^{T_i} is the entire proof. It introduces a mismatch of exactly one step at each boundary: the n=0 term (which contributes \mathbf{1}[X_0 = k]) and the n = T_i term (which contributes \mathbf{1}[X_{T_i} = k]). Since X_0 = X_{T_i} = i, these cancel perfectly. The Markov chain literally proves its own stationarity by the fact that it returns to where it started.

When Existence Fails
Transient chains. Every state is visited only finitely often almost surely. The chain drifts to infinity — no stable distribution to settle into. No stationary distribution exists.
Null recurrent chains. The chain returns to every state almost surely (f_{ii} = 1), but m_i = \infty for all i, forcing s_i = 1/m_i = 0 for all i. That’s not a probability distribution. No stationary distribution exists.
Canonical example: Simple symmetric random walk on \mathbb{Z}. Irreducible and null recurrent. If a stationary distribution existed, by symmetry it would assign equal weight to all integers — impossible for a probability measure. No stationary distribution.

Part II: Uniqueness
Theorem
If the chain is irreducible and positive recurrent, the stationary distribution constructed above is the only one.
Proof
Let \mathbf{s} be the stationary distribution from Part I, and let \mathbf{s}' be any stationary distribution. I will show s'_j = s_j for all j.
Step 1. Since \mathbf{s}'Q = \mathbf{s}', we have \mathbf{s}'Q^n = \mathbf{s}' for all n \geq 0:
s'_j = (\mathbf{s}'Q^n)_j = \sum_k s'_k (Q^n)_{kj} \qquad \text{for all } n
Step 2. Average this over n = 0, 1, \ldots, N-1:
s'_j = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_k s'_k (Q^n)_{kj} = \sum_k s'_k \left(\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (Q^n)_{kj}\right)
Step 3. By the ergodic theorem for Markov chains (which follows from positive recurrence and irreducibility):
\frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} (Q^n)_{kj} \longrightarrow s_j \qquad \text{as } N \to \infty, \text{ for all } k
This is the Cesàro convergence of time averages to the stationary distribution — it holds for all irreducible positive recurrent chains, including periodic ones.
Step 4. Since \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(Q^n)_{kj} \leq 1 uniformly, the dominated convergence theorem (or just bounded convergence for finite sums) allows passing the limit inside:
s'_j = \sum_k s'_k \cdot \lim_{N\to\infty} \left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}(Q^n)_{kj}\right) = \sum_k s'_k \cdot s_j = s_j \underbrace{\sum_k s'_k}_{=1} = s_j
So \mathbf{s}' = \mathbf{s}. \blacksquare

The Cesàro average is the key technique, and it’s worth understanding why it’s needed. For a periodic chain, (Q^n)_{kj} oscillates — it might be 0 for all odd n and positive for all even n. Pointwise limits don’t exist. But Cesàro averages smooth out the oscillation: if a sequence oscillates between 0 and 2s_j, its averages converge to s_j. Uniqueness holds even for periodic chains; only distributional convergence (Q^n \to \mathbf{1s}, not just in Cesàro sense) requires aperiodicity.

Why Irreducibility Is Needed for Uniqueness
Without irreducibility, there can be multiple closed communicating classes C_1, C_2, \ldots Each closed class C_\ell is itself a finite irreducible chain, so it has a unique stationary distribution \mathbf{s}^{(\ell)} supported on C_\ell. Every convex combination:
\alpha_1 \mathbf{s}^{(1)} + \alpha_2 \mathbf{s}^{(2)} + \cdots, \qquad \alpha_\ell \geq 0, \quad \sum_\ell \alpha_\ell = 1
is also stationary. As soon as there are two or more closed classes, there are uncountably many stationary distributions. Irreducibility — one class — is exactly what collapses this to uniqueness.

Part III: Finite Irreducible \Rightarrow Positive Recurrent
This is what makes finite chains so tractable: I never have to check positive recurrence separately.
Theorem
If \mathcal{S} is finite and the chain is irreducible, then every state is positive recurrent.
Proof in Two Steps
Step 1: All states are recurrent (not transient).
Suppose for contradiction that all states are transient. Then for each j:
E[N_j \mid X_0 = i] = \sum_{n=1}^\infty (Q^n)_{ij} < \infty
Sum over all states j \in \mathcal{S}:
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} E[N_j \mid X_0 = i] = E!\left[\sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} N_j,\Bigg|,X_0 = i\right] = E[\text{total steps taken} \mid X_0 = i] = \infty
But with |\mathcal{S}| = M < \infty:
\sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} E[N_j \mid X_0 = i] = \sum_{j} \sum_{n=1}^\infty (Q^n)_{ij} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \underbrace{\sum_j (Q^n)_{ij}}_{= 1} = \infty
Wait — this gives \infty = \infty, not a contradiction. Let me be more careful. The contradiction is:
If all states are transient, each \sum_n (Q^n)_{ij} < \infty, so:
\sum_j \sum_n (Q^n)_{ij} = \sum_n \underbrace{\sum_j (Q^n)_{ij}}_{=1} = \infty
but also = \sum_j E[N_j] < \infty \cdot M < \infty. Contradiction.
The finite sum of finite terms \sum_j E[N_j] is finite (since M < \infty and each term is finite), but we just showed it equals \infty. So not all states can be transient. By the class property of recurrence (irreducible chain: all same class), all states are recurrent.
Step 2: All states are positive recurrent (not null recurrent).
Suppose state i is null recurrent: m_i = E[T_i \mid X_0 = i] = \infty.
From the excursion construction: m_i = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} \pi_j.
With |\mathcal{S}| = M, this is a sum of M terms. So some \pi_j = \infty.
But \pi_j = E[#\text{visits to }j\text{ before returning to }i]. In a finite irreducible chain, from any state, every other state is reachable in at most M-1 steps. Between two visits to i, the chain visits at most… well, it could visit j many times. But:
By the strong Markov property, each time the chain visits j (during an excursion from i), it independently has some probability P(T_i < T_j^+ \mid X_0 = j) > 0 of returning to i before revisiting j (positive by irreducibility, finiteness). So the number of visits to j per excursion is geometric with finite mean. So \pi_j < \infty for all j.
Therefore m_i = \sum_j \pi_j < M \cdot \max_j \pi_j < \infty. Contradiction with null recurrence. So all states are positive recurrent. \blacksquare

Step 1 is the cleaner argument. The key is that a finite sum of finite numbers is finite, but the row sums of Q^n are all 1, so summing over n gives infinity — forcing at least one E[N_j] to be infinite, hence at least one state recurrent. Step 2 is subtler: I use the geometric structure of visits (strong Markov property at each return to j) to show expected visits per excursion are finite. Together they nail down positive recurrence.


The Formula s_i = 1/m_i: Proof
From the construction: s_i = \pi_i / m_i.
I claim \pi_i = 1. By definition, \pi_i = E[\sum_{n=0}^{T_i-1} \mathbf{1}[X_n = i] \mid X_0 = i]. The sum counts visits to i at times n = 0, 1, \ldots, T_i - 1. At time 0, X_0 = i — that’s one visit. For 1 \leq n \leq T_i - 1, by definition T_i is the first return time, so X_n \neq i for n = 1, \ldots, T_i - 1. Hence the sum equals 1 almost surely.
So \pi_i = 1, and:
\boxed{s_i = \frac{1}{m_i} = \frac{1}{E[T_i \mid X_0 = i]}}
\blacksquare

Summary of the Three Parts

























PartTheoremKey techniqueExistence\mathbf{s} = \boldsymbol{\pi}/m_i is stationaryIndex shift: \sum_{n=0}^{T_i-1} \to \sum_{n=1}^{T_i}; boundary terms cancelUniquenessAny other \mathbf{s}' equals \mathbf{s}Cesàro averaging of \mathbf{s}'Q^n = \mathbf{s}'; ergodic convergenceFinite \Rightarrow pos. recurrentIrreducible finite chain is always pos. recurrentPigeonhole: transience contradicts row sums of Q^n being 1
And the corollary tying everything together:
\text{Finite} + \text{Irreducible} \implies \text{Positive recurrent} \implies \text{Unique stationary distribution} \mathbf{s}, \text{ with } s_i = 1/m_i

One-Line Summary for Future Me

Existence: construct s_j = \pi_j/m_i from excursion counts and show \boldsymbol{\pi}Q = \boldsymbol{\pi} by an index shift that cancels boundary terms at X_0 = X_{T_i} = i. Uniqueness: Cesàro-average \mathbf{s}'Q^n = \mathbf{s}' and use ergodic convergence to force \mathbf{s}' = \mathbf{s}. Finite irreducible chains are always positive recurrent: transience would make \sum_j E[N_j] simultaneously finite (M finite terms) and infinite (row sums of Q^n are 1), a contradiction.

01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/09.title: 09.Google PageRank
01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/09.content:
Tags: probability stochastic-processes markov-chains applications linear-algebra
References: Blitzstein & Hwang — Introduction to Probability; Stat 110 (Harvard)
Status: 🟢 complete
Prerequisite notes: Markov Chains — Definitions and Transition Matrix · Stationary Distributions · Existence and Uniqueness of Stationary Distributions · n-Step Transition Probability


“PageRank is stationary distribution theory applied to a 50-billion-state Markov chain. The web is a directed graph; Google engineers turned it into a row-stochastic matrix and found its left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. The whole search engine is, at bottom, the Perron-Frobenius theorem at scale.”


Why This Is a Markov Chain Problem
I mentioned PageRank briefly in Markov Chains — Definitions and Transition Matrix as an example of an engineered transition matrix. Now I want to do it properly — work through the construction, identify where the theory breaks down, see exactly what fixes were needed, and understand what the stationary distribution actually measures.
The setup is simple to state. The web is a directed graph: webpages are nodes, hyperlinks are directed edges. Google’s insight was: the importance of a page is determined by the importance of the pages that link to it. A page is important if important pages link to it. That’s circular — and the resolution of the circularity is a fixed-point equation, which is exactly the stationary distribution equation \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}.

The Naive Transition Matrix
Model a random web surfer. At each step, she picks a link uniformly at random from the current page and follows it. This defines a Markov chain:
\text{State space: } \mathcal{S} = {1, 2, \ldots, N} \quad \text{(webpages, } N \approx 50 \text{ billion)}
q_{ij} = \frac{1}{\deg^+(i)} \cdot \mathbf{1}[\text{there is a link } i \to j]
where \deg^+(i) is the out-degree of page i (number of outgoing links).
In matrix form: Q is the normalized adjacency matrix of the web graph, where row i distributes 1 uniformly over the out-neighbors of i.
The PageRank vector would then be the stationary distribution \mathbf{s} satisfying \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s} — the long-run fraction of time the random surfer spends on each page. A page with high stationary probability is a page the surfer keeps returning to: it’s important.
This is the idea. Now for the problems.

Problem 1: Dangling Nodes (Pages With No Outgoing Links)
Some pages have \deg^+(i) = 0 — no outgoing links. These are called dangling nodes.
For such a page i, row i of Q is all zeros: q_{ij} = 0 for all j. But this violates the row-stochastic property: \sum_j q_{ij} = 0 \neq 1. The matrix Q is not a valid transition matrix. The random surfer gets stuck and the chain is undefined.
Fix: When the surfer reaches a dangling node, she teleports to a uniformly random page. For a dangling node i, set:
q_{ij} = \frac{1}{N} \quad \text{for all } j
This restores row-stochasticity. In matrix form: if \mathbf{a} is the vector with a_i = 1 if i is a dangling node and 0 otherwise, and \mathbf{e} = \frac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}^\top is the uniform distribution, then the patched matrix is:
Q' = Q + \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{e}
Row i is unchanged if a_i = 0 (page has outgoing links). If a_i = 1 (dangling), row i becomes \mathbf{e} = (1/N, \ldots, 1/N). Every row now sums to 1. Q' is row-stochastic.

Problem 2: Reducibility (Spider Traps and Disconnected Components)
Even with dangling nodes fixed, the web graph is not irreducible. There are many issues:
Spider traps: A set of pages that link only among themselves. Once the surfer enters, she never leaves — this is a closed communicating class, separate from the rest of the graph. Formally: a nonempty set S \subsetneq \mathcal{S} such that q_{ij} = 0 for all i \in S, j \notin S.
Example: a cycle A \to B \to C \to A with no links outside — the surfer loops forever among A, B, C.
Disconnected components: Some pages are simply unreachable from most other pages.
Consequence for stationarity: From Existence and Uniqueness of Stationary Distributions, if the chain is reducible, the stationary distribution need not be unique. Each closed class has its own stationary distribution, and every convex combination of these is also stationary. A non-unique “rank” is useless as a search ranking.
The fix must make the chain irreducible.

Problem 3: Aperiodicity
Even if the chain were irreducible, it might be periodic. A deterministic cycle A \to B \to C \to A has period 3: the surfer is at A only at times 0, 3, 6, \ldots, at B only at times 1, 4, 7, \ldots, etc. The distribution of X_n oscillates and never converges.
From Markov Chain Convergence Theorem: distributional convergence \mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \mathbf{s} requires aperiodicity in addition to irreducibility. The fix must also break periodicity.

The Google Fix: Teleportation (Damping)
Brin and Page’s solution handles all three problems simultaneously. The idea: with probability \alpha (typically \alpha = 0.85), the surfer follows a random outgoing link; with probability 1 - \alpha, she teleports to a uniformly random page on the web.
Define the Google matrix (or PageRank matrix):
\boxed{G = \alpha Q' + (1 - \alpha) \frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top}{N}}
where:

Q' is the dangling-node-patched matrix from Problem 1
\frac{\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top}{N} is the N \times N matrix with all entries \frac{1}{N} — every row is the uniform distribution
\alpha \in (0,1) is the damping factor (Google uses \alpha = 0.85)

Let me check that G is well-defined and fixes all three problems.
G Is Row-Stochastic
Row i of G:
G_{ij} = \alpha q'_{ij} + \frac{1-\alpha}{N}
Since \sum_j q'_{ij} = 1 (row-stochastic after patching) and \sum_j \frac{1}{N} = 1:
\sum_j G_{ij} = \alpha \cdot 1 + (1-\alpha) \cdot 1 = 1
All entries are positive (the \frac{1-\alpha}{N} > 0 term ensures this). So G is row-stochastic. ✓
G Is Irreducible
Every entry G_{ij} \geq \frac{1-\alpha}{N} > 0. So from any state i, there is positive probability of reaching any state j in one step. The chain is irreducible: i \to j for all i, j. ✓
(In fact, every pair of states communicates: i \leftrightarrow j for all i, j, since both i \to j and j \to i in one step.)
G Is Aperiodic
Since G_{ii} \geq \frac{1-\alpha}{N} > 0 for all i: every state has a positive probability self-loop. By the sufficient condition from Classification of States, every state is aperiodic. ✓
Conclusion
G is irreducible, aperiodic, and the state space is finite. By the Markov Chain Convergence Theorem, G has a unique stationary distribution \boldsymbol{\pi} satisfying:
\boldsymbol{\pi} G = \boldsymbol{\pi}
and G^n \to \mathbf{1}\boldsymbol{\pi} as n \to \infty. This stationary distribution is the PageRank vector.

The teleportation parameter 1 - \alpha does triple duty: it fixes dangling nodes (the surfer escapes dead ends by teleporting), ensures irreducibility (every page is reachable), and ensures aperiodicity (every page has a self-loop in the Markov sense — you can “return” in one step by teleporting back to yourself). One parameter, three problems solved. That’s good engineering informed by good mathematics.


The PageRank Equation
The stationary distribution satisfies \boldsymbol{\pi} G = \boldsymbol{\pi}, which I can unpack:
\boldsymbol{\pi} \left(\alpha Q' + \frac{1-\alpha}{N}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top\right) = \boldsymbol{\pi}
\alpha \boldsymbol{\pi} Q' + \frac{1-\alpha}{N} \boldsymbol{\pi}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top = \boldsymbol{\pi}
Since \boldsymbol{\pi} is a probability distribution, \boldsymbol{\pi}\mathbf{1} = 1:
\alpha \boldsymbol{\pi} Q' + \frac{1-\alpha}{N}\mathbf{1}^\top = \boldsymbol{\pi}
Entrywise, for each page j:
\pi_j = \alpha \sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i q'_{ij} + \frac{1-\alpha}{N}
Ignoring dangling nodes for clarity (so Q' = Q):
\boxed{\pi_j = \alpha \sum_{i : i \to j} \frac{\pi_i}{\deg^+(i)} + \frac{1-\alpha}{N}}
Reading this equation:

The first term: page j receives rank from every page i that links to it, proportional to i‘s own rank divided by i‘s out-degree. Important pages that link to j contribute more.
The second term: every page receives a baseline rank \frac{1-\alpha}{N} from the teleportation floor. No page has zero rank.

This is the recursive definition of importance: page j‘s rank depends on the ranks of pages pointing to it, which depend on the ranks of pages pointing to them, and so on. The fixed point of this recursion — the solution to \boldsymbol{\pi}G = \boldsymbol{\pi} — is exactly what the Perron-Frobenius theorem guarantees exists and is unique.

The recursion is what makes this genuinely non-trivial. “Important pages link to j, and importance is defined by which important pages link to you” is circular. The way to resolve a circular definition is to look for a fixed point — a self-consistent assignment of importance to every page simultaneously. That’s the stationary distribution. The Markov chain machinery tells me the fixed point exists, is unique, and is the limit of any iterative computation. Beautiful.


Computing PageRank: Power Iteration
The state space has N \sim 10^{10} nodes. I cannot compute G^n directly — the matrix has N^2 \sim 10^{20} entries, completely intractable.
But I don’t need G^n. I just need to find the stationary distribution \boldsymbol{\pi}. The standard method is power iteration:

Start with the uniform distribution: \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(0)} = \frac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}^\top.
Update: \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k+1)} = \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k)} G.
Repeat until convergence: |\boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k+1)} - \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k)}|_1 < \varepsilon.

By the convergence theorem, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k)} \to \boldsymbol{\pi} as k \to \infty.
The key computational observation: I never need to store G explicitly. Each update \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k+1)} = \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k)} G can be written as:
\boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k+1)} = \alpha \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k)} Q' + \frac{1-\alpha}{N}\mathbf{1}^\top
The only expensive part is the matrix-vector product \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k)} Q', which requires iterating over the (sparse) web link structure. Since the web graph is sparse (each page has O(1) links on average relative to N), this is O(N) per iteration, not O(N^2).
Rate of Convergence
From the spectral theory of n-Step Transition Probability: the rate of convergence is controlled by the second-largest eigenvalue \lambda_2 of G.
Theorem: The second eigenvalue of G satisfies |\lambda_2| \leq \alpha.
Proof: The eigenvalues of G = \alpha Q' + \frac{1-\alpha}{N}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top. The matrix \frac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top is a rank-1 matrix with eigenvalue 1 (eigenvector \mathbf{1}) and eigenvalue 0 with multiplicity N-1.
For any vector \mathbf{v} with \mathbf{v} \perp \mathbf{1} (orthogonal to the all-ones vector):
G\mathbf{v} = \alpha Q'\mathbf{v} + \frac{1-\alpha}{N}\mathbf{1}\underbrace{(\mathbf{1}^\top \mathbf{v})}_{=0} = \alpha Q'\mathbf{v}
So on the orthogonal complement of \mathbf{1}, G acts as \alpha Q'. Since Q' is row-stochastic, |Q'|_\infty \leq 1, so the eigenvalues of \alpha Q' in this subspace have magnitude at most \alpha.
Therefore all eigenvalues of G except \lambda_1 = 1 have magnitude at most \alpha. The spectral gap is at least 1 - \alpha.
Consequence: Power iteration converges at rate \alpha^k. With \alpha = 0.85:
|\boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k)} - \boldsymbol{\pi}|_1 \leq C \cdot (0.85)^k
To get 10^{-8} precision: need k \geq \frac{8\log 10}{\log(1/0.85)} \approx \frac{18.4}{0.163} \approx 113 iterations.
In practice, Google reportedly converges in 50–100 iterations. Each iteration touches the entire web graph — but only once, in a single sparse matrix-vector product. That’s the engineering miracle that made PageRank practical.

The choice \alpha = 0.85 is not arbitrary. Larger \alpha (closer to 1) means the surfer follows links more and teleports less, giving a more “link-faithful” ranking but slower convergence (smaller spectral gap 1 - \alpha). Smaller \alpha gives faster convergence but the ranking is dominated by the uniform teleportation floor — every page looks equally important. \alpha = 0.85 is the practical sweet spot. The spectral gap theorem makes this tradeoff precise: \alpha simultaneously controls the ranking quality AND the convergence rate.


The Stationary Distribution as “Democratic Vote”
There is a beautiful interpretation of \boldsymbol{\pi} beyond the random surfer model.
Claim: \pi_j is the long-run fraction of time a random surfer spends on page j.
From the Ergodic Theorem for Markov Chains (see Stationary Distributions):
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mathbf{1}[X_k = j] \xrightarrow{a.s.} \pi_j
So \pi_j is literally the proportion of web-browsing time allocated to page j by a surfer who follows the Google matrix transition rule. A page is important if a typical web surfer ends up there a lot.
Why this is a “vote”: Each link i \to j is a vote from page i for page j. But the vote is weighted: a vote from an important page (high \pi_i) is worth more than a vote from an unimportant one. The stationary distribution is the self-consistent assignment of importance that makes the weighted vote counts equal to the importance. Fixed point, again.
The formula s_i = 1/m_i from Existence and Uniqueness of Stationary Distributions gives another reading: \pi_j = 1/E[T_j \mid X_0 = j], where T_j is the return time to page j under the Google matrix dynamics. Pages with short expected return times are important. This is consistent: if you’re a popular page, you don’t have to wait long for the surfer to come back.

What PageRank Doesn’t Capture
It’s worth being honest about what the model assumes and where it breaks.
Anchor text and query relevance. PageRank measures global importance, not relevance to a query. Google’s actual search ranking combines PageRank with many other signals (TF-IDF, anchor text, user behavior, freshness, …). PageRank is one input, not the whole story.
Spam and manipulation. If a spammer creates many pages all linking to her page, she inflates her PageRank. This is called link spam. The teleportation term helps — it dilutes the influence of any finite cluster of spam pages — but it doesn’t eliminate the problem. Modern Google uses many anti-spam signals.
The time-homogeneity assumption. The web changes constantly. PageRank is computed on a snapshot; real-time recomputation is impossible. Google uses incremental updates.
Personalization. The uniform teleportation \frac{1-\alpha}{N}\mathbf{1}^\top treats all pages equally as teleportation destinations. Personalized PageRank replaces the uniform distribution with a user-specific preference vector \boldsymbol{\nu}:
G_{\boldsymbol{\nu}} = \alpha Q' + (1-\alpha)\mathbf{1}\boldsymbol{\nu}
Different users have different \boldsymbol{\nu}, giving different PageRank vectors. The mathematics is identical — just replace the uniform teleportation with a personalized one. The stationary distribution still exists and is unique (same proof: every entry is positive, so irreducible and aperiodic).

Connection to Eigenvector Centrality
PageRank is closely related to eigenvector centrality in network science. For a (non-stochastic) adjacency matrix A, the eigenvector centrality vector \mathbf{x} satisfies:
\mathbf{x} = \lambda_{\max}^{-1} A^\top \mathbf{x}
i.e., \mathbf{x} is the principal eigenvector of A^\top. This says: the centrality of a node is proportional to the sum of centralities of nodes pointing to it — exactly the PageRank recursion.
PageRank is eigenvector centrality applied to the modified, stochastified web graph. The Perron-Frobenius theorem guarantees that the principal eigenvector of a positive matrix is unique and has all positive entries — which is what makes PageRank well-defined.

This connection runs deep. The Q^n \to \mathbf{1s} convergence is the same as “power iteration on Q converges to the principal eigenvector.” The stationary distribution IS the principal left eigenvector of Q (eigenvalue 1). Linear algebra and Markov chain theory are the same theory wearing different clothes.


The Digraph Picture
It helps to draw what’s happening. For a tiny example: 4 pages {A, B, C, D}.
    A → B
    A → C
    B → D
    C → B
    C → D
    D → A

Naive Q (each row distributes uniformly over out-links):








































from\toABCDA01/21/20B0001C01/201/2D1000
This chain is irreducible (every page is reachable from every other, with some path length) and aperiodic (check: A \to B \to D \to A has length 3; A \to C \to D \to A has length 3 too; A \to C \to B \to D \to A has length 4; \gcd(3,4) = 1). No dangling nodes.
Solving \boldsymbol{\pi}Q = \boldsymbol{\pi} directly here is straightforward — a 4×4 linear system. The PageRank matrix G = 0.85 \cdot Q + 0.15/4 \cdot \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top will give slightly different values but the same qualitative picture.
Intuitively: D links to A, so A should have high rank. Both A and C link to B, so B should be high. D gets linked to by both B and C — also significant. C gets only one link (from A) — probably the lowest. This is the kind of qualitative reasoning the stationary distribution makes rigorous.

Summary























































ObjectDefinitionRoleWeb graphDirected graph on N pages; edges = hyperlinksDefines the naive chainNaive Qq_{ij} = 1/\deg^+(i) if i \to j, else 0Not always row-stochastic (dangling nodes)Dangling fix Q'Replace zero rows with \frac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}^\topRestores row-stochasticityGoogle matrix G\alpha Q' + \frac{1-\alpha}{N}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\topIrreducible, aperiodic, row-stochasticPageRank \boldsymbol{\pi}Unique stationary distribution of G\boldsymbol{\pi}G = \boldsymbol{\pi}PageRank equation\pi_j = \alpha\sum_{i \to j} \pi_i/\deg^+(i) + (1-\alpha)/NRecursive importanceComputationPower iteration: \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k+1)} = \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(k)}GConverges at rate \alpha^kSpectral gap\geq 1 - \alphaControls convergence speed; \alpha = 0.85 is the tradeoffInterpretationLong-run fraction of time a random surfer spends on page jErgodic theorem

Why I Care About This (Beyond the Application)
PageRank is a canonical example of the following meta-pattern that appears everywhere in applied probability:

Model the system as a Markov chain. (Web surfer on the link graph.)
The quantity of interest is the stationary distribution. (How often does the surfer visit each page?)
The existence and uniqueness theorem guarantees a well-defined answer. (Irreducible + positive recurrent + finite \Rightarrow unique \boldsymbol{\pi}.)
Compute iteratively via power iteration. (The convergence theorem tells me iteration works.)

This pattern appears in MCMC (MCMC and Metropolis-Hastings), in queueing theory, in Markov reward processes, in reinforcement learning (where the value function is a stationary quantity of an induced Markov chain). The underlying mathematics is always the same: find the fixed point of a linear operator, using existence/uniqueness and iterative computation.
PageRank is the most famous instance. But the lesson is the pattern, not the application.

When Brin and Page published their paper in 1998, they probably didn’t think “we are computing the left eigenvector of a row-stochastic matrix using the Perron-Frobenius theorem.” But that’s exactly what they were doing. The mathematics predates the application by decades. This is what makes pure mathematics feel magical in retrospect — it’s always already there, waiting for the application to arrive.


One-Line Summary for Future Me

PageRank is the stationary distribution of the Google matrix G = \alpha Q' + \frac{1-\alpha}{N}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top: the teleportation term (1-\alpha) fixes dangling nodes, makes the chain irreducible, and makes it aperiodic, guaranteeing a unique \boldsymbol{\pi} with \boldsymbol{\pi}G = \boldsymbol{\pi}. The spectral gap is \geq 1-\alpha, so power iteration converges in O(\log(1/\varepsilon)/\log(1/\alpha)) steps — about 100 for Google’s \alpha = 0.85.

01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/10.title: 10.Reversibility
01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/10.content:
Tags: probability stochastic-processes markov-chains reversibility
References: Blitzstein & Hwang — Introduction to Probability; Stat 110 (Harvard)
Status: 🟢 complete
Prerequisite notes: Stationary Distributions · Existence and Uniqueness of Stationary Distributions · Classification of States


“Detailed balance is the condition that says the chain looks the same run forwards and backwards. Global balance says inflow equals outflow at every state. Detailed balance says inflow equals outflow on every directed edge. The second implies the first, strictly. The gap between them is where irreversible chains live — and irreversibility turns out to be physically meaningful, not just a mathematical curiosity.”


Motivation: Two Notions of Equilibrium
From Stationary Distributions, a distribution \mathbf{s} is stationary if \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}, which entrywise says:
\sum_i s_i q_{ij} = s_j \quad \text{for all } j
Rewrite this as:
\sum_{i \neq j} s_i q_{ij} = s_j \sum_{k \neq j} q_{jk}
Left side: total probability flux flowing into state j from all other states.
Right side: total probability flux flowing out of state j to all other states.
This is global balance: at stationarity, inflow = outflow at every state. It’s a conservation law — the probability mass sitting at j doesn’t change over time because what comes in equals what goes out.
Now ask a finer question: can I require balance edge by edge, not just globally per state? That is:
s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji} \quad \text{for all pairs } i, j
This is detailed balance — and it is strictly stronger. A chain satisfying detailed balance is called reversible.
This note is about the relationship between these two conditions, why reversibility is the right framework for thinking about time-reversal, and how to use detailed balance as a computational tool.

Detailed Balance
Definition
A probability distribution \mathbf{s} satisfies detailed balance with respect to transition matrix Q if:
s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji} \quad \text{for all } i, j \in \mathcal{S}
The quantity s_i q_{ij} is the probability flux from i to j at stationarity: the probability of being in state i (which is s_i) times the probability of jumping to j given you’re in i (which is q_{ij}). Detailed balance says this flux is symmetric — whatever flows from i to j flows equally from j to i.
Theorem: Detailed Balance Implies Stationarity
If \mathbf{s} satisfies detailed balance with respect to Q, then \mathbf{s} is stationary: \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}.
Proof. Fix any state j. Sum the detailed balance condition over all i:
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} s_i q_{ij} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} s_j q_{ji} = s_j \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} q_{ji} = s_j \cdot 1 = s_j
The left side is (\mathbf{s}Q)_j. So (\mathbf{s}Q)_j = s_j for all j, i.e., \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}. \blacksquare

The proof is one line. Detailed balance is the local condition; summing it over all i gives the global condition for free. This is why detailed balance is so useful as a computational tool — if I can verify the local pairwise condition, I get stationarity for free, without solving the full balance equations \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s} as a linear system.

The Converse Is False
A chain can be stationary without satisfying detailed balance. The canonical counterexample:
Three-state cycle: \mathcal{S} = {1, 2, 3} with q_{12} = q_{23} = q_{31} = 1 and all other q_{ij} = 0.
The stationary distribution is \mathbf{s} = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) (by symmetry, or solve \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}). Check detailed balance for the pair (1,2):
s_1 q_{12} = \frac{1}{3} \cdot 1 = \frac{1}{3}, \qquad s_2 q_{21} = \frac{1}{3} \cdot 0 = 0
These are not equal. So detailed balance fails — this is an irreversible chain. Probability flows around the cycle in one direction only; the time-reversed chain would flow in the opposite direction, and the two are distinguishable.

Reversibility
The Time-Reversal of a Chain
Let (X_n)_{0 \leq n \leq T} be a Markov chain run for T steps in stationarity (i.e., X_0 \sim \mathbf{s} where \mathbf{s} is stationary). Define the time-reversed process:
Y_n = X_{T-n}, \quad 0 \leq n \leq T
Claim: (Y_n) is also a Markov chain, with transition matrix:
\tilde{q}_{ij} = \frac{s_j q_{ji}}{s_i}
Proof. First, verify the Markov property for (Y_n). Given Y_n = X_{T-n} = i and the past Y_0, \ldots, Y_{n-1} (which is the future X_{T}, \ldots, X_{T-n+1}), the future of Y is Y_{n+1} = X_{T-n-1}, which depends only on X_{T-n} = i by the Markov property of (X_n).
Now compute the transition probability:
P(Y_{n+1} = j \mid Y_n = i) = P(X_{T-n-1} = j \mid X_{T-n} = i)
By Bayes’ theorem:
= \frac{P(X_{T-n} = i \mid X_{T-n-1} = j) \cdot P(X_{T-n-1} = j)}{P(X_{T-n} = i)}
Since the chain is in stationarity, P(X_k = \ell) = s_\ell for all k, \ell:
= \frac{q_{ji} \cdot s_j}{s_i} = \tilde{q}_{ij}
\blacksquare
The reversed chain has transition matrix \tilde{Q} with entries \tilde{q}_{ij} = s_j q_{ji} / s_i.
Definition: Reversibility
A Markov chain (X_n) in stationarity is reversible if the time-reversed chain has the same distribution as the forward chain. That is, for all n and all paths i_0, i_1, \ldots, i_n:
P(X_0 = i_0, X_1 = i_1, \ldots, X_n = i_n) = P(X_0 = i_n, X_1 = i_{n-1}, \ldots, X_n = i_0)
In other words: you cannot tell whether the chain is running forwards or backwards by observing its distribution.
Theorem: Reversibility \Leftrightarrow Detailed Balance
A chain with stationary distribution \mathbf{s} is reversible if and only if it satisfies detailed balance: s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji} for all i, j.
Proof.
(\Rightarrow) Suppose the chain is reversible. Then \tilde{Q} = Q (the reversed chain has the same transitions). So \tilde{q}_{ij} = q_{ij}, i.e., s_j q_{ji} / s_i = q_{ij}, i.e., s_j q_{ji} = s_i q_{ij}. This is detailed balance.
(\Leftarrow) Suppose detailed balance holds. Then \tilde{q}_{ij} = s_j q_{ji}/s_i = q_{ij} — the reversed chain has the same transition matrix as the forward chain. The initial distribution of (Y_n) at time 0 is Y_0 = X_T \sim \mathbf{s} (stationarity). So (Y_n) and (X_n) are both Markov chains with transition matrix Q started from \mathbf{s} — they have the same distribution. \blacksquare

This theorem is the reason “detailed balance” and “reversibility” are used interchangeably. They’re the same condition, just stated in two different registers: detailed balance is the algebraic condition s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji}, and reversibility is the probabilistic condition that the chain is time-symmetric. Proving they’re equivalent is the content of the theorem.


Using Detailed Balance to Find Stationary Distributions
This is the main practical payoff. Instead of solving the linear system \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}, \sum_i s_i = 1 — which for large state spaces is a painful system — I can:

Guess a candidate \mathbf{s}.
Check s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji} for all pairs (i,j) with q_{ij} > 0.
Normalize.

If detailed balance holds, \mathbf{s} is stationary. This avoids solving the full system.
Why This Is Easier
The global balance equation \sum_i s_i q_{ij} = s_j couples all states simultaneously — it’s a system of |\mathcal{S}| equations. Detailed balance gives |\mathcal{S}|^2/2 pairwise equations, each involving only two states. For chains with special structure (birth-death, graphs with nice symmetry), these pairwise equations decouple and can be solved by telescoping.

The Birth-Death Chain: Canonical Example
A birth-death chain on {0, 1, \ldots, M} has transitions only to adjacent states:
q_{k, k+1} = p_k, \quad q_{k, k-1} = r_k, \quad q_{kk} = 1 - p_k - r_k
with p_M = r_0 = 0 (reflecting boundaries).
Claim: Every birth-death chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to some distribution.
Proof. Detailed balance for adjacent pair (k, k+1):
s_k q_{k,k+1} = s_{k+1} q_{k+1,k}
s_k p_k = s_{k+1} r_{k+1}
s_{k+1} = s_k \cdot \frac{p_k}{r_{k+1}}
For non-adjacent pairs (i, j) with |i - j| \geq 2: q_{ij} = q_{ji} = 0, so s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji} = 0 trivially. Detailed balance holds.
Telescoping to find \mathbf{s}:
s_k = s_0 \cdot \frac{p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{k-1}}{r_1 r_2 \cdots r_k}
Define \rho_k = \frac{p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{k-1}}{r_1 r_2 \cdots r_k} (with \rho_0 = 1). Then s_k = s_0 \rho_k, and normalization gives:
s_0 = \frac{1}{\sum_{k=0}^M \rho_k}, \qquad s_k = \frac{\rho_k}{\sum_{\ell=0}^M \rho_\ell}

Birth-death chains are always reversible. The intuition: transitions only go left or right, one step at a time. The only way to get from j to i is to pass through every state in between — and the same is true in reverse. There’s no “directionality” to exploit; every path from i to j has a mirror path from j to i. The topology forces reversibility.

Concrete Example: Ehrenfest Urn
M balls distributed between two urns, total d balls. State = number in urn 1. Transitions: pick a ball uniformly at random, move it to the other urn.
p_k = \frac{d-k}{d}, \quad r_k = \frac{k}{d}
The ratios:
\frac{p_{k-1}}{r_k} = \frac{(d-k+1)/d}{k/d} = \frac{d-k+1}{k}
So:
\rho_k = \prod_{j=1}^k \frac{d-j+1}{j} = \binom{d}{k}
The stationary distribution is:
s_k = \frac{\binom{d}{k}}{\sum_{\ell=0}^d \binom{d}{\ell}} = \frac{\binom{d}{k}}{2^d}
which is \text{Binomial}(d, 1/2). At equilibrium, balls are distributed binomially — exactly the maximum-entropy distribution over {0, \ldots, d} with mean d/2.
This makes physical sense: the Ehrenfest urn models diffusion. At equilibrium, the distribution of particles between two sides of a container is Binomial. Reversibility is the probabilistic statement of microscopic reversibility in physics.

A Non-Example: The Three-State Cycle
Return to the three-state cycle q_{12} = q_{23} = q_{31} = 1. I showed detailed balance fails. What is the reversed chain?
\tilde{q}_{ij} = \frac{s_j q_{ji}}{s_i} = \frac{(1/3) q_{ji}}{1/3} = q_{ji}
So \tilde{Q} = Q^\top, i.e., the reversed chain is the cycle in the opposite direction: q_{21} = q_{32} = q_{13} = 1. The forward chain cycles 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1 \to \cdots and the reversed chain cycles 1 \to 3 \to 2 \to 1 \to \cdots. These are distinguishable — the chain is not reversible.
This is the archetypal irreversible chain. In physics, irreversibility corresponds to entropy production — systems that run their dynamics in a direction determined by the arrow of time. The three-state cycle is the simplest example.

Kolmogorov’s Criterion
For a general (not necessarily birth-death) chain, there is a clean necessary and sufficient condition for reversibility that doesn’t require knowing \mathbf{s} in advance.
Theorem (Kolmogorov’s Cycle Criterion)
An irreducible Markov chain is reversible (with respect to its unique stationary distribution) if and only if for every cycle i_0 \to i_1 \to \cdots \to i_n \to i_0 in the state space:
q_{i_0 i_1} q_{i_1 i_2} \cdots q_{i_{n-1} i_n} q_{i_n i_0} = q_{i_0 i_n} q_{i_n i_{n-1}} \cdots q_{i_1 i_0}
The probability of traversing the cycle in one direction equals the probability of traversing it in the opposite direction.
Proof sketch (\Rightarrow): If detailed balance holds, multiply the detailed balance equations around the cycle:
\prod_{k=0}^{n-1} s_{i_k} q_{i_k i_{k+1}} = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} s_{i_{k+1}} q_{i_{k+1} i_k}
The left product is \prod_k s_{i_k} \cdot \prod_k q_{i_k i_{k+1}}, and similarly for the right. The s factors are the same on both sides (since the s_{i_k} appear once each on each side around the cycle). Cancel them to get the cycle condition. \blacksquare
Why this matters: Kolmogorov’s criterion is checkable from Q alone, without knowing \mathbf{s}. For complicated state spaces, checking all cycles is hard — but for small graphs it’s immediate.
For the three-state cycle: the only non-trivial cycle is 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1 (and its reverse). Forward product: q_{12} q_{23} q_{31} = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1. Reverse product: q_{13} q_{32} q_{21} = 0 \cdot 0 \cdot 0 = 0. Not equal. Not reversible. ✓

The Reversed Chain Has the Same Stationary Distribution
Claim: The reversed chain \tilde{Q} has the same stationary distribution \mathbf{s} as the forward chain Q.
Proof. Check \mathbf{s}\tilde{Q} = \mathbf{s}:
(\mathbf{s}\tilde{Q})_j = \sum_i s_i \tilde{q}_{ij} = \sum_i s_i \frac{s_j q_{ji}}{s_i} = s_j \sum_i q_{ji} = s_j \cdot 1 = s_j
\blacksquare
So reversibility is a property of a chain relative to its own stationary distribution. The forward and reversed chains share the same \mathbf{s}, even when Q \neq \tilde{Q} (i.e., even when the chain is irreversible).

Reversibility in MCMC: Why It Matters Computationally
The most important application of reversibility in modern probability is Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). The goal: sample from a target distribution \pi that I can evaluate (up to a normalizing constant) but cannot sample from directly.
The strategy: Construct a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is \pi, run it until it mixes, and treat the samples as approximate draws from \pi.
The problem: How do I construct such a chain? The detailed balance condition gives a sufficient condition that’s easy to engineer:
\pi_i q_{ij} = \pi_j q_{ji} \quad \text{for all } i, j
If I design Q to satisfy detailed balance with respect to \pi, then \pi is automatically stationary. This is how the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm works.
Metropolis-Hastings at a Glance
Given target \pi and a proposal kernel r(i, j) (symmetric for simplicity: r(i,j) = r(j,i)):

At state i, propose moving to j with probability r(i,j).
Accept the proposal with probability \min\left(1, \frac{\pi_j}{\pi_i}\right).
If rejected, stay at i.

The resulting transition probabilities:
q_{ij} = r(i,j) \cdot \min!\left(1, \frac{\pi_j}{\pi_i}\right) \quad (i \neq j)
Verify detailed balance:
\pi_i q_{ij} = \pi_i \cdot r(i,j) \cdot \min!\left(1, \frac{\pi_j}{\pi_i}\right)
Case \pi_j \leq \pi_i: \min(1, \pi_j/\pi_i) = \pi_j/\pi_i, so \pi_i q_{ij} = r(i,j)\pi_j.
And: \pi_j q_{ji} = \pi_j \cdot r(j,i) \cdot \min(1, \pi_i/\pi_j) = \pi_j \cdot r(i,j) \cdot 1 = \pi_j r(i,j). Equal. ✓
Case \pi_j > \pi_i: symmetric argument. ✓
So Metropolis-Hastings is designed to satisfy detailed balance with respect to \pi — by construction. I never need to know the normalizing constant of \pi (it cancels in the ratio \pi_j/\pi_i). The algorithm samples from distributions I can only evaluate up to a constant. This is the miracle of MCMC, and detailed balance is the mathematical mechanism behind it.

This is the reason physicists care about detailed balance. In statistical mechanics, the Boltzmann distribution \pi_i \propto e^{-E_i/kT} (where E_i is the energy of state i) is the equilibrium distribution of a physical system at temperature T. To sample from it computationally, you run Metropolis-Hastings, which satisfies detailed balance with respect to \pi — the same condition that holds for physical systems in thermal equilibrium. The algorithm is simulating thermodynamic equilibrium.


Summary













































ConceptDefinitionKey propertyGlobal balance\sum_i s_i q_{ij} = s_j for all jNecessary and sufficient for stationarityDetailed balances_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji} for all i,jSufficient for stationarity; strictly strongerReversibility(X_n) \overset{d}{=} (X_{T-n}) when started in \mathbf{s}Equivalent to detailed balanceReversed chain\tilde{q}_{ij} = s_j q_{ji}/s_iAlways has stationary dist \mathbf{s}; equals Q iff reversibleBirth-death chainsTransitions only to adjacent statesAlways reversible; s_k \propto \prod p_j/r_jKolmogorov criterionProduct of q‘s around any cycle = product in reverseCheckable from Q alone, no need to know \mathbf{s}Metropolis-HastingsMCMC algorithm built on detailed balanceSamples from \pi using only ratios \pi_j/\pi_i

One-Line Summary for Future Me

Detailed balance s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji} is the pairwise version of stationarity — it implies \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s} immediately by summing over i. A chain satisfying it is reversible: the time-reversed chain \tilde{q}_{ij} = s_j q_{ji}/s_i equals the forward chain. Birth-death chains are always reversible (telescope the pairwise equations). Kolmogorov’s criterion detects reversibility from Q alone by checking whether cycle products are direction-symmetric. MCMC (Metropolis-Hastings) is engineered to satisfy detailed balance with respect to the target distribution \pi — that’s the entire design principle.

01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/11.title: 11.Knight on a Chess Board
01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/11.content:
Tags: probability stochastic-processes markov-chains applications graphs
References: Blitzstein & Hwang — Introduction to Probability; Stat 110 (Harvard)
Status: 🟢 complete
Prerequisite notes: Markov Chains — Definitions and Transition Matrix · Stationary Distributions · Detailed Balance and Reversibility · Classification of States


“The knight is the strangest piece on the board — it’s the only one that can jump over other pieces, the only one whose reachable squares aren’t in a straight line, the only one that alternates color every move. That last fact is the mathematical heart of this problem. The chessboard is a bipartite graph, and bipartiteness is exactly periodicity. The knight has period 2.”


The Setup
A knight starts on a square of an 8 \times 8 chessboard and moves according to the standard chess rules: two squares in one direction, one square perpendicular. At each step, it picks a legal move uniformly at random from all available moves.
This is a Markov chain. The state space is \mathcal{S} = {(r,c) : 1 \leq r, c \leq 8}, with |\mathcal{S}| = 64 states.
The transition matrix Q has:
q_{(r,c),(r',c')} = \frac{1}{\deg(r,c)} \cdot \mathbf{1}[(r',c') \text{ is a legal knight move from } (r,c)]
where \deg(r,c) is the number of legal knight moves from square (r,c).
This note asks: what is the stationary distribution? Is the chain reversible? Does it converge, and to what?

The Degree of a Square
The key object is \deg(r,c) — how many knight moves are available from (r,c).
A knight at (r,c) can move to (r \pm 1, c \pm 2) and (r \pm 2, c \pm 1) — eight potential targets. Squares near the boundary have fewer legal moves because some targets fall off the board.
By direct enumeration (or symmetry):

































LocationDegreeCorner squares (e.g., a1)2Edge-adjacent-to-corner (e.g., b1, a2)3Edge squares, general4One step from corner (e.g., b2)4Near-edge interior6Central squares (e.g., d4, d5, e4, e5)8
The four corner squares have degree 2 (the most restricted). The 16 squares around the center of the board have degree 8. Degree varies from 2 to 8.

This variation in degree is why the stationary distribution is not uniform. The random knight spends more time on high-degree squares — it gets “pulled toward” the center because there are more ways to arrive there. Corners are sparsely visited: hard to reach, and easy to leave (only 2 exits each).


The Stationary Distribution
Finding \mathbf{s} via Detailed Balance
The graph structure of knight moves is undirected: if (r',c') is a legal move from (r,c), then (r,c) is a legal move from (r',c'). The adjacency is symmetric.
For an undirected graph with adjacency matrix A, define the random walk on the graph: from node i, jump to a uniformly random neighbor. The transition matrix is:
q_{ij} = \frac{A_{ij}}{\deg(i)}
Claim: The stationary distribution of this random walk is proportional to degree:
s_i = \frac{\deg(i)}{\sum_{j} \deg(j)} = \frac{\deg(i)}{2|E|}
where |E| is the number of edges.
Proof via detailed balance. Check s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji} for all i,j:
s_i q_{ij} = \frac{\deg(i)}{2|E|} \cdot \frac{A_{ij}}{\deg(i)} = \frac{A_{ij}}{2|E|}
s_j q_{ji} = \frac{\deg(j)}{2|E|} \cdot \frac{A_{ji}}{\deg(j)} = \frac{A_{ji}}{2|E|}
Since the graph is undirected, A_{ij} = A_{ji}. So s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji}. Detailed balance holds. \blacksquare
The random knight’s walk is reversible, and its stationary distribution is:
\boxed{s_{(r,c)} = \frac{\deg(r,c)}{\sum_{(r',c')} \deg(r',c')}}
Computing the Normalization
The total degree \sum_{(r,c)} \deg(r,c) = 2|E|, where |E| is the number of knight-move pairs on the 8 \times 8 board.
By enumeration (or symmetry arguments): |E| = 168 on the standard 8\times 8 board. So \sum \deg = 336.
Degree distribution on the 8 \times 8 board:



































DegreeNumber of squaresTotal degree contribution24838244208061696816128
Total: 4 + 8 + 20 + 16 + 16 = 64 squares ✓, and 8 + 24 + 80 + 96 + 128 = 336 ✓.
So the stationary probabilities:





























Degrees_{(r,c)}22/336 \approx 0.00633/336 \approx 0.00944/336 \approx 0.01266/336 \approx 0.01888/336 \approx 0.024
The knight spends 4× as much time on a degree-8 central square as on a degree-2 corner square. The ergodic theorem says this is literally the long-run fraction of moves spent on each square.

The fact that s_i \propto \deg(i) is a general theorem about random walks on undirected graphs — not special to the knight. The proof above works for any undirected graph. The knight is just a particularly nice example because the degree function has a clean geometric interpretation: degree measures how “central” a square is, and the stationary distribution reflects that centrality. This is the same logic as PageRank — high-degree nodes are more visited.


The Bipartite Structure and Periodicity
Here is the deepest structural fact about the knight’s walk.
Fact: Every knight move changes the color of the square. From a white square, the knight always lands on a black square, and vice versa.
Proof: A knight move changes (r,c) by (\pm 1, \pm 2) or (\pm 2, \pm 1). In either case, the total displacement is 1 + 2 = 3 (in taxicab distance), which is odd. The color of a square is determined by the parity of r + c: white if r+c is even, black if r+c is odd. An odd displacement changes the parity of r+c, hence changes the color. \blacksquare
This means the knight-move graph on the 8 \times 8 board is bipartite: every edge connects a white square to a black square. There are no edges within the same color class.
Consequence for the Markov chain: Starting from a white square, at even times the knight is on a white square, at odd times on a black square. The set of times the knight can return to its starting square is {2, 4, 6, \ldots} — all even. So:
\gcd{n \geq 1 : q_{ii}^{(n)} > 0} = 2
Every state has period 2. The chain is periodic with period d = 2.
This is a direct application of the theory from Classification of States: bipartiteness of the underlying graph is equivalent to period 2 of the random walk.

This is the single most important structural fact about this chain. It means the convergence theorem as stated — \mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \mathbf{s} for irreducible aperiodic chains — does NOT apply. The distribution of X_n oscillates and never converges. If I start on a white square, at every even time I’m on a white square with high probability, and at every odd time I’m on a black square with high probability. The chain never “forgets” the color of the starting square in the distributional sense.


Irreducibility
Claim: The knight’s walk on the 8 \times 8 board is irreducible — from any square, every other square is reachable.
Proof: It suffices to show that from any square (r,c), any other square (r',c') is reachable in finitely many knight moves. This is a fact about the knight-move graph being connected, which is well-known (and can be verified by exhaustive BFS). Every square of the 8 \times 8 board is reachable from every other square. \blacksquare
Note the interaction with periodicity: the knight can reach any white square from a given white square in an even number of steps, and any black square in an odd number of steps. It cannot reach a square of the same color in an odd number of steps — that’s what period 2 means.
So the chain is irreducible with period 2. The state space does not split into further communicating classes — there’s only one — but within that class, the chain alternates between two “phases” (white and black squares).

What Convergence Looks Like for a Periodic Chain
Since the chain is periodic with period 2, the distribution \mathbf{t}^{(n)} does not converge as n \to \infty. But something does converge: the Cesàro average.
Theorem (from Existence and Uniqueness of Stationary Distributions): For any irreducible positive recurrent chain (periodic or not):
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \mathbf{s} \quad \text{as } N \to \infty
And the ergodic theorem still holds:
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \mathbf{1}[X_n = (r,c)] \xrightarrow{a.s.} s_{(r,c)} = \frac{\deg(r,c)}{336}
The long-run fraction of time on each square converges, even though the distribution at any fixed time oscillates.
The Two-Step Chain Converges
For a period-2 chain, the standard fix for distributional convergence is to look at the 2-step chain (X_0, X_2, X_4, \ldots) — i.e., the chain with transition matrix Q^2.
Claim: Q^2 decomposes into two irreducible aperiodic chains: one on white squares, one on black squares.
Proof: From a white square, Q^2 takes two knight moves, landing back on a white square. Since the chain is irreducible and period 2, the white squares form an irreducible class under Q^2 — any white square is reachable from any other white square in an even number of moves. Similarly for black squares. Aperiodicity of Q^2: the period of Q^2 is \gcd{n : (Q^2)_{ii}^{(n)} > 0} = \gcd{2n : q_{ii}^{(2n)} > 0}/2 = 1 (since from any white square there exist both 2-step and 4-step returns; \gcd(2,4)/2 = 1). \blacksquare
So starting from a white square:
\mathbf{t}^{(2n)} \to \mathbf{s}^{\text{white}}, \quad \mathbf{t}^{(2n+1)} \to \mathbf{s}^{\text{black}}
where \mathbf{s}^{\text{white}} is the stationary distribution of Q^2 restricted to white squares, and similarly for black. These are:
s^{\text{white}}_{(r,c)} = \frac{\deg(r,c)}{\sum_{(r',c') \text{ white}} \deg(r',c')}, \quad s^{\text{black}}_{(r,c)} = \frac{\deg(r,c)}{\sum_{(r',c') \text{ black}} \deg(r',c')}

This is a clean illustration of the three-level convergence table from Stationary Distributions:

\mathbf{s} exists and is unique: YES (irreducible + positive recurrent)
Time averages converge to s_{(r,c)}: YES (ergodic theorem)
\mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \mathbf{s}: NO (periodic with period 2)
\mathbf{t}^{(2n)} \to \mathbf{s}^{\text{white}}: YES (2-step chain is aperiodic)



The General n \times n Board
It’s worth understanding how the analysis changes with board size. The key facts:
Irreducibility: The knight’s graph on an n \times n board is connected (irreducible) for n \geq 5. For n \leq 4, some squares are isolated or the graph disconnects — the knight cannot reach all squares from all starting positions. For example, on a 3 \times 3 board, the center square has no legal knight moves (all targets are off the board).
Periodicity: The chessboard is bipartite for all n \geq 1 (color alternation is a property of the knight move, not the board size). So the period is always 2 — on any board where the chain is irreducible.
Stationary distribution: Always proportional to degree: s_{(r,c)} \propto \deg(r,c), by the same detailed balance argument.
For the 5 \times 5 board: Minimum degree is 2 (corners), maximum is 8 (some central squares), and the chain is irreducible. Everything works exactly as for the 8 \times 8 case.

The n < 5 failure of irreducibility is a boundary phenomenon — the board is too small for the knight to maneuver freely. This is a good reminder that irreducibility is not automatic; it requires checking the graph structure. The period-2 property, however, is universal — it’s a consequence of the knight move always changing color, which has nothing to do with boundary effects.


Hitting Times: How Long to Reach a Corner?
First-step equations apply. Let h_{(r,c)} = E[\text{steps to reach a corner} \mid X_0 = (r,c)].
The four corners are the target states — label them C. Boundary conditions:
h_{(r,c)} = 0 \quad \text{for } (r,c) \in C
First-step equation for interior states:
h_{(r,c)} = 1 + \frac{1}{\deg(r,c)} \sum_{(r',c') \text{ knight-reachable from } (r,c)} h_{(r',c')}
This is a linear system of 60 equations in 60 unknowns — no closed form, but numerically solvable.
By symmetry, all four corners give the same hitting time from a given square. The hardest square to reach a corner from is intuitively a central square (far from all corners, few direct paths). The easiest is a square already adjacent to a corner.
Example: from d4 (a central square, high degree).
The knight at d4 has 8 legal moves, none of which are corners (corners are at a1, a8, h1, h8). To reach a corner, the knight must navigate from the center outward — fighting against the stationary distribution, which pulls it toward the center. Corners have stationary measure 2/336 \approx 0.006 — very small. By the formula s_{(r,c)} = 1/m_{(r,c)} from Existence and Uniqueness of Stationary Distributions, the expected return time to a corner from itself is:
m_{\text{corner}} = \frac{1}{s_{\text{corner}}} = \frac{336}{2} = 168 \text{ steps}
The expected return time to a corner is 168 steps. The expected hitting time to a corner from elsewhere will be on the same order — large, because corners are rarely visited.

m_i = 1/s_i is one of the most useful formulas I know. It converts a stationary probability into an expected return time without solving any first-step equations. For the corner: s = 2/336, so m = 168 steps. For a central degree-8 square: s = 8/336 = 1/42, so m = 42 steps. The knight returns to the center every 42 moves on average, and to a corner only every 168 moves. The center is 4× more revisited than the corners — exactly the ratio of their degrees.


Doubly Stochastic? No.
A matrix is doubly stochastic if both rows and columns sum to 1. For the random walk on an undirected graph, rows sum to 1 (by construction), but columns sum to \sum_i q_{ij} = \sum_i A_{ij}/\deg(i), which equals 1 for all j only if all degrees are equal.
The knight’s transition matrix is not doubly stochastic because degrees are not all equal (they range from 2 to 8). Consequently, the stationary distribution is not uniform — central squares have higher probability than corner squares.
This is in contrast to, say, the random walk on a regular graph (all degrees equal d), where q_{ij} = A_{ij}/d and every column sums to \sum_i A_{ij}/d = \deg(j)/d = 1. The uniform distribution is stationary for any regular graph.
Is there a related regular graph? Yes: the 8 \times 8 toroidal chessboard — wrap the board into a torus so that the board has no boundary. Every square then has exactly 8 knight-move neighbors (the 8 potential targets are all on the board, modulo wrapping). The transition matrix is doubly stochastic, and the stationary distribution is uniform: s_{(r,c)} = 1/64 for all squares.

The toroidal knight is a beautiful object: a regular random walk on a Cayley graph of \mathbb{Z}_8 \times \mathbb{Z}_8 with the generating set {(\pm 1, \pm 2), (\pm 2, \pm 1)}. It’s still bipartite (and hence period-2), still irreducible (on the torus, knight connectivity is easy to verify), but now the uniform stationary distribution makes the Fourier analysis tractable. Mixing times on Cayley graphs connect to representation theory. A rabbit hole I should explore in Random Walks on Groups.


Summary

































































PropertyValueReasonState space64 squares of 8 \times 8 boardOne state per squareTransitionUniform over legal knight movesq_{ij} = 1/\deg(i) if i \to jIrreducible?Yes (for n \geq 5)Knight-move graph is connectedPeriod2Chessboard is bipartite; knight changes color every moveReversible?YesUndirected graph \Rightarrow detailed balance with s_i \propto \deg(i)Stationary dists_{(r,c)} = \deg(r,c)/336Degree-proportional; derived by detailed balanceDistributional convergenceNo (\mathbf{t}^{(n)} oscillates)Period 2 breaks aperiodicity conditionTime-average convergenceYesErgodic theorem; holds regardless of period2-step chainAperiodic, convergesQ^2 splits into irreducible aperiodic chains on white/black squaresReturn time to corner168 stepsm = 1/s = 336/2Return time to central square42 stepsm = 1/s = 336/8

One-Line Summary for Future Me

Random knight on an 8\times 8 board: irreducible (connected graph), period 2 (bipartite — knight always changes color), reversible (undirected graph \Rightarrow detailed balance), stationary distribution s_{(r,c)} \propto \deg(r,c) (corners least visited at 2/336, center most at 8/336). Distribution \mathbf{t}^{(n)} oscillates forever; time averages converge to \mathbf{s}; the 2-step chain converges distributionally. Expected return time to a square is 336/\deg.
