01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/12.title: 12.Birth-Death Chain
01.Maths/Probability/11.Markov-chains/12.content:
Tags: probability stochastic-processes markov-chains birth-death
References: Blitzstein & Hwang — Introduction to Probability; Stat 110 (Harvard)
Status: 🟢 complete
Prerequisite notes: Markov Chains — Definitions and Transition Matrix · Stationary Distributions · Detailed Balance and Reversibility · Existence and Uniqueness of Stationary Distributions · Gamblers Ruin as a Markov Chain


“Birth-death chains are the one-dimensional Markov chains. The state space is a subset of \mathbb{Z}, transitions only go left or right by one step, and that constraint — no jumps — forces the chain to be reversible. Always. The entire theory collapses into a single telescoping recurrence, and the stationary distribution is just a product formula. Everything is explicit. There is no other family of chains where I can write down every quantity in closed form this cleanly.”


Definition
A birth-death chain is a Markov chain on state space \mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathbb{Z} — either {0, 1, \ldots, M} (finite) or {0, 1, 2, \ldots} (semi-infinite) — with the constraint that transitions only go to adjacent states:
q_{k, k+1} = p_k \quad \text{(birth probability)} q_{k, k-1} = r_k \quad \text{(death probability)} q_{k,k} = 1 - p_k - r_k \quad \text{(stay probability)} q_{k,j} = 0 \quad \text{for } |j - k| \geq 2
with boundary conditions: r_0 = 0 \quad \text{(can't go below 0)} p_M = 0 \quad \text{(can't go above } M \text{, for finite chains)}
For the chain to be valid: p_k, r_k \geq 0 and p_k + r_k \leq 1 for all k.
The name comes from population biology: state k is population size, p_k is the probability of a birth (population increases by 1), and r_k is the probability of a death (population decreases by 1). But the model appears everywhere — queues, genetics, chemical reactions, random walks.

I think of the birth-death chain as the Markov chain equivalent of a tridiagonal matrix: the transition matrix Q has nonzero entries only on the main diagonal and the two adjacent diagonals. All the structure is in those three diagonals, and the no-jump constraint is what makes everything solvable.


Irreducibility
The chain is irreducible if and only if p_k > 0 for all k < M and r_k > 0 for all k > 0 (in the finite case). In words: births are always possible (unless at the top) and deaths are always possible (unless at the bottom). Every state can reach every other via a sequence of births and deaths.
If p_k = 0 for some interior k, then state k is a barrier the chain can never cross upward — the state space splits. Similarly for r_k = 0.
I’ll assume irreducibility throughout: p_k > 0 for k < M and r_k > 0 for k \geq 1.

Reversibility: Always
Theorem. Every irreducible birth-death chain is reversible with respect to its stationary distribution.
Proof. I need to verify detailed balance s_k q_{kj} = s_j q_{jk} for all pairs (k,j).
For |k - j| \geq 2: q_{kj} = q_{jk} = 0, so both sides are zero. ✓
For adjacent pairs (k, k+1): the detailed balance condition is: s_k q_{k,k+1} = s_{k+1} q_{k+1,k} s_k p_k = s_{k+1} r_{k+1}
This is one equation per adjacent pair. I haven’t yet shown this holds — I’ll use it to find \mathbf{s} in the next section. The point is that the only non-trivial detailed balance conditions are for adjacent pairs, and there are only M of them (for a chain on {0, \ldots, M}). A birth-death chain satisfies detailed balance if and only if these M conditions hold — and I’ll construct \mathbf{s} to make them hold. \blacksquare
The structural reason for reversibility: the birth-death chain lives on a path graph (or half-line). A path graph has no cycles. By Kolmogorov’s criterion from Detailed Balance and Reversibility, reversibility requires that the probability of traversing any cycle in one direction equals the probability in the other — but there are no cycles on a path graph, so the condition is vacuously satisfied. Reversibility is a topological fact about the state space, not a special property of the rates.

This is the deepest reason to care about birth-death chains: they are always reversible, which means I always have a clean product formula for the stationary distribution. The absence of cycles is what does it. The moment the state space has a loop — like the three-state cycle — reversibility can fail. On a line or half-line, there’s nowhere for irreversibility to hide.


The Stationary Distribution: The Product Formula
Derivation
Write the detailed balance condition for each adjacent pair:
s_k p_k = s_{k+1} r_{k+1} \quad \text{for } k = 0, 1, \ldots, M-1
This gives a telescoping recurrence:
s_{k+1} = s_k \cdot \frac{p_k}{r_{k+1}}
Unrolling from k = 0:
s_1 = s_0 \cdot \frac{p_0}{r_1} s_2 = s_1 \cdot \frac{p_1}{r_2} = s_0 \cdot \frac{p_0 p_1}{r_1 r_2} s_k = s_0 \cdot \frac{p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{k-1}}{r_1 r_2 \cdots r_k}
Define the traffic intensity ratios:
\rho_0 = 1, \qquad \rho_k = \frac{p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{k-1}}{r_1 r_2 \cdots r_k} = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} \frac{p_j}{r_{j+1}} \quad \text{for } k \geq 1
Then s_k = s_0 \rho_k. Normalization \sum_{k=0}^M s_k = 1 gives:
s_0 \sum_{k=0}^M \rho_k = 1 \implies s_0 = \frac{1}{\sum_{k=0}^M \rho_k}
\boxed{s_k = \frac{\rho_k}{\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=0}^{M} \rho_\ell}, \qquad \rho_k = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} \frac{p_j}{r_{j+1}}}
This is the product formula for birth-death chains. It is completely explicit — no linear system to solve, just multiply ratios of birth and death rates and normalize.

I find it remarkable that a problem which in principle requires solving an M \times M linear system reduces to a product of M scalars. The detailed balance condition is what makes this possible: instead of the global constraint \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s} (coupling all states simultaneously), I get local constraints s_k p_k = s_{k+1} r_{k+1} (coupling only adjacent pairs), and those decouple into a one-directional recurrence.

For the Semi-Infinite Chain {0, 1, 2, \ldots}
The same formula holds, but I need the series \sum_{k=0}^\infty \rho_k to converge for a stationary distribution to exist.
Stationary distribution exists \iff \sum_{k=0}^\infty \rho_k < \infty.
If \sum_{k=0}^\infty \rho_k = \infty, the chain has no stationary distribution. Whether this means the chain is transient or null recurrent depends on further analysis — but either way, there is no limiting distribution.

Classification: When Is the Chain Positive Recurrent?
For the finite irreducible birth-death chain on {0, \ldots, M}: always positive recurrent (finite + irreducible, from Existence and Uniqueness of Stationary Distributions). The product formula always gives a valid stationary distribution.
For the semi-infinite chain on {0, 1, 2, \ldots}:





















ConditionClassification\sum_{k=0}^\infty \rho_k < \inftyPositive recurrent; stationary distribution s_k = \rho_k / \sum \rho_\ell\sum_{k=0}^\infty \rho_k = \infty, \sum_{k=0}^\infty 1/(p_k \rho_k) = \inftyNull recurrent\sum_{k=0}^\infty \rho_k = \infty, \sum_{k=0}^\infty 1/(p_k \rho_k) < \inftyTransient
The second and third conditions come from the theory of one-dimensional random walks — the quantities \sum 1/(p_k \rho_k) appear when computing expected hitting times and absorption probabilities via first-step equations.

The transience/null-recurrence distinction for semi-infinite chains is the one piece of this theory I find genuinely unintuitive. You’d think: if \sum \rho_k = \infty, the chain must drift to +\infty and be transient. But null recurrence is the sneaky middle case — the chain wanders to +\infty but always comes back, just with infinite expected return time. The simple symmetric random walk on \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} (constant p_k = r_k = 1/2) is the canonical null recurrent birth-death chain.


Examples
Example 1: The Simple Random Walk (Gambler’s Ruin)
p_k = p, r_k = q = 1-p for all k \in {1, \ldots, N-1}, with absorbing boundaries p_N = r_0 = 0.
\rho_k = \left(\frac{p}{q}\right)^k
For p \neq q:
s_k = \frac{(p/q)^k}{\sum_{\ell=0}^N (p/q)^\ell} = \frac{(p/q)^k \cdot (1 - p/q)}{1 - (p/q)^{N+1}}
But wait — the Gambler’s Ruin has absorbing states at 0 and N. Those are absorbing, not reflecting. The stationary distributions are \delta_0 and \delta_N (all mass at the absorbing boundaries). The product formula above applies when I think of the chain as having reflecting boundaries — i.e., states 0 and N push back into the interior.
For the reflecting version (r_0 = 0, p_N = 0, p_k = p, r_k = q for interior states):
\rho_k = (p/q)^k, \qquad s_k = \frac{(p/q)^k}{\sum_{\ell=0}^N (p/q)^\ell}
For the fair walk p = q = 1/2: \rho_k = 1 for all k, so s_k = 1/(N+1) — the uniform distribution. This confirms: the simple symmetric random walk on {0, \ldots, N} with reflecting boundaries has the uniform stationary distribution. Makes sense: all states have the same degree in the path graph (interior states have degree 2, except the endpoints which have degree 1 — actually the endpoints have a self-loop in the reflecting version, restoring degree 2).

Pedantic but worth noting: for the reflecting boundary at 0 with p_0 = 1 (deterministically go to 1), then r_1 = q gives \rho_1 = p_0/r_1 = 1/q, which breaks the symmetry slightly. The clean uniform result requires p_0 = p (same birth probability at the boundary), which is the lazy/reflecting boundary convention. The details matter for the normalization.

Example 2: The Ehrenfest Urn
M balls, d total, state = number in urn 1. From Detailed Balance and Reversibility:
p_k = \frac{d-k}{d}, \quad r_k = \frac{k}{d}
\rho_k = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} \frac{(d-j)/d}{(j+1)/d} = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} \frac{d-j}{j+1} = \binom{d}{k}
s_k = \frac{\binom{d}{k}}{2^d} = \text{Binomial}(d, 1/2) \text{ PMF at } k
The stationary distribution is \text{Binomial}(d, 1/2). This is the equilibrium distribution of balls between two chambers — the maximum entropy distribution consistent with d balls and equal probability of being in either urn.
Example 3: M/M/1 Queue (Semi-Infinite)
A queueing model: customers arrive at rate \lambda (Poisson), each served at rate \mu. State = number of customers in system. In discrete time approximation:
p_k = \lambda, \quad r_k = \mu \quad \text{for all } k \geq 1, \qquad p_0 = \lambda, \quad r_0 = 0
Let \rho = \lambda/\mu (traffic intensity).
\rho_k = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\right)^k = \rho^k
The series \sum_{k=0}^\infty \rho^k = \frac{1}{1-\rho} converges if and only if \rho < 1.
For \rho < 1: positive recurrent, stationary distribution s_k = (1-\rho)\rho^k — a Geometric distribution on {0, 1, 2, \ldots} with parameter 1-\rho.
For \rho \geq 1: no stationary distribution. The queue grows without bound — arrivals outpace service, the system never reaches equilibrium.
\boxed{s_k = (1-\rho)\rho^k, \quad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots \qquad \text{(for } \rho < 1\text{)}}
The mean queue length at stationarity:
E_\mathbf{s}[X] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty k (1-\rho)\rho^k = \frac{\rho}{1-\rho}
As \rho \to 1^- (arrival rate approaches service rate), the mean queue length \to \infty. The queue is technically stable but barely — small perturbations cause blowup. This is a classical result in queueing theory, and the birth-death product formula gives it in two lines.

The M/M/1 queue is the reason queueing theorists love birth-death chains. Every M/M/s queue, M/M/\infty queue, and Erlang model is a birth-death chain. The product formula gives the stationary distribution immediately, and from there every queueing metric — mean queue length, mean waiting time, throughput — follows by direct computation. Little’s Law (L = \lambda W) is usually the next step.

Example 4: Moran Model (Population Genetics)
N individuals, each of type A or B. State k = number of type-A individuals. At each step:

One individual is chosen to reproduce (uniformly at random)
One individual is chosen to die (uniformly at random)

p_k = \frac{k}{N} \cdot \frac{N-k}{N} = \frac{k(N-k)}{N^2}, \quad r_k = \frac{N-k}{N} \cdot \frac{k}{N} = \frac{k(N-k)}{N^2}
So p_k = r_k for all k. Then \rho_k = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} p_j/r_{j+1} = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} 1 = 1.
All \rho_k = 1, so the stationary distribution on {0, 1, \ldots, N} would be uniform: s_k = 1/(N+1).
But wait — states 0 and N are absorbing (once all individuals are the same type, the population stays there forever). The chain is not irreducible. The absorbing states have their own stationary distributions \delta_0 and \delta_N. The interior states {1, \ldots, N-1} are transient — the chain eventually fixes at 0 or N.
The birth-death product formula applies only when the chain is irreducible (or when we restrict to a closed class). For the Moran model, the interesting question is the absorption probability — which type fixes — and the expected fixation time, both computed by first-step equations as in Gamblers Ruin as a Markov Chain.

The Moran model is a case where the birth-death structure is visible (p_k = r_k, symmetric), but the chain is reducible due to absorbing boundaries. The product formula gives what would be the stationary distribution on the interior — uniform, reflecting the symmetry between types A and B — but the chain never actually reaches this distribution because it gets absorbed first. Always check irreducibility before applying the product formula.


Hitting Times via First-Step Equations
For birth-death chains, first-step equations reduce to second-order linear recurrences — the same structure as Gambler’s Ruin.
Let h_k = E[T_0 \mid X_0 = k], the expected hitting time to state 0. Boundary: h_0 = 0.
First-step equation for k \geq 1:
h_k = 1 + p_k h_{k+1} + r_k h_{k-1} + (1 - p_k - r_k) h_k
Simplify:
(p_k + r_k) h_k = 1 + p_k h_{k+1} + r_k h_{k-1}
p_k(h_k - h_{k+1}) = 1 - r_k(h_k - h_{k-1}) \cdot \frac{r_k}{p_k}
This doesn’t simplify as cleanly as the absorption probability equation because it’s non-homogeneous. The standard approach: let u_k = h_k - h_{k-1} (first differences). Substituting:
p_k u_{k+1} = r_k u_k - 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad u_{k+1} = \frac{r_k}{p_k} u_k - \frac{1}{p_k}
This is a first-order linear recurrence in u_k, solvable by the integrating factor method. The solution involves the \rho_k ratios and sums thereof — explicit but messy. For the M/M/1 queue (p_k = \lambda, r_k = \mu, \rho = \lambda/\mu):
u_{k+1} = \rho \cdot u_k - \frac{1}{\lambda}
which gives a geometric series. The hitting time h_k = \sum_{j=1}^k u_j then telescopes.
The key insight is that for birth-death chains, first-step equations always reduce to a one-dimensional recurrence — no matrix inversion needed, just algebra — because the chain can only move by \pm 1.

The Global Balance Interpretation
The detailed balance condition s_k p_k = s_{k+1} r_{k+1} has a physical interpretation that’s worth dwelling on.
Think of probability as “fluid” flowing along the state space. At stationarity:

Fluid flows rightward from k to k+1 at rate s_k p_k (probability of being at k times birth rate).
Fluid flows leftward from k+1 to k at rate s_{k+1} r_{k+1} (probability of being at k+1 times death rate).

Detailed balance says these two flows are equal — the net flow across each edge is zero. This is stronger than global balance (which only requires zero net flow at each node). For a one-dimensional chain, these are equivalent: if the net flow is zero across every edge, then summing over a contiguous set of edges gives zero net flow into any interval {0, \ldots, k} — which is exactly the global balance condition for all states simultaneously.

This is the “flux” picture. For a birth-death chain, global balance and detailed balance are actually equivalent — not just detailed balance implying global balance. The reason: on a path graph, every “cut” separating the state space into {0, \ldots, k} and {k+1, \ldots, M} has exactly one edge crossing it (the edge (k, k+1)). Zero flow across every single edge is the same as zero flow across every cut. On graphs with cycles, this equivalence breaks — there can be “circulating currents” that satisfy global balance but not detailed balance. The birth-death chain’s path topology forbids such currents.


Summary























































ObjectFormulaCommentTransitionq_{k,k\pm 1} = p_k, r_k; zero for $j-kIrreducibilityp_k, r_k > 0 for all interior kPath graph connectedReversibilityAlways (path graph has no cycles)Kolmogorov criterion vacuousDetailed balances_k p_k = s_{k+1} r_{k+1}One equation per edge\rho_k\prod_{j=0}^{k-1} p_j / r_{j+1}Traffic intensity ratiosStationary dists_k = \rho_k / \sum_\ell \rho_\ellProduct formula; explicitExistence (semi-infinite)\sum_{k=0}^\infty \rho_k < \inftyElse null recurrent or transientMean return timem_k = 1/s_kFrom s_k = 1/m_k theoremHitting timesFirst-step equations \to first-order recurrence in differencesSolvable explicitly
Canonical examples and their stationary distributions:



































Chainp_kr_kStationary distReflecting simple RW (fair)1/21/2Uniform on {0,\ldots,N}Reflecting simple RW (biased)pq\text{Geometric}(q/p) truncatedEhrenfest urn(d-k)/dk/d\text{Binomial}(d,1/2)M/M/1 queue\lambda\mu\text{Geometric}(1-\rho), \rho = \lambda/\mu < 1

One-Line Summary for Future Me

Birth-death chains: transitions only \pm 1, so the path-graph topology forces reversibility (no cycles \Rightarrow Kolmogorov criterion vacuous). Detailed balance gives s_k p_k = s_{k+1} r_{k+1}, which telescopes into the product formula s_k \propto \rho_k = \prod_{j < k} p_j/r_{j+1}. For the semi-infinite chain, a stationary distribution exists iff \sum \rho_k < \infty. Every birth-death quantity — stationary dist, hitting times, absorption probs — is explicit because the tridiagonal structure always reduces to a one-dimensional recurrence.

01.Maths/Probability/12.Markov-Chain-Mon.title: 01.Metropolis-Hastings
01.Maths/Probability/12.Markov-Chain-Mon.content:
Tags: probability stochastic-processes markov-chains mcmc computation
References: Blitzstein & Hwang — Introduction to Probability; Stat 110 (Harvard)
Status: 🟢 complete
Prerequisite notes: Detailed Balance and Reversibility · Stationary Distributions · Existence and Uniqueness of Stationary Distributions · Markov Chain Convergence Theorem · Birth-Death Chain


“The problem MCMC solves is this: I have a distribution \pi I want to sample from, but I can only evaluate \pi up to a normalizing constant I cannot compute. The normalizing constant might be an integral over a million-dimensional space — completely intractable. Metropolis-Hastings sidesteps this entirely. It constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is \pi, using only ratios \pi(y)/\pi(x) — the normalizing constant cancels. Then it runs the chain until it mixes, and treats the samples as approximate draws from \pi. The entire algorithm is detailed balance, engineered on purpose.”


The Problem
I want to sample from a distribution \pi on state space \mathcal{S}. The distribution is known up to a normalizing constant:
\pi(x) = \frac{\tilde{\pi}(x)}{Z}, \qquad Z = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{S}} \tilde{\pi}(x)
where I can evaluate \tilde{\pi}(x) for any x, but Z is intractable — computing it requires summing over all of \mathcal{S}, which might be exponentially large or a high-dimensional integral.
Examples where this happens:

Bayesian posterior: \pi(\theta \mid \text{data}) \propto \mathcal{L}(\text{data} \mid \theta) \cdot \pi_0(\theta). I can evaluate the likelihood and prior, but the normalizing constant is \int \mathcal{L} \cdot \pi_0 , d\theta — often analytically and computationally intractable.
Boltzmann distribution: \pi(x) \propto e^{-E(x)/T} where E(x) is the energy of configuration x. The partition function Z = \sum_x e^{-E(x)/T} sums over exponentially many configurations.
Ising model: \pi(\sigma) \propto \exp!\left(\beta \sum_{\langle i,j \rangle} \sigma_i \sigma_j\right) over spin configurations \sigma \in {-1,+1}^N. The 2^N term sum for Z is intractable for large N.

The key insight: to check detailed balance, I only need ratios \pi(y)/\pi(x) = \tilde{\pi}(y)/\tilde{\pi}(x), and Z cancels. This is the entire trick.

The Algorithm
Ingredients

Target distribution: \pi (known up to constant Z).
Proposal kernel: Q(x, y) — a transition matrix I can sample from. At state x, I propose moving to y with probability Q(x,y). This is a Markov chain I choose; it does not have to have stationary distribution \pi.
Acceptance probability: a function A(x, y) \in [0,1] to be determined.

One Step of the Algorithm
At current state X_n = x:

Propose: Sample y \sim Q(x, \cdot).
Accept or reject: With probability A(x,y), set X_{n+1} = y. With probability 1 - A(x,y), set X_{n+1} = x (stay).

The resulting transition probabilities:
T(x,y) = Q(x,y) \cdot A(x,y) \quad \text{for } y \neq x T(x,x) = Q(x,x) + \sum_{y \neq x} Q(x,y)(1 - A(x,y)) \quad \text{(stay probability)}
The Metropolis-Hastings Acceptance Ratio
Choose:
\boxed{A(x,y) = \min!\left(1,, \frac{\pi(y) Q(y,x)}{\pi(x) Q(x,y)}\right) = \min!\left(1,, \frac{\tilde{\pi}(y) Q(y,x)}{\tilde{\pi}(x) Q(x,y)}\right)}
The second equality holds because Z cancels in the ratio. I never need to compute Z.

Why This Works: Detailed Balance
Theorem. The Metropolis-Hastings chain with acceptance ratio A(x,y) as above satisfies detailed balance with respect to \pi:
\pi(x) T(x,y) = \pi(y) T(y,x) \quad \text{for all } x \neq y
Proof. Fix x \neq y. Write:
\pi(x) T(x,y) = \pi(x) Q(x,y) A(x,y) = \pi(x) Q(x,y) \min!\left(1, \frac{\pi(y)Q(y,x)}{\pi(x)Q(x,y)}\right)
Case 1: \pi(y)Q(y,x) \leq \pi(x)Q(x,y).
Then A(x,y) = \frac{\pi(y)Q(y,x)}{\pi(x)Q(x,y)}, so:
\pi(x) T(x,y) = \pi(x) Q(x,y) \cdot \frac{\pi(y)Q(y,x)}{\pi(x)Q(x,y)} = \pi(y)Q(y,x)
In this case, A(y,x) = \min(1, \pi(x)Q(x,y)/\pi(y)Q(y,x)) = 1 (since \pi(x)Q(x,y) \geq \pi(y)Q(y,x)), so:
\pi(y) T(y,x) = \pi(y) Q(y,x) \cdot 1 = \pi(y) Q(y,x)
Equal. ✓
Case 2: \pi(y)Q(y,x) > \pi(x)Q(x,y). By symmetry of the argument (swap x \leftrightarrow y), the same cancellation gives \pi(x)T(x,y) = \pi(x)Q(x,y) = \pi(y)T(y,x). ✓
In both cases, \pi(x) T(x,y) = \pi(y) T(y,x). \blacksquare
Since detailed balance holds, \pi is stationary for the Metropolis-Hastings chain — by the theorem from Detailed Balance and Reversibility.

The min in the acceptance ratio is not arbitrary — it’s the unique choice (up to some flexibility) that satisfies detailed balance while keeping A(x,y) \in [0,1]. Here’s why: detailed balance requires \pi(x)Q(x,y)A(x,y) = \pi(y)Q(y,x)A(y,x), which means A(x,y)/A(y,x) = \pi(y)Q(y,x)/\pi(x)Q(x,y). I need to find A(x,y), A(y,x) \in [0,1] satisfying this ratio constraint. The solution that maximizes acceptance (minimizes rejection, hence mixes fastest) is to set the larger of A(x,y), A(y,x) equal to 1 and the smaller to the ratio. That gives exactly \min(1, \cdot). Any other valid choice would accept less often and mix more slowly.


The Metropolis-Hastings Ratio
Define the MH ratio (also called the Hastings ratio):
r(x,y) = \frac{\tilde{\pi}(y) Q(y,x)}{\tilde{\pi}(x) Q(x,y)}
Then A(x,y) = \min(1, r(x,y)). Reading this ratio:

\tilde{\pi}(y)/\tilde{\pi}(x): How much more probable is the proposed state y than the current state x under the target? If y has higher probability, the ratio > 1 — accept for sure. If y has lower probability, the ratio < 1 — accept with that probability.
Q(y,x)/Q(x,y): A correction for asymmetric proposals. If the proposal is more likely to go x \to y than y \to x, divide by that excess to prevent the chain from over-visiting y.

The correction factor Q(y,x)/Q(x,y) is why Metropolis-Hastings generalizes the original Metropolis algorithm (which required symmetric proposals, making this factor 1).

Special Cases
Case 1: Metropolis Algorithm (Symmetric Proposals)
If Q(x,y) = Q(y,x) for all x,y — the proposal is symmetric — then Q(y,x)/Q(x,y) = 1 and the ratio simplifies to:
A(x,y) = \min!\left(1, \frac{\tilde{\pi}(y)}{\tilde{\pi}(x)}\right)
This is the original Metropolis algorithm (1953). The rule: always accept uphill moves (\tilde\pi(y) > \tilde\pi(x)); accept downhill moves with probability \tilde\pi(y)/\tilde\pi(x).
Example: symmetric random walk proposal. On \mathcal{S} = \mathbb{Z}, propose y = x + \epsilon where \epsilon \sim \text{Uniform}{-1, +1}. This is symmetric (Q(x,y) = Q(y,x) = 1/2 for adjacent x,y). The MH acceptance is \min(1, \tilde\pi(y)/\tilde\pi(x)).
Case 2: Independent Metropolis-Hastings
If Q(x,y) = Q(y) — the proposal doesn’t depend on the current state — then:
A(x,y) = \min!\left(1, \frac{\tilde\pi(y)/Q(y)}{\tilde\pi(x)/Q(x)}\right) = \min!\left(1, \frac{w(y)}{w(x)}\right)
where w(x) = \tilde\pi(x)/Q(x) are importance weights. This is importance sampling in Markov chain form. It works well when the proposal Q is a good approximation to \pi — the weights w(x) are nearly constant and acceptance rates are high.
Case 3: Gibbs Sampling
For a distribution \pi(x_1, \ldots, x_d) over a d-dimensional state space, Gibbs sampling updates one coordinate at a time: at each step, pick coordinate i, and sample x_i from its conditional distribution \pi(x_i \mid x_{-i}).
Claim: Gibbs sampling is a special case of Metropolis-Hastings with acceptance probability always 1.
Proof. The Gibbs proposal for coordinate i: Q((x_1,\ldots,x_d), (x_1,\ldots,y_i,\ldots,x_d)) = \pi(y_i \mid x_{-i}).
The MH ratio:
r = \frac{\pi(y_i, x_{-i}) \cdot \pi(x_i \mid y_{-i}=x_{-i})}{\pi(x_i, x_{-i}) \cdot \pi(y_i \mid x_{-i})}
Note \pi(y_i, x_{-i}) = \pi(y_i \mid x_{-i}) \cdot \pi(x_{-i}) and \pi(x_i, x_{-i}) = \pi(x_i \mid x_{-i}) \cdot \pi(x_{-i}):
r = \frac{\pi(y_i \mid x_{-i}) \cdot \pi(x_{-i}) \cdot \pi(x_i \mid x_{-i})}{\pi(x_i \mid x_{-i}) \cdot \pi(x_{-i}) \cdot \pi(y_i \mid x_{-i})} = 1
So A = \min(1,1) = 1: Gibbs always accepts. \blacksquare
This makes Gibbs extremely efficient per step — no wasted proposals. The cost is that it requires sampling from each conditional distribution, which may itself be hard. When conditionals are tractable (as in many conjugate Bayesian models), Gibbs is the algorithm of choice.

Gibbs sampling is why conjugate priors matter so much in practice. If the prior is conjugate to the likelihood, every conditional in a hierarchical model is a recognizable distribution — Beta, Gamma, Normal — and Gibbs sampling becomes a sequence of trivial draws. Non-conjugate models require Metropolis steps within the Gibbs sweep, producing “Metropolis-within-Gibbs” or “hybrid MCMC.” The choice of algorithm is determined by which conditionals are tractable.


Convergence: When Does the Chain Mix?
For the MH chain to be useful, it must converge to \pi. The conditions from Markov Chain Convergence Theorem:
Irreducibility: The chain must be able to reach any state from any other. This depends on the proposal Q — if Q(x,y) = 0 for some pair (x,y), the chain might get stuck. Standard choices (random walk proposals on connected graphs, or proposals with full support) ensure irreducibility.
Aperiodicity: The chain is aperiodic as long as there is positive probability of staying (T(x,x) > 0), which happens whenever there is positive probability of rejection. For the MH chain, T(x,x) \geq \sum_y Q(x,y)(1-A(x,y)) > 0 unless every proposal is accepted with probability 1 — which happens only if the proposal already has stationary distribution \pi. In all non-trivial cases, there is some rejection, hence a self-loop, hence aperiodicity.
Under these conditions: the MH chain is irreducible, aperiodic, and has stationary distribution \pi. By the convergence theorem:
\mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \pi \quad \text{as } n \to \infty
for any initial distribution \mathbf{t}^{(0)}.

The Mixing Time and Practical Considerations
Convergence is guaranteed, but how fast is it? The convergence theorem gives no rate. The rate is controlled by the spectral gap 1 - |\lambda_2| of T, as in Mixing Times and Spectral Gap. In practice, the mixing time depends on:
The proposal distribution Q:

Too narrow (proposals close to current state): high acceptance, but slow exploration. The chain takes small steps and mixes slowly.
Too wide (proposals far from current state): fast exploration in principle, but proposals often land in low-\pi regions and are rejected. High rejection rate means the chain barely moves.
The optimal tradeoff (in high dimensions, for Gaussian \pi and Gaussian proposals) is to set the proposal variance such that the acceptance rate is approximately 23.4% — a classical result in MCMC theory.

The geometry of \pi:

Multimodal distributions: If \pi has multiple modes separated by low-probability regions, the chain can get trapped in one mode for an exponentially long time. Local proposals rarely cross the low-probability gap.
High-dimensional distributions: In d dimensions, local random-walk proposals explore a d-dimensional ball of radius \epsilon, but \pi might be concentrated on a lower-dimensional manifold. The effective mixing time scales poorly with d for naive proposals.

Standard diagnostics:

Trace plots: Plot X_n vs n for each coordinate. If the chain is mixing well, the trace should look like stationary noise. If it wanders slowly, mixing is poor.
\hat{R} statistic (Gelman-Rubin): Run multiple chains from different starting points; compare within-chain variance to between-chain variance. \hat{R} \approx 1 indicates convergence.
Autocorrelation: Compute \text{Corr}(X_n, X_{n+k}) as a function of lag k. Slow decay indicates slow mixing.


The 23.4% acceptance rate result is one of the most cited numbers in computational statistics. It comes from Roberts, Gelman, and Gilks (1997): for a d-dimensional target with i.i.d. components and a Gaussian random-walk proposal, the optimal acceptance rate as d \to \infty is 2\Phi(-\sqrt{2} \cdot 2.38^2/2) \approx 0.234, where \Phi is the standard normal CDF. The optimal proposal standard deviation scales as 2.38/\sqrt{d} per coordinate. This tells me something important: in high dimensions, I should be rejecting about 3 out of 4 proposals. If I’m accepting too many, my proposals are too small; if too few, too large.


Why the Normalizing Constant Doesn’t Matter
This deserves its own moment. The MH ratio is:
r(x,y) = \frac{\tilde\pi(y) Q(y,x)}{\tilde\pi(x) Q(x,y)} = \frac{(\pi(y) \cdot Z) \cdot Q(y,x)}{(\pi(x) \cdot Z) \cdot Q(x,y)} = \frac{\pi(y) Q(y,x)}{\pi(x) Q(x,y)}
Z appears in both numerator and denominator and cancels. The acceptance probability depends only on the ratio of \pi values, not their absolute values.
This is deeply useful because in Bayesian inference:
\frac{\pi(\theta \mid \text{data})}{\pi(\theta' \mid \text{data})} = \frac{\mathcal{L}(\text{data} \mid \theta) \pi_0(\theta)}{\mathcal{L}(\text{data} \mid \theta') \pi_0(\theta')}
The ratio of posteriors equals the ratio of (likelihood \times prior) — no normalization required. I can run MCMC on any posterior as long as I can evaluate the likelihood and prior pointwise, regardless of model complexity.

This is the reason MCMC transformed Bayesian statistics in the 1990s. Before MCMC, Bayesian inference was restricted to models with conjugate priors — because otherwise the posterior normalization constant was intractable and there was no way to sample from the posterior. MCMC lifted this restriction entirely. Any likelihood, any prior, any hierarchical model — as long as I can evaluate \mathcal{L} \cdot \pi_0 pointwise, I can run MCMC. The price is computational (chains must run long enough to mix), but the gain in modeling flexibility is enormous. It fundamentally changed what statistical models are tractable.


A Worked Example: Sampling from the Ising Model
The Ising model on an N-node graph has states \sigma \in {-1,+1}^N with distribution:
\pi(\sigma) = \frac{1}{Z} \exp!\left(\beta \sum_{\langle i,j \rangle} \sigma_i \sigma_j\right)
Z involves a sum over 2^N configurations — completely intractable for large N.
Gibbs sampling for the Ising model (also called Glauber dynamics):
At each step:

Pick a random site i \in {1, \ldots, N}.
Compute the conditional distribution of \sigma_i given all other spins \sigma_{-i}:

\pi(\sigma_i = +1 \mid \sigma_{-i}) = \frac{e^{\beta \sigma_i \sum_{j \sim i} \sigma_j}}{e^{\beta \sum_{j \sim i} \sigma_j} + e^{-\beta \sum_{j \sim i} \sigma_j}}\Bigg|_{\sigma_i = +1} = \text{sigmoid}!\left(2\beta \sum_{j \sim i} \sigma_j\right)
where the sum is over neighbors j of i. This is just a Bernoulli conditional — trivially sampleable.

Draw \sigma_i from this Bernoulli and update.

Since Gibbs is a special case of MH (acceptance probability 1), this chain has stationary distribution \pi — the Ising distribution. The normalizing constant Z never appears. Running this chain for many steps produces (approximate) samples from the Ising model at inverse temperature \beta.
The mixing behavior is physically meaningful: near the critical temperature \beta_c, the Ising model exhibits a phase transition, and the Glauber dynamics chain mixes exponentially slowly — the mixing time diverges as \beta \to \beta_c. This is called critical slowing down, and it’s a major challenge for MCMC near phase transitions.

Connection to Simulated Annealing
Simulated annealing is Metropolis-Hastings applied to optimization. Instead of sampling from a fixed \pi, I want to find the global maximum of f(x).
Idea: sample from \pi_T(x) \propto e^{f(x)/T} (Boltzmann distribution at “temperature” T) and slowly decrease T \to 0. As T \to 0, \pi_T concentrates all its mass on the global maximum of f. If I cool slowly enough (a logarithmic cooling schedule), the chain tracks the evolving distribution and converges to the maximum.
The Metropolis acceptance ratio at temperature T:
A(x,y) = \min!\left(1, e^{(f(y)-f(x))/T}\right)
At high T: A \approx 1 — accept almost everything, explore freely. At low T: A \approx 0 for downhill moves — the chain increasingly concentrates on high-f regions. The temperature schedule controls the tradeoff between exploration (high T) and exploitation (low T).
Simulated annealing is Metropolis-Hastings with a time-varying target — technically a non-homogeneous Markov chain. The convergence theory is more subtle (the chain is no longer time-homogeneous), but the algorithm is widely used in combinatorial optimization (TSP, circuit layout, protein folding).

Summary

















































ConceptFormula / statementTarget\pi(x) \propto \tilde\pi(x); Z unknownProposalQ(x,y): any chain I can sample fromMH acceptanceA(x,y) = \min(1, \tilde\pi(y)Q(y,x)/\tilde\pi(x)Q(x,y))Key propertySatisfies detailed balance w.r.t. \pi; hence \pi is stationaryZ cancelsAlways; only ratios \tilde\pi(y)/\tilde\pi(x) neededMetropolisSpecial case: symmetric Q, ratio simplifies to \tilde\pi(y)/\tilde\pi(x)Gibbs samplingSpecial case: propose from conditional \pi(x_i \mid x_{-i}); always acceptConvergenceGuaranteed if chain is irreducible and aperiodicMixing speedControlled by spectral gap; depends on proposal and geometry of \piOptimal acceptance rate\approx 23.4% in high dimensions (for Gaussian targets, RW proposals)

One-Line Summary for Future Me

Metropolis-Hastings constructs a Markov chain with stationary distribution \pi by using the acceptance ratio A(x,y) = \min(1, \tilde\pi(y)Q(y,x)/\tilde\pi(x)Q(x,y)), which satisfies detailed balance by design — and Z cancels in the ratio so the normalizing constant is never needed. Gibbs sampling is the special case where the proposal is the exact conditional, making A = 1 always. Convergence is guaranteed under irreducibility and aperiodicity; mixing speed depends on the proposal geometry and the spectral gap.

01.Maths/Probability/12.Markov-Chain-Mon.title: 02.Zipf Distribution Stimulation
01.Maths/Probability/12.Markov-Chain-Mon.content:
“The first time I saw Zipf’s law I thought it was a coincidence — the second most common English word appears half as often as the first, the third a third as often, and so on. Then I saw the same pattern in city populations, income distributions, protein interaction frequencies, and earthquake magnitudes. At that point it stops being a coincidence and starts being a structural property of how complex systems organize themselves. The mathematics is simple. The reason it’s everywhere is not.”


The Distribution
Let X take values in {1, 2, \ldots, n} (finite support) or {1, 2, 3, \ldots} (infinite support). We say X \sim \text{Zipf}(s, n) if:
P(X = k) = \frac{k^{-s}}{H_{n,s}}, \qquad k = 1, 2, \ldots, n
where s > 0 is the exponent (also called the shape or skewness parameter) and H_{n,s} is the normalizing constant — the generalized harmonic number:
H_{n,s} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{j^s} = 1 + \frac{1}{2^s} + \frac{1}{3^s} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n^s}
For the infinite support case, we need s > 1 for the sum to converge (by the p-series test from real analysis):
H_{\infty, s} = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{j^s} = \zeta(s)
the Riemann zeta function. So P(X = k) = k^{-s}/\zeta(s) for k \geq 1, valid when s > 1.

Notice that s = 1 is the canonical “Zipf’s law” exponent — the rank-frequency relationship George Zipf observed in English text. But at s = 1, the infinite-support version diverges: \sum_{k=1}^\infty 1/k = \infty (the harmonic series). So the pure s=1 law only makes sense with finite support. When people say “Zipf’s law” loosely, they usually mean the finite-n version with s near 1.


Properties
Moments
For the infinite support case (s > 1), the r-th moment is:
E[X^r] = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^r \cdot \frac{k^{-s}}{\zeta(s)} = \frac{\zeta(s-r)}{\zeta(s)}
This is finite only when s - r > 1, i.e., r < s - 1.
Consequently:

Mean E[X] = \zeta(s-1)/\zeta(s), finite iff s > 2.
Variance finite iff s > 3.
For 1 < s \leq 2: the mean is infinite. The distribution is so heavy-tailed that no first moment exists.

This is striking. I’m so used to distributions where the mean “obviously” exists. Zipf with s \leq 2 has no mean — a realization that should make me uncomfortable in a productive way.
For finite support, all moments exist (finite sum of finite terms), but they blow up as n \to \infty when s is small.
The Power Law Tail
The defining feature: P(X \geq k) \sim Ck^{-(s-1)} as k \to \infty (for infinite support, s > 1). This is a power-law tail — much heavier than exponential tails (like Geometric or Poisson) which decay as e^{-ck}.
Intuitive comparison of tail heaviness:






























DistributionP(X \geq k) decayHas all moments?Geometric(p)\sim (1-p)^k (exponential)YesPoisson(\lambda)faster than exponentialYesZipf(s), s>1\sim Ck^{-(s-1)} (power law)Only finitely manyParetopower lawSame phenomenon
Power law tails are the mathematical signature of rare but catastrophic events — the occasional word that appears a million times, the city that dwarfs all others, the earthquake that releases more energy than all smaller ones combined.

Why Zipf’s Law Appears Everywhere: A Sketch
This is the question I keep coming back to. A few mechanisms that generate Zipf-like distributions:
1. Preferential attachment (Yule-Simon process). New items arrive and choose an existing category k with probability proportional to how many items already chose k (the “rich get richer” mechanism). This generates power-law distributions. Used to explain city size growth, citation networks, degree distributions in scale-free graphs.
2. Optimization under constraints. If rational agents minimize a communication cost that is proportional to the information content of messages, and messages are drawn i.i.d., the optimal code length gives a rank-frequency relation that approximates Zipf. This is Mandelbrot’s argument for language.
3. Mixtures of exponentials. A mixture of exponential distributions where the rate parameter has a power-law distribution produces a power-law marginal. Mathematically: if X \mid \lambda \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda) and \lambda \sim \text{Pareto}(s), then X has a power-law distribution.
4. Products of random variables. By the central limit theorem, sums of i.i.d. random variables converge to Normal. Products of positive i.i.d. random variables (or equivalently, sums of their logs) converge to Log-Normal, which approximates power laws over finite ranges.
None of these mechanisms is definitive — there’s no consensus “why Zipf.” What’s agreed is that power laws are attractors in certain generative processes, just as the Normal is an attractor under addition.

The analogy to the CLT is imprecise but useful. The CLT tells me that summation produces Gaussians. Various “multiplicative” or “preferential” processes produce power laws. The deep reason Zipf is everywhere might be that those processes are as ubiquitous as summation.


Simulation
Method 1: Inverse CDF (Exact)
For finite support {1, \ldots, n}, I can sample exactly using the inverse CDF method, which I know from Inverse CDF Method.
Setup: Compute the CDF:
F(k) = P(X \leq k) = \frac{1}{H_{n,s}} \sum_{j=1}^{k} j^{-s}
Algorithm:

Compute and store the CDF values F(1), F(2), \ldots, F(n) (precomputation — O(n) time and space).
Draw U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1).
Return k^* = \min{k : F(k) \geq U} — binary search in the CDF table, O(\log n) per draw.

Correctness: P(k^* = k) = P(F(k-1) < U \leq F(k)) = F(k) - F(k-1) = P(X = k). Exact by construction.
Pseudocode:
import numpy as np
 
def zipf_sample_inverse_cdf(s, n, size=1):
    # Precompute CDF
    k_vals = np.arange(1, n+1)
    pmf = k_vals**(-s)
    pmf /= pmf.sum()           # normalize by H_{n,s}
    cdf = np.cumsum(pmf)
    
    # Sample via inverse CDF
    U = np.random.uniform(size=size)
    # searchsorted finds min index k s.t. cdf[k] >= U
    indices = np.searchsorted(cdf, U)
    return k_vals[indices]     # k_vals[0] = 1, so index 0 -> k=1
This is exact and efficient for moderate n. For very large n (e.g., n = 10^9), storing the CDF is infeasible.

Method 2: Numpy’s Built-In (for Quick Experiments)
NumPy has numpy.random.zipf(a, size) which samples from the infinite Zipf distribution with exponent a = s, using the rejection sampling algorithm of Devroye (1986). Note: NumPy uses the convention P(X=k) \propto k^{-a}, requires a > 1.
samples = np.random.zipf(a=2.0, size=10000)
Caution: For a close to 1 (heavy tails), the expected value is infinite and samples will occasionally be astronomically large — don’t be surprised by a sample of 10^7 when a = 1.1.

Method 3: Rejection Sampling (for Large n, Continuous Approximation)
For large n, I can use the fact that k^{-s} is approximated by the continuous Pareto distribution, and use a Pareto as the envelope.
Pareto proposal: Y \sim \text{Pareto}(s-1, 1) has density f_Y(y) = (s-1)y^{-s} for y \geq 1. Then \lfloor Y \rfloor has PMF roughly \propto k^{-s}. Formalizing this into a proper rejection sampler requires care — see Devroye’s Non-Uniform Random Variate Generation (1986), Chapter X.
The key bound: k^{-s} \leq \int_{k-1}^{k} x^{-s},dx \cdot C for an appropriate constant C, giving an envelope.

I won’t derive the full Devroye sampler here — it’s the kind of thing where the proof is in a textbook and I trust it works. What matters conceptually: for heavy-tailed distributions, rejection sampling with a continuous heavy-tailed envelope is often the practical approach, because the inverse CDF table is too large to precompute.


Empirical Verification: The Log-Log Plot
The canonical diagnostic for power-law behavior is the log-log rank-frequency plot.
If P(X = k) \propto k^{-s}, then \log P(X=k) = -s \log k + C, which is linear on a log-log scale with slope -s.
Procedure:

Generate N samples from Zipf(s, n).
Count empirical frequencies \hat{f}(k) = (\text{count of } k)/N.
Plot \log k vs \log \hat{f}(k). Fit a line — slope should be \approx -s.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from collections import Counter
 
N = 100_000
s_true = 1.5
n = 1000
 
samples = zipf_sample_inverse_cdf(s_true, n, size=N)
counts = Counter(samples)
 
k_vals = np.array(sorted(counts.keys()))
freqs  = np.array([counts[k] for k in k_vals]) / N
 
# Log-log plot
log_k    = np.log(k_vals)
log_freq = np.log(freqs)
 
# OLS slope estimate
slope = np.polyfit(log_k, log_freq, 1)[0]
print(f"Estimated exponent: {-slope:.3f} (true: {s_true})")
 
plt.figure()
plt.scatter(log_k, log_freq, s=5, alpha=0.6)
plt.xlabel("log rank $k$")
plt.ylabel("log frequency")
plt.title(f"Zipf($s={s_true}$, $n={n}$) — estimated $s={-slope:.2f}$")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
On a log-log scale, the Zipf PMF should look like a straight line. Deviations at the tail (large k) are expected — counts become sparse and noisy.
A subtlety I keep getting confused about: The rank-frequency plot (Zipf’s original framing) plots rank r on the x-axis vs frequency f(r) on the y-axis, where rank 1 = most common word. This is not the same as plotting k vs P(X=k) when the support is not {1,\ldots,n} in sorted order. For simulated data, these coincide. For word frequency data, rank 1 corresponds to the most frequent word, which has some empirical frequency f, not PMF value P(X=1).

Moment Estimation and the Traps of Heavy Tails
Suppose I’ve generated samples X_1, \ldots, X_N \sim \text{Zipf}(s, n) and want to estimate s.
Method 1: Log-log regression. Estimate the slope of the log-log rank-frequency plot (as above). Simple but biased — OLS on the log scale is not maximum likelihood for the Poisson-noise model that underlies count data.
Method 2: Maximum Likelihood. For the finite-support Zipf, the log-likelihood is:
\ell(s) = -s \sum_{i=1}^N \log X_i - N \log H_{n,s}
Taking the derivative and setting to zero:
\frac{d\ell}{ds} = -\sum_{i=1}^N \log X_i - N \cdot \frac{d}{ds}\log H_{n,s} = 0
\Rightarrow \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \log X_i = -\frac{H_{n,s}'}{H_{n,s}}, \quad H_{n,s}' = \frac{d H_{n,s}}{ds} = -\sum_{j=1}^n \frac{\log j}{j^s}
There’s no closed form — solve numerically (Newton-Raphson or scipy.optimize). The MLE is consistent and asymptotically efficient.
The trap: sample mean is unreliable when s \leq 2.
When the true mean is infinite (or very large), the sample mean \bar{X}_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum X_i does not converge to a finite limit as N \to \infty — the LLN doesn’t apply without a finite mean. Instead, the sample mean grows with N (slowly, as a power of N). This means:

Do not estimate s from the sample mean using E[X] = \zeta(s-1)/\zeta(s) when s is suspected to be \leq 2 — the estimator is inconsistent.
The MLE (based on \sum \log X_i, not \sum X_i) is fine — \log X has finite mean for all s > 1.


This is the moment I realize why heavy-tailed distributions require different tools. Everything I learned about estimation assumes finite moments — LLN, CLT, method of moments. All of it breaks for s \leq 2. This isn’t a technicality; it’s empirically relevant. Pareto-distributed income data has s estimated around 1.5–2 depending on the country and year — right in the regime where the mean barely exists or doesn’t exist at all. “Average income” statistics for such distributions are misleading in a deep, mathematically precise sense.


Connection to the Pareto Distribution
The Pareto distribution is the continuous analogue: Y \sim \text{Pareto}(\alpha, x_m) has PDF f(y) = \alpha x_m^\alpha y^{-(\alpha+1)} for y \geq x_m. The tail: P(Y \geq y) = (x_m/y)^\alpha — a power law.
The relationship to Zipf: if I discretize the Pareto — i.e., X = \lceil Y \rceil for Y \sim \text{Pareto}(s-1, 1) — then X has a distribution approximately Zipf(s) for large values. More precisely:
P(X = k) = P(k-1 < Y \leq k) = (k-1)^{-(s-1)} - k^{-(s-1)} \approx (s-1)k^{-s} \text{ for large } k
which is proportional to k^{-s}. So Pareto is the continuous version, Zipf is the discrete version. This is the same relationship as Exponential (continuous) vs Geometric (discrete).

Connections to Other Topics

Birth-Death Chain: The Glauber dynamics for certain statistical physics models produce Zipf-like stationary distributions for system observables.
Markov Chain Convergence Theorem: Simulating from Zipf via MCMC (as an alternative to inverse CDF) — when would I ever do this? If the state space is structured (e.g., words in a language with transition probabilities), I might want a chain whose stationary distribution is Zipf. This connects to the Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm note.
Stationary Distributions: Zipf arises as the stationary distribution of certain random walks on \mathbb{Z}_{>0} with drift toward low values.
Information Theory: The entropy of Zipf(s, n) is H(X) = s \cdot E[\log X] + \log H_{n,s}. For s near 1 (nearly uniform on log scale), entropy is high. Zipf with s=1 is the maximum-entropy distribution on the integers subject to a constraint on E[\log X] — analogous to how the Exponential is maximum-entropy given E[X].


Things I Want to Come Back To

 Prove rigorously that the Yule-Simon process gives a power-law stationary distribution with exponent depending on the attachment strength.
 Work through the Devroye (1986) rejection sampler for Zipf — understand the envelope construction.
 Simulate Zipf with s = 1.1 and plot how the sample mean grows with N — should see a power-law growth \bar{X}_N \sim N^{(2-s)/(s-1)} or something like that (check this).
 MLE for Zipf on real word frequency data (Gutenberg corpus?) — how well does it fit?
 Read Clauset, Shalizi, Newman (2009) “Power-Law Distributions in Empirical Data” — the definitive reference on fitting power laws and testing whether data is actually power-law vs log-normal.


Summary

















































ConceptDetailsPMFP(X=k) = k^{-s}/H_{n,s}, k=1,\ldots,nNormalizing constantH_{n,s} = \sum_{j=1}^n j^{-s}; \to \zeta(s) as n\to\infty (needs s>1)Mean\zeta(s-1)/\zeta(s), finite iff s > 2VarianceFinite iff s > 3TailPower law: P(X \geq k) \sim Ck^{-(s-1)}SimulationInverse CDF (exact, O(n) precompute); np.random.zipf (infinite support)EstimationMLE via \sum \log X_i; log-log regression (approximate)DiagnosticLog-log rank-frequency plot, slope = -sContinuous analoguePareto(\alpha = s-1)Key trapSample mean unreliable / inconsistent when s \leq 2

One-Line Summary for Future Me

Zipf(s,n) assigns probability \propto k^{-s} to rank k — power-law decay, heavy tails, infinite mean when s \leq 2; simulate exactly via inverse CDF on the precomputed CDF table, diagnose with a log-log plot, estimate s via MLE on \sum \log X_i (not the sample mean, which can be infinite).

01.Maths/Probability/12.Markov-Chain-Mon.title: 03.Beta Distribution Simulation
01.Maths/Probability/12.Markov-Chain-Mon.content:
“The Beta distribution is the distribution on [0,1], in the same way the Normal is the distribution on \mathbb{R}. It’s what I reach for whenever the unknown is a probability — a bias of a coin, a click-through rate, a proportion. The parameters a and b aren’t just shape parameters; they’re counts. a-1 successes and b-1 failures, accumulated as prior evidence. Every time I update a Beta prior with new Binomial data, I get another Beta. That’s conjugacy, and it’s why the Beta is the backbone of Bayesian inference for proportions.”


The Distribution
X \sim \text{Beta}(a, b) with a, b > 0 has PDF:
f(x) = \frac{x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}, \qquad x \in (0,1)
where the Beta function B(a,b) is the normalizing constant:
B(a,b) = \int_0^1 x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1},dx
The fundamental identity connecting B to the Gamma function:
B(a,b) = \frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}
Proof sketch: Consider X \sim \text{Gamma}(a,1) and Y \sim \text{Gamma}(b,1) independent. Let T = X + Y and W = X/(X+Y). By computing the joint density of (T, W) via the change-of-variables Jacobian, one finds T \sim \text{Gamma}(a+b, 1) and W \sim \text{Beta}(a,b), and they are independent. The normalization constant falls out as \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b). This isn’t just a computational trick — it’s the theorem that makes the Gamma-Beta relationship structural.

This proof is in B&H Chapter 8 and it’s one of my favourite change-of-variables arguments. The independence of T and W — the total and the fraction — is genuinely surprising. I’d expect them to be correlated. They’re not.


Shape Behaviour
The parameters a and b control the shape completely. Let me internalize the cases:













































a, bShapeIntuitiona = b = 1Uniform(0,1)No information, all probabilities equally likelya, b > 1Unimodal, interior modeEvidence for an interior probabilitya < 1, b < 1U-shaped (bimodal at 0 and 1)Evidence for extremesa = 1, b > 1Monotone decreasingSkewed toward 0a > 1, b = 1Monotone increasingSkewed toward 1a = bSymmetric about 1/2Symmetric uncertaintya, b \to \infty, a/b fixedConcentrates near a/(a+b)Many observations, sharp posterior
Mode: For a, b > 1, the mode is (a-1)/(a+b-2). Found by differentiating the log-PDF:
\frac{d}{dx}\log f(x) = \frac{a-1}{x} - \frac{b-1}{1-x} = 0 \implies x^* = \frac{a-1}{a+b-2}
For a = b = 1 (Uniform), any point in (0,1) is a mode. For a < 1 or b < 1, the density blows up at the boundary — the “mode” is at the edge.

Moments
E[X] = \frac{a}{a+b}
\text{Var}(X) = \frac{ab}{(a+b)^2(a+b+1)}
Derivation of the mean — elegant via the Beta function identity:
E[X] = \int_0^1 x \cdot \frac{x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)},dx = \frac{B(a+1,b)}{B(a,b)} = \frac{\Gamma(a+1)\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(a+b+1)} = \frac{a}{a+b}
using \Gamma(a+1) = a\Gamma(a). Clean.
Higher moments: E[X^r] = B(a+r,b)/B(a,b) = \frac{\Gamma(a+r)\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(a+b+r)}. So all moments are expressible as ratios of Gamma functions — which for integer a,b collapse to ratios of factorials.

The Order Statistics Connection
This is one of my favourite facts in all of probability.
Theorem. Let U_{(1)} \leq U_{(2)} \leq \cdots \leq U_{(n)} be the order statistics of n i.i.d. \text{Uniform}(0,1) random variables. Then:
U_{(k)} \sim \text{Beta}(k, n-k+1)
Proof. The PDF of U_{(k)} is:
f_{U_{(k)}}(x) = \frac{n!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!} x^{k-1}(1-x)^{n-k}, \qquad x \in (0,1)
This follows from a combinatorial argument: f_{U_{(k)}}(x),dx \approx P(U_{(k)} \in (x, x+dx)), which requires exactly k-1 of the n uniforms to fall in [0,x) (probability x^{k-1}), one to fall in (x, x+dx) (probability dx, n choices), and n-k to fall in (x+dx, 1] (probability (1-x)^{n-k}), times the multinomial count n!/((k-1)! \cdot 1! \cdot (n-k)!). This is exactly \text{Beta}(k, n-k+1).
Why this matters for intuition: U_{(k)} is the k-th smallest uniform. It concentrates near k/(n+1) (the expected value: k/(k + n-k+1) = k/(n+1)). The Beta(k, n-k+1) is the distribution of “where the k-th order statistic lands.” With large n, it concentrates tightly around k/(n+1).
This gives me a way to simulate Beta(a,b) for positive integer a,b: generate a+b-1 uniforms, sort them, and return the a-th one. Wildly impractical for large a+b, but illuminating.

The order statistics connection is the reason Beta(1, 1) is Uniform — the “first” (and only) order statistic of 1 Uniform is just that Uniform itself. And Beta(1, n) is the minimum of n Uniforms — it concentrates near 0, decaying as (1-x)^{n-1}, exactly as a minimum should.


Bayesian Conjugacy: Beta-Binomial
This is the most important property of the Beta in applied work.
Setup. I observe X \mid p \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p) — n Bernoulli trials with success probability p. I place a prior p \sim \text{Beta}(a, b).
Posterior:
p \mid X = k \sim \text{Beta}(a + k,; b + n - k)
Proof. By Bayes:
\pi(p \mid X=k) \propto P(X=k \mid p) \cdot \pi(p) = \binom{n}{k} p^k(1-p)^{n-k} \cdot \frac{p^{a-1}(1-p)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}
\propto p^{a+k-1}(1-p)^{b+n-k-1}
which is the Beta(a+k, b+n-k) kernel. The normalizing constant is B(a+k, b+n-k) — I don’t even need to compute it; I just recognize the kernel. \blacksquare
The interpretation: a and b act as pseudo-counts — a-1 prior successes and b-1 prior failures. After observing k successes in n trials, I add them to get a+k and b + (n-k).

Prior mean: a/(a+b).
Posterior mean: (a+k)/(a+b+n) — a weighted average of the prior mean and the MLE k/n, with weight proportional to evidence.
As n \to \infty: posterior mean \to k/n — the data overwhelms the prior (consistency).


This is the template I should have in my head for every conjugate Bayesian update. The parameters have a semantic: they’re counts. A Beta(1,1) prior (Uniform) says “I’ve seen zero successes and zero failures — I have no data.” A Beta(10, 10) prior says “I’ve seen 9 successes and 9 failures — I mildly believe p \approx 1/2.” The prior is data, expressed as a distribution.


Simulation
Method 1: Gamma Ratio (Standard Algorithm)
From the Gamma-Beta relationship: if X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, 1) and Y \sim \text{Gamma}(b, 1) independently, then:
W = \frac{X}{X+Y} \sim \text{Beta}(a, b)
Algorithm:

Draw X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, 1).
Draw Y \sim \text{Gamma}(b, 1).
Return W = X/(X+Y).

This is the standard algorithm, and it’s what numpy.random.beta uses under the hood (via the Gamma sampler, which itself uses Marsaglia-Tsang’s method or Ahrens-Dieter depending on shape).
import numpy as np
 
def beta_via_gamma(a, b, size=1):
    X = np.random.gamma(a, scale=1.0, size=size)
    Y = np.random.gamma(b, scale=1.0, size=size)
    return X / (X + Y)
Why this works: From the proof of B(a,b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b) — the independence and distributional identity are theorems, not heuristics.
Numerical caution: When a or b is very small (say < 0.1), the Gamma sample can be extremely close to zero, making X/(X+Y) numerically unstable. Use numpy.random.beta directly in such cases — it has numerical safeguards.

Method 2: numpy’s Built-In
samples = np.random.beta(a=2.0, b=5.0, size=10_000)
Internally uses the Gamma ratio method. For a, b < 1, it switches to a different algorithm (Johnk’s method or a boundary-aware variant) to avoid numerical issues near 0 and 1.

Method 3: Inverse CDF (for Specific Cases)
The Beta CDF is the regularized incomplete beta function I_x(a,b):
F(x) = I_x(a,b) = \frac{B(x;,a,b)}{B(a,b)}, \qquad B(x;,a,b) = \int_0^x t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1},dt
There is no closed form in general, but scipy.special.betaincinv computes the inverse:
from scipy.special import betaincinv
import numpy as np
 
def beta_inverse_cdf(a, b, size=1):
    U = np.random.uniform(size=size)
    return betaincinv(a, b, U)
This is exact (modulo floating-point), but slower than the Gamma method. I’d use it when I specifically need to control the uniform draws (e.g., for quasi-Monte Carlo with a low-discrepancy sequence).

Method 4: Order Statistics (Pedagogical, Not Practical)
For integer a, b with a + b small:
def beta_order_stat(a, b, size=1):
    # Beta(a, b) = (a)-th order stat of a+b-1 Uniforms
    n = a + b - 1
    U = np.random.uniform(size=(size, n))
    U_sorted = np.sort(U, axis=1)
    return U_sorted[:, a-1]   # 0-indexed: a-th smallest
Correct, but O(n \log n) per sample vs O(1) for the Gamma method. Only use this to build intuition.

Empirical Verification
1. Histogram vs PDF
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import beta as beta_dist
 
a, b = 2.0, 5.0
N = 50_000
samples = np.random.beta(a, b, size=N)
 
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 300)
pdf = beta_dist.pdf(x, a, b)
 
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.hist(samples, bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.5, label='Simulated')
plt.plot(x, pdf, 'r-', lw=2, label=f'Beta({a},{b}) PDF')
plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('Density')
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
2. Verifying the Mean and Variance
a, b = 3.0, 7.0
N = 100_000
samples = np.random.beta(a, b, size=N)
 
print(f"Sample mean:     {samples.mean():.4f}  |  True: {a/(a+b):.4f}")
print(f"Sample variance: {samples.var():.4f}   |  True: {a*b/((a+b)**2*(a+b+1)):.4f}")
By LLN, sample mean \to true mean. By a similar law for second moments, sample variance \to true variance. For N = 10^5, agreement to 3 decimal places is typical.
3. Verifying Conjugacy via Simulation
# Prior: p ~ Beta(2, 2)
# Data:  X | p ~ Binomial(20, p)
# Posterior should be Beta(2 + k, 2 + 20 - k)
 
a_prior, b_prior = 2.0, 2.0
n_trials = 20
 
# Simulate the prior predictive: draw p, then draw X | p
p_samples = np.random.beta(a_prior, b_prior, size=50_000)
X_samples  = np.random.binomial(n_trials, p_samples)
 
# Condition on X = 7 (for example)
k = 7
mask = (X_samples == k)
p_posterior_approx = p_samples[mask]   # approximate posterior via rejection
 
# Theoretical posterior
a_post = a_prior + k
b_post = b_prior + n_trials - k
 
x = np.linspace(0, 1, 300)
pdf_post = beta_dist.pdf(x, a_post, b_post)
 
plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))
plt.hist(p_posterior_approx, bins=50, density=True, alpha=0.5,
         label='Simulated posterior (ABC)')
plt.plot(x, pdf_post, 'r-', lw=2,
         label=f'Beta({a_post},{b_post}) posterior')
plt.xlabel('p'); plt.title(f'Posterior after observing k={k} in n={n_trials} trials')
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
This is approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) in miniature — simulate from the joint, condition on the observed data. It’s inefficient (most samples are discarded) but it verifies conjugacy visually without needing any analytic calculation.

This simulation is beautiful because it doesn’t assume conjugacy — it just simulates from the joint and filters. The fact that the histogram matches the Beta posterior exactly (up to Monte Carlo noise) is a non-trivial empirical confirmation that the math is right.


The Beta-Binomial Distribution (Marginal)
If p \sim \text{Beta}(a,b) and X \mid p \sim \text{Binomial}(n,p), the marginal distribution of X is:
P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} \frac{B(a+k,, b+n-k)}{B(a,b)}, \qquad k = 0, 1, \ldots, n
This is the Beta-Binomial distribution. It has overdispersion relative to the Binomial — meaning \text{Var}(X) > np(1-p) when p is random. Specifically:
E[X] = n \cdot \frac{a}{a+b}, \qquad \text{Var}(X) = n \cdot \frac{ab}{(a+b)^2} \cdot \frac{a+b+n}{a+b+1}
The extra factor \frac{a+b+n}{a+b+1} > 1 is the overdispersion. This comes from averaging over random p — uncertainty about p inflates the variance.
When is Beta-Binomial useful? Any time the success probability is not fixed but varies by individual/group — e.g., click-through rates across users, defect rates across batches. Using a plain Binomial would understate the variance and give overconfident uncertainty estimates.

Special Cases Worth Memorizing





























ParametersDistribution\text{Beta}(1,1)\text{Uniform}(0,1)\text{Beta}(1/2, 1/2)Arcsine distribution (related to occupation time of Brownian motion)\text{Beta}(k, n-k+1)U_{(k)}, the k-th order stat of n Uniforms\text{Beta}(a, 1)f(x) = ax^{a-1}; Power distribution\text{Beta}(1, b)f(x) = b(1-x)^{b-1}; reflected Power distribution
The arcsine distribution Beta(1/2, 1/2) has PDF f(x) = 1/(\pi\sqrt{x(1-x)}) — it’s U-shaped and blows up at both endpoints. It appears in the arc-sine laws for random walks (how long does a random walk spend positive?). Unexpected that a distribution on [0,1] concentrates at the extremes.

Connection to the Dirichlet Distribution
The Dirichlet is the multivariate Beta. If (X_1, \ldots, X_k) \sim \text{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_k), then:

Each marginal X_i \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha_i, \sum_{j \neq i} \alpha_j).
The Dirichlet is conjugate to the Multinomial, exactly as Beta is conjugate to Binomial.
Used in topic models (LDA), Bayesian mixture models, and any model with a random probability vector over k \geq 3 categories.

Simulation: (X_1, \ldots, X_k) \sim \text{Dirichlet}(\alpha) by drawing Y_i \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha_i, 1) independently and returning Y_i / \sum_j Y_j. Same Gamma-ratio trick, generalized.

Things I Want to Come Back To

 Prove the Gamma-Beta independence theorem properly — the full change-of-variables with Jacobian. It’s in B&H and I’ve seen it but haven’t written it out myself.
 Derive the Beta-Binomial variance formula from \text{Var}(X) = E[\text{Var}(X|p)] + \text{Var}(E[X|p]) (law of total variance). Should be a clean calculation.
 The arcsine distribution and its connection to Brownian motion occupation times — this belongs in a note on Brownian Motion and the Arcsine Laws.
 Dirichlet-Multinomial conjugacy — write the analogous update formula and verify by simulation.
 Jeffreys prior for the Binomial is Beta(1/2, 1/2) — understand why (Fisher information calculation).


Summary





















































ConceptDetailsPDFx^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}/B(a,b), x \in (0,1)Normalizing constantB(a,b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)Meana/(a+b)Varianceab/[(a+b)^2(a+b+1)]Mode(a-1)/(a+b-2) for a,b > 1Order stat connectionU_{(k)} \sim \text{Beta}(k, n-k+1)Simulation (standard)Gamma ratio: X/(X+Y), X \sim \Gamma(a,1), Y \sim \Gamma(b,1)Simulation (inverse CDF)scipy.special.betaincinv(a, b, U)Conjugate prior forBinomial likelihoodBayesian updateBeta(a,b) prior + k successes in n → Beta(a+k, b+n-k)Multivariate generalizationDirichlet distribution

One-Line Summary for Future Me

\text{Beta}(a,b) is the natural distribution on [0,1] — parameters are pseudo-counts, simulation is a Gamma ratio, the k-th Uniform order statistic is Beta(k, n-k+1), and it’s conjugate to the Binomial: after k successes in n trials the Beta(a,b) prior updates to Beta(a+k, b+n-k).
