01.Maths/Probability/13.Poission-Process.title: 01.Poisson Process in 1 Dimension
01.Maths/Probability/13.Poission-Process.content:
Type: Stochastic Process | Domain: Probability, Statistics, Stochastic Processes
Prerequisite map: Exponential Distribution → Memoryless Property → Counting Processes → Poisson Process
Relevant books: Introduction to Probability (Blitzstein), AIMA Ch.13
Relevant courses: Harvard Stat 110 (Lectures 13–14), MIT 18.650


1. The Core Intuition
A Poisson Process on the real line (time axis) models random arrivals — events that occur:

Independently of each other
At a constant average rate \lambda (events per unit time)
Such that no two events happen simultaneously


Physical picture: Buses arriving at a stop, photons hitting a detector, emails in your inbox, radioactive decay — all modeled as Poisson processes.

Time axis:
─────┼──────────┼────┼───────────────┼───┼──────────▶
     t₁         t₂   t₃              t₄  t₅
     
Interarrivals: X₁  X₂   X₃              X₄  X₅  ~ Exp(λ) iid


2. Three Equivalent Definitions
These are not three different things — they are three lenses on the same object. Mastering all three = mastery of the Poisson process.

Definition 1 — Counting Process Definition
A counting process {N(t), t \geq 0} is a Poisson Process with rate \lambda > 0 if:

N(0) = 0
Independent increments: For 0 \leq s < t \leq u < v: N(t) - N(s) \perp N(v) - N(u)
Stationary increments: N(t+s) - N(s) \sim N(t) - N(0) (distribution depends only on length)
Poisson counts: N(t) - N(s) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))

So the number of arrivals in any interval of length \ell is: \boxed{N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda \ell)}
P(N(t) = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k}{k!}, \quad k = 0,1,2,\ldots

Definition 2 — Interarrival Definition (Constructive)
Let X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Exp}(\lambda) be the waiting times between consecutive arrivals.
Define arrival times (partial sums): T_n = X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)
Then N(t) = \max{n : T_n \leq t} defines a Poisson process.

Why Exponential? The only memoryless continuous distribution. This is what makes the Poisson process “stationary” — the process has no memory of when the last event occurred.

\boxed{P(X > t + s \mid X > s) = P(X > t)}

Definition 3 — Infinitesimal Definition
For a small interval [t, t+dt]:
P(N(t+dt) - N(t) = 1) = \lambda , dt + o(dt) P(N(t+dt) - N(t) = 0) = 1 - \lambda , dt + o(dt) P(N(t+dt) - N(t) \geq 2) = o(dt)
This says: in a tiny window, at most one event can occur, with probability proportional to \lambda , dt.

This is the definition used to derive the Poisson PMF from first principles (Stat 110 style).


3. Key Distributions
3.1 Number of Arrivals in [0, t]
N(t) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t)
E[N(t)] = \lambda t, \qquad \text{Var}[N(t)] = \lambda t
3.2 Waiting Time to n-th Arrival
T_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)
f_{T_n}(t) = \frac{\lambda^n t^{n-1} e^{-\lambda t}}{(n-1)!}, \quad t > 0
E[T_n] = \frac{n}{\lambda}, \qquad \text{Var}[T_n] = \frac{n}{\lambda^2}
3.3 Waiting Time to First Arrival
T_1 \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda), \quad E[T_1] = \frac{1}{\lambda}

4. The Superposition and Thinning Theorems
These are the power tools of Poisson processes.
4.1 Superposition (Merging)
If N_1(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_1) and N_2(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_2) are independent, then:
N_1(t) + N_2(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)

Merging two independent Poisson streams gives a faster Poisson stream.

4.2 Thinning (Splitting)
Take a \text{PP}(\lambda). Independently mark each arrival as type A with probability p, or type B with probability 1-p.
Then: N_A(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda p), \qquad N_B(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda(1-p))
And crucially: N_A \perp N_B.

Intuition: Randomizing a Poisson process gives independent Poisson processes — the randomness “decomposes cleanly.”


5. Conditioning — The Uniform Order Statistics Property
This is the deepest and most beautiful fact about the Poisson process.
Theorem: Given N(t) = n, the n arrival times T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_n are distributed as the order statistics of n iid \text{Uniform}(0, t) random variables.
\boxed{(T_1, \ldots, T_n) \mid N(t) = n ;\overset{d}{=}; (U_{(1)}, \ldots, U_{(n)})}
where U_{(1)} < U_{(2)} < \cdots < U_{(n)} are sorted draws from \text{Uniform}(0, t).
Consequence: If you know exactly n events happened in [0, t], each event’s location is a uniform draw on [0, t], independent of the others (before sorting).

Intuition: Conditioning on the count completely removes the “Poisson randomness” — all that remains is uniformly scattered points.


6. Worked Examples
Example 1 — No Arrivals
Buses arrive at rate \lambda = 3/hour. What is the probability of waiting more than 30 minutes for the first bus?
P(T_1 > 0.5) = e^{-\lambda \cdot 0.5} = e^{-1.5} \approx 0.223
Example 2 — Counting Arrivals
Emails arrive at rate \lambda = 5/hour. What is the probability of receiving exactly 3 emails in the next 30 minutes?
\lambda t = 5 \times 0.5 = 2.5 P(N = 3) = \frac{e^{-2.5}(2.5)^3}{3!} = \frac{e^{-2.5} \cdot 15.625}{6} \approx 0.2138
Example 3 — Thinning
Customers arrive at rate \lambda = 10/hour. Each is independently a “premium” customer with probability p = 0.2.

Premium customers arrive as \text{PP}(2) per hour
Regular customers arrive as \text{PP}(8) per hour
These two streams are independent

Example 4 — Uniform Order Statistics (Stat 110 Classic)
Given that exactly 1 person arrives between 12:00 and 13:00, what is the distribution of their arrival time?
T_1 \mid N(1) = 1 \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)
The arrival time is uniformly distributed across the hour — no “bunching” near start or end.

7. Derivation of Poisson PMF from Definition 3
Let p_k(t) = P(N(t) = k).
From the infinitesimal definition, write the forward Kolmogorov equations:
p_0'(t) = -\lambda p_0(t) p_k'(t) = \lambda p_{k-1}(t) - \lambda p_k(t), \quad k \geq 1
Solve for p_0: p_0(t) = e^{-\lambda t}
Solve recursively using integrating factor: p_k(t) = \frac{(\lambda t)^k e^{-\lambda t}}{k!} \checkmark

8. Poisson Process vs. Poisson Distribution



































Poisson DistributionPoisson ProcessTypeDiscrete RVStochastic processInputFixed parameter \muRate \lambda, time tOutputCount NCount N(t) for all tRelationshipN \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)N(t) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t)Extra structureNoneInterarrivals, order statistics

The Poisson distribution is a snapshot. The Poisson process is the full movie.


9. Poisson Process on a Line vs. Time
The 1D Poisson process applies equally to:

Time axis: Events at random moments
Spatial axis: Points scattered on a line (e.g., defects on a wire, stars projected onto a line)

For spatial: replace t with length \ell, and \lambda = events per unit length.
N(\ell) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda \ell)

10. Connection to Your Curriculum
Stat 110 (Blitzstein)
  └─ Lectures 13–14: Full derivation, conditioning, order statistics
  └─ Story proofs for Poisson → Exponential connection

MIT 18.650 (Statistics)
  └─ Poisson process as model for count data
  └─ MLE of λ from arrival data

CS229 (Stanford ML)
  └─ Poisson regression for count outcomes
  └─ Bayesian: Gamma prior + Poisson likelihood → Gamma posterior (conjugate)

PRML (Bishop)
  └─ Exponential family: Poisson as member
  └─ Graphical models with Poisson nodes

AIMA
  └─ Temporal probabilistic models — continuous time Markov chains build on PP
  
Introduction to Probability (textbook)
  └─ Ch.12–13: Core coverage of Poisson processes


11. Mini-Exercises
[ ] Exercise 1 — Basic PMF
Packets arrive at a router at rate \lambda = 100/second. Find:
(a) P(\text{exactly 90 packets in 1 second})
(b) P(\text{fewer than 2 packets in 10ms})
(c) Expected wait for the 5th packet.
[ ] Exercise 2 — Memoryless Property
You’ve already waited 3 minutes for a bus (rate \lambda = 1/5 min). Show that your remaining wait is still \text{Exp}(\lambda). Prove it from the definition of conditional probability.
[ ] Exercise 3 — Superposition
Type A events arrive at rate 2/hour, Type B at rate 3/hour. Find:
(a) Rate of any event
(b) P(\text{first event is Type A})
(c) P(\text{3 events in first hour, exactly 1 is Type A})
[ ] Exercise 4 — Order Statistics Property
Given N(10) = 4 events occurred in [0, 10], simulate their positions using U(0,10) and verify the empirical distribution against theory.
[ ] Exercise 5 — Conjugate Bayesian Inference
Prior: \lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta). Observe n arrivals in time t.
Derive the posterior \lambda \mid \text{data} and identify it as a Gamma distribution.

12. Key Formulas Cheatsheet
\boxed{N(t) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t)}
\boxed{P(N(t)=k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k}{k!}}
\boxed{X_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Exp}(\lambda), \quad E[X_i] = \frac{1}{\lambda}}
\boxed{T_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n,\lambda), \quad E[T_n] = \frac{n}{\lambda}}
\boxed{(T_1,\ldots,T_n) \mid N(t) = n ;\overset{d}{=}; U_{(1:n)} \sim \text{Uniform}(0,t)}
\boxed{\text{PP}(\lambda_1) \perp \text{PP}(\lambda_2) \Rightarrow \text{merged} \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)}
\boxed{\text{PP}(\lambda) \xrightarrow{\text{thin } p} \text{PP}(\lambda p) \perp \text{PP}(\lambda(1-p))}

13. Mental Model

Think of the Poisson process as nature randomly throwing darts at the time axis, where:

The rate \lambda controls the density of darts
No two darts land at exactly the same spot
Each dart is thrown independently of all others
Zooming into any sub-interval gives you the same structure, just scaled


This self-similarity and independence is what makes the Poisson process the canonical model for randomness in time.

01.Maths/Probability/13.Poission-Process.title: 02.Conditioning in Poisson Processes
01.Maths/Probability/13.Poission-Process.content:
Type: Theorem Cluster | Domain: Stochastic Processes, Probability
Prerequisite map: Poisson Process 1D → Uniform Distribution → Order Statistics → Conditioning
Parent note: Poisson Process 1D
Sibling notes: Superposition | Thinning
Relevant courses: Harvard Stat 110 (Lectures 13–15), MIT 18.650


1. The Central Question
You run a Poisson process PP(\lambda) on [0, T] and observe:
N(T) = n
You now know exactly n events happened. Where are they?

Answer (The Fundamental Conditioning Theorem):
Given N(T) = n, the n arrival times T_1 < T_2 < \cdots < T_n are distributed as the order statistics of n iid Uniform(0, T) random variables.

\boxed{(T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_n) \mid N(T) = n ;\overset{d}{=}; (U_{(1)}, U_{(2)}, \ldots, U_{(n)})}
where U_1, \ldots, U_n \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}(0, T) and U_{(1)} < U_{(2)} < \cdots < U_{(n)} are their order statistics.

2. What This Really Means
There are two equivalent interpretations — both are important:
Interpretation A — Order Statistics
The joint density of arrival times, conditioned on count n, equals the joint density of sorted uniform draws.
Interpretation B — Unordered Uniformity (Deeper)
Before sorting, the n event locations are like n iid Uniform(0,T) draws — completely unstructured, scattered uniformly.
The ordering is just an artifact of how we index them chronologically.
Without conditioning:         With conditioning N(T) = n:
Events land randomly,         Events are like n uniform darts
with random count N(T)        thrown blindly at [0, T]

─────┼──┼────┼──┼──┼──▶       ─────┼──┼────┼──┼──┼──▶
  (random # of events)            (exactly n, uniform)


Intuition: Conditioning on the count n “uses up” all the Poisson randomness about how many events occur. What’s left — the where — is maximally uniform.


3. Proof
We want the joint density of (T_1, \ldots, T_n) given N(T) = n.
Step 1 — Joint density of arrival times unconditionally.
The n arrival times of a PP(\lambda) on [0,T], given there are exactly n of them, have joint density:
For 0 < t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_n < T:
f(t_1, \ldots, t_n, N(T)=n) = \lambda^n e^{-\lambda T}
(Each event contributes \lambda from the rate; e^{-\lambda T} is the no-event probability for the gaps.)
Step 2 — Marginal P(N(T) = n).
P(N(T) = n) = \frac{e^{-\lambda T}(\lambda T)^n}{n!}
Step 3 — Conditional density.
f(t_1,\ldots,t_n \mid N(T)=n) = \frac{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda T}}{\frac{e^{-\lambda T}(\lambda T)^n}{n!}} = \frac{n!}{T^n}
for 0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n < T.
Step 4 — Recognize the distribution.
The joint density of the order statistics U_{(1)} < \cdots < U_{(n)} of n iid Uniform(0,T) is exactly:
f(u_1, \ldots, u_n) = \frac{n!}{T^n}, \quad 0 < u_1 < \cdots < u_n < T
They match. \checkmark

Key cancellation: \lambda completely vanishes from the conditional density. The rate is irrelevant once you condition on the count.


4. Conditioning on a Sub-interval
A more general and powerful result:
Setup: PP(\lambda) on [0, T]. You observe N(T) = n. What is the distribution of N(s) for s < T?
\boxed{N(s) \mid N(T) = n ;\sim; \text{Binomial}!\left(n,, \frac{s}{T}\right)}
Proof: Each of the n events (uniform on [0,T]) independently falls in [0,s] with probability s/T. Counting how many fall in [0,s] is exactly a Binomial(n, s/T).
What this says geometrically:
[0──────────s│────────────T]
 ←── s/T ──→│←── 1-s/T ──→

Each of n points independently hits [0,s] w.p. s/T
→ Binomial(n, s/T) points in [0,s]

Corollary — Expected count in sub-interval:
E[N(s) \mid N(T) = n] = n \cdot \frac{s}{T}
This is linear in s — the events are spread proportionally across [0,T].

5. Conditioning on the Past — The Memoryless Refresh
Setup: You are at time s and know N(s) = k. What happens after s?
\boxed{N(t) - N(s) \mid N(s) = k ;\sim; \text{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))}
The future is independent of the past, and the process restarts fresh from s.
This follows directly from the independent increments property of the Poisson process.
Past: known k events         Future: independent PP(λ)
─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────▶
        [0, s]        s          [s, t]
     N(s) = k known              N(t)-N(s) ~ Poisson(λ(t-s))


This is the Markov property of the Poisson process — the future depends on the past only through the current time, not through what happened before.


6. Conditioning on an Arrival — The Inspection Paradox
Setup
You arrive at a bus stop at a random time t^*. Buses follow PP(\lambda). What is the distribution of:

B = time since last bus (backward recurrence time)
F = time until next bus (forward recurrence time)

Naive (Wrong) Answer
“Average interarrival time is 1/\lambda, so I should wait 1/(2\lambda) on average.”
Correct Answer
E[F] = \frac{1}{\lambda}, \qquad E[B] = \frac{1}{\lambda}
E[F + B] = \frac{2}{\lambda}
The total interval containing t^* has expected length \frac{2}{\lambda} — twice the average interarrival time!
Why — Length-Biased Sampling
A random time t^_ is more likely to fall in a long interarrival interval than a short one. The interval containing t^_ is length-biased:
f_{\text{observed interval}}(\ell) \propto \ell \cdot f_{\text{interval}}(\ell)
For \text{Exp}(\lambda) interarrivals:
f_{\text{observed}}(\ell) \propto \ell \cdot \lambda e^{-\lambda \ell} \implies \text{Gamma}(2, \lambda)
So E[\text{observed interval}] = \frac{2}{\lambda}, split symmetrically: E[F] = E[B] = \frac{1}{\lambda}.

Paradox resolution: You don’t land uniformly among intervals — you land preferentially in long ones. The Poisson process’s memoryless property then makes F \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda) despite this bias.


7. The Ballot Problem Connection
Given N(T) = n events uniform on [0,T]:
What is the probability that event k (the k-th in chronological order) falls in sub-interval (a, b)?
P(T_k \in (a,b) \mid N(T)=n) = P(U_{(k)} \in (a,b))
where U_{(k)} is the k-th order statistic of n iid Uniform(0,T):
f_{U_{(k)}}(u) = \frac{n!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!} \cdot \frac{u^{k-1}(T-u)^{n-k}}{T^n}
This is the Beta distribution scaled to [0,T]:
U_{(k)}/T \sim \text{Beta}(k, n-k+1)
E[T_k \mid N(T)=n] = \frac{k}{n+1} \cdot T

Beautiful result: Given n events in [0,T], the expected time of the k-th event is exactly \frac{k}{n+1}T — equally spaced! The events are “spread out” on average.


8. Summary Table of Conditioning Results








































ConditionQueryDistributionN(T) = nLocation of all eventsOrder stats of n iid Uniform(0,T)N(T) = nN(s) for s < TBinomial(n, s/T)N(T) = nPosition of k-th eventBeta(k, n-k+1) scaled to [0,T]N(s) = kN(t) - N(s) for t > sPoisson(\lambda(t-s)) — independentRandom t^*Wait until next event F\text{Exp}(\lambda) (memoryless)Random t^*Total interval containing t^*Gamma(2, \lambda) (length-biased)

9. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Insurance Claims
Claims arrive at rate \lambda = 2/day. You observe N(30) = 54 claims in 30 days.
(a) Expected claims in first 10 days: E[N(10) \mid N(30) = 54] = 54 \cdot \frac{10}{30} = 18
(b) Probability of \leq 15 claims in first 10 days: N(10) \mid N(30) = 54 \sim \text{Binomial}(54, 1/3) P(N(10) \leq 15) = \sum_{k=0}^{15} \binom{54}{k} (1/3)^k (2/3)^{54-k}
(c) Expected time of 10th claim: E[T_{10} \mid N(30) = 54] = \frac{10}{55} \cdot 30 = \frac{300}{55} \approx 5.45 \text{ days}
Example 2 — Uniform Order Statistics Simulation
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 
def verify_conditioning_theorem(lam=3, T=10, n=8, n_sim=5000):
    """
    Verify: arrival times | N(T)=n  ==  order stats of n Uniform(0,T)
    """
    # Method 1: Simulate actual PP and condition on count
    pp_arrivals = []
    for _ in range(n_sim * 20):  # oversample to get N(T)=n cases
        times = []
        t = 0
        while t < T:
            t += np.random.exponential(1/lam)
            if t < T:
                times.append(t)
        if len(times) == n:
            pp_arrivals.append(sorted(times))
        if len(pp_arrivals) >= n_sim:
            break
    
    # Method 2: Direct order statistics of Uniform(0,T)
    uniform_order_stats = np.sort(
        np.random.uniform(0, T, size=(n_sim, n)), axis=1
    )
    
    pp_arrivals = np.array(pp_arrivals[:n_sim])
    
    # Compare marginal distribution of 4th arrival time
    k = 3  # 4th order statistic (0-indexed)
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 4))
    plt.hist(pp_arrivals[:, k], bins=40, alpha=0.6,
             density=True, label=f'PP conditioned on N({T})={n}')
    plt.hist(uniform_order_stats[:, k], bins=40, alpha=0.6,
             density=True, label=f'Order stat U_({k+1}) of {n} Uniform(0,{T})')
    plt.xlabel(f'T_{k+1} value')
    plt.title(f'Conditioning Theorem: T_{k+1} | N({T})={n}')
    plt.legend()
    plt.show()
    
    print(f"PP mean T_{k+1}: {pp_arrivals[:, k].mean():.4f}")
    print(f"Uniform mean U_({k+1}): {uniform_order_stats[:, k].mean():.4f}")
    print(f"Theoretical E[T_{k+1}|N={n}] = {(k+1)/(n+1)*T:.4f}")
 
verify_conditioning_theorem()
Example 3 — Inspection Paradox Verification
def inspection_paradox(lam=1.0, n_trials=100000):
    """
    Verify E[F] = 1/lambda despite the paradox intuition
    """
    forward_waits = []
    
    for _ in range(n_trials):
        # Generate a long PP
        arrivals = np.cumsum(np.random.exponential(1/lam, size=1000))
        # Pick a random observation time
        t_star = np.random.uniform(0, arrivals[-2])
        # Find next arrival after t_star
        next_arrival = arrivals[arrivals > t_star][0]
        forward_waits.append(next_arrival - t_star)
    
    print(f"E[F] empirical: {np.mean(forward_waits):.4f}")
    print(f"E[F] theoretical: {1/lam:.4f}")
    # Both ≈ 1/lambda — paradox confirmed
 
inspection_paradox()

  └─ Conjugate priors: Poisson-Gamma; conditioning on count → Gamma posterior

Introduction to Probability (textbook)
  └─ Ch.13: Order statistics; Beta as order stat of Uniform
  └─ Inspection paradox as length-biased sampling


11. Mini-Exercises
[ ] Exercise 1 — Sub-interval Count
PP(\lambda = 5/hour). You observe 20 arrivals in 2 hours.
(a) Distribution of arrivals in first 45 minutes?
(b) P(\text{at least 8 in first 45 min})?
(c) E[\text{time of 5th arrival} \mid N(2) = 20]?
[ ] Exercise 2 — Order Statistics
Prove that E[U_{(k)}] = \frac{k}{n+1} \cdot T for U_{(k)} the k-th order statistic of n iid Uniform(0,T).
(Hint: Use the Beta distribution or a symmetry argument.)
[ ] Exercise 3 — Inspection Paradox
Buses run at rate \lambda = 6/hour. You arrive at a uniformly random time.
(a) What is the expected wait for the next bus?
(b) What is the expected time since the last bus?
(c) A friend says “the average headway is 10 minutes so I expect to wait 5 minutes.” What’s wrong?
[ ] Exercise 4 — Prove the Binomial Result
Given N(T) = n, prove that N(s) \sim \text{Binomial}(n, s/T) using the Uniform order statistics theorem. Do not use the counting process definition directly.
[ ] Exercise 5 — Generalise
For a PP(\lambda) on [0, T], given N(T) = n:
Show that the number of events in disjoint sub-intervals (a_1,b_1), (a_2,b_2), \ldots, (a_k, b_k) follows a Multinomial distribution.
State the parameters explicitly.

12. Key Formulas Cheatsheet
\boxed{(T_1,\ldots,T_n) \mid N(T)=n ;\overset{d}{=}; (U_{(1)},\ldots,U_{(n)}), \quad U_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}(0,T)}
\boxed{N(s) \mid N(T) = n ;\sim; \text{Binomial}!\left(n,,\frac{s}{T}\right)}
\boxed{E[T_k \mid N(T) = n] = \frac{k}{n+1},T}
\boxed{T_k/T \mid N(T)=n ;\sim; \text{Beta}(k,, n-k+1)}
\boxed{N(t) - N(s) \perp N(s), \quad N(t)-N(s) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))}
\boxed{E[F] = \frac{1}{\lambda} ;\text{ (inspection paradox — forward wait is still Exp}(\lambda)\text{)}}

13. The Unifying Mental Model
There are two layers of randomness in a Poisson process:
Layer 1 (How many?):   N(T) ~ Poisson(λT)
Layer 2 (Where?):      Locations | N(T)=n ~ n iid Uniform(0,T)

Conditioning on Layer 1 completely decouples the layers.
Once you fix n, the process becomes a uniform scatter — no rate, no Poisson, just n uniform random points. This decomposition is what makes Poisson processes analytically tractable in virtually every applied setting.

Every hard Poisson process conditioning problem becomes easy once you invoke this decomposition: fix the count, scatter uniformly, then apply Binomial/Beta/Multinomial logic.

01.Maths/Probability/13.Poission-Process.title: 03.Superposition of Poisson Processes
01.Maths/Probability/13.Poission-Process.content:
Type: Theorem | Domain: Stochastic Processes, Probability
Prerequisite map: Poisson Process 1D → Independence →  PGF → Superposition
Parent note: Poisson Process 1D
Relevant courses: Harvard Stat 110, MIT 18.650


1. The Statement
If you have n independent Poisson processes:
N_1(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_1), \quad N_2(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_2), \quad \ldots, \quad N_n(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_n)
then their merged (superposed) process is also a Poisson process:
\boxed{N(t) = N_1(t) + N_2(t) + \cdots + N_n(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \cdots + \lambda_n)}
The merged process has rate \Lambda = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i.

2. Why This Is Non-Trivial
Summing two random processes is easy. The surprise is that the result is still a Poisson process — not just a process with the right mean, but one satisfying all three Poisson process axioms:

Independent increments ✓
Stationary increments ✓
Poisson-distributed counts ✓

This closure property is special. Summing two Binomial processes, for example, does not generally give a Binomial process.

3. Proof — Three Routes
Route 1: MGF / PGF (Cleanest)
The Probability Generating Function of \text{Poisson}(\mu) is:
G(z) = E[z^N] = e^{\mu(z-1)}
For N = N_1 + N_2 with N_1 \perp N_2:
G_N(z) = E[z^{N_1 + N_2}] = E[z^{N_1}] \cdot E[z^{N_2}]
= e^{\lambda_1 t(z-1)} \cdot e^{\lambda_2 t(z-1)} = e^{(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)t(z-1)}
This is the PGF of \text{Poisson}((\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)t). \checkmark

Key step: Independence allows factoring E[z^{N_1+N_2}] = E[z^{N_1}]E[z^{N_2}]. The PGF uniquely determines the distribution.


Route 2: Direct PMF Convolution
P(N_1(t) + N_2(t) = k) = \sum_{j=0}^{k} P(N_1 = j) \cdot P(N_2 = k-j)
= \sum_{j=0}^{k} \frac{e^{-\lambda_1 t}(\lambda_1 t)^j}{j!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\lambda_2 t}(\lambda_2 t)^{k-j}}{(k-j)!}
= e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)t} \sum_{j=0}^{k} \frac{(\lambda_1 t)^j (\lambda_2 t)^{k-j}}{j!(k-j)!}
= \frac{e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)t}}{k!} \sum_{j=0}^{k} \binom{k}{j} (\lambda_1 t)^j (\lambda_2 t)^{k-j}
= \frac{e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)t} \cdot [(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)t]^k}{k!} \checkmark
by the Binomial theorem: \sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j} a^j b^{k-j} = (a+b)^k.

Route 3: Infinitesimal Definition (Most Rigorous)
Check the three axioms for N(t) = N_1(t) + N_2(t):
Independent increments: For disjoint intervals [s,t] and [u,v]:

N(t)-N(s) = [N_1(t)-N_1(s)] + [N_2(t)-N_2(s)], independent of
N(v)-N(u) = [N_1(v)-N_1(u)] + [N_2(v)-N_2(u)]

Since N_1 \perp N_2 and each has independent increments, the sum inherits this. ✓
Stationary increments: Each component is stationary, so their sum is. ✓
No simultaneous events: P(\text{both } N_1 \text{ and } N_2 \text{ jump in } dt) = (\lambda_1 , dt)(\lambda_2 , dt) = \lambda_1 \lambda_2 (dt)^2 = o(dt) \checkmark
So at most one event occurs per infinitesimal interval. ✓
All three axioms satisfied \Rightarrow N is a Poisson process with rate \lambda_1 + \lambda_2. \checkmark

4. The Labeling / Type Probability
When you merge two streams, a natural question arises:

Given that an event just occurred in the merged process, what is the probability it came from stream i?

\boxed{P(\text{event from stream } i) = \frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \cdots + \lambda_n}}
Proof for 2 streams: In any infinitesimal interval dt:
P(\text{event from } N_1) = \lambda_1 , dt, \quad P(\text{event from } N_2) = \lambda_2 , dt
Conditioning on the merged event occurring:
P(\text{type 1} \mid \text{event}) = \frac{\lambda_1 , dt}{(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2) , dt} = \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}
This is constant — it does not depend on time, history, or how many events have occurred.

5. The Full Picture — Superposition + Thinning Duality
These two theorems are inverses of each other:
                    Thinning (p, 1-p)
          ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
          │                                  ▼
   PP(λ) ──┤                           PP(λp)  ⊥  PP(λ(1-p))
          │                                  │
          └──────────────────────────────────┘
                   Superposition (+)





















OperationInputOutputSuperpositionn independent PP’s with rates \lambda_iSingle PP with rate \sum \lambda_iThinningSingle PP(\lambda), keep each event w.p. pTwo independent PP’s: PP(\lambda p) and PP(\lambda(1-p))

Deep insight: Superposition and thinning together show that the Poisson process is closed under both merging and splitting — a hallmark of its mathematical elegance.


6. The Competition / Race Theorem
Two independent Poisson processes N_1 \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_1) and N_2 \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_2) are running simultaneously. What is the probability that the first event overall comes from N_1?
Method 1 — Exponential race:
Let T_1 \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda_1) and T_2 \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda_2) be the first arrival times, independent.
P(T_1 < T_2) = \int_0^\infty P(T_2 > t) \cdot f_{T_1}(t) , dt
= \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda_2 t} \cdot \lambda_1 e^{-\lambda_1 t} , dt = \lambda_1 \int_0^\infty e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)t} , dt = \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}
\boxed{P(T_1 < T_2) = \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_2}}
Method 2 — Labeling theorem (1 line):
The first event of the merged PP(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2) is type 1 with probability \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}, by the labeling result above. Same answer.

Generalization: For n independent exponentials, \min(T_1, \ldots, T_n) \sim \text{Exp}(\sum \lambda_i) and P(T_i = \min) = \frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_j \lambda_j}.


7. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Call Center
Two call centers A and B independently receive calls at rates \lambda_A = 4/min and \lambda_B = 6/min. Calls are routed to a single queue.

Merged arrival rate: \Lambda = 10/min
P(\text{next call is from A}) = 4/10 = 0.4
P(\text{0 calls in 30 seconds}) = e^{-10 \times 0.5} = e^{-5} \approx 0.0067
E[\text{time until 3rd call}] = 3/10 = 0.3 min

Example 2 — Competing Servers
Two servers each fail independently: Server 1 at rate \lambda_1 = 0.1/hour, Server 2 at rate \lambda_2 = 0.2/hour.

P(\text{Server 1 fails first}) = \frac{0.1}{0.3} = \frac{1}{3}
E[\text{time to first failure}] = \frac{1}{0.3} \approx 3.33 hours
After Server 1 fails, Server 2 continues at rate 0.2/hour independently

Example 3 — n Streams
Customers arrive from n cities with rates \lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n. Merged rate \Lambda = \sum \lambda_i.
Given a customer just arrived, the probability they are from city k:
P(\text{city } k) = \frac{\lambda_k}{\Lambda}
This is a Categorical distribution over cities — the arrival is like drawing a city label with these probabilities, independent of everything else.

8. Common Mistakes

























MistakeCorrectionForgetting independence requirementSuperposition requires N_1 \perp N_2. Dependent processes don’t merge cleanly.Thinking rates add only for countsThe full process (interarrivals, order statistics) is Poisson at rate \Lambda, not just counts at one time.Confusing superposition with thinningSuperposition: n \to 1 (merge). Thinning: 1 \to n (split). They are inverses.Assuming labeled streams are dependent post-mergeAfter merging, the type labels are independent of the merged process’s timing.

  └─ LOTUS and MGF proofs for Poisson sums
  └─ Practice: BH Chapter 13 problems

MIT 18.650 (Statistics)
  └─ Poisson regression: multiple sources → single count model
  └─ Superposition justifies aggregating independent count data

  └─ Queueing models for system design (M/M/1 queue uses PP arrivals)
  └─ Bayesian network: independent Poisson sources → compound model

  └─ Ch.13: Superposition theorem proof and exercises

  └─ Sensor fusion: independent noisy sensors modeled as superposed PP's


10. Mini-Exercises
[ ] Exercise 1 — Direct Calculation
Buses from Route A arrive at \lambda_A = 3/hour. Route B at \lambda_B = 5/hour.
(a) Rate of any bus?
(b) P(\text{next bus is Route A})?
(c) P(\text{exactly 4 buses in 30 minutes})?
(d) E[\text{wait for 2nd bus of any type}]?
[ ] Exercise 2 — PGF Proof
Reproduce Route 1 (PGF proof) for three independent streams \text{PP}(\lambda_1), \text{PP}(\lambda_2), \text{PP}(\lambda_3). Conclude the merged rate.
[ ] Exercise 3 — Race
Three servers fail at rates \lambda_1=1, \lambda_2=2, \lambda_3=3 per day.
(a) P(\text{Server 2 fails first})?
(b) E[\text{time until first failure}]?
(c) After the first failure, what is the distribution of time until the next failure?
[ ] Exercise 4 — Simulation
import numpy as np
 
def simulate_superposition(lambda1, lambda2, T, n_sim=10000):
    """Verify superposition: merged rate should be lambda1 + lambda2"""
    counts = []
    for _ in range(n_sim):
        # Generate arrivals from two independent streams
        n1 = np.random.poisson(lambda1 * T)
        n2 = np.random.poisson(lambda2 * T)
        counts.append(n1 + n2)
    
    empirical_mean = np.mean(counts)
    theoretical_mean = (lambda1 + lambda2) * T
    
    print(f"Empirical mean: {empirical_mean:.4f}")
    print(f"Theoretical mean: {theoretical_mean:.4f}")
    return counts
 
counts = simulate_superposition(lambda1=3, lambda2=5, T=1)
# Should verify: empirical ≈ 8
Run this. Then plot the histogram and overlay the Poisson(8) PMF. Verify they match.
[ ] Exercise 5 — Labeling Independence
Given the merged stream at rate \Lambda = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2, show that:

The type label (which stream) of the k-th event is independent of the type label of the j-th event.
(Hint: use the thinning theorem — the merged stream, when thinned, produces independent streams.)


11. Key Formulas Cheatsheet
\boxed{\sum_{i=1}^n \text{PP}(\lambda_i) = \text{PP}!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\right) \quad \text{(if mutually independent)}}
\boxed{P(\text{event is type } i) = \frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_j \lambda_j}}
\boxed{P(T_i = \min_j T_j) = \frac{\lambda_i}{\sum_j \lambda_j}, \quad \min_j T_j \sim \text{Exp}!\left(\sum_j \lambda_j\right)}
\boxed{G_{\text{Poisson}(\mu)}(z) = e^{\mu(z-1)}, \quad G_{N_1+N_2}(z) = G_{N_1}(z) \cdot G_{N_2}(z)}

12. Mental Model

Imagine n people independently and randomly throwing darts at the same timeline. Superposition asks: what does the combined dart board look like? Answer: it’s exactly what you’d get if one person threw darts at rate \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \cdots + \lambda_n — the sources become completely indistinguishable except for the fixed probability labels.

The merged process has no memory of where events came from — only the rate changes.

01.Maths/Probability/13.Poission-Process.title: 04.Thinning of Poisson Processes
01.Maths/Probability/13.Poission-Process.content:
Type: Theorem | Domain: Stochastic Processes, Probability
Prerequisite map: Poisson Process 1D → Bernoulli Trials → Independence → Thinning
Parent note: Poisson Process 1D
Sibling notes: Superposition | Conditioning
Relevant courses: Harvard Stat 110 (Lecture 14), MIT 18.650


1. The Setup
You have a Poisson process PP(\lambda). Each arriving event is independently kept with probability p, or discarded with probability 1-p.
This random filtering is called thinning (also: independent marking, Bernoulli thinning).
Original PP(λ):
────┼────┼──┼─────┼──┼────┼───┼──▶
    e₁   e₂  e₃    e₄  e₅   e₆   e₇

Each event: keep (↓) w.p. p, discard (✗) w.p. 1-p

    ✓    ✗   ✓     ✗   ✓    ✓    ✗

Kept stream PP(λp):
────┼───────┼──────────┼────┼──────▶
    e₁      e₃         e₅   e₆

Discarded stream PP(λ(1-p)):
─────────┼───────┼──────────────┼──▶
         e₂      e₄             e₇


2. The Theorem
Theorem (Thinning / Decomposition):
Let N \sim \text{PP}(\lambda). Independently mark each event as type 1 with probability p and type 2 with probability 1-p. Define:

N_1(t) = number of type-1 events in [0,t]
N_2(t) = number of type-2 events in [0,t]

Then:
\boxed{N_1(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda p) \quad \text{and} \quad N_2(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda(1-p))}
\boxed{N_1 \perp N_2}
The two thinned streams are independent Poisson processes.

3. The Surprise — Independence
The rates \lambda p and \lambda(1-p) are expected. The independence is the deep result.
Intuitively: knowing that many events were kept (large N_1) tells you nothing about how many were discarded (N_2), because each decision was made independently coin flip by coin flip.
But this intuition is incomplete — N_1 and N_2 are both functions of the same underlying process N. Why doesn’t knowing N_1 tell you something about N = N_1 + N_2 and hence about N_2?
The answer lies in the Poisson distribution’s special property:

Key algebraic fact: If N \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu) and N_1 \mid N \sim \text{Binomial}(N, p), then N_1 \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu p) and N_1 \perp N_2 = N - N_1.

This is unique to the Poisson distribution — no other distribution has this property.

4. Proof
Proof of Marginal Distributions
Fix time interval [0,t]. Let N = N(t) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t).
Each event is independently type 1 with probability p, so:
N_1 \mid N \sim \text{Binomial}(N, p)
Compute P(N_1 = k) by conditioning on N:
P(N_1 = k) = \sum_{n=k}^{\infty} P(N_1 = k \mid N = n) \cdot P(N = n)
= \sum_{n=k}^{\infty} \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k} \cdot \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^n}{n!}
= \frac{e^{-\lambda t} p^k (\lambda t)^k}{k!} \sum_{n=k}^{\infty} \frac{(\lambda t)^{n-k}(1-p)^{n-k}}{(n-k)!}
Let m = n - k:
= \frac{e^{-\lambda t} (p\lambda t)^k}{k!} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \frac{(\lambda t (1-p))^m}{m!}
= \frac{e^{-\lambda t} (p\lambda t)^k}{k!} \cdot e^{\lambda t(1-p)}
= \frac{e^{-\lambda t p} (p\lambda t)^k}{k!}
\implies \boxed{N_1 \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t p)} \checkmark
By symmetry: N_2 \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t (1-p)).

Proof of Independence
Compute the joint PMF of (N_1, N_2):
P(N_1 = j,, N_2 = k) = P(N_1 = j,, N = j+k)
= P(N_1 = j \mid N = j+k) \cdot P(N = j+k)
= \binom{j+k}{j} p^j (1-p)^k \cdot \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^{j+k}}{(j+k)!}
= \frac{(j+k)!}{j!,k!} p^j(1-p)^k \cdot \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^{j+k}}{(j+k)!}
= \frac{e^{-\lambda t p}(\lambda t p)^j}{j!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\lambda t(1-p)}(\lambda t(1-p))^k}{k!}
= P(N_1 = j) \cdot P(N_2 = k) \checkmark
The joint PMF factors — N_1 and N_2 are independent. \checkmark

5. Generalization — k-Type Thinning
Each event is independently assigned to type i with probability p_i, where \sum_{i=1}^k p_i = 1.
\boxed{N_1 \sim \text{PP}(\lambda p_1),; N_2 \sim \text{PP}(\lambda p_2),; \ldots,; N_k \sim \text{PP}(\lambda p_k)}
\boxed{N_1, N_2, \ldots, N_k \text{ mutually independent}}
Proof: Same as above using Multinomial instead of Binomial. The joint PMF factors into a product of Poisson PMFs.
Example: Customers at a store choose product A (40%), B (35%), C (25%). If customers arrive as PP(100/hour):

Product A purchases: PP(40/hour)
Product B purchases: PP(35/hour)
Product C purchases: PP(25/hour)
All three streams are mutually independent


6. Non-Constant Thinning — State-Dependent Marking
Thinning can be generalized: the retention probability p(t) varies with time.
\text{Each event at time } t \text{ is kept with probability } p(t)
Result: The thinned process is still Poisson but with a time-varying rate:
N_1 \sim \text{PP}(\lambda(t) \cdot p(t)) \quad \text{(inhomogeneous PP)}
The rate at time t becomes \lambda \cdot p(t).
Example: A server processes requests at rate 100/sec. During peak hours (8am–6pm), each request has a p(t) = 0.8 chance of being a “complex” request. Complex requests form an inhomogeneous PP with rate 80/sec during peak hours.

7. Duality with Superposition
Thinning and superposition are exact inverses:
                    SUPERPOSITION
         PP(λ₁) ──┐
                   ├──→  PP(λ₁ + λ₂)
         PP(λ₂) ──┘

                      THINNING
                              ┌──→  PP(λp)       [kept]
         PP(λ)  ──────────────┤
                              └──→  PP(λ(1-p))   [discarded]

The full picture:






























SuperpositionThinningDirectionn \to 1 (merge)1 \to n (split)Rate\lambda_1 + \lambda_2\lambda p, \lambda(1-p)IndependenceInput streams must be independentOutput streams become independentKey toolPGF factoringPoisson-Binomial-Poisson identity
Round-trip consistency:
Thin PP(\lambda) with prob p → get PP(\lambda p) and PP(\lambda(1-p)).
Now superpose them → PP(\lambda p + \lambda(1-p)) = PP(\lambda). ✓
You recover the original rate exactly.

8. The Poisson-Binomial-Poisson Identity
This is the algebraic engine behind thinning. Worth stating cleanly:
Theorem: If N \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu) and X \mid N \sim \text{Binomial}(N, p), then:
X \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu p) \quad \text{and} \quad X \perp (N - X)
This is unique to Poisson. Check: if N \sim \text{Binomial}(m, q) and X \mid N \sim \text{Binomial}(N, p), then X \sim \text{Binomial}(m, pq) but X and N-X are not independent.
The Poisson distribution is the only distribution closed under Binomial thinning with output independence.

9. Connection to the Conditioning Theorem
Thinning and conditioning are related through a beautiful symmetry.
Conditioning theorem says: Given N(T) = n, events are uniform on [0,T].
Thinning says: Thin PP(\lambda) by keeping each event with probability p = s/T (i.e., keep if event falls in [0,s]).
Then:

Kept stream = PP(\lambda \cdot s/T) on [0,T], which equals PP(\lambda) on [0,s]
This is exactly N(s)

So thinning by a spatial indicator (\mathbf{1}[\text{event} \in [0,s]]) recovers the sub-interval count, and the independence of the thinned streams recovers the independent increments property.

Deep link: The independence of increments of a Poisson process is thinning independence, when the thinning is by time sub-interval membership.


10. Worked Examples
Example 1 — Network Packets
Packets arrive at a router as PP(\lambda = 1000/sec).

60% are TCP packets
30% are UDP packets
10% are ICMP packets

TCP stream: PP(600/sec)
UDP stream: PP(300/sec)
ICMP stream: PP(100/sec)
All mutually independent.
P(\text{no ICMP in 10ms}) = e^{-100 \times 0.01} = e^{-1} \approx 0.368
P(\text{exactly 5 TCP and exactly 2 UDP in 10ms}):
= P(N_{TCP}=5) \cdot P(N_{UDP}=2) \quad \text{(by independence)}
= \frac{e^{-6} \cdot 6^5}{5!} \cdot \frac{e^{-3} \cdot 3^2}{2!} \approx 0.1606 \times 0.2240 \approx 0.036
Example 2 — Quality Control
Items produced as PP(\lambda = 50/hour). Each is defective with probability p = 0.04.

Defective items: PP(2/hour)
Good items: PP(48/hour)
Independent streams

E[\text{time until first defective}] = 1/2 hour = 30 minutes
P(\text{0 defectives in 2 hours}) = e^{-2 \times 2} = e^{-4} \approx 0.018
Example 3 — Thinning Then Race
Cars arrive on a highway as PP(\lambda = 60/min). Each is independently a truck w.p. 0.1 or car w.p. 0.9.
Truck stream: PP(6/min), Car stream: PP(54/min).
P(\text{first vehicle is a truck}) = \frac{6}{60} = 0.1 ← same as thinning probability. Always.

General rule: P(\text{first thinned event is type } i) = p_i. The race outcome probability equals the thinning probability.


11. Common Mistakes

























MistakeCorrectionAssuming independence is obviousN_1 and N_2 share the same parent N — independence is a theorem, not automaticApplying thinning without independence of marksMarks must be independent of each other and of the process historyConfusing thinning probability with conditional probabilityp is the probability of keeping an event, not the probability given some conditionForgetting thinned streams are full Poisson processesNot just the right mean — full independent increments, stationary, etc.

12. Mini-Exercises
[ ] Exercise 1 — Basic Thinning
Emails arrive as PP(\lambda = 20/hour). Each is spam w.p. 0.3 independently.
(a) Rate of spam emails?
(b) Rate of legitimate emails?
(c) Are spam and legitimate counts in any interval independent? Why?
(d) P(\text{no spam in 30 minutes})?
(e) E[\text{time until 3rd spam email}]?
[ ] Exercise 2 — Reproduce the Proof
Without looking at the note: derive N_1 \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t p) from scratch using the law of total probability. Then show independence by factoring the joint PMF.
[ ] Exercise 3 — Multinomial Thinning
PP(\lambda = 100/hour) is thinned into 3 types with p_1=0.5, p_2=0.3, p_3=0.2.
(a) Find the joint distribution of (N_1(1), N_2(1), N_3(1)).
(b) P(N_1=40, N_2=25, N_3=18) in one hour — write the expression.
(c) Are any two of the three streams correlated? Prove it.
[ ] Exercise 4 — Simulation
import numpy as np
 
def verify_thinning(lam=10, p=0.3, T=1.0, n_sim=50000):
    """
    Verify: thinned streams are independent Poisson processes
    """
    n1_counts, n2_counts = [], []
    
    for _ in range(n_sim):
        # Generate PP(lambda) on [0, T]
        n_total = np.random.poisson(lam * T)
        # Thin: each event independently kept w.p. p
        marks = np.random.binomial(1, p, size=n_total)
        n1_counts.append(marks.sum())
        n2_counts.append(n_total - marks.sum())
    
    n1_counts = np.array(n1_counts)
    n2_counts = np.array(n2_counts)
    
    print(f"E[N1] = {n1_counts.mean():.3f} | Theoretical: {lam*p*T:.3f}")
    print(f"E[N2] = {n2_counts.mean():.3f} | Theoretical: {lam*(1-p)*T:.3f}")
    print(f"Cov(N1,N2) = {np.cov(n1_counts, n2_counts)[0,1]:.4f} | Theoretical: 0")
    print(f"Corr(N1,N2) = {np.corrcoef(n1_counts, n2_counts)[0,1]:.4f} | Theoretical: 0")
 
verify_thinning()
# Covariance and correlation should be ≈ 0 — confirming independence
[ ] Exercise 5 — Uniqueness
Show that the Binomial distribution does NOT have the thinning-independence property:
Let N \sim \text{Binomial}(10, 0.5) and X \mid N \sim \text{Binomial}(N, 0.5).
Compute \text{Cov}(X, N-X) and show it is non-zero.

13. Key Formulas Cheatsheet
\boxed{N \sim \text{PP}(\lambda),; p\text{-thin} ;\Rightarrow; N_1 \sim \text{PP}(\lambda p) \perp N_2 \sim \text{PP}(\lambda(1-p))}
\boxed{k\text{-type thinning: } N_i \sim \text{PP}(\lambda p_i),\quad N_1 \perp N_2 \perp \cdots \perp N_k}
\boxed{N \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu),; X \mid N \sim \text{Bin}(N,p) ;\Rightarrow; X \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu p),; X \perp N-X}
\boxed{P(\text{first event is type } i) = p_i}
\boxed{\text{Thin then superpose: PP}(\lambda p) + \text{PP}(\lambda(1-p)) = \text{PP}(\lambda)}

14. Mental Model

Imagine a factory line (the Poisson process) producing widgets at rate \lambda. At the end of the line, a quality inspector independently flips a coin for each widget: heads → keep it, tails → scrap it.
The kept widgets form their own independent assembly line at rate \lambda p. The scrapped widgets form their own independent scrap heap at rate \lambda(1-p). The two piles have no memory of each other — because each decision was made independently.
The magic: the scrapping process has no knowledge of how many were kept, and vice versa. The independence emerges from the independence of the coin flips and the Poisson structure of the original process.

01.Maths/Probability/13.Poission-Process.title: 05.Poisson Process in Multiple Dimensions
01.Maths/Probability/13.Poission-Process.content:
Type: Theorem Cluster | Domain: Stochastic Processes, Spatial Statistics
Prerequisite map: Poisson Process 1D → Measure Theory (Basics) → Homogeneous vs Inhomogeneous → Spatial Poisson Process
Parent note: Poisson Process 1D
Sibling notes: Superposition | Thinning | Conditioning
Relevant courses: Harvard Stat 110, MIT 18.650, Stanford CS229


1. Motivation — Why Go Beyond 1D?
In 1D, the Poisson process models events in time. But many real phenomena are spatially distributed:

































ApplicationSpaceStars in the sky2D sphere projectionTrees in a forest2D planeDefects in a material3D volumeNeurons firing in a brain region3D space + time = 4DWi-Fi access points in a city2D planeCosmic ray hits on a detector2D surface
The 1D intuition extends cleanly — but the geometry becomes richer.

2. Definition — Spatial Poisson Process
Let S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d be a region in d-dimensional space. A spatial Poisson process (also: Poisson Point Process, PPP) with intensity measure \Lambda is a random collection of points {x_i} \subset S satisfying:
Axiom 1 — Poisson Counts
For any bounded region A \subseteq S:
N(A) \sim \text{Poisson}(\Lambda(A))
where \Lambda(A) is the intensity measure of A (the expected number of points in A).
Axiom 2 — Independent Scattering
For any disjoint regions A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_k \subseteq S:
N(A_1),, N(A_2),, \ldots,, N(A_k) \quad \text{are mutually independent}

These two axioms completely define the spatial Poisson process — no reference to ordering, interarrivals, or time.


3. Homogeneous vs. Inhomogeneous
3.1 Homogeneous (Stationary) PPP
The intensity measure is proportional to volume:
\Lambda(A) = \lambda \cdot |A|
where |A| is the d-dimensional volume (area in 2D, length in 1D, volume in 3D) and \lambda > 0 is the intensity (points per unit volume).
\boxed{N(A) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda \cdot |A|)}
Homogeneous = uniform density everywhere. The process looks statistically the same from any location.
3.2 Inhomogeneous PPP
The intensity varies across space via an intensity function \lambda(x) \geq 0:
\Lambda(A) = \int_A \lambda(x), dx
\boxed{N(A) \sim \text{Poisson}!\left(\int_A \lambda(x), dx\right)}
Points are denser where \lambda(x) is large.
Homogeneous (λ = const):        Inhomogeneous (λ(x) varies):

· · · · · · · · · ·            · · ·  ·· ···· ··  · ·
· · · · · · · · · ·            · ·  ·  ·   ·····  ·
· · · · · · · · · ·            ·  ·    ·  ·····  ·· ·
· · · · · · · · · ·            ·    ·   ···· ·  ·   ·
(uniform density)               (density peaks at center)


4. The d-Dimensional Setup
Key Quantities by Dimension
| Dimension | Space | Volume element | |A| for sphere/disk radius r | |---|---|---|---| | 1D | \mathbb{R} | dx | 2r (interval) | | 2D | \mathbb{R}^2 | dx,dy | \pi r^2 (disk) | | 3D | \mathbb{R}^3 | dx,dy,dz | \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 (ball) | | dD | \mathbb{R}^d | dx_1 \cdots dx_d | \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2+1)} r^d |
Count Distribution
For homogeneous PPP(\lambda) in d dimensions, in a ball of radius r centred at origin:
N(B_r) \sim \text{Poisson}!\left(\lambda \cdot \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2+1)} r^d\right)

5. The Fundamental Conditioning Theorem in dD
Theorem: Given N(A) = n, the n points in A are distributed as n iid draws from the normalized intensity measure on A:
\text{Each point} \mid N(A) = n \overset{iid}{\sim} f(x) = \frac{\lambda(x)}{\Lambda(A)}, \quad x \in A
For homogeneous PPP: Given N(A) = n, the n points are iid Uniform(A).
\boxed{(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \mid N(A) = n \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}(A)}

This is the 1D conditioning theorem, verbatim, in d dimensions. The geometry of A only affects the uniform distribution’s support.


6. Superposition and Thinning in dD
Both theorems carry over without modification:
Superposition
\text{PPP}(\lambda_1) + \text{PPP}(\lambda_2) = \text{PPP}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)
(adding point patterns from independent processes → denser homogeneous PPP)
Thinning
Each point of PPP(\lambda) is independently retained with probability p(x) (can depend on location):
\text{Retained points} \sim \text{PPP}(\lambda \cdot p(x)) \text{Removed points} \sim \text{PPP}(\lambda \cdot (1-p(x)))
Both independent. For homogeneous thinning (p(x) = p constant):
\text{PPP}(\lambda) \xrightarrow{\text{thin } p} \text{PPP}(\lambda p) \perp \text{PPP}(\lambda(1-p))

7. Nearest Neighbour Distance
One of the most important derived quantities in spatial statistics.
Setup: Homogeneous PPP(\lambda) in \mathbb{R}^d. Fix a point at the origin (or pick a random point). Let R = distance to the nearest other point.
In 2D
The probability that no point falls within radius r:
P(R > r) = P(N(B_r) = 0) = e^{-\lambda \pi r^2}
So the CDF and PDF of R:
\boxed{F_R(r) = 1 - e^{-\lambda \pi r^2}}
\boxed{f_R(r) = 2\lambda \pi r \cdot e^{-\lambda \pi r^2}, \quad r \geq 0}
This is a Rayleigh distribution (special case of Weibull).
E[R] = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\lambda}}, \qquad \text{Var}(R) = \frac{4 - \pi}{4\pi\lambda}
In dD (General)
Let \omega_d = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2+1)} be the volume of the unit ball in \mathbb{R}^d.
P(R > r) = e^{-\lambda \omega_d r^d}
f_R(r) = \lambda \omega_d d \cdot r^{d-1} \cdot e^{-\lambda \omega_d r^d}
E[R] = \frac{\Gamma(1 + 1/d)}{\left(\lambda \omega_d\right)^{1/d}}

























Dimensionf_R(r)Distribution name1D2\lambda e^{-2\lambda r} (for r>0)Exponential(2\lambda)2D2\lambda\pi r \cdot e^{-\lambda\pi r^2}Rayleigh3D4\lambda\pi r^2 \cdot e^{-\frac{4}{3}\lambda\pi r^3}Weibull

1D check: In 1D, nearest neighbour = min of left and right Exp(\lambda) gaps. By superposition and race: R \sim \text{Exp}(2\lambda). ✓


8. The Empty Space Function
Definition: F(r) = P(\text{no point of PPP within distance } r \text{ of origin})
For homogeneous PPP(\lambda) in \mathbb{R}^d:
\boxed{F(r) = 1 - e^{-\lambda \omega_d r^d}}
Same formula as the nearest-neighbour CDF — because for a homogeneous PPP, these two quantities coincide (the process looks the same from any fixed point as from a typical random point).
This is used in spatial statistics to test whether an observed point pattern is consistent with a PPP (CSR — Complete Spatial Randomness).

9. Campbell’s Theorem
A fundamental result for computing expectations of sums over PPP points.
Theorem: For PPP with intensity \lambda(x) and any measurable function f: S \to \mathbb{R}:
\boxed{E!\left[\sum_{x_i \in \text{PPP}} f(x_i)\right] = \int_S f(x),\lambda(x),dx}
Intuition: Replace the random sum over points with an integral against the intensity measure.
Example — Total signal power:
Transmitters distributed as PPP(\lambda) in 2D. Each transmitter at location x contributes signal power f(x) = |x|^{-\alpha} (path-loss model). Expected total received power:
E!\left[\sum_i |x_i|^{-\alpha}\right] = \lambda \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} |x|^{-\alpha},dx = \lambda \int_0^\infty r^{-\alpha} \cdot 2\pi r,dr = 2\pi\lambda \int_0^\infty r^{1-\alpha},dr
(Converges for \alpha > 2.)
Second moment — Campbell’s extended theorem:
\text{Var}!\left[\sum_{x_i} f(x_i)\right] = \int_S f(x)^2,\lambda(x),dx

10. Marked Poisson Process
Each point x_i of the PPP is equipped with an independent random mark m_i \sim F_m (a scalar, vector, or label).
Result: The marked process is itself a PPP on S \times \mathcal{M} (space × mark space) with intensity:
\lambda(x, m) = \lambda(x) \cdot f_m(m)
Examples:

Trees (PPP in 2D) with random heights (marks)
Wi-Fi access points (PPP in 2D) with random transmission powers
Stars (PPP in 3D) with random luminosities

Key property: Projecting back to S (ignoring marks) recovers the original PPP. Thinning by mark value recovers the thinning theorem.

11. Stochastic Geometry — Voronoi and Delaunay
Given a PPP in \mathbb{R}^2, two canonical geometric structures arise:
Voronoi Tessellation
Each point x_i “owns” the region of space closer to it than to any other PPP point:
V_i = {y \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |y - x_i| \leq |y - x_j| ;\forall j \neq i}
The Voronoi cells of a PPP(\lambda) form a random tessellation. Each cell has:
E[\text{area of cell}] = \frac{1}{\lambda}, \quad E[\text{number of sides}] = 6
Delaunay Triangulation
The dual graph of the Voronoi tessellation — connects PPP points whose Voronoi cells share an edge. Used in mesh generation, spatial interpolation.
Application in ML: Voronoi diagrams of training data → nearest-neighbour classifiers; each Voronoi cell is the decision region for one training point.

12. 2D PPP — Worked Examples
Example 1 — Stars in the Sky
Stars distributed as homogeneous PPP(\lambda = 0.01/deg²) on a 2D projection.
(a) Expected stars in a 10° × 10° patch: E[N] = 0.01 \times 100 = 1
(b) Probability of seeing exactly 3 stars in the patch: P(N=3) = \frac{e^{-1} \cdot 1^3}{3!} = \frac{e^{-1}}{6} \approx 0.0613
(c) Expected nearest-star distance (in degrees): E[R] = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\lambda}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{0.01}} = \frac{1}{0.2} = 5 \text{ degrees}
Example 2 — Wi-Fi Access Points
Access points distributed as PPP(\lambda = 0.05/m²) in a 2D office floor.
(a) Probability of no access point within 2 metres: P(R > 2) = e^{-\lambda \pi r^2} = e^{-0.05 \times \pi \times 4} = e^{-0.628} \approx 0.534
(b) Given 20 access points in a 20m × 20m room, where are they?
By conditioning theorem: each is iid Uniform on the 400m² room.
Expected position of each: centre of the room (10, 10).
Example 3 — Defects in a Material
Defects in a 3D material follow PPP(\lambda = 10^{-6}/mm³).
Volume of a 10mm × 10mm × 10mm cube: |A| = 1000 mm³.
N(A) \sim \text{Poisson}(10^{-6} \times 1000) = \text{Poisson}(10^{-3})
P(N = 0) = e^{-0.001} \approx 0.999 \quad \text{(almost surely defect-free)}

13. Python Implementation
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import poisson
 
# ── 1. Simulate 2D Homogeneous PPP ─────────────────────────────────────
def simulate_2d_ppp(lam, region=(0, 1, 0, 1)):
    """
    Simulate homogeneous PPP(lambda) on rectangle [x0,x1] x [y0,y1]
    """
    x0, x1, y0, y1 = region
    area = (x1 - x0) * (y1 - y0)
    n_points = np.random.poisson(lam * area)
    x = np.random.uniform(x0, x1, n_points)
    y = np.random.uniform(y0, y1, n_points)
    return x, y
 
# ── 2. Simulate 2D Inhomogeneous PPP (thinning method) ─────────────────
def simulate_2d_inhomogeneous_ppp(lam_func, lam_max, region=(0, 1, 0, 1)):
    """
    Simulate inhomogeneous PPP via thinning:
    1. Generate homogeneous PPP(lam_max)
    2. Thin each point: keep with prob lam_func(x,y) / lam_max
    """
    x0, x1, y0, y1 = region
    # Step 1: homogeneous envelope
    x, y = simulate_2d_ppp(lam_max, region)
    # Step 2: thin
    keep_prob = lam_func(x, y) / lam_max
    keep = np.random.uniform(size=len(x)) < keep_prob
    return x[keep], y[keep]
 
# ── 3. Nearest Neighbour Distance ───────────────────────────────────────
def nearest_neighbour_distances(x, y):
    """Compute nearest neighbour distance for each point"""
    from scipy.spatial import KDTree
    points = np.column_stack([x, y])
    tree = KDTree(points)
    dists, _ = tree.query(points, k=2)  # k=2: self + nearest
    return dists[:, 1]
 
# ── 4. Verify Nearest Neighbour Distribution ────────────────────────────
lam = 50  # points per unit area
x, y = simulate_2d_ppp(lam, region=(0, 10, 0, 10))
nn_dists = nearest_neighbour_distances(x, y)
 
r = np.linspace(0, 0.5, 200)
# Theoretical: f_R(r) = 2*pi*lambda*r * exp(-pi*lambda*r^2)
theoretical_pdf = 2 * np.pi * lam * r * np.exp(-np.pi * lam * r**2)
 
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 4))
 
plt.subplot(1, 3, 1)
plt.scatter(x, y, s=2, alpha=0.5)
plt.title(f'2D PPP(λ={lam})\nn={len(x)} points')
plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y')
 
plt.subplot(1, 3, 2)
plt.hist(nn_dists, bins=40, density=True, alpha=0.7, label='Empirical')
plt.plot(r, theoretical_pdf, 'r-', lw=2, label='Rayleigh theory')
plt.xlabel('Nearest neighbour distance')
plt.title('NN Distance Distribution')
plt.legend()
 
# Inhomogeneous: Gaussian intensity
plt.subplot(1, 3, 3)
lam_func = lambda x, y: 200 * np.exp(-((x-5)**2 + (y-5)**2) / 4)
xi, yi = simulate_2d_inhomogeneous_ppp(lam_func, lam_max=200,
                                        region=(0, 10, 0, 10))
plt.scatter(xi, yi, s=2, alpha=0.5, c='darkgreen')
plt.title(f'Inhomogeneous PPP\n(Gaussian intensity, n={len(xi)})')
plt.xlabel('x'); plt.ylabel('y')
 
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
 
# ── 5. Verify Conditioning Theorem ─────────────────────────────────────
def verify_conditioning_2d(lam=5, n_target=10, n_sim=3000):
    """Given N(A)=n, points should be Uniform(A)"""
    x0, x1, y0, y1 = 0, 4, 0, 4
    conditional_x, conditional_y = [], []
    
    while len(conditional_x) < n_sim:
        x, y = simulate_2d_ppp(lam, region=(x0, x1, y0, y1))
        if len(x) == n_target:
            conditional_x.extend(x)
            conditional_y.extend(y)
    
    # Should be Uniform(0,4) x Uniform(0,4)
    print(f"E[x] = {np.mean(conditional_x[:n_sim*n_target]):.3f} | "
          f"Theoretical: {(x0+x1)/2:.3f}")
    print(f"E[y] = {np.mean(conditional_y[:n_sim*n_target]):.3f} | "
          f"Theoretical: {(y0+y1)/2:.3f}")
 
verify_conditioning_2d()

14. Connection to ML and CS229
14.1 Stochastic Geometry in Wireless Networks
Base stations: PPP(\lambda_b) in 2D. Users: PPP(\lambda_u) in 2D. Independent.
Coverage probability (probability a random user is covered by at least one base station within radius r):
P(\text{covered}) = 1 - e^{-\lambda_b \pi r^2}
This is the empty space function — the PPP model makes this analytically tractable.
14.2 Object Detection / Point Cloud Processing
LiDAR point clouds are often modelled as inhomogeneous PPPs. Detecting an object = testing H_0: PPP vs H_1: non-PPP clustering in a region.
14.3 Neural Processes and Spike Trains
Neuron spike trains: modelled as inhomogeneous PPP(\lambda(t)) where \lambda(t) is the firing rate (a function of stimulus). Learning \lambda(t) from data = density estimation problem.
14.4 Gaussian Processes and PPP
The Cox Process (doubly stochastic Poisson process): \lambda(x) is itself a random field (e.g., a log-Gaussian process). Used in Bayesian spatial statistics and GP-based generative models in PRML Ch.3/6.

15. Summary Table













































Property1D PPdD PPPCount in regionN([0,t]) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t)N(A) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda\|A\|)IndependenceDisjoint intervalsDisjoint regionsConditioningOrder stats of Uniform(0,t)iid Uniform(A)Nearest neighbour\text{Exp}(2\lambda)Rayleigh / WeibullSuperposition\text{PP}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\text{PPP}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)Thinning\text{PP}(\lambda p)\text{PPP}(\lambda p(x))Intensityscalar \lambdafunction \lambda(x) or measure \Lambda

16. Mini-Exercises
[ ] Exercise 1 — 2D Counts
Trees are distributed as PPP(\lambda = 0.1/m²) in a forest.
(a) Expected trees in a circular clearing of radius 5m?
(b) P(\text{no trees within 3m of a random point})?
(c) Expected distance to nearest tree?
[ ] Exercise 2 — Nearest Neighbour in 3D
Molecules distributed as PPP(\lambda = 10^3/mm³) in 3D.
(a) Write f_R(r) explicitly.
(b) Find E[R].
(c) P(R > 0.05\text{ mm})?
[ ] Exercise 3 — Conditioning in 2D
PPP(\lambda = 2/m²) on a 5m × 5m room. You observe N = 15 points.
(a) Expected x-coordinate of each point?
(b) Expected number of points in the left half (x < 2.5)?
(c) Distribution of the number of points in the top-left quadrant?
[ ] Exercise 4 — Campbell’s Theorem
Interferers distributed as PPP(\lambda) in \mathbb{R}^2. Each at distance r causes interference I = r^{-4}.
(a) Use Campbell’s theorem to compute E[\text{total interference}].
(b) Does this converge? (Check the integral near r=0.)
(c) How do you fix this? (Hint: exclude a ball of radius \epsilon around origin — a guard zone.)
[ ] Exercise 5 — Simulation
Implement simulate_2d_inhomogeneous_ppp using the thinning method:

Generate homogeneous PPP(\lambda_{\max})
Retain point (x,y) w.p. \lambda(x,y)/\lambda_{\max}

Use \lambda(x,y) = 100 \cdot \mathbf{1}[x^2 + y^2 \leq 1] (uniform in unit disk, zero outside). Verify E[N] = 100\pi.

17. Key Formulas Cheatsheet
\boxed{N(A) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda |A|) \quad \text{(homogeneous, } d\text{D)}}
\boxed{N(A) \sim \text{Poisson}!\left(\int_A \lambda(x),dx\right) \quad \text{(inhomogeneous)}}
\boxed{(x_1,\ldots,x_n) \mid N(A) = n \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}(A)}
\boxed{P(R > r) = e^{-\lambda \omega_d r^d}, \quad \omega_d = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2+1)}}
\boxed{f_R(r) = \lambda \omega_d d, r^{d-1} e^{-\lambda \omega_d r^d}}
\boxed{E!\left[\sum_{x_i} f(x_i)\right] = \int f(x),\lambda(x),dx \quad \text{(Campbell's theorem)}}

18. Mental Model

Imagine a cosmic dart-thrower standing outside all of space, throwing darts uniformly at random into \mathbb{R}^d at rate \lambda per unit volume. Each dart lands independently of all others, with no memory of where previous darts landed.

Ask “how many darts in region A?” → Poisson(\lambda|A|)
Ask “given n darts in A, where are they?” → iid Uniform(A)
Ask “how far to the nearest dart?” → depends on d-dimensional ball geometry

The geometry of space enters only through the volume of regions and balls. The Poisson randomness is purely in the count; the spatial structure is purely in the uniform scatter.

01.Maths/Probability/14.Others/01.Expone.title: 01.Exponential Family
01.Maths/Probability/14.Others/01.Expone.content:
Core Definition A distribution belongs to the exponential family if its PDF/PMF can be written in the form:
                  
                

f(x \mid \theta) = h(x) \exp!\bigl(\eta(\theta), T(x) - A(\theta)\bigr)
This is the canonical form. Every term has a precise role.



Anatomy of the Formula






























ComponentNameRoleh(x)Base measureThe part that depends only on x, not \theta. Sets the “shape floor.”\eta(\theta)Natural parameterReparametrizes \theta into the exponential family’s native coordinateT(x)Sufficient statisticThe only function of x that matters for estimating \thetaA(\theta)Log-partition functionNormalization constant (in log space). Ensures the distribution integrates to 1


                  
                  The Log-Partition Function A(\theta) A(\theta) is not arbitrary — it is completely determined by h, \eta, and T:
                  
                

A(\theta) = \log \int h(x)\exp(\eta(\theta),T(x)), dx
Its derivatives generate the moments of T(x): \mathbb{E}[T(X)] = A'(\theta), \qquad \text{Var}(T(X)) = A''(\theta)
This is a profound fact — all moments come for free once you know A(\theta).



Member Distributions


                  
                  The Family Tree 
                  
                

Bernoulli — X \sim \text{Bern}(p)
P(X = x) = p^x(1-p)^{1-x}
Rewrite:
= \exp!\left(x \log\frac{p}{1-p} + \log(1-p)\right)

























ComponentValueh(x)1\eta(p)\log\frac{p}{1-p} (the log-odds)T(x)xA(p)-\log(1-p) = \log(1 + e^\eta)

Poisson — X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)
P(X = x) = \frac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!} = \frac{1}{x!}\exp(x\log\lambda - \lambda)

























ComponentValueh(x)\frac{1}{x!}\eta(\lambda)\log \lambdaT(x)xA(\lambda)\lambda

Normal — X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) (known \sigma^2)
f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\exp!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
Expand the square:
= \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\exp!\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)}_{h(x)} \cdot \exp!\left(\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}x - \frac{\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)

























ComponentValueh(x)\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-x^2/2\sigma^2}\eta(\mu)\frac{\mu}{\sigma^2}T(x)xA(\mu)\frac{\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}

Exponential — X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)
f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x} = \exp(\log\lambda - \lambda x)

























ComponentValueh(x)1\eta(\lambda)-\lambdaT(x)xA(\lambda)-\log\lambda

Quick Membership Table













































DistributionIn Exponential Family?Bernoulli✅Binomial (fixed n)✅Poisson✅Exponential✅Gamma✅Beta✅Normal✅Cauchy❌Uniform (unknown bounds)❌


                  
                  The Cauchy Exception The Cauchy distribution f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)} cannot be written in exponential family form. Its heavy tails and undefined moments mean it resists the algebraic structure the family requires. This is why the Cauchy is a canonical counterexample in statistics — it has no mean, no variance, and no sufficient statistic.
                  
                


Why This Matters — The Big Payoffs
1. Sufficient Statistics


                  
                  Fisher-Neyman Factorization T(x) is a sufficient statistic for \theta: it captures all the information in x about \theta.
                  
                

No matter how many data points x_1, \ldots, x_n you collect, you only need \sum T(x_i) to estimate \theta.
For Poisson: just keep the sample sum \sum x_i, discard everything else.


2. Conjugate Priors (Bayesian Statistics)


                  
                  Conjugacy Every exponential family distribution has a conjugate prior — a prior that, when updated with data, yields a posterior of the same family.
                  
                


























LikelihoodConjugate PriorBernoulli/BinomialBetaPoissonGammaNormal (unknown \mu)NormalExponentialGamma
This is why Bayesian inference is analytically tractable for exponential family distributions — the math closes cleanly.


3. Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)


                  
                  MLE Has a Clean Form For iid data x_1, \ldots, x_n, the MLE condition for exponential family distributions reduces to:
                  
                

\hat{\mathbb{E}}[T(X)] = \bar{T} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n T(x_i)
The MLE moment-matches the sufficient statistic. No complicated optimization needed.


4. Generalized Linear Models (GLMs)


                  
                  GLMs are Built on This Logistic regression, Poisson regression, linear regression — all GLMs assume the response comes from an exponential family distribution. 
                  
                

The natural parameter \eta is what the linear predictor \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} models directly.
This is the bridge between probability theory and machine learning.



The Natural Parametrization
When we write \eta = \eta(\theta), we can go further and treat \eta itself as the parameter:
f(x \mid \eta) = h(x)\exp(\eta, T(x) - A(\eta))
This is the natural (or canonical) parametrization. It linearizes the problem — the parameter enters the exponent linearly in \eta. This is why GLMs, variational inference, and information geometry all prefer this form.

Mental Model
Raw data x
     ↓
  T(x)  ← sufficient statistic: compress x into what matters
     ↓
η(θ) · T(x) ← dot product: parameter meets data
     ↓
  − A(θ) ← normalization enforced automatically
     ↓
  h(x) · exp(·) = valid probability distribution

The exponential family is what you get when you ask:

“What is the most general family of distributions with a fixed-dimensional sufficient statistic?”
— Pitman–Koopman–Darmois theorem


Self-Test


                  
                  Exercises 
                  
                


Write \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta) in exponential family form. Identify all four components.
Why does the Uniform(0, \theta) distribution (unknown upper bound) fail to be in the exponential family?
For Bernoulli, compute A''(\eta) and verify it equals \text{Var}(X).
If X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda), what is the sufficient statistic for \lambda? What does this mean practically?





                  
                  Answers 
                  
                


f(x \mid \alpha, \beta) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)\beta^\alpha} x^{\alpha-1} e^{-x/\beta}. So: h(x) = x^{\alpha-1}/\Gamma(\alpha), \eta = -1/\beta, T(x) = x, A = \alpha\log\beta + \log\Gamma(\alpha). (Treating \alpha as fixed, \beta as the parameter.)
The support [0, \theta] depends on the parameter \theta. Exponential family requires the support to be fixed (independent of \theta). The Fisher-Neyman factorization breaks down when the support shifts.
A(\eta) = \log(1 + e^\eta). A'(\eta) = \frac{e^\eta}{1+e^\eta} = p = \mathbb{E}[X]. A''(\eta) = \frac{e^\eta}{(1+e^\eta)^2} = p(1-p) = \text{Var}(X). ✅
T = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i (the sample sum). Practically: you don’t need to store all n observations — just their sum. The sample mean carries all the information about \lambda.




Connected Concepts

Support of Random Variables — support must be \theta-free for exponential family membership
Sufficient Statistics — the heart of why the family is powerful
Conjugate Priors — Bayesian payoff of exponential family structure
Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) — applied exponential family in ML
MLE and Method of Moments — MLE reduces to moment matching here
KL Divergence and Information Geometry — exponential families form flat manifolds
