04.ML/04.Unsupervised-learning/01.Cluste.title: 04.DBSCAN
04.ML/04.Unsupervised-learning/01.Cluste.content:
“DBSCAN asks not ‘how far are you from the centroid?’ but ‘are you surrounded by enough neighbours?’ It is a fundamentally different notion of what a cluster is — not a shape, but a region of crowding.”

Part of: Clustering · 04.Unsupervised Learning
Requires: distance metrics, \epsilon-neighbourhoods, basic graph connectivity
Connects to: 03.Hierarchical (HDBSCAN extends DBSCAN hierarchically), 01.K-Means (contrast in assumptions), 07.k-Nearest Neighbours (shared neighbourhood machinery), 02.Statistical Learning Theory (density estimation perspective)

✦ Motivation: What K-Means Cannot Do
K-Means partitions space by proximity to centroids. Its implicit assumption: clusters are convex and roughly spherical. Given two interleaved half-moons, or a ring around a core, K-Means fails categorically — not because of tuning, but because the model is wrong.
  K-Means sees this:         Reality:
  
  ●●●  ○○○                   ●●●●●●●●
  ●●●  ○○○                       ○○○
  ●●●  ○○○                   ●●●●●●●●
  
  (Two blobs — fine)         (Ring around core — impossible for K-Means)

DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) sidesteps this entirely. Its definition of a cluster: a maximal set of density-connected points. Shape is irrelevant. What matters is whether a region of space is dense.
Original paper: Ester, M., Kriegel, H.-P., Sander, J., & Xu, X. (1996). A Density-Based Algorithm for Discovering Clusters in Large Spatial Databases with Noise. KDD-96. One of the most cited papers in data mining.

✦ The Two Parameters
Everything in DBSCAN is defined in terms of two hyperparameters:

\varepsilon (epsilon): the neighbourhood radius. A point q is a neighbour of p if d(p, q) \leq \varepsilon.
\text{MinPts}: the minimum number of points required to form a dense region (including the point itself).

These two numbers are the entire model. There is no objective function being optimised, no iterative update, no convergence criterion — just a graph traversal.

✦ Definitions
Let X = {x_1, \ldots, x_n} be the dataset and d(\cdot, \cdot) a distance metric.
\varepsilon-Neighbourhood
N_\varepsilon(p) = { q \in X : d(p, q) \leq \varepsilon }
The set of all points within radius \varepsilon of p, including p itself.
Core Point
A point p is a core point if:
|N_\varepsilon(p)| \geq \text{MinPts}
Its neighbourhood is dense enough to anchor a cluster. Core points are the “interior” of clusters.
Border Point
A point p is a border point if:
|N_\varepsilon(p)| < \text{MinPts} \quad \text{but} \quad \exists \text{ core point } q \text{ such that } p \in N_\varepsilon(q)
Not dense enough to be a core, but reachable from one. Border points are the “edges” of clusters.
Noise Point (Outlier)
A point p is a noise point if it is neither a core point nor a border point. It belongs to no cluster. This is the key feature absent from K-Means and GMMs — DBSCAN has an explicit “none of the above” category.
Directly Density-Reachable
Point q is directly density-reachable from p (w.r.t. \varepsilon, MinPts) if:

p is a core point, and
q \in N_\varepsilon(p)

Note: this relation is not symmetric. q may be directly reachable from p without p being directly reachable from q (if q is a border point).
Density-Reachable
Point q is density-reachable from p if there exists a chain of points p = p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k = q such that each p_{i+1} is directly density-reachable from p_i.
Still not symmetric in general.
Density-Connected
Points p and q are density-connected if there exists a point o such that both p and q are density-reachable from o.
Density-connectedness is symmetric. This is the equivalence relation that defines cluster membership.
Cluster (Formal Definition)
A cluster C (w.r.t. \varepsilon, MinPts) is a non-empty subset of X satisfying:

Maximality: If p \in C and q is density-reachable from p, then q \in C.
Connectivity: Every pair of points in C is density-connected.

Equivalently: a cluster is a maximal set of mutually density-connected points. The clusters partition the non-noise points.

✦ The Algorithm
Input: X, ε, MinPts
Output: cluster assignment for each point ∈ X (or NOISE)

labels = {p: UNVISITED for p in X}
cluster_id = 0

for each point p in X:
    if labels[p] ≠ UNVISITED:
        continue
    
    neighbours = RangeQuery(X, p, ε)   # = N_ε(p)
    
    if |neighbours| < MinPts:
        labels[p] = NOISE              # tentative — may become border later
        continue
    
    cluster_id += 1
    labels[p] = cluster_id
    seed_set = neighbours \ {p}        # points to process
    
    while seed_set is not empty:
        q = seed_set.pop()
        
        if labels[q] == NOISE:
            labels[q] = cluster_id    # border point: was noise, now assigned
        
        if labels[q] ≠ UNVISITED:
            continue                  # already in a cluster
        
        labels[q] = cluster_id
        q_neighbours = RangeQuery(X, q, ε)
        
        if |q_neighbours| ≥ MinPts:   # q is a core point — expand further
            seed_set = seed_set ∪ q_neighbours

return labels

This is a graph BFS/DFS over the \varepsilon-neighbourhood graph, seeded only from core points. Every point is visited at most once (once labelled, it is skipped). The order of iteration does not affect which points are core points or noise — but it can affect which cluster a border point is assigned to when it is reachable from multiple clusters (this is a known ambiguity in the definition).
Complexity

Time: O(n \cdot T_{\text{query}}) where T_{\text{query}} is the cost of a range query.

With a KD-tree or ball tree: T_{\text{query}} = O(\log n) for low-dimensional data → O(n \log n) total.
In high dimensions (KD-tree degrades): T_{\text{query}} = O(n) → O(n^2) total.


Space: O(n) for labels + O(n^2) for a precomputed distance matrix (the default in sklearn for small n).


✦ Visualisation of Point Types
                ε
         ←————————→
    
    ★ ★ ★                     ★ = core point
   ★ ★ ★ ★                    ◆ = border point (in ε-neighbourhood of a core)
    ★ ★ ★   ◆                 ✕ = noise point
       ◆  ◆      ✕
              ★ ★ ★
             ★ ★ ★ ★
              ★ ★ ★

   [  Cluster 1  ]  [  Cluster 2  ]

The two clusters above could be any shape — crescents, rings, spirals — as long as internal density is sufficient.

✦ Geometric Intuition: Clusters as Level Sets
DBSCAN is equivalent to finding connected components of the level set {x : \hat{p}(x) \geq \lambda} of an implicit density estimator, where the threshold \lambda is determined by \varepsilon and MinPts.
Formally: if you construct a kernel density estimate with a uniform kernel of bandwidth \varepsilon:
\hat{p}(x) = \frac{1}{n} |N_\varepsilon(x)|
then a core point is one where \hat{p}(x) \geq \frac{\text{MinPts}}{n}. DBSCAN finds the connected components of the region where \hat{p} \geq \frac{\text{MinPts}}{n}.
This connects DBSCAN directly to density estimation (cf. 03.Density Estimation) and makes its statistical behaviour analysable. The clusters are the high-density “mountains” of the underlying distribution, separated by “valleys” of low density.

✦ Choosing \varepsilon and MinPts
This is the practical crux. Unlike K-Means where k is interpretable, \varepsilon depends on the scale of your data — there is no universal default.
MinPts
A common heuristic: \text{MinPts} = 2 \cdot d where d is the number of features (dimensionality). At minimum, MinPts \geq 3. Larger MinPts → smoother, more robust clustering; smaller MinPts → more clusters, more sensitive to noise.
The paper’s authors suggest MinPts = 4 as a default for 2D data.
The k-Distance Plot (Knee Method)
The canonical method for choosing \varepsilon:

For each point x_i, compute d_k(x_i) = distance to its k-th nearest neighbour, where k = \text{MinPts} - 1.
Sort these k-distances in descending order and plot them.
The knee (point of maximum curvature) of the resulting curve suggests the appropriate \varepsilon.

Why this works: Points in dense regions have small k-distances; outliers and noise have large k-distances. The knee separates them. Values of \varepsilon above the knee include too many points as core points (everything merges); values below miss genuine structure.
k-distance
    │  \
    │   \         ← noise points (large k-dist)
    │    \
    │     '---____  ← knee: choose ε here
    │             ‾‾‾‾‾  ← core/cluster points (small k-dist)
    └────────────────────────
                 Points (sorted)

In code:
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 
k = 4  # = MinPts - 1
nbrs = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k).fit(X)
distances, _ = nbrs.kneighbors(X)
k_distances = np.sort(distances[:, -1])[::-1]
 
plt.plot(k_distances)
plt.xlabel('Points sorted by k-distance (desc)')
plt.ylabel(f'{k}-NN distance')
plt.title('k-Distance Plot — look for the knee')
plt.axhline(y=0.5, color='r', linestyle='--', label='candidate ε')
plt.legend()
Scale Sensitivity
\varepsilon is in the same units as your distance metric. If you standardise features (zero mean, unit variance), then Euclidean distances are comparable across datasets and a starting point of \varepsilon \approx 0.3–0.5 is reasonable for 2D–10D data — but always use the k-distance plot.
DBSCAN does not handle clusters of varying density. If your data has a dense core surrounded by a sparse ring, no single \varepsilon will correctly identify both. This is the primary motivation for HDBSCAN.

✦ DBSCAN Properties
What DBSCAN Can Do That K-Means Cannot

Arbitrary shape clusters: Rings, crescents, spirals, fractals — anything connected.
Automatic k: The number of clusters is a result, not a parameter.
Explicit noise detection: Points not belonging to any dense region are labelled as outliers. This is intrinsic, not post-hoc.
No assumption of cluster shape or size: Large and small clusters coexist naturally.

What DBSCAN Cannot Do

Varying density: A single \varepsilon cannot adapt to regions of different densities.
High dimensions: The curse of dimensionality makes all \varepsilon-neighbourhoods either empty or full — the “crowding problem.” KD-trees also degrade. For d \gtrsim 10, DBSCAN becomes unreliable.
No probabilistic output: Hard assignments only, no cluster membership probability.
Parameter sensitivity: Results can change dramatically with small changes to \varepsilon near the knee.
Border point ambiguity: A border point reachable from two clusters is assigned to whichever cluster processes it first — non-deterministic over orderings.


✦ Worked Example (by hand)
Data: 8 points in \mathbb{R}^2, with \varepsilon = 1.5, MinPts = 3.
Points: A=(0,0), B=(0,1), C=(1,0), D=(5,5), E=(5,6), F=(6,5), G=(10,10), H=(0,0.5)

Step 1: Compute N_\varepsilon for each point.

N_{1.5}(A) = {A, B, C, H} → |N| = 4 \geq 3 → core
N_{1.5}(B) = {A, B, C, H} → |N| = 4 \geq 3 → core
N_{1.5}(C) = {A, B, C, H} → |N| = 4 \geq 3 → core
(check: d(C,H)=d((1,0),(0,0.5))=\sqrt{1+0.25}=1.12 \leq 1.5 ✓)
N_{1.5}(H) = {A, B, C, H} → |N| = 4 \geq 3 → core
N_{1.5}(D) = {D, E, F} → |N| = 3 \geq 3 → core
(check: d(D,F)=d((5,5),(6,5))=1 \leq 1.5 ✓)
N_{1.5}(E) = {D, E, F} → |N| = 3 \geq 3 → core
N_{1.5}(F) = {D, E, F} → |N| = 3 \geq 3 → core
N_{1.5}(G) = {G} → |N| = 1 < 3 → noise

Step 2: Run BFS from first unvisited core point, say A.

Seed set = {B, C, H}. Assign all to cluster 1.
Process B: core, N(B) = {A,B,C,H}, all already in cluster 1.
Process C: core, same neighbourhood.
Process H: core, same neighbourhood.
Seed set empty. Cluster 1 = {A,B,C,H}.

Step 3: Next unvisited point D.

Seed set = {E, F}. Assign to cluster 2.
Process E: core, N(E) = {D,E,F}, all assigned.
Process F: core, same.
Cluster 2 = {D,E,F}.

Step 4: G is labelled noise. No further unvisited points.
Result: Cluster 1 = {A,B,C,H}, Cluster 2 = {D,E,F}, Noise = {G}.

✦ Formal Correctness: The Key Lemma
Lemma: Let p be a core point and C be any cluster containing p. Then C contains all points density-reachable from p.
Proof. Suppose q is density-reachable from p via chain p = p_1, \ldots, p_k = q. By maximality of C (property 1 of the cluster definition), p_2 is directly density-reachable from p_1 = p \in C, so p_2 \in C. Since p_2 \in C and p_3 is directly density-reachable from p_2, p_3 \in C. By induction, q \in C. \square
Corollary: Each core point uniquely determines its cluster (up to the ambiguity of border points). The clustering is essentially determined by the connected components of the core-point \varepsilon-neighbourhood graph.

✦ Implementation (NumPy, from scratch)
import numpy as np
from collections import deque
 
def dbscan(X, eps, min_pts):
    """
    DBSCAN clustering from scratch.
    Returns: labels array of shape (n,), with -1 for noise.
    """
    n = len(X)
    labels = np.full(n, -2, dtype=int)   # -2 = UNVISITED
    cluster_id = 0
 
    def range_query(idx):
        """Return indices of all points within eps of X[idx]."""
        dists = np.linalg.norm(X - X[idx], axis=1)
        return np.where(dists <= eps)[0].tolist()
 
    for i in range(n):
        if labels[i] != -2:
            continue
 
        neighbours = range_query(i)
 
        if len(neighbours) < min_pts:
            labels[i] = -1   # NOISE (may be reassigned to border later)
            continue
 
        # i is a core point — start a new cluster
        labels[i] = cluster_id
        queue = deque(neighbours)
 
        while queue:
            j = queue.popleft()
 
            if labels[j] == -1:
                labels[j] = cluster_id    # border: was noise, now assigned
 
            if labels[j] != -2:
                continue                  # already labelled
 
            labels[j] = cluster_id
            j_neighbours = range_query(j)
 
            if len(j_neighbours) >= min_pts:  # j is also a core point
                queue.extend(j_neighbours)
 
        cluster_id += 1
 
    return labels
 
 
# --- Example ---
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 
X, y_true = make_moons(n_samples=300, noise=0.05, random_state=42)
labels = dbscan(X, eps=0.2, min_pts=5)
 
colors = ['steelblue', 'coral', 'grey']
for lbl, color, marker in zip([0, 1, -1], colors, ['o', 's', 'x']):
    mask = labels == lbl
    label_name = f'Cluster {lbl}' if lbl >= 0 else 'Noise'
    plt.scatter(X[mask, 0], X[mask, 1], c=color, marker=marker,
                s=20, label=label_name, zorder=3)
 
plt.legend(); plt.title('DBSCAN on two moons'); plt.tight_layout()
Production (sklearn):
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
 
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
db = DBSCAN(eps=0.3, min_samples=5, metric='euclidean', n_jobs=-1)
labels = db.fit_predict(X_scaled)
 
n_clusters = len(set(labels)) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)
n_noise = (labels == -1).sum()
print(f'{n_clusters} clusters, {n_noise} noise points')
 
# Core sample mask
core_mask = np.zeros_like(labels, dtype=bool)
core_mask[db.core_sample_indices_] = True

✦ OPTICS: Generalising DBSCAN
OPTICS (Ordering Points To Identify the Clustering Structure, Ankerst et al. 1999) addresses DBSCAN’s inability to handle varying density.
Key idea: Instead of fixing \varepsilon, OPTICS computes a reachability plot over all possible \varepsilon values simultaneously.
Define for each point p:

Core distance: d_{\text{core}}(p) =  distance to MinPts-th nearest neighbour (if |N_\varepsilon(p)| \geq \text{MinPts}; else \infty).
Reachability distance of q w.r.t. p: \text{reach-dist}_{\text{MinPts}}(q, p) = \max(d_{\text{core}}(p),; d(p, q))

OPTICS outputs points in a traversal order where reachability-distance is small between consecutive points in the same cluster. Plotting reachability vs. order reveals valleys (clusters) and peaks (cluster boundaries / noise).
Extracting clusters: cut the reachability plot at a threshold \xi (relative steepness) → clusters of varying density are correctly identified.
OPTICS is strictly more general than DBSCAN — every DBSCAN clustering is recoverable from the OPTICS ordering at the corresponding \varepsilon.

✦ HDBSCAN: The Modern Default
HDBSCAN (Hierarchical DBSCAN, Campello et al. 2013) combines OPTICS-style thinking with a proper hierarchy and automatic cluster extraction.
The Construction


Mutual reachability distance: d_{\text{mreach},k}(p, q) = \max!\left(d_{\text{core},k}(p),; d_{\text{core},k}(q),; d(p,q)\right) This “spreads out” low-density regions — sparse points are pushed far apart, dense points keep their true distances.


MST of the complete graph on X under d_{\text{mreach}} (cf. 03.Hierarchical — single linkage on mutual reachability = the MST).


Condensed cluster tree: Extract the hierarchy from the MST. At each merge, if the resulting cluster has fewer than min_cluster_size points, the smaller piece becomes noise; the larger piece continues. This condenses the full dendrogram into a tree of meaningful clusters.


Cluster selection: Each node in the condensed tree has a stability score: \text{stability}(C) = \sum_{x \in C} \left(\lambda_{\text{death}}(x) - \lambda_{\text{birth}}(C)\right) where \lambda = 1/\varepsilon (inverse distance at which a point joins/leaves). Select clusters by maximising total stability over a valid selection (no cluster and its ancestor simultaneously selected).


Soft clustering (optional): HDBSCAN can output membership probabilities, not just hard assignments — a significant advantage over vanilla DBSCAN.


HDBSCAN vs. DBSCAN








































DBSCANHDBSCANParameters\varepsilon, MinPtsmin_cluster_size, min_samplesVarying densityNoYesHierarchyNoYes (condensed tree)Soft assignmentsNoYesRuntimeO(n \log n)O(n \log n) approx.StabilitySensitive to \varepsilonMore robust
import hdbscan  # pip install hdbscan
# or: from sklearn.cluster import HDBSCAN  (sklearn >= 1.3)
 
clusterer = hdbscan.HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=5, min_samples=3,
                              prediction_data=True)
labels = clusterer.fit_predict(X_scaled)
 
# Soft cluster membership (probabilities)
soft_clusters = hdbscan.all_points_membership_vectors(clusterer)

✦ Anomaly Detection with DBSCAN
The noise label -1 is not merely a side effect — it is a first-class anomaly detector.
For anomaly detection specifically, rather than running DBSCAN and checking for noise labels, consider:
Local Outlier Factor (LOF): A score-based variant. For each point p, LOF computes the ratio of the average local density of p‘s neighbours to p‘s own local density:
\text{LOF}_k(p) = \frac{\frac{1}{|N_k(p)|}\sum_{q \in N_k(p)} \text{lrd}_k(q)}{\text{lrd}_k(p)}
where the local reachability density is: \text{lrd}_k(p) = \left(\frac{\sum_{q \in N_k(p)} \text{reach-dist}_k(p,q)}{|N_k(p)|}\right)^{-1}
\text{LOF} \approx 1: p has similar density to neighbours → inlier.
\text{LOF} \gg 1: p is in a sparser region than its neighbours → outlier.
LOF is more nuanced than DBSCAN noise labelling because it produces a continuous score rather than a binary label, and correctly handles outliers at the boundary of clusters.
from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor
lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, contamination=0.05)
outlier_labels = lof.fit_predict(X)   # -1 = outlier, 1 = inlier
scores = -lof.negative_outlier_factor_  # higher = more outlier-like

✦ The Curse of Dimensionality and DBSCAN
In high dimensions (d \gg 10), DBSCAN degrades for the same reason as KNN (cf. 07.k-Nearest Neighbours): distances concentrate. As d \to \infty:
\frac{\max_i d(x, x_i) - \min_i d(x, x_i)}{\min_i d(x, x_i)} \to 0
All pairwise distances become approximately equal. The \varepsilon-neighbourhood of any point either contains all points or no points — no intermediate density structure survives.
Practical consequence: For d > 10–20, either:

Reduce dimensionality first (PCA, UMAP) then run DBSCAN, or
Use a domain-specific distance metric that captures meaningful similarity, or
Use HDBSCAN with approximate nearest neighbours (faster and partially mitigates the curse).

DBSCAN with Euclidean distance on raw high-dimensional data is generally not meaningful.

✦ Connection to AI, ML, and Deep Learning
Outlier Removal in Training Pipelines
Before training a supervised model on real-world data, DBSCAN (or LOF) is used to remove mislabelled or corrupted training examples. Noise points disproportionately harm models like SVMs (which are margin-based) and overfit small neural networks. Running DBSCAN on the feature space and discarding noise is a standard data cleaning step in industrial ML pipelines.
Clustering Latent Representations
In self-supervised and representation learning, DBSCAN is applied to embeddings (from BERT, ResNet, VAE latent spaces) to discover emergent structure without labels. Because deep embeddings are not spherical or equal-variance, DBSCAN’s shape-agnosticism makes it more appropriate than K-Means for this purpose.
A canonical workflow in NLP:
Sentence → SBERT embedding (768-dim) → UMAP (20-dim) → HDBSCAN → topics

This pipeline underlies BERTopic — one of the most widely used topic modelling frameworks (2022–present).
Semi-Supervised Learning via Density
DBSCAN’s clusters can serve as pseudo-labels for unlabelled data. If a small number of labelled points are known, a cluster containing labelled points can propagate those labels to all unlabelled cluster members — a form of label propagation grounded in density rather than graph Laplacian.
Autonomous Driving: LiDAR Point Cloud Segmentation
In 3D point cloud processing (LiDAR data), DBSCAN is the standard algorithm for object detection and segmentation. A LiDAR scan produces \sim 10^5 3D points per frame; DBSCAN identifies connected regions of high point density corresponding to vehicles, pedestrians, and obstacles. The noise label correctly handles the ground plane and distant sparse returns.
The key reason DBSCAN is preferred over K-Means here: the number of objects in the scene is unknown and varies per frame.
Federated Learning: Client Clustering
In federated learning with non-IID data, DBSCAN is applied to gradient fingerprints (the gradient updates submitted by clients) to detect:

Byzantine clients (noise points — gradients far from any cluster)
Naturally occurring data distribution clusters

This is density-based anomaly detection applied at the system level, not the data level.
Curriculum Learning
DBSCAN can partition a training set by difficulty: dense regions (many similar examples) → easy; noise points (isolated examples) → hard or mislabelled. A curriculum learning strategy trains first on cluster interiors, progressively including border and noise points.

✦ Comparison Table




































































PropertyK-MeansGMMHierarchicalDBSCANRequires kYesYesNo (post-hoc)NoCluster shapeSphericalEllipsoidalLinkage-dependentArbitraryNoise handlingNoneNoneNoneExplicit (-1)Varying densityNoNoNoNoSoft assignmentsNoYesNoNoScales to large nYesYesNoO(n \log n)High-dimDegradesDegradesDegradesDegrades badlyDeterministicNo (init)No (init)YesYes*
*Up to border point assignment order.

✦ Exit Criterion

You know this when: you can state the formal definitions of core, border, and noise points; prove that density-connectedness is symmetric while directly density-reachable is not; implement DBSCAN from scratch using BFS; explain why no single \varepsilon handles varying density (and what HDBSCAN does about it); derive the mutual reachability distance and explain its smoothing effect; and articulate concretely why DBSCAN degrades in high dimensions and what preprocessing remedies this.


✦ References

PRML Ch. 9 (brief) — Mixture models as contrast

Breunig et al. (2000) — LOF paper: LOF: Identifying Density-Based Local Outliers

04.ML/04.Unsupervised-learning/02.Dimens.title: 00.Dimensionality Reduction
04.ML/04.Unsupervised-learning/02.Dimens.content:
✦ The Problem
A dataset X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d} has n observations and d features. In practice:

d may be in the hundreds or thousands (gene expression, images, text embeddings).
Most of the variance lives in far fewer than d directions.
Algorithms degrade in high dimensions (cf. 07.k-Nearest Neighbours — the curse of dimensionality).
Humans can only visualise \mathbb{R}^2 or \mathbb{R}^3.

Dimensionality reduction maps X \in \mathbb{R}^d \to Z \in \mathbb{R}^k with k \ll d, preserving whatever structure matters for the downstream task.
The word “preserving” hides the entire difficulty. Different methods preserve different things:



































MethodWhat it preservesWhat it sacrifices01.Principal Component Analysis(PCA)Global variance, linear structureNonlinear geometry02.Kernel PCANonlinear structure (kernel-defined)Interpretability, out-of-sample cost03.t-SNELocal neighbourhood structureGlobal distances, inter-cluster meaning04.Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)Local and some global structureMathematical guarantees (optimisation-based)05.AutoencodersTask-relevant features (learned)Interpretability
There is no free lunch here either — no method preserves everything.

✦ Why High Dimensions Are Dangerous
The curse of dimensionality (Bellman, 1957) is not a vague warning — it has precise geometric content.
Volume concentration
The volume of a unit d-ball is: V_d = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2 + 1)}
This peaks around d = 5 and then decreases to zero as d \to \infty. Almost all the volume of a high-dimensional sphere sits in a thin shell near the surface.
Formally: for a uniform distribution on the unit ball in \mathbb{R}^d, the fraction of volume within distance \varepsilon of the surface is: 1 - (1-\varepsilon)^d \to 1 \quad \text{as } d \to \infty
For \varepsilon = 0.05 and d = 100: 1 - 0.95^{100} \approx 0.994. Nearly all data lives near the boundary.
Distance concentration
For i.i.d. points drawn from a distribution in \mathbb{R}^d, as d \to \infty: \frac{d_{\max} - d_{\min}}{d_{\min}} \to 0
All pairwise distances become approximately equal. This destroys the signal for any distance-based algorithm (KNN, DBSCAN, kernel methods).
Implication for ML
To maintain a fixed data density (points per unit volume), the required sample size grows exponentially with d. A grid with 10 points per axis requires 10^d total points.
Every DR method is, at its core, a strategy for escaping these pathologies.

✦ Two Philosophies
Linear Methods
Assume the low-dimensional structure is a linear subspace of \mathbb{R}^d: z = Wx + b, \quad W \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}
Advantages: closed-form solutions, interpretable components, fast, out-of-sample projection is trivial (z_{\text{new}} = Wx_{\text{new}}).
Limitations: cannot capture curved or folded manifolds.
Methods: PCA (01.Principal Component Analysis(PCA)), Factor Analysis, ICA, Random Projections, Linear Discriminant Analysis.
Nonlinear Methods (Manifold Learning)
Assume the data lies on a nonlinear manifold \mathcal{M} embedded in \mathbb{R}^d. The intrinsic dimensionality of \mathcal{M} is k \ll d.
Advantages: can unfold complex geometry (Swiss roll, toroidal manifolds, etc.).
Limitations: no closed-form, expensive, out-of-sample extension is non-trivial or impossible.
Methods: Kernel PCA (02.Kernel PCA), t-SNE (03.t-SNE), UMAP (04.Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)), Isomap, LLE, Diffusion Maps.

✦ The Manifold Hypothesis
The central assumption underlying modern DR (and much of deep learning):

Real high-dimensional data concentrates near a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the ambient space.

Natural images do not fill \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 256} uniformly. They live near a manifold of plausible images — a tiny, structured subset of all possible pixel arrays. The same holds for text, audio, molecular structures, and financial time series.
Evidence:

Intrinsic dimensionality estimates (e.g., via two-NN estimator) of real datasets are often 10–100× smaller than the ambient dimension.
DR methods that exploit manifold structure dramatically outperform linear methods on real data visualisation tasks.
Deep networks learn increasingly compact representations in deeper layers — implicit manifold learning.

The manifold hypothesis does not say which manifold, or that the manifold is smooth, or that it is connected. It is an empirical observation, not a theorem.

✦ The Intrinsic Dimensionality Problem
Before choosing k, one should ask: what is the intrinsic dimensionality of the data?
Explained Variance (PCA-based)
Run PCA, plot the cumulative explained variance ratio vs. number of components. Choose k such that, e.g., 95% of variance is explained. This is only valid if the data structure is well-captured by PCA.
Two-NN Estimator (Facco et al., 2017)
For each point, let r_1 and r_2 be the distances to its 1st and 2nd nearest neighbours. Under the assumption that the data is locally uniform on a k-dimensional manifold:
\mu_i = \frac{r_2}{r_1}
The empirical CDF of \mu follows 1 - \mu^{-k}. Regress to estimate k. This is model-free and requires no DR to be performed first.
Correlation Dimension
Count the number of pairs of points within distance r: C(r) \propto r^k. Plot \log C(r) vs. \log r; the slope is k.

✦ Reconstruction vs. Visualisation vs. Preprocessing
DR is used for three distinct purposes, which call for different methods and different quality criteria:
1. Preprocessing for downstream ML
Goal: reduce noise, remove redundancy, speed up training, mitigate curse of dimensionality.
Criterion: downstream task performance (not DR quality per se). Use CV to select k.
Best methods: PCA (fast, deterministic, interpretable). Random projections (Johnson-Lindenstrauss) for very large d.
Warning: Fit the DR transform on the training set only. Apply the same transform to test/validation sets. DR is part of the pipeline — it can leak if misapplied (cf. 02.Pipelines and Experiments).
2. Visualisation
Goal: produce a 2D or 3D plot that reveals structure in the data.
Criterion: visual separation of known or hypothesised groups; local neighbourhood preservation.
Best methods: t-SNE, UMAP. PCA as a sanity check.
Critical warning: t-SNE and UMAP visualisations are not quantitatively interpretable. Cluster sizes, inter-cluster distances, and global layout are artefacts of the optimisation, not properties of the data. See 03.t-SNE for the full treatment.
3. Representation learning / feature extraction
Goal: learn a compact representation that captures the semantically meaningful variation in the data, for use in a downstream task.
Criterion: quality of the learned representation for the target task.
Best methods: Autoencoders (04.Representation Learning), Kernel PCA for small datasets with known kernel structure.

✦ The Geometry of Linear Projections
Any linear DR method computes a projection Z = XW^T where W \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d} has orthonormal rows (WW^T = I_k). The projection is onto the column space of W^T.
The reconstruction of X from Z is: \hat{X} = ZW = XW^TW
The reconstruction error is: |X - \hat{X}|_F^2 = |X - XW^TW|_F^2
PCA chooses W to minimise this. Every other linear method chooses a different objective — Fisher’s LDA maximises class separation, ICA maximises statistical independence — but the projection structure is the same.
The Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma tells us that a random projection to k = O(\varepsilon^{-2} \log n) dimensions preserves all pairwise distances to within a factor of (1 \pm \varepsilon) with high probability. This is a remarkable fact: you do not need to find a good projection — a random one suffices for distance preservation.

✦ Connection to AI, ML, and Deep Learning
Dimensionality reduction is not a peripheral technique — it is structurally central to modern ML in ways that are often invisible.
The Encoder-Decoder Architecture
Every autoencoder, VAE, and the encoder half of a transformer is performing learned DR. The bottleneck layer in a standard autoencoder is literally a low-dimensional projection learned end-to-end. The difference from PCA: the projection is nonlinear (via activation functions) and task-conditioned (the loss may include a downstream objective). See 04.Representation Learning.
Attention as Soft DR
The query-key-value mechanism in transformers projects the full token sequence into a lower-dimensional “attention space” and back. Multi-head attention runs h parallel low-rank projections and concatenates. The W_Q, W_K, W_V matrices are exactly the DR matrices of linear projections — learned jointly with the task.
Embeddings Are DR
Word2Vec, GloVe, BERT embeddings, image embeddings from ResNets — all of these are learned DR maps from a high-dimensional space (vocabulary \sim 10^5, image pixels \sim 10^6) to a dense low-dimensional vector (\sim 10^2–10^3). The “embedding layer” in any neural network is a DR operation.
Dimensionality Reduction for Interpretability
Principal Components of model activations are used to identify “concept directions” in neural networks (TCAV, linear probing). The geometry of the embedding space — which directions correspond to which concepts — is a DR question.
Compression and Efficiency
Knowledge distillation (training a small network to mimic a large one) is, in part, a DR problem: find a low-dimensional representation of the large network’s behaviour. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation), the dominant fine-tuning method for LLMs as of 2024, explicitly constrains weight updates to be low-rank — a DR constraint on the parameter space.

After completing these four notes, you should be able to choose the right DR method for a given problem, implement PCA from scratch, explain why t-SNE distances are meaningless, and understand the role of DR in the broader ML pipeline.

04.ML/04.Unsupervised-learning/02.Dimens.title: 01.Principal Component Analysis(PCA)
04.ML/04.Unsupervised-learning/02.Dimens.content:
“PCA does not discover structure in the data. It discovers the directions of maximum spread. Whether spread means structure is a question you must answer yourself.”

Part of: 00.Dimensionality Reduction · 04.Unsupervised Learning
Requires: linear algebra (eigendecomposition, SVD, orthogonal projections), 03.Probability Review (covariance matrix, expectations)
Connects to: 02.Kernel PCA (nonlinear extension), 03.t-SNE and 04.Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) (contrast: local vs. global), 04.Representation Learning (autoencoders as learned PCA), 04.Support Vector Machines (kernel trick appears again in Kernel PCA)

✦ The Setup
We have data X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}: n observations, d features. Assume the data is centred: \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i = 0. If not, subtract the mean first — this is not optional, it is part of the algorithm.
We want to find a sequence of orthonormal directions v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_k \in \mathbb{R}^d (with k \leq d) such that projecting the data onto these directions retains as much variance as possible.
The projected coordinates are the principal components. The directions v_j are the principal axes (also called loadings, or eigenvectors of the covariance matrix). The j-th principal component of observation x_i is the scalar z_{ij} = v_j^T x_i.

✦ Derivation I: Maximum Variance Formulation
First Principal Component
Find the unit vector v_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d such that the projected data {v_1^T x_i}_{i=1}^n has maximum variance.
The sample variance of the projections is: \text{Var}(v_1^T X) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (v_1^T x_i)^2 = \frac{1}{n} v_1^T X^T X v_1 = v_1^T \Sigma v_1
where \Sigma = \frac{1}{n} X^T X \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} is the (sample) covariance matrix (valid since data is centred).
The optimisation problem: v_1 = \underset{|v|=1}{\arg\max}\ v^T \Sigma v
Using a Lagrange multiplier \lambda for the constraint |v|^2 = 1: \mathcal{L}(v, \lambda) = v^T \Sigma v - \lambda(v^T v - 1)
Setting the gradient to zero: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial v} = 2\Sigma v - 2\lambda v = 0 \implies \Sigma v = \lambda v
So v_1 must be an eigenvector of \Sigma. Substituting back: v_1^T \Sigma v_1 = v_1^T (\lambda_1 v_1) = \lambda_1
The variance of the projection equals the eigenvalue. To maximise variance, choose v_1 as the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue \lambda_1.
Subsequent Principal Components
v_2 solves the same problem subject to v_2 \perp v_1. By induction (deflation argument), v_j is the eigenvector corresponding to the j-th largest eigenvalue \lambda_j.
Proof of orthogonality. Since \Sigma is real symmetric and positive semi-definite, the spectral theorem guarantees that its eigenvectors can be chosen to be orthonormal. The principal axes form an orthonormal basis of \mathbb{R}^d.

✦ Derivation II: Minimum Reconstruction Error Formulation
An equivalent derivation from a completely different starting point. We want a k-dimensional affine subspace S minimising the sum of squared distances from each x_i to its projection onto S.
Let V_k = [v_1 | \cdots | v_k] \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k} with orthonormal columns. The projection of x_i onto the subspace spanned by V_k is \hat{x}_i = V_k V_k^T x_i.
Reconstruction error: \mathcal{R}(V_k) = \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i - V_k V_k^T x_i|^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|^2 - \sum_{i=1}^n |V_k^T x_i|^2
The first term is constant. Minimising \mathcal{R} is equivalent to maximising \sum_{i=1}^n |V_k^T x_i|^2 = \text{tr}(V_k^T X^T X V_k) = \text{tr}(V_k^T (n\Sigma) V_k).
This is maximised when the columns of V_k are the top k eigenvectors of \Sigma — exactly the same answer as Derivation I.
The two formulations are equivalent. Maximum variance projection = minimum reconstruction error. This is not a coincidence — it is a consequence of the Pythagorean theorem in \mathbb{R}^d.

✦ Derivation III: The SVD Connection
This is the computationally important formulation. Let X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d} (centred). The thin SVD of X is:
X = U \Sigma_{\text{sv}} V^T
where:

U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}: left singular vectors, orthonormal columns (U^T U = I_r)
\Sigma_{\text{sv}} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times r}: diagonal matrix of singular values \sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_r \geq 0
V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}: right singular vectors, orthonormal columns (V^T V = I_r)
r = \text{rank}(X) \leq \min(n, d)

Now observe: \frac{1}{n} X^T X = \frac{1}{n} (U \Sigma_{\text{sv}} V^T)^T (U \Sigma_{\text{sv}} V^T) = \frac{1}{n} V \Sigma_{\text{sv}}^2 V^T
So the covariance matrix \Sigma = \frac{1}{n} X^T X has:

Eigenvectors = columns of V (the right singular vectors of X)
Eigenvalues = \lambda_j = \frac{\sigma_j^2}{n}

The principal axes are the right singular vectors of the (centred) data matrix, and the j-th eigenvalue equals \sigma_j^2 / n.
The principal component scores (projected coordinates) are: Z = X V_k = U_k \Sigma_{\text{sv},k}
where V_k and U_k are the first k columns, \Sigma_{\text{sv},k} the top-left k \times k block.
Why use SVD instead of eigendecomposition?

Numerical stability. Computing X^T X squares the condition number of X. SVD operates directly on X and is far more numerically stable when singular values span many orders of magnitude.
Efficiency when n \ll d or d \ll n. The covariance matrix is d \times d; for d = 10^4, storing and decomposing it is expensive. Thin SVD of X costs O(n d \min(n,d)) — for n \ll d, much cheaper.
Randomised SVD. For very large matrices, randomised SVD (Halko et al., 2011) computes the top-k singular vectors in O(ndk) — linear in n and d.

In practice: always use SVD. The eigendecomposition of \Sigma is presented for understanding; SVD is what you implement.

✦ The Full Algorithm
Input:  X ∈ ℝⁿˣᵈ (raw data), number of components k
Output: Z ∈ ℝⁿˣᵏ (scores), V_k ∈ ℝᵈˣᵏ (principal axes), λ ∈ ℝᵏ (eigenvalues)

1. Centre:      μ = (1/n) Σᵢ xᵢ
                X_c = X - 1μᵀ              [subtract mean from each row]

2. Decompose:   U, σ, Vᵀ = svd(X_c, full_matrices=False)
                             [thin SVD: σ is vector of singular values]

3. Sort:        (already sorted descending by numpy/scipy convention)

4. Extract:     V_k = V[:, :k]             [first k right singular vectors]
                λ = σ[:k]² / n             [eigenvalues]
                Z = X_c @ V_k              [project: scores, shape (n, k)]

5. (Optional)   X_hat = Z @ V_k.T + μ      [reconstruction]
                error = ||X_c - Z @ V_k.T||_F²


✦ Implementation from Scratch (NumPy)
import numpy as np
 
class PCA:
    def __init__(self, n_components):
        self.k = n_components
        self.mean_ = None
        self.components_ = None   # V_k: shape (k, d), rows are principal axes
        self.explained_variance_ = None
        self.explained_variance_ratio_ = None
 
    def fit(self, X):
        n, d = X.shape
 
        # 1. Centre
        self.mean_ = X.mean(axis=0)
        Xc = X - self.mean_
 
        # 2. Thin SVD
        # U: (n, r), s: (r,), Vt: (r, d)
        U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
 
        # 3. Extract top k components
        self.components_ = Vt[:self.k]             # (k, d)
        eigenvalues = s**2 / n
        self.explained_variance_ = eigenvalues[:self.k]
        self.explained_variance_ratio_ = (
            eigenvalues[:self.k] / eigenvalues.sum()
        )
        return self
 
    def transform(self, X):
        Xc = X - self.mean_
        return Xc @ self.components_.T             # (n, k)
 
    def inverse_transform(self, Z):
        return Z @ self.components_ + self.mean_   # (n, d)
 
    def fit_transform(self, X):
        return self.fit(X).transform(X)
 
    def reconstruction_error(self, X):
        Z = self.transform(X)
        X_hat = self.inverse_transform(Z)
        return np.mean(np.sum((X - X_hat)**2, axis=1))
 
 
# --- Verification against sklearn ---
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA as skPCA
import numpy as np
 
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
X = rng.standard_normal((200, 50))
 
pca_scratch = PCA(n_components=10).fit(X)
pca_sklearn = skPCA(n_components=10).fit(X)
 
# Components may differ in sign (eigenvectors are defined up to ±)
# Check that subspaces are identical
np.testing.assert_allclose(
    np.abs(pca_scratch.components_ @ pca_sklearn.components_.T),
    np.eye(10), atol=1e-10
)
print("Subspaces match.")
print(f"Explained variance ratio: {pca_scratch.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():.3f}")
Note on sign ambiguity. Eigenvectors are defined up to a sign flip (v and -v are both valid). sklearn uses a convention (largest absolute value in each component is positive) to make results deterministic. When comparing PCA implementations, compare subspaces (via |VV^T|), not individual vectors.

✦ Geometric Interpretation
PCA rotates the coordinate system to align with the axes of maximum variance of the data ellipsoid. The covariance matrix \Sigma defines an ellipsoid {x : x^T \Sigma^{-1} x = 1}. The principal axes of this ellipsoid are the eigenvectors; the axis lengths are \sqrt{\lambda_j} (the standard deviations of the projections).
Original coordinates:       After PCA rotation:

   x₂                           PC2
    │   ●  ●                      │
    │ ● ● ●  ●                ●   │
    │  ● ●● ●●         ● ●● ●●●●●─────── PC1
    │   ● ●  ●                ●   │
    └──────────── x₁               │
                           (ellipse aligned with axes)

The first k principal components define the k-dimensional hyperplane that is closest to all data points in the least-squares sense — the best-fit flat subspace.
Projection is orthogonal. The residual x_i - \hat{x}_i is perpendicular to the subspace spanned by V_k. This is not a choice — it is forced by the least-squares criterion.

✦ Explained Variance and Choosing k
The explained variance ratio of the j-th component: \text{EVR}_j = \frac{\lambda_j}{\sum_{l=1}^d \lambda_l} = \frac{\sigma_j^2}{\sum_{l=1}^d \sigma_l^2} = \frac{\sigma_j^2}{|X_c|_F^2}
The cumulative explained variance for the first k components: \text{CEV}(k) = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^k \lambda_j}{\sum_{j=1}^d \lambda_j}
How to choose k:

Threshold: Choose smallest k such that \text{CEV}(k) \geq 0.95 (or 0.99 for lossless-ish compression).
Scree plot: Plot \lambda_j vs. j. Look for the “elbow” — the point where eigenvalues level off. Components before the elbow carry signal; after it, noise.
Reconstruction error: Plot \mathcal{R}(k) vs. k and look for diminishing returns.
Downstream task: Use cross-validation on the downstream task (classification, regression) treating k as a hyperparameter.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 
pca_full = PCA(n_components=min(X.shape)).fit(X)
evr = pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_
cev = np.cumsum(evr)
 
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
 
# Scree plot
ax1.plot(range(1, len(evr)+1), evr, 'o-', color='steelblue')
ax1.set_xlabel('Component'); ax1.set_ylabel('Explained Variance Ratio')
ax1.set_title('Scree Plot')
 
# Cumulative EVR
ax2.plot(range(1, len(cev)+1), cev, 'o-', color='coral')
ax2.axhline(0.95, color='grey', linestyle='--', label='95% threshold')
ax2.set_xlabel('Number of Components'); ax2.set_ylabel('Cumulative EVR')
ax2.set_title('Cumulative Explained Variance')
ax2.legend()
plt.tight_layout()

✦ Probabilistic PCA (PPCA)
Standard PCA has no probabilistic model — it is a purely geometric operation. Probabilistic PCA (Tipping & Bishop, 1999) embeds PCA in a latent variable model:
z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_k) x | z \sim \mathcal{N}(Wz + \mu, \sigma^2 I_d)
where W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k} is the loading matrix (to be learned).
The marginal p(x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu, WW^T + \sigma^2 I_d) is a Gaussian with a rank-k plus isotropic noise covariance.
MLE solution: As \sigma^2 \to 0, the MLE of W converges to the PCA solution (up to rotation within the principal subspace). For \sigma^2 > 0, PPCA softens the projection — points close to the decision boundary have uncertain latent coordinates.
Advantages of PPCA:

Principled handling of missing data (via EM).
Defines a proper generative model — can sample from p(x).
Model selection via marginal likelihood (avoids scree-plot heuristics).
Generalises to Factor Analysis (heteroscedastic noise: \sigma^2 I \to \Psi diagonal).

The EM algorithm for PPCA:
E-step: Compute posterior p(z|x) = \mathcal{N}(M^{-1}W^T(x-\mu),\ \sigma^2 M^{-1}) where M = W^T W + \sigma^2 I_k.
M-step: Update W and \sigma^2 using the expected sufficient statistics from the E-step.

✦ Whitening
After PCA projection to k dimensions, the components z_j = v_j^T x have variance \lambda_j — they are uncorrelated but not unit-variance.
Whitening (or sphering) additionally scales each component to unit variance: \tilde{z}_j = \frac{z_j}{\sqrt{\lambda_j}} = \frac{v_j^T x}{\sqrt{\lambda_j}}
Equivalently, the whitening transform is: \tilde{Z} = Z \Lambda_k^{-1/2} \quad \text{where } \Lambda_k = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_k)
The whitened data satisfies \frac{1}{n}\tilde{Z}^T \tilde{Z} = I_k — identity covariance in the projected space.
When whitening matters:

Preprocessing for algorithms that assume spherical data (KNN, SVMs with RBF kernel, ICA).
ICA requires whitening as a preprocessing step: uncorrelated components are a necessary (not sufficient) condition for independence.
Deep learning: batch normalisation is approximately whitening per layer.

When to avoid whitening:

If some components have near-zero variance (e.g., last PCA components), dividing by \sqrt{\lambda_j \approx 0} amplifies noise catastrophically.
In reconstruction tasks: whitening is not an isometry, so reconstruction errors become hard to interpret.


✦ Limitations of PCA
1. Linearity
PCA can only find linear subspaces. The canonical example: the Swiss roll — data on a 2D curved surface embedded in \mathbb{R}^3. PCA projects onto a 2D hyperplane, collapsing the roll and destroying the intrinsic 2D structure. Kernel PCA and UMAP handle this correctly.
2. Variance ≠ Information
PCA maximises variance. But variance is not the same as signal. If a dataset has a strong nuisance factor (e.g., batch effects in genomics, illumination in images) with high variance, PC1 captures the nuisance, not the biology/content. Always interpret principal components — do not blindly trust that PC1 is the “most important” direction.
3. Sensitivity to Scale
The covariance matrix \Sigma is sensitive to the units of each feature. A feature measured in millimetres will dominate one measured in kilometres, purely due to scale. Always standardise (divide by standard deviation) before running PCA if features are in different units. If all features are genuinely comparable (e.g., pixel intensities, gene expression after normalisation), standardisation may not be needed — use judgment.
4. No Supervision
PCA ignores labels. The direction of maximum variance may be unrelated to the direction that separates classes. Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) maximises between-class to within-class variance ratio — supervised DR. For classification tasks, LDA projections are often far more useful than PCA projections.
5. Gaussian Assumption (implicit)
PCA fully characterises the data distribution only when the data is Gaussian (for which mean and covariance are sufficient statistics). For non-Gaussian data, PCA captures second-order structure but misses higher-order dependencies. ICA addresses this by seeking statistically independent (not merely uncorrelated) components.
6. Outlier Sensitivity
The covariance matrix is a second moment — quadratically sensitive to outliers. A single point far from the cluster can dramatically shift the principal axes. Robust PCA (RPCA, Candès et al., 2011) decomposes X = L + S where L is low-rank (the PCA structure) and S is sparse (the outliers). It recovers the true principal subspace even under gross corruption.

✦ Worked Example (by hand, d = 2)
Data (already centred): X = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ -1 & 1 \ 0 & -2 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
Verify centred: column means = (0, 0). ✓
Covariance matrix (n = 4): \Sigma = \frac{1}{4} X^T X = \frac{1}{4} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & -1 \ 1 & 1 & -2 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ -1 & 1 \ 0 & -2 \ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
X^T X = \begin{pmatrix} 4+1+0+1 & 2-1+0+0 \ 2-1+0+0 & 1+1+4+0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 1 \ 1 & 6 \end{pmatrix}
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 1.5 & 0.25 \ 0.25 & 1.5 \end{pmatrix}
Eigenvalues: \det(\Sigma - \lambda I) = 0
(1.5 - \lambda)^2 - 0.0625 = 0 \implies (1.5 - \lambda) = \pm 0.25 \lambda_1 = 1.75, \quad \lambda_2 = 1.25
Eigenvectors:
For \lambda_1 = 1.75: (\Sigma - 1.75 I)v = 0 \begin{pmatrix} -0.25 & 0.25 \ 0.25 & -0.25 \end{pmatrix} v = 0 \implies v_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\1\end{pmatrix}
For \lambda_2 = 1.25: v_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\-1\end{pmatrix}
Explained variance: \text{EVR}_1 = \frac{1.75}{1.75 + 1.25} = \frac{1.75}{3} \approx 0.583
PC1 explains 58.3% of variance — modest, as expected for nearly isotropic data.
Projected scores (PC1 only): Z_1 = X v_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}3 \ 0 \ -2 \ -1\end{pmatrix}

✦ Connection to AI, ML, and Deep Learning
PCA as a Special Case of Autoencoders
A linear autoencoder — an autoencoder with linear encoder z = Wx + b and linear decoder \hat{x} = W'z + b', trained with MSE loss — converges to the PCA solution. The weight matrix W at convergence spans the same subspace as the top-k principal axes (up to rotation within that subspace).
Proof sketch. The MSE loss of the linear autoencoder is exactly the PCA reconstruction error \mathcal{R}(V_k). Both are minimised by the same subspace. The autoencoder does not necessarily recover the same orthogonal basis (the rotation within the subspace is underdetermined), but it recovers the same projection.
Implication: PCA is the simplest possible autoencoder. Deep nonlinear autoencoders are learned nonlinear generalisations of PCA.
Attention and Low-Rank Structure
The self-attention mechanism projects inputs via W_Q, W_K, W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_k} where d_k \ll d (typically d_k = d / h for h heads). This is a learned linear projection — structurally identical to PCA, but optimised for the attention task rather than variance. The “d_k-dimensional attention space” is the PCA-like bottleneck of the transformer.
Covariance and Batch Normalisation
Batch normalisation (BN) standardises each feature to zero mean and unit variance across the batch. This is diagonal whitening — it only removes per-feature variance, not cross-feature covariances. Layer normalisation normalises across features, not batch. Neither is full PCA whitening (which also removes cross-covariances), but both are motivated by the same idea: controlling the covariance structure of activations stabilises training.
PCA for Overparameterised Models
Recent work on neural collapse (Papyan et al., 2020) shows that at the end of training, the last-layer features of a deep classifier collapse onto a simplex equiangular tight frame — a structured low-dimensional manifold. The PCA of the final-layer activations reflects the class structure precisely. PCA is thus a diagnostic tool for understanding what a trained neural network has learned.
Eigenfaces and Image Compression
A classical application: apply PCA to a dataset of face images (flattened to vectors). The principal components are “eigenfaces” — the directions of maximum variance across the face dataset. Representing each face as a linear combination of the top k eigenfaces achieves lossy compression and enables face recognition via nearest-neighbour search in the low-dimensional eigenface space.
This is structurally identical to the modern “embedding + nearest neighbour” paradigm — the only difference is that modern methods use nonlinear encoders (deep networks) rather than linear PCA.
LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation
LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) constrains weight updates during fine-tuning: \Delta W = AB where A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r} and B \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d} with r \ll d. This is exactly a rank-r matrix — the same constraint PCA imposes on the data matrix. The motivation: the intrinsic dimensionality of the fine-tuning update is low (cf. the manifold hypothesis), so a full-rank update wastes parameters.
Randomised PCA for Large Models
Computing PCA on the weight matrices or activation matrices of large models requires efficient algorithms. Randomised SVD (Halko, Martinsson & Tropp, 2011) computes the top-k singular vectors of an m \times n matrix in O(mnk) — much faster than the O(mn \min(m,n)) full SVD. It works by projecting onto a random k-dimensional subspace (via Johnson-Lindenstrauss) and then running exact SVD on the small projected matrix. Used in sklearn’s TruncatedSVD and in interpretability tools for large language models.

✦ Kernel PCA Preview
PCA is linear. It cannot unfold a Swiss roll or separate two concentric rings. Kernel PCA (02.Kernel PCA) extends PCA to nonlinear manifolds by the kernel trick:
Instead of computing \Sigma = \frac{1}{n}X^T X and finding its eigenvectors, compute the kernel (Gram) matrix K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j) = \phi(x_i)^T \phi(x_j) and find its eigenvectors.
The key insight: PCA in the feature space \phi(\mathcal{X}) can be performed entirely via the kernel matrix K without ever computing \phi(x) explicitly — even when \phi maps to an infinite-dimensional space (RBF kernel).
The j-th kernel PC score for x_i is: z_{ij} = \sum_{l=1}^n \alpha_{lj} k(x_l, x_i)
where \alpha_j is the j-th eigenvector of the centred kernel matrix \tilde{K}.

✦ Exit Criterion

You know this when: you can derive PCA from both the maximum-variance and minimum-reconstruction-error formulations, prove they are equivalent, implement it via SVD in ~20 lines of NumPy, explain exactly why SVD is preferred over eigendecomposing \Sigma, describe what whitening does and when it is dangerous, and state precisely what PCA cannot do and why.


✦ References
