04.ML/05.Probabilistic/02.Markov-Models.title: 02.Markov Models
04.ML/05.Probabilistic/02.Markov-Models.content:
“The future is independent of the past, given the present.” — The Markov property, in plain English


✦ Why This Note Exists
Before we can talk about speech recognition, part-of-speech tagging, biological sequence alignment, or the underpinnings of modern reinforcement learning, we need a principled way to model sequences. The Markov model is that foundation.
This note builds the full machinery — from the basic chain to Hidden Markov Models and their three canonical algorithms — with every equation derived, every assumption named, and every connection to the broader ML map made explicit.
Prerequisites: 03.Probability Review · 01.The Learning Problem
Feeds into: 01.The RL Problem · 01.Bayesian Networks · (eventually) Transformers and attention

✦ The Core Problem: Sequential Data
Most of classical ML assumes i.i.d. data: each (x_i, y_i) is drawn independently from the same distribution. That assumption collapses the moment you have:

A sentence (each word depends on preceding words)
A time series (stock prices, sensor readings)
A DNA strand (nucleotide probabilities shift with context)
A trajectory in an RL environment

You need a model that respects temporal or positional structure. Markov models are the principled answer.

✦ Part 1 — The Markov Chain
1.1 The Markov Property
Let X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_T be a sequence of random variables taking values in a finite state space \mathcal{S} = {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_N}.
Definition (Markov Property, first-order): P(X_t \mid X_{t-1}, X_{t-2}, \ldots, X_1) = P(X_t \mid X_{t-1})
The present state X_{t-1} is a sufficient statistic for predicting the future. The entire history is irrelevant — all relevant information has already been “compressed” into the current state.

Notebook margin: The first-order assumption is a modelling choice, not a law of nature. You can always extend to k-th order: P(X_t \mid X_{t-k}, \ldots, X_{t-1}). A k-th order chain over |\mathcal{S}| states is equivalent to a first-order chain over |\mathcal{S}|^k states, so we lose no generality by studying first-order chains.

1.2 The Transition Matrix
Assuming time homogeneity (transition probabilities don’t change with t), we define: A_{ij} = P(X_t = s_j \mid X_{t-1} = s_i), \quad A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}
Properties:

A_{ij} \geq 0 for all i, j
\sum_j A_{ij} = 1 for all i — each row is a probability distribution
A is called a stochastic matrix (or row-stochastic matrix)

The initial distribution \pi_0 \in \mathbb{R}^N, where (\pi_0)_i = P(X_1 = s_i), completes the model specification.
1.3 Computing Sequence Probabilities
The joint probability of a sequence x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_T follows directly from the chain rule + Markov property: P(X_1 = x_1, \ldots, X_T = x_T) = P(X_1 = x_1) \prod_{t=2}^T P(X_t = x_t \mid X_{t-1} = x_{t-1}) = (\pi_0)_{x_1} \prod_{t=2}^T A_{x_{t-1}, x_t}
This is a product of matrix entries — beautifully simple.
1.4 The Stationary Distribution
After many steps, does the chain “settle” into a stable distribution?
Definition: A distribution \pi^_ is stationary (invariant) if: \pi^_ = \pi^* A \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad (\pi^_)^T = A^T (\pi^_)^T \pi^* is the left eigenvector of A corresponding to eigenvalue 1 (which always exists for stochastic matrices by the Perron-Frobenius theorem).
Convergence: If the chain is irreducible (every state reachable from every state) and aperiodic (no cycles), then for any initial distribution \pi_0: \lim_{t \to \infty} \pi_0 A^t = \pi^*

Example — A simple 2-state weather model:
States: {Sunny, Rainy}, transition matrix: A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.1 \ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix} Row 1: if sunny today → 90% sunny tomorrow, 10% rainy.
Stationary distribution: solve \pi^* A = \pi^_, \pi^__S + \pi^__R = 1: \pi^__S = 0.833, \quad \pi^*_R = 0.167 On a long enough timescale, ~83% of days are sunny regardless of today’s weather.


✦ Part 2 — Hidden Markov Models
2.1 Motivation: When the State Is Not Observed
In a plain Markov chain, the state X_t is directly observed. But in many real problems:

In speech recognition, the underlying phoneme is hidden; we observe an acoustic signal.
In POS tagging, the underlying grammar tag (noun, verb, …) is hidden; we observe words.
In finance, “market regime” (bull/bear) is latent; we observe returns.

The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) separates the latent state sequence from the observed sequence.
2.2 Formal Definition
An HMM is a tuple \lambda = (A, B, \pi):



































SymbolNameDefinition\mathcal{S} = {s_1, \ldots, s_N}Hidden state spaceLatent states\mathcal{V} = {v_1, \ldots, v_M}Observation vocabularyObservable symbolsA \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}Transition matrixA_{ij} = P(z_t = s_j \mid z_{t-1} = s_i)B \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M}Emission matrixB_{ik} = P(x_t = v_k \mid z_t = s_i)\pi \in \mathbb{R}^NInitial distribution\pi_i = P(z_1 = s_i)
The generative process:

Sample initial state z_1 \sim \pi
Emit observation x_t \sim B_{z_t} (the z_t-th row of B)
Transition to z_{t+1} \sim A_{z_t} (the z_t-th row of A)
Repeat from step 2

The joint distribution: P(x_{1:T}, z_{1:T}) = \pi_{z_1} \prod_{t=1}^T B_{z_t, x_t} \prod_{t=2}^T A_{z_{t-1}, z_t}
Graphical structure:

  z_1  -->  z_2  -->  z_3  --> ... -->  z_T
   |          |          |                |
   v          v          v                v
  x_1        x_2        x_3             x_T

Hidden states form a Markov chain (top).
Each state independently emits an observation (bottom).

2.3 The Three Problems of HMMs
Rabiner (1989) identified three canonical problems that must be solved for HMMs to be useful in practice. Every algorithm below solves exactly one of them.





























#ProblemQuestionAlgorithm1EvaluationGiven \lambda and observations x_{1:T}, what is P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda)?Forward Algorithm2DecodingGiven \lambda and x_{1:T}, what is the most likely state sequence z_{1:T}^*?Viterbi Algorithm3LearningGiven x_{1:T}, find \lambda^* = \arg\max_\lambda P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda)Baum-Welch (EM)

✦ Part 3 — Problem 1: Evaluation (The Forward Algorithm)
3.1 Why Naïve Computation Fails
The observation likelihood is: P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda) = \sum_{z_{1:T}} P(x_{1:T}, z_{1:T} \mid \lambda)
Summing over all N^T state sequences is O(N^T) — exponential in sequence length. For N = 10, T = 100: 10^{100} terms. Completely intractable.
3.2 The Forward Variable
Define the forward variable: \alpha_t(i) := P(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_t, z_t = s_i \mid \lambda) “The probability of seeing the partial observation sequence x_1, \ldots, x_t and being in state s_i at time t.“
3.3 The Forward Recursion
Initialisation (t = 1): \alpha_1(i) = \pi_i \cdot B_{i, x_1}
Recursion (t = 2, \ldots, T): \boxed{\alpha_t(j) = \left[ \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_{t-1}(i) \cdot A_{ij} \right] \cdot B_{j, x_t}}
The bracket sums over all ways to arrive in state j at time t, then multiplies by the emission probability of x_t from state j.
Termination: P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_T(i)
Complexity: O(N^2 T) — polynomial. We’ve converted exponential summation into dynamic programming.

Derivation sketch:
\alpha_t(j) = P(x_{1:t}, z_t = j) = \sum_i P(x_{1:t}, z_{t-1} = i, z_t = j) = \sum_i P(x_t \mid z_t = j) \cdot P(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i) \cdot P(x_{1:t-1}, z_{t-1} = i) = B_{j,x_t} \sum_i A_{ij} \cdot \alpha_{t-1}(i) \qquad \square

3.4 Numerical Issues: Log-Space Computation
Products of small probabilities underflow to zero rapidly. Standard fix: work in log-space using the log-sum-exp trick: \log \sum_i e^{a_i} = a^* + \log \sum_i e^{a_i - a^_}, \quad a^_ = \max_i a_i

Notebook margin: This same trick appears in logistic regression (softmax), language model decoding, and variational inference. It’s one of the half-dozen truly universal numerical tools in ML.


✦ Part 4 — Problem 2: Decoding (The Viterbi Algorithm)
4.1 What We Want
Find the single most probable state sequence given the observations: z^*_{1:T} = \arg\max_{z_{1:T}} P(z_{1:T} \mid x_{1:T}, \lambda) = \arg\max_{z_{1:T}} P(z_{1:T}, x_{1:T} \mid \lambda)
Note: This is the joint MAP over the entire sequence — it is not the sequence of individually most probable states \arg\max_{z_t} P(z_t \mid x_{1:T}) at each time step (those are obtained by the backward algorithm and do not form a coherent sequence).
4.2 The Viterbi Variable
Define: \delta_t(i) := \max_{z_{1:t-1}} P(z_1, \ldots, z_{t-1}, z_t = s_i, x_1, \ldots, x_t \mid \lambda) “The probability of the most likely path ending in state s_i at time t, given observations so far.”
To recover the actual path, store the backpointer: \psi_t(j) := \arg\max_i \left[ \delta_{t-1}(i) \cdot A_{ij} \right]
4.3 The Viterbi Recursion
Initialisation: \delta_1(i) = \pi_i \cdot B_{i, x_1}, \quad \psi_1(i) = 0
Recursion (t = 2, \ldots, T): \boxed{\delta_t(j) = \max_i \left[ \delta_{t-1}(i) \cdot A_{ij} \right] \cdot B_{j, x_t}} \psi_t(j) = \arg\max_i \left[ \delta_{t-1}(i) \cdot A_{ij} \right]
Termination: P^* = \max_i \delta_T(i), \quad z_T^* = \arg\max_i \delta_T(i)
Backtracking (t = T-1, \ldots, 1): z_t^* = \psi_{t+1}(z_{t+1}^*)
Complexity: O(N^2 T) — identical to the forward algorithm, because we replaced \sum with \max.

Insight: Viterbi is just the forward algorithm with \sum \to \max. This swap is not cosmetic — it changes the semantics entirely from marginalisation to optimisation. The same substitution appears in belief propagation (sum-product vs. max-product) and in dynamic programming generally (shortest path vs. counting paths).


Example — POS Tagging:
Sentence: “flies like arrows”
States: {NOUN, VERB, PREP}
The word “flies” can be NOUN (“the flies”) or VERB (“he flies”). “like” can be VERB or PREP. Viterbi finds the globally most coherent assignment — e.g., VERB-PREP-NOUN — using transition probabilities between POS tags (which encode grammar) and emission probabilities (which encode lexical likelihood).


✦ Part 5 — Problem 3: Learning (Baum-Welch / EM)
5.1 The Problem Setup
Given: Observation sequences x_{1:T} (the state sequence z_{1:T} is latent).
Find: \lambda^* = (A^_, B^_, \pi^*) = \arg\max_\lambda P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda).
Direct MLE is intractable because the state sequence is hidden. This is exactly the structure EM was designed for.
Recall from 03.Probability Review: EM maximises the ELBO (Evidence Lower Bound): \log P(x \mid \lambda) \geq \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}[\log P(x, z \mid \lambda)] - \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}[\log q(z)]
In the E-step, set q(z) = P(z \mid x, \lambda_{\text{old}}). In the M-step, maximise the expected complete-data log-likelihood.
5.2 The Backward Variable
To compute the posterior P(z_{1:T} \mid x_{1:T}, \lambda), we need both a forward and a backward pass.
Define the backward variable: \beta_t(i) := P(x_{t+1}, x_{t+2}, \ldots, x_T \mid z_t = s_i, \lambda) “The probability of the future observations x_{t+1:T}, given that we’re in state s_i at time t.”
Initialisation: \beta_T(i) = 1 \quad \text{for all } i
Recursion (t = T-1, \ldots, 1): \boxed{\beta_t(i) = \sum_j A_{ij} \cdot B_{j, x_{t+1}} \cdot \beta_{t+1}(j)}
5.3 The Posterior Statistics
Using both \alpha and \beta, we can compute the two key posterior quantities:
State occupancy — probability of being in state i at time t: \gamma_t(i) := P(z_t = s_i \mid x_{1:T}, \lambda) = \frac{\alpha_t(i) \cdot \beta_t(i)}{\sum_k \alpha_t(k) \cdot \beta_t(k)}
Transition occupancy — probability of transitioning i \to j at time t: \xi_t(i,j) := P(z_t = s_i, z_{t+1} = s_j \mid x_{1:T}, \lambda) = \frac{\alpha_t(i) \cdot A_{ij} \cdot B_{j, x_{t+1}} \cdot \beta_{t+1}(j)}{\sum_{i'}\sum_{j'} \alpha_t(i') \cdot A_{i'j'} \cdot B_{j', x_{t+1}} \cdot \beta_{t+1}(j')}
5.4 The M-Step: Parameter Re-estimation
The Baum-Welch re-estimation equations are the M-step closed-form solutions (derivable by Lagrange multipliers subject to the stochastic constraints):
\hat{\pi}_i = \gamma_1(i)
\hat{A}_{ij} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \xi_t(i,j)}{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \gamma_t(i)} \quad = \frac{\text{expected number of } i \to j \text{ transitions}}{\text{expected time in state } i}
\hat{B}_{ik} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^T \gamma_t(i) \cdot \mathbf{1}[x_t = v_k]}{\sum_{t=1}^T \gamma_t(i)} \quad = \frac{\text{expected time in state } i \text{ emitting } v_k}{\text{expected time in state } i}
5.5 Convergence Properties

Guaranteed: Each EM iteration increases P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda) (or leaves it unchanged).
Not guaranteed: Convergence to the global maximum. HMM likelihood surfaces are non-convex with multiple local optima.
Practical fix: Multiple random initialisations; choose the run with highest final likelihood.


The EM lens: Baum-Welch is EM with:

Latent variable: state sequence z_{1:T}
E-step: run Forward-Backward to compute \gamma_t, \xi_t (soft assignments)
M-step: plug into re-estimation formulas (weighted MLE with soft counts) Compare to K-Means (hard assignments) vs. GMM (soft assignments). Baum-Welch is the sequential analogue of GMM’s EM.



✦ Part 6 — Continuous Observations
So far, x_t has been discrete (a vocabulary symbol). For real-valued observations (e.g., acoustic feature vectors in speech), replace the discrete emission matrix B with a continuous density:
b_i(x_t) = \mathcal{N}(x_t \mid \mu_i, \Sigma_i) \quad \text{or} \quad b_i(x_t) = \sum_m c_{im} \mathcal{N}(x_t \mid \mu_{im}, \Sigma_{im})
The Gaussian Mixture emission is standard in speech recognition. The M-step updates for \mu_i, \Sigma_i are just weighted MLE updates — same structure as GMM.

✦ Part 7 — Connection to AI and Deep Learning
7.1 Classical Applications



































ApplicationHidden StatesObservationsSpeech recognitionPhoneme sequenceAcoustic feature vectors (MFCCs)POS taggingGrammar tag sequenceWord tokensBiological sequencesFunctional region (exon/intron)NucleotidesGesture recognitionGesture phaseAccelerometer readingsFinancial regime detectionMarket regime (bull/bear/volatile)Log-returns
7.2 HMMs as a Precursor to Deep Sequence Models
HMMs encode a specific inductive bias:

Markov assumption: only one step of memory
Parametric emissions: fixed functional form (Gaussian, multinomial)
Fixed state space: N states defined ahead of time

Modern sequence models relax all three assumptions:

























LimitationHow DL addressed it1-step memoryRNNs/LSTMs: learn arbitrary-length memory via gated hidden state h_tParametric emissionNeural language models: learn emission distribution from dataFixed discrete statesContinuous latent spaces: VAEs, RNNs with dense hidden state h_t \in \mathbb{R}^dMarkov propertyTransformers: full attention over all positions — explicitly non-Markovian
Yet HMMs remain the conceptual foundation. Understanding the three HMM problems — evaluation, decoding, learning — gives you the right vocabulary for understanding attention (soft assignment over positions), CTC decoding (sequence alignment), and the ELBO in VAEs (same EM structure, continuous latent variables).
7.3 HMMs in the Modern ML Stack
HMM (1960s–1990s)
  │
  ├── Recurrent Neural Networks (1986, Elman)
  │     └── LSTM (1997, Hochreiter & Schmidhuber)
  │           └── GRU (2014) → seq2seq → Attention → Transformer (2017)
  │
  ├── CRF (2001) → BiLSTM-CRF (still used in NER)
  │
  └── Structured State Spaces (S4, Mamba, 2021–2023)
        — HMM dynamics as a continuous-time model


Mamba (2023) explicitly revisits selective state-space models, a direct generalisation of HMMs, and achieves Transformer-level performance with linear complexity. HMMs are not historical curiosities — they are the theoretical backbone of an active research direction.

7.4 RL Connection
The HMM generative model (A, B) is structurally identical to a Partially Observable MDP (POMDP):

Transition matrix A ↔ transition function P(s' \mid s, a)
Emission matrix B ↔ observation function P(o \mid s)

The Viterbi algorithm for decoding corresponds to finding the optimal policy in a degenerate POMDP. This connection deepens when we study RL with partial observability — the belief state maintained by the forward algorithm becomes the “sufficient statistic for planning.”

✦ Part 8 — Illustrated Summary
The Forward-Backward Lattice
Time:      t=1          t=2          t=3        ...   t=T
           ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐         ┌──────┐
State s_1  │α₁(1) │───▶│α₂(1) │───▶│α₃(1) │ ───▶   │αT(1) │
           └──────┘    └──────┘    └──────┘         └──────┘
                \    /        \    /
           ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐         ┌──────┐
State s_2  │α₁(2) │───▶│α₂(2) │───▶│α₃(2) │ ───▶   │αT(2) │
           └──────┘    └──────┘    └──────┘         └──────┘
                 ▲           ▲           ▲                 ▲
Observations:  x_1          x_2          x_3              x_T

Forward pass: → propagates probability left-to-right
Backward pass: ← propagates probability right-to-left
Both passes together: give full posterior γ_t(i) at every node

The Three Algorithms at a Glance
           Forward            Viterbi            Baum-Welch
           ───────            ───────            ──────────
Goal:    P(x_{1:T}|λ)      best z*_{1:T}       best λ*

How:     sum over paths    max over paths       EM: E=Forward-Backward
                                                    M=re-estimation

Replace: sum → sum         sum → max            iterate until convergence

Output:  scalar            sequence             new parameters (A,B,π)

Cost:    O(N²T)            O(N²T)              O(N²T) per iteration


✦ Complexity and Practical Notes



































OperationComplexityNotesForward algorithmO(N^2 T)Compute P(x_{1:T})Backward algorithmO(N^2 T)Needed for Baum-Welch E-stepViterbi decodingO(N^2 T)Path backtracking adds O(NT) memoryBaum-Welch (per iteration)O(N^2 T)Often needs 50–200 iterationsState space size NN^2 in complexityN is a key hyperparameter; typically 5–100
Implementation notes for Python:

Work in log-space throughout; use scipy.special.logsumexp
Multiple restarts: train 10 random models, keep the best
hmmlearn is the standard Python library; understand it well enough to reimplement it
For large-scale applications (speech), deep learning replaced HMMs; but the decoding algorithms survive as postprocessing steps


✦ Exit Criterion

You know this when: you can derive the forward recursion from first principles (chain rule + Markov property), explain why Viterbi uses \max where forward uses \sum and what that changes semantically, implement Baum-Welch’s E-step from scratch in NumPy, and describe exactly how HMMs connect to RNNs and POMDPs.

Concrete exercises:

Implement the 3-state weather HMM from scratch: initialise A, B, \pi randomly; run Baum-Welch on a synthetic sequence; verify the learned parameters recover the ground truth.
Implement Viterbi for POS tagging on a tiny corpus. Compare the Viterbi sequence to the sequence of per-step argmax posteriors \arg\max_i \gamma_t(i) — show they differ.
Derive the M-step update for \hat{A}_{ij} using Lagrange multipliers on the constraint \sum_j A_{ij} = 1.


✦ References

04.ML/05.Probabilistic/03.Gaussian-Proce.title: 03.Gaussian Processes
04.ML/05.Probabilistic/03.Gaussian-Proce.content:
“A Gaussian process is a probability distribution over functions, such that any finite collection of function values has a joint Gaussian distribution.” — Rasmussen & Williams, 2006


✦ Why This Note Exists
Every model we’ve built so far has been parametric: fix a functional form, learn a finite-dimensional parameter vector \theta. A Gaussian process takes a different path entirely — it places a prior directly over the space of functions, then conditions on data to obtain a posterior over functions.
This sounds abstract. It is not. The payoff is a model that:

makes predictions with calibrated uncertainty — the posterior variance tells you where it doesn’t know
incorporates prior knowledge about function structure through kernel design
updates exactly via Bayes’ theorem, no MCMC needed (for regression)
subsumes kernel ridge regression, spline smoothing, and RBF-kernel SVMs as special cases

GPs sit at the intersection of Bayesian inference, kernel methods, and functional analysis. Understanding them sharpens your intuition for everything that comes after — neural network weight-space vs. function-space perspectives, neural tangent kernels, and Bayesian deep learning.
Prerequisites: 03.Probability Review · 04.Support Vector Machines (kernel trick) · Linear Algebra (eigendecomposition, positive semi-definiteness)
Feeds into: 01.Kernel Methods · 05.Hyperparameter Tuning (Bayesian optimisation) · Neural Tangent Kernel (advanced)

✦ Part 1 — From Parametric to Non-Parametric
1.1 The Parametric Bottleneck
In Bayesian linear regression, we place a prior on the weight vector w \in \mathbb{R}^d: w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \alpha^{-1} I), \quad y = w^T \phi(x) + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)
This is expressive — but the function class is fixed by the choice of basis \phi(x). If you pick d = 10 basis functions, you’ve committed to a 10-dimensional function space. You can extend \phi (polynomial, RBF, Fourier features…) but you’re always choosing in advance.
The weight-space view: place a prior on w, integrate out w to get a distribution over function values.
The function-space view: place the prior directly on f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}.
The key insight is that these are equivalent when the prior on w is Gaussian — and the function-space view generalises beyond finite-dimensional w.
1.2 What Does a Prior Over Functions Mean?
A prior over functions seems infinite-dimensional and unwieldy. The Gaussian process sidesteps this through a consistency condition:
Definition (Gaussian Process): A Gaussian process is a collection of random variables {f(x) : x \in \mathcal{X}} such that for any finite set of inputs {x_1, \ldots, x_n} \subset \mathcal{X}, the joint distribution: \begin{pmatrix} f(x_1) \ \vdots \ f(x_n) \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}, K) where m_i = m(x_i) and K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j).
We write: f \sim \mathcal{GP}(m(x),, k(x, x'))
The GP is completely specified by:

Mean function m(x) = \mathbb{E}[f(x)] — often set to zero a priori
Covariance function (kernel) k(x, x') = \text{Cov}(f(x), f(x'))


The key move: you never have to work with an infinite-dimensional object. Any computation with a GP reduces to a finite-dimensional multivariate Gaussian computation on the inputs you actually care about. The Kolmogorov extension theorem guarantees that a consistent family of finite-dimensional Gaussians uniquely defines a valid stochastic process.


✦ Part 2 — The Kernel: Encoding Prior Beliefs
2.1 The Kernel as a Similarity Measure
The kernel k(x, x') encodes our prior belief about how correlated f(x) and f(x') are. If k(x, x') is large, we believe f(x) and f(x') should take similar values.
This is precisely the kernel trick from SVMs — but now it has a direct probabilistic interpretation: k is the prior covariance between function values.
Validity condition (Mercer’s theorem): k is a valid kernel iff the Gram matrix K with K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j) is positive semi-definite for all finite input sets. Equivalently, k(x, x') = \langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle_\mathcal{H} for some (possibly infinite-dimensional) feature map \phi into a Hilbert space \mathcal{H}.
2.2 Standard Kernels
Each kernel encodes a different structural assumption about f:
Squared Exponential (RBF / Gaussian) Kernel
k_{\text{SE}}(x, x') = \sigma_f^2 \exp!\left(-\frac{|x - x'|^2}{2\ell^2}\right)

Hyperparameters: \sigma_f^2 (output scale), \ell (length-scale)
Encodes: infinitely differentiable, very smooth functions
Length-scale \ell: controls how quickly the function varies. Small \ell → wiggly functions; large \ell → smooth, slowly varying functions
Feature map: corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature space (Fourier features expansion)
Caution: too smooth for many real phenomena — geological, financial, biological data often has rougher structure

Matérn Kernel
k_{\nu}(x, x') = \frac{2^{1-\nu}}{\Gamma(\nu)} \left(\frac{\sqrt{2\nu} |x-x'|}{\ell}\right)^\nu K_\nu!\left(\frac{\sqrt{2\nu}|x-x'|}{\ell}\right) where K_\nu is a modified Bessel function.

Parameter \nu: controls differentiability. \nu = 1/2 → once-differentiable (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck); \nu = 3/2 → twice; \nu = 5/2 → three times; \nu \to \infty → SE kernel
Why it matters: \nu = 5/2 is the default recommendation in practice — smoother than OU, less pathologically smooth than SE
Special cases:

\nu = 1/2: k(r) = \sigma^2 e^{-r/\ell} — exponential kernel, continuous but not differentiable
\nu = 3/2: k(r) = \sigma^2(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}r}{\ell})\exp(-\frac{\sqrt{3}r}{\ell})



Periodic Kernel
k_{\text{per}}(x, x') = \sigma_f^2 \exp!\left(-\frac{2\sin^2(\pi|x-x'|/p)}{\ell^2}\right) Encodes exactly periodic functions with period p. Combine with SE kernel (multiply) to get functions that are approximately periodic with decaying coherence — standard for seasonal time series.
Linear Kernel
k_{\text{lin}}(x, x') = \sigma_b^2 + \sigma_v^2 (x - c)(x' - c) GP with this kernel is equivalent to Bayesian linear regression through the point c. Useful as a component in additive kernel decompositions.
Rational Quadratic Kernel
k_{\text{RQ}}(x, x') = \sigma_f^2\left(1 + \frac{|x-x'|^2}{2\alpha\ell^2}\right)^{-\alpha} A scale mixture of SE kernels with different length-scales. As \alpha \to \infty, recovers SE. Useful when the signal varies at multiple scales.
2.3 Kernel Engineering
Kernels compose:

Sum: k = k_1 + k_2 → function is a sum of two independent GPs (additive structure)
Product: k = k_1 \cdot k_2 → modulation; e.g., periodic \times SE = locally periodic
Composition: k_{\text{SE}}(g(x), g(x')) for learned feature maps g → deep kernels, connection to deep learning


Notebook margin — the kernel as a scientist’s voice: When you choose a kernel, you are making a scientific claim about the structure of f. SE says “I believe f is very smooth.” Matérn-5/2 says “I believe f is three-times differentiable but not more.” Periodic says “I believe there is a repeating structure with period p.” The posterior will update these beliefs given data — but the kernel determines what it’s even possible to learn.


✦ Part 3 — GP Regression (Exact Inference)
3.1 The Setup
Observed data: \mathcal{D} = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n where y_i = f(x_i) + \varepsilon_i, \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_n^2)
Prior: f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k(x, x')) (zero mean WLOG)
Goal: compute the posterior p(f \mid \mathcal{D}) and the predictive distribution p(f_* \mid x__, \mathcal{D}) at new test points x__.
3.2 The Joint Prior
Let \mathbf{f} = (f(x_1), \ldots, f(x_n))^T and f_* = f(x__). By the GP definition: \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{y} \ f__ \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}!\left(\mathbf{0},, \begin{pmatrix} K(X, X) + \sigma_n^2 I & K(X, x__) \ K(x__, X) & k(x__, x__) \end{pmatrix}\right)
where:

K(X, X) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}: Gram matrix, K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)
K(X, x__) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}: covariance between training inputs and test point, [K(X, x__)]_i = k(x_i, x_*)
k(x__, x__): prior variance at test point

3.3 The Posterior Predictive Distribution
Using the Gaussian conditioning formula (the fundamental operation of all Gaussian inference):

Lemma (Conditional Gaussian): If \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{a} \ \mathbf{b} \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}!\left(\begin{pmatrix} \mu_a \ \mu_b \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_{aa} & \Sigma_{ab} \ \Sigma_{ba} & \Sigma_{bb} \end{pmatrix}\right) then: \mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{b} \sim \mathcal{N}!\left(\mu_a + \Sigma_{ab}\Sigma_{bb}^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - \mu_b),\ \Sigma_{aa} - \Sigma_{ab}\Sigma_{bb}^{-1}\Sigma_{ba}\right)

Applying this with \mathbf{a} = f_*, \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{y}:
\boxed{f_* \mid x__, X, \mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu__, \sigma_*^2)}
\mu_* = K(x_*, X),[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1},\mathbf{y}
\sigma__^2 = k(x__, x__) - K(x__, X),[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1},K(X, x_*)
This is the complete solution. No approximation. Exact Bayesian inference in closed form.
3.4 Interpretation — What These Equations Say
The mean \mu_*: \mu_* = K(x_*, X) \underbrace{[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1} \mathbf{y}}_{\alpha}
This is a linear combination of training outputs, weighted by the covariance between x__ and each training input. Nearby training points (large k(x__, x_i)) contribute more. This is kernel regression — the GP mean is identical to kernel ridge regression with \lambda = \sigma_n^2 / \sigma_f^2.
The variance \sigma_*^2: \sigma__^2 = \underbrace{k(x__, x__)}_{\text{prior variance}} - \underbrace{K(x__, X)[K + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1}K(X, x_*)}_{\text{variance reduction from data}}
The posterior variance is the prior variance minus what we learned from the data. The second term is always non-negative (positive semi-definiteness of K), so data never increases uncertainty. Crucially:

At a training input x_i: \sigma_*^2 \to 0 as \sigma_n^2 \to 0 (exact fit)
Far from all training data: \sigma__^2 \approx k(x__, x_*) (reverts to prior)


Worked example — 1D regression:
Prior: f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_{\text{SE}}) with \ell = 1, \sigma_f^2 = 1, \sigma_n^2 = 0.1
Training data: 5 points sampled from \sin(x) + \mathcal{N}(0, 0.1)
The posterior mean threads through the data. The posterior variance (shaded region) is:

narrow near training points (we’ve observed f there)
wide in regions with no data (we genuinely don’t know)
wider than the noise level even at training points (because we know y = f + \varepsilon, not f directly)

This is calibrated uncertainty — the 95% confidence band actually contains 95% of future observations.

3.5 Predicting at Multiple Test Points
For a vector of test points X_* = (x_{_1}, \ldots, x_{_m}): \mathbf{f}__ \mid X__, X, \mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_*, \Sigma__) \boldsymbol{\mu}__ = K(X__, X)[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1}\mathbf{y} \Sigma__ = K(X__, X__) - K(X__, X)[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1}K(X, X__)
The full posterior covariance \Sigma_* captures correlation between predictions at different test points — this is something no other standard regression model directly provides.

✦ Part 4 — Computational Complexity and the O(n^3) Wall
4.1 The Bottleneck
The posterior requires computing [K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1}. For n training points:

Matrix inversion: O(n^3) via Cholesky decomposition
Storage: O(n^2) for the kernel matrix
Prediction: O(n) per test point (after precomputing \alpha), O(n^2) for variance

For n = 10^3: trivial. For n = 10^4: feasible. For n = 10^5: painful. For n = 10^6: intractable.
In practice: use the Cholesky decomposition L L^T = K + \sigma_n^2 I (numerically stable, also gives O(n^3) but with a smaller constant than naive inversion).
4.2 Approximate GP Methods



































MethodIdeaComplexitySparse GPs (Inducing Points)Summarise n points with m \ll n inducing points ZO(nm^2)FITC / VFEVariational lower bound on the marginal likelihoodO(nm^2)Random Fourier FeaturesApproximate k(x, x') \approx \phi(x)^T\phi(x'), finite D featuresO(nD)State-space GPsConvert GP to a linear dynamical system; Kalman filterO(n) for 1D inputsStructured kernel interpolation (SKI)Interpolate onto a grid; FFT-based matrix-vector productsO(n \log n)
The inducing point / variational approach (Titsias 2009, Hensman et al. 2013) is the modern standard. The m inducing points Z are learnable — optimise them jointly with the hyperparameters.

Notebook margin — why Cholesky and not direct inversion? Numerically, K is often nearly singular (especially with the SE kernel and nearby points). Cholesky decomposition is numerically stable, reveals singularity, gives the log-determinant cheaply (sum of log diagonal), and allows efficient solves. Always use Cholesky for GP computations. Never call np.linalg.inv on a kernel matrix.


✦ Part 5 — Learning Hyperparameters: Marginal Likelihood
5.1 The Problem
The GP prior k(x, x'; \theta) has hyperparameters \theta — e.g., \theta = (\ell, \sigma_f^2, \sigma_n^2) for the SE kernel. How do we choose them?
Not cross-validation: too expensive (each CV fold requires an O(n^3) solve).
Bayesian answer: marginalise over the latent function f (already done in the posterior), then maximise the marginal likelihood p(\mathbf{y} \mid X, \theta) over \theta.
5.2 The Log Marginal Likelihood
\log p(\mathbf{y} \mid X, \theta) = -\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^T (K_\theta + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1}\mathbf{y} - \frac{1}{2}\log|K_\theta + \sigma_n^2 I| - \frac{n}{2}\log 2\pi
Three terms:

-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^T (K_\theta + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1}\mathbf{y} — data fit: how well the model fits the observations
-\frac{1}{2}\log|K_\theta + \sigma_n^2 I| — complexity penalty (Occam factor): penalises models that can explain too many datasets
-\frac{n}{2}\log 2\pi — normalisation constant

The marginal likelihood automatically balances fit and complexity — models that overfit have high fit but are penalised by the log-determinant term. This is automatic Occam’s razor.
5.3 Optimisation
Differentiate with respect to \theta and use gradient-based optimisation (L-BFGS or Adam): \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_j} \log p(\mathbf{y} \mid X, \theta) = \frac{1}{2} \text{tr}!\left[(K^{-1}\mathbf{y}\mathbf{y}^T K^{-1} - K^{-1})\frac{\partial K}{\partial \theta_j}\right]
where K = K_\theta + \sigma_n^2 I.
Gradient cost: O(n^3) per evaluation — same as the posterior. Run from multiple random initialisations (marginal likelihood is non-convex in \theta).

What the marginal likelihood does to hyperparameters:
If \ell is too small: the model is wiggly, many functions fit the data, large |K|, large complexity penalty.
If \ell is too large: the model is too smooth, fits the data poorly, large data-fit term.
The marginal likelihood finds the length-scale where these forces balance — the one that best explains the data without overfitting. This is Bayesian model selection in action.


✦ Part 6 — GP Classification
For binary classification, y \in {0, 1} and we want: p(y_* = 1 \mid x__, \mathcal{D}) = \int \sigma(f__), p(f_* \mid x__, \mathcal{D}), df__
The GP prior is the same — but now the likelihood is Bernoulli, not Gaussian. The posterior p(f \mid X, \mathbf{y}) is no longer Gaussian. Exact inference is intractable.
Approximate inference methods:

























MethodIdeaQualityLaplace approximationFit a Gaussian at the posterior modeFast, good for unimodal posteriorsExpectation Propagation (EP)Approximate each factor in the likelihood with a GaussianMore accurate than LaplaceVariational inference (SVGP)Variational lower bound, scalable with inducing pointsModern standard for large-scale GP classification
Multi-class: one GP per class (one-vs-rest) with softmax likelihood, or multi-output GP.

✦ Part 7 — Connection to Other Models
7.1 GP = Kernel Ridge Regression (in the noise-free limit)
The GP posterior mean: \mu_* = K(x_*, X)[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1}\mathbf{y} is exactly the kernel ridge regression predictor with regularisation parameter \lambda = \sigma_n^2 / \sigma_f^2. GPs give kernel ridge regression a Bayesian interpretation — and add uncertainty quantification for free.
7.2 GP = Infinite-Width Neural Networks
Neal (1994) showed: a single-hidden-layer neural network with i.i.d. priors on weights converges in distribution to a GP as the number of hidden units \to \infty. The kernel is determined by the activation function.
More recently (Lee et al. 2018, Jacot et al. 2018): deep networks trained with gradient descent correspond (in the infinite-width limit) to kernel regression with the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK). This is a GP in function space. The NTK connection is an active research area linking GPs to deep learning theory.
7.3 GP Prior on the Parameters of a Deep Network
In deep kernel learning, replace the hand-crafted feature map with a neural network: k(x, x') = k_{\text{base}}(g_\theta(x), g_\theta(x')) where g_\theta is a neural network. Jointly optimise \theta and GP hyperparameters via marginal likelihood. This combines the representational power of deep networks with GP uncertainty quantification — a practically important model class.
7.4 GP and SVMs
The SVM with RBF kernel and GP regression with SE kernel share the same kernel function. The difference:

SVM: finds a maximum-margin classifier; no probabilistic output; sparse (support vectors)
GP: full posterior distribution over f; uncertainty quantification; not sparse

For classification: GP gives calibrated class probabilities; SVM gives a hard boundary. The GP is preferred when uncertainty matters (medical diagnosis, active learning, safety-critical systems).
7.5 GP in Bayesian Optimisation
This is the primary industrial application of GPs today — used inside every major AutoML system and neural architecture search tool.
Setup: You want to minimise f(x) where f is expensive to evaluate (e.g., training a neural network with hyperparameters x). You have a budget of T evaluations.
Algorithm:

Place a GP prior on f
Observe f(x_1), \ldots, f(x_t) — update GP posterior
Choose next query x_{t+1} by maximising an acquisition function \alpha(x)
Repeat

Acquisition functions:






























FunctionFormulaBehaviourExpected Improvement (EI)\mathbb{E}[\max(f^* - f(x), 0)]Balances exploration/exploitation; most popularUpper Confidence Bound (UCB)\mu(x) + \kappa \sigma(x)Explicit exploration parameter \kappaProbability of ImprovementP(f(x) < f^* - \xi)Pure exploitation focusThompson SamplingSample \tilde{f} \sim p(f \mid \mathcal{D}), maximise \tilde{f}Simple, strong theoretical guarantees
Why GPs specifically? The acquisition function requires both a prediction \mu(x) and an uncertainty \sigma(x) at every point in the input space — not just at training points. GPs provide exactly this, in closed form, for any x.

Connection to hyperparameter tuning (Section 2.5 of the index): every time you use Optuna, Ray Tune, or a Gaussian Process optimiser to tune neural network hyperparameters, there is a GP computing posterior means and variances under the hood.


✦ Part 8 — Sampling from a GP
How do you actually draw a sample function f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k)?

Choose a grid of points X = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)
Compute the Gram matrix K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)
Add a small jitter for numerical stability: K \leftarrow K + 10^{-6} I
Compute Cholesky: L = \text{chol}(K)
Sample z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_n)
Return f = Lz

This gives a draw from \mathcal{N}(0, K) — a finite-dimensional realisation of the GP prior.
import numpy as np
 
def sample_gp_prior(x_grid, kernel_fn, n_samples=5, jitter=1e-6):
    """
    Sample functions from a GP prior.
    x_grid: (n,) array of input points
    kernel_fn: callable, k(x, x') -> scalar
    """
    n = len(x_grid)
    K = np.array([[kernel_fn(x_grid[i], x_grid[j])
                   for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)])
    K += jitter * np.eye(n)  # numerical stability
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(K)
    z = np.random.randn(n, n_samples)
    return L @ z  # (n, n_samples): each column is a function sample
 
def se_kernel(x, xp, l=1.0, sf2=1.0):
    return sf2 * np.exp(-0.5 * (x - xp)**2 / l**2)
 
x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 200)
samples = sample_gp_prior(x, se_kernel, n_samples=5)
# samples[:, i] is the i-th function sample
Try this with different kernels (SE with varying \ell, Matérn, periodic) — you will immediately develop intuition for what each kernel encodes.

✦ Part 9 — Full GP Regression Implementation
import numpy as np
 
class GaussianProcessRegressor:
    """
    Exact GP regression with SE kernel.
    Hyperparameters fixed (no marginal likelihood optimisation).
    """
    def __init__(self, length_scale=1.0, output_scale=1.0, noise_var=0.1):
        self.l   = length_scale
        self.sf2 = output_scale
        self.sn2 = noise_var
        self.L   = None  # Cholesky of (K + sn2*I)
        self.alpha = None  # (K + sn2*I)^{-1} y
 
    def _kernel(self, X1, X2):
        """SE kernel: (n1, d) x (n2, d) -> (n1, n2)"""
        diff = X1[:, None, :] - X2[None, :, :]   # (n1, n2, d)
        sq_dist = np.sum(diff**2, axis=-1)         # (n1, n2)
        return self.sf2 * np.exp(-0.5 * sq_dist / self.l**2)
 
    def fit(self, X_train, y_train):
        self.X_train = X_train
        n = len(X_train)
        K = self._kernel(X_train, X_train) + self.sn2 * np.eye(n)
        self.L = np.linalg.cholesky(K)                    # O(n^3)
        self.alpha = np.linalg.solve(
            self.L.T, np.linalg.solve(self.L, y_train))   # L L^T alpha = y
 
    def predict(self, X_test):
        K_star = self._kernel(X_test, self.X_train)        # (m, n)
        mu = K_star @ self.alpha                            # (m,)
 
        v = np.linalg.solve(self.L, K_star.T)              # (n, m)
        k_ss = self._kernel(X_test, X_test)                 # (m, m)
        cov = k_ss - v.T @ v                                # posterior covariance
 
        return mu, np.diag(cov)                             # mean, variance
 
    def log_marginal_likelihood(self, y_train):
        """Equation from Part 5. Useful for hyperparameter optimisation."""
        n = len(y_train)
        log_lik = (
            -0.5 * y_train @ self.alpha
            - np.sum(np.log(np.diag(self.L)))
            - 0.5 * n * np.log(2 * np.pi)
        )
        return log_lik

Usage: after gp.fit(X_train, y_train), call mu, var = gp.predict(X_test). The 95% confidence interval is \mu \pm 1.96\sqrt{\text{var}}.


✦ Part 10 — Deep Learning Connections (Extended)
10.1 The Weight-Space / Function-Space Duality























PerspectivePrior lives onInferencePredictionsBayesian NN (weight-space)p(w)Posterior p(w \mid \mathcal{D}) — intractable\int p(y \mid x, w) p(w \mid \mathcal{D}) dw — approximateGP (function-space)p(f) — GP priorPosterior p(f \mid \mathcal{D}) — exact GaussianExact predictive distribution
For finite-width networks, the weight-space prior induces a non-Gaussian process over functions. In the infinite-width limit, the central limit theorem makes it Gaussian — a GP. The kernel is determined by the network architecture and activation function.
10.2 Why This Matters for Modern DL

Uncertainty quantification: GPs give exact posteriors. BNNs don’t. The deep learning community’s various approaches to UQ (MC Dropout, deep ensembles, SWAG) can often be understood as approximate GP inference.
Generalisation theory: NTK analysis (a GP analysis) is currently one of the main tools for understanding why overparameterised networks generalise — a central open question in deep learning theory.
Structured prediction: GP multi-output models, GP latent variable models, and deep GPs are active research directions that directly compete with (and complement) deep learning approaches.

10.3 Where GPs Are Preferred Over Neural Networks





























ScenarioReasonSmall data (n < 10^3)GPs are non-parametric; NNs overfitCalibrated uncertainty neededExact GP posteriors vs. approximate NN uncertaintyScientific inferenceKernel design encodes domain knowledge interpretablyOptimisation (Bayesian opt.)Closed-form acquisition; cheap to evaluateInterpretability requiredKernel hyperparameters have direct physical meaning

✦ Visualising the Posterior
Prior (no data):
f(x)
 │     ~~~~
 │   ~~    ~~
 │  ~        ~   (3 sample functions, all plausible)
 │~            ~~
 └──────────────── x
   wide shaded region = prior uncertainty

Posterior (5 training points observed, marked ×):
f(x)
 │          ×
 │    ×   ~~~~×~~~
 │  ~~× ~~       ~
 │~~                ~
 └──────────────────── x
   narrow band at × (data reduces uncertainty)
   wide band far from data (prior uncertainty returns)
   mean function threads through observations

This picture — posterior mean threading through data, variance collapsing at observations and widening in unobserved regions — is the visual essence of a Gaussian Process. Any model that behaves this way is doing Bayesian inference correctly.

✦ Exit Criterion

You know this when: you can derive the GP posterior mean and variance from the Gaussian conditioning lemma, explain why the posterior variance decreases monotonically with data, implement GP regression from scratch in NumPy using Cholesky, explain what the marginal likelihood is and what the three terms mean, and describe why GPs are O(n^3) and name at least two scalable alternatives.

Concrete exercises:

Implement the full GP regressor above. Fit it to y = \sin(x) + \varepsilon on 10 training points. Plot the posterior mean and 95% confidence interval. Observe how the uncertainty widens between and beyond training points.
Sample 5 functions from a GP prior with SE kernel, then with Matérn-1/2. Plot both. Write one sentence about what you observe.
Implement the log marginal likelihood gradient with respect to \ell and \sigma_n^2 using the formula in Part 5. Use scipy.optimize.minimize to learn the hyperparameters on a dataset with a known underlying length-scale. Verify recovery.
Implement a one-dimensional Bayesian optimisation loop: GP posterior + EI acquisition + 15 iterations. Minimise f(x) = (x - 2)^2 + 0.1\sin(10x). Plot the acquisition function at each step.

04.ML/06.Advanced/01.Kernel-Methods.title: 01.Kernel Methods
04.ML/06.Advanced/01.Kernel-Methods.content:
“The kernel trick is not a trick. It is a profound insight: similarity in a rich feature space can be computed cheaply in the original space.”

Tags: kernel-methods SVM RKHS representer-theorem deep-learning machine-learning
Status: 🟢 Core
References: ESL Ch. 12 · PRML Ch. 6 · CS 229 Lecture 6–7
Prerequisites: 04.Support Vector Machines · 03.Probability Review · 02.Statistical Learning Theory

The Central Problem
Most machine learning algorithms assume a fixed, finite-dimensional feature representation. You hand the model a vector x \in \mathbb{R}^d, and it does something with it. But what if the data is not linearly separable in \mathbb{R}^d? The naive solution: map to a higher-dimensional space where it is.
\phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D, \quad D \gg d \quad (\text{possibly } D = \infty)
The brutal fact: computing in \mathbb{R}^D is expensive. If D = d^2 (all pairwise products), you’re already in trouble for modest d. If D = \infty — you literally cannot compute \phi(x) explicitly.
The kernel trick resolves this: you never need \phi(x) explicitly. You only ever need inner products \langle \phi(x_i), \phi(x_j) \rangle, and a kernel function computes this cheaply.
k(x_i, x_j) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} \langle \phi(x_i), \phi(x_j) \rangle_\mathcal{H}

1. Feature Maps and the Kernel Function
Setup
Let \mathcal{X} be the input space (e.g., \mathbb{R}^d). A feature map is \phi: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{H} where \mathcal{H} is a Hilbert space (a complete inner product space — possibly infinite dimensional).
A kernel function is any function k: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R} such that:
k(x, x') = \langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle_\mathcal{H}
for some feature map \phi. The point: we define k first, then the feature map \phi is implied by k — we may never need to construct it.
Canonical Example: The Polynomial Kernel
Let x, x' \in \mathbb{R}^2. Define:
k(x, x') = (x^\top x' + c)^2, \quad c \geq 0
Expand for x = (x_1, x_2)^\top, x' = (x_1', x_2')^\top, c = 1:
k(x, x') = (x_1 x_1' + x_2 x_2' + 1)^2 = x_1^2 x_1'^2 + x_2^2 x_2'^2 + 1 + 2x_1 x_1' x_2 x_2' + 2x_1 x_1' + 2x_2 x_2'
This is precisely \langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle where:
\phi(x) = (x_1^2,\ x_2^2,\ 1,\ \sqrt{2}x_1 x_2,\ \sqrt{2}x_1,\ \sqrt{2}x_2)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^6
Key observation: computing k(x, x') costs O(d) — one inner product and a squaring. Computing \langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle directly costs O(D) where D = \binom{d+2}{2} grows quadratically in d. The kernel saves us this cost.
The RBF (Gaussian) Kernel — An Infinite-Dimensional Feature Map
k(x, x') = \exp!\left(-\frac{|x - x'|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
Claim: This corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature map.
Proof sketch: Expand via the Taylor series of \exp:
\exp!\left(-\frac{|x|^2 + |x'|^2 - 2x^\top x'}{2\sigma^2}\right) = e^{-|x|^2/2\sigma^2} \cdot e^{-|x'|^2/2\sigma^2} \cdot e^{x^\top x'/\sigma^2}
The last factor: e^{x^\top x'/\sigma^2} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(x^\top x')^n}{n! \sigma^{2n}}. Each term (x^\top x')^n corresponds to a degree-n polynomial kernel, which has its own feature map of dimension \binom{d+n}{n}. Summing infinitely many such maps gives an infinite-dimensional \phi. Yet k(x, x') is a single exponential — O(d) to evaluate. \square
This is the fundamental power: the feature space can be infinite-dimensional while the kernel evaluation remains cheap.

2. Mercer’s Theorem — When is k a Valid Kernel?
Not every function k: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R} corresponds to a valid inner product. We need a characterisation.
Definition: Positive Semi-Definite Kernel
A symmetric function k is a positive semi-definite (PSD) kernel (also called a Mercer kernel) if for any finite set {x_1, \ldots, x_n} \subset \mathcal{X} and any c \in \mathbb{R}^n:
\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i, x_j) \geq 0
Equivalently, the Gram matrix K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} with K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j) is positive semi-definite for all choices of {x_1, \ldots, x_n}.
Mercer’s Theorem (Statement)
Let k: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R} be continuous and symmetric. Then k is a valid kernel (i.e., k(x, x') = \langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle_\mathcal{H} for some Hilbert space \mathcal{H} and feature map \phi) if and only if k is positive semi-definite.

Proof direction (necessity): If k(x,x') = \langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle, then \sum_{i,j} c_i c_j k(x_i, x_j) = \left|\sum_i c_i \phi(x_i)\right|^2 \geq 0. \square
The sufficiency direction is harder — it constructs the RKHS explicitly from k. See Section 4.

How to Check Validity

Directly verify PSD on the Gram matrix.
Use closure properties (easier in practice):

If k_1, k_2 are valid kernels, so are k_1 + k_2, \alpha k_1 (\alpha > 0), k_1 \cdot k_2
k(x, x') = f(x) k_1(x, x') f(x') for any function f
k(x, x') = \phi(x)^\top A \phi(x') where A \succeq 0



Common valid kernels:








































KernelFormulaHyperparametersLinearx^\top x'—Polynomial(x^\top x' + c)^dc \geq 0, d \in \mathbb{N}RBF (Gaussian)\exp(-\|x-x'\|^2 / 2\sigma^2)\sigma > 0Matérn(smoothness-controlled)\nu, \ell > 0Laplace\exp(-\|x-x'\| / \sigma)\sigma > 0Sigmoid\tanh(\alpha x^\top x' + c)only PSD for some \alpha, c — careful!

3. The Representer Theorem
This is the theorem that justifies using kernels for learning. It says: when you minimise a regularised loss over a function space, the optimal solution lives in the span of the training data’s feature maps.
Theorem (Representer Theorem — Schölkopf, Herbrich, Smola, 2001)
Let \mathcal{H} be an RKHS with kernel k. Consider the optimisation problem:
\hat{f} = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal{H}} \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n L(y_i, f(x_i))}_{\text{empirical loss}} + \underbrace{\Omega(|f|_\mathcal{H})}_{\text{regularisation}}
where L is any loss function and \Omega: [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R} is any strictly increasing function. Then the optimal \hat{f} has the form:
\hat{f}(\cdot) = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i k(\cdot, x_i)
for some coefficients \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in \mathbb{R}.
Proof
Decompose f \in \mathcal{H} into a component in the span of {k(\cdot, x_i)} and its orthogonal complement:
f = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i k(\cdot, x_i)}_{f_\parallel} + f_\perp
By the reproducing property of the RKHS (see Section 4):
f(x_j) = \langle f, k(\cdot, x_j) \rangle_\mathcal{H} = \langle f_\parallel, k(\cdot, x_j) \rangle_\mathcal{H} + \underbrace{\langle f_\perp, k(\cdot, x_j) \rangle_\mathcal{H}}_{= 0} = f_\parallel(x_j)
So adding f_\perp does not change any training prediction, but |f|^2_\mathcal{H} = |f_\parallel|^2 + |f_\perp|^2 \geq |f_\parallel|^2, which means f_\perp only hurts the regularisation term. Therefore the optimal solution has f_\perp = 0. \square
What this buys you: instead of optimising over an infinite-dimensional function space, you optimise over n real numbers \alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n. The learning problem reduces to finite-dimensional optimisation.

4. The Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS)
This is the natural home for kernel methods. Understanding the RKHS is understanding why the whole framework is coherent.
Construction
Given a PSD kernel k, we construct the RKHS \mathcal{H}_k as follows:
Step 1. Start with the set of all “feature functions”: for each x \in \mathcal{X}, define k_x := k(\cdot, x) as a function \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}.
Step 2. Consider the linear span: \mathcal{F} = \left{ \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i k_{x_i} \mid m \in \mathbb{N},\ \alpha_i \in \mathbb{R},\ x_i \in \mathcal{X} \right}
Step 3. Define an inner product on \mathcal{F}:
\left\langle \sum_i \alpha_i k_{x_i},\ \sum_j \beta_j k_{x_j'} \right\rangle_\mathcal{H} := \sum_i \sum_j \alpha_i \beta_j k(x_i, x_j')
This is well-defined because k is PSD.
Step 4. Complete \mathcal{F} under the induced norm |f|_\mathcal{H} = \sqrt{\langle f, f \rangle_\mathcal{H}} to get the Hilbert space \mathcal{H}_k.
The Reproducing Property
The defining property of the RKHS, which gives it its name:
f(x) = \langle f, k(\cdot, x) \rangle_\mathcal{H} \quad \forall f \in \mathcal{H}_k,\ x \in \mathcal{X}
In other words: evaluating a function f at a point x is an inner product with the kernel function k(\cdot, x). This is the reason the representer theorem proof works.
Sanity check: Set f = k(\cdot, x'). Then:
\langle k(\cdot, x'), k(\cdot, x) \rangle_\mathcal{H} = k(x', x) \checkmark
The RKHS norm |f|_\mathcal{H} has a concrete meaning: it measures the smoothness of f with respect to the kernel. The smoother the function, the smaller the norm. Regularisation with |f|_\mathcal{H}^2 is literally a smoothness penalty.

5. Kernelised Algorithms
The representer theorem + the kernel trick allows us to kernelise any algorithm that depends on the data only through inner products. We replace x_i^\top x_j \mapsto k(x_i, x_j) everywhere.
Kernel Ridge Regression
Primal: \min_{w \in \mathcal{H}} |Xw - y|^2 + \lambda |w|^2
Primal solution: \hat{w} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y — works in \mathbb{R}^d, breaks for infinite-dim \phi.
Dual: By the representer theorem, \hat{f} = \sum_i \alpha_i k(\cdot, x_i). Substituting:
\hat{\alpha} = (K + \lambda I)^{-1} y
where K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j) is the n \times n Gram matrix. Prediction:
\hat{f}(x^_) = \sum_i \hat{\alpha}_i k(x^_, x_i) = k(x^*)^\top (K + \lambda I)^{-1} y
where k(x^_)_i = k(x^_, x_i).
Cost: O(n^3) to invert (K + \lambda I) vs. O(d^3) for ridge regression. Kernel methods trade d for n in complexity — they scale with the number of samples, not the feature dimensionality.
Connection to Gaussian Processes: The kernel ridge regression predictor is identical to the GP posterior mean under an RBF prior. This is not a coincidence — they are the same model derived from different perspectives.
Kernel SVM
Recall the SVM dual:
\max_\alpha \sum_i \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j x_i^\top x_j \quad \text{s.t. } \sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0,\ 0 \leq \alpha_i \leq C
Replace x_i^\top x_j \mapsto k(x_i, x_j):
\max_\alpha \sum_i \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j k(x_i, x_j) \quad \text{s.t. } \sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0,\ 0 \leq \alpha_i \leq C
Decision function:
\hat{y}(x) = \text{sign}!\left(\sum_{i \in \text{SV}} \alpha_i y_i k(x, x_i) + b\right)
We never need \phi explicitly. We never need to work in the feature space. Everything is mediated by k.
Kernel Logistic Regression
Replace the weight vector w with \sum_i \alpha_i k(\cdot, x_i) and optimise over \alpha. The log-likelihood becomes:
\ell(\alpha) = \sum_i \log \sigma!\left(y_i \sum_j \alpha_j k(x_i, x_j)\right) - \lambda \alpha^\top K \alpha
The regularisation term \alpha^\top K \alpha = |f|^2_\mathcal{H} — this is the RKHS norm.
Kernel PCA
Standard PCA: find eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C = \frac{1}{n} X^\top X.
Kernel PCA: find principal components in the RKHS by computing the eigendecomposition of the centred Gram matrix \tilde{K}:
\tilde{K} = K - \mathbf{1}_n K - K \mathbf{1}_n + \mathbf{1}_n K \mathbf{1}_n
where (\mathbf{1}_n)_{ij} = 1/n. This centres the data in feature space without constructing \phi(x) explicitly.
The projection of a new point x^* onto the j-th principal component:
z_j(x^_) = \sum_i \alpha_j^{(i)} k(x^_, x_i)

6. Kernel Design — Encoding Prior Knowledge
The choice of kernel is a choice of inductive bias. When you pick the RBF kernel, you’re saying: “I believe the function is smooth, and similar inputs should have similar outputs, where similarity decays exponentially with Euclidean distance.” Different kernels encode different beliefs.
Stationary Kernels
k(x, x') = k(x - x') — depends only on the difference between inputs. Implies translation invariance (stationarity).

RBF: k(r) = \exp(-r^2/2\sigma^2) — infinitely differentiable. Use when the target function is very smooth.
Laplace: k(r) = \exp(-|r|/\sigma) — only once-differentiable. Better for non-smooth functions.
Matérn-\nu: interpolates between Laplace (\nu = 1/2) and RBF (\nu \to \infty). The parameter \nu controls differentiability.

Non-stationary Kernels

Linear: k(x, x') = x^\top x' — equivalent to linear models. No nonlinearity.
Polynomial: encodes feature interactions up to degree d.
Periodic: k(x, x') = \exp(-2\sin^2(\pi|x-x'|/p) / \ell^2) — for periodic functions (e.g., seasonal data).

Kernels for Structured Data
The true power of kernels: they extend machine learning to non-Euclidean inputs by defining similarity directly.

String kernels: k(s, s') =  number of common substrings of length p. Used in text classification and bioinformatics (protein sequences).
Graph kernels: k(G, G') =  a function of shared subgraph patterns. Used in chemoinformatics (molecular property prediction).
Tree kernels: for parse trees in NLP.

The definition of valid kernel is preserved: as long as the Gram matrix is PSD, any similarity function is a valid kernel — no matter how exotic the input space.

7. Computational Considerations
The O(n^3) Problem
Kernel methods require computing and storing the n \times n Gram matrix K. For large n:

Storage: O(n^2) — infeasible at n = 10^6
Inversion (kernel ridge): O(n^3) — infeasible much earlier
This is why kernel methods fell out of favour when deep learning arrived

Approximate Kernel Methods
Nyström approximation: approximate K using a low-rank factorisation:
K \approx K_{nm} K_{mm}^{-1} K_{nm}^\top
where m \ll n are randomly selected “landmark” points. Reduces to O(nm^2) computation.
Random Fourier Features (Rahimi & Recht, 2007): for shift-invariant kernels, Bochner’s theorem guarantees:
k(x, x') = \mathbb{E}_\omega!\left[e^{i\omega^\top(x-x')}\right]
Sample D random frequencies \omega_1, \ldots, \omega_D \sim p(\omega) and construct:
z(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{D}}!\left(\cos(\omega_1^\top x + b_1), \ldots, \cos(\omega_D^\top x + b_D)\right)^\top
Then k(x, x') \approx z(x)^\top z(x'). This reduces to a standard linear method in \mathbb{R}^D, costing O(nD).

8. Connection to AI, Deep Learning, and Neural Networks
Kernel methods and deep learning are more deeply connected than they might appear. Understanding this connection is important for a modern practitioner.
Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK)
The central result (Jacot, Gabriel, Hongler, 2018): An infinitely wide neural network trained by gradient descent is equivalent to kernel regression with the Neural Tangent Kernel:
k_\text{NTK}(x, x') = \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim \text{init}}!\left[\nabla_\theta f(x;\theta)^\top \nabla_\theta f(x';\theta)\right]
At infinite width:

The NTK stays constant throughout training (it doesn’t change as weights update)
The network converges to a global minimum
The final predictor is a kernel regression predictor with kernel k_\text{NTK}

What this means practically: For very wide networks, the NTK regime predicts behaviour well. For finite-width networks (real practice), the NTK drifts during training — this is called feature learning and is what makes practical deep learning powerful beyond kernel methods. The kernel regime cannot learn new features; it is fixed by the initialisation.
Deep Kernels
One response to the expressive power gap: learn the kernel. Define:
k(x, x') = k_\text{base}(\phi_\theta(x), \phi_\theta(x'))
where \phi_\theta is a neural network and k_\text{base} is a standard kernel (e.g., RBF). Train \theta jointly with the kernel machine. This is the basis of Deep Kernel Learning (Wilson et al., 2016) and gives a principled Bayesian uncertainty estimate from a deep model.
SVMs vs. Neural Networks — Historical Perspective
In the 1990s, SVMs were the dominant large-margin classifier. The shift to neural networks was driven by:

Scalability: Deep learning trains in O(n) per epoch via SGD; kernel SVMs scale as O(n^2)–O(n^3).
Representation learning: CNNs learn the right features for images; SVMs with RBF kernels cannot exploit spatial structure as efficiently.
Compositionality: Deep networks compose simple functions hierarchically; kernels are a single layer of feature mapping.

Yet SVMs with carefully designed kernels still dominate in domains with small n and structured data (e.g., genomics, cheminformatics). The choice is not doctrinal; it’s empirical.
Kernel Machines in Modern ML

Gaussian Processes (used in hyperparameter optimisation via Bayesian optimisation, as uncertainty-aware surrogates in RL and AutoML) are fully defined by their kernel.
Graph Neural Networks can be understood as learnable graph kernels.
Attention in Transformers: the scaled dot-product attention \text{softmax}(QK^\top / \sqrt{d_k})V is a data-dependent kernel. Q^\top K / \sqrt{d_k} computes kernel similarities between query and key representations. This is the connection that has been formalised in kernel attention and Performer architectures.
Support Vector Regression (SVR) is still used as a strong baseline in time series and scientific ML.


9. Worked Example — Kernel SVM vs. Linear SVM
Consider the XOR problem: 4 points in \mathbb{R}^2:
x_1 = (1,1),\ y_1 = +1 \quad x_2 = (-1,-1),\ y_2 = +1 x_3 = (1,-1),\ y_3 = -1 \quad x_4 = (-1,1),\ y_4 = -1
Linear SVM: not separable in \mathbb{R}^2 — no hyperplane separates the classes.
Polynomial kernel of degree 2: k(x, x') = (x^\top x')^2. The feature map is (for c=0):
\phi(x_1, x_2) = (x_1^2, x_2^2, \sqrt{2} x_1 x_2)
In this space:

\phi(1,1) = (1, 1, \sqrt{2}), class +1
\phi(-1,-1) = (1, 1, \sqrt{2}), class +1
\phi(1,-1) = (1, 1, -\sqrt{2}), class -1
\phi(-1,1) = (1, 1, -\sqrt{2}), class -1

Now the classes separate perfectly along the third coordinate \sqrt{2}x_1 x_2: positive class has x_1 x_2 > 0, negative has x_1 x_2 < 0. The hyperplane is w_3 z_3 = 0, i.e., the product x_1 x_2 = 0.

10. Implementation from Scratch
import numpy as np
 
# ── Kernel functions ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def rbf_kernel(X1, X2, sigma=1.0):
    """
    Compute the RBF Gram matrix between rows of X1 and rows of X2.
    K[i,j] = exp(-||X1[i] - X2[j]||^2 / (2 * sigma^2))
    """
    # ||a - b||^2 = ||a||^2 + ||b||^2 - 2 a.b
    sq_dist = (np.sum(X1**2, axis=1, keepdims=True)
               + np.sum(X2**2, axis=1)
               - 2 * X1 @ X2.T)
    return np.exp(-sq_dist / (2 * sigma**2))
 
def polynomial_kernel(X1, X2, degree=2, c=1.0):
    return (X1 @ X2.T + c) ** degree
 
def linear_kernel(X1, X2):
    return X1 @ X2.T
 
# ── Kernel Ridge Regression ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
class KernelRidgeRegression:
    """
    Dual form: alpha = (K + lambda * I)^{-1} y
    Prediction: f(x*) = k(x*)^T alpha
    """
    def __init__(self, kernel=rbf_kernel, lam=1.0, **kernel_kwargs):
        self.kernel = kernel
        self.lam = lam
        self.kw = kernel_kwargs
 
    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.X_train = X
        n = X.shape[0]
        K = self.kernel(X, X, **self.kw)
        self.alpha = np.linalg.solve(K + self.lam * np.eye(n), y)
        return self
 
    def predict(self, X_test):
        K_star = self.kernel(X_test, self.X_train, **self.kw)
        return K_star @ self.alpha
 
# ── Kernel PCA ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class KernelPCA:
    """
    1. Compute Gram matrix K
    2. Centre in feature space: K_tilde = K - 1_n K - K 1_n + 1_n K 1_n
    3. Eigendecompose K_tilde
    4. Project: Z = E_k Λ_k^{1/2}  (keep top k eigenvectors)
    """
    def __init__(self, n_components=2, kernel=rbf_kernel, **kernel_kwargs):
        self.n_components = n_components
        self.kernel = kernel
        self.kw = kernel_kwargs
 
    def fit_transform(self, X):
        self.X_train = X
        n = X.shape[0]
        K = self.kernel(X, X, **self.kw)
 
        # Centre the Gram matrix
        one_n = np.ones((n, n)) / n
        self.K_mean_rows = K.mean(axis=0)
        self.K_mean = K.mean()
        K_tilde = K - one_n @ K - K @ one_n + one_n @ K @ one_n
 
        # Eigendecomposition (K_tilde is symmetric PSD)
        eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(K_tilde)
        # Sort descending
        idx = np.argsort(eigvals)[::-1]
        eigvals, eigvecs = eigvals[idx], eigvecs[:, idx]
 
        self.eigvals = eigvals[:self.n_components]
        self.eigvecs = eigvecs[:, :self.n_components]
 
        return self.eigvecs * np.sqrt(np.maximum(self.eigvals, 0))
 
# ── Usage example ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    n = 100
    # Two concentric circles — not linearly separable
    theta = rng.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, n)
    r = rng.choice([1.0, 2.5], n)
    X = np.column_stack([r * np.cos(theta), r * np.sin(theta)])
    y = (r > 1.5).astype(float) * 2 - 1   # +1 outer, -1 inner
 
    # Kernel ridge regression with RBF kernel
    model = KernelRidgeRegression(kernel=rbf_kernel, lam=0.1, sigma=1.0)
    model.fit(X, y)
    preds = np.sign(model.predict(X))
    print(f"Accuracy: {(preds == y).mean():.2%}")
 
    # Kernel PCA for visualisation
    kpca = KernelPCA(n_components=2, kernel=rbf_kernel, sigma=1.0)
    Z = kpca.fit_transform(X)
    print(f"Projected shape: {Z.shape}")

11. Visualisation — The Kernel Trick Geometrically
Original space ℝ²                   Feature space ℝ^D (or ∞-dim)
(not linearly separable)             (linearly separable)

    ●  ○                             ○  ○  ○
  ○   ●   ○          φ: x → φ(x)    ──────────  ← separating hyperplane
    ●  ○                             ●  ●  ●

The kernel trick: we find this hyperplane WITHOUT ever moving to the
feature space. We work entirely with k(xᵢ, xⱼ) in the original space.

Decision boundary in ℝ² (from SVM dual):
  f(x) = Σᵢ αᵢ yᵢ k(x, xᵢ) + b = 0

This is a *nonlinear* curve in ℝ², induced by the kernel.
With RBF kernel, σ → 0: memorises every point (overfit)
With RBF kernel, σ → ∞: approaches linear classifier (underfit)

The bias-variance view of \sigma in the RBF kernel:

























\sigma small\sigma largeNarrow GaussiansWide GaussiansHigh variance (overfitting)High bias (underfitting)Complex decision boundarySimple (near-linear) boundaryFew effective support vectorsMany support vectors

12. Summary and Exit Criteria
The logical chain:
\text{PSD kernel} \xrightarrow{\text{Mercer}} \text{valid inner product} \xrightarrow{\text{RKHS construction}} \text{Hilbert space } \mathcal{H}_k \xrightarrow{\text{Representer theorem}} \text{finite-dim optimisation over } \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^n
The kernel trick reduces any algorithm that uses data only through inner products to kernel evaluations. Kernelise the inner products, and the algorithm works in an implicit infinite-dimensional space at the cost of O(n^2) storage and O(n^3) computation.

You know this when you can:

State Mercer’s theorem and use it to verify or refute that a given function is a valid kernel.
Derive the kernel ridge regression dual from the representer theorem — without looking it up.
Prove the representer theorem using the orthogonal decomposition argument.
Explain why the RBF kernel corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature map (via Taylor expansion of \exp).
Implement kernel ridge regression and kernel PCA in NumPy (~50 lines each).
Explain the NTK connection and what it implies about the relationship between kernel methods and infinitely wide neural networks.
Explain why Transformer attention is a form of data-dependent kernel.



References
