04.ML/08.Features/03.Feature-Selection.title: 03.Feature Selection
04.ML/08.Features/03.Feature-Selection.content:
“Perfection is achieved not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away.” — Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
In ML terms: a model that achieves the same performance with fewer features is strictly better.

Part of: 08.Feature Engineering and Data Preprocessing · 00.ML Index Prereqs: 01.Data Preprocessing · 02.Feature Engineering · 04.Bias Variance Tradeoff · 01.Linear Regression Next: 01.ML Project Workflow · 03.Model Interpretability

✦ Why Feature Selection?
You have engineered p features. Not all of them help. Some are redundant (correlated with other features — they add no new information). Some are irrelevant (independent of the target — they add only noise). Some are harmful (they carry enough noise that the model overfits to them).
The motivations for removing features are distinct and worth separating:
1. Variance reduction. Every feature is a degree of freedom. More degrees of freedom → more ways to overfit. Removing irrelevant features reduces the effective model complexity without sacrificing expressiveness. This is the bias-variance argument for feature selection.
2. Computational efficiency. Training cost scales with p (or p^2, or worse, depending on the algorithm). Fewer features → faster training and inference.
3. Interpretability. A model with 5 features is understandable. A model with 500 features is not. Clinical and legal settings often require sparse, interpretable models.
4. Avoiding the curse of dimensionality. Distance-based algorithms (KNN, SVM with RBF kernel, K-Means) degrade as p grows because all points become equidistant in high dimensions. Feature selection directly combats this.
5. Avoiding Multicollinearity. In linear models, if two features are nearly perfectly correlated, (X^TX) is nearly singular, numerical issues arise, and coefficient estimates become unstable.

✦ The Three Families
There are three fundamentally different approaches to feature selection. They differ in what information they use to score features.
Feature Selection Methods
│
├── Filter Methods
│   Score features using statistics of the data alone.
│   Model-agnostic, fast, computed once.
│   Weakness: ignores feature interactions.
│
├── Wrapper Methods
│   Score feature subsets by training and evaluating a model.
│   Model-specific, expensive, but captures interactions.
│   Weakness: O(2^p) subsets in the worst case.
│
└── Embedded Methods
    Feature selection happens during model training.
    Model-specific, efficient (no extra training loops).
    Examples: L1 regularisation, tree feature importance.


✦ 1. Filter Methods
Filter methods score each feature independently of the model, using only the relationship between the feature and the target (or between features themselves). They are computed before any model is trained.
1.1 Variance Threshold
Remove features with variance below a threshold \tau:
\text{Var}(x_j) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)^2 < \tau \implies \text{remove feature } j
Rationale: A feature with near-zero variance is nearly constant — it carries almost no information. A constant feature contributes nothing to any model.
Caveat: Variance depends on scale. If you have not standardised, a feature with small values (e.g., a probability in [0,1]) will always have low variance compared to one in [0, 10^6]. Apply after standardisation, or use a relative threshold.
import numpy as np
 
def variance_threshold(X, threshold=0.01):
    """Remove features with variance < threshold. Fit on train only."""
    variances = X.var(axis=0)
    mask = variances >= threshold
    return X[:, mask], mask
 
# Usage — fit on train, apply same mask to test
X_train_filtered, mask = variance_threshold(X_train, threshold=0.01)
X_test_filtered = X_test[:, mask]

1.2 Correlation-Based Selection
Remove features that are highly correlated with each other (redundancy) or weakly correlated with the target (irrelevance).
Pearson correlation between feature j and target y:
r(x_j, y) = \frac{\sum_i (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum_i (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)^2} \sqrt{\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2}}
r \in [-1, 1]. Remove features with |r| < \tau_{\text{relevance}}.
Redundancy: For each pair (j, k) with |r(x_j, x_k)| > \tau_{\text{redundancy}}, keep the one with higher |r(x_j, y)| and remove the other.
Critical limitation: Pearson correlation only measures linear association. A feature with a strong nonlinear relationship to the target (e.g., y = x^2) will have r(x, y) \approx 0 if x is symmetric around zero. Correlation-based selection will incorrectly discard it.
def correlation_selection(X, y, threshold=0.1):
    """Keep features with |correlation to target| >= threshold."""
    correlations = np.array([
        np.corrcoef(X[:, j], y)[0, 1] for j in range(X.shape[1])
    ])
    mask = np.abs(correlations) >= threshold
    return X[:, mask], mask, correlations

1.3 Mutual Information
Mutual information between feature X_j and target Y measures the reduction in uncertainty about Y from knowing X_j:
I(X_j; Y) = \sum_{x, y} p(x, y) \log \frac{p(x, y)}{p(x), p(y)}
For continuous variables, replace sums with integrals. In practice, estimated using k-nearest-neighbour density estimators (Kraskov et al., 2004).
Why it is superior to correlation: I(X_j; Y) = 0 if and only if X_j and Y are statistically independent — not just linearly uncorrelated. It captures any form of dependence, including nonlinear and non-monotone.
Properties:

I(X_j; Y) \geq 0 always.
I(X_j; Y) = 0 \iff X_j \perp Y.
I(X_j; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y | X_j) — the information gain about Y from observing X_j.
Symmetric: I(X; Y) = I(Y; X).

Relationship to entropy:
I(X; Y) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X, Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y)
where H(X) = -\sum_x p(x) \log p(x) is the Shannon entropy.
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif, mutual_info_regression
 
# Classification target
mi_scores = mutual_info_classif(X_train, y_train, random_state=42)
 
# Regression target
mi_scores = mutual_info_regression(X_train, y_train, random_state=42)
 
# Select top-k features
k = 20
top_k_mask = np.argsort(mi_scores)[::-1][:k]
X_train_selected = X_train[:, top_k_mask]
X_test_selected  = X_test[:,  top_k_mask]

1.4 Statistical Tests
For classification tasks, classical statistical tests can assess the independence of a feature from the class label.
Chi-squared test (for non-negative discrete features):
\chi^2 = \sum_{j} \frac{(O_j - E_j)^2}{E_j}
where O_j are observed counts and E_j = (\text{row sum}) \times (\text{col sum}) / n are expected counts under independence. High \chi^2 → reject independence → feature is informative.
ANOVA F-test (for continuous features, categorical target):
F = \frac{\text{variance between class means}}{\text{variance within classes}}
High F → means differ across classes → feature is discriminative.
Limitation of all filter methods: They score features individually. A feature that is individually uninformative but becomes informative in combination with another feature will be discarded. This is the fundamental weakness of filter methods.

1.5 Filter Method Summary















































MethodType of TargetDetects NonlinearityHandles InteractionSpeedVariance thresholdAnyN/ANoO(np)Pearson correlationContinuousNoNoO(np)Mutual informationAnyYesNoO(np \log n)Chi-squaredCategoricalNoNoO(np)ANOVA F-testCategorical classNoNoO(np)

✦ 2. Wrapper Methods
Wrapper methods treat the feature subset as a combinatorial search problem. They evaluate subsets by training a model on that subset and measuring cross-validated performance. This is model-specific and captures feature interactions — but it is expensive.
2.1 The Combinatorial Problem
For p features, there are 2^p possible subsets. For p = 50: 2^{50} \approx 10^{15} subsets — exhaustive search is impossible. All practical wrapper methods are heuristics that search this space efficiently.
2.2 Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE)
Algorithm:
1. Train model on all p features.
2. Score each feature by its importance (model-specific).
3. Remove the least important feature (or bottom k%).
4. Repeat until the desired number of features remains.

The importance score is model-specific:

Linear models: |w_j| (the magnitude of the coefficient after standardisation).
Tree-based models: mean decrease in impurity, or permutation importance.

from sklearn.feature_selection import RFE
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
 
estimator = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000)
selector  = RFE(estimator, n_features_to_select=10, step=1)
selector.fit(X_train, y_train)
 
X_train_selected = selector.transform(X_train)
X_test_selected  = selector.transform(X_test)
 
print(selector.ranking_)  # 1 = selected, k = eliminated at step k
With cross-validation — RFECV: Rather than specifying n_features_to_select, use cross-validation to select the optimal number of features:
from sklearn.feature_selection import RFECV
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
 
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5)
selector = RFECV(estimator, step=1, cv=cv, scoring='f1', min_features_to_select=1)
selector.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f"Optimal features: {selector.n_features_}")
Cost: O(p) model fits in the naive case (one per elimination step). With step=k, O(p/k) fits.

2.3 Forward Selection and Backward Elimination
Forward selection:
Start with empty set S = {}.
At each step: add the feature j ∉ S that maximises CV performance when added to S.
Stop when performance stops improving (or budget is exhausted).

Backward elimination:
Start with full set S = {1, ..., p}.
At each step: remove the feature j ∈ S whose removal causes the least CV performance drop.
Stop when performance starts dropping significantly.

Bidirectional (stepwise): Combines both — add or remove at each step, whichever improves performance most.
These are hill-climbing heuristics. They can get stuck at local optima. Forward selection is O(p^2) model fits in the worst case (each of p steps considers up to p candidates). This is feasible for moderate p (\lesssim 100) but not for p \sim 10^4.

2.4 The Leakage Trap in Wrapper Methods
This is the most common and most consequential mistake in feature selection.
Wrong:
# BUG: Feature selection uses all data including test
selector.fit(X, y)           # fitted on ALL data
X_selected = selector.transform(X)
X_train_s, X_test_s = train_test_split(X_selected, ...)
# Test set used to select features → optimistic evaluation
Correct:
# CORRECT: Feature selection inside the pipeline, inside CV
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
 
pipe = Pipeline([
    ('select', RFE(LogisticRegression(), n_features_to_select=10)),
    ('model',  LogisticRegression()),
])
# cross_val_score fits the entire pipeline on each training fold
# The RFE never sees the validation fold during its fit
scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring='f1')
Why this matters: If you select features using the full dataset, the selected features are the ones most correlated with y in the entire dataset — including the test set. The test set has leaked into the feature selection step. This inflates CV scores and produces overly optimistic estimates.
Rule: Feature selection is a step of model fitting. It must be done inside the training fold, not before the split.

✦ 3. Embedded Methods
Embedded methods perform feature selection as part of the model training process. They are more efficient than wrappers (no extra training loop) and more model-aware than filters (they consider the feature’s contribution within the model).
3.1 L1 Regularisation (Lasso)
The Lasso objective:
\hat{w} = \arg\min_{w} \left[ \frac{1}{n} |Xw - y|^2 + \lambda |w|_1 \right]
where |w|_1 = \sum_j |w_j|.
Why L1 produces sparsity (geometric derivation):
The Lasso can be written as a constrained optimisation:
\hat{w} = \arg\min_{w} \frac{1}{n} |Xw - y|^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad |w|_1 \leq t
The constraint set {|w|_1 \leq t} is an \ell^1 ball — a diamond in 2D, a cross-polytope in higher dimensions. Its extreme points (corners) are on the coordinate axes, where exactly one component of w is nonzero and all others are zero.
The unconstrained minimum (the OLS solution) is typically not on the constraint boundary. As we shrink t (increase \lambda), the constraint boundary moves inward. The first time the OLS ellipsoidal contours touch the \ell^1 ball, they almost always touch at a corner — a sparse solution.
Contrast with L2 (Ridge): The \ell^2 ball {|w|_2 \leq t} is a sphere. It has no corners. The constrained optimum can be anywhere on the sphere’s surface, and generically all components of w will be nonzero. L2 shrinks all coefficients toward zero but never sets them exactly to zero.
L2 ball (circle):          L1 ball (diamond):
        *                         *
      *   *                      /|\
     *     *                    / | \
     *  ●  *    OLS min → ●    /  |  \
     *     *                  / ● |   \   ← OLS solution likely
      *   *                  /   |    \    hits a corner → sparse
        *                   *----+----*

Connection to MAP estimation: As shown in 03.Probability Review, Lasso is equivalent to MAP estimation with a Laplace prior on w:
p(w_j) = \frac{\lambda}{2} e^{-\lambda |w_j|}
The Laplace prior has a sharp peak at zero and heavy tails — it strongly encourages sparsity while allowing a few large weights.
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso, LassoCV
 
# LassoCV selects lambda via cross-validation
lasso_cv = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=42, max_iter=10000)
lasso_cv.fit(X_train, y_train)
 
print(f"Optimal lambda: {lasso_cv.alpha_:.4f}")
print(f"Non-zero features: {(lasso_cv.coef_ != 0).sum()} / {X_train.shape[1]}")
 
# Selected feature mask
mask = lasso_cv.coef_ != 0
X_train_selected = X_train[:, mask]
X_test_selected  = X_test[:,  mask]
Elastic Net: Convex combination of L1 and L2:
\hat{w} = \arg\min_w \frac{1}{n}|Xw-y|^2 + \lambda_1 |w|_1 + \lambda_2 |w|_2^2
Adds the grouping effect: when features are correlated, Lasso arbitrarily picks one. Elastic Net tends to select correlated features together. Controlled by the mixing parameter \rho = \lambda_1 / (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2).

3.2 Tree-Based Feature Importance
Decision trees make splits by choosing the feature and threshold that maximally reduces impurity at each node. The total reduction in impurity attributed to feature j across all splits in all trees is its importance.
Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI) — also called Gini importance:
\text{Importance}(j) = \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}: \text{split on } j} p(t) \cdot \Delta I(t)
where p(t) = n_t / n is the fraction of samples reaching node t, and \Delta I(t) is the impurity reduction at that split.
For Random Forests, average over all trees:
\overline{\text{Importance}}(j) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \text{Importance}_b(j)
Known bias of MDI: High-cardinality features (many unique values) tend to score higher, even if they have no real predictive power. A random feature with 1000 unique values will have higher MDI than an informative binary feature, all else equal, because there are more possible splits. This is a well-documented deficiency.
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
import numpy as np
 
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=42)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
 
importances = rf.feature_importances_  # MDI, normalised to sum to 1
ranked = np.argsort(importances)[::-1]
for i in ranked[:10]:
    print(f"Feature {i}: {importances[i]:.4f}")

3.3 Permutation Importance
Algorithm:
1. Train model on (X_train, y_train). Record baseline score S₀.
2. For each feature j:
   a. Shuffle column j in X_val (break its association with y).
   b. Score the model on the shuffled X_val → S_j.
   c. Importance(j) = S₀ - S_j.
3. Features with large importance drop are important.
   Features with near-zero or negative drop are uninformative.

Why permutation importance is superior to MDI:

Model-agnostic: Works for any trained model, not just trees.
No cardinality bias: Shuffling a high-cardinality feature does not give it a false advantage.
Measures actual predictive contribution: It asks “how much does the model’s performance suffer if this feature is unavailable?” — which is precisely what we care about.
Evaluated on validation data: MDI is computed on training data (biased toward training fit); permutation importance is computed on held-out data.

Caveat: For correlated features, permutation importance underestimates importance. If features j and k are strongly correlated, shuffling j has little effect because k still carries the same information. The model compensates. Both features may appear unimportant individually despite being jointly essential.
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
 
result = permutation_importance(
    rf, X_val, y_val,
    n_repeats=10,        # shuffle each feature 10 times, take mean
    random_state=42,
    scoring='f1'
)
 
perm_importances = result.importances_mean
perm_std         = result.importances_std
 
# Select features with importance mean > 2 standard deviations above zero
mask = perm_importances > 2 * perm_std

3.4 Comparison: MDI vs. Permutation Importance








































PropertyMDI (Gini Importance)Permutation ImportanceComputed onTraining dataValidation / test dataCardinality biasYes — high-card features preferredNoModel-agnosticNo (tree only)YesHandles correlated featuresPoorlyPoorly (different reason)SpeedFree (computed during training)O(p \cdot n_{\text{repeats}}) model evaluationsPreferred forQuick, rough rankingProduction feature selection

✦ 4. Stability of Feature Selection
A feature selection method is stable if small perturbations to the training set produce similar selected feature sets. Unstable selection is a sign of overfitting at the feature level.
Measuring stability: Train the selector on B bootstrap samples of the training data. For each feature j, compute its selection frequency f_j \in [0, 1]. Features with f_j \approx 1 are stably selected; features with f_j \approx 0 are stably rejected; features with f_j \approx 0.5 are unstable.
\text{Stability}(j) = f_j = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}[j \in S_b]
Stability selection (Meinshausen & Bühlmann, 2010): Select only features with f_j > \pi_{\text{thr}} (e.g., 0.8). This provides finite-sample control of the false discovery rate for feature selection.
from sklearn.utils import resample
 
def stability_selection(X, y, selector, n_bootstrap=50, threshold=0.8):
    n, p = X.shape
    selection_counts = np.zeros(p)
    
    for _ in range(n_bootstrap):
        X_boot, y_boot = resample(X, y, random_state=None)
        selector.fit(X_boot, y_boot)
        # assumes selector has a boolean mask or support_ attribute
        selection_counts += selector.support_.astype(float)
    
    frequencies = selection_counts / n_bootstrap
    stable_mask  = frequencies >= threshold
    return stable_mask, frequencies

✦ 5. The Feature Selection Leakage Trap (Revisited, Precisely)
This deserves its own section because it is so commonly wrong in practice — including in published papers.
The Theorem
Let \hat{f}_{S} be a model trained on feature subset S. Let \hat{S} be the feature subset selected using the full dataset (X, y). Then:
\mathbb{E}[\text{CV error of } \hat{f}_{\hat{S}}] < \mathbb{E}[\text{true generalisation error of } \hat{f}_{\hat{S}}]
i.e., the cross-validated error underestimates the true error. The selection step has already “peeked” at the validation folds.
The Correct Procedure: Nested CV
For simultaneous feature selection and model evaluation:
Outer loop (evaluation):    Split data into K outer folds
  For each outer fold:
    Inner loop (selection): Use remaining K-1 folds for selection
      Train selector on inner training data
      Select features S_inner
    Train model on outer training data using S_inner
    Evaluate on outer test fold

Report: mean ± std of outer fold scores

In sklearn:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, mutual_info_classif
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
 
# Everything inside a single Pipeline — leakage-free by construction
pipe = Pipeline([
    ('select', SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=10)),
    ('model',  LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000)),
])
 
outer_cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores   = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=outer_cv, scoring='f1')
print(f"Unbiased F1: {scores.mean():.3f} ± {scores.std():.3f}")
The Pipeline guarantees that SelectKBest.fit() is called only on the training fold of each outer split. The mutual information scores are recomputed fresh for every fold.

✦ 6. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
6.1 Feature Selection as Regularisation
Feature selection is regularisation with a different norm. L0 regularisation:
\min_w \frac{1}{n}|Xw - y|^2 + \lambda |w|_0
where |w|_0 = |{j : w_j \neq 0}| is the number of nonzero coefficients. This directly penalises the number of features used. It is NP-hard to optimise exactly. Lasso (L1) is its convex relaxation — the tightest convex approximation to the L0 ball.
The path from L0 → L1 → L2 corresponds to increasingly relaxed sparsity constraints:

L0: exactly sparse (combinatorial)
L1: tends to be sparse (convex, tractable)
L2: never exactly sparse (smooth)

6.2 In Deep Learning: Implicit Feature Selection
Deep learning does not use explicit feature selection in the classical sense. Instead, several mechanisms implicitly select features:
Dropout: Randomly zeroes activations during training. This prevents the network from relying on any single neuron (or feature), equivalent to learning a model that is robust to feature removal. It is closest in spirit to stability selection.
Attention mechanisms (Transformers): Attention weights \alpha_{ij} measure how much position j is attended to when producing the representation for position i. High attention weight ≈ important feature. This is a soft, differentiable form of feature selection, learned end-to-end.
Sparse autoencoders: L1 penalty on the latent activations produces sparse representations — only a few neurons activate for each input. The active neurons are the “selected features” for that input. This is the basis of mechanistic interpretability research on language models (Anthropic’s “Towards Monosemanticity” and “Scaling Monosemanticity” papers).
Feature importance in XGBoost/LightGBM: These models compute MDI and permutation importance natively. The standard practice in tabular ML competitions (Kaggle) is to train a tree ensemble, extract feature importances, remove the bottom fraction, retrain, and repeat. This is iterative embedded feature selection.
6.3 The Irrelevance of Feature Selection to Overparameterised Models
Modern neural networks are massively overparameterised — far more parameters than training examples. Classical learning theory says this should overfit catastrophically. It does not, due to the double descent phenomenon (04.Bias Variance Tradeoff) and implicit regularisation from gradient descent (SGD finds flat minima).
In this regime, explicit feature selection is less critical: the model can in principle learn to ignore irrelevant features by setting their weights to near-zero. Whether it reliably does so is an active research question. In practice, for tabular data with modest n, feature selection still provides measurable benefits even for neural networks.

✦ 7. Decision Guide: Which Method?
How many features p?
│
├── p < 20
│     → Exhaustive search or Wrapper (forward/backward) is feasible
│       Use RFECV with cross-validation
│
├── 20 ≤ p ≤ 500
│     → Embedded methods: Lasso / LassoCV, or RFECV with step > 1
│       Validate with permutation importance on held-out data
│
├── 500 < p ≤ 10,000
│     → Filter first (MI or variance threshold) to get to p ~ 200
│       Then embedded (Lasso or tree importance)
│       Use Pipeline to prevent leakage
│
└── p > 10,000 (text, genomics, wide tabular)
      → Variance threshold + hashing (text)
        Lasso with coordinate descent (scales to p ~ 10^6)
        Filter: chi-squared or MI for quick pruning

Are features correlated?

Lasso arbitrarily picks one from correlated groups → use Elastic Net instead
MDI is unreliable → use permutation importance

Is interpretability required?

Yes → Lasso (sparse linear model), RFECV with logistic regression
No → Permutation importance + any model


✦ 8. Worked Example: Full Pipeline
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectFromModel, RFECV
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.model_selection import (
    train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
)
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
 
# ── 1. Simulate data: 200 samples, 50 features, 10 informative ───────────────
X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=200, n_features=50, n_informative=10,
    n_redundant=10, n_repeated=5, random_state=42
)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42
)
 
# ── 2. Strategy A: Lasso embedded selection ───────────────────────────────────
lasso_pipe = Pipeline([
    ('impute',  SimpleImputer(strategy='median')),
    ('scale',   StandardScaler()),
    ('select',  SelectFromModel(
                    LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=42, max_iter=5000),
                    threshold='mean'
                )),
    ('model',   LogisticRegression(C=1.0, max_iter=1000)),
])
 
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores_lasso = cross_val_score(lasso_pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring='f1')
print(f"Lasso pipeline CV F1: {scores_lasso.mean():.3f} ± {scores_lasso.std():.3f}")
 
# ── 3. Strategy B: Tree importance + permutation validation ──────────────────
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=42)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
 
# Permutation importance on held-out validation split
X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_train, y_train, test_size=0.2, stratify=y_train, random_state=0
)
rf.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
perm = permutation_importance(rf, X_val, y_val, n_repeats=20,
                               scoring='f1', random_state=42)
 
# Keep features where importance mean > 1 std above zero
perm_mask = perm.importances_mean > perm.importances_std
 
print(f"\nPermutation-selected features: {perm_mask.sum()} / {X_train.shape[1]}")
print(f"Expected ~10 informative features.")
 
# ── 4. Evaluate on test set (spend once) ─────────────────────────────────────
lasso_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = lasso_pipe.predict(X_test)
print("\n── Lasso Pipeline Test Performance ──")
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred))

✦ Key Facts and Theorems
Fact 1 (L0-L1 relaxation): The L1 ball is the convex hull of the L0 “ball” (union of coordinate axes). Minimising over the L1 constraint is the tightest convex relaxation of minimising over the L0 constraint. This is why Lasso is the principled convex surrogate for subset selection.
Fact 2 (Mutual information and sufficiency): I(X_j; Y) = 0 \iff X_j \perp Y. But I(X_j; Y | X_{-j}) = 0 (conditional independence given all other features) is the correct criterion for irrelevance in a multivariate model. Filter methods compute marginal MI; the conditional version is computationally intractable for large p.
Fact 3 (Lasso consistency): Under appropriate conditions (the “irrepresentable condition” on the design matrix X), the Lasso with \lambda \propto \sqrt{\log p / n} recovers the true support (set of nonzero coefficients) with probability → 1 as n \to \infty. This is the Lasso’s model selection consistency theorem (Zhao & Yu, 2006).
Fact 4 (No free lunch for feature selection): There is no universally best feature selection method. The optimal method depends on the true data-generating process — specifically, on the structure of the relationship between features and target. This is the No Free Lunch theorem applied to feature selection.

✦ Exit Criterion

You know this when:

You can derive geometrically why L1 regularisation produces sparse solutions and L2 does not.
You can implement mutual information-based filter selection from scratch and explain its advantage over Pearson correlation.
You can build a fully leakage-free feature selection pipeline using sklearn’s Pipeline and cross_val_score.
You can explain the difference between MDI and permutation importance and state when each is preferred.
You can describe the stability selection framework and explain why it controls false discoveries.
You can connect L0, L1, and L2 regularisation in a single framework and state why L0 is NP-hard.



✦ References













































SourceSectionsESL (Hastie et al.)Ch. 3.3 — subset selection; Ch. 3.4 — shrinkage (Lasso/Ridge); Ch. 7.5 — cross-validation for selectionPRML (Bishop)Ch. 3.1 — regularisation as MAP; Ch. 3.3 — Bayesian model comparisonHands-On ML (Géron)Ch. 4 — regularisation; Ch. 7 — feature importance in ensemblesIntro to ML with Python (Müller & Guido)Ch. 4 — feature selection methods in sklearnML for EngineersFeature selection in production ML pipelinesAIMA (Russell & Norvig)Ch. 18.4 — choosing a hypothesisCS 229 (Stanford)Regularisation notes; model selection and bias-varianceMeinshausen & Bühlmann (2010)Stability Selection — JRSS-BZhao & Yu (2006)On Model Selection Consistency of Lasso — JMLR

04.ML/09.Practice/01.ML-Project-Workflow.title: 01.ML Project Workflow
04.ML/09.Practice/01.ML-Project-Workflow.content:
“In theory, theory and practice are the same. In practice, they are not.” — attributed to Yogi Berra
Every algorithm in this vault is useless unless you can take it from data to a deployed, monitored, trustworthy system. This note is how you do that. Not a checklist — a way of thinking.

Depends on: 01.The Learning Problem · 02.Statistical Learning Theory · 01.Train Val Test · 03.Performance Metrics Used by: 02.Pipelines and Experiments · 03.Model Interpretability · 04.Deployment and MLOps

✦ The Shape of the Problem
Before a single line of code, the most important skill in ML is problem framing. Most project failures are not algorithmic — they are framing failures. A beautifully optimised model solving the wrong problem is waste.
The three questions to answer before anything else:

What is the task T? — classification, regression, ranking, generation, clustering?
What does success look like? — what metric P matters to the business, not just to a paper?
What data exists and is it sufficient? — do you actually have experience E?

These three questions correspond directly to Mitchell’s definition of learning: T, P, E. You are instantiating that abstract definition into a concrete system.

✦ The Workflow — A Map
Raw World
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 0: Frame the Problem                                  │
│  Task type · Success metric · Data availability            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 1: Get & Version the Data                             │
│  Sources · Provenance · Train/Val/Test split                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 2: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)                    │
│  Distributions · Correlations · Anomalies · Leakage hunt   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 3: Preprocessing & Feature Engineering Pipeline       │
│  Scaling · Encoding · Imputation · Feature construction     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 4: Baseline → Model Selection → Iteration             │
│  Always start simple · Complexity ladder · CV               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 5: Evaluation on Held-Out Test Set                    │
│  Spend the test set once · Multiple metrics · Error analysis│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 6: Error Analysis                                     │
│  Where does the model fail? Why? What data would fix it?    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 7: Deployment & Monitoring                            │
│  Serving · Distribution shift · Feedback loops             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


✦ Step 0 — Frame the Problem
0.1 Task Taxonomy
Before anything else, know which regime you are in:















































Task\mathcal{Y}Loss (canonical)BaselineRegression\mathbb{R}MSE / MAEPredict mean of training targetsBinary classification{0,1}Cross-entropyPredict majority classMulti-class{1,...,K}Cat. cross-entropyPredict most frequent classRankingOrdered pairsPairwise lossSort by popularitySequence labelling\mathcal{Y}^TToken cross-entropyMost frequent tagClustering—No supervised loss—
0.2 The Metric Must Match the Business Problem
This is where projects die. The canonical traps:
Trap 1: Optimise accuracy on an imbalanced problem. Fraud detection: 99.9% of transactions are legitimate. A classifier that always predicts “not fraud” achieves 99.9% accuracy and is useless. The right metrics are precision, recall, AUC-PR.
Trap 2: Optimise the wrong loss. If the business cost of a false negative is 100× the cost of a false positive (e.g., medical diagnosis, content moderation), your loss function should encode this asymmetry explicitly — class-weighted cross-entropy, or a custom loss.
Trap 3: Confuse online and offline metrics. A recommendation system may achieve excellent offline NDCG but perform poorly online (A/B test) because users interact with the recommendations, changing the distribution. Offline metrics are proxies; the ground truth is online behaviour.
Rule: always derive your offline metric from the business objective, and document the derivation.
0.3 The Data Audit
Before modelling, you need honest answers to:

How was the data collected? (Introduces selection bias if collection mechanism correlates with target)
How large is n? Rule of thumb: need at least \sim 10 \times d observations for a linear model to be well-posed; deep learning often needs 10^5–10^9.
Is the data labelled? If yes: who labelled it? What was their agreement (inter-annotator reliability)?
Is there a time dimension? If yes: do not shuffle randomly — preserve temporal order.
Are there ethical or legal constraints on features? (Sensitive attributes, GDPR, etc.)


✦ Step 1 — Get & Version the Data
1.1 The Train / Val / Test Split
This deserves a brief but rigorous treatment because getting it wrong corrupts everything downstream. See 01.Train Val Test for the full discussion.
The cardinal rule: your test set represents the world the model will be deployed into. It must be:

Drawn from the same distribution as deployment data
Never touched during model development
Used at most once (or very few times — each peek costs you)

The split strategy depends on the data structure:

i.i.d. data: random stratified split. Typical: 70/15/15 or 60/20/20.
Time-series data: chronological split — everything before t_0 is train, [t_0, t_1] is val, [t_1, \infty) is test. Never shuffle.
Group structure (e.g., multiple records per patient): group-aware split — all records from a patient go to the same fold. Otherwise your model learns the patient, not the disease.
Geospatial data: spatial block splits to prevent leakage through spatial autocorrelation.

Example — the patient leakage problem:
Suppose you are predicting hospital readmission. Each patient has 10 visits. If you randomly split rows, the model sees 8 visits from patient i in training and 2 in test. It learns to recognise patient i by their demographic and history — it’s doing patient matching, not generalising to new patients. Group k-fold splits by patient ID.
1.2 Data Versioning and Provenance
In any serious project, data is a first-class artefact. Version it.

DVC (Data Version Control): tracks datasets in Git, stores them in object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob)
Feature stores (Feast, Tecton, Hopsworks): centralise feature computation, prevent train-serve skew
Document every preprocessing step: transformations applied, columns dropped, imputation strategies. The pipeline itself is the documentation — use sklearn Pipeline objects (see 02.Pipelines and Experiments).


✦ Step 2 — Exploratory Data Analysis
EDA is not optional and not aesthetic. It is the stage where you discover:

Whether the problem is solvable given the data
What preprocessing the data requires
Whether the signal exists at all
Whether there is leakage

2.1 Distributions
For every feature x_j:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
 
df.describe()           # count, mean, std, min, quartiles, max
df.isnull().mean()      # fraction missing per column
df.hist(bins=50, figsize=(20, 15))  # all numeric features
sns.boxplot(...)        # outlier inspection
What to look for:

Skewness: right-skewed features (incomes, counts) hurt linear models — consider log transform
Bimodality: may indicate a hidden grouping variable that should be an explicit feature
Spikes at round numbers: often imputation artefacts (e.g., age 99 = unknown)
Feature ranges: huge range differences → must scale for distance-based models and NNs

2.2 Correlations and Target Relationships
corr = df.corr()
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True)
 
# For classification: group by target
df.groupby('target').mean()
 
# Mutual information (handles nonlinear relationships)
from sklearn.feature_selection import mutual_info_classif
mi = mutual_info_classif(X, y)
High mutual information between a feature and target is a signal worth investigating. Suspiciously high mutual information (e.g., I(x_j; y) > 0.9) should trigger a leakage investigation.
2.3 The Leakage Hunt
Data leakage is when information about the target bleeds into the features in a way that wouldn’t exist at inference time. It is the most common reason ML models fail in production.
Categories of leakage:
1. Target leakage: a feature encodes the target (possibly indirectly). Example: you are predicting loan default, and one feature is “received debt forgiveness” — which only happens after default. At inference time, this feature is 0 for all live loans, but the model learned to rely on it.
2. Temporal leakage: you use future information to predict the past. A feature computed from data after the prediction timestamp. Arises from careless joins on rolling windows.
3. Training-set contamination: preprocessing (e.g., StandardScaler) fit on the entire dataset including test. The test set “told” the scaler its statistics. Fix: fit all preprocessing only on training data.
4. Duplicate rows: if the same observation appears in both train and test sets, test accuracy measures memorisation.
Leakage detection heuristic: if your model achieves suspiciously high CV accuracy (e.g., 99% on a hard real-world problem), investigate leakage before celebrating.
Formal check: For each feature, examine: could this feature’s value at prediction time t have been derived from the target y or from events occurring after t?

✦ Step 3 — Preprocessing & Feature Engineering Pipeline
See 01.Data Preprocessing and 02.Feature Engineering for full treatment. The key principle here is pipeline discipline.
3.1 The Leakage-Safe Pipeline
All preprocessing must be fit on the training fold only and applied to all folds. The sklearn Pipeline enforces this:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
 
numeric_transformer = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('imputer', SimpleImputer(strategy='median')),
    ('scaler', StandardScaler())
])
 
categorical_transformer = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('imputer', SimpleImputer(strategy='most_frequent')),
    ('encoder', OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore'))
])
 
preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(transformers=[
    ('num', numeric_transformer, numeric_features),
    ('cat', categorical_transformer, categorical_features)
])
 
full_pipeline = Pipeline(steps=[
    ('preprocessor', preprocessor),
    ('classifier', LogisticRegression())
])
 
# Cross-validation with Pipeline: fit/transform correctly per fold
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
scores = cross_val_score(full_pipeline, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring='roc_auc')
Why this matters: if you fit the StandardScaler on the full dataset outside the pipeline, then do CV, the validation fold’s statistics have already “leaked” into the scaler. The scaler was trained on data that includes the validation samples. This is subtle and common.
3.2 The Complexity Ladder for Feature Engineering
Start minimal. Add complexity only if CV score improves:
Raw features
    → Handle missingness
    → Scale / encode
    → Log-transform skewed features
    → Interaction features (x_i · x_j)
    → Polynomial features (x_i^2)
    → Domain-specific constructions (e.g., ratios, windowed aggregates)
    → Learned embeddings (e.g., entity embeddings via NN, see deep learning)

Each step should be motivated by EDA, not applied blindly.

✦ Step 4 — Baseline → Model Selection → Iteration
4.1 The Baseline Imperative
Always start with a dumb baseline. This is not intellectual laziness — it is professional discipline.
The baseline establishes:

Whether the problem is solvable at all (if your model barely beats the baseline, the signal may not exist)
What “meaningful improvement” means quantitatively
The performance floor against which all complexity is justified

Standard baselines by task:





























TaskBaselineRegressionPredict \bar{y}_{\text{train}} for all test pointsClassificationPredict majority class (or class frequency)Time seriesPredict the last observed value (naïve forecast)RankingSort by global popularityNLPTF-IDF + logistic regression
After the dumb baseline: linear model baseline (logistic regression / ridge regression). Cheap, fast, interpretable. Sets the bar for “is nonlinearity worth it?“
4.2 The Complexity Ladder for Models
Traverse this ladder in order. Add complexity only if CV improvement justifies it:
Majority class / mean predictor
    ↓
Linear model (logistic regression / ridge)
    ↓
Tree-based models (decision tree, then random forest)
    ↓
Gradient boosting (XGBoost / LightGBM)
    ↓
Neural networks
    ↓
Ensembles / stacking

Why this order? Each step:

Is harder to train and tune than the previous
Requires more data to generalise
Is less interpretable
May not improve over the simpler predecessor

The practitioner’s heuristic: if the problem has tabular data with mixed feature types and n < 10^6, gradient boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM) is almost always the strongest out-of-the-box model. If n > 10^6 with structured data — still gradient boosting. For images, text, audio — neural networks.
4.3 Model Selection with Cross-Validation
Never use test set for model selection. Use cross-validation on the training set.
For standard i.i.d. data, stratified 5-fold or 10-fold CV is the workhorse. For time-series, forward-chaining CV:
Fold 1: train [1, t₁], val [t₁+1, t₂]
Fold 2: train [1, t₂], val [t₂+1, t₃]
Fold 3: train [1, t₃], val [t₃+1, t₄]

For simultaneous hyperparameter tuning and model evaluation, use nested CV (outer loop evaluates generalisation, inner loop selects hyperparameters). Standard CV for both gives an optimistically biased estimate.
See 02.Cross Validation and 05.Hyperparameter Tuning for details.

✦ Step 5 — Evaluation on the Held-Out Test Set
5.1 The Test Set as a Finite Resource
The test set provides an estimate of generalisation error. Every time you look at test performance and adjust the model or threshold or preprocessing accordingly, you perform implicit optimisation on the test set. After enough such peeks, test performance becomes an optimistic estimate — the variance of your peek-decisions is counted as signal.
Spend the test set once. This is the reason you need a validation set during development.
5.2 Reporting Multiple Metrics
A single metric rarely tells the full story. Standard practice:
For classification: report accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC, and AUC-PR. Disaggregate by class and by subgroup (see fairness).
For regression: report RMSE, MAE, and R^2. Also plot residuals — residual patterns reveal systematic failures invisible in summary statistics.
For probabilistic models: report calibration (reliability diagram) and log-loss. A model can have good AUC-ROC but terrible calibration — its probability estimates are unreliable even if its rankings are correct.
5.3 Statistical Significance
If your improvement over baseline is 0.3% AUC, is that real? A McNemar test (for classification), t-test over CV folds (with appropriate correction, e.g., Nadeau-Bengio), or bootstrap confidence intervals on the test metric are standard. Don’t report improvements without uncertainty estimates.

✦ Step 6 — Error Analysis

“Look at your mistakes” is one of the highest-ROI activities in ML. Ten minutes of error analysis often beats one week of architecture search.

6.1 The Error Analysis Loop
1. Collect the model's predictions on the validation set
2. Find the instances where the model is most wrong (largest loss, most confident errors)
3. Manually examine them — form hypotheses about why
4. Verify the hypotheses quantitatively
5. Fix: add data, add features, change model, adjust threshold
6. Repeat

6.2 Confusion Matrix Deep-Dive
For a classifier producing a K \times K confusion matrix:

Off-diagonal entries are errors. Which ones are large?
Which classes are confused with each other? Does this make semantic sense?
Are there systematic patterns? (e.g., model consistently confuses class 3 with class 7 — maybe these classes need a distinguishing feature)

6.3 Sliced Evaluation
Aggregate metrics hide failures in subpopulations. Always disaggregate:

By feature buckets (e.g., short documents vs. long documents, young users vs. old users)
By data source (e.g., mobile vs. desktop, US vs. EU)
By time (is performance degrading over time? This is the first sign of distribution shift)

Example: a fraud detection model with 95% overall AUC may have 70% AUC on transactions from a new merchant category that was underrepresented in training. Without sliced evaluation, this failure is invisible.
6.4 Confidence Calibration
The model’s predicted probability \hat{p} should match empirical frequency: among all instances where \hat{p} \approx 0.7, about 70% should actually be positive. Plot the reliability diagram (calibration curve):
from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve
fraction_of_positives, mean_predicted_value = calibration_curve(y_test, y_prob, n_bins=10)
plt.plot(mean_predicted_value, fraction_of_positives, "s-")
plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k:", label="Perfectly calibrated")
Overconfident models (reliability curve below the diagonal) and underconfident models have different fixes: temperature scaling, Platt scaling, isotonic regression.

✦ Step 7 — Deployment Considerations (Orientation)
See 04.Deployment and MLOps for the full treatment. The conceptual anchors:
7.1 Train-Serve Skew
The distribution of features at inference time may differ from training time. Sources:

Covariate shift: P(x) changes, P(y|x) stays the same. (e.g., user demographics shift over time)
Label shift: P(y) changes. (e.g., fraud patterns evolve)
Concept drift: P(y|x) changes. (e.g., the same symptoms now indicate a different disease post-pandemic)

All three require different interventions. Covariate shift can be corrected with importance weighting. Label shift with prior correction. Concept drift requires retraining.
7.2 The ML Flywheel
In products, ML is not a one-shot deployment — it is a continuous loop:
More data → Better model → Better product → More users → More data

This means the deployment and monitoring infrastructure is as important as the model itself.

✦ Worked Example — End-to-End Tabular Project
Problem: predict whether a hotel booking will be cancelled (binary classification).
Step 0 — Frame:

Task: binary classification
Business metric: revenue impact of false positives (overbooking costs) vs. false negatives (empty rooms). Cost-weighted F-beta score.
Data: booking records with features like lead time, ADR, special requests, customer history.

Step 1 — Data:

Historical booking data with cancellation labels.
Temporal split: train on bookings before 2018, val 2018, test 2019.
Group by booking customer — same customer must not appear in multiple folds.

Step 2 — EDA:

lead_time is heavily right-skewed → log transform.
adr (average daily rate) has outliers at 0 (free rooms) and 5000+ (typos?) → clip.
country has 170 unique values → target encoding or frequency encoding.
High mutual information: deposit_type (non-refundable → almost always kept). Investigate: is this leakage? It is not — deposit type is known at booking time.

Step 3 — Features:
Pipeline: [
    ColumnTransformer([
        ('num', StandardScaler(), num_cols),
        ('cat', OneHotEncoder(sparse=False), cat_cols)
    ]),
    LogisticRegression()
]
Step 4 — Models:





























ModelVal AUC-ROCMajority class0.500Logistic Regression0.789Random Forest0.841XGBoost0.878XGBoost + feature eng.0.891
Gradient boosting wins. Hyperparameter tuning via Bayesian optimisation: n_estimators=600, max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.05, subsample=0.8.
Step 5 — Test Evaluation: Test AUC-ROC = 0.887. Calibration is slightly off — apply isotonic regression.
Step 6 — Error Analysis: Most confident false negatives are transient bookings (1-night stays) with last-minute modifications. Feature: days_since_last_modification / lead_time. Val AUC improves to 0.894.

✦ Relation to AI / ML / Deep Learning
This workflow is not specific to tabular models — it is the universal scaffolding into which every ML system fits:
Classical ML → Deep Learning: Steps 0–2 (framing, data, EDA) are identical. Steps 3–4 change: feature engineering is largely replaced by representation learning (the neural network learns the features); model selection becomes architecture search (depth, width, attention, convolution). The stakes are higher — data requirements and compute are orders of magnitude larger, and overfitting is a more severe risk.
The deep learning practitioner’s workflow follows the same logic but with different tools:

Baseline = linear probe on pretrained features (e.g., fine-tune last layer of ResNet)
Error analysis = activation maximisation, saliency maps, attention visualisation
Evaluation = same metrics, but also robustness to distribution shift, adversarial examples
Deployment = model compression (pruning, quantisation, distillation), serving infrastructure (TorchServe, TFServing)

Supervised learning pipeline → this note:
\text{Problem} \xrightarrow{\text{frame}} (\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{D}) \xrightarrow{\text{data}} \hat{\mathcal{D}} \xrightarrow{\text{feature eng.}} \tilde{\mathcal{X}} \xrightarrow{\text{ERM}} \hat{f} \xrightarrow{\text{evaluate}} R(\hat{f}) \xrightarrow{\text{error analysis}} \text{iterate}
The formalisation from 02.Statistical Learning Theory: we are approximating the Bayes-optimal f^* = \arg\min_f R(f) by solving empirical risk minimisation \hat{f} = \arg\min_f \hat{R}(f) subject to inductive bias from \mathcal{H}, and using the entire workflow to control the generalisation gap R(\hat{f}) - \hat{R}(\hat{f}).
Reinforcement learning has a different structure but analogous concerns: environment design (analogous to problem framing), reward shaping (analogous to metric design), exploration vs. exploitation tradeoffs (analogous to model selection under uncertainty), and distribution shift from a changing policy.

✦ The Meta-Lesson
The single most important insight about ML in practice:

Data quality, problem framing, and error analysis matter more than model choice.

The history of deployed ML systems suggests roughly:

~40% of failures: wrong problem framing or metric
~30% of failures: data issues (leakage, distribution shift, quality)
~20% of failures: deployment and monitoring failures
~10% of failures: model or algorithm choices

Most of the literature — and most of the time spent in courses — addresses the last 10%.

✦ You Know This When…

You can explain why a model with 99% CV accuracy might be useless in production, and give three distinct root causes.
You can design a correct train/val/test split for a time-series group-structured dataset.
You can audit a pipeline for the five standard leakage patterns and fix each one.
You can run an error analysis session on a misclassified subset and turn observations into actionable feature engineering hypotheses.
You can implement a full sklearn Pipeline including ColumnTransformer, fit it inside a CV loop, and explain why this is necessary.
Given a business problem, you can derive the right evaluation metric and explain why accuracy alone is insufficient.
